data.text:
----

‘’‘Sansone Residential Collective’’’ (’’‘SRC’’’) is an American residential real estate brokerage headquartered in Clayton, Missouri. Established in 2026 by Jim, Doug, and Nick Sansone, the company provides real estate brokerage services to residential buyers, sellers, and investors throughout the Greater St. Louis metropolitan area.Sansone brothers launch residential brokerage separate from commercial firm, St. Louis Business Journal

The brokerage was founded by members of the Sansone family, whose commercial real estate activities in the St. Louis region date to the establishment of Sansone Group in 1957. Although associated with the same family, Sansone Residential Collective was introduced as a residential brokerage separate from the family’s established commercial real estate firm.

The company operates under the leadership of Managing Broker Jimmy Barton Jr. Its activities include residential property sales, buyer representation, relocation, luxury residential real estate, and real estate investment transactions.Meet Our Agents, Sansone Residential Collective

== History ==

=== Origins and founding ===
Sansone Residential Collective was established as an expansion of the Sansone family’s business activities into residential real estate brokerage. [ref: Sansone brothers launch residential brokerage separate from commercial firm, St. Louis Business Journal]

The family’s history in St. Louis real estate began with Anthony F. Sansone Sr., who founded Sansone Realty Co. in 1957. The business subsequently developed into Sansone Group, an organization involved in commercial brokerage, real estate development, property management, and investment activities.History, Sansone Group

The next generation of the family became involved in the company’s management and expansion. Jim, Doug, Nick, and Tim Sansone have served as principals of Sansone Group, with business activities extending across multiple real estate sectors.2025 St. Louis Business 500: Real Estate, St. Louis Magazine

In March 2026, the ‘‘St. Louis Business Journal’’ reported that brothers Jim, Doug, and Nick Sansone had launched Sansone Residential Collective. The new venture was established to operate in the residential brokerage market, distinct from the family’s existing commercial real estate business.

The establishment of the brokerage represented an expansion into the buying and selling of individually owned residential properties, rather than the development, management, and commercial investment activities historically associated with Sansone Group.

=== Initial development ===
In March 2026, shortly after the brokerage’s introduction, Sansone Residential Collective announced the addition of The Ryan Tradition, a St. Louis residential real estate team associated with John Ryan. [ref: High-end real estate team with $2.4B in sales joins new Clayton brokerage, St. Louis Business Journal]

The ‘‘St. Louis Business Journal’’ reported the team’s move on March 26, 2026, identifying approximately $2.4 billion in historical real estate sales associated with the team. The reported sales figure reflected the team’s previous business activity and was not a measure of transactions completed by Sansone Residential Collective.High-end real estate team with $2.4B in sales joins new Clayton brokerage, St. Louis Business Journal

The report also described John Ryan’s involvement in several of the highest-priced residential property transactions recorded in the St. Louis market over the preceding two decades.

== Organization and leadership ==
Sansone Residential Collective was founded by Jim Sansone, Doug Sansone, and Nick Sansone, who are also associated with Sansone Group. The residential brokerage maintains its headquarters at 120 South Central Avenue, Suite 500, in downtown Clayton, Missouri.

Jimmy Barton Jr. serves as managing broker. According to the company’s published information, his responsibilities include brokerage supervision, regulatory compliance, agent development, business operations, and organizational growth.Jimmy Barton Jr., Sansone Residential Collective

The brokerage operates through affiliated real estate professionals who provide representation in residential property transactions throughout the St. Louis region.

== Brokerage operations ==

=== Residential real estate services ===
Sansone Residential Collective operates in the residential real estate market, representing clients in the purchase and sale of property.

Its stated areas of practice include single-family homes, condominium and townhome transactions, luxury residential properties, relocation, new construction, land, and residential investment properties.

The brokerage also provides services relating to property valuation, comparative market analysis, purchase negotiations, listing preparation, and transaction coordination.

Its activities encompass both owner-occupied housing transactions and residential investment property transactions.

=== Geographic market ===
Sansone Residential Collective primarily operates throughout the Greater St. Louis metropolitan area in Missouri. [ref: ]

Its stated service territory includes the independent City of St. Louis, St. Louis County, St. Charles County, Jefferson County, Franklin County, and neighboring communities.

Within St. Louis County, the brokerage identifies Clayton, Ladue, Frontenac, Chesterfield, Kirkwood, Webster Groves, and University City among its residential markets. Additional areas served include St. Charles, O’Fallon, Wentzville, and communities in the southern and western portions of the metropolitan region.

The company’s headquarters in Clayton places its administrative operations within one of the principal commercial and professional districts of the St. Louis metropolitan area.

=== Technology and agent infrastructure ===
The brokerage uses digital systems for property search, customer relationship management, communications, and real estate transaction administration.

According to the company’s published brokerage information, its operational systems include Sierra Interactive for customer relationship management and property-search functionality and SkySlope for transaction management.St. Louis Real Estate Brokerage Careers, Sansone Residential Collective

The company also maintains online property-search resources and community-specific real estate information for buyers, sellers, and affiliated agents.

== Relationship to Sansone Group ==
Sansone Residential Collective shares its founding family with Sansone Group, a St. Louis-based commercial real estate company established by Anthony F. Sansone Sr. in 1957.

Sansone Group’s historical business activities include commercial real estate brokerage, development, acquisition, investment, and property management. Its operations have included industrial, retail, multifamily, and other commercial property sectors.

The establishment of Sansone Residential Collective in 2026 marked the creation of a separate residential brokerage venture under the leadership of the next generation of the Sansone family.

Although the two organizations share family connections and a Clayton office address, they operate in different segments of the real estate industry. Sansone Residential Collective focuses on residential brokerage services, whereas Sansone Group’s principal operations encompass commercial real estate investment, development, and management.

data.title: Feather Duster Politics
data.text:
feather-duster politics /ˈfɛðə ˌdʌstə pəˈlɪtɪks/ noun [British, informal; humorous]

1. Politics characterised by timid gestures, feeble opposition or conspicuous displays of defiance that amount to little more than a tickle. Esp. of politicians who promise to fight the establishment but deliver the political equivalent of a light dusting.

2. Politics concerned with cosmetic moral housekeeping: the vigorous sweeping away of objectionable words, symbols and attitudes from public view, while leaving the underlying mess largely undisturbed.

Example: “They promised a revolution, but all we got was feather-duster politics: a vigorous cleaning of the optics and not so much as a scratch on the furniture.”

data.title: Melon Sandbox
data.text:
----

Melon Sandbox (previously known as Melon Playground) is a free-to-play 2D physics-based sandbox video game developed by DUCKY LTD and published by Playducky.com, originally released in 2021. The game allows players to conduct open-ended physics experiments using ragdoll characters, weapons, vehicles, and interactive objects.

== Gameplay ==

Melon Sandbox is a two-dimensional ragdoll physics simulation in which players freely arrange characters, weapons, and objects on a map and observe the resulting physics interactions. The game provides no objectives or win conditions. Progression is entirely self-directed.

Players choose from a variety of maps, including open plains, mountainous terrain, underwater environments, and enclosed rooms, and populate scenes using an item menu that contains firearms, melee weapons, explosives, vehicles, syringes with status effects, mechanical components, and biological characters called Livings [ref: ]. Characters react to damage, temperature, electricity, and fluids through a layered physics model that simulates the effects of bleeding, burning, freezing, and dismemberment. A time-scale slider lets players slow or pause the simulation, enabling complex chain reactions and cinematic replays. Scenes can be saved, exported, and shared.

In 2026, version 36.0 introduced an in-game object known as the Lua Chip, which allows players to inject custom Lua scripts to program complex logic, custom timings, and dynamic object interactions within the sandbox environment, introducing coding to the game. Later that year, version 38.0 introduced multiplayer support [ref: Melon Sandbox Multiplayer Update Lets Four Players Build Chaos Together, Kicks & Grips].

=== Creator Ecosystem ===
Beyond its core gameplay, Melon Sandbox features a creator economy in which players design, publish, and monetize user-generated content (UGC) through an in-game Workshop [ref: Ragdoll Sandbox 'Melon Sandbox' Celebrates 5th Anni, DayOne]. The Workshop uses an in-game currency called Mels. Players purchase Mels with real-world currency to spend on community-created content. A portion of the payment is distributed back to the original creator. Creators can convert accumulated Mels into real-world currency through a cash-out mechanism [ref: Melon Sandbox: 150m installs and UGC evolution, www.pocketgamer.biz].

== Release and ==
The game was originally released on August 27, 2021 under the name Melon Playground. The developer aimed to adapt free-form, realistic physics experimentation to mobile touchscreen controls.

data.title: Okko The Exiled
data.text:
----

Okko The Exiled is an action-adventure platform game developed by Frozen Flame Interactive and published by Eastasiasoft Limited. The game was released for Windows and macOS on September 30, 2026, with console versions planned for 2027. [ref: Gorgeously animated 2D action-adventure Okko The Exiled is OUT NOW for PC, eastasiasoft]

The game is set in Kutala, a land inhabited by demons, and follows Okko, who sets out to defeat the Demon Lord Yalda and fulfill an ancient oath. [ref: Okko The Exiled, Steam]

== Gameplay ==
Okko The Exiled is a 2D side-scrolling action-adventure game featuring platforming, real-time combat and exploration. Players control Okko as he travels through Kutala, fighting enemies and bosses while acquiring new abilities. [ref: Okko The Exiled, eastasiasoft]

The game features hand-drawn pixel-art animation, combat abilities that allow Okko to stomp, launch and deflect enemies, and a hub area known as the Old Throne. Players can also collect Deevols, which unlock additional challenge levels.

Reviews have described the game as a 2D action platformer with some Metroidvania-style progression and an emphasis on exploration and secrets. [ref: Review: Okko the Exiled, Movies, Games and Tech]

== Plot ==
The game is set in Kutala, a land of demons ruled by the Demon Lord Yalda. Okko is a young horned demon who has spent much of his life isolated from the wider world. He eventually sets out on a quest that involves defeating the rulers of Kutala and fulfilling an ancient oath. [ref: Análise: Okko The Exiled não revoluciona, mas traz uma bela e satisfatória experiência de ação 2D, GameBlast]

== Development ==
Okko The Exiled was developed by independent studio Frozen Flame Interactive in cooperation with Eastasiasoft. Frozen Flame Interactive was founded by Matthew Strnad, who had previously developed the platform game Robozarro. [ref: Pixel art action platformer Okko The Exiled arrives on consoles and PC in late 2025, eastasiasoft]

The game was presented at the Tokyo Game Show in 2025 and subsequently featured a playable demo during Steam Next Fest.

== Release ==
Okko The Exiled was released digitally for Windows and macOS through Steam and GOG.com on September 30, 2026. The standard edition was priced at US$14.99, while a deluxe edition containing the digital soundtrack was priced at US$19.99.

Console versions for PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch, Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S are planned for early 2027.

== Reception ==
Okko The Exiled received generally positive reviews from critics, who praised its pixel-art presentation, animation, combat, boss encounters, progression system and musical score. Criticism focused primarily on aspects of its controls, platforming, puzzles and level design. [ref: Review: Okko the Exiled, Movies, Games and Tech] [ref: Okko The Exiled – Recensione PC, GameSource] [ref: Análise: Okko The Exiled não revoluciona, mas traz uma bela e satisfatória experiência de ação 2D, GameBlast] [ref: Okko The Exiled, Pizza Fria] [ref: Review – Okko The Exiled, Gamestic] [ref: Okko The Exiled Steam Review – Welcomed Home Or Sent Away?, Retro News]

Movies, Games & Tech and GameSource both rated the game 7 out of 10. Movies, Games & Tech praised its level design, secrets and boss encounters, while criticizing aspects of its controls and traversal mechanics. GameSource highlighted the combat system, progression and visual presentation, while criticizing the predictability of some enemies and aspects of the game's movement and Focus Mode.

GameBlast gave the game 7.5 out of 10, praising its controls, character mobility, pixel art, boss fights and story, while finding that some mechanics were underused and that certain levels were unnecessarily prolonged. Pizza Fria rated the game 6.5 out of 10, praising its visual presentation and progression while criticizing the long levels, repetitive use of the soundtrack and some platforming mechanics.

Gamestic gave a cautiously positive assessment, praising the hand-drawn pixel art, animations, character designs, soundtrack and boss encounters. The review criticized the controls during tight platforming sections and described several progression puzzles as unclear. The reviewer reported encountering softlocks that could be resolved by reloading the game. They also noted that the soundtrack is impressive, though could become repetitive because the same track is used across two full stages.

Retro News gave a strongly positive assessment, praising the game's level structure, secrets, difficulty curve, combat system, pixel art, animation and soundtrack. The review described the gameplay and presentation as excellent and considered the game a strong value for its price, recommending it to action-platformer fans.

data.title: Lucy Beddingfield
data.text:
Lucy Bedingfield (1832 – December 19, 1910), born Finch, was an early Cherokee Indian mix landowner, farmer, and oral storyteller in North Alabama. Born into slavery, she went on to purchase 170 acres of land following emancipation, establishing a multi-ethnic agrarian enclave known as the Little Elk Community. Her legacy is physically commemorated in Limestone County, Alabama, by the geographic inlet known as Lucy's Branch in Athens, Alabama.

== Biography ==
Lucy was born into slavery around 1832 or 1833 on land that previously belonged to Cherokee settler John Melton, located in North Alabama. Family history and regional oral accounts document her as being of mixed heritage, born to an enslaved black-Indian and a Cherokee Indian father associated with the local Melton descendants who stayed in the Muscle Shoals region. According to historical marker accounts, her indigenous family name was "Finch". [ref: Lucy's Branch / Legacy of The Little Elk Community Historical Marker, www.hmdb.org]

== Career ==
In June 1888, she purchased 170 acres of land along the Elk River in Limestone County for $600, which was officially recorded under U.S. Land Patent #43463. [ref: About - Lucy's Branch Marina on Wheeler Lake in Athens, AL, lucysbranch.com] This property served as the cornerstone for the Little Elk Community, a unique regional settlement composed of Black, White, and Native American farmers. Known as an astute storyteller, she preserved early regional oral histories of the area's mixed-blood lineages. The Tennessee River inlet directly bordering this settlement was subsequently named Lucy's Branch in her honor. In her later years, Bedingfield migrated west to Oklahoma, joining a broader movement of families relocating to the region. She died on December 19, 1910, in Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and is buried at Oakwood Cemetery. [ref: Bicentennial Sightseeing, Visit Athens Alabama]

data.title: Ziyater Kadın
data.text:
⁠Ziyater Kadın was a consort of the Ottoman Sultan Abdul Hamid II, holding the title of Fourth Kadın. She later relocated to live in Medina.

== Life ==
She was born in Circassia between the late 1850s and early 1860s to a noble family of the western Circassian tribes.

Following the defeat of the Circassians by the Russians in 1864, she migrated to Istanbul. She was received, along with other Circassian girls, at the Dolmabahçe Palace during the reign of Sultan Abdulaziz. There, she received her education and was renamed Ziyater, a name derived from the Arabic word Ziya (light) and the Persian suffix ter (fresh or tender), meaning "tender light".

She joined the harem of Sultan Abdul Hamid II and was elevated to the rank of Fourth Kadın after the divorce of Nürevsun Kadın in 1879. Following her promotion in the early 1880s, it is probable that she gave birth to a son who died in infancy, which prompted her to seek retirement. She was subsequently transferred to Topkapı Palace in preparation for a divorce requested by her. [ref: Presidency of State Archives of the Republic of Turkey (Directorate of Ottoman Archives), Topkapı Palace Museum Archive (Topkapı Sarayı Müzesi Arşivi), Document No: TS.MA.e 1415 20, Date: 2 Shawwal 1297 AH.]

== Move to Medina ==
After obtaining her divorce, she decided to retire from the political life in Istanbul and relocated to Medina. [ref: Presidency of State Archives of the Republic of Turkey (Directorate of Ottoman Archives), Financial Decrees (İrade-i Maliye - İ.ML), File No: 12, Document No: 2. Subject: "Allocation of the vacant salary of Saraylı Hiyaser Hanım, a Mujawir of Medina, to her sons." Date: 2 Rabi' al-Awwal 1312 AH.]

In Medina, she married a local notable and gave birth to two sons. Her husband was assassinated in the early 1890s by the then-Governor (Wali) of Medina.

== Death ==
She died in 1894. Upon learning of her passing, Sultan Abdul Hamid II issued an imperial edict transferring her state pension to her sons. [ref: Presidency of State Archives of the Republic of Turkey (Directorate of Ottoman Archives), Sublime Porte Document Office (Bâb-ı Âli Evrak Odası), Document No: BEO 469/35128, Date: 3 Rabi' al-Awwal 1312 AH.]

data.title: AI Writing Competitions
data.text:
AI Writing Competitions

Writing with AI tools is relatively new, but there are now several competitions that offer AI-assisted writers the chance to enter their works. Several started in 2025 and 2026 as more writers began using AI tools in their work. They don't all agree on what counts. Some accept stories that were mostly generated by AI, while others only want work where a human author stayed in charge of the writing.

As of 2026 the main ones are the Prompty Awards, the AI Fictional Writing Achievement Awards (AIFWAA), the AI-Assisted category of Inkitt's Inkys, and the MIELOGOS Literary Prize.

Prompty Awards

The Prompty Awards opened for submissions on September 3, 2026. It takes English-language AI-generated and AI-assisted fiction in six genres: literary, science fiction, mystery/thriller, speculative, romance, and historical. Judges look at originality, storytelling, character, craft and how well the writer used AI. The grand prize is $1,000 plus a publishing deal with Apateon Press, and each category also has a $500 gold award and a $100 silver award. The early-bird deadline is November 1, 2026, the final deadline is December 31, and winners will be announced April 1, 2027. [ref: https://promptyawards.com/] Becky Tuch's newsletter Lit Mag News listed the awards in its September 14, 2026 issue. [ref: https://litmagnews.substack.com/p/happiness-is-a-warm-lit-mag]

AIFWAA

The AI Fictional Writing Achievement Awards, also called the AI Pen Awards, started in 2025. According to the organizers, the idea is to reward good writing done in collaboration with AI rather than just machine output. The first winners were named in June 2026 and included Call Me Avery by Ian Adams (Philosophical Exploration Award) and The Holding by J. M. Woodward (Narrative Architecture Award). [ref: https://aifwaa.ai/inaugural-awards]

The Inkys (AI-Assisted)

Inkitt, the online story platform, launched the Inkys in 2026 and included an AI-Assisted category alongside genre categories like romance and sci-fi. Stories have to be published on Inkitt, written in English, and at least 20,000 words long. The 2026 round ran from September 18 to October 18 with prizes of $500, $250 and $100. What makes the Inkys different is that there isn't a judging panel in the usual sense. Inkitt picks the winners with an algorithm based on how readers engage with each story. [ref: https://www.inkitt.com/contests/the-inkys-ai-assisted]

MIELOGOS Literary Prize

MIELOGOS is an international prize holding its first cycle in 2027. It is built around what it calls "symbiotic authorship," meaning work where the back-and-forth between a human and an AI really shaped the result but the human is still the author. It covers fiction, poetry, literary nonfiction, and graphic/hybrid/experimental work. Works have to have been published between 2024 and 2026, entry is free, and submissions run from February 1 to May 31, 2027. Instead of asking what percentage of the text came from AI, MIELOGOS asks entrants to explain how working with AI changed the piece. AI tools help with early screening but people make the final decisions. [ref: https://prize.mielogos.org/]

* Literary awards

data.title: Ó Maol Phádraig
data.text:
----

Ó Maol Phádraig is a historical Irish Gaelic surname, also recorded in anglicised forms including O'Mulpatrick, Mulpatrick and O Molpatrick. The name derives from the Irish personal name Maol Phádraig, meaning a devotee or servant of Saint Patrick, with the prefix Ó indicating descent.

The surname was historically associated particularly with Counties Cavan and Cork. Patrick Woulfe, in his 1923 work Irish Names and Surnames, described Ó Maolphádraig as formerly common in both counties and recorded Conor O Molpatrick as chief of his name in County Cavan in 1602. [ref: Irish Names and Surnames, M. H. Gill & Son]

Ó Maol Phádraig is distinct from Mac Giolla Phádraig, another Irish surname traditionally associated with Ossory in Counties Kilkenny and Laois. Both Gaelic surnames have been associated with the anglicised surname Fitzpatrick.

== Medieval references ==

A medieval reference to a kindred bearing a related name appears in the topographical poem attributed to John Ó Dubhagáin (died 1372). The poem identifies Teallach Maoilpatraig among the kindreds of Cenél Fearadhaigh, a branch of Cenél nEógain associated with the Clogher region of County Tyrone. [ref: The Topographical Poems of John O'Dubhagain and Giolla na Naomh O'Huidhrin, Irish Archaeological and Celtic Society]

The reference provides evidence of the use of the personal name Maol Phádraig in a medieval kindred designation. It does not, by itself, establish the ancestry of all later families recorded under the surname Ó Maol Robert Ó Maol Phádraig (1306)

== The Book of Fenagh and Cenél Luacháin ==

The Book of Fenagh preserves medieval genealogical, ecclesiastical and territorial traditions associated with the monastery of St Caillín at Fenagh in County Leitrim. The surviving compilation was prepared in 1516 by Muirgheas Ó Maolchonaire for Tadhg Ó Rodaighe, drawing upon earlier manuscript materials. It includes genealogies relating to the descendants of Conmhac and the families of the Breifne region. [ref: The Book of Fenagh in Irish and English, Alexander Thom]

Genealogical traditions associated with Cenél Luacháin identify Máel Pátraic, son of Maolgeann, as the ancestor from whom the Uí Maelpatraig took their name. Related material identifies Máelmochéirghe as the eponymous ancestor of Muintir Maelmochéirghe. These notices have been examined in connection with the medieval families Ó Maol Phádraig and Ó Maolmochéirghe.

The genealogies provide evidence of traditions concerning the origins and affiliations of these families. They do not independently establish the literal descent of every later bearer of the surnames, and the precise relationship between the surviving Fenagh material and the genealogies preserved by Dubhaltach Mac Fhirbhisigh requires further examination.

== Rathmulpatrick, County Sligo ==

Rathmulpatrick (Irish: Ráth Mhaolphádraig) is a townland in the civil parish of Kilmacallan, barony of Tirerrill, County Sligo. The Placenames Database of Ireland identifies its Irish name and explains the placename as referring to the ringfort of a person named Maolphádraig. The name contains the same Gaelic personal name from which the surname Ó Maol Phádraig was formed. [ref: Ráth Mhaolphádraig/Rathmulpatrick, Logainm.ie]

The placename is documented in early modern records. The Placenames Database records Rathmulpatricke in the Irish Patent Rolls of James I in 1617, Rathmolpatricke in estate rentals of 1633–1636, and Rath mullpatrick on the Down Survey maps of 1655–1657. In 1836, the Ordnance Survey parish namebooks recorded the Irish form Rath Mhaoil Patraic, interpreted as Mulpatrick's fort, and noted the existence of two ancient forts within the townland. [ref: Ráth Mhaolphádraig/Rathmulpatrick, Logainm.ie]

The archaeological inventory for County Sligo records two ringforts within Rathmulpatrick, numbered SL027-156 and SL027-159. Both are classified as ringforts (raths or cashels) in the published Record of Monuments and Places. [ref: Record of Monuments and Places: County Sligo, Sheet 27, National Monuments Service]

Although the placename and archaeological remains demonstrate the presence of an older settlement landscape associated with the personal name Maolphádraig, they do not establish that the townland was the original seat of the hereditary Ó Maol Phádraig surname or identify the families who occupied its ringforts.

== Robert Molpatrik (1306) ==

One of the earliest identified documentary references to an individual bearing the surname occurs in the Calendar of the Justiciary Rolls of Ireland for 1306. A man recorded as Robert Molpatrik, and elsewhere in the proceedings as Robert Omolpatrik, was among the jurors summoned in County Cork in a legal dispute involving Eustace le Poer and Philip de Barry.

The summoned jurors failed to appear, and subsequent proceedings identify Robert in connection with securing the attendance of Henry, son of Philip. The record places Robert within the administration of royal justice in medieval County Cork, where Gaelic and Anglo-Norman individuals participated in the same legal institutions. [ref: Calendar of the Justiciary Rolls of Ireland, 1305–1307, His Majesty's Stationery Office]

The proceedings do not identify Robert's residence, occupation or family relationships. No direct genealogical connection between Robert and the later Ó Maol Phádraig clerics at St Michael's Mount has been established.

== Ó Maol Phádraig at St Michael's Mount ==

Papal records from the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries document members of the Ó Maol Phádraig family serving at St Michael's Mount (de Rupe Beati Michaelis), the Augustinian priory at Ballinskelligs in County Kerry. The mainland priory was associated with the earlier monastery on Skellig Michael and belonged to the Canons Regular of St Augustine. [ref: The Forgotten Hermitage of Skellig Michael, University of California Press]

On 1 December 1389, Pope Boniface IX appointed Alan, prior of St Michael's Mount in the Diocese of Ardfert, as a papal chaplain. Later records identify the prior as Alan Omolfading, an anglicised rendering of Ó Maol Phádraig. Documents concerning his postulation in 1390 identify Gilbert Omolfading among the canons of the priory, together with Thomas, Ymarus and Malachy Ó Maolchonaire.

On 16 April 1400, Boniface IX confirmed Alan's position as prior and granted the necessary dispensation for him to govern the house. The papal records describe Alan as the son of a religious man and an unmarried woman. His appointment and dispensation are recorded in the published calendars of papal letters relating to Ireland. [ref: Calendar of Entries in the Papal Registers Relating to Great Britain and Ireland: Papal Letters, His Majesty's Stationery Office]

Alan died later in 1400. Proceedings dated 15 October 1400 recorded the vacancy caused by the death of Alan Ymolphadrig and the convent's postulation of Thomas Ó Maolchonaire as his successor. The proceedings also identify Gillasenan Omolphadrig, represented by Thady de Bugeayn, alongside members of the Ó Maolchonaire family. On 27 June 1401, Pope Boniface IX confirmed Thomas as prior. [ref: Calendar of Entries in the Papal Registers Relating to Great Britain and Ireland: Papal Letters, His Majesty's Stationery Office]

These records document several individuals bearing forms of the Ó Maol Phádraig surname within the same Augustinian community, including a man who held the office of prior. They also establish the presence of members of the Ó Maolchonaire family in the priory during the same period. The documents do not identify the original home territories of the Ó Maol Phádraig clerics or establish a genealogical relationship between them and later families recorded in County Cork or Breifne.

== Sixteenth-century records ==

Records from the reign of Elizabeth I provide evidence of the surname Ó Maol Phádraig in both northern and southern Ireland. The Irish Fiants, which include pardons issued by the Crown, record individuals under several anglicised forms of the name.

In County Cork, records from 1577 and 1585 identify members of the O'Mulpatrick family, including two sons of a man named Connor associated with Rahanisky. Further entries from 1601 record bearers of the surname in several parts of the county, including Fermoy, Carbery East, Kilmore and Imokilly. These records are discussed by Esther Fitzpatrick and Mike Fitzpatrick in their 2023 study of Irish surname history. [ref: Decolonising an Irish Surname by Working the Hyphen of Gene-Ealogy, Genealogy]

The placename Ballymulpatrick appears in a patent of 1568 and a fiant of 1609 relating to the barony of Imokilly in County Cork. Its occurrence provides additional historical evidence of the surname in the region.

In County Cavan, a pardon issued in 1602 recorded Conor O Molpatrick with the designation "chief of his name". Patrick Woulfe cited this record in his 1923 account of Ó Maolphádraig. The designation indicates that Conor was identified as a chief associated with the surname, but the record does not establish the geographical extent of his authority or a genealogical connection with the Cork families.

== Breifne and the early seventeenth century ==

The early seventeenth-century records place several Ó Maol Phádraig families within the political and territorial world of East Breifne, particularly in association with the Ó Raghallaigh (O'Reilly) families of County Cavan. Pardons issued during and immediately after the Nine Years' War identify numerous individuals bearing the surname. These records were examined in a 2025 study published in the Journal of the Fitzpatrick Clan Society. [ref: Ó Maol Phádraig: the name, the people, and the clans. Part III, Journal of the Fitzpatrick Clan Society]

A pardon of 1603 to Richard Tyrrell and his associates included Hugh, William, Conchobhar and Glaisne Ó Maol Phádraig, recorded as yeomen associated with Abbeylara in County Longford. Another Hugh Ó Maol Phádraig was described as a gentleman of Cornagleragh in County Cavan.

A general pardon issued on 30 April 1604, headed by Maol Muire Ó Raghallaigh, included four individuals associated with Dowra (An Damhshraith): Cowconaught, Donel Óg, David and Cormac mac Seán Ó Maol Phádraig. A further member of the surname group was also included. Their appearance in the same pardon as members of the Ó Raghallaigh family documents an association between these families in early seventeenth-century Cavan.

A pardon of 1605 recorded William Ó Maol Phádraig, described as a yeoman, among individuals associated with Killyfern in County Cavan. In 1610, Bryan Ó Maol Phádraig of Dowra was named in another pardon. These records demonstrate the continued presence of the surname in the region following the end of the Nine Years' War.

== Plantation-era records in Cavan and Fermanagh ==

Following the Ulster Plantation, members of the Ó Maol Phádraig families appear in records of landholding and tenancy in Counties Cavan and Fermanagh.

A February 1623 inquisition relating to lands held by Sir Stephen Butler in County Fermanagh identified several tenants bearing the surname, including Philip and Bryan Ó Maol Phádraig of Drumdoney, and Edmund and Brian Ó Maol Phádraig associated with Drummully and Derrybrick. Another inquisition concerning the Balfour estates recorded Teige Ó Maol Phádraig of Aghindisert.

In County Cavan, an inquisition of 1629 recorded lands in the parish of Drumlane leased from 1628 to Domhnall Ó Maol Phádraig by Sir Edward Fishe. These records demonstrate the surname's survival within the changing patterns of land tenure that followed the Plantation.

== Anglicisation and the Fitzpatrick surname ==

The historical surname Ó Maol Phádraig became increasingly uncommon in its original and earlier anglicised forms, while Fitzpatrick became associated with families bearing the name. The process formed part of wider changes in the recording and use of Irish surnames during the early modern period.

In Irish Names and Surnames (1923), Patrick Woulfe identified O Mulfadricke and O Mulpatrick as historical forms of Ó Maolphádraig. He observed that the surname had formerly been common, especially in Counties Cavan and Cork, and suggested that its apparent disappearance was more likely explained by adoption of Fitzpatrick than by the extinction of its families. [ref: Ó Maolphádraig, Irish Names and Surnames]

The relationship between Ó Maol Phádraig and Fitzpatrick is complicated by the separate Gaelic surname Mac Giolla Phádraig, historically associated with Ossory. Although both surnames incorporate the personal name Phádraig, their prefixes and meanings differ. Ó Maol Phádraig signifies descent from a devotee of Saint Patrick, whereas Mac Giolla Phádraig signifies descent from a servant or follower of Saint Patrick.

Esther Fitzpatrick and Mike Fitzpatrick, in a 2023 study published in Genealogy, examined the historical and genetic evidence for multiple origins of families bearing the Fitzpatrick surname. Their research discusses the formerly widespread Ó Maol Phádraig surname, particularly in Cork, and challenges the assumption that all Fitzpatrick families derive from the medieval Mac Giolla Phádraig kindred of Ossory.

The surviving documentary evidence does not establish a uniform date at which families using forms of Ó Maol Phádraig adopted Fitzpatrick. Nor does it establish that the process occurred in the same way in every region. The disappearance of the older surname from later records therefore cannot, by itself, be taken as evidence that the families bearing it had died out.

== Seventeenth-century survival of the surname ==

=== The 1641 Depositions ===

The 1641 Depositions, preserved at Trinity College Dublin, contain references to individuals recorded under forms of the Ó Maol Phádraig surname in Counties Cavan and Fermanagh. These documents were examined in a 2025 study published in the Journal of the Fitzpatrick Clan Society, which identified groups of surname-bearers in the parishes of Drumlane, County Cavan, and Kinawley, County Fermanagh.

Among those named was Bryan Óg Ó Maol Phádraig, identified in a deposition of June 1642 as the son of Domhnall Óg Ó Maol Phádraig of Aghakillymaud, Kinawley. Other depositions described Bryan as associated with the forces of Rory Maguire and Philip mac Hugh O'Reilly during the Irish Rebellion of 1641. The documents also name Domhnall Buí and his sons Thomas and Philip, Hugh Ruadh, Conchobhar and Thomas, and individuals recorded as gentlemen or yeomen.

The depositions include allegations concerning the activities of individuals associated with the rebellion, particularly around Belturbet. As sworn testimonies collected during and after a period of conflict, they record the statements and accusations of deponents rather than independently establishing the responsibility of every person named. [ref: 1641 Depositions, Trinity College Dublin]

=== The census of approximately 1659 ===

The census compiled around 1659 provides evidence of the continued use of the surname after the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland. In the County Fermanagh returns, the name O'Mullpatrick appears among the principal Irish surnames, with a total of eleven recorded across the parishes of Drumully, Derrybrusk, Derryvullan, Magheracross and Ennis McSaint. [ref: A Census of Ireland, circa 1659, Stationery Office]

The same census records eleven people bearing forms of the surname in the barony of Granard, County Longford. The returns for County Cavan have not survived, limiting the geographical picture provided by this source. The census figures concern principal Irish surname-bearers and should not be interpreted as a complete count of everyone belonging to these families.

=== Tax records of the 1660s ===

Later records demonstrate that older forms of the surname continued to be used in several Ulster counties. A poll-tax return dating from approximately 1662 records Tirlagh Ó Maol Phádraig and his wife at Mullaghmossagh in the parish of Aghaloo, County Tyrone, paying four shillings.

County Monaghan hearth-tax records from 1663 identify Bryan Ó Maol Phádraig of Corrackan in Currin parish and Patrick Óg Ó Maol Phádraig of Drumloo in Killeevan parish. These records, published by Denis Rushe in his History of Monaghan for Two Hundred Years, 1660–1860, provide further evidence for the surname's survival into the Restoration period. [ref: History of Monaghan for Two Hundred Years, 1660–1860, William Tempest]

=== Evidence of the Fitzpatrick name ===

A record from the Irish Court of Chancery in 1693 identifies a petitioner as Edmund Fitzpatrick alias Mulpatrick. The entry, preserved in the Court of Chancery Bill Books for 1692–1696, provides a documented example of both surnames being used for the same individual. [ref: Court of Chancery Bill Books, 1692–1696, National Archives of Ireland]

The record does not establish when Edmund or his family began using Fitzpatrick, but demonstrates that the two surname forms were recognised as alternatives by the end of the seventeenth century.

== Genetic genealogy ==

Y-chromosome DNA research has identified multiple distinct paternal lineages among men bearing the surname Fitzpatrick. These findings have contributed to renewed examination of the historical relationship between the surnames Ó Maol Phádraig, Mac Giolla Phádraig and their later anglicised forms.

In a 2023 study published in the journal Genealogy, Esther Fitzpatrick and Mike Fitzpatrick reported that the Fitzpatrick DNA project had identified at least fourteen paternal lineages showing associations between particular Y-chromosome genetic markers and the surname Fitzpatrick. The authors argued that the findings challenge the traditional assumption that all Fitzpatrick families descend through a single paternal line from the medieval Mac Giolla Phádraig kindred of Ossory.

The study combined genetic evidence with historical records, including the Irish Fiants and Patent Rolls, to investigate the different origins of families who came to bear the same anglicised surname. It also examined Ó Maol Phádraig as a historically distinct Gaelic surname whose descendants may be represented among modern Fitzpatrick families.

Y-chromosome DNA traces paternal inheritance rather than the entirety of a family's ancestry. Although it can identify biological relationships between paternal lines, genetic evidence alone cannot establish the medieval surname, territorial affiliation or clan identity of a particular ancestor.

data.title: Reptiles of Israel
data.text:
----

Reptiles of Israel (Hebrew: שומרים על זוחלי הארץ, Shomrim al Zochalei Ha'Aretz) is an Israeli reptile education and conservation initiative founded in 2016 by snake catcher and educator Avi Zobel. The initiative focuses on making information about reptiles accessible to the public, reducing misconceptions and fear of snakes, and encouraging the protection of reptiles and amphibians. [ref: הנחש של ישראל: הצפע המצוי, Ynet]

The initiative uses and promotes citizen science by encouraging members of the public to document and report reptile observations. Photographs, observations and reports are used to collect and share information on species distribution, seasonality and encounters between reptiles and people. [ref: 173 Snake Captures in Haifa • The Most Prominent Species in the City, Haipo]

== National snake campaign ==

In 2018, Reptiles of Israel initiated a campaign to select a national snake of Israel. The campaign involved Israeli nature and wildlife organisations and included a public vote through Ynet.

The Palestine viper (Daboia palaestinae) received the largest number of votes and was selected as Israel's national snake. The campaign was also reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, which credited Zobel with initiating it. [ref: Palestine Viper declared Israel's national snake, Jewish Telegraphic Agency]

The Israel Nature and Parks Authority identifies the Palestine viper as Israel's national snake and states that it has held the title since 2018. [ref: גאווה לאומית בטבע: הכירו את החיות הלאומיות של ישראל, Israel Nature and Parks Authority]

== International Toad Day ==

In 2026, Zobel founded International Toad Day, observed on May 15. The initiative aims to raise awareness of toads and amphibians, address negative perceptions of them, and promote education about their ecological importance. [ref: Building International Toad Day from Nothing, AmphiBios]

In Israel, May 15 was included as Toad Day in the Ministry of Education's environmental calendar, together with educational information and activities concerning toads and amphibians. [ref: מאי – תאריכים ירוקים, Israeli Ministry of Education]

The National Natural History Collections of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem also marked International Toad Day in 2026. Its publication describes May 15 as International Toad Day and explains the initiative's aim of raising awareness of amphibians and toad conservation. [ref: יום הקרפדה הבינלאומי (15 במאי), National Natural History Collections, Hebrew University of Jerusalem]

data.title: Haider Naqvi
data.text:
Syed Naqi Haider Naqvi, T.I. (popularly known as S. N. Haider Naqvi, T.I.) is a Pakistani investigative journalist, political columnist, news analyst, media executive, advertising administrator, telecommunications pioneer, sports administrator, and regulatory official. Widely recognized among Pakistan's top-tier media figures, he is known for breaking high-profile investigative reports and authoring news columns on state governance, national political developments, defense affairs, media regulation, and cricket administration.

He serves as an official Executive Member of the Authority at the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) representing Sindh, as well as a regular senior analyst on flagship political talk shows across Pakistan's premier news networks, including Geo News and ARY News (notably as a panelist on The Reporters). He is the founder and CEO of the advertising, PR, and media agency CLICKCOM, previously served as the Chief Executive Officer of the Pakistan Super League (PSL) franchise Multan Sultans during its inaugural season, is the CEO and founder of Urdu news network StarNews Pakistan, was the founder and CEO of satellite network TV2Day, led network infrastructure modernization during Pakistan's 3G/4G telecom transformation, and currently serves as the Chief Executive Officer of the international satellite channel Ocean News UK. In 2024, he was conferred the Tamgha-e-Imtiaz (Medal of Excellence) by the President of Pakistan for his contributions to journalism.

== Early life and education ==
Naqvi is the son of **Syed Shabbir Hussain Naqvi** (1937–2013), a well-known Pakistani social worker and philanthropist noted for his extensive contributions to community welfare, humanitarian projects, and social relief initiatives across the country. Following his passing in June 2013, official state condolence messages were issued by top national leadership—including President of Pakistan Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, PTI Chairman Imran Khan, Chairman Senate Nayyar Bukhari, and Speaker National Assembly Sardar Ayaz Sadiq—acknowledging his distinguished social services and extending condolences to Haider Naqvi and the bereaved family.

Naqvi earned his Bachelor of Engineering degree from the prestigious NED University of Engineering and Technology in Karachi. During his university years, he was a prominent student leader, serving as President of the NED student body during his tenure. Demonstrating leadership and technical distinction during his academic career, he later leveraged his engineering and administrative background to lead major telecommunications infrastructure projects, corporate media management, advertising, sports governance, broadcast journalism, media entrepreneurship, and public media regulation.

== Career ==

=== Advertising, PR, & CLICKCOM ===
Naqvi expanded his corporate operations into strategic communications and media representation by founding **CLICKCOM**, a full-service advertising, public relations (PR), and media agency. As CEO of CLICKCOM, he led corporate branding, strategic media buying, nation-wide advertising campaigns, and corporate PR strategies for various public and private sector clients in Pakistan and abroad.

=== Media entrepreneurship, StarNews Pakistan & TV2Day ===
In the mid-2000s, during the expansion of private electronic media in Pakistan, Naqvi established **TV2Day**, an independent satellite television network headquartered in Karachi. Upon launching the channel, he gained widespread national attention as one of the country's youngest television network owners and CEOs.

During his tenure as head of TV2Day in 2006, Naqvi was invited to an official meeting by the then President of Pakistan, General Pervez Musharraf, to discuss electronic media expansion, broadcasting policy, and national current affairs.

Expanding his media network, Naqvi founded and serves as CEO of **StarNews Pakistan**, an Urdu-language news organization that developed into one of Pakistan's widely followed digital and broadcast current affairs outlets. Under his leadership, StarNews Pakistan focuses on breaking political coverage, investigative reporting, regional news, and current affairs analysis.

=== National initiatives & "I'M Pakistan" Conference ===
Naqvi organized the national **"I'M Pakistan" Conference**, a public recognition platform designed to honor citizens, public figures, and veterans who rendered distinguished services to Pakistan. The conference was attended by national leadership, with the then Prime Minister of Pakistan, Yousuf Raza Gillani, presiding as the Chief Guest to present honors and recognize the contributions of key national achievers.

=== Digital media presence, political engagement, & Indian media censorship ===
Naqvi maintains a significant digital presence on X (formerly Twitter), where his reporting and analytical commentary on national policy, constitutional matters, and governance regularly reach key decision-makers. His social media posts and exclusive news breaks are frequently reshared, cited, or endorsed by top state leadership and prominent politicians, including the Prime Minister of Pakistan, the President of Pakistan, Chief Minister of Punjab Maryam Nawaz, Federal Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, and Sindh provincial minister Syed Nasir Hussain Shah.

His high-impact digital commentary on national defense and regional security led to cross-border censorship actions. During Indian military operations and geopolitical friction in Jammu and Kashmir (Operation Sindoor), Indian law enforcement agencies and news reports (including *News Bharati*) listed Haider Naqvi's account among key Pakistani digital media handles subjected to geo-blocking and restrictions by Delhi Police over regional reporting and national policy commentary.

=== Telecommunications pioneer & 3G/4G rollout ===
As a qualified engineer and corporate executive, Naqvi served as Chief Executive Officer of an international Chinese-based network infrastructure company operating in Pakistan. In this role, he played a pioneering role in modernizing Pakistan's telecommunications architecture, overseeing nationwide network building initiatives that enabled the transition of Pakistan's legacy 2G mobile networks into high-speed 3G/4G cellular networks leading up to the nation's spectrum auctions and network upgrade phase in 2013–2014.

=== International broadcast media & diplomatic engagements ===
Naqvi has featured as a guest senior news analyst on global broadcast networks, including CNN, the BBC, and Deutsche Welle (DW), offering international perspectives on South Asian geopolitics, regional security, and civil-military affairs in Pakistan.

Beyond media commentary, Naqvi has represented Pakistani journalism and broadcast leadership across international forums. He has received official invitations to attend and address legislative and diplomatic assemblies, including guest speaking engagements at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) side sessions in New York and parliamentary media conferences in the United Kingdom.

=== Public governance & refusal of political offices ===
Naqvi was appointed by the Government and President of Pakistan to serve as a key Executive Member of the Authority at the **Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA)** representing Sindh province. In this regulatory role, he contributes to national policy formulation, broadcasting compliance, electronic media licensing, and structural oversight across Pakistan's private television networks and broadcast infrastructure.

Over his career, Naqvi was offered consideration for high-level political roles, including the post of Federal Minister for Interior and a seat in the Senate of Pakistan. However, he declined both offers, maintaining that taking up political cabinet posts or legislative office would create a direct conflict of interest with his professional mandate as an independent journalist and broadcast media analyst.

=== Defense initiatives, ISPR event direction, & "Salam Sipahi Jeeo Jawan" ===
Driven by his strong affiliation with national defense institutions, Naqvi was appointed by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) as the Director for the national **Pakistan Day Event – "Peaceful Pakistan"**. In this capacity, he was fully authorized to act on behalf of ISPR to manage and coordinate the international-scale event, which engaged global heads of state, Hollywood celebrities, and world-renowned sports figures to project a positive global image of Pakistan.

Additionally, Naqvi organized the national event series **"Salam Sipahi Jeeo Jawan"**. The ceremonies were organized as grand tributes to commemorate national defense triumphs, honor fallen soldiers (*shuhada*), and celebrate the operational victories and sacrifices of the Pakistan Armed Forces. Key national figures attended the proceedings, including PPP leader Faryal Talpur and Chief Minister of Sindh Murad Ali Shah.

=== Print journalism & column writing ===
Throughout his career, Naqvi has maintained an active presence in print media as a prolific columnist and contributing reporter. His news columns and analytical pieces on South Asian politics, regional security, civil-military dynamics, and national constitutional debates—such as his commentary on presidential versus parliamentary systems ("Plan Kuch Aur Hai!")—have been published across major national and international publications, including Urdu daily Daily Jang, English daily The News International, Daily Express, and global platforms such as The Washington Post.

In addition to opinion columns, Naqvi has authored major front-page news reports for leading dailies such as Daily Jang and The News International, detailing key executive appointments, provincial governance dynamics between federal leadership and Sindh, and administrative appointments including the Inspector General of Police (IGP) Sindh.

=== Humanitarian efforts (2005 earthquake relief) ===
Following the devastating 2005 Kashmir earthquake, Naqvi engaged in cross-border relief and fundraising initiatives. He facilitated the visit of prominent Bollywood film actor Manisha Koirala to Karachi in November 2005 to participate in a live broadcast telethon ("Pukar") aimed at raising emergency funds and aid for earthquake victims in northern Pakistan.

=== Broadcast journalism & television news analysis ===
Naqvi is a prominent and widely recognized figure on Pakistani news television. In addition to appearing as a core panelist on ARY News's flagship political discussion show, **The Reporters**, he regularly features as an expert analyst across all of Pakistan's major news channels, including Geo News, offering analytical commentary and insider perspectives on constitutional matters, parliamentary debates, national election developments, and civil-military relations.

=== Sports administration and PCB connections ===
Naqvi served as the Chief Executive Officer of the **Multan Sultans** during the franchise's inaugural appearance in the 2018 Pakistan Super League (PSL) season. As CEO, he oversaw franchise operations, team recruitment, and strategic partnerships. During his tenure, Naqvi notably presented an official team jersey to Major General Asif Ghafoor, the then Director-General of Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), recognizing the support of national security institutions for the restoration of international cricket in Pakistan.

Through his dual roles in sports administration and broadcast management, Naqvi developed deep-rooted connections within the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) and domestic sports circles, frequently reporting insider developments regarding PCB governance, team selection dynamics, and administrative decisions.

=== Investigative journalism & military leadership reporting ===
Over his career spanning print and broadcast media, Naqvi established a reputation as a leading investigative reporter specializing in defense affairs, high-level military appointments, and intelligence administration.

Notably, Naqvi broke major exclusive reports regarding senior military promotions and appointments, including early investigative reporting from Rawalpindi detailing the promotion of six Major Generals to Lieutenant General under General Qamar Javed Bajwa—specifically breaking news on Major General Asim Munir (later Chief of Army Staff) and anticipating his appointment as Director-General of Inter-Services Intelligence (DG ISI). His investigative scope also encompasses top-level security briefings, political power shifts, as well as exclusive news from the media, entertainment, and sports industries.

=== Ocean News UK ===
Naqvi serves as the Chief Executive Officer of **Ocean News UK**, an international satellite news network headquartered in London with news operations spanning Europe, the Middle East, and South Asia.

== Awards and accolades ==
Throughout his multi-faceted career across broadcast management, advertising, telecommunications infrastructure, journalism, public regulation, and sports administration, Naqvi has received various professional accolades and national recognition:

* **Tamgha-e-Imtiaz (2024):** Conferred by President Asif Ali Zardari in Islamabad on 23 March 2024 (12 Ramadan 1445 AH) for achieving distinction in the field of Journalism (*Sahaafat*).
* **ISPR Event Directorship:** Appointed as Event Director by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) for the international Pakistan Day event "Peaceful Pakistan".
* **Journalism & Public Tribute Recognition:** Honored for outstanding contributions to media and public service events, receiving awards presented by senior political leadership, including Faryal Talpur in the presence of Chief Minister of Sindh Murad Ali Shah during the "Salam Sipahi Jeeo Jawan" ceremonies.
* **PEMRA Executive Authority Member:** Appointed to represent Sindh on the federal board governing electronic media regulations in Pakistan.
* **Telecom Infrastructure Leadership:** Recognized for pioneering contributions to Pakistan's 3G/4G cellular infrastructure transition as CEO of an international network builder.
* **Youngest Media Executive Distinction:** Recognized across Pakistani media circles for becoming one of the nation's youngest television network owners and CEOs upon establishing TV2Day in the mid-2000s.
* **Sports Leadership Recognition:** Commended by national sports and administrative bodies for leading the inaugural setup of the Multan Sultans PSL franchise and promoting cricket revival in Pakistan.

data.title: Rafael Arroyo Valdespino
data.text:
Rafael Arroyo Valdespino (24 October 1892 in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico – 1949) was a Puerto Rican chemist. He published on the production of rum under the name Rafael Arroyo.

Arroyo worked at the Agricultural Experimental Station of the University of Puerto Rico in Río Piedras as fermentation chemist. In the 1940s he became head of the Experimental Station. Arroyo published Studies on Rum an other works on rum production and also held a US patent for the production of heavy rum. He died in 1949. His last works were published posthumously.

==Selected publications==
* Rafael Arroyo, Studies on Rum, University of Puerto Rico, Agricultural Experimental Station, Río Piedras, Puerto Rico, 1945.
* Rafael Arroyo, Advanced Features in Rum Fermentation, in: International Sugar Journal, Vol. 52 (1950), pp. 42-44.

== Further reading ==

data.text:
----

= The Missing Workflow =
The Missing Workflow (T/M/W or TMW) is an independent software development project founded by Italian 3D artist and technical director Danilo Caliro. It focuses on developing add-ons and workflow tools for Blender®, an open-source 3D creation application. [ref: LinkedIn, LinkedIn]

== Background ==
The Missing Workflow develops utilities intended to extend existing digital content creation tools. Its areas of development include look development, shading, lighting, UV mapping and texture color management. [ref: LinkedIn, LinkedIn]

The project focuses on integrating additional production tools within Blender®, including operations commonly associated with professional digital content creation workflows. [ref: LinkedIn, LinkedIn]

== Software ==

=== Emission Pro ===
Emission Pro is a shader-based add-on for Blender® designed for use with the Cycles rendering engine. [ref: Emission Pro — For Blender® 5.2+ and Cycles, Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

It provides controls for emissive materials, including light contribution, color variation, volumetric effects and artistic lighting adjustments. [ref: Emission Pro — For Blender® 5.2+ and Cycles, Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

The software includes configurations for general emissive surfaces, LED-style materials and electronic displays. [ref: Emission Pro — For Blender® 5.2+ and Cycles, Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

=== Color Space Converter ===
Color Space Converter is a Blender® utility for auto-assigning texture color spaces. [ref: Color Space Converter — For Blender® 4.2+, Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

It identifies texture naming conventions and uses the available OpenColorIO configuration to determine color-space assignments for different texture types. [ref: Color Space Converter — For Blender® 4.2+, Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

=== UV Edit Pro ===
UV Edit Pro is a UV editing add-on for Blender®.

It provides tools for UV projection, selection, cutting and sewing, unwrapping, transformation, texel density management and layout. [ref: UV Edit Pro — For Blender® 4.5+ and 5.0+, Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

The add-on incorporates shell-oriented editing operations, viewport overlays and interactive editing tools intended to support manual UV editing. [ref: UV Edit Pro — For Blender® 4.5+ and 5.0+, Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

== Development and distribution ==
The Missing Workflow develops and distributes its software independently through digital marketplaces, including Superhive and Gumroad. [ref: Superhive (formerly Blender Market), Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

Technical documentation and video tutorials accompany its software releases. [ref: Superhive (formerly Blender Market), Superhive (formerly Blender Market)]

data.title: Nidesh Lawtoo
data.text:
Nidesh Lawtoo (born 1976) is a philosopher and literary theorist. He is professor of Modern and Contemporary European Literature and Culture at Leiden University. His work focuses on theories of mimesis (imitation) in philosophy, literature, political theory and media studies. From 2016 to 2022 he led the European Research Council–funded project Homo Mimeticus: Theory and Criticism.

== Early life and education ==
Lawtoo was born in 1976 in Bellinzona and raised in Italian-speaking Switzerland, to a Swiss mother and a father from Mauritius. He grew up in San Vittore, in the Mesolcina valley. He studied at the University of Lausanne, where, as he later described it, he was trained at the crossroads of literary studies, philosophy and the social sciences. He received a PhD in Comparative Literature and Critical Theory from the University of Washington in 2009; his dissertation was titled "The Phantom of the Ego: Mimesis and Subjectivity in Nietzsche, Conrad, Lawrence, and Bataille".

== Academic career ==
Lawtoo was maître assistant at the University of Lausanne (2009–2013), a visiting scholar at the Humanities Center of Johns Hopkins University with a Swiss National Science Foundation fellowship (2013–2016), and assistant professor at the University of Bern (2016–2017), before joining KU Leuven. At KU Leuven he was an assistant professor of philosophy and English

From 2016 to 2022 he was principal investigator of Homo Mimeticus: Theory and Criticism (HOM), a project funded by an ERC Starting Grant (grant agreement 716181) and hosted by KU Leuven; it ran from 1 November 2016 to 30 April 2022. In 2023 he became professor at Leiden University, where he gave his inaugural lecture, "Dodo Through the Looking-Glass: A Mirror for Modern and Contemporary Culture", on 14 November 2025.

== Research ==
Lawtoo's areas of specialization include modernism, critical theory, postcolonial literature, film studies and continental philosophy, with a focus on theories of mimesis, imitation and simulation. He promotes a transdisciplinary field that he calls "mimetic studies". He has described his first major book, The Phantom of the Ego, as a Nietzschean alternative to René Girard's mimetic theory. His books engage with thinkers including Plato, Friedrich Nietzsche, Gustave Le Bon, Sigmund Freud, Georges Bataille, Girard, Philippe Lacoue-Labarthe and Jean-Luc Nancy.

=== The Phantom of the Ego (2013) ===
The Phantom of the Ego: Modernism and the Mimetic Unconscious (Michigan State University Press) argues that the modernist account of the unconscious anticipates contemporary findings on the role of mimesis in the formation of subjectivity. Rather than starting from Freud, it begins with Nietzsche and reads Joseph Conrad, D. H. Lawrence and Georges Bataille.

Reviewing the book in Modern Language Quarterly, Kurt Koenigsberger praised its reconstruction of a hidden history of the mimetic unconscious, but criticized its loose and shifting definition of modernism.

=== Conrad studies ===
Lawtoo edited Conrad's Heart of Darkness and Contemporary Thought (Bloomsbury, 2012). In Conrad's Shadow: Catastrophe, Mimesis, Theory (2016) he reads Conrad's novels, and postcolonial and cinematic works that respond to them, through the two sides of mimesis, one pathological and one therapeutic. The book shared first place in the Joseph Conrad Society of America's Adam Gillon Book Award in Conrad Studies for 2018, with Andrew Francis's Culture and Commerce in Conrad's Asian Fiction. Reviewing it in The Conradian, Yael Levin called it an important contribution to Conrad studies and praised the originality of both its theoretical paradigms and its method of presentation, while noting a tendency to treat Conrad's fiction as a point of departure for reflecting on mimesis rather than a destination.

=== Political theory ===
In (New) Fascism: Contagion, Community, Myth (2019), with a foreword by Mikkel Borch-Jacobsen, Lawtoo applies mimetic theory to authoritarian leaders and new media, taking Donald Trump as a case study. Reviewing it in L'Esprit Créateur, Bruno Chaouat called it a compelling reminder of the continued relevance of continental philosophy, sociology and psychoanalysis, while noting that the far right may imitate fascism more than embody it.

=== Violence and the unconscious ===
In two volumes published in 2023 by Michigan State University Press, Violence and the Oedipal Unconscious (subtitled The Catharsis Hypothesis) and Violence and the Mimetic Unconscious (subtitled The Affective Hypothesis), Lawtoo traces the history of the "catharsis" hypothesis and of theories of an affective, mimetic unconscious, and relates them to representations of media violence.

=== Homo Mimeticus series ===
Homo Mimeticus: A New Theory of Imitation (Leuven University Press, 2022; open access) proposes a theory of mimesis across philosophy, aesthetics and politics, and closes with a dialogue with Edgar Morin. Philipp Wolf, reviewing it in the Journal of Modern Literature, described it as a transdisciplinary study drawing on philosophy, psychology, the arts, politics and neuroscience, and singled out its attempt at a new and systematic theory of mimesis.

It was followed by two edited volumes from Leuven University Press: Homo Mimeticus II: Re-Turns to Mimesis (2024), edited with Marina Garcia-Granero, and Homo Mimeticus III: Plasticity, Mimesis and Metamorphosis with Catherine Malabou (2025), edited with Willow Verkerk. He also edited Mimetic Posthumanism: Homo Mimeticus 2.0 in Art, Philosophy and Technics (Brill, 2025), on the mimetic turn in posthuman studies. Within the HOM project he also edited special issues of Conradiana (2016), MLN (2017), CounterText (2022) and the Journal of Posthumanism (2022).

=== Mimetic inclinations ===
In a dialogue with the philosopher Adriana Cavarero, published in 2021, Lawtoo proposed the idea of "mimetic inclinations" to link mimesis to Cavarero's relational account of subjectivity; Cavarero agreed in part while voicing reservations about the risk of fusion with the other. The dialogue was continued in a 2023 special issue of Critical Horizons and a 2021 conference at KU Leuven organized by the Gendered Mimesis project in collaboration with HOM.

== Public engagement ==
Within the HOM project, Lawtoo recorded a series of video dialogues, "HOM Videos", with scholars including Jean-Luc Nancy, Edgar Morin, J. Hillis Miller, Christoph Wulf, Katherine Hayles, Adriana Cavarero and Vittorio Gallese, and, in 2025, Judith Butler. In May 2022 he gave a TEDx talk at KU Leuven, "A Mirror for the Future".

== Translations ==
His books have been translated into several languages, including:
* Italian: Il fantasma dell'Io. La massa e l'inconscio mimetico (Mimesis, 2018); (Neo)Fascismo. Contagio, comunità, mito (Mimesis, 2020); Violenza e catarsi. L'inconscio edipico and Violenza e contagio. L'inconscio mimetico (Mimesis, 2024); Homo mimeticus. Una nuova teoria dell'imitazione (Carocci, 2025)
* German: Homo Mimeticus: Eine neue Theorie der Imitation (LIT Verlag, 2024) and (Neuer) Faschismus: Ansteckung, Gemeinschaft, Mythos (LIT Verlag, 2025)
* Spanish: Homo mimeticus: Una nueva teoría de la imitación (Tirant Humanidades, 2024) and La violencia y el inconsciente: De la catarsis al contagio (Tirant lo Blanch, 2025)
* French: Les (néo)fascismes: Comment fonctionne la contagion des masses aujourd'hui ? (Hermann, 2026)
* Dutch: (Nieuw) Fascisme: Besmetting, gemeenschap, mythe (Noordboek, 2024)
* Portuguese: (Novo) Fascismo: Contágio, comunidade, mito (Documenta, 2026), translated by Sara Belo

== Awards ==
* 2009: Bruce Harkness Young Conrad Scholar Award, Joseph Conrad Society of America
* 2018: Adam Gillon Book Award in Conrad Studies (shared first place), Joseph Conrad Society of America, for Conrad's Shadow

== Selected works ==
* Conrad's Heart of Darkness and Contemporary Thought, Bloomsbury
* The Phantom of the Ego: Modernism and the Mimetic Unconscious, Michigan State University Press
* Conrad's Shadow: Catastrophe, Mimesis, Theory, Michigan State University Press
* (New) Fascism: Contagion, Community, Myth, Michigan State University Press

* Mimetic Posthumanism: Homo Mimeticus 2.0 in Art, Philosophy and Technics, Brill
* Homo Mimeticus III: Plasticity, Mimesis and Metamorphosis with Catherine Malabou, Leuven University Press

data.title: Florence Ajimobi
data.text:
Fatima Florence Ajimobi (born 5 April 1959) is a Nigerian entrepreneur, philanthropist and diplomat. She served as the First Lady of Oyo State from 2011 to 2019, during the administration of her husband, former Governor Abiola Ajimobi.

Before entering public life, she had established Grandex, which was registered in 1982 with business interests in retail, wholesale distribution and other commercial services. [ref: Life after Power…Florence Ajimobi Completes Multimillion-naira Mall – THISDAYLIVE]She is also the founder of the Access to Basic Medical Care (ABC) Foundation, established in 2011 to improve access to healthcare services. [ref: ISO accredits Ajimobi’s ABC medical laboratory, The Guardian Nigeria News - Nigeria and World News]

In 2026, she became Nigeria’s Ambassador to Austria and Permanent Representative to international organisations in Vienna.

== Early life and education ==
Florence Ajimobi was born on 5 April 1959 in Benin City, Nigeria, by a Nigerian mum into the Hajaig family of Lebanese ancestry. She grew up in Ibadan, Oyo State, where she attended Our Lady of Apostles Secondary School. [ref: 7 interesting facts about Florence Ajimobi at 60, The Nation Newspaper]

She obtained an Ordinary National Diploma (OND) from The Polytechnic, Ibadan, in 1978.

In 2013, she completed a Strategic Programme for Negotiation and Leadership at Harvard Business School, United States, where she received a certificate. She subsequently obtained a Master of Business Administration (MBA) from the London School of Business and Finance in 2014. [ref: ]

In 2017, she was awarded an honorary Doctor of Science degree in Public Administration by Ajayi Crowther University, Oyo. [ref: Ajimobi’s wife gets honorary doctorate degree, The Nation Newspaper]

== Business career ==
Florence Ajimobi began her professional career in 1979 with Femi Johnson & Company, an insurance brokerage firm. Between 1980 and 1984, she worked with Briscoe Group, Insight Communications and Edison Engineering Company, holding administrative and client service positions. [ref: Why Gov. AJIMOBI Does Not Joke With His Wife, FLORENCE, City People Magazine]

In 1984, she moved into full-time entrepreneurship, developing Grandex Group of Companies having registered the business few years earlier. The business expanded into supermarkets, wholesale distribution and warehousing, with operations in Lagos and Ibadan. Grandex later diversified into bakery operations and equipment rentals. [ref: Ex-Oyo First Lady, Florence Ajimobi, expands business, The Sun Nigeria]

== Philanthropy and healthcare ==
In 2011, Florence Ajimobi established the Access to Basic Medical Care (ABC) Foundation to improve access to healthcare services, particularly for people in underserved communities. The foundation’s activities include cancer awareness, medical screening, diagnostic services and community health outreach programmes. [ref: ISO accredits Ajimobi’s ABC medical laboratory, The Guardian Nigeria News - Nigeria and World News]

In February 2013, the Florence Ajimobi Alaanu House was inaugurated at the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan, to provide accommodation for relatives of patients receiving treatment at the hospital. [ref: Ajimobi urges Nigerians to give back to society, The Nation Newspaper]

The ABC Foundation also operates a medical diagnostic laboratory. In July 2021, The Guardian reported that the laboratory had received ISO accreditation. [ref: ISO accredits Ajimobi’s ABC medical laboratory, The Guardian Nigeria News - Nigeria and World News]

== First Lady of Oyo State ==
Florence Ajimobi served as First Lady of Oyo State from 2011 to 2019. During this period, she established the Oyo State Officials’ Wives Association (OYSOWA), through which she organised programmes focused on women’s development and empowerment. [ref: 12 govs’ wives, others for women summit in Ibadan, Punch Newspapers]

One of the association’s major activities was the annual National Women’s Summit, which brought together women from different backgrounds to discuss leadership, economic opportunities and social development. [ref: 12 govs’ wives, others for women summit in Ibadan, Punch Newspapers]

The 2017 summit reportedly attracted over 1,000 participants, including former Zimbabwean Vice President Joice Mujuru and former Liberian First Lady Jewel Howard-Taylor. [ref: Women seek more opportunities to serve Nigeria, The Guardian Nigeria News - Nigeria and World News]

== Publications ==
In April 2019, Florence Ajimobi published her memoir, My Life Like a Rainbow. The book covers her childhood, marriage, family life and experiences in public life. A book reading subsequently took place in Ibadan on 18 June 2019. [ref: Learning life’s lessons from ex-governor’s wife, Florence Ajimobi, Tribune Online]

== Diplomatic career ==
In 2026, Florence Ajimobi was appointed Nigeria’s Ambassador to Austria and Permanent Representative to international organisations in Vienna. [ref: Nigerian Ambassador Ajimobi Presents Credentials to Austrian President, Voice of Nigeria]

On 17 August 2026, she presented her credentials to the International Anti-Corruption Academy (IACA) [ref: Ambassador of Nigeria Presents Credentials, www.iaca.int]. On 17 September 2026, she presented her Letters of Credence to Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen.

In September 2026, she was appointed Nigeria’s Governor on the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for the 2026–2028 term. [ref: Nigeria Elected To IAEA Board Of Governors For 2026–2028 Term, Congratulates Ambassador Florence Ajimobi On Her Appointment As Governor, Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation]

== Personal life ==
Florence Ajimobi married Abiola Ajimobi in 1980, and the couple had five children. [ref: Gov Abiola Ajimobi, Wife, Celebrate 35th Year Of Marital Bliss, The Guardian Nigeria News - Nigeria and World News]

Her husband, who served as Governor of Oyo State from 2011 to 2019, died on 25 June 2020 in Lagos following complications from COVID-19. [ref: Ajimobi Finally Laid To Rest In Ibadan, Channels Television]

On 27 March 2025, she lost her eldest daughter, Abisola Kola-Daisi, who died in the United Kingdom. Abisola was an entrepreneur and a mother of three. [ref: UPDATED: Ex-Oyo gov Ajimobi’s daughter, Bisola, dies at 42, Punch Newspapers]
