data.title: Arrowhead 120
data.text:
The Arrowhead 120 (AH120) is a proposed frigate design developed by British defence company Babcock International in collaboration with Swedish defence company Saab AB. The design was offered for the Swedish Navy's Luleå-class frigate programme. [ref: Arrowhead 120, Babcock International] [ref: Saab in cooperation with Babcock for the Swedish Navy’s Future Surface Combatants, Saab]

In 2026 the Arrowhead 120 was one of the designs offered for Sweden's Luleå-class programme. The Swedish government subsequently selected the French Defence and Intervention Frigate (FDI) design offered by Naval Group. A contract for four FDI-based frigates was signed on 31 August 2026, and the Arrowhead 120 was not selected. [ref: Sweden inks deal with Naval Group for new frigates, Janes] [ref: Decision on negotiations with France on Luleå-class frigates for air defence role, Government Offices of Sweden]

== Design and development ==

The Arrowhead 120 was publicly presented by Babcock in 2017 as part of its Arrowhead family of naval designs. [ref: Babcock announces 'Arrowhead' – another option for the Type 31 frigate competition, Navy Lookout] The design was subsequently developed into a proposal for Sweden's future frigate requirement through cooperation between Babcock and Saab. [ref: Sweden prepares to put a foot back in blue water with frigate acquisition, Naval News]

Saab and Babcock signed a strategic cooperation agreement in September 2023 to explore joint development of advanced surface combatants. [ref: Saab signs strategic cooperation agreement with Babcock, Saab] In 2024 Saab was contracted by the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) to lead the basic design phase for the Luleå class, with Babcock providing engineering support.

The Swedish proposal combined Babcock's experience in naval architecture, ship construction and systems integration with Saab's experience in naval combat systems, sensors and weapons. Babcock's Arrowhead 140 design, which forms the basis of the Type 31 frigate programme in the United Kingdom, was cited as part of the larger design family's industrial background.

The proposed ship was intended for operations in the Baltic Sea and the High North. Babcock describes the design as incorporating features for cold-weather operation, including low-temperature steel, a strengthened ice belt and reinforcement of propulsion and steering systems.

== Design and characteristics ==

The proposed Arrowhead 120 measures 124 metres in length and has a stated displacement of 4,650 tonnes. Its construction combines a steel hull with a composite superstructure.

The Swedish configuration was based on Saab's 9LV combat management system and included an integrated mast housing radar and other electronic systems. The proposal incorporated Sea Giraffe 4A and Sea Giraffe 1X radar systems.

== Swedish frigate programme ==

The Arrowhead 120 was proposed for the Swedish Navy's Luleå-class programme, which sought to procure four new frigates to expand the navy's capabilities beyond its existing fleet of smaller surface combatants, including the Visby-class corvettes.

Saab and Babcock submitted their proposal as a joint industrial offering, with Babcock contributing ship design and construction expertise and Saab providing combat systems and Swedish equipment. [ref: More details emerge on Saab-Babcock frigate offer to Sweden, UK Defence Journal] [ref: Babcock pitches Arrowhead 120 variant for the Swedish Luleå-class frigate programme, Navy Lookout]

The principal competing proposals came from Babcock/Saab, France's Naval Group and Spain's Navantia. In May 2026 the Swedish government instructed the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration to begin negotiations with Naval Group for four frigates based on the FDI design. A contract for the four ships was signed on 31 August 2026, making the FDI the selected design for the programme.

The Arrowhead 120 therefore remained an unselected proposal rather than a class of ships ordered for the Swedish Navy.

data.title: World Time Attack Challenge
data.text:
----

The World Time Attack Challenge (known as the Yokohama World Time Attack Challenge or WTAC) is a multi-day time attack event held at Sydney Motorsport Park. It is a festival that also features a variety of categories in car culture such as drifting, demonstrations, straight-line racing, car show and a trader alley.

== History ==

=== 2008–2009: Superlap Australia ===
The origins of the World Time Attack Challenge [ref: https://www.worldtimeattack.com] can be traced back to the inaugural Yokohama Superlap event held in 2008. Conceived with limited resources and minimal event management experience, the event was organised within a matter of months and marked the beginning of a new era for time attack motorsport in Australia. With support from industry partners and grassroots workshops, the first Superlap attracted 65 competitors from across the country and was hosted at Oran Park Raceway in New South Wales.

The early format featured two primary classes—Open and Clubsprint—culminating in a Superlap shootout, which was won by Peter Lucas driving a supercharged Honda-powered Lotus Exige. Despite its relatively modest and experimental beginnings, the event quickly gained traction, supported by exhibitors and sponsors such as Advan Yokohama, Turbosmart, [ref: World Time Attack - A Walk Down Memory Lane • Turbosmart, Turbosmart] Haltech, and Royal Purple, many of whom would remain long-term partners of the event.

In 2009, the event expanded in scale and professionalism, introducing a Pro Class and attracting more competitive machinery, including Mark Berry's ADVAN/Hi Octane Nissan Skyline GT-R (R34) and the Tilton and Pulse Racing Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution entries. That year's outright victory was secured by Garth Walden in the Tilton Evolution. The 2009 event also marked the final running at Oran Park Raceway before its closure, adding historical significance to the competition.

=== 2010–Present: World Time Attack Challenge ===
Following the closure of Oran Park Raceway in 2009, the event relocated to Sydney Motorsport Park (then known as Eastern Creek International Raceway) in 2010. This transition marked a significant turning point, both in scale and ambition, as the event was rebranded as the World Time Attack Challenge (WTAC), reflecting its growing international focus.

The introduction of international competitors in 2010 elevated the competition to a global stage. Notably, Nobuteru Taniguchi piloted the HKS CT230R Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution, which set a new benchmark for time attack performance and secured overall victory. The presence of established Japanese teams and drivers signalled WTAC's emergence as a premier destination for elite time attack vehicles and engineering.

Throughout 2011 and 2012, WTAC continued to expand in both participation and technical sophistication. The Pro Class became increasingly competitive, with Australian teams rapidly developing their vehicles to challenge international entrants. Advancements in aerodynamics, tyre technology, and engine performance contributed to progressively faster lap times, reinforcing the event's reputation as a showcase of cutting-edge time attack engineering. [ref: In The Moment >> Smashing the 1:30 barrier, Speedhunters]
[ref: In The Moment>> Cyber Evo Dips Below 1:29, Scorch Breaks Down, Speedhunters]
[ref: Flash Result >> Cyber Evo Defend Their Crown, Speedhunters]
[ref: Behind The Scenes >> Life In The WTAC Pitlane, Speedhunters]

The event also grew beyond on-track competition, incorporating a larger motorsport festival atmosphere with trade exhibitions, car displays, and spectator engagement. By 2012, WTAC had firmly established itself as a globally recognised event, attracting leading teams from Japan, Australia, [ref: Australians Dominate At World Time Attack Challenge 2012, Drive] and other regions, and setting the foundation for its continued evolution as the world's premier time attack competition. [ref: WTAC 2012 - Archives Speedhunters, Speedhunters]

Between approximately 2013 and 2017, the event entered a period often characterised as an "aerodynamic arms race," with increasingly extreme vehicle designs emerging [ref: The 2017 WTAC Finals and Unlimited Aero Extremes, Headcount Coffee]
[ref: The Dust Settles At WTAC: Tilton Reigns Supreme, Speedhunters]
[ref: Welcome Back, WTAC, Speedhunters]
[ref: Flash Result: Tilton Evo Takes Third WTAC Title, Speedhunters]
[ref: The Speedhunters WTAC Wrap-Up, Speedhunters]
[ref: Open Wide & Say Ahh... The Engine Bays Of WTAC, Speedhunters]
[ref: World Time Attack Challenge 2016 - Shattering Records at Sydney Motorsport Park, DSPORT Magazine]
[ref: WTAC 2017 Starts Here, Speedhunters]
[ref: World Time Attack Challenge 2017 Is On, Speedhunters]
[ref: Why We Keep Coming Back To WTAC, Speedhunters]

Notable examples included the Scorch Racing Cyber Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution, driven by Tarzan Yamada, and the MCA "Hammerhead" Nissan Silvia, driven by Tim Slade. These vehicles featured highly advanced aerodynamic packages and bespoke engineering solutions, contributing to record-breaking performances and international attention. [ref: The Road To WTAC Starts Here, Speedhunters]
[ref: World Time Attack Challenge: The Pressure Is On, Speedhunters]
[ref: The Times Come Down At WTAC, Speedhunters]
[ref: WTAC: The Results Are In..., Speedhunters]
[ref: This One's For The Nerds: The Tech of WTAC, Speedhunters]
[ref: Re-Evaluating Fast At World Time Attack Challenge, Speedhunters]
[ref: WTAC: On The Front Line, Speedhunters]
[ref: News: HKS TRB-03 Full Attack – WTAC 2018, Narita Dogfight]
[ref: Event: World Time Attack 2018 V.1 – Pro Class Overview, Narita Dogfight]
[ref: Event: World Time Attack 2018 V.2 – One Perfect Lap, Narita Dogfight]

Despite challenges such as event disruptions during the early 2020s, WTAC has remained a prominent fixture in the global time attack calendar. It continues to attract leading teams, drivers, and manufacturers, maintaining its reputation as one of the most competitive and technologically advanced time attack events in the world. [ref: A Sneak Peek At The World Time Attack Challengers, Speedhunters]
[ref: The Return Of WTAC, Speedhunters]

== Record-Breaking Event ==
The World Time Attack Challenge has become widely recognised for record-breaking performances at Sydney Motorsport Park, with successive events producing some of the fastest closed-wheel lap times ever recorded at the circuit. In 2019, Barton Mawer set a new benchmark with a 1:19.277 lap [ref: Barton Mawer's Lap Record at Sydney Motorsport Park, Barton Mawer Motorsport] in the RP968 Porsche 968, marking one of the fastest laps ever achieved at the venue at the time. [ref: Time Crunch: The Pressure Of WTAC, Speedhunters]
[ref: Celebrating 10 Years Of World Time Attack Challenge, Speedhunters]

By 2023, Mawer further lowered the outright WTAC lap record to 1:17.8600, establishing the fastest official lap recorded on the Gardner Grand Prix Circuit configuration of Sydney Motorsport Park, beating the previous record held by Nico Hulkenberg in 2007 of 1:19.142. [ref: SMSP Lap Records]
[ref: The World Returns For WTAC 2023, Speedhunters]
This was followed by another record-break in 2024 where Barton Mawer secured a lap time of 1:17.444. [ref: EMTRON PRO CLASS - RP968 DOMINATES, World Time Attack]
[ref: Blown Away At The 2024 World Time Attack Challenge, Speedhunters]

data.title: Lilian Nneji
data.text:
----

Lilian Nneji is a Nigerian gospel singer known for her gospel music and energetic dance performances. In an interview published by PUNCH in August 2023, she discussed her early interest in music, her musical influences and the challenges she encountered while pursuing a career as a musician. [ref: Before Stardom With... Lilian Nneji, PUNCH]
== Career ==
Nneji performs gospel music and has described her musical style as encompassing different styles rather than a single specific genre. In the same interview, she discussed the role of dance in her performances and identified her single Onwere Ihe Omere Mú as one of her songs.
In September 2024, The Nation included Nneji in a list of nine Nigerian gospel singers it described as trending. [ref: Nine trending Nigerian gospel singers, The Nation]
In July 2025, Nneji spoke to PUNCH about the role of gospel music in providing consolation to Nigerians. She also discussed the inspiration behind her concert, Lilian Nneji Live in Concert, scheduled for 20 July 2025 at Solution Arena in Onipanu, Lagos. [ref: God is using gospel music to console Nigerians; Lilian Nneji, PUNCH]

data.title: Debjit Mahalanobis
data.text:
Debjit Mahalanobis is an Indian double bassist, composer, and instrument inventor who has incorporated the double bass into Hindustani classical music and Bengali folk. [ref: Meet Debjit Mahalanobis, the only full-time professional upright double bass artist in Bengal, Scroll.in] In 2018, he envisioned the Gajveena, a nine-string instrument combining elements of the double bass and the rudra veena, later which was one of the finalists at the 2026 Guthman Musical Instrument Competition at the Georgia Institute of Technology. [ref: Newly invented Gajveena makes it to the Guthman Musical Instrument competition in Atlanta, The Hindu] [ref: 2026 Finalists, Guthman Musical Instrument Competition] [ref: Check Out 10 Weird and Wonderful Finalists for the 'Pulitzer of the New Instrument World', Gizmodo]

== Early life and training ==

Mahalanobis’s paternal family includes statistician and scientist P. C. Mahalanobis, while his maternal lineage descends from Ramshankar Bhattacharya, founder of the Bishnupur Dhrupad-Dhamar gharana. [ref: About, Debjit Mahalanobis]

He started learning music informally at home on the harmonium. As a preteen, influenced by rock artists such as Led Zeppelin and The Who, he took up the guitar before moving to electric bass.

At the age of 17, he was introduced to Western classical music by his first teacher, Abraham Mazumdar. He initially studied the cello before moving to the double bass. After completing his education, he worked as a physics teacher before leaving the profession after three years to pursue music full-time.

He got mentorship under professor and conductor Hans Jürgen Nagel for a couple of years. [ref: Talented Debjit Mahalanobis and his Double Bass wonder!, GetBengal] Later he began studying Dagarvani dhrupad on the rudra veena under Bahauddin Dagar. [ref: Double the innovation: How musicians niftily weave in king-sized double bass into Indian compositions, The Hindu]

== Career ==

Mahalanobis was associated with the Calcutta School of Music. He has performed as a double bassist with several orchestras, including the Bombay Chamber Orchestra, the Indian National Youth Orchestra, the Indo-European Chamber Orchestra, the Kolkata Symphony, the South Asian Symphony Orchestra, and the Bangalore City Chamber Orchestra.

Mahalanobis recorded the main melody for the title track of the web series Taranath Tantrik after composer and filmmaker Q (Quashik Mukherjee) discovered a video of his double bass–sitar jugalbandi and approached him for the project. Mahalanobis played the melody in the studio, where it was recorded on the spot and subsequently used throughout the series. The series premiered on Hoichoi in January 2019.

Beyond orchestral performance, Mahalanobis has worked on a range of musical projects spanning contemporary music and television. In 2017, he performed on television as part of the Murshidabadi Project, a Sufi music initiative. In 2020, Sangeet Kala Mandir premiered Double Bass India, an online concert featuring his compositions. His commissioned work was also featured at the Favoriten Festival in Dortmund in 2022. In recognition of his work, he received the Chidakash Yuva Samman in 2021.

== Compositions and collaborations ==

Mahalanobis's work can be observed in Dakini 2025, an interdisciplinary short music film centred on Bengal's Bohurupi folk tradition, [ref: In 'DAKINI', Debjit Mahalanobis' Brings Double Bass Mastery To Bengali Performance Art, Homegrown] and Katha (2024), a solo double bass composition with Kathak. [ref: Debjit Mahalanobis' 'Katha' Video Tells an Unsettling Tale, Rolling Stone India]

Mahalanobis became a member of Hotel Kali, an Indo-German collaborative music project, after musician Varun Desai recommended him to Berlin-based musician Theresa Stroetges, who was seeking local collaborators during a two-month Kolkata residency organised with Goethe-Institut, Musicboard Berlin and BorderMovement. The group comprised Stroetges, Desai, Mahalanobis and Suyasha Sengupta, and released its self-titled debut album in 2021. [ref: Review: Hotel Kali Make A Stellar Case For Collaboration On Eponymous Debut Album, Wild City]

Mahalanobis has performed with DnA Machines, an electronic duo with Agnitray Chakrabarty, in which he plays a dismantlable upright electric bass. The duo performed at the World Music Day Festival at Kolkata’s Eastern Metropolitan Club in 2022. [ref: Eastern Metropolitan Club celebrates World Music Day, The Telegraph] He has also performed with JazzMahal, a Kolkata-based jazz trio featuring pianist Tazim Sheikh and drummer Aniruddha Saha, at JazzFest 2023 at the Dalhousie Institute, playing both electric and acoustic double bass. [ref: JazzFest 2023: Tunes from 'Epiphany' and a Ray-inspired 'Ode to Kolkata' shine on Day Two, The Telegraph] His performances have also explored the combination of the double bass with traditional Indian string instruments, including the Mattakokila veena and the Raas veena.

== The Gajveena ==

In 2018, Mahalanobis envisioned the Gajveena, a nine-string acoustic bass-veena designed to combine elements of the double bass and the rudra veena. Measuring 6 ft 11 in, the instrument has a 42-inch fretted fingerboard and dual resonators, and can be played with a bow or by plucking its strings. According to him, the name "Gajveena" was coined by his guru, Bahauddin Dagar.

In 2026, the Gajveena was selected as a finalist in the Guthman Musical Instrument Competition at the Georgia Institute of Technology, an international competition for new musical instrument design. It was one of ten finalists in the 2026 competition. [ref: Georgia Tech Announces Finalists in its Musical Instrument Competition, The Violin Channel]

data.title: Madeleine Dwyer
data.text:
Madeleine Dwyer is a New Zealand association football player who plays for Eastern Suburbs AFC and has represented New Zealand at under-16 and under-17 level.

== Career ==
Dwyer plays for Eastern Suburbs AFC in Auckland (since 2016). She was a member of the club's U18 youth League Squad in 2024, 2025 and 2026 [ref: 2024 Domestic Scene, Ultimate New Zealand Soccer], and the Women's First Team Squad in the 2025 and 2026 women's football seasons. [ref: Preview: Squads take shape ahead of new women's National League season, Friends of Football]

In 2024, Dwyer represented New Zealand playing for [https://www.baradene.school.nz/ Baradene College] at the [https://www.isfsports.org/sports/football ISF Football World Cup] in Dalian China. [ref: ISF Football World Cup 2024: Final Bulletin, International School Sport Federation]

In 2025 Dwyer made her debut for the Eastern Suburbs AFC women's first team against Tauranga Moana (11th May 2025, aged 15 years, 1 month and 5 days) scoring a goal on her debut [ref: ]. She was the youngest player to take the field in the final of the 2025 New Zealand Women's National League Final, where ESAFC were defeated by Auckland United 1-0 [https://www.nzfootball.co.nz/matchcentre/2025/2729091078/2729091121 Report] (29th November 2025, aged 15 years, 7 months 24 days).

In 2026, Dwyer was a member of the Auckland FC [https://aucklandfc.co.nz/womens-development-centre/ Women's Talent Development Centre] [ref: Young talent on show before national coach names U-17 World Cup squad, Friends of Football] who played a 2 game friendly series against Wellington Phoenix. Dwyer represented New Zealand in the New Zealand Secondary Schools Football tour of Melbourne in July 2026 [ref: NZ Secondary Schools Football, www.nzssfootball.co.nz]. She was a member of the Eastern Suburbs AFC Women's first team squad who won the Kate Shepherd Cup [ref: Eastern Suburbs win Kate Sheppard Cup at Christchurch indoor stadium, Stuff], and the [https://www.baradene.school.nz/ Baradene College] First XI who won the New Zealand Secondary Schools 2026 Girls’ Premier Football Tournament tournament (National Championships) [ref: 2026 Girls Premier Tournament - Home, www.sporty.co.nz].

Dwyer was selected in the New Zealand U16 squad [ref: New Zealand Announce Squad For OFC U-16 Women’s Championship 2026, New Zealand Football] for the 2026 OFC U-16 Women's Championship, held in Solomon Islands in Sept 2026. Dwyer made her international debut for New Zealand on 6th Sept 2026 starting against the host nation, Solomon Islands, and scored a goal on her international debut [ref: Match Report, Oceania Football Confederation] [ref: New Zealand score five to get underway at OFC U-16 Women's Championship, Friends of Football]. Dwyer also scored in the semi final game that qualified the team for the 2027 FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup [ref: New Caledonia and New Zealand punch Morocco 2027 tickets, www.fifa.com]

Dwyer was selected in the New Zealand U17 squad [ref: New Zealand’s FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup Squad Announced For Morocco, www.nzfootball.co.nz] for the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco (from 17 October to 7 November 2026), one of 10 players from the U-16 squad who won the 2026 OFC U-16 Championships under head coach Alana Gunn.

data.title: Nicole LeMaster
data.text:
‘’‘Nicole LeMaster’’’ is an American psychotherapist, Somatic Experiencing Practitioner, author, and dream coach. Her professional work includes somatic psychotherapy, trauma recovery, nervous-system regulation, and personal development.

== Career ==
‘’‘Nicole LeMaster’’’ is a psychotherapist, Somatic Experiencing Practitioner, author, and dream coach. Her clinical work includes somatic therapy and trauma recovery, while her separate coaching business focuses on dream work and personal development.Finding Capacity and Resilience, Carmichael TimesNicole Lemaster, Somatic Experiencing International [ref: SEI Portal, portal.traumahealing.org]

Separately, LeMaster works in the field of dream coaching through Moonbeam Dream. This coaching work is distinct from her clinical psychotherapy practice in purpose and scope. It focuses on dreams, personal development, and helping individuals explore aspirations and translate internal insights into goals and actions. It is a coaching platform rather than a clinical therapy service. [ref: SEI Portal, portal.traumahealing.org]

Although these two areas of work have different purposes and scopes of practice, both involve an interest in the relationship between internal experience and everyday life. In her clinical work, nervous-system regulation is relevant to trauma recovery and resilience; in her coaching work, the emphasis is on personal development and the process of bringing aspirations into lived experience. [ref: ]

== Media coverage ==
In August 2026, journalist Abbey Wicks profiled LeMaster in “Finding Capacity and Resilience”, published by the ‘‘Carmichael Times’’. The article discussed her work in somatic therapy, nervous-system regulation, trauma recovery, and dream coaching, as well as her book ‘‘WTF Am I Even Doing?: A Nervous System Workbook To Support Mind Body Alignment’’.Finding Capacity and Resilience, Carmichael Times

The article was also published by the ‘‘Elk Grove Citizen’’ and other publications within the same Sacramento-area publishing network.Finding Capacity and Resilience, Elk Grove Citizen [ref: ]

In December 2025, EIN Presswire published an announcement concerning LeMaster’s appearance on ‘‘Women In Power TV’’, a series hosted by Rudy Mawer.Nicole Lemaster to Appear on Women In Power TV, EIN Presswire

== Publications ==
LeMaster authored ‘‘WTF Am I Even Doing?: A Nervous System Workbook To Support Mind Body Alignment’’, which includes somatic awareness, reflective exercises, yoga practices, and chakra-related material.Books and Published Work, Nicole Lemaster

She also wrote “Forgiveness: A Personal Journey”, published by ‘‘The Science of Psychotherapy’’. The article discusses forgiveness, boundaries, self-care, embodiment, and personal growth.Forgiveness: A Personal Journey, The Science of Psychotherapy

data.title: Sumit Kumar (lawyer)
data.text:
Sumit Kumar is an Indian advocate and tax lawyer based in Kolkata. He practises at the Calcutta High Court and is the founder of The Lord's Consultancy (TLC), a tax and corporate law practice, and a partner at Harvey Legal LLP. He has written practitioner books and articles on India's Goods and Services Tax and on corporate and regulatory law.

== Education ==
Kumar holds a Bachelor of Commerce (Honours) and a Bachelor of Laws, and a Master of Laws from O.P. Jindal Global University. He is a Fellow of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India and an Associate of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India.

== Career ==
Kumar founded The Lord's Consultancy in Kolkata in 2011. The firm practises mainly in indirect taxation, including GST, customs and excise, and also handles direct tax, corporate, SEBI, FEMA and PMLA matters, with offices in Kolkata, Bengaluru and Chennai.

He practises as an advocate at the Calcutta High Court [ref: When Tax Appeal Backfires: How Far Can 'No Reformatio in Peius' Travel Under GST?, LiveLaw] and is a partner at Harvey Legal LLP. [ref: Death, Due Process and GST, The Bar Bulletin] He has appeared before the GST Appellate Tribunal, the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal and the Supreme Court of India.

== Writing ==
With his firm, Kumar has written books on Indian tax law, including the GST-TLC series, the TLC–GST Ready Reckoner 2026, the TLC Income Tax Ready Reckoner on the Income-tax Act, 2025, and GST Appellate Tribunal: Procedure Rules, 2025 – Practitioner Commentary, Drafts, Case Law & Filing Guide.

He has written for legal publications on GST, corporate and regulatory law. These include an analysis in LiveLaw of appellate enhancement under Section 107(11) of the CGST Act following Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Union of India; a column in Bar and Bench on whether the Reserve Bank of India can require Tata Sons to list; [ref: Can RBI make a private holding company go public? The Tata Sons question, Bar and Bench] an article in The Bar Bulletin on GST liability after a sole proprietor's death under Section 93 of the CGST Act; and opinion pieces for Taxmann on angel funds under the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations and on the Income-tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026. [ref: Angel Funds vis-à-vis AI-only Funds under SEBI AIF Regulations, Taxmann] [ref: Income-tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026 – What Changed and What Practitioners Should Do Now, Taxmann]

== Social work ==
Kumar is chairman and managing trustee of SEVA Foundation, a Kolkata-based charitable trust established in 2024 and registered under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which works on child education, food distribution, women's empowerment and legal awareness. [ref: About Us, SEVA Foundation]

data.title: CaseyJHayes
data.text:
Casey J. Hayes is an American music educator, choral conductor, and author. He is the A.J. Thurston Endowed Professor of Music at Franklin College in Franklin, Indiana, [ref: Casey J. Hayes, Ph.D., Franklin College] and the founding conductor and artistic director of the Vienna Gay Men's Chorus. [ref: It's gonna be …. LOUDER, Lambda Nachrichten] [ref: Künstlerische Leitung, Vienna Gay Men's Chorus] His research covers LGBTQ community choruses, inclusive music teaching, and the Jewish and LGBTQ cabaret performers of Weimar-era Germany and interwar Vienna. He was a Fulbright-Botstiber Visiting Professor of Austrian-American Studies at the University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna in 2021 [ref: Alum Chat: Katherine Baber and Casey Hayes in Discussion, Fulbright Austria] and wrote When the Music Stopped: Willy Rosen's Holocaust (2022), a historical novel about the German-Jewish cabaret artist Willy Rosen. [ref: Untold story: Franklin College professor pens book about famed musician during Holocaust, Daily Journal]

== Early life and education ==
Hayes began studying piano at age seven with teachers from the Juilliard School. [ref: Casey J. Hayes, Phi Delta Theta] He earned bachelor's and master's degrees in music education and choral conducting at Butler University in Indianapolis, where he studied with Henry Leck and James Mulholland. He received a PhD in music education from New York University's Steinhardt School in 2009. His dissertation, Building Bridges Through Song: A Qualitative Study of Educational Outreach by the New York City Ambassador Chorus, examined educational outreach by gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender choruses. [ref: Building Bridges Through Song: A Qualitative Study of Educational Outreach by the New York City Ambassador Chorus, New York University]

== Career ==
=== Early choral work and New York ===
Hayes joined his first gay chorus, the Indianapolis Men's Chorus, in January 2000, serving as its accompanist and assistant conductor. In New York he chaired the creative arts department and directed the choral and band programs at The Hewitt School, a private girls' school in Manhattan. He was co-music director of the New York City Gay Men's Chorus and musical director of its outreach ensemble, the Ambassador Chorus. [ref: Community music and the GLBT chorus, International Journal of Community Music] The chorus performed at venues including Carnegie Hall, Avery Fisher Hall, Alice Tully Hall and Radio City Music Hall during his time with it.

In 2007 Hayes founded the Gay Men's Chorus of Manhattan and served as its artistic director. The chorus gave benefit concerts to raise money for other nonprofit organizations. [ref: A City That Sings, CityBeat] In June 2009 it performed a benefit concert with the Broadway actor Malcolm Gets at the Triad Theatre in Manhattan. The concert raised money to bring students from the Sidney Lanier School, a public school in Gainesville, Florida, for children with disabilities, to New York for a 2010 performance at Carnegie Hall's Weill Recital Hall. According to the project's organizers, the hall might not have been available without these funds. [ref: Harmony through DIScovering ABILITIES: An interdisciplinary music approach for students with disabilities with the Sidney Lanier Center, ISME CMA, and NACCM, International Society for Music Education] Hayes also hosted the first meeting of the North American Coalition for Community Music, held at the Hewitt School in January 2008. He also served as musical director for the actresses Joanna Gleason and Karen Ziemba, and as a music consultant for Joan Rivers.

=== Franklin College ===
Hayes joined the faculty of Franklin College in 2009. He has served as chair of the music department and director of choral activities, conducting the Franklin College Singers, Women's Chorus and Men's Chorus. He holds the A.J. Thurston endowed professorship in music and also works as an international admissions representative for the college.

=== Community choruses in the United States ===
Hayes was artistic director of the Cincinnati Men's Chorus. The chorus roughly doubled in size during his first seasons and grew from about 30 to 80 singers over his six years with it. He then became artistic director of the Quarryland Men's Chorus in Bloomington, Indiana. He served on the board of directors of GALA Choruses and on the board of the New York State chapter of the American Choral Directors Association.

=== Fulbright and Vienna ===
Hayes was named a Fulbright-Botstiber Visiting Professor of Austrian-American Studies for 2020–21 and was hosted by the University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna from February to July 2021. [ref: Casey Hayes, Fulbright Scholar Program] His research there examined Vienna's LGBTQ and Jewish cabaret communities from the end of World War I to the 1938 Anschluss, and how émigré performers recreated Viennese cabaret in New York. [ref: Rosa Wien: Gay Rights, Schlager and Self-Exile: 1918–1938, Botstiber Institute for Austrian-American Studies] In his essay "Rosa Wien: Gay Rights, Schlager and Self-Exile: 1918–1938", published by the Botstiber Institute for Austrian-American Studies, he traced Vienna's cabaret and Schlager scene between the wars. The essay discusses "Das lila Lied" as an early gay anthem, and the gay cabaret performer Paul O'Montis, who fled Germany for Vienna and died in Sachsenhausen concentration camp in 1940.

On 17 June 2021, as part of Vienna Pride, Hayes gave the talk "A Shared Struggle: The emergence of the LGBTIQ+ rights movement in Europe and America" in the "Diplomats for Equality" series, streamed by the U.S. Embassy in Vienna. He argued that LGBTQ civil rights were not simply an American export, and that the Stonewall riots were a turning point rather than the beginning of organized resistance. [ref: Diplomats For Equality – The LGBTIQ rights movement in Europe and America, Vienna Pride] He has also lectured at the Fulbright conference in Strobl and at Pomona College. He is a research partner of the Literaturhaus Wien and its exile library, and sits on its board.

=== Vienna Gay Men's Chorus ===
In 2024, after the University of Vienna's gay choir Die Männersache was dissolved, Hayes and a core group of its singers founded the Vienna Gay Men's Chorus, with Hayes as conductor and artistic director. [ref: Über uns, Vienna Gay Men's Chorus] The tenor-bass chorus rehearses in English and German and gives an annual Pride concert. [ref: Vienna Gay Men's Chorus, Legato] It performed in the opening show of the 18th Diversity Ball at Vienna City Hall on 5 September 2026. [ref: 18. Diversity Ball bringt mehr als 3000 Gäste ins Wiener Rathaus, News]

== Writing ==
=== When the Music Stopped ===
When the Music Stopped: Willy Rosen's Holocaust was published in 2022 by Amsterdam Publishers, a Dutch press that specializes in Holocaust literature, in its New Jewish Fiction series. It was released on International Holocaust Remembrance Day. [ref: When the Music Stopped: Willy Rosen's Holocaust, Amsterdam Publishers] The novel follows Rosen from his service in World War I through his flight from Nazi Germany to the Netherlands. It covers his cabaret troupe's performances for the commandant of the Westerbork transit camp and his death at Auschwitz in 1944. Hayes called it "creative fiction" because its events, places and people are historical while its dialogue is invented.

Hayes spent about five years researching the book. He made repeated trips to archives in Germany and the Netherlands and translated Gestapo files on Rosen. He also located and reassembled scattered pages of an album compiled for the Westerbork commandant that documented Weimar-era cabaret performers held in the camp. [ref: Professor Pens Book About Famed Musician During Holocaust, U.S. News & World Report]

=== Academic writing ===
Hayes's article "Community music and the GLBT chorus" (2007) appeared in the first issue of the International Journal of Community Music. It traces the emergence and development of GLBT choruses in the United States, drawing on his outreach work with the Ambassador Chorus. He contributed the chapter "Safe Classrooms: A Fundamental Principle of Democratic Practice" to Giving Voice to Democracy in Music Education: Diversity and Social Justice in the Classroom (Routledge, 2016), edited by Lisa C. DeLorenzo. [ref: Giving Voice to Democracy in Music Education: Diversity and Social Justice in the Classroom, Routledge] He has presented at the International Society for Music Education World Conference in Kuala Lumpur (2006) and Glasgow (2016).

== Personal life ==
Hayes is married to Joseph Morris. He collects and restores antique German musical beer steins and 19th-century keyboard instruments.

== Selected works ==

* Giving Voice to Democracy in Music Education, Routledge
* Rosa Wien: Gay Rights, Schlager and Self-Exile: 1918–1938, Botstiber Institute for Austrian-American Studies
* When the Music Stopped: Willy Rosen's Holocaust, Amsterdam Publishers

The 2026–27 Cymru South season (also known as the 2026–27 Novira Cymru South for sponsorship reasons) is the upcoming seventh season of the second-tier Southern region football league in the Welsh football pyramid.

==Teams==
The league will consist of sixteen teams; twelve teams remaining from the previous season, three teams promoted from the Ardal Leagues, and one team relegated from the Cymru Premier. The top–placed team after 30 games will gain automatic promotion to the 2027–28 Cymru Premier, while the runners–up from both the Cymru South and the Cymru North face each other in a promotion play off semi–final. The winners of that game will then face the 14th–placed team from the Cymru Premier for a place in the 2027–28 Cymru Premier. [ref: JD Cymru Premier format confirmed for 2026/27, Football Association of Wales]
The three bottom teams will be relegated to the Ardal Leagues.

data.title: José Aragüez
data.text:
José Aragüez is a Spanish-born architect, author, and educator. He has developed his intellectual production and teaching career mainly in the schools of architecture at Princeton University, Columbia University, and Yale University. His writings sit at the intersection of modern and contemporary architecture, the history of science and computation, and several modes of philosophical inquiry. He is the founding principal of Spatial Infrastructure Research Office (SIRO), an architecture, urbanism, and research practice.

== Early life and education ==

José Aragüez was born in Málaga. In 2006, he completed a B.Arch./M.Arch. at the University of Granada, where his interest in conceptual architecture was nurtured under the guidance of a group of teachers including Antonio Jiménez Torrecillas and Juan Domingo Santos. Upon graduation, he received a university-wide Graduation Extraordinary Award and was also awarded a 1st National End-of-Degree Prize in Architecture from the Spanish Ministry of Culture. [ref: Order ECI/3313/2007, of 24 October, awarding the National End-of-Degree Prizes for University Education for the 2005-2006 academic year. Retrieved October 09, 2026. https://www.boe.es/diario_boe/txt.php?id=BOE-A-2007-19732] [ref: Roche, Antonio (6 November 2007). "Un Licenciado con Proyección." SUR. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://www.diariosur.es/20071106/malaga/licenciado-proyeccion-20071106.html]

In 2008 Aragüez moved to New York City to pursue post-professional studies at Columbia University. At Columbia GSAPP he studied architectural design with François Roche and Juan Herreros as well as history and theory with Mark Wigley and Kenneth Frampton, who trained him in architectural theory and critical history, respectively.

== Architecture career ==

Prior to his move to New York City, José Aragüez received an Arquia Banca Foundation grant based on holding one of the top student records in architecture in Spain. [ref: "Becas Fundación Arquia. Ganadores convocatoria 2005." Fundación Arquia. Retrieved February 27, 2026. https://fundacion.arquia.com/convocatorias/becas/convocatoria-2005/ganadores/] After a stint at the Granada-based office of Antonio Jiménez Torrecillas, it was through that grant that he relocated to Rotterdam to work for Dutch architecture firm MVRDV, in 2007. [ref: "Motorcity Alcañiz." MVRDV. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://www.mvrdv.com/projects/90/motorcity-alcaniz] In 2022 he started his own eponymous architecture practice, rebranded as Spatial Infrastructure Research Office (SIRO) in 2026. SIRO's work has focused on architectural competitions and experimental design research. The practice has entered public tenders and design competitions across Spain and in several other European countries, operating with a small team between Madrid and New York.

== Academia ==

During the 2010s Aragüez conducted doctoral studies at Princeton University under Prof. Sylvia Lavin. He also studied with Hal Foster—who introduced him to the role of 20th-century French theory in art—and wrote a dissertation on the concept of spatial organization in architecture. Aside from Lavin, his committee comprised Stan Allen, Sanford Kwinter, and Axel Kilian, then a tenure-track professor at Princeton. [ref: "Final Public Oral Exam of José Aragüez Escobar." Princeton University SoA. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://soa.princeton.edu/content/final-public-oral-exam-jos%C3%A9-araguez-escobar]

In addition to his teaching engagements, he has lectured extensively at venues including Harvard University, Yale University, Columbia University, ETH Zurich, Brno University of Technology, The Berlage, the A+D Museum in Los Angeles, MIT, Cooper Union, Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, Kyoto University, Higher Technical School of Architecture of Madrid, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, the Architectural Association School of Architecture, Rice University in Paris, Polytechnic University of Turin, and the Venice Biennale of Architecture. [ref: "The Building." Real Colegio Complutense at Harvard University. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://rcc.harvard.edu/event/building] [ref: "José Aragüez: Dispositional Intelligence." The Cooper Union. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://cooper.edu/events-and-exhibitions/events/book-talk-jose-araguez-dispositional-intelligence]

== Architectural theory ==

=== The Building (2014–2019) ===

"The Building" was an international discursive endeavor initiated by Aragüez that marked his entry into architectural discourse as an editor and theorist. Spanning six years (2014–2019), the project was launched through two symposia at the Architectural Association (London) and Columbia University GSAPP, respectively, and further developed as a theory seminar at Cornell University. These gatherings brought together architects, historians, and theorists to probe the building as a central discursive category in its own right, responding to tendencies in architectural history and theory that had shifted attention away from architectural thinking toward other fields of knowledge. [ref: "The Building at GSAPP." Columbia University GSAPP, November 2014. Retrieved October 09, 2026. * https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ebDDfsdO47A * https://thebuildingatgsapp.wordpress.com/] The initiative posited buildings as both design artifacts internal to the discipline and conceptual instruments operating within broader social, technological, and epistemological contexts.

The outcomes were compiled in a book published in 2016 as The Building by Lars Müller Publishers. [ref: Aragüez, José, ed. (2016). The Building. Lars Müller Publishers. ISBN 978-3-03778-498-3. https://www.lars-mueller-publishers.com/building] [ref: "The Building." E-flux Architecture. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://www.e-flux.com/announcements/125010/the-building] Drawing on contributors from institutions across North America and Europe, and addressing themes such as objecthood, value, digital culture, urban subjectivity, and architectural pedagogy, the volume combines theoretical essays with shorter pieces on case studies of contemporary buildings. The Building was awarded on several occasions, [ref: Valencia, Nicolás (2018). "Estos son los ganadores de la II Muestra de Investigación de la XIV BEAU." ArchDaily. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://www.archdaily.cl/cl/898825/estos-son-los-ganadores-de-la-ii-muestra-de-investigacion-de-la-xiv-beau] [ref: "Programa VI Festival Arquia Próxima." Fundación Arquia. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://fundacion.arquia.com/media/1708/programa_vi_festival_arquiaproxima-1.pdf] and it has been cited as a significant contribution to contemporary architectural culture for its effort to reposition the building as a generative site of intellectual inquiry. [ref: Epstein-Jones, Dora (2017). "On Re-centering 'the Building' in Architectural Discourse." Archinect. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://archinect.com/features/article/150013834/screen-print-57-dora-epstein-jones-on-re-centering-the-building-in-architectural-discourse] [ref: Canga, Pablo (2017). "Construir o no construir. Architecture and Thinking." Arquitectura Viva. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://coam.org/media/Default%20Files/actualidad/agenda/docs/2017/171023-the-building-arquitectura-viva-194-p59.pdf]

=== Spatial Infrastructure (2022) ===

Aragüez put forth the term "spatial infrastructure" in architecture to designate "the three-dimensional, material set of elements providing a primary articulation of space within a building's envelope prior to the introduction of partitions." [ref: "Spatial Infrastructure: An Interview with José Aragüez." urbanNext. Retrieved February 27, 2026. https://urbannext.net/spatial-infrastructure/] One of its main purposes would be to facilitate the conception of alternatives to Le Corbusier's Dom-Ino House as the quintessential spatial infrastructure of the 20th and 21st centuries. The concept appears in the central piece of a collection of essays released in 2022 under the title Spatial Infrastructure: Essays on Architectural Thinking as a Form of Knowledge. [ref: Aragüez, José (2022). Spatial Infrastructure: Essays on Architectural Thinking as a Form of Knowledge. Actar Publishers. ISBN 978-1-63840-019-6. https://actar.com/product/spatial-infrastructure/] The book assembles eight interlinked writings addressing a series of fundamental themes in architectural discourse, such as the conceptual underpinnings of a building's spatial organization, typological innovation, the philosophical dimensions of "the organic," imageability within economic systems, and the broader potential for architectural metacriticality.

Taken together, the essays argue that architectural thinking constitutes a form of knowledge in its own right, one that cuts across styles, periods, and cultural contexts. The book thus mobilizes architectural theory to encourage architects and scholars alike to reconsider the epistemological foundations of their discipline, its contributions offering both fresh perspectives on architectural history and a heuristic for future design innovation. Aragüez's Spatial Infrastructure has been described as collapsing entrenched oppositions in architectural thinking and credited with introducing "spatial infrastructure" as a productive notion for reexamining foundational questions in the discipline. [ref: Martín, Guiomar (2023). "Spatial Infrastructure is a book about the 'architecturalness' of architecture—as simple as it sounds and as complex as it gets." The Architect's Newspaper. Retrieved February 27, 2026. https://www.archpaper.com/2023/12/spatial-infrastructure-book-architecturalness-architecture/]

=== Dispositional Intelligence (2025) ===

In Dispositional Intelligence in Architecture (2025), [ref: Aragüez, José (2025). Dispositional Intelligence in Architecture. Actar Publishers. ISBN 978-1-63840-132-2. https://actar.com/product/dispositional-intelligence-in-architecture/] Aragüez crafts a theoretical framework to recast architectural design and thinking through the lens of "dispositional intelligence." In discussing the book [https://urbannext.net/the-intelligence-of-space/ in an interview with urbanNext], he explains that the concept refers to the greater or lesser sophistication of the distribution of activities and primary material elements constitutive of a building’s three-dimensional space, prior to and beyond aesthetic expression. Rather than privileging image or style, "dispositional intelligence" emphasizes relations, calibrations, and dependencies across a building’s main spatial components. It calls for architects to harness their capacity to recognize, manipulate, and strategically deploy those components in order to produce specific programmatic, phenomenological, environmental, and social effects. The book therefore makes a case for situating architectural agency in the deliberate configuration of relationships—between parts and wholes, movement of bodies and atmospheres, activities and circulation.

Simultaneously in dialogue with and in contrast to contemporary discussions on systems thinking, material computation, and postdigital design culture, Dispositional Intelligence in Architecture proposes a shift from object-centered design toward field-based and relational modes of practice. [ref: "Dispositional Intelligence in Architecture." E-flux Architecture. Retrieved February 23, 2026. https://www.e-flux.com/announcements/677348/dispositional-intelligence-in-architecture] It locates architecture’s key site of invention in the creative assemblage of material elements and program through techniques of layout, three-dimensional sequencing, and spatial negotiation. Ultimately, it provides a conceptual vocabulary for analyzing and producing buildings, favoring those that are less concerned with aesthetic novelty and more focused on performative capacity—with how they reimagine the organization of activities in space, of atmospheric experiences, and of long-term adaptability. The book received positive critical reviews. [ref: Martín, Guiomar (2026). "Periphery as Method: 'On Architecture's Dispositional Intelligence'." World-Architects. Retrieved May 18, 2026. https://world-architects.com/en/architecture-news/found/dispositional-intelligence-in-architecture-review] [ref: Barnes, Cecil (2026). "Dispositional Intelligence in Architecture – Unveiling Architectural Innovation." Bauwelt. Retrieved May 8, 2026. https://www.bauwelt.de/rubriken/buecher/Dispositional-Intelligence-in-Architecture-Unveiling-Architectural-Innovation-4374388.html] [ref: Medina Warmburg, Joaquín (2026). "Dispositional Intelligence in Architecture – A New Structural Logic." Arquitectura Viva. Retrieved May 8, 2026. https://arquitecturaviva.com/books/dispositional-intelligence-in-architecture]

== Selected awards and fellowships ==

* 2018 — XIV Spanish Architecture Biennial, awarded for The Building
* 2018 — Arquia Próxima Awards, Finalist for The Building
* 2015 — Howard Crosby Butler Traveling Fellowship, Princeton University [ref: "2015 Graduation." Princeton University School of Architecture. Retrieved October 12, 2026. https://soa.princeton.edu/content/2015-graduation]
* 2013 — Collection Research Grant, Canadian Centre for Architecture
* 2010 — William Kinne Fellows Traveling Prize, Columbia University GSAPP
* 2009 — Honor Prize for Excellence in Design, Columbia University GSAPP
* 2007 — 1st National End-of-Degree Prize in Architecture, Spanish Ministry of Culture
* 2007 — Graduation Extraordinary Award, University of Granada
* 2005 — Arquia Banca Foundation Grant, selected by student record

data.title: Ice River Complex
data.text:
The Ice River Complex (also Ice River alkaline complex) is an alkaline ultramafic intrusion in the Canadian Rockies of southeastern British Columbia, Canada, located about south of Field. Most of its roughly of exposure lies within Yoho and Kootenay national parks. [ref: Alkaline ultrabasic rocks in British Columbia: carbonatites, nepheline syenites, kimberlites, ultramafic lamprophyres and related rocks, British Columbia Ministry of Energy, Mines and Petroleum Resources, Geological Survey Branch] It was the first alkaline intrusion recognized in British Columbia and is regarded as one of the world's major alkaline complexes, notable for its layered ijolite series, carbonatites and sodalite-bearing nepheline syenites.

==Geology==
The complex is an arcuate mass about long. It intrudes Cambrian and Ordovician shales and carbonates of the Chancellor, Ottertail and McKay formations; contact metamorphism of these host rocks produced hornfels and skarns, with some limited soda metasomatism. [ref: The geology and petrology of the Ice River alkaline complex, British Columbia, Geological Survey of Canada] The complex and its host rocks were later deformed and subjected to low-grade regional metamorphism during the Columbian orogeny.

Two distinct suites are present:
* An older, rhythmically layered, feldspar-free intrusion ranging from jacupirangite through melanite ijolite to melanite urtite. It consists of repeated graded layers 10 to 200 metres thick, with nepheline increasing toward the top of each layer. Jacupirangite, the most mafic rock, contains titanaugite, titaniferous magnetite, perovskite and phlogopite. This suite is cored by a carbonatite plug and cut by carbonatite dykes.
* A younger, zoned and crosscutting syenite complex forming an elliptical pipe-like mass, grading from a greenish sodalite syenite core through pale grey nepheline syenite to darker, mafic-rich rocks at the margin, rimmed by fine-grained leucosyenite. Nepheline makes up as much as 30 per cent of these rocks and sodalite up to 20 per cent.

Carbonatites occur at several localities and are lithologically varied. Those in the layered ultramafic series include black, buff and red-weathering types; the black variety carries siderite, calcite, green berthierine and the barium zeolite edingtonite, while pyrochlore and xenotime occur in the red variety. Carbonatite associated with the syenites contains only feldspars, zeolites and rare phlogopite as silicates, with ankerite, barytocalcite and strontianite reported at some localities. Late lamprophyre dykes cut the complex and its host rocks. Carbonatites and some melanocratic syenites are enriched in niobium, rare-earth elements and strontium.

===Age===
The age of emplacement has long been debated. J. A. Allan suggested a post-Cretaceous age in 1914, and in 1959 W. C. Gussow and C. W. Hunt argued the complex was a sample of Precambrian basement. Potassium–argon and rubidium–strontium dates from the early 1960s indicated a mid-Paleozoic (Devonian–Mississippian) age. Currie (1975) obtained Early Triassic dates and preferred an emplacement age of about 245 million years, but uranium–lead zircon work reported by R. Parrish in 1986 supported the mid-Paleozoic dates as closest to the true age of emplacement.

==History of study==
The complex was described around the turn of the 20th century by G. M. Dawson (1885), A. E. Barlow (1902) and T. G. Bonney (1902). Work by J. A. Allan in 1911 and 1914 established it as one of the world's major alkaline complexes. Renewed study followed in the 1950s and 1960s, and the Geological Survey of Canada mapped it in detail in the early 1970s, [ref: Ice River alkaline complex, British Columbia (82N), Geological Survey of Canada] [ref: A preliminary report on the Ice River alkaline complex, British Columbia, Geological Survey of Canada] culminating in K. L. Currie's 1975 monograph, the most comprehensive study of the complex.

Access is difficult because of steep mountainous terrain, a lack of roads and regulations imposed by Parks Canada.

==See also==
* Carbonatite
* Geology of British Columbia

data.title: Nicole LeMaster
data.text:
‘’‘Nicole LeMaster’’’ is an American psychotherapist, Somatic Experiencing Practitioner, author, and dream coach. Her professional work includes somatic psychotherapy, trauma recovery, nervous-system regulation, and personal development.

== Career ==
‘’‘Nicole LeMaster’’’ is a psychotherapist, Somatic Experiencing Practitioner, author, and dream coach. Her clinical work includes somatic therapy and trauma recovery, while her separate coaching business focuses on dream work and personal development.Finding Capacity and Resilience, Carmichael TimesNicole Lemaster, Somatic Experiencing International [ref: SEI Portal, portal.traumahealing.org]

Separately, LeMaster works in the field of dream coaching through Moonbeam Dream. This coaching work is distinct from her clinical psychotherapy practice in purpose and scope. It focuses on dreams, personal development, and helping individuals explore aspirations and translate internal insights into goals and actions. It is a coaching platform rather than a clinical therapy service. [ref: SEI Portal, portal.traumahealing.org]

Although these two areas of work have different purposes and scopes of practice, both involve an interest in the relationship between internal experience and everyday life. In her clinical work, nervous-system regulation is relevant to trauma recovery and resilience; in her coaching work, the emphasis is on personal development and the process of bringing aspirations into lived experience. [ref: ]

== Media coverage ==
In August 2026, journalist Abbey Wicks profiled LeMaster in “Finding Capacity and Resilience”, published by the ‘‘Carmichael Times’’. The article discussed her work in somatic therapy, nervous-system regulation, trauma recovery, and dream coaching, as well as her book ‘‘WTF Am I Even Doing?: A Nervous System Workbook To Support Mind Body Alignment’’.Finding Capacity and Resilience, Carmichael Times

The article was also published by the ‘‘Elk Grove Citizen’’ and other publications within the same Sacramento-area publishing network.Finding Capacity and Resilience, Elk Grove Citizen [ref: ]

In December 2025, EIN Presswire published an announcement concerning LeMaster’s appearance on ‘‘Women In Power TV’’, a series hosted by Rudy Mawer.Nicole Lemaster to Appear on Women In Power TV, EIN Presswire

== Publications ==
LeMaster authored ‘‘WTF Am I Even Doing?: A Nervous System Workbook To Support Mind Body Alignment’’, which includes somatic awareness, reflective exercises, yoga practices, and chakra-related material.Books and Published Work, Nicole Lemaster

She also wrote “Forgiveness: A Personal Journey”, published by ‘‘The Science of Psychotherapy’’. The article discusses forgiveness, boundaries, self-care, embodiment, and personal growth.Forgiveness: A Personal Journey, The Science of Psychotherapy

data.title: The Last Recruit (band)
data.text:
----

An independent story

== Built from the ground up. ==
The Last Recruit is an independent rock band from Leigh-on-Sea, founded by school friends brought together through a shared passion for music, recording and live performance. The band has evolved from performing grunge covers in local youth venues into writing, recording and independently releasing original music spanning pop, alternative rock, grunge and metal.

The short version

== A timeline ==

== of the noise. ==
Key points in the band's evolution, from the first name to the next chapter.

# 2024Celestial Horizon formed.
# 2025The Last Recruit name and new era began.
# 2026Life album released.
# 20262016 single released.
# 2026+The Descend era.

01

== The Genesis ==
The band's journey began in 2024 under the name Celestial Horizon. Inspired by bands such as Nirvana, Green Day and other alternative rock acts, the original lineup performed covers at school events, Music-on-Sea performances and local venues around Southend and Leigh-on-Sea. These early performances established the band's energetic live reputation and sparked an ambition to begin writing original material.

02

== Rebirth & the DIY philosophy ==
In 2025 the group adopted the name The Last Recruit, marking the beginning of a new era. Around the same time, the band experienced the departure of its founding bassist, Thomas Layton. Instead of bringing the project to an end, frontman Nicolas Rodrigues and drummer Sam Risbin continued writing together. They also welcomed a new bassist named Charlie.The philosophy was simple: create the best recordings possible using whatever equipment was available.Determined to learn every stage of music production, Nicolas spent months teaching himself recording, editing, mixing and mastering through experimentation rather than formal training.

03

== The making of Life ==
This approach led to the creation of the band's debut album, Life. Recorded almost entirely in Nicolas' bedroom over approximately six months, the project represented the band's first full-scale original release. Most of the album was recorded using microphones placed in front of amplifiers and vocal performances.

=== The Life tracking station ===
A glimpse into the original bedroom studio.

Early bedroom studio

Musically, Life surprised many people familiar with the band's live performances. While audiences knew The Last Recruit as a grunge and alternative rock band, the album explored a far more melodic and pop-influenced direction.

04

== Fog & friction ==
Among the songs featured on Life, “Field of Fog” and “Hole of the Bump” stand as the album's two defining pieces, together capturing its central themes and emotional identity.

“Field of Fog” reflects on memory, nostalgia and childhood. The song contrasts the warmth of early memories with the uncertainty of growing older. By contrast, “Hole of the Bump” explores physical pain and discomfort.The completion of Life marked a turning point. Every lesson learned during the album became the foundation for future releases.Although Life represented a major creative achievement, its commercial release proved to be the band's greatest logistical challenge. During digital distribution, repeated moderation issues forced the removal of two completed recordings: “50s Ghosts” and a professionally recorded version of “Life”.

05

== The 2016 bridge ==
Following the completion of Life, The Last Recruit entered a new stage of development. The knowledge gained from months of recording, mixing and experimenting during the album's production allowed the band to work with a much faster and more refined creative process. This evolution became clear with the standalone single 2016, a song that represented the connection between the melodic world of Life and the heavier direction of the upcoming Descend era.

Unlike the six-month production period of Life, 2016 was completed in approximately one week. The speed of the recording process demonstrated how much Nicolas' production workflow had developed, allowing the band to move from writing an idea to releasing a finished track far more efficiently. Shortly after completion, the song became available on streaming platforms, marking one of the fastest releases in The Last Recruit's history.

The production of 2016 combined the band's established bedroom recording methods with support from Belfairs Academy's music department. The majority of the track—including vocals, guitars, bass, editing, mixing and mastering—was completed by Nicolas inside his bedroom studio using his personal recording setup.

The drums were performed by Sam Risbin and recorded inside one of Belfairs Academy's music classrooms. With the assistance of a music teacher, two Zoom microphones were used to capture the drum performance before the recordings were combined into a stereo track and transferred back to Nicolas for editing and integration into the final production. This collaboration became another example of The Last Recruit's DIY approach: combining available resources, education and independent creativity to create original music.

=== The 2016 & Descend setup ===
The recording environment as the sound evolved.

Recording setup for 2016

The accompanying photograph depicts the recording setup used throughout the production of 2016. The only major difference is the absence of the large monitor, which was introduced later during the production of The One Who Waits and became part of the studio setup for all recordings that followed.

Musically, 2016 occupies a unique position within The Last Recruit's catalogue. Rather than belonging entirely to either the Life or Descend eras, the song acts as a bridge between them. It carries the melodic songwriting, cleaner production and experimental approach developed during Life, while introducing the heavier guitar tones, stronger rock influence and increased intensity that would later define Descend.

The creation of 2016 marked a major milestone for the band. It proved that the lessons learned during Life had permanently changed the way The Last Recruit created music. The song was not only a new release, but evidence of the band's progression: a point where improved production skills, faster workflows and evolving musical identity began to merge into a new era.

06

== A return to roots ==
During the creation of 2016, The Last Recruit were also working on Descend, a project that marked another major evolution in both songwriting and production. Returning to the band's heavier roots, Descend explores rock and metal while showcasing a significantly more detailed production style.

Outside the studio, The Last Recruit has continued to perform throughout Essex, appearing at venues and events including the Palace Theatre, The Fickle Pickle Club, Music-on-Sea performances and community events.

07

== An independent progression ==
Everything associated with The Last Recruit has been built independently. The band writes its own songs, records and produces its own music, designs artwork, manages releases, develops promotional material and maintains its own online presence without the support of a record label.

The story of The Last Recruit is ultimately one of continuous progression. From humble beginnings as school friends performing covers to independently producing and releasing original music across multiple genres, the band continues to evolve.

data.title: Robert Van Gulick
data.text:
----

----

Robert Van Gulick is a philosopher and professor of philosophy at Syracuse University. [ref: Robert Van Gulick, Syracuse University College of Arts and Sciences] His work is primarily in the philosophy of mind and philosophy of cognitive science, particularly consciousness, self-awareness and functionalism. [ref: Robert N. Van Gulick Curriculum Vitae, Syracuse University College of Arts and Sciences]

Van Gulick is associated with the Higher-Order Global States (HOGS) model of consciousness, which combines elements of higher-order and global-state approaches to conscious awareness. [ref: Higher-Order Theories of Consciousness] [ref: Consciousness] The model has subsequently been discussed in academic literature on higher-order and self-representational theories of consciousness. [ref: Same old, same old: the same-order representation theory of consciousness and the division of phenomenal labor, Synthese] [ref: Phenomenal consciousness with infallible self-representation, Philosophical Studies] [ref: The Oxford Handbook of the Philosophy of Consciousness, Oxford University Press]

== Education and career ==

Van Gulick received an A.B. in philosophy from Princeton University in 1970. He earned an M.A. in 1973 and a Ph.D. in philosophy in 1976 from the University of California, Berkeley. His dissertation was titled Functionalism as a Theory of Mind.

He taught at Rutgers University from 1976 to 1984 and joined Syracuse University in 1984. He became a professor of philosophy at Syracuse in 1995. From 2008 to 2010, he held Syracuse's William P. Tolley Distinguished Teaching Professorship in the Humanities. [ref: William P. Tolley Distinguished Teaching Professor in the Humanities, Syracuse University College of Arts and Sciences]

Van Gulick served as president of the Society for Philosophy and Psychology in 2002. [ref: Past Officers, Society for Philosophy and Psychology]

== Philosophical work ==

Van Gulick has written on consciousness, self-awareness, functionalism, intentionality, emergence and the relationship between phenomenal experience and cognitive organization.

=== Higher-Order Global States ===

Van Gulick developed the Higher-Order Global States model as an account of the relationship between consciousness and higher-order awareness. In contrast to standard higher-order accounts that posit a distinct higher-order representation of a lower-order mental state, HOGS treats the relevant higher-order content as arising within the organization of a larger global state.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy interprets Van Gulick's account as one in which globally available first-order states acquire a higher-order dimension through their incorporation into representations of the self and its relationship to the environment. It also notes some ambiguity in the theory concerning the precise relationship between the original first-order state and the resulting higher-order global state.

The HOGS model has been discussed in subsequent work on higher-order and self-representational theories of consciousness. Josh Weisberg examined the model in Synthese as a form of same-order representation theory and considered its combination of global availability and self-awareness. Chad Kidd considered HOGS alongside other self-representational models in Philosophical Studies, including whether its account of integrated conscious states addresses problems involving self-misrepresentation.

Tom McClelland discusses HOGS in The Oxford Handbook of the Philosophy of Consciousness, situating it within self-representational theories and describing the role that integration into a subject's broader mental economy plays in the account. Later authors have continued to compare aspects of HOGS with alternative accounts of higher-order representation and self-consciousness. [ref: Quotational higher-order thought theory, Philosophical Studies] [ref: Pre-Reflective Self-Consciousness: A Meta-Causal Approach, Review of Philosophy and Psychology]

Van Gulick later connected HOGS with Global Neuronal Workspace theory. In an editorial introducing a 2022 special issue on self-consciousness, Stefan Lang and Klaus Viertbauer describe his contribution as combining HOGS with the Global Neuronal Workspace framework and developing a virtual-self integration account of the conscious subject. [ref: Editorial: Self-Consciousness Explained—Mapping the Field, Review of Philosophy and Psychology]

== Selected publications ==

* Van Gulick, Robert (1988). "A Functionalist Plea for Self-Consciousness". The Philosophical Review. 97 (2): 149–181..
* Van Gulick, Robert (1989). "What Difference Does Consciousness Make?". Philosophical Topics. 17 (1): 211–230..
* Van Gulick, Robert (1995). "How Should We Understand the Relation Between Intentionality and Phenomenal Consciousness?". Philosophical Perspectives. 9: 271–289..
* Van Gulick, Robert (2000). "Inward and Upward: Reflection, Introspection, and Self-Awareness". Philosophical Topics. 28 (2): 275–305..
* Van Gulick, Robert (2001). "Reduction, Emergence and Other Recent Options on the Mind/Body Problem: A Philosophical Overview". Journal of Consciousness Studies. 8 (9–10): 1–34.
* Van Gulick, Robert (2004). "Higher-Order Global States (HOGS): An Alternative Higher-Order Model of Consciousness". In Gennaro, Rocco J. (ed.). Higher-Order Theories of Consciousness: An Anthology. John Benjamins Publishing Company. pp. 67–92..
* Van Gulick, Robert (2009). "Functionalism". In McLaughlin, Brian P.; Beckermann, Ansgar; Walter, Sven (eds.). The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Mind. Oxford University Press. pp. 128–151..
* Van Gulick, Robert (2012). "Subjective consciousness and self-representation". Philosophical Studies. 159 (3): 457–465..
* Van Gulick, Robert (2014). "Getting it All Together – Phenomenal Unity and the Self". Analysis. 74 (3): 491–498..
* Van Gulick, Robert (2022). "Consciousness and Self-awareness—an Alternative Perspective". Review of Philosophy and Psychology. 13 (2): 329–340..

== References ==

== External links ==

data.title: Dr Jamilu Isyaku Gwamna
data.text:
Dr. Jamilu Isyaku Gwamna (MFR), known as the Sardaunan Gombe, is a Nigerian economist, businessman, and politician from Gombe State. [ref: Jamilu Isyaku Gwamna, The Guardian Nigeria] He is noted for his leadership in the Nigerian power sector and his political involvement in Gombe State. [ref: Gombe APC picks Jamilu Gwamna as consensus guber candidate ahead of Pantami, The Cable]

== Background and Education ==
Gwamna was born in Jekada Fari, Gombe Local Government Area, Gombe State.
He holds a B.Sc. in Accounting, an M.Sc. in Business Economics and Finance, and a Ph.D. in Economics from London Metropolitan University (2008).
He is a recipient of the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR).

== Career ==
=== Business and Public Service ===
Gwamna served as Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Kano Electricity Distribution Company (KEDCO), one of the 11 electricity distribution companies created during the Goodluck Jonathan-era privatization. KEDCO covers Kano, Jigawa, and Katsina States.
He has been described as the “visible brain behind the successes” of KEDCO.

== Political Career ==
Gwamna has been active in Gombe State politics since the Fourth Republic.
He contested for Governor of Gombe State under the All Nigeria People’s Party (ANPP) in 2007 and later participated in the People’s Democratic Party (PDP) primaries in 2019.

On 9 December 2022, he defected from the PDP to the All Progressives Congress (APC) with a large group of supporters and served as the Tinubu Presidential Campaign Coordinator for Gombe State in the 2023 general elections.

In April 2027, Gwamna was reported as the APC consensus candidate for the Gombe State governorship race. [ref: APC picks consensus candidates for 2027 Gombe elections, Premium Times Nigeria] [ref: APC unveils consensus 2027 governorship candidate in Gombe, Punch Newspapers]

data.title: Constantime
data.text:
----

Constantime is an independent watchmaking brand and atelier founded in 2025 in Târgu Mureș, Transylvania, Romania, by Alin Constantin Mureșan. [ref: Het Dracula-horloge? Constantime zet Transsylvanië op de horlogekaart, 0024 Horloges] [ref: Mecanism elvețian, ADN transilvănean, După Afaceri Premium] Its first model, Constantime Genesis, was produced as a limited series of 25 pieces. [ref: Constantime: un atelier de ceasornicărie independentă construit în Târgu Mureș, Club Antreprenor]

Constantime makes small-series mechanical watches and uses references to Transylvanian architecture and history in their design. The watches use Swiss mechanical movements combined with components made and finished in the atelier, particularly the dials and hands; leather straps are made by a local artisan in Transylvania. [ref: CONSTANTIME Genesis participă la Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève 2026. Constantin A. Mureșan duce în premieră un brand românesc de orologerie de la Târgu Mureș pe scena internațională, LuxuryOnline]

== History ==

The first ideas that later developed into Constantime date to around 2017, when Alin Constantin Mureșan began considering the possibility of creating a watch that would carry his own design and personal imprint. [ref: Constantime Genesis: A Watch Born Beneath the Vaults of Transylvania, MrWatchMaster] The project developed over several years from an interest in watch design and mechanical movements into a dedicated watchmaking brand and atelier. [ref: Românul care a construit un ceas pentru Nadia Comăneci, iar acum și-a lansat propriul brand premium: CONSTANTIME, start-up.ro]

The name Constantime combines “Constantin”, part of the founder's name, with the English word “time”. [ref: Un orologer artizan român a creat un ceas pentru Nadia Comăneci cu primul 10 olimpic din istoria gimnasticii, Newsweek România]

== Transylvanian identity and Genesis ==

Transylvania became part of the identity of Constantime because the brand was created and developed in the region. Its architecture and history became a source of shapes and details used in the watches. [ref: Un ceas creat la Târgu Mureș duce simbolurile Transilvaniei la „Oscarurile” orologeriei, Cuvântul Liber]

The design of Genesis draws on the fortified architecture of Transylvania, including vaulted ceilings and arches found in medieval castles and fortified churches. Its sword-shaped hands and polished elements also refer to historical weapons associated with the region.

The name Genesis refers to the beginning of the Constantime project. The model was produced as a series of 25 numbered pieces; Constantime states that the number also refers to 2025, the year in which the brand was founded. [ref: Constantime Watches, Constantime]

== Watchmaking and production ==

The production process begins with raw brass used for the dial. The dial is machined, engraved, polished, coloured and finished in the Târgu Mureș atelier. The hands are also made and finished in the atelier.

These locally produced components are combined with a stainless-steel case, a Swiss mechanical movement and a leather strap made by a Transylvanian artisan. Constantime currently sources its cases externally, while developing its own case design with the aim of having future cases produced locally.

The atelier has stated that it intends to increase the proportion of components developed and produced locally and to expand its work on mechanical movements from finishing and customisation toward more complex modifications.

== Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève ==

In 2026, Constantime Genesis was entered in the Challenge category of the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG) and was included in the official selection. [ref: Un artizan din Târgu Mureș a creat un ceas unic pentru Nadia Comăneci, dedicat primului 10 din istoria gimnasticii, Revista LOR]

Alin Constantin Mureșan described the entry as an opportunity to present a project developed in Transylvania to an international watchmaking audience.

== Nadia Comăneci commemorative watch ==

In 2026, Constantime created a one-off mechanical watch for Romanian gymnast Nadia Comăneci to mark the 50th anniversary of the first perfect 10 in modern Olympic gymnastics, achieved at the 1976 Montreal Games. [ref: Mureș: Ceas personalizat pentru Nadia Comăneci cu primul 10 olimpic, creat de un artizan independent de ceasuri mecanice, AGERPRES]

The central design element was placed on the small-seconds subdial, which reproduced the “1.00” shown by the electronic scoreboard in Montreal. The scoreboard had not been designed to display a score of 10.00, so Comăneci's result appeared as 1.00. The design also incorporated her competition number.

The watch was personally presented to Comăneci by Alin Constantin Mureșan during anniversary events held in Onești, Romania.
