Gaggz Pal

Gaggz Pal is an independent Punjabi singer, music artist, and creative entrepreneur. He has gained widespread digital recognition across multiple social media platforms, accumulating a combined community of over half a million followers and subscribers across YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook.

Gaggz Pal developed a passion for music, digital media, and visual arts early in life. Over his professional career, he successfully blended his artistic background in digital design and custom creation with his passion for Punjabi music. As an independent recording artist, Gaggz Pal releases Punjabi music singles distributed globally through major digital streaming platforms (such as Spotify, Apple Music, and iTunes). data.title: Charles Lynn Webb
data.text:
----

Charles Lynn Webb, is an American attorney who previously served as a Georgia judicial officer. His career has included work as a Fulton County prosecutor, DeKalb County Recorder's Court judge, and private-practice attorney. [ref: Georgia courts directory 2013-2014 - Digital Library of Georgia, dlg.usg.edu] [ref: Charles L. Webb, Law Office of Charles L. Webb]

== Early life and education ==
Webb was born and raised in White Springs, Florida, and attended Hamilton County High School.

Webb attended Edward Waters College (1991, summa cum laude) and then Florida State University, where he earned his MPA and J.D. in 1995. [ref: Find a Florida Bar Lawyer, The Florida Bar]

Webb was admitted to practice law on November 1, 1996.

Webb is currently listed as a member of good standing.

== Prosecutorial Career ==
Webb began his career as a prosecutor with the Fulton County Solicitor General's Office before joining the Fulton County District Attorney's Office in 1998. [ref: ]

During his time with the office, Webb served as a senior assistant district attorney in the Major Case Division, where his work included serious felony cases.

== Judicial Career ==
Webb served as a judge on the DeKalb County Recorder's Court in June 2010.

== Private practice and criminal defense ==
In 2010, Webb represented a defendant in an appellate court where the conviction was affirmed. [ref: Brown v. State (Ga. Ct. App. 2010), Justia Law]

In 2014, in a highly publicized fatal hit-and-run trial, Webb represented the defendant, who was acquitted. [ref: Man found not guilty in fatal hit-and-run, WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta]

In 2016, Webb represented a defendant charged with misdemeanor disorderly conduct in the Mothers's Day brawl inside Kiku Japanese steakhouse. [ref: 4 facing charges in Mother's Day brawl, WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta]

In 2019, Webb represented a defendant in DeKalb County on charges of aggravated assault, aggravated battery, and possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, which resulted in a jury acquittal. [ref: State of Georgia v. Michael Lester Austin, Jr., DeKalb County Superior Court, Case No. 18CR-2097-10, Jury Verdict, June 12, 2019.]

== Professional recognition ==
In 2004, the Fulton County District Attorney's Office named Webb its Lawyer of the Year.

In 2022, Webb received the Pinnacle Leadership Award from the Fortitude Educational and Cultural Development Center, Inc. [ref: Past Honorees, FECDC]

Webb was recognized as a Top 100 member by the National Trial Lawyers. [ref: Charles Webb - Georgia (Atlanta) - The National Trial Lawyers Top 100, The National Trial Lawyers]

data.title: Kyoto University Design School
data.text:
Kyoto University Design School () is the name used for educational activities centered on the Collaborative Graduate Program in Design at Kyoto University. The interdisciplinary five-year doctoral program began in April 2013 under Japan's Program for Leading Graduate Schools.

== History ==

Kyoto University established the Unit of Design, a faculty organization supporting the new program, in November 2012. Plans for the program were reported by the Asahi Shimbun and Sankei Shimbun in early 2013. A Design Innovation Base opened at Kyoto Research Park (KRP) in April 2013, followed by the establishment of the Design Innovation Consortium in March 2014 to support collaboration with industry and public-sector organizations. MEXT's project period was fiscal 2012–2018, and the program received an overall rating of A in its 2019 post-project evaluation. The Unit of Design was subsequently reorganized within Kyoto University's cross-graduate education framework. The Collaborative Graduate Program in Design continues to be listed among Kyoto University's graduate education programs.

== Organization ==

The program involves four graduate schools: the Graduate School of Informatics (informatics), the Graduate School of Engineering (mechanical engineering and architecture), the Graduate School of Management (management), and the Graduate School of Education (psychology).

The Design Innovation Consortium supports collaboration outside the university. The Advanced Scientific Technology & Management Research Institute of Kyoto (ASTEM) is its managing organization, and KRP serves as its secretariat.

== Education ==

The program's curriculum combines design approaches from five disciplines with methods intended for use across disciplinary boundaries. Ishida et al. (2017) describe design as a "lingua franca" among specialists from different fields. Mountford et al. (2020) cited Ishida et al. (2017) in their discussion of interdisciplinary education in engineering. Their study of European doctoral research networks also identified the importance of developing a shared language across disciplines. The program uses the concept of "+-shaped people" to describe specialists who can work across disciplines while retaining expertise in their own fields.

Coursework is organized into three categories. Design methodology covers the concepts, philosophy, and history of design. Broad-area design introduces methods such as ethnography, data analysis, and simulation. Domain design covers methods specific to the participating disciplines.

During the first two years, students undertake field-based learning (FBL) and problem-based learning (PBL) using topics drawn from faculty projects. From the third year, they participate in open innovation projects with external organizations. The curriculum also includes multidisciplinary field internships in Japan and abroad. Doctoral research is conducted in each student's home graduate school, with guidance from researchers in other disciplines.

A Design Innovator Index was developed to assess students' competencies, drawing in part on the United Kingdom's Researcher Development Framework. It consists of 24 items in four areas: intelligence, personality, engagement, and governance.

The Summer Design School, a separate workshop first held in 2011, brings together participants from different disciplines to address social problems. The 2026 three-day event was scheduled for 16–18 September.

== Collaborations ==

From 2014, Kyoto University's Unit of Design and Hong Kong Baptist University's Department of Computer Science jointly held annual Design for Sustainability workshops. National Cheng Kung University joined in 2017. Kyoto University and the University of the Ryukyus also held joint design workshops beginning in 2013, addressing topics including employment and regional revitalization. Kyoto City University of Arts was a formal partner of the Unit of Design, contributing faculty to the Design School and later participating in its organizing committee.

data.title: Billy Valentine
data.text:
William Denom, known professionally as Billy Valentine, is an American singer, songwriter and producer who rose to fame in the 1970s and 1980s as half of The Valentine Brothers. He has written for acts including Ray Charles and the Neville Brothers, [ref: Music Interview: Billy Valentine, HiFi Plus] and has done vocal work for television shows including Boston Legal and Sons of Anarchy [ref: BILLY VALENTINE, The Voice Heard On Sons Of Anarchy Releases A New Album Of Unique Covers!, Skylight Webzine] in addition to releasing multiple solo albums. [ref: Billy Valentine, Discogs]

Valentine was born in West Virginia [ref: Billy Valentine Biogrpahy, All Music], and grew up with 12 siblings in Columbus, Ohio where his parents ran a nightclub called Club Faces. [ref: ‘I’m a messenger. That’s my calling’: 80s hitmaker Billy Valentine on his socially conscious comeback, The Guardian]

He currently resides in Los Angeles, and maintains a regular presence on the nightclub performance circuit. [ref: Billy Valentine, CodaMusic]

data.title: Ashirbek Muminov
data.text:
Ashirbek Kurbanovich Muminov (Kazakh: Әшірбек Құрбанұлы Муминов; born 18 July 1959) is a historian specializing in medieval Islam in Central Asia. His research includes Hanafi scholarship, Islamic manuscripts and the history of Islamic education.⁠[1]⁠[2]⁠[10]

= Early life and education =
Muminov grew up in Tashkent and attended Secondary School No. 1, where he studied Arabic from the second grade. He completed school in 1976 with a gold medal.⁠[1]⁠[10]

He entered the Arabic section of the Faculty of Oriental Languages at Tashkent State University in 1976 and graduated with honours in 1982. He qualified as an Arabic philologist and a teacher of Arabic and English languages and literature.⁠[7]

From 1987 to 1990, he undertook postgraduate research at the Leningrad branch of the Institute of Oriental Studies of the USSR Academy of Sciences under Stanislav Mikhailovich Prozorov. He defended his Candidate of Historical Sciences dissertation in Leningrad on 29 March 1991. It examined al-Kafawi’s Kata’ib a‘lam al-akhyar as a source for the history of Islam in Transoxiana.⁠[7] [ref: ИВР РАН (Санкт-Петербург) - Personalia, www.orientalstudies.ru]

On 24 June 2003, he defended his Doctor of Historical Sciences dissertation at Tashkent Islamic University. The study examined the significance of Hanafi scholars in the urban life of central Transoxiana.⁠[7]

= Academic career =
Muminov began his research career in 1982 at the Abu Rayhan Beruni Institute of Oriental Studies in Tashkent, working in the department responsible for source studies and cataloguing Oriental manuscripts. Detailed biographical accounts record research employment in 1982–1985 and 1990–1991.⁠[10] [ref: Ташкент-Алматы-Астана-Стамбул: Путь исламоведа, Qojalar.kz]

From 1991 to 1993, he headed the Department of Oriental Philology at Ahmed Yasawi University in Turkestan.⁠[10] He was an associate professor in the Department of Islamic Studies at Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies from 1993 to 2005.⁠[8] [ref: ]

In 2005, he became deputy director of the R. B. Suleymenov Institute of Oriental Studies in Almaty, serving until 2013.⁠[8]⁠[10] From 2013 to 2016, he headed the Department of Religious Studies at L. N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University in Astana.⁠[8] In 2016, IRCICA identified him as consultant to its director general on Central Asian studies.⁠[2] [ref: ]

= International research appointments =
In 1998, Muminov was a visiting professor in the Fourth Section of the École pratique des hautes études (EPHE), at the Sorbonne in Paris, working with F. Déroche. He returned to the institution in 2002 as a visiting professor in its Fifth Section, working with D. Aigle.⁠[8]

The Alexander von Humboldt Foundation records a research fellowship at Ruhr University Bochum, hosted by Stefan Reichmuth, with sponsorship beginning on 1 October 1999. Muminov’s CV dates the research visit to 1999–2001.⁠[8]⁠[9]

In 2006, he was a visiting scholar at Indiana University, researching Islamization and sacred genealogies in Central Asia. He also held a visiting professorship at Zentrum Moderner Orient in Berlin in 2011.⁠[8]

He was a Fulbright Visiting Scholar at Indiana University Bloomington from September 2011 to June 2012. From September 2012 to June 2013, he held a senior fellowship at Koç University’s Research Center for Anatolian Civilizations in Istanbul.⁠[8]

In April–June 2015, he was a visiting scholar at Nanjing University in China.⁠[8]

= Research =
From 2001 to 2008, he participated in the “Manuscript heritage of Central Asia” project at CNRS in Paris, directed by Maria Szuppe. He subsequently participated in the project “Manuscript traditions of Iran, India and Central Asia” (2009–2012), directed by Szuppe and Nalini Balbir.⁠[8]

Muminov collaborated with Bakhtiyar Babadjanov and Anke von Kügelgen on the 2007 volume Disputes on Muslim Authority in Central Asia (20th Century). The collection presents texts documenting religious debates in Soviet Central Asia. In a 2008 review, Canat Mahaşeva discussed its use of manuscripts and printed works preserved in private collections.⁠[4] [ref: (XX.yy. Orta Asya Müslüman Din Adamlarýnýn Polemikleri: Kritik Edisyon ve Kaynak Araþtýrmasý),, Ankara Üniversitesi İlahiyat Fakültesi Dergisi]

He also conducted research with Devin DeWeese on the Islamization of Central Asia and sacred lineages, published in the two-volume work Islamization and Sacred Lineages in Central Asia (2008 and 2013).

He co-edited Saduaqas Ghïlmani’s biographical collection with Allen Frank and Aitzhan Nurmanova. Published by IRCICA in 2018, the two-volume edition contains the Arabic-script Kazakh text and an English translation.⁠[5] In 2026, he edited Galiya Kambarbekova’s catalogue of Turkic manuscripts in Kazakhstan’s National Library.⁠[6] [ref: Biographies of the Islamic Scholars of Our Times, shop.ircica.org]

= Recognition =
In 2016, his book Hanafi Madhhab in the History of Central Asia won first place in the Islam category of the regional Book of the Year competition for Russian-language scholarship on Islam and Iran. The award was presented on 1 December 2016.⁠[3] [ref: ]

= Languages =
His CV lists Kazakh, Uzbek and Russian as native languages, and Arabic, Turkish and English as fluent languages. It also records reading knowledge of German, French, Persian and the Turkic languages of Central Asia.⁠[8]

data.title: Faydor Litvin
data.text:
----

Faydor L. Litvin (January 21, 1914 – April 26, 2017) was a scientist who dedicated his life to the development of the modern theory of gearing and contributed to the theory of mechanisms. [ref: Celebrating the life of Distinguished Professor Emeritus Faydor Litvin, Mechanical and Industrial Engineering]

Born in Belarus, he emigrated to the United States in 1979 at the age of 65. He then worked as a professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and as the founding director of the Gear Research Center at the University of Illinois at Chicago. He continued his research until his retirement at the age of 93. [ref: Remembering UIC Distinguished Professor Emeritus Faydor L. Litvin, Gear Research Laboratory]

He was an expert in kinematics and the theory of gearing, with research on high-precision gear mechanisms used in the rotorcraft, aerospace, and automotive industries.

== Early life and education ==
Litvin was born in Belarus in 1914 to Jewish parents.

In 1928, at the age of 14, he moved to Leningrad, now Saint Petersburg, to pursue further education. He supported himself while continuing his studies.

He graduated from Leningrad Polytechnic Institute with distinction in 1937. He defended his PhD in 1944 and received his Doctor of Technical Science degree in 1954.

From 1963 to 1979, he served as department head and professor of mechanical engineering at the Institute of Precision Mechanics and Optics in Leningrad. There, he laid the mathematical foundations of his work on advanced gear geometry and kinematics.

== Career in the United States ==
In 1979, at the age of 65, Litvin fulfilled his long-standing wish to leave the Soviet Union. When asked how he could leave his prominent position and face an uncertain future, he replied: "It was easy. There was an ocean of blood between me and that country."

Born during World War I, he lived through the Russian Revolution, pogroms, Stalin's purges, World War II, and the Holocaust, in which his parents were killed.

He moved to the United States and joined the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Illinois at Chicago as a professor. He founded and directed the Gear Research Center. There, together with his PhD students, he conducted research in collaboration with NASA, the U.S. Army, and the rotorcraft industry for 27 years. His technology helped reduce noise, vibration, and stress and was used in an upgraded attack helicopter operated by the U.S. Army.

Litvin mentored 100 PhD students, 50 in Russia and 50 in the United States, as well as visiting scholars from around the world. His students went on to hold teaching and research positions in the United States, Italy, Spain, Russia, Bulgaria, Poland, Hungary, China, Taiwan, and Australia. They described themselves as belonging to the "elite school of Litvin."

== Publications and inventions ==
Litvin had more than 350 publications, including 10 monographs, and held 26 patents. His monograph The Theory of Gearing went through six editions.

During World War II, he developed an invention that enabled the efficient transmission of radar coordinates to antiaircraft artillery instrumentation used by Soviet troops at the front. To test it, he traveled to Leningrad during the siege, crossing Lake Ladoga under heavy bombardment.

In his book Development of Gear Technology, he dedicated a chapter to scientists who had contributed to mechanical engineering, some of whom had received little recognition during their lifetimes. He researched their lives, sometimes contacting third-generation descendants. Portraits of these scientists formed a gallery in his Gear Research Center.

== Research and engineering contributions ==
Litvin's work replaced empirical trial-and-error gear design methods with mathematical models based on differential geometry.

His research focused on the simulation of meshing and tooth contact analysis. It introduced the localization of bearing contact and predesigned parabolic transmission functions. [ref: Generation and tooth contact analysis of spiral bevel gears with predesigned parabolic functions of transmission errors, NASA] [ref: Computerized Design and Generation of Low-Noise Gears with Localized Bearing Contact, NASA] His algorithms allowed computer numerical control machines to grind gears, reducing operational noise, wear, and vibration.

== Collaboration with NASA ==
In the 1980s, Litvin began collaborating with NASA's Glenn Research Center and the U.S. Army Research Laboratory. His geometric models were used to optimize planetary gear trains and spiral bevel gear drives to improve the reliability, safety, and acoustic performance of helicopter transmissions.

== Awards and honors ==
Litvin was an ASME Fellow, an associate editor of Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering, and a member of the honorary editorial advisory board of Gearing and Transmissions.

His awards included 12 from NASA, the Thomas Bernard Hall Prize from the Institution of Mechanical Engineers in the United Kingdom, the Edison Award, and the IFToMM Merit Award from the International Federation for the Promotion of Mechanism and Machine Science.

In 1985, he was recognized as an "Outstanding New Citizen" by the Citizenship Council of Metropolitan Chicago for his work at UIC. He received an honorary doctorate from the University of Miskolc in Hungary in recognition of his influence on the development of noncircular gear research in Hungary. In 2001, he was named UIC's Inventor of the Year.

== Personal life and interests ==
Litvin was married for nearly 78 years to Shifra Litvin, whom he had met in third grade. His wife, his lifelong companion and close friend, died 14 days before their 78th wedding anniversary. He was devoted to his family and took pride in his son and daughter, four grandchildren, and seven great-grandchildren.

He taught himself to read as a child, and his desire to learn continued into his later years. At the age of 100, he translated Goethe's writing from German into English. His interests included art, literature, and religion. He also wrote poetry.

Former students remembered Litvin for his wisdom, kindness, and cultural interests. His former student Vincenzo Parenti Castelli, a professor at the University of Bologna, wrote: "Somebody said that we are little people on the shoulders of a giant. He was such a giant!"

data.title: Max Shelton
data.text:
----

Max Shelton is an Australian agricultural scientist with research interests in tropical pastures and the use of Leucaena leucocephala as feed for beef cattle. Much of his career was spent at the University of Queensland [ref: Five decades of leucaena R&D: Is it time to move on?, Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation] where he was involved in the research and development of new cultivars, including an insect-resistant variety, [ref: Insect-resistant forage crop almost ready for commercial release, ABC News] and led research projects in South-East Asia. [ref: Improving smallholder cattle fattening systems based on forage tree legume diets in eastern Indonesia and northern Australia, Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research] In 2022, Shelton was awarded the AW Howard Medal for significant contributions to the advancement of pastures in Australia. [ref: Grants, scholarships and awards from the AW Howard Memorial Trust, Primary Industries and Regions South Australia] [ref: People on the move in the grain industry, Grain Central]

== Research and career ==
Shelton graduated with honours from a degree in agricultural science at the University of Queensland in 1968. He then completed a PhD at the University of Queensland in 1972 [ref: Factors influencing competition between upland rice (Oryza sativa Linn.) and undersown stylo (Stylosanthes guyanensis Aubl.), The University of Queensland] on the integration of stylo pasture in farming systems in North-East Thailand. He returned to the University of Queensland in 1978 in the Department of Agriculture, taking up a tenured lectureship in pasture science in 1986. He retired in 2016 as associate professor. [ref: Celebrating the contribution of Dr Max Shelton, Beef Central]

Shelton's career focused on the development and management of forage tree legumes in livestock production. With colleagues he bred a new psyllid-resistant variety of Leucaena called Redlands. [ref: 'Redlands' leucaena lifts beef productivity and profitability in coastal Queensland, Beef Central] He was also involved in the release of three other new pasture plant varieties (Sesbania cv Mt Cotton and Leucaena cvv Tarramba, and Wondergraze). Shelton worked with smallholder farmers in Indonesia to improve nutrition for cattle through better pasture management. He has delivered a series of courses to graziers in northern Queensland and advised them on the establishment and management of grazed leucaena pastures.

Shelton has also carried out research on the environmental impact of cattle production, including methane production [ref: Leucaena: The productive and sustainable forage legume, Meat & Livestock Australia] and how leucaena-based grazing systems can be used to sequester carbon. [ref: Soil organic carbon and total nitrogen under Leucaena leucocephala pastures in Queensland, Crop & Pasture Science] [ref: The sequestration and turnover of soil organic carbon in subtropical leucaena-grass pastures, Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment] In addition, Shelton has investigated the drought-resistance potential of leucaena for farmers in dry, tropical regions. [ref: Drought fodder crop takes centre stage, UQ News]

data.title: Joseph B. Rasmussen
data.text:
Joseph B. Rasmussen is a Canadian aquatic ecologist. He is Professor Emeritus of Biological Sciences at the University of Lethbridge, where he held a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems and directed the Water Institute for Sustainable Environments. He developed stable-isotope methods now widely used to quantify food web structure and trophic position, and applied tracer-kinetic models to the study of contaminant biomagnification and in situ fish bioenergetics. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 2016.

Rasmussen was appointed in 2010 to a federal advisory panel reviewing environmental monitoring of the Athabasca oil sands, one of six scientists named by then-environment minister Jim Prentice. In 2024, University of Lethbridge researchers named a newly described species of parasite, Myxobolus rasmusseni, after him in recognition of his career in aquatic biology.

== Early life and education ==
Rasmussen studied zoology at the University of Alberta in the 1960s and 1970s, completing an honours BSc and an MSc in limnology, and went on to a PhD in aquatic ecology at the University of Calgary in 1983.

== Career ==
Rasmussen joined the Department of Biology at McGill University in 1984 as an NSERC postdoctoral fellow, and was later promoted to full professor. During his time at McGill, he worked on lake zoobenthos, stable-isotope food web ecology, and contaminant biomagnification, and in 1998 was among the faculty who established the McGill School of Environment.

He moved to the University of Lethbridge in 2003 to take up a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems, renewed in 2010, and to direct the Water Institute for Sustainable Environments. He later chaired the Department of Biological Sciences before retiring in 2019 as Professor Emeritus.

Later in his career, Rasmussen's group turned toward the conservation of native salmonids in western Canada, studying how introduced brook trout affect bull trout (Salvelinus confluentus) populations and how rainbow trout introductions affect the genetics of native westslope cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarkii lewisi), and tracing selenium from coal mining through mountain stream food webs. This work fed into his appointment to the federal oil sands review panel and to provincial panels on environmental monitoring and selenium impacts on Athabasca rainbow trout.

== Research ==
In the 1980s, whether persistent contaminants biomagnify up aquatic food webs was disputed; some chemists argued, from equilibrium partitioning, that it was thermodynamically implausible. Rasmussen and collaborators built kinetic models accounting for uptake, elimination, and bioenergetics to show that biomagnification is expected for contaminants that are readily assimilated but slowly eliminated, and that much lake-to-lake variation in fish PCB and mercury levels can be explained by food web structure.

His group adapted nitrogen stable-isotope (δ¹⁵N) methods, until then used mainly in marine geochemistry, to freshwater food webs, showing that δ¹⁵N signatures track trophic position more efficiently than traditional stomach-content analysis while also predicting mercury bioaccumulation; they also showed that comparing trophic position across different food webs requires correcting for variation in baseline isotope signatures. Combining isotope measurements with long-term lake data, the group traced how species introductions, such as smallmouth bass, reshaped the trophic position of native lake trout, and his student Anthony Ricciardi produced widely cited estimates of extinction rates among North American freshwater fauna. Rasmussen's group also extended radiotracer bioenergetics techniques to estimate feeding rates and metabolic costs of wild fish populations in the field.

== Awards and honours ==
* Fellow, Royal Society of Canada (Academy of Science, Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences division), 2016.
* Ingrid Speaker Award for Outstanding Research Achievement, University of Lethbridge, 2012.
* Frank H. Rigler Memorial Award, Society of Canadian Limnologists, 2010.
* Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems, 2003 (renewed 2010).

In 2024, a newly discovered myxozoan parasite infecting fathead minnows in southern Alberta was named Myxobolus rasmusseni in his honour by researchers Molly Tilley and Cameron Goater. Goater, a longtime colleague, described Rasmussen as one of the most decorated aquatic biologists in the country.

== Selected publications ==
* Rasmussen, J. B., Rowan, D. J., Lean, D. R. S., & Carey, J. H. (1990). Food chain structure in Ontario lakes determines PCB levels in lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush) and other pelagic fish. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences, 47(10), 2030–2038.
* Cabana, G., & Rasmussen, J. B. (1994). Modelling food chain structure and contaminant bioaccumulation using stable nitrogen isotopes. Nature, 372, 255–257.
* Cabana, G., & Rasmussen, J. B. (1996). Comparing aquatic food chains using nitrogen isotopes. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 93(20), 10844–10847.
* Vander Zanden, M. J., & Rasmussen, J. B. (1999). Primary consumer δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N and the trophic position of aquatic consumers. Ecology, 80(4), 1395–1404.
* Vander Zanden, M. J., Casselman, J. M., & Rasmussen, J. B. (1999). Stable isotope evidence for the food web consequences of species invasions in lakes. Nature, 401, 464–467.
* Ricciardi, A., & Rasmussen, J. B. (1999). Extinction rates of North American freshwater fauna. Conservation Biology, 13(5), 1220–1222.
* Rowan, D. J., & Rasmussen, J. B. (1996). Measuring the bioenergetic cost of fish activity in situ using a globally dispersed radiotracer (¹³⁷Cs). Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences, 53(4), 734–745.
* Luek, A., Rowan, D. J., & Rasmussen, J. B. (2014). NP fertilization stimulates anaerobic selenium reduction in an end-pit lake. Scientific Reports, 7(1), 10502.

His publications have been cited more than 28,500 times, with an h-index of 75, according to Google Scholar.

data.title: Deep Structure Theory
data.text:
Deep Structure Theory (DST), also known as Neuropsychological Deep Structure Theory, is a unifying analytical framework that models how mental states emerge as compiled electromagnetic oscillatory activity relating to the structure and function of underlying neural circuitry. It is a local instance of dynamic complex systems theory that applies to how the brain generates the mind and was introduced by the cognitive neuroscientist and psychotherapy researcher Oliver Boxell. [ref: Deep Structure Theory: An introduction to a unifying theoretical framework for the analysis of human neuropsychology., Journal of Mind and Behavior]

The term "deep structure" was popularized in formal linguistics by Noam Chomsky in his theory of generative grammar, although this referred only to a core syntactic structure that could be expressed as different surface sentence forms. Boxell radically extends and deepens the idea in DST by developing it into a standard model for the entirety of the mind in which core conceptual meaning representations can be re-coded into integrated language, mathematics, music and sound patterns, or visuospatial and sensorimotor patterns. Furthermore, while Chomsky viewed mental representation in isolation, DST describes deep structure as the product of integrated, co-evolved representational and real-time processing subsystems. As such, the DST paradigm is able to stipulate systems for memory, learning, and sustained developmental patterns over time, in which the emergence of consciousness appears and plays a mediating role. The relationship between micro- and macro- neural circuits and compiled oscillations as the encoding of deep structure also makes DST more explicit about how the mind emerges from the structure and function of the brain, although generative grammar also more loosely viewed deep structure as somehow relating to the structure of the brain.

=== Basic Technical Outline ===
Universal deep structure algorithms: Boxell imports three core algorithms from X-Bar Theory (namely the complement, specifier, and adjunct rules), as well as binary switches, but views them as domain-general faculty for core meaning rather than a language-specific one. As such, in DST these formal algorithms derive abstract mental information structure as encoded by compiled neural oscillations. In common with dynamic complex systems theories generally, these neurosymbolic structures are computed as branching computations of nodes (units of information) that form binary tree representations.

Phase transitions: The domain-general faculty for core meaning occurs in the Information-Phase (I-Phase) of deep structural computation. One of the main functions of the I-Phase is conceptual or thematic role assignment, in which the deep structural tree incorporates theta theory and predicate logic. As some of these I-Phase computations reach a neural activation threshold filter known as theta (Φ) they transition into the Spellout-Phase (S-Phase), where the core meaning derivations are re-rendered into modality-specific deep structural forms through the addition of abstract features to the nodes, producing language, mathematics, music and sound patterning, and visuospatial and sensorimotor patterning. The I-to-S phase transitions in DST subsume transformations and phase analysis from the Minimalist Program and extend it as per-propositional chunking to all neurocognitive domains as a general computational working memory constraint.

Linearization: Some I-Phase and especially S-Phase computations reach another neural threshold filter called omega (Ω) that precipitates the deletion of branches from the deep structural tree representations to create a linear string of nodes. Subsets of deep structures that undergo this transition become self-aware or conscious, in-line with fundamental neurobiological research on consciousness that finds it appears when activation thresholds are reached in conjunction with highly distributed macrocircuits. [ref: What is the readiness potential?, Trends in Cognitive Sciences] [ref: Unconscious determinants of free decisions in the human brain, Nature Neuroscience] [ref: Piercing of Consciousness as a Threshold-Crossing Operation, Current Biology] [ref: Neural correlates of evidence accumulation during value-based decisions revealed via simultaneous EEG-fMRI, Nature Communications]

Memory: The sustained strength of transient neural circuit structures upregulates the strength of branch connections between nodes in deep structural tree derivations. Using Marvin Minsky's typology, Boxell calls the strength of branch connections "k-lines" (knowledge lines). [ref: K-Lines: A theory of memory, Cognitive Science] Just as neural circuits upregulate k-lines, k-line strengths can downregulate neural circuit connectivity strength; at both the neurobiological and emergent neuropsychological levels, frequency, recency, and saliency are proposed as the main filters that determine connectivity strengths. The ephemeral nature of k-lines show how the processing subsystem is instrumental in forming part of the nature of the deep structures that are built along with the actual representational algorithms that constrain their nature.

Learning and development: A real-time episode of learning involves the re-weighting of k-line branch attachments between nodes of deep structural trees. These can be transient but if frequency, recency, and saliency build up these learned connections to a critical mass threshold known as alpha (α), then the deep structural tree derivations involved become entrained into the developmental trajectory of the individual and further episodes of learning and development can build on them. Cycles of the α, Φ, and Ω thresholds running through I-Phase, S-Phase, and linearization process developmental curves over time, which Boxell (2025) relates to neuroconstructivism and its preceding models such as Piaget's cognitive development theory and Mahoney's cognitive constructivism. This mechanism also accounts for highly entrained components of human nature such as personality and identity.

Bidirectional crosstalk with natural systems: Direct two-directional interactions between neuronal cells and circuits, immune cells, endocrine molecules, microbiota and their metabolites, and the central nervous system mean that emergent deep structural mental states from these circuits' activity can influence — and be influenced by — a range of biological and biochemical systems. [ref: Neuropsychological Deep Structure: The Electromagnetic Emergence of Human Nature, Psychopathology, and the Scope of Clinical Mental Health Intervention., University of Rochester] This accounts for placebo effects and somatoform conditions, for example. Additionally, Piattelli-Palmarini and Vitielo identify a mathematical isomorphism between Quantum Field Theory and the features of Chomskyan X-Bar Theory and the Minimalist Program that are in turn incorporated into DST. [ref: Quantum field theory and the linguistic Minimalist Program: a remarkable isomorphism, Journal of Physics: Conference Series] Boxell (2025) suggests that this isomorphism may therefore transitively apply to DST as well, which is in-keeping with Piatelli and Vitielo's suggestion that it relates to electromagnetic oscillatory activity and could be connected to a more general neural phenomenon than language in isolation. If so, then the isomorphism may provide evidence of a high level of parsimony between the deep structural account of neuropsychology and quantum electrodynamics.

=== Psychopathology ===
DST views psychopathology as a form of "oscillopathy" or "rhythmopathy," terms introduced by Buzsáki and Vöröslakos (2023, p.926). [ref: Brain rhythms have come of age, Neuron] Boxell identifies four main etiological pathways, as follows:

* Genetically predetermined: When the genome codes for protein synthesis that impacts key neural circuit formations, clinically diagnosable mental states emerge in the form of neurodevelopmental disorders. Examples include intellectual disability disorders, Down's syndrome, or Williams Syndrome.
* Chemically induced: The introduction of substances that can impact synaptic or neural transmission will influence the structure and function of neural circuits and in turn the emergent deep structural mental states. Most psychiatric conditions have a chemically induced version.
* Neurodegenerative: Molecular or cellular pathologies that impact the structure and function of neural circuits will in turn produce pathological emergent deep structural states. Examples include Alzheimer's disease, Lewy Bodies dementia, other dementias, and traumatic brain injuries.
* Epigenetic predispositions/trauma-induced: The genome has code that is switched on or off by interaction with environmental stimuli. When the I-Phase encodes interpersonal-emotive trauma, the associated pain expresses phenotypes for neural circuits responsible for the S-Phase that use its neurocognitive modalities (such as language or visuospatial patterns) to produce symptomatic narratives — namely, defensive patterns of deep structural information processing that redirect the underlying I-Phase to "anesthetize" the pain of the trauma. There are a variety of such responses, each corresponding to a psychiatric disorder. Additionally, bidirectional crosstalk between relevant neural circuits and other biological systems mean that microbiota and their metabolites, endocrine responses, immunological responses, central nervous system responses may all impact neural structure and function directly or indirectly via interfacing with the genes that express them.
The deep structural account of psychopathology is predicted by findings that psychometric, genomic, neurocognitive, and neural circuit data across mental disorders all load onto a common latent variable known as the p-factor. [ref: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP): A Quantitative Nosology Based on Consensus of Evidence, Annual Review of Clinical Psychology] [ref: Toward the future of psychiatric diagnosis: the seven pillars of RDoC, BMC Medicine] As such, Boxell argues that mental disorders are different variants of the same core set of underlying neuropsychological representational and processing systems.

The Deep Structure Psychotherapy Model, also formulated by Oliver Boxell, provides a framework to apply these etiological pathways to clinical diagnosis and treatment. [ref: Deep Structure Psychotherapy. In B. Owens & K. Campbell (eds). The Encyclopedia of Mental Health Trainings, Certifications, and Credentials, Vol. 3., ONB] For measurement of deep structural states to enhance psychometrics, different technologies are used including reaction time latencies, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG). The model itself establishes some key principles of emergent neuropsychology that can be used to integrate efficacious components of traditional forms of psychotherapy together and it also enables the formulation of augmentative techniques to prime clinical target deep structures into their antidotes additively alongside the traditional interventions to boost efficacy further.

data.title: Justin Humphreys
data.text:
Justin Humphreys is an American drag racer who competed in the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) Sport Compact and Pro Stock categories, as well as the NOPI Outlaw category. He won the 2005 NHRA Sport Compact Modified championship before entering NHRA Pro Stock competition in 2007. In Pro Stock, he won the 2008 NHRA Carolina Nationals at zMAX Dragway in Concord, North Carolina, and the 2010 Pro Stock Showdown at Las Vegas Motor Speedway. He was nominated for NHRA Rookie of the Year in 2007. [ref: Richard Maskin joins Justin Humphreys, Motorsport.com] [ref: Charlotte: GM Racing final report, Motorsport.com] [ref: Justin Humphreys defeats Johnny Gray to Win Pro Stock Showdown, Dragzine]

== Racing career ==

=== Sport Compact racing ===

Humphreys competed in the NHRA Xplod Sport Compact Drag Racing Series in the Modified category, driving a 2003 Lexus GS 300. In 2005, he won the NHRA Sport Compact Modified championship. He continued competing in Sport Compact racing before moving into NHRA Pro Stock competition in 2007.

=== NHRA Pro Stock ===

Humphreys entered NHRA Pro Stock competition in 2007, driving a Pontiac GTO for RaceRedi Motorsports. The car was sponsored by Knoll-Gas Energy. Engine builder Richard Maskin joined the team's program, while Eric Luzinski initially served as crew chief.

During his rookie season, Humphreys competed in multiple national events and was nominated for the NHRA Rookie of the Year award. [ref: Memphis: Justin Humphreys preview, Motorsport.com]

At the 2007 NHRA Finals in Pomona, California, Humphreys reached the Pro Stock final round and finished as runner-up to Jeg Coughlin Jr. [ref: Humphreys, Glidden Bradenton test wrap-up, Motorsport.com]

=== Bob Glidden and the Pontiac GXP ===

In 2008, Humphreys competed in a Pontiac GXP. Veteran Pro Stock racer Bob Glidden joined the RaceRedi Motorsports team during the final six races of the 2007 season and continued working with the team in 2008 as crew chief. [ref: Humphreys, Glidden Bradenton test wrap-up, Motorsport.com]

By April 2008, Humphreys was among the top ten drivers in the Pro Stock season standings after the first four events. [ref: Las Vegas: Justin Humphreys preview, Motorsport.com]

=== 2008 Carolina Nationals ===

On September 14, 2008, Humphreys won the Pro Stock category at the inaugural NHRA Carolina Nationals at zMAX Dragway in Concord, North Carolina. It was the first NHRA national event held at the newly constructed dragway.

Driving the RaceRedi Motorsports Pontiac GXP, Humphreys qualified 11th and defeated Rob Mansfield, Jim Yates and Jeg Coughlin Jr. to reach the final against Kurt Johnson. Johnson's car developed a starter-drive problem and could not stage for the final. Humphreys staged his car and completed the run to secure his first NHRA Pro Stock national-event victory. He became the 51st first-time winner in NHRA Pro Stock history, and the victory was Pontiac's 189th in the category.

=== Pro Stock Showdown ===

In February 2010, Humphreys won the Pro Stock Showdown at The Strip at Las Vegas Motor Speedway, driving a Pontiac GXP. In the final round, he defeated Johnny Gray after Gray's car lost traction. Humphreys recorded a 6.79-second run in the final.

=== 2015 K&N Horsepower Challenge standings ===

Humphreys was listed in the NHRA's 2015 K&N Horsepower Challenge standings in 36th place with 95 points. [ref: 2015 K&N Horsepower Challenge Standings, National Hot Rod Association]

=== Return to racing ===

After being away from professional racing for several years, Humphreys returned to NHRA Pro Stock competition in 2014. Larry Morgan contacted him and asked him to drive Morgan's Pro Stock car at the Charlotte event. Humphreys accepted the offer. His competition license had expired during his absence, so he worked with Morgan at Rockingham Dragway to renew it before returning to competition. [ref: Humphreys relapses: Returns to addictive Pro Stock racing, Competition Plus]

== Personal life ==

Humphreys is from Monrovia, Maryland. He competed in professional drag racing with RaceRedi Motorsports, his racing team. [ref: Seattle: Justin Humphreys preview, Motorsport.com] [ref: Humphreys relapses: Returns to addictive Pro Stock racing, Competition Plus]

data.title: Johnny O'Reilly
data.text:
----

Johnny O'Reilly (born 22 October 1970) is an Irish filmmaker and journalist. [ref: Our man in Moscow, The Irish Times] [ref: 'I want to see out the war': Irish filmmaker moved to Ukraine from Russia when 'the pessimists were proved right', The Irish Times] [ref: Red Letter Day, The Sunday Times] He wrote and directed the Russian-language feature films Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) and The Weather Station (2010), as well as the Academy Award-shortlisted short film The Terms (2002). [ref: The Terms Shortlisted for Oscars, IFTN] His feature documentary Kherson was shot over four years in southern Ukraine. As a journalist, he has spent two decades covering politics and culture in Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine for publications including The Times, The Sunday Times, Rolling Stone, and The Irish Times.

== Early life and education ==
O'Reilly grew up in Dublin, Ireland. He studied Russian and Classics at Trinity College Dublin. In 1993, while still a student, he worked in Moscow as a freelance reporter covering the Russian constitutional crisis. In 1996, he completed graduate film studies at New York University. He worked at The Sunday Times for two years before pursuing a full-time career in filmmaking. In 2006, he relocated to Moscow, where he lived for ten years.

== Career ==

=== Filmmaking ===
O'Reilly first gained international recognition with the short film The Terms (2002), based on a short story by Irish writer Mike McCormack. The film was shortlisted for the 74th Academy Awards and received multiple international festival awards.

His feature directorial debut was the Russian-language thriller The Weather Station (2010), described by Variety as a whodunit set in an arctic meteorological outpost and filmed near Simferopol in Crimea. [ref: The Weather Station, Variety]

In 2016, he wrote and directed Moscow Never Sleeps, an ensemble drama set during Moscow City Day celebrations that follows several interconnected stories over a single day and stars prominent Russian actors.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, O'Reilly began work on the documentary feature Kherson, following civilians, soldiers, and families living through the occupation and liberation of Kherson city.

=== Journalism and cultural initiatives ===
O'Reilly has spent more than two decades reporting from Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and the wider former Soviet region, covering politics, culture, society, and conflict across Eastern Europe. His journalism has appeared in international media outlets, including The New York Times, Rolling Stone, The Sunday Times, The Times, The Irish Times, MarketWatch, and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

In 2008, he co-founded the Irish Film Festival in Moscow, an annual cultural initiative that ran for eleven years, evolving into a nationwide arts festival across multiple Russian cities.

=== Russian television incident ===
In August 2015, O'Reilly appeared live on Russian state television to discuss Moscow Never Sleeps. During the interview, he referred to the imprisonment of Ukrainian filmmaker Oleg Sentsov as a political imprisonment, after which the broadcast was abruptly cut short. [ref: Russian TV Cuts Away After Irish Director Backs Jailed Ukrainian Filmmaker Oleg Sentsov, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: Russian TV cuts off Irish director after backing jailed filmmaker, The Irish Times] The incident received international media coverage in outlets such as The Irish Times and The Hollywood Reporter. [ref: Russian TV Cuts Away After Irish Director Backs Jailed Ukrainian Filmmaker Oleg Sentsov, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: Russian TV cuts off Irish director after backing jailed filmmaker, The Irish Times]

== Filmography ==

* CO/MA (2004) – Feature film; co-director
* The Weather Station (2010) – Feature film; writer, director
* Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) – Feature film; writer, director
* Kherson – Documentary feature; writer, director, producer

data.title: Ella Yurman
data.text:
----

[[File:Ella Yurman.jpg|thumb|Yurman performing at Club Cumming in 2024]]

Ella Yurman (born ) is an American talk show host, writer, and comedian. She is known for hosting Going Down with Ella Yurman and Late Stage Live! With Ella Yurman, as well as for her 2025 Teen Vogue interview of Vivian Wilson.

Yurman has been cited as a prominent Gen Z influencer by Cosmopolitan, and her interview of Wilson earned her a GLAAD Media Award nomination in 2026 for outstanding journalism.

==Talk shows==
Late Stage Live! With Ella Yurman is a queer volunteer-run monthly show focusing on current events and politics for a primarily Gen Z audience. [ref: Late Stage Live! With Ella Yurman Wants to Be the Next Daily Show — But Make It LGBTQ+, Teen Vogue] The structure of the show follows the format set by The Late Show, opening with a monologue from Yurman, followed by a guest segment, and has a rapid-fire, irreverent tone throughout. The show is filmed at Brooklyn Information & Culture, airs on Brooklyn Public Access, [ref: Late Night Gets a Much-Needed Queer Makeover With ‘Late Stage Live!’, Jezebel.com] and episodes are published on YouTube for free.

Before creating the show, Yurman was writing for the YouTube series Some More News, and thought "there’s only so much I could be doing as a writer in a room writing for yet another cishet white guy." [ref: Ella Yurman, Teen Vogue] She was inspired to start the show having noticed there were no trans late night talk show hosts, or prominent trans commentators on politics. She approached playwright and comic Reid Pope and comedy writer Rima Parikh, whom she knew from New York stand up comedy circles, to write for the show. Neither Yurman nor head writer Pope had prior experience in television production. [ref: From a Tiny Studio in Brooklyn, Late Stage Live! Is Queering Late Night, [[Them (magazine)]

Guests who have appeared on Late Stage Live! show include New York City Councilmember Chi Ossé in October 2024. Topics covered include the marijuana industry and prison abolition, and it has a left-wing perspective with anti-capitalism and Palestinian liberation principles.

Yurman also hosts Going Down with Ella Yurman, the succession of Late Stage Live!, which was described as a "very good YouTube news series" by New York magazine's The Cut in 2025. [ref: What’s ‘Going Down’ With Ella Yurman: The Gen-Z New’s Cast Bringing Independent Journalism Back – Off Record Media]

T4T, an all-trans stand-up comedy show based in Brooklyn, was founded by Yurman and Terrence Dugan in 2022. [ref: T4T celebrates three years of transgender comedy, creating safe spaces at the Bell House, Brooklyn Paper] [ref: Trans Comedians Laugh Amidst the Horrors, Autostraddle] In 2024, Yurman left the show to focus on Going Down.

==Interview of Vivian Wilson==
[[File:Vivian Jenna Wilson - February 2025.jpg|thumb|Vivian Wilson, pictured a month before her March 2025 interview by Yurman in Teen Vogue]]
Yurman interviewed Vivian Wilson for Teen Vogue as the cover story for its March 2025 issue. [ref: Vivian Jenna Wilson on Being Elon Musk’s Estranged Daughter, Protecting Trans Youth and Taking on the Right Online, Teen Vogue] [ref: The 7 best takedowns of a chaotic 2025, Salon.com] The interview quickly gained attention on social media, and was covered by The New York Times, [ref: An Interview With Elon Musk’s Daughter Was Months in the Making, The New York Times] New York magazine's The Cut, [ref: 100 Days, 100 Small Victories: The political wins, works of art, and acts of defiance bringing us relief, joy, and even hope under Trump 2.0., [[The Cut (publication)] highlighted as a great read by Politico, [ref: The rival Biden forgot, Politico] and included by Salon in its list of "the 7 best takedowns of a chaotic 2025" for its impact on the public image of Elon Musk, Wilson's disowned father.

Yurman remarked to The New York Times of the interview that "I think a lot of coverage of trans people these days, even high-profile trans people, ends up centering their transness so much that it reduces them to two-dimensional figures without interiority. Most of all, I wanted this piece to give Vivian a chance to be herself in front of the world." The interview was nominated for the 37th GLAAD Media Awards in 2026 in the category Outstanding Online or Print Journalism Article in 2026. [ref: Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry Among Winners at 37th Annual GLAAD Media Awards, IGN.com]

==Reception==
In a 2024 article, Jezebel called Yurman "a generational talent with the sort of stage presence and charisma that make her one to watch". She was cited as a prominent gen Z influencer by Cosmopolitan in 2025. [ref: Introducing Cosmopolitan’s 2025 Z-Stars, [[Cosmopolitan (magazine)] She has also been featured in The New York Times, Politico, and Teen Vogue.

data.title: Konstantinas Šakenis
data.text:
----

Konstantinas Šakenis (27 November 1881 – 7 July 1959) was a Lithuanian engineer, teacher and politician. He served as Lithuania's Minister of Education from 1927 to 1934, State Controller from 1934 to 1940, and Speaker of the Seimas from 1936 to 1940.

Educated at the Imperial Petersburg Institute of Technology in Saint Petersburg, Šakenis taught physics at various schools in Vilnius, Voronezh, Kaunas, Panevėžys from 1912 to 1926. In 1920, he published a three-part Lithuanian physics textbook for gymnasiums. He was active in the Lithuanian public life. During World War I, he was a member of the Lithuanian Society for the Relief of War Sufferers. He was a member of the central committees of the Party of National Progress (1920–1924) and its successor the Lithuanian Nationalist Union (1928–1933).

In December 1926, Šakenis became a member of the Third Seimas when he filled the vacancy left by Antanas Smetona who became the president of Lithuania. In April 1927, he became the Minister of Education. During his seven-year tenure, Lithuania implemented mandatory primary education and improved teachers' education and licensing. Šakenis was seen as a strong supporter of president Smetona and implemented educational policies favoring the Lithuanian Nationalist Union, most notably the prohibition of all political and social organizations in schools. After the ministry, Šakenis was the State Controller and the Speaker of the Fourth Seimas. He held both positions until the Soviet occupation of Lithuania in June 1940.

He was arrested by the Soviet NKVD during the June deportation in 1941. He was sentenced to ten years in prison and lifetime in exile, but was released in 1956 and returned to Lithuania. He wrote poetry and finished his memoir, which were posthumously published in 1990s after Lithuania regained independence.

==Biography==
===Early life and education===
Šakenis was born on in the village of, in the Vabalninkas volost of what was then the Kovno Governorate of the Russian Empire (now Biržai District Municipality, Lithuania). His family were royal peasants who had greater personal freedoms than serfs and sought education. His uncles Ferdinandas was deported to Siberia for participating in the Uprising of 1863, Juozas was a military doctor educated at Moscow University, and Pelicijonas worked for the railroad. Šakenis was the eldest of six siblings. His brother Julijonas became a Roman Catholic priest.

Šakenis was first educated by a daraktorius at a clandestine school at his home. In September 1892, he enrolled at Šiauliai Boys' Gymnasium. There he was friends with the future engineer and belonged to a small group of Lithuanian students that promoted the use of the Lithuanian language.

He graduated from the gymnasium with a silver medal in June 1900 and enrolled in the Faculty of Physics and Mathematics at the University of St. Petersburg. He joined a society of Lithuanian students that distributed and promoted Lithuanian press which was illegal due to the Lithuanian press ban and was its vice-chairman. He was expelled in early 1901 for taking part in an anti-Tsarist student unrest, but was able to get readmitted. In 1902, he voluntarily transferred to the Mechanics Faculty of the Imperial Petersburg Institute of Technology. There he studied with his friends Gravrogkas, Steponas Kairys, and.

His studies were temporarily interrupted by the Russian Revolution of 1905. He then worked at the Vilija factory of Petras Vileišis, as well as assisted in editing and publishing the first Lithuanian daily Vilniaus žinios. After completing his practicum at and as an assistant locomotive engineer at Radviliškis–Mažeikiai railway, Šakenis graduated in May 1910.

===Early career===
After graduation, Šakenis moved to Vilnius. In late 1911, he obtained teaching position at the 1st Vilnius Gymnasium and later at the Vilnius Girls' Gymnasium where he taught physics and cosmography. In 1912, he also worked as an engineer on the construction of the headquarters of the Saulė Society in Kaunas. During this time, he participated in the activities of the Lithuanian Mutual Aid Society of Vilnius.

At the start of World War I, Šakenis was elected to the audit committee of the Lithuanian Society for the Relief of War Sufferers. He organised trade workshops and schools on behalf of the Lithuanian Society. In 1915, the Russian gymnasiums along with Šakenis were evacuated to Russia. From September 1915 to June 1918, he served as an inspector of the Lithuanian gymnasium in Voronezh. For nearly a year, he was also an acting principal of the gymnasium while Pranas Mašiotas was recuperating. In late 1917, Šakenis helped edit published by the Party of National Progress.

Šakenis returned to Vilnius in June 1918 and became a teacher of mathematics and physics at the Vilnius Vytautas the Great Gymnasium. At the same time, he wrote a three-part textbook on physics in Lithuanian as there was an urgent need for Lithuanian-language educational materials. At the start of the Lithuanian–Soviet War, Šakenis evacuated to Kaunas.

From June 1919 to July 1925, Šakenis worked at the Lithuanian railways under the Ministry of Communications. At the same time, he taught courses on physics and railroad at the Kaunas Higher Technical School (present-day. In fall 1919, Šakenis participated in drafting plans for a Lithuanian university. These plans were initially rejected leading to the establishment of Higher Courses (they were reorganized into the University of Lithuania in 1922). However, Šakenis did not teach at either the courses or the university. He was hired by the university as senior assistant in early 1925 but chose the position of gymnasium's principal.

In 1922, he became a council member of the Trade and Industry Bank. In July 1925, he replaced Jonas Yčas as the principal of three gymnasiums in Panevėžys (Boys', Girls', and Russian) that shared the same premises. He continued in this role until December 1926. However, already in 1925, he returned to Kaunas and obtained a position with the Ministry of Education.

===Political career===
Šakenis was active in the Party of National Progress and was a member of its central committee from 1920 to 1924. In 1924, the party was reorganized into the Lithuanian Nationalist Union. On its ticket, he ran in the May 1926 election to the Third Seimas in the Panevėžys district. He was listed second to Antanas Smetona and was not elected. Following the December 1926 coup, Smetona became the President of Lithuania and Šakenis took his seat in the Seimas. Šakenis was officially sworn in on 30 December 1926, but was not active in the proceedings.

====Minister of Education====
Smetona dissolved the Seimas on 12 April 1927 which caused a government crisis and a new cabinet was formed on 3 May 1927. Šakenis became the Minister of Education and served under prime ministers Augustinas Voldemaras and Juozas Tūbelis until 12 June 1934 when the cabinet resigned in the aftermath of the attempted coup by voldemarininkai. At the same time, from 1928 to 1933, Šakenis was a member of the central committee of the Lithuanian Nationalist Union. According to the memoirs of general Stasys Raštikis, Šakenis was usually quiet and agreed with the president Smetona.

During his tenure as minister, Lithuania carried out some key reforms in education, including implementation of the mandatory primary education. While the law on the mandatory education was adopted in 1922, it was implemented during Šakenis' tenure. In 1931, the government announced that the implementation was complete. Other accomplishments included expansion of trade schools, improvements to teachers' education and licensing, enhancement of physical and material school resources, opening of the in 1927 and of the in 1934, reorganization of the Kaunas Music School into the. He chaired a committee which organized the celebrations of the 500th death anniversary of Grand Duke Vytautas the Great in 1930 and supervised construction of the Vytautas the Great War Museum. He supported activities of the Scout Association of Lithuania and the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union allowing them to operate in all public schools from October 1928.

Šakenis also implemented several policies that benefited the Lithuanian Nationalist Union. Most notably, on 30 August 1930, he issued a circular prohibiting all political and social organizations in schools. This was primarily aimed against the Catholic youth association Ateitis, but also affected socialist and nationalist groups. Only the scouts, whose supreme chief was president Smetona, were allowed to operate in schools. The circular elicited official protests from the Holy See arguing that it violated the Concordat of 1927. Ateitis continued to be active among students, despite police investigations and threats of expulsion.

During Šakenis' tenure, the government adopted a new statute of the University of Lithuania which significantly curtailed its autonomy and increased influence of the Ministry of Education. In another move against the Lithuanian Christian Democratic Party, the Faculty of Theology and Philosophy was significantly reduced in August 1931: five of 22 departments were cut, and the number of senior professors reduced from 37 to 19.

====State Controller and Speaker of the Seimas====
From 12 June 1934 to 15 June 1940 (or 17 July), Šakenis served as the State Controller of Lithuania.

From 1 September 1936 to 1 July 1940, Šakenis was a member of the Fourth Seimas and its Speaker. Elected after nearly a decade, the Seimas was primarily an advisory body to the president. On a few occasions, Šakenis publicly declared that the main function of the Seimas was to assist the president, and not to represent the will of the Lithuanian people. He chaired most of the Seimas sessions and, as state controller, presented annual state budgets for approval but only on a few occasions participated in discussions on specific laws.

Šakenis was a member of various societies, including chairman of the, member of the board of the Scout Association of Lithuania and, and benefactor of the student's association. In September 1930, he was one of the co-founders of the Lithuanian Nationalist Fund which provided financial aid to students who supported the Lithuanian Nationalist Union. He also organized the construction of a primary school in Vabalninkas. Completed in 1936, it was named in his honor in 1937.

On 15 June 1940, during the government's last meeting before the Soviet occupation, Šakenis was among the few ministers who spoke in favour of armed resistance rather than compliance with the Soviet ultimatum.

After the occupation, Šakenis was dismissed from his government roles and moved to his birthplace in Veleniškiai. The new Soviet regime sharply criticized him. For example, Antanas Sniečkus speaking to the People's Seimas referred to Šakenis as a "spineless" "political fool" who helped politicians swindle government's money. In both roles, the controller and speaker, Šakenis was replaced by Liudas Adomauskas who helped to transform Lithuania into a Soviet socialist republic.

===Soviet persecution===
On 14 June 1941, during the June deportation, Šakenis was arrested by the Soviet NKVD. On 3 March 1946, he was sentenced to ten years in prison and lifetime exile according to the Article 58 by the Special Council of the NKVD. He was imprisoned in various Siberian Gulag camps, including in near Nizhnyaya Poyma (part of Kraslag) in the Krasnoyarsk Krai and near Tayshet (part of Ozerlag) in Irkutsk Oblast. In May 1951, he was exiled to in the Krasnoyarsk Krai and later to in Tomsk Oblast where he was able to reunite with his family.

He was released in July 1956 and returned to Lithuania in poor health. He lived in Troškūnai where he died on 7 July 1959. He was buried in Vabalninkas in his family grave. In 2008, his grave was added to the Registry of Cultural Property.

==Publications==
===Physics textbook===
In 1920, Šakenis published three-part physics textbook for Lithuanian gymnasiums. He continued to edit and improve it, and there were five editions published before 1940. It remained the primary physics textbook used in gymnasiums for the entire interwar period. The textbook was based on the Russian textbook by, but information was presented differently and included Lithuanian examples (for example, the transatlantic flight of Lituanica). In later editions, the book included some advanced topics like the four-dimensional space by Hermann Minkowski and the theory of relativity by Albert Einstein.

Writing the book was difficult because there was no established Lithuanian terminology. Šakenis consulted with other specialists (, Pranas Mašiotas, ) and linguist Jonas Jablonskis. As such, the book is valued for its contribution to the Lithuanian terminology.

===Historical studies===
Šakenis published two historical studies.

While still a student in Saint Petersburg, Šakenis received a special permit to study archives the Lithuanian newspaper Aušra at the Imperial Public Library. He published a few articles in Vilniaus žinios in 1905–1906 and a larger study "Aušra" ir jos gadynė for the 50th anniversary in 1933.

Vabalninkas ir jo apylinkė praeityje ligi Lietuvos nepriklausomybės atgavimo, a local history of the Vabalninkas area, was published by the Lithuanian Historical Society in 1935.

===Poetry and memoir===
Šakenis was interested in poetry. In 1909, he translated a few poems by Adam Mickiewicz and published them in Viltis. He published the full translation of Pan Tadeusz in 1924. Critics in the magazine Kultūra valued the translation not for its poetic qualities, but for faithfulness to the original.

During his imprisonment and exile in Siberia, Šakenis composed poetry but was unable to write it down due to lack of paper. He was able to write down about 12,000 lines of poetry after he returned to Lithuania in 1956. These poems were published by his son, Romualdas Šakenis, in 1995 as Vaizdai ir mintys nelaisvėje (Images and Thoughts in Confinement). Though simple and unrefined, his verses include elements of local heritage, provide historical insights, and showcase his patriotism. The book includes 69 translated poems by Mikhail Lermontov, Alexander Pushkin, Nikolai Nekrasov, Aleksey Apukhtin, Afanasy Fet, Nikoloz Baratashvili, Raphael Patkanian, Victor Hugo, and others.

His memoir Iki "Vaizdų ir minčių nelaisvėje" (Before "Images and Thoughts in Confinement") were published in 1997. The memoir, started in 1934 and continued after his return from Gulag camps, cover the events up to 1925.

===Other===
In 1911, encouraged by Antanas Smetona and Jonas Basanavičius, Šakenis wrote a study on Polonization carried out by the bishops of Vilnius. The manuscript was taken by the Italian priest Aurelio Palmieri and used in his publications.

In addition, Šakenis published articles in various Lithuanian newspapers, including Vilniaus žinios, Viltis, Vairas, Lietuvos ūkininkas.

==Legacy==
His son Romualdas worked to build a memorial stone and reconstruct a granary in his birth village of Veleniškiai. A memorial museum dedicated to Šakenis was opened in Veleniškiai on 6 July 2000.

On 26 July 1943, Šakenis sent a birch bark letter to his wife for his son's 11th birthday. The letter is preserved at the and was included among 148 such letters in a multinational application to include them in the Memory of the World Register by UNESCO in 2023. His imprisonment and deportation was highlighted in the permanent exhibition of the Ninth Fort.

Streets named after Šakenis are located in Kaunas, Vilnius, and Vabalninkas. A memorial plaque was affixed to the house in Kaunas where he lived in 1930–1940 for his 125th birth anniversary.

==Personal life==
In 1928, Šakenis married Stanislava Šakenienė Giedraitytė (1900–1982) in a ceremony officiated by Vladas Mironas. The wedding was attended by many government officials and is noted as one of the last events where president Antanas Smetona and prime minister Augustinas Voldemaras were still on friendly terms before their falling out in early 1929.

Šakenienė was from a well-connected family. Her brother was the Minister of Defense in 1930–1934, while her sister was married to the engineer and professor. Šakenienė was also a cousin of Sofija Smetonienė, the first lady of Lithuania. Historians discuss these relationships when analyzing the impact of family ties on politicians' careers.

Educated at the University of Lithuania, Šakenienė became one of the first Lithuanian women surgeons. She chaired the Lithuanian Society for the Care of the Blind from 1930 to 1940.

Šakenienė together with her son Romualdas and daughter Rita were deported in June 1941 to Komarovka in, Tomsk Oblast. Both children escaped to Lithuania in 1947 and Šakenienė followed in 1948. However, she was quickly caught and sentenced to three years in prison. The children were arrested in summer 1952 and deported to where they reunited with their parents in 1953. The family returned to Lithuania in 1956.

==Awards==
Šakenis was awarded:
* Order of Vytautas the Great, 2nd class (1930)
* Order of the Three Stars, 1st class (1932)
* Order of the Iron Wolf by the Scout Association of Lithuania (1934)
* Order of the Lithuanian Grand Duke Gediminas, 1st class (1938)
* Riflemen's Star (1938)

data.title: Oregon State–Washington State football rivalry
data.text:
----

----

The Oregon State–Washington State football rivalry is an American college football rivalry game played in the states of Oregon and Washington between the Oregon State Beavers in Corvallis and the Washington State Cougars in Pullman.

First played in 1903, the game is one of the most played rivalries in NCAA football, historically being part of the Northwest Championship. The two schools have historically been apart of the same conference, with them being members of the Pacific Coast Conference from 1916 to 1959, the Athletic Association of Western Universities from 1964 to 1968, the Pac-8 Conference from 1968 to 1978, the Pac-10 Conference from 1978 to 2011, the Pac-12 North Division from 2011 to 2021, and the Pac-12 Conference from 2011 onwards.

The individual matchup between the two schools gained national attention after 10 out of the 12 original teams in the Pac-12 moved to other NCAA conferences in 2024, leaving the two teams as the only ones still in the conference. [ref: College football conference realignment breakdown for 2024-25: Teams in new conferences, NCAA] The matchup has not been officially named yet, with suggestions including "The Land-Grant Rivalry", "The Cascade Cup", "The War on I-84", or "The Columbia River Rivalry". [ref: Buddy-buddy time is over. Washington State-Oregon State is now a real rivalry., The Spokesman-Review] [ref: Rivalry game wins are meaningful, no matter who the opponent is, The Spokesman-Review]

Although the teams do not compete for a trophy on the field, the winning team's alumni association is given the "No Name Trophy", consisting of basalt and granite rock taken from the Columbia River, weighing more than 50 pounds. [ref: Take home the rock: WSU takes on the Beavers in Corvallis - A new trophy is introduced for the WSU vs. OSU rivalry, Daily Evergreen] [ref: ‘Let’s go win the rock’: Behind the new WSU-Oregon State rivalry trophy, Yakima-Herald Times] The concept of the trophy going to the winning team's alumni association is used by Oregon State in the Platypus Trophy.

Like many rivalry games, the game is played during the final week of the college football season, being played in that slot every year since 2025 following the collapse of the Pac-12.
==Series history==
The rivalry was first played in 1903, and has been played 111 times through 2025. They have played each other in 1903, 1905, and annually since 1910, except for in 1918, 1925, 1926, 1943, 1944, 1987, 1997, 1998, 1999, and 2002. Oregon State and Washington State played each other twice in 1945 and in 2025. Washington State leads the series [ref: Washington State-Oregon State, The Sideline]

The game is usually played at either Reser Stadium in Corvallis or Martin Stadium in Pullman. However, nine games were played in Portland, Oregon, and the 2011 game was played at CenturyLink field in Seattle in an effort to increase revenue for the two teams. [ref: Cougs pumped to play at CenturyLink, The Spokesman-Review]

Even though Washington State currently leads the series, Oregon State had several notable win streaks throughout it's history. Oregon State won the first four games they played against each other from 1903 to 1911, before Washington State broke the streak by winning 10-9 in 1912.

Oregon State had two notable win streaks, from 1960 to 1964, and from 1966 to 1971 under coaches Tommy Prothro and Dee Andros. The only time that Washington State won between 1960 and 1971 was in 1965, where they won 10-8 in Corvallis.

Washington State's largest win streak was from 1983 to 1993 under coaches Jim Walden, Dennis Erickson, and Mike Price, where they won 10 consecutive games until Oregon State beat them 21-3 on November 12, 1994. [ref: Oregon State vs Washington State, Fueled By Sports]

The 2023 Matchup, marred by rumors of conference realignment, and being jokingly dubbed the "Pac-2 Championship Game", was the first matchup in the rivalry's history in which both teams were ranked. The game was filled with pageantry, with the Washington State band playing the Oregon State fight song before the game. The Cougars would defeat the Beavers 38-35.

In 2024, Oregon State and Washington State became the only teams remaining in the Pac-12 Conference, [ref: Oregon State, Washington State last standing in depleted Pac-12, KGW8] leading to them being nicknamed the "Pac-2" by media outlets, to the point that a game between the two teams during the 2023 football season was jokingly dubbed the "Pac-2 Championship Game" by fans. [ref: How Pac-2 moves forward after leverage play as College Football Playoff updates 12-team expansion model, CBS Sports] [ref: What happens when realignment leaves a college football team behind, ESPN] [ref: College football abandoned them, but the Pac-2 refuses to go away, The Washington Post] The new attention to the game led to them forming a rivalry against each other. [ref: How the rebuilt Pac-12 looks to be 'in a tier of its own', ESPN] [ref: Washington State-Oregon State rivalry has some unexpected connections this year, Yahoo Sports] [ref: This Rivalry Is Really Weird., Youtube - Pac-12 Conference] Ahead of the game that year, Washington State head coach Jake Dickert said "Oregon State’s not our buddy." and "It’s one of our biggest rivals now". [ref: Abandoned rivals reunion pits Oregon State, Washington State, CBS Sports / Field Level Media] Washington State would lose in upset fashion 41-38.

In 2025, due to scheduling constraints brought on by their "Pac-2" independent nature, Oregon State and Washington State played each other twice in the regular season, the third time in FBS history two teams played each other in the regular season. [ref: Why do Washington State and Oregon State play each other twice in 2025?, Yahoo Sports] The teams split their matchups 1-1, each earning themselves a share of the Pac-12 title. Following Oregon State's win, Oregon State players were quoted as saying "They say it's a rivalry, but a rivalry is if you're winning and losing, but we've been winning every time." [ref: "They say it's a rivalry, but a rivalry is if you're winning and losing, but we've been winning every time." Somehow behind only 60 yards of passing Oregon State and company pulled off the win tonight vs. WSU. The team had A LOT to say postgame:, X]

In 2026, six new schools joined the Pac-12, marking the start of conference play in the new rebuilt league. [ref: New-Look Pac-12 Returns for First Week of Conference Play, Front Office Sports] Ahead of their first meeting in 2026, it was announced the winning teams alumni association would receive the "No Name Trophy", a 50 pound plus rock based trophy consisting of basalt and granite rock taken from the Columbia River.
