data.title: Drag Syndrome
data.text:
Drag Syndrome is a British drag performance collective composed of drag queens and drag kings with Down syndrome. The collective was founded in London in 2018 by choreographer and artistic director Daniel Vais and developed from his work with performers with Down syndrome through Culture Device Dance Project. [ref: Drag Syndrome: A collective opening up drag for people with Down's Syndrome, Dazed] [ref: The Drag Troupe For Kings and Queens With Learning Disabilities, Vice]

The group's performances combine drag, dance, lip-sync, costume, movement, humour and audience interaction. Since its formation, Drag Syndrome has performed in the United Kingdom and internationally at queer nightlife venues, festivals, Pride events and cultural institutions. Appearances have included Glastonbury Festival, RuPaul's DragCon UK, Berghain in Berlin, Somerset House in London and the Münchner Kammerspiele in Munich. [ref: Line-Up 2023, Glastonbury Festival] [ref: Prepare To Be Blown Away By The Power Of Drag Syndrome, British Vogue] [ref: Drag Syndrome, Somerset House]

The collective has received media attention for its relationship to disability, sexuality, gender, artistic autonomy and queer culture. It has been profiled by outlets including Dazed, British Vogue, The Guardian, The Standard, PAPER, Gay Times, PinkNews, Vice and ITV News. [ref: Drag Syndrome: Inside the UK's first Down's syndrome drag night, ITV News]

==History==

===Formation and first performances===

Drag Syndrome developed from Culture Device Dance Project, an artistic company founded by Daniel Vais involving dancers and performers with Down syndrome.

According to accounts published by Vice and Dazed, the idea developed after Vais attended an event with actor and dancer Sarah Gordy where they saw drag performers. Gordy expressed an interest in experimenting with drag, and Vais subsequently discussed the idea with other artists from Culture Device. The performers began researching drag and developing their own stage identities.

Drag Syndrome gave its first public performance on 29 March 2018 at vFd, formerly Vogue Fabrics, an LGBTQ+ performance space in east London. Vice reported that the sold-out performance featured six artists. Following the response to the first event, the project developed into an ongoing performance collective.

A second event, Drag Syndrome 0.2, was held at Vogue Fabrics on 31 May 2018.

ITV News profiled the collective in June 2018, including performer Otto Baxter, whose drag persona is Horrora Shebang.

The collective subsequently became part of London's queer nightlife and performance scene and appeared at London Pride, the Royal Vauxhall Tavern and other queer cultural events.

Later in 2018 the collective performed at Alternative Miss World at Shakespeare's Globe.

PAPER published a feature on the group during its first year. Vais described the performers researching drag and developing individual characters rather than treating drag solely as costume. [ref: Drag Syndrome Shines a Light on Inclusivity, PAPER]

===International expansion===

During 2019 Drag Syndrome increased its activity outside London and the United Kingdom.

ITV News Wales covered members of the collective during a performance in Cardiff in June 2019. [ref: The drag act changing the way people think about Down's syndrome, ITV News Wales]

The collective also appeared at Montréal Pride in Canada. By November 2019, Dazed described Drag Syndrome as being on an international tour following performances in Britain and continental Europe.

The Dazed feature profiled Vais and performers including Horrora Shebang, Justin Bond and Gaia Callas and discussed the development of their individual drag identities.

The collective subsequently continued touring internationally, appearing at Pride events, theatres, festivals, clubs and cultural institutions.

===Michigan discrimination dispute===

In 2019, Drag Syndrome was scheduled to perform in Grand Rapids, Michigan, as part of a disability drag event organised by DisArt.

Peter Meijer, owner of the Tanglefoot Building where the performance was scheduled to take place, prevented Drag Syndrome from performing at the venue. Meijer said he had concerns about whether the artists were able to give "full and informed consent" to participate in drag. [ref: ACLU files formal complaint against Peter Meijer, Michigan Public]

DisArt and the American Civil Liberties Union of Michigan challenged the decision, and the ACLU filed a formal discrimination complaint.

Members of Drag Syndrome publicly rejected the suggestion that they were incapable of deciding whether they wished to perform drag. [ref: Drag collective Drag Syndrome kicked out of US venue after owner thought the performers didn't give their 'full and informed consent', Attitude]

The dispute generated international coverage and discussion about autonomy, sexuality and the rights of people with intellectual disabilities.

===DragCon and British Vogue===

In January 2020, Drag Syndrome performed at the inaugural RuPaul's DragCon UK in London.

Filmmaker Jess Kohl followed members of the collective during the event for a short documentary titled Drag Syndrome, commissioned by British Vogue for its 2020 Pride film series.

The film followed the performers preparing for and performing at DragCon UK and explored their individuality, gender expression and artistic practice.

Kohl said that one aim of the film was to move away from patronising responses towards people with intellectual disabilities and instead present members of the collective as complex artists exercising their own agency.

The film was released by British Vogue on 23 June 2020. [ref: Meet Drag Syndrome As They Perform At RuPaul's DragCon UK, British Vogue]

The film later appeared at Fashion Film Festival Milano, where Kohl received the Best Director award. [ref: Fashion Film Festival 2021: tutti i vincitori, Vogue Italia]

===2021–2023===

Following the disruption to live performance caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, Drag Syndrome returned to live performances and international touring.

By 2022, a frequently presented line-up included Lady Mercury, Nikita Gold, Davina Starr, Justin Bond, Lady Francesca and Horrora Shebang.

In May 2022, Drag Syndrome appeared at the Mittenmang International Theatre Festival in Bremen, Germany. The programme listed Lady Mercury, Nikita Gold, Davina Starr, Justin Bond and Jonny Medals among the performers. [ref: Drag Syndrome & maquillage queervaganza: Drag Night Mittenmang, Mittenmang International Theatre Festival]

In August 2022 the collective staged a day-long programme at Somerset House in London as part of This Bright Land. The programme featured Nikita Gold, Lady Mercury, Justin Bond, Lady Francesca, Horrora Shebang and Davina Starr and combined drag performances with talks, music and guest appearances.

Drag Syndrome returned to RuPaul's DragCon UK in January 2023. The Guardian documented the collective as part of a photographic feature on the event. [ref: 'Let's celebrate love': RuPaul's DragCon UK – a photo essay, The Guardian]

In June 2023 Drag Syndrome performed at Glastonbury Festival, appearing in the Shangri-La programme.

===2024–present===

In January 2024, Drag Syndrome performed as part of the All Abled Arts programme at the Münchner Kammerspiele in Germany.

The collective returned to the theatre in June 2024 for That's Drag! Extravaganza, alongside German guest performers including Rocky Black, Pinay Colada, Earl van Grey, KingTenu and Victoria Hell. [ref: That's Drag! Extravaganza, Münchner Kammerspiele]

Rocky Black, a Germany-based drag king, appeared with Drag Syndrome as a guest artist in connection with this German activity.

On 18 June 2024, Drag Syndrome performed at the opening of Krake Festival at Berghain in Berlin. [ref: Krake Festival Opening, Berghain]

In July 2024, The Guardian published a photographic feature about the collective featuring Nikita Gold, YouGo Boss, Justin Bond, Lady Francesca, Sheeza Bet, Davina Starr and Lady Mercury. The performers discussed their experiences of drag, performance and disability in their own words. [ref: 'Our message? Be fabulous!': drag artists with Down's syndrome – in pictures, The Guardian]

In 2025, the Barbican Centre in London hosted a screening of Saskia Boddeke's film Inside My Heart followed by a ScreenTalk featuring Drag Syndrome performers Annalie Huberman-Hertz (YouGo Boss) and Francis Majekodunmi (Lady Francesca) with Vais. [ref: Inside My Heart + ScreenTalk, Barbican Centre]

During 2025, Drag Syndrome announced that it would stop accepting new UK bookings, citing difficulties obtaining sufficient financial and institutional support for disabled artists.

In March 2026, The Guardian reported that Drag Syndrome had joined UnMute, a live music roster established to improve professional opportunities for disabled musicians and performers. The collaboration enabled the collective to resume taking UK bookings. [ref: 'No one's tried this before': a new live music roster aims to ensure opportunities for disabled musicians, The Guardian]

Annalie Huberman-Hertz, who performs as YouGo Boss, was quoted in the article discussing professional opportunities for disabled artists.

==Artistic practice==

Drag Syndrome's artists perform through individual drag personas developed according to their own interests, performance styles and identities.

Performances typically incorporate dance, movement, lip-sync, costume, make-up, music, comedy and audience interaction.

Early reporting on the collective emphasised that the performers researched drag and developed individual characters rather than being assigned identities by the artistic director.

In the 2019 Dazed profile, members discussed their individual approaches to drag. Horrora Shebang described a performance identity influenced by horror and darker aesthetics, while Gaia Callas discussed costume, glamour and transformation.

Justin Bond, the drag king persona of Ruby Codiroli, has described Drag Syndrome as a professional artistic group. In a 2020 feature with The Standard, Codiroli discussed the importance of being treated with professional respect rather than being viewed primarily through disability. [ref: I'm a Londoner: How a drag community of performers with Down's Syndrome is challenging stereotypes, Evening Standard]

The collective's work has frequently been discussed in relation to the autonomy and sexuality of people with intellectual disabilities. Media coverage has addressed assumptions that disabled adults should be separated from queer culture, sexuality or forms of performance associated with provocation and self-expression.

The collective's approach places emphasis on performers controlling their own stage identities and artistic personas.

==Performers==

Drag Syndrome has operated with a changing ensemble since its formation in 2018. Artists perform under individual drag personas, and different combinations of performers have appeared in different shows, tours and periods of the collective's history.

Artists documented as having performed with Drag Syndrome include:

Horrora Shebang — Otto Baxter
Justin Bond — Ruby Codiroli
Lady Francesca — Francis Majekodunmi
Gaia Callas — Danny Smith
Frozita Honkong — Sam Barnard
George the Lord
Gymma Black
Nikita Gold — Nick McKerrow
Lady Mercury — Adam Wild
Davina Starr — Davis Simpson
Jonny Medals — Holly Riseborough
YouGo Boss — Annalie Huberman-Hertz
Sheeza Bet
Lady Felicia
Rocky Black — Germany-based guest artist

The official Drag Syndrome artist archive documents a number of the collective's early and long-standing performers. [ref: Artists, Drag Syndrome]

Horrora Shebang, Justin Bond and Gaia Callas were profiled by Dazed during the collective's early period of international touring.

The 2022 Mittenmang International Theatre Festival identified Lady Francesca as Francis Majekodunmi, Lady Mercury as Adam Wild, Nikita Gold as Nick McKerrow, Davina Starr as Davis Simpson, Justin Bond as Ruby Codiroli and Jonny Medals as Holly Riseborough.

The Barbican Centre identifies Francis Majekodunmi as Lady Francesca and Annalie Huberman-Hertz as YouGo Boss.

YouGo Boss, Sheeza Bet, Nikita Gold, Justin Bond, Lady Francesca, Davina Starr and Lady Mercury were documented in The Guardian in 2024.

Lady Felicia has also been publicly documented as a Drag Syndrome performer in research on disability and performance. [ref: Research, Alison Mahoney]

Rocky Black appeared with Drag Syndrome in Germany as a guest artist and is included in the historical performer list while retaining that distinction.

The ensemble has changed over time, and inclusion in the historical list does not necessarily indicate current permanent membership.

==Selected performances==

Selected appearances by Drag Syndrome include:

Vogue Fabrics / vFd, London — first performance, 29 March 2018
London Pride — 2018
Alternative Miss World, Shakespeare's Globe — 2018
Oslo, Norway — 2018
Royal Albert Hall, London — 2019
Montréal Pride — 2019
RuPaul's DragCon UK — 2020
Mittenmang International Theatre Festival, Bremen — 2022
Paris Pride — 2022
Somerset House, London — This Bright Land, 2022
WHOLE Festival, Germany — 2022
RuPaul's DragCon UK — 2023
Glastonbury Festival — 2023
Münchner Kammerspiele, Munich — 2024
Krake Festival at Berghain, Berlin — 2024

==Media and publications==

Drag Syndrome has been the subject of coverage in newspapers, magazines, fashion publications, LGBTQ+ media, television and documentary film.

One of the earliest television reports about the collective was broadcast by ITV News in June 2018.

In September 2018, PinkNews published a profile of Otto Baxter and his drag persona Horrora Shebang, discussing his experiences performing with Drag Syndrome. [ref: What it's like being a drag queen with Down's Syndrome, PinkNews]

Vice published a substantial feature about the collective in December 2018, documenting its formation, first performance and early artistic development.

In January 2019, LGBTQ Nation published a feature on Drag Syndrome and its growing international activity. [ref: 'Drag Syndrome' is a fierce drag show where all the performers have Down's Syndrome, LGBTQ Nation]

In June 2019, Gay Times published a dedicated feature about the collective. [ref: Drag Syndrome are the revolutionary group defying expectations, Gay Times]

Later that year, Dazed published an extensive feature by Tom Rasmussen examining Drag Syndrome's origins, international touring and the individual drag personas of its performers.

Drag Syndrome also appeared in Attitude. Reporting on the 2019 Michigan discrimination dispute noted that the collective had previously appeared as one of the publication's cover subjects during its anniversary series.

In 2020, photographer Eimear Lynch photographed the collective for Dazed, with styling by Sophie Cochevelou and make-up by Jack Oliver. [ref: Drag Syndrome, Dazed]

The same year, Drag Syndrome appeared in King Kong Garçon, a publication associated with King Kong Magazine. The editorial was created by Berlin-based Contemporary Ct Collective and featured Gymma Black, George the Lord, Frozita Honkong, Gaia Callas, Lady Francesca, Justin Bond and Horrora Shebang. [ref: Berlin's Contemporary Ct Collective shine a light on Drag Syndrome in the latest issue of King Kong Garçon, It's Nice That]

In March 2020, The Standard published a profile of Justin Bond focusing on Drag Syndrome, professional performance and stereotypes surrounding Down syndrome.

In June 2020, British Vogue released Jess Kohl's short documentary Drag Syndrome as part of its Pride film series.

The documentary subsequently received recognition at Fashion Film Festival Milano.

In 2022, Drag Syndrome was the subject of a fashion editorial in DSECTION Magazine, photographed by Cameron McNee. [ref: Drag Syndrome, Models.com]

The Guardian documented Drag Syndrome at RuPaul's DragCon UK in a photographic essay in January 2023.

In July 2024, The Guardian published a dedicated photographic feature about Drag Syndrome. The feature presented a number of the performers discussing their work, identities and experiences in their own words.

In 2025, Drag Syndrome appeared in Novembre Magazine Issue 17 in an editorial photographed by Jules Moskovtchenko and styled by Patricia Villirillo. The editorial featured Davina Starr, Lady Francesca, Nikita Gold, Justin Bond, YouGo Boss and Daniel Vais. [ref: Inside Novembre issue 17: Drag Syndrome by Jules Moskovtchenko & Patricia Villirillo, Novembre]

Drag Syndrome was also featured as a cover subject for Issue 17 of Novembre Magazine. [ref: Novembre Magazine Issue 17, Novembre]

Other publications and media outlets that have covered Drag Syndrome include NBC News and a range of LGBTQ+, arts, fashion and disability publications.

==Books and academic publications==

Drag Syndrome has been featured in books concerning drag and LGBTQ+ culture and has been discussed in academic writing on contemporary drag and disability performance.

In 2020, Drag Syndrome was featured on page 34 of Dan Jones's 50 Drag Queens Who Changed the World: A Celebration of the Most Influential Drag Artists of All Time, published by Hardie Grant. [ref: 50 Drag Queens Who Changed the World: A Celebration of the Most Influential Drag Artists of All Time, Hardie Grant]

The inclusion placed Drag Syndrome among drag performers selected by Jones for their influence on the development and visibility of the art form.

In 2021, Drag Syndrome was featured in Dom&Ink's Queer Power: Icons, Activists & Game Changers from Across the Rainbow, published by HarperCollins. [ref: Queer Power: Icons, Activists & Game Changers from Across the Rainbow, HarperCollins]

The collective is also discussed in Mark Edward and Stephen Farrier's edited academic volume Contemporary Drag Practices and Performers: Drag in a Changing Scene, Volume 1. The book examines Drag Syndrome and Horrora Shebang within a wider discussion of contemporary drag practice and the expansion of drag beyond conventional assumptions about who participates in the form. [ref: Contemporary Drag Practices and Performers: Drag in a Changing Scene, Volume 1, Methuen Drama]

The volume discusses Drag Syndrome's participation in Andrew Logan's 2018 Alternative Miss World at Shakespeare's Globe and considers the collective in relation to disability, queer visibility and contemporary performance practice.

==Reception and cultural impact==

Coverage of Drag Syndrome has frequently focused on the relationship between assumptions about intellectual disability and the performers' artistic and personal autonomy.

Early reporting by Vice documented the performers' involvement in researching and constructing their own drag personas.

Dazed described Drag Syndrome in 2019 as a professional drag collective of drag kings and queens with Down syndrome and examined how the performers developed distinct artistic identities.

In British Vogue, filmmaker Jess Kohl argued against reducing the performers to sentimental or patronising representations of disability. Her film instead focused on their personalities, sexuality, gender expression and professional practice.

The 2019 Michigan controversy brought particular attention to questions of consent and autonomy. The ACLU of Michigan challenged the decision to prevent the performers from appearing on the basis of assumptions about their intellectual disabilities.

In the 2024 Guardian feature, members of the group discussed performing as a form of self-expression, professional ambition and cultural participation.

The collective has also been discussed within broader debates about employment and professional opportunities for disabled artists. In 2026, The Guardian reported on Drag Syndrome's involvement with the UnMute roster and barriers the collective had encountered in securing sustainable UK bookings and support.

data.title: Amorji Nike
data.text:
Amorji Nike (also spelled Amoji Nike) is a town in Enugu East Local Government Area of Enugu State, Nigeria. It is one of the communities that make up the Nike region in Enugu East. [ref: Construction the 13km Nike Lake junction – Amorji Nike – Adoration Pilgrimage Centre Road, Enugu State Government] [ref: Enugu East LGA, Enugu State Government] It constitutes a political ward known as Amorji Ward within Enugu East LGA. [ref: ENUGU EAST LOCAL GOVERNMENT Human Resources Data Form - Wards, Enugu East Local Government]

== History and Administration ==
Amorji Nike is part of the Nike clan, which comprises several towns and villages in Enugu East and Enugu North LGAs. The town is recognized as an autonomous community in Enugu East.

== Villages ==
Amorji Nike is made up of several villages, including:
* Amube
* Umunwoka
* Isienu
* Akama
* Ngonogo
* Umuifi

== Infrastructure ==
The Enugu State Government constructed the 13km Nike Lake Junction – Harmony Estate – Amorji Nike – Adoration Pilgrimage Centre – Orie Emene Road to link Amorji Nike with Enugu metropolis and ease traffic in Abakpa Nike. [ref: Ugwuanyi maintains high throttle on infrastructure devt in Enugu amid COVID-19, Business Day]

== Traditional leadership ==
The community is headed by a traditional ruler. The current traditional ruler is HRH Igwe Titus Okolo, Eze Oha 1 of Amorji Nike. [ref: Whoever steals yam in my domain will be isolated forever – Enugu monarch, Punch Newspapers]

== Religion ==
The area hosts several churches including Assumption Parish, Nkwor Nike under the Catholic Diocese of Enugu. [ref: Catholic Diocese of Enugu - Parishes, Catholic Diocese of Enugu]

data.title: Arunachal church burnings, 1968–1978
data.text:
Between 1968 and 1978, Christian communities in the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), renamed Arunachal Pradesh in January 1972, faced a period of persecution [ref: Christianity and social change in northeast India: a study of the role of Christianity in social change among the Khasi-Jaintia Hill tribes of Meghalaya, Vendrame Institute; Firma KLM Private Ltd.] [ref: The Illustrated Weekly Of India(january-july)1988] that included church burnings, [ref: Togo Basar's Articles from Arunachal Pradesh, India: The History of Untold Misery and Persecutions to Christians in Arunachal Pradesh India, Togo Basar's Articles from Arunachal Pradesh, India] a crackdown on missionaries, and arrests of pastors and converts, alongside standing Inner Line restrictions on missionary entry. [ref: Indian Christians Stopped an Anticonversion Law. Until Now., Christianity Today] [ref: Identity Crisis: A Law Banning Conversion Sparks Fears of Religious Divide, Global Press Journal] Journalistic accounts associate the crackdown with the tenure of K. A. A. Raja, the territory's first chief commissioner and later first lieutenant governor. [ref: Preach, Fifty Two] It has also been documented by the Government of Arunachal Pradesh including Bundle-Con-1970-73, titled as Confidential Files, which contains 16 files. Among them is a 1970 confidential file titled "National Integration, Protection of culture and religious faiths of the people of NEFA". [ref: National Integration-Protection of culture and religious faiths of the people of NEFA, Confidentials Files, State Archives of Arunachal]

== Overview ==
According to Christianity Today, police burned churches, looted homes, and attacked Christian families between 1968 and 1974, [ref: North East India: Combating the Converts, Christianity Today] with 47 churches reportedly torched in a single region in 1974. [ref: ] [ref: North East India: Combating the Converts, Christianity Today] A former Adi policeman, Takeng Taggu, later recalled having burned churches and arrested missionaries on government orders during this period before he himself converted. A 1990 dispatch by the Catholic agency UCA News, the main contemporaneous Christianpress account, reported substantially higher decade-long totals. [ref: Despite persecution, Christianity flourishes in Arunachal Pradesh state, UCA News]

The period overlapped with the founding of the Donyi-Polo revival among the Tani communities and the entry of RSS-affiliated organisations, developments later linked by scholars to the administrative climate of the time. [ref: The Institutionalization of Tribal Religion: Recasting the Donyi-Polo Movement in Arunachal Pradesh, Asian Ethnology] [ref: BJP and Donyi-Polo: New Challenges to Christianity in Arunachal Pradesh and Northeast India, International Bulletin of Mission Research] [ref: ]

In 1978, when Arunachal Pradesh was still a union territory administered directly by the central government, accounting for this incident, its legislature passed the Arunachal Pradesh Freedom of Religion Act, which prohibits conversion by force, inducement, or fraud. [ref: Philosophy for NEFA] [ref: A decades-old law and politics of religion in BJP-ruled Arunachal Pradesh, Deccan Herald] The period thus is also regarded as the culmination for the passing of the Arunachal Pradesh Freedom of Religion Act, [ref: BJP and Donyi-Polo: New Challenges to Christianity in Arunachal Pradesh and Northeast India, International Bulletin of Mission Research] which is an attempt to prohibit proselytism. [ref: State Anti-conversion Laws in India, Law Library of Congress, Global Legal Research Directorate] [ref: The Catholic Church in Northeast India: 1890-1990: a Multidimensional Study, Firma KLM]

data.title: Heidrick & Struggles
data.text:
Heidrick & Struggles International Incorporated, commonly called Heidrick & Struggles, is an American executive search and management consulting company headquartered in Chicago, Illinois, United States, with offices in 56 offices across the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia as of 2026. [ref: The Big 5 Executive Search Firms, Hunt Scanlon Media]

==History==

Heidrick & Struggles was founded in 1953 in Chicago by Gardner Heidrick and John E. Struggles, both of whom were former employees of American management consulting firm Booz Allen Hamilton. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles Company Overview & News, Forbes] [ref: Headhunting: A Brief History of a Profession, Eurogalenus]

From the late 1950s through the 1960s, Heidrick & Struggles opened offices in Los Angeles, San Francisco and New York City. In 1968, the firm established its first international office in London.

In 1999, the firm completed an initial public offering (IPO) and began trading on the NASDAQ under the ticker symbol HSII. [ref: Forbes: Headaches and Struggles, Forbes] [ref: Internet Cos., CONSOL Energy, Heidrick & Struggles Plan IPOs, Bloomberg] On April 30, 1999, the IPO closed with 4.2 million shares offered at $14/share. [ref: Internet deals shrug off technology scare, Deseret News] As of 2005, the company had more than 50 offices in six continents. [ref: Headhunters and How to Use Them: A Guide for Organisations and Individuals, John Wiley & Sons]

In January 2013, Heidrick & Struggles purchased Senn Delaney Leadership Consulting Group, a Huntington Beach organizational culture advisory firm, in an all cash deal for $53.5 million. [ref: Senn Delaney bought for $53.5 million, Orange County Register]

In September 2017, Heidrick & Struggles acquired 2GET, an executive search firm in Brazil. [ref: Heidrick acquires one of largest executive search firms in Brazil, Staffing Industry Analysts (SIA)] In December 2021, the company entered into an agreement to acquire two executive search and leadership consulting companies, RosExpert in Russia and WE Partners in Ukraine and Kazakhstan. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles Enters Agreement to Acquire RosExpert in Russia and WE Partners in Ukraine and Kazakhstan, Hunt Scanlon Media]

In March 2022, the company posted global revenues of $1 billion. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles Reports 61 Percent Revenue Rise; Names Diversity Leader, Hunt Scanlon Media]

In April 2021, the company acquired Business Talent Group, an online marketplace for on-demand independent consultants. [ref: Heidrick buys Business Talent Group, entering the on-demand talent platform space, Staffing Industry Analysts (SIA)] In January 2023 Heidrick & Struggles acquired Atreus, an executive interim management firm based in Germany. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles Plans to Acquire Atreus, Hunt Scanlon Media]

In 2024, the company appointed Tom Monahan as chief executive officer. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles’ new president shares what he learned about going for a CEO job, Fortune]

In December 2025, the company agreed to be acquired by an investor group led by Advent International and Corvex Private Equity, ending 26 years as a public company. [ref: Heidrick & Struggles soars after $1.3 billion go-private deal]

== Research studies ==
Heidrick & Struggles regularly conducts studies and research focused on industry trends.

In March 2026, Heidrick & Struggles found in their "Closing the CEO capability gap" study that, in 2025, one in five Fortune 500 companies appointed CEOs that had international work experience. [ref: Global experience enhanced CEO Ariane Gorin’s leadership skills, Fast Company]

In April 2026, Heidrick & Struggles released the findings of their 2025 "Private Equity–Backed Chief Financial Officer Compensation Survey". The survey found that, on average, CFOs working in PE-backed firms in the United States took home cash pay of $604,000 in 2025, an increase of 5% year over year. [ref: ] That same month, the company released a report on "High-End Independent Talent." It found a 151% increase in demand for interim leaders since 2021, with human resources being the top business function seeking interim leadership support. [ref: ]

In May 2026, the company’s "CEO & Board Confidence Monitor" found that of the approximately 2,000 CEOs and directors surveyed, only four out ten expressed confidence that CEO succession planning had positioned organizations properly for the future. [ref: The leadership pipeline is under pressure, Fast Company]

data.title: Terrence Portelli
data.text:
Terrence Portelli is a Maltese politician and asset recovery manager [ref: Maltese voters have 39 candidates for Europe, 13 of which are independents, Malta Today] who served as leader of Imperium Europa, a far-right political party in Malta, from February 2025 to March 2026. He previously contested the 2024 European Parliament election as a candidate for the party.

== Political career ==
In September 2023, Portelli, alongside Normal Lowell (as planned candidates for the 2024 elections), spoke at an Imperium Europa press conference in front of the Great Siege Monument in Valletta. He presented the party as the only solution for Malta, highlighting the need to address forces dividing identity and to “rekindle the fire of masculinity and femininity in society”. [ref: Imperium Europa claims it is the only solution for Malta, [[TVM (Malta)]

=== European Parliament candidacy ===
Portelli contested the 2024 June European Parliament election in Malta as a candidate for Imperium Europa. [ref: 2024 elections: Malta heads to the polls for MEP and Local Council elections, BusinessNow.mt] [ref: CANDIDATES FOR MEP ELECTION 2024 - NATIONAL (MEP), Electrical Commission of Malta] [ref: Scandal-hit Malta struggles with next EU commissioner candidate, Euractiv] Malta elects six Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) using the single transferable vote system. [ref: 39 candidates, including 9 from PL, 8 from PN, to contest EP election, The Malta Independent]

Portelli’s campaign included opposition to further European Union integration. He advocated for Malta's withdrawal from the eurozone and the reintroduction of the Maltese lira, which he proposed should be backed by gold. He also supported changes to Malta's political system based on the model of Athenian democracy. [ref: Election Playbook: In the land of the F-Living, Malta Today]

In a May 2024 interview with the Times of Malta, Portelli criticized established political figures, referring to them as "puppet politicians" and "leeches". He spoke of rounding them up and handing them over to their “enemy,” and framed it in historical terms (comparing it to Arminius). He also opposed foreign military involvement and financial support in international conflicts and criticized European security policies. [ref: 'We will round you up': far-right MEP candidate's threat to political 'leeches', Times of Malta]

During debates organized by the National Youth Council in late May, Portelli raised issues concerning Malta’s current media transparency and allotted freedom of expression. [ref: ‘If someone says ABC, media has to report ABC’, says Imperium Europa candidate, Maltadaily.mt] He also argued that continued immigration could result in Malta's native population becoming a minority. [ref: Maltese becoming minority in their own country, says Imperium Europa’s Terrence Portelli, Malta Daily]

==== Results ====
Portelli himself received 147 first-preference votes (0.06%). He was eliminated early in the first-round counting process after receiving a small number of transferred votes, finishing with around 154–158 votes in total. [ref: Official: all the first-count votes in the European Parliament elections, Times of Malta] Nearly all of the party’s support went to Norman Lowell, who obtained 6,669 first-preference votes but was also eliminated later without reaching the quota required for election (37,180 votes). [ref: Norman Lowell Lost 1,569 Votes Since Last European Parliament Election, Lovin Malta]

=== Leadership of Imperium Europa ===
On 9 February 2025, Portelli became leader of Imperium Europa, succeeding the party's founder, Norman Lowell. His tenure followed a period of declining electoral support for the party.

Portelli resigned as party leader in March 2026, citing personal reasons and limited time. [ref: Terrence Portelli Resigns As Imperium Europa Leader, Eman Cross Takes Over, Lovin Malta] He was succeeded by Eman Cross, who was selected by the party's executive council. [ref: Expelled by Imperium Europa in 2021, Cross returns to lead far-right party, Times of Malta]

data.title: Delta Institute
data.text:
----

Delta Institute is a Dutch think tank working on government digitization and innovation policy. The organization began in October 2023 as Recoding Government (), an initiative of Alexander Klöpping and tech entrepreneur Onno Eric Blom. It has operated under its current name since April 2026. [ref: 'Overheid digitaal zeer gebrekkig', Kamer komt met plannen, NOS Nieuwsuur] [ref: Commissie Digitale Zaken wil historische digitale hervorming van de overheid, iBestuur] [ref: Wetgevingsoverleg over de Jaarverslagen en Slotwetten 2025 van de ministeries EZ, BZK en JenV, voor zover het onderwerpen betreft die zien op digitalisering, House of Representatives of the Netherlands] [ref: Omdat de toekomst er niet vanzelf komt: waarom we verdergaan als Delta Instituut, Delta Institute]

== Founding and manifesto ==
On 9 October 2023, Klöpping and Blom published an opinion piece in the newspaper NRC which said that the Dutch government's IT infrastructure was outdated, and argued that information technology is a core government task. [ref: Het kan niet langer zo doorgaan met de ict-incompetentie van de overheid, NRC] [ref: Manifest over ict-onkunde wekt beroering, Binnenlands Bestuur] On the same day they released the manifesto Recoding Government, which called for better pay and more policy influence for programmers inside government. [ref: Manifest over ICT-incompetentie van de overheid wil politiek wakker maken, iBestuur] [ref: Manifest tegen ICT-onkunde overheid aangeboden aan 'volgend kabinet', AG Connect] The article reached the House of Representatives three days later, in a committee debate of the standing committee on Digital Affairs, where the state secretary promised a written response. [ref: Verslag van een commissiedebat, gehouden op 12 oktober 2023, over digitaliserende overheid, House of Representatives of the Netherlands] [ref: Reactie Manifest 'Herprogrammeer de Overheid', House of Representatives of the Netherlands]

The group presented the manifesto to members of that committee on 13 February 2024. [ref: Aanbieding manifest m.b.t. ICT-problematiek bij de overheid door de groep 'Herprogrammeer de Overheid', House of Representatives of the Netherlands] On 16 December 2024, committee members released the document Ons Digitaal Fundament (), which proposed a central Digital Service. NOS and iBestuur both reported that the document came out of cooperation with the foundation. MP Barbara Kathmann called the manifesto "the stone in the pond" and credited it with pushing the House to press the cabinet for major IT reform. Klöpping currently sits on the organization's advisory board, whilst Blom runs the organisation. [ref: Position paper Herprogrammeer de Overheid t.b.v. rondetafelgesprek Nederlandse Digitaliseringsstrategie, House of Representatives of the Netherlands] The coalition agreement of January 2026 announced a Dutch Digital Service, a competitive pay scale for IT specialists, mandatory review of IT projects above five million euros, and centralized digital procurement. [ref: Coalitieakkoord: Nieuwe Digitale Dienst moet regie pakken over IT Rijk, iBestuur] [ref: Coalitieakkoord: CIO krijgt meer sturing én verantwoordelijkheid, AG Connect] The Dutch Digital Service launched in the summer of 2026. [ref: Digitale Dienst gaat toch zelf aan de slag met eigen iters, Binnenlands Bestuur]

== National AI Delta Plan ==
The idea for a National AI Delta Plan came up over dinner with minister of infrastructure and water management Vincent Karremans at the Ministry of Economic Affairs, in Summer 2025. Six tech entrepreneurs and researchers, Blom among them, wrote the plan; the foundation covered part of the cost. Karremans received it in November 2025. [ref: Tijdens een etentje bij minister Karremans bedachten zes techbro's een AI-plan. Dat is nu regeringsbeleid, Trouw] [ref: Nationale AI Deltaplan: soepel ontslagrecht moet Nederland aantrekkelijk maken voor ai-hoofdkantoren, Computable] It runs to 52 recommendations, built with input from more than sixty experts. [ref: Beleidsmonitor: Het Nationaal AI Deltaplan van Nederland, Kenniscentrum Data & Maatschappij] [ref: Nationaal AI Deltaplan moet Nederland aan top van Europa brengen, BNR Nieuwsradio] The newspaper Trouw reported that the Jetten cabinet folded the plan into the coalition agreement "almost word for word."

== National Agency for Disruptive Innovation ==
The foundation was one of the outside partners in a Ministry of Economic Affairs study of a National Agency for Disruptive Innovation (NADI), envisioned as a Dutch counterpart to DARPA. Minister Karremans sent the findings to the House of Representatives in February 2026 and left the decision on whether to actually establish it to the next cabinet. NADI was subsequently mentioned in the coalition agreement. [ref: Beslisnota bij Bevindingen verkenning naar een Nationaal Agentschap voor Disruptieve Innovatie (NADI), Ministry of Economic Affairs / House of Representatives of the Netherlands] [ref: Bevindingen verkenning naar een Nationaal Agentschap voor Disruptieve Innovatie (NADI), House of Representatives of the Netherlands]

== Name change ==
In April 2026 the organization announced it would carry on as Delta Institute, with a broader thematic scope. Government documents have used that name since. [ref: Antwoorden op vragen commissie van de V-100 over AI en de impact op toekomstige generaties (Kamerstuk 26643, nr. 1522), House of Representatives of the Netherlands] The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate said the institute spent 2026 carrying out several actions from the AI Delta Plan, including work on an ELLIS Institute as a European AI research center. [ref: Verslag van een commissiedebat, gehouden op 25 juni 2026, over Innovatie, House of Representatives of the Netherlands] The foundation is based at the Marineterrein in Amsterdam.

data.title: Medy Renaldy
data.text:
----

Medy Renaldy (born 31 december 1996) is an Indonesian content creator, illustrator, and entrepreneur. He is widely known for his review content on toys, particularly action figures and rare collectible items on the YouTube and TikTok platforms. In addition to his digital career, Medy is also known as the 2nd Runner-up for Abang Jakarta Timur (East Jakarta Young Ambassador) in the 2018 Abang None Jakarta competition. [ref: Profil Medy Renaldy, Kreator Konten Indonesia beserta Fakta Menariknya, kumparan] [ref: Medy Renaldy: Viral Toy Content Creator & Collector on YouTube and TikTok, duniagames.co.id]Medy is also on the 2026 Forbes 30 under 30 Asia list for social media. [ref: Forbes 30 Under 30 2026: Social Media, Marketing & Advertising, Forbes]
== Early life and education ==
Medy Renaldy was born in Jakarta on December 31, 1996. He is an alumnus of Trisakti University, Faculty of Industrial Technology, majoring in Industrial Engineering at the class of 2014. [ref: Profil Medy Renaldy: Biodata, Kekayaan, Fakta Menarik, dan Foto Masa Muda, Inilah.com]

He has been pursuing his hobby of collecting action figures since he was in junior high school. [ref: 10 Potret Medy Renaldy, Kreator Spesialis Review Mainan, IDN Times] His first collection was an action figure of Sheriff Woody from the Toy Story film, which was a gift from his parents. His current collection includes various characters, ranging from Iron Man, Captain America, to the Annabelle Doll. [ref: Medy Renaldy: Bukan Sekadar Konten Kreator, Tapi Pengusaha Kreatif Inspiratif, kabarbaik.co]

During college, Medy did not only focus on academics but was also active outside of campus. In 2018, he represented East Jakarta in the Abang None Jakarta competition and successfully achieved the 3rd Place position as well as earning the Favorite Winner title. [ref: Penghargaan Abang None DKI Jakarta Favorit, FTI Trisakti]

== Career and business ==

=== Illustrator and Entrepreneur ===
Before becoming a full-time content creator, Medy worked as an illustrator. He has enjoyed drawing since 2014 and often painted portraits of important figures and celebrities, such as Jokowi, Will Smith, Najwa Shihab, and Benyamin.

In 2017, he founded MR Creative Lab, a service for creating realistic face illustrations and for a gallery of his artworks. [ref: Instagram, www.instagram.com] Due to his talent in drawing, he was invited to appear on the talk show Hitam Putih on Trans7 hosted by Deddy Corbuzier in 2018.

In addition to digital content, Medy also founded a business into the culinary field by founding Soto Susu Bu Tin restaurant in January 2020, which serves Soto Betawi with a special recipe from his mother.

=== Content Creator ===
Medy has had a YouTube channel since October 2, 2011, but he became consistent in uploading content since 2020. He focuses his content on reviews, unboxing, and stories about expensive, rare, and high-quality toy collections from various franchises such as Marvel, Harry Potter, and Toy Story. [ref: Kronologi Medy Renaldy Dihujat karena Bulu Babi, IDN Times]

In September 2024, Medy had the opportunity to meet American YouTuber, IShowSpeed, during his visit to Jakarta, and Medy gave him a Cristiano Ronaldo action figure as a gift. [ref: 3 Fakta Menarik Action Figure Ronaldo yang Dihadiahkan Medy Renaldy ke IShowspeed, medcom.id]

As of 2 October 2026, Medy Renaldy's YouTube channel has over 5 million subscribers and 774 of videos that have reached a billion views total. [ref: Medy Renaldy, YouTube] His TikTok account also has over 11 million followers. [ref: Medy's tiktok, TikTok]

== Public attention and controversy ==

=== Customs Incident ===
Medy once became the focus of media and collector communities after he expressed his disappointment with the Customs and Excise authorities. [ref: Kemenkeu beri bukti kasus paket mainan Megatron bukan ulah Bea Cukai, Antara News] The incident occurred in April 2024 when a Megatron toy package, which was a gift shipment from the producer, was detained by the authorities and the toy box was reportedly damaged. [ref: Paket Mainan Megatron Milik Youtuber Rusak, Bea Cukai Beri Klarifikasi, Bisnis.com] Medy claimed he was asked to send an invoice for an item that was actually a gift. [ref: Influencer Medy Renaldy Respons Video Pembongkaran Mainan Megatron, ekonomi]

=== Appeal to Stop Playing Roblox ===
In October 2025, Medy once again sparked public debate after uploading a video on TikTok containing a serious appeal to the public, especially adults, to stop playing the online game Roblox. Medy expressed concerns about the psychological and social impact of the game. He presented three main reasons: [ref: Medy Renaldy Mode Serius, Ingatkan Bahaya Main Roblox: Stop Sekarang Kalau Mau Selamat, Wartakotalive.com]

* Potential indicator of a lack of social interaction, referring to study results linking internet gaming disorder to loneliness.
* The trend of mountain climbing simulations in Roblox was considered insulting to the nature-loving community.
* Potential for gaming disorder characterized by a chaotic lifestyle.

Medy's statement sparked pros and cons, and it emerged around the same time as a ban from the minister of primary and secondary education (Mendikdasmen) regarding the game Roblox for children, which also became a concern for the Deputy Minister of Communication and Digital Affairs. [ref: Indonesian government warns children, parents against ‘violent’ Roblox]

== Personal life ==
Medy Renaldy officially married Charera Prilly, a TikToker and influencer, on Tuesday, February 25, 2025. Their marriage ceremony (akad nikah) was held intimately in Bali, with the backdrop of Uluwatu Beach. [ref: 5 Fakta Pernikahan Medy Renaldy dan Charera Prilly, Popbela.com]

The wedding attracted attention because Medy incorporated elements of his hobby. Their wedding rings were delivered by his favorite Transformer toy. In the reception held that evening, Medy also used Marvel characters (Thor, Deadpool, Doctor Strange, and Iron Man) as an analogy to express his feelings to Charera, further reinforcing his personal branding as a toy collector. [ref: Medy Renaldy dan Charera Resmi Menikah, Popmama.com]

data.title: Niklas Elmehed
data.text:
Niklas Elmehed is a Swedish painter. He is known for his paintings of vinyl and gold leafed Nobel Prize illustrations and portraits which become feature of Nobel Prize ceremonies held every year in the month of October. [ref: Meet Niklas, the artist behind the Nobel Prize portraits, The Business Standard] [ref: Nobel Prize: Meet the artist behind laureates’ illustrations, Yahoo News Singapore]
== Career ==
Elmehed pursued fine arts in Sweden. [ref: Who is Niklas Elmehed: The man behind the iconic illustrations of the 2025 Nobel laureates, The Times of India] He also developed an interest in science, history and journalism. He developed sketch drawings using black and white charcoal, while pursuing his higher studies at the KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. [ref: Behind Niklas Elmehed’s gold portraits of Nobel Prize winners, The Hindu] It was through mastering the craft of sketch drawings using black and white charcoal, he was inspired to paint drawings with the element of gold foil. He obtained his master's degree at both KTH Royal Institute of Technology and Royal Institute of Art.

He began painting the official portraits of Nobel Prize laureates in 2012. It was revealed that the Nobel Committee had come up with the solution of using paintings instead of relying on photographs in order to publish the images of Nobel Prize laureates officially and in 2012, Niklas was hired as an art director by the Nobel Media as one of the fewest steps taken by the Nobel Committee to address the longstanding issues related to poor quality photographs, photographs with copyright issues and low resolution images of the award winners that usually circulate online. Niklas had been tasked with the visual content during the Nobel Prize ceremonies ever since he took charge as art director in 2012. In 2017, Niklas came up with the idea of using gold foil in his portraits, when the Nobel Committee had decided that the main color to be incorporated during the prize announcements would be gold in a landmark move, following the transition of Nobel Prize which went through a graphical rebranding procedure. [ref: Meet The Artist Behind Those Gold-Leafed Nobel Prize Illustrations, NDTV] His paintings on Noble Prize laureates are frequently displayed and featured in news media outlets after the announcement of Noble Prize winners. His job role is monitored under close supervision and the job role also inculcates on the concept of strict confidentiality as he is one of the fewest individuals to learn about the official Nobel Prize winners well in advance before the official public announcements.

In 2025, Elmehed unveiled “The Golden Wall”, where he displayed and exhibited the portraits of Nobel Prize winners at the Nobel headquarters located in Stockholm, Sweden. He conducted a live painting performance at the Nordic Pavilion of World Expo 2025 in Osaka, Japan. He also displayed his work at the TEDxPatras 2025, where he delivered glimpses of visual storytelling to a large target audience. [ref: ] He also serves as a freelance artist for the Sweden men's national football team.

data.title: Brookie (food)
data.text:
----

A brookie is type of bar cookie and hybrid dessert that combines aspects and ingredients from cookies and brownies. The batter of a brownie and the dough of a cookie are usually made separately and then combined before baking. This can either be done by layering the batter and dough or by scooping one after the other into the pan. [ref: The Vanderbilt Hustler, Reaching Out] [ref: brookie, dictionary.cambridge.org]

Brookies are usually baked in square or rectangular baking pans, like brownies. This causes brookies to be similar in size and shape to brownies. Brookies often have a fudgy or cakey texture, like brownies, while also keeping the chewy texture from cookies.

The brownie batter is often made with cocoa powder, sugar, eggs, flour and other ingredients. The cookie dough may include flour, eggs, brown sugar, and other ingredients. [ref: Turn leftover Creme Eggs into a gooey ‘brookie’ traybake, The Independent] [ref: The Vanderbilt Hustler, The New Gold Standard] In addition, they may also be made with chocolate chips, rolled oats, nuts, or dried fruits. Brookies are often baked and served like brownies, and they may be served with a variety of accompaniments such as milk, ice cream, fruit, coffee or whipped cream. [ref: ]

== Variations ==
Multiple variations of the brookie have been created. Many recipes substitute or add ingredients to have different flavors, textures or variations that meet dietary needs.

Vegan brookies are brookies made without any animal products. They are made to replace the butter, eggs, and milk chocolate chips using substitutes like apple sauce, vegetable oil, vegan butter and vegan chocolate chips.

Pumpkin swirl brookies are pumpkin or pumpkin spice flavored brookies. They are made with canned pumpkin puree and can additionally have cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice, pumpkin pie spice, ginger, cottage cheese, butterscotch chips and other spices. Pumpkin swirl brookies and typically more orange than regular brookies.

Peanut butter brookies are made by adding peanut butter to the brownie batter. Peanut butter brookies can also be made with various other nut butters like almond butter, walnut butter, cookie butter, and others nut butters. [ref: Pic's Really Good Recipe Book, Random House New Zealand]

Brookies themselves can also be made into ice cream by blending or cutting brookies and adding it to the ice cream as it is being churned. [ref: Carvel Drops New Brookie Ice Cream Flavor That´s a Mashup of Two Favorite Desserts] This ice cream can then be made into milkshakes by blending the brookie ice cream with milk. [ref: Milkshake Recipes: 100 Creamy and Irresistible Milkshake Recipes for Every Craving and Occasion, Brad Hoskinson]

== History & Popularization ==
The brookie was invented in the late 20th century, in the United States, the exact origins are unknown. Many restaurants and bakeries claim to have invented the brookie. The earliest known mention of a brookie was in 1988, where The Vanderbilt Hustler shows a menu from Rafferty's Bar & Restaurant with the brookie listed as a dessert. [ref: The Vanderbilt Hustler, Celebrating a Century of Service to the Vanderbilt Community.]

In 2006, Joanna Crumley's Praline Brookies, a brookie variant combining pecan pralines and brookies, placed as a top 100 finalist competing for the $1,000,000 grand prize in the 42nd Pillsbury Bake-Off. [ref: Hubbard resident wins 2019 Pillsbury Bake-Off dessert category, becomes finalist, Statesman Journal] [ref: Praline Brookies Recipe, Pillsbury]

In 2014, Milk and Brookies was founded by Jovon English, Marques Brooks, Naimah Harris and Tisa Smart-Washington. [ref: milk + brookies, Milk + Brookies] In 2015, Milk and Brookies went on season 7 of Shark Tank seeking $100,000 for 20% equity. This offer was turned down. [ref: Week 4: Table 87, EZ-Pee-Z, Milk + Brookies, Dude Products] Later, in 2016 Milk and Brookies participated in the 2nd annual CookieCon in Los Angeles, California. [ref: Visit milk + brookies at LA Cookie Con 2016, milk + brookies]

In 2016, Harry Foster baked brookies for MasterChef Australia Series 8. [ref: Team Challenge: Royal Children's Hospital Fête]

data.title: Natalya Kusch
data.text:
Natalya Kusch (also known as Natalya Fichtenbaum-Kusch, Natalie Kusch and Natasha Kush) is a Ukrainian ballet dancer and ballet teacher. [ref: Audition Artistic Directors March 2024, BalletStage Listed as Natalya Fichtenbaum-Kusch.] [ref: Vorstellungen mit Natalie Kusch, Vienna State Opera performance archive] [ref: Von der Primaballerina in Oberwölbling, ORF Niederösterreich] She has worked as a soloist with the Vienna State Ballet, a principal dancer with Queensland Ballet, and a senior artist with the Australian Ballet. [ref: Der Körper ist mein Instrument!, Die Niederösterreicherin] [ref: Annual Report 2014, Queensland Ballet "The Company" section, PDF page 14.] [ref: Annual Report 2015, The Australian Ballet "Directors, Artists and Employment Statistics" section.]

== Biography ==

=== Training and Vienna State Ballet ===
Kusch was born in Nikopol, Ukraine. She trained in Dnipro and continued her studies at the ballet conservatory in St. Pölten under Shida Mubaryakova. Before her engagement in Vienna, she worked at the opera and ballet theatre in Dnipropetrovsk and at theatres in Magdeburg and Cairo. [ref: Natalia Kush, Odesa National Academic Opera and Ballet Theater]

From 2005 to 2013, she danced with the ballet company of the Vienna State Opera and the Vienna State Ballet. She was promoted to soloist under Manuel Legris. On 26 June 2011, she performed the title role in Giselle at the Vienna State Opera. [ref: Gisela / Giselle oder Die Wilis / Willis am 26.06.2011, Vienna State Opera performance archive] The opera's performance archive lists 131 performances under the name Natalie Kusch between 2006 and 2013. [ref: Personenverzeichnis: Kusch, Natalie, Vienna State Opera performance archive Entry lists 131 performances from 25 December 2006 to 3 March 2013.] She also appeared in the filmed ballet sequences for the Vienna Philharmonic's 2011 New Year's Concert. [ref: Neujahrskonzert: Premiere für Schloss Laudon, ORF Wien]

=== Australia and international guest appearances ===
In 2013, Kusch joined Queensland Ballet in Brisbane as a principal dancer at the invitation of Li Cunxin. In 2014, she danced Juliet in Kenneth MacMillan's Romeo and Juliet, opposite Steven McRae. [ref: Queensland Ballet: Romeo and Juliet, Dance Australia] In 2015, she joined the Australian Ballet as a senior artist. [ref: Kusch joins the AB; Cubans come to Brisbane, FollowSpot] In March of that year, she performed the title role in Maina Gielgud's production of Giselle in Melbourne, partnered by Chengwu Guo as Albrecht. [ref: Australian Ballet – Giselle – Melbourne, DanceTabs]

In 2017, she appeared as a guest artist with the Royal New Zealand Ballet in the title role of Roland Petit's Carmen. [ref: Carmen. Royal New Zealand Ballet, Michelle Potter … on dancing] In September of the same year, she performed Carmen at the Teatro dell'Opera di Roma. [ref: Carmen 2016-17 Soirée Roland Petit, Archivio Storico del Teatro dell'Opera di Roma Cast and performances from 8 to 14 September 2017.] In 2018, she performed a duet from the ballet with Michele Satriano at the Benois de la Danse festival on the historic stage of the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow. [ref: Под сенью Петипа, Музыкальная жизнь]

Her other engagements included Universal Ballet in Seoul and, from 2019, the ballet company of the State Theatre in Košice. In 2020, she joined the opera and ballet theatre in Odesa. [ref: Natalya Kusch, Attitude Ballet Studios Vienna] In 2023, she danced Aurora in The Sleeping Beauty on an Australian and New Zealand tour with the Royal Czech Ballet. [ref: Kusch returns with the Royal Czech Ballet, Dance Australia]

=== Teaching ===
Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Kusch left the country in 2022 and moved to Munich, where she taught at the Munich International Ballet School. She returned to Austria in 2023. She works as a coach with Europaballett St. Pölten, where she coached the principal roles in a 2024 production of Swan Lake. [ref: Team, Europaballett St. Pölten "Trainer und Lehrer" section.]

=== Personal life ===
On 27 June 2023, Kusch married Thomas Fichtenbaum.

data.title: Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience & Institution
data.text:
Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience and Institution is a 1976 book by American poet, scholar, and essayist Adrienne Rich that examines motherhood from the lens of personal experience, anthropology, and feminist theory. Rich researched and wrote the book over a 4 year period because she felt that motherhood “was a crucial, still relatively unexplored, area for feminist theory.” [ref: Of woman born: motherhood as experience and institution, W. W. Norton & Company] It has been described by the Los Angeles Times as a landmark work in the literature of motherhood. [ref: Adrienne Rich dies at 82; feminist poet and essayist, Los Angeles Times]

== Summary ==

Of Woman Born begins with a foreword describing one of the book’s central aims: to begin to fill in the gap between the universal experience of motherhood and what is known about it: “We know more about the air we breathe, the seas we travel, than about the nature and meaning of motherhood.” The foreword also describes the book’s aim to create a distinction between motherhood as an experience, which Rich defines as “the potential relationship of any woman to her powers of reproduction and to children” and motherhood as an institution—the social and political systems that define, limit, and control the experience of motherhood.

=== Anger and Tenderness ===
Using entries from her journal, Rich illustrates the conflicting feelings she experienced as a young mother of three in the 1950’s: tenderness and anger, ambition and weariness, power and powerlessness. She describes how, from an early age,  she struggled to bridge the gap between the feminine ideals of the 1950’s, and her own vision of herself as a serious, independent poet. She describes the outline of her young adult life: married to a Cambridge academic at the age of 22, three children by the age of 29, her decision to be sterilized after her third child, her struggle to write while raising young children. Rich then examines the many assumptions her younger self had accepted as inevitable: that her experience as a mother was simply “the human condition;” that motherhood and child care had always looked this way; that mothers acted on instinct alone; that the only person developing in the mother-child relationship was the child. Rich ends the chapter citing her hope and belief that culture will come to see female biology “as a resource, rather than a destiny.”

=== The Sacred Calling ===
Rich traces the shifting roles of women in the United States and England over the 19th century, and illustrates how women went from essential, widely-skilled, productive members of their homesteads in pre-industrial eras to isolated individuals whose role was limited to “the specialization of motherhood.” She describes how the growth of factories in the Industrial Revolution separated the home from the “man’s world” of wage-earning, ambition, and power, and created the ideal of the home as the “woman’s sphere” of refuge and retreat, a relatively recent concept in human history. “The home thus defined had never before existed. It was a creation of the Industrial Revolution, an ideal invested with the power of something God-given, and its power as an idea remains unexpunged today.” She identifies the repercussions of this shift for women and mothers: isolation, loneliness, powerlessness, and a narrow definition of a woman’s capacities.

===The Kingdom of the Fathers ===
In this chapter, Rich explores the roots, characteristics, and consequences of patriarchy, which she defines as “the power of the fathers.” She identifies the advent of private property and inherited wealth as key foundations of patriarchal order, and a tendency to think in “positive-negative polarities”—rational/irrational, powerful/powerless—as key characteristics. Power itself, Rich states, and power over others, “is a primal relationship under patriarchy,” most often exemplified through a man’s control over his wife and children. Monotheism, in which an all-powerful, usually male god, causes this patriarchal power structure to become “internalized as ‘conscience,’ ‘tradition,’ ‘the moral law within.” Rich discusses how women have mostly experienced power as a negative force. She identifies the renewed interest in matriarchal and pre-patriarchal cultures that characterized feminist and counter-culture movements of the 1960’s and 1970’s as efforts “to reintegrate what has been named the unconscious, the subjective, the emotional with the structural, the rational, the intellectual.”

=== The Primacy of the Mother ===
Rich examines how the field of anthropology has opened an awareness of other societies not based on patriarchal order or lineage, either in the form of pre-patriarchal or matriarchal societies. She cites the importance of this work to women and to feminist studies: “If women were powerful once, a precedent exists; if female biology was ever once a source of power, it need not remain what it has since become: a root of powerlessness.” She cites the work of JJ Bachofen and Robert Briffault as foundations for early feminist anthropological works like Helen Diner’s Mothers and Amazons and Elizabeth Gould Davis’ The First Sex. Noting that the existence of a “true universal matriarchy” is impossible to prove, Rich reflects instead on woman-centered or “gynocentric” periods of human culture “when Woman was venerated in several aspects, the primal one being maternal.” Rich argues that in these periods, women’s essential roles in the survival and thriving of human communities—through fertility, child nurturance, food production and preservation—were highly valued as “the transformations necessary for the continuation of life.” Rich identifies this “transforming power,” versus “power over others” as hallmarks of women-centered versus male-centered societies.

=== The Domestication of Motherhood ===
Expanding on the previous chapter, Rich lays out several theories that attempt to explain how human societies shifted from female-centered to male-centered over time. She examines Friedrich Engels’ theory of private ownership and patrilineal inheritance, theories that posit the early protective role of human males as an origin of male dominance, and the work of psychologists Erich Neumann and Karen Horney, that cite the life-giving powers of females as a source of both reverence and fear. Taking up early religion and mythology, Rich traces the shift from mother-goddess to male-centered monotheism in Egypt and Greece, the disappearance of female figurines as objects of worship, and a shift in the image of the divine family—the mother figure changing from the all-giving, self-sustaining “Great Mother” to an unequal, subordinate role increasingly limited to the domestic and maternal.

=== Hands of Flesh, Hands of Iron ===
Turning to the history of childbirth, Rich points out that, until the 18th century, “childbirth was overwhelmingly the province of women.” She identifies several reasons for this: women’s extensive first-hand experience with childbirth and female anatomy; cultural taboos against men’s involvement in the labor process; the perception of midwifery as beneath the dignity of male physicians, who were brought into childbirth cases only in emergencies. She examines how the establishment of Christianity in the Middle Ages created impediments to safe childbirth practices on several fronts: by viewing midwifery, attached to the female body and its reproductive organs, as an unclean profession; by prioritizing the baptism of the infant, even in utero, over the life and health of the mother; and by a limited understanding of female anatomy due to the Church’s prohibition of cadaver dissection. Rich traces the beginning of obstetrics as a male profession to 1663, when a court physician attended to the birth of a favorite mistress of Louis XIV, creating demand in the upper classes for the man-midwife, a lucrative profession that relied on the knowledge and practices of female midwives. Rich relates the controversial history of the forceps, invented in England in the 1600’s by man-midwife Peter Chamberlen, whose family kept the device a closely-guarded secret until 1721. The growing use of forceps in the late 1700’s set off a debate in the midwife community, who claimed the tool was overused, misused, and often harmful to the mother of the infant, as argued by Elizabeth Nihell in her 1760 Treatise on the Art of Midwifery. >Rich closes the chapter with a history of puerperal fever, often called “childbirth fever,” which reached epidemic proportions over the 18th and 19th centuries, as childbirth moved from home births guided by midwives to hospital births attended by physicians who did not yet understand the link between bacteria and infection. Rich notes that even the male physicians who investigated the deadly impact of contagion on mothers giving birth—Alexander Gordon, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Ignaz Philipp Semmelweis—were ignored or attacked by the male obstetric community until the end of the 19th century, when bacterial infection became widely understood.

=== Alienated Labor ===
In this chapter, Rich examines the ways women have been alienated from the process of childbirth over the course of history. She notes that most male-dominated societies have framed childbirth as a woman’s most important contribution to the family, lineage, or society, and how this emphasis has led many modern women to view the choice as “an inescapable either/or: motherhood or individuation.” Rich discusses how negative cultural attitudes around pregnancy,  childbirth, and pain—as punishment for original sin, as physical defilement, as fear of death—further remove women from a healthy relationship to the process. She examines the physical and psychological repercussions of the introduction of anesthesia in childbirth in the late 19th century, the backlash from the midwife community, and the subsequent evolution of modern natural childbirth practices. Rich describes her personal experience giving birth under general anesthesia for all three of her pregnancies in the 1950’s, lamenting the ways medical technology—from artificial induction to anesthesia—often create a cascading effect of complications that require further intervention. She argues for a perspective that views birth not as “a sudden crisis to be handled by others,” or the central event of a woman’s life, but “as a continuum, interwoven inextricably with the entire spectrum of a woman’s life”, and one event in the unfolding of a woman’s evolving relationship to her body, sexuality, and strength.

=== Mother and Son, Woman and Man ===
Through examples from literature, psychology, religion, and popular culture, Rich argues that the mother-son relationship has often been regarded as either overly sentimental or toxic, characterized by control, suffering, and guilt. She explores the long shadow cast by Freud over the psychology of the mother-son relationship, a framework she argues is reductive, narrowly biological, and regressive. She looks at changes in perspective on mother-son relations led by developments in psychology and the women’s movement of the 1970’s, and the difficult questions faced by feminist mothers raising boys in a male-dominated culture. She argues against the assumption that feminists hate men, stating “it is absurd to think that women on the path of feminism wish to abandon their sons, emotionally or otherwise.” On the path of individuation from child to man, Rich imagines a choice for sons that is broader than aggression and defense over fear and feeling, instead offering the chance to realize “that strength and vulnerability, toughness and expressiveness, nurturance and authority, are not opposites, not the sole inheritance of one sex or another.” Taking up the question of what women who are beginning to challenge the values of patriarchy truly want for their sons, she concludes that the answer is “to discover new ways of being men even as we are discovering new ways of being women.” To that end, she urges an end to the separation of a public “male” world and a private “female” one, and a refusal of “the traditional separation between ‘love’ and ‘work.”

=== Motherhood and Daughterhood ===
Rich begins the chapter with a description of her relationship with her own mother, a talented concert pianist and composer who sacrificed her career to marry and raise children according to her husband’s strict rules, and the anger she felt towards her mother for not protecting her from her father’s overbearing demands. She then explores the physical and psychological bonds that can lead to “the deepest mutuality and the most painful estrangement”< between mothers and daughters, citing Virginia Woolf, Emily Dickinson, and Sylvia Plath as examples. She defines matrophobia as the fear of becoming one’s mother, and explains the cultural and economic issues that make this fear prevalent. She describes the loss of the mother-daughter bond as “the essential female tragedy,” as illustrated by the Greek myth of Demeter and Kore and the subsequent importance of the Eleusinian mysteries of ancient Greece. She discusses how women who have felt “unmothered” may look for mother-figures in their own lives, or by mothering others in various helping professions. She maintains that although the intense bond between mothers and daughters can be destructive, “there is no reason why it is doomed to be.” She argues that the nurture of daughters requires “trust and tenderness” and “courageous mothering”, and that a mother’s “primary bequest to her daughter” is the quality of her own life, “because a woman who can believe in herself, who is a fighter, and who continues to struggle to create livable space around her, is demonstrating to her daughter that these possibilities exist.” She closes the chapter with a discussion of the reasons women may choose not to have children, their important contributions to the lives of women, and the equal importance of non-biological mother figures in a woman’s life.

=== Violence: The Heart of Maternal Darkness ===
Using a 1974 case of infanticide as an example, Rich explores the history of infanticide, from legal infanticide practiced as population control in Sparta, Rome, Japan, and China, to infanticide by mothers who faced excommunication or execution due to religious laws against unwed mothers, and infanticide in response to poverty. Rich argues that infanticide, rather than being exclusively an act of psychosis, is often a response to depression, lack of reproductive choice, and desperate economic conditions. On abortion, Rich argues that abortion laws across the globe have fluctuated in keeping with a country’s economic and military needs, citing the Soviet Union, Japan, and China as 20th century examples, and advocates for safe, widely available, effective birth control. In her closing arguments, Rich urges women to examine the forces that shape the experience of motherhood, and to distinguish between what is natural and what is imposed by society. “The institution of motherhood cannot be touched or seen,” she states, arguing that economic dependence, laws limiting reproductive choice, lack of social benefits for mothers and adequate childcare, unequal pay, and the isolation of full-time motherhood are “connecting fibers of this invisible institution, and they determine our relationship to our children whether we like to think so or not.” Rich sees hope in what women have managed to maintain for themselves and their children—“the tenderness, the passion, the trust in our instincts, the evocation of a courage we did not know we owned, the detailed apprehension of another human existence, the full realization of the cost and precariousness of life.” In closing, she argues that these qualities can and should effect positive change in the world at large: “The mother’s battle for her child—with sickness, with poverty, with war, with all the forces of exploitation and callousness that cheapen human life—needs to become a common human battle, waged in love and in the passion for survival.”

== Legacy ==
Of Woman Born has been described by the Los Angeles Times as a landmark work in the literature of motherhood. Writing in 2018, literary critic Sandra Gilbert stated that Of Woman Born "was, and is, a groundbreaking feminist study that brilliantly exemplifies the innovative scholarship energized by what has come to be called the 'second wave' of the women's movement." [ref: Essential essays: culture, politics, and the art of poetry, W.W. Norton & Company]

In a 2021 essay for Ploughshares, scholar Cynthia R. Wallace noted that, "When Of Woman Born came out, Rich had already been a widely acclaimed poet for a quarter of a century, but this book received more attention than any of her previous publications and polarized reviewers. It's hard to overstate how influential the book was among readers, activists, and later, scholars." [ref: Rereading Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience and Institution, Ploughshares]

== Reception ==

=== Critical response ===
Writing in the New York Review of Books in 1976, the critic Helen Vendler labeled Of Woman Born as "partisan writing" that often lapsed into "a rhetoric of sentimentality," while acknowledging that "the book has a certain cumulative force, not so much on account of its theorizing as because of its undeniable feelings and its inarguable social facts." [ref: Myths for Mothers, The New York Review of Books] In The New York Times Book Review, Francine Du Plessix Gray wrote "Of Woman Born is almost two books, one moving, one maddening," praising the book's autobiographical writing while criticizing its "unoriginal muddled polemics against patriarchy." [ref: Amazonian prescriptions and proscriptions, The New York Times] In The Village Voice, Jane Lazarre called the book "compelling and compassionate," and "the best analysis I have seen of what we mean when we speak of patriarchy." [ref: Reading Adrienne Rich: reviews and re-visions, 1951-81, University of Michigan Press] The 1976 Kirkus review predicted that "Dynamic, woman-centered, frequently persuasive and even disarming, this is certain to spark controversy for its uncompromising stance and its more surprising documented findings." [ref: Book Reviews, Sites, Romance, Fantasy, Fiction, Kirkus Reviews]

=== Public response ===
On its publication in October 1976, Of Woman Born sold well, was translated into numerous foreign languages, and was released as a mass-market paperback in 1977. [ref: The power of Adrienne Rich: a biography, Nan A. Talese/Doubleday] A tenth anniversary edition was released by Norton in 1986 with a new introduction by Rich, and re-issued in 1995. [ref: Of woman born: motherhood as experience and institution, W.W. Norton & Company] A new edition was released by Norton in 2021, with a new foreword by author Eula Biss and an introduction by author Dani McClain.

data.title: Halcyon Veil
data.text:
Halcyon Veil is an American independent record label founded in 2015 by Rabit and Lane Stewart. Originally based between Houston, Texas, and Los Angeles, the label was associated with a hybridized style of club music sometimes described as "post-club," releasing work by artists including IVVVO, MHYSA, Angel-Ho, and 700 Bliss. The label's output has since broadened to include indie rock, hip-hop, and pop, continuing a consistent focus on music resistant to genre classification. Resident Advisor described the label as having grown from an outpost for experimental club music into a freeform, community-oriented network [ref: Label of the month: Halcyon Veil, Resident Advisor], while Bandcamp Daily characterized it as a distributed entity that, while rooted in Houston, has "always looked outward, almost like a pirate radio station. [ref: Halcyon Veil's Decade of Mutant Club Hybrids, Bandcamp Daily]"

== History ==
Halcyon Veil was formed in 2015, after Stewart and Burton met on Twitter, Burton proposing starting a label within minutes of meeting in person. [ref: A Houston Chorus: Mother Rabit Dreams a Garden, Fact (UK magazine)] The label's debut release was Angel-Ho's EP Ascension the same year. [ref: ANGEL-HO's New Track Is About the Lack of Safe Space for Queer People of Color in Cape Town Clubs, Vice] Its early catalog was closely associated with the "deconstructed" or "post-club" scenes of the mid-2010s, situating the label alongside a wider network of artists including Chino Amobi and Elysia Crampton. [ref: The Rise of Conceptronica, Pitchfork] Rabit and Chino Amobi's The Great Game: Freedom from Mental Poisoning, released on the label in 2015, was later cited by critic Matthew Phillips as a defining work of what he termed "neofuturism," an aesthetic he traced through artists including Arca, Lotic, and Holly Herndon. By the end of the decade, the label's roster had expanded to include artists such as IVVVO, whose 2019 single "Forever Your Mouth" was played by Aphex Twin during his Coachella set that year. [ref: Setlist.fm - Aphex Twin Setlist, Setlist.fm]
