data.title: Glenn Cohen (psychologist)
data.text:
Glenn Richard Cohen (born October 26, 1964) is an American-Israeli psychologist and former officer of the Mossad (Israel's national intelligence agency).

Following the Hamas attack on Israel of 7 October 2023, Cohen was designated as the first mental health professional to meet returning hostages upon their release, and subsequently led the team of psychologists that debriefed the hostages released from Gaza captivity between November 2023 and October 2025. [ref: 'Resilience is in the Jewish people's DNA': The man helping Israel's freed hostages heal, The Jewish Chronicle]

==Biography==

Cohen was born and raised in New York City. He studied at Ramaz high school and was an avid basketball player. [ref: How do you debrief a hostage?, The Jewish Standard] In 1982, he made aliya to Israel. After a year studying at Yeshiva, he enlisted to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in 1984. [ref: What we know about captivity in Gaza – with Glenn Cohen, Call Me Back with Dan Senor]

=== Education ===
Cohen earned his undergraduate degree (B.A) in Psychology and Geography from The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and his graduate degree (M.A) in Clinical Psychology from Bar-Ilan University, specializing in combat-related PTSD. [ref: The Blogs: Ex-Mossad Chief Psychologist Delivers Message of Hope and Resilience]

==Military and Intelligence Career==

Cohen graduated from the Israeli Air Force flight academy and served for seven years as a search and rescue helicopter pilot. [ref: Glenn Cohen on Hostages, Trauma, and the Psychology of Survival, The Algemeiner] After his discharge, he was recruited by the Mossad where he served for 30 years, [ref: Glenn Cohen on Hostages, Trauma, and the Psychology of Survival, The Algemeiner] retiring as Chief Operational Psychologist. [ref: ] He retired from the Mossad in 2015.

==October 7 Hostage Crisis==

===Emergency Reserve Duty===

Following the Hamas October 7 attack in 2023, Cohen was called up to serve in IDF emergency reserve duty in the Hostage Negotiation Unit, serving for over five months. He was the first psychologist to meet returning hostages as they crossed back into Israel. [ref: 'Humanitarian intelligence': Debriefing head lays out protocol for questioning freed hostages, The Jerusalem Post] [ref: ]

===Debriefing Protocol: "Humanitarian Intelligence"===

Cohen authored the protocol for the psychological recovery and debriefing of returning hostages, and led the team that debriefed hostages released from Hamas captivity. He coined the term 'humanitarian intelligence' to describe an intelligence-gathering approach that centers on the trauma victim's wellbeing, contrasting it with existing US protocols that prioritize security debriefing immediately upon a hostage's return.

Cohen drew on lessons from the reception of Israeli POWs after the 1973 Yom Kippur War, noting that those POWs had described their treatment upon return as one of the worst aspects of their captivity experience.

Cohen has also written about post-traumatic growth (PTG), arguing that national trauma can serve as a catalyst for societal renewal. [ref: From national PTSD to national post-traumatic growth: Israel must turn pain to power, The Jerusalem Post]

data.title: Josh Pacewicz
data.text:
Josh Pacewicz is an American sociologist, who is an Associate Professor of Sociology and Urban Studies at Brown University and a 2020 Guggenheim Fellow. His research interests are in the areas of political sociology, historical sociology, urban sociology, the sociology of law, and American political development. [ref: ]

== Education and Career ==
Pacewicz holds a bachelor’s degree from The University of Texas-Austin, Plan II Honors program. He graduated from the University of Chicago with a Ph.D in Sociology in 2010. His dissertation was supervised by Andrew Abbott, Elisabeth Clemens, Andreas Glaeser, and Susan Gal. [ref: Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the Post-Keynesian Society, University of Chicago Press]

From 2010 to 2012, Pacewicz was an ASA Postdoctoral Fellow on the Current Economic Crisis at Stanford University, under the supervision of Mark Granovetter. [ref: Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the Post-Keynesian Society, University of Chicago Press] He joined the faculty at Brown University in 2012.

== Research Areas and Books ==
Pacewicz’s research focuses on American statecraft and subnational governance, especially the interplay between federal policy and party politics, municipal finance, political advocacy and expertise, and more generally the democratic process. His research relies primarily on interviews with legislators, state agency employees, municipal officials, and other policy workers. Pacewicz has written about qualitative case selection and comparison [ref: What Can You Do With a Single Case? How to Think About Ethnographic Case Selection Like a Historical Sociologist, Sociological Methods & Research] [ref: After Positivism: New Approaches to Comparison in Historical Sociology, Columbia University Press], and he is the author of two books about American political development and federalism.

In his 2016 book Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the post-Keynesian Society, Pacewicz examines municipal and partisan politics in two Rust Belt cities during the 2008 and 2012 election cycles. [ref: Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the Post-Keynesian Society, University of Chicago Press] The book shows how changes in American federalism—the corporate merger waves that followed 1970s-era financial deregulation and changes in the prevailing logics of inter-governmental finance—eroded the traditional base of both political parties, thus creating an opening for activists to take over grassroots politics, especially within the GOP. Partisans and Partners was a co-winner of the American Sociological Association’s Theory prize. [ref: Past Awards, ASA Theory Section]

His 2027 book, Divided States: Doing Federalism in Red and Blue America, centers officials who interpret and administer federal rights and programs in the states and documents their ongoing efforts to make real the promises of flagship social programs and civil rights guarantees. [ref: global.oup.com] In Republican states, this resulted in policies that were less extreme than legislators’ frontstage rhetoric, but also contributed to an extremist and antidemocratic reorientation among Republicans, who used the architecture of state government to decouple legislative initiatives from their street-level consequences.

== Awards ==
Pacewicz’s articles have received prizes from the American Sociological Association’s Historical-Comparative Section (2016) and Community and Urban Sociology Section (2015 and 2021). [ref: ] [ref: ] He has won an award from the Society for the Advancement of Socio-Economics (SASE) and was a 2020 Guggenheim Fellow. [ref: annual prize, Oxford Academic] [ref: Guggenheim Fellowships: Supporting Artists, Scholars, & Scientists, www.gf.org]

data.title: Dhukal Wirrpanda
data.text:
Dhukal Wirrpanda (born 1957) is a Yolŋu elder and artist from the Dhudi-Djapu clan in North East Arnhem Land (associated with the Baniyala and Dhuruputjpi homelands). [ref: About the artist: Dhukal Wirrpanda, Annandale Galleries]

Dhukal Wirrpanda is the grandson (son in Yolŋu terms) of Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda, the Yolŋu leader at the centre of the landmark High Court of Australia case Tuckiar v The King (1934). Dhukal Wirrpanda is the protagonist and narrator of the documentary film Dhakiyarr vs The King. Nine ceremonial larrakitj hollow-log coffins) that Wirrpanda painted, along with seven other elders, were permanently installed in the foyer of Supreme Court of the Northern Territory during a Wukidi (reconciliation) ceremony at the end of the film. He has continued to advocate for Indigenous rights, reconciliation, and official recognition of historic Aboriginal deaths in custody. [ref: One of Australia's oldest cold cases: why after 90 years a family is still waiting for justice, The Guardian] [ref: Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda’s family calls for fresh probe into mystery disappearance, ABC News]

== Early life ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda was born in 1957 (some records cite 1955) to his father, Djungi.

He was born in North East Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, and raised on his ancestral Dhudi-Djapu clan homelands in Dhuruputjpi, approximately 200 kilometres southwest of Yirrkala. [ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda: Yalata (91x52cm Bark), Art Ark] [ref: Dhangultji at Dhuruputjpi, 1996 by Dhukal Wirrpanda, Galuma Maymuru, Art Gallery of New South Wales] Since the 1980s he has lived, worked and exhibited alongside his late wife, Galuma Maymuru.

== Artistic methods and themes ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda works include bark painting, wood carving and ceremonial hollow-log poles (larrakitj), using natural earth pigments and ochres sourced from his ancestral lands. His artistic practice is deeply connected with the ancestral stories, ceremonies and knowledge of the Dhudi-Djapu clan. [ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda: Yalata (91x52cm Bark), Art Ark]

His work frequently depicts the sacred ecology and seasonal transformations of his homelands around Dhuruputjpi in north-east Arnhem Land.

A portion of his mature practice centred on the Wukidi series, which depicts the ancient ancestral tsunami narrative and inland mortuary site integral to Dhudi-Djapu ceremonies. In this story, the ancestral hunters Balurruwuy and Yangamawuy were swept inland by a catastrophic wave and transformed into standing stone pillars. [ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda, Wukidi Tsunami, 2005, Deutscher and Hackett]
[ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda Sold at Auction Prices, Invaluable]

In addition to inland freshwater narratives, Wirrpanda's work engages deeply with sea country and maritime ecologies. In his contribution to the Saltwater collection, Gapuwarriku at Lutumba (1997-98), Wirrpanda depicts turtle hunters who successfully return with their catch. [ref: Djapu Turtle Hunt (1998) by Dhukal Wirrpanda, Australian National Maritime Museum] [ref: Gapuwarriku at Lutumba (1998) by Dhukal Wirrpanda, Australian National Maritime Museum] Anthropologist Howard Morphy noted that Wirrpanda uses the imagery the turtle shell, the connecting rope and the cleansing tide as a rich metaphor for Yolŋu mortuary ceremonies and the renewal of life. [ref: Saltwater Country – Paintings From Yirrkala, Art+Australia]

== Exhibitions ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda's early exhibition history includes participation in the 1984 Baniyala Artworks showcase at the Crafts Council Gallery in Sydney.

Alongside his late wife, fellow artist Galuma Maymuru, Wirrpanda co-created Dhangultji at Dhuruputjpi in 1996, a carved and painted wood installation that reflects the sacred ecology and ownership of their clan lands.

In 1997, he was featured in the landmark exhibition Native Title: Yirrkala Bark Paintings at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia in Sydney, highlighting the intersection of customary law, land rights, and contemporary bark painting. [ref: Native Title: Yirrkala Bark Paintings (1997), Museum of Contemporary Art Australia]

From 1998 to 1999, his work was included in A Material Thing: Objects from the Collection at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, showcasing sculptural works and cultural objects.

In 1998, Wirrpanda's bark paintings Djapu Turtle Hunt and Gapuwarriku at Lutumba were exhibited in the Saltwater: Yirrkala Bark Paintings of Sea Country project, created by Yolŋu artists to assert sea rights and sacred coastal ownership following illegal fishing intrusions at Garranali. These paintings then featured in the touring exhibition of the same name. [ref: Saltwater Country - Paintings From Yirrkala, Art+Australia]

Also in 1998, Wirrpanda and Galuma Maymuru held a joint exhibition titled In Memory of Narritjin – Bark Paintings and Carvings at the William Mora Gallery in Melbourne.

In 2000, Wirrpanda and Galuma Maymuru's collaborative carved sculpture Nyapalingu Wapitja Pair was exhibited at the 2000 Olympic Arts Festival in Sydney. [ref: Nyapalingu Wapitja Pair, Deutscher and Hackett]

In 2003, he was exhibited in the group showcase Buwayak (Invisibility) at Annandale Galleries in Sydney, which focused on the spiritual and cultural presence of Yolŋu art.

In 2025, he was featured in Yolŋu Power: The Art of Yirrkala at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, celebrating the enduring power and political agency of Yirrkala artistic traditions.

In addition to group exhibitions, Wirrpanda's commercial exhibition history includes Yolngu Bark at the Ben Grady Gallery in Canberra (2001), a dual showcase with Galuma Maymuru at Framed Darwin Gallery (2002), and Arnhem Land Ochres at Mina Mina Art Gallery in Brunswick Heads (2006).

Internationally, Wirrpanda’s work has been featured in European exhibitions, including the group showcase Sillage held at Arts d’Australie in Paris in 2022. [ref: Sillage Exhibition, Arts d'Australie, Stephane Jacob]

== Collections ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda's bark paintings and larrakitj (ceremonial poles) are held in major public collections both in Australia and internationally, including:
* Australian National Maritime Museum, Sydney, holds Djapu Turtle Hunt (1998) and Gapuwarriku at Lutumba (1998) as part of the permanent collection.
* British Museum, London holds Mana and Wan'kawu – shark and freshwater goanna at Dhurruputjpi. [ref: Bark painting: Mana and Wan'kawu – shark and freshwater goanna at Dhurruputjpi, British Museum]
* Art Gallery of New South Wales, Sydney, holds the collaborative sculpture Dhangultji at Dhuruputjpi (1996), created with Galuma Maymuru.
* Queensland Art Gallery and Gallery of Modern Art, Brisbane, holds Wukidi ga Yingapungapu I (2005). [ref: Wukidi ga Yingapungapu I by Dhukal Wirrpanda, Queensland Art Gallery / Gallery of Modern Art]
* National Gallery of Australia, Canberra.
* National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne.
* Supreme Court of the Northern Territory, Darwin. [ref: Dh'a'kiyarr Wirrpanda Monument, Monument Australia]
* JW Kluge Collection at the University of Virginia, United States, holds commissioned works. [ref: A Personal Reflection on the Origins of Maḏayin, Kluge-Ruhe Aboriginal Art Collection]
* Kerry Stokes Collection, Perth.

In 2018, his 1986 bark painting in the British Museum collection was loaned for the international exhibition Shine on Me: The Sun and Us at the Deutsches Hygiene-Museum in Dresden, Germany.

== Awards ==
Between 1996 and 2005, Dhukal Wirrpanda's work was selected multiple times for inclusion in the prestigious Telstra National Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander Art Awards at the Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory in Darwin (in 1996, 1997, 1998 and 2005).

== Publications ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda's artwork and cultural contributions are featured in key exhibition catalogues and texts on Indigenous Australian art, including:
* Saltwater: Yirrkala Bark Paintings of Sea Country: Recognising Indigenous Sea Rights (1999), published by Buku-Larrŋgay Mulka Centre in association with Jennifer Isaacs. [ref: Saltwater: Yirrkala Bark Paintings of Sea Country: Recognising Indigenous Sea Rights, Buku-Larrŋgay Mulka Centre in association with Jennifer Isaacs Publishing]
* Art from the Land: Dialogues with the Kluge-Ruhe Collection of Australian Aboriginal Art (1999), edited by Howard Morphy and Margo Smith Boles and published by the University of Virginia / MSquared. [ref: Art from the Land: Dialogues with the Kluge-Ruhe Collection of Australian Aboriginal Art, University of Virginia / MSquared]
* Spirit Country: Contemporary Australian Aboriginal Art (1999) by Jennifer Isaacs and published by Fine Arts Museums. [ref: Spirit Country: Contemporary Australian Aboriginal Art, Fine Arts Museums]
* Galuma Maymuru, Dhukal Wirrpanda: Bark Paintings and Ceremonial Poles (2007) by Galuma Maymuru and Dhukal Wirrpanda, introduction by Bill Gregory, and published by Annandale Galleries in association with Buku-Larrŋgay Mulka Centre). [ref: Galuma Maymuru, Dhukal Wirrpanda: Bark Paintings and Ceremonial Poles, Annandale Galleries]
* Saltwater: Paintings of Sea Country: The Recognition of Indigenous Sea Rights (2014), edited by Jennifer Isaacs and published by Buku-Larrŋgay Mulka. [ref: Saltwater: Paintings of Sea Country: The Recognition of Indigenous Sea Rights, Buku-Larrŋgay Mulka Centre]
* Mad̲ayin: Waltjan̲ ga Waltjan̲buy Yolnuwu Miny'tji Yirrkalawuy = Eight Decades of Aboriginal Australian Bark Painting from Yirrkala (2022), edited by Wukun̲ Wan̲ambi, Henry Skerritt and Kade McDonald, and published by the Kluge-Ruhe Aboriginal Art Collection of the University of Virginia. [ref: Mad̲ayin: Waltjan̲ ga Waltjan̲buy Yolnuwu Miny'tji Yirrkalawuy = Eight Decades of Aboriginal Australian Bark Painting from Yirrkala, Kluge-Ruhe Aboriginal Art Collection of the University of Virginia / DelMonico Books]
* Yolŋu Power: The Art of Yirrkala (2025), edited by Cara Pinchbeck and published by the Art Gallery of New South Wales. [ref: Yolŋu Power: The Art of Yirrkala, Art Gallery of New South Wales]

== Advocacy for Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda ==

Dhukal Wirrpanda is a direct descendant and successor clan leader of Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda, a Dhudi-Djapu leader who disappeared in 1934 following his release from Darwin's Fannie Bay Gaol after his murder conviction was overturned by the High Court of Australia in Tuckiar v The King. [ref: After 91 years, there are still more questions than answers over the death of Aboriginal man Dhäkiyarr, The Conversation]

=== 2002 audio documentary ===
In 2002, Wirrpanda met Sydney academic Tom Murray, who was visiting Arnhem Land.

Wirrpanda wanted to hold a traditional funeral ceremony for Dhakiyarr, which in Yolŋu culture is important because, as Wirrpanda explained, "all of the bones and strength and spirit of a person flows back into the land". [ref: Dhakiyarr vs the King: Press Kit & Study Guide, Film Australia]

Murray worked with Wirrpanda to produce a radio documentary titled Dhakiyarr vs the King and Territory, which was broadcast on Hindsight, ABC Radio National's social impact program (and again in 2013). [ref: Tuckiar (Dhakiyarr) v the King and Territory, Hindsight]

The audio documentary, focused on the family and their pain, drew attention to the case. Murray assisted Wirrpanda to record a video letter, so they could make their case in their own words to the Chief Minister of the Northern Territory, Clare Martin.

In the video letter, Dhukal requested the return of Dhakiyarr's remains or permission to hold a formal reconciliation ceremony at the Supreme Court of the Northern Territory in Darwin. [ref: A healing from the past, for the future, The Sydney Morning Herald] Martin agreed to the request and facilitated access for the historic Wukidi (reconciliation) ceremony to take place at the Supreme Court.

=== 2004 documentary film ===
With the reconciliation ceremony set to take place, Murray partnered with co-director Allan Collins and Dhakiyarr's family to develop a feature-length documentary film.

The documentary film Dhakiyarr vs The King examines the historical intersection between Yolŋu customary law and the Australian legal system through the experiences of the Wirrpanda and McColl families. Dhukal Wirrpanda served as one of the protagonists and narrators for the film.

Scenes from the reconciliation ceremony form the climax of the film. In June 2003, more than 200 Yolŋu people followed in Dhakiyarr's "footsteps" (as described in the film), from Arnhem Land to Darwin, to restore Dhakiyarr's honour and confront historical injustices. They were joined by 30 descendants of Albert McColl, the policeman Dhakiyarr speared seventy years before, as well as Chief Minister Martin, judges from the Northern Territory Supreme Court and the High Court of Australia.

Nine ceremonial larrakitj (hollow-log coffins), prepared and painted by Dhukal and Wuyal Wirrpanda alongside elders from six joining clans, were permanently installed in the foyer of Supreme Court of the Northern Territory to restore Dhakiyarr's honour and guide his spirit home. [ref: Dh'a'kiyarr Wirrpanda Monument, Monument Australia] It was in the Supreme Court of the Northern Territory where Dhakiyarr was once made 'invisible'. Or, as Wirrpanda described it, where "they treated him like a man without a footprint".

The film premiered at the 2004 Sydney Film Festival [ref: Dhakiyarr vs the King – Sydney Film Festival Archive, Sydney Film Festival] where it won the Rouben Mamoulian Award. [ref: Dhakiyarr vs the King, Screen Australia] The film also won the 2004 New South Wales Premier's Audio/Visual History Prize. [ref: NSW Ministry for the Arts Annual Report 2004–05, New South Wales Parliament] In 2005, it screened at the Sundance Film Festival, [ref: Dhakiyarr vs the King – Sundance Film Festival Archives, Sundance Institute] as well as a number of other international film festivals in the US, UK, Canada and Taiwan. [ref: Dhakiyarr vs the King (2004), National Library of Australia Web Archive]

The film was also broadcast on the Australian Broadcasting Corporation and streamed on ABC iview, [ref: Dhakiyarr vs The King, Australian Broadcasting Corporation] [ref: Dhakiyarr versus the King, The Age] and is also available on streaming service Kanopy [ref: Dhakiyarr vs The King, Kanopy] and from the National Film and Sound Archive. [ref: Dhäkiyarr vs the King, National Film and Sound Archive] In France, the film is distributed for public screening and cinema exhibition by the association Documentaire sur grand écran. [ref: Dhakiyarr vs the King (2004), Documentaire sur grand écran]

Opening the film at Federation Square in Melbourne, Dhukal and Wuyul Wirrpanda declared it to be "the film that they had always wanted to make," reflecting on the film's role as an Indigenous-led vehicle for truth and historical reconciliation. [ref: Macquarie University Research Excellence Awards Spotlight, Macquarie University]

=== 2025 coronial inquiry ===
Following Northern Territory coronial findings into Dhakiyarr's disappearance handed down in early 2025, Wirrpanda and his family expressed disappointment over the coroner's decision not to hold a formal inquest or invite submissions from Indigenous family members. Legal scholars noted that despite findings that Dhakiyarr was not "in care or custody" at the time of his disappearance, he remained under state care at the Kahlin Aboriginal Compound when he went missing.

=== New investigation commenced in 2025 and is ongoing ===
Wirrpanda has continued public campaigns calling for official accountability, wanting Dhakiyarr's death to be recognised as an Aboriginal death in custody. Alongside fellow clan leader Djambawa Marawili, he has also advocated for the Northern Territory government to establish a reconciliation centre in Dhakiyarr's name to foster cross-cultural understanding between Yolŋu and non-Indigenous Australians.

In December 2025, Northern Territory police announced a new investigation into the mysterious disappearance of Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda. [ref: NT police restarts investigation into Yolngu leader, ABC News]

=== Educational adoption and legal impact ===

The High Court decision in Tuckiar v The King and its subsequent appeal remain a foundational case study in Australian legal education, widely taught across law faculties to illustrate principles of procedural fairness, legal ethics, the presumption of innocence, and the duties of counsel.

The documentary film Dhakiyarr vs The King, featuring Wirrpanda as lead protagonist and narrator, has been adopted as a foundational educational resource across Australian law faculties and by professional legal bodies, including the New South Wales Bar Association for professional education in legal ethics and Indigenous rights. [ref: Dhakiyarr vs the King @ NSW Bar Association, Macquarie University Research Portal] [ref: Tuckiar v The King and Legal Ethics, NSW Bar Association News]

Wirrpanda continues to present his family's history to legal audiences. For a recent film screening with the NSW Bar Association, he travelled several hours from his remote homeland at Dhuruputjpi to the community of Baniyala in East Arnhem Land in order to access a reliable communications link and address event attendees directly via a video link.

==See also==

== References ==

== External links ==

* [https://www.nfsa.gov.au/collection/item/dhakiyarr-vs-the-king Dhäkiyarr vs the King] at the National Film and Sound Archive

data.title: Furuichi clan
data.text:
The Furuichi clan (, Furuichi-shi, also read Furuchi-shi) is a clan of Japan. Place names called Furuichi-gō existed in of Kawachi Province, in Higashinari () of Settsu Province, in Shiga District of Ōmi Province, and elsewhere, and the name derives from them. [ref: ]

== Furuichi clan of Yamato ==

The Furuichi of Yamato were a (provincial warrior) family based at Furuichi in Soekami District, Yamato Province, the present-day in Nara. They were (armed clerics) attached to the branch of Kōfuku-ji, and they built.

=== Origins and base ===
The site of Furuichi was once a market called. When its lord, the monzeki (abbot) of the Daijō-in, moved the market inside the Daijō-in's own district as the South Market (), the former site came to be called Furuichi ("old market"). [ref: 『戦乱と人物』、高柳光寿博士頌寿記念会 編、1968年、149頁]

As for the family's origin, the says that they were of the Kiyohara clan and descendants of Prince Toneri, and the (in the [ref: ]) says that they were descendants of, who had lived at Furuichi. Both, however, are sources of the early modern period, and there is no confirmation.

The home settlement of Furuichi-gō was surrounded by a moat and contained five machi (wards); village heads (shōya) and deputies (daikan) were placed there. They collected taxes but also represented the community, and the wards and villages ran annual observances such as festivals on their own., stressing this autonomy, argues that the Furuichi clan's control over the settlement has been overestimated, and that the moat around it should be seen as one of the moated villages (kangō) found widely in Yamato. He also holds that Furuichi Castle was not large enough to take in the town below it, and that it is reasonable to regard it as confined to the area of the aza (sub-district) named (old castle), the site of the present housing estate.

=== Successive heads ===
When the family began to use the name Furuichi is unknown, but the name appears in Shōchū 2 (1325). On the 4th day of the 12th month of the same year, the Daijō-in abbot left the (Zenjō-in) and moved to this Tajima-no-kimi (). Inaba Nobumichi sees this as a case in which the abbot relied on Tajima-no-kimi, a gobōnin (retainer of the abbot) who appears to have been the core of the abbot's armed force, and argues that the Daijō-in depended on the strength of the Furuichi. [ref: 中世寺院の権力構造, [[Iwanami Shoten] In Shitoku 3 (1386), took office as one of the (executive officers of the shuto assembly) together with and others, and the family had become the leading shuto of the Daijō-in side.

When the Daijō-in monzeki and the Tsutsui clan came into conflict from Kakitsu 2 (1442), Inken's grandson fought on Kyōkaku's side.

Insen died in Kyōtoku 2 (1453), and his son succeeded him. When the Ōnin War began in Ōnin 1 (1467), In'ei joined the Western Army. In'ei tightened his control over his retainers, for example by taking judicial authority within the house into his own hands, but, perhaps because this provoked opposition from kinsmen and vassals, he retired in Bunmei 7 (1475).

After In'ei's retirement his younger brother Chōin became head of the family. Since the Ōnin War the kokujin of Yamato had been divided into the Tsutsui faction and the Ochi faction, and Chōin acted as a leading figure of the Ochi faction second only to. At first the Ochi faction had the upper hand, and under Chōin the Furuichi reached their peak, but in Meiō 6 (1497) they were defeated in battle by the Tsutsui faction and went into decline. A peace was then concluded among the kokujin of Yamato, excluding the Furuichi, and Chōin sided with and, commanders of the Hosokawa clan who invaded Yamato, and fought against the Yamato kokujin.

After Chōin was killed in battle in Eishō 5 (1508), fighting between the Tsutsui side and the Ochi side broke out again in Yamato, and Chōin's successor joined the Ochi side. Furuichi Castle, the family seat, was taken several times during this period, and under Kōin it became difficult to hold. The Furuichi came to rely mainly on on the ridge (the of the sources) and on and Ōji () in the eastern hills (). Thereafter the Furuichi alternately fought and made peace with the Tsutsui side, and when Matsunaga Hisahide, a retainer of the Miyoshi clan, advanced into Yamato in Eiroku 2 (1559), they followed him.

=== Character of their power ===

==== Kinsmen and retainers ====
Asakura Hiroshi tentatively calls the league centred on the Furuichi the "Furuichi faction" (Furuichi-tō). Unlike the six leagues that served as sponsors () of the, no connection with the festival appears in the sources, but the entry for the 1st day of the 10th month of Meiō 6 (1497) in the names, as kokujin belonging to this league, the Furuichi, Yamamura, Nagai (), Tsubao (), Yamada (),,, Fukuzumi (), Uryū, Banjō () and Kushira (). Asakura cautions, however, that this is not the whole membership. Of these, the Kushira clan is described as distant relatives of the Furuichi through a brother in an entry of the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki for the 29th day of the 9th month of Bunmei 13 (1481) listing the relatives of shuto and kokumin.

Tanaka Keiji divides the Furuichi kin into "traditional kinsmen" and "fictive kinsmen". The former were the Yamamura,,, Yoshida,, Inoue, Nagata (Inagaki) and Nagai.

These kinsmen were permitted by the main line to use a double surname prefixed with "Furuichi", such as Furuichi Yamamura, Furuichi Nagata, Furuichi and Furuichi Inoue. Many were also allowed to use "In" (), the character shared by the Furuichi in their personal names, and some styled themselves with court-type titles such as Chikuzen-no-kami or Ōmi-no-kami.

Among the vassals, the wakatō () ranked as samurai in social status. In a roster of the 5th day of the 11th month of Bunmei 12 (1480), two wakatō are classed as "of samurai status" (), and they were entitled to ride on horseback; there is even a case of one bearing the title Yamashiro-no-kami. By contrast, chūgen and (quiver bearers) were of commoner (bonge) status, and there was a clear gap between the two groups. Whereas earlier scholars saw the wakatō as commoners seeking samurai status, Tanaka holds that in Yamato hereditary samurai formed the core of the wakatō, with newly risen samurai around them.

The origins of the wakatō fall into four groups: cadet branches of the Furuichi kin; cadet branches of shuto and other than the Furuichi kin; men of local landholding families (dogō); and men promoted from commoner status. and came from local landholding families, and was promoted from commoner status. In the grant of titles of the 12th month of Meiō 2 (1493), of the kin was made Ōmi-no-kami and the wakatō was made Zusho-no-suke; these were official appointments, not self-assumed titles.

There were also cases of vassals rising in status. The had originally been wakatō of the Koizumi () but rose to the status of shuto and kokumin; the Daijō-in Jisha Zōjiki for the 9th day of the 12th month of Bunmei 14 (1482) says, "the were originally wakatō of the Koizumi, and have risen" (). On this occasion the invoked their marriage ties with Furuichi In'ei, and they belonged to both the Tsutsui side and the Furuichi side.

In the 8th month of Eishō 3 (1506), these kinsmen and vassals were attacked in their home villages. The records that on the 16th, through the work of the Tsutsui foot soldiers (ashigaru), "Furuichi Yamamura, Fujiwara, Yokoi, Nagai and the rest" () were burned without exception, and that the Tsutsui force went straight on into Nara, where Furuichi Tango-dono, who was in Nara, crossed and fled. [ref: 『多聞院日記』第1巻（巻1至11）英俊ほか著、辻善之助 編、三教書院、1935年、[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/pid/1212359/1/103 コマ103]（国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション）。]

==== Control of the retainer band ====
It was in In'ei's time that the kin and retainers came to be firmly bound together. In a case of killing between retainers at Furuichi Castle in Chōroku 2 (1458), the party who struck did not settle the matter by private fighting, but first petitioned the lord, obtained permission, then killed his opponent and reported afterwards. The relatives of the side that was killed in return likewise chose litigation rather than revenge. The Furuichi judged the cases by their own authority: the killing done with permission was left unpunished, while the other, even though it was self-defence, was ruled a capital offence and the culprit was executed on the spot. Tanaka Keiji sees this ruling, which rejected self-help through private fighting to this degree, as an early form of the law of (equal punishment of both parties to a quarrel). A power that suppressed self-help to this extent would normally not appear until Toyotomi Hideyoshi's sword hunt, and in that respect, he says, the Furuichi's justice was about 130 years ahead of the country as a whole.

Control extended to the kin as well. In Bunshō 1 (1466),, a powerful kinsman who had long supported In'ei since he became head as a child, was expelled for defying In'ei's wishes. In Bunmei 2 (1470), two vassals were executed and thirty kinsmen and wakatō were driven out., who recorded this, called it pitiable but unavoidable, which suggests that such punishments by the Furuichi were regarded as natural. Tanaka sees these as moves of the same kind as the Mōri clan's destruction of the Inoue family (Tenbun 19, 1550), and notes that the Furuichi's control came more than 80 years earlier.

==== Economic base ====
Furuichi, their home base, was a key point of communication commanding the road. From here the Furuichi gained control over the bashaku, who were both carriers of goods and petty merchants, and over the toll barriers (seki) on the roads.

In the 4th month of Bun'an 4 (1447), Insen received at Furuichi the former abbot Kyōkaku, who had been driven out of the Daijō-in. Kyōkaku spent the 27 years until his death in Bunmei 5 (1473) at the in Furuichi. In the 7th month of the same year, when bashaku uprisings (ikki) broke out in Yamato, Ōmi, Kawachi, Yamashiro and elsewhere, a rumour arose that Kyōkaku and Insen had set the bashaku in motion to destroy Nanto (Nara), and the shuto assembly imposed a censure (shūkan) on the two. Kyōkaku was indignant at the uprising in his diary and the charge was false, but Tanaka Keiji considers that Insen, who was closely tied to the bashaku, may well have organised and supported it.

As for toll barriers, it was Kyōkaku who could appoint the (agent) of the Kizu (Kizu) ferry, and holding his person was the basis of the Furuichi's control. In Bunmei 4 (1472) they held the main barrier at, and together with their advance into southern Yamashiro from Bunmei 2 (1470), they appear to have held the de facto position of shugodai (deputy governor), backed by Hatakeyama Yoshinari and Ōuchi Masahiro of the Western Army. In Meiō 2 (1493), after the collapse of the Yamashiro Province uprising, they were formally appointed shugodai of Yamashiro. They also set up new barriers in southern Yamashiro, and whenever Jinson went up to the capital or an abbot travelled down, he asked Chōin or the kinsman Inoue Ōmi-no-kami for passage through the barriers. In the 10th month of Entoku 2 (1490) they set the bashaku of Shimokoma and Kizu in motion and caused an uprising.

==== Quarters within the temple ====
Sons of the Furuichi, as shuto of the Daijō-in side, entered the Kōfuku-ji quarters (bōsha) generation after generation:, son of Inken (胤憲); Chōin, son of Insen; and, adopted son () of In'ei; relatives of the Furuichi served as its head until the Tenshō era. Kyōkaku, too, noted that the Hosshin-in had a historical connection with the Furuichi. [ref: 『史料纂集』［第10］第1（）、続群書類従完成会、1971年]

The authority to appoint and dismiss the head lay with the Daijō-in. It was the Furuichi, however, who chose the successor, and the chosen successor paid the Furuichi a fee of 200 hiki. There is also a case in which Jinson demanded the fee for a change of head from the Furuichi rather than from the monks of the quarters. Hatakama Kazuhiro sees these as evidence that the Furuichi regarded the Hosshin-in as part of their family's property.

The Hosshin-in was also the Furuichi's base in Nara. It became customary for the Kasuga lecture (Kasuga-kō) of the shuto assembly to be held at the Hosshin-in with the Furuichi as the presiding officer (tōyaku), and meetings of the scholar-monks (gakuryo) and of the roppō were also held there. [ref: 『大乗院寺社雑事記 第11巻』、辻善之助 編・校訂、角川書店、1964年]

=== Culture ===
When Kyoto became a battlefield in the Ōnin War, many court nobles took refuge with their sons who were serving as abbots and temple heads in Nara, and men of culture such as renga masters came and went with them. Nanto already had a foundation in the renga gatherings dedicated to Tenjin and the performing arts of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival, and with the addition of the culture of the capital, tea, renga,, Noh and kemari spread rapidly. Ishii Tomoko called this era the "Nanto Renaissance" and placed Chōin as its embodiment.

His position as head (tōryō) of the was not unrelated to this. The kanpu shuto were warrior monks permitted to marry; they carried out policing and justice throughout the province, proclaimed debt cancellations (tokusei), and took part in maintaining the temple and the shrine, and they also held the right to stage new sarugaku and the performing arts of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The tōryō was the one who carried these out.

In the tea ceremony, Chōin is known as a senior disciple of Murata Jukō. The names him as one of Jukō's disciples, saying "Furuichi Harima of Nanto in Washū is Jukō's foremost disciple, a man of taste and a master" (). The ("Letter on the heart"), in which Jukō set out his precepts on tea, is also addressed to "Furuichi Harima Hōshi". The shows that Chōin owned many famous utensils associated with Jukō, such as,, and; he seems to have been his patron as well as his disciple.

His elder brother In'ei was fond of. It was one of the events of Urabon: a tea room was set up in a bathhouse, furyū decorations were placed in the bath, tea was served and a banquet was held. The records of Bunmei 1 (1469), when it was at its height, repeatedly show In'ei serving as the host (tōyaku), and it was also an event to relieve the tedium of Kyōkaku, who was living in retirement at Furuichi. There is no case of Chōin himself hosting rinkan chanoyu, but in the 1st month of Bunmei 13 (1481) he acted as "tea master" () and held a large gathering, bearing all the costs himself.

In Noh he supported the Konparu troupe (). Furuichi patronage predated Chōin, but he was only two years apart in age from Konparu Zenpō, and he is said to have supported him strongly, even using his own authority. Zenpō's collection of talks on the art, the, contains comments on Chōin's chanting, which shows that Chōin learned utai from Zenpō. He is also said to have been a skilled player of the shakuhachi.

The Furuichi also cultivated, and Insen held renga gatherings within Furuichi Castle. His sons In'ei and Chōin also practised renga and the tea ceremony. Court nobles (kuge) and performers who had come down to Nara to escape the Ōnin War are said to have taken part in the gatherings Chōin hosted. Konparu Zenchiku and his son also sat in the monthly renga gatherings held at the Furuichi residence. Chōin was on close terms with, from whom he received the. Chōin held renga gatherings not only at his own residence but also at temples where he was in retreat and in camp during battles. Three of his verses were included in the under the name "Gon-no-risshi Chōin".

=== Genealogy ===
A genealogy of the Furuichi is appended to volume 3 of the. Insei () does not appear there and has been added on the basis of the.

== Furuichi clan of Kaga ==
=== Overview ===
The Furuichi of Kaga began with the migration of (), a descendant of Furuichi Harima-no-kami, lord of. Taneie served the kanpaku Konoe Nobutada and was given the post of naishi, then served Tōdō Takatsugu, later lord of the Tsu Domain in Ise, and afterwards moved to Kaga. [ref: 『加賀藩史稿』第13巻、尊経閣、1899年] The family crest is the same maru ni kaede as that of the Yamato Furuichi.

Taneie's son was a warrior who served Maeda Toshitsune, the second lord of the Kaga Domain, in the early Edo period. His common name was. He entered Toshitsune's service young with a stipend of 3,630 koku, and on his lord's death he followed him in death (junshi, by suicide) at the age of 34. [ref: 『金沢古蹟志 第11編』、金沢文化協会、1934年、59-61頁] His heir was his younger brother, a samurai who served Maeda Tsunanori and a Confucian scholar who studied under Zhu Shunshui. [ref: 『加賀藩史料 第3編 (寛永十八年～寛文二年)』、清文堂出版、1980年、571頁] [ref: 『金沢古蹟志 第11編』、金沢文化協会、1934年、60-61頁] Kanemoto also died of illness in his thirties and the Kaga Furuichi came to an end, but descendants of of the Echizen Furuichi, described below, served the successive lords of the Kaga Domain. [ref: 先祖由緒并一類附帳【帙492】、古市甚太郎（尚一）・古市友作（政忠）、1868年]

=== Genealogy ===

== Furuichi clan of Echizen ==

The origin of the Echizen Furuichi is uncertain, but several Furuichi are recorded in the records of the estates owned by Kōfuku-ji in Echizen Province.

The "Echizen Province Asuwa District Office Notice" (), dated 24 November 951 (Tenryaku 5, 10th month, 23rd day), is a report from the district office of Asuwa District to the estate revenue officers of Tōdai-ji. It states that the Tōdai-ji estates in the district,, and, lay within the jōri grid but were "originally either wasteland or marshland", with no tenants to cultivate them, and that in particular was "something never heard of". [ref: 大日本古文書]

Eight people signed at the end of this notice: a member of the Ikue clan serving as kengyō and general steward of the; five acting dairyō (; two of the Ikue clan, two of the Asuwa clan and one of the Furuichi clan); and two acting shōryō (of the Ikue and Hata clans). The Furuichi name appears among the five acting dairyō. [ref: 『福井市史 資料編 2 (古代・中世)』、福井市、1989年] [ref: 『東南院文書 第３櫃第20巻 越前国足羽郡庁牒』、東大寺、951年]

In the Muromachi period, the family administered (the present area of Awara) and (the present Mikuni-chō in Sakai) of the, a Kōfuku-ji estate, and within the. [ref: 『大和志料 上巻』、奈良県 編、1914年、412頁] [ref: 『福井県郷土叢書 第10集 (北国庄園史料)』、福井県立図書館, 福井県郷土誌懇談会 共編、1965年] In the early Sengoku period, however, on 23 July 1470 (Bunmei 2, 6th month, 25th day), Asakura Takakage, who was close to completing the conquest of Echizen, informed that he had decided that "the whole of the Tsuboe estate shall be held by Asakura". [ref: 『大乗院寺社雑事記 第4巻』、辻善之助 編・校訂、1964年、450-451頁] This marked the decline of Kōfuku-ji and the end of the estate culture.

In the Sengoku period,, a son of Furuichi Harima-no-kami (whether Chōin or In'ei is unknown), was taken into the service of Asakura Yoshikage with 500 koku but was killed at the battle of against the Kaga Ikkō-ikki; 's heir was taken into the service of Mukai Suruga-no-kami () of Echizen with 300 koku.

Among the retainers of, first lord of the Ōno Domain in Echizen, the name appears. [ref: 『下総町史 原始古代・中世編 史料集』、下総町史編さん委員会 編、1990年、698頁] 's ancestors, like, were retainers of the Asakura family (Takakage and Yoshikage): died in battle at the main gate of Ichijōdani, and was killed at in Nomi District, Kaga Province. Their family crest, maru no uchi ni mitsu yahazu (three arrow nocks in a circle; ), was granted by Takakage.

In present-day Fukui Prefecture, there have been settlements of families named Furuichi since before the Meiji period at Togano-chō () and Shikununo-chō () in Fukui (Ichijōdani Asakura Family Historic Ruins) and at Sakai-chō in Sakai (near the Mukai family residence ). Togano produced the educator,, and, who ran the kimono shop in Echizen Fuchū (Echizen). Their family temple is the.

== Furuichi clan of Himeji ==
=== Expansion of the Yamato Furuichi into Kawachi and Kii ===
The ancestor of the Himeji Furuichi was, who belonged to Matsunaga Hisahide, shugo of Yamato and lord of Furuichi Castle. [ref: 『姓氏家系大辞典 第5巻』、太田亮 著、1942年、5306-5307頁] In Tenshō 5, after the death of Matsunaga Hisahide, Kageharu's son moved to Kawachi and took up farming. 's son (later ) studied medicine in Kyoto, took the art name, [ref: 『漢方の臨床 34(12)(400)』、東亜医学協会、1987年、899頁] and moved to Kishū. [ref: 『古市公威』、故古市男爵記念事業会 編、1937年]

=== To Edo as a samurai-rank physician ===
In the 2nd month of Genna 3, 's son was born in Kishū. Gensei deepened his learning and medicine in Nagasaki, and in the Kan'ei era he was taken into the service of Sakai Tadayo, lord of Kawagoe in Bushū. From fallen Yamato kokujin, the Furuichi thus became "samurai whose profession was medicine" (samurai-rank physicians, ), and came to revere Gensei as the "restorer of the family".

=== Establishment of the Himeji Furuichi ===
In Kan'en 2, in the time of Gensei's son and of, when was transferred to Himeji, the Furuichi followed him and served in Edo as retainers of the Himeji Domain. The Furuichi house that moved to the Himeji Domain, while continuing to live permanently in Edo, held important posts such as oku-toshiyori and motojime-yaku (equivalent to kanjō bugyō), received several increases in stipend, and maintained and developed the family name.

=== Move to Himeji in the Bakumatsu and Restoration period ===

In Bunkyū 3, amid the turmoil of the Bakumatsu, the Himeji Domain announced a policy of recalling retainers stationed permanently in Edo () to the castle town. The Furuichi family complied, left the Edo residence and moved within the enclosure of Himeji Castle. The head of the family, Furuichi, held high posts having served as sakite monogashira and motojime-yaku, and had established his position in the domain through increases in stipend.

From the Bakumatsu into the Meiji period, the heads of the family and their close relatives repeatedly lacked sons, and the family adopted heirs from other houses again and again. 's nephew (later renamed ) was adopted into the Furuichi family in Tenpō 14. He excelled in letters and arms and valued integrity; he served as an omote koshō (page) and also as an organiser of Western-style drill, and at the age of 42, on the retirement of his adoptive father, he moved to Tokyo.

had one son and one daughter: the son was Kōi and the daughter. Kōi was the first president of the College of Engineering of the Imperial University (the predecessor of the University of Tokyo Faculty of Engineering) and head of the Civil Engineering Bureau of the Home Ministry, and he has been called the highest authority in modern civil engineering.

== Furuichi clan of Kagoshima and Tanegashima ==

The ancestors of the Furuichi of Kagoshima and Tanegashima were of the Yamato Furuichi, who came to the island in the Sengoku period, [ref: 『籾井家日記』、野々口政太郎 等校、1931年] and Furuichi Kai-no-kami and his son, of the Mogami family. [ref: 『鹿児島県史料集 13』、鹿児島県史料刊行委員会 [編]、1973年、135-136頁]
became a retainer of Tanegashima Tokitaka, and in 1562 (Eiroku 5), when Tokitaka's daughter left Tanegashima to become the second wife of her cousin Shimazu Yoshihisa, he accompanied her, settled at Kokubu (present-day Kirishima, Kagoshima Prefecture) and became a retainer of Yoshihisa. [ref: 『種子島家譜 第1巻』、鮫島宗美 訳、1962年、28頁]
Furuichi Kai-no-kami and came to the island in 1552 (Tenbun 21) on the orders of Shimazu Tadayoshi, and served as intermediaries with Konoe Taneie, Shikibu-no-taifu and others, petitioning for court rank for Shimazu Takahisa (). [ref: 『鹿児島県史料集 11』、鹿児島県史料刊行委員会 [編]、1973年、76頁] Nagato-no-kami later changed his surname to Mogami and called himself Mogami.

On Tanegashima, the of the main Tanegashima Furuichi line is preserved as an Important Cultural Property of Japan.

Furuichi Shizuko, who in 1886 founded the Komagome Kindergarten (now Usagi Kindergarten), the first kindergarten in Japan, was also from Tanegashima.

data.title: Jordan Zietz
data.text:
Jordan Zietz is an entrepreneur and the co-founder and CEO of LemonLime, a San Francisco-based artificial intelligence startup. [ref: LemonLime, Y Combinator] [ref: AI Startup Apologizes for Offering Job Interviews in Exchange for Company Tattoos, The Wall Street Journal] A 2024 graduate of Stanford University, he drew criticism in July 2026 after promoting an offer of job interviews to party guests who got LemonLime tattoos. [ref: Tech CEO in hot mess over tattoo-for-job-interview tit for tat, USA Today]

Before LemonLime, Zietz gained national attention as the 44th Stanford Tree, the university's unofficial mascot, a role from which he was suspended in 2022 for displaying a banner that read "Stanford Hates Fun" on the field during a football game. [ref: ‘Stanford Hates Fun’: Students Revolt After Tree Mascot Suspension, The Wall Street Journal] [ref: Stanford student suspended from serving as Tree mascot, ESPN; Stanford Tree mascot suspended for holding 'Stanford hates fun' sign during game, CBS Sports; Stanford's beloved tree mascot suspended for antics taking place during Arizona State game, Sports Illustrated] His other prior ventures include founding GameReef and All-Star eSports League, and co-founding the social app Confetti. [ref: Jordan Zietz is solving the problem plaguing gamers nationwide, Kidpreneurs] [ref: Competing for College: South Florida high school senior creates esports league for students to earn scholarships, WSVN] [ref: A Startup Offered Job Interviews to Anyone Willing to Get Its Logo Tattooed. 7 People Took the Deal, Inc.]

== Early life and education ==
Zietz is a Florida native and attended Pine Crest School. [ref: Business Spotlight: Eau Resort & Spa managers give their best for Habitat, The Coastal Star] He studied management science and engineering at Stanford University, receiving a Bachelor of Science degree in 2024. [ref: 134th Commencement: List of Conferred Degrees and Degree Candidates, Stanford University] [ref: CEO apologizes for offering interviews to people who got tattoos of his AI company logo, San Francisco Chronicle] From 2021 to 2024, he was a member of the editorial board of The Stanford Flipside, a student satirical newspaper. [ref: Staff, The Stanford Flipside] In April 2023, he appeared as a contestant on Wheel of Fortune, representing Stanford during the show's College Week Spring Break episodes. [ref: College Week Spring Break 4]

=== Stanford Tree ===

During the 2022–23 academic year, Zietz served as the 44th Stanford Tree, the official mascot of the Leland Stanford Junior University Marching Band and the unofficial mascot of the university. [ref: Stanford Tree gets the axe, suspended until January, The Stanford Daily] [ref: Meet the sapling: Bravery and new beginnings with Emily Rodriguez ’26, the 45th Stanford Tree, The Stanford Daily]

On October 22, 2022, during the Stanford University football game against Arizona State, Zietz and three other students, including Arizona State's mascot, carried a 40-foot banner across the field which read "Stanford Hates Fun". [ref: Inside “Stanford’s War On Fun”: Tensions mount over University’s handling of social life, The Stanford Daily] The slogan referred to student complaints about the university administration's handling of social life.

Following the stunt, the band's executive committee suspended Zietz from the role. The committee said the decision concerned his use of the position "for personal benefit" and was unrelated to the banner's message.

A student-led campaign protested Zietz's suspension and the university's social-life policies at the November 5 football game against Washington State, including the creation of a petition calling for Zietz's reinstatement which attracted over 700 signatures. [ref: ‘Stanford Hates Fun’ protests campus social life restrictions during football game, The Stanford Daily]

In 2023, Zietz judged auditions for the role and selected Emily Rodriguez as his successor.

== Career ==

=== Early businesses ===
Zietz started his first business, GameReef, through a Young Entrepreneurs Academy program supported by the Boca Raton Chamber of Commerce. In 2019, he founded the All-Star eSports League, which offered free, sponsor-funded competitions through which high school esports clubs could compete against one another and pursue college scholarships.

Zietz later co-founded Confetti, a social networking platform.

=== LemonLime ===
In early 2026, Zietz co-founded San Francisco artificial intelligence startup LemonLime alongside co-founder Daniela Muñoz. The company develops software to automate sales and marketing for small businesses. The company joined Y Combinator's Summer 2026 batch.

==== Tattoo controversy ====
In July 2026, during Y Combinator's Startup School weekend, Zietz hosted an afterparty at LemonLime's San Francisco office. Y Combinator told Inc. that it had neither sponsored the party nor included it in Startup School. In a since-deleted LinkedIn post, Zietz wrote that the company had brought a tattoo artist to the party and offered an "instant interview" to anyone who got a LemonLime tattoo; according to the post, seven people received tattoos. [ref: Tech founder responds to backlash after guaranteeing ‘instant interview’ to anybody getting company tattoo, The Independent] [ref: A Y-Combinator startup offered job interviews in exchange for getting a tattoo—because they want employees ‘just as crazy as we are’, Fast Company] Zietz told Inc. that he, Muñoz and other LemonLime team members also received tattoos.

The post drew widespread criticism online. [ref: YC-backed AI startup faces backlash after founder offered interviews for tattoos, then apologized, Fortune] [ref: YC founder asks desperate job seekers to tattoo themselves for an interview, The San Francisco Standard] Zietz later deleted the posts and apologized. [ref: Startup Founder Apologizes After Offering Interviews to People Who Got Tattoos, Gizmodo] He described the event as "reckless" and said it had shown poor judgment by appearing to tie a permanent tattoo to a job opportunity. He said participants had chosen their own tattoos, that no one had been asked to get the company logo, that interviews had been available to everyone and that LemonLime would cover removal costs for anyone who later regretted a tattoo. In an August 2026 interview with Wired, Zietz said that some of those tattooed had not been seeking jobs. [ref: The Job-Interview Tattoo Guy Everyone Got Mad at Finally Explains Himself, Wired]

data.title: Hışva Han
data.text:
Hışva Han, also known as Lala Mustafa Pasha Inn, is a historic Ottoman inn in the Şahinbey district of Gaziantep, Turkey, south of Gaziantep Castle. The oldest surviving inn in the city centre, it was commissioned by Lala Mustafa Pasha in the second half of the 16th century. Although the building has no construction inscription, it is believed to have been built between 1563 and 1577. [ref: Gaziantep, TDV İslâm Araştırmaları Merkezi] [ref: Hışva Han – Gaziantep, Kültür Portalı]

Part of the Lala Mustafa Pasha külliye, Hışva Han is a single-storey building with a central courtyard, constructed from black and white dressed stone. Originally used for trade, accommodation and storage, it was restored by Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality and reopened in August 2016 as a complex housing a hotel, restaurant and shops. [ref: Hışva Hanı, Tarihi ve Kültürel Eserler]
[ref: Anadolu’da Yolcu Hanından Konaklama Yapısına Hışvahan: Kültürel Mirasın Korunmasına Yönelik Bir Yaklaşım, İdealkent]

data.title: Hacksaw (1971 movie)
data.text:
Hacksaw is a 1971 American television Western produced by Walt Disney Productions for The Wonderful World of Disney. [ref: The Wonderful World of Disney Television, Hyperion Books] Directed and produced by Larry Lansburgh, the film originally aired on NBC in two parts on September 26 and October 3, 1971. [ref: Disney A to Z: The Official Encyclopedia: Third Edition, Disney Editions] [ref: Hacksaw (television), D23]

Tab Hunter was at a low point in his career when he made the film, being seen as a has-been and having to take out trade ads to get work. [ref: Hacksaw, Turner Classic Movies]

Filming took place in the Canadian Rockies, at the Calgary Stampede, the Radium Hot Springs, the Simpson River, and in Steamboat Springs, Colorado. [ref: Tab Hunter, Colorado Springs Gazette-Telegraph] [ref: Disney Movie Is Filmed With Local Personalities At Steamboat Springs, Colorado Springs Gazette-Telegraph] [ref: Disney, The Robesonian] [ref: Hacksaw, Turner Classic Movies]

Randy Sparks of The New Christy Minstrels came out of retirement to write three songs for the film: "Hacksaw", "Race Song" and "Love Song". [ref: Disney Hour Composer Home From Retirement, The Robesonian] [ref: Christy Minstrel creator composes songs for 'Hacksaw', The Anderson Herald] [ref: Sparks, The Daily Capital News] [ref: Casse-Cou, Chronique Disney]

The film is currently available in on Disney+. [ref: Hacksaw, Disney+] In a review, Common Sense Media felt that while it's "wholesome," kids might find scenes in the film "a little dull." [ref: Hacksaw Movie Review, Common Sense Media]

The Register-Herald described it by writing “a cowboy living in the Canadian Rockies captures and attempts to break a wild mountain stallion,” [ref: Disney's World, Beckley Post-Herald The Raleigh Register] with the Daily News adding “for the big chuck wagon race at the Calgary Stampede.” [ref: Trains Stallion for Chuck Wagon Race In Disney Episode, Red Bluff Tehama County Daily News]

The Robesonian called it a “two-part stallion drama,” [ref: Daughter Of Famed Film Comedian Now Starring On 'World Of Disney', The Robesonian] [ref: Expert Horseman, Actor Takes New Disney Role, The Robesonian] and the Delaware County Daily Times referred to it as a “two-part western adventure.” [ref: Tab in film, Delaware County Daily Times]

data.title: Dante Kraven
data.text:
Dante Kraven is an Oregonian artist that offers his work for charity organizations. His commissioned work can be seen in hotels, parks, and museums around the world. He takes his inspiration from his work as a guide and outdoor specialist for research teams. He is an avid volunteer with both religious functions and community services. In his spare time in the summers he leads outdoor retreats through his local church helping troubled youths and young adults.

He is the oldest in a set of twin boys, twin brother is Raphael. His parents were immigrants from Ireland and France. They met at a religious fundraiser and immediately hit it off. They were married within 6 month of meeting and had their first set of twins within a year.

Recently (May 2026) he submitted multiple pieces to an auction held by North American Orthodox Church which generated a little over $500,000 for the organization.

His stated goal for his art is to inspire young people to get outdoors and enjoy the world created by God for them and to share images and experiences to those who can no longer venture experience the wild places around the world. He has visited almost 2 dozen countries and lead research teams in 5. He hopes that at least in one child they see his work and develop a sense of “wanderlust” to go see what’s out there.

== References ==

Taken from North American Orthodox newsletter and from a local news interview available on YouTube.

data.text:

data.title: George Ergemlidze
data.text:
George Ergemlidze (, Giorgi Ergemlidze) is a Georgian singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and record producer from Tbilisi. He works mainly in synthwave and alternative pop. He wrote the house song "My Queen", released in 2008 by Soulful Mood Recordings and in 2010 as a remix package with Portuguese DJ Ricky Teixeira on AudioBite Records, and fronted the Tbilisi band Mutual Friends. His solo albums include Eclectic (2012), Marsidan (2015), Dear WE (2020), Digitized (2022) and Looking Back in Time (2026).

== Early life ==
Ergemlidze is the son of Nugzar Ergemlidze, whom the music site beehype described as one of the foremost Georgian pop and rock composers of the Soviet era. Nugzar Ergemlidze, born in Batumi in 1955, is also a painter; he studied design at the Tbilisi State Academy of Arts and worked as an editor at Georgian state television and radio from 1982 to 2004.

Ergemlidze played the piano from early childhood. He has said that seeing Queen's performance at Live Aid when he was about ten shaped his musical taste, and that at 13 he taught himself to arrange and produce music on a computer.

== Career ==
=== "My Queen" (2008–2010) ===
In 2008, at the age of 20, Ergemlidze took part in the television talent show Star Academy, where, by his own account, he was told he did not have enough talent to succeed. The same year his song "My Queen" was released as a single by the Russian label Soulful Mood Recordings, under the name Darwin Marcus.

In 2010 My Queen (Remixes), credited to Ricky Teixeira featuring George Ergemlidze, was released on 28 September 2010 by AudioBite Records through its AudioBite Soulful imprint, with mixes by Teixeira, Groove Technicians, BBwhite, Ramiro Bernabela, and DJ Troby & Francesco Cofano. Ergemlidze is credited as vocalist, writer and composer.

=== Mutual Friends ===
At around the age of 20, Ergemlidze and a friend formed a band; he was the founder, leader and singer of Mutual Friends. In June 2011 the band played Alter/Vision's Tbilisi Open Air festival, alongside 19 other bands from Georgia and abroad. He later said the band became quite popular, but that he left to go solo because music was a hobby for the band but his career.

=== Solo work (2012–present) ===
He began his solo career under the name Ergland, releasing the album Eclectic in 2012, before switching to his own name for Marsidan, released on 3 March 2015.

From 2017 he moved toward synthwave. He sent his song "Violet Star" to the YouTube channel and label NewRetroWave, which then had about 300,000 subscribers; according to Ergemlidze, the upload received 20,000 views within two hours, which he regards as the moment his international career began. Reviewing the song in June 2017, beehype called it an energetic, catchy throwback to the 1980s that drew on A-ha and Duran Duran in a synthwave style. He released the EP Violet Star in September 2017, and NewRetroWave went on to publish more of his songs, including "Violet Star", "In My Sleep", "Strangers", "People on the Moon", "Somewhere Here" and "Rainy Town". He was the featured vocalist on "Falling Awake" by DJ Ten, from the album Trinity (Deluxe Edition), released by NewRetroWave on 30 March 2018. He also sang on two songs by the Los Angeles synthwave group Lunr1982: "Morning Light", released on the compilation RetroSynth Records Volume 3 on 9 September 2018, and "November Is Mine" (with Shyguys) in 2019. In 2019 he was the featured vocalist on "Time Slowing Down" by Ultraboss, from the album Slave to the Passion (Rosso Corsa Records).

He released the EPs Simplicity and Simplicity II in 2019, and the albums Dear WE on 11 November 2020 and Digitized on 9 December 2022. In August 2022, "In My Sleep", entered for Georgia, won the 17th edition of the Eurovision Times Song Contest, an online contest run by the blog The Eurovision Times, finishing first of 39 entries.

The EPs Inhale (2023) and Exhale (2024) were released by RetroReverb Records. In August 2024 the digital audio workstation FL Studio added instruments recreated from his songs and samples of his vocal phrases to its "Retrowave Featured Artists" pack for its FLEX plug-in; according to Ergemlidze, he was one of seven artists worldwide chosen for the pack. His album Looking Back in Time was released on 1 May 2026.

Ergemlidze directs and edits his own music videos, including those for "Violet Star", "In My Sleep", "If You Hear Me", "Agreed Then Denied", "Into the Unknown", "I Can Be" and "Stolen Skies".

=== Audio software ===
Ergemlidze also develops audio plug-ins for music production, including the free delay effect Rice Cake Delay and the saturation plug-in EYETURATE, released in 2026 for Windows and macOS.

== Musical style ==
His early work includes Georgian-language pop and rock with Mutual Friends and house music with "My Queen". His later work is synthwave and alternative pop influenced by 1980s synth-pop. He sings in English, saying he wants to reach as wide an audience as possible, and has criticised the expectation among some Georgian music critics that local artists should sing only in Georgian.

data.title: Rossin Bicycles
data.text:
Rossin or Rossin Bicycles was the manufacturer of road-racing bicycles beginning in 1974 and was known for new racing and time trial bicycle designs.

== History ==
Vittorio Ghezzi, Giuseppe Ghezzi, Domenico Garbelli, and Alberto Inzaghi in 1973 recruited Mario Rossin to join in creating a new company to manufacture competitive bikes to supply their Italian amateur racing teams. [ref: Rossin Brand History, Registro Storico Cicli] [ref: Rossin Bikes, The Spoken]

Mario Rossin was formerly a bicycle racer and had served as chief builder at Colnago bicycles. His work with fitting top racers at Colnago including Eddy Merckx built his reputation for skilled craftsmanship.

The original five-member partnership reduced to Domenico Garbelli and Mario Rossin by 1980. Rossin acquired the Pogliaghi brand in November 1983 from Sante Pogliaghi when he retired, bringing the Pogliaghi production and Sante's expertise including road, track and tandem bike designs to the Rossin factory. [ref: Pogliaghi Super Record SLX, Bicycle Guide]
Later still, Alcide Basso of Basso Bikes bought the Poglaighi brand and remaining Pogliaghi production from Rossin in November 1989. [ref: Red-Hot Italian Iron, Bicycle Guide]

Rossin incorporated aerodynamic features into frame designs, developed new specialty time trial bikes designs such as the Futura CX, introduced the first disk wheels in 1983 and was among the first to add an onboard computer.
[ref: The High-tech Bicycle, Harper & Row]
[ref: Italian Racing Bicycles: The People, The Products, The Passion, Velo Press]
[ref: 1001 Bicycles to Dream of Riding, Universe Pub]
[ref: Cars, Trains, Ships, And Planes, A Visual Encyclopedia of Every Vehicle, DK Publishing]

In 1992 Rossin SRL was acquired by FINROSS SRL. GRUPPO BICI obtained the Rossin brand by 2000. Master frame builder Mario Rossin passed away in 2018. [ref: Cycling: Cavenago has said goodbye to Mario Rossin, bicycle manufacturer and sportsman, Cavenago Di Brianza, November 15, 2018]

==Trademark==
The Rossin brand logo design was influenced by the label on Royal-Cola bottles and by the wording on Rossignol skis. Rossingnol protested, so the logo design was changed in 1977. [ref: Rossin Brand History, Registro Storico Cicli]

Rossin advertising included the slogan "Biciclette per vincere" or "Bicycles to Win."

The trademark consists of the word "ROSSIN" in stylized characters, or two polygons, one inside each other, containing an artistic letter "R". [ref: Global Brand Database, WIPO]

==Production overview==
Rossin desiged and produced in Italy traditional steel racing bicycles, time trial bicycles specialized for triathlons and later, carbon fiber racing bicycles. [ref: The Bicycle Book-The Definitive Visual History, DK-Penguin Random House] Rossin was also the first Italian bicycle brand to produce in 1984 a distinct mountain bike model.

GRUPPO BICI reintroduced Rossin bicycles with a line-up of new design carbon fiber road bikes, along with traditional steel road bike frames and mountain bikes in 2011. The last Rossin bicycles were produced between 2017-2019.

== Sponsored Teams 1975-1999 ==
Rossin bikes were used by racing champions including De Vlaeminck, Van Poppel, Berzin, Ugrumov, Virenque, Argentin, Kelly, and Kuiper.

data.title: Miljan Krpić
data.text:
----

Miljan Krpić (Serbian Cyrillic: Миљан Крпић; born 3 July 2003) is a Serbian professional footballer who plays primarily as a centre-back for Nemzeti Bajnokság I club ETO FC Győr, where he has served as captain. He was part of the ETO side that won the 2025–26 Nemzeti Bajnokság I. [ref: „Ez egy újabb lehetőség, hogy bizonyítsuk, hogy képesek vagyunk újra bajnokságot nyerni” – az ETO csapatkapitánya bizakodva várja a Fradi elleni meccset, 24.hu]

== Club career ==
Krpić began playing football with Hajduk Kula, where he was a youth teammate of Miloš Kerkez. He subsequently spent time in the youth systems of TSC Bačka Topola and Hungary's Puskás Akadémia. [ref: Együtt fociztak gyerekként – Az ETO erőssége Kerkez nyomdokán járna a magyar válogatottban, Kisalföld] He started as a defensive midfielder before moving to centre-back. [ref: Mađari bi da nam ga "ukradu", a on sanja Partizan, B92.sport]

Krpić began his senior career with TSC under coach Žarko Lazetić. He played in the 2022–23 Serbian SuperLiga season, when TSC finished second, and later joined Voždovac. Following Voždovac's relegation from the SuperLiga, he moved to newly promoted ETO FC Győr in the summer of 2024.

Krpić initially had a limited role at ETO. During the winter preparation period of the 2024–25 season, coach Balázs Borbély reorganized the defence and used Krpić at centre-back. By the spring he had become a regular starter; Kisalföld described him as one of the club's leading players and noted his composure and ability to carry the ball out of defence. He suffered an ankle-ligament injury during a UEFA Conference League qualifying match against Rapid Wien in 2025 and was sidelined for about two months.

ETO won the 2025–26 Hungarian league title. In 2026, after the departure of Milán Vitális, Krpić took over as team captain. An independent Kisalföld match report also recorded him wearing the armband in ETO's 4–0 league win over Nyíregyháza on 2 August 2026. [ref: Lőttek, láttak, győztek – négygólos győzelemmel nyitott otthonában az ETO, Kisalföld]

== International eligibility ==
Krpić holds Serbian and Hungarian citizenship. In March 2026, Kisalföld examined why he had not been selected for Hungary despite public speculation about a call-up. The newspaper reported that his Hungarian ancestry was too distant to meet FIFA's ancestry requirement and that his periods of residence in Hungary had not been continuous. Under the residency route described by the newspaper, his five-year qualifying period restarted when he joined ETO in 2024, making 2029 the earliest point at which he could become eligible to represent Hungary. [ref: Miért nem játszhat Miljan Krpic a magyar válogatottban?, Kisalföld]

data.title: ProxyAI
data.text:
ProxyAI is a hosted customer-support software service. Its WordPress integration provides automated answers based on published website content, human handoff and support-ticket management. [ref: ProxyAI Chat Assistant, WordPress.org]

== Product and features ==
ProxyAI is a customer-support chatbot platform for online stores and websites. It answers visitor questions using site content and, when connected to a store catalogue, can provide product information such as variants, prices and stock status. Its commerce features include order-status assistance and shopping-cart or checkout support. The platform also offers human handoff, a shared agent inbox [ref: Agent Tasks, ProxyAI Help], support tickets, helpdesk connections, and a knowledge base for documents such as policies and manuals [ref: Add-Ons, ProxyAI Help]. Additional features include moderation controls, visitor and usage reporting, voice and messaging channels, and Agent Tasks for scheduled or event-triggered workflows. [https://wordpress.org/plugins/proxyai/ WordPress plugin listing], [https://apps.shopify.com/proxyai Shopify App Store listing] [ref: ProxyAi, Shopify App Store], feature and add-on guides

== Integrations ==
ProxyAI offers integrations for WordPress, Shopify and Wix [ref: Wix, ProxyAI Help]. The WordPress plugin provides a dashboard within WordPress administration and supports WooCommerce features when WooCommerce is installed. The Shopify app runs inside Shopify administration and connects the chatbot to the store catalogue, orders and cart. The Wix integration places a chat bubble on a Wix site and can connect to Wix Stores for product and checkout assistance. ProxyAI also supports web chat, voice, WhatsApp, Telegram, LINE, Messenger, Instagram and Discord. WordPress plugin listing, Shopify guide, Wix guide, channel integrations [ref: Channel Integrations, ProxyAI Help]

Shopify supports building a cart during chat. Wix can prepare a checkout link, but its guide says it cannot modify an existing shopper cart.

data.title: Manuel da Silva Rosa
data.text:
Manuel da Silva Rosa (born 1961), also known as Manuel Rosa, is a Portuguese-American historian, author, and researcher known for his publications on Age of Discovery subjects and the identity and origins of Christopher Columbus.

Rosa holds a doctorate in Insular and Atlantic History (15th–20th centuries) from the University of the Azores and he is associated with CHAM Açores, part of the Centre for the Humanities (CHAM – NOVA FCSH). His research examines the historical identification of the Genoese Cristoforo Colombo with Don Cristóbal Colón, the Admiral and Viceroy of the Indies.

His books on Columbus have been published in Portugal, Spain, Poland, Lithuania, Brazil, and the United States.

== Biography ==

Manuel da Silva Rosa was born in Vila do Valverde, Madalena, on Pico Island in the Azores, in 1961. He emigrated to the United States in 1973.

In addition to his historical research, Rosa is a poet, musician, and producer.

He began independently investigating the origins and identity of Christopher Columbus in 1991.

== Academic career and research ==

=== Doctoral research ===

On April 12, 2023, Rosa defended his doctoral dissertation in Insular and Atlantic History (15th–20th centuries) at the University of the Azores.

The dissertation, entitled CRISTOFORO COLOMBO versus CRISTÓBAL COLÓN: Cristoforo Colombo, the weaver from Genoa, was not Don Cristóbal Colón, the navigator from Iberia, examined the documentary and biographical evidence traditionally used to identify the Genoese Cristoforo Colombo with the navigator Don Cristóbal Colón.

His doctoral supervisors were João Paulo Oliveira e Costa, professor at NOVA University Lisbon, and Avelino de Freitas de Meneses, professor at the University of the Azores.

The dissertation was approved unanimously with distinction by the examining committee.

[ref: Manuel da Silva Rosa defendeu provas de doutoramento em História Insular e Atlântica (séculos XV-XX), Notícias UAc]

=== Research into Christopher Columbus ===

Rosa's historical investigations challenge the conventional identification of Don Cristóbal Colón, Admiral and Viceroy of the Indies, with Cristoforo Colombo, a member of a Genoese family associated with the wool trade.

His research examines royal correspondence, legal proceedings, genealogical records, chronicles, heraldry, and other archival evidence relating to the navigator.

Rosa argues that the surviving documentary record does not establish a continuous biographical connection between the Genoese Cristoforo Colombo and Don Cristóbal Colón. His conclusions differ from the conventional historical identification of Christopher Columbus as Genoese.

In Portugal na História: Uma Identidade (2022), historian João Paulo Oliveira e Costa discussed Rosa's research and its examination of the documentary evidence concerning Columbus's origins.

[ref: Portugal na História: Uma Identidade, Temas e Debates]

=== DNA investigations ===

Between 2003 and 2005, Rosa participated as a Portuguese historical researcher in investigations associated with the University of Granada's studies of the remains attributed to Christopher Columbus.

The investigations examined genetic evidence in connection with competing hypotheses about the navigator's origins.

=== Lectures and media appearances ===

Rosa has presented his research at academic conferences and public lectures in Europe and the United States.

On April 11, 2014, he delivered a lecture entitled "The Fraud of Columbus' History and Identity Exposed" at Duke University, sponsored by Mi Gente and the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies.

[ref: The Fraud of Columbus' History and Identity Exposed, Duke University]

His research has also been discussed in interviews with BBC Radio and WNPR and in television documentaries produced in Spain and Poland.

=== Santa María investigations ===

In 2014, Rosa contributed historical information to investigations concerning claims by underwater explorer Barry Clifford that he had discovered the remains of Columbus's flagship, the Santa María, off the coast of Haiti.

Rosa questioned the identification of the wreck and proposed an alternative interpretation of the vessel's fate.

His research was examined by UNESCO and Haitian authorities as part of their assessment of the archaeological claims.

[ref: La Santa María pudo haber sido quemada y no hundida, Diario de Navarra]

== Publications ==

=== Books ===

* O Mistério Colombo Revelado. With Eric James Steele. Ésquilo, Portugal, 2006. ISBN 978-9728605865.

* Colombo Português: Novas Revelações. Ésquilo, Portugal, 2009. ISBN 978-9898092533.

* Colón: La Historia Nunca Contada. Ésquilo, Spain, 2010. ISBN 978-9898092663.

* Kolumb: Historia Nieznana. Rebis, Poland, 2012. ISBN 978-8375107227.

* Colombo Português: Novas Revelações. Digital edition, Association Cristovao Colon, United States, 2012.

* Colombo: História do Mistério, Censura e Invenção. Volume I: Os Pontos Cardeais. Association Cristovao Colon, United States, 2013.

* Kolumbas: Atskleistoji istorija. Charidbė, Lithuania. ISBN 978-9955739449.

* Columbus: The Untold Story. Outwater Media Group, United States, 2016. ISBN 978-0578179315.

* Colombo: Mistério Resolvido. Arandis Editora, Portugal, 2017.

* Portugal e o Segredo de Colombo. Alma dos Livros, Portugal, 2019.

* Rozwiązana tajemnica Kolumba, syna Warneńczyka. Exemplum, Poland, 2020.

* Columbus in the Crosswinds. Comissão Cultural da Marinha, Portugal, 2024. ISBN 9789899065185.

* 1494: D. João II e o Segredo do Brasil. Alma dos Livros, Portugal, 2024.

* COLUMBUS versus COLÓN. Association Cristovao Colon, United States, 2024.

* 1494: D. João II e o Segredo do Brasil. Brazilian edition, Caravelas Editora, 2026.

* COLOMBO — Um Príncipe Português. Alma dos Livros, Portugal, 2026.

=== Academic articles ===

* Rosa, Manuel (2015). "Unraveling Riddles and Falsities of Christopher Columbus: His Nobility, the Location of Natividad, and the Santa Maria's True Fate." e-Legal History Review, No. 19, January 2015.

* Rosa, Manuel (2015). "A Will Without a Way: A Critical Review of How the Christopher Columbus Mayorazgo of 1498 Continues to Perpetrate a Fraud Against Historians and History." e-Legal History Review, No. 21, June 2015.

== Awards and recognition ==

* 1976 – Boston Globe Art Merit Award.

* 2002 – Lockheed Martin Lightning Award.

* 2015 – Special Recognition Award, American Institute of Polish Culture.

* 2016 – Columbus: The Untold Story included in IndieReader's selection of the best self-published books of 2016, published by The Huffington Post.

* 2017 – Independent Press Award, World History category.

* 2017 – MediaTravel Columbus Award, Łódź, Poland.

* 2018 – New York City Big Book Award.

* 2024 – Globe of Independence Award.
