data.title: Syed Tanveer Hussain Shah
data.text:
Syed Tanveer Hussain Shah

Syed Tanveer Hussain Shah, also published as Syed T. Shah and Tanveer H. Shah, is a software engineer and former university educator whose academic research has addressed educational leadership and the application of data analytics in higher education. He previously served as an Assistant Professor at the University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir and later worked at Microsoft. [ref: Borderless]

Education

Shah earned a Doctor of Education (Ed.D.) degree in Educational Administration from Dowling College in New York in 2016. His doctoral research examined the relationship between business analytics and decision-making among university executives, particularly in relation to student retention. [ref: Proquest]

Academic career

Shah worked at the University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir as a systems analyst beginning in 2003. Following his doctoral studies in the United States, he returned to the university and served as an Assistant Professor at its Institute of Education from 2017 to early 2018. [ref: LinkedIn]

In 2018, Shah relocated to the United States and subsequently joined Microsoft as a software engineer. [ref: Borderless]

Research

Shah’s academic work has focused on educational leadership, institutional decision-making, and big data analytics. [ref: School leadership journal]

In 2014, he co-authored Creating a Model that Empowers School Leaders with Muhammad Riaz, Mary Kelly, and Elsa-Sofia Morote. The paper was included in the proceedings of the Canada International Conference on Education (CICE-2014), held at Cape Breton University in Nova Scotia, Canada. Related research appeared in the International Journal for Cross-Disciplinary Subjects in Education under the title Presenting a Model That Leads School Leaders’ Empowerment. [ref: Conference proceedings]

In 2016, Shah completed his doctoral dissertation, Big Data Business Analytics and Informed Decision Making: Comparisons Between University Executives with High and Low Student Retention. [ref: Doctorate dissertation]

His chapter Big Data Analytics in Higher Education was published by IGI Global in 2018 in Maximizing Social Science Research Through Publicly Accessible Data Sets. The chapter examines the use of analytics to support university management and decision-making. [ref: IGI Global]

Selected publications

data.title: Red Rising (series)
data.text:
Red Rising is a science fiction novel series by American author Pierce Brown. Set in a future in which humanity has colonized the Solar System, the series depicts a hierarchical society divided into genetically and socially stratified groups known as Colors. The story follows a rebellion against the ruling class and the political, military, and social conflicts that result. [ref: Brown, Pierce, The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]

The series began with Red Rising in 2014, followed by Golden Son (2015) and Morning Star (2016). Brown continued the narrative with Iron Gold (2018), Dark Age (2019), and Light Bringer (2023). [ref: Red Rising, Publishers Weekly] [ref: Iron Gold, Publishers Weekly]

== Publication ==
The first three novels form the original trilogy. The later novels continue the story after the rebellion against the Society and expand the narrative to include the political challenges of governing the newly established Republic.

== Setting and themes ==
The novels take place in a future in which humanity has colonized the Solar System. Society is divided into Colors, hereditary castes associated with different social roles. Golds occupy the ruling class, while Reds perform much of the labor that supports the established order. The hierarchy is maintained through political power, social conditioning, and the use of technology.

The first novel follows Darrow, a Red miner on Mars who discovers that the social order rests on a deception. He undergoes physical transformation and training to infiltrate the Gold elite, with the aim of undermining the ruling system from within.

The series combines elements of dystopian fiction and space opera with political intrigue, military conflict, and classical imagery. The Science Fiction Encyclopedia compares aspects of the first novel with earlier science fiction and with the young-adult dystopian genre, while noting its emphasis on action, personal sacrifice, and the protagonist's rise through the social hierarchy.

Recurring themes include class conflict, revolution, authoritarianism, loyalty, sacrifice, and the difficulty of creating a stable political order after the overthrow of an established regime.

== Plot ==
=== Original trilogy ===
The original trilogy follows Darrow, a member of the Red caste who works underground on Mars. After learning that the surface has long been habitable for the ruling Golds, he joins a revolutionary movement and undergoes extensive surgery and training to infiltrate Gold society.

In Red Rising, Darrow enters the Institute, an institution where young Golds compete in a violent test of leadership and survival. Golden Son follows his increasing involvement in Gold politics and military affairs. Morning Star continues the conflict between the rebellion and the Society.

=== Second series ===
The second series takes place after the initial rebellion has succeeded in overthrowing the Society's rule on Mars. The new Republic faces the challenge of extending its political order across the Solar System while confronting opponents of the revolution.

Iron Gold broadens the narrative through multiple points of view and examines the aftermath of revolution. Its plot includes military campaigns, political disputes within the Republic, and the experiences of people whose lives have not improved as much as the revolution promised.

Dark Age and Light Bringer continue the military and political conflicts among the competing factions of the Solar System.

== Characters ==
The novels feature characters from several castes and political factions. The later books expand beyond Darrow's perspective to portray the consequences of the rebellion for different groups within the Solar System.

* Darrow — A Red-born revolutionary who infiltrates the Gold ruling class and becomes a central military leader.
* Virginia au Augustus — Known as Mustang, a Gold leader associated with the Republic.
* Sevro au Barca — Darrow's ally and a prominent member of the Howlers.
* Cassius au Bellona — A Gold swordsman whose personal relationships and political loyalties affect the conflict.
* Adrius au Augustus — Known as the Jackal, a political strategist and adversary of Darrow.
* Lysander au Lune — A major character in the later novels whose political ambitions influence the struggle over the future of the Solar System.
* Lyria of Lagalos — A Red whose experiences offer a perspective on the effects of the revolution on ordinary people.
* Ephraim ti Horn — A former soldier whose storyline explores survival and the consequences of political upheaval.

== Reception ==
=== Critical reviews ===
Red Rising received reviews from professional book-review publications. Publishers Weekly described the novel as an action-driven science fiction story, but criticized its originality and plausibility. The review discussed Darrow's background as a Red miner, the caste system on Mars, and his recruitment to infiltrate Gold society.

In its entry on Pierce Brown, the Science Fiction Encyclopedia discusses the first trilogy's relationship to young-adult dystopian fiction and earlier science fiction. It describes the narrative as combining action, personal sacrifice, and the protagonist's rise within a rigid social order.

Publishers Weekly reviewed Iron Gold as a continuation of the original trilogy's setting. Its review highlighted the novel's expanded points of view, political tensions, and focus on individual characters amid large-scale military events.

=== Commercial performance ===
Dark Age appeared on Publishers Weekly bestseller charts in August 2019. The publication's science fiction list placed the novel at No. 2 for the week of August 12, 2019. [ref: Publishers Weekly Bestseller Lists: Science Fiction, Publishers Weekly]

Light Bringer also appeared on Publishers Weekly hardcover fiction bestseller charts following its 2023 publication. The chart records its position on the list. [ref: Publishers Weekly Bestseller Lists: Hardcover Fiction, Publishers Weekly]

== Adaptations ==
=== Board game ===
A tabletop game based on Red Rising was published by Stonemaier Games in 2021. The game adapts characters and castes from the novels into a card-based strategy game. [ref: Red Rising Game Review, Meeple Mountain]

A review by Meeple Mountain discussed the game's card-based mechanics, components, and relationship to the source material. [ref: Red Rising Game Review, Meeple Mountain]

=== Screen adaptation ===
A screen adaptation of Red Rising has been pursued. Coverage of the adaptation has discussed the challenges of translating the novels' large cast, detailed social hierarchy, and expansive setting to the screen. [ref: The Red Rising Movie Is Going To Be Really Hard To Get Right, For A Few Reasons, CinemaBlend]

data.title: Kelley Dennison
data.text:
Kelley Anne Dennison is an American political candidate, licensed massage therapist, small-business owner, and activist from Colorado. [ref: Kelley Dennison, Ballotpedia] [ref: Kelley Dennison for Congress, Kelley Dennison for Congress] She became the Republican nominee for Colorado's 2nd congressional district in the 2026 United States House of Representatives election. [ref: Kelley Anne Dennison wins GOP race for Colorado’s 2nd Congressional District] Her campaign has focused on economic affordability, environmental conservation, family policy, education reform, and constitutional rights. [ref: Kelley Dennison, 27-year-old massage therapist, is Republican nominee to face Rep. Joe Neguse in 2nd District, Colorado Public Radio]

== Early life and education ==
Dennison is a Colorado native who has described growing up in a family where political issues and public affairs were openly discussed. [ref: 2nd Congressional District: Republican Kelley Dennison, Colorado Public Radio] According to her campaign interviews, her interest in politics developed partly through high school civics and history classes and concerns about the rising cost of living. [ref: At 27, Estes Park's Dennison brings an unconventional face to Colorado GOP politics, Estes Valley Voice]

She attended Estes Park High School and completed professional training in massage therapy at the Academy of Natural Therapy, receiving a certificate in 2023. [ref: Kelley Dennison, Ballotpedia]

== Career ==

=== Business and massage therapy ===
Before entering electoral politics, Dennison worked as a licensed massage therapist and small-business owner. Her professional background includes operating Wind Bear Holistic Healing, abusiness associated with massage and holistic wellness services.

She has presented her experience working directly with clients and running a small business as a basis for understanding the financial pressures faced by ordinary workers, families, and entrepreneurs.

=== Entry into politics ===
Dennison's first reported involvement in electoral politics included working as a campaign staffer for Republican congressional candidate Adam DeRito. She subsequently decided to run for Congress herself, citing concerns about affordability, government accountability, and the limited participation of younger Americans in politics.

Her candidacy attracted attention because she entered a high-profile congressional race without having previously held elected public office.

== Political career ==

=== 2026 congressional campaign ===
In 2026, Dennison sought the Republican nomination for Colorado's2nd congressional district. She won the Republican primary on June 30, 2026, defeating Christina Blunt and becoming the party's nominee for the general election against Democratic incumbent Joe Neguse.

The race drew attention because the district had historically favoured Democrats. In the 2024 election, Neguse won nearly 70% of the vote, making Dennison's campaign a challenge in a district where Republicans faced a significant electoral disadvantage.

Dennison promoted a grassroots campaign aimed at engaging younger voters and residents of Colorado's mountain communities. She also advocated for greater participation by members of Generation Z in political life.

== Political positions ==
Dennison's campaign platform includes several major policy areas. The following summarizes positions she has publicly expressed; it does not imply that the proposals have been enacted.

=== Economic affordability ===
Dennison has advocated increasing the supply of housing, reducing regulations that she believes increase construction costs, and limiting large corporate investors' purchases of starter homes. Shehas also emphasized the cost of living for working families and younger Coloradans.

=== Environmental conservation ===
She supports responsible land use, conservation of forests and headwater ecosystems, and protection of watersheds. She has also emphasized the relationship between environmental stewardship, water security, and Colorado's outdoor recreation economy.

=== Family and education policy ===
Her campaign supports pro-family policies, greater parental involvement in education, and efforts to improve educational quality and practical career preparation. She also identifies veterans and senior citizens as groups deserving stronger support.

=== Constitutional rights and term limits ===
Dennison supports Second Amendment rights and has signed the U.S. Term Limits pledge, committing to support a constitutional amendment limiting congressional service. Her campaign frames these positions around individual liberty and government accountability.

=== Immigration and government accountability ===
She supports secure borders, enforcement of immigration laws, and more efficient legal immigration pathways. She has also called for greater transparency in government and cooperation across party lines.

== Public image and political significance ==
Dennison has been described in media coverage as an unconventional, younger Republican candidate. Her candidacy combines conservative positions on gun rights and government regulation with an emphasis on housing affordability, environmental conservation, and outreach to younger voters.

Her background as a small-business owner rather than a career politician has been a prominent part of her campaign identity. She has argued that ordinary citizens should participate more actively in public affairs instead of leaving political leadership exclusively to established politicians.

== Electoral status ==
As of October 18, 2026, Dennison is the Republican nominee in the 2026 general election for Colorado's 2nd congressional district.

data.title: Rorisons
data.text:
Rorisons (formerly Rorisons RMD) is a family owned agricultural lime and fertiliser company based in Mount Maunganui, New Zealand. It quarries limestone at Aria in the King Country and supplies lime, fertiliser and soil testing services to farms in the central North Island.

== History ==

The business traces its origins to I M Rorison Ltd, a transport company that Ian Marshall Rorison and his wife Nora started in Tokoroa in 1950, carting timber and fertiliser. [ref: Rorisons, RuralHQ]
In 1957 the family moved to Tauranga, where the company became a bulk haulage business and was soon renamed Rorison Mainline Limited. [ref: Progress, Power, Pride, New Zealand Trucking]

In the mid 1960s Rorison took over a lime and serpentine quarry at Aria, about nine kilometres inland from Piopio. Its lime was sold as Rorison Aglime, and its serpentine was supplied to fertiliser works as a source of magnesium for serpentine superphosphate.

During a farming downturn in 1971, the New Zealand Lumber Company took over Rorison Mainline. Rorison kept the Aria quarry through Rorison Mineral Developments Limited (RMD) and later rebuilt the trucking fleet. The restructured business was based at Mount Maunganui. He died in 1982, and his son Gary took over management of the business.

By 2009 the company, trading as Rorisons RMD under managing director Mike Rorison, described itself as a third generation family business. That year its lime and LimeMag, a lime and serpentine blend, received BioGro and Asure organic certification. The company said the Aria quarry held the only commercially quarried serpentine seam in the North Island. [ref: A soil solution to fit fertiliser budget, SunLive]

In 2013 Rorisons RMD agreed to manufacture Hatuma Dicalcic Phosphate, a fertiliser from the Hawke's Bay company Hatuma, at its Aria quarry. [ref: Environmentally friendly fertiliser comes to the King Country, Sustainability Matters] The company now describes itself as a fourth generation family business. [ref: About Rorisons, Rorisons] Mike Rorison is managing director and Rona Rorison a director, and Matt and Kate Rorison also work in the business. [ref: Our Team, Rorisons]

I M Rorison bulk haulage truck.jpg|An I M Rorison Ltd bulk haulage truck and tipping trailer, 1950s
Rorisons Mainline truck at wharf.jpg|Rorisons Mainline truck No. 64 beside the ship Imperial Star, about 1970

== Operations ==
Rorisons has sites at Aria and on Aria Road near Piopio in the King Country, and its head office is in Mount Maunganui in the Bay of Plenty. [ref: Rorisons, Rorisons] It supplies farms in the Waikato, King Country, Taranaki, Bay of Plenty and Hawke's Bay regions, both directly and through rural consultants and spreading contractors.

Products include agricultural lime and lime based products such as CalciMag and CalciFeed, lime for aerial topdressing, limestone aggregates for farm tracks, fertilisers sourced in New Zealand and overseas, and custom fertiliser blends, including [https://www.biogro.co.nz BioGro] certified organic options. These are supplied for dairy, sheep and beef, and cropping farms, both conventional and regenerative. The company also offers soil and herbage testing, fertiliser recommendations and nutrient management advice.

data.title: 2027 Atlantic hurricane Season
data.text:
The 2027 Atlantic hurricane season is the future event for the annual Atlantic hurricane season in the Northern Hemisphere. The season officially begins on June 1, 2027, and ends on November 30, 2027. These dates, adopted by convention, historically describe the period in each year when most subtropical or tropical cyclogenesis occurs in the Atlantic Ocean (over 97%). The National Hurricane Center (NHC) will begin issuing regular Tropical Weather Outlooks on May 15, 2027, about two weeks prior to the start of the season.

In advance of, and during, each hurricane season, several forecasts of hurricane activity are issued by national meteorological services, scientific agencies, and noted hurricane experts. These include forecasters from the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)'s Climate Prediction Center, Tropical Storm Risk (TSR), the United Kingdom's Met Office, and Colorado State University (CSU). The forecasts include weekly and monthly changes in significant factors that help determine the amount of tropical storms, hurricanes, and major hurricanes within a particular season.

According to NOAA and CSU, the average hurricane season between 1991 and 2020 contained about 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes and 3 major hurricanes (Category 3 and higher), as well as an accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) index of 72–111 units. Broadly speaking, ACE is the measure of the power of a tropical or subtropical cyclone multiplied by the length of time it existed. ACE is only calculated for full advisories on specific tropical or subtropical cyclones reaching wind speeds of 39 mph (63 km/h) or higher. NOAA typically describes a season as above-average, average, or below-average depending on the cumulative ACE index, but the number of tropical storms, hurricanes or major hurricanes can also be considered.

data.title: Hurricane Trudy (2026)
data.text:
Hurricane Trudy is an active hurricane west of Mexico. It is the twenty-first named storm, twelfth hurricane, and tenth major hurricane of the 2026 Pacific hurricane season.

==Meteorological history ==

On October 6, at 06:00 UTC, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) stated a tropical wave entered the East Pacific south of Guatemala, and started monitoring it for development in the next 7 days. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/xgtwo/gtwo_archive.php?basin=epac&fdays=7¤t_issuance=202610060600] On October 12, the NHC noted the disturbance gained a surface low and stated it had a very high chance of development. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/xgtwo/gtwo_archive.php?basin=epac&fdays=7¤t_issuance=202610120600] The next day, at 15:00 UTC, the NHC upgraded the low pressure area to a tropical depression, designating it as Twenty One-E. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.001.shtml]Six hours later, the depression intensified into a tropical storm and was given the name Trudy. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.002.shtml] By October 14, Trudy had been upgraded to Category 1, and rapidly strengthened to Category 3 the next day, with it expected to further strengthen into a Category 4. [ref: Hurricane Trudy approaches Mexico’s coast: What you need to know about its path, El Cronista]

However, the eye started to decay and it was no longer visible around 18:35 UTC. At the same time The Hurricane Hunters flew into the storm, and noticed that Trudy rapidly weakened below major hurricane strength. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.update.10161833.shtml] [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.014.shtml]

== Preparations ==
On October 15, The National Hurricane Center issued Tropical Storm Watches for southern Mexico. [ref: Hurricane Trudy strengthens; warnings issued along Pacific Coast, nj] The next day they were upgraded into Hurricane Warnings, with tropical storm watches and warnings being issued for additional areas around the coast. data.title: Kenneth Nelson (academic)
data.text:
Kenneth Tommy Nelson is a Swedish sociologist and the Barnett Professor of Social Policy at the University of Oxford. He is head of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention and a fellow of St Cross College, Oxford. [ref: Professor Kenneth Nelson, Department of Social Policy and Intervention] [ref: Professor Kenneth Nelson, St Cross College] He also holds a professorship at the Swedish Institute for Social Research (SOFI) at Stockholm University. [ref: Kenneth Nelson appointed professor at the University of Oxford, Stockholm University]

Nelson's research concerns comparative social policy and the welfare state, particularly poverty, social inequality, minimum-income protection and social rights.

== Education and career ==

Nelson studied sociology and social work at Stockholm University and completed a doctorate in sociology there in 2004. His dissertation, Fighting Poverty: Comparative Studies on Social Insurance, Means-tested Benefits and Income Redistribution, examined the anti-poverty effects of different forms of social protection across welfare states. [ref: Fighting Poverty: Comparative Studies on Social Insurance, Means-tested Benefits and Income Redistribution, Stockholm University] He subsequently worked at the Swedish Institute for Social Research (SOFI), becoming professor of sociology in 2014.

In 2023, Nelson joined the University of Oxford as Barnett Professor of Social Policy and became a fellow of St Cross College, Oxford. He subsequently became head of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention.

Nelson has held a number of positions in academic organisations and publishing. He served as a board member and co-chair of the European Network for Social Policy Analysis (ESPAnet), and is a member of the Board of Governors of the Foundation for International Studies on Social Security (FISS). [ref: ESPAnet – European Network for Social Policy Analysis] [ref: Foundation for International Studies on Social Security] He is a co-editor of the Journal of European Social Policy. [ref: Journal of European Social Policy: Editorial Board, SAGE Publications] Nelson has also served on the board of the Swedish Sociological Association, including as its president from 2020 to 2022, and is a former president of the Nordic Sociological Association. [ref: Sveriges sociologförbund]

Nelson directs the Social Policy Indicators (SPIN) database, a cross-national collection of institutional social-policy data maintained at Stockholm University. [ref: Social Policy Indicators Database, Stockholm University] [ref: The Social Policy Indicators (SPIN) database, International Journal of Social Welfare]

== Research ==

Nelson's research focuses on the development and consequences of welfare states and social policy from a comparative perspective. His work has examined poverty, income inequality, social rights, minimum-income protection, health, employment and intergenerational relations.

A substantial part of his research concerns the comparative measurement of social policy, including the use of institutional indicators of social rights and benefit entitlements to analyse differences between welfare states. [ref: Social citizenship rights and social insurance replacement rate validity: pitfalls and possibilities, Journal of European Public Policy] Through SPIN, Nelson has contributed to comparative data on the institutional structure of social protection across countries. [ref: The Social Policy Indicators (SPIN) database, International Journal of Social Welfare]

=== Minimum income protection ===

Nelson has conducted comparative research on minimum-income benefits and the relationship between social assistance, poverty and broader welfare-state institutions. His work has examined the adequacy of social assistance in relation to poverty thresholds and the relationship between minimum-income benefits and material deprivation. [ref: Social Assistance and EU Poverty Thresholds 1990–2008: Are European Welfare Systems Providing Just and Fair Protection Against Low Income?, European Sociological Review] [ref: Counteracting material deprivation: The role of social assistance in Europe, Journal of European Social Policy]

With Ive Marx, Nelson edited Minimum Income Protection in Flux (2012), a comparative study of changes in minimum-income protection in Europe. [ref: Minimum Income Protection in Flux, Palgrave Macmillan] The book was subsequently discussed in the academic literature, including in an independent review in the Journal of Social Policy. [ref: Review of Minimum Income Protection in Flux, Journal of Social Policy]

Nelson's later work with Rense Nieuwenhuis developed a framework for analysing benefit coverage that distinguishes coverage from the generosity of social benefits. [ref: Towards a new consolidated framework for analysing benefit coverage, Journal of European Social Policy]

=== Intergenerational social policy ===

Nelson has also studied the distribution of social protection between generations. With Simon Birnbaum, Tommy Ferrarini and Joakim Palme, he co-authored The Generational Welfare Contract: Justice, Institutions and Outcomes (2017), which examines how welfare states distribute social protection across childhood, working life and old age. [ref: The Generational Welfare Contract: Justice, Institutions and Outcomes, Edward Elgar]

The book's analysis of intergenerational social policy and the relationship between provision for different age groups was discussed in several scholarly reviews. [ref: Review of The Generational Welfare Contract: Justice, Institutions and Outcomes, Basic Income Studies] [ref: Review of The Generational Welfare Contract, Journal of Social Policy] [ref: Review of The Generational Welfare Contract: Justice, Institutions and Outcomes, Community, Work & Family] [ref: Review: Simon Birnbaum, Tommy Ferrarini, Kenneth Nelson and Joakim Palme, The Generational Welfare Contract, Intergenerational Justice Review]

=== Other research ===

Other areas of Nelson's research include the relationship between welfare states and health. Research with Johan Fritzell examined the association between minimum-income benefits and mortality, while work with Tommy Ferrarini and Ola Sjöberg examined unemployment insurance and self-rated health. [ref: Welfare states and population health: The role of minimum income benefits for mortality, Social Science & Medicine] [ref: Unemployment insurance and deteriorating self-rated health in 23 European countries, Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health]

More recent research has examined the relationship between social policy and climate change, including the role of social protection in addressing the distributional consequences of decarbonisation and public support for environmental taxation. [ref: Social sustainability in the decarbonized welfare state, Global Social Policy] [ref: Decarbonization Politics for All: Means-Tested Social Assistance, Eco-Social Values, and Public Support for Increased Fossil Fuel Taxes in Europe, Regulation & Governance]

== Selected publications ==

* Minimum Income Protection in Flux, Palgrave Macmillan
* The Generational Welfare Contract: Justice, Institutions and Outcomes, Edward Elgar
* Social Policy in Changing European Societies: Research Agendas for the 21st Century, Edward Elgar
* Social Sustainability in Ageing Welfare States, Edward Elgar

data.title: Applied Optoelectronics
data.text:
----

Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. (AOI) is an American company that designs and manufactures fiber-optic networking products and optical semiconductor components. It is headquartered in Sugar Land, Texas, and its common stock trades on the NASDAQ under the symbol AAOI. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. Common Stock (AAOI), Nasdaq] The company was founded in 1997 by Chih-Hsiang (Thompson) Lin and completed its initial public offering in 2013. [ref: Form DEF 14A (proxy statement), Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. / SEC]

The company's products include optical transceivers for data centers, equipment for cable television (CATV) broadband networks, and lasers and components for telecommunications and fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) applications. [ref: Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. / U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission] As of December 31, 2025, the company had 4,691 employees. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics: Number of Employees 2012-2025, MacroTrends]

== History ==
Applied Optoelectronics was incorporated in Texas on February 28, 1997, by Chih-Hsiang (Thompson) Lin, who had worked as a research scientist and research associate professor at the University of Houston. The company reincorporated in Delaware in March 2013.

In 2000, AOI opened its headquarters and manufacturing facility in Sugar Land, Texas. [ref: AOI Opens New Manufacturing Facility, Moves Operations, Compound Semiconductor] Its early operations focused on semiconductor lasers and optical components.

AOI began trading on the Nasdaq on September 26, 2013, under the symbol AAOI. Its initial public offering was priced at $10 per share, below the proposed range of $13 to $15. The company sold 3.6 million shares and received approximately $33.5 million in net proceeds. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics sets pricing for IPO, PE Hub] [ref: Applied Optoelectronics shares fall after $36M IPO, www.ksl.com] [ref: Applied Optoelectronics - 10-Q quarterly report FY2013 Q3, companiesmarketcap.com]

In 2016, the company's two largest customers accounted for approximately three-quarters of its revenue, while its ten largest customers accounted for more than 95%. [ref: Microsoft is a big customer of Hortonworks and Applied Optoelectronics, CNBC]

In August 2017, AOI disclosed a slowdown in demand from a large data center customer, after which its stock price declined. [ref: Mad About Your Loss in Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) Stock? Don't Sue!, Nasdaq] The company subsequently disclosed quality issues involving certain lasers and transceivers. Shareholders filed securities class-action lawsuits against AOI and two of its officers. [ref: In re Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. Securities Litigation — Stipulation and Agreement of Settlement (S.D. Tex.), SEC filing / official settlement site] One consolidated action was settled for $15.5 million, with the settlement funded by the company's directors' and officers' insurance.

In December 2022, AOI entered a supply agreement with a technology customer to manufacture certain lasers, and in June 2023 it signed a further agreement covering design and assembly services. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) enters supply agreement with Microsoft Corporation, StreetInsider]

In March 2025, AOI entered into a transaction agreement with a customer that included a warrant to purchase up to 7,945,399 shares at an exercise price of $23.6954 per share, exercisable until March 13, 2035. [ref: Form 8-K (Amazon transaction agreement and warrant), Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. / SEC]

== Products ==

=== Optical transceivers ===
AOI manufactures optical transceivers for data center and networking applications. Its products include transceivers with data rates ranging from 40G to 1.6T and use form factors including SFP, QSFP, QSFP-DD and OSFP. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics demonstrating new transceiver product portfolio at OFC, www.semiconductor-today.com]

In the first quarter of 2026, the company reported its first volume shipment of 800G products. [ref: 1AAOI - Applied Optoelectronics Inc, Morningstar] In March 2026, AOI announced a volume order for 1.6T data center transceivers. [ref: AOI receives first volume order of 1.6T data center transceivers, Light Reading]

=== Semiconductor components ===
AOI manufactures semiconductor laser chips and optical components used in its products. It fabricates lasers using a combination of molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD), and supplies lasers and laser subassemblies to other equipment and transceiver manufacturers.

=== Cable broadband ===
AOI supplies equipment for hybrid fiber-coaxial cable television networks. In September 2022 it introduced HFC products under the Quantum Bandwidth brand, including amplifiers and remote-management software. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics Showcases New Family of HFC Products Under Its 'Quantum Bandwidth' Brand Name, www.gophotonics.com] [ref: AOI adds smarts to cable amps with 'QuantumLink', Light Reading]

In July 2025 Charter Communications certified AOI's 1.8 GHz amplifiers and QuantumLink software for deployment in its network. [ref: Charter certifies AOI's 1.8 GHz amplifiers for cable upgrades including extended Docsis, Telecompaper] [ref: AOI Certified by Charter Communications, Converge Digest] In 2026 AOI announced that it was supporting Mediacom's with Quantum Bandwidth amplifiers and software for a DOCSIS 4.0 network upgrade. [ref: Mediacom advances DOCSIS 4.0 network upgrades with AOI Quantum Bandwidth, Fierce Network]

== Manufacturing and operations ==
AOI has manufacturing and research-and-development facilities in the United States, Taiwan and China. Its Sugar Land, Texas headquarters houses laser and laser-component fabrication, data center transceiver production, and research and development. Through subsidiaries, the company operates facilities in Taipei, Taiwan and Ningbo, China, and maintains a research-and-development facility in Atlanta, Georgia. [ref: 1.8GHz Cable Plant Signal Generator, Digicomm]

AOI is developing a 210,000-square-foot manufacturing facility adjacent to its Sugar Land headquarters. The Office of the Governor of Texas said the project represented more than $279 million in capital investment and was expected to create about 500 jobs. [ref: $20M state grant to fuel semiconductor expansion in Sugar Land, create 500 jobs, KPRC] In April 2026 the company was awarded a $20,852,518 grant from the Texas Semiconductor Innovation Fund to support the expansion. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics Gets $21M Grant to Help Build $280M Plant in Texas, Industrial Equipment News]

In 2026, AOI added three buildings between Pearland and Missouri City, Texas, to its Houston-area operations and reported plans to increase its combined 800G and 1.6T transceiver production capacity. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics Q1 2026 Earnings Report, Marketbeat.com] [ref: AOI Expands Its Houston-Area Footprint to 900,000 Square Feet to Increase Capacity and Support Future Growth, investors.ao-inc.com]

== Finances ==
AOI reported 2025 revenue of $455.7 million, compared with $249.4 million in 2024. Its 2025 GAAP gross margin was 30%, and its net loss was $38.2 million, compared with a $186.7 million net loss in 2024. [ref: AOI Reports Record Q4 2025 Revenue, Expands Datacenter Capacity for 2026, Converge Digest]

For the first quarter of 2026, AOI reported revenue of $151.1 million and a GAAP net loss of $14.3 million, and it completed a public equity offering that raised approximately $382.4 million. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) Financials 2026 - Income Statement and Balance Sheet $AAOI, www.marketbeat.com] [ref: Form 8-K (First Quarter 2026 results), Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. / SEC]

data.title: Oscar Lindsey
data.text:
Oscar Robert Lindsey (born May 1, 2002) is an American singer, songwriter, and multi-instrumentalist. [ref: Oscar Lindsey on Apple Music, Apple Music] Born and raised in Nashville, Tennessee, to a musical family, Lindsey has released five studio albums. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Artist Page, Mom + Pop Music] He is best known for his indie folk-rock sound, characterized by introspective lyricism. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Interview, Official Charts] Alongside his music, Lindsey has documented an interest in liminal spaces, creating numerous videos exploring the concept. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Official YouTube Channel, YouTube]
== Early life ==
Raised by his father, Grammy-nominated American country music songwriter and record producer Chris Lindsey, and his mother, American author and songwriter Aimee Mayo, Lindsey gained experience with music at a young age, though he has admitted that he did not truly love music until he was in middle school. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Chats Blissfully Melancholic New Album 'Sunshine', Ones to Watch] [ref: Oscar Lindsey Live in the Library, WUTC] [ref: Tape Recorders, OCD and Bo Burnham: In Conversation with Oscar Lindsey, Strand Magazine] At age 14, inspired by Bo Burnham, he decided to learn all of Burnham's songs on the piano before later shifting to the guitar. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Instagram Post, Instagram] [ref: Oscar Lindsey on Sunshine, Virality and Life, The Music Box Media] In high school, he made comedy songs and rap music on GarageBand. His first self-released projects were the EP Tony Tapes and its single "23 to Go". Once Lindsey learned how to use DistroKid to distribute music onto Spotify, he took a short hiatus and began making more serious music in 2022 after discovering The Beatles. The Beatles became one of his biggest influences alongside Paul Simon, Ween, Todd Rundgren, Mac DeMarco, Elliott Smith, and Alex G—influences that became prominent in his work.
== Career ==
=== 2022–2025: Independent releases and Glitter ===
In 2022, Lindsey self-released the singles "Petals" and "All of My Friends", as well as the EP Airbag. In 2022, according to Lindsey, he was arrested for painting graffiti; he came out of the experience wanting to commit fully to music, and the following year he released his debut studio album, Look I Caught A Fish. [ref: Oscar Lindsey – Live set at the beach, YouTube]

Ahead of the album's March 8, 2023 release, he issued the lead single "Big Star". Recorded on a tape machine to achieve a lo-fi sound, Look I Caught A Fish began a prolific string of independent releases. He followed it later that year with his second album, Dinosaur (December 4, 2023), which included the single "If I Was a Bird", as well as the standalone single "If I Could Hold You Again" featuring his brother, Levi Lindsey. In 2024, he self-released his third studio album, Rocky Mountain Toast (April 11), and the EP Magic Eight Ball (September 7).

For his fourth album, Glitter, Lindsey decided to take a more serious approach by spending significantly more time on its production. As Lindsey stated, "Glitter was the first one where I was like, 'Okay, I want to step everything up.'" Self-released on July 19, 2025, Glitter was Lindsey's first project to be professionally mixed and recorded entirely on a computer, with the exception of the track "I Wanna Feel". [ref: Oscar Lindsey Instagram Post, Instagram] The album was supported by two singles, "Ruby" and "Forever's Such a Long Time", both of which were released with accompanying music videos. The music video for "Forever's Such a Long Time" was shot on 8mm film by Christian Modica, who also directed the video alongside Lindsey as co-director. [ref: Oscar Lindsey - Forever's Such a Long Time (Official Video), YouTube] Following the release of Glitter, from September 2025 to March 2026, Lindsey showcased his interest in liminal spaces and filmmaking by releasing a series of YouTube videos covering liminal spaces, nostalgia, and various niche topics.

=== 2026–present: Mom + Pop Music and Sunshine ===
In May 2026, Lindsey signed with the independent music booking agency Ground Control Touring, [ref: Oscar Lindsey Artist Page, Ground Control Touring] [ref: Oscar Lindsey Instagram Post, Instagram] and later that month, he signed with the New York-based independent record label Mom + Pop Music. While Lindsey's previous albums had been recorded on GarageBand, his next album, Sunshine, was recorded using Logic Pro. On June 12, 2026, Lindsey released "Metal Through Her Lips", the lead single from Sunshine, via Mom + Pop Music. [ref: Metal Through Her Lips - Single by Oscar Lindsey, Apple Music] The song went viral on TikTok, which helped further launch his career. Speaking about the song's social media popularity, Lindsey said, "It makes more sense looking at it retroactively, but I just had no idea that it was gonna happen. I always believed in myself and thought it would happen, but I'm just grateful that it happened now." Leading up to the release of Sunshine, he released the singles "Flip a Coin" and "Painting the Walls" under Mom + Pop Music. [ref: Oscar Lindsey to Release SUNSHINE LP, Shares New Single, BroadwayWorld] On October 16, 2026, Lindsey released the self-produced album Sunshine via Mom + Pop Music, marking his label debut. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Serves Up Vulnerability with a Side of Indie Charm on Sunshine, Jammerzine] Lindsey described the album as "every phase of an early-20s, fed-up love story." Rather than performing every instrument himself as he had done on his previous releases, Lindsey collaborated on the album with James Eichman and several other musician friends. Sunshine was also Lindsey's first project to receive a vinyl release. [ref: Sunshine by Oscar Lindsey, Bandcamp]
== Discography ==
=== Studio albums ===

* Sunshine (2026)

=== Extended plays ===

data.title: Ouled Djellal ( sheep )
data.text:
The Ouled Djellal (also known as the Algerian Arab or Western Thin-tailed) is a breed of domestic sheep native to the steppe and high plains of Algeria. It is the most dominant, widespread, and economically important sheep breed in the country, accounting for approximately 63% to 65% of the national flock with an estimated population of over 11 to 12 million head. It is primarily kept for meat production and wool, and is highly favored for its exceptional adaptability to arid and semi-arid pastoral systems.

== History ==
The breed takes its name from the town of Ouled Djellal, located southwest of Biskra, which represents its historical cradle. Historical hypotheses suggest that the thin-tailed, fine-wooled ancestors of the breed may have been originally introduced to North Africa from Italy by the Romans during the fifth century.

Due to its high commercial profitability and productivity, the breed expanded dramatically over the late 20th and early 21st centuries. Driven by the mechanization of the steppe and changing transportation infrastructures, its population increased from roughly 10 million in 1989 to over 11–12 million head, overrunning the geographical ranges of smaller native breeds. Today, it has spread far beyond its central-eastern Algerian origin into the western steppes and cross-border regions of western Tunisia.

== Characteristics ==
The Ouled Djellal is a large, long-legged, and slender thin-tailed breed explicitly built for high mobility and long-distance walking across sparse rangelands. It is entirely unicolored white, with white skin, a thin head, a convex or sub-convex facial profile, and long, drooping ears. The fleece is white and consists of a light, refined, carpet-grade wool. Rams generally display strong, spiral horns, whereas the ewes are typically polled (hornless).

At maturity, rams average 81 kg (with some selection strains reaching up to 140 kg) in weight and stand approximately 84 cm tall at the withers. Ewes average 49 kg (ranging up to 75 kg in optimized systems) and stand about 74 cm tall.

The breed is an exceptionally hardy and active forager, showing remarkable tolerance to extreme heat and prolonged nutritional stress in arid environments. Under standard management systems, ewes demonstrate high maternal capacity and produce an average litter size of 1.5 lambs. Lambs display excellent growth potential and rapid fattening profiles, typically starting at a birth weight of 3.5 kg and scaling efficiently to 30 kg by five months of age. Ewes also maintain a substantial dairy performance, lactating for approximately 180 days and yielding around 75 kg of milk.

== Economic Importance ==
The Ouled Djellal serves as the definitive cornerstone of Algerian agropastoralism and food security. It is the absolute reference breed for the national Eid al-Adha holiday market, commanding the highest buyer demand, commercial volume, and investment yields across local livestock corridors. Its meat is highly valued, and the breed produces a heavier, fat-retentive carcass profile compared to smaller regional types.

== Genetic Homogenization Impact ==
The commercial superiority of the Ouled Djellal has driven a widespread trend toward livestock homogenization across the North African steppes. To maximize economic returns, pastoralists throughout western Algeria have systematically introduced heavy Ouled Djellal rams into native western herds. This aggressive crossbreeding practice has resulted in severe genetic dilution and the absorption of smaller indigenous breeds—most notably pushing the native, high-meat-quality Hamra breed to the brink of extinction.

data.title: Kirenia Alvarez
data.text:
Kirenia Álvarez, known professionally as KIKI, is a Cuban visual artist based in Miami, Florida, who works in pigmented epoxy resin. She is the founder of KIKI by Kirenia Alvarez LLC, and her brand name, KIKI BY KIRENIA ALVAREZ, is a federally registered trademark for works of art of epoxy resin. Álvarez describes her resin wall pieces as "jewelry for walls".

== Background ==
Álvarez was born on November 16, 1983, in Guanabacoa, Havana, Cuba. Her family won the United States visa lottery and emigrated to the U.S. in March 1998; she was raised in Hialeah, Florida, where she attended Hialeah High School. She studied Web Page Design at Florida National College in 2001. Álvarez began working in the banking industry in 2008, starting as a receptionist, and worked in that field for about fifteen years. In a 2025 interview, she said she discovered epoxy resin as an artistic medium during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, and that developing her first resin piece took more than six months.

== Career ==
Álvarez works from Miami, Florida, through her company KIKI by Kirenia Alvarez LLC, organized in Florida in 2021. In 2022, the mark KIKI BY KIRENIA ALVAREZ was registered with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (Reg. No. 6728425) for "works of art of epoxy resin".

In June 2021, her work went on sale at the Kendall branch of El Dorado Furniture in Miami; according to the artist's announcements at the time, her first two pieces there sold on July 4, 2021.

Her work has been presented at the Carnaval on the Mile juried art festival in Coral Gables.

Álvarez has discussed her work in Spanish-language media in South Florida, including a 2025 segment on Telemundo 51's Cuéntale a Marilys, a 2021 interview on MEGA TV with Jasmina Marazita, and an appearance on UniVista TV's El Show de Carlucho in 2022. In June 2025 she was the subject of a full episode of Emigrante Podcast, "Joyas de Pared, el Arte de Kirenia Alvarez" (Wall Jewelry: The Art of Kirenia Alvarez).

== Style and technique ==
Álvarez produces wall works in pigmented epoxy resin, building layered, high-gloss surfaces, frequently with gold-toned accents and onyx- or geode-like effects.

== Awards and recognition ==
* First Place, Mixed Media category, Carnaval on the Mile, Coral Gables (2023), for a resin depiction of La Catrina. The festival's awards program, run by the Kiwanis Club of Little Havana, grants first, second and third place awards in its Fine Arts Village categories. The festival's official winners board, published on Carnaval Miami's official event page, names her "1st Kiki Alvarez" in the Mixed Media category and shows her holding the first-place blue ribbon.
* In April 2021, she appeared on the cover of DMH Magazine.

== Exhibitions ==
* Carnaval on the Mile (juried art festival), Coral Gables, Florida, 2023.

data.title: Dionfest
data.text:
Dionfest is an English-language website covering festivals, cultural traditions, religious observances, regional fairs and related subjects in India and other parts of the world. Founded by Abhay Ramola, the website was launched on 4 January 2026. Its articles explore festival dates, historical backgrounds, customs, rituals and cultural significance.

The website's coverage extends beyond festival descriptions to include environmental issues associated with celebrations, sustainable event practices, cultural heritage, festival travel, planning advice and educational articles about traditions and communities. Its regional coverage includes festivals and fairs in Uttarakhand, alongside articles about Indian and international celebrations.

== History ==

DionFest was founded by Abhay Ramola and launched on 4 January 2026. The website was established as a digital publication focused on festivals, cultural traditions and subjects connected with public celebrations.

Ramola has an undergraduate academic background in history, having completed a Bachelor of Arts degree in the subject. His interest in historical events and cultural traditions is reflected in the website's coverage of regional festivals and celebrations in different parts of the world.

The website covers local festivals and fairs in Uttarakhand, including events associated with Uttarkashi and the Rawain Valley. It also publishes articles about festivals in other parts of India and internationally.

== Content and coverage ==

DionFest publishes informational articles about festivals and related cultural, historical, environmental and practical subjects.

=== Festivals around the world ===

The website covers festivals and celebrations from different countries and regions. Articles explore festival dates, origins, historical context, rituals, customs and the ways celebrations are observed by local communities.

Its international coverage includes festivals in Asia and other parts of the world, with individual articles examining the distinctive traditions and cultural practices associated with particular events.

=== Indian festivals ===

DionFest covers religious celebrations, seasonal festivals, regional fairs and other cultural observances in India. Articles discuss the background of festivals, traditional practices, community participation and variations in how celebrations are observed across regions.

The coverage includes both widely observed celebrations and regional events associated with particular communities and traditions.

=== Local festivals and fairs in Uttarakhand ===

Regional festivals form part of the website's coverage of Indian cultural heritage. Its articles include local fairs and religious traditions associated with Uttarakhand, particularly the Uttarkashi district and the Rawain Valley.

One event covered by the website is the Danda Devrana Mela, a religious fair associated with Rudreshwar Maharaj. The website's article describes the event's rituals, traditional music, folk dances, procession and significance to surrounding communities.

Ramola has also written about his personal connection with the fair and his childhood in Naugaon. His account describes his experience of the event and aspects of the surrounding regional traditions.

=== Cultural traditions and heritage ===

DionFest publishes articles exploring the stories, beliefs and customs associated with festivals. Topics include the historical development of celebrations, traditional practices, community identity and the cultural meanings attached to rituals.

The website also covers cultural heritage and exploration, including information intended to help readers understand traditions and the historical context of places associated with celebrations.

=== Environmental impact of festivals ===

DionFest covers environmental issues associated with festivals and large public celebrations. Topics include air pollution, noise pollution, waste generation, water use and the environmental footprint of events.

Articles examine how travel, food, energy consumption and event operations can affect the environment. This coverage also considers the challenges of managing waste and protecting nearby communities and natural environments during celebrations.

=== Green festivals and sustainability ===

The website publishes material about sustainable festival practices and approaches to reducing the environmental impact of celebrations. Topics include waste reduction, reusable materials, responsible resource use and environmentally considerate event planning.

This subject area explores ways to consider sustainability while respecting cultural traditions and the significance of celebrations to local communities.

=== Festival waste management ===

Waste management is another subject covered by DionFest. Articles discuss festival waste, including plastic, food waste and discarded flowers associated with religious and cultural events.

The coverage considers waste reduction, responsible disposal and recycling as part of broader discussions about the environmental effects of public celebrations.

=== Climate and festivals ===

DionFest examines the relationship between festivals, climate and resource consumption. Relevant topics include emissions associated with travel and event operations, energy use, accommodation and other factors that contribute to the environmental footprint of celebrations.

=== Festival travel, tips and advice ===

The website publishes practical articles for readers researching festivals or planning visits to cultural events. These include guidance on researching destinations, preparing for remote locations, considering accommodation and transport, understanding local customs and planning festival trips.

The articles complement the website's cultural coverage by addressing practical questions that arise when people research or attend celebrations.

=== Festival planning and research ===

DionFest also covers methods of researching and planning cultural experiences. Topics include verifying festival dates, consulting reliable sources, preparing itineraries and understanding the local context of events.

The information is intended to help readers approach festivals with greater awareness of their history, customs and practical requirements.

=== Environmental awareness and responsible celebrations ===

Some articles address responsible participation in festivals and the environmental considerations associated with public gatherings. Subjects include reducing waste, respecting sacred places, supporting local communities and considering the effects of tourism on cultural and natural environments.

== Editorial approach ==

DionFest publishes explanatory articles about festivals, cultural traditions and related subjects. The website maintains editorial information describing its approach to research, fact-checking, corrections and editorial standards.

Its coverage combines historical information with, in some cases, firsthand observations of regional festivals. Historical claims, dates and other factual details should be checked against reliable sources, including official announcements and published research where available.

== Founder ==

Abhay Ramola is the founder of DionFest. His interests include history, festivals and cultural traditions. His coverage of regional celebrations in Uttarakhand includes events he has attended personally.

data.title: Akido (healthcare company)
data.text:
Akido (formerly Akido Labs) is an American healthcare technology company based in Los Angeles, California. The company develops artificial intelligence software for clinical care and operates a network of healthcare services. Its products include ScopeAI, a clinical support system designed to assist with patient interviews, medical assessments, and treatment recommendations.

== History ==

Akido was founded in 2015 and emerged from work associated with the University of Southern California's Digital Health Lab. Initially, the company developed data and software tools for healthcare providers and public-service organizations, including tools intended to identify people at risk of adverse health or social outcomes. [ref: The AI Doctor Will See New York Ride-Share Drivers Now, The Wall Street Journal]

In 2022, the company shifted toward directly delivering healthcare services after acquiring a multispecialty medical practice in Southern California. It developed a healthcare network combining clinical services with its technology.

In May 2025, Akido announced a $60 million Series B funding round led by healthcare investment firm Oak HC/FT. The company said the funding would support the expansion of ScopeAI and its clinical network. [ref: Akido Raises $60 Million Series B to Expand Reach of ScopeAI, Business Wire] [ref: Akido: $60 Million Series B Secured For Health AI Platform, Pulse2]

In July 2026, the company announced that it was dropping "Labs" from its name and expanding its AI-supported healthcare model under the Akido and Akido Medical brands. [ref: Akido Announces the First AI-Native Health System in the US, PR Newswire]

== Products and services ==

=== ScopeAI ===

ScopeAI is a clinical artificial intelligence system developed by Akido. It guides patient interviews, suggests follow-up questions, organizes clinical information, and generates proposed diagnoses, tests, and treatments for review by a licensed clinician. According to reporting by the Wall Street Journal, physicians retain authority to approve, modify, or reject its recommendations.

Akido has used ScopeAI in clinical settings that include conventional clinics, street medicine programs, and services for populations that may have difficulty accessing healthcare. In 2025, the company announced plans to use the system in a healthcare program for rideshare drivers in New York City.

=== Healthcare services ===

Akido operates healthcare services in conjunction with its technology. Its programs have included street medicine for people experiencing homelessness and partnerships with community organizations. In January 2026, CalMatters reported on the use of ScopeAI in street medicine programs in California, including its role in helping outreach workers gather patient information for subsequent physician review. [ref: Can AI help make homeless Californians healthier?, CalMatters]

In 2025, Akido partnered with community organizations to launch an AI-assisted street medicine program in the San Francisco Bay Area. [ref: Akido Labs launches AI-powered street medicine program in SF, Fierce Healthcare]

== Reception and concerns ==

Supporters of AI-assisted clinical care argue that these systems may help clinicians serve more patients and improve access to care in underserved communities. Akido’s partnerships have included organizations serving people experiencing homelessness and workers with limited time to seek medical attention.

The use of AI to support diagnosis and treatment has also raised questions about accuracy, privacy, bias, informed consent, and the quality of care for vulnerable patients. In its 2026 reporting, CalMatters described concerns from healthcare and AI researchers about the risks of using diagnostic AI with people experiencing homelessness, including the need for appropriate human oversight and safeguards.

data.title: Jeffry Burchard
data.text:
----

Jeffry Burchard is an architect, urban designer, and educator. He is managing partner and design principal at Machado Silvetti and an Associate Professor in Practice of Architecture at the Harvard Graduate School of Design. [ref: Jeffry Burchard, Harvard Graduate School of Design] In 2020, he received the American Institute of Architects Young Architects Award, a national award recognizing early-career architects for leadership and contributions to the profession. [ref: Young Architect Award, American Institute of Architects] [ref: AIA Announces Winners of the 2020 Young Architects Award, Traditional Building]

== Education and academic career ==

Burchard studied architecture at the University of Idaho before completing the post-professional Master in Architecture II program at the Harvard Graduate School of Design, graduating with distinction in 2008.

He began teaching at Harvard GSD as a Design Critic in Architecture in 2012. He was appointed Assistant Professor in Practice of Architecture in 2017 and promoted to Associate Professor in Practice of Architecture in 2023. His teaching has included architecture core studios, thesis, and professional practice. [ref: Announcing GSD Faculty Appointments and Promotions for the 2023-2024 Academic Year, Harvard Graduate School of Design]

== Architectural career ==

After completing his graduate studies at Harvard, Burchard joined Machado Silvetti, initially working as senior project designer on New York University's Global Center for Academic and Spiritual Life. He later became a partner and principal of the practice and subsequently managing partner and design principal.

His work at Machado Silvetti has included architecture and urban-design projects in the United States and internationally. Harvard GSD identifies Burchard as project architect and urban designer for both the Tun Razak Exchange financial district in Kuala Lumpur and the Vietnamese-German University campus in Binh Duong Province, Vietnam.

In early 2025, Burchard and Stehanie Randazzo Dwyer succeeded founders Jorge Silvetti and Rodolfo Machado in the ownership and leadership of Machado Silvetti. According to The Architect's Newspaper, this succession followed a long-term process in which ownership and responsibility was gradually transferred to Burchard and Randazzo Dwyer. The two retained the companies name in order to continue the firm's identity. [ref: How are architecture firms using succession planning to build sustainable futures for their practice?, The Architect's Newspaper]

== Selected work ==

=== Denver Art Museum ===
Burchard was directly involved in the renovation and expansion of the Denver Art Museum campus. He focused on a new welcome center and working on the Gio Ponti-designed Martin Building. He was later interviews by public-radio station KUNC regarding the challenges of adapting the landmark museum without stripping it of its architectural character. [ref: Denver Art Museum Looks To Renovate A Work Of Art: Itself, KUNC]

The projects glass welcome center was later discussed on Engineering News-Record where Burchard was quoted on the decision to create a self-supporting glass enclosure and on the relationship between the new elliptical structure and the surrounding museum buildings. [ref: Glass Welcome Center Becomes Denver Art Museum's New 'Front Door', Engineering News-Record]

=== Downtown Cary Park ===

Burchard played a substantial role in the Machado Silvetti design team for Downtown Cary Park in Cary, North Carolina which was developed with OJB Landscape Architecture. [ref: Downtown Cary Park, American Institute of Architects]

In 2026, the seven-acre park was examined as a new civic center for Cary in Metropolis and the project's architecture and urban context was discussed with Burchard. [ref: In North Carolina, an Iconic Park Completes a Community, Metropolis] Subsequently, the project received national recognition from the AIA for regional and urban design.

=== Provincetown projects ===

Burchard has also worked on his fair share of redevelopment and preservation projects, specifically in Provincetown, Massachusetts. The Provincetown Independent reported on a waterfront redevelopment proposal designed by Burchard in 2023 and discussed how he intended to reconnect the site with Provincetown's historic maritime and industrial character. [ref: With More Space, Barker Unveils a Bigger Plan for the Waterfront, The Provincetown Independent]

The newspaper also covered Burchard's renovation design for the historic Lancy House at 230 commercial street. This article released in 2026 also included Burchard's plans to restore elements of its nineteenth-century Second Empire exterior while simultaneously adapting the building for its new public and commercial uses. [ref: Approvals Are in Hand, But Lancy House Renovations Hit Delays, The Provincetown Independent]

== Professional recognition ==

Burchard was one of few recipients of the AIA Young Architects Award back in 2020. The AIA describes the award as recognizing young architects who have demonstrated exceedingly impressive leadership skills and have made significant contributions to the profession early in their careers. This selection was also reported by independent architecture and building-industry publications. [ref: AIA gives Young Architects, Associates Awards, Metal Architecture]

data.text:
Lutheran High School of St. Charles County (commonly abbreviated Lutheran St. Charles and LHS), is an American private high school in St. Peters, Missouri. Founded in 1980, it is owned and operated by congregations of the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod.

== Academics ==
According to Niche's 2027 rankings, Lutheran St. Charles is the 59th best high school in Missouri and the 35th best in the St. Louis area. [ref: 2027 Lutheran High School of St. Charles County Rankings, [[Niche (company)]

== Athletics ==
Lutheran St. Charles is a full member of the Missouri State High School Activities Association (MSHSAA) and the Archdiocesan Athletic Association. The school's athletic teams are known as the Cougars. [ref: Athletics, Lutheran High School of St. Charles County] The Cougars have won a total of eleven state titles in six MSHSAA-sponsored different sports. [ref: MSHSAA Lutheran St. Charles High School State Championships, Missouri State High School Activities Association]

In 2021, LHS's soccer team beat St. Pius X 3–0 to win the Class 1 state championship. [ref: Soccer season wraps up with state championship games, Sports Illustrated] Just a few weeks later, the football team won the school's first and only state title in the sport after defeating Lamar 33–27 in the Class 2 state championship game. [ref: ‘We did it’; Lutheran St. Charles wins first-ever state football title, Fox 2 Now]

data.title: Finna
data.text:
Finna is a national search service and digital library platform that brings together the collections of archives, libraries, museums and research institutes in Finland. Its main public site, Finna.fi, lets anyone search, view and in many cases download material from more than 470 organisations through a single interface. The National Library of Finland maintains and develops the service, the Ministry of Education and Culture funds it, and CSC – IT Center for Science provides part of the technical operation.

Finna grew out of the ministry's National Digital Library project (2008–2017). It opened in beta in 2012 and launched formally in October 2013. As of September 2026 it held more than 19 million records, of which about four million had digital content available online. Searching and viewing need no account. Descriptive metadata exposed through its open API is released under the CC0 public domain dedication and needs no registration, while the reuse of images and other digital objects depends on licences and rights statements set by each contributing organisation.

== History ==

=== National Digital Library ===
Finna began as the public customer interface of the National Digital Library (Kansallinen digitaalinen kirjasto, KDK), a content and service project of the Ministry of Education and Culture that ran from 2008 to 2017. When the project ended, Finna became a separate unit of the National Library of Finland.

The project first planned to build the interface on off-the-shelf commercial software. In autumn 2011 the product chosen through competitive tendering did not meet the requirements, and the developers switched to open-source software. Within a few months they had built a demonstration system on VuFind. Development on the open-source stack started at the beginning of 2012, and a test version of the Finna.fi interface opened to the public later that year. The service entered beta production in December 2012.

=== Name ===
Candidate names included Etsin, Vipunen, Iso Jytky and Hakuli, and the developers used Morgan as a working title. The service received the name Finna on 4 May 2012, after which the finna.fi domain was registered.

=== Launch and growth ===
Finna launched formally in October 2013 after about eleven months in beta. The first partners were the Jyväskylä University Library, the National Archives of Finland, the National Library of Finland, the Finnish Forest Museum Lusto and other museums of the Kantapuu database, the National Board of Antiquities (now the Finnish Heritage Agency), the Tuusula Museum of Art and the Finnish National Gallery. More than 7.6 million records were searchable at launch. The University of Jyväskylä received the first organisation-specific Finna view.

The first version of the open API was built in 2015 and opened to the public on 3 February 2016, together with a search filter for more than 200,000 openly licensed images. In 2016 the Vaski libraries became the first public library consortium to use Finna as their online library. After the National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI) added its material, Finna also began to carry video; KAVI later moved its film database Elonet onto its own Finna view.

In 2017 Finna introduced Finna Street, a location-based search for historical photographs, and the National Board of Antiquities published more than 100,000 images in the service. A new management interface and a redesigned appearance followed in 2018.

Demand for digital material rose during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. That year Finna launched Finna Luokkahuone ("Finna Classroom"), a landing page of learning material for teachers, and began to include the Library of Open Educational Resources. A vision for 2021–2024, published in April 2020, set three focus areas: access to information and lifelong learning, user experience, and cooperation. At the end of 2021, 421 organisations contributed material, and the Shortcut to research page for open research publications and research material opened. The Finnish Food Authority and the Finnish Environment Institute became the first research institutes to join in 2022.

=== Since 2023 ===
Finna marked its tenth anniversary in 2023, when it held material from more than 470 customer organisations. A further vision for 2025–2028 was published in November 2023. In May 2024 Finna.fi added a Northern Sámi user interface and search support, funded by the Alfred Kordelin Foundation; the Sámi Museum Siida and the libraries of Lapland opened Northern Sámi interfaces at the same time.

In April 2024 the Helmet libraries of the Helsinki Metropolitan Area opened a new online library on the Finna platform. Several public libraries also dropped their own mobile apps in 2024, and by the end of that year 84% of Finnish municipal libraries used Finna as their online library.

In September 2026 the National Library released a redesigned Finna with a new brand and visual identity by the agency Werklig. The redesign streamlined the page structure and aimed to improve accessibility and use across devices.

== Organisation and funding ==
The National Library of Finland administers Finna and develops it together with the participating organisations, which remain responsible for their own content. All participating organisations form the Finna consortium; its steering body is the Finna consortium group, made up of representatives of the customer organisations. The Ministry of Education and Culture funds the service.

An organisation joins Finna by contract. Joining is free of charge for archives, libraries and museums in the administrative sector of the Ministry of Education and Culture.

In the original design of the National Digital Library, Finna was the public interface, and a separate service called Formula aggregated Finnish material to Europeana.

== Content ==
Finna.fi combines books, journals and articles, theses, photographs, works of art, museum objects, archival documents, maps, sheet music, sound recordings, video, games, learning material and research data. National databases in the index include Fennica, the Finnish national bibliography, and Viola, the Finnish national discography.

The figures below come from the public Finna API on 18 October 2026. They count records after deduplication: Finna merges matching records from different sources, mainly books, into a single search result.
