data.title: Have I Been Squatted
data.text:
----

Have I Been Squatted Inc. is a privately held cybersecurity company that works on domain intelligence. It builds a platform for finding typosquatted and lookalike domains, along with the websites and infrastructure tied to them, that may be used for phishing, brand impersonation, or other abuse. According to the company's documentation, its monitoring draws on domain permutations, Domain Name System (DNS) data, Certificate Transparency logs, registration data, website analysis, and passive infrastructure telemetry. [ref: Getting started with Have I Been Squatted, Have I Been Squatted Documentation]

The service started in 2022 as a public tool for spotting typosquatted domains. The company that now runs it, Have I Been Squatted Inc., was founded in 2024. [ref: About, Have I Been Squatted] [ref: Have I Been Squatted, LinkedIn]

The company also publishes research on phishing, malicious infrastructure, malware delivery, and domain-name security. Its work has been covered by BBC News, The Register, Recorded Future News, BleepingComputer, and FreightWaves. [ref: Phishing operation with links to Russia, Armenia compromised Western cargo companies, researchers find, Recorded Future News] [ref: Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers, The Register]

== History ==

Have I Been Squatted began in 2022 as an experimental tool for finding possible typosquats. Users entered a domain name and the tool generated variations of it, showing registrations that could be used to impersonate the original organization. The company says the project was first released after an experiment was shared on Hacker News, and that it grew as security practitioners started using it. Part of the tool was built on twistrs, an open-source Rust library for generating domain-name permutations that the company still maintains on GitHub. [ref: Have I Been Squatted, GitHub]

Have I Been Squatted Inc. was founded in 2024 to develop and run the service on a commercial basis. [ref: Terms of Service, Have I Been Squatted]

The commercial service moved beyond one-off typosquatting searches to continuous monitoring and investigation of external infrastructure, and later added tools for investigations, alerts, and domain takedowns.

== Platform ==

The platform looks for internet infrastructure that may be impersonating an organization, its domains, or its brands. Customers add domains for monitoring, and the platform regularly generates permutations of them and checks for related registrations and infrastructure. It adds context to what it finds using DNS records, HTTP responses, WHOIS and RDAP registration data, Certificate Transparency observations, screenshots, classification data, and passive infrastructure telemetry.

Monitoring is not limited to typos of a protected domain. The platform also surfaces domains found through Certificate Transparency, passive DNS, and other infrastructure signals.

Separately from monitoring, the platform includes tools for investigating individual domains and larger datasets. Infrastructure it identifies can be classified, investigated, and linked to alerts or response work. The company later added workflows for submitting domain takedown requests and tracking their progress.

== Threat intelligence research ==

=== Diesel Vortex ===

In February 2026, Have I Been Squatted and the threat intelligence group Ctrl-Alt-Intel published an investigation into a cybercrime operation they called Diesel Vortex. The group went after freight and logistics companies in the United States and Europe, using phishing sites built to take over accounts on load boards, fleet-management systems, fuel-card services, and other logistics platforms. [ref: Russian cybercrime ring targeted freight firms in US, Europe, report says, FreightWaves]

According to Recorded Future News, Have I Been Squatted researchers found an exposed.git directory belonging to the operation. It held source code and the group's communications, which showed how the campaign was organized and indicated that the group was building a phishing-as-a-service platform to support a wider criminal operation.

FreightWaves reported that the campaign had compromised 1,649 unique credentials, drawn from 3,474 stolen login pairs. The investigation also identified 52 deployed phishing domains, more than 75,000 targeted contact email addresses, and 35 confirmed attempts at fraud using Electronic Funds Source checks.

The exposed material pointed to an organized operation, with separate roles and infrastructure for stealing credentials, communicating with logistics staff, and managing victim sessions. Recorded Future News reported that the compromised accounts could be used for freight diversion, double brokering, and check fraud.

Have I Been Squatted and Ctrl-Alt-Intel worked with technology and security companies to disrupt the campaign's infrastructure. Recorded Future News named Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), Cloudflare, GitLab, IPinfo, and Ping Identity among those involved.

In April 2026, BleepingComputer referred to the Diesel Vortex investigation in its report on an FBI warning about a sharp rise in cyber-enabled cargo theft. It cited Have I Been Squatted's finding that the group had used dozens of phishing domains against freight and logistics operators since 2025. [ref: FBI links cybercriminals to sharp surge in cargo theft attacks, BleepingComputer]

=== Recruitment malware campaigns ===

In August 2026, Have I Been Squatted published a technical analysis of a malware campaign that used a fake hiring process to target a job seeker in the Web3 sector. The attackers approached the victim on LinkedIn, ran what looked like a normal interview process using Calendly and Google-hosted services, and then sent technical assessment material that was malicious. [ref: From fake interview to signed ClickOnce: inside a three-payload Windows chain, Have I Been Squatted]

On Windows, the attack used a digitally signed ClickOnce application. Installing it eventually delivered three payloads: a version of NeedleStealer, a separate information stealer written in Rust, and a custom Go remote-access trojan with remote shell access, file management, proxying, keylogging, and hidden virtual network computing.

The same infrastructure could also serve a macOS delivery chain that ended in Odyssey Stealer. The researchers said the mix of legitimate online platforms, signed software, and targeted social engineering made the fake recruitment process far more convincing than ordinary phishing.

In September 2026, BBC News cited analysis by Have I Been Squatted in a report on fake recruitment scams. The report followed a victim who was approached on LinkedIn and lost about £18,000 in cryptocurrency after installing malicious software during what seemed to be a real hiring process. It highlighted the attackers' use of genuine Google services and digitally signed software. [ref: I lost my savings after a job interview scam, BBC News]

=== Internationalized domain name and Chromium research ===

In October 2026, Have I Been Squatted published research on how Chromium-based browsers handle internationalized domain names (IDNs). They tested whether deceptive lookalike domains could get past Chromium's protections and be shown to users in Unicode, rather than in their Punycode form, which is easier to recognize as suspicious. [ref: Turning IDN edge cases into typosquats, Have I Been Squatted]

The researchers found edge cases involving two characters: the Cyrillic letter ө, used in languages such as Kazakh and Mongolian, and the Latin letter ƙ, used in languages such as Hausa. Using these characters, they built lookalikes of well-known domains that passed Chromium's display checks.

Have I Been Squatted registered 20 proof-of-concept lookalike domains for the research, including ones resembling Apple, SpaceX, Okta, and Nike. The Register covered the findings on October 10, 2026, explaining how the two characters could get around Chromium's checks for suspicious internationalized domains.

Chromium runs several checks before deciding whether to show an internationalized domain in Unicode. One set looks for characters and scripts often used for impersonation. Another reduces each domain to a simplified comparison string, called a skeleton, and compares it against a built-in list of popular domains.

The research found that Cyrillic ө was missing from Chromium's whole-script lookalike list, so adding it to an otherwise confusable Cyrillic domain could stop that check from triggering. The Latin ƙ caused a related problem at the skeleton stage. Its hook was kept as a combining mark, so the skeleton never exactly matched the ASCII domain it imitated.

The researchers also looked at Chromium's Safety Tips, which warn users when they navigate to a site by comparing it, exactly and approximately, against well-known sites and sites the user visits often. They found cases where a lookalike differed enough from the comparison skeleton to avoid a warning, as well as limitations affecting domains with fewer than five characters before the top-level domain.

As part of the work, the company analyzed the.com zone for internationalized domains and found about 162,000 pairs in which an IDN resembled an ASCII.com domain. The researchers noted that this did not mean 162,000 malicious typosquats, since such pairs can include legitimate multilingual domains and defensive registrations.

The research also compared email clients. Gmail showed the tested internationalized sender domains in Unicode, while Outlook Web showed the same domains as Punycode A-labels. The Register noted that the two services had made different trade-offs in how they present internationalized email domains to users.

== Public and open-source tools ==

Alongside its commercial service, Have I Been Squatted releases free and open-source security tools.

twistrs is a Rust library for generating and enumerating domain-name permutations. It is released under the MIT License, hosted in the company's public GitHub organization, and was one of the building blocks of the original typosquatting service.

In December 2025, the company launched certgrep, a free search service for Certificate Transparency data. It lets users search certificate records with regular expressions, wildcards, and substring queries. The company built it after using similar functionality internally to find domains that matched suspicious patterns. [ref: Announcing certgrep, Have I Been Squatted]

The company also maintains an open-source Python software development kit for its application programming interface (API). It gives programmatic access to features including domain-squatting analysis, domain investigation, and Certificate Transparency search. [ref: haveibeensquatted-python, GitHub]

data.title: Sara Mitich
data.text:
----

Sara Mitich (born November 26, 1988) is a Canadian actress who is best known for her roles in Star Trek: Discovery, The Expanse, and Murdoch Mysteries. Mitich is the host of Gratitude & Growth, [ref: https://gratitudegrowth.com/about the website for Gratitude & Growth] and the author of 21 Days of Gratitude: Simple Exercises for a More Positive Life.

==Early life==
Sara Mitich was born in 1988 in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada [ref: https://youvebeenhooked.wordpress.com/2016/07/11/5x5-with-the-hook-sara-mitich/ an interview with Sara] and she is the youngest out of three girls. Her parents are from Serbia. She wanted to be a ballerina from a young age, and she attended the National Ballet School of Canada. As an adult, she attended the University of Toronto and Sheridan college for acting. She starred in various short films, such as Mind Games, Plastic, and Prick.

==Career==
===Murdoch Mysteries===
In Murdoch Mysteries, Mitich portrays Lillian Moss, a suffragette attempting to flee from her past life. Her character, Moss, and potential romantic partner, Emily Grace—played by actor Georgina Reilly —meet while protesting for women's rights, and the two grow close while working together. The pair decide to move to London, England, although Mitich's character is killed before the pair are able to leave Toronto.

===The Expanse===
In The Expanse, Mitich portrays a character named Gia, a prostitute who appears in four episodes of season one. In addition to her job, she also serves as a language tutor to Dimitri Havelock—portrayed by actor Jay Hernandez—a detective on the planet Ceres. She is later attacked by another character and is visited by Havelock while she recovers in the hospital. When asked about portraying Gia, Mitich has said that the "learning the language and gestural language was challenging." She also mentions that the role of Gia is one that she has learned keep perspective with and not to judge them. [ref: Revealed in an interview with Mitich on [https://starrymag.com/sara-mitich-the-expanse/ Starry Mag's website]]

===Star Trek Discovery===
Throughout the series Star Trek: Discovery, Mitich had the opportunity to play two different characters, Lieutenant Commander Airiam and Lieutenant Nilsson. She portrayed Airiam during the first season of the show, before being recast as Lt. Nilsson from season two onwards. Airiam was a female human cyborg, who also served as an officer aboard the USS Discovery. According to Darren Franich, a critic at Entertainment Weekly, Airiam is "the greatest background character in Trek history since the glory days of the Deep Space 9 bar." [ref: http://ew.com/tv/2019/01/11/star-trek-discovery-canon Entertainment Weekly]

As for Nilsson, her background is similar to Mitich's own—a ballerina who went to a prestigious school of dance, and ended up with a differing career path. [ref: Issue 204, Star Trek Magazine] Her character succeeds Airiam as a spore drives ops officer aboard the USS Discovery. Occasionally, Nilsson would be left in charge of the bridge of her ship. She later moves and serves aboard the USS Voyager, leaving her pet tribble behind.

===Control===

In Control, Mitich portrays a woman named Eileen. She wakes up in a room, where she is given numerous tasks to complete by an unseen entity. Failure to do so would result in her daughter, Eve, being killed. Working with her husband Roger, the pair must work together to save their daughter and uncover the secret behind her memory loss. Eileen has latent psychic abilities, and the organization that trapped her is determined to see what she can do. [ref: Revealed on [https://kemodoent.com/film/control/ Kemodo Entertainment's official website]]

==Personal life==
Mitich is an accomplished equestrian. She also enjoys kickboxing, yoga, and Pilates.

===Gratitude & Growth===
Mitich is the host of the self-growth brand named Gratitude & Growth, a personal development platform focused on mindfulness, emotional regulation, and presence. The project began as a podcast and later expanded into a broader brand offering written content, community resources, and tools for personal growth.Her work with Gratitude & Growth has been featured by publications including Tiny Buddha [ref: https://tinybuddha.com/author/sara-mitch/ Tinybuddha's website] and The Elephant Journal.

Hopscotch Air is a FAA-certificated air carrier based in New York, flying a fleet of technologically-advanced Cirrus SR22 aircraft. Launched in 2009, the company performs about fourteen hundred revenue legs a year throughout the northeast. Because of the type of aircraft it flies, along with the regional nature of its service, Hopscotch Air says it can offer fares far below that of traditional private aviation. Hopscotch Air currently has bases in New York and Boston. It's planning to expand service to southern states later early 2027.

In the spring of 2026, Hopscotch Go Corporation, the parent company of Hopscotch Air, received qualification for a Regulation A+ filing from the Securities and Exchange Commission. Regulation A+ allows the company to raise capital from the general public,

Andrew Schmertz, a former reporter with NY1 News and former business reporter with the ABC affiliate service, ABC News One, leads the company as Chief Executive Officer. Doug Okin is the co-founder. Robert Bergen is the Director of Operations and Asael Greenberg in the Chief Pilot.

Hopscotch Air previously had marketing relationships with the New York Islanders, Bridgeport Islanders, and Swiss International Airlines.

data.title: Republican Movement of Venezuela
data.text:
The Republican Movement (RM) is a Venezuelan political party with republican and liberal leanings. Its ideological and institutional platform is based on the defense of fundamental individual rights [ref: Movimiento Republicano - English, www.movimientorepublicano.org]—private property, liberty, and life—the restoration of republican institutions, the market economy, and the strict separation of powers.

== Political Principles and Ideology ==
The Republican Movement bases its doctrine on five fundamental pillars set forth in its statements of organizational principles:
# Defense of Individual Rights: It considers the safeguarding and protection of private property, individual liberty, and the right to life to be essential and non-negotiable conditions—the pillars for the full exercise of citizens’ rights.
# Institutional Framework and the Republic: Promotes the revival of the republican model based on the premise that all citizens are free and equal before the law, thereby laying the foundation for a robust rule of law.
# Libertades económicas y civiles: It explicitly advocates for the free market, freedom of action and enterprise, freedom of thought, religious freedom, and the fundamental right to freedom of movement within the country, in addition to guaranteeing unrestricted access to justice.
# Separation of Powers and Alternation in Office: It upholds the strict necessity of a division and independence of public powers that allows for mutual and effective checks and balances. It also supports the democratic election of state officials for fixed terms of office.
# Transparency and Public Administration: Calls for rigorous oversight of public spending and absolute transparency in state administrative expenditures. Promotes active citizen participation aimed at fostering respect for institutions and legitimizing a responsible political class in the country. [ref: Movimiento Republicano reafirma su compromiso con la participación electoral en Anzoátegui - El Tiempo, eltiempove.com]

data.title: Employee 24/7
data.text:
Employee 24/7 is an American custom software and business automation company based in Tallahassee, Florida. It builds custom software and advanced automation intended to address businesses' operating costs and to create new recurring revenue streams for clients.

Hurd has described the company rule that "every solution must be engineered to return at least $2 for every $1 spent", and that the company will not sell a solution that does not meet that threshold. "Most vendors sell tools; we sell the outcome," Hurd said in 2026.

== History ==
Employee 24/7 was founded in February 2026 in Tallahassee, Florida, by Waymon Hurd III. Before founding the company, Hurd worked for more than 15 years in call centers, logistics, customer service and sales, and for more than seven years as a licensed financial professional.

== Business model ==
The company sells custom software and automation projects to small and medium-sized businesses, and says it serves clients in more than 50 industries. Employee 24/7's stated return standard is that every solution must be engineered to return at least $2 for every $1 a client spends. The company says its most successful clients have seen returns of $6 to $8 for every $1 spent. Prospective clients are offered a tailored demonstration and a free trial before payment.

== Products ==
GymMeals247 is the company's flagship product, a recurring-revenue platform for gym owners that provides personalized meal plans under the gym owners' own brand at zero cost to them.

== Recognition ==
In October 2026 the company was profiled in two Business Life magazine features describing its return-on-investment standard and the GymMeals247 platform. On October 15, 2026, the American Recognition Awards named Employee 24/7 the Best Custom Software Company in Florida for 2026.

Saleh Hasaballah (Arabic: صالح حسب الله) is an Egyptian lawyer at the Court of Cassation and writer. He is a member of the Egyptian Writers Union and the founder of the Egyptian Sports Lawyers Association.

== Career ==
Hasaballah practices law before the Egyptian Court of Cassation and the Supreme Constitutional Court. He is a member of the Egyptian Writers Union and has authored works in the legal field.

He founded the Egyptian Sports Lawyers Association (رابطة المحامين الرياضيين) in Egypt to promote sports activities among lawyers and to provide legal support in sports law.

== Legal activism ==
In 2011, following the 25 January Revolution, Hasaballah filed a complaint to Attorney General Abdel Meguid Mahmoud requesting an investigation into former interior ministers who served after the revolution, on suspicion of concealing incriminating evidence related to the killing of demonstrators.

According to Egypt Independent, the Attorney General ordered investigations into Mahmoud Wagdy and Mansour El-Essawy and the head of national security, based on the complaint filed by Hasaballah. [ref: Attorney general orders investigation into former interior ministers, Egypt Independent]

data.title: Louis Brown
data.text:
= Louis Brown: King of Clubs =
Louis Brown (c. 1934–1986) was a British nightclub proprietor associated with London's West End nightlife during the 1960s, 1970s and early 1980s. He was known for his association with La Valbonne, a nightclub in Soho, and his venues which attracted entertainers, musicians and other prominent figures. He was known for his distinctive ideas and designs within his clubs making a name for himself as the King of Clubs.

== Career ==
Louis Brown was a British nightclub entrepreneur who became a prominent figure in London's West End nightlife during the 1960s and 1970s. Working alongside business partner Leonard Bloom, he established and operated a number of nightclubs, including La Poubelle, Le Kilt and the Scotch of St James, before opening La Valbonne in Soho in 1967.

Known for his distinctive approach to nightclub design and entertainment, Brown developed venues that attracted musicians, celebrities and fashionable clientele. His business interests later extended beyond London to Skindles Hotel in Taplow, Berkshire, where he established Studio Valbonne as a nightclub and entertainment venue. Brown continued to operate his nightclub businesses into the 1980s and died in 1986.

=== Skindles ===
Brown was also involved in the ownership and management of Skindles Hotel, a historic riverside hotel in Taplow, Berkshire, during the 1970s. Under his involvement, the establishment formed part of his wider interests in the hospitality and nightclub industries. In 1978, plans were proposed for an extension comprising 81 additional bedrooms, reflecting efforts to redevelop the property as a hotel and leisure destination. Skindles subsequently closed in 1995.

=== La Valbonne ===
La Valbonne was a nightclub at 62 Kingly Street in Soho, London, which opened in 1967 and became Louis Brown's best-known establishment. The venue was noted for its elaborate interior, featuring multiple bars, tropical plants, large fish tanks and a heart-shaped swimming pool incorporated into the dance floor. It attracted musicians, entertainers and other prominent figures, and appeared in Pete Walker's 1970 film Cool It Carol.

=== Other clubs ===
Le Kilt was a Soho nightclub associated with Louis Brown and his business partner Leonard Bloom. Situated on Greek Street, it formed part of Brown's expanding portfolio of West End entertainment venues during the 1960s and 1970s. The club operated within London's emerging discothèque culture, which increasingly centred on recorded music, dancing and fashionable nightlife.

La Poubelle was an early London discothèque associated with Louis Brown. It opened in 1959 and is described in historical accounts as one of London's earliest venues devoted to recorded-music dancing. Located initially on Great Marlborough Street, near Oxford Circus, the club attracted socialites and helped establish the discothèque format that subsequently spread throughout the capital.

The Scotch of St James opened in Mason's Yard, Mayfair, in July 1965 and became a prominent nightclub and live-music venue during London's Swinging Sixties. Associated with Louis Brown's nightclub interests, it attracted musicians and other figures from the British and American music scenes. American guitarist Jimi Hendrix famously joined musicians for an impromptu performance there on his arrival in England in September 1966.

=== Relationship with Peter Stringfellow ===
Brown's La Valbonne nightclub reportedly attracted the interest of fellow nightclub entrepreneur Peter Stringfellow. A retrospective account states that Stringfellow regarded the venue as influential and that Brown offered to sell it to him however the deal never fulfilled.

== Personal life ==
Brown was known for his enthusiasm for music, nightlife and entertainment. His professional interests extended beyond running venues to the atmosphere and technology of the nightclub experience, including the development of elaborate lighting effects and distinctive interior designs. This was shown through his desire for cars when being seen driving his Jaguar E-Type and his Rolls-Royce Silver Cloud.

== Legacy ==
Louis Brown was an ambitious and influential figure in London's nightclub scene, whose establishments helped shape the atmosphere of fashionable nightlife during the Swinging Sixties and the decades that followed.

With a distinctive vision for entertainment, music and interior design, he created venues that offered more than a traditional nightclub experience, transforming them into destinations for celebrities, musicians and London's social elite. La Valbonne became the defining example of his approach, while his involvement with the Scotch of St James and Skindles extended his influence across London's West End and beyond.

His ability to combine striking surroundings with an atmosphere of exclusivity and excitement reflected the changing character of British nightlife during a period of significant cultural transformation. Although many of the venues associated with Brown have since closed or disappeared, their place in the history of the era remains a testament to his entrepreneurial ambitions and his contribution to the development of the modern nightclub experience.

This allowed him to be known within the entertainment industry as the King of Clubs.

data.title: North Beach Terror Toad
data.text:
----

The North Beach Terror Toad is a newly reported cryptid from North Beach Maryland. The story went viral on Reddit and has sparked discussion between Maryland Locals and Cryptid Fans alike.

The post was made on r/maryland and quickly blew up and gained 100k views and many replys. The post goes as follows:

I reported this on encounter atlas but wanted to share this here to see if anyone else has seen this thing.

This was summer of 2024. Me and my best friend Joe were in the North Beach/Chesapeake Beach area for the few days leading up to and including the 4th of July. The night of the 2nd, we decided to take a walk and smoke a blunt we had been saving. We were both 21 years old at the time and going into our Junior Year of college. I say that so you understand that we were dumb and at that age were you feel invincible.

As we were approaching the Wetlands Overlook Park, walking along the side of the road, we both caught sight of an odd silhouette. At first we both were freaked out because we thought it must be a kid who was lost and scared in the dark. We both started jogging towards the figure and as we got closer (we had been walking for a while and our eyes were adjusted to the dark) we both stopped. We were probably 8 feet from the figure and now could make out details. It was probably 3-3.5 ft tall and was dark green. The face resembled a toad but it almost appeared like it had a small elephant trunk in place of the nose. the arms were lanky, with the knuckles almost dragging on the floor, and the hands each had 3 fingers that ended in claws. The legs were short and stumpy. The thing had ears like a bat, coned and pointed, but they were much larger than a bats ears. Its eyes were large and they glowed a super bright white. We stood staring at the thing for a good 10 seconds before it put its hands on the ground and sprung off, and with two big jumps it disappeared into the marsh.

I remember that much because it was so odd and otherworldly that I took in every detail. I know how so crazy this sounds and so i have only ever told close family and friends. The reason I am writing this now, is that my fiancée and I are moving to North Beach in a few months and I had to know if anyone has seen thing. I know what I saw.

After the post went viral, the OP put an update along with a rough sketch:

Edit: I feel like I should add a few things.

I was smoking weed, not anything that would have given me visions of hallucinations. We also were not even high at the time of the event.

I swear this is truthful.

I would never lie about something like this, and really debated coming forward with this account.

I work as a naturalists in Anne Arundle County and I know what normal animals look like.

I am not offended by the jokes or people not believing me. I know how crazy it sounds so the jokes are inevitable. I appreciate those who do believe me and have offered kind words and theories.

North Beach has its own cryptid now ig. The North Beach Terror Toad sounds nice

I also did a quick drawing of what the thing looked like. I am a terrible artist

== Description ==

* Size & Color: Roughly 3 to 3.5 feet tall and dark green.
* Face: Resembled a toad but featured a small, elephant-like trunk instead of a normal nose.
* Upper Body: Lanky arms that almost dragged on the ground, ending in three-fingered clawed hands, accompanied by coned, pointed bat-like ears.
* Lower Body: Short, stumpy legs.

== References ==

data.title: Mitti de Putt
data.text:
Mitti de Putt (Punjabi: ਮਿੱਟੀ ਦੇ ਪੁੱਤ) is a 2026 Indian Punjabi-language action drama film directed by R. Malkana and written by Amar Hundal, Ryan Khan and Raj S. Jhinjar. Produced by Iqbal Cheema and Amar Hundal, it stars Dev Kharoud, Sharan Kaur and Vikramjeet Virk, alongside Yograj Singh, Anita Meet and Mahabir Bhullar.

The film was released in Indian cinemas on 18 September 2026. It received mixed review from critics, with praise for its action sequences, performances and production quality, while criticism was directed at its screenplay.

== Plot ==
The story follows two villages whose rivalry has persisted across generations over land and pride. Left with his family destroyed, Bikkar Singh vows to bring his mother home and confront the man responsible.

== Cast ==

* Dev Kharoud as the protagonist, Bikkar Singh
* Vikramjeet Virk as the antagonist, Jang Singh, Bikkar's uncle
* Pardeep Cheema as Sarwan, Jang's second son
* Aman Sutdhar as Shera, Jang's first son
* Deepak Kamboj as Kartar, Bikkar's cousin
* Sharan Kaur as Basant Kaur, Bikkar's wife
* Anita Meet as Bikkar's mother, Jang's sister
* Yograj Singh as Bikkar's paternal grandfather
* Mahabir Bhullar as Jang's father
* Ashish Duggal
* Aman Dhaliwal
* Dilawar Sidhu as Gindar
* Manjit Singh
* Vikramjit Khehra
* Ravinder Mand
* Rang Dev
* Sukh Dandiwal
* Ravneet Kaur
* Harinder Bhullar
* Gurinder Makna
* Jasbir Gill

== Production ==
Mitti de Putt was produced by Iqbal Cheema and Amar Hundal under the banners of Liv Lyf Films and Zora Studios. R. Malkana directed the film, with Amar Hundal responsible for the story and screenplay. Ryan Khan and Raj S. Jhinjar contributed additional screenplay and dialogue work.

The film's technical crew included cinematographer Sukh Kamboj, editor Gurjeet Hundal and composer Avvy Sra. Siraj Sayed served as action director. The production was promoted through official teasers released by Zora Studios and Dharma Productions in August 2026.

== Release ==
The film was released in Indian cinemas on 18 September 2026. Dharma Productions handled distribution across India, while The Next Film Studios handled overseas distribution. The film was also released in the United States on a limited theatrical basis.

== Reception ==
Critical response

Viewer reviews praised the film's action choreography, particularly its hospital fight sequence. Some audience reviews also commended its soundtrack and the presentation of the central family feud, while negative reviews criticised the characterisation, dialogue and motivations behind the conflict.

The Times of India covered the film before its release, describing it as a revenge saga centred on family, culture and loyalty. Actor Vikramjeet Virk characterised the film as a tribute to the strength, pride and spirit of Punjabi people.

Audience rating

As of October 2026, Mitti de Putt had received positive audience ratings across several online platforms. On IMDb, the film was rated 9.5 out of 10 from approximately 882 votes. On BookMyShow, it received a rating of 9.5 out of 10 from more than 1,200 votes.

data.title: Doro (chatbot)
data.text:
----

Doro is a Canadian artificial intelligence chatbot designed to act as a mental-health coach for people experiencing early signs of anxiety and depression. It was developed by Razroze Inc., a startup founded in 2023 by brothers Rastin and Ramtin Rassoli and based at Velocity, the University of Waterloo's startup incubator in Kitchener, Ontario. The app conducts sessions by text or voice, draws on techniques from cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy, and assigns users small tasks between sessions.

== History ==
Rastin Rassoli began developing Doro in 2023 while studying computer science and psychology at the University of Waterloo, after earlier helping to build Joyi, an app delivering short psychology lessons to teenagers, during a co-op placement. He continued the work through the university's Enterprise Co-op program with the support of a CA$30,000 government grant. A first version was released to about 100 trial users in June 2024, followed by a wider release in September 2024, when the University of Waterloo's Campus Wellness service began offering the app to students.

By late 2024 the university reported that Doro had been deployed at some 30 mental-health clinics in Ontario and Alberta, and in January 2025 the student newspaper Imprint reported that the app had more than 2,000 users. Mobile apps for iOS and Android followed in 2025, and in August 2025 the Waterloo Region Record reported that the company had signed a contract with a chain of clinics in Alberta. By 2026 the company was working with hospital systems in Canada and the United States and collaborating with University of Waterloo researchers on clinical applications, according to the university.

== Features ==
Doro replaces questionnaire-style intake with a conversational assessment and delivers exercises drawn from about 20 psychotherapeutic techniques, such as journalling or the TIPP skill for managing panic, while tracking each session. It is positioned as an early-intervention tool for people whose symptoms have not reached a clinical diagnosis, rather than as treatment for diagnosed conditions. The developers state that the chatbot maintains a defined therapeutic stance and conversational boundaries rather than acting as a general-purpose assistant.

If a user's symptoms indicate a crisis, the app stops the session and directs them to a built-in directory of crisis helplines organized by country and province, or to a therapist in their region. Doro also partners with therapists, providing them with summaries of a user's prior conversations, and its exercises include prompts to attend social events and build connections outside the app.

== Reception ==
In September 2024, CBC News profiled Doro in a report on AI mental-health apps for students; experts quoted in the report said such apps cannot replace conventional treatment and raised concerns about safety, privacy and the lack of regulation of AI mental-health apps generally. In a 2025 episode of the TVO series Big If True on AI chatbots and therapy, host Molly Thomas tested the app; when she described thoughts of self-harm, it directed her to crisis resources. The Waterloo Region Record also covered the startup in 2025.

== References ==

data.title: Operations & Intelligence
data.text:
Operations & Intelligence / O&I (Operatiën & Inlichtingen) was a Dutch stay-behind organization that originated in 1946/1947 from the resistance against the German occupation during World War II and was disbanded by Prime Minister Lubbers in 1992. [ref: Dr. D. Engelen, De Nederlandse stay behind-organisatie in de koude oorlog 1945-1992 Ministerie van Algemene Zaken, Ministerie van Defensie & Rijksarchiefdienst/PIVOT The Netherlands, National Archives, Institutional Investigation (Dutch). The Hague, 2005. ISBN 90-5909-0489.] [ref: https://www.rudi-harthoorn.nl/operatien-inlichtingen/] In fact, there were two separate organizations, namely Operations and Intelligence, which were eventually coordinated by a single person but each had its own task. [ref: https://www.defensiebond.nl/binnenland/erkenning-voor-ex-leden-stay-behind-organisatie/] Until approximately the mid-1980s, they were referred to simply as O and I; since then, service A and service B. In the media, O&I was often compared to the Italian Operation Gladio, although the Dutch network differed from it in important respects. [ref: Onderzoek naar Stay Behind-organisatie Ministerie van Defensie, NIMH, 2 February 2024.]

Operations & Intelligence was tasked with keeping the population as resilient as possible against communist propaganda and passing on information regarding political developments to the 'government in exile'. Furthermore, the organization was to attempt to disrupt and mislead the occupier's apparatus of authority wherever possible. Armed resistance was not the primary objective, but as the Soviets approached, members of the organization were to receive sufficient weapons from hidden depots to avoid being slaughtered defenseless. One such underground weapons depot, consisting of 19 crates, was discovered by chance in 1983 in the woods near Rozendaal. Three years earlier, in 1980, a similar weapons find had already been made in Haelen.

==History==

[[Image:LouisEinthoven.jpg|thumb|150px|Louis Einthoven]]
Operations & Intelligence originated from the Dutch resistance against the German occupier during the Second World War and was intended as a continuation of the work of the Intelligence Bureau (BI) and the Special Assignments Bureau (BBO). At the initiative of the head of the BI, Jan Somer, Section IIIC of the General Staff was established on May 13, 1946, of which he himself became the first head. Alongside the already existing Sections IIIA and IIIB of the General Staff, GS IIIC was responsible for setting up a stay-behind organization and gathering military intelligence in and about foreign countries.

GS IIIC consisted of Section I (Operations) and Section II (Preparation), with the head of Section I also becoming the head of the military section of the Foreign Intelligence Service (BID), established in February 1946, since formally only the BID was authorized to gather intelligence via foreign agents. In 1948, Section IIIC was renamed Section G7, and as of July 1, 1949, Section General Affairs (SAZ). This became the Intelligence branch (I, later B) of what had come to be called Operations & Intelligence since the early 1950s.

Former BBO agent Henk Veeneklaas, alias David van Eyck, also considered it advisable not to let the knowledge and experience gained during the war regarding operations in hostile/occupied territory be lost. As Commander of the Netherlands Armed Forces, Prince Bernhard referred him in the summer of 1945 to Louis Einthoven, who was then in the process of setting up the National Security Bureau (BNV).

Together with British officers of the Special Operations Executive (SOE), preparations were subsequently made for a stay-behind organization aimed at sabotage actions in case the Netherlands were occupied again. Funding for this was initially channeled through Einthoven's security service, which knew about Somer's General Command IIIC from the outset, whereas Somer only discovered the existence of the new organization led by Einthoven in the course of 1949. The latter became the Operations (O, later A) branch of Operations & Intelligence.

==Organization & structure==
For security reasons, both branches of O&I were heavily compartmentalized, and employees did not know each other's real names, partly as a result of the lessons learned from the Englandspiel. Coordination at the top was eventually established, but there was no close cooperation between the two organizations, let alone integration.

Since 1949, both branches of O&I were funded from the resources of the General Staff of the Department of War, later the Department of Defense, while until 1964 there was also a financial contribution from the CIA, which used the code name SYRUP-SYNTHOSIS for O&I.

The military and civilian personnel of the I-branch were formally employed by the Ministry of Defence, whereas (current or former military) employees of the O-branch were paid by Defence but were not employed by it. Because it was expected that the occupying forces would intern the intelligentsia, they recruited only people who did not hold a title or leadership position.

The implementing organization was formally housed within the General Staff of the Armed Forces and made use of the accommodation (Villa Maarheeze in Wassenaar) of the Foreign Intelligence Service (IDB).

The ultimate responsibility for 'establishing, modifying, and dissolving an organization in peacetime, charged with the preparation of a stay-behind organization in wartime' was shared by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence.

===Coordination===
[[Image:Max van der Stoel.jpg|thumb|150px|Max van der Stoel (here in 1983) the last coordinator of O&I]]
At the insistence of Louis Einthoven, it was decided in the late 1940s that the activities of O&I would be coordinated on behalf of the Prime Minister and the Minister of War and Navy/Defence by the Chief of the General Staff (CGS), assisted by the Joint Planning Board (JPB). In 1956, coordination was placed in the hands of the newly established position of Coordinator of Intelligence and Security Services, who, as a senior civil servant, is part of the Prime Minister's cabinet.

Following disputes regarding the management of both branches, Prime Minister Marijnen established the Ruppert Commission on July 8, 1964, named after its chairman, Marinus Ruppert, a member of the Council of State. This commission investigated whether a stay-behind organization was still desirable at all, and if so, how it should be organized. The commission concluded that O and I should continue to exist side by side and that a delegate should be appointed to lead the O branch and also coordinate both branches.

In accordance with this advice, Prime Minister De Jong appointed Ruppert himself as delegate of O, and thereby as coordinator, effective March 1, 1967. From January 1, 1974, to April 29, 1988, these positions were held by Theo van Lier, who was a Member of Parliament for the PvdA and, like Ruppert, a member of the Council of State and had been involved in the resistance. At the time of the dissolution of O&I in 1992, Minister of State Max van der Stoel was the coordinator.

===Foreign relations===
Initially, both O and I worked closely with the British secret services, joined by the Americans in 1951, resulting in a tripartite consultation. For consultation with other Western European stay-behind organizations, there was initially the Western Union Clandestine Committee (WUCC), but in 1949 this was taken over by the Clandestine Planning Committee (CPC) and later the Allied Clandestine Committee (ACC) of NATO.

Although formally only the Foreign Intelligence Service (BID) was authorized to gather foreign intelligence, the I branch also did so and O&I entered into cooperative relationships with foreign services, such as with MI6 in 1948 and with the CIA in 1949. In the early 1950s, the O branch carried out covert operations together with the BID in which agents were dropped behind the Iron Curtain to gather intelligence and support the anti-communist resistance. O's involvement may have been necessary because the BID did not have its own military instructors, whereas for O it was a good opportunity to practice operations in hostile territory. The fact that the dropped agents were often fascists and former Nazis was apparently not a problem for the many former resistance fighters in O.

In April 1972, a retired flag officer of the Royal Netherlands Navy, known by the pseudonym Mulder, was appointed to represent O & I externally, particularly within the NATO ACC. There, he served as the spokesperson for the National Clandestine Service (NCS), which was to assist the Dutch government in exile during wartime and, via the National Section (NS) at NATO's Allied Clandestine Base (ACB), to direct the field organization remaining in occupied Netherlands. As of August 1, 1978, "Mulder" was succeeded by Theo van Lier, who was already Head of O and Coordinator. An instruction regarding the NCS from Prime Minister Lubbers and Minister of Defence Van Eekelen dating from 1987, in which both branches are by then referred to as Service A and Service B, is the last known internal document concerning the organization.

===Operations O (Later A)===

The O organization, which fell under the Ministry of General Affairs (the Prime Minister), was focused on carrying out sabotage, raids, and assassinations in occupied territory. To this end, O had sections for Sabotage, Psychological Warfare, Communications, Falsification, Operational Financing, Security, and Codes. Ton Herstel, former chairman of the Council for Journalism and NCRV, was attached to O as an instructor in psychological warfare.

In mid-1952, the staff of the O-branch consisted of 21 people and possessed 28 American transceivers from the Second World War, as well as 17 modern Philips radios. Scattered throughout the country were 21 secret underground caches, in which, among other things, a few thousand kilograms of explosives and a quantity of weapons, as well as a total of 10 million guilders in paper money and 400,000 guilders in gold ten-guilder coins, were to be hidden. In 1988, there were 39 caches that were to be filled with sabotage material by the Marechaussee, plus approximately 15 caches containing money, gold, and gemstones for a total of 40 million guilders.

The O branch was initially housed in an attic on the Oudegracht in Utrecht, but later moved to the law firm of co-founder Bootsma at Keizersgracht 729 in Amsterdam. From 1979 to 1984, the staff of the O service (about twelve people) was based on a floor of a villa at Koninginneweg 184 near the Vondelpark under the guise of a historical study society, the Hendrik van Borsele Foundation. The last known office address of O was the heavily guarded Marine Etablissement Amsterdam (Kattenburg) near the central station in Amsterdam. The organization, by then designated as Service A, numbered about 30 staff members and about 30 field staff members who were intended to be a reflection of the various worldviews.

Since 1967, the head of the O branch was designated as a delegate and was appointed by the Minister of Defence, in consultation with the Prime Minister. Since 1967, he also served as coordinator of both branches of Operations & Intelligence. In this capacity, the following served:

*1947-1962: Louis Einthoven (also head of the BVD)
*1962-1967: Major General (Ret.) Willem den Boer (alias Bax)
*1967-1973: Marinus Ruppert
*1974-1988: Mr. Theo van Lier
*1988-1992: Max van der Stoel

====Weapons stockpiles====
For sabotage purposes, the O branch possessed thousands of kilos of explosives and weapons, which were stored in forty secret underground storage locations. A weapons depot discovered by chance on April 4, 1980, on the De Bedelaar estate (in Haelen) turned out, as became officially known in November 1990 but was suspected soon after its discovery, to be part of O. After this discovery, it was decided to dismantle the forty storage locations and concentrate the explosives in a central storage facility with the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee.

However, during the clearing out, it became apparent that various storage locations had been plundered and that many explosives and weapons were missing. Presumably, these fell into the hands of criminals such as Sam Klepper and John Mieremet and the Amsterdam Delta Group (according to the Dutch judiciary, Etienne Urka, Mink Kok, and Jan Femer belonged to this group).

In 1992, during a raid on a farm in Oudebildtzijl, Friesland, a large supply of drugs was found alongside a stockpile of approximately 130 kilos of explosives (mainly Semtex) and grenades. Nothing was known about the origin of these weapons—even to the IRT team that knew about the drugs—but according to Public Prosecutor Fred Teeven, it had to be investigated whether these weapons originated from "Gladio depots." Criminal Mink Kok was involved in the discovery of the weapons, with whom Teeven (with the permission of the Public Prosecution Service ) made a deal in 1998.

On September 9, 2007, KRO Reporter broadcast a documentary about Operations & Intelligence, which revealed that weapons and explosives from a secret depot in the Scheveningse Bosjes in The Hague had fallen into the hands of organized crime. The case came to light when police arrested Sam Klepper and John Mieremet in 1991. The Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) covered up the arms heist—the largest in Dutch history—at the time to avoid 'unwanted publicity in the Gladio sphere'.

===Information (I, later B)===
[[Image:Maarheze.jpg|thumb|Villa Maarheeze in Wassenaar, where the General Affairs Section (SAZ) was housed]]
The Intelligence branch originated from Section IIIC of the General Staff of the Armed Forces, established in 1946, which was renamed Section G7 in 1948 and Section General Affairs (SAZ) in 1949.

In the 1970s and 1980s, SAZ consisted of approximately thirty staff members and some 125 agents tasked with preparing a stay-behind intelligence organization. In the event of an impending occupation, they would not form the stay-behind organization themselves; instead, they were the 'peace organization,' tasked with recruiting and training secret agents. These secret agents were referred to as the 'field organization.' In the event that the Netherlands were occupied, they would constitute the actual 'remaining force,' directed and supported by the staff operating from unoccupied territory.

The head of the I-branch, or the General Affairs Section, was initially appointed by the Chief of the General Staff (CGS) and, since 1968, by the Commander of the Land Forces (BLS). Serving as such were:

*1946-1948: JM Somer
*1948-1962: Cavalry Captain JJL Baron van Lynden
*1962-1970: Lieutenant Colonel GA van Borssum Buisman
*1970-1981: JWA Bruins
*(the names of later heads are not known)

In the event of escalating international tension, the organization's staff would relocate to Great Britain or the United States to direct the agent network in occupied territory from there. At the height of the Cold War, the agent network consisted of approximately two hundred people.

Seventeen agencies had been appointed for the preparations, most of which, however, consisted of only one person:

*I secretariat and transport
*II lines (escape routes from occupied Netherlands)
*III intelligence networks
*IV radio connections
*V reproduction
*VI radio technology
*VII intelligence operations via the BID
*VIII code matters
*IX security (field safety)
*X air filtration (infiltration and exfiltration to and from occupied Netherlands via the air)
*XI sea filtration (idem from sea)
*XII special network (for highly specialized intelligence work, for example in the economic or financial field)
*XIII short-term networks (short-term intelligence networks, such as Dorpsplein)
*XIV accounting
*XV financial networks (ensure sufficient funds to keep the other networks running)
*XVI weather network
*XVII documentation/falsification, microphotography etc.

===Dissolution===
The Dutch organization managed to operate in secret for 35 years. Even the ministers were unaware of its existence. After the existence of the Italian Operation Gladio was revealed in November 1990, then-Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers confirmed the existence of a Dutch stay-behind organization in a letter dated November 13, 1990, to the Parliamentary Committee on Intelligence and Security Services.

Lubbers explicitly stated that the difference with the stay-behind organizations in several other European countries was that the Dutch organization was not under NATO command. In the event of war and occupation, it would fall exclusively under the authority of the Dutch government in freedom. In his letter, Lubbers also pointed out a material and organizational difference between Gladio and the Dutch setup. The Dutch organization operated according to the 'single agent' principle, which is not suitable for group activities under NATO leadership, which was apparently the case with the Italian Gladio. The Netherlands has always rejected this subordination to NATO.

At the time the organization's existence was confirmed, downsizing was underway following the end of the Cold War. Formally, the organization was dissolved in early 1992: for service A (formerly the O-branch) by means of a letter dated March 13, 1992, from Prime Minister Lubbers; and for service B (formerly the I-branch) via a letter dated April 3, 1992, from Minister of Defence Ter Beek. The field staff of service B also received a letter of thanks from Prince Bernard. The winding-up process continued until 1994.

For Operations & Intelligence, the dissolution came as a surprise, as Prime Minister Lubbers had indicated in March 1991 that he wanted the organization to continue in a streamlined form. Service B had moved into new premises at the Fort De Bilt gendarmerie complex in Utrecht just a few months before the dissolution.

Service B had also just begun distributing advanced cryptographically secured radio equipment to agents, enabling them to maintain contact with the Allied Clandestine Base (ACB) entirely independently. This equipment, known as the AZO-90 (Automatische ZendOntvanger 1990), had been developed since 1980 in close cooperation with other European stay-behind organizations, the CIA and MI6, and was manufactured by the German company Telefunken. The cost was around 80 million euros, with the Dutch contribution amounting to 10 million euros.

==Aftermath==
Shortly after Operations & Intelligence was disbanded in 1994 and some employees were on leave, two of them (including a major) committed blackmail involving food poisoning at Nutricia. They were arrested and convicted. To prevent others from engaging in similar activities, they were all reinstated to active service.

In response to parliamentary questions in 1997, the State Secretary for Education, Culture and Science ordered an investigation into the archives of O&I, but these turned out to have been almost entirely destroyed after the closure in 1992. Invoking the Public Access to Government Information Act (Wob), KRO Reporter managed to uncover a large number of secret O&I archive documents, some of which were published online. MPs Teeven and Boekestijn of the VVD and Van Velzen of the SP submitted parliamentary questions regarding this matter following the KRO broadcast on September 11 and 13, 2007, respectively.

In 2005, the Ministry of General Affairs, the Ministry of Defence and the National Archives jointly published a so-called PIVOT report on Operations & Intelligence, written by intelligence historian Dick Engelen.

The television programme Andere Tijden devoted two episodes to Operatie & Inlichtingen and the Historisch Nieuwsblad also paid attention to this organisation.

data.title: Francesco Corvino
data.text:
----

Francesco Corvino is a British-Italian storyworld director and architect. He specializes in narrative worldbuilding, creative direction and IP development across film, television, videogames and experiential entertainment, for international clients.. [ref: About, Francesco Corvino / Eicon Design]

Corvino has contributed storyworld development to major productions, including Shōgun, Blade Runner 2049, Ready Player One, Game of Thrones season 4, The Martian, Thor: Ragnarok and Birdman (film). In 2019, he won an Art Directors Guild Award for his contribution on Ready Player One and in 2025 he won a Visual Effects Society Award for his work on Shōgun. [ref: Visual Effects Society Announces Winners of the 23rd Annual VES Awards, Visual Effects Society]

== Background and approach ==
Corvino holds a Master of Architecture (M.Arch) and specializes in storyworld direction, a multidisciplinary design approach that integrates narrative, character design, setting, history, visual style, and internal rules to build cross-media franchises and intellectual properties.

Developing this workflow while freelancing across film and video game productions, Corvino structured the approach to address cross-departmental coordination challenges, production delays, and budget overruns. The primary objective of storyworld direction is to align creative decisions across departments to maintain narrative consistency and production efficiency.

== Career ==

=== Films ===

Corvino contributed to the storyworlds of films such as Edge of Tomorrow (2014), Maleficent (2014), Birdman (2014), The Martian (2015), Thor: Ragnarok (2017), and Blade Runner 2049 (2017). [ref: Francesco Corvino, IMDb] He helped shaping the world of Steven Spielberg's Ready Player One (2018), supporting the art department led by production designer Adam Stockhausen, which won the Art Directors Guild Award for Excellence in Production Design for a Fantasy Film. [ref: 23rd Annual ADG Awards Nominees & Winners (2019), Art Directors Guild]. His film credits also span several of Disney's live-action reimaginings—including Cinderella, Beauty and the Beast, Dumbo, and Pinocchio, alongside Mary Poppins Returns—as well as major franchise tentpoles such as Lucasfilm's The Mandalorian and The Amazing Spider-Man 2.

Throughout his career, Corvino has collaborated directly with many filmmakers and production designers. He closely worked with production designer Gemma Jackson on major productions, including the biographical war drama Lee (2023), as well as the HBO Victorian science-fiction series The Nevers (2021), and the Netflix historical drama Death by Lightning. He also has a long-standing collaboration with director Christian Ditter, with whom he developed the storyworld for the film adaptation of Michael Ende's fantasy novel Momo.

As of 2025, Corvino is in charge of the storyworld development of HEADS, a retro-futuristic stop-motion animated feature film being developed by Nihil Declarandum and Mackinnon & Saunders and endorsed by Guillermo del Toro.

=== Television ===
In television, Corvino's work includes select contributions to high-profile historical dramas and fantasy series. Collaborating with Irish visual effects studio SSVFX, he designed the digital historical recreation of Osaka Castle and its city for the FX historical drama Shōgun [ref: Shōgun (2024) Full Cast & Crew, Metacritic]. The series won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Special Visual Effects in a Season or a Movie, and Corvino—alongside Manuel Martinez, Phil Hannigan, and Keith Malone—won the Visual Effects Society Award for Outstanding Created Environment in an Episode, Commercial, Game Cinematic, or Real-Time Project at the 23rd Annual VES Awards in 2025 [ref: Creative Arts Emmys: 'Shōgun' Dominates With 14 Wins, Variety]

His other notable television work includes contributing digital matte painting to the fourth season of HBO's Game of Thrones (2014) through Rodeo FX, whose visual effects team won a Primetime Emmy Award [ref: Game Of Thrones – Awards & Nominations, Academy of Television Arts & Sciences]
, and serving as a concept designer for the second season of Netflix's Wednesday (2025).

=== Video games ===
In interactive media, Corvino contributed narrative and storyworld development to the Meta Quest gaming showcase 2023.

As of 2024, he works with Absurd Ventures, the multimedia company founded by Rockstar Games co-founder Dan Houser, and he's involved in the storyworld development of the studio's upcoming open-world video game project.

=== Experiential entertainment ===
Outside of screen media, leveraging his architectural background, Corvino has designed environments for location-based entertainment and experiential installations. His projects include storyworld development for Pearl Quest, an immersive dark ride developed for China's Wanda Group in Qingdao, the Sphere in Las Vegas and the design of the visitor destination experience at the renovated Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid, in collaboration with Balich Wonder Studio. Corvino was also involved in the design of Netflix House, Netflix's permanent experiential entertainment and retail venues.

In live spectacle and theatrical entertainment, Corvino worked with the creative company Dragone on the cultural spectacle Souk Wonders. Additionally, he was involved in the development of the immersive theatrical adaptation of Grease, staged at Battersea Power Station in London, translating the original intellectual property into a multi-space, environmental narrative experience.

=== Teaching and speaking ===
Corvino has contributed extensively to industry education in storyworld and concept design as an instructor for The Gnomon Workshop. [ref: Francesco Corvino, The Gnomon Workshop] He has authored three specialized professional masterclass titles for the platform: Creating Worlds for Film & TV, Cinematic Illustration for Film and Matte Painting Techniques for Concept Design. [ref: Tutorial: Creating Worlds for Film & TV, CG Channel]

In addition to masterclasses, Corvino has delivered guest lectures on concept art and architectural worldbuilding at academic institutions, including Bournemouth University. In December 2024, he was a featured speaker at the London screen industry conference FOCUS, participating in the "In Brief: Groundbreakers" panel alongside Academy Award winners Simon Hayes and Frances Hannon, as well as industry technologist Terry White. [ref: First Look at FOCUS 2024 Conference Programme, FOCUS London]

data.title: A. Jordan Wright
data.text:
Andrew Jordan Wright, professionally known as A. Jordan Wright, is an American clinical psychologist most noted for his award-winning work in the field of psychological testing and assessment. He has won awards from the Association of Psychology Training Clinics (APTC), the American Psychological Association's Society of Clinical Psychology (SCP), and the Society for Personality Assessment (SPA) for his contributions to the field of psychology, training, and assessment, and he is a fellow of the American Psychological Association and the Society for Personality Assessment, as well as a Diplomate of the American Board of Psychological Assessment (ABPA) and the American Board of Professional Psychology. He is currently a clinical associate professor and program director of the combined clinical/counseling psychology PhD program at New York University and the founding director of NYU's training clinic, the NYU Center for Counseling and Community Wellbeing. He also serves as the chief clinical officer at Parallel Learning, a technology and service company in the special education space.

== Education ==
Wright received his master of arts in psychology in education in 2001 from Teachers College, Columbia University, followed by his PhD in clinical psychology in 2006 from Columbia University.

== Career ==
After receiving his PhD and license as a New York State psychologist, Wright joined the faculty of Teachers College, Columbia University, where he coordinated the psychological testing and assessment curriculum for the PhD program in clinical psychology (2006–2011). During this time, he also served as the director of mental health for The HOPE Program, a workforce development program in downtown Brooklyn that helps chronically under- and unemployed adults reintegrate into the workforce (2007–2011). He then joined the faculty of SUNY Empire State College, where he served as the statewide department chair of psychology and coordinated the online psychology program (2011–2017). He joined the faculty of New York University in 2017, where he founded and runs the Center for Counseling and Community Wellbeing, directs the PhD program in combined clinical/counseling psychology, and coordinates the psychological testing and assessment curriculum.

In 2011, Wright published his first book, Conducting Psychological Assessment: A Guide for Practitioners (Wiley Publishers), which came out in its second edition in 2020. Following the success of his first book, he collaborated with Gary Groth-Marnat on the sixth edition of the Handbook of Psychological Assessment (Wiley Publishers), the most widely used textbook in graduate psychological assessment coursework.

== Scholarship ==
Wright's scholarship focuses on two primary areas (and their intersection): psychological testing and assessment (including evidence-based assessment, tele-assessment validity, and cultural factors in the assessment process) and social justice (including LGBTQIA+ issues in psychology). He has authored many peer-reviewed journal articles, including "Evidence-based clinical psychological assessment (EBCPA): Review of current state of the literature and best practices" (2022) in Professional Psychology: Research and Practice, "Queering psychological assessment" (2024) in Professional Psychology: Research and Practice, and "Equivalence of remote, digital administration and traditional, in-person administration of the WISC-V" (2020) in Psychological Assessment. He is the co-author of the Wright-Constantine Structured Cultural Interview (WCSCI), a qualitative, structured interview to collect information about clients' culturally lived experience as part of a psychological assessment process.

== Professional service ==
Wright has served as president of the Society of Clinical Psychology (2025), chair of the American Psychological Association's Board of Educational Affairs (2022), and president of the American Board of Psychological Assessment (2025–present). He has also served on the executive board of the Society for Personality Assessment (2025–2027). He chaired a task force at the American Psychological Association that developed educational and training guidelines for psychological assessment in health service psychology, published in American Psychologist (2020), led guidance development for psychological tele-assessment during COVID for APA (2020), and was the lead author of the process-oriented competency framework (POCF), a new set of competencies for education and training in health service psychology, published in 2025 in Training and Education in Professional Psychology.

== Recognition ==
Wright is a fellow of the American Psychological Association and the Society for Personality Assessment. He holds board certification from the American Board of Psychological Assessment and the American Board of Professional Psychology in Clinical Psychology. He is also a diplomate of the American Board of Psychological Assessment (ABPA; 2012) and the American Board of Professional Psychology (ABPP; 2022). In 2024, he won the Association of Psychology Training Clinic's Jean Spruill Achievement Award, their highest honor, as well as the American Psychological Association Society of Clinical Psychology's Award for Distinguished Contribution to Assessment Psychology. In 2025, he won the Society for Personality Assessment's Distinguished Service and Contribution to Personality Assessment Award.

== Selected books ==

* Wright, A. J., & Raiford, S. (2021). Essentials of psychological tele-assessment. Wiley Publishers.
* Wright, A. J. (2020). Conducting psychological assessment: A guide for practitioners (2nd ed.). Wiley Publishers.
* Wright, A. J. (Ed.) (2019). Essentials of psychological assessment supervision. Wiley Publishers.

data.title: Poker affiliate
data.text:
A poker affiliate (also poker partner; in decentralized, club-based apps usually a poker agent) is a person or company that brings users to online poker and receives a commission for it from a poker room or club. The practice belongs to the wider affiliate marketing industry serving online gambling operators.

== Terminology ==
With centralized poker rooms, the intermediary is called an affiliate or partner. It works under an agreement with the operator: a player signs up through its link or promo code and is assigned to it.

In decentralized (club-based) poker apps the common term is agent. Such an intermediary represents one or more clubs, recruits members, sells and buys back chips, and in return receives a share of the rake. Trade press describes this environment as an ecosystem of clubs, agents, super agents and unions.

== History ==
Poker room partner programmes spread alongside the growth of online poker in the 2000s. Competition among partners popularised rakeback — a refund of part of the commission, paid out of the intermediary's own earnings.

During the 2010s several operators stopped paying rakeback through partners in favour of in-house loyalty schemes. In 2012 the relaunched Full Tilt Poker replaced partner deals with a VIP system paying players directly. The Merge Gaming network followed suit in January 2013.

From the late 2010s, decentralized poker apps, also known as club apps, became widespread; in them any user can open a club of their own. Games there are organised by club operators and their alliances, known as unions, while agents bring in new players. Alongside amateur communities, the scene includes companies that run clubs and unions as a professional business.

== Compensation models ==
In online gambling, poker included, partners are paid under one of three schemes:
* CPA (cost per acquisition) — a one-off fee for each new customer who meets the operator's condition, such as a first deposit;
* revenue share (revenue sharing) — a percentage of net revenue generated by the referred audience; in poker this comes mainly from rake;
* hybrid — a combination of the first two models.

For large firms both main models matter about equally: in 2019 revenue share brought Catena Media 43% of its revenue and CPA 40%.

An affiliate or agent may share part of its earnings with players as rakeback. Some operators have restricted this, substituting their own loyalty programmes.

== Agent model ==
In decentralized apps the developer supplies only the software platform; everything else is handled by users. A typical hierarchy:
* app — software and tables;
* union — a shared pool spanning several clubs;
* club — admits players and settles with them;
* agent — finds an audience, sells and buys back chips.

As a rule, each agent has its own ID, which players use to join a club and become assigned to that agent. From the rake those players pay, the club gives the agent a share, part of which the agent may return to them as rakeback. Deposits and withdrawals are handled by club administrators, sometimes through agents.

== Roles compared ==
{| class="wikitable"
! !! Affiliate !! Agent
|-
| Setting || Centralized poker rooms || Decentralized apps
|-
| Referral method || Partner link or promo code || Joining a club by ID
|-
| Flow of funds || Directly through the room's cashier || Within the club, including via the agent
|-
| Income || CPA, revenue share or hybrid || Share of rake from the club or union
|}
Sources:

== Regulation ==
Treatment of partners varies by jurisdiction. In 2014 the New Jersey Division of Gaming Enforcement ruled that flat-fee intermediaries register as vendors, while those paid by revenue share or on a hybrid basis need an ancillary licence.

The United Kingdom has no separate licence for partners; the government's 2023 white paper confirmed that licensed operators remain accountable for their marketing.

* Online poker

data.title: Francis Verney (died 1559)
data.text:
Francis Verney (1531/34 – 1559) was an English politician. He sat as MP for Buckinghamshire in 1555 and possibly Buckingham in March 1553. [ref: VERNEY, Francis (1531/34-59), of Salden in Mursley, Bucks. and London., History of Parliament Online]

He also served as sewer of the chamber by 1547 until his death; and member of the household of Princess Elizabeth in 1554.

He was the fourth son of Sir Ralph Verney (died April 1546) and the brother of Edmund Verney. He possibly married Margaret, the daughter of Sir Nicholas Vaux, 1st Baron Vaux of Harrowden, and widow of Sir Francis Pulteney of Misterton, Leicestershire with a marriage licence dated 2 April 1548.
