data.title: Have I Been Squatted
data.text:
----

Have I Been Squatted Inc. is a privately held cybersecurity company that works on domain intelligence. It builds a platform for finding typosquatted and lookalike domains, along with the websites and infrastructure tied to them, that may be used for phishing, brand impersonation, or other abuse. According to the company's documentation, its monitoring draws on domain permutations, Domain Name System (DNS) data, Certificate Transparency logs, registration data, website analysis, and passive infrastructure telemetry. [ref: Getting started with Have I Been Squatted, Have I Been Squatted Documentation]

The service started in 2022 as a public tool for spotting typosquatted domains. The company that now runs it, Have I Been Squatted Inc., was founded in 2024. [ref: About, Have I Been Squatted] [ref: Have I Been Squatted, LinkedIn]

The company also publishes research on phishing, malicious infrastructure, malware delivery, and domain-name security. Its work has been covered by BBC News, The Register, Recorded Future News, BleepingComputer, and FreightWaves. [ref: Phishing operation with links to Russia, Armenia compromised Western cargo companies, researchers find, Recorded Future News] [ref: Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers, The Register]

== History ==

Have I Been Squatted began in 2022 as an experimental tool for finding possible typosquats. Users entered a domain name and the tool generated variations of it, showing registrations that could be used to impersonate the original organization. The company says the project was first released after an experiment was shared on Hacker News, and that it grew as security practitioners started using it. Part of the tool was built on twistrs, an open-source Rust library for generating domain-name permutations that the company still maintains on GitHub. [ref: Have I Been Squatted, GitHub]

Have I Been Squatted Inc. was founded in 2024 to develop and run the service on a commercial basis. [ref: Terms of Service, Have I Been Squatted]

The commercial service moved beyond one-off typosquatting searches to continuous monitoring and investigation of external infrastructure, and later added tools for investigations, alerts, and domain takedowns.

== Platform ==

The platform looks for internet infrastructure that may be impersonating an organization, its domains, or its brands. Customers add domains for monitoring, and the platform regularly generates permutations of them and checks for related registrations and infrastructure. It adds context to what it finds using DNS records, HTTP responses, WHOIS and RDAP registration data, Certificate Transparency observations, screenshots, classification data, and passive infrastructure telemetry.

Monitoring is not limited to typos of a protected domain. The platform also surfaces domains found through Certificate Transparency, passive DNS, and other infrastructure signals.

Separately from monitoring, the platform includes tools for investigating individual domains and larger datasets. Infrastructure it identifies can be classified, investigated, and linked to alerts or response work. The company later added workflows for submitting domain takedown requests and tracking their progress.

== Threat intelligence research ==

=== Diesel Vortex ===

In February 2026, Have I Been Squatted and the threat intelligence group Ctrl-Alt-Intel published an investigation into a cybercrime operation they called Diesel Vortex. The group went after freight and logistics companies in the United States and Europe, using phishing sites built to take over accounts on load boards, fleet-management systems, fuel-card services, and other logistics platforms. [ref: Russian cybercrime ring targeted freight firms in US, Europe, report says, FreightWaves]

According to Recorded Future News, Have I Been Squatted researchers found an exposed.git directory belonging to the operation. It held source code and the group's communications, which showed how the campaign was organized and indicated that the group was building a phishing-as-a-service platform to support a wider criminal operation.

FreightWaves reported that the campaign had compromised 1,649 unique credentials, drawn from 3,474 stolen login pairs. The investigation also identified 52 deployed phishing domains, more than 75,000 targeted contact email addresses, and 35 confirmed attempts at fraud using Electronic Funds Source checks.

The exposed material pointed to an organized operation, with separate roles and infrastructure for stealing credentials, communicating with logistics staff, and managing victim sessions. Recorded Future News reported that the compromised accounts could be used for freight diversion, double brokering, and check fraud.

Have I Been Squatted and Ctrl-Alt-Intel worked with technology and security companies to disrupt the campaign's infrastructure. Recorded Future News named Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), Cloudflare, GitLab, IPinfo, and Ping Identity among those involved.

In April 2026, BleepingComputer referred to the Diesel Vortex investigation in its report on an FBI warning about a sharp rise in cyber-enabled cargo theft. It cited Have I Been Squatted's finding that the group had used dozens of phishing domains against freight and logistics operators since 2025. [ref: FBI links cybercriminals to sharp surge in cargo theft attacks, BleepingComputer]

=== Recruitment malware campaigns ===

In August 2026, Have I Been Squatted published a technical analysis of a malware campaign that used a fake hiring process to target a job seeker in the Web3 sector. The attackers approached the victim on LinkedIn, ran what looked like a normal interview process using Calendly and Google-hosted services, and then sent technical assessment material that was malicious. [ref: From fake interview to signed ClickOnce: inside a three-payload Windows chain, Have I Been Squatted]

On Windows, the attack used a digitally signed ClickOnce application. Installing it eventually delivered three payloads: a version of NeedleStealer, a separate information stealer written in Rust, and a custom Go remote-access trojan with remote shell access, file management, proxying, keylogging, and hidden virtual network computing.

The same infrastructure could also serve a macOS delivery chain that ended in Odyssey Stealer. The researchers said the mix of legitimate online platforms, signed software, and targeted social engineering made the fake recruitment process far more convincing than ordinary phishing.

In September 2026, BBC News cited analysis by Have I Been Squatted in a report on fake recruitment scams. The report followed a victim who was approached on LinkedIn and lost about £18,000 in cryptocurrency after installing malicious software during what seemed to be a real hiring process. It highlighted the attackers' use of genuine Google services and digitally signed software. [ref: I lost my savings after a job interview scam, BBC News]

=== Internationalized domain name and Chromium research ===

In October 2026, Have I Been Squatted published research on how Chromium-based browsers handle internationalized domain names (IDNs). They tested whether deceptive lookalike domains could get past Chromium's protections and be shown to users in Unicode, rather than in their Punycode form, which is easier to recognize as suspicious. [ref: Turning IDN edge cases into typosquats, Have I Been Squatted]

The researchers found edge cases involving two characters: the Cyrillic letter ө, used in languages such as Kazakh and Mongolian, and the Latin letter ƙ, used in languages such as Hausa. Using these characters, they built lookalikes of well-known domains that passed Chromium's display checks.

Have I Been Squatted registered 20 proof-of-concept lookalike domains for the research, including ones resembling Apple, SpaceX, Okta, and Nike. The Register covered the findings on October 10, 2026, explaining how the two characters could get around Chromium's checks for suspicious internationalized domains.

Chromium runs several checks before deciding whether to show an internationalized domain in Unicode. One set looks for characters and scripts often used for impersonation. Another reduces each domain to a simplified comparison string, called a skeleton, and compares it against a built-in list of popular domains.

The research found that Cyrillic ө was missing from Chromium's whole-script lookalike list, so adding it to an otherwise confusable Cyrillic domain could stop that check from triggering. The Latin ƙ caused a related problem at the skeleton stage. Its hook was kept as a combining mark, so the skeleton never exactly matched the ASCII domain it imitated.

The researchers also looked at Chromium's Safety Tips, which warn users when they navigate to a site by comparing it, exactly and approximately, against well-known sites and sites the user visits often. They found cases where a lookalike differed enough from the comparison skeleton to avoid a warning, as well as limitations affecting domains with fewer than five characters before the top-level domain.

As part of the work, the company analyzed the.com zone for internationalized domains and found about 162,000 pairs in which an IDN resembled an ASCII.com domain. The researchers noted that this did not mean 162,000 malicious typosquats, since such pairs can include legitimate multilingual domains and defensive registrations.

The research also compared email clients. Gmail showed the tested internationalized sender domains in Unicode, while Outlook Web showed the same domains as Punycode A-labels. The Register noted that the two services had made different trade-offs in how they present internationalized email domains to users.

== Public and open-source tools ==

Alongside its commercial service, Have I Been Squatted releases free and open-source security tools.

twistrs is a Rust library for generating and enumerating domain-name permutations. It is released under the MIT License, hosted in the company's public GitHub organization, and was one of the building blocks of the original typosquatting service.

In December 2025, the company launched certgrep, a free search service for Certificate Transparency data. It lets users search certificate records with regular expressions, wildcards, and substring queries. The company built it after using similar functionality internally to find domains that matched suspicious patterns. [ref: Announcing certgrep, Have I Been Squatted]

The company also maintains an open-source Python software development kit for its application programming interface (API). It gives programmatic access to features including domain-squatting analysis, domain investigation, and Certificate Transparency search. [ref: haveibeensquatted-python, GitHub]

data.title: Border (2026 film)
data.text:
Border (; also known as Bian jing) is a 2026 Mandarin- and Mongolian-language drama film written and directed by Ah Biao in his feature debut. [ref: San Sebastian Competition Title 'Border' Boards Reel Suspects for Global Sales, [[Variety (magazine)] [ref: Ah Biao, Fred Cavayé, Jesse Eisenberg, Amanda Kernell, Gabriel Martins and Tony Vahl also to compete for the Golden Shell, San Sebastián International Film Festival] [ref: Bian jing / Border, San Sebastián International Film Festival] The film stars Zheyan Li, Feng Qi, Han Sanming, Gang Zheng and Tao Guo.

According to the official poster billing block, the film was produced by Jenny Man Wu, with Lili Tong, Tyler Hill and Xue Ma as producers, and Yaohua LI (also credited as LI Yaohua; Chinese: 李要华), Jing Yang and Hao Zhou as co-producers; Dongmei Li, Nan Xin and Ning Wu are credited as associate producers. [ref: Borderless Films, official poster billing block for Border.]

Produced by Borderless Films as a Hong Kong–United States–South Korea co-production, Border was selected for the Official Selection of the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival, where it had its world premiere and won the festival's Special Jury Prize. [ref: San Sebastian Adds Jesse Eisenberg, Fred Cavayé, Amanda Kernell Films to Golden Shell Race, [[Variety (magazine)] [ref: Jesse Eisenberg & 'Les Misérables' Added To San Sebastián Competition, [[Deadline Hollywood] [ref: San Sebastián: Mike Leigh's 'Tender Loving Care' Wins Golden Shell & Best Screenplay, [[Deadline Hollywood] [ref: 'Tender Loving Care', by Mike Leigh, carries off the Golden Shell at the San Sebastián Festival's 74th edition, San Sebastián International Film Festival] Paris-based sales company Reel Suspects handles worldwide sales.

==Plot==
In a forgotten town where men keep their feelings buried and speak little, a broke young miner drifts through a numb routine. His life is disrupted by the arrival of an enigmatic young woman, who awakens a dormant curiosity. He follows her onto a darker path, leaving behind the only world he knows, unaware that she is not who she appears to be.

==Cast==
* Zheyan Li
* Feng Qi
* Han Sanming (credited as Sanming Han)
* Gang Zheng
* Tao Guo

==Production==
Border is the feature debut of Ah Biao, a director, screenwriter and cinematographer born in Shanxi, China, in 1990 and based in Bangkok.

According to the San Sebastián International Film Festival catalogue, production companies are Borderless Films Ltd. (Hong Kong / China; Jenny Man Wu) and Mala Productions LLC (United States; Tyler Hill and Hao Zhou). Co-production companies include Yangtze Visual Culture Co. Ltd. (Japan; Jing Yang) and Yilu Partners Co. Ltd (South Korea; Xue Ma). Yaohua LI is credited as a co-producer. International sales are handled by Reel Suspects (France).

Principal individual credits on the official poster billing block include:

According to Variety, the film is a Hong Kong–United States–South Korea–Japan co-production; the festival listing identifies the production countries as Hong Kong, the United States and South Korea, while also listing a Japanese co-production company. The runtime is 78 minutes; original languages are Mandarin Chinese and Mongolian.

==Release==
Border was announced for the Official Selection (in competition) of the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival on 14 August 2026, joining titles by directors including Mike Leigh, Pablo Larraín, Nicole Garcia and Yeşim Ustaoğlu. On 11 September 2026, Variety reported that Reel Suspects had boarded worldwide sales on the film; Variety also reported that it was among titles in contention for the Sebastiane Award.

The film had its world premiere in San Sebastián on 23 September 2026, with further festival screenings through 26 September, including a presentation with the film delegation at the Kursaal. [ref: Pelikula: "Border", Kulturweb] [ref: Border (Bian Jing), DMovies] At the festival press conference, Ah Biao said he aimed to express emotions and interpersonal distances rather than tell a conventional plot-driven story, and described the title's "border" as primarily figurative; producer Jenny Man Wu and cast members including Han Sanming also spoke at the event. [ref: El cineasta Ah Biao reivindica en 'Border' el cine de emociones: "La historia no es importante", Europa Press] [ref: Ah Biao: "Existen fronteras entre las personas", San Sebastián International Film Festival]

On 26 September 2026, Border won the Special Jury Prize (Premio especial del jurado) at the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival. [ref: Mike Leigh's 'Tender Loving Care' Sweeps San Sebastian Awards, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: Mike Leigh's 'Tender Loving Care' Wins Big at San Sebastián, [[Variety (magazine)] [ref: San Sebastian 2026: The Awards, The Film Verdict] [ref: "Tender loving care", de Mike Leigh, se lleva la Concha de Oro, Orain / EITB] The festival jury described the film as "bold in both cinematic form and sexual explicitness that in the confidence of its vision reveals a major new voice in world cinema".

==Reception==
Following its San Sebastián premiere, Border received coverage from international film critics writing in English, Spanish, French, Basque and other languages.

Writing for DMovies from the festival, Nataliia Serebriakova placed the film in the tradition of contemporary Chinese slow cinema and noted Ah Biao's austere visual style, while arguing that its narrative and characters remained underdeveloped.

Diego Batlle of Otros Cines described the debut as austere and demanding, comparing its approach in places to early Jia Zhangke, and welcomed it as an unusual Chinese first feature in San Sebastián's main competition despite finding it uneven. [ref: Festival de San Sebastián 2026: Crítica de "Border" ("Bian jing"), película de Ah Biao (Competencia Oficial), Otros Cines]

Diego Lerer of Micropsia similarly highlighted the film's rigorous mise-en-scène and long takes, comparing aspects of its tone to Jia Zhangke and Aki Kaurismäki, and called Ah Biao's command of staging unusually assured for a first feature while noting that the film would likely divide audiences. [ref: 'Border' San Sebastian Review: Ah Biao's Stark Portrait of Loneliness and Desire, Micropsia] [ref: San Sebastián 2026: crítica de 'Border' ('Bian Jing'), de Ah Biao (Competición), Micropsia]

In The Film Verdict, Stephen Dalton described Border as a starkly beautiful but overly cryptic exercise in lo-fi noir minimalism, praising its visual compositions while finding the drama maddeningly opaque. [ref: Border, The Film Verdict]

Writing for the French site Le Polyester, Nicolas Bardot praised Ah Biao's use of minimalism and visual storytelling, while noting that key plot points remain deliberately opaque; he linked the film's harsh immersion to earlier Chinese cinema such as Li Yang's Blind Shaft and early work by Diao Yinan. [ref: ]

A review for View of the Arts argued that the film's silences are sometimes eloquent and sometimes distancing, praising Zheyan Li's performance and Ah Biao's cinematography while finding the emotional connection between characters and audience incomplete. [ref: 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival: "Border" Review, View of the Arts]

Ricardo Fernández of El Contraplano praised the film's coherent visual depiction of isolation but argued that its extreme narrative reduction emptied the central relationships of emotional force. [ref: 'Border': Emociones bajo tierra, El Contraplano]

Writing in Basque for Berria, Lander Garro described the film as an austere formal exercise built around frozen pre-action poses and a deliberately cold mise-en-scène, calling it interesting but close to boredom. [ref: 'Bian Jing / Border', Berria]

data.title: 2026 Narathiwat attack
data.text:
On July 22, Unknown assailants attacked the Buketa Sami checkpoint killing five paramilitary personnel and injuring six others, no group claimed responsibility for the attacks; however, authorities suspected two men responsible for the attack.

== Background ==

The Provinces of Narathiwat, Yala province and Pattani province are Thailand's only Muslim majority provinces, in those regions an insurgency by Malay insurgents have claimed the lives of 7,000+ people since 2004 [ref: Thai authorities hunt for suspects after an attack in troubled south kills 5 soldiers, Manila Bulletin]

Thai spokeswoman, Ratchada Thanadirek stated that in the past two to three months that a series of violent attacks were perpetrated by a "terrorist network seeking to instil fear among the public and target state officials" [ref: Five soldiers killed in bomb attack in Thailand’s restive south, The Straits Times]

A day before the attack occurred, a car explosion occurred in front of a Police station causing minor injuries and property damage [ref: Five Thai soldiers killed in bomb attack, Dawn]

== Attack ==
The attack occurred on 6:45 PM, when unidentified assailants used pipe bombs and firearms during the attack, The attack resulted in the deaths of five Thai rangers while six civilians were wounded, including a ten-year-old boy [ref: Thailand: 5 soldiers killed in attack on security checkpoint, DW], a three-year-old girl and a senior citizen [ref: Five Thai rangers killed in armed attack in Narathiwat, Bernama], The attack also lasted for ninety seconds before ending [ref: CCTV shows nine attackers raiding Narathiwat checkpoint in 90 seconds, The Star] after the attack, Emergency teams immediately transported the wounded to hospitals [ref: 5 paramilitary troops killed in southern Thailand checkpoint attack, Anadolu Agency]

After the attack, The assailants seized three AK-47 rifles, Three bullet-proof vests and three cellphones from the paramilitary personnel [ref: Thai authorities hunt for suspects after an attack in troubled south kills 5 soldiers, The Washington Post]

Government forces reported that the pick-up truck used to transport the assailants was found abandoned and set on fire, 13 miles away from the attack site [ref: Thailand launches manhunt after 5 soldiers killed, civilians injured in deep south, South China Morning Post]

== Victims ==
The names of the victims killed were identified as [ref: Five rangers killed, civilians injured in Narathiwat checkpoint attack, Nation Thailand]

* Theerayut Somakerd
* Sakiriya Jena
* Wimon Dabthong
* Nattasit Kaewsena
* Salahuding Pi

Names of the Victims injured [ref: Five Thai rangers killed, civilians injured in Narathiwat checkpoint attack, The Star]

* Habib Hina
* Muhammad Ali Abrue
* Farhah Abrue
* Muhammad Hafit Hina
* Awatif Bueraheng

== Aftermath ==
Thai government forces sealed off the checkpoint after the attack and launched investigations to identify the assailants

On July 24, Thai authorities imposed martial law in Narathiwat following the attack as to pursue the assailants, this was issued by Major General Yod-Arwut Phuengpak [ref: Thailand imposes martial law in southern province after attack kills 5 paramilitary troops, Anadolu Agency]

Peacetalks with Insurgents in the area were also postponed indefinitely as a result of the attack [ref: Deadly raid puts peace talks on hold, Bangkok Post]

== Reactions ==
Thai Prime Minister, Anutin Charnvirakul condemned the attacks calling it a "brazen act of terrorism" and "a serious threat to national security"

== References ==

data.title: 1879–80 Birmingham Senior Cup
data.text:
The 1879–80 Birmingham Senior Cup was the fourth season of the oldest county cup competition still active and the third oldest in the world overall. [ref: Birmingham County FA Cups, BCFA] [ref: The History of the Birmingham Senior Cup 1876 to 1905, Grorty Dick. ASIN:B00L3AL7YE] Aston Villa beat Saltley College 3–1 in the final.

Villa beat Excelsior 8–1 in the second round. On 14 February 1880, Aston Villa beat Newport (Salop) 7-0 in the third round [ref: Matches played on Saturday, Birmingham Evening Mail, 16 February 1880, p3] and Walsall Swifts in the semi-finals. [ref: "Gossip on rural pastimes", The Leeds Mercury, 26 March 1880, p2]

The Saltley Collegians reached the final, beating Stoke in the third round, in a tie delayed to allow the students to return to college after a mid-term break. [ref: Football jottings, Nottingham Evening Post] In the semi-finals the club lost 3–0 to Derby at the Aston Lower Ground, [ref: Birmingham Challenge Cup, Derby Daily Telegraph] but a protest was made that one of the Derby players was "cup-tied", having already played for Wednesbury Strollers in the Sheffield Challenge Cup, against the rules of the competition which barred any player from representing more than one side in competitive matches. [ref: Football, Birmingham Daily Gazette] The protest was upheld and the college team put into the final, where it faced Aston Villa at the Aston Lower Grounds in what was seen as a "certainty" for the Villans; [ref: Birmingham Association Cup, Nottingham Evening Post] the Aston side duly won 3–1. [ref: Birmingham Association Challenge Cup Final Tie, Birmingham Gazette] [ref: Aston Villa v Saltley College 3–1, Play Up Liverpool] The match was the college's high point in football.

Wednesbury Strollers reached the last six in 1879–80 losing heavily to the professional Walsall Swifts, by which time the Swifts were seen as the strongest side in Walsall. [ref: Football, Birmingham Evening Mail] The semi-final stage (because of an inequality of entrants) had three teams, but Swifts were doubly unlucky with the draw – they missed out on the bye to the final, and were drawn to face Aston Villa, by then the strongest side in the Midlands. Villa duly won 2–1 in front of 6,000 at the Aston Lower Grounds, scoring twice in two minutes. [ref: Birmingham Association Cup, Nottingham Evening Post]

data.title: Muriel Horrell
data.text:
----

Muriel Agatha Horrell (13 December 1910 – May 1994) was a South African pilot, military officer and race relations researcher. She served in the South African Women’s Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) [ref: Flying High: The Story of the Women's Auxiliary Air Force 1939-1945, Military History Journal] during the Second World War, attaining the rank of major and serving in South Africa, Kenya, Egypt and Italy. She was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) in 1947 for her wartime service. After the war, Horrell worked for the South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) for almost four decades, where she researched apartheid legislation and compiled the Institute's annual Survey of Race Relations, which became a widely used reference on South African social, political and economic conditions. She received honorary degrees from the University of Natal and the University of the Witwatersrand in recognition of her contributions to race relations research.

== Early life ==
Horrell was born on 13 December 1910 in Pretoria, South Africa, to Katherine (née Sutherns) and Lloyd Leslie Horrell, the eldest of five children. She attended Pretoria High School for Girls and then completed a Bachelor of Science at the University of the Witwatersrand, followed by a teacher’s diploma at the Johannesburg Teacher Training College. [ref: Muriel Horrell A tribute, Race Relations News]  She taught for just over eight years in Pretoria  and helped develop a geography syllabus as a member of a provincial committee. She was also an active Girl Guide leader serving as a District Captain, keen sports woman, and accomplished rider.

==WAAF and wartime service==
Horrell developed an early passion for aviation and is reputed to have been the first South African woman granted an airline pilot’s licence qualifying as a Flight Officer in 1938. She was active in the South African Women’s Aviation Association (SAWAA) and was a flight officer and lecturer. At the outbreak of World War ll on 1 September 1939, Egerton-Bird, a prominent member of the (SAWAA) had telegraphed General Jan Smuts offering the SAWAA’s services to the government. On 10 May 1940, the establishment of the South African Women’s Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) was gazetted, [ref: Government Notices, The Union of South Africa Government Gazette] and Horrell was enlisted in 1940. [ref: Transnational Race Relations: Muriel Horrell’s Journey toward Understanding Reserves and Reservations in South Africa, Africa, and the United States, American Studies] The WAAF’s wartime activities included communications, intelligence, link-trainer instruction, armament training, and technical work on aircraft, in addition to clerical and logistical roles such as dispatch riding and administration.

In December 1940, Horrell led the first detachment of WAAFs to be sent north where they established a camp in Nairobi, Kenya. She was posted to Cairo in 1941 as deputy director of the WAAF in the Middle East. [ref: Muriel Horrell – chronicler of the banal evil of apartheid, queen of a million footnotes., Daily Maverick]

In April 1942, the WAAF and South African Air Force (SAAF) administrative functions were merged, with only a few officers remaining in the directorate. With the El Alamein offensive toward Alexandria and Cairo in June 1942, Horrell oversaw the evacuation of around 800 WAAF personnel from Cairo to Aswan.

In December 1943, Horrell was appointed as WAAF Staff Officer responsible to Air Headquarters Services back in Pretoria with the rank of Major. When mobilisation began, she visited WAAF contingents in Algeria and Italy in 1945 as part of a demobilization team.

==Demobilisation and postwar work==
After being demobilised on 15 May 1946, Horrell began working as a technical officer for the National War Memorial Health Foundation. The Foundation originated with a proposal to establish a living war memorial that provided health services to all South Africans, including non-European communities. Its guiding principles were that it be living, national, and support fundamental human rights. [ref: The National War Memorial Health Foundation., South African Medical Journal] In this role, she helped to plan health promotion projects and travelled widely throughout the country.

On 14 November 1947, Horrell was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) for her wartime service [ref: Central Chancery of the Orders of Knighthood, The London Gazette] in recognition of her organisation and evacuation of WAAFs from Cairo during the El Alamein campaigns.

Following the election of the National Party (South Africa) in 1948 the government announced that the Foundation would receive no further grants other than those promised by the defeated Prime Minister, Jan Smuts. Due to dwindling funds, staff were advised to seek other employment, and Horrell accepted a post as Technical Assistant at the South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR). [ref: The South African Institute of Race Relations 1929–1979: A short history., South African Institute of Race Relations.]

The IRR, founded in 1929, is an organisation dedicated to researching socio-economic issues and improving race relations in South Africa. In a 1989 interview, Horrell stated: “I’ve always believed that one must be involved to effect change.” [ref: Muriel Horrell, Researcher extraordinary, Race Relations News]

In 1949, Horrell began at the IRR in the newly established role of technical assistant (renamed as research officer from 1959).  One of Horrell’s first tasks at IRR was to document the effects of the Group Areas Act. Horrell  travelled extensively across South Africa to observe the social and economic consequences of this legislation.

She took over compiling the annual Survey of Race Relations, and is named as initiating the change of  the Survey to a report on the state of the nation and making the report essential to all students of South African Affairs. [ref: An Enduring Scandal, South African History Online] From 1959, this role was that of research officer which she executed alone until the last six years of her twenty-eight year service when she had assistance. The Survey of Race Relations is an annual publication documenting socio-economic, demographic, and political trends in South Africa, including politics, employment, industrial relations, education, health, living conditions, and crime. The  Surveys were objective and rigorous with facts fully authenticated, referencing ministerial statements, official reports and parliamentary records. Horrell extended the IRR’s research and collection of factual information, producing 41 booklets and fact papers on topics such as the homelands, trade unions, passive and violent resistance, and the rights of black women. In addition to research, she prepared parliamentary questions, reported on legislation affecting race relations, met with local and international visitors, and gave lectures when invited.

In her 1994 obituary, John Kane-Berman, executive director of IRR, called her “the Queen of a Million Footnotes”, noting that “her name appears in more academic books and journal articles in more languages than any other person who has written about South Africa”. [ref: Apartheid watchdog dies, The Star] An editorial in the Cape Times in 1976 stated that in the Survey, “the facts speak for themselves, too often with spine-chilling eloquence, but their presentation is rigorous and objective.”

In 1964, she received a travel grant from the Carnegie Foundation to study underdeveloped communities in Africa and the United States. She visited Kenya, Northern Rhodesia, Rhodesia and Tanganyika, newly independent nations, examining the challenges and opportunities of postcolonial development. Her research included political, social and economic analysis of each African country she visited. In the United States, she researched Native American reservations and compared them with African reserves/homelands, and an in depth analysis of the Civil Rights movement. During her time in the United States, she embarked on a speaking tour, and attended many meetings with academics, senior human rights, political and church leaders as well as South African exiles.

==IRR and apartheid-era research==
In 1971, Horrell was awarded an honorary Master of Social Science degree by the University of Natal, and in 1974, she received an honorary Doctor of Philosophy from the University of the Witwatersrand “for her contributions to the study and improvement of race relations in South Africa.”

In 1972, she was sponsored by the University of Gothenburg, the Scandinavian Institute of African Affairs (now called the Nordic Africa Institute)  and the Swedish Mission Board to give a series of addresses in Sweden.

In 1973, the IRR was one of four anti-apartheid civil society organisations investigated by the Schlebusch Commission. The SAIRR Council stated that the Schlebusch Commission was a ‘totally unsuitable vehicle for a task of this nature’. They criticised the use of a select committee of Parliament, the in-camera nature of hearings, and the inability of affected entities to review the evidence against them. [ref: Our History, IRR]

==Later life and death==
Horrell retired from full-time work at the Institute in 1977 but continued contributing chapters on religion to The Survey of Race Relations until her 80s. She remained active in improving race relations through the  St John’s Ecumenical Church. Horrell died in May 1994 in Johannesburg, South Africa, aged 83.

data.title: Robert Peckham (MP)
data.text:
----

Sir Robert Peckham (by 1516 – 10 September 1569) was an English politician. He sat as MP for Buckinghamshire in April 1554. [ref: PECKHAM, Sir Robert (by 1516-69), of London, Biddlesden and Denham, Bucks., History of Parliament Online]

He was knighted on 2 October 1553.

== Family and education ==
He was the first son of Sir Edmund Peckham of Denham by Anne, the daughter of John Cheyne of Chesham Bois, Buckinghamshire. He was the brother of Henry Peckham (MP for Wycombe). He was admitted into Gray's Inn in 1533., he married Mary, the daughter of Edmund Braye, 1st Baron Braye.

== Political career ==
He also served as clerk comptroller of the counting house by 1540 till 1543; justice of the peace for Buckinghamshire from 1542 till 1547, quorum in 1558/59; commissioner of subsidy in 1543, commissioner of relief in 1550; escheator in Bedfordshire and Buckinghamshire from 1545 till 1546; sheriff from 1556 till 1557; member of the Privy Council from August 1553 till November 1558.

data.title: Thomas Lavyngton
data.text:
Thomas Lavyngton () was an English politican. He sat as MP for Reading in March 1416, 1417, 1420, May 1421, 1422, 1423, 1425, 1427, 1429, 1431, 1435, and 1442. [ref: LAVYNGTON, Thomas, of Reading, Berks., History of Parliament Online]

He also served as justice of the peace for Berkshire from 13 November 1448 till June 1449, and 22 March 1452 till January 1454; commissioner of oyer an terminer in Oxfordshire, and Berkshire in January 1450; commissioner to impound goods of the Bishop of Salisbury in July 1450; and tax collector of Berkshire in August 1450. He also possibly served as Mayor of Reading from Michaelmas 1421 till 1422, and 1426 till 1427.

Before 1426, he married Denise.

data.title: David Plummer
data.text:
David Alexander Plummer. [ref: SUSSEX WILDLIFE TRUST - Charity 207005, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk] is a British wildlife photographer, filmmaker, author, naturalist and conservationist. His work encompasses wildlife photography, natural history filmmaking, fieldcraft and conservation education [ref: Fieldcraft AKA how to watch wildlife without disturbing it - Sussex Wildlife Trust], with particular expertise in birds, especially owls, and butterflies.

Plummer's wildlife photographs have appeared in specialist publications and the national and international press [ref: 7 Years of Camera Shake, Discover Wildlife] [ref: I made the choice to grab life by the horns, The i] [ref: ProZone Interview: David Plummer, N-Photo]. He was shortlisted for Wildlife Photographer of the Year in 2016 and is the author of 7 Years of Camera Shake (2017) [ref: 7 Years of Camera Shake, The Times], which documents his photographic work following his diagnosis of Parkinson's disease in 2009. His television and film work includes contributions to BBC natural history productions, including Wild Isles (2023) [ref: Wild Isles], as well as wildlife consultancy and documentary filmmaking.

Plummer was the subject of 15 Years (2023) [ref: 15 YEARS - Living with Parkinson’s Disease as a Wildlife Photographer (Short Documentary)], a short documentary directed by Katie Mayhew that received a Golden Wing Grand Award at the [https://msmke.net Hungarian Special Film Festival] [ref: Ezen a fesztiválon három patkány is lehetett díjnyertes, index.hu]. He also appeared in Shaking Hands with the Devil [ref: Shaking Hands With The Devil – A documentary on Parkinson's & Witchcraft in Kenya, Africa], a documentary examining the stigma surrounding Parkinson's disease in Kenya [ref: ], which received a Bronze Judges' Award at the 2024 [https://smileymovement.org/charityfilmawards Smiley Charity Film Awards] [ref: Smiley Charity Film Awards, Smiley Charity Film Awards]. In 2025, he contributed to Super Nature, a feature-length documentary directed by Ed Sayers that premiered at the BFI London Film Festival [ref: Super Nature, Screen Scotland].

Plummer previously worked as a resident wildlife photographer at the [https://knepp.co.uk Knepp Estate] rewilding project in West Sussex. He has served as a trustee of Sussex Wildlife Trust since March 2024 [ref: Trustees and President - Sussex Wildlife Trust] and contributed to the Parkinson's UK garden at the 2026 RHS Chelsea Flower Show, which received the BBC/RHS People's Choice Award for Best Show Garden [ref: ].

== Early life ==
Plummer developed an interest in wildlife during childhood, spending time observing insects, breeding butterflies and studying animals in their natural habitats. His early interest in wildlife photography was influenced by the work of British bird photographer Eric Hosking, whom he heard interviewed on BBC Radio [ref: David Plummer: From Amateur to Professional, www.naturettl.com].

He began experimenting with photography using a second-hand Prinzflex 35mm single-lens reflex camera. Initially photographing wildlife and plants in his local surroundings, he developed his photographic techniques through observation and field experience [ref: Wildlife Photographer Proves Parkinson’s Is No Obstacle, Medium].

Plummer began his working career at the age of 17 as a police cadet, subsequently serving as a police officer for the Metropolitan Police. He then transferred to the Caribbean, where he continued working as a police officer, before pursuing a professional career in wildlife photography [ref: Woodland Bird Photography with David Plummer].

His early photographic work concentrated on British wildlife, particularly in Kent and Sussex, before expanding to international locations, including Africa, South America and the Galápagos Islands [ref: 7 YEARS OF CAMERA SHAKE - DAVID PLUMMER, wildimportance].

== Career ==

=== Wildlife photography ===
Plummer established his career photographing wildlife in Britain and internationally, with particular interests in birds, mammals and animal behaviour [ref: 6 world-class wildlife shots taken by a photographer with Parkinson's, Parkinson's Europe]. His work has taken him to locations including the Pantanal wetlands of Brazil, where he has photographed wildlife since the late 1990s.

He readily adopts fieldcraft, animal behaviour and the use of hides and camouflage into his photographic approach [ref: Fieldcraft AKA how to watch wildlife without disturbing it - Sussex Wildlife Trust].

He previously worked at the Knepp Estate in West Sussex, where he was involved in wildlife photography, photographic safaris and fieldcraft instruction [ref: The Knepp Estate, West Sussex, Bird Photographer of the Year].

Plummer’s observations of fallow deer at the Knepp Estate were featured in the companion book to the BBC natural history series Wild Isles. The book quotes his accounts of the annual deer rut and the behaviour of competing males. [ref: Wild Isles, William Collins]

In 2016, Plummer was shortlisted for Wildlife Photographer of the Year. The following year he published, 7 Years of Camera Shake: One Man's Passion for Photographing Wildlife, a collection of more than 200 photographs taken following his diagnosis of Parkinson's disease in 2009. The book features wildlife photographed in Britain and internationally, accompanied by accounts of his photographic experiences [ref: ].

=== Film and Television ===
Plummer has worked as a wildlife consultant, photographer and filmmaker on natural history television productions and documentary films. His work has included contributions to BBC programmes, including Springwatch and Wild Isles (2023), for which he provided footage of tawny owls [ref: Trustees and President - Sussex Wildlife Trust].

He has worked with wildlife presenter Hamza Yassin on several BBC productions. In 2023, he appeared in Hamza: Strictly Birds of Prey [ref: Hamza: Strictly Birds of Prey from the Cairngorms to urban London, Silverback Films], sharing his knowledge of tawny owl behaviour and assisting with filming at his wildlife garden in West Sussex [ref: Hamza: Strictly Birds of Prey review – a solid hour of utter loveliness from the Strictly winner, The Guardian]. In 2025, he contributed to Hamza's Hidden Wild Isles [ref: Hamza's Hidden Wild Isles], assisting with the observation of wild badgers in Sussex for the episode Spring, featuring Yassin and his two nieces. He also appeared in Winter, in which Yassin returned to Plummer's garden to film wild tawny owls.

Plummer has appeared on BBC television programmes, including BBC Breakfast and The One Show. In 2010, he assisted with wildlife photography in Scrag Copse [ref: Parkinson's sufferer talks about his new wildlife photography book, The Argus]. In March 2016, he demonstrated wildlife photography techniques using a floating hide on The One Show [ref: Floating hide – Spy in the lake]. He also appeared on the programme to discuss his experience of living with Parkinson's disease and his photographic career [ref: Time In The Wild]. In September 2017, he was interviewed on BBC Breakfast [ref: Interview on BBC Breakfast] about his book 7 Years of Camera Shake, his career and his experience of Parkinson's disease. He later appeared on BBC Breakfast [ref: Interview on BBC Breakfast with David Plummer & Dr Fothergill-Misbah - Shaking Hands with The Devil] to discuss Shaking Hands with the Devil, a documentary examining the experiences of people living with Parkinson's disease in Kenya.

Plummer has also been interviewed on BBC radio, including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Radio 2's Jeremy Vine programme [ref: Jeremy Vine - Hiding Parkinson's - BBC Sounds, BBC], BBC Sussex and BBC Southern Counties Radio [ref: https://davidplummer.co.uk/media-profile/radio/, David Plummer].

In 2018, Plummer appeared in an advertising campaign for Huawei's P20 Pro smartphone, produced by German advertising agency Jung von Matt [ref: #FotosMitWahrerGröße präsentiert von HUAWEI und der Deutschen Parkinson Gesellschaft] [ref: #FotosMitWahrerGröße: Das ist die erste Arbeit von Jung von Matt für Huawei - HORIZONT, www.horizont.net]. The campaign featured his work photographing a wolf and highlighted the phone's AI-assisted camera technology in relation to his experience of Parkinson's disease [ref: Apps und Gadgets: So hilft smarte Technik Menschen mit Handicap - WELT, DIE WELT]. Five photographs taken during filming were auctioned to raise funds for the German Society for Parkinson's and Movement Disorders.

Plummer was credited as a wildlife consultant on Wilding (2023) [ref: Title: Wilding Director: David Allen Year: 2023 Production company: Passion Pictures Time: 1:13:21 Available to watch on Amazon Prime], a documentary directed by David Allen about the rewilding of the Knepp Estate in West Sussex.

In 2023, Plummer appeared alongside artist Alex Echo and musician Nigel Bates in Passion, Purpose & Parkinson's [ref: Passion, Purpose & Parkinson's, FilmFreeway], a short documentary directed by Olz McCoy about their experiences of pursuing creative careers following Parkinson's diagnoses [ref: CVP: The freedom to film, Definition].

The same year, Plummer was the subject of 15 Years [ref: 15 YEARS - Living with Parkinson’s Disease as a Wildlife Photographer (Short Documentary)], a short documentary directed by Katie Mayhew examining his photographic career and the challenges presented by Parkinson's disease [ref: Katie Mayhew: Framing the wild’s untold tales, British Cinematographer]. The film received a Golden Wing Grand Award at the 2023 Hungarian Special Film Festival [ref: Díjazottak 2023 / Award winners 2023, msmke.net] and was screened at the IN THE PALACE International Short Film Festival in 2024 [ref: 15 Years, inthepalace.com].

Plummer also featured in Shaking Hands with the Devil, a documentary directed by Olz McCoy examining the stigma and discrimination experienced by people with Parkinson's disease in Kenya. The film was nominated in the Golden Pier Short Documentary category at the 2024 Cannes Film Awards [ref: 2024, Cannes Film Awards] and received a Bronze Judges' Award at the 2024 Smiley Charity Film Awards.

In 2025, Plummer contributed to Super Nature, a feature-length documentary directed by Ed Sayers and filmed on Super 8. The film premiered at the BFI London Film Festival in October 2025 and was released in UK cinemas in September 2026. [ref: Super Nature, Screen Scotland]

=== Conservation and education ===

Plummer's work includes wildlife conservation, environmental education and photographic tuition.

His involvement with conservation organisations includes his work at the Knepp Estate rewilding project in West Sussex and his support for Sussex Wildlife Trust through photography, filmmaking and educational activities [ref: Wildlife photographer David Plummer and his love for Sussex, Great British Life]. On 6 March 2024, he was appointed a trustee of Sussex Wildlife Trust, a conservation charity working to protect wildlife and habitats across Sussex [ref: Specialist Wildlife Guide Naturalist Film Consultancy & Photography, David Plummer] [ref: SUSSEX WILDLIFE TRUST - Charity 207005, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk].

Plummer is a Gardens and Greenspaces Ambassador [ref: ] for [https://www.wealdtowaves.co.uk Weald to Waves], a Sussex nature-recovery initiative seeking to connect habitats across the county. In this role, he promotes wildlife-friendly gardening and habitat creation [ref: ].

At his home in West Sussex, he has developed a wildlife garden used for observing, photographing and filming wildlife. He shares his experience of wildlife gardening and habitat creation through educational activities and advice [ref: ].

His educational work includes photographic tuition and fieldcraft instruction, with guided wildlife photography experiences focused on observing animals in their natural environments.

In 2026, Plummer contributed to the development of the Parkinson's UK garden at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show. Garden designer Arit Anderson visited his wildlife garden in Sussex to discuss how gardening helps him manage Parkinson's disease and how adaptations to outdoor spaces can support people living with the condition [ref: RHS Chelsea Flower Show - 2026: 1. Countdown to RHS Chelsea Flower Show 2026]. The garden received the BBC/RHS People's Choice Award for Best Show Garden [ref: Arit Anderson wins RHS/BBC People’s Choice award 2026, www.rhs.org.uk].

== Parkinson's disease and advocacy ==
Plummer was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2009. He has spoken publicly about the effects of the condition on his life and career, including the physical challenges associated with wildlife photography [ref: A Leopard Doesn't Change Its Spots, Reader's Digest] [ref: Life Through a Lens, PosAbility].

His experience of living with Parkinson's is documented in his book 7 Years of Camera Shake and in several television and documentary productions.

He has also participated in Parkinson's disease awareness activities through interviews and documentary appearances. He also gives public talks on wildlife photography, conservation and his experiences of living with Parkinson's disease [ref: ] [ref: David Plummer Wildlife Photographer Public Speaker & Motivational talks, David Plummer]

data.title: Matija Strlič
data.text:
Matija Strlič (born 1968) is a Slovenian heritage scientist and analytical chemist. He is Professor of Analytical Chemistry at the University of Ljubljana and Honorary Professor of Heritage Science at University College London (UCL). [ref: About Us, Heritage Science Laboratory Ljubljana, University of Ljubljana] [ref: People at the Institute for Sustainable Heritage, University College London]

His research focuses on the application of scientific methods to cultural heritage, including studies of degradation of historic paper and other heritage materials, effects of the environment and climate on collections, heritage values and the study of historical odours. [ref: The smell of history, Chemistry World]

Strlič studied chemistry at the University of Ljubljana and received a PhD in chemistry from the university in 2000. [ref: Prof Matija Strlic, University College London]

He joined University College London in 2007 and worked at UCL's Institute for Sustainable Heritage. In 2010, Strlič was course director of UCL's newly established MRes programme in Heritage Science. [ref: New Masters in Heritage Science at UCL Centre for Sustainable Heritage, Conservation DistList] He was a co-investigator on the Science and Engineering in Arts, Heritage and Archaeology (SEAHA) Centre for Doctoral Training, an EPSRC-funded centre established at University College London in partnership with the University of Oxford and the University of Brighton. [ref: Announcing SEAHA – Centre for Doctoral Training in Science and Engineering in Arts, Heritage and Archaeology, UCL Digital Humanities] He was also a member of the SEAHA Steering Committee. [ref: 2nd International SEAHA Conference: Book of Abstracts, University College London] He was Deputy Director of UCL Institute for Sustainable Heritage until 2019. [ref: Matija Strlic – About, University College London]

He also taught on the MSc in Conservation for Archaeology and Museums at UCL Institute of Archaeology (2008-2019). [ref: Matija Strlic – Teaching, University College London]

Strlič served as a Senior Research Fellow at the Smithsonian Institution's Museum Conservation Institute between 2020 and 2022. [ref: Good pollution: Smells in museums, Columbia University Graduate School of Architecture, Planning and Preservation]

At the University of Ljubljana, Strlič is Professor of Analytical Chemistry and leads the Heritage Science Laboratory Ljubljana. He is listed among the teaching staff of the Chair of Analytical Chemistry [ref: Chair of Analytical Chemistry, University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Chemistry and Chemical Technology], where he has taught courses in Analytical chemistry (since 1997) and Natural sciences for conservators (since 2019).

He heads the Centre of Excellence in Green Heritage Science [ref: GreenHer CoE, "[https://greenher.uni-lj.si/about-us/ About us]", University of Ljubljana. Accessed 19 September 2026.], an interinstitutional Centre established in Slovenia and funded by the European Commission through the Teaming instrument of the Widening programme. [ref: European Commission, "[https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101136457 GreenHer Centre of Excellence: Green Heritage Science]", CORDIS, grant agreement No. 101136457, 2025.]

He is member of the European Academy of Sciences and Arts [ref: European Academy of Sciences and Arts, "[https://euro-acad.eu/fileGreetings.php?path=JcjqsJxxDEVPYnM7ciBE New Members Elected by the Senate]", 2024.] and is Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry and the International Institute for Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works. Strlič has been included in the Stanford–Elsevier list of the world's top 2% of scientists, [ref: Top 2% Scientists, TOPSCINET] and his Scopus author profile records more than 190 publications. [ref: Author details: Strlic, Matija, Scopus]

In 2002, Strlič received the Zois award for outstanding scientific contributions in chemistry, [ref: Nagrade in priznanja za izjemne dosežke v znanstveno-raziskovalni in razvojni dejavnosti – 2002, Ministrstvo za šolstvo, znanost in šport] and in 2015, he received the Ambassador of Science of the Republic of Slovenia Award. [ref: Nagrade in priznanja za izjemne dosežke v znanstveno-raziskovalni in razvojni dejavnosti – 2015, Ministrstvo za izobraževanje, znanost in šport] In 2026, Strlič received the Research Collaboration Index Arts & Humanities Subject Award in recognition of his highly collaborative and cross-disciplinary research. [ref: Arts & Humanities Subject Award, Research Collaboration Index]

data.title: St. John's Episcopal Church (Park Slope)
data.text:
St. John's Episcopal Church, known locally as St. John's Park Slope, is a parish of the Episcopal Church at 139 St. John's Place in the Park Slope neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York City. Founded in 1826 in what was then the village of Brooklyn, it is the second-oldest Episcopal parish in Brooklyn, after St. Ann's. Since 1870 the congregation has worshipped in a Gothic Revival brownstone church, attributed to the architect Edward Tuckerman Potter, which lies within the Park Slope Historic District, designated by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1973. The parish belongs to the Episcopal Diocese of Long Island.

== History ==

=== Founding ===
In 1826 the Rev. Evan Malbone Johnson sold his farm in Newtown to pay for a new church in Brooklyn. The first St. John's, a wooden building at Washington and Johnson Streets, opened for worship on September 24, 1826. The parish was incorporated on April 16, 1827, as "The Rector, Church Wardens and Vestrymen of Saint John's Church at Brooklyn", and the church was consecrated by Bishop John Henry Hobart on July 10, 1827. Its name was chosen by drawing lots. Johnson served as rector for twenty-one years without salary; known locally as "the Domine", he was said to have married some two thousand couples.

The young parish was active in the life of the village. In the 1820s it joined Presbyterian, Baptist and Dutch Reformed congregations in founding the Brooklyn Sunday School Union. By about 1837 its Sunday school kept a lending library of some 400 volumes open to the public, and in 1831 Johnson's wife, Maria, founded the Women's Benevolent Society, whose 1841 silver collection plates the parish still owns. Johnson also led the petition to open Myrtle Avenue, which succeeded despite some four hundred objectors.

In 1843, when pew rents were keeping poorer people out, Johnson asked the vestry that no one who came to the church "shall ever apply... and not be supplied with a seat", and the vestry agreed. The same year, in a private letter to John Jay, he wrote that, whatever his earlier opinions, he had come to believe that "God hath made of one blood" the whole human race. He befriended the Black priest Alexander Crummell, inviting him to preach, and between 1846 and 1853 he was among the clergy who argued that St. Philip's Church, a Black congregation in Manhattan, should be admitted to the convention of the Diocese of New York; St. Philip's vestry formally thanked him. He resigned from St. John's in 1847 to found St. Michael's, a free church in Brooklyn.

=== Dissension and recovery ===
After the death of the rector Thomas T. Guion in 1862, the parish was divided: vestrymen resigned, meetings failed to reach a quorum, and several priests declined calls to serve as rector. Bishop Horatio Potter asked George Franklin Seymour to recover the parish from "the distressing condition into which internal dissension had brought it". Seymour raised more than $13,000 in a single year, served until 1866, and later became Bishop of Springfield.

=== Move to Park Slope ===
In 1868 the parish sold its building and began holding mission services near Prospect Park. Under the rector Alexander Burgess, later Bishop of Quincy, it bought lots at Seventh Avenue and Douglass Street (now St. John's Place) in 1869, and the cornerstone of a new chapel was laid on June 15, 1869. The chapel opened on January 16, 1870, with about six hundred people present and Bishop Abram Newkirk Littlejohn preaching. The parish's histories attribute its design to Edward Tuckerman Potter, who had earlier been engaged to design a church the parish planned, and never built, on DeKalb Avenue. A larger church planned for the Seventh Avenue corner was never built, and the corner lots were later sold. The Brooklyn Theatre was built on the site of the first church and burned on December 5, 1876, in one of the deadliest fires in the city's history; the site was later occupied by the Brooklyn Daily Eagle building.

In 1885 the parish began enlarging the chapel with a nave and chancel, giving the building a cruciform plan. Trinity Church, Wall Street, which had helped the parish in 1832, lent it $8,000 in 1872 and forgave the loan in 1910. The parish carried a mortgage for forty-six years. During the Great Depression the rector's salary was small and sometimes paid in food, but the mortgage was paid off in 1931 and the church was consecrated by Bishop Ernest M. Stires on December 27 of that year.

=== Twentieth century ===
From the 1950s, Anglicans who had immigrated from the Caribbean became a large part of the congregation and sustained it as many earlier members moved away. The parish's own history acknowledges that the newcomers "were not always welcomed" at first. On December 16, 1960, the 1960 New York mid-air collision brought one of the airliners down at Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place, a block from the church. A new Hillgreen-Lane organ, the gift of an anonymous donor, was dedicated in 1962, and in 1963 a bequest of more than $400,000 from Mrs. Palen Nelson established the parish endowment. A series of sacrament windows by Payne Studios was installed between 1965 and 1971.

Around 1970 St. John's joined St. Augustine's Church and the Richmond Foundation in sponsoring the Park Slope North Child Development Center, the first day-care center built from the ground up in New York City under the 1969 Youth Facilities Act; it served about 250 children and was later named for Helen Carey, wife of Governor Hugh Carey. Brian McAnuff, a composer published by Oxford University Press, was music director from about 1971 to 2009. The parish celebrated its sesquicentennial in 1976 with a history by its rector, the Rev. Clifford A. Buck, who served from 1958 until his death in 1985.

Under the Rev. Clarence H. Powers (1987–2013), the parish helped found the Brooklyn Episcopal AIDS Committee in 1989, the first such committee in the diocese, and in the late 1980s buried in its garden people with AIDS, some of whom had been abandoned by their families. It ran a weekly food ministry and Thanksgiving dinners for homeless and elderly neighbors, and launched a parish website in 1996. In 1992 it bought a fire-damaged brownstone on Seventh Avenue for classrooms and youth programs; the purchase divided the congregation, but the building served for a decade and was sold in 2003 for nearly three times its cost, paying for a new boiler, a kitchen and the restoration of the garden. A room for young children added about 2008 was followed in June 2009 by ten baptisms on a single day. Several parishioners from this period were later ordained. A 2010 tornado damaged the bell-cote and garden; insurance funded the church's first full repainting in decades, and the restoration was completed in 2012, the year Powers published a second parish history.

=== Twenty-first century ===
The Rev. Shelley McDade came to St. John's as priest-in-charge in 2015 and later became rector, serving until 2020, when she was called to All Saints' Church in Rehoboth Beach, Delaware. The Rev. Ben DeHart became rector in 2023; in 2024 The Living Church reported on the parish's renewed growth. The parish marked its bicentennial on May 17, 2026, which the New York State Senate recognized in a resolution sponsored by Senator Zellnor Myrie noting its "strong Caribbean legacy".

== Architecture ==
The church is built of brownstone in the Gothic Revival style; the Landmarks Preservation Commission's records date it to 1869. The cornerstone, laid in 1869, is inscribed "JESUS ✝ CHRIST". The original chapel was enlarged from 1885 with a nave and chancel. A memorial window to Guion depicts St. John, and the Holy Family windows in the nave memorialize the Nelson family. A shrine to Our Lady was dedicated in September 1971 by the exiled Bishop of Haiti. A Jardine tracker organ installed in 1893 was replaced by the Hillgreen-Lane organ in 1962.

data.title: Aspergillus sigurros
data.text:
Aspergillus sigurros is a species of fungi in the family Aspergillaceae. [ref: Updating the taxonomy of Aspergillus in South Africa, Studies in Mycology] It was described by Cobus M. Visagie in 2020 in a scientific paper dedicated to Keith A. Seifert titled Updating the Taxonomy of Aspergillus in South Africa and named after Keith's favorite band, Sigur Rós. [ref: Light shed on the dark territory of fungal diversity with 7 new species to science, FBIP] When inhaled from mold by humans, it can cause Aspergillosis. [ref: Mayo Clinic, mayoclinic]

data.title: Niedax
data.text:
Niedax Holding GmbH serves as the parent company of the Niedax Group and is headquartered in Linz am Rhein, Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany. The group has remained family-owned since it was established in 1920 and manufactures products for electrical and building installation technology. The Niedax Group operates at 81 sites, including 25 production facilities, in over 30 countries. It has joint ventures with FEMI-CZ and Steelline, both based in Italy, as well as with the R&M Electrical Group in Southampton, UK, and ABB in North America. [ref: ABB and Niedax’s joint venture—Abnex—ready to take on North America’s cable tray demands, Electrical Business]

The company develops and produces cable management systems for use in buildings, industrial facilities, and infrastructure projects. [ref: Niedax: Unabhängigkeit von Stahlindustrie, Wirtschaftswoche]

== History ==
Niedax was founded in Berlin in 1920 by engineers Alexander Niedergesäß and Fritz Axthelm as Niedergesäß & Co. OHG. The company initially manufactured fastening materials for the electrical industry. [ref: Mittelständler Niedax: „Mein Ziel war es, mit einer Milliarde Umsatz in Rente zu gehen. Jetzt will ich zwei.“, Wirtschaftswoche]

After World War II, the company was rebuilt and opened a branch in Linz am Rhein. [ref: Linz am Rhein. Die Geschichte der Stadt von der Frühzeit bis zur Gegenwart, Böhlau] A hot-dip galvanising facility began operations in St. Katharinen in 1975. By the end of the 1970s, production had been relocated to St. Katharinen, while the company's administration remained in Linz am Rhein. [ref: Niedax Group investiert kräftig in Linzer Standort, Rhein-Zeitung] [ref: Seit 1955 in Linz, Rhein-Zeitung] In 1995, Bruno Reufels and Egon Winggen took over the company's management from Franz Kolmer following his retirement. [ref: Ein Unbequemer geht, Rhein-Zeitung]

From 1995 onwards, Niedax began expanding its international operations. [ref: Niedax Group: Auf dem Weg zur ersten Umsatzmilliarde, Unternehmeredition] The company acquired Elektraplan in 1996 and the Dutch firm Alinco in 1999. [ref: Mit kleinen Klemmen zum Erfolg, Rhein-Zeitung] On 1 January 2000, it took over the Kleinhuis Group, based in Lüdenscheid, followed by Rico GmbH & Co. KG in 2004. [ref: Niedax steuert auf Expansionskurs, Rhein-Zeitung] [ref: Expansionskurs bringt neue Jobs, Rhein-Zeitung] Most of the larger acquisitions were made during periods of economic crisis, particularly the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. During this time, Niedax also bought two steel service centres.

Egon Winggen retired in 2007 and was succeeded by Alexander Horn, who joined Bruno Reufels as managing director. [ref: Egon Winggen prägte die Geschichte der Niedax-Gruppe, Rhein-Zeitung]

A new operational management team took up its duties on 1 January 2023. [ref: Niedax leitet den Generationswechsel ein, Elektrowirtschaft] Since the summer of 2023, the Niedax Group has been purchasing CO2-reduced steel from various suppliers and processed the material at its own production facilities. [ref: Die Niedax-Group bezieht CO2-reduzierten Stahl von Thyssenkrupp Steel, TGA-Fachplaner.de] [ref: UK steel maker delivers low-CO2-emissions steel to cable management firm, Envirotec Magazine]

In 2024, Niedax took over the Spina Group, an Italian manufacturer of cable management systems and distributor of electrotechnical materials for industrial facilities. [ref: Niedax übernimmt italienische Spina Group, Elektro.net] In November 2024, Niedax and ABB established the joint venture Abnex Inc., which brings together the two companies' North American cable tray businesses. [ref: ABB and Niedax Group Partner on Cable Tray Systems, Automation World] [ref: ABB, Niedax Launch Abnex Inc. for North American Cable Management, Mexico Business News] [ref: ABB and Niedax’s joint venture—Abnex—ready to take on North America’s cable tray demands, Electrical Business]

In 2025, Niedax opened a new site in Rahms, which primarily houses administrative and sales functions as well as a newly built technology campus. Since its completion, the site has served as the coordination centre for the group’s European infrastructure projects. Niedax Infrastruktur GmbH was established in connection with the development. [ref: Niedax Group erschließt neuen Standort in Deutschland, VG Asbach] [ref: Neuer Technologie Campus & Experience Center „Synnoscape“, I-Magazin]

In 2026, Niedax started working on a fibre-optic network for critical infrastructure in Germany. In April 2026, the Niedax subsidiary Netz33 GmbH began to work on a roughly 130-kilometre test route in Niedergörsdorf, Brandenburg. Along this route, Netz33 is testing technologies for the protection of data connections against sabotage, disruptions, and other security risks. [ref: Test für krisensicheres Glasfaser-Netz in Brandenburg, Süddeutsche Zeitung] [ref: Test Segment: Brandenburg Building Crisis-proof Fiber Optic Network, teltarif.de]

== Corporate structure ==
Niedax Holding GmbH, based in Linz am Rhein, serves as the parent company of the Niedax Group and has remained entirely family-owned since it was founded.

The group is organised in several corporate levels. Niedax Verwaltungs GmbH sits below the parent company and manages Niedax Beteiligungs GmbH & Co. KG. This company, in turn, holds a stake in Niedax GmbH & Co. KG, which consolidates most of the group's shareholdings.

Niedax has 81 locations in more than 30 countries, including 25 production facilities. [ref: Who we are – introducing the Niedax Group, Niedax Group] The group operates joint ventures with the Italian companies FEMI-CZ and Steelline, R&M Electrical Group in Southampton, United Kingdom, and ABB in North America. As of September 2023, the group had around 2,700 employees. The group consists of 68 directly or indirectly owned subsidiaries across Europe, North America, Asia, and the Middle East.

== Business areas ==
The Niedax Group is active in the production and distribution of cable management systems as well as electrotechnical installation and fastening materials made from metal, PVC, and glass fibre. [ref: Niedax Group investiert Millionen in Stahl-Service-Center, Hidden Champions] The systems are used in industrial facilities, office buildings, and infrastructure projects. [ref: Unter Strom, GoingPublic.de]

A number of subsidiaries operate in the steel service sector, where they process steel for external industrial customers and for the group's own cable tray manufacturing.

The distribution business covers international trading in electrotechnical products together with services including planning and installation.

Infrastructure represents a further area of activity and includes the construction of data centres and the expansion of general network infrastructure. [ref: Kritische Infrastruktur: Niedax plant sicheres Glasfasernetz entlang der Schiene, Rhein-Zeitung]

Niedax products have been installed in projects including the Gotthard Base Tunnel and the Elbphilharmonie.

data.title: Los Lupeños de San José
data.text:
----

Los Lupeños de San José is a Mexican Folklórico dance company based in San Jose, California. Founded in 1969 by Susan V. Cashion and Ramón Morones Ortiz, it developed as a study and performance group dedicated to Mexican folk dance [ref: Did you know? Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]. The company operates under [http://CashionCulturalLegacy.org Cashion Cultural Legacy] and is based at the Mexican Heritage Plaza in East San Jose [ref: Did you know? Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]

== History ==

=== Foundation and early activities ===
Cashion and Morones met in Guadalajara, Mexico, where they studied folklórico. They established Los Lupeños in San José in 1969. Cashion also taught at Stanford University while continuing to direct the company. [ref: The Role of Folklorico and Danzantes Unidos in the Chican@ Movement, University of California, Merced]

The company's early activities included music education as well as dance. In a study of women in California mariachi, Cynthia Reifler Flores describes Cashion's efforts to establish a community mariachi ensemble to accompany the dancers. Instruction was open to interested participants, including women and musicians of different backgrounds. Barbara Pérez-Díaz, whose career is examined in the study, participated as both a dancer and musician. A surviving program documents the company's December 4, 1971 concert at the San Jose Civic Auditorium, with performances by Mariachi Tequilatlán and Mariachi Uclatlán. [ref: Barbara Perez-Díaz y Rebeca Gonzales. Women Pioneers of Mariachi in California. The Cultural and Transnational Implications, KARPA]

An April 1983 article in the San José newspaper Our Paper described the company as the oldest organized Mexican Folklorico dance company in the Nation. [ref: Los Lupenos Return Triumphantly to San Jose, Our Paper]

=== Folklórico organizations and collaborations ===
The founders participated in networks connecting folklórico practitioners across the United States. In a note about the early years of the Asociación Nacional de Grupos Folklóricos [https://angfdance.com/ (ANGF)], dance scholar Gabriela Mendoza-García identifies Cashion and Morones among the California practitioners contacted for the March 1974 national gathering at the University of New Mexico. Her account also reproduces a photograph of Los Lupeños performing Yucatán dances at ANGF in 1975. [ref: Creation, Growth, and Inspiration: The Beginnings of the Asociación Nacional de Grupos Folklóricos (1974–1976), Gabriela Mendoza-Garcia Ballet Folklorico]

Cashion and Morones organized collaborative folklórico concerts in San José in 1977 and brought visiting teachers from Mexico for performances and workshops. Eve Marie Delfin's history distinguishes these gatherings from the later Danzantes Unidos Festival, organized by John Estrada and Sue Welsh at UCLA in 1979. [ref: About Us, Danzantes Unidos] Delfin also documents Los Lupeños' subsequent role in hosting the festival in San José during the 1980s. [ref: The Role of Folklorico and Danzantes Unidos in the Chican@ Movement, University of California, Merced]

=== Transition to Cashion Cultural Legacy ===
In 2014, 501c3 Non profit organization [http://cashionculturallegacy.org Cashion Cultural Legacy] acquired Los Lupeños. A March 2015 interview in In Dance reported the appointment of Samuel Cortez as artistic director. Managing director Tony Ferrigno described the company's work as researching, learning, and staging folk dances, producing concerts, and providing community education through Los Lupeños Academy. [ref: Did you know? Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]

== Repertoire and performance ==
By 2026, the repertoire encompassed dances from almost every regions of Mexico and works based on early California history. Cashion described the company's interpretation as shaped by its California dancers' experiences as well as Mexican traditions. [ref: From Mexico to California and Back: A Look at Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]

The founders created Mextizol, a dance drama about mestizo culture that premiered in the mid-1970s and toured the southwestern United States in several versions. [ref: Archiving Fellowships Blog: Cashion Cultural Legacy, Part 1, Dance/USA] A 2001 Los Angeles Times review examined the company's performance at Caltech. [ref: Ballet Folklorico Los Lupenos Whirls Through Regional Traditions, Los Angeles Times]

The Library of Congress documents musician Artemio Posadas's work accompanying the company and advising it on traditional son huasteco music and dance. [ref: Artemio Posadas: Mexican music and dance from California, Library of Congress]

=== Californio repertoire ===
The company's repertoire has included dances associated with Mexican California. A 2004 newspaper announcement listed its dancers in Fandango IV—Songs & Dances from Mexican California at the Presidio of San Francisco, alongside Coro Hispano de San Francisco, Conjunto Nuevo Mundo, and Cascada de Flores. [ref: Take a green tour through the city, SFGATE]

In November 2023, with the help of a National Endowment for the Arts grant, the company presented Los Californios, Carnaval del Cascarón as part of Etnofonías, Los Sonidos de México at the Mexican Heritage Plaza. The concert program describes the suite as a tribute to Mexican traditions of Alta California and credits collaborators including Los Arribeños de San Francisco. [ref: Etnofonías Concert Program, Los Lupeños de San José]

== Education and cultural preservation ==
Los Lupeños Academy offers folklórico instruction at the Mexican Heritage Plaza. Its classes serve students of all ages and they are offered in partnership with the Mexican Heritage Plaza. Cashion Cultural Legacy also operates the Los Lupeños Juvenil youth ensemble. [ref: Archiving Fellowships, Dance/USA]

In 2006, the Alliance for California Traditional Arts awarded Los Lupeños a Living Cultures grant to inventory its costume and prop collection and improve storage. ACTA described the collection as consisting largely of handmade traditional costumes accumulated since the company's founding. [ref: Los Lupeños de San José, Alliance for California Traditional Arts]

== Archives and exhibitions ==
The San José Public Library's California Room lists the Los Lupeños de San José Records, a collection containing administrative papers, correspondence, newspaper clippings, photographs, ephemera, and audiovisual material. [ref: Los Lupeños de San José Records, San José Public Library] [ref: California Room Collections, San José Public Library] In 2024, a Dance/USA archiving fellowship supported work on Cashion Cultural Legacy's digital records, including naming conventions and organization of archival files.

In 2026, San José State University's Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Library listed ¡Que Viva!: Honoring Mexican Heritage Through Music and Dance, a photographic exhibition at its Africana, Asian American, Chicano, Native American Studies Center featuring Los Lupeños and Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán. [ref: ¡Que Viva!: Honoring Mexican Heritage Through Music and Dance, San José State University Events]

data.title: Triton (programming language)
data.text:
Triton is an open-source domain-specific language and compiler for writing compute kernels for graphics processing units (GPUs). Triton is widely adopted in deep learning frameworks because of its portability and accessibility, including by notable LLM frameworks such as vLLM.

Kernels are written as decorated Python functions that operate on blocks ("tiles") of data, and it differs from lower level languages like CUDA in that much of the scheduling within a block is handled automatically.

Triton began as the doctoral research of Philippe Tillet at Harvard University and was further developed at OpenAI, which released version 1.0 in 2021. It is now the default GPU code-generation target for PyTorch's torch.compile. and the subject of a book by Harshwardhan Fartale, published by Manning.

Triton supports Nvidia and AMD GPUs, [ref: triton-lang/triton: Compatibility, GitHub] and Intel maintains an out-of-tree backend for its own GPUs. [ref: Learn How to Build and Run the Open Source OpenAI Triton Backend for Intel GPUs, Intel Developer]

== Example ==

The code below illustrates how a softmax kernel could be written in Triton.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def softmax_kernel(out_ptr, in_ptr, in_stride, out_stride, n_cols,
BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
row = tl.program_id(0)
cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
mask = cols torch.Tensor:
n_rows, n_cols = x.shape
out = torch.empty_like(x)
BLOCK = triton.next_power_of_2(n_cols)
softmax_kernel[(n_rows,)](out, x, x.stride(0), out.stride(0), n_cols,
BLOCK=BLOCK)
return out

Writing the kernel this way produces a single GPU kernel that computes the maximum, exponentials, sum and division in one pass, reading the input from memory once. A naive PyTorch implementation built from separate tensor operations launches each step as its own kernel, reading and writing intermediate results to memory between them. [ref: Fused Softmax, Triton documentation] In practice, PyTorch's built-in torch.softmax avoids this by calling a dedicated hand-written CUDA kernel. [ref: aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/SoftMax.cu, GitHub]

In CUDA, a row-wise softmax requires explicit synchronisation between the threads that cooperatively compute each row's maximum and sum; in Triton the compiler handles the synchronisation and shared-memory management.
