data.title: University at Buffalo Student Association
data.text:
The University at Buffalo Student Association Inc., commonly known as the Student Association or SA, is the undergraduate student government of the University at Buffalo (UB), a public university in New York. It represents undergraduate students, recognizes and funds student organizations, and operates campus events and services. [ref: About us, University at Buffalo Student Association] Under its bylaws, every UB undergraduate is a member of the association. [ref: University at Buffalo Student Association Inc. By-Laws, University at Buffalo Student Association]

SA is incorporated separately from the university and has federal 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status. [ref: Student governments become not-for-profit, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)] [ref: University At Buffalo Student Association Inc, Nonprofit Explorer] In 2026, it oversaw more than 200 undergraduate clubs and operated on an annual budget of approximately $4.5 million, funded primarily by a mandatory student activity fee. [ref: UB students vote to increase $109 mandatory student activity fee to $115, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

== History ==

=== Early history and student control of funds ===

The exact founding date of the Student Association is not established in published sources. University Archives holds a collection of SA minutes, correspondence, and other records dating from 1961 to 1967, showing that the organization was active by the early 1960s. [ref: Student Association Records, 1961–1967, University at Buffalo Libraries] The university's Black Student Union, founded in 1967, was recognized by SA in 1968 and had approximately 1,000 members by 1969. [ref: Black Student Union Collection, University at Buffalo Libraries]

In 1970, students established Sub-Board I (SBI), a corporation that administered funds for UB's student governments. SBI was created to move control of student activity-fee money away from the Faculty Student Association (FSA), and it later operated services including legal consultations, a safety shuttle, an off-campus housing service, and student radio. [ref: UB to replace Sub-Board I with Faculty Student Association as student government fiscal agent, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

=== Nonprofit incorporation and fiscal-agent transition ===

In March 2013, the SA Senate voted 13–0, with two abstentions, to seek student approval to incorporate SA as an independent nonprofit. Supporters said that incorporation would separate the association's liabilities from the university and allow SA to enter contracts in its own name. [ref: SA pushes to become not-for-profit, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)] A subsequent student referendum approved incorporation with 90 percent support.

The organizational change was completed in 2019. UB replaced SBI, which had served as fiscal agent for 49 years, with the FSA on July 1, and UB's student governments incorporated as nonprofit organizations legally separate from the university. SA's Senate became the corporation's board of directors. The Internal Revenue Service recognized SA as tax-exempt in December 2019.

=== Recent governance changes ===

In January 2025, the Senate voted 17–0, with one abstention, to divide the existing vice-presidential office into three positions responsible for advocacy, clubs, and events. The change expanded the executive board from three elected officers to five beginning with the 2025–26 term. President Samin Bhuya argued that the change would broaden representation, while vice president Killian Hannigan said that dividing the portfolio would create a clearer chain of command. Senator Jack Koscinski initially questioned whether the additional offices were necessary. [ref: SA Senate splits VP role into three positions: advocacy, events and clubs, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

In October 2025, the Senate voted 19–1, with two abstentions, to permit the president and treasurer, acting jointly, to remove a club-council coordinator. President Aisha Adam supported the change as a way to address coordinators who did not perform their duties. An earlier version had failed the preceding spring amid concerns that it would concentrate too much authority in the executive board. [ref: SA council coordinators now subject to removal by e-board, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

The REAL party swept all five executive offices in April 2026 in an election with 4,937 voters, which then-president Aisha Adam described as record turnout. The elected board consisted of Jack Koscinski as president, Na'Dia Carter as vice president for advocacy, Pranavan Balachandran as vice president for clubs, William Dong as vice president for events, and Laron Fomby as treasurer. [ref: 'REAL' party sweeps SA's 2026–27 e-board elections, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

After Koscinski resigned in July 2026, Carter became acting president. Fomby announced that the special presidential election would be held alongside the regular Senate election and the student-activity-fee referendum in September, saying that combining the votes would avoid a series of back-to-back elections. [ref: Student Association president, senators up for election Sept. 14 to 18, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)] Charlene Okine won the presidency with 1,296 votes, approximately 38 percent of the votes cast in a four-candidate race. During the same election period, undergraduates voted both to retain the mandatory student activity fee and to increase it from $109 to $115 per semester.

== Governance and organization ==

SA is governed by its elected officers, a Senate, and an Executive Committee. The association's bylaws operate as both the constitution of the student government and the governing document of the nonprofit corporation.

=== Executive branch ===

The executive board consists of the president, vice president for advocacy, vice president for clubs, vice president for events, and treasurer. Officers are elected annually by the undergraduate student body and serve one-year terms. Candidates must be full-time UB students. [ref: Student Government, University at Buffalo Student Association]

The president is SA's chief executive officer and official representative and oversees the executive branch and staff. The vice president for advocacy coordinates student-rights and student-welfare work and serves as a liaison to university administrators. The vice president for clubs assists recognized organizations, advises students forming new clubs, and administers club sanctions and recognition under SA policy. The vice president for events oversees association-wide programming. The treasurer is SA's chief financial officer and administers disbursement of the budget, monitors financial transactions, enforces internal controls, and is charged with safeguarding SA assets.

=== Senate ===

The Senate has 24 voting seats. Twelve are held ex officio by the five executive officers and the coordinators of SA's seven club councils; the other twelve senators are elected at large by undergraduates in the fall. The Senate elects a chair from among its at-large members. Under the bylaws, it is also the nonprofit corporation's board of directors.

The Senate allocates the annual budget, approves budget changes and line transfers, reviews recognized clubs, adopts and amends policies, hears certain club appeals, changes election rules, and may suspend an officer. It may also pass resolutions concerning academic policy, student rights, and student welfare. Regular meetings are scheduled every other Wednesday during the fall and spring semesters, and any person may address the body when recognized by the chair.

=== Executive Committee and oversight ===

The Executive Committee comprises the five executive officers and the Senate chair. It may act when the Senate cannot meet, including outside the fall and spring semesters or when delay would create a financial or other loss. Its authority is limited: it cannot amend the bylaws, suspend or remove elected officials, fill vacancies, set Senate compensation, or change election, conflict-of-interest, or whistleblower rules. The Senate or an independent audit committee is responsible for overseeing annual independent audits and reviewing financial-reporting controls.

=== Club councils and administrative departments ===

Recognized clubs are grouped into seven councils: Academic, Engineering, Hobby, International, People of Color, Special Interest, and Sports. Clubs in each council elect a coordinator, who represents the council in the Senate. [ref: Departments, University at Buffalo Student Association]

SA's administrative departments include Media and Marketing, Entertainment, Production, Student Affairs, Club Services, Finance, Office Staff, and professional staff. These units plan events, provide equipment and publicity, process club expenditures, support student organizations, and provide institutional continuity. SA policy requires decisions concerning club recognition and discipline to be made without regard to a club's viewpoint.

== Funding, clubs, and programs ==

SA is funded principally by UB's mandatory undergraduate student activity fee. In 2019, an analysis of the association's general ledger by The Spectrum described a $4.2 million budget supported by a fee of $104.75 per student per semester. [ref: How does the Student Association spend its $4.2 million?, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)] The fee remained $109 per semester for seven years before students approved an increase to $115 in September 2026. This initiative was led by Treasurer Laron Fomby. About 3,400 students participated in that referendum: 2,310 voted to keep the fee mandatory, and 2,248 voted for the increase.

Fomby announced the proposal to increase the fee in August 2026 and argued that the approximately $4.5 million budget had become inadequate as the number of recognized clubs and the cost of major events increased. He reported that, during preparation of the 2026–27 budget, approximately $250,000 had been redirected from Bullsapalooza to club allocations, raising the club-budget pool from $850,000 to $1.1 million. Supplemental funding was increased by 52 percent to approximately $145,000, while the Comedy Series and Student Choice Speaker programs were discontinued because of their cost and attendance. Fomby rejected a moratorium on recognizing new clubs and characterized the proposed six-dollar fee increase as a compromise. [ref: SA will ask students to raise mandatory activity fee from $109 to $115, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

For the fiscal year ending in July 2025, SA's federal tax filing reported revenue of $4,370,562, expenses of $4,965,260, and net assets of $5,566,803. SA uses its budget to fund more than 200 clubs and to operate events and services. Association-wide programs have included Fest concerts, Bullsapalooza, International Fiesta, a homecoming carnival, a speaker series, legal consultations, reduced-price tickets, and equipment services for clubs.

Event policy has changed in response to costs and leadership transitions. President Samin Bhuya ended the former practice of holding both a fall and spring Fest after the 2024 Spring Fest and 2025 Fall Fest each cost more than $500,000. In 2026, SA postponed Fall Fest until the spring following Koscinski's resignation and scheduling conflicts with UB Athletics. Fomby said that approximately $525,000 would be reserved for the rescheduled concert and that performers from several genres would replace the previous headliner-centered format. [ref: SA's 2026 Fall Fest delayed, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

== Controversies and legal disputes ==

=== 2012 mobile-application contract ===

In March 2012, SA treasurer Sikander Khan and vice president Meghan McMonagle signed a $297,500 contract with Virtual Academix for a mobile application and five years of maintenance. SA president JoAnna Datz stopped the agreement before money was paid and submitted an internal report to police. The report estimated that a comparable product would have cost between $50,000 and $150,000. The Erie County District Attorney's Office and University Police investigated and reported that they found no criminal conduct. [ref: SA Scandal: There's No App For That, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

The SA Senate began a recall process and suspended Khan's pay. He resigned as treasurer on April 20, five days after the recall petition began; the incoming treasurer was appointed to finish the term. [ref: SA Treasurer Resigns, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

=== InterVarsity recognition dispute ===

In April 2012, the Senate derecognized the campus chapter of InterVarsity Christian Fellowship after a dispute over the chapter's requirement that its officers affirm a doctrinal statement. The dispute began after the chapter's treasurer said that he had felt pressured to resign because he did not agree with the statement. SA policy prohibited clubs from excluding students from membership, and the Senate treated the officer requirement as inconsistent with that rule. [ref: InterVarsity Re-Instated as New York University Decides Leaders Are Different than Members, Christianity Today]

In July, the Student-Wide Judiciary reversed the Senate's decision and restored the club's recognition. The judiciary concluded that SA's membership rule did not bar a religious organization from applying belief-based requirements to its leaders, as distinct from its general membership. [ref: IVCF re-recognized as official SA club, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

=== 2013 presidential resignation ===

President Nick Johns resigned on September 18, 2013, while an impeachment petition carrying more than 2,000 signatures was circulating. He had been accused of harassment, improperly accepting gifts, mishandling SA funds, favoritism in hiring, absenteeism, and falsifying documents. Johns denied wrongdoing, describing the allegations as unsubstantiated and the evidence as circumstantial, but said that a prolonged fight would damage the organization. Vice president Lyle Selsky became interim president, while treasurer Siddhant Chhabria assumed additional management responsibilities; a special presidential election was scheduled for October. [ref: After Johns' resignation, Student Association looks ahead, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

=== 2019 fiscal-agent transition ===

UB's 2019 decision to dissolve SBI and transfer fiscal-agent responsibilities to the FSA prompted opposition from SA leaders, SBI employees, and students. SA president Gunnar Haberl and treasurer Tanahiry Escamilla said that excluding student leaders from the decision was unacceptable and raised a potential conflict of interest because several members of the university review committee also held FSA roles. University officials said SBI lacked a contractual relationship with UB, that the existing arrangement did not comply with State University of New York guidance, and that the transition would reduce fees paid by student groups.

Students held a rally and circulated a petition to preserve SBI and its services. UB maintained that student governments would continue to set their budgets and programming priorities and that students would retain representation on the FSA board. [ref: UB Students Rally to Save SBI, Spectrum News 1 Buffalo] The transfer proceeded on July 1, 2019, alongside SA's incorporation as an independent nonprofit.

=== 2020 presidential suspension ===

In February 2020, SA's board of directors indefinitely suspended president Yousouf Amolegbe after its Rules, Administration and Government Oversight Committee reported nine policy violations, including alleged conflicts of interest involving his role in the entertainment company RAGE Boyz. The board voted 12–1, with four abstentions. Amolegbe denied the conflict-of-interest allegations and criticized the procedure used to suspend him. [ref: Student Association president indefinitely suspended for alleged conflict-of-interest violations, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

The suspension divided board members and students and left some presidential duties unassigned under the bylaws then in effect. Vice president Georgia Hulbert and treasurer Kendra Harris assumed many of the president's operational responsibilities. Hulbert voted for the suspension, while Harris voted against it and argued that the timing would disrupt SA's busiest semester. In March, Harris moved three times to reinstate Amolegbe, but each motion failed. At that point he had been suspended for more than five weeks, and no final removal vote had occurred. [ref: SA president remains suspended after three failed motions to reinstate, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

=== Young Americans for Freedom litigation ===

In March 2023, SA adopted a club-recognition rule that generally prohibited clubs outside the Academic, Engineering, and Sports councils from affiliating with outside organizations. The rule affected chapters of political, humanitarian, and public-service groups. It was adopted weeks after the UB chapter of Young Americans for Freedom (YAF) hosted conservative commentator Michael Knowles, although the policy did not name YAF or Knowles. President Becky Paul-Odionhin defended the rule as a means of protecting other SA clubs from consequences arising from directions imposed by outside affiliates; critics alleged that it was aimed at YAF. [ref: University at Buffalo Clubs Caught in Free Speech Crossfire, Inside Higher Ed]

YAF and several members filed a federal lawsuit in June 2023 against SA and three university officials, alleging violations of the First Amendment and Fourteenth Amendment. [ref: UB student group files second lawsuit against university, WGRZ] SA repealed the outside-affiliation rule before it took effect and restored the chapter's recognition, but the plaintiffs amended their complaint to challenge replacement requirements governing clubs' legal status and officers' acknowledgment of SA policies. [ref: Federal judge dismisses YAF's lawsuit against SA, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

In December 2024, the United States District Court for the Western District of New York dismissed the action for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and failure to state a claim and denied the plaintiffs' request for a preliminary injunction. [ref: University at Buffalo Young Americans for Freedom v. University at Buffalo Student Association Inc., No. 1:2023cv00480, Document 59, Justia] The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the dismissal in an unpublished summary order in November 2025. [ref: Young Americans for Freedom at UB loses legal fight at federal appeals court, The Buffalo News]

=== 2026 executive-board compensation debate ===

During the spring 2026 semester, president Aisha Adam made three attempts to increase each executive-board member's annual stipend from $19,500 to $24,180. She argued that the president and treasurer routinely worked substantially more hours than their compensation covered. The first proposal failed after an hour-long debate, and a second received 10 votes in favor and four against but did not reach the 13 votes required under the bylaws. The third attempt received 12 votes in favor and one against, again falling one vote short. [ref: SA Senate fails to pass resolution by one vote in third attempt to raise e-board wages, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

Treasurer and president-elect Jack Koscinski did not take a formal position but called Adam's argument compelling and estimated that he worked 30 to 50 hours per week. Incoming vice president for advocacy Na'Dia Carter supported higher compensation in principle but said the incoming board should accept the result if students and senators did not trust it with a raise. In August, incoming treasurer Laron Fomby said that the proposal would not be revived during the 2026–27 year and that he was instead considering lower stipends for the three vice-presidential offices.

=== 2026 resignation and policy reforms ===

Incoming president Jack Koscinski resigned effective July 31, 2026, shortly after fellow executive-board members and staff sent a no-confidence letter to SA senators and university officials. The letter was signed by treasurer Laron Fomby, vice president for advocacy Na'Dia Carter, vice president for clubs Pranavan Balachandran, vice president for events William Dong, chief of staff Mya Glynn, and administrative assistant Gabriela Paz; Fomby provided it to The Spectrum. The letter alleged financial mismanagement, attempted fraud, biased hiring practices, and other misconduct. Koscinski denied the allegations except that he acknowledged having made jokes about firing staff during his preceding term as treasurer; he said he had apologized and characterized the dispute as an internal power struggle. UB said that it was reviewing the allegations. [ref: SA president quits amid allegations of misspending, misconduct, attempted fraud, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

Fomby said that he had begun a review of expenditures approved during Koscinski's term as treasurer and Aisha Adam's term as president. He cited business-class rail tickets and three group dinners as examples of spending that he believed benefited the officers personally. Adam and Koscinski disputed that characterization, citing accessibility and health reasons for the rail upgrades, university approval of the dinners, and completion of the annual audit. UB later declined to disclose whether an investigation existed or what its result may have been, citing confidentiality and privacy law. [ref: SA Senate reforms finance, staff policies, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

Carter became acting president after the resignation. In September, Carter and Fomby introduced five policy changes responding to the allegations, all of which the Senate approved by a 14–0 vote. The measures generally limited SA-funded travel to economy class except where legally required as an accommodation, ended discretionary per-diem payments, restricted meal purchases for executive officers and non-UB guests, reassigned control of access to SA office rooms, and required broader approval to suspend or dismiss professional staff. Adam responded that the travel resolution formalized existing procedures and that the disputed upgrades had been accessibility accommodations that would remain permitted under the new rule.

data.title: Pealeism
data.text:
Pealeism, known by its namesake as Practical Christianity, or more commonly Positive Thinking, is a non-denominational Christian revivalist and new religious movement based on the preaching of Norman Vincent Peale’s ministry, especially his book The Power of Positive Thinking. It emerged in the 1940s advocating for Christian revival in the United States, primarily emphasizing the practical aspects of Christian faith to improve daily life. Pealeism reached its height during the early Fourth Great Awakening before declining throughout the 1960s. [ref: Surge of Piety: Norman Vincent Peale and the Remaking of American Religious Life, Yale University Press]

== History ==
=== Opposition to the New Deal ===
From 1942 on, Norman Vincent Peale’s contacts in business, politics, industry, and religion developed in to a movement around his ministry. In 1945, Peale and his wife, Ruth Stafford Peale, established Guideposts magazine, which featured personal accounts of how faith had helped people confront difficulty.

Peale associated Christian faith with American civic life, capitalism, anti-communism, opposing U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, and participated in conservative organizations including the Committee for Constitutional Government and Spiritual Mobilization. [ref: Norman Vincent Peale Was A Conservative Hero Known Well Beyond His Era, NPR] He belived Christian revival could counter the influence of communism by encouraging Americans to treat Christian faith as integral to personal wellbeing.

=== Post-World War II era and Cold War ===
After World War II, the Pealeist movement grew to include the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic and Foundation for Christian Living, which was the administrative arm of Peale’s ministry. The two organizations allowed Peale to preach to business executives, industrial workers, and youth outside his immediate congregation. In 1951, Peale renamed the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry and served as its president until 1962. The foundation promoted cooperation between clergy and psychiatrists, supported pastoral counselling, and sought to establish Christian faith as integral to mental health.

These approaches were further popularized by books his books, The Real Art of Happiness in 1950, and seminally, The Power of Positive Thinking in 1953.

Peale’s relationships with Federal Bureau of Investigation director J. Edgar Hoover and U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, increased his public visibility and brought his views on religion and national identity to influential circles. He supported campaigns presenting the United States as “one nation under God,” which was part of a broader political and cultural trend towards the prominence of religious language in public life during the 1950s. Peale’s emphasis on rugged individualism and success also appealed to business audiences, since he argued that prayer could inform business decisions, strengthen workplace relations, and address professional challenges.

=== Decline and institutional reorganization ===
Peale’s ministry remained active after the 1950s, but growth in public religious observance declined during the 1960s. In contrast, debates about secularism, science, and societal role of religion became more prominent. The foundation’s claims that Christianity was important to mental health were increasingly criticized by intellectuals.

Peale stepped down as president of the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry in 1962. The foundation subsequently faced financial difficulties by the late 1960s and struggled to maintain the level of support in had the decade prior, reflecting broader changes in the relationship between Christian revivalism and mental-health care.

In 1972, the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry merged with the Academy of Religion and Mental Health to create the Institutes of Religion and Health. However, the organization ended in 1975, though a substantially altered counselling institution continued.

Peale continued to lecture, write, and participate in religious and media activities until he retired as senior minister of Marble Collegiate Church in 1984. He also received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the United States’ highest civilian honour. He died on 24 December 1993 at the age of 95 at his home in Pawling, New York.

In 1995, the Peale Center for Christian Living merged with Guideposts under the leadership of Peale’s wife.

=== 2016 United States presidential election and influence on Donald Trump ===
Peale’s influence received renewed attention during Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign through the latter’s public accounts of his religious upbringing. Trump attended Marble Collegiate Church with his family, and repeatedly identified Peale as a significant spiritual influence. [ref: How Trump got religion — and why his legendary minister’s son now rejects him, The Washington Post] Peale’s influence continues to be relevant in discipline about Christianity’s role in contemporary American conservatism. [ref: ]

== Beliefs ==
Pealeism’s institutional leadership was theologically liberal, [ref: A Better Definition of Religion, Open Publications of UTS Scholars] [ref: After Cloven Tongues of Fire: Ecumenical Protestantism and the Modern American Encounter with Diversity, The Journal of American History] with its namesake articulating his views through Faith is the Answer, A Guide to Confident Living, The Art of Real Happiness, and The Art of Living. These developed from his alma mater’s appreciation of Boston personalism; especially works by Marcus Aurelius, Ralph Waldo Emerson and William James, which were treated as an intellectual authority for the Methodist interpretation of Christ's real presence in the Eucharist. [ref: God's Salesman: Norman Vincent Peale and the Power of Positive Thinking, Oxford University Press] Peale further developed on this doctrine by incorporating practices and concepts from the Unity Church and Christian Science. Doing so, he emphasized the practical, rather than creedal, aspects of Christianity to improve life as popularized through his movement’s seminal work, The Power of Positive Thinking. [ref: Lehmann, William Jr. (1958) The Theology of Norman Vincent Peale, Concordia Theological Monthly: Vol. 29, Article 8. https://scholar.csl.edu/ctm/vol29/iss1/8]

Peale’s ministry has also been politically non-partisan since 1984. In an interview with Christian Science Monitor, he explained that if he could change what he did in his career, “(I wouldn't) get involved with a politician. A minister should deal (only) with the human soul.” [ref: Preacher's preacher most enjoys helping people one-to-one - CSMonitor.com, www.csmonitor.com] Before then however, especially during the early Fourth Great Awakening, his preaching religiously justified politically conservative values of Americanism, anti-communism, Christian nationalism, and laissez-faire individualism.

=== Theology ===
==== God as a person ====

God wasn’t a doctrinally defined subject within Pealeism, merely portrayed as personal in nature and emphasized through simple prayer language, forgiveness, and role as the Father. Peale further described God as a ubiquitous, natural, creative, and vital force, able to renew individuals mentally through continuous engagement. [ref: Business Ethics and the Protestant Spirit: How Norman Vincent Peale Shaped the Religious Values of American Business Leaders, Journal of Business Ethics]

==== Jesus as a teacher ====

Jesus Christ’s role of the Son of God wasn’t heavily emphasized either, instead being portrayed as the “Great Teacher” and embodying the “art of living;” a life of confidence, trust, and idealism, with followers meant to be living “in Christ.” Here, Christ taught how to live healthily and let go of guilt that affects mental well-being.

==== Nature of the soul ====
Given Christ’s role, Pealeism rejected original sin, instead grounding the soul's nature in lived experience and thought. Humans were therefore seen as capable of improvement through their thoughts and beliefs. Positive thinking therefore provided personal strength, while emotional pain, feelings of inferiority, fear, and negative thought engendered weakness.

==== Sin and mental state ====
This meant sin was actually a lack of mental wellness, which was believed to undermine personal livelihood and fulfillment, while moral failure was specifically emotional turmoil and lack of personal success. It could thus be remedied through moral knowledge of general precepts, conscience, reason, the teachings of Jesus, practical experience, and primarily faith; including trust in God’s forgiveness, personal confidence, and the settled expectation of improvement in one’s lived circumstances. Faith was sometimes equated with self-confidence or surrendering to God to overcome fear and act constructively. The regular reading and memorizing of uplifting biblical passages, along with church attendance was also recommended to support mental adjustment.

==== Universalism and salvation ====
Pealism’s understanding of sin led it to hold what is now criticized as a universalist stance on salvation, [ref: Norman Vincent Peale, Apostle of Self-Esteem, Way of Life Literature] with human beings sometimes described as “citizens of eternity,” not entirely meant to corporeally exist. Peale claimed that all people receive salvation after death, arguing this is the soul’s true state, with his eschatology being otherwise vague and simplified instead of systematic.

==== Approach to prayer ====
Prayer itself was presented as a simple, disciplined technique rather than a devotional practice, with followers urged to be specific, regular, and purposeful in its use. It was framed a means of sustained self-reflection and understanding of God, influencing personal conduct, and fostering positive mental focus per the principles of Matthew 7:7-8 and Philippians 4:13.

==== Role of the bible ====
Scripture itself had a selectively critical role, with Peale’s ministry publishing the King James Bible. He praised the text as the best source of insight into human beings and as a source of curative power. And it was claimed this for the New Testament because the disciples of Christ copied his practice of “the art of living” in to its books. Peale even described the Bible as working “like penicillin,” excusing harmfully infectious thinking by providing practical wisdom, positive imagery, and remedial thought.

=== Politics ===
Peale argued through his preaching that the free market, business success, and economic growth were compatible with Christianity. In a 1950 article titled Let the Church Speak Up for Capitalism, he argued for a more active Christian justification of capitalism. His ooverall approach helped connect Protestant values with prevailing America’s business culture, as his preaching emphasized self-improvement, confidence, and perseverance.

After 1936, he also presented Christianity being in political conflict with communism. He specifically argued that Christian faith could counter communist influences by strengthening social stability and reinforcing national identity. This iteration of religious nationalism helped promote the idea that individual faith and faith in God were equivalent to faith in the United States. Peale argued that this improved individual health and strengthened the United States.

Since 1984, however, the organizations making up Peale’s ministry have largely refrained from partisan politics. Guideposts editor-in-chief Edward Grinnan explained that the publication does not cover such issues. [ref: The P Word, Guideposts Articles] The only public policy stance taken by the associated Blanton-Peale Institute & Counselling Center is to advocate for universal mental health care. [ref: ]

In 2016 however, Peale’s son John Stafford Peale, who was vice-president of the Peale Foundation and identifies with the Democratic Party, personally disavowed Trump’s invocation of his father’s influence. He claimed that what Trump espoused wasn’t related to his father’s preaching. [ref: How Trump got religion — and why his legendary minister’s son now rejects him, The Washington Post]

== Controversy ==
=== Psychological soundness ===
Despite the popularity of The Power of Positive Thinking, Peale’s approach was criticized by theologians, psychologists, psychiatrists, and other religious commentators. Some argued that his techniques reduced otherwise complicated emotional and social problems to appear readily solvable. They objected to the emphasis on avoiding negativity, arguing that optimism couldn’t simply dismiss anxiety, grief, anger, and suffering. Other critics questioned if these techniques were scientifically sound.

=== Credibility of the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry ===
The American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry experienced difficulties reconciling Christian counselling with psychiatry. Some medical professionals and researchers objected to its claims about the role of faith in treating mental illness, particularly questioning the veracity of its evidence for faith healing and the tendency to wards faith as a necessity for mental health. The foundation also faced disagreements over its research methods, professional standards, and the degree to which evangelism should be part of counselling.There was also misgivings within the foundation, including the precision of its scientific and clinical goals. Overall, this weakened the movement’s premise that Christian faith and psychology could be treated as a unified scientific approach.

=== 1960 United States presidential election and anti-Catholicism ===
During the 1960 United States presidential election, Peale was controversially associated with the Citizens for Religious Freedom, a group of Protestant clergy who objected to the candidacy of John F. Kennedy because he was Roman Catholic. They argued a Catholic president could be unduly influenced by the Holy See, which was widely criticized as religiously prejudiced, and damaged Peale’s reputation. He withdrew from the group and offered to resign as minister of Marble Collegiate Church, although they didn’t accept his resignation. Peale later described his involvement as a serious mistake. [ref: Norman Vincent Peale, 'Minister to Millions,' Dies: Religion: Mixing faith and psychology, author of 'The Power of Positive Thinking' spread inspiration worldwide., Los Angeles Times] [ref: National Affairs: Test of Religion, TIME] [ref: Protestant Clergy Vs. the Catholic Candidate, JFK, Time]

=== Theological criticism ===
Critics such as Reinhold Niebuhr argued that Peale’s overly emphasized self-assurance and individual success over obligations to Christian faith and role of original sin. Some regarded his approach as reducing religion to reassurance and practical achievement.

== Notable adherents ==
* Scott Adams - cartoonist, author, and commentator
* Helen Hadsell - contestant, author, public speaker
* Bobby Schuller - lead pastor on Hour of Power (2012-present), senior pastor of Shepherd’s Grove (2013-present)
* Robert Schuller - lead pastor on Hour of Power (1970-2006), senior pastor of Crystal Cathedral (1980-2006)
* W. Clement Stone - businessman, philanthropist, and author
* Donald Trump - chairman of The Trump Organization (1971-2017), Co-Chairman of the New York Vietnam Veterans Memorial Commission (1982-1985), 45th and 47th President of the United States (2017-2021, 2025-2029)
* Fred Trump - chairman of The Trump Organization (1929-1971)

data.title: Ferdowsi's Grandeur
data.text:
Ferdowsi's Grandeur (Persian: ) is a sculpture of the Persian poet Ferdowsi, made by Mohsen Saraji and commissioned by Hossein Sabet for the science square of Ferdowsi University of Mashhad, Iran. A May 2025 report in The Independent Persian described it as a 38-metre fibreglass statue that had not been installed. [ref: مجسمه‌ای‌ که هرگز نصب نشد؛ قامت ایستاده فردوسی، خط قرمز گنبد, The Independent Persian]

== Construction ==
Work began in autumn 2019. According to the Saraaj centre's project account, fabrication was completed in Azar 1399 (November–December 2020) and involved more than 250 components. [ref: فردوسی, Saraaj]

== Proposed installation ==
In May 2020, the Iran Book News Agency reported objections by university academics and students to the proposed scale and location. Critics questioned its suitability for an educational setting and argued for prioritising university facilities. The report also covered university president Mohammad Kafi's defence of the project and his explanation that a private donor was financing it. [ref: ماجرای ساخت مجسمه 40 متری فردوسی در دانشگاه فردوسی مشهد چیست؟, Iran Book News Agency]

In May 2024, Iran International reported that Ahmad Alamolhoda characterised the proposed university statue as an attempt to present Ferdowsi in opposition to Imam Reza. [ref: نماینده خامنه‌ای در خراسان رضوی: برخی می‌خواستند فردوسی را مقابل امام رضا مطرح کنند, Iran International]

In a Mehr News Agency report republished by Expressna on 31 August 2025, Razavi Khorasan governor Gholamhossein Mozaffari supported installing the statue and said there was no obstacle to doing so. He rejected comparisons between the monument and the Imam Reza shrine, while calling for consideration of the location and implementation details. [ref: استاندار خراسان رضوی: نصب مجسمه فردوسی هیچ مانعی ندارد, Expressna]

Didban Iran reported that Mohammad Javad Khosravi, mayor of Tehran's District 22, said the municipality had sought to transfer the statue from Mashhad for installation in the Chitgar heights or at Chitgar Lake, but that the statue had not been made available to it. [ref: مدیران شهری پایتخت: مجسمه فردوسی در حال از بین رفتن است/ نه در مشهد از آن استفاده کردند، نه آن را به تهران دادند, Didban Iran]

data.title: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, NTU
data.text:
The School of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) is an academic unit of Nanyang Technological University (NTU) in Singapore. The school was established in 1981 as the School of Civil and Structural Engineering. It was renamed to the School of Civil and Environmental Engineering in 2002.

CEE is ranked sixth in the world for Civil and Structural Engineering in the QS World University Rankings by Subject in 2026. [ref: ]

Professor Lim Teik Thye currently serves as Acting Chair of the School. Professor Ioannis Brilakis will assume the role of Chair from January 2027 [ref: New Leadership: Welcoming Professor Ioannis Brilakis as the Next Chair of CEE, School of Civil and Environmental Engineering]. Professor Brilakis is currently the Laing O'Rourke Professor of Construction Engineering and Director of the Construction Information Technology Laboratory within the Department of Engineering at the University of Cambridge [ref: Ib340, Department of Engineering].

== History ==
The late Emeritus Professor Chen Charng Ning was the founding dean of NTU's then School of Civil and Structural Engineering. In 2020, the NTU endowment fund was launched in honour of the late engineering dean which started off with $1m donation [ref: New NTU endowment fund in honour of late engineering dean kicks off with $1m donation, The Straits Times].

== Organisation and management ==
The school functions under NTU’s College of Engineering and is led by a chair with associate chairs for undergraduate and graduate programmes, faculty, and research [ref: organisation, Default].

data.title: Ahmed Hassan El Omairi
data.text:
Ahmed Hassan Al-Amiri

Ahmed Hassan Al-Amiri, also known as Ahmed Hassan, is an Egyptian digital content creator interested in promoting the tourism and heritage attractions of Matrouh Governorate, particularly the Siwa Oasis. data.title: EasyAudit
data.text:
EasyAudit is an American information security compliance company headquartered in Miami Beach, Florida. It provides a managed compliance service that combines a dedicated human compliance lead with an AI-based platform to help organizations prepare for third-party audits and certifications against frameworks including SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, NIST Cybersecurity Framework and ISO 9001. The company was founded by Christian Khoury, a former Deloitte risk advisory consultant, who serves as chief executive officer.[1]

The company describes its approach as "Autonomous Compliance" and positions the service as an alternative to both compliance automation software, such as Vanta and Drata, and to readiness assessments sold by consulting firms.[2] EasyAudit does not perform audits or issue certifications; those remain the responsibility of independent auditors and accredited certification bodies.

History

EasyAudit was founded in 2023 by Christian Khoury and Tyson Graham. Khoury previously worked in risk advisory at Deloitte.[1] According to the company, it was started because its founders were unable to hire the compliance expertise they needed and built a service to replace it.[2]

The company initially launched as an AI-based compliance software product that generated self-assessment reports, security controls and policy documents from a company questionnaire.[3] It later repositioned from selling software to delivering an outcome-based managed service, in which a named compliance lead manages each engagement and the platform executes recurring work.[2]

In 2026, EasyAudit introduced a free diagnostic engagement it calls the Compliance Simulation, and a guarantee under which customers do not pay if they are not audit-ready by an agreed date.[2]

Products and services

EasyAudit sells a single managed service built from three parts: a dedicated compliance lead who owns the engagement and coordinates with the customer and its auditor; an AI assistant the company calls the AI Compliance Officer, which collects evidence, drafts documentation and monitors controls; and an underlying platform that stores controls, evidence, mappings and audit history.[2]

The platform is organized around a single framework-agnostic control library, called the EasyAudit Framework, into which each supported standard is mapped. The company states that one control in the library can satisfy requirements from up to seven frameworks, so that evidence collected once applies across all of them.[4] Supported frameworks include SOC 1, SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800-53, and NIST SP 800-171.[4]

Other platform functions include an onboarding questionnaire that builds a company profile, AI-generated controls and policies tailored to that profile, continuous monitoring through read-only integrations with Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Microsoft 365, risk assessment, vendor risk management, a public trust center, and a Model Context Protocol connection that lets third-party AI assistants read the compliance data.[4]

Before a contract, prospective customers can take part in the Compliance Simulation, a diagnostic in which EasyAudit reviews existing policies and connected systems and returns a gap analysis, scope, timeline and price. Where eligible, the timeline is backed by a guarantee that the customer does not pay if it is not audit-ready by the agreed date.[2] The company states that formal certification and audit opinions remain with the independent auditor.[2]

Business model and market

EasyAudit charges a subscription fee for the managed service rather than billing by the hour, and ties part of that fee to delivering audit readiness by an agreed date.[2] The company has said it competes mainly with compliance consulting firms, including the Big Four accounting firms and specialist firms such as Coalfire, and A-LIGN, whose paid readiness assessments it aims to replace with its free Simulation, and secondarily with compliance automation software vendors such as Vanta, Drata and Secureframe.[2]

Its customers are mid-market organizations in regulated industries, typically with 500 to 10,000 employees, including insurance, data centers, business process outsourcing, pharmaceutical services and companies pursuing ISO 42001 for AI management systems. The company primarily serves the United States, with secondary markets in Canada and Latin America, and supports English and Spanish.[2]

data.title: Terenc Pepa
data.text:
----

Terenc Pepa (born 8 October 1987) is an Albanian landscape and cultural heritage photographer, certified commercial drone pilot, and information technology engineer. [ref: Terenc Pepa, fotografi që fokuson shpirtshëm hiret e bukurive tona t’hyjshme, Star Plus TV] [ref: Terenc Pepa, fotografi që fokuson shpirtje dhe hire të bukurisë shqiptare, ABC News Albania] His work focuses primarily on documenting the landscapes, historical sites, and regional culture of Shkodër and Northern Albania. [ref: Terenc Pepa, fotografi profesionist që profesionalisht na sjell Shkodrën në çdo hir të saj adhurues, Albert Vataj]

== Early life and education ==

Pepa was born in Shkodër, Albania, on 8 October 1987. He received artistic training during his secondary education at the Prenkë Jakova artistic school (Shkolla Artistike "Prenkë Jakova") in Shkodër before pursuing formal studies in computer engineering and information technology.

Pepa later completed European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) certification as an unmanned aircraft (drone) pilot, incorporating specialized high-altitude aerial photography and videography into his documentation of the mountainous terrain of the Albanian Alps. [ref: About – Terenc Pepa Photography, terencpepa.com]

== Photography and visual promotion ==

Pepa has documented landscapes, architectural sites, and cultural heritage across Northern Albania for over a decade. His imagery frequently highlights regional landmarks including Rozafa Castle, Lake Shkodër, the Shala River, Theth, Valbona Valley National Park, the Kelmend region, and the historic urban core of Shkodër.

Journalist and cultural critic Albert Vataj has written multiple profiles detailing Pepa's photographic style, emphasizing his technical use of drone cameras at dawn and dusk to record natural light patterns over historical ruins, rivers, and national parks in Northern Albania.

Pepa's visual work has been utilized in destination marketing campaigns, institutional archives, and promotional projects supported by public institutions and international development bodies:
* Government and regional institutions: The Municipality of Shkodër (Bashkia Shkodër), the Shkodër Regional Council (Këshilli i Qarkut Shkodër), the National Agency of Protected Areas (Agjencia Kombëtare e Zonave të Mbrojtura – AKZM), and projects backed by the Minister of State for the Protection of Enterprise (Ministria e Shtetit për Mbrojtjen e Sipërmarrjes).
* International and non-governmental organizations: Visual production and heritage documentation for the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the Institute for Habitat Development (Co-PLAN), and the Italian humanitarian organization VIS Albania.

== Information technology and digital media ==

Parallel to his work in photography, Pepa has worked in system administration, web development, and broadcasting infrastructure. He has provided IT and video transmission support for regional broadcaster Star Plus TV and served as digital media administrator and webmaster for the multi-sports club KF Vllaznia Shkodër. He is also the founder and developer of the regional portal Shkodër.info.

== Awards and recognition ==

* Shkodra Tourism Awards: Awarded "Tourism Influencer of the Year" for regional digital promotion and travel photography of Northern Albania.
* Creative History Balkans Tour: Third prize in the regional photography contest organized by the Creative History Balkans initiative for a photograph documenting Rozafa Castle.
* World Bank Cultural Heritage Competition: Third prize in a photographic competition supported in collaboration with the World Bank.

== References ==

data.title: Usman Iqbal
data.text:
Usman Iqbal is a Pakistani-born health informatics researcher and academic. He is a Professor of Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence at Bond University, where he leads the Evidence-Based Practice Professorial Unit at Gold Coast Hospital and Health Services.

== Education ==
Usman graduated with a Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) from the Federal Urdu University of Arts, Science and Technology. He subsequently earned an MBA in healthcare administration and a PhD in health informatics from Taipei Medical University. He also holds a postgraduate certificate in global health informatics from the Harvard–MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology.

== Academic career ==
Usman held academic positions at Taipei Medical University and co-founded the Taiwan chapter of the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) collaborative. He subsequently worked in government on digital health initiatives before joining Bond University. He also holds an adjunct academic appointment at the University of New South Wales.

His research focuses on digital health, biomedical informatics, patient safety, and artificial intelligence in healthcare. In 2020, he co-authored a paper proposing "earlier medicine", an approach that uses artificial intelligence and predictive analytics to support earlier identification of health risks and intervention. In 2026, he was the lead author of an evidence gap map of digital health interventions for patient engagement, published in npj Digital Medicine.

Usman was elected a Fellow of the International Academy of Health Sciences Informatics in 2023. In 2019, he received Taiwan's Plum Blossom Card in recognition of his contributions as a high-level foreign professional.

data.text:
== Sunkind India Limited ==
Sunkind India Limited is an Indian renewable energy company headquartered in Gurugram, Haryana. The company works in the solar energy sector, delivering engineering, procurement, and construction (solar EPC services), operations and maintenance (O&M), and commercial renewable energy project solutions for industries and institutions. Its business activities also include solar mounting structures and photovoltaic module manufacturing, with planned expansion into battery energy storage systems. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, official website.]

The company operates under the brand of Sunkind Energy and describes its activities as covering several stages of the renewable energy value chain, including solar project development, equipment manufacturing and renewable power generation. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Sunkind Energy: EPC operations and project portfolio.]

== History ==
Sunkind Energy was established in Sept 2019 to develop solar energy solutions for industrial and commercial customers in India. Its early operations included rooftop photovoltaic installations and hybrid rooftop systems. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, About Us: company history and leadership.]

2020: In 2020 the company completes its first set of hybrid rooftop systems, laying the foundation for execution excellence. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Investor information and financial disclosures.]

2021: Company delivers a major 3 MWp rooftop project, expanding its capabilities and building trust across sectors.

2022: Company launches Strucmax and establishes in-house mounting structure manufacturing, completing 18+ MWp of projects in a single year. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Strucmax: solar mounting structures.]

2023: Sunkind recorded strong growth, delivered 20+ MWp of solar projects, and moved into a new corporate headquarters.

2024: Company executes 75+ MWp of projects and completes its first project under an operating expenditure (OPEX) model.

2025: Sunkind crosses 150+ MWp in project capacity, expands group manufacturing capabilities, and strengthens its position as a future-ready clean energy company.

== Business activities ==

=== Solar engineering, procurement, and construction ===
Sunkind's principal business as of 2026 is providing Solar EPC services. The company provides turnkey solar power installations services including engineering, equipment procurement, construction, installation and commissioning.

Its project portfolio includes rooftop solar systems, ground-mounted photovoltaic installations and off-site solar projects. The company also provides solutions under capital expenditure (CAPEX) and operating expenditure (OPEX) arrangements.

Under the CAPEX model, customers finance and own their solar installations. Under OPEX arrangements, solar assets may be developed and operated under contractual structures designed to reduce the customer's initial capital requirement.

=== Operations and maintenance (O&M) ===
Sunkind India Limited provides integrated and external operations and maintenance services for solar power plants. These services include plant inspections, module cleaning, remote monitoring, equipment repairs and performance management. The services are designed to support system availability, energy generation and long-term plant performance.

=== Solar mounting structures ===
Strucmax is the part of Sunkind Energy group's and a solar mounting structure manufacturing business. It manufactures mounting systems used to support photovoltaic modules in solar power installations.

The company describes its products as modular, in-house-engineered structures designed for installation efficiency and structural durability. The business is part of the group's efforts to integrate equipment manufacturing with solar EPC operations.

=== Photovoltaic module manufacturing ===
Sunkind Photovoltaics is a part of Sunkind energy group and photovoltaic module manufacturing business. Its activities focus on manufacturing solar modules for use in renewable energy installations. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Sunkind Photovoltaics.]

The company describes its manufacturing approach as including automated production processes and quality control. Its published product information includes high-efficiency TOPCon and bifacial solar module technologies. [ref: pv magazine India, Sunkind India Limited secures long-term supply access to 1 GW TOPCon DCR solar cells, 29 May 2026.]

=== Battery energy storage ===
Batt-Li is the part of Sunkind Energy group's plan for building lithium-ion batteries for renewal energy storage business. The company is actively investing in commercial and industrial energy storage solutions (BESS). [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Batt-Li: battery energy storage.]

=== Project portfolio ===
Sunkind's solar EPC portfolio includes installations for industrial, commercial, institutional and power-sector customers. The company's project listings identify clients across industries such as steel, textiles, automotive manufacturing, packaging, aluminium, healthcare, hospitality and food processing.

The company lists projects in more than 16 states and union territories. Its published portfolio includes both commissioned installations and projects under execution.

=== State-wise presence ===

=== Manufacturing and vertical integration ===
Sunkind has diversified from solar EPC installation to downstream manufacturing of solar components. The proposed battery storage business, Batt-Li, will participate in the production of battery storage. In effect, the company downstreams its project realizations into selected components, a move described as a backward-integration initiative.

data.title: Blue Alto Farewell 2026
data.text:
----

= Blue Alto Farewell 2026 =
[https://youtube.com/@[user] Blue Alto Farewell 2026] is a proposed name for an alleged incident associated with a school farewell held on 23 April 2026 in Rawalpindi, Punjab, Pakistan. Accounts provided by a student describing the incident concern a disagreement among friends over transportation to an after-party and the reported departure of a group in a blue Suzuki Alto. The circumstances surrounding the incident have not been independently verified, and the proposed name has not been established as a widely used or officially recognized title.

== Background ==
The account places the alleged incident at or near the parking area by the gate of Army Public School and College (APSAC), Ordnance Road, in Rawalpindi. The event was reportedly associated with a Grade 12 farewell.

According to the account, a group of four friends planned to attend an after-party following the farewell. The account alleges that three members of the group left in a blue Suzuki Alto while the fourth, identified in the account as Unas Rizwan, was left behind.

== Alleged incident ==
The account further alleges that the circumstances surrounding the group’s departure became disputed. It describes disagreement over whether the friends had arrived at the agreed time and whether they had seen or collected the student who was reportedly left behind.

The account also claims that injuries were observed afterward. However, no independent documentation has been provided to establish how the injuries occurred or whether they were connected to the alleged incident. The available information does not establish that an assault took place or determine responsibility for any harm.

== Disputed accounts and online discussion ==
According to the account, the students involved gave differing explanations of the events, including disagreements about their timing and whether they had seen the student in question. The account also describes discussion and speculation among students on social media.

A YouTube channel using the name “Blue Alto” has been identified by the person providing the account as a possible source of related material. The channel’s content, the context of any relevant videos, and claims that material was subsequently deleted have not been independently verified.

== Documentation and investigation ==
The person providing the account reports having photographs, chat records, timestamps, and written statements related to the alleged incident. These materials have not been independently examined for this draft.

No independently verifiable news reports or publicly available official investigation documenting the alleged incident were identified during the research conducted for this draft. The official school website confirms the institution’s identity but does not, by itself, establish that the alleged incident occurred.

== Sources ==

# Army Public School & College (Boys), Ordnance Road, Rawalpindi. Official website: https://apsordrd.edu.pk/ This source provides institutional information; it has not been identified as documenting the alleged incident.
# “Blue Alto” YouTube channel. https://youtube.com/@[user] Identified by the person providing the account as a possible source for further research. The relevance and reliability of its content have not been independently established.

data.text:
Freshdi is an online multi-category business-to-business (B2B) marketplace connecting global suppliers and buyers. [ref: About Us, Freshdi] Its earlier documented activities focused on supply chain traceability and agricultural distribution in Vietnam. [ref: Ứng dụng nền tảng số để kết nối tiêu thụ nông sản Việt, VOV2]

== History and activities ==

=== Traceability and agricultural supply chain (2022–2023) ===
In February 2022, Vietnam's National Numbering and Barcodes Center (NBC) announced a cooperation agreement with Freshdi to apply barcode standards, blockchain technology, and big data to supply chain management and product traceability. [ref: Ký kết hợp tác giữa NBC và Freshdi, National Numbering and Barcodes Center]

During this period, Vietnamese media outlets including VietQ and VOV2 reported on Freshdi's implementation of digital tools to connect agricultural producers with distributors and to verify supply chain participants. [ref: Ứng dụng công nghệ Blockchain trong truy xuất nguồn gốc, Journal of Intellectual Property and Innovation] In February 2023, the Thanh Hóa youth organization collaborated with Freshdi Vietnam to establish a QR code-integrated portal introducing local specialty agricultural products. [ref: Tỉnh đoàn, Hội LHTN tỉnh Thanh Hóa phối hợp Freshdi Việt Nam hỗ trợ xây dựng Cổng đặc sản Thanh Hóa ứng dụng công nghệ 4.0, Thanh Hóa Youth Union]

=== Digital transformation initiatives ===
In June 2023, at the launch event for a digital transformation handbook for the food processing and distribution sector, Freshdi representatives presented sales management solutions and tools for marketing Vietnamese agricultural products to small and medium-sized enterprises. [ref: Ra mắt sổ tay chuyển đổi số ở lĩnh vực chế biến và phân phối thực phẩm, VietnamPlus] [ref: Sổ tay chuyển đổi số – Cẩm nang hữu ích cho doanh nghiệp nhỏ và vừa trong lĩnh vực chế biến và phân phối thực phẩm, Kinh tế và Dự báo]

In December 2025, Nhân Dân reported Freshdi Vietnam's participation in the VietLeap business matching event within the artificial intelligence ecosystem. [ref: Kết nối, tăng cường hợp tác cho hệ sinh thái trí tuệ nhân tạo tại Việt Nam, Nhân Dân]

== Corporate structure ==
According to the terms of use on its official website, the platform is operated by Freshdi Asia Pte. Ltd., a company registered in Singapore. [ref: Terms of Use, Freshdi] Operations and domestic partnerships in Vietnam are conducted through Freshdi Vietnam Joint Stock Company.

data.title: Abdulmalek Majeed Hameed
data.text:
----

Abdulmalek Majeed Hameed (Arabic: عبد الملك مجيد حميد), also referred to in news coverage as Abdulmalek Majeed, is an Iraqi cybersecurity commentator whose interviews and public statements have focused on online extortion, information security and the protection of social media accounts. [ref: مختص بمكافحة الابتزاز الإلكتروني: أساليب المبتزين مختلفة والإبلاغ المبكر خط الدفاع الأول, Iraqi News Agency] [ref: عبد الملك مجيد: الابتزاز الإلكتروني لم يعد مجرد جريمة تُرتكب خلف الشاشات، بل تحدياً مجتمعياً يمس الأسرة والشباب والمؤسسات, Ashur News Agency]
According to a 2026 report by Third River News Agency, Majeed began his technical activities in 2014, focused on information security in 2015, and was reported to hold a CEH v11 certification. [ref: خبير أمن المعلومات عبد الملك مجيد يقدم وصاياه لمكافحة الابتزاز الالكتروني, Third River News Agency]
== Media coverage ==

=== Iraqi News Agency interview ===
On 16 August 2026, the Iraqi News Agency published an interview with Majeed conducted by journalist Ahmed Smeisim. The discussion addressed different methods of online extortion, the risks associated with social media, and the importance of reporting threats and protecting personal information.

=== Newspaper interviews ===
In 2026, the Iraqi newspaper Al-Haqiqa published an interview featuring Majeed under the title "Hidden Wars of Electronic Extortion: Abdulmalek Majeed Recounts the Story of Confrontation". The interview discussed online extortion, public awareness and digital security. [ref: حروب الابتزاز الإلكتروني الخفية... حكاية المواجهة يرويها عبد الملك مجيد, Al-Haqiqa]

In September 2026, Al-Nahar newspaper also published material about Majeed in issues 3787 and 3789, including an interview about electronic extortion and its effects on society. [ref: جريدة النهار العدد 3787 في 20-9-2026, Al-Nahar] [ref: جريدة النهار العدد 3789 في 22-9-2026, Al-Nahar]

=== Other news coverage ===
On 18 September 2026, the Ninth News Agency published an article titled "Abdulmalek Majeed: From Digital Security Awareness to Combating Online Extortion". [ref: عبد الملك مجيد.. من ثقافة الأمن الرقمي إلى مكافحة الابتزاز الإلكتروني, Ninth News Agency]

In September 2026, Third River News Agency published reports quoting Majeed on the risks of artificial intelligence-generated images and methods of protecting individuals from online extortion. [ref: خبير الأمن السيبراني عبد الملك مجيد يحذر: الذكاء الاصطناعي أصبح سلاحاً جديداً بيد المبتزين عبر الصور المزيفة, Third River News Agency] [ref: خبير أمن المعلومات عبد الملك مجيد يقدم وصاياه لمكافحة الابتزاز الإلكتروني, Third River News Agency]

== Public commentary ==
Majeed has discussed the use of social engineering, account compromise and manipulated digital images in online extortion. In interviews, he has emphasized account security, protection of personal information, and early reporting of extortion attempts.

== Early life and background ==
Majeed was born in Baghdad, Iraq, in 1997. According to Third River News, he began his activities in technology in 2014, initially sharing educational material through social media. The publication reports that he subsequently focused on information security and online extortion prevention beginning in 2015. [ref: خبير أمن المعلومات عبد الملك مجيد يقدم وصاياه لمكافحة الابتزاز الالكتروني, Third River News]

== Cybersecurity activities ==
Majeed has discussed cybersecurity awareness, personal data protection, and the risks associated with online extortion. [ref: خبير أمن المعلومات عبد الملك مجيد يقدم وصاياه لمكافحة الابتزاز الالكتروني, وكالة النهر الثالث الإخبارية]

In an August 2026 interview with Ashur News Agency, he described his involvement in assisting individuals affected by online extortion and promoting safer digital practices. [ref: عبد الملك مجيد: الابتزاز الإلكتروني لم يعد مجرد جريمة تُرتكب خلف الشاشات ، بل تحدياً مجتمعياً يمس الأسرة والشباب والمؤسسات, Ashur News Agency]

His public statements have addressed online impersonation, account security, fraudulent links, and the misuse of artificial intelligence to create manipulated images and videos.

== Digital safety awareness ==

Majeed has advocated stronger awareness of online risks, including the use of secure passwords, two-factor authentication, and caution when interacting with unfamiliar links.

He has also emphasized the importance of preserving evidence and contacting the appropriate authorities when responding to online extortion.

data.title: Stun Siva
data.text:
----

Stun Siva (also credited as Stun Shiva) is an Indian stunt choreographer and actor who works mainly in Tamil cinema, and also in Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada films. He received the Tamil Nadu State Film Award for Best Stunt Coordinator for Kannukkul Nilavu (2000) and, with Peter Hein, the IIFA Award for Best Action for the Hindi film Ghajini.

== Career ==

=== Stunt choreography ===
Siva began his career in the Tamil film industry as a stunt performer and assistant. In a 2018 interview with The Times of India, he said that he became a stunt master with the 1997 film Love Today. A 2008 India Today feature on Chennai's stunt directors included him among the city's leading action choreographers and described how stunt professionals progressed in the industry. In 2016, The Times of India discussed his work and experience in an article on Tamil cinema's action choreographers.

He received the Tamil Nadu State Film Award for Best Stunt Coordinator for Kannukkul Nilavu (2000). For the 2008 Hindi film Ghajini, he and Peter Hein won the IIFA Award for Best Action at the 2009 IIFA technical awards.

His later work includes the action sequences of Nelson Dilipkumar's Jailer (2023); a review in Odisha Plus said that the film relied heavily on his action direction and that the action complemented the narrative.

=== Acting ===
Siva has also appeared as an actor, including in Vettaiyaadu Vilaiyaadu (2006). In Champion (2019), directed by Suseenthiran, he played the antagonist. In an August 2019 interview with The Times of India, he discussed his performance in Goli Soda 2 and said it led to him being cast as a lead actor.

=== Directing ===
In 2015, Siva announced his directorial debut, an action film with a romance track, launched in the presence of producer Kalaipuli S. Thanu and director Prabhu Solomon. The film, titled Karate Karan (also spelled Karatekaaran), was described as a Tamil remake of The Karate Kid, with his sons Kevin and Steven in the lead roles; Siva said that Jackie Chan had sent his good wishes to the team. In 2018, The Times of India reported on his continued work on the film.

== Personal life ==
Siva's sons, Kevin Kumar and Steven Kumar, are also stunt choreographers and martial artists.

== NutraLabs ==

NutraLabs Aust Pty Ltd is an Australian contract manufacturing company based in Braeside, Victoria.https://abr.business.gov.au/ABN/View?id=86684751942 1https://www.dairysafe.vic.gov.au/licensee-register?licence_type=manufacturer&order_by=licence_no&start=230&view=searchresults 2 The company provides formulation, dry powder blending and packing services for food, health, wellness, sports nutrition and nutraceutical products.https://nutralabs.com.au/services/ 3https://nutralabs.com.au/ 4

History NutraLabs Aust Pty Ltd was established in Victoria in 2025.https://abr.business.gov.au/ABN/View?id=86684751942 1 The company's Australian Business Number became active on 22 February 2025.https://abr.business.gov.au/ABN/View?id=86684751942 1 The company operates a manufacturing facility at 254 Governor Road, Braeside, Victoria.https://www.dairysafe.vic.gov.au/licensee-register?licence_type=manufacturer&order_by=licence_no&start=230&view=searchresults 2 The company was co-founded by Danny Rotman and Sam Briskin. Before establishing NutraLabs, Rotman co-founded Omniblend, another Australian contract manufacturing business, in 2008, which he subsequently sold. Briskin previously founded Hitex Confectionery, a contract manufacturer of protein bars, which he sold in 2023.

In 2026, Rotman was quoted by The New Daily in reporting on increases in whey protein prices and international demand for protein products.https://www.thenewdaily.com.au/life/health/2026/06/18/global-protein-costs 5

== Services and operations ==
NutraLabs provides contract manufacturing services for dry food, beverage, health, wellness, sports nutrition and nutraceutical products.https://nutralabs.com.au/services/ 3https://nutralabs.com.au/ 4 Its operations include product formulation and development, dry powder blending, private-label manufacturing and powder packing.https://nutralabs.com.au/services/ 3https://nutralabs.com.au/food-product-development/ 6

Products manufactured by the company include baking and dairy blends, protein powders, sports nutrition products, pre-workout powders, electrolyte powders and other dry nutritional blends.https://nutralabs.com.au/ 4 The company manufactures existing formulations and provides formulation and product development services for new or modified products.https://nutralabs.com.au/food-product-development/ 6

Its powder-packing capabilities include jars and tubs, buckets, composite containers, doy bags, pillow and block-bottom bags and sachets.https://nutralabs.com.au/ 4

== Regulatory and compliance ==
NutraLabs Aust Pty Ltd is licensed by Dairy Food Safety Victoria. The regulator's register lists the company's manufacturing facility at 254 Governor Road, Braeside, under licence number 10000470.https://www.dairysafe.vic.gov.au/licensee-register?licence_type=manufacturer&order_by=licence_no&start=230&view=searchresults 2

NutraLabs Aust Pty Ltd is registered with the Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry as an export dairy processing establishment. The department's register lists the company's facility at 254 Governor Road, Braeside, as establishment number 3589, with its registered operation covering the blending of dried milk and dried milk products.https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/dairy-export-registered-processing-establishments.pdf 7

NutraLabs Aust Pty Ltd is also listed by the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology as an Australian establishment certified by Halal Certification Authority Australia for powder blends. The register lists the approval as valid until 31 December 2028.https://www.moiat.gov.ae/-/media/site/moiat/halalapprovedslaughter/halalapproved.ashx 8

NutraLabs Aust Pty Ltd holds BRCGS Global Standard Food Safety Issue 9 certification for its Braeside facility. Certificate C826535, issued by DNV Business Assurance Italy S.r.l., covers the blending and packing of dairy-based and non-dairy powders in plastic pouches, jars, bags, foil sachets and composite cans. The facility achieved an A audit grade following an announced audit conducted on 17 November 2025. The certificate is valid until 29 December 2026, subject to its certification conditions.https://directory.brcgs.com/ 9

data.text:
----

Noor Mahnun Anum was born on 1964, Malaysia. She is a Malaysian painter that creates figurative works of domestic scenes and still life, fusing realism, allegory and whimsical. [ref: Noor Mahnun Anum - Biography, Yeo Workshop]

== Biography ==
Noor Mahnun Anum was born on 1964, in Kelantan, Malaysia.

Before Anum was an artist, she studied architecture in the USA. On 1989, she begin her Masters in Fine Art at Hochschule für Bildende Künste, Braunschweig and graduated on 1996. Anum had her first residency at Rimbun Dahan in Kuang, Selangor, from 2000 - 2001. From 2002 - 2003, she received a scholarship from the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs for a printmaking course at II Bisonte, Florence.

== Solo Exhibitions ==
Anum's had her solo exhibitions Anum at Yeo Workshop, Singapore (2025), Disco Lombok Still Life at The Edge Galerie, Kuala Lumpur (2017) and September at The Back Room (2021).

Most recently, her work was showcased at Merdeka Textile Museum in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
