data.title: Shamsiddin Kamoliddin
data.text:
----

= The Scientific Achievements of Professor Sh. S. Kamoliddin and His Contribution to Scholarship =
One of the principal strengths of Sh. S. Kamoliddin’s scholarly work is that, despite his foundational education in Oriental studies, which provided him with knowledge of several Eastern languages and the skills needed to work with primary sources, he has never confined his research interests to historiography and historical source studies alone.

While working on his doctoral dissertation between 1990 and 1993, following the joint recommendation of Orientalist P. G. Bulgakov and archaeologist E. V. Rtveladze, he began employing an interdisciplinary research approach. This approach incorporated written sources and archaeological findings, as well as evidence from historical toponymy, cartography, numismatics, anthropology, ethnography, and other auxiliary historical disciplines.

The comprehensive study and comparative analysis of different types of sources, together with his distinctive methodological approach, have enabled him to develop research conclusions that sometimes differ from positions widely accepted in international historiography. Examples of his research findings include the following:

1. The Early Presence of Ancient Turks in Central Asia

According to the document, a prevailing view in international historiography holds that the ancient Turks arrived in Central Asia during the Turkic Khaganate period, from the mid-sixth to the mid-eighth century. Kamoliddin’s toponymic and linguistic research into the historical place names of Central Asia led him to conclude that ancient Turkic populations had lived in the region since at least the Bronze Age and formed part of its early indigenous population.

He proposed that, following the arrival of Aryan-speaking groups, some of these populations were displaced beyond Central Asia, mainly to the north and east, while a larger portion remained in the region under Aryan rule.

2. The Contribution of Ancient Turks to Settled and Urban Culture

The document describes a view in historiography that ancient Turks lived exclusively nomadic lives, primarily engaged in animal husbandry, and made no contribution to settled agricultural and urban culture.

Through interdisciplinary research and comparative analysis of historical terminology in Turkic and Iranian languages, Kamoliddin concluded that ancient Turks had developed traditions in agriculture, horticulture, metallurgy, handicraft production, and urban construction. He argued that they made a significant contribution to the development of settled agricultural and urban culture in Central Asia.

3. The Role of Medieval Turks in the Cultural Development of the Muslim World

The document discusses the view that medieval Turks were primarily associated with raids and warfare and made little contribution to world culture and civilization.

Kamoliddin’s research in historiography and historical source studies led him to argue that medieval Turks played an active role in the cultural flourishing of the Muslim world commonly referred to as the “Muslim Renaissance.” He considered them initiators and important participants in this process, which he attributed to the interaction of different cultures within the Islamic world. He further argued that the experience acquired by Turkic peoples during the Turkic Khaganate period, from the mid-sixth to the mid-eighth century, contributed to their role in the later cultural development of the Abbasid Caliphate, which existed from the mid-eighth century to the early thirteenth century.

4. The Origins of the Samanid Dynasty

The document notes that the Samanid dynasty, which ruled Transoxiana and Khorasan during the ninth and tenth centuries, is generally regarded in historiography as having Iranian origins.

Based on a comprehensive examination of written, archaeological, numismatic, ethnographic, and other historical evidence, Kamoliddin proposed that the Samanids had Oghuz-Turkic origins.

According to his interpretation, the dynasty’s ancestor, known as Saman-Khudat or Saman-Yabgu, descended from the Turkic yabghus of Tokharistan, whom he associated with the Ashina clan, the ruling family of the Turkic Khaganate. Kamoliddin further proposed that this ancestor bore the Turkic name Arkuk and practiced Buddhism or Manichaeism before converting to Islam. The document also states that, according to its interpretation, he wore his hair in a braid in accordance with an ancient Turkic custom and was nicknamed “Kakuldar” by the surrounding Iranian population, a term interpreted as “the possessor of a braid.”

5. The Historical Development of the Terms “Uzbek” and “Uzbekistan”

The document discusses the claim that the ethnonym “Uzbek” and the place name “Uzbekistan” were introduced by Russian Bolsheviks during the national-territorial delimitation of Turkestan in 1924.

Kamoliddin’s research in historical geography and cartography led him to argue that the term “Uzbek” was already used among Turkic peoples as a personal name in the twelfth century.

According to his interpretation, the names “Uzbek,” “Uzbekia,” or “Uzbekistan” began to be used in the fourteenth century in connection with the Golden Horde during the reign of Öz Beg Khan, when his subjects came to be known as Uzbeks.

The document further states that, in the fifteenth century, the term “Uzbek” was used to designate the population of the Uzbek Ulus, which emerged in the Dasht-i Qipchaq steppes following the disintegration of the Golden Horde.

From the beginning of the sixteenth century until the middle of the eighteenth century, the terms “Uzbek” and “Uzbek” as a geographical designation were used in connection with the Shaybanid and Astrakhanid states of Central Asia. Subsequently, until the Russian conquest of the region between 1855 and 1875, the term served as a collective designation for the Uzbek khanates centered in Bukhara, Samarkand, Khiva, Balkh, and Kokand.

data.title: Napleton
data.text:
----

Napleton is a small rural hamlet on the southern side of Kempsey, about 3–4 miles south of Worcester. It is part of Kempsey and is in the WR5 postal district.

Historical records have it as "Appelton" in 1275 and 1327, which directly translates to apple settlement or orchard. [ref: Worcestershire place names]

Napleton Grange is a substantial period house on Napleton Lane which was once the home of Edward Elgar (composer) who lived in Kempsey from 1923–1927. Napleton Grange dates back to around 1440 and is a property on the ‘Elgar Route’ which takes people through notable places and houses linked to the composer. Edward Elgar was appointed Master of the King’s music in 1924, during his time in Napleton, and the Civic Fanfare was composed whilst he was living there. [ref: https://elgarroute.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Elgar-Route-Leaflet-Web.pdf? ]

Napleton House is the main house of the hamlet and is believed to have been built on the site of a roman villa. It was once owned by the Marquess of Blandford. [ref: Unspoilt Georgian country house]

Napleton House also has a Site of Special Scientific Interest in the grounds [ref: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/693153fc5b5198836f304020/annex-b-restrictions-relating-to-licensed-actions-on-or-around-protected-sites-in-worcestershire-2025.pdf ] - Napleton Meadows.

data.title: Cedric Harris (software architect)
data.text:
Cedric Harris is an American software architect, inventor, entrepreneur, and author. He is the founder and chief executive officer of ElephantSqlDB, Inc., an Austin, Texas–based database software company, and was formerly chief research officer of Everything Blockchain, Inc.

== Education ==
Harris received a Bachelor of Science in computer software engineering from Tuskegee University.

== Career ==
=== 832 Energy Technology Consultants ===
Harris founded 832 Energy Technology Consultants, a Houston-based firm through which he worked as a software architect and engineer for United Airlines.

=== Everything Blockchain ===
In June 2021, Everything Blockchain, Inc. acquired 832 Energy Technology Consultants, and Harris was named the company's chief research officer while continuing to operate the business.

=== ElephantSqlDB ===
Harris founded ElephantSqlDB, Inc., which operates with its subsidiary Dataark Systems, LLC. In August 2025, the company announced the general availability of ElephantSqlDB, a software-as-a-service database that it describes as using a "quantum-asymptotic" architecture based on a variant of Grover's algorithm run on Nvidia GPU simulation technology. The company stated it had been accepted into the Nvidia Inception program. The product is unrelated to the earlier ElephantSQL PostgreSQL hosting service. Harris's books Beyond the Asymptote describe the asymptotic algorithms underlying the platform.

== Patents ==
Harris is a named inventor on U.S. patents relating to blockchain platform services, including "Blockchain platform as a service (BPaaS)" [ref: Blockchain platform as a service (BPaaS)] and "Blockchain platform service". [ref: Blockchain platform service]

== Publications ==
* Beyond the Asymptote, Volume I (ISBN 979-8-9952815-0-4)
* Beyond the Asymptote, Volume II: The Implementation Edition (ISBN 979-8-9952815-1-1)

== Speaking engagements ==
In August 2023, Harris spoke at the Executive Next Practices (ENP) Institute's 3rd Annual Growth Summit, "Platform Leaps During Market Turbulence," held at UC Irvine Beall Applied Innovation.

data.title: Pitch Recognition (baseball)
data.text:
----

{Infobox baseball
| name = Baseball Pitch Recognition Timeline
| image = Pitch Recognition Timeline.png
| caption = “Approximate sequence of visual perception, pitch recognition, swing decision, swing adjustment, and contact during baseball batting. Timing values are and vary by pitch speed, pitch type, and batter characteristics.”
| sport = Baseball

}

Pitch recognition in baseball refers to the perceptual ability of batters to detect visual cues from a pitcher’s pitching motion, arm angle and hand position at pitch release, and spin of the ball to identify the pitch type thrown (e.g. fastball, curveball, slider, changeup). Batters subconsciously generate predictions about the trajectory and speed of different pitch types to anticipate where and when the ball will cross the hitting zone. [ref: Müller, S. & Abernethy, B. “Expert Anticipatory Skill in Striking Sports: A Review and a Model.” *Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport* 83(2): 175–187 (2012).]

Pitch recognition helps batters decide whether to execute a full bat swing or a checked swing based on anticipating that the pitch will or will not be in the strike zone. Because batters often must check a swing mid-motion, the decision whether to swing usually must occur very early in the pitch’s trajectory.

== Timing constraints ==

Sports scientists estimate that a batter typically needs **about 150 milliseconds** to initiate and complete a swing. Given that a 95 mile-per-hour fastball takes roughly **400 milliseconds** to travel from pitcher to home plate, this leaves only about **250 milliseconds** for recognition and decision making (i.e. “the blink of an eye”). [ref: Adair, Robert K. The Physics of Baseball (2002).]

Because of highly constrained swing decision time, many hitting coaches teach a mental sequence of “yes, yes, YES,” describing hitters' intent to swing unless pitch recognition cues contradict it, changing the hitters' intent to “yes, yes, NO” if the pitch is clearly outside the strike zone. [ref: The Batter's Box Mindset: How to Win Every Battle at the Plate in Baseball and Softball]

== Pitch repertoire and deception ==

Pitch recognition is both more difficult and more critical because modern professional pitchers often throw five or more types of pitches, each with distinct velocity, movement, and spin signatures. For instance, a cut fastball may travel only a few mph slower than a pitcher’s fastball but exhibit late horizontal movement in the opposite direction of the pitcher's pitching arm. The subtle, late nature of such movement increases difficulty for hitters to distinguish early signals. [ref: Cut fastball, MLB.com]

An example of pitch movement deceiving hitters is Mariano Rivera, whose reliance on a cut fastball contributed to his dominance as a relief pitcher. [ref: Cut fastball, The New York Times]

== Conceptual contrasts ==

=== vs. Plate discipline ===
Plate discipline is a measure of a batter’s ability to swing at strikes and refrain from swinging at balls. One statistic often used is the walk-to-strikeout ratio (BB/K). A BB/K of 1 walk per 2 strikeouts (0.5) is generally acceptable, while a ratio greater than 1 is rare and denotes strong plate discipline. Historical examples of hitters with elite career BB/K ratios include:

- Ted Williams: ≈ 2.85
- Wade Boggs: ≈ 1.90
- Tony Gwynn: ≈ 1.84
- Joe Morgan: ≈ 1.82
- Barry Bonds: ≈ 1.66
- Juan Soto: ≈ 1.08 [ref: MLB Hitters Sorted By Best Walk To Strikeout Ratio For Career]

While plate discipline can be measured as an outcome, pitch recognition refers to the underlying perceptual skill that influences not only swing decisions but also swing adjustments. Historically, Tony Gwynn of the San Diego Padres was notable for making solid contact with a variety of pitch types and locations. [ref: Tony Gwynn was a pure contact hitter]

=== vs. Visual skills ===
Visual faculties such as dynamic tracking, contrast sensitivity, and peripheral vision are often considered the hardware; pitch recognition is the software that interprets sensory input, matches patterns, and activates decision pathways. Both can be trained, but they are conceptually distinct and may require separate assessment and training. [ref: Tremblay, M., Couëpel, B., Abboud, J. et al. "What are the Individual Characteristics or Skills Associated with Baseball Batting Performance? A Scoping Review." *Sports Med* Open 11, 150 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-025-00947-1.]

== Testing and training methods ==

Academic research has found sports vision training programs that target visual skills to be effective for improving performance in a range of sports skills. [ref: Lochhead, L., Feng, J., Laby, D. M., & Appelbaum, L. G. (2024). "Training vision in athletes to improve sports performance: a systematic review of the literature." *International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology*, 1–23. https://doi.org/10.1080/1750984X.2024.2437385].
Sports science studies that specifically investigate perceptual-cognitive skills, such as pitch recognition, typically use the experimental method of **video-occlusion** in which observers view video clips showing a batter’s perspective that are cut off (occluded) at various times before, at, or after pitch release. Participants must guess pitch type or predict ball/strike. Experts often outperform novices under occlusion conditions, suggesting superior early cue sensitivity. [ref: Müller, S. & Abernethy, B. “Expert Anticipatory Skill in Striking Sports: A Review and a Model.” *Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport* 83(2): 175–187 (2012).] The video-occlusion method developed by sports science researchers also is used by college and professional baseball organizations to test batters' pitch recognition ability. [ref: Sport Expertise and Skill Learning Evidence Provides Unique Opportunities to Develop Baseball Players]

Beyond research and testing uses, video-occlusion has been studied as a method of training perceptual-cognitive skills in a variety of sports [ref: Müller, S., Morris-Binelli, K., Hambrick, D.Z. et al. "Accelerating Visual Anticipation in Sport Through Temporal Occlusion Training: A Meta-Analysis." *Sports Medicine* 54, 2597–2606 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-024-02073-6(2006).] Studies that specifically investigated baseball pitch recognition found that both vision training [ref: Clark JF, Ellis JK, Bench J, Khoury J, Graman P (2012) "High-Performance Vision Training Improves Batting Statistics for University of Cincinnati Baseball Players." *PLoS ONE* 7(1): e29109. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0029109] and video-occlusion methods [ref: Fadde, P. J. “Interactive Video Training of Perceptual Decision-Making in the Sport of Baseball.” *Technology, Instruction, Cognition and Learning* 4(3-4): 265-285 (2006).] improved the batting statistics of college baseball players.

Awareness of pitch recognition as a critical component of baseball batting has furthered by Major League Baseball’s adoption of an **automated ball-strike system (ABS)** starting with the 2026 season. [ref: ABS Challenge System starting 2026, MLB.com]

== See also ==
* PITCHf/x — historical pitch-tracking system
* Statcast — modern pitch and player tracking
* Automated Ball-Strike System

== References ==

== Further reading ==

* Müller, S., Dekker, E., Morris-Binelli, K., Piggott, B., Hoyne, G., Christensen, W., et al. (2023). *Attributes of Expert Anticipation Should Inform the Design of Virtual Reality Simulators to Accelerate Learning and Transfer of Skill*. *Sports Medicine*, 53(2).
* Müller, S., Fadde, P. J., & Harbaugh, A. G. (2017). *Adaptability of Expert Visual Anticipation in Baseball Batting*. *Journal of Sports Sciences*, 35(17): 1682-1690.
* Fadde, P. J. (2016). *Instructional Design for Accelerated Macrocognitive Expertise in the Baseball Workplace*. *Frontiers in Psychology*, 7: 292.

According to his personal website, Allen started his first company at the age of 17 and began working as an artificial intelligence engineer at 19. He did not attend university. His website also describes his participation in hackathons and his work as a judge at TreeHacks at Stanford University.

=== The20hr.co ===
In an account published on 9 August 2025, Allen described developing The20hr.co with a group of friends during a hackathon in Sweden. The project was a tool for personalised outreach on LinkedIn. According to Allen, the team built, launched and sold the project within 20 hours, with Revel acquiring it. [ref: The20hr.co, Henry Allen]

=== Vultur ===
Allen's personal website describes Vultur as his current project and connects its development to his interest in how people share opportunities.

data.title: Nagarukhra
data.text:
----

Nagarukhra (; ) is a town and a local government area in the Nadia district in the Indian state of West Bengal. It operates under the Kalyani subdivision and the Haringhata CD block. The town is share the part of the area covered by the Kolkata Metropolitan Development Authority (KMDA) in the Region and is administered by two Gram Panchayats. [ref: Kolkata Metropolitan Development Authority, KMDA]

== History ==
The earliest known historical identity of the area is associated with Ukrah (or Ookra). Historical accounts connected with the Mughal administration, including references in the Ain-i-Akbari, indicate that Ukrah was documented as a pargana during the Mughal period. [ref: History of Nadia, Nadia District Administration]

During the early 18th century, Ukrah became associated with the Zamindari system of Bengal. Local historical accounts connect the Ukrah Zamindari with Raghuram, a descendant of Bhavananda Majumdar. Following the Battle of Plassey in 1757 and the East India Company's acquisition of the Diwani of Bengal in 1765, the region came under British revenue and administrative control. British geographic surveys associated with James Rennell recorded the name of the area as Ukhra or Aukerah, documenting its continued presence during the colonial period. [ref: Rennell and the Surveyors of India, The Geographical Journal]

The Jamuna River played an essential role in the development of the settlement by providing opportunities for transportation and agriculture. Over time, a local market (ganj) developed. It is historically suggested that as the settlement grew into an important local center, the prefix "Nagar" (meaning town) was added to the older name Ukhra, forming "Nagarukhra".

Throughout the 19th century, Nagarukhra and the surrounding Nadia region became part of the colonial economy, particularly noted for "Indigo cultivation" (neel kuthis). The partition of India in 1947 impacted the territorial status of Nadia. The district was briefly associated with East Pakistan in early boundary arrangements before the Radcliffe Award placed most of Nadia, including Nagarukhra, in India on 18 August 1947. [ref: Partition of British India, The National Archives]

== Geography ==
Nagarukhra is situated in the southern part of the Nadia district within the flat alluvial landscape of the lower Ganges basin. The surrounding terrain has minimal relief, characterized by fertile alluvial deposits and low-lying agricultural land. Groundwater and topographical studies identify the lowest recorded ground-surface elevation in the district near Nagarukhra, at approximately 14 metres above mean sea level. [ref: Ground Water Information Booklet, Nadia District, West Bengal, Central Ground Water Board, Ministry of Water Resources, Government of India]

The settlement is closely associated with the Jamuna River, a key geographical feature of the locality, and is located near the administrative boundary between Nadia and North 24 Parganas districts. [ref: District Census Handbook Nadia, Census of India 2011, Series 20, Part XII A, Directorate of Census Operations, West Bengal]

=== Climate ===
Nagarukhra experiences a humid tropical climate (Köppen climate classification Aw), typical of southern West Bengal. Summers are hot and humid, the monsoon season brings substantial rainfall, and winters are mild and dry. According to local climate data, the annual mean temperature is approximately 26.3 °C, with an average annual precipitation of 1,550–1,560 mm. July is generally the wettest month, while December is the driest. [ref: Climate Summary for Nagarukhra, Weatherbase.com]

== Civic and revenue administration ==
The civic administration of the wider town and its adjoining areas is managed by two rural local bodies: Nagarukhra-I and Nagarukhra-II Gram Panchayats. Law and order for the entire Nagarukhra area and surrounding villages are maintained by the Nagarukhra Police Station. [ref: Nadia District Police, West Bengal, Nadia District Police]

=== Revenue office ===
For land and revenue administration, the core central part of the town corresponds to the Ukrah mouza (Jurisdiction List or JL No. 77). This specific mouza houses the local Revenue Inspector (RI) office, which manages the land records and revenue matters for the immediate region under the state's land reforms department. [ref: Mouza Information, Land and Land Reforms Department, Banglarbhumi]

=== Postal services ===
The town operates a delivery post office serving the local residents and surrounding villages. It functions under the Department of Posts with the designated PIN code 741257. [ref: Locate Post Office: Nagarukhra, India Post]

=== Electricity board ===
The area's power supply and electrical infrastructure are overseen by a regional Customer Care Center (CCC) of the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (WBSEDCL). [ref: WBSEDCL Customer Care Centers, WBSEDCL]

== Demographics ==
Nagarukhra encompasses multiple mouzas (revenue villages) spread across the Nagarukhra-I and Nagarukhra-II Gram Panchayats.

According to the 2011 Census of India, the two Gram Panchayats together recorded a total population of 40,766 (with 19,825 people in Nagarukhra-I and 20,941 in Nagarukhra-II). Within this larger administrative boundary, the specific core mouza of Ukrah (JL No. 77) independently recorded a population of 13,548. In this core area, the literacy rate was 83.91%, with male literacy at 88.55% and female literacy at 78.96%. [ref: Primary Census Abstract at Town, Village and Ward Level, West Bengal – District Nadia, 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India]

The predominant languages spoken in the area are Bengali and Hindi, with Bengali being the principal medium of everyday communication, education, and local administration.

== Notable persons ==
* Anil Ghorai (1957–2014) – Eminent Bengali writer and novelist who spent his formative years in Nagarukhra after his family moved there in 1962. He is widely recognized for his literary works depicting the lives of marginalized communities. [ref: Eminent Bengali writer Anil Ghorai passes away, The Times of India]
* Manas Kumar Ganguly – Politician affiliated with the Indian National Congress, who contested from the Haringhata Assembly constituency in the 1971 and 1977 West Bengal Legislative Assembly elections. [ref: Statistical Report on General Election, 1971 to the Legislative Assembly of West Bengal, Election Commission of India]
* Chanchal Debnath – Local politician and former Nadia district Zilla Parishad office-bearer, associated with regional administrative and development initiatives in the area. [ref: Nadia Zilla Parishad, Nadia District Administration]

== Education ==
Nagarukhra has educational institutions providing education from the primary level to the higher secondary level. The locality has both co-educational and girls' schools, serving Nagarukhra and the surrounding areas. [ref: School Directory: Nadia District, Banglar Shiksha]

== Healthcare ==
Basic healthcare is managed through Nagarukhra Primary Health Centre - a state-run primary healthcare center. For advanced medical requirements, residents utilize the sub-divisional hospitals in Kalyani. [ref: Health & Family Welfare Department, Government of West Bengal, Department of Health & Family Welfare, West Bengal]

== Culture ==
=== Nagarukhra Lok Utsav ===
The cultural landscape of the town is notably marked by the annual Nagarukhra Lok Utsav (Folk Festival). This regional festival is organized to celebrate and preserve traditional Bengali folk arts, music, and local crafts, attracting participants and visitors from the surrounding districts. The event plays a significant role in maintaining the cultural heritage of the area. [ref: Local festivals of Nadia, Nadia District Administration]

=== Other Festivals ===
Alongside standard urban festivities. Major religious and cultural festivals of West Bengal, including Durga Puja, Kali Puja, and Saraswati Puja, are celebrated widely across the town with active community participation.

== Transport ==
Nagarukhra is strategically linked to neighboring urban & rural centers via road networks. The Kanchrapara-Nagarukhra-Bongaon Intercity Road, Nagarukhra-Habra Road & Nagarukhra-Gopalnagar Road are vital arterial route connecting the town directly to the nearby towns & villages. State highways and local routes also connect the area to Kolkata, Barrackpore, Kalyani, Habra, Barasat, and Bongaon. For daily transit, the town relies on public buses, auto-rickshaws, and e-rickshaws. The nearest Railway station of Nagarukhra is Habra railway station, Kanchrapara railway station & Kalyani Jn. railway station.

The Kanchrapara–Nagarukhra–Bongaon Intercity Road passes through the locality and links the National Highway network in North 24 Parganas and Nadia. The route connects with NH 112 near Gaighata and NH 12 near Barajaguli and continues towards Kanchrapara and connect with Kalyani Expressway and after cross the Hooghly River it's connects with the GT Road. [ref: Road Network of West Bengal, Public Works Department]

data.title: Jim Gloyd
data.text:
----

Jim Gloyd is an American writer, actor, producer, director and author. He wrote, produced, co-directed and starred as Bruce in the 2020 drama The Wager. His other screen credits include the voice role of Tsayid in Cadia: The World Within (2019) and Dr. Molder in Clay Zombies (2021). [ref: The Wager, Rotten Tomatoes] [ref: The Wager, Apple TV] [ref: Jim Gloyd, IMDb]

== Career ==
Gloyd developed The Wager from a short story he had written. In 2018, the Scioto Post reported that the film was being produced by Clean Screen Productions, a company created by Gloyd, and that filming was planned in Circleville, Ashville and Columbus, Ohio. The report also covered the casting of former heavyweight boxing champion James "Buster" Douglas. [ref: "Buster" Douglas Cast in Local Film "The Wager", Scioto Post]

Pickaway County Board of Commissioners minutes from April 2019 document Gloyd's request to use the county Engineer's Office in Circleville for filming The Wager. [ref: April 2, 2019 Minutes, Pickaway County] The film was released in 2020. Apple TV and Rotten Tomatoes credit Gloyd as a director and actor, while Rotten Tomatoes also credits him as producer and screenwriter.

The Wager received local television coverage on Good Day Columbus on ABC6, where Gloyd appeared to discuss the film. Dove.org later reviewed the film and identified Gloyd among its actors, writers, directors and producers. The production and release were also covered by the Circleville Herald. [ref: Local filmmaker talks about his movie "The Wager", ABC6 / Good Day Columbus] [ref: The Wager, Dove.org] [ref: Ashville man to shoot inspirational film in Pickaway, Circleville Herald] [ref: Locally sourced movie to be released next week, Circleville Herald]

In addition to The Wager, Gloyd voiced Tsayid in the fantasy film Cadia: The World Within, which also featured Corbin Bernsen and James Phelps. He later appeared as Dr. Molder in the 2021 horror-comedy Clay Zombies. [ref: Cadia: The World Within, Apple TV] [ref: Cadia: The World Within Cast, TV Guide] [ref: Clay Zombies, Apple TV] [ref: Clay Zombies, Tubi]

== Books and children's projects ==
Gloyd's published works include Becoming Free from the Judas in Me, co-authored with Shawn Harper and published in 2010, and The Wager: And 11 Other Short Stories, co-authored with William C. Canfield and published by Glory Publishing in 2025. His bibliography also includes the children's title Sammy the Witness: The Fish That Outlived Methuselah!. [ref: Jim Gloyd, Goodreads] [ref: Saving Satan's Backsliders: Becoming Free From the Judas in Me, PR.com] [ref: The Wager: And 11 Other Short Stories, AbeBooks]

Gloyd is also credited as a writer on the animated television project The Chronicles of the Tiny Ones: Sammy the Witness, listed as a current project on his IMDb profile. The related published children's title Sammy the Witness: The Fish That Outlived Methuselah! is listed in his Goodreads bibliography.

== Music ==
Gloyd releases independent music under the project name 100 Days Ahead. Public listings under his name include the tracks "Warning Lights", "Burned Again" and "My Superhero". [ref: 100 Days Ahead tracks, Slaps]

== Awards and recognition ==
At The Actors Awards in September 2020, Gloyd received Best Performance of Fest and Best Actor in a Drama for The Wager. [ref: September 2020 Winners, The Actors Awards] The Vegas Movie Awards' August winners archive lists The Wager and Gloyd for Best 1st Time Producer. [ref: August Edition — Winners of Excellence, Vegas Movie Awards]

data.title: Radio Swammerdam
data.text:
Radio Swammerdam is een Amsterdams wetenschapsradioprogramma en podcast. Het programma wordt sinds 2 mei 2010 gemaakt door een redactie van Amsterdamse studenten en recent afgestudeerden met interesse in wetenschap, journalistiek en radio. In de uitzendingen worden wetenschappers geïnterviewd over hun onderzoek, met als doel wetenschappelijke onderwerpen toegankelijk te maken voor een breder publiek.

Geschiedenis

Radio Swammerdam werd opgericht in 2010 en is vernoemd naar de zeventiende-eeuwse Amsterdamse natuuronderzoeker Jan Swammerdam. Swammerdam deed onderzoek naar onder meer insecten en menselijke fysiologie en hield in Amsterdam een rariteitenkabinet bij.

Het programma ontstond als studenteninitiatief en wordt sindsdien grotendeels vrijwillig gemaakt. De redactie bestaat uit Amsterdamse studenten en net afgestudeerden, vaak met een achtergrond in wetenschap, journalistiek of academisch onderzoek.

Format

Elke aflevering staat in het teken van een wetenschappelijk onderwerp. In de uitzending schuiven een of meerdere onderzoekers aan om hun onderzoek toe te lichten. De gesprekken duren doorgaans ongeveer een uur en richten zich op het toegankelijk maken van academische kennis voor luisteraars buiten het specifieke vakgebied.

Naast interviews bevat het programma regelmatig columns of vaste rubrieken. De onderwerpen lopen uiteen van natuurwetenschappen en geneeskunde tot geesteswetenschappen, sociale wetenschappen en maatschappelijke vraagstukken.

Uitzending en distributie

Radio Swammerdam wordt uitgezonden op Radio SALTO, op zondag van 11:00 tot 12:00 uur. De opnames vinden plaats in Pakhuis de Zwijger in Amsterdam. Afleveringen zijn daarnaast terug te luisteren als podcast via onder meer Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Pocket Casts en andere podcastplatforms.

Redactie

De redactie wisselt per seizoen en bestaat uit studenten en pas afgestudeerden uit Amsterdam. Volgens de eigen omschrijving wordt het programma vrijwillig gemaakt door mensen met een passie voor onderzoek, journalistiek en radio.

Activiteiten

Hoewel de meeste afleveringen studio-interviews zijn, verzorgt de redactie ook veel specials: afleveringen opgenomen op locatie. In 2026 organiseerde de redactie onder meer een evenement in de Universiteitsbibliotheek van de Universiteit van Amsterdam onder de titel Radio Swammerdam Slaat Alarm: Pas Op Voor De Negentiende Eeuw!.

Naam

De naam verwijst naar Jan Swammerdam (1637–1680), een Amsterdamse natuuronderzoeker die bekendstaat om zijn werk op het gebied van anatomie, insectenonderzoek en microscopie. De verwijzing sluit aan bij het wetenschappelijke karakter van het programma.

data.title: Goran Gatalica
data.text:
Goran Gatalica (born 2 September 1982) is a Croatian writer, poet and haiku poet. He has also worked in physics, chemistry and education. He is a member of the Croatian Writers' Association and Matica hrvatska. [ref: Gatalica Goran, Društvo hrvatskih književnika]

== Life and work ==

Gatalica was born in Virovitica, Croatia, and completed his elementary and secondary education in Daruvar. He studied at the University of Zagreb, where he obtained master's degrees in Physics and Chemistry Teaching in 2009 and Chemical Engineering in 2011. He subsequently enrolled in doctoral studies. He has worked at the Institute of Physics, the Ruđer Bošković Institute and the Faculty of Chemical Engineering and Technology of the University of Zagreb.

Gatalica writes poetry in Croatian, including in the Kajkavian dialect, as well as haiku. His work has appeared in Croatian and international literary journals, collections and anthologies.

His poetry has been discussed in Croatian literary criticism. In Vijenac, Ljerka Car Matutinović reviewed his collection Kozmolom, discussing its prose-poetry form, metaphorical imagery and existential themes. [ref: Kozmičko iščitavanje svijeta, Vijenac]

Darija Žilić discussed Gatalica's collection Odsečeni od svetla in Vijenac, including its use of the Kajkavian dialect and its distinctive vocabulary and imagery. [ref: Ares briše svet med zvezdami, Vijenac]

Ružica Martinović-Vlahović reviewed Noćni jasmin / Night Jasmine in Kolo, discussing the collection's 113 haiku, its organization around the four seasons and its relationship to traditional and contemporary haiku. [ref: Zbirka poetskih trofeja, Kolo]

His first poetry collection, Krucijalni test, was published in 2014 by Matica hrvatska Daruvar. In 2015, it received the Slavić Award for the best first book published in 2014. [ref: Nagrada Dana hrvatske knjige – Slavić, HRČAK]

His second collection, Kozmolom, was published in 2016. In 2017, it received the Kvirin Award at the Kvirin Poetry Meetings in Sisak. The award was reported by Novi list. [ref: Kvirinovi susreti: Miroslavu Mićanoviću plaketa, nagrađen i Goran Gatalica, Novi list]

In the same year, Gatalica received the Dragutin Tadijanović Poetry Award from the Foundation of the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts. The award was reported by the Croatian news agency HINA. [ref: Pjesnik Goran Gatalica laureat ovogodišnje Nagrade "Dragutin Tadijanović", HINA]

His third poetry collection, Odsečeni od svetla, was published in 2018 by the Croatian Writers' Association and received the Katarina Patačić Literary Award for the best Kajkavian book published in 2018.

His fourth collection, Jezero zmešaneh noči, was published in 2020. His fifth book, Noćni jasmin / Night Jasmine, was published in 2022. The collection received the Krunoslav Sukić recognition for Book of the Year 2021/2022 from the Center for Peace, Nonviolence and Human Rights in Osijek. [ref: Goranu Gatalici priznanje Krunoslav Sukić za knjigu godine 2021./2022., SiB.hr]

Gatalica has received awards in international haiku competitions. The Bashō-an International English Haiku Competition in Japan lists him among its award recipients. [ref: Bashō-an International English Haiku Competition, Koto City Culture and Community Foundation]

In 2023, Gatalica received the Katanogahara Monogatari Award at the fourth Star Haiku Contest in Katano, Japan. The award was reported by Croatian Radiotelevision. [ref: Pjesnik Goran Gatalica osvojio nagradu Katanogahara Monogatari, Hrvatska radiotelevizija]

In 2025, Gatalica received the John Bird Dreaming Award at the third John Bird Dreaming Haiku Competition in Australia. Croatian Radiotelevision reported the award. [ref: Hrvatskom književniku Goranu Gatalici prva nagrada za haiku u Australiji, Hrvatska radiotelevizija]

His sixth poetry collection, Povratak u Getsemani / Returning to Gethsemane, was published by Tonimir in Varaždinske Toplice in 2025. The Croatian National Bibliography records the publication as an 88-page volume. [ref: Hrvatska nacionalna bibliografija: Niz A – knjige, 2025, National and University Library in Zagreb]

The book was selected as one of the finalists for the 2025 Tin Ujević Award of the Croatian Writers' Association. [ref: Izabrano 11 finalista Nagrade Tin Ujević, Društvo hrvatskih književnika] It subsequently received the Duhovno hrašće Award at the Poetry Meetings in Drenovci. [ref: Šlisuriću Povelja Visoka žuta žita, Gatalici Duhovno hrašće, Večernji list]

Gatalica has also worked as an editor of haiku publications. Since 2020 he has edited the Haiku Meridians column in Iris magazine, and since 2021 he has edited the Haiku Circles column and a monthly haiku competition in Lanterna magazine.

data.title: Colonial fascism
data.text:
The colonial fascism is a term used to describe various historical regimes in Haiti, such as the presidency of Louis Borno or the subsequent government of François Duvalier. [ref: The Roots of Haitian Despotism, Lynne Rienner Publishers]

== Development ==
There is significant controversy regarding which political movements and governments in Africa, if any, can be considered fascist. The American historian and political scientist Robert Paxton, a scholar on the subject of fascism, rejects the view that Idi Amin’s government in Uganda was fascist in nature. [ref: Robert O. Paxton, The Anatomy of Fascism, 2004, p. 191] The Coalition for the Defence of the Republic and the larger nascent Hutu Power movement, an ultranationalist and Hutu-supremacist movement that organized and carried out the Rwandan genocide with the aim of exterminating the Tutsi people of Rwanda, has been described as an example of “tropical fascism” in Africa. [ref: Judging war, judging history: behind truth and reconciliation, Stanford University Press] Other examples of colonial fascism are the Brazilian Integralist Action party, Egyptian militarism, [ref: Fascism and Nasserism: Ideological Influence or Alternative Explanations?] [ref: Egypt’s New Constitutional Amendments: Moving toward Totalitarianism, Arab Center Washington DC] [ref: The record of collaboration of King Farouk of Egypt with the Nazis and their ally, the Mufti] and the Integralist movement in Brazil, one of the far-right movements that had the greatest impact in its place of origin. [ref: UN ENSAYO BIBLIOGRÁFICO SOBRE EL INTEGRALISMO BRASILEÑO, Revista Ayer] [ref: EL FASCISMO TROPICAL: LITERATURA Y AÇÃO INTEGRALISTA BRASILEIRA, Revista Ayer]

== See also ==
* Brazilian integralism
* Nazism in the Americas
* Islamofascism

data.title: Ameen Laghari
data.text:
----

= Ameen Laghari =
Ameen Muhammad Laghari (Sindhi:امين لغاري also spelled Amin Laghari/Leghari) is a Sindhi author and researcher [ref: امين لغاري, انسائيڪلوپيڊيا سنڌيانا]. He has served as In-charge secretary of the Sindhi Language Authority an autonomous body under the Government of Sindh and Its deputy director of research and publication. [ref: "Secretories - Sindhi Language Authority", Sindhi Language Authority] [ref: "Introduction to Contributors", Kalachi Research Journal (Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai Chair, University of Karachi)].

== Early life and education ==
Laghari was born on 7 June 1966 in Sanghar, Sindh, Pakistan [ref: "امين لغاري", SindhSalamat Kitab Ghar]. He did his early schooling from primary school of village and completed his matriculation, Intermediate education and BA from high school and Degree College Sanghar. He pursued master's degree in mass communication from University of Sindh in 1991.

== Career ==
In 1992 Laghari joined Sindhi Language Authority (SLA), Statutory body of Government of Sindh as Research Assistant. From 14 March to 23 May 2018, he served as In-charge Secretary of Sindhi Language Authority and again from 9 February to 22 June 2023. [ref: "سيڪريٽري", Sindhi Language Authority]. During his tenure he served under renowned scholars and literary figures including Dr NA Baloch, Dr Ghullam Ali Allana and Ishaq Samejo [ref: Sindhi Language Authority hosts farewell in honour of Deputy Director Amin Leghari, The Nation] [ref: Sindhi Language & Literature at a Glance, Scribd]. As deputy director of Research and Publication he was involved in Research and Publication on Sindhi Language including contributing to authority's Sindhi Boli Research Journal. He also participated in conferences on Sindhi language and its revival [ref: "Sindhi language, Indus Script and Endangered Indigenous languages", UNESCO International Decade of Indigenous Languages 2022–2032] [ref: Sindhi Language, Indus Script and Endangered Indigenous Languages International Conference – Proceedings / Program, sl.sindhila.org]. Laghari retired from Sindhi Language Authority on December 22, 2025 [ref: "Sindhi Language Authority Hosts Farewell In Honour Of Deputy Director Amin Leghari", UrduPoint].

data.title: Jarrett Bell
data.text:
Jarrett Bell is an American sports journalist and NFL columnist for USA Today, where he has worked since 1993. [ref: Staff Profile: Jarrett Bell, USA Today] He is a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame selection committee and a recipient of the Pro Football Writers of America (PFWA) Bill Nunn Jr. Award. [ref: Bill Nunn Memorial Award Winners, Pro Football Hall of Fame]

== Early life and education ==
Bell was raised in Detroit, Michigan. [ref: Jarrett Bell (@[user]) on X, X (formerly Twitter)] During his youth, he worked at Olympia Stadium as an equipment manager for the Detroit Jr. Wings and as an assistant in the Detroit Red Wings public relations department.

He attended Michigan State University, graduating in 1981 with a bachelor's degree in Human Communication. [ref: USA Today Columnist Jarrett Bell On His 30 Years Covering The NFL, KUT Radio] In 1979, he studied abroad at the University of London under The Guardian's Contemporary Mass Media program. [ref: Jarrett Bell, posthillpress.com]

== Career ==
Bell began his journalism career as a staff writer for The Dallas Times Herald. [ref: Sports Journalist Jarrett Bell First Black Man To Receive Bill Nunn Jr. Writer's Award, blackenterprise.com] In 1989, he became the editor of The Dallas Cowboys Weekly. From 1990 to 1992, he covered the San Francisco 49ers for The Marin Independent Journal.

In 1993, Bell joined USA Today as a national NFL columnist, covering league games, business operations, and executive profiles.

From 2013 to 2017, Bell was a contributor for ESPN, appearing as a panelist on NFL Insiders and SportsCenter. [ref: 2020 PFWA Off-Field Award nominees announced, profootballwriters.org] He has also appeared as a commentator on CBS Sports, NBC Sports, CNN, and NFL Network. He was a regular guest on the Baltimore Ravens pregame show on WBAL from 2001 to 2018. [ref: Jarrett Bell: Getting personal with the NFL, iheart.com]

Bell was featured in two documentaries, “The Forgotten Four” and “Minister of Defense: The Reggie White Story.” He also had a cameo role in the movie Invincible.

==Author==
Bell co-wrote Reggie Williams' memoir, Resilient by Nature: Reflections from a Life of Winning On and Off the Football Field, released in 2020, for which he received an Outstanding Book Award from the National Association of Black Journalists.

== Committees and honors ==
Bell has served on the Pro Football Hall of Fame Selection Committee since 1997. [ref: HOF Selection Committee member Jarrett Bell joins the show, Pro Football Hall of Fame YouTube] He was a member of the 26-person Blue Ribbon Panel that selected the NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team and serves on the media panel that selects the Super Bowl MVP. The National Association of Black Journalists honored Bell with a Salute to Excellence Award in 2020.

In 2022, the PFWA awarded Bell the Bill Nunn Jr. Award for long and distinguished career contributions to professional football reporting. [ref: 'I got a story for you': USA TODAY Sports' Jarrett Bell wins prestigious Bill Nunn Jr. Award] [ref: USA Today's Jarrett Bell wins writers' award for service, yahoo.com] He is the first Black journalist to receive the award. He received first-place honors from the Associated Press Sports Editors (APSE) in 2020 and has received multiple writing awards from the National Association of Black Journalists (NABJ).

data.title: Crossley-Kegresse half-track
data.text:
----

The Crossley-Kégresse half-track was an experimental half-track using the Kégresse track tested by the British army in the late 1920s. The production vehicles were produced by Crossley Motors in the United Kingdom and delivered to the army from 1926. The Kégresse track was licensed from Citroën in France, which employed its inventor Adolphe Kégresse.

== Development ==

Kégresse half-tracks were also extensively used by the French army, [ref: ] [ref: ] including the later Citroën P17 and P107 utility half-tracks. [ref: Le grand album des Citroën-Kégresse sous l'uniforme, Histoire & Collections] In 1923, the British army purchased Kégresse half-track vehicles from Citroën for testing, but ultimately decided they were not satisfactory for its purposes and commissioned Crossley Motors to produce a new vehicle using the licensed track from Citroën.

In the British army, the Crossley vehicle could replace horses for haulage work that otherwise only animals could do, one of the first such attempts in the world. The Kégresse track had a two-speed gearbox while the standard gearbox had four speeds, giving a total of eight forward speeds. It was otherwise driven like a truck. It was used as a general service vehicle, a staff car, and an artillery tractor. [ref: ]

== Service history ==

=== Trials and field exercises ===

Test trials began at least as early as October 1924. [ref: ] In February 1925 comparative cross-country and road trials took place in which the Crossley-Kégresse half-track placed first, ahead of the fully tracked Vickers Light Dragon Mark II. By November 1925, it had been found "capable of traversing the most difficult country at a very fair speed" in government trials. [ref: ] In later trials, it proved capable of pulling a heavy QF 4.5-inch howitzer across open country, including through a stream. [ref: ] In 1926, it was demonstrated to the heads of government of the British Dominions at Camberley, equipped to tow a QF 3.7-inch mountain howitzer.

It was among the first vehicles used to equip the British army's interwar Experimental Mechanised Force (EMF), the first mechanised combined arms brigade in the world. At the Force's formation in 1927, the Crossley half-track was used by the machine-gun battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry, [ref: ] and the 9th Field Brigade of the Royal Artillery, allowing these previously non-mechanised infantry and artillery units to manoeuvre alongside the 3rd and 5th battalions of the Royal Tank Corps in a prototype of a modern combined arms mechanised force. Operating with the 'fast group' it maintained a daily average cross-country speed of 10 mph over 30 miles. This was "the first mechanised formation to be born in the world, and was the mother of all 'armoured divisions'".

=== Shanghai deployment ===

Between February and May 1927, tensions arose in China. The EMF's 11 and 80 batteries, armed with QF 18-pounder guns, were re-equipped with Crossley-Kégresse half-tracks and Burford-Kégresse half-tracks, replacing their fully tracked Vickers Light Dragon Mark IIs, and shipped to China as part of the Shanghai Defence Force. This Force was withdrawn in January 1928. In 1928 and 1929, the remaining Vickers Light Dragon Mark IIs towing artillery in the EMF in the UK were also replaced with Burford- and Crossley-Kégresse half tracks.

== Legacy ==

In 1927, the British War Office ordered a related Crossley vehicle in which drive wheels could be fitted with chain tracks, intended to reproduce the functionality of the Crossley-Kégresse vehicle in a more flexible format. [ref: ] The half-track Crossley-Kégresse left British army consideration in the early 1930s, as part of a general shift away from half-tracks to fully tracked vehicles by the army.

At least two examples of the half-track have survived and been preserved, one by the Norfolk Tank Museum and another by the British army's Royal Logistics Corps Museum, both in the United Kingdom. Official Ministry of Supply photographs of the vehicle are held in the collections of the Imperial War Museum. [ref: ]

== References ==

* Moving the Guns: The Mechanisation of the Royal Artillery, 1854-1939, HMSO
* British Military Transport, 1829–1956, HMSO
* Men, Ideas and Tanks: British Military Thought and Armoured Forces, 1903–39, Manchester University Press
* The Tanks: The History of the Royal Tank Regiment and its Predecessors Heavy Branch Machine-Gun Corps Tank Corps & Royal Tank Corps 1914–1945 (1914–1939), Praeger

data.title: Enzo Cacciola
data.text:
----

Enzo Cacciola (born 12 December 1945) is an Italian artist associated with Analytical Painting. Since the 1970s, his work has incorporated industrial materials including cement and asbestos, later extending to materials such as Multigum and denim. [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia processo e provocazione, Il Giornale dell'Arte] He participated in the international exhibition Analytische Malerei in Düsseldorf in 1975 and in documenta 6 in Kassel in 1977. [ref: Angela Madesani, curator, The Golden Nightingale. Ricostruzione di una mostra, Progettoarte-Elm, Milan, 10 May–29 June 2018, reconstructing Palma Bucarelli's project for the third Golden Nightingale prize in Platres, Cyprus, in 1973, https://www.progettoarte-elm.com/eng/exhibitions/the-golden-nightingale-ricostruzione-di-una-mostra (accessed 14 July 2026); Klaus Honnef and Catherine Millet, Analytische Malerei (Genoa: Edizioni Masnata/La Bertesca, 1975); documenta, documenta 6, 24 June–2 October 1977, https://documenta.de/en/retrospective/documenta-6 (accessed 14 July 2026).]

== Life and career ==
Cacciola held his first solo exhibition at Galleria La Bertesca in Genoa in 1971. In 1973, Palma Bucarelli included him with Paolo Cotani, Marco Gastini, Carmengloria Morales and Gianfranco Zappettini in her project for the third Golden Nightingale prize in Platres, Cyprus. [ref: Gli analitici di Palma, Il Gionale delle Arte]

In 1975, Cacciola participated in Analytische Malerei in Düsseldorf, curated by Klaus Honnef and Catherine Millet. Two years later, he took part in documenta 6 in Kassel. [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia processo e provocazione, Il Giornale dell'Arte]

Cacciola has also been active in local government in Rocca Grimalda. He served as mayor from 1995 to 2004, returned to the office in 2020, and was elected again in May 2026. [ref: Le elezioni comunali nei paesi dell’Alessandrino: tutti i sindaci eletti, La Stampa] [ref: Comune di Rocca Grimalda, www.comune.roccagrimalda.al.it]

== Work ==

=== Early geometric and analytical work ===

During the late 1960s and early 1970s, Cacciola developed geometric-concrete works incorporating elements such as neon. His attention to the division of pictorial space led to multipart works in which the wall behind the individual elements formed part of the composition. In the Superfici integrative of the early 1970s, the work therefore depended on its surrounding architectural context. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 9–10; Corà, Uncini Cacciola, 9–10.]

Cacciola's work developed within the Italian current of Analytical Painting, whose practitioners examined painting through its material and structural components rather than through representation. His particular focus was the relationship between the support, the physical surface, the materials used and the sequence of operations through which the work was made. [ref: Meneguzzo, Pittura Analitica. I percorsi italiani 1970–1980; Giorgio Bonomi et al., Pensare Pittura. Una linea internazionale di ricerca negli anni '70 (Cinisello Balsamo: Silvana Editoriale, 2009).] In the Asbesti works of 1974, he combined asbestos-containing mixtures with a restricted range of muted pigments. [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia, processo e provocazione - Il Giornale dell'Arte, Il Giornale dell'Arte] From 1975, he applied unpigmented cement directly to canvas, with the resulting layers and drips retaining visible traces of the working process. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 12.]

In his text Processo operativo (1975), Cacciola described the materials, manual procedures, and working times involved in producing his cement paintings, treating the process itself as a constituent element of the work. [ref: Corà, Uncini Cacciola, 9–11; Salvatore Russo, "Enzo Cacciola Interviewed," Art International Contemporary Magazine, no. 3 (May–June 2022): 14.]

Photography became integral to this process. Cacciola photographed successive stages in the application of cement and displayed the resulting sequences as components of the work itself. He later extended the combination of photography and painting to the site-related cycles begun in 1979. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 16–17.]

In a diary entry published in KUNSTFORUM International in 1975, Klaus Honnef wrote that, despite his initially ambivalent response to Cacciola's work, the artist's method corresponded closely to the principles Honnef had formulated for Analytical Painting. [ref: Klaus Honnef, "Tagebuch," KUNSTFORUM International 14, no. 3 (1975): 168; reproduced and translated in Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 13–14.]

At documenta 6, Cacciola delegated the selection of the work shown in his allotted space to Honnef and Weiss. The curators chose a sixteenth-century Venetian Venus attributed to Titian's workshop from the Wallraf-Richartz-Museum in Cologne. It was accompanied by Cacciola's Processo operativo, which explained the transfer of the artist's decision-making role to the curators. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 14–15; documenta 6, vol. 1, 58.]

In the early 1980s, Cacciola temporarily turned to figurative painting; works from this period were included in Achille Bonito Oliva's Pittura in radice in 1981. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 18–20; Bonito Oliva, Pittura in radice.]

=== Site-related work ===

Beginning with a cycle produced on Taboga Island, Panama, in 1979, Cacciola also developed a site-related practice outside the studio. The method involved gathering materials locally, preparing and applying them by hand to unstretched canvas, allowing the works to dry and documenting the process photographically. [ref: Andrea Daffra, "Un punto di vista geografico sull'opera pittorica di Enzo Cacciola," in Enzo Cacciola: I colori della terra / Los colores de la tierra (Genoa: De Ferrari Editore, 2024), 21.]

In July 1980, he exhibited 36 horas de pintura en San Giacomo at the Foro Cultural Contreras FONAPAS in Mexico City. The installation comprised thirty-six cement paintings produced during a continuous thirty-six-hour working session, accompanied by a photographic sequence documenting the process. [ref: Andrea Daffra, "Il segno della materia. L'opera come testimonianza storica," in Daffra and Valenti, eds., Enzo Cacciola. Paesaggi di pittura, 37–42; Daffra, "Un punto di vista geografico," 21–22.]

In 2017, Cacciola produced a group of unstretched paintings at the Bay of Pigs in Cuba using white Nanodur cement and locally sourced materials. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 25; Daffra, "Il segno della materia," 45–46, note 52.]

During a working stay at Estancia El Milagro in La Candelaria, Salta Province, in 2022, he collected locally occurring rocks and mineral material, ground them into coloured particles and applied them to canvas. The resulting works were shown at the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Salta in Los colores de la tierra in February 2024. [ref: Daniele Crippa, "Cacciola è ora in Argentina," in Andrea Daffra, Enzo Cacciola: I colori della terra / Los colores de la tierra (Genoa: De Ferrari Editore, 2024), 9-13; Gobierno de la Provincia de Salta, "Segui disfrutando Vacaciones en Cultura."]

=== Later industrial materials ===
Around 2000, Cacciola developed the Multigum series, [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia, processo e provocazione - Il Giornale dell'Arte, www.ilgiornaledellarte.com/Articolo/-Enzo-Cacciola-tra-materia-processo-e-provocazione] [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia, processo e provocazione - Il Giornale dell'Arte, www.ilgiornaledellarte.com/Articolo/-Enzo-Cacciola-tra-materia-processo-e-provocazione] combining canvas, vinyl resin, threaded rods and bolts. In later works he also introduced denim as a support, using it with both cement and other industrial materials. [ref: Russo, "Enzo Cacciola Interviewed," 15.] [ref: Enzo Cacciola: Structura (Soresina: DAV - Dipartimento Arti Visive, 2024), discussion of the Cementi bianchi su jeans; Casamonti, Centurione Scotto Boschieri and Bignotti, eds., Arte Jeans, 12; Bruno Corà, ed., Uncini Cacciola. Strutture e superfici del cemento (Pietrasanta: Edizioni Armanda Gori Arte, 2023), 10-11.]These works extended his longstanding use of unconventional industrial materials within painting.

== Selected exhibitions ==
1971 - Enzo Cacciola, Galleria La Bertesca, Genoa (first solo exhibition). [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 9.]

1973 - The Golden Nightingale, third edition, Platres, Cyprus; project selected by Palma Bucarelli. [ref: Madesani, The Golden Nightingale. Ricostruzione di una mostra.] [ref: Gli analitici di Palma - Il Giornale dell'Arte, Il Giornale dell'Arte]

1975 - Analytische Malerei, Düsseldorf, curated by Klaus Honnef and Catherine Millet. [ref: Honnef and Millet, Analytische Malerei.]

1977 - documenta 6, Kassel. [ref: documenta, documenta 6; documenta 6, vol. 1, 58.]

1980 - 36 horas de pintura en San Giacomo, Foro Cultural Contreras FONAPAS, Mexico City. [ref: Daffra, "Il segno della materia," 37–42.]

1981 - Pittura in radice, Galleria Forma, Genoa, curated by Achille Bonito Oliva. [ref: Bonito Oliva, Pittura in radice.]

2024 - Los colores de la tierra, Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Salta, Argentina. [ref: Gobierno de la Provincia de Salta, "Segui disfrutando Vacaciones en Cultura."]

== Public collections ==
Works by Cacciola are held in the permanent collection of the Museo d'Arte Contemporanea di Villa Croce in Genoa. [ref: Make it new! Tomas Rajlich e l’arte astratta in Italia, Genova Smart]

== Further reading ==
documenta 6. Vol. 1: Malerei, Plastik/Environment, Performance. Kassel, 1977.

Bonito Oliva, Achille. Pittura in radice. Milan: Uni Editrice, 1981.

Corà, Bruno, ed. Uncini Cacciola. Strutture e superfici del cemento. Pietrasanta: Edizioni Armanda Gori Arte, 2023.

Bonomi, Giorgio, Claudio Cerritelli, Marco Meneguzzo, Alberto Rigoni, Franco Sborgi and Sandra Solimano. Pensare Pittura. Una linea internazionale di ricerca negli anni '70. Cinisello Balsamo: Silvana Editoriale, 2009.

Meneguzzo, Marco. Pittura Analitica. I percorsi italiani 1970–1980. Cinisello Balsamo: Silvana Editoriale, 2007.

Fiz, Alberto. Enzo Cacciola: Works 1970–2015. Cinisello Balsamo: Silvana Editoriale, 2015.

Daffra, Andrea, and Paola Valenti, eds. Enzo Cacciola. Paesaggi di pittura. Panama - Città del Messico - Cuba. Genoa: De Ferrari Editore, 2022.

Daffra, Andrea. Enzo Cacciola: I colori della terra / Los colores de la tierra. Genoa: De Ferrari Editore, 2024.

data.title: Oil and Gas Free Zones Authority
data.text:
Oil and Gas Free Zones Authority (OGFZA) is the federal government of Nigeria agency responsible for the regulation of oil and gas free zones. It was established in 1996 under the Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act. The Act designated the Onne/Ikpokiri area of Rivers State as an oil and gas export free zone. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

== History ==

The Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act was enacted on 29 March 1996. The Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Authority to operate and manage Onne Oil and Gas Frr Zone. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

== Regulatory jurisdiction ==

Regulators and free-zone operators are at odds over the geographic and sectoral scope of OGFZA's mission.

A media analysis in The Guardian Newspaper suggested the debate centered on ambiguities and overlaps between the OGFZA and NEPZA laws. It further mentioned that instead of combining OGFZA with NEPZA, the federal government had kept it as a distinct organization in response to a previous public-sector reform initiative. [ref: OGFZA and NEPZA bills: Matters arising, The Guardian]

In subsequent years, the two free-zone regulators' disagreement persisted. Punch revealed in 2021 that a Senate committee had criticized the ongoing disputes between NEPZA and OGFZA and demanded changes to their enabling legislation to make their different roles more clear. [ref: NEPZA, OGEFZA crisis, an economic sabotage, says NASS, Punch]

== Disputes involving free-zone operators ==

In the oil and gas free-zone system, OGFZA has also been involved in regulatory issues with operators.

An audit of Intels Nigeria Limited's operations from 2006 to 2016 was mandated by OGFZA in 2017. The authority claimed violations of free-zone rules, according to The Guardian Newspaper. The claims were refuted by Intels. [ref: Fresh trouble for Atiku's INTELS as OGFZA alleges rules' violation, The Guardian]

Intels later vowed to sue the authority, according to Punch Newspaper. The company contested a number of issues, including the renewal of its operating license, OGFZA charges, and regulatory rulings pertaining to foreign employees employed by businesses in the One Free Zone. [ref: Intels threatens to sue OGFZA over malicious allegations, Punch]

Following OGFZA's revocation of operating licenses, the case subsequently entailed immigration action against foreign workers of Intels and a number of related businesses. [ref: FG revokes residence permits of expatriates in Atiku, others' firms, Punch]

== Petroleum-sector regulatory overlap ==

Nigeria's post-2021 petroleum regulatory framework has also raised concerns about OGFZA's jurisdiction.

A jurisdictional dispute between OGFZA and the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority was resolved in June 2026 by the Senate Committee on the Downstream Petroleum Sector. According to Punch, the committee was looking for a framework to address statutory obligations that overlap between the two bodies. [ref: Senate promises to end conflict between petroleum sector regulatory agencies, Punch]

The disagreement centered on whether the regulatory framework run by petroleum-sector organizations or the free-zone laws of OGFZA applied to operations conducted within oil and gas free zones. [ref: Senate promises to end conflict between petroleum sector regulatory agencies, Punch]

== Functions ==

The authority is tasked with overseeing the designated export free zone and managing authorized businesses within it under the Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act. Its statutory powers include approving firms, issuing licences, enacting regulations and managing provisions governing the movement of commodities and allowed activities within the free zone. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

Additionally, the Act permits the authority to assume duties previously carried out by NEPZA in relation to the export of gas and oil from Nigerian export processing zones. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

== Free Zones Under OGFZA ==

# Onne Oil and Gas Free Zone, Rivers State
# Warri Oil and Gas Free Zone, Delta State
# Notore Industrial City, Rivers State
# Eko Support Services Free Zone, Lagos State
# Liberty Oil and Gas Free Zone, Akwa Ibom State
# Brass Oil and Gas City, Bayelsa State
# BESTAF Industrial Free Zone, Lagos State
# Secured Bunkering Anchorage Free Zone, Lagos State
# Orashi Special Energy Free Zone, Imo State
# Dangote Industries Free Zone, Lagos State

The Onne/Ikpokiri area in Rivers State was the free zone specifically designated by the 1996 Act. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

The zone grew out of the logistics and services related to oil and gas operations at Onne Port. Its management served as the foundation for OGFZA's subsequent attempts to exert regulatory authority over additional Nigerian free zones connected to oil and gas. [ref: 20 Years After, NEPZA to Hands off Oil and Gas Free Zones, ThisDay]

data.title: Eleanor Sillerico
data.text:
Eleanor Sillerico Mayta, known professionally in the United States as Eleanor Sillerico, is a Bolivian-American civil engineer and tunnel construction manager [ref: Meet Eleanor Sillerico: A Global Career in Tunneling Engineering, smetnet.org] who worked on the construction of the Elizabeth Line railway in London, [ref: Elizabeth Line Innovations: Moving the Industry Forward, mottmac.com] United Kingdom and the Metro Purple Line extension in Los Angeles, California. [ref: "'Construction of Tunnels Means Sacrifice': Meet Eleanor Sillerico, Civil Engineer and Construction Manager", RT&S newspaper] Sillerico has also worked on tunneling projects in Bolivia, Spain and Georgia. [ref: Latinos en Metro: Para la ingeniera Eleanor Sillerico, cada tunel es un desafio fascinante, Hispanic LA newspaper] [ref: Eleanor Sillerico - Why I Build Beneath, UCA Underground Construction Association] Her most recent tunneling project is the Hudson River Tunnel Project connecting New Jersey and New York City. [ref: Premio Ing. Walter Gonzalez incentiva la excelencia académica, El Diario newspaper] [ref: Premio Ing. Walter Gonzalez incentiva la excelencia académica, El Diario newspaper]

==Early Life and Education==
Sillerico was born in La Paz, Bolivia in 1978. Her father is a civil engineer. [ref: Latinos en Metro: Para la ingeniera Eleanor Sillerico, cada tunel es un desafio fascinante, Hispanic LA newspaper] Her brother Rodrigo Sillerico Mayta is a violinist and conductor of the Bolivia Clasica orchestra and an associate of the concert pianist Ana-Maria Vera.

Sillerico attended high school at, and graduated from, Unidad Educativa Parroquial San Jose, a Roman Catholic high school sponsored by the Oblates of St. Joseph religious order, located in the Villa Victoria working class neighborhood of the Max Paredes macro district of the city of La Paz. [ref: Premio Ing. Walter Gonzalez incentiva la excelencia académica, El Diario newspaper] She received her degree as a civil engineer from the Higher University of San Andrés (Universidad Mayor de San Andres) in La Paz, Bolivia in 2002. Sillerico won the 2002 Premio Ing. Walter Gonzalez for academic excellence at the UMSA university in La Paz, Bolivia. [ref: Premio Walter Gonzalez: la Excelencia Académica de Ingenieria Civil, La Razon] [ref: Premio Ing. Walter Gonzalez incentiva la excelencia académica, El Diario newspaper] She completed advanced studies at the Centro de Estudios y Experimentacion de Obras Publicas (CEDEX) and the Technical University of Madrid (UPM), earning master's degrees in geotechnics and tunneling engineering. [ref: Eleanor Sillerico Mayta, InfluentialWomen.com]

data.title: Pavel Florjančič
data.text:
Pavel Florjančič (born 11 August 1947) is a Slovenian painter known primarily for his work in realism, photorealism, and hyperrealism. His work is particularly associated with still-life painting, with an emphasis on light, reflections, and the material qualities of depicted objects. [ref: Pavel Florjančič »V iskanju univerzalne lepote«, Sokolski dom Škofja Loka] [ref: Pavel Florjančič, Loški muzej Škofja Loka]

== Early life and education ==
Florjančič was born on 11 August 1947 in Virlog near Škofja Loka, Slovenia. From 1962 to 1966, he attended the School of Design in Ljubljana, where he studied applied graphic design. He later continued his education at the Department of Art Education of the Pedagogical Academy in Ljubljana.

Between 1970 and 1975, he worked as an art teacher at an elementary school in Škofja Loka. In 1975, he obtained the status of an independent cultural worker as a painter, and in 1977 he received a state scholarship for further artistic training in Paris.

In 1979, together with artists including Franc Berčič - Berko, Herman Gvardjančič, Franc Novinc and Ive Šubic, he became one of the founding members of the Association of Artists of Škofja Loka (Združenje umetnikov Škofja Loka, ZUŠL). [ref: Zgodovina ZUŠL, Združenje umetnikov Škofja Loka]

From 1986 onward, he collaborated with galleries in Munich and later exhibited elsewhere in Europe and in the United States. He lives and works in Škofja Loka.

== Artistic work ==
Florjančič's painting is based on close observation of the physical world and a highly detailed realist painting technique. Still lifes form a central part of his body of work. Recurring motifs include glass, fruit, flowers, bottles, drinking glasses, musical instruments and other everyday objects.

Light is an important element in his work. Art historian and critic Damir Globočnik, writing in connection with the exhibition V iskanju univerzalne lepote ("In Search of Universal Beauty"), highlighted Florjančič's treatment of light, reflections on glass surfaces and the realistic depiction of the material qualities of objects.

In 2007, art historian Boštjan Soklič wrote about Florjančič's work in the journal Loški razgledi on the occasion of the artist's 60th birthday. [ref: Razstava Pavla Florjančiča ob umetnikovi 60. letnici, Loški razgledi]

== Exhibitions ==
Since the 1970s, Florjančič has participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions in Slovenia and abroad. His solo exhibitions have included presentations at the Ivan Grohar Gallery in Škofja Loka, galleries in Linz and Vienna, an exhibition in New York in 2016, and an exhibition at the Šivec House Gallery in Radovljica in 2019.

In 2007, the Ivan Grohar Gallery in Škofja Loka organised an exhibition marking his 60th birthday. The exhibition and his work were also covered by the Slovenian newspaper Gorenjski glas. [ref: Tihožitja, ki so živa, Gorenjski glas]

In 2020, his exhibition V iskanju univerzalne lepote was presented at the Sokolski dom Gallery in Škofja Loka.

== Awards and recognition ==
In 2020, the Association of Artists of Škofja Loka, with the support of the Municipality of Škofja Loka, awarded Florjančič the Grohar Award for his lifetime artistic achievement and his contribution to the association.

data.title: Rachel Pepper
data.text:
----

Rachel Ann Pepper is a Judge at the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales, Australia. She was appointed to the Court in 2009. [ref: Judicial officers and decision makers, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

== Early life and education ==
Rachel Pepper was born in Canada and immigrated to Australia in the early 1980s. She completed her secondary education at Swanbourne Senior High School in Perth, Western Australia, graduating in 1984. [ref: SWEARING IN CEREMONY OF RACHEL ANN PEPPER AS A JUSTICE OF THE LAND AND ENVIRONMENT COURT OF NEW SOUTH WALES, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

She graduated from the Australian National University with a Bachelor of Arts, majoring in French, in 1992 and a Bachelor of Laws with First Class Honours in 1994. [ref: Judicial speeches and papers, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

== Legal career ==
Pepper practised as a solicitor with Allen Allen & Hemsley in 1995. In 1996, she served as associate to Justice Michael McHugh in the High Court of Australia. [ref: ANU]

She was called to the New South Wales Bar in 1997, reading with John Marshall and Justin Gleeson. She practised as a barrister at 7 Wentworth Chambers and 12 Wentworth Selborne Chambers until her appointment to the Court in 2009. [ref: LEC Swearing in ceremony]

Between January 2017 and April 2018, Pepper served as Chair of the Scientific Inquiry into Hydraulic Fracturing of Onshore Unconventional Gas Reservoirs and Associated Activities in the Northern Territory. [ref: Home, Northern Territory Government]

In 2021, she was made a fellow of the Australian Academy of Law. [ref: Rachel Pepper, Australian Academy of Law]

== Professional activities ==
Pepper serves on the editorial board of the Australian Journal of Administrative Law and is the Environment Section Editor of the Australian Law Journal. [ref: Environmental Law, The Australian Law Journal]

From 2009 to 2018, she was a Co-Consulting Editor of the Australian Environment Review published by LexisNexis. [ref: Co-consulting Editors, Australian Environment Review]

She has served on the committee of the Australian Institute of Administrative Law and was its President. [ref: National Executive, Australian Institute of Administrative Law] She is also a member of the Ngara Yura Committee of the Judicial Commission of NSW [ref: Ngara Yura Committee members, Judicial Commission of New South Wales] and a judicial member of Football Australia. [ref: Constitution, Football Australia]

Pepper served as Secretary of the Australian Association of Constitutional Law from 2013 to 2017 and as Vice President from 2017 to 2018. [ref: UNSW]

She was elected to the NSW Bar Council in 2000 and served until her appointment to the bench in 2009, including as Secretary from 2005 to 2009. [ref: ANU alumnae trailblazers in law: an intimate discussion, Australian National University]

From 2019 to 2023, Pepper was a board member of Twenty10. She also served as Vice President of ACON from 2001 to 2003. [ref: ACON Annual Report 2001/2002]

Pepper has authored and edited books, journal articles, book chapters and other publications in the fields of environment, administrative, constitutional, criminal and discrimination law [ref: Thomson Reuters]. She has also participated in the teaching and training of judges from overseas in environmental law and environmental dispute resolution through programs supported by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Asian Development Bank. [ref: 2022 IUCN Academy of Environmental Law Colloquium]

== Academic appointments ==

Pepper is an Adjunct Professor at the University of Sydney Law School [ref: University of Sydney Law School].

She has been a judicial fellow and visiting scholar at the Australian National University College of Law [ref: ANU Law School] and Melbourne University Law School [ref: Melbourne University Law School]. She has also taught law courses at the University of New South Wales, the University of Technology Sydney and the University of Sydney. [ref: University of Sydney Law School]
