data.title: Sema Kiliçkaya
data.text:
----

Sema Kılıçkaya (also written Sema Kiliçkaya or Sema Kilickaya), born on 31 January 1968 in Antakya (formerly Antioch), Turkey, is a French novelist, translator, and teacher of Turkish origin.

Writing in French from what she calls an "in-between-three" position between Turkish, Arabic, and French, Kılıçkaya draws on an identity shaped by the Turkish–Syrian borderlands and the Antakya region. Her novels explore exile, the relationship to one's mother tongue, and the transmission of migration memory. She received the Prix Seligmann against racism in 2014, awarded at the Sorbonne, for Le Royaume sans racines and the France-Turquie Literary Prize in 2018 for La Langue de personne.

== Biography ==

=== Early life ===

Sema Kılıçkaya was born on 31 January 1968 in Antakya (the ancient Antioch), in the southeastern Turkish province of Hatay, near the Syrian border. According to a 2024 interview with the French research outlet Observatoire de la Turquie Contemporaine, she grew up in a household that was both Turkish-speaking and Arabic-speaking, reflecting the multicultural character of the Antakya region. In 1972, at the age of four, she emigrated to France with her parents as part of the Turkish economic migration of the Trente Glorieuses. The family settled in the Haute-Marne department in eastern France.

=== Literary career ===

Her first book, Anadolu. Contes, récits et anecdotes de Turquie (2004, Publisud), a collection devoted to the oral heritage of Anatolia, received extensive coverage in the Turkish national daily Hürriyet when it was released.

Her first novel, Le Chant des tourterelles (The Song of the Turtle Doves, 2009, L'Arganier), spans three generations of women and traces the fate of a Turkish family between Syria and Turkey. It was shortlisted for the Prix Senghor first-novel prize in 2009.

Le Royaume sans racines (The Kingdom Without Roots, 2013, In Octavo), drawing on her observation of a Turkish community transplanted to Haute-Marne, earned her the Prix Seligmann against racism in 2014. The distinction, awarded by the Chancellery of the Universities of Paris, was covered as a major event in the French-Turkish press by Hürriyet (which ran a front-page report and a follow-up piece on the Sorbonne ceremony of 5 February 2015) and by edebiyathaber.net.

Quatre-Vingt-Dix-Sept (Ninety-Seven, 2015, In Octavo) is a political family novel centred on Alèv, a young Alevi woman, and the memory of the 1937–38 Dersim events as transmitted to later generations.

La Langue de personne (Nobody's Language, 2018, Emmanuelle Colas) is set in a family of Turkish origin in eastern France in the aftermath of the Charlie Hebdo attacks. It won the 2018 France-Turquie Literary Prize. It was the subject of a scholarly critical reading in the peer-reviewed academic journal Hommes & Migrations, published by the French National Museum of the History of Immigration, and of an extended literary essay on Kedistan.

== Reception ==

The academic journal Hommes & Migrations has read Kılıçkaya's work as a fictional exploration of the "invisibilised stories" of working-class migrant families in rural France, arguing that her novels stage language itself as the central object of migration — both wound and shelter — and that her writing constitutes "an ethical inquiry into the possibility of a shared idiom."

The Turkish daily Hürriyet, reporting on the Sorbonne ceremony of 5 February 2015, described Le Royaume sans racines as a novel that "brings to French readers a face of Turkey that remains invisible in dominant narratives" and framed the Prix Seligmann as a rare recognition of a Turkish-born author writing in French about the migrant condition. An earlier Hürriyet report on the announcement of the same prize characterised the distinction as "a major recognition from France for a Turkish writer."

The Turkish literary outlet edebiyathaber.net devoted an essay to the paradox of Kılıçkaya's reception, noting that her prize-winning novel had, at the time, no Turkish edition and remained unknown to Turkish-language readers despite its critical success in France.

The online magazine Kedistan described La Langue de personne as "a language novel" in which the search for a shared idiom becomes an ethical and political question, and situated it within a broader French-Turkish literary field concerned with post-migratory identity.

The Observatoire de la Turquie Contemporaine, in a 2024 interview-portrait, presented her body of work as one of the most sustained French literary meditations on the memory of Turkish rural migration to Europe and on the specifically Anatolian, Turkish–Arabic-speaking origins of the diasporic experience.

Her novels have also been featured on national radio: RFI devoted an episode of its summer series Littérature sans frontières – Une terre, une auteure to her work and to the biographical trajectory that informs it.

== Bibliography ==

=== Novels ===

* Le Chant des tourterelles, Paris, L'Arganier, 2009; reprinted by In Octavo — shortlist Prix Senghor 2009
* Le Royaume sans racines, Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule, In Octavo, 2013 (reprinted 2018) — Prix Seligmann 2014
* Quatre-Vingt-Dix-Sept, In Octavo, 2015
* La Langue de personne, Paris, Emmanuelle Colas, 2018; paperback: J'ai lu, 2018 — France-Turquie Literary Prize 2018
* Les Pluies sauvages, Le Pythagore, 2020
* L'Affaire Benjamin S., 2023

=== Other works ===

* Anadolu. Contes, récits et anecdotes de Turquie, Paris, Publisud, 2004
* Drôles d'oiseaux, short story in Une enfance turque, Bleu autour, 2016
* 25 Thématiques d'anglais contemporain, textbook, 2018
* Preface to Leila Salhi, Comprendre les Turcs – Guide de voyage interculturel, 2019

== Awards and honours ==

* 2009 — Shortlist, Prix Senghor, for Le Chant des tourterelles.
* 2014 — Prix Seligmann against racism, injustice and intolerance, awarded by the Chancellerie des universités de Paris, for Le Royaume sans racines. Ceremony held at the Sorbonne on 5 February 2015.
* 2018 — France-Turquie Literary Prize, for La Langue de personne.

data.title: Shaz Saleem
data.text:
= Shaz Saleem =
Shaz Saleem (also known as Shazada Saleem) is a British community activist, charity founder and former Conservative Party politician. He served as a councillor for Kingswinford North and Wall Heath on Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council from 2021 and was appointed cabinet member for highways and public realm in May 2022.[1][2] [ref: ]

Saleem founded The Saleem Foundation, a charitable organisation registered in 2019 that supports individuals and community groups across Birmingham and the Black Country.[3][4] His community activities have included charitable fundraising, youth engagement, mental health awareness and environmental projects. [ref: ]

== Background ==
Saleem has longstanding connections with Kingswinford and the Dudley borough in the West Midlands. [ref: ]

Before entering local government, he was involved in the private hire and taxi industry and community organisations. [ref: ]

In a March 2026 interview with the University of Derby's StoryHub, Saleem described his grandfather as an important influence on his involvement in charitable activities. His grandfather died in 2016, and Saleem subsequently established a foundation in his memory.[4] [ref: ]

== Political career ==

=== Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council ===
Saleem was elected as a Conservative councillor for Kingswinford North and Wall Heath in the 2021 local elections.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

In May 2022, he was appointed cabinet member for highways and public realm on Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council. His responsibilities included matters relating to highways and public spaces within the borough.[1] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

In February 2023, Saleem was suspended from the Conservative Party and resigned from his cabinet position. He subsequently served as an independent councillor.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

=== Legal proceedings ===
In March 2025, Saleem appeared at Walsall Magistrates' Court charged with two offences relating to allegedly threatening or offensive voicemail messages sent in June 2023. [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

Saleem denied both charges. On 6 March 2025, District Judge Michael Wheeler found him not guilty.[6] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

=== Return to the Conservative Party ===
In February 2026, the Express & Star reported that Saleem had rejoined the Conservative Party. He stated that he intended to support Conservative candidates in the 2026 local elections rather than stand as a candidate himself.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

== Charitable activities ==

=== The Saleem Foundation ===
Saleem founded The Saleem Foundation in 2019 in memory of his grandfather, who died in 2016.[4] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

The foundation was registered with the Charity Commission for England and Wales on 29 April 2019 under charity number 1183167.[3] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

According to its registered charitable objectives, the foundation supports charities, voluntary organisations and disadvantaged individuals across Birmingham and the Black Country. Its activities include assistance relating to health, disability, financial hardship, age and other circumstances affecting personal welfare.[3] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

In a March 2026 interview with StoryHub Derby, Saleem described the foundation's involvement in food distribution, mental health awareness campaigns, charitable fundraising and community activities.[4] [ref: ]

=== Community projects ===
Saleem has been associated with a number of community initiatives, including activities aimed at reducing loneliness, engaging young people and improving local environments. [ref: ]

These include The Saleem Foundation's Cuppa Club, established to provide opportunities for social interaction, particularly among older residents experiencing isolation.[4] [ref: ]

Other activities have included litter-picking initiatives, food assistance and awareness campaigns concerning mental health and domestic abuse.[4] [ref: ]

=== Fundraising ===
Saleem has participated in charitable fundraising activities, including boxing events. [ref: Councillor hoping to deliver a knockout for Mayor’s charities, Dudley Council News]

In March 2022, Dudley Council publicised his participation in a charity boxing event at Kingswinford School in support of PAPYRUS Prevention of Young Suicide and the Mayor of Dudley's charities.[7] [ref: Councillor hoping to deliver a knockout for Mayor’s charities, Dudley Council News]

In March 2026, Dudley Council announced a further charity boxing event involving Saleem and council leader Patrick Harley, scheduled for August 2026 at Dudley Town Hall. [ref: Charity boxing showdown raises almost £28K, Dudley Council News]

The event took place on 21 August 2026. On 27 August, Dudley Council reported that it had raised £27,685 for charitable causes, with further income from ticket sales still to be confirmed.[8] [ref: Charity boxing showdown raises almost £28K, Dudley Council News]

The proceeds were intended to benefit charities supported by the Mayor of Dudley and the former mayor, with an additional donation allocated to Birmingham Children's Hospital.[8] [ref: Charity boxing showdown raises almost £28K, Dudley Council News]

== Awards and recognition ==
Saleem received a High Sheriff Award in 2025 in recognition of his community activities, as reported by the Express & Star in February 2026.[2] [ref: Former Dudley councillor and community activist returns to the Tories, Express and Star]

His voluntary work has included involvement in charitable fundraising, activities addressing social isolation and local community projects.[4] [ref: Former Dudley councillor and community activist returns to the Tories, Express and Star]

data.title: StarTree
data.text:
[https://startree.ai/ StarTree] is a company that offers a managed real-time analytics platform based on Apache Pinot.

StarTree was founded in 2019 by Kishore Gopalkrishna [ref: Announcing StarTree, www.linkedin.com] and Xiang Fu who were the original creators of Apache Pinot. StarTree is headquartered in Mountain View, California, and has received funding from Bain Capital, CRV, GGV and Sapphire Ventures. [ref: Leading Real-time Analytics Through Innovation, StarTree]

StarTree adds additional capabilities to Apache Pinot including improved management tools, scalable upserts, and the ability to connect to external Iceberg or Delta Lake tables [ref: ]. StarTree is available as a fully managed service or can be deployed on private cloud infrastructure.

Common use-cases include serving customer-facing applications, observability systems, and real-time metrics. StarTree is used by companies including Grab [ref: Grab’s Real-Time Metrics for Marketplace Observability Insights, Efficiently Connected], Life360, Together.ai, and Razorpay [ref: User Stories, StarTree]

data.title: Hojat Amani
data.text:
Hojat Amani (Persian: حجت امانی; born 30 July 1978) is an Iranian contemporary artist, researcher, and educator. His artistic practice encompasses painting, photography, digital imagery, installation, and Persian calligraphy. His work draws on Persian miniature painting, Qajar-era visual culture, Persian poetry, and Islamic artistic traditions, reinterpreting historical imagery through contemporary visual forms. [ref: Hojat Amani, Fallen angels, from the series Angels in Paradise, 2012, Los Angeles County Museum of Art] [ref: Between Tradition and Modernity, Haleh Gallery] In February 2017, the Iranian newspaper Shargh reported his appointment as acting head of the Saba Cultural and Artistic Institute, affiliated with the Iranian Academy of Arts. [ref: حجت امانی سرپرست مؤسسه صبا شد, Shargh]

== Life and education ==

Amani was born in Lorestan, Iran, in 1978, according to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. He studied painting at the University of Art in Isfahan and later pursued graduate studies in art. Haleh Gallery's biographical account lists a bachelor's degree completed in 2004 and a master's degree in fine arts completed in 2008.

According to his professional curriculum vitae, Amani holds a PhD in comparative and analytical art history, with a focus on the Middle East, a master's degree in art research, and a bachelor's degree in painting. His studies also included fine art and Persian calligraphy.

Amani's research and artistic practice focus on Persian calligraphy, Islamic aesthetics, traditional Iranian painting, and the relationship between historical visual traditions and contemporary art.

== Career ==

Amani has worked as an artist, researcher, and educator. His professional curriculum vitae lists academic appointments at Tarbiat Modares University in Tehran and Isfahan University of Arts, as well as teaching activities in Pakistan and Germany. It also records research and administrative roles associated with the Iranian Academy of Arts.

In February 2017, Shargh reported that Amani had been appointed acting head of the Saba Cultural and Artistic Institute, an institution affiliated with the Iranian Academy of Arts. The newspaper described him as an artist from Lorestan with a background in art research and Persian calligraphy. It also discussed his work across painting, photography, calligraphy, installation, and other media.

Amani's listed professional activities include research on Persian calligraphy and Iranian visual culture, participation in art conferences, teaching traditional calligraphy, and contributing to exhibitions and cultural programmes.

== Artistic practice ==

Amani works across painting, photography, digital imagery, installation, and calligraphy. His art draws on Persian poetry, miniature painting, historical portraiture, and Islamic cultural traditions, bringing these references into dialogue with contemporary visual culture.

=== Persian miniature painting and Qajar imagery ===

Amani has developed works that reinterpret Safavid and Qajar portraiture through contemporary visual strategies. In its presentation of his exhibition Between Tradition and Modernity, Haleh Gallery described his portraits as a transformation of historical Persian miniature painting into a modern visual language, drawing a comparison with the use of existing popular images in Andy Warhol's pop art.

His work also engages with representations of women in Iranian visual history. The Museum of Islamic Art in Doha included discussion of Amani's work in its exhibition Qajar Women: Images of Women in 19th-century Iran, which ran from 8 April 2015 to 11 June 2016. The exhibition explored historical Qajar representations of women and their continuing influence on contemporary artists. The museum identified Amani, alongside Shadi Ghadirian and Mahmood Sabzi, as an artist who adapts Qajar visual aesthetics to comment on modernity, femininity, and the relationship between past and present. [ref: Qajar Women: Images of Women in 19th century Iran, Museum of Islamic Art]

=== Angels and photography ===

One of Amani's recurring subjects is the angel, interpreted through Iranian cultural and religious traditions. His series Angels in Paradise includes Fallen Angels (2012), a digital image in the collection of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA).

LACMA's curatorial notes describe Amani's angels as figures that reflect human shortcomings and explain that his imagery draws on traditional Iranian Muslim beliefs about angels accompanying human beings throughout their lives. In Fallen Angels, a contemporary woman is depicted with wings formed from golden leaves, combining symbolic imagery with references to the natural world.

In February 2014, Amani participated in the Colombo Art Biennale in Sri Lanka. In a report published by The Sunday Times, journalist Adilah Ismail discussed his work under the heading “Angelic touch to human worldliness”. The article described photographs featuring people posed against angel wings incorporating intricate Persian calligraphic details, linking spiritual imagery with everyday human experience. [ref: 'Making history' around Colombo, The Sunday Times]

=== Calligraphy and nature ===

Amani's practice also explores the relationship between Persian calligraphy and nature. In November 2016, The Indian Express covered an exhibition at Egg Art Studio in New Delhi that addressed the relationship between humans and wildlife. The newspaper described Amani's contribution as an image of a woman transforming into a bird, formed using the flowing lines and lyrical qualities of traditional Persian calligraphy. [ref: A lonely planet, The Indian Express]

Amani has also researched traditional Iranian scripts, including Ta'liq, and has described the revival and promotion of this calligraphic tradition as part of his artistic and scholarly work.

== Research ==

Amani's listed research projects include:

* Nastaliq Inscriptions of Iran, commissioned by the Iranian Academy of Arts.
* Aesthetics of Iranian Mosques from the Early Centuries to the Fifth Century AH.
* Tones of Shahnameh Reading in Lorestan, commissioned by the Iranian Academy of Arts.

His research interests include the history of Islamic art, Persian calligraphy, Iranian architecture, traditional painting, and contemporary visual culture.

== Books ==

Amani's listed publications include:

* Ungeteilte Himmel (2016), with Professor Dr. Wenzel, associated with Goethe University Frankfurt.
* The Book of the Mythical World: Myth in the Islamic Lands of Italy and Spain (2021), Mahkameh Publications.
* An Introduction to the Calligraphy Method of Mirza Shafi Tabrizi (2018), Naskh Publications, Iranian Academy of Arts, Tehran.

== Selected scholarly articles ==

Amani's listed academic and critical publications include:

* “Discourse Study of the Formation of Haft Awrang by Norman Fairclough’s Discourse Analysis Approach” (2025).
* “Analysis and Review of Erol Akyavaş's Calligraphic Works in Modern Turkey” (2022).
* “New Qajarism in Iranian Contemporary and Modern Visual Arts,” Journal of Art and Civilization of the Orient, volume 10 (2022).
* “Renovation of Traditional Turkish Painting Art in Contemporary Turkey,” Bagh-e Nazar, volume 18 (2022).
* “Changing the Meaning in Contemporary Iranian Calligraphy Discourse,” with Hasan Bolkhari and Sedaqat Jabari, JACO, issue 31 (2021).
* “Evolution of Traditional Painting in Contemporary Turkey,” with Sara Farahmand, Bagh-e Nazar (2021).
* “Developments of Islamic Calligraphy in Contemporary Turkey,” with Sara Farahmand, JACO, issue 32 (2020).
* “Nasta'liq Style Calligraphy in Qajar Period,” For Tomorrow Magazine, issue 25 (2020).
* “Pakistani New Art,” For Tomorrow Magazine, issue 21 (2018).

== Lectures and presentations ==

Amani's listed lectures and presentations include:

* “Review and Criticism of Traditionalist Views on Islamic Calligraphy,” Nazar Institute, Tehran (2023).
* “Intertextual Analysis of the Rosary of Particles by Ziauddin Emami,” University of Sistan and Baluchestan (2023).
* “Impact of Calligraphy on Treatise of Mahmoud bin Muhammad,” Isfahan University of Arts (2022).
* Webinar on calligraphy movements and treatises, University of Sistan and Baluchestan (2022).
* Webinar on the Neo-Miniature movement in Middle Eastern art, University of Sistan and Baluchestan (2021).
* National webinar on the Harufiyeh art movement, Visual Arts Secretariat (2021).
* “The Effect of Miniature Painting on Modern Middle Eastern Art,” Isfahan University of Arts (2021).
* “Integration of Arts in Iranian Primary Schools,” with Omid Karimi, Congress on Iranian Islamic Architecture, Tehran (2018).
* “Ta'liq Calligraphy and Khajeh Ekhtiar,” National Congress, Gonabad, Iran (2017).
* “Persian Paintings and Calligraphy,” HKDM University, Freiburg, Germany (2016).
* “Persian Calligraphy,” Pädagogische University, Freiburg, Germany (2016).
* “New Qajarism in Iranian Modern Art,” Museum of Islamic Art, Doha, Qatar (2015).
* “The Physics of Angels,” with Catherina Wenzel (2014).
* “Islamic Calligraphy,” Karachi Visual Art University, Pakistan (2014).
* “Islamic Calligraphy from Past to Present,” Raudondaris Castle, Lithuania (2013).
* “Environmental Art in Iran,” 2nd Kathmandu International Art Festival, Nepal (2012).

== Workshops ==

Amani's listed workshops include:

* Persian Painting and Calligraphy Workshop, KCCC Gallery, Klaipėda, Lithuania (2013).
* “Making History” workshop, 3rd Colombo Art Biennale, Sri Lanka (2014).
* Persian Calligraphy Workshop, Baroti Art Gallery, Klaipėda, Lithuania (2011).
* Performance art inspired by the poetry of Rumi, Chowkandi Art Gallery, Karachi, Pakistan, with actress Kiaf Qaznavi (2014).

== Artist residencies ==

Amani's listed artist residencies include:

* London, England (2010).
* Lithuania, supported by the Lithuanian Communication and Culture Center (2011).
* Kathmandu, Nepal (2012).
* Karachi, Pakistan (2014).

== Selected exhibitions ==

Amani has participated in solo and group exhibitions in Iran and internationally. The following list is based on his supplied exhibition record and includes events documented by institutional and press sources.

* Still Life, solo exhibition, March Art Gallery, San Francisco, United States (2022).

data.title: Stark Future
data.text:
----

Stark Future S.L. is a Spanish manufacturer of high-performance electric motorcycles headquartered in Sant Boi de Llobregat, near Barcelona. Founded in 2019 by Swedish entrepreneur Anton Wass and engineer Paul Soucy, the company is best known for the Stark VARG platform, a family of electric motocross, enduro and supermoto motorcycles. [ref: Spanish electric motorcycle company revolutionises motocross and mobility, European Investment Bank]

In 2025 the company reported its first profitable quarter and full-year revenue of €115 million, and in March 2026 it became the first electric manufacturer to win an FIM world championship title when it secured the Manufacturers' title in the FIM SuperEnduro World Championship.

== History ==

=== Founding (2019–2021) ===
Anton Wass, who grew up near Stockholm, had earlier co-founded the motorcycle parts e-commerce group Pierce AB, owner of the online retailer 24MX. [ref: A Peek Behind the Golden Ring: Visiting Stark Future Headquarters, Motorcycle.com] He founded Stark Future in Barcelona in 2019 with the stated aim of building electric motorcycles that outperform the best combustion-engined competitors rather than asking riders to compromise for sustainability. The company name derives from the Swedish word stark ("strong"); varg is Swedish for "wolf".

The Stark VARG was unveiled on 14 December 2021 as an electric motocross bike producing up to 80 hp, a figure the company claimed made it the most powerful production motocross motorcycle available. [ref: Stark Varg: This electric motocross bike from Sweden throws shade at its gas-powered competition, Notebookcheck] Wass later described the launch as the most successful of any motorcycle company in history.

=== Production ramp and Eicher investment (2022–2023) ===
Deliveries were originally scheduled for September 2022 but were delayed by production and quality problems; the company reportedly rejected roughly 90% of an initial batch of 1,000 frames from a supplier, and the first VARG MX customer units were delivered in May 2023.

On 29 December 2022 Eicher Motors, the Indian parent company of Royal Enfield, agreed to invest €50 million for an approximately 10.35% stake in Stark Future, taking a board seat and entering a technical collaboration agreement covering research and development, technology sharing and manufacturing. [ref: Eicher Motors to invest over Rs 440 cr in electric bike firm Stark Future, Business Standard] [ref: Eicher Motors Announces Strategic Investment in Stark Future, Cycle News] In June 2023 the company signed a €20 million loan with Banco Santander to expand production.

=== Expansion and profitability (2024–2025) ===
In September 2024 the European Investment Bank signed a €40 million credit facility with Stark Future, backed by the EU's InvestEU programme, to fund research, development and the scale-up of manufacturing capacity in Sant Boi de Llobregat over 2024–2027. [ref: Spain: EIB and Stark Future sign a €40 million loan to invest in innovation and new solutions for the electric motorcycle sector, European Investment Bank] [ref: Barcelona-based electric motorbike company Stark Future secures €40M from EIB, Silicon Canals] The street-legal VARG EX enduro model was launched in December 2024.

In April 2025 the company reported its first profitable month, with monthly revenue of €18.3 million and EBITDA of €2.8 million. [ref: Stark Future Achieves Record Profitability for All-Electric Motorcycle Manufacturer, RideApart] On 15 July 2025 Stark Future announced its first profitable quarter, reporting Q2 2025 revenue of €47 million and EBITDA of €4.5 million, with revenue more than doubling year on year; the company described itself as the fastest electric vehicle manufacturer to reach profitability. [ref: Stark Future Smashes EV Profitability Records in Q2 to Challenge Legacy Powersports, Cycle News] [ref: This electric motorcycle company just did what no one else could, Electrek] Electrek noted that the "largest electric-only motorcycle manufacturer" claim excludes large Asian scooter-focused makers such as Yadea and NIU.

A further equity round in 2025, drawn mainly from existing shareholders together with new investors connected to the MotoGP paddock, took total capital contributions past €100 million. [ref: Stark Future exceeds €100 million in total capital contributions with the latest equity investment round, The Pack] In October 2025 the company launched its third model, the road-legal VARG SM supermoto.

For the full year 2025 Stark Future reported revenue of €115 million, up 77% year on year, with fourth-quarter growth of 97% and profitability in five of the final nine months; the company said it had taken more than 3% of the global enduro segment within a year and around 50% of the enduro market in Germany. [ref: Stark Future Posts Record Growth and Profitability Accelerating Path to Global Scale, Cycle News] Revenue roughly tripled year on year in the first quarter of 2026. [ref: This EV Dirt Bike Startup Just Tripled Revenue, And Went Profitable, RideApart]

== Products ==
All current models share the VARG platform: a liquid-cooled electric motor with carbon-fibre sleeve and integrated inverter, a 7.2 kWh lithium-ion battery in a magnesium honeycomb casing, a steel frame with forged aluminium subframe, and a handlebar-mounted, Android-based waterproof touchscreen (the "Arkenstone") used to select power maps and receive over-the-air updates. [ref: 2025 Stark Varg EX and SM Coming to US Market, Motorcycle.com] Models are offered in a standard (60 hp) and "Alpha" (80 hp) configuration.

* VARG MX (unveiled December 2021; deliveries from May 2023) – the original motocross model, quoted at up to 80 hp and around 938–978 Nm of torque at the rear wheel. A revised MX 1.2 chassis followed with altered frame flex characteristics. [ref: Stark VARG MX 1.2, Stark Future]
* VARG EX (launched December 2024) – a street-legal enduro variant on 21/18-inch wheels, weighing about 120 kg. [ref: Bike Check: Stark VARG EX Brings Electric Power to Hard Enduro, Zona Enduro]
* VARG SM (launched 14 October 2025) – a road-legal supermoto on 17-inch wheels with KYB suspension and Brembo brakes, weighing 124.5 kg; the company claims the highest power-to-weight ratio of any production supermoto. It is A1-licence compliant in Europe, priced from €12,990, and from US$12,999 in North America. [ref: Stark VARG SM launched as street-legal electric motorcycle with jaw-dropping specs, Electrek] [ref: Stark Future takes it to the street with VARG SM electric Supermoto, Powersports Business] [ref: 2025 Stark Varg SM Review – First Ride, Motorcycle.com] [ref: Stark Varg SM 2025 – Electric supermoto with 80 hp and record power-to-weight ratio, Motorcycles.news]
* Factory Edition (2026) – a limited run of 500 MX and EX units with KYB Factory A-Kit suspension, matching the specification raced by the factory team. [ref: Stark Future, Stark Future]

The company has stated that further models are in development, including a travel enduro (Stark Älg) and a road-going sport model (Stark Lo).

== Racing ==
Stark's racing programme is led by Racing Director Sébastien Tortelli, a two-time motocross world champion who joined the company as test manager.

=== SuperEnduro ===
Stark was initially refused entry to the FIM SuperEnduro World Championship in early 2024 when the FIM reversed a rule change that would have admitted electric motorcycles; electric machines were admitted from 2025. [ref: How Stark Varg is Winning World Titles, GritShift] In March 2026, at the final round in France, Stark won the 2026 FIM SuperEnduro World Championship Manufacturers' title, the first world championship title for an electric motorcycle manufacturer. Riders Eddie Karlsson and Toby Martyn finished fourth and fifth in the Prestige standings on the VARG EX, competing against KTM, Husqvarna, Triumph and Honda machinery ridden by, among others, Billy Bolt and Jonny Walker. [ref: Stark wins 2026 FIM SuperEnduro World Championship Manufacturers' title, Visordown] [ref: Stark Claims FIM SuperEnduro Manufacturers' Title, Cycle News] [ref: Stark becomes first-ever e-motorcycle to win SuperEnduro title, Powersports Business]

=== Hard Enduro and Erzbergrodeo ===
In 2026 Stark contested the FIM Hard Enduro World Championship with Karlsson and Martyn. At the Erzbergrodeo, which opened its main event to electric motorcycles for the first time in 2026, Karlsson finished ninth and became the first rider to complete the event on an electric motorcycle; Martyn finished twelfth. Stark riders also swept the podium of the event's Rocket Ride hillclimb.

=== Supercross ===
In August 2025 the FIM World Supercross Championship announced Stark Future as its seventh team and the first fully electric team to race against combustion-engined motorcycles in an FIM-sanctioned supercross series. [ref: World Supercross Announces Landmark Team Deal and Stark Future Electric Debut, FIM World Supercross Championship] At its debut at the 2026 season opener in Calgary, Canada, Stark riders took five of six holeshots and Michael Hicks scored the manufacturer's first overall podium in the SX2 class; rivals attributed part of the start advantage to the venue's altitude, which did not penalise the electric powertrain. [ref: 2026 FIM World Supercross Round 1 Results, Cycle News] [ref: Anstie kickstarts SX2 title defence with victory, [[Racer X (magazine)] In September 2026 Stark announced a factory team for the 2026 Australian Supercross Championship, becoming the first all-electric manufacturer in that series after Motorcycling Australia approved electric motorcycles to race alongside combustion machines. [ref: Stark Future Joins 2026 Australian Supercross Championship, Motorcycle.com]

=== Records ===
In November 2025 Swiss rider Jiri Zak set a Guinness World Record for the highest altitude reached on a motorcycle, riding a VARG to 6,721 m on Ojos del Salado.

== Notable riders ==
Freestyle motocross pioneer Travis Pastrana published a review of the VARG, [ref: Video: Travis Pastrana reviews the Stark Varg, GateDrop] and the bike has featured in comparison tests at Pastrana's Maryland compound alongside Ken Roczen and Carson Brown. [ref: Can a Stark Varg Beat a 500cc 2-Stroke Suzuki Around Pastranaland?, RideApart] Retired supercross racer Blake Wharton conducted an early ride evaluation for Cycle World. [ref: Stark Varg Electric Motocross Bike First Ride, Cycle World]

== Key people ==
* Anton Wass – Founder and Chief Executive Officer [ref: Team, Stark Future]
* Paul Soucy – Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer
* Sébastien Tortelli – Racing Director
* Andres Espuelas – Chief Operations Officer
* Dennis Nylund – Chief Revenue Officer
* Morgan Karlsson – Chief Marketing Officer
* Max Cichon – Chief Financial Officer
* Victor Val – Chief Legal Officer

== Operations ==
The company operates a 20,000 m² factory in Sant Boi de Llobregat where both battery packs and complete vehicles are produced in-house, and by 2025 sold through around 400 retail locations in more than 50 countries. [ref: Stark VARG: April 2025 Sales Surge Past $20M] Stark states that the factory runs on renewable energy and that it is reducing plastic in its products, including a compostable bio-nylon crash guard. [ref: Radically Fast, Sustainable and Built to Last, Groundbreakers]

== Reception ==
Early press tests praised the VARG's performance while noting the adjustment required in riding technique and charging logistics; Dirt Bike Magazine observed that a full day of amateur racing on one charge was possible only with careful power management. [ref: Stark Varg Electric MX Bike: Full Test, Dirt Bike Magazine] Ars Technica described the VARG EX as extremely fast and capable but "a little too unrefined". [ref: The electric Stark Varg EX is brutally fast but a little too unrefined, Ars Technica]

data.title: Agata Zając
data.text:
Agata Zając (also written Agata Zajac; born 1995) is a Polish orchestral and operatic conductor based in the United Kingdom. She won second prize in conducting at the Princess Astrid International Music Competition in Trondheim in 2026 and second prize and the audience prize at the Siemens Hallé International Conductors Competition in Manchester in 2023. She has held fellowships and assistantships with the NDR Elbphilharmonie Orchester, the Barcelona Symphony Orchestra, the Royal Northern College of Music and the Tanglewood Music Center.

== Early life and education ==
Zając was born in Poznań. She began her musical education as a violinist at music schools in Poznań, and in 2015 began studying orchestral conducting at the Ignacy Jan Paderewski Academy of Music in Poznań in the class of Marcin Sompoliński, graduating with a master's degree in July 2020. She has also studied in masterclasses and conducting academies with Paavo Järvi (Tonhalle Conductors' Academy, Zürich, 2022), Marin Alsop (NOSPR conducting workshops, 2021), Peter Eötvös, Jorma Panula, Johannes Schlaefli and Mark Heron. In 2018 she received scholarships from the Polish Minister of Culture and National Heritage and the Marshal of the Greater Poland Voivodeship.

== Career ==
=== Early career in Poland ===
From April 2018 Zając worked as an assistant conductor at the Warsaw Chamber Opera on three premieres, including a historically informed reconstruction of Stanisław Moniuszko's Halka (Vilnius version) on period instruments, which was broadcast by TVP Kultura in 2019. In 2018 she received a special prize at the Malta International Conducting Masterclass and Competition, after which she assisted the Greek conductor Michalis Economou with the Malta Philharmonic Orchestra and the Greek Radio Symphony Orchestra; in 2019–20 she assisted him on a New Year concert tour of China with the Athens Philharmonia Orchestra, conducting one of its eleven concerts.

She was resident conductor of the Toruń Symphony Orchestra in the 2020/21 season and of the Sudeten Philharmonic (Filharmonia Sudecka) in Wałbrzych in 2021/22, under a residency programme of the National Institute of Music and Dance.

=== Fellowships and assistantships ===
In 2022 Zając was appointed Mills Williams Junior Fellow in Conducting at the Royal Northern College of Music in Manchester for the 2022/23 season, selected from more than 120 applicants. In the summer of 2023 she was a Conducting Fellow at the Tanglewood Music Center, where she conducted the Tanglewood Music Center Orchestra in works including Rachmaninoff's Isle of the Dead.

She was assistant conductor to Ludovic Morlot at the Barcelona Symphony Orchestra in the 2023/24 and 2024/25 seasons, and one of three Conductor Fellows of the NDR Elbphilharmonie Orchester in Hamburg under Alan Gilbert in 2024/25. She is represented by TACT Artists Management.

=== Guest conducting ===
Zając has conducted orchestras including The Hallé, the Britten Sinfonia, the National Symphony Orchestra of Ireland, the orchestra of the Teatro Regio di Torino, the Grazer Philharmoniker, the Orchestre national de Metz Grand Est, the Pfalzphilharmonie Kaiserslautern, the Real Filharmonía de Galicia, the Siemens Türkiye Symphony Orchestra (at its first concert, in Istanbul in November 2023), the Polish National Radio Symphony Orchestra, the Szczecin Philharmonic and the Poznań Philharmonic.

Her scheduled appearances in the 2026/27 season include the Orquestra Gulbenkian in Lisbon and the NDR Radiophilharmonie, with which she conducts the opening concert of the Harzburger Musiktage in Wolfenbüttel in May 2027.

== Competitions and awards ==
* 2018 – Special prize, Malta International Conducting Masterclass and Competition
* 2021 – Special distinction, International Conducting Competition "Città di Brescia – Giancarlo Facchinetti"
* 2023 – Second prize and audience prize, Siemens Hallé International Conductors Competition, Manchester
* 2026 – Second prize, Princess Astrid International Music Competition (conducting), Trondheim

== Repertoire ==
Zając's repertoire includes symphonic and operatic works, with an emphasis on Central and Eastern European music and Polish composers, including Grażyna Bacewicz.

data.title: Fortitude Valley (TV series)
data.text:
Fortitude Valley is an upcoming Australian television crime drama for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) releasing in 2027. Produced by Moving Floor Entertainment, the series follows Ethan Tobane, an up and coming detective who is following the footsteps of his father the series explores family secrets, corrupting power and complicated truths of the underbelly of peoples lives. [ref: Hunter Page-Lochard, Kat Stewart find their way to Moving Floor Entertainment’s ‘Fortitude Valley’, if.com.au]

== Plot ==
Ethan Tobane a rising star in the Queensland Police Service, following in the footsteps of his father, Ethan admired his father but when he learns his father may have been corrupt during his time on the service. Ethan is forced to investigate a murder in an abandoned government building, Ethan explores the facts and intertwining details of his fathers possible involvement. [ref: Australia’s ABC orders Princess Pictures comedy and Moving Floor crime thriller, C21media] [ref: ]

== Cast ==
On 23 February 2026, Hunter Page-Lochard and Kat Stewart where named as the main leads for the series. [ref: Valley to take gritty lead role in shadowy new crime drama series, couriermail.com.au] On 31 March 2026 production announced that John Kim had joined the cast in the role of Gavin Chang. [ref: John Kim Joins Hunter Page-Lochard & Kat Stewart In Australian Drama ‘Fortitude Valley’, Deadline] On 9 June 2026, Rupert Everett had joined the cast. [ref: Rupert Everett makes his way to 'Fortitude Valley', IF Magazine]
* Hunter Page-Lochard as Ethan Tobane
* Kat Stewart as Heather Briggs
* John Kim as Gavin Chang
* Rupert Everett as James Demming
* Charlie Bridgewater as Charlie Roy

== Production ==
On 23 February 2026, ABC announced that the series would enter production in April 2026 with production funding secured by Screen Queensland. [ref: ABC series ‘Fortitude Valley’ to commence production in Brisbane, Screen Queensland] [ref: Fortitude Valley, Screen Australia]

The series was being produced by Moving Floor Entertainment with Hunter Page-Lochard sharing co-writing credits with Stephen Irwin and Leigh McGrath.. [ref: Brisbane Crime Thriller Fortitude Valley Heads to ABC in 2027, With Filming Beginning in April, Fortitude Valley News] The series would be shot on location with filming taking place in Queensland. [ref: Brisbane Crime Thriller Fortitude Valley Heads to ABC in 2027, With Filming Beginning in April, Fortitude Valley News]

ABC announced that it would air on ABC and its on demand streaming service ABC iView in 2027. [ref: ABC unveils Fortitude Valley – A gritty new crime series set in Brisbane’s underbelly, FilmInk] Rachel Okine head of scripted at the ABC said the ABC was excited to return to Brisbane for filming. [ref: John Kim Joins Cast of Australian Crime Drama 'Fortitude Valley', Resonate Voices]

On 1 April 2026, the series was one of 91 projects that had received further funding for production development. [ref: ]

On 21 October 2026, the series was apart of the lineup of shows set to air on the ABC in 2027. DCD Rights in the UK had secured the rights for the series distribution in the UK.

= Nick Paley =

Nick Paley is an American screenwriter, director, and editor. He co-wrote the screenplay for the Oscar-nominated feature Marcel the Shell with Shoes On [ref: ] (2021) with Marcel's creators Dean Fleischer Camp and Jenny Slate. [ref: Jenny Slate Can’t Wait for You to See ‘Marcel the Shell with Shoes On’, Vanity Fair] [ref: How 'Marcel the Shell' went from viral sensation to 2022's most adorable movie star, Los Angeles Times] [ref: A Beautiful Collage of Obstacles and Heartbreaks: An Interview with ‘Marcel the Shell with Shoes On’ creators Dean Fleischer-Camp and Nick Paley, Script Magazine] Nick is the creator, showrunner, director, executive producer, and writer of the Hulu television series Phony (2026– present). [ref: Hulu Press] [ref: Phony creator says Connie Britton explores a darker side of motherhood in ‘crazy, fun mystery’ (exclusive), Entertainment Weekly] He also served as both a director and editor on Broad City (2019). [ref: How ‘Broad City’ Filmed an Entire Episode as a Social Media Story, The Hollywood Reporter]

== Early Life and Education ==
Paley was born and raised in Northern Vermont and graduated from New York University with a film degree.

== Career ==
Paley worked as an editor and director on television projects before collaborating with filmmaker Dean Fleischer Camp on Marcel the Shell with Shoes On. Camp and Paley met while working in television editing.

Paley co-wrote Marcel the Shell with Shoes On with Camp and Jenny Slate. The screenplay was developed through an iterative process in which Paley and Camp wrote sections, recorded Slate improvising dialogue as Marcel, and revised the script using material from those sessions. The process continued over several years. [ref: How 'Marcel the Shell' went from viral sensation to 2022's most adorable movie star, Los Angeles Times] [ref: ‘Marcel the Shell’ made it to the big screen by staying small, The Washington Post] The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Animated Feature, A New York Film Critics Association Award [ref: 'Marcel The Shell With Shoes On' Wins Best Animated Feature From New York Film Critics Circle], and Paley won an Annie Award for Outstanding Achievement in Writing for an Animated Feature. [ref: ‘Guillermo Del Toro’s Pinocchio’ Wins Five Trophies Including the Top Prize at the 50th Annie Awards, The Hollywood Reporter]

Paley’s television work includes editing and directing on Broad City, Hack Into Broad City [ref: Nick Paley List of Movies and TV Shows - TV Guide, www.tvguide.com], Inside Amy Schumer [ref: TV Review: ‘Inside Amy Schumer’, Variety], and Brody Stevens: Enjoy It!. [ref: Brody Stevens: Enjoy It! credits - Metacritic, www.metacritic.com] He has been nominated for two Emmys for editing and producing, [ref: Telvision Academy Bios - Nick Paley, Telvision Academy] and won an American Cinema Editors award. [ref: ACE Eddie Awards: ‘Mad Max’ & ‘The Big Short’ Take Top Prizes; TV Trophies To ‘Mad Men’, ‘Amy Schumer’ – Winners List, Deadline]

Paley created the Hulu mystery-comedy series Phony, which premiered on October 20, 2026. The series stars Connie Britton and Sam Nivola. It follows a teenager who, after a car accident, suspects that his mother has been replaced by an impostor. [ref: ‘Phony’ Trailer: Sam Nivola Suspects Connie Britton Is An Imposter In Hulu’s Coming-Of-Age Mystery, The Playlist] Paley wrote the first two episodes, directed half of the first season, and executive-produced the series; Anthony King served as co-showrunner. In an interview with TV Insider, Paley said the series’ emotional premise drew on a childhood fear of losing his mother. [ref: What Is Hulu's 'Phony' Based On? Creator of Connie Britton Series Explains (Exclusive), TV Insider]

data.title: Operational risk quantification
data.text:
== Introduction ==

Operational risk quantification refers to the statistical and analytical methods used to assess an organization's potential financial losses related to operational risk — losses arising from internal failures (fraud, processing errors) or from external events beyond the organization's control (natural disasters, pandemics). In banking, for example, a borrower's default is classified as credit risk rather than operational risk, whereas an error made in granting a loan is classified as operational risk.

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision formally defined operational risk in the Basel II Accords (2004) as "the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events." [ref: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards, Bank for International Settlements] Basel II requires banks to quantify this risk in order to determine a portion of their regulatory capital and economic capital under Pillar 2 (ICAAP), the equity institutions must hold to absorb losses.

Institutions combine qualitative approaches, such as Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA), with quantitative approaches, such as the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) and the Loss Distribution Approach (LDA).

Since the 2020s, in response to the emergence of systemic threats linked to climate risks and dependence on technological service providers, these methodologies have integrated forward-looking scenario analyses. These practices are framed by new supervisory standards (such as the European regulation DORA, Digital Operational Resilience for the financial sector and Amending regulations) and rely technically on machine learning and Big data processing.

== Typology of methodological approaches ==

Financial institutions employ various methodological approaches to quantify their exposure to operational risk. The choice of model depends on the depth of historical data [ref: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework – Comprehensive Version, Bank for International Settlements], regulatory constraints [ref: 2023 EU-wide stress test – Methodological Note, EBA], and the institution's internal objectives regarding resilience [ref: Building operational resilience: Impact tolerances for important business services (PS6/21), Bank of England].

Quantitative models are divided into two main categories. Statistical methods jointly evaluate the frequency and severity of historical losses, while forward-looking scenario analyses estimate the impact of rare but critical events, such as cyberattacks, compliance litigation, or system failures [ref: Scenario Analysis in the Measurement of Operational Risk Capital: A Review, Journal of Operational Risk]. Both approaches frequently rely on modeling techniques, such as Monte Carlo simulation, to generate loss distributions [ref: Loss Distribution Approach for Operational Risk, SSRN Electronic Journal]. Under Basel III, banks using such models must calculate capital requirements at a 99.9% confidence level [ref: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards, Bank for International Settlements].

The implementation of these mathematical models raises several technical challenges documented by supervisory authorities [ref: Operational Risk: Supervisory Guidelines for the Advanced Measurement Approaches, Bank for International Settlements]:
*The scarcity of historical loss data and reporting bias in externally sourced data, which are especially pronounced for extreme, low-frequency events;
*The high sensitivity of capital requirements to distributional assumptions, notably the shape of the severity distribution's tail and the choice of dependence (correlation) structure between risk categories;
*The difficulty of combining statistical loss data with qualitative inputs, such as business environment and internal control factors (BEICFs).

To address these limitations, banking and insurance institutions no longer use these models in isolation. They combine quantitative measures with qualitative assessments within a comprehensive risk management framework.

=== Loss Distribution Approach (LDA) ===

The Loss Distribution Approach (LDA) estimates the total distribution of operational losses from historical data by modelling frequency and severity separately. Frequency is typically modelled with a Poisson or negative binomial distribution, while severity is fitted to heavy-tailed distributions such as the Lognormal, Weibull, or Pareto law [ref: Quantitative Risk Management: Concepts, Techniques and Tools, Princeton University Press].

The aggregate loss for a given period is modelled as:

: S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i

where N is the (random) number of loss events, drawn from the frequency distribution, and each Xi is an individual loss severity, drawn independently from the severity distribution. Because this sum has no closed-form solution for most distribution choices, banks estimate it via Monte Carlo simulation, drawing repeatedly from both distributions to build an aggregated loss distribution and read off the capital requirement at the 99.9th percentile.

Extreme Value Theory (EVT) is commonly used to model the tail of the severity distribution, which are the low-frequency, high-severity losses that drive most of the capital charge. Copulas allow the model to capture dependence between different types of incidents, and a Bayesian approach can blend expert judgment with sparse historical data [ref: Modeling Operational Risk Using Bayesian Inference, Springer].

LDA's reliance on historical data is also its main weakness: a single extreme, unprecedented event can render the model's assumptions obsolete overnight. In January 2008, Société Générale disclosed a €4.9 billion loss linked to unauthorised trading positions built up by trader Jérôme Kerviel (an amount that dwarfed any severity scenario the bank's internal model had been calibrated to expect) [ref: L'affaire Kerviel, un traumatisme pour le contrôle des risques, Le Monde].

Episodes like this, where the past offered no guide to the future, pushed supervisors to gradually phase out internally modelled approaches like LDA in favour of the standardised SMA [ref: Standardised Measurement Approach for operational risk, Bank for International Settlements].

=== Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) ===

The Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) was introduced by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) in December 2017 during the finalization of the Basel III accords, replacing all previously existing approaches — including the Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) — with a single, non-model-based method [ref: Basel III: Finalising post-crisis reforms, Bank for International Settlements]. In Europe, it is transposed by the CRR3 regulation, applicable from 2025 [ref: Regulation (EU) 2024/1623 amending Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 as regards requirements for operational risk (CRR 3), Official Journal of the European Union].

Under the SMA, capital requirements are calculated in two steps. First, the Business Indicator (BI) — a proxy for the bank's size derived from its income statement — is converted into a Business Indicator Component (BIC) using marginal coefficients that rise with the BI's size, in a structure similar to a progressive tax scale [ref: Standardised approach — Calculation of the standardised approach, Bank for International Settlements]:

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Bucket !! BI range !! Marginal coefficient
|-
| 1 || ≤ €1 billion || 12%
|-
| 2 || €1–30 billion || 15%
|-
| 3 || > €30 billion || 18%
|}

For a bank with a BI of €35 billion, for example, the BIC comes to:

: BIC = (1 × 12%) + (29 × 15%) + (5 × 18%) = €5.37 billion

as given in the BCBS's own worked example.

Second, the BIC is multiplied by an Internal Loss Multiplier (ILM), which factors in the bank's own loss history: the ILM equals 1 when the bank's historical losses match what would be "expected" for a bank of its size, rises above 1 for banks with a heavier loss record, and falls below 1 for banks with a lighter one. Within the European Union, however, CRR3 disregards historical loss data for all institutions when calculating minimum own funds requirements — effectively fixing the ILM at 1 across the board, to keep the framework harmonised and comparable throughout the Union.

The BCBS designed the SMA to reduce the excessive variability in risk-weighted capital calculations that had built up under the AMA's more flexible, internally modelled approach, and to make banks' capital ratios easier to compare. Supervisors still require banks to supplement this standardised calculation with forward-looking scenarios as part of their internal capital adequacy assessment process (ICAAP) [ref: Guidelines on ICAAP and ILAAP].

=== Expert-based scenarios ===

Since 17 January 2025, the European DORA regulation (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) has required financial institutions to model scenarios of severe disruption to critical services [ref: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA), Official Journal of the European Union]. Article 26 of the same regulation gives one concrete example of this shift: financial entities identified by supervisors as systemically important must run a threat-led penetration test (TLPT) — a live, adversarial simulation of a real cyberattack against production systems — at least once every three years, covering some or all of their critical or important functions.

Unlike the LDA or the Standardized Measurement Approach, expert-based scenario analysis isn't tied to historical data at all: it draws on the judgment of internal or external experts to gauge the probability and impact of rare, emerging, or unprecedented events — a major cyberattack, the failure of a critical third-party provider, a systemic shock [ref: Operational Risk Management: Best Practices in the Financial Services Industry, John Wiley & Sons].

One common technique is reverse stress testing: rather than starting from a cause and estimating an impact, the expert starts from an outcome — the point at which the bank would become insolvent or unable to operate — and works backward to estimate how likely that outcome is [ref: Guidelines on common procedures and methodologies for the supervisory review and evaluation process (SREP)]. Because these are, by definition, low-frequency, high-severity events, the confidence level used to quantify them is aligned with the same 99.9% threshold Basel III applies elsewhere — meaning the institution is expected to be able to withstand a shock that would statistically occur only once every thousand years.

In practice, this takes the form of workshops or interviews bringing risk managers and business-line experts together; their judgments are converted into probability-severity pairs, which feed into a simulated loss distribution. The COVID-19 pandemic offered a real-world test of the method starting in 2020: no bank had comparable historical loss data for a modern pandemic, so the business continuity plans put in place during the crisis relied heavily on this kind of forward-looking, judgment-based scenario work rather than on past-loss statistics.

These scenarios feed directly into the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), underpinning stress tests and recovery plans. The European Banking Authority (EBA) and the Bank of England both require banks to quantify these impact tolerances rigorously enough to check they're consistent with the bank's stated risk appetite [ref: Revised Guidelines on common procedures and methodologies for SREP].

To sharpen these projections, institutions increasingly combine expert judgment with mathematical tools — Monte Carlo simulation, for instance, to test different business configurations or gauge the payoff of security investments. The same analyses feed into risk-appetite calibration, testing dependencies between different failure modes, and assessing whether continuity plans hold up under resilience frameworks such as the Bank of England's PS6/21 policy statement of March 2021.

=== Exposure-based scenarios ===

Exposure-based methodologies have been promoted by ORX, an industry association of more than 100 financial institutions worldwide, in a reference report published in April 2023 [ref: Exploring Risk Exposure Methodologies, ORX]. These approaches tie potential losses to identifiable, measurable business drivers rather than to historical loss events or expert judgment alone.

Unlike traditional expert-based scenarios, the Exposure, Occurrence, Impact (XOI) model breaks risk down into three observable and auditable variables [ref: Operational Risk Modeling in Financial Services: The Exposure–Occurrence–Impact Method, Wiley]:
* Exposure (X): the volume of units at risk — for example, the total number of transactions processed over a given period.
* Occurrence (O): the probability of failure per unit, typically estimated from historical rates and adjusted for the effectiveness of current controls.
* Impact (I): the financial loss per affected unit.

The estimated total loss is the product of these three factors: Loss = X × O × I. A joint report by the European Central Bank and the European Banking Authority illustrates the scale these variables can take in practice: across the European Economic Area, fraud affected credit transfers at a rate of 0.001% of transaction value in the first half of 2023, while total payment fraud across all instruments (card payments, credit transfers, direct debits, cash withdrawals and e-money) reached €4.3 billion in 2022 and €2.0 billion in the first half of 2023 alone [ref: ECB and EBA publish joint report on payment fraud]. To capture the uncertainty in exposure-based estimates, institutions typically use Monte Carlo simulation to generate a distribution of possible losses, from which the 99.9th percentile defines the economic capital needed to cover an extreme, "once-in-a-thousand-years" loss [ref: Operational Risk Management, Wiley].

This approach also allows institutions to set precise impact tolerances. For payment systems specifically, the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI) set a maximum recovery time of two hours for critical payment services — a benchmark the Bank of England treats as distinct from, but complementary to, the broader impact tolerances firms must set for themselves under its own operational resilience framework.

== Summary: Application Matrix ==

The following table summarizes how each approach is typically applied within an operational risk management framework [ref: Operational Risk Management: Best Practices in the Financial Services Industry, John Wiley & Sons]:

SMA and LDA are primarily associated with capital calculation. SMA provides the regulatory capital requirement under Pillar 1, while LDA remains widely used by large institutions for their internal capital estimates (Pillar 2) due to its statistical structure that allows for modeling the entire loss distribution.

Scenario analysis, for its part, is employed for forward-looking assessments, particularly ICAAP, risk appetite calibration, and supervisory stress testing. It enables the quantification of low-frequency, high-severity events that are imperfectly captured by historical data.

At the same time, structured scenario methods (such as the XOI approach) and exposure-based models strengthen this forward-looking dimension by linking potential losses to their operational drivers—internal processes, information systems, or dependence on third-party providers. These approaches are integrated into operational resilience frameworks to evaluate tolerance thresholds and business recovery capabilities in the event of a major shock.

For its part, the Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA) process indirectly feeds quantitative models. By identifying major exposures and vulnerabilities in control systems at all levels of the organization, the RCSA provides the qualitative input data necessary for developing scenarios, calculating internal capital, and defining risk appetite. This process maps the control environment in which statistical models are subsequently applied [ref: Operational Risk Management: Best Practices in the Financial Services Industry, John Wiley & Sons].

In practice, financial institutions never rely on a single tool but combine these different approaches in an integrated manner. This complementarity is required by supervisors to meet regulatory requirements, justify capital adequacy, and test the overall resilience of the institution against severe but plausible crisis scenarios.

== Expansion of the scope of quantification ==

The evolution of operational risk quantification reflects a progressive convergence between regulatory simplification, model sophistication, and supervision that is now focused on resilience. Since the introduction of the Basel II framework, methodologies have transitioned from formulas based on volume indicators toward forward-looking approaches that integrate endogenous data and exogenous exposure vectors [ref: Operational Risk Management: Best Practices in the Financial Services Industry, John Wiley & Sons].

Driven by digital transformation, the scope of quantification now integrates advanced cybersecurity metrics. Modeling is no longer limited to compensating for financial losses but extends to measuring the institution's survival capacity. This assessment relies on standardized performance indicators such as Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO). In Europe, the DORA regulation institutionalizes this approach by mandating threat-led penetration testing to validate these tolerance thresholds.

The urgency of these measures is highlighted by the continuous increase in the average cost of a data breach in the global financial sector, which reached $5.9 million in 2023—a 15% increase compared to 2020 [ref: Cost of a Data Breach Report 2023]. For example, the ransomware attack targeting the provider ION Trading in 2023 paralyzed the clearing activities of dozens of banks, illustrating the need to precisely quantify these technological interdependencies [ref: EBA Guidelines on ICT and security risk management (EBA/GL/2019/04)].

At the same time, the operational risk taxonomy has formally integrated Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM). The massive outsourcing to cloud computing service providers now generates a major systemic concentration risk. Indeed, approximately 70% of Cloud computing services in the European financial sector are concentrated among three dominant providers: AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud [ref: Cloud outsourcing and the risks to financial stability]. To address this phenomenon, quantification increasingly relies on Graph theory to identify Single Points of Failure (SPoF) within outsourcing chains. Major incidents, such as the 2021 OVHcloud data center fire in Strasbourg, now serve as case studies for modeling data loss and estimating failover costs in the event of a critical provider's hardware failure [ref: EBA Guidelines on outsourcing arrangements (EBA/GL/2019/02)].

Additionally, climate and environmental risks are the subject of intense methodological developments aimed at translating climate shocks into tangible operational losses. Physical risk involves quantifying direct damage to banking infrastructure. For example, in 2023, natural disasters generated $380 billion in global economic losses, a significant portion of which was uninsured, thereby increasing the risk of net loss for exposed financial institutions [ref: 2024 Climate and Catastrophe Insight]. Concurrently, transition risk captures the increase in legal and non-compliance risks. This component notably includes fines and litigation related to greenwashing. The $25 million fine imposed by the SEC in 2022 on DWS, Deutsche Bank's asset management subsidiary, for misleading statements regarding its ESG criteria, marks the definitive entry of climate compliance into the quantitative calculation of operational risk [ref: Principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks, Bank for International Settlements].

Ultimately, operational risk management models are evolving from a strictly retrospective and segmented approach toward a systemic and forward-looking analysis. This new architecture is no longer limited to calculating a simple regulatory capital requirement. It allows institutions to define rigorous impact tolerances, thereby ensuring the maintenance of critical functions even in the event of an extreme but plausible shock, in accordance with the operational resilience principles issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision [ref: Principles for Operational Resilience, Bank for International Settlements].

== Role of technology, data, and automation ==

The volume of financial data is growing exponentially. According to the research firm IDC, data generated by financial institutions recorded an average annual growth rate of 26% between 2018 and 2025 [ref: Harnessing Data Analytics in Financial Services to Drive Customer Loyalty, International Banker]. This proliferation of unstructured information (Big data) is transforming the quantification of operational risk. Institutions are massively deploying machine learning algorithms. These models ingest millions of transactions per second to identify weak signals. In the area of anti-money laundering (AML), the impact is significant. The integration of deep learning has allowed some institutions to reduce false positives in the detection of suspicious transactions by up to 60% [ref: Opportunities and Challenges of New Technologies for AML/CFT].

At the same time, behavioral analysis monitors the digital habits of employees. It detects anomalies in login patterns or access to sensitive data. This proactive monitoring aims to prevent massive internal fraud. Historically, the absence of these algorithmic safeguards allowed for major lapses, such as the unauthorized positions held by trader Kweku Adoboli, which cost UBS $2.3 billion in 2011 [ref: UBS rogue trader Kweku Adoboli jailed over 'UK's biggest fraud', The Guardian].

Historically, collecting loss events required tedious manual processing. Today, natural language processing (NLP) automates the analysis of written or vocal communications. Algorithms extract semantics from emails, instant messages, and customer complaints. They automatically categorize incidents according to regulatory taxonomy. This technology has become indispensable given the proliferation of alternative communication channels. Between 2021 and 2023, the SEC imposed more than $200 million in fines on Wall Street banks for the unmonitored use of applications like WhatsApp by their employees [ref: SEC Charges 11 Wall Street Firms with Widespread Recordkeeping Failures, SEC Press Release]. The integration of NLP now makes it possible to ingest these massive flows to instantly detect transgressive vocabulary or systemic compliance failures [ref: Report on Big Data and Advanced Analytics].

Furthermore, Graph theory is used to model complex technological interdependencies. Operational losses rarely occur in isolation. Algorithms reveal hidden correlations between various internal and external factors. They map software supply chains to anticipate contagion effects. The 2020 cyberattack on the software company SolarWinds perfectly illustrates this hyper-connectivity risk. The malicious infiltration of a single update from this IT provider compromised the networks of thousands of companies and government agencies worldwide [ref: What you need to know about the biggest hack of the US government in years, The Guardian]. Network modeling helps anticipate these cascading vulnerabilities and evaluate a bank's global exposure to technology-driven systemic risk [ref: Fundamental Models in Financial Risk Management, John Wiley & Sons].

However, the integration of these technologies introduces a major vulnerability: model risk. The opacity of certain predictive algorithms poses a regulatory challenge described as the "black box" effect. A poorly calibrated model can lead to colossal financial and reputational losses. In 2012, a faulty high-frequency trading algorithm caused Knight Capital to lose $440 million in just forty-five minutes [ref: SEC Charges Knight Capital With Violations of Market Access Rule, SEC Press Release]

In addition, artificial intelligence algorithms can replicate discriminatory biases. In 2019, the credit-granting algorithm for the Apple Card, managed by Goldman Sachs, was investigated by New York regulators for alleged gender-based discrimination [ref: A Viral Tweet Accused Apple's New Credit Card of Being 'Sexist.' Now New York State Regulators Are Investigating, Time]. To prevent such lapses, authorities require strict explainability of automated decisions, independent model validation, and the systematic maintenance of human oversight [ref: Newsletter on artificial intelligence and machine learning, Bank for International Settlements]

== Notes and references ==

data.title: Somasekhar Sundaresan
data.text:
Somasekhar Sundaresan (born 23 December 1972) is an Indian jurist serving as a Permanent Judge of the Bombay High Court. After his appointment as an Additional Judge to that high court in November 2023, Sundaresan was confirmed as a Permanent Judge in September 2025. [ref: Hon'ble Sitting Judges: Somasekhar Sundaresan, J., High Court of Bombay] [ref: Advocate Somasekhar Sundaresan sworn in as additional judge of Bombay HC, The Indian Express] [ref: President appoints 6 Permanent Judges for Bombay High Court, SCC Online] He has also practiced as a regulatory and commercial lawyer giving advice on takeovers, securities laws and corporate insolvency rules in Mumbai. [ref: Somasekshar Sundaresan of JSA leaves the firm to begin counsel practice, The Economic Times]

== Early life and education ==
Sundaresan graduated with a Bachelor of Commerce from RA Podar College of Commerce & Economics in 1993. He then earned his law degree from Government Law College, Mumbai in 1996. While pursuing his law degree, Sundaresan worked in finance journalism as a business editor for The Times of India from 1994 to 1998. [ref: Somasekhar Sundaresan, Partner, J. Sagar Associates, on work of a transactional lawyer, responsibilites of a Partner, and his transition from Journalism to Law, SuperLawyer]

== Career ==

=== Legal ===
In 1999, Sundaresan joined Udwadia, Udeshi & Berjis (now Argus Partners) as a partner, advising on company law and foreign exchange regulations. From 2002 until August 2016, he served as a partner at J. Sagar Associates. Sundaresan's practice there had a focus on transactional governance and regulatory litigation before the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the Competition Commission of India and the Securities Appellate Tribunal.

=== Public policy and regulatory committees ===
Sundaresan has served on multiple Indian government advisory committees. He was a part of the SEBI Takeover Regulations Advisory Committee in 2010 to draft the revised substantial acquisition code. [ref: SEBI appoints committee to revamp Takeover Code; Achutan, Somasekhar Sundaresan and Kumar Desai represent the legal community, Bar and Bench] [ref: Report of the Takeover Regulations Advisory Committee, Securities and Exchange Board of India] Sundaresan provided advice to the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission under Justice B.N. Srikrishna between 2011 and 2013, which prepared the draft Indian Financial Code. [ref: Who tried to clip the RBI governor's wings?, Mint] He was also a member of SEBI's High-Level Committee on Insider Trading Regulations in 2013, chaired by Justice N.K. Sodhi. [ref: Report of the High Level Committee to Review the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 1992, Securities and Exchange Board of India] Sundaresan was appointed by the Supreme Court of India to a six-member expert panel, reviewing securities market regulatory mechanisms after allegations against the Adani Group in 2023. [ref: Supreme Court forms expert panel to probe any regulatory failure on Adani issue, The Hindu]

=== Judicial ===
Sundaresan was recommended for elevation to the bench by the Bombay High Court Collegium in October 2021. The file was returned for reconsideration by the Union Government due to views expressed by Sundaresan on social media regarding pending court matters. In January 2023, the Supreme Court Collegium, headed by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, strongly reiterated his name, stating that airing critical views on government policy does not compromise judicial independence or imply bias. [ref: Advocate Somasekhar Sundaresan appointed as an Additional Judge of the Bombay High Court, The Hindu] Sundaresan was then sworn in as an Additional Judge on 28 November 2023, before becoming a Permanent Judge on 18 September 2025.
