data.title: August Nimtz
data.text:
----

August H. Nimtz (born 1942) is an American political scientist. He is a professor of political science and of African American and African studies at the University of Minnesota.

His first book, Islam and Politics in East Africa (1980), based on fieldwork in the Tanzanian town of Bagamoyo, focused on the political role of its Sufi brotherhoods. Since 2000 Nimtz has written mainly about Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin. His books include Marx and Engels: Their Contribution to the Democratic Breakthrough (2000), a two-volume study of Lenin's electoral strategy (2014), a comparison of Marx and Frederick Douglass written with Kyle A. Edwards (2024), and a reply to Cedric Robinson's Black Marxism (2026).

== Early life and career ==
Born in 1942 [ref: August Nimtz: History and Contingency in the Making of a Black Communist, Minneapolis Interview Project] to a New Orleans family, [ref: Double Ring Ceremony Unites Nimtz-Towns In New York City, The Louisiana Weekly] Nimtz grew up under Jim Crow laws, attending schools that were segregated by law. [ref: "Black Marxism" Under Debate, 40 Years On, Cosmonaut] He took a Bachelor of Arts at Purdue University in 1963 [ref: Receiving Degrees, New Orleans States-Item] and a Ph.D. in political science at Indiana University in 1973. [ref: August H. Nimtz, jr. Islam and Politics in East Africa: The Sufi Order in Tanzania. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press. 1980. Pp. xvi, 234. $20.00, The American Historical Review] His doctoral research was based on fieldwork in the Tanzanian coastal town of Bagamoyo, where he lived in 1969 and 1970 and later visited. [ref: Islam in Tanzania - Islam and Politics in East Africa. The Sufi Order in Tanzania. By August H. Nimtz Jr. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 1980. Pp. xvi + 234, The Journal of African History] His first book was a shortened and revised version of the thesis.

Nimtz has taught at the University of Minnesota since 1971. He is a professor of political science and of African American and African studies there. [ref: August Nimtz, College of Liberal Arts, University of Minnesota] In 2002 he received the Horace T. Morse-University of Minnesota Alumni Association Award for Outstanding Contributions to Undergraduate Education. [ref: Distinguished Teachers Morse-Alumni, Scholars Walk]

Nimtz was a member of the Socialist Workers Party (SWP) from 1972 to 1995. He co-chaired the Minnesota Committee on Southern Africa from 1976 to 1978 and the Twin Cities chapter of the National Black Independent Political Party from 1981 to 1983. [ref: Voter's guide: City primary election, Minneapolis Star and Tribune] He twice ran for office for the SWP: for mayor of Minneapolis in 1985, [ref: Mayor, Minneapolis Star and Tribune] and the next year as running mate to Tom Jaax, its candidate for governor of Minnesota. [ref: Socialist candidate for governor wants public steel control, The Duluth News-Tribune]

== Works ==
Nimtz's first book came out of his doctoral fieldwork and was about Islam and politics in Tanzania. His later books are about Marx, Engels and Lenin, and several of them are about race and slavery in the United States.

=== Islam and politics in East Africa ===
Nimtz's first book Islam and Politics in East Africa: The Sufi Order in Tanzania came out in 1980. It examines the political role of the tariqa, or Sufi brotherhood, in East Africa under German and British colonial rule and through independence. [ref: Review of Islam and Politics in East Africa: The Sufi Order in Tanzania, The International Journal of African Historical Studies] Nimtz argues that the reason the brotherhoods grew was because they gave leadership roles to African Muslims, which they could not get within mainstream Islam. [ref: Review of Islam and Politics in East Africa: The Sufi Order in Tanzania, The American Political Science Review] The book ends with thirteen propositions meant to apply beyond East Africa. Norman R. Bennett reviewed the book in the American Historical Review and called it a major contribution that went well beyond earlier guesswork about the brotherhoods. Ibrahim Abu-Lughod called the book an important study in the American Political Science Review and C. C. Stewart wrote that the book opened a debate that had not been possible before in East Africa.

Bennet and Stewart felt the thirteen propositions at the end of the book were weak. Bennett wrote that they were commonsense conclusions from evidence and the latter called several of the propositions circular. Abu-Lughod wrote that the book stopped at the independence struggle and did not cover what happened to the brotherhoods afterwards. Marguerite Ylvisaker reviewed the book in the International Journal of African Historical Studies and wrote that she doubted Nimtz's claim that the split between "black" and "white" was the basic division in Swahili society. She also added that women's membership got only a brief mention.

=== Marx scholarship ===
Marx and Engels: Their Contribution to the Democratic Breakthrough was published in 2000. It argues that Marx and Engels were leading figures in the democratic movement of the nineteenth century and that what they went through in the revolutions of 1848 and 1849 shaped their later ideas. [ref: Review of Marx and Engels: Their Contribution to the Democratic Breakthrough, Science & Society] [ref: The Philosophy and Politics of Freedom, Monthly Review] The book follows their work in the Communist League, the revolutions themselves as well as Engels's work after Marx died. It includes a chapter that compares Marx with Alexis de Tocqueville. Paul Le Blanc reviewed the book in Monthly Review and wrote that it works both as a guide to the Marx/Engels Collected Works and as a political biography. Reviewing the book in Science & Society Mehmet Tabak called it a full account of their party work. Bradley J. Macdonald reviewed the book in Perspectives on Politics and credited Nimtz with putting their ideas back into the working-class struggles of the time. [ref: Review of Marx and Engels: Their Contribution to the Democratic Breakthrough, Perspectives on Politics]

Tabak, Le Blanc and Macdonald all thought that Nimtz claimed more than his evidence supported. Tabak said working-class organisation came before Marx and Engels and was developed largely independently of them. Le Blanc objected to the book's definition of the working class and also disagreed with what it says about the dictatorship of the proletariat. Macdonald said Nimtz had mistaken what Marx and Engels meant to do for what they actually achieved. He further wrote that his case against the "Marxologists" only works if books such as the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and Capital are left out.

Marx, Tocqueville, and Race in America: The 'Absolute Democracy' or 'Defiled Republic (2003) grows out of the comparison in the earlier book. The book compares Tocqueville's writings on the United States with Marx's on slavery and the Civil War. [ref: Marx, Tocqueville, and race in America: the "absolute democracy" or "defiled republic", Berkeley Law Library catalogue] In a survey of Marx scholarship in English, Paul Blackledge described the book as an expansion of one chapter of Marx and Engels, and summed up its argument as being that Marx and Engels understood the American democracy of their day better than Tocqueville because they saw how much slavery and racism mattered. [ref: Marx for Today, Routledge] Richard Boyd, in Perspectives on Politics, praised the chapters on Marx and Engels. He called them detailed, and wrote that Nimtz recounts Marx's support for the Union cause with grace and passion. [ref: Review of Marx, Tocqueville and Race in America: The "Absolute Democracy" or "Defiled Republic", Perspectives on Politics] Boyd was much harder on the treatment of Tocqueville, which he called a straw man. In his opinion Nimtz attacks Tocqueville for views he did not hold. He also wrote that Democracy in America is treated as though it were only concerned with political institutions. He further objected that Nimtz applies a double standard on race, excusing Marx's racial insults while calling Tocqueville's views straightforwardly racist.

Nimtz wrote The Communist and the Revolutionary Liberal in the Second American Revolution: Comparing Karl Marx and Frederick Douglass in Real-Time (2024) with Kyle A. Edwards. The book traces Douglass from Garrisonian abolitionism to what the authors call revolutionary liberalism, and Marx from radical democracy to communism. It argues that the two converged during the Civil War and then diverged again. [ref: Marx and Douglass in Their Time, Against the Current] Jason Dawsey wrote a review of the book in Against the Current. He singled out the attention the book gives to Marx's journalism in the New York Daily Tribune and Die Presse, which he thought a useful corrective to recent scholarship's focus on the Grundrisse and Capital. Dawsey disliked the authors' talk of a "mind-meld" between the two men. He also wanted more on what was happening elsewhere in the world at the time.

"Black Marxism": A Marxist Critique (2026) is a reply to Cedric Robinson's Black Marxism: The Making of the Black Radical Tradition (1983). It gathers work Nimtz published over four decades, along with autobiographical writing and new essays. The centrepiece is his 1984 review of Robinson in the Journal of African Marxists, one of the first responses to that book. A 2002 essay answers the charge that Marx was Eurocentric. The volume closes with a new essay, "Revisiting Black Marxism Four Decades Later". Reviewing the book in Cosmonaut, Gary Levi called it the strongest available answer to charges about Marx's views on race. However, he wrote that Nimtz's strengths as a political historian do not carry over into the account of the years since the 1970s. He also found the claim that the United States is less racist and more tolerant than ever to be one-sided. Seth Sandronsky reviewed it in CounterPunch. For him the core of the book was its reading of what Marx and Engels wrote about the divisions between English and Irish workers, and between black and white workers in the United States. [ref: On Cedric Robinson's "Black Marxism", CounterPunch]

=== Lenin scholarship ===
Lenin's Electoral Strategy from Marx and Engels through the Revolution of 1905 and Lenin's Electoral Strategy from 1907 to the October Revolution of 1917 appeared in 2014. Both are subtitled The Ballot, the Streets or Both, and both deal with Lenin's leadership of the Bolshevik wing of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in the four Russian state Dumas. [ref: Vladimir Lenin as Democratic Vanguard Revolutionary, New Political Science] According to Nimtz Lenin used elections and parliaments for revolutionary ends more than anyone else, and that he took his lead from Marx and Engels. He describes Lenin's position as revolutionary parliamentarism: standing in elections while rejecting what Engels called parliamentary cretinism, the belief that winning seats could replace struggle outside parliament. [ref: Review of Lenin's Electoral Strategy from Marx and Engels through the Revolution of 1905 and Lenin's Electoral Strategy from 1907 to the October Revolution of 1917, Perspectives on Politics]

William W. Sokoloff, writing in New Political Science, called the books politically relevant. Bradley J. Macdonald in Perspectives on Politics contrasted the two volumes favorably against the stereotypical image of Lenin as a Jacobin, a believer in willpower and a hero of the anti-liberal crowd. Derrick Morrison, in Against the Current, called the books handbooks for anti-austerity activists. [ref: Election and Revolution, Against the Current] Sokoloff and Macdonald each had reservations. Sokoloff found Nimtz needlessly harsh towards other scholars. He also said Nimtz identifies too closely with Lenin so that the resulting Lenin is never wrong. Macdonald thought there was too much quotation of Lenin and also found the case for Lenin's present-day relevance weak. Todd Chretien said Nimtz was too absolute in tracing the split in the Second International mainly to disagreements about elections. [ref: Revolutionary parliamentarism? Lenin, the Bolsheviks, and the electoral arena, International Socialist Review]

=== Other works ===
In Marxism versus Liberalism: Comparative Real-Time Political Analysis (2019) Nimtz applies a method he calls comparative real-time political analysis. It compares rival figures against each other over the same events, and asks three questions of each: what they wrote, what their actions achieved as those events unfolded, and how accurately they read them. The book pairs Marx and Engels with Tocqueville on the French side of the European Spring, Marx with John Stuart Mill on the American Civil War, Lenin with Max Weber on the Russian Revolution of 1905, and Lenin with Woodrow Wilson on 1917 and the end of the First World War. [ref: The Democratic Quest: Marxism Versus Liberalism, New Politics] Matthew E. Strauss reviewed it in New Politics. The method, he thought, worked best in the comparison chapters and credited Nimtz with being open about its limits. He pointed out that Nimtz treats Domenico Losurdo's Liberalism: A Counter-History as an opponent when the two books complement each other.

Nimtz has also authored articles in academic journals. He wrote an article in Science & Society in 2015 on the first clash between Marxism and anarchism. He argued that the popular account, which traces the split to the debates of the First International, exaggerates their importance of those debates. He wrote that Marx and Engels never publicly confronted Mikhail Bakunin on what divided them. [ref: V. I. Lenin's Struggle Against Anarchism, International Critical Thought] There was a symposium on the article the following year. [ref: Revisiting Marxism and Anarchism, Science & Society]

== Selected publications ==

*Marx and Engels: Their Contribution to the Democratic Breakthrough, State University of New York Press
*Marx, Tocqueville, and Race in America: The "Absolute Democracy" or "Defiled Republic", Lexington Books
*Lenin's Electoral Strategy from Marx and Engels through the Revolution of 1905: The Ballot, the Streets or Both, Palgrave Macmillan
*Lenin's Electoral Strategy from 1907 to the October Revolution of 1917: The Ballot, the Streets or Both, Palgrave Macmillan
*The Ballot, the Streets or Both: From Marx and Engels to Lenin and the October Revolution, Haymarket Books
*Marxism versus Liberalism: Comparative Real-Time Political Analysis, Palgrave Macmillan
*The Communist and the Revolutionary Liberal in the Second American Revolution: Comparing Karl Marx and Frederick Douglass in Real-Time, Brill

data.title: Alex Pongrass
data.text:
Alexander "Alex" Pongrass (10 November 1923 – 9 June 2000) was a Hungarian-born Australian businessman and football administrator. Co-founder of the National Soccer League (NSL) alongside Frank Lowy. Pongrass was a long-time chairman of St George-Budapest Soccer Club.

== Early life ==
Born into a Jewish family in 1923, he was the second of three brothers. He began a textile apprenticeship and studied bookkeeping.

In 1939, following the outbreak of World War II, 16-year-old Pongrass left home to work in his uncle’s newspaper distribution business. His parents later perished in the Auschwitz concentration camp. His brother, George, survived internment in the Dachau concentration camp.

In 1944, during the German occupation of Hungary, Pongrass joined the Jewish underground resistance. Utilising forged identity papers, he posed as a liaison officer with the SS guards command. He successfully escorted Hungarian Jews to the protection of Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who saved thousands of Jews from execution and forced death marches by issuing protective Swedish passports. [ref: Obituary - Alexander (Alex) Pongrass - Obituaries Australia, oa.anu.edu.au] [ref: Biographies of 22 outstanding Hungarian migrants, Hungarian Immigration in Australia.]

== Business career ==
Partnering with his brother George, Alex established an engineering works in Sydney (later Pongrass Brothers Pty Ltd). During the 1960s and 70s, the company expanded into commercial boatbuilding, metal furniture, and plumbing, eventually employing over 600 people.

== Football administration ==
=== St George-Budapest ===
Pongrass served as a benefactor and chairman of the St George-Budapest Soccer Club. In 1958, he became president for over 40 years until the late 1990s. Under his leadership, the club became an powerhouse in Australian football, constructing its own rectangular venue, St George Stadium at Barton Park, which hosted local and international fixtures. [ref: Australian Professional Leagues, SFCU] [ref: The impact of football 'visionary' and recent Hall of Fame inductee Alex Pongrass AM, Football Australia] [ref: Alex Pongrass AM into the Football Australia Hall of Fame, St George Football Club] [ref: From Socceroos and Pele to a drug den. Now this stadium has been reborn, The Sydney Morning Herald]

Pongrass is credited with elevating the professional standards of the sport in Australia by actively recruiting top-tier, professional coaching talent. He hired national team manager Rale Rasic and Hungarian-Australian coach Frank Arok. During his tenure, St George-Budapest won five NSW First Division championships and captured the National Soccer League title in 1983. Pongrass also acted as a long-time mentor to Australian football legend Johnny Warren.

=== Foundation of the National Soccer League ===
On 5 April 1975, Pongrass and Hakoah's Frank Lowy convened a meeting of clubs where attendees signed a resolution of intent that led to the launch of the National Soccer League (NSL) in 1977. [ref: Minutes of Special Meeting on the Australian National Soccer League, Soccer News via Facebook] The NSL became the first national club competition of any football code in Australia.
== Honours ==
* In the 1988 Australia Day Honours, Pongrass was awarded the Member of the Order of Australia (AM) in recognition of his services to the game.
* In November 2024, he was posthumously inducted into the Football Australia Hall of Fame as a participant at Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium. [ref: Football Australia Hall of Fame, Wikipedia]

== Death ==
Pongrass passed away in Sydney on 9 June 2000. [ref: Family notices, The Sydney Morning Herald]

data.title: Drew Smith
data.text:
----

Drew Smith (born 1950) is an English food writer, critic, editor, broadcaster and translator. He was The Guardian restaurant columnist, editor of The Good Food Guide, and presenter and investigative journalist of Channel 4’s Food File TV programme. His books include Oyster, a Gastronomic History of the World (with Recipes); Soupology, Six Broths for 70 Soups; and Modern Cooking: From the First Backstreet Bistros of Lyons to the Finest Restaurants. He also translated La Mère Brazier: The Mother of Modern French Cooking, by Eugénie Brazier into English and acted as a consultant editor on the first translation of The Talisman of Happiness, by Ada Boni.

== Food journalism and broadcasting ==
Smith was appointed editor of The Good Food Guide in 1981, [ref: ] after winning the restaurant writer of the year award at the Glenfiddich Food and Drink Awards. [ref: ] He held the post of editor until 1989 [ref: FOOD & DRINK / Undercover with a guide leader: 'The Good Food Guide', The Independent].
Whilst at The Good Food Guide [ref: All Consuming: The instant Sunday Times bestseller: Why We Eat the Way We Eat Now, Random House], Smith coined the term Modern British Cooking to describe regional and traditional British cuisine.. He had strong views on some regional cuisine, describing in 1982 that the lack of good food options in the North East England was a "black hole of gastronomy". [ref: A Geordie gourmet, The Independent]

In 1981 he was appointed restaurant columnist for The Guardian [ref: Drew Smith, Caterer & Hotelkeeper], where he stayed until 1990. When Smith inspected the London branch of Maxim's restaurant in 1983 without wearing a tie, the door staff presented Smith with a selection of public school ties to borrow while dining. The Guardian's headline on the resultant review went: "Sunshine, at £18, I’ll eat it stark naked with chopsticks if I like." [ref: From veggie fritters to fish ice-cream: 200 years of Guardian food, The Guardian]

In 1991 Smith launched Channel 4’s investigative food programme Food File. [ref: Channel 4 8:30: Food File, The Times] Notable episodes include one that explored The Mediterranean diet for the first time on British TV, and an exposé of the potential harm of saturated fats. [ref: Television - Eschewing the fat: Food File, Channel 4, The Times]

Smith is also known for his radio and podcast work. He presented A beginner’s guide to the oysters on BBC Sounds and was featured on the BBC’s The Food Programme. [ref: A beginners guide to the oyster, BBC]

Smith has contributed to newspapers and magazines, including The Sunday Times, The Guardian and The Independent, as well as being cited in several books [ref: The Sociology of Tourism: Theoretical and Empirical Investigations, Routledge] and articles about food and hospitality.

== Books ==
Smith is a book author and editor. His works include Oyster, a Gastronomic History of the World (with Recipes) [ref: A potted history of the oyster in London, The Standard] – voted one of American Vogue’s books of the year – Soupology, Six Broths for 70 Soups [ref: Broth to Bowl by Drew Smith] and Modern Cooking: From the First Backstreet Bistros of Lyons to the Finest Restaurants.
He was instrumental in bringing two European classic recipe books to English audiences for the first time: La Mère Brazier: The Mother of Modern French Cooking, a French classic by Eugénie Brazier [ref: La Mère Brazier, Elwin Street Productions] [ref: The Queen of the French Kitchen, The Daily Beast], the first woman awarded six Michelin stars [ref: Mère Brazier, guide.michelin.com], which Smith translated into English and was named the 2018 book of the year by The Observer. He also published
The Talisman of Happiness by Ada Boni [ref: The Book That Taught Nonna to Cook Is Coming to America, The New York Times], for which he served as consultant editor on the first English translation of the Italian cooking book.
Smith also collaborated on a series of books with Dr Stephan Domenig of the FX Mayr clinic in Austria, exploring the benefits of the alkaline diet.
He is currently editor-at-large for book publisher Elwin Street Productions.

== Other work ==
Smith is one of the founders of the Guild of Food Writers and acted as Head of Food Policy at the London Docklands Development Corporation from 1999 to 2001.

== Awards ==
Glenfiddich Food and Drink Awards, restaurant critic of the year 1979, 1982, 1985.

data.title: Hackelia latifolia
data.text:
Hackelia latifolia, commonly known as Forest Hound's Tongue, [ref: Species: Hackelia latifolia (Forest Hound's-Tongue), bie.ala.org.au] is a species of flowering plant in the borage family. The species is native to Australia. [ref: A new Cynoglossum species, and transfers to Hackelia in eastern Australian Boraginaceae, Australian Systematic Botany]

== Distribution ==
The plant is endemic to Australia and is found in Victoria, New South Wales, and Queensland.

== Description ==
Hackelia latifolia has a trailing habit with stems to 1m long, stems have numerous prickly and hairlike hooks sometimes called setae. Leaves are oval shaped (ovate to broad-ovate) and contain similar prickly hairs. [ref: VicFlora: Hackelia latifolia, vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au]

The flowers are small, with usually white sepals.

== References ==

data.title: CE-103
data.text:
CE-103 is an analog of modafinil, a member of a series of structurally related heterocyclic derivatives. [ref: Structure-Activity Relationships of Novel Thiazole-Based Modafinil Analogues Acting at Monoamine Transporters, Journal of Medicinal Chemistry]

CE-103 inhibits dopamine reuptake with an IC50 of 14.73 μM, an IC50 of 420.1 μM at the norepinephrine transporter (NET), while its effect on serotonin transporter (SERT) is negligible, therefore it is a modestly selective dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Sprague Dawley rats given CE-103 at doses 1 and 10 mg/kg showed an increased working memory index in a radial arm maze. Administration of the compound also decreased levels of complexes containing phosphorylated dopamine transporter (pDAT) and D1 receptor, while significantly increasing levels of complexes containing D2 receptor and D3 receptor. [ref: A heterocyclic compound CE-103 inhibits dopamine reuptake and modulates dopamine transporter and dopamine D1-D3 containing receptor complexes, Neuropharmacology]

It is closely related to CE-123, being a positional isomer.

data.title: 2026–27 Arkansas Razorbacks men's basketball team
data.text:
----

The 2026–27 Arkansas Razorbacks men's basketball team will represent the University of Arkansas during the 2026–27 season. The Razorbacks will be led by third year head coach John Calipari, and play their home games at Bud Walton Arena in Fayetteville, Arkansas as a member of the Southeastern Conference.

==Previous season==

Arkansas finished John Calipari's second season with a record of 28-9 and ranked No. 15. The Razorbacks won the SEC Tournament championship for only the second time (their first since 2000), and made it to the Sweet 16 for the second consecutive season. [ref: Arkansas runs aways from Vandy, claims second SEC Championship, Southeastern Conference]

Freshman guard Darius Acuff would earn SEC Freshman of the Year and SEC Player of the Year honors, and would be named a first team All-American, which had not happened since Sidney Moncrief earned first team honors in 1979. [ref: Acuff Voted 1st Team AP All-America]

Acuff was drafted with the seventh overall pick in the NBA Draft by the Sacramento Kings. Teammates Meleek Thomas and Trevon Brazile were also drafted by the Cleveland Cavaliers and Denver Nuggets, respectively. [ref: https://www.espn.com/nba/draft/rounds]

==Offseason==

====2026 Recruiting Class====

As of May 20, 2026, Arkansas has signed all 4 players to their 2026 recruiting class. [ref: https://www.on3.com/college/arkansas-razorbacks/basketball/2026/commits/] Shooting guard/small forward JJ Andrews, the son of former NFL offensive lineman Shawn Andrews, is the No. 1 player in Arkansas and a 5-star recruit. He was named a McDonald's All-American. Arkansas also signed small forward Abdou Toure, a high 4 star recruit and Top 50 player nationally, who is also the #1 player in Connecticut. 7'0" power forward Miikka Muurinen, a 5-star player, signed with Arkansas on May 19, and 5 star combo guard Jordan Smith Jr, who is also a McDonald's All-American, signed on May 20. Arkansas has the top class on 247Sports, the No. 2 class on Rivals/On3 (just behind Duke), and No. 1 on ESPN.

The 2026-27 Penn State Nittany Lions basketball team will represent Penn State University during the 2026-27 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. They will be led by fourth-year head coach Mike Rhoades, and will play their home games at Bryce Jordan Center located in State College, Pennsylvania as members of the Big Ten Conferene (B1G).

== Previous season ==

The Nittany Lions finished the 2025–26 season 12–20, 3–17 in Big Ten play to finish in 18th place. data.title: Mallard x Pacific black duck hybrid
data.text:
A mallard x pacific black duck hybrid is the hybrid offspring between a feral or domestic mallard (Anas platyrhynchos), and a pacific black duck (A. superciliosa) (abbreviated as PBD [ref: How Hybrid Ducks are Threatening the Future of Native Ducks, The Hobart + Launceston Independent Local] or sometimes called the grey duck). Hybrid ducks can result from the crossing of either a mallard drake x a female pacific black duck, or a pacific black drake x a female mallard. [ref: The breeding performance of Grey duck, Anas superciliosa, mallard, Anas platyrhynchos, and their hybrids in captivity, Academia] Though hybrid ducks are fertile, [ref: Identifying Mallard x Pacific Black Duck Hybrids, eBird] [ref: Ducks, Northern Midlands Council] [ref: Ducks, Derwent Estuary Program] they are not widely considered a unique species, and are classified under the same genus as their parent species. The mallard is known to hybridise with twenty-six species of waterfowl, with most being dabbling ducks of the genus Anas.

== History ==
Originally occurring in Eurasia and North America, the northern mallard was introduced to areas overlapping with the range of the Polynesian and Australasian occurring pacific black duck throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, being introduced to Australia in the 1860s (as early as 1862), and to New Zealand in 1867. The mallard was introduced to Australia and New Zealand as a gamefowl, but also through efforts by acclimisation societies as a means of creating an environment reminiscent of the native Europe of many settlers. [ref: Mallard, Australian Museum] Both species are dabbling ducks of the genus Anas that occupy ecologically similar niches in their respective ranges, and have naturally come into contact in areas of distributive overlap. In both Australia and New Zealand, its range increased rapidly in the 1950s as agricultural areas were developed in the post-war period. Historic records indicate that hybridisation increased significantly following this range expansion, with rates of hybridisation being less than 3% in New Zealand prior to 1958.

=== Introduction to Australia ===
The mallard was introduced to Australia as early as 1862, and saw prolific expansion into wetlands across the continent. The species was introduced incrementally to each state, first arriving in Victoria as early as 1864 with additional introduction efforts in 1971–72 where it has seen the most distributive expansion and success. It was introduced to Sydney and Perth before 1900 and before 1912 respectively, and has since become widespread in the proximity of each capital. The mallard has been noted to have spread throughout South Australia and Queensland too, occurring as far north as Maryborough in the latter, though it has only formed non-breeding populations in the state. The species can also be found uncommonly in Tasmania and the King and Flinders Islands north of the state. Lord Howe Island, Macquarie Island, and Norfolk Island all possess introduced mallard populations as well. While they occur here only in small densities, they have already contributed to a drastic decline in native pacific black duck populations regardless. Much of the hybrids present on Lord Howe Island in particular appear to be descended from New Zealand stock, and may have migrated from the mainland. [ref: The occurrence of hybridisation between the Pacific Black Duck (Anas superciliosa) and other dabbling ducks (Genus: Anas) in Australia, Victoria University] The lack of phenotypic expression and diversity of purebred pacific black ducks on the island may indicate that the species has become locally extinct there.

=== Introduction to New Zealand ===
The mallard is stated to have been introduced to New Zealand as early as 1867. Interbreeding with the native pacific black duck population began soon after introduction, with the first hybrid ducks being reported as early as 1885. The Natural History of Canterbury did not mention the mallard in its 1927 edition, indicating that the initial introduction of mallards may have been to some degree unsuccessful, though, the pacific black duck is noted as having declined in numbers due to hunting. [ref: Hybridisation, and the Conservation of the Grey Duck in New Zealand, UC Research Repository] Mallards were introduced from North America again in the 1920s–40s, and subsequent introduction of Australian feral populations occurred sometime in the 20th century as well. These later introductions were more significant, and may have been more successful due to the pacific black duck population having already been extricated from some areas due to hunting. New Zealand mallards have experienced significant introgression from hybridisation since their introduction, becoming no longer genetically consistent with the original stock of northern mallards introduced throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, constituting a novel genetic cluster (often referred to as a hybrid swarm) today.

==== Purposeful hybridisation ====
In 1967, the former New Zealand Wildlife Service (NZWS) commenced a controlled hybrid breeding programme in order to "establish objective criteria for the identification of hybrids". The programme was conducted at the Pūkaha National Wildlife Centre (at the time known as the Mount Bruce Native Bird Reserve) near Masterton, and involved the assemblage of a stock of both species for purposeful interbreeding. Ducks were housed in two large aviaries equipped with freshwater terraces of a maximum depth of 2cm (0.8in) fed by a stream and bolstered by boulders to discourage erosion and allow "loafing" behaviour (a position assumed by a contented duck during relaxation). Artificial and natural nesting sites were provided in the form of tin hutches, open faced boxes separated by hessian to reduce visibility of ducks between pairs, and areas of dense long grass or other foliage in order to create ideal conditions for breeding. Nests were readily accepted by pairs of both species, which were fed crushed oyster shells and granulated lime in order to meet individual calcium demands characteristic of laying three or more clutches at a heightened frequency. Though nests were occupied quickly, pacific black duck pairs did not lay at all in the first year of the study, whereas mallards did, likely having adapted to captivity faster comparatively. While mallards typically laid larger clutches than pacific black ducks, hybrid females (a group referred to in the study as F1) tended to lay clutches between the size of both parent species. High embryo fatality was recorded among clutches resulting from crosses between pacific black duck drakes and F1 females, indicating gametic incompatibility resulting from backcrossing. Despite this however, backcrossing F1 females with mallard drakes resulted in higher rates of embryonic development and hatchling survival comparatively to backcrossing with pacific black drakes. Backcrossed hybrids were found to produce viable offspring that progressed to hatching, whereas F1 x F1 pairs laid fertile clutches that did not hatch.
== Appearance ==
Mallard x pacific black duck hybrids are typically visually distinct from both parent species, however, the expression of phenotypical traits from either parent species varies significantly between individuals. Hybrids are often said to express traits more in common with mallards than black ducks, [ref: Hybridization, Introgression, and Morphometric Differentiation between Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) and Grey Duck (Anas superciliosa) in Otago, New Zealand, The Auk – Advances in Ornithology] however, two morphologically distinct hybrid populations in the Otago region of southeast New Zealand have been noted to resemble mallards and pacific black ducks respectively. The phenotype of a hybrid is not always indicative of its genetic makeup, with analysis of hybrid mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) conducted in 2019 finding that; while an individual may express morphological characteristics congruent with one parent species, it may possess the mtDNA of the other. [ref: Can grey duck (Anas superciliosa) x mallard (mallard) hybrids be recognised in the field?, Notornis]

=== Legs and bills ===

It is often stated that hybrid ducks are easily distinguished by their bright orange legs, which are considered to exclusively occur in hybrids. Purebred pacific black ducks can express orange legs, though they are far less saturated than those of mallards, and sampling of phenotypes among the species indicates a prevalence of olive-green, grey, of khaki coloured legs over oranges or yellows in New Zealand populations. In Tasmania, the only duck species that possesses bright orange legs akin to those of the mallard is the Australasian shoveler (Anas rhynchotis). [ref: Living with Ducks, Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania] A 2019 study conducted by the Ornithological Society of New Zealand that analysed the phenotypic expression of hybrids to quantify the recognisability of their traits in the wild found that; 95.8% hybrid drakes possessed bright orange legs characteristic of mallards. Orange-tinged legs may appear more frequently amongst hybrid ducks that are superficially identical to pacific black ducks, though if the individual does not express any other tells of hybridisation, the morphological distinction is usually best left ignored. Legs can however, be used in the distinction between purebred pacific black ducklings and juveniles, which exclusively possess grey legs compared to the orange-tinged legs of hybrid ducklings.

The bill is another point of scrutiny in determining a mallard x pacific black duck hybrid. In purebred pacific black duck, the bill is almost always a solid slate grey colour with subtle green undertones, appearing very apparently different from the variable shades of bright yellows, oranges, browns, and brown-greys of female mallards and drakes. Obvious hybrids usually possess blotchy bills with a colouration more reminiscent to mallards, while more cryptic hybrids tend to only have mallard-adjacent colouration around the base and tip of the bill.

=== Plumage ===
While female mallards and some individual pacific black ducks may appear superficially similar due to morphological consistencies between their dappled tan, brown, and dark greyish brown plumage, both parent species are very easily separated by facial markings. Among both female pacific black ducks and drakes, a pair of lateral black bars are apparent on the face, with a thick superciliary bar extending from the base of the bill and streaking through the eye before ceasing around the ear, and a thinner partially less defined black bar extending from the gape, separating the cheek into two prominent cream patches. Female mallards possess a singular, lighter coloured, fair less defined bar streaking through the eye. Hybrid ducks are likely to share traits from both species, and may sport a darker face with less developed or absent cheek bars, typically making for an obvious tell. Another sexually monomorphic trait of pacific black ducks is the black crown of feathers along the top of the skull. It is normally solidly coloured in purebred pacific black ducks, and exhibits dappling or streaking by lighter feathers to various degrees amongst hybrid ducks.

Per the 2019 ornithological study, 86% of females and 52% of drakes derived from the interbreeding of mallard drakes x female pacific black ducks, and 16% of females and 24% of drakes derived from pacific black drakes x female mallards possessed facial plumage more in common with pacific black ducks than mallards. Additionally, 36% of examined purebred pacific black ducks possessed facial mottling and dark napes that are more frequently identified in hybrids. Mallard drakes are well-known for their vibrant green heads and chestnut coloured breasts and throats which make them easily distinguishable from both female pacific black ducks and drakes. Consequently, a duck that possesses a green head but otherwise has a phenotype congruent with a pacific black duck, is certainly a hybrid (pictured). Additionally, Yellow-orange legs have been found to be linked to the partial or total expression of a green head in drakes.

Pacific black ducks possess very slight cream-coloured edging around each of their darker coloured body feathers, with the trims being more pronounced among females. These trims are further broadened in hybrids, where streaking amongst dark body feathers often results in the creation of an overall lighter coloured plumage. Hybrids may also possess upcurled tail feathers, a trait common with mallards. Hybrid ducks derived from crossing between a wild pacific black duck and a domestic mallard will often have far lighter breast, throat, and underbelly feathers common with the solid white plumage of the domestic parent.

=== Wings ===
Both species possess an irridescent speculum, a rectangular patch of coloured feathers located in the secondary flights of some birds (most well known in dabbling ducks). In pacific black ducks, the speculum is usually a beetle green with purplish indigo accents, whereas in mallards it is often more of a blue-green. Speculums are not necessarily a reliable tell of hybridisation, as the angle at which they are viewed in direct sunlight may skew the perception of their colour. The plumage around the speculum is less similar between species, with pacific black ducks typically having thick black trailing edges framing the speculum with occasional thinner borders of light tan, while mallard speculums are framed with thick white trailing edges. Amongst hybrids, the latter is more commonly expressed. 59% of hybrids derived from mallard drakes x female pacific black ducks examined in the 2019 study possessed speculum edging common with both purebred pacific black ducks as well as mallards, where the lighter buffing varied from low to high thickness between individuals derived from the cross. 68% of hybrids derived from pacific black drakes x female mallards exhibited speculum edging common in female mallards. Wing patterning varies significantly between hybrid individuals and is often more obviously indicative of hybridisation when referenced against parent species.

== Threats to pacific black duck population ==
As both pacific black ducks and mallards exist in similar environments in their native ranges, the species come into frequent contact in the advent of distributive overlap, resulting in the proliferation of hybrid ducks which compete for resources with their native parent species.

=== Genetic introgression and outcompetition of pacific black ducks in New Zealand ===
The New Zealand pacific black duck (A. s. superciliosa) has already suffered massive population reduction from most of its native range following the introduction of mallards. [ref: Native Pacific black ducks at risk in Tasmania due to introduced species, ABC News Australia] As of 1958, the introduced mallard constituted 53% of both species combined population in Otago, increasing to 82% in 1977. In 1981–82, plumage analysis indicated that a hybridisation rate of 51% had accumulated between the species, with the proportion of pacific black ducks in the collective population having decreased to just 4.5%, a density believed to be unsustainable for the species. As of 2025, pure genetic pockets of pacific black duck were recorded from just 9% of sites examined in the core of their range in the western portion of South Island. [ref: Anthropogenic Hybridization Contributes to the Naturalization of Introduced Domestic Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) at the Expense of Native New Zealand Gray Ducks (A. s. superciliosa), PubMed] Across both North and South Island, pacific black ducks constitute 6–10% of collective population samples, demonstrating the extent to which the species has been outcompeted by the mallard. Analysis of the genetic vulnerability of New Zealand mallards indicate that the populations possess a higher predisposed resilience to selective pressures and ecological change than pacific black ducks, raising concerns that they may completely outcompete them.

While the breeding cycles of both species are generally asynchronous (beginning a month earlier in breeding populations of mallards), degradation and extirpation of native forests and wetlands as a result of urbanisation and agricultural expansion likely disarmed any reproductive isolation between the two species as their distributive overlap has continued to increase since initial introduction. Pacific black ducks are more suited to undisturbed habitat comparatively to the more adaptable mallard, raising concerns that the former will suffer more extensive loss due to climate change as a result of further ecological disturbances. During breeding cycles, mallard drakes have been known to court to female pacific black ducks, though the inverse interaction does not occur at a reliably observable frequency, with a 5:2 ratio of mallard drake x female pacific black duck pairings occurring in the Waikato region of New Zealand. This mating bias may indicate forceful copulation of female pacific black ducks by mallard drakes, or a bypassing of courtship behaviour entirely in favour of mating. This conclusion is favoured by behavioural changes undergone by pacific black ducks when outnumbered by mallards observed in Australia, including a reluctance to feed and fleeing from interspecies confrontation, both indicative of mallard dominance. Mallard drakes are also often connoted as being "more aggressive" than pacific black drakes, typically in relation to their mating habits and related territorial nature. [ref: 'Aggressive' hybrid ducks spreading through Tasmania's waterways, Pulse Tasmania] The propensity of female mallards to lay replacement clutches within thirteen days between clutches while more than half of female pacific black ducks surveyed by the NZWS did not lay replacement clutches at all additionally increases potential for outcompetition.

=== Genetic introgression and outcompetition of pacific black ducks in Australia and Tasmania ===
Initially, it was considered that the hybridisation between both species was restricted to urban areas in Australia due to introduced mallards being derived mostly from released domestic stock, however, phenotypic analysis of South Australian populations and New South Wales specimens has determined that hybridisation does occur in rural duck populations. The overall frequency of hybridisation between mallards and Australian pacific black ducks (A. s. rogersi) is 1.5%, considerably lower than the frequency of hybridisation in New Zealand populations. New Zealand hybrids have been found to be present on Australia's east coast, and further migration events may have potential to increase hybridisation rates. Currently, hybridisation amongst Australian duck populations is considered to be a low threat, and a survey on the comparative population densities of both species in urban parks throughout Melbourne found that pacific black ducks outnumbered mallards at all sites.

A prominent driver of the mallard's distributive expansion and the proliferation of hybrids in Australian and Tasmanian waterways has been the purposeful accommodation of mallard populations by humans. Mallards are often fed by humans in urban parks, causing them to become acclimatised to reliable food sources and further increasing their distribution by allowing them to breed in areas of regular food stability. Mallards have also been known to outcompete pacific black ducks in feeding grounds, as they are larger bodied and more aggressive. In mainland Australia, mallards have not yet shown the propensity to exclude pacific black ducks entirely from urban parks were both species occur, though they exhibit dominant nesting and feeding tendencies. Mallard overpopulation as a result of overfeeding has also become a threat to duck habitat in Tasmania as well as some parts of mainland Australia, as large flocks of mallards trample native vegetation. Waterways that are overstocked with mallards are also subject to algal blooms, increased potential for harbouring botulism, and general quality degradation as a result of waste produced by the birds. In January of 1998, a newsletter by Hunter Bird Observers Inc. based in New Lambton, New South Wales, reported that a density of upwards of five hundred mallard x pacific black duck hybrids were inhabiting the junction of Lake Macquarie and Dora Creek, with the reason given for their inhabitation being feeding. [ref: Newsletter, Hunter Bird Observers Club Inc.]

In Tasmania, purebred pacific black duck populations are similarly threatened by genetic extirpation. Concern has been raised locally over the seemingly increasing rarity of purebred pacific black ducks in Hobart and the Derwent estuary as hybrid sightings increase. Much of the hybridisation occurring in Tasmania has been a direct result of illegal dumping of domestic mallards in natural or urban wetlands, or the mismanagement and subsequent loss of domestic mallards into the wild.

== Mitigation of hybridisation ==
In the May of 1998, the New Zealand Fish and Game Council alongside the Department of Conservation issued an official nationwide hunting season for hybrid ducks in order to attain a sample of the morphological and phenotypical characteristics of the ducks for future study and referral. Thousands of individuals were killed, with 1,992 being used in the Ornithological Society of New Zealand's study on the morphology of the hybrid and its recognisability in the field. 2,000 specimens shot in the season were sampled in a 2007 study, concluding that 74% of ducks sampled from the west coast, and 99% of ducks sampled from South Island exhibited hybrid morphology. The programme did not meaningfully reduce the hybrid population, which has continued to grow.

In conserving purebred populations of pacific black ducks, the Derwent Estuary Program and Tasmanian Government among other independent ecological preservation bodies recommend not to feed ducks of any species in order to prevent potential hybridisation from occurring between mallards and pacific black ducks seeking the same food sources. Feeding wild ducks is also generally advised against as it causes nutritional deficiencies which can result in deformations such as angel wing.The Tasmanian Government strongly advises owners of domestic ducks to "adequately contain" them in order to avoid potential further introduction of mallards into existing feral populations. This advice is frequently repeated as a measure to mitigate hybridisation and restrict potential opportunities for pacific black ducks to become outcompeted in their native range. Alternatively, muscovy ducks (Cairina moschata var. domestica), a breed that cannot hybridise with the pacific black duck, can also be kept.

== Natural hybridisation ==

The mallard and pacific black duck are known to naturally coexist on the Mariana Islands, an archipelago off the eastern coast of the Philippines and a part of the extremities of both species' distributions. It is hypothesised that the Mariana mallard (Anas oustaleti), an extinct dabbling duck once endemic to the archipelago may have in reality been a subspecies created from the hybridisation between the mallard and pacific black duck. [ref: Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Removing the Mariana Mallard and the Guam Broadbill From the Federal List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife, Federal Register] The taxonomic validity of the Mariana mallard is heavily debated, and it is currently undecided whether or not the population constituted a wholly new species, subspecies, or a hybrid swarm. The United States Fish and Wildlife Service designates the Mariana mallard as a subspecies; (A. p. oustaleti). Among the population, all females and a majority of drakes exhibited a phenotype congruent with pacific black ducks, though possessed bright orange legs and lacked cheek barring, both common in known hybrids. Conversely, a smaller percentage of males exhibited a phenotype congruent with male mallards, including the appearance of the speculum and general plumage. The variability of phenotypes and the propensity of the morphology of the Mariana mallard to match descriptions of known hybrids may support the conclusion that the population was the result of hybridisation.

data.text:
The Quartier des Archives is the 11th administrative district of Paris, located in the 3rd arrondissement, in the Marais. [ref: [https://www.lefigaro.fr/histoire/archives/2016/11/18/26010-20161118ARTFIG00308-le-marais-un-quartier-insalubre-sauve-par-andre-malraux-en-1962.php Le Marais: un quartier insalubre sauvé par André Malraux en 1962]] Its name refers to the Archives Nationales housed in the Hôtel de Soubise and the Hôtel de Rohan, to the west of the district. [ref: [https://www.persee.fr/doc/gazar_0016-5522_2019_num_254_2_5864 Le quadrilatère des Archives nationales à Paris, un site historique en mutation]]

The district is bordered:

* to the south by the Rue des Francs-Bourgeois and the Rue du Pas-de-la-Mule (border with the 4th arrondissement);
* to the east by the Boulevard Beaumarchais (border with the 11th arrondissement);
* to the north by the Rue Pastourelle, Rue de Poitou, and Rue du Pont-aux-Choux (border with the Quartier des Enfants-Rouges);
* to the west by the Rue des Archives (border with the Quartier Sainte-Avoye). [ref: [https://www.leparisien.fr/paris-75/paris-75004/a-paris-la-rue-des-archives-va-t-elle-concurrencer-l-avenue-montaigne-15-01-2016-5454753.php A Paris, la rue des Archives va-t-elle concurrencer l'avenue Montaigne ?]]

data.title: XFarm Technologies
data.text:
xFarm Technologies is a Swiss company with headquarters in Manno, operating in the agricultural technology sector. [ref: Una pioggia di milioni per una startup insediata in Ticino, Corriere del Ticino] It develops digital farm management tools used by farmers and agri-food supply chain operators, including farm management software (xFarm), Internet of Things (IoT) field sensors, decision support systems (DSS) and supply chain analytics software. [ref: xFarm Technologies, la startup agritech chiude il round Serie C da 36 milioni di euro - StartupItalia, StartupItalia]

Founded in 2017 as xFarm by Matteo Vanotti, xFarm Technologies took its current form in 2021, following the merger with the Italian company Farm Technologies. [ref: Digital ag platforms xFarm & Farm Technologies merge to become 'Spotify of agtech', AgFunderNews] [ref: xFarm merges with Farm Technologies to create leading agri-tech company, Startupticker] Between 2019 and 2024, the company raised funding in three rounds of €3 million, [ref: Agritech, xfarm chiude round da 3 mln con United Ventures, Fortune Italia] €17 million, [ref: xFarm, scommessa svizzera da 17 milioni sulla fattoria «smart», Il Sole 24 Ore] €36 million, [ref: La startup agritech xFarm Technologies raccoglie 36 milioni di euro per l'espansione globale, Forbes Italia] [ref: xFarm raises €36m to build superapp for farmers, Sifted] and it expanded internationally, acquiring Greenfield Technologies (Spain) [ref: xFarm integra a la extremeña Greenfield Technologies para consolidarse como líder europeo en el agrotech, elEconomista.es] and SpaceSense (France) in 2024, [ref: Agritech xFarm Technologies merges with Greenfield and Spacesense to hone its Geospatial AI, Tech.eu] [ref: XFarm Technologies cresce all'estero con SpaceSense in Francia e Greenfield in Spagna, Il Sole 24 Ore] and Checkplant (Brazil) in 2025. [ref: Suíça Xfarm Technologies Entra no Brasil para Investir em Agricultura Digital, Forbes Brasil]

At the time of the Checkplant transaction, the company reported supporting more than 500,000 farms across 8.3 million hectares. Since July 2025, xFarm Technologies has been a certified B Corporation. [ref: xFarm Technologies SA - Certified B Corporation - B Lab, www.bcorporation.net]

== History and international expansion ==

Matteo Vanotti, who serves as the company's chief executive officer, founded xFarm in 2017 to support the management of his family's farm in Monferrato, Piedmont. [ref: ] In 2019, the company closed a €3 million funding round led by United Ventures.

In 2021, xFarm merged with Farm Technologies, an Italian company developing agronomic algorithms, thus becoming xFarm Technologies. At the time, the company reportedly supported around 80,000 farms across one million hectares.

In 2022, xFarm Technologies closed a €17 million Series B round led by Swisscom Ventures. At the time, the company was active in Switzerland, Italy and Spain, where it had local branches. [ref: Swiss-Italian startup xFarm Technologies secures €17 million, Startupticker]

In April 2024, the company acquired both SpaceSense, a French company specializing in geospatial artificial intelligence and satellite-based climate intelligence, and Greenfield Technologies, a Spanish company active in soil characterization.

In October 2024, xFarm Technologies closed a €36 million Series C round led by Partech with existing and new investors, [ref: XFarm Technologies punta sull'intelligenza artificiale. 450 mila aziende sulla piattaforma, la Repubblica] [ref: XFarm lève 36 millions d'euros pour son application de gestion agricole, L'Usine Digitale] including Mouro Capital, the venture arm of Banco Santander, linked to the creation of a fintech and insurtech division dedicated to risk and credit management services for farmers. [ref: Mouro Capital (Santander) aterriza en la 'agrotech' suiza xFarm en una ronda de 36 millones, La información]

In March 2025, xFarm Technologies officially entered the Latin America market through the acquisition of Checkplant, a Brazilian company operating the Farmbox platform in Brazil, Colombia and Paraguay. [ref: Europeia xFarm e brasileira CheckPlant fecham "M&A da agricultura digital", AgFeed] [ref: xFarm si espande in America Latina, accordo con Checkplant, L'Informatore Agrario]

== Products and services ==
xFarm Technologies develops xFarm, a farm management platform available as both a mobile and a web application, supporting agronomic, administrative, economic and environmental management of farms. [ref: Farm-Management mit KI: Satelliten, Sensoren, Modelle, top agrar] [ref: Catalyzing Digital Innovation in AgTech: The Case of XFARM as a Digital Innovation Ecosystem, Research and Innovation Forum 2025 Vol2] The company also provides a line of IoT devices, including weather stations, soil moisture sensors and leaf wetness sensors, [ref: Enablers to Digitalization in Agriculture: A Case Study from Italian Field Crop Farms in the Po River Valley, with Insights for Policy Targeting, Agriculture] [ref: Dai sensori all'intelligenza artificiale: "Controlliamo 700 ettari di frutteti", Il Resto del Carlino] complementing the software and feeding data into forecasting models and DSS. In addition, xFarm Technologies provides satellite imagery for remote field monitoring.

In December 2025, the company launched an artificial intelligence assistant available via the WhatsApp messaging service and connected to the xFarm platform, allowing farmers to record field operations through text or voice messages, and receive alerts on weather conditions, insect attacks and plant disease risks. [ref: Agricoltura, arriva nuovo assistente virtuale basato sull'intelligenza artificiale - Mondo Agricolo - Ansa.it, Agenzia ANSA]

=== Supply chain projects ===
xFarm Technologies developed the Barilla Farming platform for the soft wheat supply chain behind Barilla's Mulino Bianco products, involving 2,600 farms in Italy, France, Austria and Eastern Europe in the traceability project. [ref: Barilla, con XFarm diventa hi-tech la filiera del grano tenero di Mulino Bianco, Il Sole 24 ORE] In 2024, a new collaboration started on the basil supply chain used for Barilla's pesto, involving 25 supplying farms and cooperatives across 310 hectares. [ref: Barilla con xFarm Technologies digitalizza l'intera filiera del basilico, Italiafruit News]

Other projects include the digitalization of the Granlatte dairy chain for Granarolo, covering around 600 farms, gathering herd data, supporting feed crop planning and sustainability assessments, [ref: Granarolo mette in pista 300 milioni di investimenti in 3 anni, Il Sole 24 Ore] and a supply chain digitalization program with the rice producer Riso Gallo. [ref: Riso Gallo si affida a xFarm Technologies per la digitalizzazione della filiera, Agrisole - Il Sole 24 Ore] The company took part in the Agrometeo monitoring project with Conserve Italia and the University of Bologna, [ref: Agrometeo: Conserve Italia presenta i primi risultati su difesa fitosanitaria, rese e consumi idrici, Italiafruit News] with the installation of 600 sensors across 700 hectares of orchards to support irrigation and crop protection decisions, and a project for the tomato processor Tomato Farm, involving 200 growers. [ref: Filiera del pomodoro digitalizzata, accordo Hubfarm e xFarm - Notizie - Ansa.it, Agenzia ANSA]

The xFarm platform was also used by Lavazza, combined with blockchain technology, in a traceability pilot on two coffee farms in Brazil. [ref: Using the Transparency of Supply Chain Powered by Blockchain to Improve Sustainability Relationships with Stakeholders in the Food Sector: The Case Study of Lavazza, Sustainability]

=== Other collaborations ===
In 2023, xFarm Technologies signed an agreement with the fertilizer producer Yara for the development of digital tools for nutrient use efficiency. [ref: Accordo tra Yara e xFarm, L'Informatore Agrario] In the same year, the company entered a three-year project with Dyson Farming in the United Kingdom, to collect and process farm operations data. [ref: Dyson Farming increases profit to £5.2m in 2023, Farmers Weekly] In 2024, xFarm Technologies joined Bunge's regenerative agriculture program in Brazil, providing farmers with field sensors and DSS fed by the resulting data. [ref: Bunge signs strategic partnership with xFarm Technologies - Revista Cultivar, Revista Cultivar]

== Awards and recognition ==

In 2022, xFarm Technologies entered the Top 100 Swiss Startup Award ranking. [ref: xFarm Technologies SA, www.top100startups.swiss] In December 2024, it was named Startup of the Year at SIOS24 Winter organized by StartupItalia. [ref: ] In 2025, it was ranked 37th in the Sifted 100: DACH & CEE leaderboard. [ref: Sifted 100: DACH & CEE — Fastest-Growing Startups 2025, sifted.eu]

data.title: Boeotia Football Clubs Association
data.text:
Boeotia Football Clubs Association (Greek: Ένωση Ποδοσφαιρικών Σωματείων Βοιωτίας) is the governing body of association football in the regional unit of Boeotia, Greece. [ref: Ε.Π.Σ. Βοιωτίας, Ελληνικό Ποδόσφαιρο] Based in Livadeia, it is a member of the Hellenic Football Federation (HFF). It is responsible for organizing local league championships and the local Cup, as well as youth championships. It also coordinates the regional representative teams (Youth and Children), which compete at the national level.

== History ==
It was founded as an independent association in 1973; [ref: Ιστορική Αναδρομή, EPS Boiotias] in previous years, specifically from 1928 to 1973, teams from the Boeotia region participated in competitions organized by the Euboea Football Clubs Association (as the Euboea–Boeotia FCA).

Under its jurisdiction are the regional Cup and league competitions. In the men's category during the 2024–25 season, two divisions existed: the A Category with 11 clubs [ref: Βαθμολογία, EPS Boiotias], and the B Category with two groups of 12 and 14 clubs each.

data.title: Volunteers in Technical Assistance (VITA)
data.text:
Volunteers in Technical Assistance (VITA) was an American nonprofit organization that provided technical assistance for international development. It emerged in 1959 from a group of scientists and engineers linked to General Electric. VITA became an early organization associated with appropriate technology. [ref: Imagining the future through revisiting the past: the value of history in thinking about R(R)I's possible future(s), Journal of Responsible Innovation]

==History==
VITA developed from discussions among scientists and engineers at General Electric in Schenectady, New York. Some also taught at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. [ref: Engineering and Sustainable Community Development, Morgan & Claypool Publishers series SYNTHESIS LECTURES ON ENGINEERS, TECHNOLOGY, AND SOCIETY] The group began receiving requests for technical advice from charities. The United States Agency for International Development contracted it to study solar cookers in 1960. [ref: Imagining the future through revisiting the past: the value of history in thinking about R(R)I's possible future(s), Journal of Responsible Innovation]

VITA later expanded outside the United States. It had affiliated groups in several countries by 1968. In 1969, the Office of Economic Opportunity commissioned VITA to undertake work in the United States.

== Activities ==
VITA maintained a roster of volunteers used by more than 120 private relief organizations by 1991. These included CARE, the Red Cross, Catholic Relief Services and Save the Children. [ref: DOCTORS WHO RESPOND TO SUFFERING ABROAD, The Washington Post] VITA also used computer networks to distribute technical information. The Washington Post in 1993 reported that the organization used the Internet in its work. It advised countries on subjects such as crop production and water facilities. [ref: GETTING CAUGHT UP IN THE INTERNET, The Washington Post]

The organization also worked on projects linking development with environmental conservation. The Christian Science Monitor in 1995 reported on VITA's work near the Perinet nature reserve in Madagascar. VITA trained local guides for ecotourism. It also oversaw a program that directed part of national park revenue to village projects. [ref: Poor Nations Confront Choice of Trees or Jobs, Christian Science Monitor]

== Merger ==
VITA in 2005 joined with EnterpriseWorks Worldwide. The combined organization became known as EnterpriseWorks/VITA. [ref: Simple Ways to Keep Food Cool, Voice of America] EnterpriseWorks/VITA later merged with Relief International in 2009. [ref: ]

data.title: John Grosett
data.text:
John Rock Grosett ( – September 1866) was an British soldier and politician. He sat as MP for Chippenham from 1820 till 1826. [ref: GROSETT, John Rock (?1784-1866), of Lacock Abbey, nr. Chippenham, Wilts.; Spring Garden and Petersfield, Jamaica, History of Parliament Online]

== Political career ==
He served as cornet of the 13th Dragoon in 1804 and was promoted to lieutenant in 1805, he retired in 1807; he served as member of assembly in Jamaica from 1831 till 1844; and member of council.

== Family ==
He was the second but only surviving son of the merchant Schaw Grosett (died 1820) and Mary, the daughter of Thomas Rock, a Bristol merchant. On 19 February 1810, he married his first cousin Mary Spencer (died 31 October 1820), the daughter of Edward Shirley and they had at least four sons (three predeceased him) and at least two daughters (whom predeceased him). On 20 July 1825, he married Christina Maria de Kantzow and they had at least one son whom predeceased him.

data.title: Julius Yasir Ballo
data.text:
----

Julius Yasir Ballo (born April 20, 2003), known as JuJu Ballo, is an American professional boxer from San Diego, California, of Iraqi and Chaldean Catholic descent. A multi-time USA Boxing National Champion and 2021 Junior Pan American Games gold medalist as an amateur, he turned professional in 2025 after signing with Top Rank. He was undefeated through his first four professional fights as of August 2026. He frequently appears on the same fight cards as his cousin, fellow professional boxer Jonathan "Jonny" Mansour.

== Early life ==
Ballo was born in San Diego and raised in the city's East County area, including the communities of Lakeside and El Cajon. [ref: East County boxer Julius Ballo set to make pro debut, FOX 5 San Diego] [ref: El Cajon cousins will fight Saturday in Detroit, The San Diego Union-Tribune] His father, Yasir Ballo, immigrated to the United States from Iraq and boxed as an amateur before opening Bomber Squad Boxing Academy in El Cajon, where Julius trains under Berlin Kerney. [ref: Julius Ballo has a plan, and it doesn't involve settling for less than No. 1, BoxingScene] Ballo has said he began boxing at age three. The Ballo family also owns El Pueblo Mexican Food, a restaurant chain with five locations. The family is of Iraqi and Chaldean Catholic descent, part of a Chaldean community with a significant presence in both San Diego and Detroit; San Diego County is home to the second-largest Chaldean community in the United States, and Detroit the largest. [ref: Undefeated boxing cousins to make Detroit debut at Fox Theatre in August, ClickOnDetroit / WDIV Local 4]

== Amateur career ==
Ballo won USA Boxing's National Championships in 2021, 2022, and 2023, and has been described in later coverage as a three-time national champion. [ref: Julius Ballo signs co-promotional deal with Overtime Boxing and Top Rank, BoxingScene] He was named USA Boxing's Youth Athlete of the Year for 2021. He won gold at the 2021 Junior Pan American Games in Cali, Colombia, and closed his amateur career with the 2024 National Golden Gloves championship. The Ring reported that Ballo had more than 200 amateur bouts while representing Team USA; [ref: Julius Ballo, backed by Top Rank, in store for big plans, [[The Ring (magazine)] BoxRec lists his amateur record at 51 wins and 8 losses. [ref: Julius Ballo, BoxRec] Ballo's promotional team has described him as having been ranked the No. 1 pound-for-pound amateur boxer in the United States out of an estimated 55,000 amateur competitors, though this ranking has not been independently verified.

Among his amateur wins was a decision over Jahmal Harvey, who was already a world amateur champion at the time and went on to represent the United States at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Ballo did not qualify for the Olympic roster himself, an outcome he later described as one of the more disappointing results of his amateur career.

== Professional career ==

=== Signing with Top Rank ===
In January 2025, Ballo signed with Top Rank. He is managed by James Prince and his father, Yasir Ballo. By 2026, Ballo's own social media following was reported by his team at more than 1.2 million combined across Instagram and TikTok.

=== 2025: Professional debut ===
Ballo made his professional debut on July 26, 2025, at the Madison Square Garden Theater in New York, defeating Brandan Ayala by unanimous decision over four rounds. [ref: Julius Ballo, BoxRec] Ahead of the fight, he told TMZ Sports he intended to "make my name up there in the pound-for-pound list." [ref: Team USA Boxer Julius 'Juju' Ballo Vows to Make Statement In Pro Debut, TMZ Sports]

On December 13, 2025, Ballo defeated Juan Centeno by unanimous decision over six rounds in Hollywood, California. Centeno stepped in as a late replacement opponent, and Ballo moved up two weight classes to make the fight; all three judges scored the bout 60-53. [ref: Chaldean boxing prospects Jonny Mansour and Julius Ballo win professional bouts on same night in Los Angeles, SyriacPress] [ref: Chaldean cousins Mansour, Ballo deliver knockout show for fans, Times of San Diego]

=== 2026: SD Fight Night and Detroit debut ===
On April 18, 2026, Ballo headlined an event billed as SD Fight Night at Frontwave Arena in Oceanside, California, a card he co-promoted with his father, defeating Roman Reyes by unanimous decision over six rounds to improve to 3-0. [ref: Julius Ballo breaks down Roman Reyes over six rounds, BoxingScene] [ref: SD Fight Night full card set for Saturday in Oceanside, CA, FIGHTMAG] Discussing his motivation for continuing to box, Ballo told BoxingScene, "I don't have to do this. I drive a quarter-million-dollar car, and live in a multi-million-dollar house. I don't have to do this sport. I do it because I love it, and I am addicted to that winning feeling." [ref: Julius Ballo boxes because he wants to, not because he has to, BoxingScene]

On August 29, 2026, Ballo made his Detroit debut at the Fox Theatre, on a card promoted by Salita Promotions with G2G Promotions that was marketed toward Metro Detroit's Chaldean and Middle Eastern communities and again shared with Mansour. [ref: Coming For the Knockout, Chaldean News] [ref: Chaldean boxing cousins Ballo, Mansour ready to put on show in the Motor City, Times of San Diego] Ballo said of the booking: "Fighting in Detroit is more than just another bout for me, this is an opportunity to represent my family, my Iraqi and Chaldean roots, and to give back to a community that's supported us from day one of this journey." In the co-main event, Ballo defeated Julian Gomez-Clemons by shutout unanimous decision over six rounds, with all three judges scoring the bout 60-54, before a sellout crowd reported as the largest for a boxing event in the Fox Theatre's history. [ref: Fight Action Fills Fox Theatre In Detroit for Salita Promotions, NY Fights] Ahead of the bout, The Ring reported that Ballo aimed to become a multi-division world champion and to position himself for a featherweight world title opportunity by 2028.

== Personal life ==
Ballo is of Iraqi and Chaldean Catholic descent. His father, Yasir Ballo, boxed as an amateur after immigrating to the United States and later opened Bomber Squad Boxing Academy in El Cajon, where Julius trains and where his father has also worked alongside him as a co-promoter. He remains close with his cousin, professional boxer Jonny Mansour, with whom he trained as a youth and now frequently shares fight cards.

data.title: Anuromyzus acantholimonis
data.text:
Anuromyzus acantholimonis is a species of aphid belonging to the tribe Macrosiphini in the family Aphididae. The species was discovered in the Mount Ida region of Balıkesir Province, Turkey, and was first scientifically described in 2026 by Şahin Kök, Shalva Barjadze and Andrey V. Stekolshchikov. [ref: Revision of the genus Anuromyzus Shaposhnikov, 1959 (Hemiptera: Aphididae), Zootaxa]

[[File:Acantholimon_ulicinum_kz02.jpg|left|thumb|Acantholimon ulicinum, the host plant of Anuromyzus acantholimonis]]

The species was found on Acantholimon ulicinum, at an elevation of 1,705 metres on Sarıkız Peak in the Mount Ida range. [ref: Kaz Dağları'nda yeni bir böcek türü keşfedildi, Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University] It was scientifically described from wingless, viviparous females. It is the second known species of the genus Anuromyzus, which previously contained only.

data.title: Dabloons
data.text:
----

Dabloons is a collaborative online role-playing game and Internet meme that became popular on TikTok in November 2022. [ref: Hello traveler…have ye heard about TikTok Dabloons?, The Verge] Within the game, participants collect and spend an imaginary currency called "dabloons" via "encounters" with videos featuring cats as merchants or other characters. [ref: What are dabloons? A guide to TikTok’s new favourite meme currency, Dazed] Its name comes from doubloon, a Spanish gold coin. [ref: What are dabloons?: Tiktok's new imaginary economy explained, The Guardian]

The Internet trend started from an image of a cat with an outstretched paw, which was posted to Instagram in April 2021 with the caption "4 dabloons". Players kept track of their own dabloons balances, and TikTok's recommendation algorithm also supplied personalized encounters to players. Users also collaboratively added thieves, lotteries, government agencies, and rival factions to the game.

Large dabloons giveaways led to fictional hyperinflation, rising prices, and debt. The fictional economy of dabloons was analyzed in a 2026 study in the journal Convergence. [ref: Dabloons, autopsy of a TikTok meme: Self-excitation and self-destruction in social media cultures, Convergence]

data.title: Giovanni Kasermann
data.text:
Giovanni Kasermann was a luthier in Naples, Italy during the first half of the 20th century specializing in mandolins [ref: Imposta sui redditi di ricchezza mobile elenco dei contribuenti privati possessori di redditi incerti e variabili delle categorie B e C (esclusa la rivalsa), Italia: Direzione generale imposte dirette]. His workshop was located at Via Carbonara 112 in Naples, Italy, and he was an active luthier until at least 1951 [ref: Dictionnaire universel des luthiers, Bruxelles: Les Amis de la Musique].

His instruments from the early 1900s bear various labels marked "Fratelli Häsermann," while later instruments in the 1910s to 1940s are labeled "Giovanni Kasermann." His craftsmanship featured classic Neapolitan mandolin styles apparent on his decorative bowlback mandolins, but he is also credited with employing a novel double-top design [ref: Mandolin patents in Italy between 1870 and 1930: between real innovations and commercial strategy., "Il periodo d'oro del mandolino" curated by Ugo Orlandi].

An advertisement for Kasermann's workshop published in the 1922 Musique-Adresses Universel states, "A distinguished workshop for Neapolitan mandolins. Unsurpassed concert mandolins for soloists, featuring a marvelous tone and absolutely perfect intonation in every position—a level of quality never before attained in such instruments. We also offer mandolas, mandoloncellos, lutes, mandolones, and guitars, as well as tortoiseshell picks and high-quality musical strings for all types of instruments." [ref: Musique-Adresses Universel, Paris: Office Général de la Musique]

Aside from plucked instruments, Kasermann also made at least one violin that was exhibited at the 1937 Exhibition of Modern and Contemporary Violin Making in Cremona, Italy [ref: Italian Violin Makers, London: Paul Hamlyn] [ref: Le Celebrazioni stradivarianne a Cremona, Turris].
