data.title: Neo-Krautrock
data.text:
----

Neo-Kraut Rock (later Neo-Krautrock) was invented and coined by the predecessor of Düsseldorf band Vibravoid, Lightshow Society Düsseldorf in the late 1980s. [ref: Vibravoid, Djournal] [ref: Kiss the Sun: Il lungo viaggio dell'heavy psych 1980–2000, Tsunami Edizioni] The first use of the designation is documented in 1988 to describe a new German-only Düsseldorf musical style that follows the original Kraut Rock tradition of the 1960s and 1970s but still draws on its ideas. [ref: Neo Psychedelic Neo Kraut Rock – Live at Casino, self-published] Later use extends the genre for international bands that focus on the Motorik rhythms of NEU! and Can.

== History ==
The word Kraut was used in world wars I and II to humiliate Germans as a derogatory term. [ref: kraut, Dictionary of Canadianisms on Historical Principles] In 1971 German agency Popo Music put ads in UK Melody Maker and US Billboard to promote the new German music named Kraut Rock spelled in 2 Words. [ref: Der Klang der Revolte: Krautrock und Pop avantgarde, Schott Music] The music was a German interpretation of psychedelic rock incorporating various styles. In the 1980s this term became derogatory and bands like Eloy hated by press and audience. [ref: Eloy, Progressive Rock & Progressive Metal E-Zine] German magazine Musikexpress repeatedly used Kraut Rock for sounds regarded as passé. [ref: Krautrock: German Music in the Seventies, University of Michigan Press] In 1997 David Bowie appeared on Germany's highest-rated television show Wetten, dass..?, where his question about Neu! received only one response from the audience, his question about Harmonia was met with complete silence. [ref: Don't Mention The War (41): David Bowie bei Wetten dass…? über Neu! und Harmonia, Die Tageszeitung Popblog]
In 1988 Düsseldorf band Lightshow Society Düsseldorf first introduced the designation Neo-Kraut Rock in the two word spelling on a concert flyer. In 1990 the group was renamed to Vibravoid who kept using the designation to describe their style which is rooted in the traditions of Düsseldof Kraut Rock that emerged around the first psychedelic club on mainland Europe, Creamcheese. [ref: Der "Lichtraum (Hommage à Fontana)" und das „Creamcheese“ im museum kunst palast: Zur Musealisierung der Düsseldorfer Kunstszene der 1960er Jahre, transcript Verlag] [ref: The Vibravoid – Neo Kraut Rock Psychedelia: Band Info, Vibravoid] In 1994 German magazine Intro reviewed the Vibravoid demo tape Void Forum and quoted “the band calls it Neo Kraut Rock”. [ref: Review of Vibravoid, Intro] In 1999, Smag Lifestyle Magazin described Christian Koch of Vibravoid as a "Neo-Kraut Rock Musiker". [ref: WP8: UFO CLUB, Smag Lifestyle Magazin] Another Düsseldorf group associated with the term Neo-Kraut Rock and Düsseldorf as a so called “Neo-Kraut Hub” was Kreidler who declined being part of that scene. [ref: Joachim Henn, review of Kreidler, Weekend, Intro, November 1996, reproduced in Kreidler's press archive.] In 2009 Vibravoid released the Kraut Rock Sensation EP which documents the first German release consisting solely of Kraut Rock coversongs. In the October 2009 issue of Prinz magazine reviewed the release in the context of the contrasting contemporary reception of Kraut Rock in Germany and Britain. The article noted that, “while entire Krautrock parties were being held in Britain, the music remained a niche phenomenon in its German country of origin” and that Vibravoid have load the cover songs with new “coolness”. [ref: Von Düsseldorfern... Hocherhitztes Kraut, Prinz]

== International use ==

Despite the German origin and the limitation to German music the designation was used in contrast for international bands from the 1990s onwards. British groups lke Stereolab and Loop incorporated Kraut Rock influences into their music and were described by press as a “Krautrock” revival, picking up the one word spelling. [ref: The Cambridge Companion to Krautrock, Cambridge University Press] [ref: Never Fade Out: Loop's Robert Hampson Interviewed, The Quietus]

In 1998 an early international occurrence of the exact expression "Neo-Krautrock" is documented in an interview with Cul de Sac. The interviewer applied the terms "Neo-Krautrock" and "Post-Rock" to the band's music, while the band rejected these classifications. [ref: Cul de Sac interview: Glenn Jones, Perfect Sound Forever]

== Contemporary use of “Neo-Krautrock” ==

The term “Neo Krautrock” was later also used beyond the historical West German scene, while the motorik sound associated with Neu! increasingly became a “shorthand for Krautrock” in international reception. [ref: 'I always wanted to be different', The Guardian]

In 2006, WDR produced the documentary Kraut und Rüben - Über die Anfänge deutscher Rockmusik as a history of the music that emerged in West Germany. The documentary describes "Kraut Rock" as German only phenomenon in the late 1960s and 1970s with a wide spectrum of musical styles. [ref: Kraut und Rüben – Über die Anfänge deutscher Rockmusik, WDR Rockpalast] In a later Rockpalast epsiode, WDR uses the designation for Tokyo-based group Minami Deutsch under the tile "Krautrock aus Japan" (Krautrock from Japan) although the band does not belong geographically and chronologically to the 1970s Kraut Rock scene in West Germany. [ref: Krautrock aus Japan: Minami Deutsch, WDR]

Berlin band Camera was described by British magazine The Quietus as a "contemporary neo-krautrock outfit" and discussed its music in relation to the Motorik approach associated with Neu!. The article noted that the anti-establishment and political dimensions associated with bands such as Neu!, Faust, Can and Amon Düül had been filtered out as later bands adopted their musical vocabulary. [ref: Camera — Radiate!, The Quietus]

data.title: Michael E. Smith (U.S. Navy admiral)
data.text:
= Michael E. Smith (U.S. Navy admiral) =
Michael E. Smith is a retired United States Navy rear admiral and national security advocate. He served in the United States Navy for more than three decades, including as commander of Carrier Strike Group Three and president of the Navy's Board of Inspection and Survey. After retiring from active military service, he became involved in national security advocacy and founded National Security Leaders for America.

== Military career ==
Smith graduated from the United States Naval Academy in 1983 and subsequently completed nuclear power training. His early assignments included service aboard the guided-missile cruiser USS Texas and the destroyer USS Leftwich. He participated in Operation Desert Storm and later served in assignments connected with U.S. naval operations in the Mediterranean and the Persian Gulf.

Smith commanded the destroyer USS Porter and Destroyer Squadron 23. He also served as sea combat commander for the Nimitz Strike Group and as deputy task force commander for coalition maritime operations in the northern Persian Gulf.

His senior staff assignments included work in the offices of the Chief of Naval Operations, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the U.S. Pacific Fleet, and U.S. Pacific Command. He served as director of the Navy's Strategy and Policy Division and later commanded Carrier Strike Group Three.

His final active-duty assignment was president of the Board of Inspection and Survey, which evaluates the material condition and operational readiness of Navy ships and submarines. Smith retired from active duty in 2015. His military awards include the Bronze Star Medal for combat service.

== Post-military career ==
Following his retirement from the Navy, Smith worked in national security advocacy and writing. He has contributed commentary on national security and East Asian affairs to publications including 38 North and The National Interest. He has also served as president of the American College of National Security Leaders.

Smith founded and leads National Security Leaders for America, an organization of former senior national security officials that advocates for democratic institutions and constitutional principles.

== Political advocacy ==
Smith became publicly involved in presidential politics during the 2024 United States presidential election. Through National Security Leaders for America, he participated in efforts opposing Donald Trump's return to the presidency. The organization endorsed Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris.

Smith has also publicly criticized actions by the Trump administration that he argues threaten democratic norms, the nonpartisan character of the armed forces, and national security. His public commentary has addressed military leadership, civil-military relations, and the consequences of political decisions for the U.S. military.

data.title: Linxens
data.text:
----

Linxens is a French technology company that manufactures components and develops technologies used in smart cards, identification products, radio-frequency identification (RFID), and other electronic applications. Its products have included microconnectors, antennas, RFID inlays and tags, and components used in payment cards, SIM cards and identification products. [ref: Linxens France SA, Bloomberg]

Linxens originated from the Microconnections division of French connector manufacturer FCI. In 2011, the division was sold to private equity firm Astorg and established as a stand-alone business. The company was later renamed Linxens and was acquired by CVC Capital Partners in 2015. In 2018, Tsinghua Unigroup agreed to acquire Linxens from CVC.

== History ==

=== Microconnections and Astorg ===

Linxens originated from the Microconnections division of FCI, a French manufacturer of electrical connectors. In 2011, private equity firm Astorg acquired the division from FCI, separating Microconnections from its former parent and establishing it as a stand-alone business. [ref: Astorg Partners scelle le rachat des microcircuits de FCI, L'Agefi]

FCI had previously been the connector subsidiary of the French industrial group Areva before being acquired by Bain Capital in 2006. [ref: Astorg négocie en exclusivité le rachat des microconnexions de FCI, L'Agefi]

At the time of the Astorg transaction, Microconnections had reported revenue of €202 million for 2010. L'Agefi described it as the world leader in the production of flexible connectors for smart cards.

The business was subsequently renamed Linxens. [ref: REFILE-LPC-Banks line up around 1 bln euros of debt for CVC Linxens buy, Reuters]

=== Acquisition by CVC Capital Partners ===

In 2015, CVC Capital Partners entered into an agreement to acquire Linxens from Astorg. [ref: CVC to Buy French Tech Firm Linxens in $1.7 Billion Deal, The Wall Street Journal] [ref: CVC valoriserait 1,5 milliard d’euros son LBO sur le français Linxens, L'Agefi]

The Wall Street Journal reported that the transaction valued Linxens at approximately €1.5 billion ($1.66 billion) and that CVC had pre-empted an auction process being run by Astorg.

Reuters reported that Linxens had approximately 1,100 employees, five manufacturing facilities and three research and development centres in Europe and Asia at the time.

Between 2010 and 2014, Linxens's annual sales increased from approximately €200 million to €253 million, according to L'Agefi. The company had manufacturing operations in France and Singapore and had also acquired Thai company KNL, which specialized in contactless technology.

L'Agefi reported that Linxens was benefiting from the expansion of smart-card use in China and the United States. Europe and Asia accounted for approximately 49 percent and 51 percent of its sales respectively.

=== Acquisition by Tsinghua Unigroup ===

In 2018, Chinese semiconductor company Tsinghua Unigroup moved to acquire Linxens from CVC. [ref: Chinese chipmaker Tsinghua Unigroup to buy France's Linxens for $2.6 billion - sources, Reuters]

The proposed acquisition received coverage in the French press. Le Figaro described Linxens as a French technology "pépite" and reported on the proposed transaction. [ref: Un chinois convoite Linxens, une pépite de la tech française, Le Figaro]

Reuters reported that Tsinghua Unigroup had agreed to acquire Linxens for approximately €2.2 billion. The proposed acquisition also raised questions over whether the French government would regard Linxens as a strategic company and therefore subject the transaction to foreign-investment controls.

The French government did not object to the transaction. According to a Finance Ministry official cited by Reuters, Linxens was not considered strategic because it manufactured passive components rather than semiconductors. [ref: France not objecting to sale of Linxens to Chinese group, Reuters]

=== Tsinghua restructuring ===

Tsinghua Unigroup later experienced serious financial difficulties and defaulted on bond obligations in 2020. The group entered a court-supervised restructuring process in China in 2021. [ref: China's Tsinghua Unigroup says creditors back restructuring plan, Reuters]

A consortium led by Wise Road Capital and JAC Capital was subsequently selected as the strategic investor in Tsinghua Unigroup's restructuring.

The restructuring was completed in 2022, with Wise Road Capital and JAC Capital among the investors in the reorganized group.

== Operations ==

Linxens manufactures components used in smart cards and other electronic products. Its smart-card products have included connectors used in banking cards, SIM cards, identification cards and health cards.

The company also develops Internet of Things (IoT) and RFID technologies. Bloomberg describes Linxens France's activities as including IoT modules, authentication and traceability platforms, and RFID inlays and tags.

Bloomberg lists automotive, logistics, luxury goods, transportation, supply chain, food and beverage, and healthcare among the sectors served by Linxens France.

The company has operated manufacturing and research facilities in Europe and Asia.

== Tsinghua Unigroup International litigation ==

Linxens Holding SAS was involved in legal proceedings in the British Virgin Islands arising from the liquidation of Tsinghua Unigroup International Co. Ltd. (TUI).

In September 2020, Linxens provided financing to TUI. TUI subsequently made a payment of approximately US$125.9 million to Linxens in December 2020. [ref: BVI Case Law Update, Baker & Partners]

After TUI entered liquidation, its joint liquidators challenged the payment to Linxens as an unfair preference.

In 2026, the Commercial Division of the High Court of Justice of the British Virgin Islands ruled in Luke Almond et al. v Linxens Holding SAS that the payment should be set aside as an unfair preference. In reaching its decision, the court considered TUI's cash-flow insolvency at the time of the payment and whether the transaction had occurred in the ordinary course of business.

== Passport supply-chain scrutiny ==

In 2026, the Financial Times investigated Linxens's role in the supply chain for electronic passports and its ownership following the restructuring of Tsinghua Unigroup. [ref: UK and European passports linked to restricted Chinese investors, Financial Times]

The Financial Times reported that Linxens produces inlays used in biometric passports. The inlays contain chips and antennas that allow the passports and the personal data they contain to be read electronically, although the chips themselves are supplied by another manufacturer.

The report examined Linxens's links to Wise Road Capital and JAC Capital, which led the investor group involved in the restructuring of Tsinghua Unigroup. Both investment firms were added to the United States Department of Commerce's Entity List in 2024 over national-security concerns relating to semiconductor technology.

The Financial Times reported that Linxens's ownership had raised concerns among some security specialists and British politicians about the passport supply chain. Linxens stated that it did not have access to the transport or personalisation keys used for passport chips and said that its operations complied with applicable security requirements.

== Labour dispute in France ==

In 2026, employees at the Linxens plant in Buchelay, Yvelines, took industrial action during a dispute concerning employment and working conditions. [ref: Buchelay: une semaine de grève chez Linxens contre la violence managériale et la régression sociale, Infos Yvelines]

data.title: Zingroll
data.text:
Zingroll is an American streaming platform for AI-generated films and series. The platform is known for it's short-form and episodic content produced with generative video tools.

The company was founded by Harshit Yadav, who had previously built the consumer applications Airfeed and LitFeed. It maintains offices in San Francisco and Delhi.

Its investors include Accel, Andreessen Horowitz's Speedrun programme, Google, Z Fellows and Network VC.

== History ==

Zingroll was founded by Harshit Yadav, an entrepreneur based in San Francisco who had previously built 2 consumer applications, Airfeed and LitFeed. The platform launched on iOS and subsequently on Android. Its early positioning centred on free access to movies and series. The application was later repositioned around personalised generation, allowing a user to appear as the protagonist of a movie generated from a single photograph.
== Atoms AI Cohort ==

In March 2026, Zingroll was named one of five startups selected for the Atoms AI Cohort 2026, a partnership between Accel and Google's AI Futures Fund announced in November 2025 to support early-stage companies building AI products connected to India. The programme received more than 4,000 applications and each selected company became eligible for up to $2 million in funding from Accel and the AI Futures Fund together with up to $350,000 in Google cloud and AI compute credits.

Accel partner Prayank Swaroop told TechCrunch that roughly 70% of the rejected applications were "wrappers" and that many of the remainder fell into crowded categories such as marketing automation and AI recruitment. Jonathan Silber, co-founder and director of Google's AI Futures Fund, said the selected companies aligned with areas where Google expected deeper real-world adoption of AI. The Free Press Journal characterised Zingroll as the creative outlier of the group.

The cohort opened on 11 March 2026 at Google's Ananta campus in Bengaluru with virtual speaker series running through April and May 2026 and a concluding programme in Mountain View, California in June. Announcing the selection, Accel described Zingroll as a streaming platform for AI-native films and shows. The selection was also reported by The Indian Express, YourStory, Analytics India Magazine, Moneycontrol and IT Voice.

== Platform and technology ==

Zingroll distributes films and series produced with generative tools. The application is distributed free of charge, offers trailers and original series, with in-app purchases. The application allows a user to upload a photograph and receive an episodic film in which they appear as the lead character.
== Funding ==

Zingroll raised $250,000 in pre-seed funding. In November 2025, the Ukrainian-American firm Network VC announced an investment in the company. Its founder, Oleksandr Soroka, said the firm backs founders who change how audiences create and experience content. Its listing
with a16z Speedrun names Accel, a16z Speedrun, Google and Z Fellows among its backers, and it appeared among the companies presenting at the a16z Speedrun 2025 demo day. Selection for the Atoms AI Cohort in March 2026 carried eligibility for up to $2 million in further investment and up to $350,000 in Google compute credits.

data.title: 2023 Shell oil platform protest
data.text:
The 2023 Shell oil platform protest was a Greenpeace action in which activists boarded and occupied a Shell oil platform being transported across the Atlantic Ocean.

== Historical background ==

In 2018, Shell began investing in the redevelopment of the Penguin oil and gas field, northeast of the Shetland Islands. It authorized the construction of the Penguins FPSO, the company's first manned installation in the UK North Sea in 30 years. [ref: Shell approves development of Penguins oil, gas field in North Sea, Reuters] [ref: Shell hits Greenpeace protestors on Penguins FPSO with injunction, Energy Voice]

Construction of the platform was completed by China's Offshore Oil Engineering Company in November 2022. The 34,000-tonne FPSO was then transported from China by Dutch shipping company Boskalis with its vessel the White Marlin. [ref: Greenpeace activists end 13-day occupation of Shell's oil platform, Offshore Energy] [ref: Greenpeace Activists Board Heavy-lift Vessel Carrying Shell's Penguins FPSO, Offshore Engineer] The platform was said to allow Shell to develop eight new wells at the Penguins field, with expected output reaching up to 45,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. [ref: Shell Gives North Sea Shot in Arm With Field Redevelopment, Bloomberg]

== Boarding and protest ==

On January 31, 2023, six Greenpeace activists approached the White Marlin in three boats launched from the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise. The platform was still in route to the North Sea and in the Atlantic Ocean north of Gran Canaria at the time. Four of them used ropes to climb onto the deck. [ref: Footage shows the moment Greenpeace activists scaled a Shell oil platform that was being transported in 'rough conditions' in the Atlantic, Business Insider] The four activists occupied the vessel's cargo and displayed a banner reading "Stop Drilling. Start Paying."

Shell sought an injunction against Greenpeace while the four activists occupied the platform. The injunction required two of Greenpeace's ships to stay clear of the White Marlin. After the injunction, two more activists boarded using a chartered trimaran and small boats which were not listed in the injunction. [ref: More Greenpeace Protestors Board Heavy-Lift Vessel Carrying Shell FPSO, The Maritime Executive] The following day, a court issued an order barring further boardings and requiring the six activists to leave the platform upon its arrival in Norway.

The activists set up a wind turbine on the platform to power their communications equipment. [ref: Activists disembark Shell Penguins FPSO after 13-days, Energy Voice] Other activists who did not board sailed out to confront the White Marlin without boarding it. The occupation ended on February 12, 2026 when the vessel docked at Haugesund, Norway. No arrests were made after the activists left the platform.

== Litigation and settlement ==

In February 2023 Shell sent a claim to Greenpeace $120,000 over damage it claimed was caused during the occupation. In November 2023 Shell filed a lawsuit against Greenpeace, seeking $2.1 million for legal, safety and security costs it incurred because of the protest. [ref: Shell sues Greenpeace for $2.1 million after boarding oil vessel, Reuters] Shell also asked the court to bar Greenpeace from protesting at its offshore infrastructure.

Shell offered to settle for $1.4 million if Greenpeace agreed to never protest against against future Shell infrastructure at sea or port, but Greenpeace refused the settlement, calling it a strategic lawsuit against public participation. [ref: Shell sues Greenpeace after FPSO boarding, Splash247] In a December 2023 filing Shell reduced the claim to about $1 million. [ref: Greenpeace to donate £300,000 to RNLI as part of lawsuit settlement with Shell, Civil Society]

The lawsuit was settled out of court in December 2024 with Greenpeace donating £300,000 to the Royal National Lifeboat Institution and accepting no liability or paying anything directly to Shell. The activists involved agreed not to travel within 500 metres of three Shell North Sea sites for five years. [ref: Greenpeace settles lawsuit with Shell over North Sea protest, Riviera Maritime Media]

data.title: Mereological Fallacy
data.text:
The mereological fallacy is a conceptual error within the philosophy of mind, in which psychological capacities of a person or animal are attributed to the brain or another part of the organism. The argument is associated with neuroscientist Max Bennett and philosopher Peter Hacker, whose Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience (2003) criticises such attributions in cognitive neuroscience. [ref: Naming Our Concerns about Neuroscience: A Review of Bennett and Hacker's Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience, Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior]

Bennett and Hacker distinguish the cognitive processes that enable thinking, from the organism that exercises those capacities. Their argument has been disputed by various philosophers including Daniel Dennett and John Searle. [ref: What Is Cognitive Psychology?, Athabasca University Press]

== Argument ==
According to Bennett and Hacker, the circumstances under which psychological descriptions apply to people and other animals are part of what gives those descriptions their meaning. They argue that describing a brain as perceiving, or deciding, transfers these descriptions to something that does not meet their conditions of application. The resulting statements, on their account, are conceptually confused rather than empirically false. [ref: Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience, Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews]

Bennett and Hacker accept that neural processes make psychological capacities possible. On their account, neuroscience investigates how neural activity enables an animal to see or remember. They claim that it doesn't explain those capacities by assigning sight or memory to the brain itself. They also argue that treating these expressions as harmless metaphors does not resolve the problem when the expressions are used when explaining phenomena like perception or memory.

Harry Smit and Hacker later clarified that the error isn't a strictly invalid inference, it is more precisely, an inappropriate attribution of a property, which may then produce mistaken inferences. In their usage, fallacy has a broader use than in formal logic. [ref: Seven Misconceptions About the Mereological Fallacy: A Compilation for the Perplexed, Erkenntnis Abstract and note 1.]

== Background ==

Bennett and Hacker's account draws on Ludwig Wittgenstein's discussion in Philosophical Investigations of the circumstances in which sensations and other psychological attributes can be ascribed to living beings. Smit and Hacker relate their terminology to Anthony Kenny's earlier discussion of the homunculus fallacy. They prefer the mereological terminology because the objection concerns part–whole relations, without requiring the postulation of a miniature person inside the organism.

The argument was debated in Neuroscience and Philosophy: Brain, Mind, and Language (2007), which included criticisms by Dennett and Searle and a reply by Bennett and Hacker. [ref: Minds, Brains, and Capacities: Situated Cognition and Neo-Aristotelianism, Frontiers in Psychology]

== Reception ==

Reviewing Bennett and Hacker's book, David W. Schaal welcomed its criticism of dualism and its attention to behavioural criteria for psychological concepts. He nevertheless questioned some restrictions the authors placed on the use of memory concepts in research on non-human animals.

Daniel Dennett defends a modified use of psychological vocabulary for subpersonal mechanisms. On his account, attributing simplified forms of belief to brain components can help explain a person's capacities without treating each component as a complete thinker.

John Searle challenges the role assigned to behavioural criteria. He argued that the evidence used to attribute a psychological state should be distinguished from the state itself, and that Bennett and Hacker's argument confuses these issues.

Paul Churchland appeals to information-processing descriptions in computer science, arguing that talk of storing, retrieving and manipulating information can have an intelligible technical use. Bennett and Hacker respond that producing results consistent with a rule differs from following that rule with understanding. Discussing this exchange, Michael R. W. Dawson argues that a functional explanation decomposes a system's capacities into simpler operations, which need not resemble the behaviour of the system as a whole.

Rom Harré questions whether brains, although parts of human bodies, should also be described as parts of persons. He proposes reformulating the issue through relationships between meanings and the roles of bodily organs in human activities. His account permits describing the hippocampus as an organ for remembering, without identifying neuroscience with psychology. [ref: Behind the Mereological Fallacy, Philosophy Abstract.]

Hans-Johann Glock defends the category-mistake objection to attributing cognition to brains and their parts, while rejecting the further claim that the brain cannot be described as the organ of cognition.

* Embodied cognition
* Philosophy of neuroscience

data.title: Hoba (film)
data.text:
----

Hoba (stylized in all caps; also known as The Vile) is a 2025 Emirati supernatural psychological horror film written and directed by Majid Al Ansari. The film follows a woman who descends into paranoia after her husband brings home a second wife, sensing a dark presence following the other woman. It was based on an original screenplay written by Al Ansari and Johnnie Alward and stars Bdoor Mohammad, Sarah Taibah, and Iman Tarik.

The film was produced by Image Nation Abu Dhabi and Spooky Pictures. Hoba premiered at Fantastic Fest 2025 in Austin, Texas. After playing at festivals, it was released theatrically in the United Arab Emirates on October 30, 2025, and in Saudi Arabia in November 2025.

== Synopsis ==
Amani (Bdoor Mohammad), a wife and mother living in suburban Abu Dhabi, finds her husband Khalid (Jasem AlKharraz) returning home with a pregnant second wife, Zahra (Sarah Taibah), without her knowledge or consent. Feeling betrayed, Amani tries to reassert herself as the household's matriarch as her daughter, Noor (Iman Tarik), begins growing closer to Zahra after being bullied at school. After seemingly paranormal events, Amani's sanity unravels, as she becomes convinced that a malevolent supernatural presence has followed Zahra into their household.

== Cast ==
* Bdoor Mohammad as Amani
* Jasem AlKharraz as Khalid
* Iman Tarik as Noor
* Sarah Taibah as Zahra

== Production ==
=== Development ===
Hoba was directed by Majid Al Ansari. Al Ansari cited Fatal Attraction and What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? as his inspirations for the film, which explores themes such as polygamy, greed, betrayal, and trauma.

=== Filming and collaboration ===
The film was produced by Image Nation Abu Dhabi and Spooky Pictures. [ref: Image Nation Abu Dhabi Pacts With Spooky Pictures on Chloe Okuno’s Thriller ‘Watcher’, Variety] [ref: Image Nation, Spooky Pictures Set For ‘Late Night With the Devil’ (EXCLUSIVE), Variety] It was the first Arabic-language Emirati film co-produced by the two companies. Steven Schneider and Roy Lee served as producers and provided creative input. Additional producers include Derek Dauchy and Rami Yasin, with Mohamed Hefzy and Yasir Al Yasiri serving as executive producers.

== Release ==
=== Film festivals ===
Hoba had its world premiere at Fantastic Fest 2025 at the Alamo Drafthouse in Austin, Texas, in September 2025. In October 2025, the film was screened at the Sitges Film Festival in Spain and the BFI London Film Festival. [ref: ] In December 2025, the film was also screened at the Gulf Film Festival.

The film was also screened at the Emirates Airline Festival of Literature in January 2026, where Al Ansari participated in a Q&A following the screening.

=== Theatrical release ===
Hoba was released in UAE cinemas on October 30, 2025. The film opened in Saudi Arabia in November 2025, and was distributed by Telfaz11. In October 2026, it was announced that Dark Sky Films had acquired U.S. distribution rights for the film.

== Reception ==
The film received positive reviews from critics, including coverage in Variety and Deadline. On the review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, it has an approval rating of 100% based on 11 reviews.

data.title: Perimenopause
data.text:
----

Perimenopause is the phase during which the ovaries gradually reduce their hormonal activity, a period of physical and psychological changes preceding menopause. It begins with a persistent difference of seven days or more in the length of consecutive menstrual cycles and it ends after the occurrence of one year of amenorrhea, when menopause is reached. [ref: Executive summary of the Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop + 10: addressing the unfinished agenda of staging reproductive aging, The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism] The fluctuating hormone levels, particularly variations in the level of circulating estrogen, can cause a wide range of symptoms, including heavy and irregular bleeding, mood and memory changes, decreased libido, vasomotor symptoms and genitourinary symptoms. [ref: Management of perimenopausal and menopausal symptoms, BMJ] [ref: Perimenopause, Canadian Medical Association Journal] Perimenopause is a normal part of reproductive aging rather than a disease. [ref: European Society of Endocrinology clinical practice guideline for evaluation and management of menopause and the perimenopause, European Journal of Endocrinology]

== Signs and symptoms ==
The most commonly reported symptoms include hot flashes, sleep changes, vaginal dryness, and adverse mood. While these are the most commonly discussed perimenopausal symptoms, women may experience many others, and the type and severity of symptoms vary widely among individuals.

=== Hot flashes and night sweats ===
Hot flashes and night sweats, together known as vasomotor symptoms, are among the most common symptoms of perimenopause. [ref: Perimenopause: From Research to Practice, Journal of Women's Health] Moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms often begin during perimenopause and last on average seven to eleven years.

=== Sleep changes ===
Sleep changes are another perimenopausal symptom that can affect the quality of life of women in their early perimenopausal stage. [ref: Management of Menopausal Symptoms: A Review, JAMA] [ref: Sleep Disturbance and Perimenopause: A Narrative Review, Journal of Clinical Medicine] Studies indicate that insomnia is more common during perimenopause than before it. Although women begin to notice sleep changes in their 40s, they become worse with the menopausal transition. However, there is no clear consensus on whether these changes in sleep pattern are directly related to menopause or due to estrogen withdrawal or other hormonal changes, or simply related to ageing. The hot flashes at night are one cause of sleep disturbance.

=== Vaginal dryness and reduced libido ===
Although vaginal dryness or dyspareunia is a common issue reported among postmenopausal women, women in their perimenopausal stage also experience vaginal dryness, even though the estrogen levels are not consistently low as in postmenopause. [ref: Vaginal dryness: a review of current understanding and management strategies, Climacteric] Unlike hot flashes and adverse moods, vaginal dryness and sleep difficulties are less likely to get better without ongoing treatment.

Reduced libido is also reported.

=== Adverse mood ===

Perimenopause is associated with an increased vulnerability to depressive symptoms and major depressive episodes compared with premenopause. [ref: Cognition and mental health in menopause: A review, Best Practice & Research Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology] A history of depression is a major risk factor. [ref: Guidelines for the evaluation and treatment of perimenopausal depression: summary and recommendations, Menopause] Depressive symptoms frequently co-occur with vasomotor symptoms, sleep disturbance and psychosocial stressors. [ref: Promoting good mental health over the menopause transition, The Lancet]

=== Cognition ===
Cognitive complaints such as "brain fog" and memory lapses are also reported. A 2026 meta-analysis of 26 studies found poorer cognitive outcomes in perimenopausal than in premenopausal women, although this effect appeared only in studies using the STRAW+10 staging criteria; overall, no difference was found compared with postmenopausal women. [ref: Cognitive functioning in perimenopause: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis, Psychology and Aging]

== Diagnosis ==
Diagnosis is primarily clinical. In otherwise healthy women over 45, the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends diagnosing perimenopause based on vasomotor symptoms and irregular periods, without laboratory tests. [ref: Menopause: identification and management, www.nice.org.uk] Other causes of menstrual irregularity, such as pregnancy, thyroid disease and hyperprolactinemia, should be considered.

== Management ==

Menopausal hormone therapy is commonly used as a treatment for women who experience symptoms of perimenopause such as hot flashes, sleep disturbance, vaginal dryness and mood changes, and can improve the quality of life. However, most evidence on hormone therapy derives from postmenopausal populations, and it has not been specifically optimised for perimenopause. [ref: Management of the Perimenopause, Clinical Obstetrics and Gynecology] Women who experience irregular bleeding may benefit from oral contraceptives, which can also provide contraception, since pregnancy can occur during perimenopause.

==== Non-hormonal pharmacological options ====
Non-hormonal options for hot flashes include gabapentin and neurokinin 3 receptor antagonists such as fezolinetant. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) can reduce hot flashes and are also used to treat perimenopausal depression.

==== Non-pharmacological approaches ====
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is also recommended for hot flashes. [ref: The 2023 nonhormone therapy position statement of the North American Menopause Society, Menopause (New York, N.Y.)]

== Society and culture ==
Historically, there has been limited public and clinical information about menopause and the perimenopausal transition, and awareness of perimenopause specifically remains low, although it is a life stage that most women who reach midlife will eventually go through. [ref: An exploration of women's knowledge and experience of perimenopause and menopause: An integrative literature review, Journal of Clinical Nursing]

Public discussion has expanded in recent years, with growing attention to its impact on quality of life and on workplace participation. [ref: An empowerment model for managing menopause, The Lancet] A 2025 literature review for the UK Department for Work and Pensions found evidence that menopause symptoms can affect women’s confidence and wellbeing at work. [ref: Menopause in the Workplace Literature Review, GOV.UK] The Menopause Society has issued workplace recommendations for employers, including flexible working arrangements and awareness training. [ref: Menopause and the workplace: consensus recommendations, Menopause (New York, N.Y.)]

== References ==

data.title: Kim Tae-ho
data.text:
Kim Tae-ho (; 1948 – 4 October 2022) was a South Korean abstract painter associated with Dansaekhwa, the Korean monochrome painting movement. He is best known for his Internal Rhythm () series, begun in the 1990s, in which more than twenty layers of paint are built up in a grid and then cut back with a blade to expose the colours beneath. [ref: ‘벌집 회화’로 유명한 단색화 작가 김태호 전 홍익대 교수 별세, Kyunghyang Shinmun] [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily] The cell-like surfaces of these works led critics to call them "beehive paintings". [ref: ‘벌집 회화’로 유명한 단색화 작가 김태호 전 홍익대 교수 별세, Kyunghyang Shinmun] [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] He taught painting at Hongik University from 1987 to 2016. [ref: ‘벌집 회화’로 유명한 단색화 작가 김태호 전 홍익대 교수 별세, Kyunghyang Shinmun]

== Early life and education ==
Kim was born in Busan in 1948 and lived there until middle school. He then moved to Seoul to attend Seoul Arts High School, where he met Park Seo-bo and became his student. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] [ref: Kim Tae Ho – Biography, Galerie Françoise Livinec]

He studied painting at Hongik University's College of Fine Arts under the abstract painter Yoo Young-kuk and Dansaekhwa painters including Ha Chong-hyun and Chung Sang-hwa. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] He graduated in 1972 and completed a master's degree in art education at Hongik's Graduate School of Education in 1984. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] [ref: ‘벌집 회화’로 유명한 단색화 작가 김태호 전 홍익대 교수 별세, Kyunghyang Shinmun]

== Career ==
Kim held his first solo exhibition in 1977, presenting his Form series. In 1982 he won the grand prize at the Gonggan (Space) Print-Making Competition. [ref: Kim Tae Ho – Biography, Galerie Françoise Livinec]

He taught in Hongik University's painting department from 1987 to 2016. After retiring, he headed the Kim Tae-ho Formative Research Institute (). [ref: ‘벌집 회화’로 유명한 단색화 작가 김태호 전 홍익대 교수 별세, Kyunghyang Shinmun] He lived and worked in Paju, Gyeonggi Province. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho, Pearl Lam Galleries]

Korean critics generally place him among the "post-Dansaekhwa" painters who followed the movement's first generation, alongside artists such as Lee Bae and Lee Kang-so. [ref: 김태호 후기 단색화 작가 별세, Seoul Shinmun] [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily] In 2021 one of his Internal Rhythm paintings sold for ₩210 million at a Seoul Auction sale. From 2021 he also produced NFT digital works. [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily]

== Style and technique ==
Kim's work is commonly divided into three periods: Form paintings made with spray paint, Form works made with hanji (Korean mulberry paper), and the acrylic Internal Rhythm series from the mid-1990s onward. [ref: Equilibrium Shifts: a Solo Exhibition by Kim Tae-Ho, Pearl Lam Galleries]

=== Form in spray paint ===
Begun in 1977, the Form () series hid figurative subjects beneath horizontal bands, an image inspired by the metal shutters covering commercial and bank buildings. Kim made these works mainly with a spray technique. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] [ref: Kim Tae Ho – Biography, Galerie Françoise Livinec]

=== Form in hanji ===
Kim then carried the Form series into hanji, layering the paper onto canvas and shifting his focus from image to material and surface texture. This work led to the Internal Rhythm series. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] [ref: Kim Tae Ho – Biography, Galerie Françoise Livinec]

=== Internal Rhythm ===
For the Internal Rhythm () series, begun around 1995, Kim drew a fine pencil grid on the canvas. He then applied 20 or more layers of acrylic paint in alternating vertical and horizontal strokes. Once the paint had partly set, he cut into the raised ridges with a specially made carving blade. [ref: 김태호 Kim Tae Ho, ARTN Edition] [ref: 화제의 전시: 김태호 개인전 '질서의 흔적', YTN] The cuts reveal the buried colours inside small cell-like pockets between the grid lines. [ref: ‘벌집 회화’로 유명한 단색화 작가 김태호 전 홍익대 교수 별세, Kyunghyang Shinmun] Seen from a distance, a work reads as a single colour; at close range, the hidden layers become visible. [ref: 김태호 Kim Tae Ho, ARTN Edition]

== Death ==
In September 2022, Kim collapsed while visiting Busan. He died there on 4 October 2022, aged 74. [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily] [ref: ‘벌집 회화’로 유명한 단색화 작가 김태호 전 홍익대 교수 별세, Kyunghyang Shinmun] The Korean press reported a stroke as the cause of his collapse, while ArtAsiaPacific reported that he died of sepsis. [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily] [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] His solo exhibition Traces of Order (), then on view at Pyo Gallery in Seoul, was extended to 27 October as a memorial exhibition. [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily] Park Seo-bo publicly mourned his former student. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific] [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily]

== Selected exhibitions ==
* 2022 – Traces of Order, Pyo Gallery, Seoul [ref: 화제의 전시: 김태호 개인전 '질서의 흔적', YTN] [ref: '포스트 단색화 거장' 김태호의 유작전, The Korea Economic Daily]
* 2022 – Two-person exhibition with Choi Myoung-young, Jeju Dam Studio Gallery, Seogwipo [ref: 제주서 만나는 '한국 단색화의 거장'... 최명영ㆍ김태호 2인전 개최, Bravo My Life]
* 2022 – Internal Rhythms, The Columns Gallery, Singapore [ref: 김태호 단색화, 선(禪)에서 존재론으로, Lee Seoul Gallery via Newswire]
* 2022 – Internal Rhythm – Fractal Microcosmos, Lee Seoul Gallery, Seoul [ref: 김태호 단색화, 선(禪)에서 존재론으로, Lee Seoul Gallery via Newswire]
* 2020–21 – Equilibrium Shifts, Pearl Lam Galleries, Hong Kong [ref: Kim Tae-Ho (1948–2022), ArtAsiaPacific]
* 2018–19 – The Aesthetics of Lining, Metaphysical Art Gallery, Taipei [ref: Kim Tae Ho – Biography, Galerie Françoise Livinec]
* 2016 – Internal Rhythm, Gallery Date, Busan [ref: Kim Tae Ho – Biography, Galerie Françoise Livinec]

== Collections ==
Kim's works are held in public collections including the British Museum, London; the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea; the Seoul Museum of Art; the Busan Museum of Art; the Daejeon Museum of Art; the Shimonoseki City Art Museum, Japan; and the museum of the Guangzhou Academy of Fine Arts, China. [ref: Kim Tae-Ho, Pearl Lam Galleries]

data.title: Salaspils Research Reactor
data.text:
The Salaspils Research Reactor () is a former pool-type research reactor in Salaspils, Latvia. It was built for the Institute of Physics of the Latvian Academy of Sciences and operated from 26 September 1961 to 19 June 1998. [ref: Development of nuclear energetics in Latvia] [ref: Par Salaspils kodolreaktora likvidēšanas un demontāžas koncepciju, Likumi.lv] Research at the reactor covered nuclear physics, radiation chemistry and radiobiology.

The facility was partly dismantled after its closure, but decommissioning was still in progress in August 2025. [ref: IAEA Mission Says Latvia Committed to Safe and Responsible Management of Radioactive Waste, Sees Areas for Further Enhancement, International Atomic Energy Agency] [ref: Republic of Latvia National Report on the implementation of the obligations under the Convention on Nuclear Safety for the 10th Review Meeting of the Contracting Parties]

== Establishment and research ==
The Soviet government authorised construction of the reactor in 1958. It was based on the IRT design developed at the Institute of Atomic Energy in Moscow. The reactor first reached criticality on 26 September 1961. Reconstruction in the mid-1970s increased its thermal power to 5 MW. [ref: 60 gadi kopš Salaspils kodolreaktora iedarbināšanas, LSM.lv]

Alongside research in nuclear physics, radiation chemistry and radiobiology, the reactor was used to develop radiation dosimeters and produce radioactive preparations for medical use. Latvian scientists also developed a radiation loop that supplied gamma rays for irradiation experiments and work on industrial irradiation processes.

The reactor provided training for specialists from North Korea, Iraq and Libya, which had acquired IRT reactors from the Soviet Union.

== Closure and decommissioning ==
In May 1995, the Latvian government ordered preparations to dismantle the reactor and prohibited further purchases of nuclear fuel. [ref: Par pasākumiem Salaspils zinātniski pētnieciskā atomreaktora likvidācijas sagatavošanai, Likumi.lv] The reactor shut down permanently on 19 June 1998. The government approved a decommissioning plan on 26 October 1999 and revised it in 2004.

Unused nuclear fuel was returned to Russia in 2005, followed by the spent fuel in 2008. By 2019, the reactor had been partly dismantled and was awaiting final decommissioning, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Funding shortages and the need for additional capacity at the Radons radioactive waste repository near Baldone delayed completion of the dismantling work. [ref: Salaspils reaktoram aprit 60; līdz demontāžai vēl vismaz 10 gadi, LSM.lv] Decommissioning remained in progress in August 2025, when Latvia's radiation regulator reported delays in completing the dismantling design.

data.title: Bedrock Robotics
data.text:
----

Bedrock Robotics is an American company, based in San Francisco, that develops sensor, computing and machine learning systems to automate heavy construction equipment, beginning with excavators. [ref: The AI Boom Has a Dirt Problem. This $1.75 Billion Startup Says Robots Can Fix It, Inc.] It was founded in 2024 by former Waymo engineers.

In August 2026 excavators equipped with the company system were working without an operator in the cab on three commercial sites in Texas and Nevada. [ref: First came self-driving cars. Now, Waymo veterans are building autonomous construction equipment., Business Insider] [ref: Bedrock Robotics deploys fully autonomous excavators on jobsites, Construction Dive] Independent observers described the deployments as an early-stage and limited test, noting that their productivity and need for human intervention had yet to be tested across more projects and over longer periods. [ref: Autonomous excavators are digging with empty cabs, Fox News]

== History ==
Bedrock Robotics was founded in 2024 by Boris Sofman, Ajay Gummalla, Kevin Peterson and Tom Eliaz. Three of the four had previously worked at Waymo, where Sofman led the autonomous trucking program and Peterson led perception for that division. Sofman had earlier co-founded the consumer robotics company Anki, which shut down in 2019. [ref: Ex-Waymo engineers launch Bedrock Robotics with $80M to automate construction, TechCrunch] Kevin Peterson also previously co-founded Marble, a robotics company acquired by Caterpillar Inc. in 2020. [ref: Caterpillar Acquires Robotic Specialist Marble Robot Inc, RER Magazine]

In July 2025, Bedrock announced $80 million in combined seed and Series A funding led by Eclipse and 8VC; at the time it was testing its system in Arkansas, Arizona, Texas and California with four contractors. In 2026, the company raised $270 million in a Series B round, giving it a valuation of $1.75 billion. [ref: Bedrock, an A.I. Start-Up for Construction, Raises $270 Million, The New York Times]

Bedrock began field-testing its system on contractors' projects with human operators driving equipped excavators to collect training data and later with the machines digging autonomously while a safety operator remained in the cab. The company also used a test site at Proto-Town, an industrial campus in Lockhart, Texas. [ref: 'Startup Cowboys' Are Making This Texas Town the New Tech Hotspot, The Wall Street Journal] As of December 2025, the system had been installed on excavator models from 20 to 80 tons. [ref: Bedrock Robotics Moves Earth With Autonomous Excavators, Engineering News-Record]

By mid-2026, Bedrock had approximately 50 equipped machines working on projects in six states. In July 2026, a Bedrock-equipped Caterpillar 352 excavator dug to a preset grade and loaded a dump truck for several hours with no one in the cab and no remote intervention; its productivity varied from lower to higher than that of a human operator. In August 2026, excavators using the company system were operating without onboard operators on three commercial sites in Texas and Nevada.

== Technology ==
Bedrock's system, which the company calls the Bedrock Operator, consists of cameras, lidar, GPS receivers and onboard computers added to an excavator, together with machine-learning software. The kit interfaces with the drive-by-wire hydraulic controls used on modern excavators. [ref: These Driverless Construction Vehicles Could Speed the Data Center Boom, [[The Information (website)]

When no operator is in the cab, a remote worker monitors several machines and can take control of one that has stalled; the machines stop automatically if a person or unauthorized object comes too close.

== Reception and analysis ==
Independent observers describe Bedrock's technology as being in its early stages, limited to no-operator excavators on three sites, and wrote that it was unclear whether autonomous machines could adapt to unpredictable construction sites reliably and cheaply enough for contractors to adopt them.

Vineet Kamat, a professor of construction management at the University of Michigan, called the deployments "a limited test" and said that contractors working on thin margins would need to be sure of a return on investment before spending a few hundred thousand dollars on robotic equipment. Fernanda Leite, a civil engineering professor at the University of Texas at Austin, said she expected sites in the near term to combine highly automated systems with highly skilled workers.

Fox News columnist Kurt Knutsson wrote that it remained to be seen whether the near-human productivity reported by the company would hold across more job sites, how intervention rates would change as one person monitored a larger fleet, and whether the machines could work safely around people over long periods.

=== Regulatory considerations ===
Because the machines operate on private construction sites rather than public roads, Bedrock does not face the same regulatory issues as robotaxis and autonomous trucks. Bryant Walker Smith, an associate professor of law at the University of South Carolina who studies automation, noted that it was unclear how Occupational Safety and Health Administration rules referring to an equipment "operator" would apply when one person remotely monitors several machines and intervenes only when something goes wrong.

data.title: The detention of Reza Valizadeh
data.text:
----

The detention of Reza Valizadeh is the Iranian government's ongoing incarceration of Reza Valizadeh (also known as Abdolreza Valizadeh), an Iranian-American journalist. The Iranian government has detained Valizadeh in Iran since September 2024, where he was sentenced in December 2024 to ten years in prison on charges of “collaborating with a hostile government.” [ref: Iranian court jails Iranian-American journalist for 10 years, lawyer says, Reuters] [ref: Reza Valizadeh, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty] In May 2025, the U.S. Department of State designated Valizadeh as wrongfully detained. [ref: From inside Iran's Evin Prison, journalist Reza Valizadeh pleads for medical help for him and other American captives - CBS News, www.cbsnews.com] [ref: Concerns mount over Iranian-American journalist Reza Valizadeh, wrongfully detained in Iran - CBS News, www.cbsnews.com] Valizadeh's detention has received sustained coverage from international media outlets and press freedom organizations.

== Valizadeh's journalism career ==
Valizadeh began his journalism career in Iran. He was arrested in 2007 in connection with a blog post critical of then-President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s security team. [ref: Imprisoned for telling the truth: A Q&A with Iranian-American journalist Reza Valizadeh’s brother, Committee to Protect Journalists]  Following the 2009 Iranian presidential election and the protests known as the Iranian Green Movement, he left Iran and later received asylum in France.

After leaving Iran, Valizadeh worked for international Persian-language media outlets, including Radio France Internationale, Voice of America Persian, and Radio Farda. [ref: Reza Valizadeh, UANI] His Iran-focused reporting for Radio Farda included stories on corruption, protests, and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

== Arrest, trial, and sentencing ==
On March 6, 2024, Valizadeh returned to Iran for the first time since 2009 to visit his aging parents.  He was arrested by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in Tehran on September 22, 2024.  Following his arrest, Valizadeh was held in Evin prison without access to his lawyer. [ref: U.S. Confirms Reports That Iran Arrested an Iranian-American Citizen, The New York Times]  Iranian intelligence interrogated Valizadeh while he was detained and pressured him to cooperate against his former employer, Radio Farda.  Valizadeh reportedly refused to cooperate.

On December 14, 2024, an Iranian court found Valizadeh guilty of “collaborating with a hostile government,” charges that stemmed from his work at a U.S.-funded radio outlet. [ref: Iran sentences an Iranian-American journalist to 10 years in prison, AP News]  The court sentenced Valizadeh to ten years in prison.  Valizadeh’s sentence also included restrictions on his residence, travel, and political-party membership following his imprisonment.  Valizadeh's attorneys have noted concerns about the fairness of his trial, including that the judge acted as both prosecutor and adjudicator for a trial lasting less than an hour.  Valizadeh’s appeal of his conviction was denied in January 2025.

== Detention conditions and health ==
Valizadeh has been held primarily in Evin Prison in Tehran since his arrest, a facility commonly used to hold political prisoners and foreign detainees.  During his imprisonment, Valizadeh has endured solitary confinement and repeated interrogation. [ref: Advocacy groups push for jailed Americans to be included in U.S.-Iran negotiations, The Washington Times]  He has suffered from deteriorating health conditions while imprisoned, including coughing, asthma-related breathing issues, persistent back pain, and dental problems. Conditions at Evin Prison, including unsanitary housing, polluted water, contaminated food, and inadequate medical treatment, have reportedly exacerbated Valizadeh’s health conditions. [ref: CPJ alarmed by new prison recording from Reza Valizadeh in Iran’s Evin Prison, Committee to Protect Journalists]

Valizadeh was briefly transferred to Fashafouyeh Prison following Israeli airstrikes on Evin Prison in June 2025, before being returned to Evin Prison. Valizadeh’s family believes that the strike and Valizadeh’s subsequent transfer contributed to his worsening asthma.

== Public attention and advocacy on behalf of Valizadeh ==
Valizadeh’s detention has received coverage from Reuters, the Associated Press, CBS News, Fox News, the Washington Post, Al Jazeera, and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. [ref: US detainees in Iran risk becoming collateral damage in war, families and supporters fear, AP News] [ref: American journalist detained in Iran as Supreme Leader Khamenei threatens US, Israel, State Department says, Fox News] [ref: Iran jails journalist Reza Valizadeh for ‘hostile’ US collaboration, Al Jazeera] Press freedom organizations have also called attention to his case. [ref: Reza Valizadeh, Foley Foundation]  The United States Department of State formally designated Valizadeh as “wrongfully detained” in May 2025, which authorizes the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs to coordinate activities across the Executive Branch to seek Valizadeh’s release. [ref: Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs, United States Department of State]  On January 20, 2026, attorneys for Valizadeh filed a petition with the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention on his behalf.

In June 2026, CBS News published a recording in which Valizadeh, speaking from Evin Prison, requested medical assistance for himself and other detained Americans.  In the recording, Valizadeh questioned why his and other Americans’ release had not been addressed in broader negotiations to end the 2026 Iran war.  These concerns were echoed in a June 19, 2026 Washington Post opinion column by Valizadeh’s attorney. [ref: ]
