data.title: Salah El Moncef
data.text:
Salah El Moncef is a writer, literary scholar, editor and visual artist. He was born in Kuwait City and is based in France.His books include [https://journals.openedition.org/transatlantica/707 Atopian Limits] (2002), [https://www.atoponbooks.com/the-offering The Offering] (2015), [https://www.forewordreviews.com/reviews/now-and-then/ Now and Then] (2022), [https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/mqr/2023/01/an-enormous-enigmatic-signifier-salah-el-moncefs-benghazi/ Benghazi] (2022) and [https://www.atoponbooks.com/the-woman-from-warsaw The Woman from Warsaw] (2026). He also published the study [https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0969725X.2021.1988410 Art as Pharmakon] in 2021. Reviews and scholarly discussions of Salah El Moncef’s fiction have focused on memory, loss, migration, and the effects of colonial rule and fascist violance. [ref: Salah EL MONCEF BIN KHALIFA, Nantes Université] [ref: Review of Atopian Limits, Transatlantica] [ref: Memory, Trauma, and the Diasporic Subject, Los Angeles Review of Books] [ref: An Enormous, Enigmatic Signifier: Salah el Moncef's Benghazi, Michigan Quarterly Review] [ref: The Art of World-Building: Salah el Moncef's The Woman from Warsaw, Michigan Quarterly Review] [ref: Salah el Moncef, official author site (used only for routine biographical and publication data).]

Moncef teaches English studies and creative writing at Nantes Université, where he works as a Maître de Conférences. His research focuses on contemporary American literature, diasporic writing, migration, and transnational identities. He is also the General Issue Editor of Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities and an editor of the Routledge series Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities. The journal has featured his paintings on its covers and included his artwork as illustrations in its issues. [ref: Nantes Université, institutional profile/CV: maître de conférences in English studies and creative writing; research on diasporic literatures, migration, and transnational identities.] [ref: Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities – About this journal, Taylor & Francis] [ref: Routledge, Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities, series page.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue I 2024." Angelaki 29.5 (2024), artwork list and acknowledgements.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue II 2025." Angelaki 30.6 (2025), artwork list and acknowledgements.]

== Education and academic career ==
A biographical note in The Matrix in Theory states that Moncef recieved the Presidential Prize for Distinction in the Humanities in 1987. It also mentions that he held a Fulbright fellowship at Indiana University Bloomington from 1988 to 1993. Indiana University also lists him among its alumni who completed a PhD in English.. [ref: Salah El Moncef, Genders archive] [ref: Myriam Diocaretz and Stefan Herbrechter, eds., The Matrix in Theory (Rodopi, 2006), contributor note for Salah el Moncef bin Khalifa.] [ref: Benghazi, PhD alumni publications]

Moncef later started teaching English and creative writing in Nantes, France. His work focuses on American literature and culture, along with migration, diasporic writing, and the experiences of people living between different cultures.

== Scholarship and editorial work ==
During the 1990s, Moncef wrote articles on Ezra Pound, John Updike’s Rabbit at Rest, Paul Auster’s Moon Palace, and Thomas Harris’s Hannibal Lecter novels. His work appeared in journals such as boundary 2, Arizona Quarterly, Angelaki, and Genders. In 2002, he published Atopian Limits: Questions of Self, Complexity, and Contingency in Postmodern American Narrative, bringing together some of his work on postmodern American fiction. [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Gold, Representation, and the Reversible Dynamic of Symptomatic Return in Ezra Pound." boundary 2 22.1 (1995): 117–142.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Sounding the Black Box: Linear Reproduction and Chance Bifurcations in Rabbit at Rest." Arizona Quarterly 51.4 (1995): 69–108.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Lecter Knows Worst: Justice, Marginal Value, and the Law in the Series of Thomas Harris's Silence of the Lambs." Genders, 5 July 1999.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Figures in (De)composition: The Genesis of the Paradoxical Self in Paul Auster's Moon Palace." Angelaki 4.3 (1999): 75–91.]

Jean-Yves Pellegrin reviewed Atopian Limits in Transatlantica. He discussed how the book looks at American fiction and the work of writers such as Paul Auster, Ken Kesey, John Updike, Thomas Harris, Gore Vidal, and Kathy Acker.

In 2005, Moncef co-edited Présence et représentation with Jacques Gilbert. The following year, he co-edited Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture with Michele Bottalico. Antonio C. Márquez reviewed the second book in Aztlán and discussed Moncef’s chapter, “The Hybrid Self at the Crossroads." [ref: Antonio C. Márquez, review of Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture, Aztlán 32.2 (2007): 213–216.] [ref: WorldCat, bibliographic record for Présence et représentation, Jacques Gilbert and Salah el Moncef (Peter Lang, 2005).]

His later work included chapters on mestiza and cyborg identeties and The Matrix trilogy. He also wrote about The Truman Show, Gloria Anzaldúa, and Don DeLillo’s novels Underworld and Falling Man. In 2020, he wrote the entry “Minor Literature” for the Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Literature.

His 2016 article Litarature as Antidote looks at Falling Man and its themes of trauma, grief, and recovery. In 2021, Angelaki published his study Art as Pharmakon: Viral Tirror, Trauma, and Healing in the DeLillian Age. He also explored transnational identities in a two-part essay, “Nomadismes et identités transfrontalières,” published in Amerika in 2010. [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Minor Literature." Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Literature, published 29 May 2020.] [ref: Art as Pharmakon: Viral Terror, Trauma, and Healing in the DeLillian Age, Angelaki] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Literature as Antidote: Reflections on Don DeLillo's Falling Man." International Journal of Humanities and Social Science Research 2 (2016): 87–113.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Life after 'Truman'?" Revue française d'études américaines 102 (2004): 117–125.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "The Matrix Trilogy and the Triumph of Virtual Reason." In The Matrix in Theory (Rodopi, 2006): 227–248.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Mestizas and Cyborgs R Us." In (Re)Mapping the Centres (2000): 125–136.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Übermenschen, Mestizas, Nomads." Angelaki 8.3 (2003): 41–57.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Don DeLillo's Underworld and the Inscriptions of the Commonplace." Angelaki 13.1 (2008): 149–165.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Nomadismes et identités transfrontalières (première partie)." Amerika 2 (2010).] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Nomadismes et identités transfrontalières (deuxième partie)." Amerika 2 (2010).]

Other researchers have also referred to Moncef’s work in their studies of literature and cultural theory. In a 2010 essay on Paul Auster’s Moon Palace, Pal Hegyi discussed Moncef’s article “Figures in (De)composition” and used the terms “monadic unfolding” and “nomadic self-containment. [ref: Extended mise-en-abyme in Paul Auster's Moon Palace, AMERICANA: E-Journal of American Studies in Hungary]

In 2023, Joshua M. Hall discussed the ideas of Anzaldúa and Nietzsche presented in Moncef’s article “Ubermenschen, Mestizas, Nomads.” A 2026 article by Yvonne Liao, Julia T. S. Binter, Olivia Irena Durand, and Helena F. S. Lopes on colonial port cities also cited his “Minor Literature” entry, along with the work of Deleuze and Guattari. [ref: Anzaldúa's Snake-Bridge as Alternative to Mestizaje, The Journal of Aesthetic Education] [ref: Port cities storytelling: Drawing on materials of neglect, Journal of Global History]

=== Scholarly reception ===
Cary Wolfe wrote the preface to Atopian Limits, titled “Total Systems and Dense Instances.” In it, he looks at how the book uses systems theory, complexity, and contingency to study contemporary American fiction. [ref: Cary Wolfe, "Total Systems and Dense Instances," preface to Salah El Moncef, Atopian Limits: Questions of Self, Complexity, and Contingency in Postmodern American Narrative (Peter Lang, 2002).]

Other researchers have also discussed Moncef’s work. In an article on John Updike’s fiction published in Studies in American Fiction, C. Parker Krieg discussed Moncef’s reading of Rabbit at Rest. In Textual Practice, Alan Lopez wrote that his reading of a passage from Frantz Fanon’s work was greatly influenced by Moncef’s earlier analysis of Peter Weir’s film The Truman Show. [ref: Energy Futures: John Updike's Petrofictions, Studies in American Fiction] [ref: Alan Lopez, "Kindred spirits: Fanon's postcolonialism," Textual Practice 29.5 (2015): 949–972, note 37.]

Moncef was listed as an editor of Angelaki for “General Issue 2008 I”.He continued to be named as General Issue Editor in later issues through 2025. Routledge also lists him as an editor of the book series Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities.. [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "General issue 2008 I." Angelaki 13.1 (2008): 1.]

== Fiction ==

=== The Offering ===
The Offering was first published in 2015. The novel follows Tariq Abbassi, a Tunisian poet and restaurant owner living in France. It deals with migration, his hopes as a writer, problems in his marriage, grief, and memory. The book includes an introduction by scholar Mari Ruti. [ref: Mari Ruti, introduction to The Offering, by Salah el Moncef.]

Stefan Mattesich wrote a review essay about the novel in Angelaki. In the Los Angeles Review of Books, Stephen Watt discussed how the story deals with trauma and diaspora, including what he calls “happy forgetting.” Wade A. Bell Jr., writing in Moderna Språk, describes Tariq as a divided person shaped by life across different countries and cultures. [ref: Wade A. Bell Jr., review of The Offering, Moderna Språk 111.1 (2017): 206–208.] [ref: Stefan Mattesich, review essay on The Offering, Angelaki 20.4 (2015).]

=== Now and Then and Benghazi ===
Now and Then (2022) includes two works of fiction, Benghazi and The Night Visitor, along with two essays, “A Bridge Too Near” and “The Voice of Exile.” In her review for Foreword Clarion Reviews, Amy O’Loughlin discusses the book’s themes of migration, nationalism, and identity across different countries. BlueInk Review praised the book’s descriptive writing but questioned whether the stories and essays fit well together as a whole. [ref: Review of Now and Then, Foreword Clarion Reviews] [ref: Now and Then, BlueInk Review]

Benghazi was also published as a separate novella in 2022. Told by Mariam Khaldoon, the story follows her family and her friendship with Esther Sanz during Italian rule in Libya, including Benito Mussolini’s visit to Benghazi in 1937.

In Michigan Quarterly Review, Watt looks at the novella through Paul Ricœur’s ideas about memory and the introduction by Mari Ruti. He describes the characters as people who live between cultures and never feel fully at home. Kirkus Reviews praised the book’s setting and the relationship between a father and daughter, but felt that some parts of the story were too slow and drawn out. [ref: Review of Benghazi by Salah el Moncef, Kirkus Reviews]

Moncef’s novelette Sleepwalking was published in the journal Short Story in 2011. [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Sleepwalking." Short Story 19.1 (2011): 30–53, University of Northern Iowa ScholarWorks.]

=== The Woman from Warsaw ===
Atopon Books published The Woman from Warsaw in 2026. The novel is set mainly in Benghazi during the Second World War. Mariam tells the story of her teenage years under Italian Fascist rule and her relationship with Esther, a Jewish woman who moved there from another country. The book has four sections, beginning with Benghazi, and builds on the family story and wartime setting introduced in the earlier novella. [ref: The Woman from Warsaw, Atopon Books]

In Michigan Quarterly Review, Watt explains how the novel uses Mariam’s memories to tell the story of Fascist racial laws, wartime bombings, and Esther’s experiances. He also discusses Esther’s independence and shows how Benghazi was once a city where people from different backgrounds lived together. He describes Mariam’s telling of the past as an act of “right remembering.”

== Visual art ==
Moncef’s paintings have appeared on the covers of Angelaki and as illustrations inside the journal. In General Issue I 2024 (volume 29, issue 5), Birth 3 appeared on the cover, while Three Flights Up and Fantasy Rhino were included inside. General Issue II 2024 (volume 29, issue 6) featured Phoenician Mask 3 on the cover and included Humpty Dumpty, Iris Out, and Passage Pommeraye. General Issue I 2025 (volume 30, issue 5) included Fantasy Rhino 3 (Kinderszenen), while General Issue II 2025 (volume 30, issue 6) included Strange Attractors 9 (Space). [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue II 2024." Angelaki 29.6 (2024), artwork list and acknowledgements.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue I 2025." Angelaki 30.5 (2025), artwork list and acknowledgements.]

data.title: Rajmata (Novel)
data.text:
Rajmata () is a historical novel by Neelam Karki Niharika. This book was published on March 30, 2026, by FinePrint. [ref: Neelam Karki ‘Niharika’’s New novel Rajmata Released, SpotlightNepal] It won the Kabi Danda Puraskar, 2083 B.S. [ref: राजमाता उपन्यासलाई कविडाँडा आख्यान पुरस्कार, Ekantipur] This book is based on the life of the heroic women whom history overlooked or the state failed to recognize.

==Synopsis ==
Before Nepal acquired its present geographical shape, it experienced many ups and downs. At times it expanded, at other times it fragmented, and it had to endure the fate of being divided. During different historical periods, small kingdoms emerged and disappeared. The powerful conquered the weak, and many dynasties took control of the reins of government. They ruled either independently, jointly, as tributary states, or as semi-autonomous kingdoms. The names of the royal families that conquered these kingdoms and the records of their remarkable achievements have been preserved in history [ref: ‘अध्ययन गर्दै जाँदा थाहा भयो – महिला सवालमा इतिहास पनि पक्षपाती रहेछ’ – नीलम कार्की निहारिका, ‘अध्ययन गर्दै जाँदा थाहा भयो – महिला सवालमा इतिहास पनि पक्षपाती रहेछ’ – नीलम कार्की निहारिका]. Some women, too, found opportunities to have their names engraved on stone inscriptions, copper plates, or written in the colophons of manuscripts, alongside those of their husbands or sons. Occasionally, they are also mentioned in royal genealogies.

Over time, archaeologists unearthed historical documents through excavation and research, and historians carefully recorded them in books with great dedication and perseverance.

By weaving together those historical pages, while also giving due importance to certain heroic women whom history overlooked or the state failed to recognize, Rajmata presents a beautiful garland of interconnected stories [ref: निहारिकाको नयाँ कृति ‘राजमाता’] [ref: History, Memory, and Marginal Voices: ‘Rajmata’ Reframes Nepal’s Past Through a Feminine Lens, History, Memory, and Marginal Voices: ‘Rajmata’ Reframes Nepal’s Past Through a Feminine Lens]

==Award==
Kabidanda Akhyan Puraskar of 2083 was awarded to Rajmata. The award was given by Kabidanda Sahitya Samaj and the award money is 200,160 Rupees.

data.title: The Once and Future World Order
data.text:
== The Once and Future World Order ==
The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West is a 2025 book by international relations scholar Amitav Acharya, [ref: ] published by Basic Books in April 2025. [ref: The Once and Future World Order, John Murray Press] The book explores the historical development of world order across different civilizations and regions, beginning with ancient Sumer and Egypt and extending through Persia, Greece, India, China, Rome, the Islamic world, Africa, the Americas, and Europe to the contemporary international system. [ref: The once and future world order: why global civilization will survive the decline of the West, Basic Books] The book examines the development of political ideas, institutions, and practices associated with relations among states and societies, including diplomacy, trade, political organization, war, and interstate cooperation, and concludes with a discussion of the changing international order and the implications of declining Western dominance.

== Contents ==
The book consists of an introduction and fourteen chapters, tracing the development of different world orders and interactions among societies throughout history, before turning to the contemporary international system and its possible future.

The book begins by underscoring that different ideas and institutions so commonly associated with today’s US-led “Western” world order emerged in non-Western civilizations thousands of years before the rise of the West. These range from peace treaties and interstate cooperation to freedom of the seas and environmental protection. Acharya argues that these contributions have often been overlooked in the mainstream history of international relations and world orders.

The book examines how the dominance of the European perspective over the last 500 years has contributed to two forms of historical misrepresentation: the sin of commission and the sin of omission. The sin of commission is largely the misinterpretation or distortion of the achievements of non-Western cultures and civilizations. The sin of omission occurs when fundamental facts about them are overlooked. A significant portion of the book is a chronicle of these sins. Acharya reveals what has been distorted, obscured, or omitted about non-Western civilizations. At the same time, the book considers the achievements and failures of both Western and non-Western civilizations. It also examines how the illusion of benevolence has repeatedly become a common denominator of imperial discourse. [ref: Review of the Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West, International Studies Review]

The civilizations explored in this book can be classified into four broad categories. Parallel civilizations coexist independently, with little interaction among them. Congruent civilizations exhibit accidental similarities despite the vast physical distance between them. Interactive civilizations can be known for their markedly asymmetrical relationships. Finally, a convergent civilization in theory entails the merging of civilizational values on the basis of parity of esteem.

In its discussion of the contemporary world order, the book identifies three schools of thought regarding the future of the United States as a preeminent power. The first, so-called “cry-wolf” school, postulates that the theory about the decline of the United States is nothing new. It has come and gone, but the United States remains the leading power, with no reason to assume that the future will be any different. The second is the “bionic-man” argument, which concedes that America is indeed on the decline, but it is likely to rebound. The third, the “Roman Empire” analogy, suggests that the US’s decline will be slow, like that of the Roman Empire, and may take up to two centuries.

The book also explores three fears in the West today about the end of the American-led Western order: the fear of the rise of the “civilization states,” the fear of the Chinese-built and Chinese-led order, and the fear of “chaos, violence, and conflict.” Although the future may not be “a garden of peace”, Acharya suggests, based on his examination of historical world orders, that the emerging order may be more humane and, almost certainly, no less so than the current world order.

data.title: Object Shows (Web Series)
data.text:
Originating from the indie web series [https://www.tvguide.com/tvshows/battle-for-dream-island/1060525925 Battle for Dream Island], the microgenre of object shows was conceptualized sometime during 2008 with Total Firey Island, and officially became a noted trope during 2011-2013. The most major parts of the style are anthropomorphic objects with black stick-line limbs and "doodle" faces. They were animated on Adobe Flash the majority of the time, however as of now they are made on a variety of platforms such as the animation app Flipaclip, sometimes even using unconventional applications such as Google Slides, another early software used in the 2011-2013 era. The first and most well-known object show, BFDI, was created by Cary and Michael Huang. [ref: BFDI 2: Barriers and Pitfalls]

The official community, or often referred to as a fanbase of the microgenre, is the Object Show Community, commonly shortened to OSC. The TikTok branch of the fandom is referred to as OSCTT (Standing for Object Show Community Tiktok). Other object shows, such as Inanimate Insanity (the unofficial 'sister show' to BFDI) or One (called hfjone to avoid confusion and to clarify its creator, Cheesy Hfj) are common examples of it.

As of 2020 and onwards, the Object Show Community has experienced a massive growth in interest, with Gen Alpha taking root in it. There are also many major controversies tied to the fandom, though are not listed.

data.title: Bogos
data.text:
Bogos (Bogo; associated with the Bilen people) is a historical region in present-day Eritrea, centered on the area around Keren. The region is known for its unique social institutions, customary laws and historical traditions. Werner Munzinger, a nineteenth-century explorer and ethnographer, documented the customs, legal practices and political history of the Bogos in his work Über die Sitten und das Recht der Bogos, published in 1859.

Bogos developed within the larger historical context of the northern Horn of Africa, where highland communities, pastoral societies and regional powers maintained fluctuating political and commercial relationships. Munzinger's writings, along with the historical and linguistic research of Leo Reinisch, provide accounts of the region's traditional history, kinship structures and customary institutions.

In the nineteenth century, Bogos became increasingly involved in the political rivalries affecting the northern Ethiopian and Eritrean borderlands. The region's history was linked to the expansion of Egyptian authority, the policies of Ethiopian rulers and the changing balance of power in the surrounding territories. Historical accounts by Munzinger and later studies of Eritrea provide sources for examining these developments and their effects on local communities.

The social organization of Bogos was closely linked to customary law, kinship and community traditions. Munzinger's account describes rules regarding marriage, inheritance, property, family relations and compensation for injury and homicide, making it an important early source for the study of the region's traditional legal institutions.

Hassan Rilwan is a Nigerian public administrator who served as the Executive Secretary of the Kaduna State Scholarship and Loans Board from 2019 to 2022 under Governor Nasir Ahmad el-Rufai. [ref: El-Rufai appoints Hassan Rilwan as ES Kaduna Scholarship Board, Blueprint Newspaper] [ref: Kaduna spends N800m on 42 students to study overseas, Vanguard Newspaper] He subsequently served as Special Adviser to the Governor.

== Early life and career ==
Rilwan is an Associate Fellow of the Nigerian Leadership Institute and an alumnus of the Young African Leaders Initiative (YALI) fellowship. [ref: Hassan Rilwan Profile, The Future Awards Africa] In 2009, he served on the Federal Government Ministerial Committee on the establishment of the Almajiri Education System, which was established to integrate traditional Islamic education with modern school curricula across Northern Nigeria.

== Public service ==
In September 2019, Governor Nasir Ahmad el-Rufai appointed Rilwan as Executive Secretary of the Kaduna State Scholarship and Loans Board.

During his tenure, the board managed state-sponsored merit-based international scholarships for foreign postgraduate studies and implemented policy adjustments to protect educational funding during the COVID-19 pandemic. [ref: Kaduna says COVID-19 won't affect scholarships, loans, Punch Newspapers] In August 2021, under his leadership, the board coordinated the emergency security evacuation of tertiary institution students of Kaduna origin from Jos, Plateau State during inter-communal unrest. [ref: Jos crisis: Kaduna evacuates students from Plateau, Vanguard Newspaper]

Following his term at the scholarship board, Rilwan was appointed Special Adviser within the Kaduna State Government.

data.title: Ulaa Browser
data.text:
Ulaa Browser [ref: ] is a privacy-focused web browser developed by Zoho Corporation, an Indian technology company known for products such as Zoho Books, Zoho Mail and Zoho Workplace. It is designed to provide a safer, more private and more productive browsing experience by combining regular web browsing with built-in privacy protection, advertisement blocking, tracker prevention and productivity features. Like Google Chrome, Ulaa is based on the Chromium browser engine, which means most modern websites should work similarly in both browsers. However, Ulaa adds its own features and customisations to improve privacy and help users manage their online activities. It is available for Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS, making it suitable for personal computers, office systems and mobile devices. One of its main attractions is that users can access many privacy and productivity features without having to install several separate browser extensions. [ref: https://ulaa.com/#privacy] [ref: Zoho launches privacy-centered browser ‘Ulaa’ to challenge Google, Microsoft and Apple, BusinessLine] [ref: https://www.business-standard.com/technology/tech-news/privacy-centred-web-browser-ulaa-to-remain-free-for-end-users-without-ads-123051000818_1.html]

== Privacy and Advertisement Blocking ==
One of Ulaa's principal features is its built-in advertisement and tracker blocking functionality. Websites may use advertisements, tracking scripts, cookies, and other technologies to display content, measure visitor activity, or personalise services. Ulaa's protection mechanisms are intended to block certain advertisements and tracking elements, reducing some forms of online tracking and potentially improving page-loading performance. [ref: https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/startup/government-agencies-enterprises-keen-on-adopting-zohos-ulaa-web-browser-10731491.html]

The browser provides privacy settings that allow users to adjust the level of protection. More restrictive settings may interfere with website functionality when a website depends on scripts or other resources that are blocked. Consequently, users may occasionally need to adjust protection settings for particular websites. [ref: After Arattai, Zoho's Google Chrome killer tops App Store charts. Here's what makes Ulaa browser special, mint] [ref: Zoho CEO Sridhar Vembu launches new 'Private Browser' in India; forays into AI tools powered by ChatGPT - BusinessToday, Business Today]

Advertisement blocking does not guarantee that all advertisements will be removed. Similarly, tracker prevention does not provide complete anonymity or prevent every method of collecting information about browsing activity. [ref: Zoho launches Ulaa web browser, unveils AI strategy, The Times of India] [ref: 'Trust me, bro': Zoho's Sridhar Vembu promises user privacy security in Arattai Messenger soon, Deccan Herald] [ref: Ulaa: Everything you need to know about Zoho’s Google Chrome rival, The Indian Express]

data.title: Mobile application security
data.text:
Mobile application security (mobile AppSec) is the discipline of protecting mobile apps, the data, and backend services they connect to from reverse engineering, tampering, malware, and runtime attacks across an app's development lifecycle. It sits between two broader fields: application security, which covers building and verifying secure software generally, and mobile security, which covers protecting the device, operating system, and network layers a mobile app runs on. Mobile application security narrows that scope to the app itself. It focuses on the compiled binary sitting on a device the developer does not control, along with the code and secrets packaged inside it.

Standards bodies and industry analysts publish guidance specifically addressing mobile application security, distinguishing it from broader application security and mobile security concerns. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) maintains "OWASP Mobile Application Security" as a separate dedicated project from its general Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS), on the grounds that mobile apps raise concerns, such as binary exposure and reverse engineering, that its web-focused standards do not fully address. [ref: Introduction to the OWASP Mobile Application Security Project - OWASP Mobile Application Security, mas.owasp.org] Gartner has similarly tracked "mobile application security testing" as a distinct technology category in its [https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/8151129 Hype Cycle for Application Security], along with Application Shielding. The analyst firm has published a dedicated market guide for it, separate from its general application security testing and mobile device management coverage. [ref: Gartner Mobile Application Security Testing Guide, NowSecure]

This distinction matters in practice because a mobile app, unlike a server-side web application, ships an executable copy of itself onto a device that is fully accessible to an attacker. The attacker can install the app, decompile it, attach a debugger, run it on an emulator, or modify and repackage it, without ever touching the developer's own infrastructure. Mobile application security therefore largely focuses on defending against this class of client-side attacks, on top of the concerns it already shares with web and API security, such as insecure data storage, weak authentication, and insufficient transport-layer protection.

== Overview ==

Smartphones are used to access sensitive personal and financial information, including banking and payment services, as well as enterprise systems and data. [ref: Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, NIST] That has made mobile apps a target. Attackers steal credentials and payment data, extract and run fraud at scale through farmed emulators and automated bots, or take a legitimate app, repackage it with malicious code, and redistribute it. Academic work on mobile malware traced reverse engineering, tampering, and repackaging as recurring attack methods more than a decade ago; [ref: Suarez-Tangil, Guillermo; Tapiador, Juan E.; Peris-Lopez, Pedro; Ribagorda, Arturo (2014). "Evolution, Detection and Analysis of Malware for Smart Devices". IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials. 16 (2): 961–987.] mobile app security vendors have continued to report the same categories, along with API exploitation, as ongoing attack vectors. [ref: ]

Mobile application security is usually treated as spanning the entire software development life cycle, from secure design and coding through automated testing in continuous integration pipelines to hardening release binaries and monitoring apps once they reach stores such as the Google Play Store and the Apple App Store. Once an app is published, the developer has limited visibility into how it is used or attacked after it leaves the build pipeline, unless the app is built to report threat telemetry back.

== Why mobile apps require dedicated security practices ==

Several properties of the mobile environment set app security apart from traditional web or server application security.

* The client is untrusted and physically exposed. A mobile app binary can run on a device the attacker controls, so decompilers, disassemblers, and static analysis tools can be pointed directly at the compiled code. An attacker can read an app's logic, extract embedded API keys and cryptographic material from the binary, and reverse-engineer its business logic without ever touching a server.

* The binary itself can be patched and redistributed. Because the application binary is under the attacker's control, the app can be repackaged and republished under a different name, for example, to strip out license checks, bypass in-app purchases, inject malware, or intercept and alter data before it reaches the server. Academic literature has documented repackaging and cloning Android apps as a distinct malware-distribution route. [ref: Crussell, Johnathan; Gibler, Clint; Chen, Hao (2012). "Attack of the Clones: Detecting Cloned Applications on Android Markets". University of California, Davis. http://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~hchen/paper/esorics2012.pdf]

* The runtime environment is hostile by design. On a rooted or jailbroken device, or inside an emulator, debugger, or dynamic instrumentation framework, an attacker can watch and modify an app's behavior while it runs, even where the code itself resists static analysis.

* Distribution and the device population are both harder to control than on the desktop. Apps are typically installed through official stores but can equally be sideloaded from third-party marketplaces or direct downloads, and the resulting devices span a wide range of OS versions, manufacturers, and hardware capabilities, such as whether a hardware-backed secure element is present, in a way that a single web server environment does not have to contend with.

* Resources are constrained. Mobile devices have far less battery life, memory, and processing power than servers, and users notice when an app is slow or large, so security controls have to be engineered with performance and app size in mind.

Many standard web application security controls, discussed at greater length in application security, still apply to a mobile app's backend and API layer. On their own, though, they are not sufficient; the client binary needs its own layer of defense. For device- and network-level risks, a mobile app inherits them simply by running on a phone, such as SIM-based attacks, Bluetooth exploits, or rogue Wi-Fi access points; see mobile security.

== The mobile application security lifecycle ==

Mobile AppSec practices are usually mapped across the phases of app development and its life after release, extending the general application-security lifecycle described in the application security article.

* Design and requirements. Threat modeling for mobile-specific risks, such as what happens if a device is rooted, an API key is extracted, or backend API endpoints are exposed.

* Development. Secure coding practices, secure API communications (such as certificate pinning and short-lived tokens), and platform-provided secure storage (such as the Android Keystore system and the Apple Keychain), while avoiding hardcoded secrets.

* Build and integration. Automated security testing built into the pipeline, with code-hardening protections applied as part of the release build.

* Pre-release testing. Static application security testing (SAST), Dynamic application security testing (DAST), Interactive application security testing (IAST), and manual penetration testing of the compiled binary before submission to an app store.

* Release. Runtime protections, such as runtime application self-protection (RASP), so the shipped binary can detect and respond to hostile conditions on its own.

* Post-release monitoring. Detecting threats against apps already installed on user devices, including counterfeit or modified copies circulating outside official stores, since a published app cannot be patched instantly the way a server can.

== Common threats and attack techniques ==

For threats that target the underlying device, operating system, or radio/network stack, as opposed to a specific app, such as SS7 and IMSI-catcher attacks, Bluetooth exploits, or malicious firmware, see mobile security. The list below is specific to the app binary and its own network and storage behavior.

* Reverse engineering. Decompiling or disassembling an app to read its source logic, extract algorithms, or find embedded secrets.

* Repackaging and code tampering. Modifying a decompiled app, for example, to bypass license checks, remove ads, inject malware, or redirect payments, then redistributing it, often through unofficial app stores.

* Dynamic instrumentation and hooking. Intercepting, inspecting, or modifying an app's behavior at runtime, including bypassing certificate pinning, root/jailbreak detection, or authentication checks.

* Man-in-the-middle attacks against app traffic. Intercepting network traffic between the app and its backend, typically over insecure or compromised Wi-Fi, to read or alter data in transit.

* Insecure data storage. Tokens, credentials, or personal data left unencrypted in local storage, logs, backups, or caches, recoverable by an attacker with physical or malware access to the device.

* API and backend abuse. Since many mobile apps are thin clients for a backend API, attackers often find API weaknesses by first reverse-engineering the mobile client to see how it talks to the server.

* Malicious and cloned apps. Fake or trojanized versions of legitimate apps built by repackaging a genuine app with malicious code, then distributed to trick users into installing them.

* Emulator and bot abuse. Running an app inside an emulator or automation framework, or directing an AI agent, at scale to commit fraud, such as fake account creation, credential stuffing, or abuse of promotions and loyalty programs. This kind of automated abuse increasingly targets a mobile app's backend API directly, bypassing the app's own interface since APIs are built for automation and often expose more functionality than the UI does.

* Supply chain risk. Vulnerabilities introduced through third-party SDKs, open-source libraries, or compromised build tooling, as distinct from vulnerabilities in the app's own first-party code.

== OWASP Mobile Top 10 (2024) ==

The OWASP Foundation's Mobile Top 10 project publishes a periodically updated list of the most critical mobile application security risks, based on incident reports, vulnerability data, and expert review. [ref: OWASP Mobile Top 10, OWASP Foundation] The 2024 revision lists:

# M1: Improper Credential Usage
# M2: Inadequate Supply Chain Security
# M3: Insecure Authentication/Authorization
# M4: Insufficient Input/Output Validation
# M5: Insecure Communication
# M6: Inadequate Privacy Controls
# M7: Insufficient Binary Protections
# M8: Security Misconfiguration
# M9: Insecure Data Storage
# M10: Insufficient Cryptography

Compared with the 2016 list, the 2024 revision adds supply chain security and binary protection as distinct top-level categories, reflecting the growing prominence of reverse engineering, tampering, and third-party dependency risk in reported incidents. OWASP maintains two closely related mobile projects alongside the Top 10 list. The Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) sets out security requirements for mobile apps, used by architects and developers as a foundational requirement and by testers as a benchmark. [ref: OWASP MASVS - OWASP Mobile Application Security, mas.owasp.org] The [https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/ Mobile Application Security Testing Guide (MASTG)] is a detailed manual of testing techniques and test cases aligned with the MASVS, covering static and dynamic analysis and reverse-engineering methodology for iOS and Android. [ref: OWASP MASTG - OWASP Mobile Application Security, mas.owasp.org]

== Core defensive domains ==

OWASP's MASVS groups app-level security requirements into several categories, including storage, cryptography, authentication, network communication, platform interaction, code quality, privacy, and resilience. Most of what the security industry calls "mobile app protection" falls under the resilience category specifically, since it addresses reverse engineering and tampering rather than the more general engineering concerns covered elsewhere in MASVS. [ref: MASVS-RESILIENCE: Resilience Against Reverse Engineering and Tampering - OWASP Mobile Application Security, mas.owasp.org]

=== Secure development and code quality ===

Standard practices include avoiding hardcoded secrets, validating input and output, using platform-provided secure storage APIs, and enforcing certificate pinning for network calls. Apple and Google have published secure coding guidance for Android [ref: Privacy checklist, Android Developers] and iOS [ref: Security, Apple Developer Documentation] app development, as well as for cross-platform frameworks such as React Native and Flutter.

=== Resilience: hardening, runtime self-protection, and attestation ===

OWASP's MASVS-RESILIENCE category covers a cluster of related techniques aimed at making an app harder to reverse engineer or tamper with, rather than a single technique.

Code obfuscation is one component, an application of the general concept of software obfuscation to mobile binaries. Common techniques include:

* Name obfuscation and code shrinking rename classes, methods, and fields using meaningless identifiers and remove unused code. On Android, Google's open-source R8 compiler has been the default code shrinker and obfuscator in the Android Gradle Plugin since 2019 and remains compatible with existing ProGuard configuration rules.

* Control-flow obfuscation, which restructures an app's logic so its execution flow is hard to follow even with a decompiler.

* String and resource encryption, so embedded secrets cannot simply be read out of the binary.

* Polymorphic protection, which varies the obfuscation applied between builds so a technique that worked against one release does not automatically work against the next.

A second component is runtime application self-protection (RASP): defenses built into the app itself that detect and react to hostile conditions while it is running, on top of whatever protections were applied at build time. Common checks include rooted or jailbroken devices, debuggers, emulators, dynamic hooking frameworks, tampering with the app's code signing or checksum, and execution in an unexpected or repackaged environment. Depending on what it finds, an app can log and alert, restrict its functionality, or shut down.

A third component is app attestation: platform features such as Google's Play Integrity API [ref: Play Integrity API, Android Developers] and Apple's DeviceCheck and App Attest services [ref: DeviceCheck, Apple Developer Documentation] provide baseline OS-level checks that let a backend server cryptographically check that a request comes from an unmodified copy of the app running on a real device, helping rule out emulators, patched binaries, and automated bots. In defense-in-depth security architectures, these platform baselines are frequently complemented by additional runtime checks and monitoring to address broader threat vectors.

OWASP's own MASVS documentation frames these resilience controls as defense-in-depth measures that sit alongside sound security architecture, never in place of it. The absence of obfuscation or anti-tampering does not by itself constitute a vulnerability, and OWASP states directly that such techniques "must not be used as a substitute for proper security architecture." The same documentation also notes that resilience measures can reduce the transparency of what a compiled app is doing and make independent code review harder, which is a particular concern for apps in public-interest sectors such as government or health.

=== Testing ===

Gartner defines mobile application security testing as covering static, dynamic, and behavioral analysis of an app before or after development. Applied to mobile apps specifically, static and dynamic techniques are adapted as discussed in more detail in Testing methodologies below; behavioral testing observes an app's runtime behavior for signs of abuse rather than checking it against a fixed rule set.

=== Post-release monitoring ===

Once an app is published, its security is no longer only a pre-release concern. Ongoing visibility into how it is being attacked or abused, for example through counterfeit or repackaged copies circulating outside official stores, unusual traffic suggesting bot or fraud activity, or attacks attempted against instrumented apps on real user devices, functions as a further layer of defense, since a shipped mobile binary cannot be patched the instant a new attack technique surfaces the way a server usually can.

== Testing methodologies ==

Mobile app security testing draws on the same broad categories as general application security, static application security testing (SAST), dynamic application security testing (DAST), interactive application security testing (IAST), and software composition analysis (SCA). Applied to mobile apps, each is adapted somewhat. SAST tools work against decompiled or disassembled mobile binaries. Because there is no server-side source code to inspect, they look for issues such as hardcoded secrets, insecure API usage, and insufficient obfuscation directly in the compiled app. DAST tools exercise a running app on an emulator or physical device, observing network calls, local data storage, and platform API usage. Unlike a single-server environment, mobile DAST must account for a wide range of OS versions and device models. IAST tools instrument the app runtime during automated or manual testing to identify vulnerabilities while code executes in real time. SCA flags known-vulnerable third-party mobile SDKs against public vulnerability databases such as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE). Manual penetration testing and reverse engineering, following methodologies such as the OWASP MASTG, still catch logic flaws and bypasses that automated tools miss. This kind of testing is commonly integrated into continuous integration pipelines to evaluate builds on each commit, well before a periodic audit would catch the same problem.

== Standards, frameworks, and regulation ==

Mobile application security is shaped by open community standards alongside formal regulatory requirements.

* OWASP's MASVS and MASTG open standard and testing methodologies specific to mobile apps.

* NIST guidance, including Special Publication 800-124 Revision 1, Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise. [ref: Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, National Institute of Standards and Technology]

* The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), which applies to apps handling payment card data and mandates secure development, vulnerability management, and protection of client-side code. [ref: Document Library, PCI Security Standards Council]

* The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), which applies to apps handling protected health information in the United States and requires technical safeguards against unauthorized access. [ref: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, "HIPAA Security Series". https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/ocr/privacy/hipaa/administrative/securityrule/techsafeguards.pdf]

* Data protection regulations such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) govern what data an app collects, how it is stored, and user consent. [ref: European Union, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4 May 2016, pp. 1–88; see in particular Articles 5, 6, 7, 25 and 32.] [ref: Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL), "Recommandation relative aux applications mobiles", Délibération no. 2024-061 of 18 July 2024.] This overlaps with the "Inadequate Privacy Controls" category in the OWASP Mobile Top 10. [ref: OWASP Foundation, "M6: Inadequate Privacy Controls", OWASP Mobile Top 10, 2024 release. https://owasp.github.io/www-project-mobile-top-10/2023-risks/m6-inadequate-privacy-controls]

* Platform requirements set directly by Apple and Google through their app store review guidelines, [ref: App Review Guidelines, Apple Developer] [ref: Android Apps on Google Play, play.google.com] which define mandatory baseline security and privacy requirements for published apps.

== Industry and tooling ==

Several companies sell commercial tools in the domains above spanning mobile application security testing, app shielding, code hardening, runtime application self-protection (RASP), and app attestation.

The OWASP Foundation remains a vendor-neutral nonprofit and does not endorse any of the companies that build tools against its standards. It recognizes organizations as "[https://mas.owasp.org/MASTG/0x02c-Acknowledgements/#mas-advocates MAS Advocates]" for their sustained contributions to the Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) and Mobile Application Security Testing Guide (MASTG).

== Standard guidance and baseline controls ==

Industry guidance published by the OWASP Foundation and NIST outlines common baseline controls for mobile application security:

* Client-side threat modeling: Frameworks emphasize evaluating risks specific to the client binary, such as reverse engineering or device compromise, alongside traditional server and API risks.

* Credential and secret management: Published standards advise against hardcoding API keys or cryptographic secrets in code, recommending platform secure-storage features (like Android Keystore and Apple Keychain) and short-lived tokens instead.

* Code hardening: Guidance recommends applying obfuscation and protection mechanisms to release builds, varying techniques between releases to prevent repeated exploitation.

* Network transport security: Standards call for Transport Layer Security (TLS) coupled with certificate or public-key pinning to protect communication channels.

* Runtime environmental checks: Security baselines include controls that detect rooted or jailbroken operating systems, active debuggers, emulators, and dynamic instrumentation tools.

* Platform attestation: Architectural recommendations incorporate platform attestation APIs to verify binary and device integrity before fulfilling backend requests.

* Automated pipeline testing: Frameworks advise integrating automated security scanning into continuous integration pipelines rather than relying solely on periodic manual audits.

* Post-release threat visibility: Guidance highlights the need for ongoing monitoring of repackaged binaries and anomalous traffic patterns following publication.

* Dependency management: Standards emphasize continuous vetting of third-party SDKs and open-source libraries to mitigate supply chain risks.

OWASP's own guidance notes that while hardening and resilience measures provide critical defense-in-depth, they serve to complement rather than replace secure underlying software architecture.

data.title: Parneet Khaira
data.text:
Parneet Kaur Khaira, known professionally as Parneet Khaira, is an Australian model, children's author, youth advocate and social media content creator based in Brisbane, Queensland. Her work has focused on youth empowerment, cultural diversity, environmental awareness and community engagement. In 2025 she won the title of Miss Australia Legacy International 2025.

== Early life and education ==
Khaira moved to Australia at the age of three and grew up there. She has spoken publicly about her Punjabi heritage and about her upbringing in Australia and her strong connection to the country she calls home. Khaira has expressed an interest in Australian public life, community affairs and contributing to the country through public service and civic engagement.

== Career ==

=== Modelling and pageantry ===
Khaira began modelling at a young age and has taken part in Australian pageants. In July 2025, she won the title of Miss Australia Legacy International 2025. In 2026, StarCentral Magazine profiled her as one of the finalists in its coverage of the National Miss Australia competition. StarCentral Magazine also published an earlier article about candidates for Queens of Australia 2025.

=== Writing ===
Khaira is a children's author whose books address confidence, kindness, self-belief and environmental responsibility. Her titles include You're Too Young and It Starts With You. Earlier reporting also identified Fearless and Fierce as a children's book associated with her youth advocacy initiative.

=== Digital media ===
Khaira creates social media content about fashion, beauty, modelling and lifestyle. She has also used her platforms to promote advocacy initiatives, community projects and youth empowerment. [ref: Instagram, www.instagram.com]

== Advocacy and community work ==
Khaira began volunteering for charitable causes in her early teens. Her community interests have included youth empowerment, disability inclusion, cultural understanding, environmental sustainability and education.

She founded Fearless Future, an initiative that addresses bullying, racism and self-doubt and encourages confidence and inclusion among young people. Earlier media coverage referred to the initiative as Fearless Vibez. Media reports have also described book donations to schools in India, environmental initiatives and awareness efforts on social issues affecting young people.

== Political involvement ==
Khaira has taken part in political and community activities in Queensland, including involvement with the Liberal National Party (LNP) and its youth organisation, Young LNP. [ref: Instagram, www.instagram.com]

== Youth diplomacy ==
Khaira has plans to take part in the Change the World Academy programme in New York City in 2027. [ref: ] The programme runs Model United Nations conferences, in which students debate international issues, practise negotiation and explore diplomacy.

data.title: J M Barrie and the Lost Boys
data.text:
----

J. M. Barrie and the Lost Boys (also published as J. M. Barrie & the Lost Boys: The Real Story Behind Peter Pan) is a 1979 biographical work by British writer and filmmaker Andrew Birkin, researched by Birkin and Sharon Goode, examining the relationship between J. M. Barrie, creator of Peter Pan, and the five sons of Arthur and Sylvia Llewelyn Davies, who inspired the character. The book grew out of Birkin's research for The Lost Boys (1978), his three-part BBC docudrama on the same subject.

== Background ==
Birkin first explored Barrie's relationship with the Llewelyn Davies family in The Lost Boys, a three-part BBC drama he wrote, broadcast in October 1978 and starring Ian Holm as Barrie. Drawing on the extensive research undertaken for that production — including Barrie's private notebooks, family letters and diaries, and recorded interviews with surviving members of the family and their circle — Birkin expanded the material into a full-length documentary biography, published the following year.

== Synopsis ==
The book traces Barrie's growing closeness to the Davies boys — George, Jack, Peter, Michael and Nico — from their first meetings in Kensington Gardens through Barrie's eventual role as their guardian following the deaths of both parents. Structured around primary documents and photographs reproduced alongside the narrative, it follows the family's story to the deaths in adulthood of three of the five brothers, and the shadow these cast retrospectively over the creation of Peter Pan.

== Publication history ==
The book was first published in the United Kingdom by Constable in 1979, and in the United States by Crown Publishers. Birkin later assigned his rights in the work to the Great Ormond Street Hospital Children's Charity, which holds the copyright to Peter Pan. A revised edition, with a new preface and additional illustrations, was published by Yale University Press in 2003, to coincide with the centenary of Peter Pan.

== Critical reception ==
The book received widespread critical praise on publication and on its 2003 reissue. In Time, Gerald Clarke's review, headlined "The Lost Man", called it "one of the year's most complex and absorbing biographies", [ref: The Lost Man, [[Time (magazine)] while Eve Auchincloss, writing in The Washington Post, described it as "a terrible and fascinating story". [ref: Review of J. M. Barrie and the Lost Boys, The Washington Post] In his review "Barrie, poet of death" for The Listener, the author Ronald Blythe called the book "a lesson in revelations. Having created one of television's masterpieces, The Lost Boys, Andrew Birkin follows it up, not with the now customary book of the programme, but with its documentation set out in another form but with an equally compelling artistry. It is indicative of the author's creative use of restraint that this astonishing history justifies his claim of 'love story' from beginning to end." [ref: Barrie, poet of death, The Listener] Blythe later nominated the book in The Guardian as being "my most unforgettable read of the year." [ref: Books of the Year, The Guardian] The writer and director Caroline Thompson wrote in the Los Angeles Times that "this stunningly constructed biography is a story of obsession and the search for pure childhood; touching, moving, charming, a revelation." [ref: Review of J. M. Barrie and the Lost Boys, Los Angeles Times] The Oxford Companion to Children's Literature calls it "the most candid and perceptive biography to have been written of Barrie". [ref: The Oxford Companion to Children's Literature, Oxford University Press] Writing privately to Nico Llewelyn Davies on 13 June 1979, the editor and biographer Rupert Hart-Davis called it "unquestionably the best book on the subject, and unlikely ever to be surpassed." [ref: Letter from Rupert Hart-Davis to Nico Llewelyn Davies, 13 June 1979, reproduced in facsimile at [https://www.jmbarrie.co.uk jmbarrie.co.uk].]

data.title: Kiran Bhat
data.text:
----

Kiran Bhat (born 21 April 1990) is an Indian-American novelist, poet, short-story writer, literary critic and translator, who has written the poetry collections Autobiografia (2019), Speaking in Tongues (2022), [ref: Indian literature page-turners 2022, The New Indian Express] and the novel We of the Forsaken World (2020). [ref: Kiran Bhat's Book Launch: We of the Forsaken World, Global Atlanta] [ref: I like the idea of channeling the sorts of stories that humans like to come back to: Kiran Bhat, author, Girar, Kitaab] [ref: Author Kiran Bhat and Book: We of the Forsaken World, [[Khabar (magazine)] He is also the author of the ongoing serialized online novel Girar. [ref: Kiran Bhat Is Writing the Diversity of Our World, Electric Literature] In 2026, he received the International Writer of the Year award at the Peoples' Awards, held at the House of Commons in London. [ref: Kiran Bhat Honored with International Writer of the Year Award, Khabar]

== Early life ==
Bhat was born to doctors Anu and Subra Bhat and raised in Jonesboro, Georgia, United States, and partly in Karnataka, India. [ref: Circling the World: An Interview with Kiran Bhat, PRISM international] [ref: I try to compress our globe into a single narrative fictional space: Author Kiran Bhat, NRI Pulse] Bhat graduated from New York University. [ref: NRI writer's travelogue 'Tirugata' released in city, Star of Mysore]

== Career ==
In 2013, Bhat published his first book, titled Early Stories, which is a collection of stories written during his college years and subsequent time period he spent traveling. [ref: Traitor to Tradition, Resister to Remorse: A Conversation with Kiran Bhat, [[Asymptote (magazine)]

In 2019, he released the poetry collection Autobiografia and the Mandarin-language poetry collection Kiran Speaks.

In 2020, Bhat published a Portuguese story collection titled Afora, Adentro and his novel We of the Forsaken World. [ref: World traveling author makes stop at Edinboro, Edinboro Now] [ref: A Poetic Call for Peace, [[The Wire (India)] It is a short story cycle involving sixteen narratives based in four imagined places replicating the industrialising parts of our world. [ref: 'The Will to Survive Is a Force That Never Discriminates': Literature and Global Environmental Refugees and Other 'Forsaken' Peoples, Heavy Feather Review]

In 2021, Bhat started working on a new novel, titled Girar. [ref: With Girar, Author Kiran Bhat Is Reinventing Storytelling and Publishing, NRI Pulse] Girar is being released as a digital novel in monthly installments, with each story set in another country of the world. [ref: Kiran Bhat Interviewed, [[BOMB (magazine) 20 December 20 2022] [ref: Lounge Interview: Kiran Bhat, Author, Traveller and Polyglot, Kitaab]

Bhat published the poetry collection Speaking in Tongues: Poems in Spanish, Mandarin, and Turkish through the publisher Red River in 2022. [ref: Book Review: Speaking in Tongues: Poems in Spanish, Mandarin and Turkish, [[Outlook (Indian magazine) 12 November 2022] Bhat also contributed the poem "A Reporter Asked" to the poetry anthology Amity: Peace Poems, which was edited by Sahana Ahmed and published in December 2022.

Bhat curates for the Yatha Katha Literature Festival in Mumbai, and is co-chair of the Environmental Sustainability Subcommittee of the Global Indian Council. [ref: Kiran Bhat nominated for a Peoples' Award in U.K., Khabar]

== Awards ==
In 2026, Bhat was nominated for International Writer of the Year in the Public Life category of the Peoples' Awards, an annual event bringing together members of the diaspora community and Members of Parliament. He received the award at a ceremony held at the House of Commons; the organizers stated that he was the first person of Indian origin living outside the United Kingdom to receive it.

== Selected bibliography ==
* Early Stories (2013) [ref: Early Stories, eBookit.com]
* Accepting My Place (2017) [ref: Accepting My Place, eBookit.com]
* Tirugaatha (2019) [ref: Kiran Bhat, Cordite Poetry Review]
* Autobiografia (2019) [ref: Autobiografía - Bhat, Kiran, National Library of Spain]
* We of the Forsaken World (2020) [ref: We of the Forsaken World by Kiran Bhat, Dactyl Review] [ref: On the Page: The Novelist-Poet Questions in Kiran Bhat's Seminal Work We of the Forsaken World, Modern Diplomacy]
* Girar (2021)
* Speaking in Tongues (2022)

=== Book contributions ===
* Yearbook of Indian Poetry in English: 2020–2021 by Many Poets [ref: Yearbook of Indian Poetry in English: 2020–2021, Hawakal]
* The Best Asian Short Stories 2021 by Zafar Anjum [ref: The Best Asian Short Stories 2021, Kitaab]
* Amity: Peace Poems (2022)

== Personal life ==
Bhat is of Kannadiga origin. He has traveled to 177 countries and held residence in 25 cities. He currently resides in Mumbai, India, which he considers home. He speaks 12 languages, including English, Hindi, Kannada, Spanish, Portuguese, Mandarin, Japanese, and Turkish.

== Academic career ==
Igor Đurčik worked at the Evangelical Theological Seminary in Osijek, Croatia. [ref: Promocija novog broja časopisa "Religija i tolerancija", Udruženje novinara Srbije] [ref: Koncept nade modernog sveta u dinamici religije neba i religije zemlje, Religija i tolerancija] He was a professor at the Protestant Theological Faculty in Novi Sad. [ref: Uticaj hrišćanstva na evropsku kulturu i civilizaciju (Implikacije Milanskog edikta), Central and Eastern European Online Library] Đurčik has also professor at the Balkan Theological Faculty in Niš, as the lecturer for the course Metodologija istraživačkog rada (Research Methodology). data.title: Pagurixus jerviensis
data.text:
----

Pagurixus jerviensis is a species of hermit crab in the family Paguridae. It was described in 1984 by the carcinologists Patsy A. McLaughlin and Janet Haig as part of their revision of the genus Pagurixus, and is known from Jervis Bay and other parts of the coast of New South Wales, Australia, as well as Lord Howe Island. Australian specimens had previously been misidentified as Eupagurus lacertosus, a distinct species, before being recognised as new. [ref: A review of Pagurixus (Decapoda, Anomura, Paguridae) and descriptions of new species, Crustaceana]

==Taxonomy==

The genus Pagurixus was established by Melin in 1939 as a monotypic subgenus of Eupagurus, with Eupagurus (Pagurixus) boninensis from the Bonin (Ogasawara) Islands as its only species. Several additional species from across the Indo-Pacific were subsequently referred to the subgenus, but almost all were known from one or very few specimens, and the group remained poorly understood.

In their 1984 review of the group, based on material from major museums in the United States, Europe and Australia, McLaughlin and Haig concluded that Pagurixus warranted generic rank. Alongside redescriptions of the previously named species, they described P. jerviensis as new. The species has since been treated as valid in the world checklist of anomuran decapod crustaceans. [ref: Annotated checklist of anomuran decapod crustaceans of the world (exclusive of the Kiwaoidea and families Chirostylidae and Galatheidae of the Galatheoidea). Part I – Lithodoidea, Lomisoidea and Paguroidea, The Raffles Bulletin of Zoology]

Australian material now assigned to P. jerviensis had earlier been reported in the literature as Eupagurus lacertosus or Pagurus lacertosus, for example by Pope (1947), Dakin and coauthors (1948–1960), Griffin (1967) and Healy & Yaldwyn (1970), but these records did not represent that species, P. lacertosus (Henderson, 1888).

The holotype is a male (shield length 2.6 mm) collected by P. Berents on 24 May 1980 at a depth of 18 m on the north face of Bowen Island, Jervis Bay, New South Wales; it is deposited in the Australian Museum in Sydney (registration AM P33836). Paratypes from Jervis Bay, Shell Harbour, Long Reef near Collaroy, the open New South Wales coast and Lord Howe Island are held in the Allan Hancock Foundation (Los Angeles), the Rijksmuseum van Natuurlijke Historie (Leiden), the United States National Museum and other collections.

==Etymology==

The specific name evidently refers to Jervis Bay, the type locality of the species.

==Description==

Pagurixus jerviensis is a minute species: the shield, the hardened anterior portion of the carapace, measured 1.0–4.3 mm in length in the material examined. As in other hermit crabs, the soft abdomen is protected by an empty gastropod shell. Like other species of the genus, it shows pronounced sexual dimorphism in the right cheliped: the right chela of large males becomes swollen or elongate and loses much of the armature seen in females and small males, with the corneous cutting teeth replaced by strong calcareous teeth.

Within the genus, P. jerviensis belongs to the group of species lacking rows of setae on the underside of the terminal segment of the antennular peduncle. It is distinguished from its congeners by the short, stout dactyls of the second pereopods, each with 7–10 corneous spines on the ventral margin, by the dorsal row of spines on the dactyl of the left chela, and by the telson, whose terminal margins are straight and armed with 2–4 strong spines, sometimes accompanied by a few spinules. Females have paired gonopores.

==Distribution and habitat==

The species is known from the coast of New South Wales, including Jervis Bay (Bowen Island and Boat Harbour), Shell Harbour and Long Reef near Collaroy,and from Lord Howe Island in the Tasman Sea. Known records span the intertidal zone to a depth of about 22 m.

data.title: Yannick Fierling
data.text:
----

Yannick Fierling (born February 1, 1971, in Sarreguemines, France, is a French business executive and engineer. He is the president and chief executive officer of Electrolux Group. [ref: Electrolux names appliances veteran Fierling as new CEO, Reuters] [ref: Yannick Fierling, un Français nommé à la tête d'Electrolux, L'Usine Nouvelle]

== Early life and education ==
Fierling holds two master's degrees in mechanical engineering from the Université de Technologie de Compiègne in France and Virginia Tech in the United States. [ref: European Commission - Brussels Economic Forum 2025 - Yannick Fierling, ec.europa.eu] He also holds a degree in finance for executives from INSEAD in France. [ref: 15th Global Peter Drucker Forum, 15th Global Peter Drucker Forum]

== Career ==
Fierling began his career in 1996 at SKF. He then joined Whirlpool Corporation in 2000, where he held various senior leadership roles over 15 years.

In 2015, he was appointed CEO of Haier Europe. He stepped down in April 2024. [ref: Yannick Fierling steps down as CEO of Haier Europe, Haier Europe]

In August 2024, Electrolux Group announced that Fierling would succeed [https://sv.wikipedia.org/en/Jonas%20Samuelson Jonas Samuelson] as president and CEO. He joined the company in October 2024 and formally assumed the role on January 1, 2025. [ref: KBBFocus - Yannick Fierling announced as new president & CEO of Electrolux Group, kbbfocus.com]

Fierling delivered the opening keynote speech, focused on “Sustainability in the Spotlight” at IFA Berlin 2025. [ref: Top international speakers and visionary topics at IFA 2025, IFA Berlin 2027 - Innovation For All]

He is an advocate for changes to the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism. [ref: Så blev en skruv en ny regelmardröm, Affärsvärlden]

data.title: Regent International School, Dubai
data.text:
Regent International School is a private, co-educational British-curriculum school in The Greens, Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Operated by Fortes Education, the school provides education from Foundation Stage 1 through Year 13, serving children aged approximately 3 to 18. It follows the National Curriculum for England, leading to General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE), International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE) and A-level qualifications. [ref: Regent International Private School L.L.C, Knowledge and Human Development Authority] [ref: Regent International School, Get Information about Schools] [ref: IGCSE or GCSE – What is the Difference?, Regent International School]

The school was rated Very Good overall in its 2023–24 inspection by Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA). The UK Department for Education also lists a British Schools Overseas inspection report for the school dated 12 February 2026; Regent states that it received an Outstanding judgement under that framework. [ref: Regent International Private School L.L.C: Summary of Inspection Findings 2023–2024, Knowledge and Human Development Authority] [ref: British schools overseas: accredited schools inspection reports, UK Department for Education] [ref: Principal's Message, Regent International School]

== History ==

Regent International School was established in the early 1990s. The KHDA's current school directory and a 2015 British Schools Overseas inspection report give its opening year as 1992, although a 2016–17 KHDA report gives 1993. [ref: Regent International School, Dubai: British Schools Overseas inspection report, CfBT Education Trust] [ref: Regent International Private School: Inspection Report 2016–2017, Knowledge and Human Development Authority]

Regent was originally a school with both primary and secondary education. In 2016, the secondary division was relocated to the newly opened Sunmarke School, another Fortes Education institution. Regent subsequently offered a primary-focused programme, before expanding again into secondary education and Sixth Form provision. [ref: Sunmarke School: Value-for-money premium school, Gulf News] [ref: Making the move from Primary to Secondary? Here's how we do it!, Regent International School]

The school is led by principal David Williams, who previously held teaching and leadership roles at Regent, including Head of Lower School and Vice Principal. [ref: Mr. David Williams, Regent International School]

== Curriculum ==

Regent International School follows the English National Curriculum through its Foundation Stage, Primary, Secondary and Sixth Form phases.

=== Early Years Foundation Stage ===

The Early Years Foundation Stage (FS1 and FS2) serves children aged approximately three to five. Teaching follows the British EYFS framework and incorporates play-based learning, language development and opportunities for independent exploration. The school describes its early years provision as informed by the Curiosity Approach. [ref: Early Years Foundation Stage, Regent International School]

=== Primary education ===

Primary education covers Years 1 to 6, including Key Stage 1 (Years 1–2) and Key Stage 2 (Years 3–6). The curriculum includes English, mathematics and science, alongside humanities, creative subjects, computing and physical education. Regent also provides cross-curricular projects and extracurricular activities. [ref: Primary School, Regent International School]

=== Secondary education ===

Secondary schooling includes Key Stage 3 (Years 7–9) and Key Stage 4 (Years 10–11). Students study the National Curriculum for England and work towards GCSE or IGCSE examinations. Assessment during Key Stage 3 includes classroom testing and end-of-year examinations. [ref: How Is Progress Measured in Years 7 to 9? A Parent's Guide to Key Stage 3 Assessment, Regent International School]

=== Sixth Form ===

In Years 12 and 13, the school offers A-level courses as part of its post-16 British curriculum pathway. Its Sixth Form provision includes university and career guidance. [ref: Regent International School, Regent International School]

== Educational approach ==

=== Positive Education ===

Regent integrates Positive Education into its teaching and pastoral provision. The approach incorporates student wellbeing, resilience, character development and social and emotional learning alongside academic studies.

=== Technology and creative education ===

The school's programmes cover science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM), including activities involving coding, robotics and design technology. It also offers opportunities in music, drama, media and performing arts. [ref: Our Campus, Regent International School] [ref: Free Extracurricular Activities, Regent International School]

=== Extracurricular activities ===

Regent runs sports, science, creative arts, language and enrichment clubs. Its published extracurricular programme includes football, basketball, netball, swimming, Model United Nations, debating, robotics, musical theatre, visual arts and the Duke of Edinburgh's International Award.

== Campus and facilities ==

Regent International School is located in The Greens, Dubai. The campus includes more than 77 purpose-built activity rooms, an assembly hall and specialist teaching spaces for science, design technology, food technology and the arts. It also has music studios, drama rooms, art spaces and separate libraries for the Foundation Stage, Primary and Secondary phases.

Sports facilities include two multipurpose sports decks, an outdoor sports pitch, a semi-Olympic swimming pool and a learner's pool. Indoor and outdoor play zones support physical education and recreation. The campus is also used by the Fortes Pro Sports Academy.

== Inspections and accreditation ==

=== Knowledge and Human Development Authority ===

Regent is regulated and inspected by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority. Its 2023–24 inspection gave the school an overall rating of Very Good. The same inspection rated its provision for inclusion Outstanding and its wellbeing provision Very Good. [ref: Inspection ratings, wellbeing and inclusion ratings 2023–2024, Knowledge and Human Development Authority]

The inspectors reported outstanding attainment and progress in the Foundation Stage, while attainment and progress in English, mathematics and science were generally rated Very Good across Primary and Secondary. The inspection also identified areas for development in Islamic Education and Arabic.

[ref: Regent International Private School: Summary of Inspection Findings 2022–2023, Knowledge and Human Development Authority]

=== British Schools Overseas ===

Regent appears in the UK Department for Education's register of British Schools Overseas, which lists an inspection report dated 12 February 2026. The school reports that the inspection rated it Outstanding. A previous British Schools Overseas inspection took place in November 2015.

== Student achievement ==

In December 2024, Khaleej Times reported that Regent student Arina Gavrilenko received a Pearson Outstanding Learner Award following the 2023–24 Pearson Edexcel examination series, with the highest mark globally in mathematics and the highest mark in science in the Middle East. The report also noted recognition for other Regent students in the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations. [ref: Regent International School students win international award, Khaleej Times]
