data.title: Arab Cycling Federation
data.text:
The Arab Cycling Federation (ACF) is an Arab federation concerned with the sport of cycling. It was founded in 1975 by a group of national Arab cycling federations and operates under the umbrella of the Union of Arab National Olympic Committees. Its headquarters was originally in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, before moving to Cairo, Egypt, then to Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and finally to Sharjah. [ref: الشهراني نائباً أول لرئيس الاتحاد العربي للدراجات, Okaz] In July 2018 the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) officially recognized the federation's championships and races.

== Members ==
* Iraq – 1976
* United Arab Emirates – 1975
* Saudi Arabia – 1975
* Syria – 1975
* Jordan – 1982
* Palestine – 1983
* Bahrain – 1983
* Kuwait – 1977
* Qatar – 2002
* Lebanon – 1977
* Yemen – 1988
* Oman – 1987
* Egypt – 1975
* Somalia – accession pending
* Libya – 1975
* Algeria – 1975
* Morocco – 1975
* Tunisia – 1975
* Sudan – 1975
* Mauritania – 2017

== Presidents of the Federation ==
* Prince Bandar bin Abdulrahman
* Dr. Khalid Al-Turki
* Sheikh Faisal bin Hamid Al Qasimi
* 2025 – present: Dr. Yasser Omar Al-Dokhi [ref: Yasser Al Doukhi elected President of Arab Cycling Federation, Sharjah 24] [ref: Arab Cycling Federation General Assembly elects new leadership, The Peninsula]

== Board members ==
President of the Federation: Dr. Yasser Omar Al-Dokhi

First Vice President: Abdulaziz Al-Shahrani

Second Vice President: Mohammed Katem

Third Vice President: Fatima Al-Ghanem

Members: Dr. Tarek Al-Khayyat, Youssef Harb, Dr. Ahmed Jaber, Jamal Al-Kuwari, Mohammed Aidaroos

Secretary-General: Dr. Ashraf Mohammed Sayed Imam

== History of the Federation ==
The Arab Cycling Federation was the first Arab sports federation to come into being. The idea of establishing it was brought to the first Arab Cycling Tour of Lebanon in 1955 by the Syrian administrator Rashid Dashan, and after the tour ended it was taken forward with Ismail Taher (Egypt), Abdel Hafiz Al-Turki (Libya), Saadi Al-Douri (Iraq) and Nassif Majdalani (Lebanon).

The Arab Federation was founded on Wednesday, 11 January 1956, in Cairo, during the third Egypt International Cycling Race. Its administrative committee was formed of Ismail Taher (Egypt) as president; Tayseer Mashnouq (Syria), Nassif Majdalani (Lebanon), Saadi Al-Douri (Iraq) and Masoud Al-Zentouni (Libya) as vice-presidents; Joseph Saadeh (Lebanon) as deputy for motorcycles; Sayed Zaki (Egypt) as secretary-general; Shaker Abdel Hay (Egypt) as assistant secretary-general; and Abdullah Abdel Hay as assistant secretary for motorcycles.

Several meetings were held to activate the federation's role and activity, the last of which took place in Beirut in April 1966, but they did not achieve the desired goals, and the federation's activity subsequently ceased after an unsuccessful experience.

Following an invitation from the Saudi Cycling Federation to the presidents of Arab cycling federations, the founding conference to re-establish the Arab Federation was held in Riyadh from 28 to 30 October 1975. The meeting was a complete success and the federation was re-founded, with Prince Bandar bin Abdulrahman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud (Saudi Arabia) chairing the board of the new Arab Federation. He was succeeded as president by Dr. Khalid Ibrahim Al-Turki (Saudi Arabia), and then by Sheikh Faisal bin Hamid Al Qasimi (UAE) from June 1997.

Following an invitation from the Egyptian Cycling Federation and a number of Arab federations to hold an extraordinary general assembly in Cairo in 1997, to discuss reviving the Arab Federation, which had been inactive for more than six years, the general assembly elected a new board of directors and moved the headquarters to Cairo. This continued until 2003, when the general assembly in Tunis decided to attach the headquarters to the presidency in the United Arab Emirates, which has headed the federation since 1997. The signs of change in the federation's course soon became clear to all, reflecting everyone's desire to activate its role, support its progress and achieve the goals of raising the standard of Arab cycling to the best levels. The federation saw a qualitative leap thanks to the redrafting of many regulations in line with the new stage, and the regular implementation of championship and course programs.

== Objectives of the Federation ==
To spread and promote the sport in the Arab countries.

To prepare technical and administrative cadres.

To work on raising the technical level of the Arab player.

To strengthen relations among member federations, offering advice and counsel and settling any disputes that may arise between them.

To consolidate relations with the Union Cycliste Internationale and with continental and international federations.

To coordinate among member federations and unify their positions at Arab and continental meetings.

To support member federations when they take part in international and continental events.

To encourage scientific research and authorship, and to enrich the Arab library with books and translations on the sport, supporting authors and translators.

== References ==

data.title: Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna
data.text:
----

The Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna (LGWA) is a proposed gravitational-wave observatory that would detect low-frequency gravitational waves by measuring vibrations of the Moon with an array of ultra-sensitive seismic sensors deployed on the lunar surface. It is intended to operate in the 1 mHz–1 Hz frequency band.

The project was proposed in 2020 and is intended to bridge the frequency gap between space-based detectors such as LISA and terrestrial observatories such as LIGO, KAGRA, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer.

== History ==

=== Early theoretical work ===
The idea of using an entire celestial body for detecting gravitational waves was proposed by Joseph Weber. Weber suggested that the Earth or the Moon could act as natural resonant antennas, with gravitational waves exciting their normal modes and the resulting motion being measured by sensitive gravimetric instruments.
Subsequent theoretical studies examined the response of planetary bodies to gravitational waves. Freeman Dyson derived the response of a free surface to an incident gravitational wave, while Ari Ben-Menahem later developed a treatment for a spherically symmetric Earth and showed that gravitational waves could excite low-order spheroidal modes of the planet.

=== Lunar seismology and experimental attempts ===
The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package deployed seismometers on the Moon between 1969 and 1977, providing the first long-term record of lunar seismic activity. Among the instruments flown during the Apollo program was the Lunar Surface Gravimeter, which was partly conceived for gravitational-wave investigations.
The gravimeter suffered an engineering failure that prevented the experiment from operating as intended. Later analyses concluded that its sensitivity would not have been sufficient to detect astrophysical gravitational-wave signals, although Apollo seismic data were subsequently used to place limits on low-frequency gravitational-wave backgrounds.

=== Modern developments ===
Interest in planetary-body gravitational-wave detection was renewed with advances in seismology and precision sensing technologies. Studies explored the use of terrestrial seismic networks for low-frequency gravitational-wave searches and re-examined the response of the Earth and Moon to gravitational waves.
In the 2020s, detailed analyses of the lunar seismic environment, gravitational-wave response, and detector sensitivity led to the development of the Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna concept.

=== LGWA proposal ===
LGWA was proposed by Jan Harms and collaborators in response to a European Space Agency call for lunar science concepts. The proposal outlined a gravitational-wave observatory operating in the millihertz-to-hertz frequency range using the Moon as the detector test mass.

== Science objectives ==

=== Lunar science ===

A major component of the LGWA science programme is the study of the Moon's internal structure and seismic properties.

==== Seismic sources ====

Seismic observations conducted during the Apollo missions demonstrated that the Moon remains seismically active. More than 13,000 seismic events, collectively known as moonquakes, were identified from data acquired between 1969 and 1977.
Lunar seismic sources are generally classified into three categories: deep moonquakes, shallow moonquakes, and meteoroid impacts. Deep moonquakes are correlated with tidal stresses induced by the Earth-Moon system, while shallow moonquakes are less frequent and their origin remains incompletely understood.
Because the Moon lacks a substantial atmosphere, meteoroid impacts generate seismic signals that can be detected across the lunar surface and provide information on the present impact environment of the Earth-Moon system.
The distribution of seismic activity across the Moon remains only partially constrained because the Apollo seismic network operated exclusively on the lunar near side.

==== Internal structure ====

Data from the Apollo seismic experiments provided the first direct constraints on the Moon's internal structure, revealing a differentiated body composed of crust, mantle and core.
Seismic analyses led to the development of reference models of the lunar interior, including the Very Preliminary Reference Moon Model, which combines seismological and geodetic observations to describe the Moon's internal density and seismic velocity profiles.
Current models indicate a crust approximately 40 km thick and a small core with an estimated radius of about 380 km, although substantial uncertainties remain for the deepest regions of the Moon owing to the limited coverage of the Apollo seismic network.

==== Formation history ====

The Moon's internal structure provides important constraints on theories of its origin. Seismic, geodetic and geochemical evidence indicates that the Moon is a differentiated body with a crust, mantle and core, suggesting that it formed through a high-energy event followed by extensive melting and internal differentiation.
Several hypotheses have been proposed for the Moon's formation, including capture, co-accretion, fission and giant-impact models. Among these, the giant-impact hypothesis, in which the Moon formed from debris produced by a collision between the proto-Earth and a planetary body, is the most widely studied explanation.
The composition and internal structure of the Moon remain important tests of competing formation scenarios.

==== Geological processes ====

The principal geological processes affecting the Moon include impact cratering, regolith formation, volcanism, tectonic deformation and mass-wasting phenomena such as landslides.
Impact cratering is the dominant surface-modifying process and is largely responsible for the production and evolution of the lunar regolith. Although lunar volcanism is no longer active, geological and geochemical evidence indicates that extensive volcanic activity occurred during the Moon's history, with some volcanic deposits dating to about two billion years ago.
Tectonic structures such as thrust faults, wrinkle ridges and grabens indicate that the Moon has undergone prolonged crustal deformation. Recent studies have also suggested that some tectonic and mass-wasting processes may still be active.

=== Low-frequency gravitational-wave detection ===

[[File:LGWA_Characteristic_Strain.png|thumb|350px|right|Characteristic strain sensitivity of the Lunar Gravitational Wave Antenna compared with other gravitational-wave detectors.]]

The Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna is designed to operate in the decihertz frequency band between approximately 1 mHz and 1 Hz. This frequency range is expected to contain sources that are inaccessible or only partially accessible to existing gravitational-wave detectors.

Proposed targets include the early inspiral phases of compact binary systems, white-dwarf mergers, tidal disruption events, and other transient astrophysical phenomena.

==== Compact binaries ====
Compact binary systems containing white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes are among the principal sources expected in the LGWA frequency range.
At decihertz frequencies, these systems are observed during the late stages of their inspiral, before entering the sensitivity bands of ground-based gravitational-wave detectors. Observations at these frequencies can provide information on the masses, orbital evolution and formation channels of compact binaries.
White-dwarf binaries, including double white-dwarf and white-dwarf–neutron-star systems, are regarded as important sources of low-frequency gravitational waves.

==== White-dwarf mergers and Type Ia supernovae ====

Binary systems containing white dwarfs are expected to be important sources of gravitational waves in the decihertz band.
As orbital energy is lost through gravitational-wave emission, some double white-dwarf systems eventually merge. Such mergers have been proposed as progenitors of several classes of stellar transients, including some models of Type Ia supernovae.
Gravitational-wave observations can provide information on the masses and merger rates of these systems, offering an independent approach to studying the origin of Type Ia supernovae.
White-dwarf mergers may also produce a variety of other outcomes, including massive white dwarfs, neutron stars and other transient phenomena, depending on the masses and compositions of the binary components.

==== Massive and intermediate-mass black holes ====

Binary systems containing massive and intermediate-mass black holes are expected to be important sources of low-frequency gravitational waves.
Massive black-hole binaries are thought to form during galaxy mergers and emit gravitational waves as their orbits shrink prior to coalescence. Observations of such systems can provide information on the growth of black holes and the assembly history of galaxies.
LGWA is also expected to be sensitive to intermediate-mass black holes and to extreme and intermediate mass-ratio inspirals, in which a compact object orbits a much more massive black hole. These systems are regarded as potential probes of black-hole formation and evolution in dense stellar environments and galactic nuclei.

==== Tidal disruption events ====

A tidal disruption event (TDE) occurs when a star passes sufficiently close to a black hole to be disrupted by tidal forces.
Most observed TDEs have been identified through electromagnetic emission produced as stellar debris is accreted by the black hole. Gravitational-wave emission is expected to accompany some disruption events, particularly those involving white dwarfs and intermediate-mass black holes, whose signals are predicted to peak in the decihertz frequency range.
Observations of such systems could provide information on the properties of intermediate-mass black holes and the dynamics of stars in galactic nuclei.

==== Core-collapse supernovae and relativistic jets ====

Core-collapse supernovae are expected to produce gravitational waves through asymmetric collapse, turbulence and anisotropic neutrino emission during the explosion of massive stars. Most of the gravitational-wave signal from these events lies at frequencies above the LGWA band, but low-frequency emission associated with the gravitational-wave memory effect may extend into the decihertz range. Combined observations with low- and high-frequency detectors could therefore provide information on both the explosion mechanism and the properties of the newly formed compact remnant.
Relativistic jets produced in phenomena such as gamma-ray bursts and some supernovae have also been proposed as sources of low-frequency gravitational-wave memory signals.

==== Gravitational-wave cosmology ====

Gravitational-wave observations can be used to measure cosmological distances independently of traditional electromagnetic methods through the use of so-called standard sirens.
The combination of luminosity distances derived from gravitational-wave signals with source redshifts can provide measurements of cosmological parameters, including the Hubble constant.
Sources observable in the decihertz band may offer accurate distance estimates and improved sky localisation, enabling both direct identification of host galaxies and statistical cosmological analyses.
Low-frequency gravitational-wave observations may also contribute to studies of the stochastic gravitational-wave background and tests of cosmological models beyond the standard cosmological framework.

==== Fundamental physics ====

Low-frequency gravitational-wave observations can be used to test predictions of general relativity and search for possible deviations from the theory in the strong-field regime. The long inspiral signals observable in the decihertz band are particularly sensitive to effects that may arise in alternative theories of gravity.
Gravitational-wave measurements may also be used to investigate the properties of black holes through observations of their inspiral and ringdown phases, providing tests of the no-hair theorem and measurements of black-hole multipole moments.
In addition, compact-object mergers and extreme mass-ratio inspirals have been proposed as probes of dark matter through their potential interaction with dense dark-matter environments surrounding black holes.

=== Multi-band gravitational-wave astronomy ===

LGWA is intended to complement both space-based observatories such as LISA and ground-based detectors including LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA.
By observing compact binaries in a frequency range intermediate between those instruments, LGWA is intended to enable multi-band studies of gravitational-wave sources, improving measurements of source parameters and providing additional tests of general relativity.

== Mission architecture ==

Unlike laser-interferometric observatories, LGWA is designed to detect gravitational waves through measurements of the Moon's seismic response to passing gravitational waves.

=== Mission concept ===
The baseline concept consists of an array of four seismic stations deployed within a permanently shadowed region (PSR) near one of the lunar poles. Each station would be equipped with two orthogonal horizontal inertial sensors, allowing the array to measure ground motion and reduce the effects of local seismic noise through correlated observations between stations.

=== Instruments ===

Each LGWA station is designed to carry two orthogonal horizontal Lunar Inertial Gravitational-wave Sensors (LIGS) mounted on a levelled platform.
The sensors are intended to measure horizontal ground displacements with sub-picometre sensitivity and to operate in the cryogenic environment of permanently shadowed lunar craters.
The baseline designs employ suspended proof masses with either interferometric or superconducting readout systems, combined with cryogenic cooling and superconducting actuation technologies to minimize instrumental noise.
Two baseline implementations, based on niobium and silicon mechanical suspensions respectively, have been studied as part of the instrument development programme.

=== Deployment site ===

The baseline LGWA concept places the observatory within a permanently shadowed region (PSR) near one of the lunar poles.
PSRs are cratered areas that receive little or no direct sunlight and maintain some of the coldest and most thermally stable conditions on the Moon.
These regions were selected because their low temperatures and reduced thermal variations are expected to minimize environmental noise and improve the performance of the cryogenic inertial sensors.
Candidate deployment sites have been investigated using lunar topography, illumination and thermal models to identify locations that combine permanently shadowed areas with nearby access to solar power resources.

=== Noise mitigation ===
A principal design goal of LGWA is the reduction of seismic and environmental noise.
The four-station configuration is intended to allow correlated measurements between stations and suppression of the lunar seismic background through array-analysis techniques.
The selection of permanently shadowed regions as deployment sites is also intended to minimize thermal disturbances and provide stable cryogenic operating conditions for the sensors.

== Comparison with Other Detectors ==

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Comparison with existing and planned detectors
|-
! Detector !! Technique !! Frequency band !! Environment
|-
| LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA || Laser interferometry || ~10 Hz–1 kHz || Earth
|-
| Einstein Telescope || Underground laser interferometry || ~1 Hz–10 kHz || Earth (underground)
|-
| Cosmic Explorer || Laser interferometry || ~5 Hz–10 kHz || Earth
|-
| LISA || Interferometric spacecraft || ~0.1 mHz–0.1 Hz || Space
|-
| DECIGO || Interferometric spacecraft || ~0.1–10 Hz || Space
|-
| LGWA || Lunar inertial sensors || ~1 mHz–1 Hz || Moon
|}

LGWA differs from existing and proposed gravitational-wave observatories in that it uses seismic measurements of the Moon rather than long-baseline laser interferometry. Its proposed frequency coverage overlaps with that of concepts such as DECIGO while employing a fundamentally different detection technique.

== Development status ==
As of 2024, LGWA remained in the mission study and technology-development phase.
The project is being developed by an international collaboration and is supported by studies of lunar environmental conditions, instrument technologies and mission deployment concepts.
In 2024, the Italian Space Agency (ASI) and the Gran Sasso Science Institute (GSSI) announced support for preparatory studies related to lunar science missions, including LGWA.

== Soundcheck ==

Soundcheck is a proposed pathfinder mission for LGWA intended to characterize the geophysical environment of permanently shadowed regions near the lunar poles and to demonstrate technologies required for a future lunar gravitational-wave observatory.
The mission is designed to measure seismic ground motion, temperature variations and magnetic-field fluctuations in a permanently shadowed region, where the baseline LGWA observatory is planned to operate. Data collected by Soundcheck are intended to improve understanding of the lunar seismic background, assess environmental conditions relevant to gravitational-wave detection, and support the selection and design of future LGWA deployment sites.

data.title: Tsismis Central
data.text:
Tsismis Central (formerly Pinoy Circle Showbiz) is a Philippine entertainment news website and social media brand that covers local showbiz news, celebrity stories and Philippine television. Its name comes from tsismis, the Filipino word for gossip. The site publishes in Taglish, a mix of Tagalog and English, and runs on the Blogger platform. [ref: Tsismis Central]

== History ==
=== Pinoy Circle (2015) ===
The brand began in June 2015 as Pinoy Circle, a Filipino website and video page that posted short videos about news and stories from the Philippines.

=== Pinoy Circle Showbiz (2016) ===
In 2016, Pinoy Circle started Pinoy Circle Showbiz, a separate page for entertainment content. It covered showbiz news about Filipino celebrities and recaps of Philippine teleseryes.

=== YouTube channel hack (2024) ===
In December 2024, the Pinoy Circle YouTube channel was hacked. The hackers renamed the channel and used it to stream fake videos of Elon Musk promoting a cryptocurrency giveaway, a scam that hit many YouTube channels at the time. The owners were not able to get the channel back because of limited support from YouTube, and the brand moved its work to its other pages.

=== Rebrand to Tsismis Central (2026) ===
In September 2026, Pinoy Circle Showbiz was rebranded as Tsismis Central and moved to its own domain, tsismiscentral.com. Under the new name it posts short-form videos, called reels, which are shared on Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and X.

== Content ==
Tsismis Central publishes:
* Showbiz news about Filipino actors, singers and public figures, based on reports from Philippine news outlets such as GMA Network and ABS-CBN.
* TV recaps of Philippine teleseryes, with a summary of each episode and its air date.
* Reels, short videos about the day's top showbiz stories, which are also placed inside the matching articles on the website.

== See also ==
* Entertainment journalism
* Television in the Philippines

data.title: Pemamek
data.text:
Pemamek Oy is a Finnish engineering company that designs and manufactures welding automation and production automation systems for heavy metal fabrication. Its products are sold under the PEMA brand. The company is headquartered in Loimaa, Southwest Finland, and has been owned by the Heikonen family since the late 1980s. [ref: Leadership And Governance - Pemamek] [ref: ”Ei riitä, että olemme Suomen paras – pitää olla champions league -tasoa”, Perheyritysten liitto] Its customers include shipyards, manufacturers of wind turbine towers and foundations, and makers of heavy equipment, boilers and pressure vessels. [ref: ] [ref: ]

In the financial year ending March 2026, the parent company Pemamek Oy reported revenue of €155.2 million and had 386 employees. [ref: Pemamek - yritystiedot, päättäjät, taloustiedot, Finder] The company states that around 90 per cent of its sales are exports.

== History ==

=== Origins and ownership changes (1970 to 1989) ===
Pemamek was founded in 1970 in Loimaa. The company describes its origins as a small business making welding positioners, devices that hold and rotate a workpiece during welding. According to Pekka Heikonen, the current chairman, the company had about ten employees when he joined in 1978.

In 1982 Pemamek became part of Korpivaara Oy, and Heikonen became its factory manager. The conglomerate Amer acquired Korpivaara in 1984. In late 1988 Amer decided to divest three of its metal industry businesses, and Pemamek's business passed to Heikonen.

=== Automation and growth (1980s to 2010s) ===
Pemamek began developing robotic solutions in the 1980s. During the 1990s automation became its core product line. Through the 2010s, demand from shipyards was a major driver of growth, and staff numbers passed 200. Customers in this period included the Meyer Turku shipyard. [ref: Pemamek kasvaa aimo askelin Loimaalla, Loimaan Lehti]

A factory extension completed in early 2017 increased production space by half. Jaakko Heikonen had become chief executive in spring 2016. In the 2017-18 financial year the company expected revenue of about €50 million, compared with €35-40 million in earlier years, and employed 190 people.

On 1 May 2019 Juha Mäkitalo, previously chief executive of the sheet metal machinery maker Finn-Power, succeeded Jaakko Heikonen as CEO. Heikonen remained vice chairman of the board. Revenue for the financial year 2018-19 was €77 million, with 230 employees. [ref: Juha Mäkitalo Appointed As New CEO Of Pemamek - Pemamek]

=== Diversification into wind energy (2016 onwards) ===
In 2023 Yle reported that the company had decided some six or seven years earlier that it depended too heavily on the cyclical shipbuilding industry, and had turned to the growing wind power market. [ref: Kan Finland bli en stormakt för grön teknik? Vi besöker familjeföretaget som ser enorm efterfrågan, Svenska Yle] In June 2022 Pemamek announced €15 million of investment in a factory extension and product development, aimed at demand from the wind industry. The extension brought the Loimaa factory to 27,000 square metres. [ref: Windtech International - Pemamek invests in factory expansion and R&D to meet demand from the wind market, www.windtech-international.com] The new hall, completed in December 2022, has a ceiling five metres higher than the older halls, to accommodate production lines for large offshore wind foundations.

In spring 2023 Pemamek announced orders for production lines for XXL monopile foundations from Sif Holding of the Netherlands and Haizea Wind Group of Spain. Staff numbers grew from just over 200 to nearly 350 within a few years.

=== Recent developments (2024 to present) ===
In June 2026 Pemamek acquired the business operations of Mach Machines, a North American robotic welding integrator. The combined operation was to move to a larger facility in Blue Ash, Ohio. [ref: Pemamek X Mach Machines - Pemamek Joins Forces With Mach Machines] In October 2026 Jaakko Heikonen and Pemamek were named among the finalists of the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year competition in Finland. [ref: Pemamek kisaa kovassa seurassa, Loimaan Lehti]

== Operations ==
Pemamek's headquarters and factory are in Loimaa, beside Finnish national road 9, with engineering offices in Tampere and Turku. [ref: Contact - Pemamek] Design, manufacturing and testing of its systems take place in Finland. Export contracts often include installation, commissioning and maintenance at the customer's site.

=== International presence ===
In 2023 Finnvera reported that Pemamek had subsidiaries in the United States, Germany, Spain and Italy, and sales companies in Brazil and Poland. As of 2026 the company lists sales or service offices in Germany, the United States, Brazil, Poland, Spain, Italy, and the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Its Spanish operation trades as Pemamek Iberia.

The June 2026 purchase of Mach Machines' business added a team in Ohio; the combined US operation was to relocate to Blue Ash, Ohio.

== Products and technology ==
Pemamek makes equipment that automates welding and the handling of large, heavy steel parts. Welding joins metal parts by melting them together along a seam. On thick steel structures such as ship hulls or wind turbine foundations, a single seam can require many passes, so manual welding is slow and physically demanding. Pemamek's products either move the workpiece so that it can be welded in the best position, carry the welding equipment along the seam, or use industrial robots to perform the weld. [ref: ]

=== Handling and positioning equipment ===
The company's standard product range includes:

* Welding positioners, which grip a workpiece and tilt or rotate it so that the welder or a welding machine can reach each seam from the most favourable angle.
* Roller beds, sets of motorised and free-running rollers that turn tubes, pipes and other cylindrical parts during welding, painting or assembly.
* Column and booms, a vertical column with a horizontal arm that carries a welding head over a workpiece, commonly used together with roller beds for long circumferential and longitudinal seams on cylinders.

=== Robotic and line systems ===
For larger projects Pemamek supplies robotic welding stations and complete production lines. A smaller project is typically a robotised or automated welding cell, while a larger one is a full production line delivered as a project. Examples include:

* Shipbuilding panel lines. Ship hulls are assembled from flat steel panels stiffened with welded profiles. A panel line moves plates through stations that join them, attach the stiffeners and weld them, often with robots mounted on gantries. The line supplied for Harland & Wolff's Belfast yard combines robotic welding portals, automated material handling and welding equipment. [ref: Harland & Wolff modernisation sees new robotic welding line]
* Wind tower and foundation lines. Monopile foundations for offshore wind turbines are large steel tubes, which in 2023 Finnvera described as reaching more than 15 metres in diameter. They are made by rolling and welding thick plate into cylindrical sections and joining the sections end to end.
* Robotic welding stations for heavy equipment and general fabrication, such as the PEMA Skytrack range.

=== Software ===
Pemamek also sells welding control software under the name PEMA WeldControl.

== Financial information ==
Pemamek Oy is privately held and its financial year ends on 31 March. The figures below are for the parent company Pemamek Oy, as reported by the business information service Finder. [ref: Pemamek - yritystiedot, päättäjät, taloustiedot, Finder] In June 2026 the company stated its annual revenue as approximately €200 million.

data.title: Caleb Landon
data.text:
Caleb Landon is an American real estate investor and entrepreneur. He is the founder of Landon Capital Group, a firm that acquires and operates manufactured housing communities through investor syndications, and the president and co-founder of Lotly Software, a property management software company for mobile home parks. [ref: Why Mobile Home Parks Continue to Outperform with Caleb Landon] [ref: About Lotly, Lotly]

== Early life and education ==
Landon began taking classes at Jessup University in Rocklin, California, at age 11, and later graduated from the university. [ref: Featured Online Stories, Jessup Magazine]

== Career ==
After high school, Landon worked as an intern and analyst at a mobile home park syndication firm for about two years, underwriting acquisitions. [ref: How He Built 250 Mobile Home Park Units From a College Dorm, Investor Fuel] [ref: Efficient Mobile Home Park Syndications with Caleb Landon] He left in early 2023, while still in college, to start his own firm, Landon Capital Group. He raised just under $400,000 from friends, family and other investors for his first acquisition.

As of 2026, Landon Capital Group operated seven communities, three in Michigan, three in Iowa and one in Texas, totaling more than 250 home sites, with Landon as sole general partner. Its most recent acquisition at that time was a $2.8 million purchase funded in part by about $1.1 million raised from roughly 20 investors.

Landon is the president and co-founder of Lotly Software LLC, a company based in Rocklin, California, that develops property management software for mobile home parks, covering functions such as tenant screening, rent collection, maintenance requests and resident communication. At Lotly he leads product, engineering and Fair Credit Reporting Act compliance. Lotly Software also operates RentalApplication.ai, a pay-per-report tenant screening service for landlords and property managers, [ref: About, RentalApplication.ai] and MHPSales.ai, an AI voice agent that handles sales inquiries for manufactured homes by phone, text and email. [ref: MHPSales.ai, Lotly Software LLC] In an interview, Landon said the company's software products were developed using AI-assisted programming.

data.title: WorkwithUSAID.gov
data.text:
WorkwithUSAID (launched as WorkwithUSAID.org and later WorkwithUSAID.gov) was a free online resource hub run by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) to help organizations learn how to partner with the agency and compete for its contracts, grants and cooperative agreements. Launched on 4 November 2021 by the Industry Liaison team in USAID's Office of Acquisition and Assistance and developed by the digital product studio Miew under USAID's Partnerships Incubator, [ref: USAID's Partnerships Incubator – Kaizen, A Tetra Tech Company, Anthem Awards] the platform offered a self-assessment tool, a searchable directory of prospective partners, aggregated funding opportunities, a private-sector portal, and a library of plain-language guidance, later translated into Arabic, French, Portuguese and Spanish. [ref: WorkwithUSAID, Partnership for Public Service] [ref: Case Study: Partner Engagement – WorkwithUSAID.gov, USAID Office of Acquisition and Assistance, Industry Liaison team] Nearly 20,000 organizations from more than 160 countries applied to join its Partner Directory, and the Partnerships Incubator program behind the site won a Gold Anthem Award for innovation in 2025. The site also received an honorable mention in Fast Companys 2023 World Changing Ideas Awards. [ref: World Changing Ideas Awards 2023: General Excellence finalists and honorable mentions, Fast Company] The site was shut down in 2025 during the Department of Government Efficiency's dismantling of USAID.

== Background ==
USAID worked with roughly 3,000 partner organizations a year in more than 100 countries. [ref: USAID wants to make it easier for partners to compete for its grant money, Federal News Network] Its funding was nonetheless concentrated among a small number of large implementers; in fiscal year 2021, 20 organizations received about 70 percent of the agency's funding. Prospective partners, particularly local organizations in partner countries and groups with no prior federal experience, reported that USAID's processes and language were complex and legalistic, that language barriers kept them from acting on opportunities in their own countries, and that entry points such as unsolicited proposals were difficult to use.

The platform supported the agency's New Partnerships Initiative and its broader effort to "localize" foreign assistance by directing more funding to local and first-time partners. [ref: 2023 USAID Customer Experience (CX), Performance.gov] USAID's designation as a federal High Impact Service Provider (HISP) in 2021 made the platform one of the agency's customer-experience commitments under the President's Management Agenda.

== History ==
=== Development and launch ===
The site was developed through USAID's Partnerships Incubator, a program for which Kaizen, A Tetra Tech Company, served as prime contractor. [ref: WorkwithUSAID.org Fact Sheet, USAID] Miew, a digital product studio with offices in Chicago and Porto, was the program's development lead and designed and built the platform. The site was initially hosted outside government systems.

WorkwithUSAID.org launched on 4 November 2021, as part of Administrator Samantha Power's "New Vision for Global Development" announcement. [ref: Advocacy Advisor: End of Year 2021, Humentum] USAID's chief acquisition officer, Mark Walther, described it as a site where "organizations can do self assessments and have other resource tools available to see how ready they are to partner directly with the agency". [ref: How procurement supports the mission at USAID, Federal News Network] The Industry Liaison team used a "hub and spoke" model: the website served as the central source of content, which was then distributed through social media, an email newsletter, webinars and industry events, with feedback from those channels and from user surveys used to shape new content. Power promoted the site in early 2022 as "a free, USAID-funded resource hub that empowers partners with the knowledge and networks to navigate how to work with USAID". [ref: Launch of WorkwithUSAID.org: Recent Initiative Announced by USAID Administrator Samantha Power, USAID Alumni Association]

In its first 13 months (to 15 December 2022) the site recorded about 1.7 million pageviews, approved 3,277 Partner Directory profiles and logged 2,464 completed pre-engagement assessments. Nearly 80 percent of directory members reported no previous USAID partnership experience, and about 60 percent were local organizations.

=== Expansion ===
In 2023 USAID expanded the platform, adding a funding feed that pulled solicitations from SAM.gov and Grants.gov by API, a page where prime partners could post subcontracting "sub-opportunities", an events calendar, and a portal for submitting and internally routing unsolicited proposals. [ref: USAID 2023 High Impact Service Provider Action Plan, Performance.gov] It also added a Corporate Partnering Portal to connect private-sector companies with USAID and its programs; the portal averaged about 175 unique users a month after launch. [ref: USAID 2024 High Impact Service Provider Action Plan, Performance.gov] Ruth Buckley, a USAID deputy assistant administrator, described the platform in 2024 as one of the agency's "big, big innovations". [ref: USAID Gathering CX Feedback Through Online Resource Hub, MeriTalk] In November 2024 the site was migrated from contractor hosting onto AidNet, USAID's internal network infrastructure.

=== Translation ===
The site launched full French, Spanish and Arabic versions in March and April 2024, followed by Portuguese in January 2025. [ref: Case Study: Multilingual Website – WorkwithUSAID.gov, USAID Office of Acquisition and Assistance, Industry Liaison team] Translation combined machine translation with human proofreaders for each language. Because USAID's Office of the Chief Information Officer prohibited direct API connections between the production site and outside translation software, the team translated content in the cloud-based tool Crowdin in a pre-production environment and manually copied it into the live site, which ran on the Strapi content management system. Lacking a FedRAMP-authorized cloud option once the site moved onto USAID servers, the team selected an on-premises system, Trados GroupShare, on the advice of colleagues at the State Department; its rollout was on hold as of early 2025. By then the site offered more than 450 non-English resources.

=== Humanitarian exchange and shutdown ===
In partnership with DEMAC (Diaspora Emergency Action and Coordination), the platform was developing a humanitarian exchange to help organizations coordinate and support one another during crises, with an initial launch planned in Ukraine.

In early 2025 the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) led the dismantling of USAID, and WorkwithUSAID.gov was shut down before the humanitarian exchange could launch. The agency's remaining functions were merged into the United States Department of State on 1 July 2025. [ref: USAID officially shuts down and merges remaining operations with State Department, NPR]

Other plans announced before the shutdown included personalized content based on a user's location, sector and organization type; Login.gov sign-in; automated matching of partners to funding opportunities; and integration with USAspending.gov to show which partners received funding.

== Features ==

* Pre-Engagement Assessment – a self-evaluation questionnaire of about 48 questions that generated a customized report on an organization's readiness to receive USAID funding.
* Partner Directory – a vetted public directory where approved organizations could create profiles to be found by USAID staff and potential teaming partners.
* Funding Feed – USAID solicitations drawn from SAM.gov and Grants.gov.
* Sub-opportunities – subcontracting roles posted by prime partners through an online form.
* Unsolicited submissions portal – a form for submitting unsolicited proposals, which were routed internally to the relevant USAID office.
* Corporate Partnering Portal – a private-sector section connecting companies with USAID and its programs.
* Resource library – explainer videos, guides and policy documents on topics such as federal procurement regulations and obtaining a Unique Entity Identifier, along with a "Start here" checklist offered in English and eight other languages.
* Events and blog – listings of in-person and virtual events and articles on partnership stories and agency news.

== Usage and impact ==
Nearly 20,000 organizations from more than 160 countries applied to join the Partner Directory, of which about 8,800 had been approved by February 2025. More than 2,200 approved members were headquartered in the United States, including more than 1,600 that had never worked with USAID, more than 800 U.S. small businesses and more than 180 veteran-owned businesses. According to the Anthem Awards entry, the Partnerships Incubator connected more than 8,000 organizations to $1.6 billion in funding.

Between November 2021 and February 2025 the site recorded 703,187 users, about 8.29 million page views and 1.22 million sessions. Over the same period it published 288 blog articles and 453 multilingual resources, and handled 790 unsolicited submissions and 486 sub-opportunities. The associated Work with USAID LinkedIn group grew to more than one million members, and the team's email newsletter reached about 136,000 subscribers.

== Awards and reception ==

* Anthem Awards (2025) – Gold, Innovation; awarded to USAID's Partnerships Incubator, entered by Kaizen with Miew credited
* Fast Company World Changing Ideas Awards (2023) – Honorable Mention, General Excellence

Writing for the Brookings Institution in 2023, Justin Fugle described the site as "a key effort to expand USAID's local partner base", noting that more than 5,000 organizations had registered, over 60 percent of them local entities. [ref: A USAID localization model finally emerges, Brookings Institution] Devex cited the site among USAID's localization measures, describing it as "intended to help potential partners understand the agency better". [ref: USAID and localization: A progress report, Devex] In 2023 testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Elana Aquino of the peacebuilding organization Peace Direct acknowledged the platform but said local organizations still struggled to compete with international NGOs familiar with USAID's processes. [ref: Testimony before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations]

User surveys reported in 2022 found satisfaction varied by experience level: about 78 percent of current USAID prime partners and 71 percent of subcontractors were satisfied with the site, compared with about 42 percent of organizations that had never worked with the agency.

data.title: TX2
data.text:
----

TX2 was born as Timothy Evan Thomas in Cort Collins, CO. He is most widely known as the American alternative rock singer and songwriter TX2. He gained attention in the early 2022 through a combination of social media promotion, viral singles, and touring within the alternative rock and metalcore scenes. TX2’s music mixes pop punk, emo, alternative rock, rap, numetal, metalcore and electronic music, often focusing on themes of mental health, identity, alienation, criminalisation of the queer in the USA, internet culture, and social criticism.

TX2 signed with Hopeless Records in July 2023 and later toured with artists including Ice Nine Kills, In This Moment, The Word Alive, and Beartooth.

TX2 originally released music independently as a solo artist before launching TX2 as a band with multiple members. Early releases built a following online, particularly on TikTok, where TX2 became known for his often over the top videos and provacative song lyrics.

In 2023, the single “I Would Hate Me Too” became one of TX2’s breakout songs online and helped expand the band’s audience beyond social media. During this period, TX2 released several singles and EPs while touring nationally and expanding into Europe.

In 2023, TX2 toured with Magnolia Park on a United States tour, before featuring on their track 'Life In The USA'.

In June of 2024 TX2 played Download Festival in the United Kingdom, and Aftershock Festival in California. That same year, TX2 appeared on the Kiss of Death Tour Part 2 tour alongside Ice Nine Kills, In This Moment, and Avatar.

TX2 released the single “MAD” featuring Spencer Charnas of Ice Nine Kills on August 28, 2024.

Additional collaborations during this period included “Vendetta”, featuring Johnny 3 Tears of Hollywood Undead, and “THIS ISN’T ABOUT DRUGS (I SWEAR)”, featuring From First to Last.

In 2025, TX2 joined the touring festival Summer of Loud alongside Beartooth, Parkway Drive, Killswitch Engage, I Prevail, The Devil Wears Prada, The Amity Affliction, and Alpha Wolf. TX2 also performed at the Vans Warped Tour stop in Long Beach, California.

In July and August of 2025 TX2 toured with The Word Alive and later announced the project’s first headline tour across Europe and the United Kingdom.

TX2 frequently collaborates with other artists. Recent collaborations include "Feed" featuring DeathByRomy, "Nice Guy" featuring Ekoh, "The End Of Us" featuring Andy Biersack of Black Veil Brides, and "Murder Scene" featuring Joshua Roberts of Magnolia Park.

TX2 released his debut album End Of Us in February 2026 on Hopeless Records, before allegedly parting ways to release under an independent name.

On April 25, 2026 TX2 kicked off their North American tour with Black Veil Brides, As December Falls, and From Ashes To New.

TX2 has received polarized reactions within the alternative and metalcore scene. Supporters have praised his openness about mental health, identity, and online harassment, while critics have pointed out his heavy use of social media and his confrontational online persona.

Kerrang! described Evan Thomas as a “much-hyped altrock icon-in-waiting” in a feature discussing TX2’s debut album End Of Us. Revolver included TX2 in its 6 Best New Songs Right Now feature in 2025.

TX2’s music combines alternative, emo, pop punk, rap, numetal, metalcore, and electronic influences. His sound and style has been associated with the emo revival, metalcore, and TikTok alternative music scenes. More recent music has shown a shift in TX2's style, with their song 'Evil Is Contagious' being made with a ska punk instrumental co-created with Reel Big Fish.

TX2 lists Green Day, My Chemical Romance, Linkin Park, Limp Bizkit, and Eminem as his influences.

TX2 consists of 4 key members:
Singer - Timothy Evan Thomas (Active since 2017)
Drums - Ethan Church (Active since 2025)
Guitar - Cameron Rostami (Active since early 2022)
Bass - Courtney Lee Howard (Active since late 2023)

The band released their debut album, titled "End Of Us" and it consists of 13 tracks titled:
1. Feed (feat. DeathbyRomy)
2. Nice Guy (feat. Ekoh)
3. REJECT VAMPIRISM (interlude)
4. HOSTAGE (they will not erase us)

8. Singing Along
9. Lost Souls
10. Die Alone

data.title: Tokyo Peace Exhibition
data.text:
The, also known in English as the Peace Memorial Tokyo Exposition and the Peace Commemorative Exposition, was an exposition held from March 10 to July 31, 1922, at Ueno Park, Tokyo, to commemorate the Allied victory in the First World War. Organized by an official exposition bureau (, Hakurankai Jimukyoku), it opened at the moment Japanese delegates were returning home from the Washington Naval Conference, becoming the largest and most popular Japanese exposition held to that time, with more than eleven million visitors—a record for a Taishō era exhibition.

== Background ==

According to historian Frederick R. Dickinson, the exposition grew out of the optimism of the early 1920s, when Japan's participation in the Washington Naval Conference of 1921–22 was seen at home as a triumph of international cooperation and disarmament, and The Tokyo Asahi described the fair as representing "the best of world culture" and "a harbinger of dazzling beauty." [ref: World War I and the Triumph of a New Japan, 1919-1930, Cambridge University Press] By the Taishō era the state-building exhibitions of the Meiji period had given way to exhibitions as entertainment and spectacle, and the Tokyo Peace Exhibition was conceived on a correspondingly grand scale: costing roughly 6 million yen, with almost fifty pavilions, two triumphal gates, and a natural lake covering some 110,000 square metres, it was described as the largest Japanese exposition to date. [ref: Peace Commemorative Exposition, Ueno Park, Tokyo, 1922, Old Tokyo]

The exposition opened on March 10, 1922, shortly after the conclusion of the Washington Naval Conference, timed to coincide with the return of Japan's delegates and with the annual cherry blossom season at Ueno. At the opening ceremony, festival chairman Prince Kan'in Kotohito, flanked by celebratory pine, plum and bamboo, tolled a dedicated "peace bell" and released doves, declaring that world sentiment was weary of "the ghastly evils of war" and full of "admiration for the happiness of peace." Official English-language materials dated the event "March 10–July 31, 1922". [ref: MeijiShowa]

== Grounds and exhibits ==

The grounds were divided into two sections. The first, laid out on the heights of Ueno Park, was dominated by a peace tower designed by the architect Sutemi Horiguchi, a leading figure of the Bunriha ("Secessionist") architecture group influenced by the Vienna Secession; the tower was modelled on the Wedding Tower at Darmstadt. The five entrances were arched in the shape of Mount Fuji. A second section surrounded Shinobazu Pond, around which clustered the exhibition's most popular attractions, from the Hokkaido pavilion and colonial exhibits to amusement rides; a contemporary account in The Japan Magazine likened the shoreline buildings to "architectural oddities, with unexpected humps in the roofs and extraordinary bumps in walls." [ref: The Tokyo Peace Exhibition, The Japan Magazine]

Pavilions and special buildings included those of Japan's colonies and overseas territories—Taiwan, Karafuto, Korea, Manchuria–Mongolia, and the South Seas mandate—as well as prefectural pavilions, industrial and machinery halls, an agricultural and sericulture hall, a "foreign lands" building, the Sumitomo pavilion, and a section of modern "culture houses" (, bunka jūtaku), together with airplane demonstrations and a touring hydroplane ride over the pond. [ref: Heiwa Kinen Tokyo Hakurankai (The Peace Memorial Tokyo Exposition), Unpinning History: Japanese Posters in the Age of Commercialism, Imperialism, and Modernism] Meiji-era and colonial pavilion architecture, photography, and even the exposition's official map—designed by Koijūrō Yoshida—were widely reproduced in commemorative postcards, albums, and administrative reports.

== Attendance and legacy ==

The exposition drew more than 11 million visitors, a record for a Taishō-period exhibition, making it the most popular Japanese exposition of its era. Its cherry-blossom backdrop fed a wider cultural shift identified by Dickinson, in which the cherry blossom became newly associated with the "culture of peace" of the 1920s. The exposition was commemorated in souvenir postcards, photographic albums, posters (including an official poster by the graphic designer Sugiyama Sueo), and map prints.

The opening of the exposition coincided with the debut on April 2, 1922, of Japan's oldest weekly magazines: the inaugural covers of Sunday Mainichi and its rival Shūkan Asahi both carried photographs taken at the fair. [ref: Japan's savvy, salacious shukanshi, Number 1 Shimbun] Images and printed records of the exposition are held in archives including the Library of Congress and the Stanford University Libraries. [ref: Formosa Bldg. (i.e. Building) Peace Expos., Tokyo, Library of Congress] [ref: Tōkyō Hakurankai Jimukyoku kyoka Heiwa Kinen Tōkyō Hakurankai ekibijō hikae, Stanford University Libraries]

data.title: ClokIt USA American building information and property documentation company
data.text:
----

ClokIt USA, LLC is an American company developing digital solutions for building information management, field documentation, and property records. The company focuses on organizing information associated with commercial buildings, including site surveys, photographs, physical conditions, and historical property documentation. Its stated objective is to create a digital record of buildings that can be maintained and referenced as properties undergo changes over time.

== Overview ==
ClokIt USA operates in the building documentation and property technology sectors. Its approach centers on collecting and organizing physical building information to support access to records throughout a property's lifecycle. [ref: ]

Commercial properties may undergo renovations, changes in occupancy, equipment replacement, and other modifications. Records associated with these changes can include architectural drawings, field reports, inspection photographs, and utility documentation.

ClokIt USA's proposed digital information system is intended to bring these types of records together in an organized format.

== Field investigation and documentation ==
Field investigation is one of the activities associated with ClokIt USA's approach to building information management.

Documentation may include:

* Existing building conditions and architectural features
* Electrical, plumbing, and mechanical systems
* Utility infrastructure and service information
* Site photographs and field observations
* Interior and exterior building characteristics
* Existing conditions relevant to renovations or tenant improvements

These records can provide reference information for architects, engineers, construction professionals, property managers, and other parties involved in building-related projects.

== Digital building records ==
A central concept promoted by ClokIt USA is the creation of a persistent digital history for individual properties.

The concept involves associating records with a specific building so that information generated during investigations, modifications, and ongoing property operations can remain accessible for future reference.

This approach is related to broader developments in digital property records, facility information management, and construction documentation technology.

== Development ==
ClokIt USA has described its work as an effort to connect building documentation with long-term property information management.

Additional independently published information is needed to document the company's founding, organizational development, commercial milestones, and broader industry activities.

data.title: Kawanthissa Tusker
data.text:
Kawanthissa (also spelled Kavanthissa or Kavantissa) was a wild Sri Lankan elephant associated with the Galgamuwa area of Sri Lanka's North Western Province. He was known for his prominent tusks and attracted public attention.

== Background ==

Kawanthissa was known in the Galgamuwa area and received attention from residents and wildlife enthusiasts. News reports described public concern about his welfare following an injury in 2026. [ref: Outrage and calls for investigation following tragic death of iconic Kawanthissa, The Sunday Times]

== Injury and death ==

In September 2026, Kawanthissa was reportedly found with an injury to his right foreleg in the Galgamuwa area. Wildlife officials and veterinarians treated the injury and monitored his condition. [ref: Ailing tusker Kavanthissa in critical condition, public urged to stay away, Daily Mirror]

Subsequent reports described a deterioration in the elephant's condition, including reduced food intake and diarrhoea, while veterinary treatment continued. [ref: Ailing tusker Kavanthissa in critical condition, public urged to stay away, Daily Mirror]

Kawanthissa died in October 2026 while receiving veterinary care. His death prompted public concern and calls for an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his treatment. [ref: Outrage and calls for investigation following tragic death of iconic Kawanthissa, The Sunday Times]

== Investigation ==

Following Kawanthissa's death, Sri Lanka's Environment Ministry announced an independent investigation into the circumstances of his treatment and whether any errors or deliberate wrongdoing had occurred. [ref: Independent probe into tusker Kawanthissa's death, Daily Mirror]

On 19 October 2026, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake appointed an expert committee to investigate the elephant's death, examine its possible causes, and determine whether lapses or negligence had occurred during treatment. The committee was also tasked with making recommendations concerning wild elephant welfare and conservation. [ref: President appoints committee to probe Kavanthissa's death, Daily Mirror]

The committee was expected to submit its findings and recommendations to the President within 30 days. The appointment of the committee did not establish the cause of death or prove that negligence had occurred. [ref: President appoints committee to probe Kavanthissa's death, Daily Mirror]

data.text:
= Shaz Saleem =
Shaz Saleem (also known as Shazada Saleem) is a British community activist, charity founder and former Conservative Party politician. He served as a councillor for Kingswinford North and Wall Heath on Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council from 2021 and was appointed cabinet member for highways and public realm in May 2022.[1][2] [ref: ]

Saleem founded The Saleem Foundation, a charitable organisation registered in 2019 that supports individuals and community groups across Birmingham and the Black Country.[3][4] His community activities have included charitable fundraising, youth engagement, mental health awareness and environmental projects. [ref: ]

== Background ==
Saleem has longstanding connections with Kingswinford and the Dudley borough in the West Midlands. [ref: ]

Before entering local government, he was involved in the private hire and taxi industry and community organisations. [ref: ]

In a March 2026 interview with the University of Derby's StoryHub, Saleem described his grandfather as an important influence on his involvement in charitable activities. His grandfather died in 2016, and Saleem subsequently established a foundation in his memory.[4] [ref: ]

== Political career ==

=== Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council ===
Saleem was elected as a Conservative councillor for Kingswinford North and Wall Heath in the 2021 local elections.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

In May 2022, he was appointed cabinet member for highways and public realm on Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council. His responsibilities included matters relating to highways and public spaces within the borough.[1] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

In February 2023, Saleem was suspended from the Conservative Party and resigned from his cabinet position. He subsequently served as an independent councillor.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

=== Legal proceedings ===
In March 2025, Saleem appeared at Walsall Magistrates' Court charged with two offences relating to allegedly threatening or offensive voicemail messages sent in June 2023. [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

Saleem denied both charges. On 6 March 2025, District Judge Michael Wheeler found him not guilty.[6] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

=== Return to the Conservative Party ===
In February 2026, the Express & Star reported that Saleem had rejoined the Conservative Party. He stated that he intended to support Conservative candidates in the 2026 local elections rather than stand as a candidate himself.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

== Charitable activities ==

=== The Saleem Foundation ===
Saleem founded The Saleem Foundation in 2019 in memory of his grandfather, who died in 2016.[4] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

The foundation was registered with the Charity Commission for England and Wales on 29 April 2019 under charity number 1183167.[3] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

According to its registered charitable objectives, the foundation supports charities, voluntary organisations and disadvantaged individuals across Birmingham and the Black Country. Its activities include assistance relating to health, disability, financial hardship, age and other circumstances affecting personal welfare.[3] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

In a March 2026 interview with StoryHub Derby, Saleem described the foundation's involvement in food distribution, mental health awareness campaigns, charitable fundraising and community activities.[4] [ref: ]

=== Community projects ===
Saleem has been associated with a number of community initiatives, including activities aimed at reducing loneliness, engaging young people and improving local environments. [ref: ]

These include The Saleem Foundation's Cuppa Club, established to provide opportunities for social interaction, particularly among older residents experiencing isolation.[4] [ref: ]

Other activities have included litter-picking initiatives, food assistance and awareness campaigns concerning mental health and domestic abuse.[4] [ref: ]

=== Fundraising ===
Saleem has participated in charitable fundraising activities, including boxing events. [ref: Councillor hoping to deliver a knockout for Mayor’s charities, Dudley Council News]

In March 2022, Dudley Council publicised his participation in a charity boxing event at Kingswinford School in support of PAPYRUS Prevention of Young Suicide and the Mayor of Dudley's charities.[7] [ref: Councillor hoping to deliver a knockout for Mayor’s charities, Dudley Council News]

In March 2026, Dudley Council announced a further charity boxing event involving Saleem and council leader Patrick Harley, scheduled for August 2026 at Dudley Town Hall. [ref: Charity boxing showdown raises almost £28K, Dudley Council News]

The event took place on 21 August 2026. On 27 August, Dudley Council reported that it had raised £27,685 for charitable causes, with further income from ticket sales still to be confirmed.[8] [ref: Charity boxing showdown raises almost £28K, Dudley Council News]

The proceeds were intended to benefit charities supported by the Mayor of Dudley and the former mayor, with an additional donation allocated to Birmingham Children's Hospital.[8] [ref: Charity boxing showdown raises almost £28K, Dudley Council News]

== Awards and recognition ==
Saleem received a High Sheriff Award in 2025 in recognition of his community activities, as reported by the Express & Star in February 2026.[2] [ref: Former Dudley councillor and community activist returns to the Tories, Express and Star]

His voluntary work has included involvement in charitable fundraising, activities addressing social isolation and local community projects.[4] [ref: Former Dudley councillor and community activist returns to the Tories, Express and Star]

data.title: Max Shelton
data.text:
----

Max Shelton is an Australian agricultural scientist and former Associate Professor at the University of Queensland. He is known for his research on tropical pastures and the development of a new insect-resistant cultivar of Leucaena leucocephala, a variety called Redlands [ref: Insect-resistant forage crop almost ready for commercial release, ABC News], which is used in cattle farming. In 2022, Shelton was awarded the AW Howard Medal for significant contributions to the advancement of pastures in Australia. [ref: Leucaena research pioneer Max Shelton receives national honour, Beef Central]

== Research and career ==
Shelton graduated with honours from a degree in agricultural science at the University of Queensland in 1968. He then completed a PhD at the University of Queensland in 1972 [ref: Factors influencing competition between upland rice (Oryza sativa Linn.) and undersown stylo (Stylosanthes guyanensis Aubl.), The University of Queensland] on the integration of stylo pasture in farming systems in North-East Thailand. He returned to the University of Queensland in 1978 in the Department of Agriculture, taking up a tenured lectureship in pasture science in 1986. He retired in 2016 as associate professor. [ref: Celebrating the contribution of Dr Max Shelton, Beef Central]

Shelton's career focused on the development and management of forage tree legumes in livestock production. With colleagues he bred a new psyllid-resistant variety of Leucaena called Redlands. [ref: 'Redlands' leucaena lifts beef productivity and profitability in coastal Queensland, Beef Central] [ref: Associate Professor Max Shelton on his pest resistant Leucaena forage research, ABC Rural] He was also involved in the release of three other new pasture plant varieties (Sesbania cv Mt Cotton and Leucaena cvv Tarramba, and Wondergraze). Shelton worked with smallholder farmers in Indonesia to improve nutrition for cattle through better pasture management. [ref: Improving smallholder cattle fattening systems based on forage tree legume diets in eastern Indonesia and northern Australia, Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research]
He has delivered a series of courses to graziers in northern Queensland and advised them on the establishment and management of grazed leucaena pastures. [ref: Five decades of leucaena R&D: Is it time to move on?, Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation]

Shelton has also carried out research on the environmental impact of cattle production, including methane production [ref: Leucaena: The productive and sustainable forage legume, Meat & Livestock Australia] and how leucaena-based grazing systems can be used to sequester carbon. [ref: Soil organic carbon and total nitrogen under Leucaena leucocephala pastures in Queensland, Crop & Pasture Science] [ref: The sequestration and turnover of soil organic carbon in subtropical leucaena-grass pastures, Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment] In addition, Shelton has investigated the drought-resistance potential of leucaena for farmers in dry, tropical regions. [ref: Drought fodder crop takes centre stage, UQ News]

data.title: MT-ND4 m.11232TC
data.text:
----

MT-ND4 m.11232T>C (also written 11232T>C or m.11232T>C) is a rare mutation in the mitochondrial gene MT-ND4. It changes one amino acid (leucine to proline at position 158) in the ND4 protein, which is part of complex I in the mitochondria. When the mutation is present in essentially all of a person's mitochondria (homoplasmic), it has been linked to a high risk of severe, permanent brain injury after sevoflurane anesthesia. [ref: Effects of a Mitochondrial Genetic Variant on Sevoflurane Hypersensitivity, Anesthesiology]
__TOC__
==History==
Starting in 2025 and 2026, doctors began reporting cases of previously healthy children and young adults who woke up slowly or never fully recovered after routine surgery. Many developed damage to the basal ganglia, movement problems, cognitive decline, or died. Almost all of them had received sevoflurane, and testing showed they carried the same m.11232T>C mutation. The patients shared maternal Venezuelan ancestry (often linked to the state of Carabobo). Because mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother, the mutation is passed down that way.

Lab experiments with cells from these patients found that sevoflurane at normal anesthetic levels almost completely shut down the part of mitochondrial energy production that depends on complex I. Propofol did not cause the same sharp drop. A few patients who had already been injured by sevoflurane later had surgery with propofol-based intravenous anesthesia and did not have the same acute brain injury again.

Professional groups have responded. The American Society of Anesthesiologists and the Society for Pediatric Anesthesia recommend asking about maternal Venezuelan ancestry and considering avoiding all volatile anesthetics in those patients until more is known [ref: ]. The FDA has also issued an alert about the risk [ref: FDA Alerts Health Care Providers to Cases of Neurologic Complications from General Anesthesia Linked to Genetic Variant in Patients of Maternal Venezuelan Ancestry, FDA]. Targeted genetic testing for the mutation is now available from some labs.

Not every person with the mutation has been shown to react, and researchers are still working out exactly how high the risk is and whether other anesthetics are also dangerous. Before these cases, the mutation was listed as a variant of uncertain significance. The new clinical reports and lab data are what changed that assessment.

== References ==

data.title: WD J1011+2845
data.text:
WD J1011+2845 also known as SDSS J1011+2845 is a cool White dwarf star located approximately 48 Light-years(approx. 15 parsecs) from Earth in the constellation Leo Minor. In a study published in October 2026, a research team led by the University of Warwick identified it as potentially the reddest-colored star ever recorded, exhibiting a distinct deep salmon-pink hue to human vision.

While the majority of nearby white dwarfs appear white or pale blue, [ref: Astronomers reveal surprising true colours of white dwarfs, warwick.ac.uk] WD J1011+2845 is a rare exception due to its unique atmospheric composition consisting largely of carbon, giving it a spectral type of DQ, indicating that it is a white dwarf that is carbon rich. The star features a deep Convection zone that has dredged up carbon from its core to the surface. Under intense atmospheric density and pressure, these carbon molecules heavily distort the star's light, absorbing shorter wavelengths of light and squeezing nearly all of its emitted visible light beyond 600 nanometers. This creates its characteristic salmon-pink hue.

=== Designation ===
The designation WD J1011+2845 follows the standard naming system established by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) for white dwarfs. The WD prefix identifies the object as a White dwarf, while the J indicates the positioning using the modern J2000 coordinates epoch. The numbers 1011+2845 represent the star's precise celestial coordinates in the sky: a Right ascension of 10 hours 11 minutes, and a Declination of +28° 45 minutes.

=== Discovery and Characteristics ===
WD J1011+2845 was analyzed as part of a spectroscopic survey of 151 white dwarfs within 20 Parsecs of Earth. The research group, led by astrophysicist Dr. Mark Hollands, utilized light-spectrum data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey alongside color vision models to determine how the star's atmospheric elements would filter light to the human eye. [ref: Green, Pink And Purple: Astronomers Reveal Surprising True Colors Of White Dwarf Stars - Eurasia Review, www.eurasiareview.com]

Unlike other color-shifted white dwarfs whose unusual hues are caused by temporarily accreted planetary debris (such as WD J1330+6435, a chartreuse-green white dwarf identified in the same study [ref: First Green Star Adds to Milky Way's Rainbow, Newser]), the salmon-pink coloring of WD J1011+2845 is driven by internal stellar forces. Because the carbon is continually supplied from within the star's interior, astronomers project that WD J1011+2845 will retain its distinctive salmon-pink color for billions of years.

data.title: Qingdao Haier Biomedical
data.text:
Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co., Ltd. (SSE: 688139) is a Chinese medical technology and life sciences enterprise operating under the healthcare ecosystem of Haier Group. [ref: Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co Ltd Company Profile, Reuters] Headquartered in Qingdao, Shandong, the company manufactures cold-chain storage equipment, biological safety equipment, automated laboratory equipment, and digital healthcare solutions. [ref: Listing Announcement: Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co., Ltd. (688139), Shanghai Stock Exchange]

Its systems are utilized globally across academic research institutes, biopharmaceutical companies, medical institutions, blood donation centers, and public health agencies. In October 2019, Haier Biomedical completed its initial public offering on the Science and Technology Innovation Board (STAR Market) of the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

== History ==
Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co., Ltd. was established on October 28, 2005, under the former name Qingdao Haier Special Electrical Appliances Co., Ltd. The company initially focused on biomedical refrigeration and subsequently expanded its operations into biobanking, healthcare cold-chain management, molecular diagnostics, and laboratory solutions.

* 2008: Provided biobanking solutions to the China Marrow Donor Program.
* 2011: Secured World Health Organization (WHO) Performance, Quality and Safety (PQS) prequalification for medical refrigerators and freezers; a company-developed refrigerator was carried aboard the Shenzhou-8 spacecraft.
* 2015–2017: Initiated research and development into internet-connected monitoring solutions and entered the point-of-care testing market.
* 2019: Completed its initial public offering on the Shanghai Stock Exchange STAR Market under stock code 688139.
* 2020–2023: Acquired Chongqing Sandawell Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. in 2020 and a stake in Suzhou Houhong Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd. in 2023 to expand pharmacy and cold-storage automation.
* 2024–2026: Expanded research into automated laboratory instruments and bioprocess technology applications.

== Operational Sectors and Product Categories ==
Haier Biomedical designs, manufactures, and distributes laboratory and medical equipment across four primary sectors:

=== Sample and Biobanking Solutions ===
* Cryogenic storage systems, including ultra-low temperature freezers operating at -86°C and -150°C, and hydrocarbon-based ecological freezers.
* Automated full-temperature-range biobanking systems for high-throughput sample preservation and retrieval.
* Specialized cryogenic systems deployed in research facilities and specialized environments.

=== Research and Biomanufacturing Solutions ===
* Cell processing workstations, cell culture systems, and cell preservation equipment.
* Laboratory safety and biosafety equipment, including CO₂ incubators, refrigerated centrifuges, Class II biological safety cabinets, and laminar flow clean benches.
* Biopharmaceutical consumable tracking systems and sterile preparation equipment.

=== Healthcare and Hospital Pharmacy Solutions ===
* Automated hospital pharmacy dispensing systems and medication management cabinets.
* Digital medical imaging equipment and clinical workflow support software.

=== Blood Management and Public Health Networks ===
* Internet-connected blood bank refrigerators and plasma freezers for inventory tracking across blood centers and hospitals.
* Solar-powered vaccine refrigerators, mobile vaccination vehicles, and immunization clinic equipment designed for public health infrastructure. [ref: Cold Chain Equipment Guide, UNICEF Supply Division]

== Global Operations and Partnerships ==
Haier Biomedical operates across more than 160 countries and territories. The company maintains regional technical support hubs and distribution networks in North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, the Middle East, and Africa.

The company has collaborated with international organizations—including the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and GAVI—to supply solar-powered vaccine refrigeration equipment and cold-chain infrastructure to health systems in developing economies.

== Sustainability ==
Haier Biomedical publishes annual environmental and governance performance disclosures. Its sustainability initiatives focus on:
* Transitioning refrigeration product lines to natural hydrocarbon refrigerants to lower global warming potential.
* Manufacturing zero-electricity, solar-direct-drive cold-storage equipment for off-grid medical infrastructure.
* Implementing green manufacturing processes certified under international environmental management standards.
