data.title: Lee Su-yeon (picture book illustrator)
data.text:
----

Lee Su-yeon (born 1982) is a South Korean picture book author, illustrator, and graphic novelist. Her work focuses on emotions and memories, growth and healing, employing watercolor and anthropomorphic animal characters to portray the inner lives of her characters. Her notable works include Breakfast On the Moon, Two Friends on My Shoulders, I Sell Furniture Somehow, and It Rains and the Grass Grows.

== Life and Career ==
Lee was born in Seoul and studied for an MA at the Camberwell College of Arts in the United Kingdom. She teaches picture book making and graphic novel courses at Hankyoreh Education and Chungkang College of Cultural Industries.

In addition to writing and illustrating her own works, Lee illustrates books by other authors. Her works include 《우리 마을에 온 손님》 (Visitors in Our Village) and 《커다란 집》 (The Big House), both written by Park Hye-sun and 《많은 사람들이 바다로 가》 (Many People Go to the Sea), written by Kim Gaemi.

《내 어깨 위 두 친구》 (Two Friends on My Shoulders) was mentioned in the 2023 White Ravens catalogue selected by the International Youth Library in Munich. Her graphic novel 《어쩌다 보니 가구를 팝니다》 (I Sell Furniture Somehow), based on her experience working as a furniture salesperson in her twenties, was featured in the 2025 Book Illustrators Gallery at the Asian Festival of Children's Content (AFCC).

In 2026, Lee participated in a discussion program featuring children's literature creators from South Korea and Australia in Sydney.

== Awards and Recognition ==

* 2025년 — Selected for dPICTUS 100 Outstanding Picturebooks, 《많은 사람들이 바다로 가》 (Many People Go to the Sea).

* 2025년 — Selected for the BolognaRagazzi Awards' The BRAW Amazing Bookshelf, 《커다란 집》 (The Big House)
* 2023년 — Selected for The White Ravens, 《내 어깨 위 두 친구》 (Two Friends on My Shoulders)
* 2022년 — Selected for the AFCC Book Illustrators Gallery, 《너는 나의 모든 계절이야》 (You Are My Every Season)

== Artistic Style ==
Lee explores deep emotions, relationships, growth, and healing through her writing and image making. She observes everyday events and shifts in characters' feelings, portraying people's inner lives through anthropomorphic characters. Lee seeks to express a range of emotions through her characters and share stories of empathy and comfort with readers.

data.title: Tito Bautista
data.text:
Tito Bautista is a Filipino-American technology executive, information technology consultant and entrepreneur based in Las Vegas, Nevada. Over a career of more than three decades he worked on enterprise systems for companies in the media, automotive, insurance, finance and telecommunications industries, led the consulting firm TechSite America, and served as chief operating officer of Web Deposition, a developer of software for remote participation in legal depositions. He is a named co-inventor on a United States patent application for the secure real-time broadcast of deposition testimony. [ref: System and method for secured peer-to-peer broadcast of instantaneous testimony in text format (US 2011/0258442 A1), Justia Patents]

== Early life and education ==
Bautista was born in Manila, Philippines. He attended San Beda in Manila for his secondary education, graduating in 1971, and went on to earn a bachelor's degree in business administration from De La Salle University in 1976.

In 1977 his family emigrated to the United States, one of many Filipino families who left the country during the period of martial law under Ferdinand Marcos, which had been declared in 1972 and was accompanied by political repression and economic instability.

== Career ==

=== Move into information technology ===
In his first years in the United States, Bautista worked as an accountant. He later enrolled at the Chubb Institute in Short Hills, New Jersey, a technical school known for training career-changers in computer programming, where he studied computer systems analysis and programming between 1980 and 1982. After earning his certificate he left accounting for the information technology industry, a shift that allowed him to combine his background in finance with systems design.

=== Enterprise consulting ===
Through the 1980s and 1990s Bautista worked as an information technology consultant and project leader for several large corporations in the New York metropolitan area, including companies in the telecommunications, media, insurance, finance and automotive industries.

=== TechSite America and work in the Philippines ===
From 1992 to 2014 Bautista was president of TechSite America, a Los Angeles–based IT consulting firm that placed business and systems consultants with corporate clients and coordinated offshore programming and call-center teams.

Through TechSite, Bautista was involved in early efforts to computerize the Philippine Bureau of Customs, a project undertaken with the United Nations Development Programme, the Science and Technology Advisory Council of the Philippines in New York, Stevens Institute of Technology, Hewlett-Packard and the Swiss inspection firm SGS. He also promoted the introduction of electronic data interchange (EDI) in the Philippines, under which import, export, brokerage and financial documents were exchanged electronically between trading partners. EDI later became one of the standard channels for lodging electronic entries with the Bureau of Customs. [ref: Customs Reforms and Modernization: The Philippine Experience, CAREC Program]

=== Web Deposition ===
From 2009 to 2013 Bautista served as chief operating officer of Web Deposition, a Los Angeles company that developed a cloud-based platform allowing attorneys and other participants to join live depositions remotely. The software captured, encrypted and transmitted audio, video and transcript data from remote proceedings, and the company stated it could cut the cost of attending depositions by as much as 70 percent compared with in-person attendance.

With colleagues Allan Casilao and Monday U. Abengowe, Bautista is listed as a co-inventor on a patent application filed in April 2010 and published in October 2011 for a "system and method for secured peer-to-peer broadcast of instantaneous testimony in text format," which describes capturing and authenticating a witness's testimony and transmitting it in real time to authorized remote participants. [ref: US20110258442A1, Google Patents] The approach anticipated remote and virtual depositions, which became widespread in the U.S. legal profession during the COVID-19 pandemic.

=== Jets Inc. ===
In October 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Bautista founded Jets Inc., doing business as Jets Air Pro, an environmental technology company in Las Vegas. The company supplied air purification and sanitizing systems using UV-C light and ionizers, many connected through Internet of Things sensors, and consulted on indoor-air-quality measures for businesses, schools and public venues. It operated until December 2022.

=== Later work ===
In recent years Bautista has focused on artificial intelligence strategy, advising organizations as a fractional chief AI officer and developing AI-driven products. He also produces and presents Consciousness + AI, a YouTube documentary series examining questions in the philosophy of mind, including the hard problem of consciousness, integrated information theory, panpsychism and whether artificial intelligence systems could be conscious. [ref: Consciousness + AI, YouTube]

== Volunteer work ==
Bautista volunteers as a tax counselor with AARP Foundation Tax-Aide, a program in which trained volunteers prepare and file tax returns free of charge for older adults and taxpayers with low to moderate incomes. [ref: AARP Foundation Tax-Aide Sites Open Nationwide, Providing Free Tax Prep to Millions of Older Adults, AARP] The work draws on the accounting background with which he began his career in the United States.

== Writing ==
Bautista is the author of Journey Towards a Dream, a book published on Kindle about migration and the pursuit of the American Dream, drawing on the experience of those who leave their home countries for the United States. [ref: Journey Towards a Dream, Amazon Kindle]

== Recognition ==
In 2022 Bautista and Jets Air Pro received recognition in the health category of the Anthem Awards, and he received leadership awards associated with the Internet 2.0 and Health 2.0 conferences.

== Personal life ==
Bautista lives in Las Vegas. He has three sons: Carlo, Michael and Gino.

* Filipino Americans

* [https://www.youtube.com/@[user] Consciousness + AI] on YouTube

data.title: International Northern Ssireum Federation
data.text:
----

International Northern Ssireum Federation (INSF) is a United States-approved non-profit organization established to preserve and internationalize "Northern Ssireum" (including Tti-ssireum and Sokswae), a traditional style of Korean wrestling rooted in the northern regions of the Korean Peninsula and Manchuria.

== Overview and Status ==
The federation operates a global governance framework with participation from 19 countries to systematize and standardize Northern Ssireum.

INSF is registered as a non-governmental organization (NGO) with the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA). It is also officially listed in the database of the Union of International Associations (UIA) under Organization ID: AA7728. The UIA profile defines the organization's primary aim as the preservation and globalization of Northern Ssireum, recognizing its identity within the context of UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.

== Core Activities ==
=== UN High-Level Political Forum (HLPF) Side Event ===
On July 9, 2026, INSF hosted an official side event at the United Nations High-level Political Forum (HLPF). The event focused on the sustainable transmission of traditional wrestling heritage along the Silk Road and highlighted the role of physical culture in achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

=== International Competitions ===
The federation organized the International Northern Ssireum Championship to commemorate UN International Youth Day. Additionally, to celebrate the joint inscription of Ssireum on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, the federation hosted the 2nd International Northern Ssireum World Championships to mark the "2026 UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage Day."

=== Academic Research and Publications ===
INSF conducts research focusing on the technical and historical connections between Korean Ssireum and other Eurasian traditional wrestling styles, such as Central Asian Kurash, Pakistani Kushti, and Mongolian Bokh.
* The research findings have been published as a book series titled The Warrior's Path: Silk Road Traditional Wrestling and Physical Culture on Amazon.
* Academic papers and archived materials from the "Silk Road Warrior Arts Research Project" are indexed and preserved with Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) in the Zenodo repository operated by CERN.

== See also ==
* Ssireum
* Silk Road
* Intangible cultural heritage

== References ==
[ref: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA) Official NGO Database.]
[ref: Union of International Associations (UIA) Yearbook Profile (Org ID: AA7728).]
[ref: "Connecting Eurasia: Silk Road Living Heritage and Sustainable Ssireum Transmission", UN HLPF Official Side Events Schedule, July 2026.]
[ref: International Northern Ssireum Federation, [user] et al. (2026). The Warrior's Path (1): Silk Road Traditional Wrestling and Physical Culture. Amazon Publishing.]
[ref: "Silk Road Warrior Arts Research Project Community", Zenodo (CERN) Digital Repository.]

data.title: Network Tasman
data.text:
Network Tasman Limited is a New Zealand electricity distribution company based in Hope, near Richmond, in the Tasman District. It owns and operates electricity distribution infrastructure supplying homes and businesses across the Nelson and Tasman regions in the northern South Island.

The company is wholly owned by Network Tasman Trust [ref: About the Trust - Network Tasman], a consumer trust established in 1993 [ref: Energy Companies (Tasman Energy Limited) Vesting Order 1993, New Zealand Legislation] following restructuring of the New Zealand electricity industry. The trust holds the company's shares on behalf of eligible electricity consumers in the historic Tasman network area.

Network Tasman adopted its present name in 1998, following the separation of the electricity distribution and retailing operations of Tasman Energy Limited. The company's history can be traced to the establishment of electricity supply in the region in 1908 [ref: History of Network Tasman - Network Tasman].

On 31 March 2026, Network Tasman amalgamated with Nelson Electricity Limited, combining two previously separate electricity distribution businesses. The amalgamated company reported 53,809 electricity connections as at 31 March 2026 [ref: Amalgamation of NTL and NEL - Network Tasman] [ref: Network Tasman Announces 2026 Annual Results - Network Tasman].

== History ==

=== Early electricity supply, 1908–1958 ===
The origins of electricity distribution in the Tasman region date to 1908, when Kōhatu farmer Robert Ellis introduced electric power to his home. In 1911, Ellis obtained a licence to supply electricity commercially through the Waimea Electric Supply and Manufacturing Company, using a waterwheel at a flourmill. The company continued operating independently until 1933.

Other electricity undertakings developed during the early twentieth century, principally under local authority ownership. Motueka Borough Council began generating electricity in 1921, followed by Murchison County Council, which commissioned the Six-Mile hydroelectric scheme in 1922.

Nelson City Council established a coal-fired electricity generating station at Wakefield Quay in 1923, beginning the development of a separate municipal electricity supply system for central Nelson.

The Golden Bay Electric Power Board was established in 1925, with the Pupu hydroelectric scheme commissioned in 1929. The Waimea Electric Power Board was established in the same year, absorbing existing electricity supply undertakings in Brightwater and Motueka.

Development of electricity generation continued during the following decades. Construction of the Cobb hydroelectric scheme began in 1935, with the project completed by the government in 1944. A hydroelectric plant was commissioned at Maruia Falls in 1951.

A major development occurred in 1958 when the Nelson and Tasman electricity supply system was connected to New Zealand's national electricity grid, reducing the region's dependence on local generating schemes [ref: History of Network Tasman - Network Tasman] [ref: Nelson Electricity buyout welcomed - Network Tasman].

=== Consolidation of electricity authorities, 1963–1988 ===
During the second half of the twentieth century, electricity supply authorities in the region were progressively consolidated.

In 1963, the Waimea Electric Power Board merged with the Murchison electricity undertaking. In 1976, the Waimea and Golden Bay electric power boards amalgamated to form the Tasman Electric Power Board.

The combined authority was responsible for electricity distribution across a geographically extensive area, incorporating rural communities, coastal settlements and growing urban centres.

In 1988, the Tasman Electric Power Board became Tasman Energy [ref: History of Network Tasman - Network Tasman].

=== Electricity industry reform, 1990–1998 ===
Reform of New Zealand's electricity industry during the early 1990s led to the commercialisation of regional electricity authorities.

Under the Energy Companies Act 1992, electricity authorities were required to adopt corporate structures. Tasman Energy considered alternative ownership arrangements, including private ownership, local authority ownership and a consumer trust.

In 1992, the company's directors recommended that the business be owned through a trust representing electricity consumers. Following public consultation, the Tasman Electric Power Trust was established on 30 April 1993 to hold the shares in the company on behalf of consumers.

Sir Wallace Rowling, a former Prime Minister of New Zealand and former Member of Parliament for Tasman, became the trust's founding chair.

Further electricity industry reforms [ref: www.beehive.govt.nz] in 1998 - the Bradford reforms - required electricity distribution businesses to be separated from electricity retailing activities. Tasman Energy retained the electricity distribution network and sold its retailing business to Contact Energy.

The distribution company was renamed Network Tasman Limited, while the Tasman Electric Power Trust became Network Tasman Trust [ref: ].

=== Network Tasman from 1998 ===
Following the 1998 restructuring, Network Tasman continued developing and maintaining the region's electricity distribution infrastructure under consumer trust ownership.

The company retained responsibility for the electricity network, while electricity retailers supplied electricity to consumers and issued electricity bills.

Network Tasman subsequently developed interests in related infrastructure and services, including fibre-optic communications networks and electricity metering [ref: History of Network Tasman - Network Tasman].

In 2025, the company acquired full ownership of Nelson Electricity Limited, which had been jointly owned with Marlborough Lines since 1996. The businesses amalgamated in March 2026 [ref: Amalgamation of NTL and NEL - Network Tasman].

=== Electricity network ===
Network Tasman owns and operates electricity distribution infrastructure across the Nelson and Tasman regions. Its infrastructure includes overhead electricity lines, underground cables, substations, transformers and associated equipment.

Following the 2026 amalgamation with Nelson Electricity, Network Tasman operates two network areas.

The Tasman network serves approximately 43,000 electricity connections across the wider Tasman and Golden Bay areas, including Murchison, Richmond, Stoke, Tāhunanui, Atawhai and surrounding communities.

The Nelson network serves approximately 10,000 connections in central Nelson, previously supplied by Nelson Electricity Limited.

Although the networks are operated by the same company, they retain separate distribution pricing arrangements, reflecting differences in network characteristics and costs [ref: Amalgamation of NTL and NEL - Network Tasman].

Electricity retailers remain responsible for selling electricity to consumers, while Network Tasman maintains and develops the physical distribution network.

Network Tasman also operates fibre-optic communications infrastructure and has interests in electricity metering and related businesses [ref: Network Tasman Announces 2026 Annual Results - Network Tasman].

== Network Tasman Trust ==
Network Tasman Trust is the consumer ownership trust that holds all shares in Network Tasman Limited.

Established on 30 April 1993 [ref: Energy Companies (Tasman Energy Limited) Vesting Order 1993, www.legislation.govt.nz] as the Tasman Electric Power Trust, it was created following electricity industry restructuring and public consultation on the future ownership of Tasman Energy.

The trust was renamed Network Tasman Trust in 1998 [ref: History of Network Tasman - Network Tasman].

Its beneficiaries are eligible electricity consumers in the historic Tasman network area, encompassing the wider Tasman and Golden Bay regions, Murchison and parts of Nelson outside the former Nelson Electricity network.

The beneficiary arrangements are established by the trust deed and were not changed by the amalgamation with Nelson Electricity in 2026 [ref: About the Trust - Network Tasman].

Network Tasman Trust is governed by six trustees. Five trustees are elected by eligible electricity consumers, while the sixth is appointed by the three largest electricity consumers. Elected trustees serve six-year terms, with elections taking place every three years for two or three positions on a rotating basis [ref: About the Trust - Network Tasman].

Network Tasman Trust is separately governed by its trustees [ref: ].

The trust appoints the directors of Network Tasman Limited and monitors the company's performance. As of October 2026, Sarah Smith is chair of Network Tasman Limited, having been appointed a director in August 2017 and becoming chair in December 2023 [ref: Board of Directors - Network Tasman]. Oliver Kearney is the company's chief executive, having held the position since 2016

It also reviews the company's Statement of Corporate Intent [ref: Statement of Corporate Intent - Network Tasman] and undertakes 5-yearly of the company's ownership arrangements [ref: Ownership Review - Network Tasman]. In 2026 an independent review was undertaken by Key Business Partners [ref: Ownership review - Key Business Partners, Network Tasman Limited]. The review considered alternative ownership structures, including listed and unlisted company ownership, local authority ownership, a cooperative structure and continued consumer trust ownership.

The review recommended retaining the existing trust ownership arrangements. Network Tasman Trust invited public submissions, which closed on 6 October 2026, and provided an opportunity for submitters to be heard on 16 October [ref: Ownership Review - Network Tasman].

All submissions received supported retention of consumer trust ownership. Following its consideration of the review and public consultation, Network Tasman Trust confirmed in October 2026 that the existing consumer trust ownership structure would be retained.

Network Tasman Limited is required to operate as a commercially successful business under the Energy Companies Act 1992 [ref: Energy Companies Act 1992, www.legislation.govt.nz].

=== Founding trustees and Sir Wallace Rowling ===
Sir Wallace Rowling, who served as Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1974 to 1975, was the founding chair of the Tasman Electric Power Trust in 1993.

Rowling had longstanding connections with the region, having been born in Motueka and represented the Tasman electorate in Parliament. He was also a director of Tasman Energy during the transition to consumer trust ownership.

Following Rowling's death in 1995, Sir Peter Malone became chair of the trust from 1995 to 2005.

In 1997 the Trust established the Sir Wallace Rowling Scholarships in his memory [ref: Sir Wallace Rowling Scholarship - Network Tasman].

=== Network Tasman Charitable Trust ===
The Network Tasman Charitable Trust is a separate charitable entity established in 2006 to provide grants and scholarships supporting eligible individuals and community organisations.

The charitable trust supports community activities across a range of areas, including education, sport, culture and community services.

Its trustees are appointed by Network Tasman Trust [ref: ].

The charitable trust also administers the Sir Wallace Rowling Scholarships, which assist students undertaking tertiary education who have demonstrated academic achievement, leadership and participation in cultural, sporting or community activities [ref: ].

== Nelson Electricity Limited ==
Nelson Electricity Limited originated from the municipal electricity undertaking operated by Nelson City Council.

In 1923, the council established a coal-fired generating station at Wakefield Quay, marking the beginning of municipal electricity generation and distribution in Nelson.

The city's electricity network subsequently developed under council ownership, separately from the rural electricity supply authorities that later became Tasman Energy and Network Tasman. [4]

In 1991, Nelson City Council leased the Nelson Electricity network to CitiPower, a subsidiary of Capital Power [ref: Citipower Ltd, Nelson (Subsidiary Company Of Capital Power Ltd), Archives Online].

In 1996, the council sold Nelson Electricity to Tasman Energy and Marlborough Electric, the predecessors of Network Tasman and Marlborough Lines. The Commerce Commission cleared the proposed acquisition in June 1996 [ref: Marlborough Electric and Tasman Energy cleared to acquire Nelson Electricity Ltd, www.comcom.govt.nz].

Following the transaction, Network Tasman and Marlborough Lines each held a 50% interest in Nelson Electricity. The sale ended Nelson City Council's ownership of the city's electricity distribution business [ref: Nelson Electricity buyout welcomed - Network Tasman] [ref: Commerce Commission Decision 340 - Transalta Corporation of Canada and Contact Energy Limited, www.comcom.govt.nz].

=== Acquisition by Network Tasman in 2025 ===
In February 2025, Network Tasman announced an agreement to acquire Marlborough Lines' 50% shareholding in Nelson Electricity for NZ$26.7 million.

The transaction took effect on 31 March 2025, making Nelson Electricity a wholly owned subsidiary of Network Tasman. The acquisition ended almost three decades of joint ownership by the two electricity distribution companies.

Nelson Electricity initially continued operating as a separate legal company, with services provided by Network Tasman [ref: Nelson Electricity buyout welcomed, Top South Now]. On 31 March 2026, Network Tasman Limited and Nelson Electricity Limited legally amalgamated into a single electricity distribution company.

Following amalgamation, the former Nelson Electricity distribution area became Network Tasman's Nelson network, while the existing Network Tasman distribution area continued as the Tasman network [ref: Amalgamation of NTL and NEL - Network Tasman].

The Commerce Commission considered the implications of the amalgamation for the regulatory price-quality arrangements applicable to electricity distribution businesses. The amalgamation consolidated the two businesses under common ownership and management, while maintaining distinct distribution pricing arrangements for the two network areas [ref: Nelson Electricity and Network Tasman merger – Impact on the default pricequality path, www.comcom.govt.nz] [ref: Draft regulatory settings for merged Network Tasman–Nelson Electricity, www.comcom.govt.nz].

=== Consumer ownership following amalgamation ===
Although Network Tasman acquired and amalgamated Nelson Electricity, the transaction did not change the beneficiaries of Network Tasman Trust.

The trust was established in 1993 to hold the shares in the electricity distribution company on behalf of consumers in the historic Tasman network area.

Nelson Electricity had previously been owned by Nelson City Council, but the council's sale of the business in 1996 ended the indirect municipal ownership interest of Nelson residents.

Consequently, consumers in the former Nelson Electricity network are not beneficiaries of Network Tasman Trust.

The trust's consumer distributions, trustee voting arrangements and Sir Wallace Rowling Scholarships continue to apply to eligible consumers within the Tasman network area, as defined by the trust deed. [2][6]

== Financial performance ==
For the financial year ended 31 March 2026, Network Tasman reported operating revenue of NZ$70.8 million, compared with NZ$69.7 million in the previous year.

The company reported an operating surplus after tax of NZ$12.2 million, compared with NZ$23.1 million in 2025. The previous year's result included a one-off non-cash revaluation gain associated with the acquisition of Nelson Electricity.

Total assets at 31 March 2026 were NZ$382 million, compared with NZ$371 million the previous year.

Net operating cash flow was NZ$20.1 million, while capital expenditure totalled NZ$18.8 million.

Network Tasman reported 53,809 customer connections at year-end, compared with 53,334 in 2025.

During the financial year, the company paid NZ$14.1 million in electricity distribution discounts to eligible consumers and a dividend of NZ$2.1 million to Network Tasman Trust.

The company also reported costs associated with repairing electricity distribution infrastructure damaged by severe weather events [ref: Network Tasman Announces 2026 Annual Results - Network Tasman].

data.title: Brian Patrick Hall
data.text:
----

Brian P. Hall was a values researcher, author, and professor emeritus of pastoral counseling at Santa Clara University. He was an ordained Episcopal priest and served as chairman of Values Technology. [ref: Values Shift: A Guide to Personal and Organizational Transformation, Wipf and Stock Publishers] With Benjamin Tonna, he developed the Hall–Tonna Inventory of Values, an assessment intended to identify values priorities and describe aspects of personal development. [ref: Review of Transition-Related Assessment Instruments, Transition Research Institute, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]

== Career and publications ==
Hall's work concerned pastoral counseling, values, and personal and organizational development. His publisher describes his work with Values Technology as applying values theory to religious and corporate leadership.

Hall authored The Genesis Effect: Personal and Organizational Transformations and Values Shift: A Guide to Personal and Organizational Transformation. Resource Publications published editions of both books in 2006. The Genesis Effect discusses relationships between values and personal and institutional growth, while Values Shift addresses values, leadership, and organizational change. [ref: The Genesis Effect: Personal and Organizational Transformations, Wipf and Stock Publishers]

== Hall-Tonna Inventory of Values ==
The Hall–Tonna Inventory of Values was developed to identify individuals' values priorities. A 1995 review described the version then available as a computer-scored assessment containing 77 forced-choice items addressing 125 values, eight developmental stages, and seven developmental cycles. It could be administered individually or in groups.

=== Applications in research ===
In a 1991 article in the Journal of School Leadership, Robert P. Craig and Cynthia J. Norris described using the inventory in a university preparation program for prospective school administrators. They examined participants' values clusters in relation to leadership classifications and argued that the process could help participants clarify the philosophical foundations of their educational practice and career decisions. [ref: Values Perception and Future Educational Leaders, Journal of School Leadership]

In 2014, Corne Thomas, Sanetta Henrietta Johanna du Toit, and Susanna Maria van Heerden discussed the Hall–Tonna Values Map in research on leadership and person-centred residential care. The authors used the framework to interpret relationships between organizational values and leadership styles, associating its self-initiating phase with interpersonal relationships, shared responsibility, and recognition of individuality. [ref: Leadership: The key to person-centred care, South African Journal of Occupational Therapy]

=== Evaluation ===
Eleanor E. Sanford reviewed the inventory in the 1992 Eleventh Mental Measurements Yearbook. A summary of her assessment appeared in Teresa A. Dais and Paula D. Kohler's 1995 Review of Transition-Related Assessment Instruments. The summary recorded a recommendation for the instrument while also reporting that further technical information and evidence of validity were needed. It noted Sanford's caution that additional empirical support was necessary before using the inventory to predict or judge individuals' values development and change.

== Selected publications ==
* The Genesis Effect: Personal and Organizational Transformations, Resource Publications
* Values Shift: A Guide to Personal and Organizational Transformation, Resource Publications

data.title: 2007 Ji-Paraná Tornado
data.text:
The Ji-Paraná Tornado was an strong tornado phenomenon occurred on September 24, 2007, causing destruction in the region of Ji-Paraná, in Rondônia. The tornado caused over 1 million reais (BRL) in damages. [ref: ]

== Synoptic Setup ==

The tornado and storms were caused by a Cold front that came from the south. Before the tornado, it was a warm 80⁰F, indicating the possibility of storms. When the Cold front arrived, it caused a line of instability in the state, thus causing the tornado. [ref: ]

== Damage in the city and information ==

The tornado ripped roofs off houses and businesses, overturned cars, knocked down power poles near a gas station, hurled road signs a distance away, and uprooted large trees, suggesting an E/F2 classification. [ref: ]
and left more than 10 families homeless. [ref: ]
The tornado also caused an estimated 1 million reais in damage at the time.
Shortly after the tornado, a Microburst with winds of 149 km/h (92 mph) hit the city. [ref: ]
It possibly hit Rondolândia, which also suffered electrical power outages.

== Trajectory ==

The tornado started in the Ji-Paraná River and quickly moved towards the eastern part of the city, uprooting trees, knocking down power poles, etc.
The tornado traveled more than 8km to Nova Colina, affecting a rural area before dissipating.
[ref: ]

data.title: Chef Nepal
data.text:
= Chef Nepal (TV Series) =
Chef Nepal is a competitive cooking reality TV show produced by Dharma Pictures. Created and produced by Dharma Raj Pandey, the program began broadcasting on Kantipur TV on 8 September 2023. It featured amateur cooks and culinary enthusiasts competing in a series of cooking challenges, with their dishes evaluated by judging paned led by Nepali celebrity masterchef Santosh Shah as master judge. [ref: ‘Chef Nepal’ to air on Kantipur Television, kathmandupost.com] [ref: ‘Chef Nepal’ to air from today on Kantipur Television, kathmandupost.com] [ref: Chef Nepal: So Happy to Finally See a Cooking Reality Television Show, NeoStuffs]

The competition also featured Bhanse Laxman Prasad Bhandari and Chef Ganesh Bahadur Dhakal as judges. Its first season concluded in July 2024, with Ajuihang Rai winning the competition. [ref: राईलाई सेफ नेपालको उपाधि, Naya Patrika News]

== Background and Development ==
The development of Chef Nepal preceded its television premier by several years. In an interview published by Kantipur daily newspaper in September 2023, producer Dharma Raj Pandey described an earlier attempt to develop a cooking competition for Nepali television. He said the concept had initially been researched several years before production began but had been set aside because of the market conditions at that time. [ref: ‘सेफ नेपाल’ आजदेखि, Ekantipur]

The project was subsequently revived under Dharma Pictures. Public announcements about the program appeared in 2022, with early reports naming Himalayan Television as the prospective broadcaster. [ref: टीभी रियालिटी शो ‘सेफ नेपाल’को मास्टर जजमा सन्तोष साह अनुबन्धित, Online Khabar]

In October 2022, Onlinekhabar reported that masterchef Santosh Shah had joined the production as master judge. Chef Santosh Shah had received international attention through the BBC television competition MasterChef: The Professionals. The Program also announced the involvement of Chef Ganesh Dhakal, Bhanse Laxman Bhandari and actress Priyanka Karki, who was described in contemporary reporting as an executive producer and celebrity judge.

In July 2023, Kantipur Television and Dharma Pictures entered into an agreement to broadcast the programme. The agreement was signed at Kantipur Television's office in Tinkune, Kathmandu, by the broadcaster's chief executive, Shishir Pachhai, and Shah, representing the program as masterjudge.

== Production ==
Chef Nepal was developed and produced by Dharma Raj Pandey through Dharma Pictures. Siddhartha Pudasaini was identified as the program's director at the time of its television debut.

A competition kitchen and filming set were established at Royal Thai Hospitality in Bhaktapur. The facility was used for contestant cooking challenges and the judges' assessments.

The program experienced delays between its initial announcement and television broadcast. In a review published shortly after the first episode, entertainemnt writer Neeraj Pun reported that financial constraints had affected the production's original schedule.

The series eventually premiered on Kantipur Television in September 2023.

== Competition Format ==
The first season was designed primarily for home cooks, students and amateur cooking enthusiasts rather than established professional chefs.

According to reporting published before the premier, the organiser received more than 500 applications through an online audition process. Approximately 100 applicants were shortlisted for subsequent selection round

Participants were required to prepare dishes for a panel of judges, who assessed their culinary performance and determined which contestants would advance. The competition progressed through auditions, elimination rounds and later cooking challenges.

The announced format included 18 episodes; two audition episodes, four elimination episodes, then competition episodes and two finale episodes. This represented the production plan reported before broadcast rather than a confirmed final episode total.

Contestants advanced from the initial selection pool to a Top 16 stage, followed by a Top 8 stage and the final competition. The program included dishes from different Nepali communities and culinary traditions.

== Judges and Presenters ==
The competition's principal judges were:

* Masterchef Santosh Shah: Nepalese chef known internationally for his participation in BBC's Masterchef: The Professionals. He served as master judge.
* Chef Ganesh Bahadur Dhakal: Chef and Hospitality entrepreneur associated with Royal Thai Hospitality and Baan Thai Restaurants.
* Bhanse Laxman Prasad Bhandari: Nepalese chef popularly known as Bhanse Laxman

Actress Priyanka Karki was associated with the program in executive production and celebrity judgin capacity during its development and initial presentation. But she did not appear in any episode of the series broadcasted in Kantipur Television. There is no any report available for her absence in the show.

In july 2024, Onlinekhabar reported that Rakchya Upreti would present the program's remaining episodes following an interruption to the broadcast schedule. [ref: फुड रियालिटी शो ‘सेफ नेपाल’को बाँकी एपिसोड बिहीबारदेखि, Online Khabar]

== Broadcast History ==
Chef Nepal began airing on Kantipur Television on 8 September 2023. The original schedule provided for a weekly Friday evening broadcast at 9 PM.

The program's television run extended in 2024. Its broadcast schedule was interrupted, and the remaining episodes were subsequently announced for transmission on Kantipur Television in July 2024.

Contemporary news reports also documented the involvement of commercial partners and related digital activities. These arrangements accompanied the television production but were separate from the competition itself.

== Season 1 Results ==
The first season concluded in July 2024.

Ajuihang Rai, a contestant from Udayapur, was declared the winner after advancing through the competition's elimination and final rounds. The result was reported by Naya Patrika following the grand finale.

Republica subsequently identified Bikesh Manandhar as First runner-up and Ingwa Subba as second runner-up. [ref: Australian ambassador congratulates winners of Chef Nepal, www.myrepublica.nagariknetwork.com]

The Competition also featured Australian Ambassador to Nepal Felicity Volk as a guest during its fourteenth episode. Following the conclusion of the first season, Volk met members of the production team and contestants and congratulated the winners and runners-up.

== Reception ==
Following the program's premier, entertainment website NeoStuffs published as assessment of its first episode.

Writer Neeraj Pun welcomed the development of an original Nepali cooking competition and gave a generally favorable assessment of its initial production. His review also identified aspects of the program's visual presentation that could have been improved, particularly the limited close-ip coverage of food prepared by contestants.

The series received coverage from several Nepali news publications throughout its development, broadcast and conclusion. Kantipur, The Kathmandu Post, and Onlinekhabar reported on the production and television launch, while Naya Patrika and Republica documented events following the comptition's final stages.

In July 2025, The Kathmandu Post published a feature about Navina Gyawali, a visually impaired cook and entrepreneur who had participated in Chef Nepal. The article described her progression through the competition and later culinary activities. [ref: Who can stop a determined woman? No one, kathmandupost.com]

== Subsequent programming ==
In May 2025, Kantipur reported that applications had opened for a follow-up television project titled Chef Nepal: The Professionals. [ref: 'शेफ नेपाल'को आवेदन खुला, Ekantipur]

Unlike the original competition, which primarily featured amateur cooks, the proposed new edition was intended for experienced professional chefs. The organizers announced that applicants would need at least five years of professional culinary experience.

The follow-up production was presented as a separate competition under the Chef Nepal name. At the time of the announcement, it was in the application stage.

== External Links ==

* [https://www.chefnepal.com/ Chef Nepal - Official Website]
* [https://www.chefnepal.com/shows-chef-nepal Chef Nepal- Television Program Information]

data.title: National Employment Law Project
data.text:
The National Employment Law Project (NELP) is an American nonprofit organization focused on employment law, labor policy, and workers' rights. Founded in 1969, it conducts research and advocates for policies concerning wages, unemployment insurance, workplace safety, employment discrimination, and enforcement of labor laws. [ref: About Us, National Employment Law Project]

== History ==

NELP was founded in 1969 by students at Columbia Law School in New York City as a legal clinic serving workers. During the 1970s and 1980s, it provided litigation assistance, legal research, training, and expert testimony to legal-aid attorneys throughout the United States. The organization subsequently expanded its work in labor-policy research and advocacy. [ref: NELP's History of Fighting for Racial & Economic Justice, National Employment Law Project]

== Policy and advocacy ==

=== Minimum wage and employment standards ===

The NELP has advocated for increases to federal and state minimum wages. In 2014, The Washington Post reported that the organization's federal advocacy coordinator, Judith Conti, had criticized the Obama administration's initial proposal to raise the federal minimum wage to $9 per hour as insufficient. [ref: The inside story of how the White House learned to love the minimum wage, The Washington Post]

=== Wage-theft enforcement ===

The NELP has participated in California's Strategic Enforcement Partnership, a collaboration between the state's labor commissioner, worker centers, and legal-aid organizations to investigate wage theft and other labor-law violations.

A 2022 CalMatters investigation described NELP's role in coordinating participating organizations and their wage-theft investigations. The report identified Amaya Jennifer Lin, a NELP campaign manager, as a coordinator of the partnership. [ref: To fight wage theft California gets strong assist from worker centers, CalMatters]

=== Workplace safety ===

The NELP has also researched enforcement of workplace health and safety regulations. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the organization published research examining staffing levels at the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). In October 2020, The New Yorker cited NELP's research on the decline in federal workplace-safety inspectors and interviewed its worker-health-and-safety program director, Deborah Berkowitz. [ref: Trump's Labor Secretary Is a Wrecking Ball Aimed at Workers, The New Yorker]

[user] is an independent game developer who creates adult visual novels. The developer's first release is the interactive smartphone game My Girlfriend Meets My Friend.

My Girlfriend Meets My Friend

My Girlfriend Meets My Friend is a 2D adult visual novel built with the Unity game engine for Windows, macOS, and Android. Chapter 1 was released as a free-to-play title on itch.io, with a second chapter in development and funded through Patreon.

In the game, the player character invites his girlfriend, Hannah, to stay at his apartment after her landlady tells her she must move out for building repairs. Soon after she arrives, the player character's boss, Harry, calls him into the office for an emergency overtime shift to test client mobile software over several days. This leaves Hannah alone in the apartment with the player's friend and roommate, Ace.

Gameplay takes place entirely through a simulated phone screen. Players read and reply to text messages, view photo and video attachments, use a decryption tool to read hidden chats, check a forum, and watch IP surveillance cameras. The first chapter includes more than 220 images and videos. Dialogue choices change character stats such as Lewd, Love, Will, NTR (Netorare), and NTS (Netorase), which determine which story path the player gets.

data.title: Vidani
data.text:
----

Vidani (Marathi: विडणी) is a prominent and heavily populated village located in the Phaltan taluka of Satara district in the Indian state of Maharashtra. Situated in the agrarian heartland of the Deccan Plateau, the village is renowned for its intensive sugarcane cultivation, its historical ties to the Maratha Empire, and the ancient Uttareshwar Temple. It also serves as a critical rural hub for agricultural research, acting as an implementation site for institutions like the Nimbkar Agricultural Research Institute (NARI). [ref: Census of India 2011: Data from the 2011 Census, including cities, villages and towns, Census of India]

== History ==

The history of Vidani is deeply intertwined with the broader history of the Phaltan region, which was a prominent Maratha princely state ruled by the Nimbalkar dynasty prior to Indian independence. Historical records from the Satara District Gazetteer suggest that Vidani, alongside neighboring agrarian settlements, served as an important revenue-generating village for the Phaltan state due to its proximity to the fertile Nira River basin. [ref: Satara District Gazetteer, Gazetteers Department, Government of Maharashtra]

The village's most significant historical monument is the Uttareshwar Temple, believed to date back several centuries. Local lore and architectural evidence suggest the temple faced vandalism in the 17th century by the Bijapur general Afzal Khan during his military campaign against Shivaji Maharaj.

== Geography and Climate ==

Vidani is geographically positioned at, sitting at an average elevation of 550 meters (1,800 feet) above sea level. It is located 72 kilometers northeast of the Satara district headquarters, 11 kilometers east of Phaltan city, and approximately 242 kilometers southeast of the state capital, Mumbai.

The village spans a total geographical area of 2,186.6 hectares (21.87 sq km). Rather than a single densely packed core, the settlement is distributed among a primary center and several decentralized hamlets (locally referred to as wadis or vastis), including Mazeri, and Pawarwadi.

=== Climate ===

Vidani experiences a hot semi-arid climate. The region falls squarely within the rain-shadow zone of the Western Ghats, making it relatively dry for most of the year.

* Summer (March to May): Extremely hot and dry, with daytime temperatures frequently exceeding 38°C (100°F).

* Monsoon (June to October): Characterized by erratic and generally low rainfall, averaging between 400 mm to 500 mm annually. Due to the scant rainfall, the village relies entirely on canal irrigation. [ref: Climate and Rainfall Data for Satara District, India Meteorological Department, Pune]

* Winter (November to February): Mild and pleasant, with nighttime temperatures dropping to around 12°C to 15°C.

== Demographics ==

As per the 2011 Census of India, Vidani has a total population of 10,439 individuals, spread across 2,080 households. It is one of the most heavily populated rural centers in the Phaltan subdivision.

* Gender: The population consists of 5,398 males and 5,041 females, yielding a sex ratio of 934 females for every 1,000 males, which is roughly on par with the regional average.

* Children: The population of children aged 0-6 years is 1,124, making up 10.77% of the total population. The child sex ratio stands at 855.

* Literacy: The overall literacy rate in Vidani is an impressive 80.44%, which is higher than the national average. Male literacy is 86.08%, while female literacy is 74.43%.

* Social Stratification: Scheduled Castes (SC) constitute 13.84% of the population, while Scheduled Tribes (ST) account for 0.34%.

== Economy and Agriculture ==

The economy of Vidani is heavily reliant on agriculture and allied agro-industries.

=== Cash Crops and Irrigation ===

Sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum) is the dominant cash crop. Despite being in a drought-prone region, sugarcane cultivation thrives here due to a robust network of artificial irrigation supplied by the Neera Right Bank Canal, which draws water from the Veer Dam. [ref: Irrigation and Water Management in the Nira Basin, Water Resources Department, Maharashtra] The harvested sugarcane primarily supplies the cooperative and private sugar mills in the taluka, notably the Shriram Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana and New Phaltan Sugar Works.

Other secondary crops include sorghum (jowar), pearl millet (bajra), onions, maize, and wheat.

=== Dairy and Allied Sectors ===

Dairy farming is a critical supplementary source of income. Almost every farming household maintains livestock, and the village features several milk collection centers that supply major state cooperatives like Govind Milk and Milk Products, headquartered in Phaltan.

Vidani also serves as an important field-testing ground for the Nimbkar Agricultural Research Institute (NARI). NARI's interventions in the village include the introduction of high-yield sweet sorghum varieties and the distribution of the "Nari Suvarna" sheep breed, which has significantly improved the economic resilience of marginal farmers.

== Civic Administration and Utilities ==

Vidani is governed by a Gram panchayat (village council) under the Panchayati Raj system. The village is divided into multiple wards, each electing a Gram Panchayat member. The Sarpanch serves as the head of the village administration.

* E-Governance: Vidani has digitized many of its administrative functions. Residents can access land records (7/12 extracts), pay property taxes, and obtain domicile certificates through the state's online Maha-e-Seva Kendras.

* Healthcare: The village is served by a Primary Health Centre (PHC) and several private dispensaries. Severe medical cases are referred to the sub-district hospital in Phaltan.

* Water Supply: The village is currently being upgraded under the central government's Jal Jeevan Mission, ensuring piped drinking water connections to every household. [ref: Jal Jeevan Mission Dashboard - Satara District, Ministry of Jal Shakti]

== Education ==

Educational facilities in Vidani are well-developed for a rural setting. The primary education sector is managed by the Satara Zilla Parishad, which runs multiple Marathi-medium primary schools distributed across the main village and its wadis.

For secondary and higher secondary education, the Uttareshwar High School serves local students, eliminating the need to travel to Phaltan city for basic schooling. For higher education (undergraduate and technical degrees), students primarily commute to Phaltan or Baramati.

== Culture and Society ==

=== Uttareshwar Temple ===

The cultural epicenter of the village is the ancient Uttareshwar Temple, dedicated to Lord Shiva. The temple features elements of traditional Hemadpanti dry-stone masonry. It is considered a Jagrut Devasthan (an awakened, active shrine) by the locals. The temple complex undergoes a massive transformation during the annual Maha Shivaratri festival, drawing devotees from across the district.

=== Warkari Tradition ===

Vidani is deeply embedded in the Warkari tradition of Maharashtra. The village sits close to the Palkhi Marg, the designated route for the annual procession of Sant Dnyaneshwar's palanquin traveling from Alandi to Pandharpur. During the monsoon months, the villagers of Vidani mobilize collectively to offer Annadaan (free food), medical aid, and shelter to the thousands of traveling pilgrims (warkaris). [ref: Warkaris receive warm welcome in Phaltan villages, The Times of India]

Other major festivals celebrated with fervor include Ganesh Chaturthi, Diwali, and the local village Yatra (fair) held in honor of the village deity, featuring traditional wrestling matches (Kusti) and folk performances.

== Transport ==

Vidani is well-connected to nearby urban centers via road networks.

* Road: State transport (MSRTC) buses regularly ply between Phaltan and Vidani. The expansion of National Highway 160 nearby has improved overall connectivity to major cities like Pune (110 km) and Solapur (175 km).

* Rail: The nearest railway station is the Phaltan Railway Station (Station Code: PLLD), which operates on the local Lonand-Phaltan line. The nearest major railway junction with nationwide connectivity is Pune Junction.

* Air: The closest domestic and international airport is Pune Airport (PNQ), located approximately 115 kilometers away.

data.title: 2007 Ji-Paraná Tornado
data.text:
The Ji-Paraná Tornado was an strong tornado phenomenon occurred on September 24, 2007, causing destruction in the region of Ji-Paraná, in Rondônia. The tornado caused over 1 million reais (BRL) in damages. [ref: Tornado atinge Rondônia com ventos de 150 km/h, apolo11]

== Synoptic Setup ==

The tornado and storms were caused by a Cold front that came from the south. Before the tornado, it was a warm 80⁰F, indicating the possibility of storms. When the Cold front arrived, it caused a line of instability in the state, thus causing the tornado. [ref: Tornado atinge Rondônia com ventos de 150 km/h, apolo11]

== Damage in the city and information ==

The tornado ripped roofs off houses and businesses, overturned cars, knocked down power poles near a gas station, hurled road signs a distance away, and uprooted large trees, suggesting an E/F2 classification. [ref: Tornado causa destruição em Rondônia, Jornal do Brasil]
and left more than 10 families homeless. [ref: Ji-Paraná conta com estrago de tempestade, G1]
The tornado also caused an estimated 1 million reais in damage at the time.
Shortly after the tornado, a Microburst with winds of 149 km/h (92 mph) hit the city. [ref: Tornado atinge Rondônia com ventos de 150 km/h, apolo11]
It possibly hit Rondolândia, which also suffered electrical power outages.

== Trajectory ==

The tornado started in the Ji-Paraná River and quickly moved towards the eastern part of the city, uprooting trees, knocking down power poles, etc.
The tornado traveled more than 8km to Nova Colina, affecting a rural area before dissipating.
[ref: Tornado atinge Rondônia com ventos de 150 km/h, apolo11]

==Series overview==

==Plot==
When Oscar makes the life-altering decision to leave behind his modest background and economic hardships in Bosnia, he carries with him a singular, unwavering dream: to attend medical school and build a secure, meaningful future. Arriving in the pristine and seemingly immaculate city of Lund, Sweden, he expects an orderly transition into European university life. Instead, he quickly discovers that reality is far more eccentric, unpredictable, and chaotic than he ever could have imagined.
Plunged headfirst into a whirlwind of high stakes academics, stark cultural shifts, and sudden independence, Oscar finds his daily routine instantly upended by a colorful ensemble of personalities. He moves into a quirky, lived in apartment shared with Erik a laid back engineering student sporting a distinct California accent and strong, unyielding opinions on pizza toppings. Between Erik's mischievous pranks and culinary debates, Oscar's home life is never dull. Adding to the turbulence is Nora, a deadpan, scheming letting agent who treats housing like a high-stakes chess match and thrives on absolute administrative chaos. Under their watch, Oscar learns that nothing in Sweden goes quite according to plan.
Meanwhile, his deep, lifelong bond with his childhood best friend, Selma, faces entirely new tests across geographic borders and shifting distances. As they navigate the complexities of life apart, buried feelings inevitably bubble to the surface. But everyday life brings its own absurd hurdles, from bizarre local traditions emerging from the shadows to disrupt their peace to the persistent, haunting echoes of a mysterious recurring dream that blurs the delicate line between fate and reality.
As old boundaries are crossed and unexpected foundations are built, Oscar must learn to navigate a complex labyrinth of personal and professional choices. Will his resilience, romance, and newfound friendships be enough to conquer the challenges ahead? Tune in to watch how this captivating international journey unfolds!

data.title: Ihab I. Hassan
data.text:
Ihab I. Hassan, also known as Barkah Barcor, is a Toronto-based author, engineer, and entrepreneur. He is the author of eleven books, including the memoir Tangled Web: My Fight to Break Free From Four Scams, and the founder of New Dimensions Solutions and Barkah Barcor Publishing. [ref: Amazon author page, "Ihab Hassan" — https://www.amazon.com/author/scammed-victims]

== Writing career ==
Hassan works as an engineer and cybersecurity professional. After he was defrauded in four separate scams, he wrote Tangled Web: My Fight to Break Free From Four Scams, a memoir describing how each fraud worked and how he recovered. [ref: Better Read Than Dead (bookstore listing with synopsis and ISBN 9798339950998) — https://betterread.com.au/book/tangled-web-my-fight-to-break-free-from-four-scams-by-ihab-hassan.do] [ref: Ryefield Books listing, ISBN 9798339950998 — https://www.ryefieldbooks.com/books/tangled-web-my-fight-to-break-free-from-four-scams-by-ihab-hassan/9798339950998]

His subsequent books focus on fraud prevention and recovery, including Scam-Proof Your Life: How to Outsmart Fraudsters in a Digital Age (also published in French as Protégez votre vie contre les arnaques), Exposing the Web: Unmasking the Scammers of Our Digital Age, and Rising After the Fall: Reclaiming Your Life After Betrayal and Scams. [ref: Bookshop.org listing, "Exposing the Web", ISBN 9798265759450 — https://bookshop.org/p/books/exposing-the-web-unmasking-the-scammers-of-our-digital-age-ihab-hassan/50829acf4a65d4f1] His later books include The Power of One Star, about online reviews and reputation, and Before We Vanish, co-authored with Fayza Hassan. [ref: Open Library author record, Ihab Hassan — https://openlibrary.org/authors/OL16639151A/Ihab_Hassan]

== Business career ==
Hassan is the founder of New Dimensions Solutions, the company behind the SKID SAFE non-slip coating line, sold via ndclean.com and ndclean.ca. [ref: New Dimensions Solutions — https://www.ndclean.com] [ref: Crunchbase company profile, New Dimensions Solutions — https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/new-dimensions-solutions] He also founded Barkah Barcor Publishing, the imprint under which his books appear. [ref: Barkah Barcor Publishing — https://barkahbarcorpublishing.com] Earlier in his career he founded two companies in Saudi Arabia, Mount Sinai Company and Innovation Foundation Factory.

data.title: Memorial Park (Providence, RI)
data.text:
Memorial Park is a public park in Providence, Rhode Island, located along the Providence River. The park features monuments dedicated to Rhode Island residents who fought in World War I, World War II, and the Korean War. [ref: Memorial Park, www.goprovidence.com] The park is managed by the City of Providence Parks Department. [ref: ]

== History ==
The park was opened in 1996 in front of the Providence County Courthouse after significant redevelopment resulting from the Providence River Relocation Project. [ref: Providence River Relocation, CNU] [ref: Cret’s wandering WWI shaft, Architecture Here and There] Following the destruction of Memorial Square, the park became the new home for a 150-foot tall memorial honoring more than 700 Rhode Island residents who died in World War I. [ref: World War I Monument, Memorial Square, Providence, Providence County, RI, Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. 20540 USA] The monument was designed by the French-American architect Paul Cret and built in 1929. The monument was disassembled starting in 1987 before being rebuilt in 1986. [ref: War Memorials Will Shine Bright for WaterFire Salute to Veterans - WaterFire Providence, waterfire.org] [ref: RI monuments on the move, The Providence Journal]

Two years after the park opened, the Rhode Island legislature allocated money to the Korean War Memorial Commission of Rhode Island. The memorial was built on the park's northern side by a Massachusetts-based sculptor and dedicated on October 8, 1998. [ref: Rhode Island Korean War Memorial, Photograph by Sylvie Watts] The memorial is flanked by the flags of Providence, the State of Rhode Island, the United States, and South Korea. [ref: Rhode Island Korean War Memorial, Photograph by Sylvie Watts]

In 2007, following contributions from Brown University, the City of Providence, the CVS Corporation, and other entities, a World War II memorial was dedicated on Veterans Day. [ref: Rhode Island World War II Memorial, Photographs by Edan Larkin] [ref: WWII Monument, www.bensavelkoul.nl] [ref: Brown University Contributes $50,000 to R.I. WWII Memorial, archive2.news.brown.edu] The memorial is surrounded by a stone wall featuring the seals of all of Rhode Island's cities and towns and the number of people who served from that town. Construction of the memorial was led by Joseph Corrente, a World War II and Korean War veteran who had earlier been co-chairman for the construction of the Korean War monument. [ref: JOSEPH CORRENTE Obituary (2009) - CRANSTON, RI - The Providence Journal, Legacy.com] [ref: When the Written Word Fails: Human Histories of WWII · The World War II Memorial in Providence: Untold Stories and Desperate Remembrance · Commemorative Works of Providence, commemorativeworksprovidenceri.digitalscholarship.brown.edu]

The Rhode Island Holocaust Memorial opened next to the World War II memorial in August 2015. [ref: Rhode Island Holocaust Memorial, Photographs by Sophia Siegel] The memorial incorporates prominent elements of Holocaust remembrance, including railroad tracks and entrance gates. [ref: The Rhode Island Holocaust Memorial in Providence, RI, Public Art Archive] [ref: Rhode Island Dedicates Holocaust Memorial In Providence, TPR: The Public's Radio]

=== Proposed Vietnam War memorial ===
After years of stalled efforts in the Rhode Island General Assembly to establish a memorial for Vietnam War veterans from Rhode Island, the state government announced on August 19, 2026, that a memorial would be constructed across the Providence River from Memorial Park. [ref: Last Honors with Providence's War Memorials, Rhode Island Monthly] [ref: Rhode Island’s Vietnam veterans have waited decades for a memorial. Now they know where it will be. • Rhode Island Current, Rhode Island Current] [ref: State of Rhode Island General Assembly, www.rilegislature.gov]

data.title: Adv Nivedida Subramanian
data.text:
= Adv Nivedida Subramanian =
Nivedida Subramanian is an Indian lawyer and politician associated with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), India. She served as Kerala state president of the BJP’s women’s wing, Mahila Morcha, and later as president of the party’s Thrissur North district unit in Kerala. In September 2026, the Government of India appointed her as a member of the National Commission for Women (NCW). [ref: Baptised in Emergency Fire, Nivedita Braces for Battle in Guruvayur, The New Indian Express] [ref: Notification S.O. 5257(E): Appointment of Members, National Commission for Women, The Gazette of India] [ref: ] [ref: NCW (@[user]) on X, X (formerly Twitter)]
== Early life and family ==
Subramanian is from Guruvayur in Thrissur district, Kerala. Her mother, Radha Balakrishnan, was active in the Bharatiya Jana Sangh and later held a leadership position in the BJP’s women’s organisation. Her father, Balakrishnan, was also reported to have been associated with the Jana Sangh. The family’s political involvement meant that Subramanian was exposed to party workers and political activity from childhood. [ref: ]

In 1975, during the Emergency declared by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, Radha Balakrishnan was arrested after taking part in protests against the Emergency. Subramanian, then approximately three years old, accompanied her mother to Palakkad Fort prison. In an interview published in 2016, Subramanian recalled that she remained with her mother in prison and that the experience had stayed with her. [ref: Nivedida Subramanian, BJP's Experimental Candidate For Ponnani, TimelineDaily]

Subramanian has described the experience as an early encounter with political adversity. The episode has subsequently been highlighted in profiles of her political career.

== Education and legal career ==
Subramanian holds a bachelor’s degree and a law degree. A 2016 profile reported that she was then pursuing a master’s degree in law at Annamalai University. A 2026 report by Madhyamam states that she obtained an LL.M. in labour law from Annamalai University, an LL.B. from Mangalore University, and an MBA in human resources from ICFAI University.

She has worked as an advocate in the civil and criminal courts at Chavakkad. Madhyamam reported that she had practised there for more than 12 years and had been a Supreme Court-accredited mediator since 2014. She also served as vice-president of the Chavakkad Bar Association. A company disclosure by Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL) described her as a lawyer, mediator and social-service participant, and recorded her tenure as a non-executive independent director. She was reappointed to the board with effect from 28 March 2025, and her tenure ended on 27 March 2026. [ref: Statutory disclosure: Board of Directors, Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited] [ref: Integrated Filing (Governance): Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited, National Stock Exchange of India] [ref: MRPL reappoints four independent directors to its board, FilingReader]

== Political career ==

=== BJP Mahila Morcha ===
Subramanian became a prominent figure in the BJP’s Kerala women’s organisation, Mahila Morcha, and served as its state president. Her mother, Radha Balakrishnan, had also held a leadership role in the organisation as a former state president.

As Mahila Morcha state president, Subramanian publicly advocated greater participation by women in BJP activities. In a 2021 Times of India report on the party’s efforts to expand its women’s cadre in Kerala, she said that social media was being used to interact with women volunteers and involve them in party activities. The report also discussed the role of the Sabarimala protests and local political mobilisation in the party’s outreach to women. [ref: Kerala: BJP claims its women cadre is blooming, The Times of India]

Her profile within the state BJP became more visible around the Mahila Sangamam, a large women’s gathering organised by Mahila Morcha in Thrissur on 3 January 2024. The New Indian Express reported that Subramanian was a principal organiser of the event, which the BJP had promoted as a gathering of two lakh women. The newspaper described the programme as a significant organisational moment for her within the party. India Today subsequently reported that the BJP’s women-focused event in Thrissur was seen by party sources as Subramanian’s initiative and quoted her discussing the party’s campaign approach towards women voters. [ref: Kerala Mahila Morcha president Nivedida steals the show at women’s conference, The New Indian Express] [ref: Modi in Thrissur, BJP on cloud nine: What next?, India Today]

The event brought her into greater public view alongside senior BJP leaders during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Thrissur. Contemporary reporting connected her role in organising the gathering with her standing in the state unit.

=== Thrissur North district president ===
On 27 January 2025, the BJP’s Kerala unit appointed Subramanian president of its Thrissur North organisational district. She was one of four women among the 27 district presidents named that day. [ref: BJP ‘doubles’ Kerala districts to 30, Christian push evident as it appoints 27 unit heads, @[user]]

=== Elections ===
Subramanian first contested an election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly in 2016 as the BJP candidate from Guruvayur. The New Indian Express published a profile of her candidacy that year, discussing her legal career, family background and childhood experience during the Emergency. She received 25,490 votes (17.26%) and finished third, behind K. V. Abdul Khader of the CPI(M), who won the seat, and P. M. Sadiqali of the IUML. [ref: Guruvayoor, Vidhan Sabha 2016 — IndiaVotes, www.indiavotes.com]

==== 2024 Lok Sabha election ====
In the 2024 Indian general election, Subramanian contested the Ponnani Lok Sabha constituency in Kerala as the BJP candidate. She secured 124,798 votes, approximately 12.16% of the votes polled, finishing third behind Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) candidate M. P. Abdussamad Samadani and Communist Party of India (Marxist) candidate K. S. Hamza. [ref: General Election 2024: Statistical Report, Constituency-Wise Detailed Results, Election Commission of India] [ref: 6 out of 9 Kerala women candidates upped vote share in LS polls, BJP shines, Onmanorama]

Her candidature coincided with an increase in the BJP’s electoral performance in the constituency compared with the previous general election. In 2019, the party’s candidate, Rema, had secured 110,603 votes, or 10.87% of the vote. In 2024, the BJP’s vote total increased by 14,195, while its vote share rose by 1.29 percentage points to 12.16%. [ref: Ponnani Lok Sabha Constituency, Elections.in] This represented an increase of approximately 12.8% in the party’s absolute vote total over its 2019 performance.

Ponnani has historically been a strong constituency for the IUML, and the BJP has faced electoral challenges in the region. In an interview with Onmanorama following the election, she described her candidature as a symbol of women’s empowerment and resilience, and argued that voters should assess women candidates on their merit and commitment rather than solely on their political affiliations. She also presented the BJP’s message in terms of development without discrimination.

Onmanorama noted that the BJP’s vote share in Ponnani had increased across the 2019 and 2024 elections, when the party fielded women candidates. The 2024 result therefore marked a further improvement in the party’s vote total and vote share in the constituency.

== National Commission for Women ==
On 24 September 2026, the Ministry of Women and Child Development issued a notification appointing Nivedida Subramanian and Archna Mishra as members of the National Commission for Women under the National Commission for Women Act, 1990. The notification specified a term of three years from the date of assumption of office, or until the age of 65, or until further orders, whichever occurred first.

Subramanian took charge as a member on 1 October 2026 at the Commission’s headquarters in New Delhi. Madhyamam reported that she was the first member of the Commission from Kerala.

In an interview with Manorama Online published the following day, Subramanian said that she had been asked to submit an application but had not been certain that she would receive the appointment. She described work concerning women’s protection and intervention on women’s issues as an area of particular interest. The interview also recorded her intention to take issues such as cyber abuse seriously. [ref: ‘വനിതാ കമ്മിഷനിലെ പദവി അപ്രതീക്ഷിതം, അപേക്ഷ സമർപ്പിക്കാൻ പറ‍ഞ്ഞിരുന്നു’: ഏറ്റവും താൽപര്യമുള്ള മേഖലയെന്ന് നിവേദിത സുബ്രഹ്മണ്യം, @[user]]

The NCW’s official website subsequently listed her as a member of the Commission. [ref: ]

== Personal life ==
In a 2016 interview with The New Indian Express, Nivedita said that her husband and in-laws died in a road accident in 2007. She also spoke about the death of her mother, Radha Balakrishnan, in 2012, and the difficulties she faced raising her three children after these losses.

data.title: Adrian Crutchfield
data.text:
Adrian Crutchfield is an American saxophonist, flutist, composer, and horn arranger from Roanoke, Virginia. Working across jazz, funk, R&B, hip-hop, and pop, he is best known as the final saxophonist and horn arranger to perform and record with Prince and The New Power Generation from 2012 to 2016. [ref: Bio – Adrian Crutchfield, adriancrutchfield.com] Fellow saxophonist Dave Koz has called him "one of the most highly anticipated up-and-coming musicians of his generation." [ref: Bio: Adrian Crutchfield, Music Mentor Group]

==Early life and education==

Crutchfield was born and raised in Roanoke, Virginia, where his passion for the saxophone was ignited at age four. During a concert, jazz artist Kenny G noticed the young Crutchfield in the audience, invited him on stage, and gifted him his first saxophone after playing a childish melody on it for the boy. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, Antigua Winds]

Around age ten, Crutchfield and his family relocated to Charlotte, North Carolina, where he was able to pursue his musical education more formally. He attended the Northwest School of the Performing Arts from sixth through eleventh grade. He subsequently graduated from the North Carolina School of the Arts (Conservatory) in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

He went on to pursue higher education at Florida State University, graduating in 2008 with a Bachelor of Arts in Music with a concentration in jazz, contemporary media, and commercial music.

==Career==

===Work with Prince===

Crutchfield served as the final saxophonist and horn arranger for Prince and The New Power Generation from 2012 until Prince's death in 2016. He was featured on several of Prince's later works, including the 2017 Grammy-nominated album Hit-N-Run Phase 2. In 2026, he was credited for overdubbing horn parts on the posthumous Prince album Timeless, a contribution that became the subject of controversy, as Prince's estate had initially stated the album would feature no new overdubs. [ref: Timeless (Prince album)]

===Other collaborations===

Beyond his work with Prince, Crutchfield has performed and toured with a diverse roster of artists including Lionel Richie, Bette Midler, CeeLo Green, Anthony Hamilton, Fantasia Barrino, KC and JoJo, Adina Howard, Regina Belle, Bootsy Collins, Young Jeezy, Jonathan Butler, Peter White, The Avett Brothers, Kenny Lattimore, Maysa Leak, Paul Jackson Jr., and Nathan East. Bette Midler has described his performance style as "divine." [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, ArtistCard]

He is featured as both a soloist and section player on Bootsy Collins' album World Wide Funk. In the jazz world, he has performed alongside Branford Marsalis, Brian Culbertson, Kim Waters, Mike Phillips, Alex Bugnon, Jeff Lorber, and the groups Fourplay and The Gap Band featuring Charlie Wilson. He also appears on the 2025 re-release of Brian Culbertson's Sensuality, contributing tenor saxophone.

Crutchfield collaborated with rapper Big K.R.I.T. on the 2022 neo-soul/hip-hop studio album Digital Roses Don't Die, playing flute on two tracks. On "Wind (Interlude)," he provides the backing flute instrumentation for the poetic, atmospheric interlude; on "More Than Roses," his flute arrangements appear alongside a live horn section and strings that form the song's lush, soulful soundscape. He is also a featured artist on the track "Dishonest Mistake" from the 2017 studio album Resurrection by Adina Howard. [ref: Resurrection (Adina Howard album)]

===Solo career===

Crutchfield released his debut album, Private Party, in 2009, blending jazz, neo-soul, and hip-hop influences. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, Légère Reeds] His second album, Leap, followed in 2017 and was described as a genre-defying project showcasing his neo-soul sound. He released his third album, Lover, in 2022.

In 2025, Crutchfield signed with Trippin 'n Rhythm Records and released Slick, his fourth studio album and label debut. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield – Slick, Smooth Jazz Daily] His single "Sooo Good" reached number one on the Billboard charts in August 2026, holding the position for three consecutive weeks. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, adriancrutchfield.com] He subsequently achieved a second number-one single with "Hypnotic." His collaborative single "Colors," featuring saxophonist BK Jackson, guitarist Lemek, and multi-instrumentalist Ryan La Valette, also reached number one on the Billboard charts.

data.title: Africa International Housing Show
data.text:
The Africa International Housing Show (AIHS) is an annual housing and construction exhibition and conference held in Abuja, Nigeria. It was founded by Festus Adebayo.

== History ==
Adebayo said the event began as the Abuja Housing Show and was renamed after participants from other countries attended. The 2026 edition was presented as the show's 20th anniversary. At its opening, Adebayo said the event had started with 10 participants and had grown into an exhibition featuring 350 companies.

== Editions ==
The 2022 edition, described as the 16th, focused on capital market financing for housing and the effects of climate change on affordable housing. Adebayo said it would include 31 international speakers and more than 400 exhibitors.

The 2023 edition was themed "Beyond Rhetoric To Homes; Making Housing Happen". Adebayo said the organisers were partnering with the International Finance Corporation on green housing finance.

The 19th edition was scheduled for 27 July to 1 August 2025 at the Transcorp Hilton Hotel under the theme "Reimagining Housing Through Innovation, Collaboration, and Policy". The organisers expected about 40,000 participants and 200 exhibitors from 21 countries.

The 20th edition opened in Abuja on 15 July 2026.

== Housing TV Africa ==
The Africa International Housing Show launched Housing TV Africa, a television channel focused on housing. At the 2026 opening, Adebayo described it as the continent's first dedicated housing television channel.
