= About =
Patrick Mathias, professionally known as Password, is an African songwriter, record producer, singer-songwriter, and Creative Architect whose work bridges mainstream African music, contemporary gospel, and culture-shaping creativity.

In 2013 Password was crowned the ultimate prize winner of the MTN SongStar contest with Don Jazzy and afterwards, he got widespread recognition for his contribution to the Davido single ‘Gobe’, which peaked at #1 on MTV Base’s Official Naija Top Ten Chart. He has continued to write for artists such as Darey, Praiz, General Pype, and other A-list artists in the industry.

With a career spanning songwriting, production, performance, and creative development, Password has contributed [ref: Password] to records across diverse musical landscapes. His credits include Davido’s “Gobe,” Vector’s “Dad & Dot,” Ada Ehi’s “Congratulations” featuring Buchi, Chinyere Udoma’s “Eze Mmuo”, Praiz’s “Somebody,” and General Pype’s “Champion.” His wider catalogue includes collaborations with artists such as Darey, Olamide, Tiwa Savage, and Jeff Akoh, alongside contributions to film soundtracks, including Hoodrush and Journey to Self.

Beyond the studio, Password is the founder of Kingdom Pop Culture (KPC), a creative ecosystem at the intersection of faith, culture, and contemporary music. Through KPC, he is building a platform that develops talent, nurtures creative community, and equips a new generation of artists to shape cultural narratives through music, media, and storytelling.

His own artistic expression is rooted in the conviction that music should do more than entertain—it should awaken hope, inform identity, and leave a lasting imprint on people and culture. This philosophy informs his evolving body of work, including Cogitations, an Urban Gospel album exploring faith, purpose, identity, and the realities of a generation through an authentic contemporary sound.

As an artist and creative entrepreneur, Password is committed to building work and platforms that transcend trends, expand the possibilities of African music, and demonstrate that faith and cultural relevance can coexist with excellence, innovation, and global ambition.

His mission is to create timeless work that outlives trends, informs identity, and leaves humanity more hopeful than he found it.

data.title: .werkkzeug
data.text:
.werkkzeug ("werkkzeug" is german for "tool") - procedural content generation program for demos. It was developed between 2000-2007 by a German group called ".theproddukt" (a branch of Farbrausch). Only 3 releases of the program were made,.werkkzeug 1.200,.werkkzeug 1.201, and.werkkzeug 3 TE (Texture Edition). In April of 2012, the Source Codes for.werkkzeug 3 and.werkkzeug 4 were released on Github, along with other tools and libraries used for their demos.

This software is mostly known for the award winning game, ".kkrieger", it is also known for ".detuned™" for playstation 3, and other competition winning demos, such as "fr-041: debris"

==.werkkzeug 1.200-1.201 ==
.werkkzeug 1 was the first edition of the program, having a fast and powerful 3d engine, ability to import from.JPEG and.OGG files, an advanced texture and mesh generator, ability to export as.exe and.kk1 files, and other features. [ref:.theprodukkt, www.theprodukkt.com]

The source code for.werkkzeug 1.200-1.201 hasn't been released.

==.werkkzeug 3 ==
.werkkzeug 3 was first released as.werkkzeug 3 TE (Texture Editon) [ref: An archive of theprodukkt's website, talking about.werkkzeug 3 TE.] [ref: The downloads for.werkkzeug 3 TE on the werkkzeug.com website linked on theprodukkt.com.], a limited edition that only had the capability to create textures and test them on simple 3d models. The full version of.werkkzeug3 features a macro-language that allows to make interactive programs, such as video games instead of just demos. In 2004, with the help of a special branch of.werkkzeug 3, a first-person shooter game under the name ".kkrieger" was made, with only 96KB of size.

.werkkzeug 3 is one of the most powerful tools for procedural texturing, having some even appear photorealistic.

The source code for.werkkzeug 3 is open, one having the general version of the program, and another having one built specifically for the making of.kkrieger. [ref: The general.werkkzeug 3 repository., GitHub] [ref: The.kkrieger branch of.werkkzeug 3., GitHub]

==.werkkzeug For mobile ==
.werkkzeug for mobile [ref:.theprodukkt, www.theprodukkt.com] has never been released publicly, but the source code for it has been released. It was built for making small demos or commercial games for mobile devices, altough.theprodukkt hadn't used this version for anything. This version was seemingly a branch of.werkkzeug 3, as the source files for it are in the /werkkzeug3 repository.

==.werkkzeug 4 ==
.werkkzeug 4 is the most recent version of the program, having the most realistic and low in file size results. Many projects such as fr-041: debris and Detuned have been made in it. It was built on the "Altona" framework found in the github repository [ref: fr_public/altona_wz4/altona at master · farbrausch/fr_public, GitHub].

== External links ==

data.title: European Academy of Childhood-onset Disability
data.text:
----

The European Academy of Childhood-onset Disability (EACD), formerly known as the European Academy of Childhood Disability, is an international multidisciplinary professional association focused on childhood onset disability. Established in 1989, it promotes research, education and cooperation among professionals working with people with childhood-onset disabilities in Europe and beyond. [ref: About us, European Academy of Childhood-onset Disability]Its members work in fields including medicine, health profession, social work, education and research. EACD has more than 500 members representing over 35 countries. [ref: Welcome to the European Academy of Childhood Disability, EACD Education]
__TOC__
== History ==
British child neurologist Brian Neville was EACD's founding chair and served from 1989 to 2000. He was succeeded by British developmental paediatrician Martin Bax, who chaired the academy from 2000 to 2008. [ref: Our organisation, European Academy of Childhood-onset Disability] Bax was also the editor of Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology. [ref: Martin Bax obituary, The Guardian]EACD was registered as a charitable organization in the United Kingdom in 1992 and as an international not-for-profit association in Belgium in 2021. In 2014, it joined the American Academy for Cerebral Palsy and Developmental Medicine and the Australasian Academy of Cerebral Palsy and Developmental Medicine in establishing the International Alliance of Academies of Childhood Disability. [ref: 'Better Together': achieving a global professional network for childhood disability, Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology] In 2016, EACD hosted its 28th annual meeting in Stockholm jointly with an international cerebral palsy conference and the alliance's first international meeting. [ref: Past meetings, EACD Education]

== Activities and education ==
EACD organizes an annual meeting hosted in a different European city every year. The meetings include presentations of research, educational courses and discussions involving clinicians and researchers. [ref: EACD Annual Meeting, European Academy of Childhood-onset Disability] The 38th annual meeting, held at the University of Galway in Ireland in June 2026, attracted approximately 1,300 delegates from 62 countries. A further 350 people participated in its public Experience Village, which was co-designed with people with lived experience and offered accessible activities, demonstrations and disability-related information. [ref: EACD Galway 2026 Wrap-Up, EACD Education]

Education is a central part of the academy's work. EACD maintains a digital educational platform that provides access to lectures, webinars, presentations from annual meetings, clinical resources and other material relating to childhood-onset disability. Its archives make educational content from previous meetings available beyond the annual congresses. [ref: EACD Education, EACD Education]In addition to its annual meetings, EACD organizes training for early-career researchers and clinicians. Summer schools were held in Pisa, Italy, in 2019 and 2022 and in Poznań, Poland, in 2023, [ref: Summer School for Early Career Researchers focusing on Childhood-onset Disabilities, European Academy of Childhood-onset Disability] and an autumn school at the University of Pisa 2025 on digital technologies and artificial intelligence in evidence-based medicine and rehabilitation. [ref: Autumn School 2025, EACD Education]

EACD has initiated clinical-practice recommendations relating to childhood-onset disabilities. These include recommendations on the definition, diagnosis, assessment and treatment of Developmental Coordination Disorder, first published in 2012 and subsequently updated as international recommendations in 2019. [ref: European Academy for Childhood Disability (EACD): recommendations on the definition, diagnosis and intervention of developmental coordination disorder, Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology] [ref: International clinical practice recommendations on the definition, diagnosis, assessment, intervention, and psychosocial aspects of developmental coordination disorder, Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology]

Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology is an official journal of EACD and several other professional organizations concerned with paediatric neurology and childhood disability. [ref: Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology: Overview, Wiley Online Library]

data.title: Whatsaheart
data.text:
= whatsaheart =
Kei Kim (born August 13th, year is unknown) is an New Zealand-based faceless alternative-pop/shoegaze artist, whose fame originates from popular tracks like "for her [ref: ]" and "snakelike (the stars collide) [ref: ]". He has an average of 650,000 monthly listeners on Spotify. He is an independent artist who produces his own tracks on the music production platform BandLab. He writes, produces, and releases his own songs independently. [ref: whatsaheart Lyrics, Songs, and Albums, Genius]

Whatsaheart began his music career in early 2023 with the single "formyslxts", followed by "pxssesive" a month later in early February, along with a remix of the same track with featured artist "SSJ Twiin" two weeks later. Later in summer 2023, he released his 2nd most streamed single on Spotify [ref: whatsaheart, Spotify] titled "for her", totalling over 30 million streams. He then beat his own record with the single "snakelike (the stars collide)" in spring 2024 that reached over 55 million streams, making it his most famous track. In winter 2024, he released his 3rd most streamed single on Spotify, "taking over me". He is however also known for other tracks like "WHXRE" (unreleased) and "lovesick", a song that is the first track on the "lovesick EP", released in 2024. Whatsaheart has a wide variety of unreleased songs, most of which can be found on music streaming platforms like SoundCloud, Audiomack, or YouTube.

== Early Life ==
Kei Kim was born in a small town in New Zealand, on August 13th. The exact birth year is unknown. Kim explained his first real interest in music was in his early childhood, when a soundtrack from famous video-game franchise Sonic the Hedgehog titled "I Am... All Of Me" by Japanese-American rock band Crush 40. A vivid childhood memory of his was playing the song with an air-guitar, while standing on his bed. Growing up, he developed a growing interest in the music group Daft Punk and was a big fan of theirs for a long time. He also mentions that Daft Punk was one of his main inspirations to become a faceless artist. As Kim's music taste evolved, he became a big fan of American rapper and singer XXXTentacion. Kim said he admired Onfroy's self-awareness, talent, and how he wanted to change himself for the better. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

He then went on to discover famous Australian band Chase Atlantic. He explained attending a live performance and being in awe of their performance. He said he wished to be in the band's position and how he would've enjoyed performing live on stage also. Kim highlights that witnessing that performance hadn't necessarily been a direct inspiration for him to begin making music of his own, but rather that it helped him develop the idea in his head. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

== Musical career ==
Kim's musical history dates back to his early childhood. As he was part of a musically-involved family, he had easy and direct access to various musical instruments. His first ever experience with a real instrument was when he played the drums when he was part of his school's band. Kim's involvement with music didn't stop there, however. Before that, Kim recalls covering songs from his PlayStation and recording these covers on his phone. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

Later on, he would again record these covers on the music producing platform BandLab and post said covers to the public. As he stayed consistent with his covers, he started building himself a small community around his identity and music. And although Kim enjoyed the community of people he'd managed to form, he kept believing he could achieve something bigger. This belief led him to opening a TikTok account to advertise his music. He however then took the page down after receiving negative backlash. Approximately a month after closing his first page, Kim decided to try again and opened a second TikTok account, which is a major checkpoint in Kim's musical career. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

When asked in an interview, Kim explained he didn't have any songs he liked more than others, and believed all of his tracks were individually valuable for his career and where he is now. He did however note that he considers "for her" and "pxssesive" important releases in his career. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

== Musical style and discography ==
Whatsaheart's musical genres generally include alternative pop and rock, shoegaze, with occasional alternative metal influences. When asked about influences and inspirations, Kim hightlighted the popular anime Bleach and Japanese video game Kingdom Hearts. He also mentions being a big anime fan overall and enjoying video games. [ref: the whatsaheart interview]

He occasionally uses Light Yagami's (main character in popular manga and anime "Death Note") laugh as an element in some of his tracks like "WHXRE" and "pxssesive".

Reoccurring topics in his tracks are love, heartbreak, and romantic obsession. Some tracks that highlight these topics well are "pxsession", "obsessixn", "toxic", "LOVE GUN", and "sky (falling for you)". Albums with similar focuses are the "lovesick" EP and "katsubō". [ref: whatsaheart - discography]

== Collaborations ==
Most of whatsaheart's tracks have been produced with no featured artist*s, but he still has made some collaborations with other shoegaze/alternative artists. Examples are the "The Carter Brothers [ref: ]" album, produced in collaboration with shoegaze artist Snave, popular single "sharp fangs [ref: ]" featuring alternative hip-hop artist removeface, and a remix of single "Realize [ref: ]" released by artist Trxy!, featuring whatsaheart and Softcult.

In 2024, American rapper Odetari posted a TikTok clip of a song on his computer with the caption "@[user]", but there is no further information on this possible collaboration from either artists. [ref: TikTok - Make Your Day, www.tiktok.com]

== Social media ==
Whatsaheart's official TikTok account ([https://www.tiktok.com/@[user] @[user]]) has approximately 400,000 followers, and almost 11 million likes. His Instagram account ([https://www.instagram.com/whatsaheart3/ @[user]]) has 150,000 followers and two posts. He mostly uses these platforms to advertise his upcoming releases and show support to his fandom and community. [ref: Whatsaheart TikTok Page]

Muayad "Mo" Abbas is a real estate development executive and university lecturer known for his involvement in residential, hospitality, and mixed-use developments in the United States and international markets. He is Managing Director of Development at OKO Group and a lecturer at the University of Miami School of Architecture. [ref: Bisnow's Hurricane Irma Miami State of the Market, Bisnow] [ref: Former Ritz president leads new North Miami project, The Real Deal] [ref: Rafael Moneo Reveals Design of His First Condo Tower in Miami, ArchDaily]

== Career ==

=== Related International ===
Abbas previously served as Vice President of Related International, the international development arm of the Related Group, overseeing real estate operations in Panama, Colombia, and Argentina. [ref: Bisnow's Hurricane Irma Miami State of the Market, Bisnow]

=== Urbanis Advisors and Apeiron Living ===
Abbas founded Urbanis Advisors, a real estate development and advisory firm. He subsequently co-founded Apeiron Living, a luxury residential and hospitality venture conceived in collaboration with Horst Schulze, co-founder and former president of the Ritz-Carlton Hotel Company, and Michael Bedner, co-founder of Hirsch Bedner Associates (HBA). [ref: Former Ritz president leads new North Miami project, The Real Deal] [ref: Rafael Moneo Reveals Design of His First Condo Tower in Miami, ArchDaily] [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club wins approval, plans to launch sales, The Real Deal]

The founders conceived Apeiron as a hospitality and residential brand combining luxury living with personalized service, health and wellness, preventive medical care, and arts and cultural programming. The concept was designed primarily for affluent, active older adults seeking a residential environment that supported independent living and aging in place -- coined as Limitless Living.

The brand emphasized architecture, hospitality, wellness, and curated experiences as pillars of an integrated residential lifestyle. Apeiron's proposed wellness program included medical services coordinated with the Cleveland Clinic. [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club wins approval, plans to launch sales, The Real Deal]

Apeiron at the Jockey Club in Miami, Florida, was the venture's flagship development and a model for potential expansion into other U.S. markets. The proposed redevelopment of the historic waterfront property included serviced residences, hospitality amenities, wellness facilities, dining, cultural programming, and a marina. [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club wins approval, plans to launch sales, The Real Deal]

The architectural design was led by Pritzker Architecture Prize recipient Spanish architect Rafael Moneo. [ref: Rafael Moneo Reveals Design of His First Condo Tower in Miami, ArchDaily]

The development faced legal challenges from existing condominium associations seeking to block construction. In June 2020, Florida's Third District Court of Appeal upheld the trial court's rulings, affirming Apeiron Miami LLC's development and its property rights at the Jockey Club. [ref: Jockey Club residents reignite lawsuit against next-door landowner, The Real Deal] [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club Developer Wins Key Ruling from Appeals Court, Carlton Fields] [ref: Developer Wins Key Ruling from Appeals Court in Miami-Dade, Council on Vertical Urbanism]

=== Mast Capital ===
Abbas subsequently served as Senior Vice President of Development at Mast Capital, a Miami-based real estate investment and development firm.

During his tenure, he led the development of Cipriani Residences Miami, an 80-story, 397-residence luxury condominium tower in Miami's Brickell neighborhood, designed by Arquitectonica. [ref: Mast Capital, www.mastcapital.com] [ref: ] [ref: Mast Capital, www.mastcapital.com]

The project was in collaboration with the Cipriani family. Led by Giuseppe Cipriani, the family's hospitality organization partnered with Mast Capital to establish its first ground-up residential development in the United States.

=== OKO Group ===
In 2025, Abbas joined Vlad Doronin's OKO Group as Managing Director of Development, overseeing a portfolio of luxury residential, hospitality, and mixed-use developments. His responsibilities encompass development strategy, design, entitlements, construction, and project execution. [ref: About us, OKO Group]

== Academic career ==
Abbas is a lecturer at the University of Miami School of Architecture, where he teaches real estate entrepreneurship in the Master of Real Estate Development + Urbanism (MRED+U) program.

His teaching focuses on real estate development, entrepreneurship, and practical applications of development strategy. As part of his teaching, he has organized student visits to residential and hospitality developments in Miami providing students with exposure to the development process and project execution. [ref: ] [ref: Research Portal, scholarship.miami.edu] [ref: ]

data.title: Sam Ven
data.text:
== References ==

Sam Ven () is a Cambodian social work administrator and child protection advocate. [ref: Management Team - This Life Cambodia, This Life Cambodia] He serves as the Children and Families Section Lead at This Life Cambodia (TLC), a non-governmental organization specializing in community-led developmental programs. Ven is recognized for directing structural social assistance programs focused on juvenile rehabilitation, diversionary alternative sentencing, and family preservation for marginalized populations affected by parental incarceration. [ref: Sam Ven - Global Social Service Workforce Alliance, Global Social Service Workforce Alliance] Community programs managed under his administration have provided social support, case tracking, and integration services to approximately 3,000 families throughout Cambodia. [ref: Celebrating Recognition: Sam Ven's Impact on Social Service..., This Life Cambodia]

== Early life and education ==
Ven was raised in a rural village in Cambodia during the post-Khmer Rouge reconstruction period. His early formal education was disrupted by localized civil conflicts and geographic displacement. Despite prevailing socio-economic barriers in his community, he completed his secondary education and subsequently graduated with a Bachelor's Degree in Business Administration. His early exposure to community instability influenced his later career pivot toward professional social welfare and advocacy systems.

== Career ==

=== Non-governmental organization work ===
Ven entered the non-profit sector by volunteering for localized non-governmental organizations (NGOs) targeting substance harm reduction and urban marginalized populations. In 2012, he formally joined the professional staff of This Life Cambodia (TLC).

He initially served as a Program Officer for three years, tracking legal case management for minors entangled in the provincial criminal justice system. He was subsequently promoted to Program Coordinator, where he led the "This Life Beyond Bars" team, before being appointed to the organization's Senior Management Team as a section leader.

=== Program management and strategy ===
As the Section Lead for Children and Families, Ven oversees five operational community initiatives and manages a department of approximately 30 professional social service workers. His administrative portfolio focuses heavily on the "This Life in Families" (TLIF) and "This Life Beyond Bars" (TLBB) frameworks.

Operating across several provinces—including Siem Reap, Banteay Meanchey, and Phnom Penh—these initiatives concentrate on:
* Institutionalization Prevention: Administering structural family livelihood assessments and educational grants to prevent the placement of children into residential care institutions (orphanages) when primary caretakers face imprisonment.
* Kinship Care Optimization: Developing strategic case management networks to safely retain vulnerable minors within extended family or biological structures.
* Juvenile Reintegration: Coordinating life skills, vocational training, and post-release support metrics inside juvenile correctional spaces to mitigate youth recidivism rates.

== Advocacy and public engagement ==
Ven frequently acts as a civil society liaison to Cambodian state judicial and correctional bodies concerning statutory reforms for minor offenders. In December 2023, he represented TLC at the Annual Meeting of the Siem Reap Provincial Administration, engaging in policy talks with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Tea Seiha. [ref: On 25th and 26th December 2023, Mr. Sam Ven..., This Life Cambodia Official Communication] Ven advocated for structural alternatives to detention at the immediate point of youth arrest, alongside educational reforms inside prisons to alleviate structural institutional overcrowding.

Additionally, he coordinates public human rights broadcasts detailing juvenile justice frameworks alongside national ministries, such as the Department of Juvenile Rehabilitation under the Ministry of Social Affairs, Veterans and Youth Rehabilitation (MoSVY). [ref: Rights of the child in the conflict with the law and the progress, Cambodian Center for Human Rights] According to organizational performance indexes, programs under his managerial oversight have systematically verified the community tracking and safe reintegration of more than 1,500 vulnerable children.

data.title: Howard Lamar (Artist)
data.text:
Howard Lamar (September 7, 1947 – November 15, 2018) was an American painter and sculptor associated with Ojai, Carmel-by-the-Sea, and Santa Barbara, California. Working across painting, sculpture, glass, and ceramics, Lamar developed a colorful figurative style characterized by personal narrative and recurring symbolic imagery. [ref: Off the Wall: Art in Unusual Places, Santa Barbara Independent] [ref: Howard Lamar, Focus on the Masters Arts Archive & Library] Critics and arts organizations identified influences in his work from European Modernists including Marc Chagall, Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso, and Wassily Kandinsky.

== Early life and career ==
Lamar was born in Greenville, South Carolina, on September 7, 1947. A 1983 profile in the Sedona Red Rock News reported that he had drawn and painted since childhood and described him as a self-taught artist whose success in competitions encouraged him to pursue art full-time. [ref: Sedona Red Rock News, 1983-06-15, Sedona Red Rock News]

Lamar's early work included small, largely Impressionistic landscape watercolors. Focus on the Masters Arts Archive & Library later described his earliest exhibitions as watercolors displayed on a blanket and noted the substantial changes in his work over the course of his career.

By 1983, Lamar was exhibiting paintings, drawings, and sculpture at the Forms Gallery at Hozho in Sedona, Arizona. The Sedona Red Rock News described his work at the time as symbolic and narrative and reported that, after feeling constrained by the two-dimensional limitations of pictorial media, he had expanded into sculpture. The same profile noted earlier exhibitions in Beverly Hills and at the Santa Barbara Museum of Art.

== Carmel and Ojai ==
During the 1990s, Lamar operated the Howard Lamar Studio in Carmel-by-the-Sea, California. A 1995 interview in LEADERS identified him with the Carmel studio and discussed his preference for maintaining artistic control over his work rather than adapting it to the prescriptions of dealers or the commercial art market. [ref: The 'Maverick' Artist, LEADERS]

Around 2000, the Dallas Observer reported that a body of Lamar's work known as The Dallas Collection had been donated for an auction benefiting the Shakespeare Festival of Dallas and a matching grant from the McDermott Foundation. The works were also placed on public display at Samuell-Grand Park during the festival's summer performances. The newspaper identified Lamar at the time as a Carmel, California, artist. [ref: Blink, Dallas Observer]

Lamar subsequently returned to Ojai, where he operated Galerie Lamar. In 2004, he was selected for documentation by Focus on the Masters, a nonprofit arts education and archival organization that documents the lives and work of contemporary artists. Lamar's documentation took place in 2004, and the organization's archive holds extensive material concerning his career and work.

== Artistic practice and influences ==
Lamar worked in a range of media during his career, including painting, sculpture, glass, and ceramics. [ref: The Business of Art, LEADERS]

Writing about an exhibition of Lamar's work in Santa Barbara in 2008, Heather Jeno of the Santa Barbara Independent described his style as combining playful imagery and lighthearted colors with a distinctive symbolic language. She noted affinities with Chagall and Kandinsky and described Lamar's use of whimsical figures, animals, abstracted dots and lines, narrative compositions, and flattened or tilted pictorial planes.

Focus on the Masters similarly identified elements of Chagall, Matisse, and Picasso in Lamar's work while noting the development of his own recognizable expression and symbolism.

In 2024, art critic Abigail Leali examined Lamar's work in two essays for MutualArt Magazine. In “Returning, Reflecting, Rebuilding: The Art of Howard Lamar,” Leali considered Lamar's use of symbolism and the relationship between representation, abstraction, and the viewer's encounter with the work. [ref: Returning, Reflecting, Rebuilding: The Art of Howard Lamar, MutualArt] In a subsequent essay, “Howard Lamar and the Lineage of French Modernism,” she examined his work in relation to the French Modernist tradition, particularly the influence of Picasso and Matisse, and discussed his use of iconography as a means of visual communication. [ref: Howard Lamar and the Lineage of French Modernism, MutualArt]

== Iconography ==
Recurring symbols became a prominent feature of Lamar's work. In a 2015 interview with LEADERS, Lamar said that his icons had begun appearing when he was in his late twenties and had continued to develop as his exploration of different themes evolved. [ref: The Universal and The Esoteric, LEADERS]

Lamar divided the icons into what he called “universal” and “esoteric” groups. The first included familiar forms such as the sun, moon, hearts, stars, flowers, and cats. The second included symbols particular to his own work, including the Bird of Discernment, Energy, No-Time, and Infinity. Lamar described the meanings of the icons in relation to the themes he explored within individual works.

Leali subsequently discussed Lamar's iconography as part of his broader approach to visual communication, emphasizing the relationship between symbolic meaning and the viewer's experience of the work.

== Meta-Liminalism ==
Later in his career, Lamar used the term Meta-Liminalism to describe aspects of his investigation of perception and consciousness. In a 2015 interview with LEADERS, Lamar said that he had coined the term “meta-liminal” in 2007 and discussed it in relation to shifting points of observation, identity, awareness, consciousness, comprehension, and definition. Leali later discussed Meta-Liminalism in her critical examination of Lamar's work, including its relationship to perception, symbolic communication, and the viewer's participation in meaning.

== Microsoft Alumni Foundation ==
In 2014, Lamar became an artist partner of the Microsoft Alumni Foundation in connection with its sixth annual Reunion with a Purpose, held at Microsoft's corporate headquarters in Redmond, Washington. Marylou Brannan, then executive director of the Foundation, described Lamar as an “artist partner.” [ref: Howard Lamar Fine Art, Galerie Lamar]

The October 17 event brought together hundreds of Microsoft alumni and current and former company leaders to recognize philanthropic and nonprofit work within the Microsoft alumni community. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer participated in the event, while Microsoft Alumni Network chairman Jeff Raikes discussed the alumni community's philanthropic activities. [ref: Microsoft Leadership and Hundreds of Alumni Reunite to Celebrate Philanthropy and Community Engagement at Microsoft Alumni Foundation's Reunion with a Purpose, Microsoft Alumni Foundation]

Lamar's work was presented in connection with the event. A published event photograph shows Nadella, Raikes, Ballmer, and recipients of the Foundation's 2014–15 awards standing in front of Lamar's painting Kindness and Generosity.

In 2017, Lamar presented dozens of works spanning multiple media at An Evening of Art and Celebration in Austin, Texas. CultureMap Austin reported that the presentation drew from approximately five decades of Lamar's work and highlighted his Kindness & Generosity series. [ref: Art-lovers convene at stately Seven Oaks estate for an elegant party, CultureMap Austin]

== Death ==
Lamar died in Santa Barbara, California, on November 15, 2018, at the age of 71.

Nika Sikharulashvili is a Georgian footballer born in Gurjaani, Georgia. He is currently playing for Iberia 1999 as a midfielder. [ref: Instagram, www.instagram.com]

== Early Life ==
Nika Sikharulashvili moved to Tbilisi and joined the Dinamo Tbilisi academy. He developed quickly and was later called up for the Georgian U19 team. [ref: [ინტერვიუ] ნიკა სიხარულაშვილი: "მე როგორი ფეხბურთიც მომწონს და რაც ჩემს წარმოდგენაშია, დემჩენკოს ხელში ზუსტად ასე ვთამაშობთ"..., Lelo.Ge]

== Club Career ==
Nika Sikharulashvili started at Dinamo Tbilisi's Reserve team in 2023, later then being promoted to the first team. After scoring 5 goals in 43 matches, Dinamo Tbilisi sent him on a loan to Greek club Makedonikos F.C. [ref: ნიკა სიხარულაშვილი, ეროვნული ლიგა]

In Makedonikos, Nika Sikharulashvili scored 1 League goal in the 2024-25 Super League Greece 2 against PAS Giannina FC on December 14, 2024 and he played 1 match in the league. [ref: ] Outside of the league, he played 1 match domestically. Makedonikos returned him to Dinamo Tbilisi because he was on loan. [ref: Instagram, www.instagram.com]

After coming back to Dinamo Tbilisi, he was in the reserve team. After scoring 2 goals in 12 Matches, Nika Sikharulashvili transferred to Iberia 1999, his current club. [ref: ნიკა სიხარულაშვილი, ეროვნული ლიგა]

In Iberia 1999, he was first in the reserve team. In the Liga 3, he scored 4 goals in 3 matches and Andriy Demchenko promoted him to the first team. [ref: Georgian Footy (@[user]) on X, X (formerly Twitter)] For Iberia 1999, he became a starter. In 2026 Erovnuli Liga, he has scored 2 goals in 12 matches, scoring against Torpedo Kutaisi [ref: ტორპედო - იბერია 1999 / 2026-08-15 21:00, ეროვნული ლიგა] and Meshakhte Tkibuli. [ref: მეშახტე - იბერია 1999 / 2026-10-10 15:30, ეროვნული ლიგა] For Iberia 1999, he started playing and being a starter in European competitions. Against Flora Tallinn in the 2026-27 UEFA Champions League Qualifying first round, Iberia 1999 won 3-2 in the first leg. [ref: Flora vs Iberia (2-3) Jul 8, 2026 Player Ratings and Stats, FootballCritic] At home, Nika Sikharulashvili scored a brace to secure a 2-2 draw in the second leg and a 5-4 win on aggregate. [ref: Slovan vs Iberia (1-1) Jul 29, 2026 Match Stats, FootballCritic] After losing the 2026-27 UEFA Champions League Qualifying second round, They faced Larne in the 2026-27 UEFA Europa League Qualifying third round. [ref: ] The first match ended in a 0-0 draw at away, at home in the Mikheil Meskhi Stadium, the match went to extra time after 1 goal from each side and Nika Sikharulashvili scored the winner in the 102nd minute and Iberia 1999 were guaranteed to qualify for an European competition because if they lost the Europa League Play-off, there was a 2026-27 UEFA Conference League spot. [ref: ] In the second leg, they lost 1-2 at home and Iberia 1999 qualified for the 2026-27 UEFA Conference League league phase. [ref: ] He played the full match against Sint-Truiden in the 2026-27 UEFA Conference League where they lost 2-0 at away. [ref: ] Against Mjallby AIF in the 2026-27 UEFA Conference League league phase, he won a penalty which was scored by Iberia 1999's captain, Giorgi Jinjolava. Mjallby AIF equalized late in the match. data.title: Ahmed Sajidan Jarjis Rafsan
data.text:
Ahmed Sajidan Jarjis Rafsan (born 1 July 2003), who also uses the name Sajidan Rafsan, is a Bangladeshi social entrepreneur, humanitarian organizer, researcher and student activist. He is the founder and executive leader of the Shirin Sajmila International Foundation (SSIF), a nonprofit that works in disaster relief, disability rehabilitation, maternal healthcare, civic engagement and youth mobilization in South Asia, the Middle East and Africa. He also founded ApexStride, a company that develops prosthetics for flood-prone regions.

Rafsan is a senior at St. Olaf College in Minnesota, in the class of 2027. He also works on cancer genomics as a data scientist at the Dana–Farber Cancer Institute.

==Early life and education==
Rafsan was born in Chittagong, Bangladesh, and grew up mostly in the Mehedibagh area of the city. His mother, Shirin A. Chowdhury, was a professor of management at the University of Chittagong and had survived cancer three times. She later suffered from uterine carcinosarcoma. His sister, Sajmila Jishmam Uzma, was a third-year electrical and electronic engineering student at the university.

He went to school in Chittagong, mainly at Cantonment English School and College and Chittagong Cantonment Public College. At 13 he started a small school for local children in the yard of the family home. It grew into a nonprofit that taught children from low-income families and offered rehabilitation services and inclusive education models. The initiative was first called Dream Foundation, and SSIF is its later form. In 2018 he spoke on the entrepreneurship panel at the Glocal International Teen Conference, which is organized in Nepal. He was invited as a ninth-grade student.

The United World Colleges (UWC) are an international network of schools that teach the International Baccalaureate to students chosen through national committees. After his SSC examinations in 2019, Rafsan won a full scholarship to UWC Changshu, in the city of Changshu near Shanghai in China, and began there in August 2019. He took a year out when his mother's cancer returned, and he finished the second year at UWC Maastricht in the Netherlands. He then received a full scholarship to St. Olaf College. He is a Davis UWC scholar there, and in 2023 he was named a Weber Scholar at the college's Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community. In November 2025 the college described him as a junior studying economics and political science, and the Davis scholars report lists him under quantitative economics. He studied data science and economics.

==Family loss and healthcare==
On 10 July 2022 Rafsan was in India with his mother and sister, who were hit by a bus as they crossed a street. He and his brother were on the other side of the road. The accident happened in Kolkata, and his mother was badly hurt. His sister died of her injuries. His mother, partly paralyzed and still ill, died on 22 August 2022, within 40 days of the accident. She died at Imperial Hospital in Chittagong.

Rafsan has said that his time in public, local and private hospitals in Bangladesh and India showed him inequalities in access, cost and care, and that this shaped his later public health and humanitarian work. After the deaths he renamed the organization the Shirin Sajmila International Foundation, after his mother and sister.

==Humanitarian and social work==
SSIF is a United States 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Rafsan founded it in 2016. SSIF says it has reached more than 700,000 people through programs in disaster response, disability rehabilitation, maternal healthcare, education, public health and civic engagement. It works in Bangladesh and has led refugee support in Egypt for Sudanese and Syrian communities. It also works in Kashmir, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and other countries.

SSIF worked with the World Health Organization, local government and military partners during the 2024 floods in Bangladesh, giving emergency relief, medical care, menstrual hygiene supplies and rehabilitation support to families in districts including Feni and Noakhali. Its website says a 15-member medical team runs regular camps in flood-affected areas with the Bangladesh Army, and that it sent 20 tons of medicine to Feni with the World Health Organization and the government.

Rafsan was one of the key young organizers of protest mobilization during the July 2024 uprising and a medical-response coordinator, and SSIF gave medical and legal help to injured student protesters. During and after the uprising, SSIF launched Bir Chattala Shajai, a civic and public art movement. It mobilized more than 100,000 young people, mainly in Chittagong and Dhaka, for murals, graffiti and other civic work.

In July 2025, after a plane crashed into Milestone School and College in Dhaka, Rafsan wrote on Facebook about Sabuja Begum, a school employee who was badly burned while rescuing children. SSIF said it was paying for her care and her family's expenses.

==ApexStride==
Rafsan started ApexStride in 2023 to build repairable prosthetic systems for humid, flood-prone places. It also works on mobility rehabilitation and accessibility for people with disabilities. A Bangla feature article described his aim as restoring "freedom of movement" and dignity for people with disabilities. He has talked about the work on Bangladeshi television, including Channel 24's Prosongo Chattogram in September 2026.

In April 2026 ApexStride won second prize, US$7,500, at the Ole Cup, St. Olaf's student pitch competition. In 2026 it took first place and US$25,000 at the Fowler Global Social Innovation Challenge in San Diego, a competition named for the philanthropist Ron Fowler, against teams from more than 25 countries. It was named World Champion and Global Grand Prize winner, and the prize money was to support its prosthetics and healthcare work.

==Research==
At St. Olaf, Rafsan is a research investigator with the Caribbean Studies Lab, part of the Caribbean Studies Network, which Professor Kristina Medina-Vilariño started in 2013. He co-founded the lab. The lab's work covers Caribbean migration, identity formation, diasporic memory and digital archiving. His own work also covers climate precarity, migration governance, public health and digital inequity.

He and Medina-Vilariño presented the lab at the Caribbean Digital XII conference, held at Northeastern University in Boston on 4–5 December 2025. St. Olaf was the only undergraduate institution on the program. In July 2026 he spoke at the fourth continental conference of Harvard's Afro-Latin American Research Institute (ALARI), held 22–24 July in Cali, Colombia, as one of the youngest panelists and the only participant from Bangladesh.

==Prizes and shortlists==
In 2025 SSIF was shortlisted in the Health category of the 2026 Zayed Sustainability Prize, which carries a US$1 million award. Rafsan received a Projects for Peace grant through the Kathryn W. Davis program. In 2026 he was among the 25 finalists, all under 25, in the third cycle of The World Around's Young Climate Prize.

Julian Lual

**Julian Lual** (born April 16, 2002) is a Canadian college basketball player who most recently played for the Alcorn State Braves of the Southwestern Athletic Conference (SWAC). He previously played for McCook Community College and the Arkansas State Red Wolves.

## Early life and high school career

Lual was born in Canada and grew up in Calgary, Alberta, where he attended Central Memorial High School. He later moved to the United States to complete his high school career at Central Pointe Christian Academy in Kissimmee, Florida.

## College career

### McCook Community College (2020–2022)

Lual began his collegiate career at the junior college (JUCO) level with McCook Community College in Nebraska. As a freshman in the pandemic-shortened 2020–21 season, he appeared in 25 games, averaging 10.0 points and 5.7 rebounds per game. He broke out during his sophomore season (2021–22), starting all 31 games and averaging 14.1 points, 8.9 rebounds, and 1.9 assists per game. He recorded 15 double-doubles on the year, earning All-Region IX accolades and attracting Division I recruiting interest.

### Arkansas State (2022–2024)

In 2022, Lual transferred to NCAA Division I program Arkansas State under head coach Mike Balado, later playing under Bryan Hodgson. During the 2022–23 season, he appeared in 32 games (six starts), averaging 4.9 points and 3.0 rebounds in 18.2 minutes per game. The following season (2023–24), he retained a rotational role on a Red Wolves team that reached the Sun Belt tournament championship game, averaging 4.5 points and 2.2 rebounds over 32 appearances.

### Alcorn State (2024–2025)

For his final year of collegiate eligibility, Lual transferred to Alcorn State for the 2024–25 season. He appeared in 22 games for the Braves, contributing 5.2 points and 3.0 rebounds per game before concluding his collegiate career.

data.title: Prof. Mamoon Abdelhalim Wagih
data.text:
Mamoon Abdel Halim Mohamed Wagih (; born 13 November 1960) is an Egyptian linguist and academic specializing in Arabic grammar, morphology and lexicography. He is a professor emeritus at Fayoum University, a former dean of its Faculty of Dar Al-Uloom, and a member of the Academy of the Arabic Language in Cairo. He has served as scientific director of the Historical Dictionary of the Arabic Language. [ref: مأمون وجيه, مجمع اللغة العربية بالقاهرة] [ref: مأمون عبد الحليم محمد وجيه, Fayoum University] [ref: صلاح فضل ومأمون وجيه ضمن تشكيل مؤتمر مجمع اللغة العربية بالشارقة, أخبار اليوم]

== Early life and education ==
Wagih was born on 13 November 1960 in a village in the Tanta district of Gharbia Governorate, Egypt. He studied at Tanta University, receiving a bachelor's degree in Arabic language in 1984 and a master's degree in Arabic grammar in 1989. In 1996, he earned a doctorate in Arabic grammar from Cairo University through a joint-supervision programme involving the School of Oriental and African Studies at the University of London.

== Academic career ==
Wagih joined the Faculty of Dar Al-Uloom at Fayoum as an assistant lecturer in 1990. Following his doctorate, he became a lecturer in 1996. From 1999 to 2009, he held academic appointments at the Faculty of Sharia and Islamic Studies in Al-Ahsa, part of Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University in Saudi Arabia.

He returned to Fayoum University in 2009 and was promoted to professor in September 2011. He subsequently headed the Department of Grammar, Morphology and Prosody and served as dean of the Faculty of Dar Al-Uloom from 2012 to 2015. He also served as editor-in-chief of the faculty's academic journal. Fayoum University records his appointment as professor emeritus in August 2021. [ref: أ.د. مأمون عبد الحليم محمد, Fayoum University]

== Academy of the Arabic Language ==
In October 2013, Wagih was appointed an expert on dictionary committees at the Academy of the Arabic Language in Cairo. He was elected to membership in 2016, succeeding Mahmoud Ali Makki. His work at the Academy has included committees concerned with the Great Arabic Dictionary, Arabic poetic vocabulary and historical lexicography.

== Historical Dictionary of the Arabic Language ==
Wagih has served as scientific director of the Historical Dictionary of the Arabic Language (), a project documenting the historical usage and semantic development of Arabic vocabulary. The project has involved Arabic language academies and received support from the Emirate of Sharjah. [ref: مقدمة المدير العلمي, المعجم التاريخي للغة العربية]

The first eight volumes were presented in Sharjah on 5 November 2020. In a November 2021 interview with Youm7, Wagih discussed the dictionary's methodology, including its treatment of word origins and changes in meaning across historical periods. [ref: المدير العلمى للمعجم التاريخى للغة العربية فى حواره لـ"اليوم السابع", Youm7]

== Research and publications ==
Wagih's research includes Arabic syntax, morphology, grammatical analysis of classical poetry and comparisons between classical Arabic grammatical traditions and modern linguistic approaches. His publications have addressed metathesis, ellipsis, syntactic ambiguity, constituent ordering and grammatical evidence in pre-Islamic poetry.

=== Selected books ===

* دراسات في علم التصريف (Studies in Arabic Morphology).
* ظاهرة الإعلال والإبدال: دراسة تحليلية (The Phenomena of I'lal and Ibdal: An Analytical Study).
* العروض والقافية بين التراث والتجديد (Arabic Prosody and Rhyme: Between Tradition and Renewal).
* منصوبات الأسماء: دراسة في ضوء التراث النحوي (Nouns in the Accusative Case: A Study in the Light of the Arabic Grammatical Tradition).

=== Selected research ===

* القلب المكاني في البنية العربية — research on metathesis in Arabic morphology.
* قرائن الحذف في البنية والتركيب — research on ellipsis in Arabic linguistic structures.
* مسوغات التقديم الإجباري في التراكيب العربية — research on obligatory fronting in Arabic syntax.
* شواهد امرئ القيس في التراث النحوي — research on grammatical evidence from the poetry of Imru' al-Qais.
* أثر الرواية الشفهية للشعر الجاهلي في تعديل الحكم النحوي — research on oral transmission of pre-Islamic poetry and grammatical judgments.

== Poetry ==
Wagih is also the author of a poetry collection titled غضبة النيل (The Wrath of the Nile), which contains 26 poems according to the Academy of the Arabic Language.

Plucked is an upcoming American dark comedy period film written, produced, and directed by Usher Morgan and Katie Vincent. The film stars Vincent in the lead role, alongside Jared Canfield, J. Anthony Crane, Catherine Curtin, Susan Gallagher, Bryant Carroll, and Tony D. Head. [ref: Plucked Teaser Trailer: Stranger Things' Catherine Curtin Stars in Comedy Movie, Yahoo Entertainment]

The film was independently produced by Dark Passage Films and is scheduled to be released theatrically in the United States on November 13, 2026. [ref: Plucked Teaser Trailer: Stranger Things' Catherine Curtin Stars in Comedy Movie, ComingSoon.net] [ref: 'Plucked' Dark Comedy Film Stars Katie Vincent, Jared Canfield, J. Anthony Crane, Catherine Curtin – Trailer and Release Date, Movie Vine]

==Premise==
In Gilded Age New York, a rebellious woman (Vincent) is trying to divorce her emotionally unstable husband (Canfield). Consequently, a civilized evening violently spirals into pandemonium. [ref: Plucked (2026) film review, Screen Critix]

==Cast==

==Early reviews==
In early reviews, critics praised the film's dialogue, performances, and blend of period drama and dark comedy. [ref: Plucked, Rotten Tomatoes]

Carl Burgess of Screen Critix awarded the film 4.5 out of 5 stars, calling it "an impressive return from Morgan and Vincent" that showed "considerable growth in scale and visual confidence." Alton Williams, a critic with Battle Royale With Cheese described it as an "entertaining and increasingly unpredictable film that finds plenty of drama within the walls of a single home." Williams also praised Vincent's performance in the film. [ref: Plucked: Review, Battle Royale With Cheese]

The New York Amsterdam News "Curtain Raiser" critic Lapacazo Sandoval noted the film's $300K micro budget, and wrote that Plucked is "“a deliciously vicious dinner party in a world you can’t resist entering.” [ref: 'Plucked' Review: A Gilded Age Dinner Party Worth Crashing, AmNews Curtain Raiser]

Jason Knight of UK Film Review awarded the film 4 out of 5 stars, praising its period setting, cinematography, and performances, particularly those of Vincent and Canfield; noting that the first half of the film was somewhat slow-paced, he felt the remainder of the film made up for it. [ref: Plucked, UK Film Review]

Lucy Lost () is an upcoming French animated mystery historical film, directed by Olivier Clert and produced by Xilam Animation. The film's script was written by Clert and Helen Blakeman.

It is an adaptation of the 2014 children's novel Listen to the Moon by British author Michael Morpurgo, set during World War I.

==Plot==
Lucy lives with her family in a village on a small, isolated island. Her extraordinary gifts are met with rejection by the villagers. When she meets Milly, a little girl only she can see, Lucy embarks on a great adventure to uncover the secret of her mysterious powers.

The English dub of the film will be recorded in the United Kingdom. [ref: Olivier Clert’s Annecy competition title 'Lucy Lost' sells widely including Germany, Italy, Spain, China, Japan, Screen Daily]

==Production==
Marc du Pontavice first read Listen to the Moon in 2017, when he was having a drink with an artist Xilam collaborated with, and he recommended it to du Pontavice [ref: 'Lucy Lost' Producer & Director Share the Secrets of Their Magical Animated Mystery (Exclusive First Look), Animation Magazine] and that he thought the "themes of family, love and memory against a backdrop of vivid landscapes, would translate beautifully to the screen". After acquiring the rights to the book, his original idea was to adapt the novel into a 10-episode television miniseries as announced in 2019 [ref: « Lucy Lost »: découvrez le projet au Cartoon Forum !, Xilam], which was originally to be directed by Jean-Christophe Dessaint and it would be fully animated in CGI, with a final 2D rendering. [ref: Xilam finds Lucy Lost in Morpurgo book, C21Media] Helen Blakeman came on board for the script of the project then a miniseries in 2020. [ref: Xilam's 'Lucy Lost' Taps Bafta-Winning Writer Helen Blakeman (EXCLUSIVE), Variety]

Du Pontavice struggled due to its bifurcated structure, which was across two parallel narrative threads and that the crew had great difficulty adapting the story, which worked very well in the novel but was hard to translate to the screen. [ref: Xilam's Buzzy 'Lucy Lost': 'From Europe, We Can Explore a More Emotionally Driven Form of Family Storytelling', Variety] [ref: Festival d’Annecy 2026: pourquoi «Lucy Lost» d’Olivier Clert bouleverse le public, Radio France Internationale] The original budget as a miniseries was $6 million. [ref: What we're watching at MIPTV, Kidscreen] After meeting Olivier Clert in 2022, he convinced him to make it into a theatrical movie instead, by deciding that they would tell Lucy's story and by uniting the different narrative strands of the book by bringing Milly, who exists in another plot of the novel, directly into the Lucy's world, which du Pontavice really liked, where Clert developed it by creating a complete storyboard, editing it with voice acting and music, making it look like a movie. [ref: How Olivier Clert's Storyboarding Instincts Cracked Xilam's 'Impossible' 'Lucy Lost' Adaptation, Cartoon Brew] Clert joined the project later, after seeing some early visual materials at Xilam, as he was drawn to their timeless quality. Originally, he was only going to contribute as a storyboard artist, but he soon became more deeply involved in developing the story.

The film was fully animated in a mix of traditional animation and 3D [ref: Sneak Peek: French Producer Marc du Pontavice Gives Us the Scoop on His New Movie 'Lucy Lost', Animation Magazine], with some parts of the animation were done at Gao Shan Pictures in Réunion in the Indian Ocean and cleanup and color were carried out at Xilam's studio in Vietnam. Olivier Clert personally created the storyboard for the entire film, single-handedly drawing and planning the staging for its 1,800 shots. Adobe After Effects was used to create the wind in the feature film, while the voices were recorded before the animation was completed and voice casting tests were conducted for the film's child roles. The film's art direction of the production was directed by Joyce Colson [ref: Rising Stars of Animation 2025, Animation Magazine], with graphics created by Jade Khoo and animation direction by Carlo Toselli. [ref: ] [ref: 'Lucy Lost' review: Charming, playful animated adaptation of Michael Morpurgo novel 'Listen To The Moon', Screen Daily]

The film's team did not show the visuals to the book's author Michael Morpurgo until they had a completed animatic, which was a first animated version of the storyboard and they received a compliment from Morpurgo, who said he wished to have seen the film before he wrote the book. Du Pontavice noted that, during the writing, storyboarding and production of the film, the story and the book upon which it was based took on new relevance given the conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran between 2022 and 2026, unfolding in a world becoming increasingly polarized and rife with suspicion, hatred and rejection. He also said the film is a response to the fear of artificial intelligence in animation, given that it is a feature film that is absolutely impossible to create using AI, both technically and artistically and that artificial intelligence is incapable of venturing into this territory. One element not originally in the book was Lucy having white hair caused by trauma; this detail was absent from the original novel. When the film's director, Olivier Clert, began developing the story, he read a book on the folktales and legends of the Isles of Scilly and came across the story the children tell in the film, that white hair is the mark of a witch and cited by Marc du Pontavice as a well-identified psychological phenomenon, given that people of all ages experience a total loss of hair pigmentation due to trauma. Although this was not in the book and was added for the film, Morpurgo liked it.

The film's original score was composed by Anne-Sophie Versnaeyen; the first phase of recording took place at Studio Polyson in Montreuil. For the session, Jean-Michel Tavernier assembled a small 14-piece string section, conducted by Gisèle Gérard-Tolini, alongside a 6-piece woodwind group and an 8-piece brass section. Several soloists joined the orchestral ensemble, chosen for their unique timbres and ability to enrich the film's soundscape, including singer Isabel Sörlig, Marc Chouarain on the Cristal Baschet, and a nyckelharpa player. The viola and ukulele parts were recorded by the Versnaeyen herself. The second phase took place at Studio British Grove in London; the session involved recording a larger string section with 33 musicians conducted by Andrew Skeet, known for his work with the band The Divine Comedy. The Trinity Boys & Girls Choir, a group of 15 young
singers, was also recorded in London, lending the soundtrack a choral dimension. Orchestration was handled by the film's composer Anne-Sophie Versnaeyen and Ben Foskett, while recording and mixing were carried out by Fiona Cruikshank, Vincent Joinville, and Cédric Culnaërt.

==Release==
The film will be released in France on 28 October 2026 by distributor Le Pacte. Canal+ and Ciné+ OCS signed on for the French pay television rights. [ref: Xilam's Adaptation of Michael Morpurgo's 'Lucy Lost' Sets Sail with Sales & Distribution Partners, Animation Magazine] It was screened at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival as a Family Screening. [ref: Xilam's 'Lucy Lost' Heads to Prestige Festivals Ahead of France Release, Animation Magazine] It will make its UK premiere on 10 November 2026, at the Manchester Animation Festival. [ref: MAF Adds Animation Nation Forum, 'Lucy Lost' & 'Cat in the Hat' to 2026 Program, Animation Magazine]

The film's soundtrack will be released by Milan Records in digital, CD, and vinyl formats, with the vinyl version featuring exclusive cover art. The CD and vinyl editions will be released on October 30, while the digital album will launch two days earlier, coinciding with the film's premiere, on October 28.

==Reception==
===Critical reception===
The film received a positive reception with the critics. In his review for Variety, Guy Lodge praised the film's visual style, noting the influence of classic Studio Ghibli, particularly in the character designs and drawing parallels to When Marnie Was There. He also mentioned the liberties director Olivier Clert and co-screenwriter Helen Blakeman took with Michael Morpurgo's original novel, changes that worked well from a cinematic standpoint, but noted that "children much younger than the book's preteen target audience may be left a little adrift." Lodge notes that the film takes its time revealing its hand during a leisurely paced first half, but he says is not a bad thing.

Wendy Ide, writing for Screen Daily, praised the character design, noting that it evokes certain female protagonists from Studio Ghibli, but she pointed out that it represents a missed opportunity to give the film a more distinctive visual identity. Ide praised Anne-Sophie Versnaeyen's score for the feature film, noting how it tells its own story, such as at the beginning of the film, where the use of the harp lends Lucy's journey a delicate yet unsettling quality, while also gaining body and substance through richer orchestration as Lucy's friendship with Milly develops.

Mariana Conti Takahashi (July 23, 1985) is a Brazilian sociologist and politician affiliated with the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL). [ref: Vereadora do PSOL detida por Israel diz em carta que está bem 'na medida do possível', O Globo] [ref: Mariana Conti envia vídeos sobre reuniões de Vini ao MP, Jornal Correio da Manhã] [ref: Brazilian delegation joins international flotilla to Gaza: 'This is the largest mission in history', Brasil de Fato] She served as a city councilwoman in Campinas, and in 2026, she was elected to the Legislative Assembly of São Paulo (Alesp). [ref: Com mais de 126 mil votos, vereadora Mariana Conti é eleita deputada estadual, Central Brasileira de Notícias] [ref: Por 21 votos a 8, fracassa tentativa da ultradireita de cassar Mariana Conti por integrar Flotilha a Gaza, CSP-Conlutas] [ref: Eleições 2026: veja quem são os deputados estaduais eleitos por SP, Agência Brasil]

== Biography ==

=== First years and education ===
Mariana Conti Takahashi was born on 23 July 1985 in the city of Campinas, in the interior of São Paulo. She is one of four children born to an electrical engineer and a sociologist. [ref: Mariana Conti critica violência política de gênero dentro da Câmara, Correio Popular] She grew up in Americana, a city bordering Campinas, and enrolled at the State University of Campinas (Unicamp) in 2004 to study social sciences. [ref: MARIANA CONTI TAKAHASHI, Instituto de Filosofia e Ciências Humanas da Unicamp] During her undergraduate studies, she participated in the student movement and served as coordinator of the university’s Central Student Council. [ref: Mariana Conti (Psol) é eleita deputada estadual após três mandatos como vereadora de Campinas, Todo Dia]

In 2015, she completed her master’s degree in sociology with a thesis titled Florestan Fernandes: Imperialism and Class Struggle in the Era of Monopoly Capital, also at Unicamp, where the sociologist Florestan Fernandes had studied. [ref: Florestan Fernandes: imperialismo e luta de classes na era do capital monopolista, State University of Campinas] In 2021, the university reported that Mariana was an administrative employee on leave to serve her elected term and that she was pursuing a Ph.D. [ref: Reitor recebe parlamentares para estreitar diálogo com lideranças políticas, Unicamp]

=== Politics ===

Mariana began her political activism while still a young woman, as part of the student movement at Unicamp. Between 2004 and 2007, she helped coordinate the Central Student Council, getting involved in protests related to public education, free public transportation, and the defense of women’s rights. [ref: conheça Mariana, Mariana Conti 50100] Later, she became active in party politics with the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL).

Mariana Conti initially ran for city councilor in Campinas in the, but was not elected. [ref: Apuração - Campinas (SP): 2008, Folha de S. Paulo] In the 2010 general elections, she ran for federal deputy representing São Paulo and was elected as an alternate. [ref: Candidados a deputado federal do estado São Paulo, [[G (website)] In, she ran again for city councilor in Campinas and was elected as an alternate, even though she was the sixth-highest-voting candidate, her party did not meet the electoral threshold. [ref: Apuração em tempo real - 1° turno - Campinas, Universo Online] In 2014, she ran for federal deputy and, once again, served as an alternate. [ref: Resultado das Apurações dos votos das Eleições 2014 em SP para Governador, Senador, Deputados Federais e Deputados Estaduais, [[G1 (website)]

In the, Mariana Conti was elected to the as a member of the PSOL with 6,956 votes; she was the fourth-highest vote-getter for the City Council and the only woman elected to that legislature. [ref: Em Campinas, a única mulher eleita para Câmara é de esquerda e socialista, Esquerda Online] [ref: UOL Eleições 2016 Campinas/SP: Apuração de votos, resultado, prefeito e vereadores eleitos, [[Universo Online] In 2018, she ran for the first time for the position of state representative in the 2018 São Paulo state elections as a candidate for the PSOL. [ref: Resultado da votação para Mariana Conti em São Paulo, Gazeta do Povo] She received 35,307 votes and was elected as an alternate. [ref: ]

In the, she was reelected with 10,886 votes, becoming the candidate with the most votes for the in that election. [ref: Com mulher como candidata mais votada pela 1ª vez, Câmara de Campinas tem número recorde de vereadoras eleitas, [[G1 (website)] It was the first time a woman had received the most votes for city council in the history of Campinas. During her second term, she participated in debates and initiatives related to women’s rights, human rights, public education, and public services. In 2022, she chaired a public hearing of the Campinas City Council aimed at discussing the activities and history of neo-Nazi and fascist organizations in the municipality. [ref: TRANSCRIÇÃO DA 62ª AUDIÊNCIA PÚBLICA DE 2022, REALIZADA PELA "COMISSÃO PARLAMENTAR DE INQUÉRITO PARA INVESTIGAR AS AÇÕES VIOLENTAS DE GRUPOS NEONAZISTAS E FASCISTAS EM CAMPINAS" EM 21 DE NOVEMBRO, SEGUNDA-FEIRA, ÀS 09H39, NO TEATRO BENTO QUIRINO, À RUA LUZITANA, 1.505 E 1.555, PARA TRATAR SOBRE O TEMA: "HISTÓRICO DAS ORGANIZAÇÕES FASCISTAS DO BRASIL E COMBATE INSTITUCIONAL"., Câmara Municipal de Campinas] [ref: CPI que investiga crescimento do fascismo em Campinas tem audiência pública dia 23 de junho, Carta Campinas] In the 2022 São Paulo state elections, she ran again for a seat in the Legislative Assembly of São Paulo. [ref: ] She received 43,988 votes and was once again elected as an alternate. [ref: ] In that same election, Mariana had previously announced her candidacy for governor of São Paulo. [ref: Vereadora de Campinas se coloca como candidata ao governo de SP após desistência de Boulos, Carta Campinas] Mariana withdrew her candidacy after the PSOL declared its support for Fernando Haddad (PT). [ref: Pela unidade e por candidatura própria do PSOL, Mariana Conti retira pré-candidatura ao Governo Paulista, Mariana Conti] [ref: PSOL aprova apoio à candidatura de Haddad em São Paulo, CNN Brasil]

In the, she was reelected to the with 14,356 votes, becoming the city’s top vote-getter for the second consecutive time. [ref: Vereadora mais votada em Campinas, Mariana Conti prevê avançar em questões ambientais e diz que 'feminismo é imparável', [[G1 (website)] With this result, she began her third consecutive term as a city councilmember in 2025. [ref: Campinas (SP): veja lista dos vereadores eleitos nas Eleições 2024, Universo Online]

In October 2025, Mariana Conti took part in the Sumud Global Flotilla, which included other national and international public figures such as Brazilian activist Thiago Ávila and Swedish activist Greta Thunberg. [ref: Vereadora de Campinas participa de missão que vai desafiar bloqueio de Israel para levar ajuda humanitária a Gaza, O Globo] [ref: Prominent Brazilian presence in Global Sumud Flotilla to Gaza, The Palestinian Information Center]

In the 2026 São Paulo state elections, she ran for office and was elected state representative with 126,344 votes, ranking as the 30th-highest vote-getter among those elected to the Legislative Assembly of São Paulo. [ref: ]

data.title: Jules Bourdais
data.text:
Jules Désiré Bourdais (born April 6, 1835 in Brest, France; died June 2, 1915 in Paris) was a French architect.

Bourdais is best known for designing the Trocadéro Palace with Gabriel Davioud and for creating a design for a stone column for the 1889 World's Fair, the Colonne Soleil (Sun Column), which would have rivaled the Eiffel Tower.

==Biography==
Jules Désiré Bourdais was born on April 6, 1835, in Brest, France, to Jean Julien Bourdais, a ship's captain and officer of the Legion of Honour, [ref: Recherche - Base de données Léonore, www.leonore.archives-nationales.culture.gouv.fr] and Fanny Marie Louise Valéri. Bourdais graduated from the École Centrale Paris in 1857. He married Blanche Marie Juliette Fauvelet de Charbonnière in 1867.

Between 1868 and 1870, Bourdais designed the Saint-Pierre-ès-Liens church and the Protestant church in Nègrepelisse. During the Franco-Prussian War in 1870, Bourdais served as a lieutenant in the engineering corps. Between 1876 and 1878, Bourdais and Gabriel Davioud designed the town hall for the 19th arrondissement of Paris and in May 1876, Bourdais and Davioud won a competition to design the Trocadéro Palace.

In 1881, Bourdais created a design for a "sun column" – a granite tower topped with a beacon that would be capable of illuminating all of Paris as far as Neuilly-sur-Seine, Levallois-Perret, and the Bois de Boulogne. In 1886, with the support of engineer Amédée Sébillot, [ref: Musée d'Orsay: Jules Bourdais, Phare monumental] Bourdais submitted his design proposal to a competition for the 1889 World's Fair, but lost to Gustave Eiffel's proposal for the Eiffel Tower.

Bourdais died at his residence in the 16th arrondissement of Paris on June 2, 1915, [ref: Visionneuse - Archives de Paris, archives.paris.fr.] and was buried in the Montmartre Cemetery. [ref: Cimetière de Montmartre-Répertoire annuel d'inhumation: Aaron-Bourgeois (1912-1920)]

data.title: Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter
data.text:
The Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter (MPSD; ) is a non-university research institute of the Max Planck Society (MPG). It is located in the Hamburg district of Bahrenfeld, on the campus of the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY). The institute primarily conducts basic research in the natural sciences, in experimental and theoretical physics and chemistry. Its focus is on very fast physical processes and chemical reactions that can be studied by ultrafast spectroscopy using pulsed radiation sources such as the nearby free-electron lasers FLASH and European XFEL.

== History ==
The institute grew out of an existing Max Planck Society research group for structural dynamics at the University of Hamburg. The decision to establish an independent institute with five research departments and up to 120 permanent positions was announced in November 2012. The institute was officially founded on 1 January 2014 and initially consisted of two departments, headed by its two founding directors: Condensed Matter Dynamics, led by Andrea Cavalleri, and Atomically Resolved Dynamics, led by R. J. Dwayne Miller. The Theory Department under Ángel Rubio was added on 1 November 2014. Miller's department was dissolved when he left the MPSD on 30 June 2020. On 15 June 2021, Philip Moll was appointed director of the Microstructured Quantum Matter Department.

In 2024, Jie Shan and Kin Fai Mak were recruited as further directors. They joined the institute fully on 1 January 2025 and lead two jointly run departments of Nanoscale Quantum Materials, focusing on optics (Shan) and transport (Mak), bringing the number of departments to five.

== Building ==
Since its founding, the MPSD has used space in the neighbouring Center for Free-Electron Laser Science (CFEL) building, which it shares with DESY and the University of Hamburg. A separate institute building next to the CFEL, designed by hammeskrause architekten, was completed in 2023; a foundation slab up to 1.5 metres thick keeps its laboratories free of vibrations. The building was officially opened on 13 May 2024. Of its total construction cost of €54 million, the City of Hamburg contributed €37 million and the Max Planck Society the rest. The extension allowed the institute to grow from three to five departments.

== Departments ==
{| class="wikitable"
|+ Departments of the MPSD
! Department !! Director !! Period
|-
| Condensed Matter Dynamics || Andrea Cavalleri || since 2014
|-
| Theory || Ángel Rubio || since 2014
|-

| Nanoscale Quantum Materials – Optics || Jie Shan || since 2025
|-
| Nanoscale Quantum Materials – Transport || Kin Fai Mak || since 2025
|-
| Atomically Resolved Dynamics (former) || R. J. Dwayne Miller || 2014–2020
|}

== Doctoral training ==
The MPSD hosts the International Max Planck Research School for Ultrafast Imaging and Structural Dynamics (IMPRS-UFAST), a structured doctoral programme founded in 2011 for doctoral students with backgrounds in physics, chemistry and biology.
