data.title: Have I Been Squatted
data.text:
----

Have I Been Squatted Inc. is a privately held cybersecurity company that works on domain intelligence. It builds a platform for finding typosquatted and lookalike domains, along with the websites and infrastructure tied to them, that may be used for phishing, brand impersonation, or other abuse. According to the company's documentation, its monitoring draws on domain permutations, Domain Name System (DNS) data, Certificate Transparency logs, registration data, website analysis, and passive infrastructure telemetry. [ref: Getting started with Have I Been Squatted, Have I Been Squatted Documentation]

The service started in 2022 as a public tool for spotting typosquatted domains. The company that now runs it, Have I Been Squatted Inc., was founded in 2024. [ref: About, Have I Been Squatted] [ref: Have I Been Squatted, LinkedIn]

The company also publishes research on phishing, malicious infrastructure, malware delivery, and domain-name security. Its work has been covered by BBC News, The Register, Recorded Future News, BleepingComputer, and FreightWaves. [ref: Phishing operation with links to Russia, Armenia compromised Western cargo companies, researchers find, Recorded Future News] [ref: Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers, The Register]

== History ==

Have I Been Squatted began in 2022 as an experimental tool for finding possible typosquats. Users entered a domain name and the tool generated variations of it, showing registrations that could be used to impersonate the original organization. The company says the project was first released after an experiment was shared on Hacker News, and that it grew as security practitioners started using it. Part of the tool was built on twistrs, an open-source Rust library for generating domain-name permutations that the company still maintains on GitHub. [ref: Have I Been Squatted, GitHub]

Have I Been Squatted Inc. was founded in 2024 to develop and run the service on a commercial basis. [ref: Terms of Service, Have I Been Squatted]

The commercial service moved beyond one-off typosquatting searches to continuous monitoring and investigation of external infrastructure, and later added tools for investigations, alerts, and domain takedowns.

== Platform ==

The platform looks for internet infrastructure that may be impersonating an organization, its domains, or its brands. Customers add domains for monitoring, and the platform regularly generates permutations of them and checks for related registrations and infrastructure. It adds context to what it finds using DNS records, HTTP responses, WHOIS and RDAP registration data, Certificate Transparency observations, screenshots, classification data, and passive infrastructure telemetry.

Monitoring is not limited to typos of a protected domain. The platform also surfaces domains found through Certificate Transparency, passive DNS, and other infrastructure signals.

Separately from monitoring, the platform includes tools for investigating individual domains and larger datasets. Infrastructure it identifies can be classified, investigated, and linked to alerts or response work. The company later added workflows for submitting domain takedown requests and tracking their progress.

== Threat intelligence research ==

=== Diesel Vortex ===

In February 2026, Have I Been Squatted and the threat intelligence group Ctrl-Alt-Intel published an investigation into a cybercrime operation they called Diesel Vortex. The group went after freight and logistics companies in the United States and Europe, using phishing sites built to take over accounts on load boards, fleet-management systems, fuel-card services, and other logistics platforms. [ref: Russian cybercrime ring targeted freight firms in US, Europe, report says, FreightWaves]

According to Recorded Future News, Have I Been Squatted researchers found an exposed.git directory belonging to the operation. It held source code and the group's communications, which showed how the campaign was organized and indicated that the group was building a phishing-as-a-service platform to support a wider criminal operation.

FreightWaves reported that the campaign had compromised 1,649 unique credentials, drawn from 3,474 stolen login pairs. The investigation also identified 52 deployed phishing domains, more than 75,000 targeted contact email addresses, and 35 confirmed attempts at fraud using Electronic Funds Source checks.

The exposed material pointed to an organized operation, with separate roles and infrastructure for stealing credentials, communicating with logistics staff, and managing victim sessions. Recorded Future News reported that the compromised accounts could be used for freight diversion, double brokering, and check fraud.

Have I Been Squatted and Ctrl-Alt-Intel worked with technology and security companies to disrupt the campaign's infrastructure. Recorded Future News named Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), Cloudflare, GitLab, IPinfo, and Ping Identity among those involved.

In April 2026, BleepingComputer referred to the Diesel Vortex investigation in its report on an FBI warning about a sharp rise in cyber-enabled cargo theft. It cited Have I Been Squatted's finding that the group had used dozens of phishing domains against freight and logistics operators since 2025. [ref: FBI links cybercriminals to sharp surge in cargo theft attacks, BleepingComputer]

=== Recruitment malware campaigns ===

In August 2026, Have I Been Squatted published a technical analysis of a malware campaign that used a fake hiring process to target a job seeker in the Web3 sector. The attackers approached the victim on LinkedIn, ran what looked like a normal interview process using Calendly and Google-hosted services, and then sent technical assessment material that was malicious. [ref: From fake interview to signed ClickOnce: inside a three-payload Windows chain, Have I Been Squatted]

On Windows, the attack used a digitally signed ClickOnce application. Installing it eventually delivered three payloads: a version of NeedleStealer, a separate information stealer written in Rust, and a custom Go remote-access trojan with remote shell access, file management, proxying, keylogging, and hidden virtual network computing.

The same infrastructure could also serve a macOS delivery chain that ended in Odyssey Stealer. The researchers said the mix of legitimate online platforms, signed software, and targeted social engineering made the fake recruitment process far more convincing than ordinary phishing.

In September 2026, BBC News cited analysis by Have I Been Squatted in a report on fake recruitment scams. The report followed a victim who was approached on LinkedIn and lost about £18,000 in cryptocurrency after installing malicious software during what seemed to be a real hiring process. It highlighted the attackers' use of genuine Google services and digitally signed software. [ref: I lost my savings after a job interview scam, BBC News]

=== Internationalized domain name and Chromium research ===

In October 2026, Have I Been Squatted published research on how Chromium-based browsers handle internationalized domain names (IDNs). They tested whether deceptive lookalike domains could get past Chromium's protections and be shown to users in Unicode, rather than in their Punycode form, which is easier to recognize as suspicious. [ref: Turning IDN edge cases into typosquats, Have I Been Squatted]

The researchers found edge cases involving two characters: the Cyrillic letter ө, used in languages such as Kazakh and Mongolian, and the Latin letter ƙ, used in languages such as Hausa. Using these characters, they built lookalikes of well-known domains that passed Chromium's display checks.

Have I Been Squatted registered 20 proof-of-concept lookalike domains for the research, including ones resembling Apple, SpaceX, Okta, and Nike. The Register covered the findings on October 10, 2026, explaining how the two characters could get around Chromium's checks for suspicious internationalized domains.

Chromium runs several checks before deciding whether to show an internationalized domain in Unicode. One set looks for characters and scripts often used for impersonation. Another reduces each domain to a simplified comparison string, called a skeleton, and compares it against a built-in list of popular domains.

The research found that Cyrillic ө was missing from Chromium's whole-script lookalike list, so adding it to an otherwise confusable Cyrillic domain could stop that check from triggering. The Latin ƙ caused a related problem at the skeleton stage. Its hook was kept as a combining mark, so the skeleton never exactly matched the ASCII domain it imitated.

The researchers also looked at Chromium's Safety Tips, which warn users when they navigate to a site by comparing it, exactly and approximately, against well-known sites and sites the user visits often. They found cases where a lookalike differed enough from the comparison skeleton to avoid a warning, as well as limitations affecting domains with fewer than five characters before the top-level domain.

As part of the work, the company analyzed the.com zone for internationalized domains and found about 162,000 pairs in which an IDN resembled an ASCII.com domain. The researchers noted that this did not mean 162,000 malicious typosquats, since such pairs can include legitimate multilingual domains and defensive registrations.

The research also compared email clients. Gmail showed the tested internationalized sender domains in Unicode, while Outlook Web showed the same domains as Punycode A-labels. The Register noted that the two services had made different trade-offs in how they present internationalized email domains to users.

== Public and open-source tools ==

Alongside its commercial service, Have I Been Squatted releases free and open-source security tools.

twistrs is a Rust library for generating and enumerating domain-name permutations. It is released under the MIT License, hosted in the company's public GitHub organization, and was one of the building blocks of the original typosquatting service.

In December 2025, the company launched certgrep, a free search service for Certificate Transparency data. It lets users search certificate records with regular expressions, wildcards, and substring queries. The company built it after using similar functionality internally to find domains that matched suspicious patterns. [ref: Announcing certgrep, Have I Been Squatted]

The company also maintains an open-source Python software development kit for its application programming interface (API). It gives programmatic access to features including domain-squatting analysis, domain investigation, and Certificate Transparency search. [ref: haveibeensquatted-python, GitHub]

== References ==

== External links ==

*
* [https://github.com/haveibeensquatted Have I Been Squatted on GitHub]

data.title: Kenneth Morrow
data.text:
= Kenneth “K” Morrow =

Kenneth (Ken) “K” Morrow is an American author/writer/inventor specializing in the production, cultivation and study of the cannabis plant, hashish production, terpene/cannabinoid/flavonoid isolation and pharmaceutical applications. He is the founding owner of Trichome Technologies, a molecular research and development company.

Kenneth Morrow, who has also written under the pen name “K,” is an author/writer, botanist, horticulturist, agronomist, cannabis formulation specialist, consultant, and the founding owner of Trichome Technologies. His book [https://www.amazon.com/Marijuana-Horticulture-Fundamentals-Comprehensive-Cultivation-ebook/dp/B0HJMWBD32 Marijuana Horticulture Fundamentals: A comprehensive guide to cannabis cultivation and hashish production] is a highly regarded informational source. He has written for multiple periodicals for decades and is considered a respected information source (see list below). Informational links to many of the articles and media interviews and programs mentioned in the detailed biographical notes compiled by @[user]. More information and articles can be found at [https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/magazine CannabisBusinessTimes.com] and [https://muckrack.com/kenneth-morrow Morrow’s Muckrack profile].

= Kenneth Morrow’s Early Years =
To understand what Kenneth “K” Morrow has built you have to understand the world he built it in. Not the world of licensed dispensaries and compliance departments and seed-to-sale tracking software — that world didn't exist yet. Not the world of venture capital and celebrity strains and Instagram marketing. That world was decades away.

The world Morrow came from was completely illegal. Every transaction happened in cash. Every relationship depended on trust. Every pound moved was a risk taken in service of something the people taking the risk genuinely believed in. Morrow operated in this world and was thirteen years old when he started.

In 1978, in the ninth grade, with his mother's permission, Morrow began cultivating cannabis hydroponically. He ordered a Hydropot system from the back of a [https://hightimes.com/ High Times Magazine] — a busboy tray, lava rock, a fish aquarium aerator, a little Miracle-Gro. It was the only hydroponic system he ever purchased. Everything after that he built himself.

Morrow had access to cannabis that most people his age had never encountered. And he wasn't just consuming it. He was studying it. Between 1978 and 1981, his early experiences with the plant ranged across blond and red hashish from Lebanon, Afghan hash, and multiple old world cultivars — Panamanian, Mexican, Columbian, Thai. These were not recreational curiosities. They were reference points. Each one told him something about what the plant was capable of, each raised the bar on what he was trying to achieve.

In 1980 or 1981, he took his first hit of an unusually clean, clear amber honey oil. The flavor was extraordinary. The cleanliness was extraordinary. The potency was extraordinary. That oil became the defining standard of everything that followed — the reference point that set the bar for flavor, cleanliness, and potency that he would spend the next four decades building toward and ultimately surpassing.

By the mid-1980s, as growers were introducing commercial scale operations and high quality trim was becoming more abundant, Morrow began trafficking cannabis. He was fifteen years old and continued through the late eighties and into the early nineties. But trafficking was never the point. The plant was the point. His focus was moving steadily away from flower and toward the trichome — toward what lived in the resin, toward what the plant was actually capable of when you knew how to capture it properly.

He continued his dry sieve education throughout this period, pursuing super refined extracts with the particular obsession of someone who has tasted what is possible and cannot accept anything less. And through all of it — the trafficking, the cultivation, the extraction experiments — he was doing something that would define his legacy more than any single technique: he was documenting everything, developing repeatable and consistent and predictable processes, and building a foundation of knowledge that could be passed forward.

In a world where there was no patent office to run to, no institution to credential him, no legal framework to protect what he was building — Morrow built it anyway. And he gave it away.

= The 1990s =
In the early 1990s, Morrow continued learning while pushing further into the question that consumed him: what was the best possible way to capture the active ingredients in the trichome?

Then in 1994, Morrow received very basic water hash isolation instructions. What he did with those basic instructions was entirely his own. He employed a titanium water chiller to replace ice, maintaining the water at precise temperatures throughout the extraction process. He utilized fresh frozen plant material — harvested and immediately frozen rather than dried — to minimize contamination and preserve the aromatic terpene compounds that the drying process destroyed. The result was a superior aromatic and flavorful isolate of extraordinary quality. He was producing it years before any commercial separation equipment existed for this process, because that equipment hadn't been invented yet. He was building everything himself because he had to.

In 1995 he was fully utilizing fresh frozen cannabis to make hashish — and the results were unlike anything commercially available, because nothing commercially available was built on the foundation he had constructed.

In 1994, Morrow established Trichome Technologies. With it came a conscious philosophical commitment that would govern everything: he would prioritize trichome production, environmental control, repeatability, and consistency over yield or appearance. This was not a commercial calculation. It was a craftsman's declaration. He was building advanced indoor hydro and aeroponic systems of a sophistication that had no parallel in any legal industry, because no legal industry existed. He was doing it underground because the work was worth doing right regardless of whether anyone would ever know his name.

Morrow also began a breeding program during this period that would eventually total over two hundred proprietary cultivars. One of those cultivars was a standout clone he originally called Purple Kush — a stabilized resin forward line that would go on to become one of the most recognized cannabis strains in the world. Widespread plagiarism of the name eventually forced a rename to Ultra Violate, and by the time that happened the genetics had already spread globally. The name changed. What he had built did not.

In early 1994, Morrow had also begun investigating solvent extraction, ultimately starting to extract utilizing butane — years before the dab culture had a name, years before standardized tools existed for the process. He was documenting solvent extraction as chemistry: repeatability, safety, stability. He was writing down what he was doing because he believed the knowledge belonged to the people who needed it.

Around 1997 or 1998, Morrow was in the parking lot outside a Berkeley indoor garden shop when he met a woman named Mila Jansen. They got to talking. He showed her a sample of his ice water hash — before she had anything like it, before commercial separation bags of any kind were available for sale anywhere. He showed her what he had built. What was possible. It was so pure, she initially did not believe it was made with just ice and water.

Mila Jansen would go on to develop the Ice-O-Lator. Later, Marcus "Bubbleman" Richardson would develop Bubble Bags — the mainstream commercial product that brought the water hash separation technique to mass market and put it in the hands of growers around the world.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pjZd8MpL96Y Neither] the Ice-O-Lator nor the Bubble Bags were Morrow's invention, but both existed downstream of that moment in that parking lot where Morrow showed someone what he had been building in the underground for years and shared it freely because that was what you did when you believed the knowledge was more important than the credit. The knowledge moved outward. The products got names. Morrow’s name was not on them.

In 1996 Morrow became the first cannabis grower ever interviewed on a [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vb-qSgu9Dd4&t=64s segment of 60 Minutes]. To understand what that meant you have to understand what 60 Minutes was in 1996 — not just a television program but the most watched and most culturally authoritative news magazine program in America, the place where the country went to have important stories confirmed as real. A cannabis grower appearing on 60 Minutes was something the culture had never imagined possible. And Morrow appeared in shadow, voice altered, face completely hidden — nationally visible and completely anonymous. The knowledge he had spent nearly two decades building was acknowledged on the most watched news program in America. The craftsman who built it could not be seen. That image — the expertise present and recognized, the person behind it legally erased — was the pre-legalization era compressed into a single frame.

In 1997 he appeared again on television, this time on CNN on a show titled [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pjZd8MpL96Y Higher Times]. That same year, he became the second private individual ever to have cultivars and extract samples tested by the University of Mississippi. To understand why this mattered requires understanding what the University of Mississippi cannabis laboratory actually was. It was not simply a testing facility. It was the only federally sanctioned cannabis research laboratory in the entire United States — the sole institution with federal authorization to study the plant scientifically. For any private individual to have their material tested there was extraordinarily rare. For a craftsman operating entirely underground in Northern California to achieve it represented a legitimacy that no other form of recognition in the cannabis world could match. The results documented at that laboratory carried a weight that no dispensary award or community recognition could replicate — because they were produced by the one institution the federal government itself had authorized to tell the truth about the plant. His G-13 cultivar tested at 27.2% THC. His water hash tested at 68.6% THC. These were not just impressive numbers. They were proof of concept — documented by the most credible source available — for everything he had been building since 1978. Also in 1997, Morrow entered his first competition and made an extraordinary debut at the [https://castatefair.com/california-cannabis/ California Cannabis Awards], simultaneously claiming first, second, and third place. He continued to compete through 2000, accumulating nine awards in total.

On September 8, 1998, he was formally deputized as an agent of the Oakland Cannabis Buyers Cooperative. To understand what this meant requires understanding what the OCBC was. The Oakland Cannabis Buyers Cooperative was one of the most important medical cannabis institutions in the country at the time — a dispensary and patient advocacy organization operating at the center of the legal and political fight to protect what Prop 215, California's Compassionate Use Act, had created. Being recognized and formally deputized by the OCBC carried genuine weight within the medical cannabis community. It meant that the most serious and visible institutional players in the movement had determined that Morrow Morrow's work was credible, essential, and worthy of formal protection. The official language of his deputization declared him a duly authorized officer of the City of Oakland, immune from civil and criminal liability under Section 885d of the Federal Controlled Substances Act. Everyone involved understood what that paper was worth against a federal government that didn't recognize it. He went back to work anyway. That same year, 1998, he created the first branded hash — KIF. A name on a product. His standard, made visible.

In October 1999 Morrow was featured in [https://hightimes.com/ High Times Magazine] in a piece titled "Return to Trichome Tech." In January 1999 the same magazine named Trichome Technologies the Best Growroom in the 25-year history of the magazine and that same month he was the subject of another feature titled "Trichome Tech: A Scientific Approach to Growing." Two features in the same month in the most widely read cannabis publication on earth. He was not seeking the spotlight. The work was too significant to ignore.
= The 2000s =
The 2000s arrived and with them a new phase of Morrow’s contribution to the culture he had been building from the inside out. Morrow began teaching through magazines beyond High Times, Cannabis Now, Greenhouse Management, Cannabis Business Times, along with Red Eye Express, Burst High in Japan, Skunk, Heads, Canamo and many more publications across multiple countries. His step-by-step methods moved the culture forward while it stayed underground. He was building the technical library of an industry that did not yet legally exist, writing it down carefully enough that the people who came after would have something to build on.

Through the early 2000s, Morrow published technical work on purging standards, solvent behavior under vacuum, and wax and lipid contamination — writing extraction as chemistry, repeatability, safety, and stability at a time when most people in the industry were still learning what those words meant in this context.

In April 2000, a High Times feature titled "Trichome Technologies Guide to Making Hash" explained the process of both dry sieving and the concept of making water hash without the use of extraction bags — A process he developed before any separation bags were commercially available anywhere. This article was later included in the book Hashish by Robert C. Clarke and republished multiple times. It documented what Morrow had been doing for years and put it into the permanent record of the craft.In October 2000 another High Times feature titled "Harvest Time at Trichome Tech" followed.

In 2002, Butane Hash Oil (BHO) hit print. Morrow published the first BHO article ever to be published in [https://www.ebay.co.uk/itm/256468693227 Red Eye Express magazine], titled "Captain Butane Saves the Day." Pre-dab culture. Before standardized tools. Solvent extraction documented as a craft process before the industry existed to commercialize it. He had been doing this for years. He was now making sure everyone else could, too.

In 2004, Morrow smuggled cultivation books and cannabis genetics into Cuba — a story published as a feature in both [https://rollitup.org/t/marijuana-into-cuba-a-mission-from-jah.544967/ High Times and Red Eye Express] and republished multiple times. He went where the plant needed to go.

By the mid-2000s, the world around Morrow was beginning to change in ways that would eventually transform everything he had helped build underground into the foundation of a legal billion dollar industry. California's medical cannabis market was maturing. Dispensaries were professionalizing. The Cole Memorandum would signal a conditional federal retreat that opened the door to serious outside investment. The language of the industry was shifting from medicine to commerce, from craft to scale. The knowledge Morrow had spent decades developing and freely sharing was increasingly being absorbed into an industry that was moving fast and looking forward and not particularly interested in where any of it came from. He kept building anyway. He kept documenting. He kept pushing the frontier.

In October 2012, Morrow co-authored a High Times article titled "Waxes and Lipids and Fats, Oh My — The Quest for Pure BHO." Then came the vacuum oven pivot — a moment that quietly reshaped the entire concentrate industry. To understand what Morrow did, it helps to know what a vacuum drying oven actually was before he got to it. Vacuum drying ovens were industrial and pharmaceutical pieces of equipment — used in food processing, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and laboratory research to remove moisture and solvents from materials under controlled heat and reduced pressure. Nobody in the cannabis world was using them. The connection between what those machines could do and what cannabis extraction needed had not been made. Morrow made it.

Morrow became the first person to reconfigure an Across International Vacuum Drying Oven specifically for cannabis extracts. He added a digital vacuum gauge for precision monitoring, stronger internal hoses and clamps to handle the demands of cannabis processing, staged heat application to protect volatile terpene compounds, and vacuum pressure control to manage the purging process with a level of precision that no previous method could achieve. His proof of concept turned into an industry standard that others followed immediately. Every commercial cannabis extraction operation running a vacuum oven today is running it in a configuration that traces back to what Morrow built in his facility and documented for the world.

In July 2013, a High Times feature entitled "Art and Science of Cleaning Concentrates Part 2" became the first mention of vacuum drying ovens, thin layer evaporation, and winterization in the history of the magazine. He was writing the technical future of an industry that was only beginning to understand what it was becoming. In October 2013, Trichome Technologies became the first trademarked cannabis company and consulting company in history. The underground craftsman who had no legal framework to protect what he was building when he started now had his name on the first trademark in the industry he had spent decades building from nothing.

July 2014, High Times included a feature entitled "Kings of Concentrate — Dab Report." In the High Times 40th anniversary issue (November 2014), Trichome Technologies was chosen as number one of the "Greatest Pot Gardens of All Time" and the most innovative grow from their 40 years of ground-breaking cultivation coverage. That was forty years of coverage by the most important cannabis publication in the world, and the best they had ever seen was Morrow’s. Also in 2014, Morrow received the Chalice award for contributions to the industry. That same year he developed micro-encapsulated cannabinoid and terpene formulations and became the first person to enter separated cannabinoids and terpenes in competition at the [https://cannabiscup.com/seattle/ High Times Cannabis Cups Seattle].

In 2015, Morrow’s research expanded into bioavailable and water soluble isolates of cannabinoids pushing the frontier forward again into territory the industry would not fully follow him for years. Beginning in 2015, he became a columnist for [https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/magazine Cannabis Business Times] magazine and joined their [https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/about-us board of advisors], a role he holds to the present day. On December 15th, 2015 Morrow was given the Trailblazer Award by High Times magazine.

In 2016, Morrow’s Marijuana Horticulture Fundamentals, a 400-plus page book that sold 15,000 copies was published and is now available in [https://www.amazon.com/Marijuana-Horticulture-Fundamentals-Comprehensive-Cultivation-ebook/dp/B0HJMWBD32 eBook format]. This was the definitive technical reference written by the man who had been building the technical foundation since before most of his readers were adults. Also in 2016, Morrow became the first person to perform and patent a terpene isolation method for cannabis. The first. Not a refinement of someone else's work. Not an improvement on an existing process. The first. In a field where he would go on to hold multiple patents, this was the one that opened the door, establishing that the isolation of individual terpene compounds from cannabis was not just possible but achievable with the rigor and repeatability that serious science required.

In 2017, Morrow was recognized as an award-winning journalist and continued contributing to major cannabis reference works — the cover of Ed Rosenthal's [https://www.amazon.com/Big-Book-Buds-Marijuana-Varieties/dp/0932551394 Big Book of Buds], Jason King's [https://www.amazon.com/Cannabible-Collection/dp/1580088376 Cannabible], Jorge Cervantes’ Grow Basics and [https://www.amazon.com/Cannabis-Encyclopedia-Definitive-Cultivation-Consumption/dp/1878823396 Cannabis Encyclopedia], Greg Green's [https://www.amazon.com/Cannabis-Grow-Bible-Definitive-Recreational/dp/1937866785 Cannabis Grow Bible] Volumes 1 and 2, and Robert C. Clarke's revised [https://www.amazon.com/Hashish-2nd-Robert-Connell-Clarke/dp/B003G53Y5E Hashish].

According to the [https://vault.hightimes.com/ High Times archives], Kenneth Morrow has contributed over 65 articles and over 290 images. He is one of the most prolific non-staff contributors in the history of the magazine. In an industry that produced no shortage of people seeking recognition, he was the one who showed up in the record more than most — not because he was chasing the spotlight but because the work kept demanding to be documented.

=== Legalization and Corporatization ===
By the time the legal recreational market opened in California on January 1, 2018, the industry Morrow had technically helped build from the ground up was operating at a scale he could not have imagined when he ordered that Hydropot in 1978. Commercial extraction facilities with automated vacuum ovens. Industrial scale BHO operations. Terpene isolation labs. Concentrate brands worth tens of millions of dollars. The entire technical architecture of what those facilities were doing — the processes, the equipment configurations, the extraction chemistry, the purification standards — all traced back through the underground years to work that Morrow had done, documented, and given away freely because he believed the knowledge belonged to the people who needed it. His name was on none of the equipment.

The corporate era arrived with its lobbyists and its greenhouse complexes and its political access and its burner distributions and its price collapses, and it absorbed the technical foundation of the craft community the same way it absorbed everything else — without acknowledgment, without compensation, without so much as a footnote. The extraction facilities running today are running on his processes. The vacuum ovens in those facilities are configured the way he configured the first one. The terpene isolation methods are built on his patents. The water hash techniques trace back to what he was producing in 1995 before any separation bags existed anywhere. Morrow kept working.

An August 2018 High Times feature entitled "The Great Terpene Swindle" by Trichome Technologies exposed a company which had notoriously sold hydrosols to unsuspecting customers disguised as pure terpenes. The legal market had arrived, the corporate era was fully underway, and Morrow was still doing what he had always done: watching, documenting, calling out what was wrong when no one else would. He was still protecting the consumer and still holding the standard.

The September 2018 High Times “710” awards special issue listed Kenneth “K”Morrow among the "Pioneers" of cannabis.

In August 2021,“Breeding The Culture: K Of Trichome Technologies,” a [https://beardbrospharms.com/k-trichome-technologies/ Beard Bros. Pharms column] featured Morrow.

The Cannthropology column in the September 2024 [https://leafmagazines.com/learn/history/cannthropology-terp-titan-kenneth-k-morrow/ Leaf Magazine] featured Morrow as "Titan of Terps.”

=== The Quiet Architect ===
There is a particular kind of person who builds things that outlast them without needing credit for the building, who documents what they know not because documentation serves their career but because the knowledge belongs to the people who need it. Such a person shows someone a technique in a parking lot and doesn't think about what that moment might eventually become. Such a person writes the first article on BHO extraction and the first article on terpene isolation and the first guide to water hash not because a publisher is paying well but because the information needs to exist in the world and he is the one who has it. This same person breeds over two hundred proprietary cultivars and watches one of them — Purple Kush, later forced to rename as Ultra Violate when plagiarism made the original name impossible to protect — spread across the global cannabis culture while his name gets left behind.

This person is Kenneth Morrow, deputized by the Oakland Cannabis Buyers Cooperative with a document that means nothing against a federal government that doesn't recognize it and goes back to work anyway. Morrow, who reconfigures the first vacuum oven for cannabis extraction and holds the first terpene isolation patent and appears on 60 Minutes in shadow because the knowledge is important enough to share nationally but the law makes the person sharing it invisible. And it is Morrow who helped build the system they still use and whose name is on none of the equipment running it.

A quiet architect with a lasting impact, Kenneth Morrow helped build the technical backbone of modern cannabis cultivation and extraction long before the spotlight arrived. Genetics, extraction, purification, formulations, education — others followed trends.

Kenneth “K” Morrow helped build the system still used today.

data.title: Michael Oberlaender
data.text:
== Michael S. Oberlaender ==
Michael S. Oberlaender is a cybersecurity executive and author. In March 2021 he was appointed chief information security officer (CISO) of LogMeIn. He is the author of the Global CISO series of books on CISO leadership, strategy and communication with boards.

== Career ==
Coverage of Oberlaender's 2021 appointment at LogMeIn described him as a 30-year industry veteran who had held CISO and advisory positions at other organizations, including Vodafone Deutschland, Cisco and Netskope. The coverage did not give his titles or dates at those companies.

== LogMeIn ==
In March 2021, LogMeIn named Oberlaender its chief information security officer. He was described as leading a global security team covering IT security, security operations, assurance, engagement, governance, risk management and compliance, and as responsible for the security of the company's internal systems and software products. LogMeIn's chief information officer, Ian Pitt, described him as a strategic partner for improving the company's software development lifecycle.

== Board and advisory roles ==
At the time of his LogMeIn appointment, Oberlaender was reported to serve on the board of the ISACA Greater Houston Chapter. In July 2024, Netenrich named him among the founding members of its Security Advisory Council. He is also listed as a speaker by SecureWorld.

== Certifications and memberships ==
Coverage of his 2021 appointment listed professional certifications including CISM, CISSP, CISA and CRISC, and memberships in (ISC)², ISACA, ISSA and InfraGard. These details are reported as of March 2021.

== Books ==
Oberlaender is the author of the Global CISO series.

* Global CISO — Strategy, Tactics, & Leadership: How to Succeed in InfoSec and CyberSecurity. Security Management reviewed the book in October 2020. The reviewer, Ben Rothke, described it as a playbook-style guide for new and experienced CISOs covering strategy, people, regulation, business goals and budgets, and noted its emphasis on security as an ongoing effort rather than a one-time project.
* Premier CISO — Board & C-Suite: Raising the Bar for Cybersecurity. Security Management reviewed the book in February 2025, describing it as the third volume in the series and as a practical guide to working with boards and executives. The review presented its central idea as CISOs earning board trust by communicating in business terms. Help Net Security discussed the book in a September 2024 interview with Oberlaender and included it in a March 2025 list of ten books for security leaders.

== Media appearances ==
In a September 2024 interview with Help Net Security, Oberlaender discussed fitting security into business processes, building a security strategy from scratch, and aligning with frameworks such as ISO, NIST and CIS. In March 2026, Fortra published a question-and-answer interview with him covering how he entered cybersecurity, the evolution of the CISO role, security culture, threats from artificial intelligence and quantum cryptography, limited CISO access to boards, and reliance on outsourced virtual CISOs.

= Who Is Lurkhs? =

== Overview ==
Lurkhs, known online by the username @[user], is a gaming content creator who uses TikTok to share content and develop his presence within online gaming communities. His public identity is centered around gaming, digital content creation, and building a recognizable personal brand. Through his online activity, Lurkhs is working to grow his audience and establish himself as a creator in the gaming space. [ref: Lurkhs]

Lurkhs maintains a distinction between his online identity and his private life, choosing to be recognized by his creator name rather than publicly sharing personal information. His TikTok account serves as the primary platform through which viewers can discover his content and follow his activity.

== Gaming Background ==
One of the main gaming communities associated with Lurkhs is Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege, a tactical first-person shooter developed by Ubisoft. The game features competitive team-based matches in which players rely on strategy, communication, map knowledge, and individual mechanical skill.

Rainbow Six Siege has developed a substantial content-creation community, with creators sharing gameplay highlights, competitive moments, entertaining clips, and videos showcasing different aspects of the game. Platforms such as TikTok have become an important part of this community, allowing creators to present shorter videos to audiences beyond the people they encounter in-game.

Gaming content can appeal to different types of viewers, including experienced competitive players, casual gamers, and people discovering a game for the first time. For creators associated with the Siege community, developing a recognizable style and maintaining an identifiable online presence can help distinguish their content from the many other videos published daily.

== TikTok and Social Media Presence ==
Lurkhs publishes content under the TikTok username @[user]. His profile provides a central location for viewers to access his videos and follow his development as a content creator.

TikTok allows gaming creators to reach audiences through short-form videos, where editing, pacing, entertainment, and the presentation of gameplay can influence how viewers respond to a post. Videos can reach people who do not already follow an account, giving smaller creators opportunities to introduce themselves to new audiences.

Lurkhs's account has approximately 1,100 followers. This audience represents the community he has developed around his online identity so far. Follower counts can change over time as creators publish new content, gain exposure, and attract viewers with similar interests.

His public-facing brand is built around the Lurkhs username. Maintaining a consistent creator identity across videos and online communities can make it easier for viewers to recognize an account and associate new content with the same creator.

== Content Creation and Audience Growth ==
Building an audience on social media involves more than simply uploading videos. Gaming creators often need to consider the type of content they publish, how videos are edited, which moments are most entertaining to viewers, and how their content fits into the wider gaming community.

Short-form gaming videos can feature impressive gameplay, humorous situations, close matches, unexpected moments, and highlights that communicate an experience in a short amount of time. The format also allows creators to experiment with different approaches and discover which styles connect most effectively with their audiences.

For creators in competitive gaming communities, consistency and recognizable presentation can contribute to long-term development. A distinct username, recognizable editing style, and an understanding of the intended audience can help create a more unified online presence.

Lurkhs's continued activity on TikTok provides a platform for developing his content and reaching additional viewers. As his library of videos grows, his account can serve as a record of his creative development and progress within the gaming content community.

== Personal Brand and Online Identity ==
The Lurkhs name functions as the central element of his online identity. Rather than relying on publicly available personal details, his creator profile allows audiences to associate his name with his published content.

An online gaming brand can extend beyond individual videos. A consistent name and presentation can help a creator maintain recognition across social media, gaming communities, and other digital platforms. These elements can become increasingly important as a creator develops new content, collaborates with other players, or explores additional opportunities within gaming.

Privacy is also an important consideration for online creators. Keeping personal information separate from a public creator identity allows someone to participate in online communities while maintaining boundaries around their life outside social media. Lurkhs's public identity is therefore centered on his creator name and online activity.

== Future Development ==
The gaming content industry continues to provide opportunities for creators to develop audiences through social media. TikTok, in particular, allows videos to reach viewers outside an account's existing follower base, making it possible for creators to expand their presence as their content evolves.

For Lurkhs, continued development can involve refining his content style, experimenting with different gaming videos, engaging with viewers, and establishing a consistent identity within the communities he participates in. Audience growth can vary depending on the content published, viewer interest, and how widely individual videos are shared.

As his online presence develops, the Lurkhs name remains the primary identifier for his public content. His TikTok profile provides the most direct way to view his published videos and follow changes to his audience.

data.title: Charles Lee Bevins
data.text:
----

22:11, 25 April 2026 (UTC)[user] Charles Lee Bevins is an American physician-scientist and immunologist known for his contributions to the study of antimicrobial peptides and innate immunity, particularly the role of defensins in epithelial host defense. His work on antimicrobial peptides has been described in independent scientific coverage as part of a broader shift in biomedical research that recognized endogenous antibiotics as key components of host defense.

== Early life and education ==

Bevins earned a Bachelor of Arts in biology from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County in 1976. He received both his MD and PhD in biochemistry from the University of Maryland School of Medicine in 1983 [ref: 1998 recipient of alumni award], where his doctoral mentor was Ralph M. Pollack [ref: Detection of a transient enzyme-steroid complex during active-site-directed irreversible inhibition of 3-oxo-delta 5-steroid isomerase, Biochemistry].

He completed residency training in pediatrics at the University of California, San Francisco and conducted postdoctoral research at the National Institutes of Health under the mentorship of Michael A. Zasloff [ref: LinkedIn Biography] [ref: Peptides from frog skin, Annu Rev Biochem].

== Career and research ==

Bevins began his academic career at the University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine, where he served as Assistant Professor of Pediatrics and Genetics. He later held a faculty research position at the Cleveland Clinic before joining the University of California, Davis in 2003, where he became Professor of Microbiology and Immunology in the School of Medicine and was later named Distinguished Professor [ref: University Website].

His research has focused on antimicrobial peptides and innate immunity at epithelial surfaces. Early work from his laboratory demonstrated that epithelial cells produce antimicrobial peptides, including tracheal antimicrobial peptide (TAP) [ref: Tracheal antimicrobial peptide, a cysteine-rich peptide from mammalian tracheal mucosa: peptide isolation and cloning of a cDNA, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A], supporting the concept that mucosal surfaces contribute actively to host defense.

Bevins’ work on antimicrobial peptides was discussed in contemporaneous scientific coverage as part of a group of discoveries that helped establish endogenous antimicrobial peptides as a major component of innate immunity.

Subsequent independent reviews of antimicrobial peptides have described these molecules as central components of innate immunity and host–microbe interactions, reflecting the emergence of the field to which Bevins contributed.

Bevins has also contributed to studies of defensins in intestinal immunity [ref: Paneth cells of the human small intestine express an antimicrobial peptide gene, J. Biol. Chem.] [ref: Defensin-6 mRNA in human Paneth cells: implications for antimicrobial peptides in host defense of the human bowel, FEBS Lett] [ref: Protection against enteric salmonellosis in transgenic mice expressing a human intestinal defensin, Nature], defensin function in the male reproductive tract [ref: A common mutation in the defensin DEFB126 causes impaired sperm function and subfertility, Sci Transl Med] [ref: Multifunctional glycoprotein DEFB126--a curious story of defensin-clad spermatozoa, Nat Rev Urol], the role of defensins in shaping the microbiota [ref: Enteric defensins are essential regulators of intestinal microbial ecology, Nat Immunol] [ref: The potter's wheel: the host's role in sculpting its microbiota, Cell Mol Life Sci], and host–microbe interactions [ref: Human α-defensin 6 promotes mucosal innate immunity through self-assembled peptide nanonets, Science], including research on Paneth cell function [ref: Paneth cells, antimicrobial peptides and maintenance of intestinal homeostasis, Nat Rev Microbiol] and inflammatory bowel diseases [ref: Reduced Paneth cell alpha-defensins in ileal Crohn's disease, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A].

== Media coverage and impact ==
Bevins’ research has been featured in independent scientific and general media. A 1993 feature in The Journal of NIH Research highlighted his work on antimicrobial peptides as part of an emerging field of “endogenous antibiotics.”

His research on the human defensin DEFB126 and its role in fertility was later covered by The New York Times in 2011.

== Honors and recognition ==

Bevins has received numerous honors for his research and mentorship, including:

* National Institutes of Health MERIT Award [ref: NIH Reporter]
* Distinguished Professor, University of California, Davis
* School of Medicine Research Award (University of California, Davis)
* Dean’s Awards for Excellence in Teaching and Mentoring (University of Pennsylvania, 1996 [ref: PENN Award]; University of California, Davis, 2007)

He has also served in leadership roles in the scientific community, including co-chairing a Gordon Research Conference on Antimicrobial Peptides in 2001 [ref: 2001 GRC].

== Selected contributions ==

Bevins is known for contributions to:

* Discovery and characterization of epithelial antimicrobial peptides
* Studies of defensins and Paneth cell biology
* Mechanisms of innate immunity at mucosal surfaces [ref: Inducible expression of an antibiotic peptide gene in lipopolysaccharide-challenged tracheal epithelial cells, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A]

== Selected publications ==
* Bevins, CL, Salzman, NH. "The potter’s wheel: The host’s role in sculpting its microbiota." Cell Mol Life Sci. 2011.
* Bevins CL, Salzman NH. "Paneth cells, antimicrobial peptides and maintenance of intestinal homeostasis." Nature Reviews Microbiology. 2011.
* Clevers, HC, Bevins, CL. "Paneth cells: maestros of the small intestinal crypts." Annu Rev Physiol. 2013.
* Salzman, NH, Bevins, CL. "Dysbiosis--a consequence of Paneth cell dysfunction." Semin Immunol. 2013.

== References ==

[ref: Taylor R. "Drugs 'R' Us: Finding New Antibiotics at the Endogenous Pharmacy." Journal of NIH Research. June 1993.] [ref: Belluck P. "Study Links Male Infertility to a Missing Protein." The New York Times. July 20, 2011.] [ref: Zasloff M. "Antibiotic peptides as mediators of innate immunity." Nature. 2002.] [ref: Hancock REW, Chapple DS. "Peptide antibiotics." Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy. 2000.] [ref: Ganz T. "Defensins: antimicrobial peptides of innate immunity." Nature Reviews Immunology. 2003.]

data.title: Linda mwananchi movement
data.text:
Linda Mwananchi is a Kenyan political movement established in 2026. The movement has been associated with opposition politics in Kenya and has participated in political mobilization and civic engagement activities ahead of the 2027 general election. In 2026, the movement adopted The Equitable Party as its political party vehicle and initiated a rebranding process under the name Linda Mwananchi. [ref: Political parties registrar approves Linda Mwananchi Movement Party name change - Breaking Kenya News] [ref: The Equitable Party to Rebrand to Linda Mwananchi Movement, Sifuna Confirms - Kenyans.co.ke, www.kenyans.co.ke]

== History ==

Linda Mwananchi emerged in 2026 amid political realignments within Kenya's opposition. The movement has been associated with Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, who has participated in its public activities and political engagements. [ref: Linda Mwananchi endorses Sifuna as 2027 presidential candidate, The Standard]
In September 2026, the Political Parties Disputes Tribunal issued a ruling concerning matters related to the movement's registration following a dispute involving the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties. [ref: ‘Linda Mwananchi movement’ name row heads to political parties tribunal, Citizen Digital]

== Activities ==

The movement advocates for citizen participation in governance, constitutionalism, accountability, and public involvement in democratic processes.

Linda Mwananchi has organized political rallies, public forums, and civic engagement events in different parts of Kenya. Its activities have focused on issues relating to governance, leadership, and preparations for the 2027 Kenyan general election.

Politicians associated with the movement have included Babu Owino, James Orengo, George Natembeya, and Bonny Khalwale. [ref: Linda Mwananchi group settles on Sifuna as its 2027 presidential candidate, Citizen Digital]

== Organization ==

The movement's activities have involved a combination of elected political leaders, party officials, and youth representatives. [ref: From broad-based to united opposition: How young women are shaping the 2027 General Election, Daily Nation] Media reports have identified Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna as one of the principal figures associated with the movement's public activities, alongside other politicians who have participated in its rallies and civic engagement programmes.

The movement has also incorporated youth representatives into its organizational structure. According to media reports, these representatives have participated in public outreach, civic education initiatives, and communication activities carried out under the Linda Mwananchi banner. [ref: Sifuna Picks Pauline Njoroge, Three Women For Linda Mwananchi Communication Team]

As of 2026, the movement's organizational structure continued to evolve alongside efforts to establish itself as a political organization ahead of the 2027 Kenyan general election. [ref: Linda Mwananchi endorses Sifuna as 2027 presidential candidate, The Eastleigh Voice]

== Reception ==

Linda Mwananchi has received media coverage in discussions concerning opposition politics, youth participation in governance, and political developments ahead of the 2027 general election. [ref: Linda Mwananchi leaders now prioritise individual interests ahead of 2027 elections, Daily Nation]

data.title: Gaetan Algoet
data.text:
Gaetan Algoet

Gaetan Algoet (born 7 January 1964) is a Belgian author and maritime researcher known for his work on historical shipwrecks, piracy, and geographical reconstructions. His work is based on early historical and mythological sources. He has published works in Dutch, English, German, and French. He is active as an independent researcher based in Belgium.

== Biography ==
Algoet was born in Germany. He worked for the Belgian Air Force. He is also certified Dive Master.

His interest in maritime research began in the Dominican Republic, where he met Czech marine archaeologist Lubos Kordac. He invited Algoet to conduct archival research on the French shipwreck La Viette with the American organization North Caribbean Research (NCR). This led to their first collaborative publication.

In 2009, Algoet made his debut as an author in cooperation with Lubos Kordac. Their book Verborgen en verloren schatten in de Dominicaanse Republiek was published in 2010 by Free Musketeers.

Over the following years, Algoet published through various Dutch and Belgian publishers before establishing his own imprint, Algoet Publishing. His works cover maritime history, piracy, and historical geography, including studies on Hispaniola, the Spanish Plate Fleet, and medieval legends.

In 2026, Algoet received regional media attention for his independent geographical reconstruction of the location of Avalon. This is a legendary island described in medieval chronicles. His findings were featured by the Belgian regional broadcaster ROBtv. [ref: ROBtv. "Locatie van mythisch eiland Avalon na 1500 jaar gevonden door Gaetan Algoet uit Begijnendijk." 2025. https://www.robtv.be/nieuws/locatie-van-mythisch-eiland-avalon-na-1500-jaar-gevonden-door-gaetan-algoet-uit-begijnendijk-chatgpt-geeft-mij-98-tot-99-procent-kans-204211]

== Works ==
=== Dutch-language works ===

* Verborgen en verloren schatten in de Dominicaanse Republiek (2010, with Lubos Kordac)
* Avalon onthuld – Het verloren Koninkrijk
* De Rode Piraat
* De grootste kaperbuit aller tijden - Piet Heyn en de Zilvervloot (2026)
* Amerika onthuld
* Historische scheepswrakken rond Hispaniola
* Tussen Velt en Bergh: 200 jaar verbonden
* Het Piratenleven Onthuld (three-volume series)
* De Slag in de Baai van Maimón
* Het geheim van de broederschap

=== International editions ===

* A Hundred Giants: The French Huguenot Experience in Florida: 1562–1565 (2018, with T. L. Armstrong and R. H. Baer Florida: Signum Ops)
* Avalon Revealed – The Lost Kingdom
* Avalon enthüllt – Das verlorene Königreich
* Avalon Révélé – Le Royaume Perdu
* The Pirate Life Revealed – 17th Century
* The Pirate Life Revealed – 18th Century
* Battle in Maimon Bay
* Piet Heyn (2026 Florida: Signum Ops)

== Reception ==
Algoet’s archival research on historical shipwrecks, including the Nuestra Señora de la Concepción, is cited on the English Wikipedia in the articles San Miguel (1551 shipwreck) and List of shipwrecks in the 16th century.

His research was referenced in the Brazilian historical study A Profundeza Do Mar Azul (2020) by historian and archaeologist Dalton Delfini Maziero. He cited Algoet’s work on early colonial shipwrecks. [ref: Maziero, Dalton Delfini. A Profundeza Do Mar Azul. Google Books. https://www.google.be/books/edition/A_Profundeza_Do_Mar_Azul/f5r7DwAAQBAJ?hl=nl&gbpv=1&dq=Ga%C3%ABtan+Algoet&pg=PT91&printsec=frontcover]

Algoet is listed as a contributing author by Field Manor, a historical museum in Florida, which highlights his co-authorship of A Hundred Giants: The French Huguenot Experience in Florida: 1562–1565. [ref: Field Manor Museum. "The Ais People." https://www.fieldmanor.org/the-ais-people]

He is also included on the Signum Ops Authors Page, an American platform documenting contributors to historical and archaeological publications. [ref: Signum Ops. "Authors Page." http://www.signumops.com/authors.html]

A maritime researcher on the TreasureNet forum described Algoet as “a marine archaeologist and very reliable man,” noting his expertise in early Dutch script and archival interpretation. [ref: TreasureNet Forum. "Any early Dutch script experts here?" https://www.treasurenet.com/threads/any-early-dutch-script-experts-here.162427/]

Standaard Boekhandel, a major Belgian bookseller, published a redactional description of Algoet’s book Avalon onthuld – Het verloren Koninkrijk, summarizing his methodology and referencing regional media coverage. [ref: Standaard Boekhandel. "Avalon onthuld – Het verloren Koninkrijk." https://www.standaardboekhandel.be/p/avalon-onthuld-9789403850023]

* Official website: http://www.GaetanAlgoet.eu

data.title: Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh
data.text:
Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh is a Palestinian-American journalist and media entrepreneur. He is the founder and editor-in-chief of @[user], a digital media publication and social media news outlet focused on news and culture for Muslim audiences. [ref: Meet the Accidental Editor in Chief of Muslim Media, Wired] [ref: Content creators surge past legacy media as news hits a tipping point, The Washington Post] He founded the publication while studying journalism at Rutgers University and was named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list in Media in 2021. [ref: Filling a Media Void for Young Muslims, Rutgers University Foundation] [ref: Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh, Forbes]

==Early life and education==

Al-Khatahtbeh is a first-generation Palestinian American. His mother was a Palestinian refugee and his father immigrated to the United States from Jordan.

He began his undergraduate studies at Rutgers University–Newark before transferring to Rutgers University–New Brunswick, where he studied journalism. He graduated from Rutgers in 2020 with a degree in journalism.

While a student, Al-Khatahtbeh became interested in creating media focused specifically on Muslim communities. According to Rutgers, after the 2017 executive order restricting travel from several Muslim-majority countries, he wrote an article about the policy for a journalism class and sought a Muslim-focused publication in which to publish it. His difficulty finding such an outlet contributed to his decision to develop his own publication.

==Career==

===Muslim===

Al-Khatahtbeh launched Muslim in February 2019 while he was a junior at Rutgers. The project initially included a weekly newsletter covering news related to Muslims before expanding into an online publication and social media network.

In April 2020, PAPER profiled Al-Khatahtbeh and the publication, describing Muslim as a media platform aimed primarily at Millennial and Generation Z Muslim audiences. Al-Khatahtbeh told the magazine that he created the platform in response to what he saw as a lack of Muslim-led coverage of issues affecting Muslim communities. [ref: Finally, a New Platform by Muslims for Muslims, PAPER]

Religion News Service also profiled Al-Khatahtbeh and Muslim in 2020, reporting that the publication was intended to reach young Muslims across different racial, sectarian and religious backgrounds. [ref: Meet Muslim, a new online publication for the Gen Z ummah, Religion News Service]

In 2020, Muslim drew wider attention after reporting on the use of a song containing a recitation of an Islamic hadith during Rihanna's Savage X Fenty fashion show. Forbes subsequently cited the story in its profile of Al-Khatahtbeh.

By 2021, the publication had expanded significantly on social media. Business Insider reported that the @[user] Instagram account had grown to more than 750,000 followers within two years and that the publication had expanded to platforms including TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat. [ref: How the 22-year-old who owns the @[user] Instagram handle used it to launch a disruptive media company, Business Insider]

Al-Khatahtbeh has also spoken publicly about the moderation of Palestinian content on social media platforms. During the 2021 Israel–Palestine crisis, the Columbia Journalism Review reported that Al-Khatahtbeh said he had documented thousands of instances in which Instagram users reported censorship or restrictions involving Palestine-related content. [ref: Social networks accused of censoring Palestinian content, Columbia Journalism Review]

In 2023, The Washington Post featured Al-Khatahtbeh in an article examining the growth of independent social-media news creators and their increasing role in how younger audiences consume news. The newspaper described him as one of a broader group of independent creators reshaping digital news consumption and reported that @[user] had accumulated millions of followers on Instagram and TikTok.

Al-Khatahtbeh was subsequently quoted by The Washington Post in its reporting on social-media moderation during the Israel–Gaza war, including concerns about restrictions affecting Palestinian and pro-Palestinian content. [ref: In Israel-Hamas war, social media isn't neutral, The Washington Post]

In May 2025, Meta restricted access to the @[user] Instagram account in India following a legal request from the Indian government. Agence France-Presse reported that users in India were shown a notice saying that access had been restricted because of a legal request. Al-Khatahtbeh publicly criticized the decision as censorship. [ref: Meta blocks major Muslim Instagram page in India amid rising conflict, The Guardian]

A 2026 profile in Wired examined Al-Khatahtbeh's development of Muslim from a student media project into a large social-first media operation. At the time of the profile, Wired reported that the publication had more than 12 million followers across its social-media platforms, including 6.7 million on Instagram.

==Recognition==

In 2021, Al-Khatahtbeh was included in Forbes 30 Under 30 list in the Media category for his work building Muslim. Rutgers later reported that he was the youngest person included on the Media list that year.

He also received grant support from the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation for the development of Muslim.

== References ==

data.title: Rick Robertson
data.text:
Richardson Robertson III, professionally known as Rick Robertson, is an American architect and principal of Robertson Partners Architects. His work includes private residences and proposals for large-scale urban development drawing on Neoclassical, Beaux-Arts, and other classical architectural traditions. His projects include the Fleur de Lys estate in Los Angeles and proposed residential developments in California and New York.

== Career and residential architecture ==

Robertson designed Fleur de Lys, a French-inspired estate in Los Angeles, which was featured in Matt Tyrnauer’s 2002 Vanity Fair article “Versailles on the Pacific”. [ref: Tyrnauer, Matt. “Versailles on the Pacific.” Vanity Fair, April 2002.] The Los Angeles Times also reported on the estate and Robertson’s work. [ref: Ryon, Ruth. “Now Anchored in Hollywood.” Los Angeles Times, December 13, 1998.]

Jeff Hyland’s The Legendary Estates of Beverly Hills includes a chapter on Fleur de Lys describing its site, architecture, construction, and landscape. [ref: Hyland, Jeff. The Legendary Estates of Beverly Hills. New York: Rizzoli, 2008. Chapter: “Carolwood Drive: Fleur de Lys.”] The property was assembled from six adjacent parcels to create a site of approximately five acres.

In 2014, the Los Angeles Times reported that Fleur de Lys had sold for $102 million. The article identified Robertson as its architect and quoted his description of the house as a Neoclassical design conceived as a decorative arts museum rather than one based on a traditional French floor plan. [ref: Beale, Lauren. “Westside mansion sells for $102 million, highest Southland price.” Los Angeles Times, April 1, 2014.]

In April 2007, C Magazine published Degen Pener’s profile “Classical Artist,” examining Robertson’s career, architectural philosophy, and use of classical precedents in residential and urban design. [ref: Pener, Degen. “Classical Artist.” C Magazine, April 2007.]

Robertson designed a Mediterranean-style house in Tulsa, Oklahoma, for Bobby and Leslie Lorton. Southern Accents featured the residence in “Together in Tulsa” in its May–June 2007 issue, discussing its limestone exterior, classical detailing, and the clients’ interest in historical architectural accuracy. [ref: Fox, Marion Laffey. “Together in Tulsa.” Southern Accents, May–June 2007.]

In January–February 2014, Veranda published “Glamorous Texas Home,” featuring a Dallas residence designed by Robertson. The article credited Beverly Field with the interior design, Nancy Perot with the text, and Max Kim-Bee with the photography. [ref: Perot, Nancy. “Glamorous Texas Home.” Veranda, January–February 2014. Interior design by Beverly Field; architecture by Richardson Robertson III; photography by Max Kim-Bee.]

In 2010, the Los Angeles Times featured a French Normandy-style residence designed by Robertson at Lake Arrowhead, California. [ref: Marshutz, Scott. “Home of the Week: Chateau on Lake Arrowhead.” Los Angeles Times, September 5, 2010.] In 2019, the newspaper identified him as the architect of a Mediterranean-style residence in Los Angeles’s Bird Streets neighborhood offered for sale by former motorcycle racer John Kocinski. [ref: Flemming, Jack. “Retired motorcycle racer John Kocinski asks $30 million for Bird Streets abode.” Los Angeles Times, January 16, 2019.]

== Classical architecture and urban design ==

In December 2007, Angeleno published Gaby Baum’s “The Limestone Cowboy,” a feature examining Robertson’s design for City House, a proposed residential tower in downtown Los Angeles. [ref: Baum, Gaby. “The Limestone Cowboy.” Angeleno, December 2007, pp. 102–103.] The article discussed the project’s limestone cladding, bas-relief decoration, and granite cobblestone motor court in the context of Robertson’s approach to classical architecture.

Baum examined Robertson’s preference for a prominent entrance and a formal motor-court arrival sequence, contrasting this arrangement with modern buildings whose service functions are organized around rear alleys. The article also discussed his architectural philosophy in relation to contemporary modernist architecture and architects including Thom Mayne and Frank Gehry.

The feature presented City House as an example of Robertson’s advocacy of what he called a “New Beaux Arts” approach, incorporating historical architectural references, traditional materials, and ornamental detail into a contemporary high-rise design. The article documented his application of these principles to proposed urban development as well as residential architecture.

In 2009, Robertson published The Future of Classicism: New Beaux Arts, The Architecture of Richardson Robertson III, a 300-page book documenting his architectural work, including houses, estates, new towns, and proposed skyscrapers. [ref: Robertson, Richardson III. The Future of Classicism: New Beaux Arts, The Architecture of Richardson Robertson III. Blurb, 2009. [https://www.blurb.com/b/728925-the-future-of-classicism-new-beaux-arts-the-archite Book listing].]

Robertson’s City House and Olympic proposals received coverage in several publications. In April 2006, Los Angeles Times staff writer Roger Vincent reported on a proposed $500-million residential development at the southeast corner of Olympic Boulevard and Grand Avenue in downtown Los Angeles. [ref: Vincent, Roger. “Developer Promises Two Condo High-Rises Nearby.” Los Angeles Times, April 24, 2006.] The plans comprised City House, a proposed 60-story tower, and the Olympic, a proposed 50-story tower, with a combined total of 330 residential units. The report described plans for limestone cladding and discussed Robertson’s classical architectural approach in contrast with contemporary glass-and-steel high-rises, including his interest in precedents such as Los Angeles City Hall.

Steve Cutler’s “New York Living Goes Global,” published in New York Living Magazine in December 2006–January 2007, described plans for the Olympic, a proposed 49-story tower with 150 condominium apartments, and City House, a proposed 60-story tower with 180 units. The article discussed their limestone exteriors and classical detailing, Robertson’s references to New York museums and the former Pennsylvania Station, and his comments on the projects. [ref: Cutler, Steve. “New York Living Goes Global.” New York Living Magazine, December 2006–January 2007, pp. 34–35.]

In May 2006, David Brussat discussed Robertson’s proposed towers in The Providence Journal article “Angeleno inspiration for Providence,” considering their designs in the broader context of classical architecture in contemporary American cities. [ref: Brussat, David. “Angeleno inspiration for Providence.” The Providence Journal, May 18, 2006, p. B5.]

In May 2003, Urban Land published Brad Berton’s “Northern Gateway,” an article about Las Lomas, a proposed master-planned community in Los Angeles County that identified Robertson as the project’s architect. [ref: Berton, Brad. “Northern Gateway.” Urban Land, May 2003, pp. 74–78.]

Robertson developed the Setauket Village Center proposal to redevelop the Route 25A retail district in Setauket, Long Island. [ref: Mastrosimone, Peter C. “A New Vision of Setauket Unveiled: Village center and park could remake Route 25A.” The Village Times Herald, October 9, 2003, pp. A1, A13.] In October 2003, The Village Times Herald described his plan to bring together three shopping plazas with apartments or condominiums above shops, a village green, gardens, a pond, and an amphitheater. The article characterized the design as a Beaux-Arts reinterpretation of early American architecture incorporating Tudor and shingle-style elements. It also quoted Robertson on modern architecture and Long Island’s changing development pattern.

In November 2003, Newsday reported on the proposed village-center development in “Big Plans Afoot for East Setauket”. [ref: Wotapka, Dawn. “Big Plans Afoot for East Setauket.” Newsday, November 10, 2003.] Later that month, the newspaper’s editorial board published “A Model for Revitalizing LI Towns,” presenting the proposal’s combination of housing above retail space and a community park as a potential model for downtown revitalization. [ref: Klurfeld, James M., and Richards, Carol R. “A Model for Revitalizing LI Towns.” Newsday, November 28, 2003, p. A42.]

== Other architectural projects ==

In 2013, the Los Angeles Times reported on Robertson’s design for a proposed 25,000-square-foot penthouse at the W Hollywood. The planned residence included four bedrooms, a ballroom, a screening room, a trophy room, a fitness center, and a beauty parlor. [ref: Lelyveld, Nita. “Above it all in Hollywood.” Los Angeles Times, May 19, 2013.]

In a 2008 article about Château Élysée in Los Angeles, The New Yorker included Robertson’s observations on the building and its architectural character. [ref: Goodyear, Dana. “Château Scientology.” The New Yorker, January 14, 2008.]

== Awards and honors ==

A 2007 C Magazine profile reported that Robertson received the Los Angeles Star of Design Award from the Pacific Design Center. The article also reported that his design for the Fleur de Lys estate in Holmby Hills earned him recognition from the French government for his contributions to French-style architecture.

Your Pink Bits (YPB) is an Australian intimate skincare brand launched in 2024. [ref: Your Pink Bits launches Intimate Brightening Cream, What She Just Said] The company produces cosmetic skincare products for external intimate and body skin and has been featured in Australian beauty and lifestyle publications in connection with the growth of the intimate skincare category. [ref: From Face to Everywhere: Why Skincare Is Going South -]

== History ==
Your Pink Bits launched in Australia in late 2024 following approximately two years of research and development. [ref: Make Merry Monday #67: Eat, Drink, Buy, Try, Visit & Read, Onya Magazine] The brand entered the market with its Intimate Brightening Cream, a cosmetic skincare product developed for external intimate skin.

At launch, media coverage focused on the brand's use of conventional skincare ingredients and Australian botanical extracts within the emerging intimate skincare category. In 2025, Eat Live Escape included Your Pink Bits in its coverage of the expansion of skincare beyond traditional facial care, discussing the brand in the context of increasing consumer interest in specialised intimate skincare.

== Products ==
The company's principal product is an intimate brightening cream developed for use on external intimate and body skin. The product is marketed for areas including the bikini line, inner thighs, underarms and external buttock and perianal areas. [ref: Natural Intimate Skin Brightening & Lightening Cream, Your Pink Bits®]

The company describes the product as a cosmetic product for the appearance of dark spots and uneven-looking skin tone. Its listed ingredients include vitamin C, turmeric extract, Australian finger lime extract, papaya enzyme and aloe vera.

== Reception ==
The launch of Your Pink Bits received coverage from Australian beauty and lifestyle publications. What She Just Said covered the launch of the brand's Intimate Brightening Cream in November 2024., while Bondi Beauty included the product in its 2024 beauty stocking-filler guide as part of its coverage of intimate beauty products. [ref: 9 of the Best Beauty Stocking Fillers]

In 2025, Eat Live Escape discussed Your Pink Bits in a feature examining the expansion of skincare beyond facial care and the growth of specialised intimate and body skincare. Onya Magazine subsequently featured the brand in its Make Merry Monday lifestyle series.
