data.title: The Castillejos Oppidum
data.text:
----

The settlement of Los Castillejos, located in the municipality of Sanchorreja in the province of Ávila in Spain, was a hill fort or oppidum (also known as a castro) where people lived between the late Chalcolithic or Early Bronze Age and the fifth century BC. Although some archaeological excavations have taken place, the ruins are hardly visible here. [ref: Guía. Castro de Los Castillejos. Sanchorreja, Ávila]

The oppidum of “Los Castillejos” is one of the most important archaeological sites in the province of Ávila. The stratigraphic sediments have a depth of 2.0 meters. The range of the sediments can be traced from the late Chalcolithic or early Bronze Age until the fifth century BC, when the settlement was gradually abandoned by its inhabitants without any signs of cultural Romanization. [ref: Vetones: historia y arqueología de un pueblo prerromano, UAM Ediciones]

These people are considered as the predecessor of what would become later the Vettones, who founded new relevant settlements in the province of Avila like La Mesa de Miranda, Las Cogotas, Ulaca or El Raso.

The first archaeological excavations took place in the decade of 1930 by Joaquín María de Navascués, Emilio Camps Cazorla, and Juan Cabré. But the first findings were not published until 20 years later by Juan Maluquer [ref: El Castro de los Castillejos en Sanchorreja. Estudio de las excavaciones realizadas por D. Juan Cabré, D. Joaquín María de Navascués, y D. Emilio Camps, de 1931 a 1935]. An additional archaeological excavation took place later in the years 1981, 1982 and 1985 by F. J. González-Tablas Sastre.

The archaeological findings include many different types of ceramics, personal items made of bronze (buttons, needles, brooches, belt buckles), and utensils made of iron (axes, knives).

Some metal recipients found in the settlement, the ceramic techniques and types used, as well as one of the belt buckles with the representation of a griffin, are typical samples of western cultures like the Phoenicians, which had colonies around the Mediterranean area of the Iberian Peninsula at that time. Therefore, those items found at Los Castillejos are a confirmation that there was some type of exchange between the people who lived here and the coastal inhabitants of the Peninsula.

== References ==

GONZÁLEZ-TABLAS SASTRE, F.J. y DOMÍNGUEZ CALVO, A.; Los Castillejos de Sanchorreja. Campañas de 1981, 1982 y 1985. Acta Salmanticensia 117. Salamanca. 2002.

data.title: Cryptocurrency Operation in Texas
data.text:
Cryptocurrency Operations in Texas

Cryptocurrency operations in Texas include areas such as cryptocurrency mining, trading, and business services. The development of cryptocurrency related services is largely attributed to Texas’s energy system, business environment, and state regulations. Originally starting with the Bitmain mining center in Rockdale in 2018, and boosted by China's refusal to continue operations in 2021, The state of Texas has seen an increase in operations, mostly in cryptomining. Because of this growth, an increase in jobs has occurred, alongside a rise in environmental concerns and scams.

== History ==
In December of 2017, it was announced that the town of Rockdale would lose the Alcoa smelting factory. The facility, founded in 1952, was the lifeline of the city, and brought in jobs which, in turn, doubled the population. This crippled the town's economy, and left many without a reliable source of income. This would soon change, as on October 21, 2019, things would change for Rockdale, as Bitmain (Now Bitdeer), a notable cryptocurrency equipment manufacturer and cryptomining company, announced plans to purchase the rusting Alcoa factory and convert it into a cryptomining facility. This marked the start of cryptocurrency's rise in Texas, as the Bitmain facility, despite taking three years to build alongside multiple delays, proved that large scale operations could be made. [ref: Mayor of Rockdale says Bitcoin mining saved the town’s economy, Cryptopolitan]

On May 31, 2021, China, then the world's leading cryptomining nation, would pass a law stating that cryptocurrency trading, mining, and related services would be permanently banned amid energy consumption, financial regulation, and illegal activity. [ref: The China Bitcoin Ban: A History of Shifting Regulations, OKX]
Upon hearing this news, Greg Abbott, Governor of Texas, would state that “Texas is open for Crypto business.” on X, signaling the start of many cryptomining operations in Texas and the United States. [ref: A North Texas community will vote to form a city in an effort to quiet down a crypto mine, The Texas Tribune]

On October 7, 2021, Core Scientific Holding Co. announced that the company, alongside the city of Denton, agreed to make a cryptomining facility. [ref: Crypto mine to be turned into $6B data center in Denton, Dallas Buisness Journal]Although the Core Scientific cryptocurrency mine was the largest mine announced in 2021, multiple cryptocurrency mining companies such as Riot, Cipher Mining, US Bitcoin, Rhodium, and Bitdeer announced and began to construct cryptomines. Notable examples include the creation of the Alborz, Bear, Chief and Odessa sites. [ref: Bitcoin Mining Companies in 2026: MARA, Riot, CleanSpark and the Public Crypto Miners Explained, Miner Compare]

On April 16, 2022 The Fort Worth City Council voted in favor of buying crypto equipment and actively mining cryptocurrency. With the council accepting a donation of three Bitcoin mining machines from the Texas Blockchain Council. “The goal wasn’t to make money, that wasn’t the primary objective. It was for people to know about the city, know that Fort Worth is a dynamic, forward-thinking city and doing innovative things that no other cities have done. So in that sense, it’s been very successful.” Stated Carlo Capua, chief of strategy and innovation. [ref: Fort Worth was the first city to adopt bitcoin mining to attract attention. Was it worth it?, Fort Worth Report]

Throughout 2022, multiple cryptocurrency plants were made, most notably with Cipher Mining. Cipher Mining would create the Alborz and Chief cryptomines in early 2022, with the Alborz mine starting mining operations on August 9, and the Chief mine becoming operational in mid October. Cipher Mining would also create the Bear mine, which would start construction in mid 2022. Alongside opening their most notable operation, the Odessa cryptomining facility. The facility started mining cryptocurrency on November 29, and has been expanded multiple times, most recently in 2024. [ref: Cipher Mining, A Bitcoin Miner Installs 40-MW Wind Powered Site In Texas, DC Forecasts] Compute North would create the Upton County cryptomine in February, and would eventually file for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy on September 22, leading to their assets being seized and given to rivals. [ref: Compute North Post-Mortem: When Hosting Customers Went Broke First, Idea Proof]A joint effort by MARA and US Bitcoin would lead to the construction of the Granbury mine in mid April, [ref: MARA-Granbury, MARA] And Riot would begin construction of the Corsicana mine, with groundbreaking beginning in October. [ref: Construction of Navarro County Bitcoin Mining Site Met by Protesters, NBC DFW] By the end of 2022, there were at least twenty seven mining operations within Texas as reported by the Texas Comptroller. [ref: Cryptocurrency in Texas: Opportunities and Challenges in Mining Digital Coins, Texas Comptroller]

On January 1, 2023, Bitcoin hit an all time low with a price of $16,625.08. This sparked many debates over the ethics and profitability of cryptomining within the state. The drop in price, combined with rising electricity costs, increased the break even price and profit margin, allowing for major operations to be delayed or run on a shorter platform than usual. [ref: A Visual Look Back on Bitcoin in 2023, Coin Market Cap]

As of April 2023, five of the ten biggest cryptocurrency mines in the world were within Texas's borders. According to the CGAA journal, more electricity was being consumed by facilities, shown by the top five mines using a total of 1,212 MW of power — the equivalent to the electricity use of over 240,000 Texas homes. [ref: Bitcoin Mining in Texas: Understanding the Energy and Economic Impact, CGAA]

On September 26, 2023, CNBC would state that national and international cryptomining companies were moving operations to Texas. [ref: Texas paid bitcoin miner Riot $31.7 million to shut down during heat wave in August, CNBC]Operations in Nebraska, North Carolina, and Kentucky would be moved, and European and Asian companies were actively attempting to buy land and build cryptomines in Texas.

During November 8 and 9 of 2023, Texans voted on, and passed, Proposition 7. Proposition 7 would create the Texas Energy Fund, alongside a grid and generation policy. A majority of all funds generated would go towards dispatchable power generation for cryptocurrency mines, with additional funding for microgrids and grid work for public electricity utilities. [ref: Texas voters approve $10B energy fund, with most going to build gas-fired power plants, Utility Dive]

On February 22, 2024, Riot Platforms and the Texas Blockchain Council (TBC) filed a lawsuit against the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Energy Information Administration (EIA) due to a misleading and "unnecessary" survey meant to collect data from crypto mining companies on energy use, alongside sensitive operational details. Riot and the Texas Blockchain Council would also state that the survey violated numerous laws such as the Administrative Procedure Act and PRA.
On March 24, The DOE and EIA agreed to withdraw the survey after a court hearing on February 28 in Waco, TX. [ref: Texas Blockchain Council v. Department of Energy, New Civil Liberties Alliance]

On May 1, 2024, nine citizens of Hood County sued MARA, specifically the Granbury cryptomine, over health, property-values and regulation infractions. Residents cited migraines, tinnitus, insomnia, anxiety, and hearing loss, alongside declining property values and an harmful impact on livestock behavior and farm operations. The Granbury mine had faced complaints before, most notably in April of 2024 where county inspector John Shirley issued 37 citations to the facility, with a majority of complaints being based off of noise pollution. [ref: Texas Homeowners Sue MARA Over Granbury Bitcoin Mine Noise, The Chain Observer–Crypto News]

Between May and August of 2024, The Texas Observer stated that the Corpus Chrisi cryptomine was using 127,500 gallons per day, well above the city’s threshold of 100,000 gallons/day. This would add up to an estimated 11.56 million gallons of water used between May and August. During this time, Corpus Christi was in the midst of a drought, and public resources were often strained. [ref: Last Year, a Corpus Christi Cryptomine Guzzled over 11 Million Gallons. Now, Its Water Usage Is Being Kept Secret, The Texas Observer]

On November 21, 2024, The Public Utility Commission of Texas passed a registration rule stating that all cryptomining operations had to register to report information such as location, ownership and electricity demand to ERCOT by February 1, 2025. The rule, inspired by the February 22 lawsuit, allowed regulators a better view of operations and their impact within the state. [ref: Crypto miners must register with state and reveal power usage under new Texas rule, The Texas Tribune]

From December of 2024 to February of 2025, Chris Jones, a former technician at Riot’s Corsicana facility filed multiple complaints to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Texas Attorney General’s Office, and the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA). Jones alleged that Riot was misusing public funds, altering financial information, and had unsafe electrical infrastructure within their facilities. Alongside how he was fired after stating the previously stated claims on social media. [ref: The Crypto Racket, The American Prospect]

On May 15 of 2025, the Texas Attorney General’s office sided with journalists seeking records to cryptomining operations in the state. The Attorney General's office also stated that the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) had not shown that releasing the requested information would expose critical-infrastructure weaknesses. [ref: State utility commission sues Texas attorney general to avoid releasing data on crypto companies’ power use, The Texas Tribune] PUCT would respond with a lawsuit on June 27, stating that releasing the requested information, specifically regarding electricity management and locations, would put statewide power infrastructure at risk. [ref: Texas agency sues to stop release of data center records that it says could aid terrorists, The Texas Tribune]

In August of 2025, residents near MARA's Granbury mine revived a plan to incorporate Mitchell Bend as a town, hoping that creating a local government could address noise concerns brought by the cryptomine. [ref: Bitcoin Business Tries to Derail Hood County Neighborhood’s Incorporation, Texas Scoreboard] In response, MARA would file a federal lawsuit on October 7 of 2025, claiming that the proposed town intentionally targeted and would disrupt operations. After review, county judge Ron Massingill allowed to election to proceed, with November 4 being chosen as the election date. [ref: MARA Sues to Block Texas County Vote Creating Town Around Its Bitcoin Mine, The Energy Magazine] On the day of the election, Hood County residents voted to reject the incorporation proposal, with a 62% of 138 votes majority. [ref: North Texas community votes against forming a city to regulate a noisy Bitcoin mine, The Texas Tribune]

From April 2 to May 28 of 2026, the Public Utility Commission and Texas Water Development Board conducted a voluntary survey on electricity and water use by data centers and cryptocurrency-mining facilities that planned to operate through 2030. The survey asked about facility location, power demand, cooling and water use. [ref: Texas PUC Sues Paxton to Keep Data Center Locations Confidential, Texas Policy Research]

On October 5 of 2026, the Public Utility Commission sued Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office over the release of information regarding the facility’s location and water-usage. The commission argued that releasing the information given would create a security risk to multiple facilities and companies. [ref: Texas agency sues to stop release of data center records that it says could aid terrorists, The Texas Tribune]

== Architecture ==
=== Mining ===
By far the most notable characteristic of cryptomines are the large, but dense, rows of buildings that house the cryptomining equipment, alongside air conditioning units that sit inside or outside the buildings. Cryptomines in Texas use many nationally and globally recognised equipment, such as ASIC miners, GPU mining rigs, Power Supply Units, and advanced cooling systems. [ref: Top Tools for Cryptocurrency Mining in 2025: The Complete Guide, Gate] The cooling systems are vital to the mines operations, and are responsible for keeping the expensive equipment from overheating by using immersion cooling (found in some facilities) and standard air conditioning fans. [ref: 8 Most Profitable Crypto Mining Machines: Expert Tested for 2025, Mineshop] Cryptomines also use ethernet switches, routers, and fiber optic cables for network connection and better coordination between machines. The fiber optic cables can also link up to industrial grade servers and monitoring software that track hashrates, temperatures, power usage, and network connectivity. [ref: Mining Machinery: ATEX/IECEx Certified Guide (2026), Intrinsically Safe]

=== Facility setup ===
Operations are often set up close to or on active or previously active electricity infrastructure, such as power plants, factories, and industrial parks, with many key components being upgraded and reused. By doing so, electricity can be easily used and distributed among the facilities buildings, and facilities can save money on infrastructure and utilities implementation. In terms of power distribution, electricity flows from city or county based grids to substations and Air Conditioning, offices, and communication and control centers. The most notable part of the flow of electricity is the mining equipment, which are housed in dense rows. Cryptomining computers and equipment reside within the buildings, and are in constant operation. [ref: Cryptocurrency in Texas: Opportunities and Challenges in Mining Digital Coins, Texas Comptroller] Inside and outside the buildings are hundreds of air conditioning units that run constantly, alongside immersion-cooling systems providing additional cooling power. [ref: Riot Platforms: The Company Behind the Most Energy Intensive Bitcoin Mine in the U.S., Greenpeace]

Cryptomining facilities can also serve a multipurpose role. In January of 2026, Riot announced that a building part of its Rockdale facility was undergoing renovations to become an AMD data-center lease. [ref: Riot to convert cryptomine site in Texas to HPC, signs 25MW lease with AMD, Data Center Dynamics] Multiple cryptomines have also undergone renovations, with some mines being fully converted to data centers. Core Scientific's Denton campus is a great example, with the 78 acre site undergoing a full conversion that, when completed, would create one of the largest data centers in the country. The campus alone would house multiple tenants such as OpenAI and CoreWeave, and feature space for computing power beside data operations. [ref: Denton Data Center Campus: From Core Scientific Crypto Mining Site into a Major U.S. AI Hub, Construction Review]

== Economics ==
=== Profitability ===
A key aspect of the profitability of cryptomines is electricity. Texas has a deregulated power market alongside large amounts of renuable and nonrenuable energy. Because of this, energy is available at a cheap cost, which helps miners reduce operating costs. [ref: Cheap Electricity Made Texas a Hub for Crypto Mining and Data Centers but New Regulations Could Slow Growth, Crypto Citizens Network] Large mining operations can also sign up and participate for ERCOT demand-response and electricity management programs. The demand-response program is particularly designed to support cryptomining facilities by financially incentivizing them to shut down part, or all of, their operations during times of high electricity demand. [ref: Texan Bitcoin miners profit by using less electricity; advocates say all Texans should get the same chance, The Texas Tribune] During the August of 2023 heatwave, Riot earned about $31.7 million by scaling back electricity demand within the Rockdale cryptomine. In August alone, Riot would mine $8.9 million worth of Bitcion across it's operations. [ref: Texas paid bitcoin miner Riot $31.7 million to shut down during heat wave in August, CNBC] By doing so, cryptomines can make money off of ERCOT based incentives, alongside mining cryptocurrency and avoiding expensive power. Despite many financial motivations, profitability is not guaranteed when Bitcoin prices fall, network difficulty rises, and electricity costs increase. [ref: Bitcoin Miners Texas Grid Curtailment Faces an Incentive Cliff, Watcher News]

=== Upkeep ===
Keeping systems cool is the biggest challenge that cryptomines face. Cryptomining machines turn all of their operating power into heat, and combined with Texas's heatwaves, can prove to be a major challenge for cryptomines. Air Conditioning, especially for the mining equipment, is often a carefully planned mix of fans, ventilation, intake filters, and water-system maintenance. [ref: How to Design Optimal Airflow for a Bitcoin Mining Facility, Hashrate Index] The intake filters in particular are crucial to cryptomining, as they are often replaced and checked on for dust and other particles. If left unchecked, dust-clogged filters restrict airflow and can contribute to overheating or equipment damage.

Cryptomining facilities also deal with electrical infrastructure upkeep, as numerous substations, transformers, switchgear, and high-voltage connections mean constant inspections and maintenance. Because of this, one possible infrastructure failure could cause a large portion of the mine to shut down. Hardware in particular is a constant repair-and-replacement job. Fans, power supplies, cables, and mining hash boards can fail, so operators need spare parts, repair staff, and plans for emergencies or replacements. [ref: How a Texas Bitcoin Mining Facility Used A Multi-Layered Filtration Approach to Protect Air Intakes From High Wind Dust Infiltration, Smith Filer Corporation]

== Operations ==
=== Location ===
Many cryptomines, such as Riots Rockdale facility, uses and adds onto previously made electricity infrastructure to save money and advance operations quicker. MARA's Granbury, McCamey, and Garden City mines follow this rule, as they operate close to power plants to provide a steady flow of electricity. [ref: Cryptocurrency in Texas: Opportunities and Challenges in Mining Digital Coins, Texas Comptroller] Most cryptomines operate near rural towns, and are sometimes close to lakes for easier water consumption.

As previously stated, most cryptomines are based in rural Texas, with the Odessa and Fort Worth mines being the only two urban based cryptomining facilities. According to Bloomberg in September of 2024, western Texas had a reported seven cryptomines, the most by region in the state. South central Texas had four cryptomines, and north and north central Texas were tied with three cryptomines in each region. [ref: Texas Tug of War: Grid Juggles Solar Boom and Power-Hungry Data Centers, Bloomberg] It is theorized that there are more cryptomines within far western Texas and the Texas panhandle, but no publicly shared information has been released regarding that theory.

=== Size ===
The size of cryptomines vary drastically, and can vary based on land used, total land area, and electricity usage. The largest cryptomine in Texas as of October 2026 (By size and electricity usage) is Riot Platforms Rockdale facility, which uses an average of 700 megawatts to support operations across 200 total acres of land. [ref: Rockdale, Riot Platforms] The largest cryptomine based off of total land area is Riots Corsicana campus, spanning 858 acres meant for cryptomining and data operations. [ref: Riot Platforms acquires additional 238 acres at Corsicana, Texas, campus, Data Center Dynamics] It is unknown what the smallest cryptomine is, as the state of Texas's registration system focuses on large facilities, so it doesn’t provide a complete list of smaller operations.

=== Ownership ===
Riot is the biggest cryptomining company in Texas, with the two biggest cryptomines in both electricity usage and size, Rockdale and Corsicana, being under Riots jurisdiction. [ref: Corsicana, Riot Platforms] MARA is also significant, as the Granbury, Garden City, and Hartford cryptomines used a combined 594 megawatts of power, alongside the King Mountain location that MARA uses but does not own. Bitdeer, despite founding the first cryptomine in Texas, operates a cryptomine close to Riots Rockdale mine, alongside a few smaller operations in Milam county. [ref: MARA- Portfolio, MARA] Cipher Digital, despite being the smallest of the four, operates the Odessa cryptomine. Cipher Digital has previously conducted cryptomining operations at the Black Pearl facility up until February of 2026, as the site has been transformed into a data center for Amazon. [ref: Bitdeer Announces Acquisition of 200 Acres Near Rockdale Facility in Milam County, Texas to Support AI/HPC Infrastructure Development, Bitdeer]

== Laws ==
Texas is one of the most crypto‑friendly U.S. states. However, Texas lacks clear and specific laws, regulations, and consequences for electricity use, grid connections, and the facility’s location and equipment. Because of this, cities and counties are often left to develop and enforce their own laws regarding cryptomining operations. There are some laws set by ERCOT and the state of Texas, however, those laws primarily focus on electricity usage and electricity management and not cryptomining operations.

=== State of Texas ===
Arguably the most important Texas based cryptomining law is Senate Bill 6. Passed into law on June 20, 2025, the bill addresses the "Large electricity loads" crypromining and data centers have on Texas's energy grid. With grid reliability, cost allocation, and coordination and interconnections all being addressed. [ref: Texas Senate Bill 6: Understanding the Impacts to Large Loads and Co-located Generation, Baker Botts] Another notable law is the PUCT registration rule, which requires all cryptomining facilities to register as a "Large electric load" center if the facility uses more than 75 MW to operate and can stop at least 10% of its actual or anticipated peak demand during crucial events. By registering, facilities must constantly update their ownership, site details, power-use data, and demand forecasts to ERCOT. Violations include fines up to $25,000 USD per day. [ref: 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.114 - Registration of Virtual Currency Mining Facilities, Cornell Law School]

Outside of addressing large electricity loads, Texas has passed no laws related to noise pollution, expansions, water usage, and environmental impact that are associated with cryptomining. Leaving counties and cities to develop and enforce their own laws.

=== Counties ===
Most county based cryptomining laws primarily focus on industrial land-development and facility operations, whether they cover a cryptomining facility depends on the wording of each measure implemented by the county. Counties may not, however, pass their own noise ordinances for unincorporated areas. Instead, counties rely on state law, which states that noise is unreasonable if it exceeds 85 decibels after a peace officer has given notice.

Hood county is a great example. In June 18, 2025, the county obtained permission from the state to sign into law a bill that would regulate the size of an industrial lot, water and electric utilities and management, and the size of buildings developed. The rules target a variety of possible operations, not just cryptomining within the county. [ref: 2025 Texas Statutes Local Government Code Title 7 - Regulation of Land Use, Structures, Businesses, and Related Activities. Subtitle B - County Regulatory Authority. Chapter 231 - County Zoning Authority. Subchapter K. Development Regulations in Hood County Section 231.223. Development Regulations Generally, JUSTIA]

In Austin county, lawmakers paused data center projects over community and environmental impacts concerns. Under a proposed law, developers must submit and certify that the needed equipment complies with specified state restrictions before construction can begin. Whether the law covers cryptomining depends on whether that project fits the definition of an AI data center. [ref: AUSTIN CO. COMMISSIONERS ENACT MORATORIUM ON DATA CENTERS, BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS, KWHI]

=== Cities ===
Just like counties, most city based rules primarily apply to data centers and industrial uses. Because of this, whether or not a cryptomining facility is included depends on the facility’s location and how city codes and ordinances define it.

In El Paso, the city adopted a policy in June of 2026 that would require data centers to obtain a special-use permit, clearly outline noise mitigation, and install a 300-foot buffer from homes or ecological sites. In addition, developers must provide plans for water and energy use, emissions, noise, and water treatment. Although it does not specifically address cryptomining facilities, it does outline key areas for data centers and the many similarities they share. [ref: El Paso adopts tougher rules for future data center developments, El Paso Matters]

Granbury would pass a law similar to El Paso's in July of 2026, with the law semi-addressing the MARA cryptomining facility, and possible data centers, close to the town. Granbury would state that rule regarding noise mitigation, site planning, water systems, data and equipment storage, and energy usage. [ref: Addressing truth's and rumors about Data Centers in Granbury, City of Granbury]

Fort Worth has similar regulations, with city staff proposing laws that would ban cryptocurrency mining within the city on June 2, 2026. Alongside outlining areas for further industrial usage and place a greater emphasis on major operations that would benefit the city. As of October 18, 2026, the city was still debating a possible short term ban on cryptomining and data center infrastructure. [ref: Fort Worth could ban cryptocurrency mining. Data centers might be here to stay, Forth Worth Report]

== Controversies ==
=== Scams ===
In 2025 alone, Texas lost $1 Billion to cryptocurrency scams. The rise in cryptocurrency infrastructure has ties to this, specifically with investments and fake business operations from those claiming to be legitimate entities. [ref: What to know as cryptocurrency scams rise in Texas, The Texas Tribune] Central Texas in particular is often the site of large scams due its age and education demographics, allowing for easy targeting. Because of this, the FBI has taken additional steps to alert citizens in the region. [ref: Head of Local FBI talks of ‘massive increase’ in crypto scams in Central Texas, KXAN Austin] Social engineering, the act of using words and trust to influence people, has repeatedly been used, specifically in large financially based scams.

Common scams in the state of Texas include kiosk scams, investment scams, and law enforcement scams. A deep concern amongst Texas law enforcement is Crypto Marketing, where "Promoters of securities tied to cryptocurrencies recruit investors to pitch the investments, often to friends and family and through social media and blogs." as stated by the Texas State Securities Board. [ref: Cryptocurrency Scams, Texas State Securities Board]

=== Electricity and Environmental Impact ===
A major criticism of the rapid growth of cryptomining is its impact on Texas's power supply and energy grid. Bitcoin mines often draw hundreds of megawatts and add substantial demand, sometimes by surprise, to ERCOT's (Electric Reliability Council of Texas) grid and energy monitoring systems. ERCOT, in response, has passed new laws, regulations, and plans to better manage the multiple cryptocurrency mines scattered throughout the state. One notable example is Texas’s 2025 SB 6, a document outlining the state's plan for better management of crypto facility related power supplies. [ref: Cryptocurrency in Texas: Opportunities and Challenges in Mining Digital Coins, Texas Comptroller] This plan, however, does not specifically outline any protocols for emergencies or potential crises. In 2023 alone, all cryptomines in Texas used 2,717 megawatts of power, enough to power roughly 680,000 homes and far surpassing anywhere else in North America. [ref: A North Texas community will vote to form a city in an effort to quiet down a crypto mine, The Texas Tribune]

Another major criticism is crypto mines environmental impact. In a 2022 study conducted by Nature, 32 out of the 34 largest cryptocurrency mines in the United States relied heavily on gas, coal, and oil based power. In Texas alone, Dallas and Houston were heavily cited as having the worst crypto-based pollution rates in the nation, with San Antonio and Austin not too far behind. [ref: The environmental burden of the United States’ bitcoin mining boom, Nature Communications] An estimated 1.1 million Texans in Houston and Dallas are to suffer from cryptomining based pollution, with pollution spilling into rural Texas and neighboring states. A notable type of pollution attributed to cryptomining is noise, which, similar to data centers, is often attributed to the large amounts of power and water needed to keep systems running without failure. To keep systems in line, large amounts of fans are used to keep equipment from overheating. Many cryptomining facilities have faced backlash over noise pollution, with audio levels ranging from 35-60 dB being produced from facilities. This prolonged sound interference has been linked to sleep disturbance, stress, and mental fatigue among those close to operations. [ref: Data centers and cryptocurrency mining in Texas drive strong power demand growth, US Energy Information Administration]

=== Crypto companies in politics ===
During the 2024 Federal Elections, cryptomining companies spent $133 million in supporting Republican canadates. Most notably Donald Trump and Senator Ted Cruz, who is belived to own at least three cryptomining machines near the town of Iraan in went texas. In 2023, Cruz disclosed a purchase of an estimated $50,000 to $100,000 in Bitcoin following an endorsement by the Texas Blockchain Council. [ref: The Crypto Racket, The American Prospect]

data.title: Gary Meier
data.text:
----

Gary Meier was an Australian soccer goalkeeper who played for Sydney Olympic FC during the club's debut season in the National Soccer League (NSL).

=== Career ===
Meier featured prominently as the primary goalkeeper for Sydney Olympic in the 1977 NSL season, the inaugural year of Australia's first national professional soccer competition. He appeared in all 26 league matches and recorded 8 clean sheets, contributing to the team's defensive efforts despite finishing 12th in the 14-team league. [ref: ]

He is recognised as one of the club's historical defensive stalwarts and was inducted into the Sydney Olympic FC Hall of Fame. [ref: ]

No further details about Meier's career (such as other clubs, birth date, or international appearances) appear in publicly available sources.

data.title: Ringgold Telephone Company
data.text:
Ringgold Telephone Company (doing business as RTC) is an independent local exchange carrier and Internet service provider based in Ringgold, Georgia. Founded in 1912, the company provides fiber-optic broadband, telephone service, and managed IT services to residential and commercial customers in Catoosa County and adjacent areas in Northwest Georgia.

== History ==
The company was established in 1912 by Jim Evitt Sr., a Catoosa County pharmacist, with eight initial telephone lines. [ref: Ringgold Telephone marks century of service, Chattanooga Times Free Press] Following his death, his son, Jim Evitt Jr., assumed control of the utility. In 1950, RTC transitioned from manual switchboards to an automated dial exchange, serving approximately 250 subscriber lines. [ref: Annual Report of the Georgia Public Service Commission, State of Georgia]

Following the death of Jim Evitt Jr. in 1973, his daughter, Alice Evitt Bandy, became president of the company. [ref: Local family keeps Ringgold connected for three generations, The Catoosa County News]

During the late 1990s, the company expanded from basic analog telephone service into data transmission. In 2000, RTC completed a regional infrastructure upgrade making DSL broadband available across its 122-square-mile (320 km) exchange footprint. [ref: Rural Telcos Bridge the Digital Divide, Telephony Online] In 2003, RTC expanded into IPTV and digital television distribution over copper and hybrid infrastructure. [ref: RTC selects Amino for IP set-tops, Light Reading]

In June 2004, the company relocated operations from downtown Ringgold to an expanded operations facility on Evitt Parkway. In April 2025, RTC moved its corporate headquarters back to downtown Ringgold, acquiring and renovating the former Chrysler dealership building on Nashville Street. [ref: Ringgold Telephone Company returns to historic downtown hub, Chattanooga Times Free Press]

== Network and services ==
RTC operates an optical fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) network covering over 55 percent of Catoosa County. [ref: Broadband Deployment Data: Catoosa County, GA, Federal Communications Commission] Its network provides symmetric gigabit broadband, voice-over-IP (VoIP), hosted private branch exchange (PBX), and enterprise data links with service-level agreements.

The company also provides network hardware installation, commercial security integration, and structured cabling for regional businesses and public institutions in the greater Chattanooga metropolitan area.

data.title: Injection waterproofing of concrete structures
data.text:
Injection waterproofing of concrete structures is a repair technique in which liquid resins or cementitious grouts are introduced into cracks, joints and voids in concrete to restrict or prevent water penetration. Injection systems are used in the repair of concrete structures where leakage occurs through localized defects. Depending on the repair objective, the injected material may provide water sealing, flexible filling or structural bonding. [ref: Injection products and systems, Deutsches Institut für Bautechnik]

Injection waterproofing forms part of the broader field of waterproofing and pressure grouting. The selection of injection material depends on the condition of the structure, the characteristics of the defect, the presence of flowing water and the required performance of the repair. [ref: Guide for the Selection of Grouts to Control Water Leakage Through Cracks in Concrete Structures, International Concrete Repair Institute]

== Operating principle ==
Injection waterproofing involves introducing a sealing material into a crack, joint or void through purpose-installed injection ports or packers. The material is delivered under controlled pressure and is intended to occupy the accessible leakage path. [ref: Injection Waterproofing: How It Works and When to Use It, knowledge.semeonidis.com]

Depending on its chemical composition, the injected material may react with water, expand, cure into a flexible seal or form a rigid bond between adjacent concrete surfaces. Different material systems are used for sealing and structural repair, and these functions are not necessarily interchangeable.

The method can be used to address leakage through defects in concrete structures. Injection may also be considered where an existing waterproofing layer is inaccessible and a suitable injection system has been designed for its repair. [ref: Technical Evaluation Method for Physical Property Changes due to Environmental Degradation of Grout-Injection Repair Materials for Water-Leakage Cracks, Applied Sciences]

== Injection materials ==

=== Polyurethane resins ===
Polyurethane injection materials are used in certain water-sealing applications, including the treatment of leaking cracks in concrete. Some formulations react with water and expand to fill accessible cavities. Other formulations produce flexible seals that can accommodate limited movement. [ref: Evaluation of polyurethane resin injection for concrete leak repair, Case Studies in Construction Materials]

Fast-foaming polyurethane materials may be used to control flowing water before additional sealing treatment, depending on the selected repair system.

An experimental study published in Case Studies in Construction Materials in 2019 investigated polyurethane resin injection for concrete leakage repair. The research reported a reduction in water penetration in the tested concrete specimens following injection treatment. [ref: Evaluation of polyurethane resin injection for concrete leak repair, Case Studies in Construction Materials]

=== Epoxy resins ===
Epoxy resins are used for repairing cracks in concrete where a rigid, force-transmitting bond is required. [ref: Construction products detail, DIBt]

Unlike flexible sealing materials, conventional structural epoxy systems are intended to bond crack surfaces and restore continuity between concrete elements. Their suitability depends on the moisture condition, crack stability and other characteristics of the substrate. [ref: Construction products detail, DIBt]

Epoxy injection is therefore associated primarily with structural crack repair, although certain epoxy systems may also contribute to sealing applications.

=== Acrylic gels ===
Acrylic-based injection gels are used in selected sealing applications where swelling properties and compatibility with permanently damp conditions are required.

Certain acrylic gel systems can absorb and release water, making environmental moisture conditions important to their intended performance.

These materials are classified separately from rigid structural injection products.

=== Cementitious grouts ===
Cement-based injection materials include cement suspensions and other hydraulic-binder formulations.

They are used for particular crack- and void-filling objectives, depending on the required material properties and repair design.

The suitability of cementitious injection depends on the dimensions of the defect, the intended repair function and the properties of the selected grout.

== Applications ==
Injection waterproofing is associated with repairs to concrete structures affected by water penetration through cracks, construction joints or connected voids. [ref: Injection Waterproofing: How It Works and When to Use It, knowledge.semeonidis.com]

Applications described in technical literature include underground structures, tunnels, retaining walls, tanks and other concrete elements exposed to water. [ref: Properties and Application of Chemical Grouting Materials for Construction Joint Leakage, Advances in Materials Science and Engineering]

The method may provide an alternative to external access where the leakage path can be reached from the accessible face of the concrete structure.

Its applicability depends on the identified defect and whether the injection material can adequately penetrate and seal the relevant pathway.

== Repair procedure ==
A typical injection repair includes preliminary assessment of the defect, selection of a suitable injection system, preparation of the concrete surface, installation of injection ports and controlled introduction of the repair material.

Injection equipment delivers the selected material through installed packers. The pressure and method of application depend on the product, substrate and repair objective.

After injection and curing, the repaired area may be inspected to evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment.

Quality control can involve observations during application, material testing and examination of the completed repair, depending on the specified requirements.

== Limitations ==
Injection waterproofing does not necessarily resolve the underlying causes of cracking or water penetration.

The performance of an injection repair depends on the properties of the selected material, the condition of the concrete, the geometry and movement of the defect, and the environmental exposure of the repaired structure.

Research on grout-injection repair materials has identified hydrostatic pressure, groundwater flow, thermal effects, chemical exposure, substrate movement and moisture conditions as factors that may influence long-term performance.

Consequently, material selection and repair design must consider the expected conditions of service. A material intended for structural bonding may not provide the flexibility required at a moving joint, while a flexible water-sealing material may not restore structural strength.

The distinction between water-sealing and structural repair is an important aspect of selecting an appropriate injection system.

* Waterproofing
* Pressure grouting
* Concrete
* Damp proofing
* Structural repair

The Koipuram Palliyodam is a prominent snake boat (palliyodam) from Koipuram village, situated on the northern bank of the Pamba River in Pathanamthitta, Kerala. The boat is famously known by its popular moniker, "Madachadi Chundan" (meaning "the chundan that jumped over bunds"). It is strictly owned, maintained, and operated by the 569th Number NSS Karayogam Koipuram.The vessel is believed to carry the blessings of the local deity of [https://www.justdial.com/Pathanamthitta/Nellickal-Koipuram-Devi-Temple-Koipuram/9999PX468-X468-251014154949-I6A1_BZDET Koipuram-Nellickal Devi Temple] [ref: Aranmula Vallamkali - Official Website of Aranmula Palliyoda Seva Sangam, Aranmula Vallamkali]

The boat regularly participates in the prestigious annual Aranmula Uthrattathi Vallamkali (snake boat regatta) and the ritualistic Vallasadya feast offerings dedicated to the Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple. Throughout its racing history, the Koipuram Palliyodam has established a reputation as one of the most highly competitive and formidable boats in the waters of the Pamba River.

Koipuram has a rich maritime heritage, with the village owning and operating a snake boat for the last several centuries. It belongs to the lineage of the very first boats built in the Aranmula region of Kerala. The current version of the boat was last reconstructed in 2014 by the renowned craftsman "Ayroor Chellappan Achari".

data.title: Boo! (Naré song)
data.text:
"Boo!" is the debut single by Armenian singer Naré. It was released as a single on 23 September 2026.

It was Armenia's winning entry for the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2026 in Ta' Qali, Malta. Naré won the competition with a total of 202 points, a combined total from 1st in the public vote and 3rd in the national juries, earning Armenia its third overall victory at the contest.

data.title: Zenas Ayansipe Olatunde
data.text:
Zenas Ayansipe Olatunde (born 18 December 2004) is a Nigerian technology entrepreneur and software developer. He is the founder and chief executive officer of Nova Inc, the Houston-based technology company behind Nova Payments, Nova Domains, Agent Exchange and the Nova social application. [ref: Zenas Ayansipe O. — AI Developer / Researcher, Nova Inc] [ref: Nova Inc — The Nova Ecosystem, Nova Inc]

== Early life and education ==
Olatunde is from Oyo State, Nigeria. He attended Holiness Foundation Nursery and Primary School and Baptist Medical Center Secondary School. He studied at The Oke-Ogun Polytechnic, Saki (TOPS), where he earned a National Diploma (ND) in Animal Health and Production and a Higher National Diploma (HND) in Animal Production Technology.

== Career ==
Olatunde founded Nova Inc in 2023 and serves as its chief executive officer. [ref: Nova Inc — The Nova Ecosystem, Nova Inc] Under Nova Inc he has developed a group of software products known as the Nova Ecosystem: Nova Payments, a payment platform for merchants; Nova Domains, a domain-name service; Agent Exchange, a marketplace in which autonomous AI agents post jobs, bid, hold payment in escrow and deliver work; Agent Store, a marketplace for hiring AI agents; and Nova, a short-video social application with an integrated wallet and marketplace. [ref: Agent Exchange — the agent-to-agent job market, Nova Inc] [ref: AgentExchange repository, GitHub]

His published open-source work, distributed across his GitHub accounts kilomene, Mceeomoba and segz7448, centres on AI automation and autonomous agent systems. It includes Nova-bot, an autonomous agent system with agent, backend and deployment components; [ref: Nova-bot repository, GitHub] AgentLine, a permanent-address system for AI agents; [ref: AgentLine repository, GitHub] Universal-AGT and Termux-AGT, platforms for deploying agents to persistent hosts; [ref: Termux-AGT repository, GitHub] social-media automation tooling; automated trading agents; and NVT, an Android messaging and calling application. His work also includes the continued pre-training of a language model for Android deployment.

== Nova Inc ==

Nova Inc is the parent company for Olatunde's products. Its services include payments, domain names, an agent-to-agent job market and a social application, presented together as the Nova Ecosystem. [ref: Nova Inc — The Nova Ecosystem, Nova Inc]

data.title: Isobel Shaw
data.text:
Isobel Shaw (née O'Beirne; born 1943) is an Irish-born travel writer and guidebook author based in Switzerland. She is known for her guidebooks to Pakistan, including the Pakistan Handbook [ref: Pakistan handbook, Murray] (1989) and the Pakistan Trekking Guide [ref: Pakistan trekking guide: Himalaya, Karakoram, and Hindu Kush, Vanguard Books] (1993). The Pakistan Handbook was shortlisted for the Thomas Cook Travel and Guide Book Awards. [ref: Thomas Cook Travel Book Awards, The Weekend Telegraph] In 2005 she received the Pakistan Society Award for the advancement of public knowledge and understanding of Pakistan in the United Kingdom. [ref: Pakistan Society Awards, The Pakistan Society]

Early life and education

Shaw was born Isibéal Mairéad O'Beirne in County Meath, Ireland, and grew up at Kilcarty House, Kilmessan near Dunsany. Her father lectured in criminal law at the University of Cambridge. [ref: Sister Benedict's Connemara farm, Meath Chronicle] Her elder sister, Maeve O'Beirne, became a Benedictine nun at Kylemore Abbey in Connemara as Sister Benedict, and for many years managed the abbey farm. Shaw studied Anthropology and English at the University of Cambridge, UK.

Career

Early travel writing

Shaw's husband worked in international development, and the couple lived in Tanzania, the United States, Indonesia and Pakistan. Isobel worked as a freelance journalist during these postings. In Indonesia she co-wrote Spotlight Indonesia [ref: Spotlight Indonesia, Elsevier] (1978) with David Brownlow, and she was profiled in The Indonesian Times [ref: Profile: Isobel Shaw, The Indonesian Times] in 1977.

Pakistan guidebooks

Shaw lived in Pakistan from 1978 to 1981 and returned frequently afterwards. She wrote A Traveller's Guide to Pakistan [ref: A Traveller's Guide to Pakistan, Asian Study Group] with Hilary Adamson, published in 1981 by the Asian Study Group, while she was living in Pakistan. She then wrote the Collins Illustrated Guide to Pakistan, [ref: Collins illustrated guide to Pakistan, Collins] published in 1989 by Collins in the United Kingdom and published by Passport Books in the United States as Pakistan. [ref: Pakistan, Passport Books] The Collins edition was reviewed in The Sunday Telegraph by Fitzroy Maclean who described it as "no superficial summary, but a thoughtful study which brings both the country and people alive". [ref: How to discover Eastern Promise, The Sunday Telegraph]

Shaw's Pakistan Handbook was published by John Murray in London and The Guidebook Company in Hong Kong in 1989. A US edition was published by Moon Publications 1990 and a second edition was published in 1998. [ref: Moon Handbooks: Pakistan, Avalon Travel Publishing] The book was reviewed in The Daily Telegraph in 1990 and was described as "a comprehensive guide to travel within the country". [ref: Good Guides, The Daily Telegraph] The book was shortlisted in 1990 in the guidebook category of the Thomas Cook Travel and Guide Book Awards. Other writers on the region have recommended Shaw's work, with Laura Stone calling her "the best guidebook writer on Pakistan". [ref: Himalaya by Bike: A Route and Planning Guide for Cyclists and Motor Cyclists, Trailblazer Publications, Trailblazer Publishing]

For the next two decades, Shaw worked as a tourism consultant to the Government of Pakistan and as a tour guide specializing in the mountains of Central Asia [ref: Environmental protection of the Himalaya: a mountaineers' view, Indus Publ. Co].  She gave a keynote address at the Pakistan Tourism Convention in Karachi in October 1993 and received a Friends of Pakistan award there. [ref: Knowing Pakistan: the way only a foreign trekker could, The News International] She contributed the tourism chapter to Environmental Protection of the Himalaya: A Mountaineers' View (1994), the chapter on tourism to Old Roads, New Highways: Fifty Years of Pakistan [ref: Old roads, new highways: fifty years of Pakistan, Oxford University Press] (Oxford University Press, 1997), and the Pakistan section of Insight Guides: South Asia. [ref: South Asia, APA Publications] Her work was profiled in She magazine (1993) and The News International (1993).

Trekking guides

Shaw began trekking seriously in Northern Pakistan in 1987 and within five years had covered most of the main routes in the Karakoram and Hindu Kush. Her Pakistan Trekking Guide (1993) organized about a hundred treks accessible from the mountain airports of Chitral, Gilgit and Skardu. In The American Alpine Journal, Gene and Betsy White wrote that the authors "present a sympathetic and positive portrait of Pakistan, its people and its scenic beauty", and that the book "should be required reading" for anyone planning to visit Pakistan as a tourist, trekker or resident. [ref: AAC Publications - Pakistan Trekking Guide, publications.americanalpineclub.org] In the Alpine Journal, Trevor Braham called it "well-researched" and said the sketch maps earned it "full marks". [ref: Review of Pakistan Trekking Guide by Isobel Shaw and Ben Shaw, Alpine Journal]

In 1990 Shaw led an expedition up the Baltoro Glacier to Concordia near K2 with the Swiss mountaineer André Roch, who was then aged 84. Shaw's Trekking Guide to the Karakoram and Hindu Kush of Northern Pakistan [ref: Trekking Guide to the Karakoram and Hindu Kush of Northern Pakistan, Vanguard Books] was published by Vanguard Books in 2013 and drew on further journeys to Northern Pakistan made after 1993.

Lectures

Shaw has given lectures on Pakistan and Central Asia to audiences including the Royal Geographical Society in London and the Société de Géographie de Genève, in Switzerland. [ref: Le Kirghizistan, dans les traces d'Ella Maillart aux sources du fleuve Syr-Darya, par Isobel SHAW, Société de Géographie de Genève] In January 2000 she addressed the Geneva society on a journey across Kyrgyzstan by jeep, on horseback and on foot. The journey followed the 1932 route of the Swiss traveller Ella Maillart to the sources of the Syr Darya.

Style and themes

Reviewers have noted that Shaw's route descriptions are based on personal experience, with other sources credited where used. Her guides combine practical detail with information on Pakistan's history, peoples, religions and languages. Her writings stress the hospitality of Pakistanis towards visitors and includes advice for women travelling in conservative areas, drawn from her own travels.

Personal life

Shaw married Robert Shaw in 1964 and has three children, Dominique (born 1966), Katharine (born 1967) and James Benedict (born 1969). Her son Ben Shaw is co-author of both of her trekking guides. She has lived in Switzerland since 1981.

Selected works

* Spotlight Indonesia (with David Brownlow). Pergamon Press, 1978.
* A Traveller's Guide to Pakistan (with Hilary Adamson). Asian Study Group, Islamabad, 1981.
* An Introduction to Pakistan. The Guidebook Company, Hong Kong, 1988.
* Collins Illustrated Guide to Pakistan. Collins, London, 1989. ISBN 0-00-215217-7. US edition: Pakistan, Passport Books, Chicago, 1989. ISBN 0-8442-9918-9.
* Pakistan Handbook. John Murray, London; The Guidebook Company, Hong Kong, 1989. ISBN 0-7195-4751-2. 2nd edition: Moon Publications, Chico, CA, 1998. ISBN 1-56691-069-2.
* Pakistan: aux sources de la civilisation de l'Indus. Olizane, Geneva, 1990. ISBN 2-88086-065-2.
* Pakistan Trekking Guide (with Ben Shaw). The Guidebook Company / Odyssey, Hong Kong, 1993.
* Odyssey Illustrated Guide to Pakistan. Odyssey, Hong Kong, 1996; 5th edition, Local Colour, Hong Kong, 1999.
* Trekking Guide to the Karakoram and Hindu Kush of Northern Pakistan (with Ben Shaw). Vanguard Books, Lahore, 2013. ISBN 978-969-402-559-9.

Chapters

* "Tourism", in Victoria Schofield (ed.), Old Roads, New Highways: Fifty Years of Pakistan. Oxford University Press, Karachi, 1997.
* "The Impact of Tourism", in Aamir Ali (ed.), Environmental Protection of the Himalaya: A Mountaineers' View. Indus Publishing, New Delhi, 1994. ISBN 81-7387-012-8.
* "Pakistan", in Insight Guides: South Asia. APA Publications, 1988.

Awards and honours

* 1990: Shortlisted, Thomas Cook Travel and Guide Book Awards (guidebook category), for Pakistan Handbook
* 1993: Friends of Pakistan award, Pakistan Tourism Convention, Karachi

data.title: Have I Been Squatted
data.text:
----

Have I Been Squatted Inc. is a privately held cybersecurity company that works on domain intelligence. It builds a platform for finding typosquatted and lookalike domains, along with the websites and infrastructure tied to them, that may be used for phishing, brand impersonation, or other abuse. According to the company's documentation, its monitoring draws on domain permutations, Domain Name System (DNS) data, Certificate Transparency logs, registration data, website analysis, and passive infrastructure telemetry. [ref: Getting started with Have I Been Squatted, Have I Been Squatted Documentation]

The service started in 2022 as a public tool for spotting typosquatted domains. The company that now runs it, Have I Been Squatted Inc., was founded in 2024. [ref: About, Have I Been Squatted] [ref: Have I Been Squatted, LinkedIn]

The company also publishes research on phishing, malicious infrastructure, malware delivery, and domain-name security. Its work has been covered by BBC News, The Register, Recorded Future News, BleepingComputer, and FreightWaves. [ref: Phishing operation with links to Russia, Armenia compromised Western cargo companies, researchers find, Recorded Future News] [ref: Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers, The Register]

== History ==

Have I Been Squatted began in 2022 as an experimental tool for finding possible typosquats. Users entered a domain name and the tool generated variations of it, showing registrations that could be used to impersonate the original organization. The company says the project was first released after an experiment was shared on Hacker News, and that it grew as security practitioners started using it. Part of the tool was built on twistrs, an open-source Rust library for generating domain-name permutations that the company still maintains on GitHub. [ref: Have I Been Squatted, GitHub]

Have I Been Squatted Inc. was founded in 2024 to develop and run the service on a commercial basis. [ref: Terms of Service, Have I Been Squatted]

The commercial service moved beyond one-off typosquatting searches to continuous monitoring and investigation of external infrastructure, and later added tools for investigations, alerts, and domain takedowns.

== Platform ==

The platform looks for internet infrastructure that may be impersonating an organization, its domains, or its brands. Customers add domains for monitoring, and the platform regularly generates permutations of them and checks for related registrations and infrastructure. It adds context to what it finds using DNS records, HTTP responses, WHOIS and RDAP registration data, Certificate Transparency observations, screenshots, classification data, and passive infrastructure telemetry.

Monitoring is not limited to typos of a protected domain. The platform also surfaces domains found through Certificate Transparency, passive DNS, and other infrastructure signals.

Separately from monitoring, the platform includes tools for investigating individual domains and larger datasets. Infrastructure it identifies can be classified, investigated, and linked to alerts or response work. The company later added workflows for submitting domain takedown requests and tracking their progress.

== Threat intelligence research ==

=== Diesel Vortex ===

In February 2026, Have I Been Squatted and the threat intelligence group Ctrl-Alt-Intel published an investigation into a cybercrime operation they called Diesel Vortex. The group went after freight and logistics companies in the United States and Europe, using phishing sites built to take over accounts on load boards, fleet-management systems, fuel-card services, and other logistics platforms. [ref: Russian cybercrime ring targeted freight firms in US, Europe, report says, FreightWaves]

According to Recorded Future News, Have I Been Squatted researchers found an exposed.git directory belonging to the operation. It held source code and the group's communications, which showed how the campaign was organized and indicated that the group was building a phishing-as-a-service platform to support a wider criminal operation.

FreightWaves reported that the campaign had compromised 1,649 unique credentials, drawn from 3,474 stolen login pairs. The investigation also identified 52 deployed phishing domains, more than 75,000 targeted contact email addresses, and 35 confirmed attempts at fraud using Electronic Funds Source checks.

The exposed material pointed to an organized operation, with separate roles and infrastructure for stealing credentials, communicating with logistics staff, and managing victim sessions. Recorded Future News reported that the compromised accounts could be used for freight diversion, double brokering, and check fraud.

Have I Been Squatted and Ctrl-Alt-Intel worked with technology and security companies to disrupt the campaign's infrastructure. Recorded Future News named Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), Cloudflare, GitLab, IPinfo, and Ping Identity among those involved.

In April 2026, BleepingComputer referred to the Diesel Vortex investigation in its report on an FBI warning about a sharp rise in cyber-enabled cargo theft. It cited Have I Been Squatted's finding that the group had used dozens of phishing domains against freight and logistics operators since 2025. [ref: FBI links cybercriminals to sharp surge in cargo theft attacks, BleepingComputer]

=== Recruitment malware campaigns ===

In August 2026, Have I Been Squatted published a technical analysis of a malware campaign that used a fake hiring process to target a job seeker in the Web3 sector. The attackers approached the victim on LinkedIn, ran what looked like a normal interview process using Calendly and Google-hosted services, and then sent technical assessment material that was malicious. [ref: From fake interview to signed ClickOnce: inside a three-payload Windows chain, Have I Been Squatted]

On Windows, the attack used a digitally signed ClickOnce application. Installing it eventually delivered three payloads: a version of NeedleStealer, a separate information stealer written in Rust, and a custom Go remote-access trojan with remote shell access, file management, proxying, keylogging, and hidden virtual network computing.

The same infrastructure could also serve a macOS delivery chain that ended in Odyssey Stealer. The researchers said the mix of legitimate online platforms, signed software, and targeted social engineering made the fake recruitment process far more convincing than ordinary phishing.

In September 2026, BBC News cited analysis by Have I Been Squatted in a report on fake recruitment scams. The report followed a victim who was approached on LinkedIn and lost about £18,000 in cryptocurrency after installing malicious software during what seemed to be a real hiring process. It highlighted the attackers' use of genuine Google services and digitally signed software. [ref: I lost my savings after a job interview scam, BBC News]

=== Internationalized domain name and Chromium research ===

In October 2026, Have I Been Squatted published research on how Chromium-based browsers handle internationalized domain names (IDNs). They tested whether deceptive lookalike domains could get past Chromium's protections and be shown to users in Unicode, rather than in their Punycode form, which is easier to recognize as suspicious. [ref: Turning IDN edge cases into typosquats, Have I Been Squatted]

The researchers found edge cases involving two characters: the Cyrillic letter ө, used in languages such as Kazakh and Mongolian, and the Latin letter ƙ, used in languages such as Hausa. Using these characters, they built lookalikes of well-known domains that passed Chromium's display checks.

Have I Been Squatted registered 20 proof-of-concept lookalike domains for the research, including ones resembling Apple, SpaceX, Okta, and Nike. The Register covered the findings on October 10, 2026, explaining how the two characters could get around Chromium's checks for suspicious internationalized domains.

Chromium runs several checks before deciding whether to show an internationalized domain in Unicode. One set looks for characters and scripts often used for impersonation. Another reduces each domain to a simplified comparison string, called a skeleton, and compares it against a built-in list of popular domains.

The research found that Cyrillic ө was missing from Chromium's whole-script lookalike list, so adding it to an otherwise confusable Cyrillic domain could stop that check from triggering. The Latin ƙ caused a related problem at the skeleton stage. Its hook was kept as a combining mark, so the skeleton never exactly matched the ASCII domain it imitated.

The researchers also looked at Chromium's Safety Tips, which warn users when they navigate to a site by comparing it, exactly and approximately, against well-known sites and sites the user visits often. They found cases where a lookalike differed enough from the comparison skeleton to avoid a warning, as well as limitations affecting domains with fewer than five characters before the top-level domain.

As part of the work, the company analyzed the.com zone for internationalized domains and found about 162,000 pairs in which an IDN resembled an ASCII.com domain. The researchers noted that this did not mean 162,000 malicious typosquats, since such pairs can include legitimate multilingual domains and defensive registrations.

The research also compared email clients. Gmail showed the tested internationalized sender domains in Unicode, while Outlook Web showed the same domains as Punycode A-labels. The Register noted that the two services had made different trade-offs in how they present internationalized email domains to users.

== Public and open-source tools ==

Alongside its commercial service, Have I Been Squatted releases free and open-source security tools.

twistrs is a Rust library for generating and enumerating domain-name permutations. It is released under the MIT License, hosted in the company's public GitHub organization, and was one of the building blocks of the original typosquatting service.

In December 2025, the company launched certgrep, a free search service for Certificate Transparency data. It lets users search certificate records with regular expressions, wildcards, and substring queries. The company built it after using similar functionality internally to find domains that matched suspicious patterns. [ref: Announcing certgrep, Have I Been Squatted]

The company also maintains an open-source Python software development kit for its application programming interface (API). It gives programmatic access to features including domain-squatting analysis, domain investigation, and Certificate Transparency search. [ref: haveibeensquatted-python, GitHub]

data.title: Volkan Gurses
data.text:
----

Volkan Gurses is a physicist, engineer, and entrepreneur whose research concerns with studying the fundamental limits of technologies and developing technologies that approach these limits. [ref: Information Technologies at the Fundamental Physical Limits, California Institute of Technology] [ref: Bill Gross Business Plan Competition Winners, Caltech Office of Technology Transfer and Corporate Partnerships] He is a postdoctoral researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the California Institute of Technology.

Gurses received a Bachelor of Science in electrical engineering with the Research Option from the Georgia Institute of Technology in 2020. He subsequently earned a Master of Science in electrical engineering in 2022 and a Doctor of Philosophy in electrical engineering with a minor in physics in 2026 from the California Institute of Technology. [ref: Volkan Gurses, Caltech Holistic Integrated Circuits Laboratory] [ref: One Hundred Thirty-Second Commencement, California Institute of Technology]

He studies the physical limits of sensing, communication, and computing and develops integrated photonic and electronic systems designed to approach them. His research includes quantum phased arrays for manipulating quantum light, [ref: Tiny chip could enable super-secure quantum Wi-Fi, New Scientist] [ref: Quantum Wi-Fi Future: Quantum Tech Could Power Super-Secure Wireless Communication, The Quantum Insider] [ref: Quantum Promises “Unhackable” Wireless Networks, Microwave Product Digest] [ref: An on-chip phased array for non-classical light, Nature Communications] quantum coherent transceivers, and monolithic classical–quantum computers.

In 2015, he won first prize in physics in TÜBİTAK's national secondary-school research competition [ref: Yapay yerçekimi TÜBİTAK'ta ödül getirdi, Milliyet] and an EIROforum prize at the European Union Contest for Young Scientists. [ref: EUCYS prizewinner visits CERN, CERN Bulletin] His venture Foundation won Caltech's 2026 business-plan competition.

In October 2026, Gurses wrote "How far can we push computing?" for MIT Technology Review, discussing the fundamental physical limits of computing and communications. [ref: How far can we push computing?, MIT Technology Review]

= Malik Sumeed =

Malik Sumeed is an Indian journalist and editor from Jammu and Kashmir. He serves as Senior Managing Editor of Kashmir News Bureau (KNB), a Srinagar-based digital news agency. His reporting has covered politics, Defence, entertainment, and social issues in Jammu and Kashmir. [ref: Malik Sumeed - IMDb, IMDb] [ref: ]

== Career ==

Sumeed began his journalism career in the entertainment sector and later expanded into political and public affairs reporting. He has been associated with Kashmir News Bureau and The Kashmir Scenario. [ref: Enable JavaScript to use search, www.google.com] [ref: ]

According to professional journalism profiles, he has worked in journalism for nearly a decade and has reported on politics, entertainment, and sports. His bylined articles have appeared in Kashmir News Bureau and The Kashmir Scenario. [ref: ] [ref: GK correspondent among 24 journalists complete DCC 2026, www.greaterkashmir.com] [ref: 24 पत्रकारों का डिफेंस कॉरेस्पोंडेंट्स कोर्स संपन्न, तीनों सेनाओं के साथ हुआ प्रशिक्षण - mobile, punjabkesari]

== Entertainment Journalism ==

Sumeed gained attention for covering the Indian television and film industry from Jammu and Kashmir. Media reports have described him as one of the few Kashmir-based journalists focusing on entertainment journalism and celebrity interviews. [ref: Defence Correspondents Course Concludes in Assam, https://onlykashmir.in/] Recently Malik Sumeed completed the Important Defence Correspondent Course organised by Ministry of Defence throughout DPR.

He has stated that he interviewed several actors, singers, and film personalities during his early reporting career. [ref: www.imdb.com] [ref: 24 journalists complete defence training in Assam's Tezpur: 3-week course covered Army, Navy, Air Force operations and responsibilities, Bhaskar English]

== Journalism and Editorial Work ==

As Senior Managing Editor of Kashmir News Bureau, Sumeed has overseen reporting on regional politics, governance, education, and social issues. His published work includes coverage of employment, education, and public policy matters in Jammu and Kashmir. data.title: James Storer (footballer)
data.text:
----

James Lee Storer (born 4 October 2004) is an Irish professional footballer who plays as a goalkeeper for EFL League One club Plymouth Argyle. [ref: ]

==Club career==
===Youth career===
Born in Buxton, Storer began his career in the youth setup of Port Vale progressing from Under-9 from Under-13 levels with The Valiants, before he departed the club in 2018 to join Premier League Wolverhampton Wanderers. [ref: Premier League football beckons for Vale Academy..., Port Vale FC] On 21 July 2021, after progressing quickly through the ranks at Wolves; Storer signed a two–year scholarship. [ref: Meet Wolves Academy’s 2021/22 scholars, wolves.co.uk] On 27 October 2022, Storer signed his first professional contract with the club.

===Wolverhampton Wanderers===

On 1 November 2021, almost four months after signing his scholarship; Storer was named amongst the first team substitutes for a Premier League game against Everton at Molineux - with Wolves running out 2–1 winners. [ref: ] He didn't feature for the first team again after that and on 5 June 2025, Storer was offered a new deal, [ref: Wolves confirm 2025 retained list, wolves.co.uk] which he signed the following month. [ref: Storer and Benjamin Sign Extensions Before Loan Moves from Wolves, alwayswolves.co.uk] The following 6 June 2026, Storer was named on the retained list following the conclusion of the 2025–26 campaign. [ref: Wolves confirm 2026 retained list, wolves.co.uk]

===Darlaston Town (loan)===
On 2 August 2024, Storer sealed his first loan stint away from Wolves as he joined Northern Premier League Division One Midlands side Darlaston Town on a three–month loan deal. [ref: Darlaston sign young Wolves keeper on three months loan, darlastontown1874fc.com] The loan came to an end in January 2025 and Storer went onto make 26 appearances across all competitions for The Citizens. [ref: Darlaston Town – Appearances – James Storer – 2024-2025, footballwebpages.co.uk]

===Chester (loan)===
On 10 January 2025, Storer joined National League North side Chester on loan for the rest of the season, [ref: Jimmy Storer joins Chester FC on loan!, chesterfc.com] he went onto feature 25 times in all during his time at the Deva Stadium before he returned to parent club, Wolves. [ref: James Storer: Chester FC: playmakerstats.com, playmakerstats.com]

===Greenock Morton (loan)===
On 15 July 2025, Storer was loaned out to Scottish Championship side Greenock Morton on a season–long loan, [ref: James Storer joins on loan, chesterfc.com] he made his professional debut later the same day as he played the full 90 minutes of the Scottish League Cup Group opener against Stenhousemuir, in which Morton ran out 3–0 winners. [ref: Greenock Morton 3–0 Stenhousemuir, bbc.co.uk] This was followed by his senior debut in league football on 2 August 2025, as Storer featured in Greenock Morton's 0–0 draw against Dunfermline Athletic on the opening day of the Scottish Championship season. [ref: Greenock Morton 0–0 Dunfermline Athletic, bbc.co.uk] He went onto make 32 appearances in all during his temporary stay at Cappielow and was voted Greenock Morton's Young Player of the Year on 8 May 2026. [ref: 🏆 Young Player of the Year. Following a stand out season, James Storer has been voted as the 2025/26 Young Player of the Year! Congratulations, Jimmy 👏]

===Plymouth Argyle===
On 26 June 2026, Storer left Wolverhampton Wanderers on a permanent basis as he signed for League One side Plymouth Argyle on a free transfer; penning an initial two-year deal. [ref: James Storer signs for Argyle, pafc.co.uk] [ref: Storer signs for Plymouth Argyle, wolves.co.uk] On 25 August 2026, Storer made his debut in English professional football as he played the full 90 minutes during Plymouth Argyle's 4–2 loss against Premier League side Coventry City in Round One of the EFL Cup. [ref: ] [ref: Plymouth Argyle 2-4 Coventry City, bbc.co.uk]

==International career==
Born in Buxton, Storer is of Irish descent. On 30 May 2022, he was called up to the Republic of Ireland U19s for two friendly internationals against Iceland at the Pinatar Arena. [ref: U19s set for Iceland double header, rissc.org] He was unused substitute for the first game which Ireland won 3–0, [ref: Republic of Ireland U19 3–0 Iceland U19, extratime.com] and played the full 90 minutes in the second which Ireland lost 1–0. [ref: Republic of Ireland U19 0–1 Iceland U19, extratime.com]

data.title: Andrea Lankford
data.text:
Andrea Lankford is an American author and former Park Ranger for the National Parks Service. [ref: Andrea Lankford, Andrea Lankford] She is the author of five books [ref: When hikers vanish, how modern searches really work, Police1] including the New York Times best seller [ref: Hardcover Nonfiction Books - Best Sellers - Books - Sept. 10, 2023 - The New York Times, The New York Times] Trail of the Lost: The Relentless Search to Bring Home the Missing Hikers of the Pacific Crest Trail [ref: The Relentless Search to Bring Home the Missing Hikers of the Pacific Crest Trail, Grand Central Publishing].

== Personal Life ==
Lankford is originally from Tennessee and holds degrees in Forestry and Nursing. [ref: Andrea Lankford, Andrea Lankford]

She lives in California. [ref: Andrea Lankford, Andrea Lankford]

== Career ==
Lankford worked as a National Park Service ranger for twelve years in National Parks that included the Grand Canyon, Zion and Yosemite National Park. [ref: 'I was born to do this': national park rangers on their triumphs and tragedies, The Guardian] She received awards for her work as a ranger investigator and introduced the “Heat kills, hike smart” public education program, targeted at day hikers visiting the Grand Canyon. [ref: Andrea Lankford, Andrea Lankford] [ref: Public Service Announcement Campaigns: Activities and Financial Obligations for Seven Federal Departments, www.govinfo.gov] [ref: Preparing for a day hike at Grand Canyon: what is useful?, In: Cole, David N.; McCool, Stephen F.; Borrie, William T.; O’Loughlin, Jennifer, comps. 2000. Wilderness science in a time of change conference—Volume 4: Wilderness visitors, experiences, and visitor management; 1999 May 23–27; Missoula, MT. Proceedings RMRS-P-15-VOL-4. Ogden, UT: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station. p. 221-225]

After leaving the Parks Service, Lankford worked as a concierge nurse for 14 years, working primarily in Los Angeles. [ref: Andrea Lankford, Andrea Lankford]
