data.title: Louis Brown
data.text:
----

Louis Brown (c. 1934–1986) was a British nightclub proprietor associated with London's West End nightlife during the 1960s, 1970s and early 1980s. He was known for his association with La Valbonne, a nightclub in Soho, and his venues which attracted entertainers, musicians and other prominent figures. He was known for his distinctive ideas and designs within his clubs making a name for himself as the King of Clubs.

== Career ==
Louis Brown was a British nightclub entrepreneur who became a prominent figure in London's West End nightlife during the 1960s and 1970s. Working alongside business partner Leonard Bloom, he established and operated a number of nightclubs, including La Poubelle, Le Kilt and the Scotch of St James, before opening La Valbonne in Soho in 1967.

Known for his distinctive approach to nightclub design and entertainment, Brown developed venues that attracted musicians, celebrities and fashionable clientele. His business interests later extended beyond London to Skindles Hotel in Taplow, Berkshire, where he established Studio Valbonne as a nightclub and entertainment venue. Brown continued to operate his nightclub businesses into the 1980s and died in 1986.

=== Skindles ===
Brown was also involved in the ownership and management of Skindles Hotel, a historic riverside hotel in Taplow, Berkshire, during the 1970s. Under his involvement, the establishment formed part of his wider interests in the hospitality and nightclub industries. In 1978, plans were proposed for an extension comprising 81 additional bedrooms, reflecting efforts to redevelop the property as a hotel and leisure destination. Skindles subsequently closed in 1995. Here on the Taplow Society archive it mentions the restoration Brown had on Skindles and what he did with it. https://www.taplowsociety.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/NL41.pdf

=== La Valbonne ===
La Valbonne was a nightclub at 62 Kingly Street in Soho, London, which opened in 1967 and became Louis Brown's best-known establishment. The venue was noted for its elaborate interior, featuring multiple bars, tropical plants, large fish tanks and a heart-shaped swimming pool incorporated into the dance floor. It attracted musicians, entertainers and other prominent figures, and appeared in Pete Walker's 1970 film Cool It Carol.

=== Other clubs ===
Le Kilt was a Soho nightclub associated with Louis Brown and his business partner Leonard Bloom. Situated on Greek Street, it formed part of Brown's expanding portfolio of West End entertainment venues during the 1960s and 1970s. The club operated within London's emerging discothèque culture, which increasingly centred on recorded music, dancing and fashionable nightlife. http://lesenfantsterribles.adrianstern.com/lekilt.pl

La Poubelle was an early London discothèque associated with Louis Brown. It opened in 1959 and is described in historical accounts as one of London's earliest venues devoted to recorded-music dancing. Located initially on Great Marlborough Street, near Oxford Circus, the club attracted socialites and helped establish the discothèque format that subsequently spread throughout the capital.http://lesenfantsterribles.adrianstern.com/lapoubelle.pl

The Scotch of St James opened in Mason's Yard, Mayfair, in July 1965 and became a prominent nightclub and live-music venue during London's Swinging Sixties. Associated with Louis Brown's nightclub interests, it attracted musicians and other figures from the British and American music scenes. American guitarist Jimi Hendrix famously joined musicians for an impromptu performance there on his arrival in England in September 1966. http://lesenfantsterribles.adrianstern.com/otherclubs.pl

Samantha's Club was a London nightclub operating around the late 1960s and early 1970s. A retrospective account published in 2025 recalls the club as a basement venue off Regent Street, featuring soul music performances and a distinctive DJ booth constructed from the body of a Jaguar E-Type car. The account places the club within London's fashionable nightlife scene at the end of the 1960s. Louis Brown's precise role in Samantha's, including the extent of his ownership or management, https://ninebattles.com/2026/09/29/samanthas-club-new-burlington-street-what-clubs-and-venues-do-you-remember-in-london/http://lesenfantsterribles.adrianstern.com/samanthas.pl

=== Relationship with Peter Stringfellow ===
Brown's La Valbonne nightclub reportedly attracted the interest of fellow nightclub entrepreneur Peter Stringfellow. A retrospective account states that Stringfellow regarded the venue as influential and that Brown offered to sell it to him however the deal never fulfilled.

== Personal life ==
Brown was known for his enthusiasm for music, nightlife and entertainment. His professional interests extended beyond running venues to the atmosphere and technology of the nightclub experience, including the development of elaborate lighting effects and distinctive interior designs. This was shown through his desire for cars when being seen driving his Jaguar E-Type and his Rolls-Royce Silver Cloud.

== Legacy ==
Louis Brown was an ambitious and influential figure in London's nightclub scene, whose establishments helped shape the atmosphere of fashionable nightlife during the Swinging Sixties and the decades that followed.

With a distinctive vision for entertainment, music and interior design, he created venues that offered more than a traditional nightclub experience, transforming them into destinations for celebrities, musicians and London's social elite. La Valbonne became the defining example of his approach, while his involvement with the Scotch of St James and Skindles extended his influence across London's West End and beyond.

His ability to combine striking surroundings with an atmosphere of exclusivity and excitement reflected the changing character of British nightlife during a period of significant cultural transformation. Although many of the venues associated with Brown have since closed or disappeared, their place in the history of the era remains a testament to his entrepreneurial ambitions and his contribution to the development of the modern nightclub experience.

This allowed him to be known within the entertainment industry as the King of Clubs.

== References ==

data.title: 2022– Georgian political crisis
data.text:
The 2022–Georgian political crisis is an ongoing political crisis in the country of Georgia. The crisis began on 25 February 2022, with protests against the Georgian government over what critics perceived as insufficient support for Ukraine in the Russo-Ukrainian War, which had begun a day earlier. The foreign policy pursued by the ruling Georgian Dream party, including growing economic ties with Moscow and deteriorating relations with Ukraine and the European Union, has faced criticism from major Georgian opposition parties. These criticisms have arisen amid the ongoing Russian-Georgian conflict stemming from the 2008 Russo-Georgian War and the Russian occupation of Georgian territories. The ruling party has rejected accusations of pursuing a pro-Russian policy, justifying its approach as necessary to preserve peace and stability.

In June 2022, the European Union declined to grant Georgia candidate status, citing the need for further progress in aligning with EU policies. The ruling party faced further protests in June and July 2022 over its failure to secure EU candidate status. Amid deteriorating relations with the West, in March 2023, the ruling party proposed a foreign agents law that would require non-governmental organizations (NGOs) to register as "foreign agents" if they received more than 20% of their funding from abroad. Many NGOs in Georgia receive funding from Western donors. The ensuing protests forced the Georgian Parliament to withdraw the bill. In December 2023, the European Union subsequently granted Georgia candidate status.

In February 2024, the ruling Georgian Dream party replaced Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili with Irakli Kobakhidze. In April 2024, the foreign agents bill was reintroduced and subsequently passed despite continued protests. The 2024 Georgian parliamentary and presidential elections further strained the political situation in the country, with the ruling party claiming victory while the opposition alleged electoral fraud. On 28 November 2024, during a press briefing, Prime Minister Kobakhidze announced the suspension of talks on Georgia's accession to the European Union until 2028, sparking further protests. The Second Kobakhidze government responded by adopting a series of restrictive laws targeting protesters and taking steps to consolidate power.

==Background==
By the time the crisis began, Georgian Dream had been the ruling party in Georgia since defeating Mikheil Saakashvili's United National Movement (UNM) in the 2012 parliamentary election. Having announced its intention to continue Georgia's existing bid for accession to the European Union and NATO, Georgian Dream also advocated combining a pro-European foreign policy with a more conciliatory approach towards Russia than that of its more firmly anti-Russian predecessors. [ref: Georgia's elections pit anti-Russian president versus conciliatory challenger, The Christian Science Monitor] Bidzina Ivanishvili, a Georgian billionaire who founded the Georgian Dream party and led it to victory in the 2012 elections, has faced accusations of being a Russian oligarch because he amassed his wealth, estimated at $7 billion, in Russia during the 1990s. Ivanishvili has rejected these accusations. [ref: Bidzina Ivanishvili: Georgia's billionaire 'puppet master' betting the house on Moscow, The Guardian] After briefly serving as prime minister from 2012 to 2013, Ivanishvili resigned from office, although he continued to be regarded as the éminence grise of Georgian politics, exerting influence over the ruling party from behind the scenes. For a time, Ivanishvili and Georgian Dream managed to avoid accusations of being pro-Russian. [ref: Popular Oligarchy: Why the Public Still Supports Georgian Dream, Georgian Institute of Politics] However, in 2019, the Georgian government faced major protests following the participation of Russian MPs in a session of the Interparliamentary Assembly on Orthodoxy held in the Georgian Parliament, during which Russian MP Sergei Gavrilov delivered a speech from the parliamentary speaker's chair. [ref: Who is the Russian Orthodox communist who provoked protests in Tbilisi?, JAM News] Georgia also experienced political crises in 2020 and 2021, marked by a sharp increase in political polarization between the government and the opposition. [ref: At New Year Reception, Zurabishvili Talks 'National Accord', Civil Georgia]

Tensions between Georgia and Russia have remained high due to the legacy of Russian imperial and Soviet rule over Georgia, as well as Russia's support for separatist movements in the Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia. [ref: What Happened: The Russia-Georgia Conflict, Gfsis.org]

==Georgia and the Russian invasion of Ukraine==
Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Georgian government condemned Russian actions and provided humanitarian assistance and diplomatic support to Ukraine. However, it did not join the sanctions imposed on Russia, a decision that coincided with an influx of Russian capital and the arrival of Russians seeking to avoid military mobilization. [ref: The Background on the Protests in Georgia, The New York Times] [ref: Ruling party head vows to "defend Ukraine's interests" on "all int'l platforms to the end", Agenda.ge] [ref: Before Ukraine there was Georgia. In 2008 Russia invaded Georgia and occupied 20% of our territory – Irakli Garibashvili, Rustavi2.ge] Although Russian migration had some positive socioeconomic effects, including strong economic growth and the appreciation of the Georgian currency [ref: These economies are booming as Putin's war drives migrants and money out of Russia, CNBC], its negative consequences, such as rising real estate prices and concerns over national security, placed additional strain on longstanding tensions between Georgians and Russians. [ref: How the war in Ukraine affects the real estate market in Georgia, JAM News] [ref: Russians fleeing Putin's war add new strain to old tensions in nearby Georgia, USA Today]

Since the start of the war, Georgia has seen an increase in trade with Russia. In 2022, Georgian exports to Russia rose by 7%, while imports increased by 79%, deepening Georgia's economic reliance on Russia. By contrast, trade between the European Union and Russia declined to approximately one-third of its previous volume, with Russia's share of EU imports falling from 9.5% to 1.7%. [ref: როგორია "ქართული ოცნების" ანტიდასავლური პროპაგანდა და რა არის რეალობა?, Publika] [ref: TI Georgia: Georgia's Economic Dependence on Russia Increased in 2022, Civil Georgia] Additionally, trade between Georgia and Russia continued to grow rapidly in 2023. [ref: How the Georgian Government, Once a US Ally, Became an Adversary, Against the Wishes of Its Protesting Citizens, Just Security] In May 2023, Russia abolished visa requirements for Georgian citizens and lifted the flight ban that had been in effect since July 2019. [ref: Russia Abolishes Visa Regime and Lifts Ban on Airline Flights with Georgia Starting May 15, Civil Georgia] Although Georgia did not join the economic sanctions imposed on Russia, it initially "acted fully in accordance with the financial sanctions" imposed by the United States and other countries. [ref: 2022 Investment Climate Statements: Georgia, US Department of State] However, in 2024, reports emerged alleging that the National Bank of Georgia was facilitating Russian importers' efforts to circumvent Western financial sanctions by settling transactions in rubles.

On 28 February 2022, the Georgian authorities denied landing permission to a Ukrainian charter flight sent to transport Georgian volunteers from Georgia to Ukraine. Georgian Dream officials argued that allowing the flight would risk drawing Georgia into the war. [ref: The Ukrainian charter sent to fly Georgian volunteers was not allowed to land in Tbilisi, Mtavari Arkhi] [ref: მდინარაძე: სახელმწიფოს ნებართვით მოხალისეების გაგზავნა ომში ჩართვის განაცხადი იქნებოდა, Radio Freedom] In response, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy decided to recall Ukraine's ambassador to Georgia. [ref: ზელენსკიმ საქართველოდან ელჩი გაიწვია კონსულტაციებისთვის, Radio Freedom]
==Initial protests against the Georgian Dream==
On 25 February 2022, large-scale protests began in front of the Georgian Parliament in Tbilisi in solidarity with Ukraine. Large crowds demanded the resignation of Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili over his statement that Georgia would not join Western sanctions against Moscow, which he made earlier that day. The demonstrations continued for six consecutive days and took on an anti-government tone, reflecting growing frustration with the Georgian authorities' perceived inadequate response to the Russian invasion. [ref: Outpouring of anger in Georgia over Government inaction on Ukraine, OC Media] [ref: Thousands Of Georgians Protest Russia's Invasion Of Ukraine] [ref: Protesters In Tbilisi Decry Georgian Government's Inadequate Support For Ukraine, RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty] Elene Khoshtaria, leader of the opposition Droa party, addressed the crowd, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili and his administration. She called for immediate and effective measures to support Ukraine, including closing Georgian airspace to Russian aircraft, and urged Georgia to apply for EU membership. [ref: PM's resignation, closing sky for Russia, EU membership application – large-scale rally in Tbilisi, JAMnews]

==Tensions with European Union==
During the 2020 election campaign, Georgian Dream pledged to apply for European Union membership in 2024. Following Ukraine's announcement of its application four days after the start of the Russian invasion, Georgian opposition politicians called on the Georgian government to submit a similar application. [ref: Ex-PM Says Georgia Should Ask for 'Immediate' EU Membership, Civil Georgia] However, Georgian Dream reacted reluctantly, arguing that not all the necessary commitments for submitting an application had been fulfilled and describing Ukraine's bid as a "political gesture" by the European Union in response to the war. The party argued that this rationale did not apply to Georgia, which was not directly involved in the conflict. It therefore initially maintained that Georgia would adhere to its original schedule for applying for EU membership. [ref: No EU Application Before 2024, Kobakhidze Says, Civil Georgia] Nonetheless, Georgian Dream soon yielded to public pressure and announced on 2 March 2022 that Georgia would apply for EU membership, citing "the changed situation in the world". [ref: Georgia, Moldova Formally Apply for EU Membership Amid Russia's Invasion of Ukraine, Radiofreeeurope/Radioliberty] [ref: Georgia formally applies for EU]

Relations with the European Union soon deteriorated. On 9 June 2022, the European Parliament adopted a six-page resolution accusing the Georgian government of undermining press freedom in the country. It also recommended that the European Council impose sanctions on Bidzina Ivanishvili over what the resolution described as "his role in the deterioration of the political process in Georgia", the "level of control he exerts over the government and its decisions, including those on the politically motivated persecution of journalists and political opponents", and his "exposed personal and business links to the Kremlin, which determine the position of the current Government of Georgia towards sanctions on Russia". [ref: EP's Georgia Press Freedom Resolution Calls for Ivanishvili Sanctions, Civil.ge] In the same month, the European Union granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova but deferred its decision on Georgia, citing the need for further reforms by the Georgian government. [ref: Georgia's EU Candidate Status Postponed, Pending Reforms, Georgia Today] This decision prompted the opposition to mobilize against the government. [ref: Rattled by Ukraine war, Georgia wrestles with tighter societal controls, The Christian Monitor] A series of protests was organized in June and July 2022 by the non-governmental organization (NGO) Shame Movement. [ref: Tens of Thousands Rally in Tbilisi to Support European Integration, Jamestown] The organizers blamed the Georgian government for the country's failure to obtain EU candidate status and called for its resignation and replacement by a technocratic interim government of "national accord" tasked with implementing the EU's conditions for granting candidate status. [ref: Pro-EU Rally Calls for PM Garibashvili to Resign, Civil Georgia]

On 14 December 2022, the European Parliament again called on the European Council to impose sanctions on Bidzina Ivanishvili, accusing him of contributing to the deterioration of Georgia's democratic political process. It also called on the Georgian government to release imprisoned former president Mikheil Saakashvili, citing the deterioration of his health during his imprisonment, and allow him to receive treatment at a specialized medical facility abroad. [ref: European Parliament approves resolution on implementation of Georgia-EU Association Agreement, Agenda.ge]

The third European Parliament resolution criticizing Georgian Dream was adopted on 14 February 2023. It accused the Georgian government and Bidzina Ivanishvili of intentionally mistreating imprisoned former president Mikheil Saakashvili and reiterated calls for his release, as well as for the imposition of personal sanctions on Ivanishvili. [ref: European Parliament resolution calls for imposition of sanctions against Bidzina Ivanishvili]

The Georgian Dream party criticized the European Parliament's resolutions. Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili described them as "irresponsible and offensive towards our people". [ref: Georgian leaders lash out after ominous signs on EU candidacy, Eurasianet] [ref: ] Georgian Dream parliamentarian Dimitri Khundadze questioned Georgia's pursuit of EU membership, stating: "We won't give up our dignity to get [candidate] status! [...] No one will intimidate Bidzina Ivanishvili or the Georgian state with threats of sanctions!". [ref: Supporters question Georgia's EU aspirations over Ivanishvili sanctions threat, OC Media] [ref: Georgian PM: time of Georgian authorities serving foreign interests "over", OC Media] [ref: PM Garibashvili says Saakashvili Arrived to Georgia to "Stage a Coup", Formula News]
==Foreign agent law controversy in 2023==

On 2 August 2022, in response to the protests and the European Parliament's resolutions, the sovereignist faction People's Power was established within the parliamentary majority. The faction proposed legislation to regulate foreign influence by establishing a special registry to monitor politically active organizations receiving foreign funding, many of which were funded by Western donors. [ref: Sovereignist Revival, Civil.ge] [ref: Georgia has a huge Western-funded NGO sector and regular outbreaks of violent protest, is there a link?, Azerbaycan24] [ref: "სიმართლის მთქმელი" 9 დეპუტატი და "ოცნება" უმრავლესობის გარეშე, რადიო თავისუფლება] The group published a series of open letters accusing the United States and the European Union of attempting to overthrow the Georgian government. [ref: Ivanishvili supporters accuse the US of attempting coup in Georgia, OC Media] The group questioned American funding to Georgia, arguing that much of it was directed towards NGOs to promote the American agenda under the guise of "strengthening democracy". It claimed that this practice contradicted the principles of democracy and popular sovereignty. [ref: Georgian society should be interested in US aid goals, People's Power says, 1tv] [ref: According to the dictionary of pseudo-liberals, an independent court means an externally managed court, an independent media means an externally managed media - People's Power, Rustavi2.ge] [ref: Georgian Dream departees: American funding in Georgia is not aimed at strengthening the democratic system, but at undermining it, Interpressnews] People's Power described several Georgian NGOs and political parties, including Mikheil Saakashvili's United National Movement, as "American agents". The group also accused the European Union and the United States of attempting to pressure Georgia by withholding EU candidate status to secure Saakashvili's release following what it described as a failed coup attempt. It defended the 2021 arrest of Mikheil Saakashvili on charges of corruption and abuse of power and rejected allegations of his mistreatment, saying that he was deliberately endangering his health through a hunger strike initiated in protest against his arrest. The People's Power movement also accused the United States and the European Union of interfering in Georgia's internal affairs by undermining the country's judiciary. [ref: Georgia is envisioned for a certain role that we shall play under the dictation of the Embassy – new statement of the People's Power, Rustavi 2] [ref: "ხალხის ძალის" განცხადებით, სააკაშვილის პარტნიორებს ორი მიზანი აქვთ: გათავისუფლება ან ლიკვიდაცია, Radio Freedom] [ref: Former ruling party MPs accuse US Embassy of "attacking the Govt", interfering in judiciary, 1tv] Judicial reform was among the twelve conditions set by the EU for granting Georgia candidate status. However, People's Power argued that the proposed reforms were aimed at "subjugating the Georgian judiciary to foreign control". [ref: People Power Says USAID-backed Rule of Law Project "Attack on Sovereignty", Civil.ge] In September 2022, the ruling Georgian Dream party questioned the credibility of influential NGOs, including Transparency International and the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED), accusing them of aligning with the opposition and violating political neutrality by calling for the formation of a technocratic interim government. Irakli Kobakhidze, the party's chairman at the time, also questioned the transparency of their foreign funding. [ref: ირაკლი კობახიძის განცხადებით, რამდენიმე დიდი არასამთავრობო ორგანიზაციის ფინანსური შემოსავლები კითხვის ნიშნებს აჩენს, Interpressnews] [ref: Brief - Ruling Party Contests Civic Space, Civil Georgia]

While the government argued that the foreign agents bill was necessary to ensure public disclosure and transparency, the opposition, along with Western embassies and politicians, opposed the legislation, comparing it to the Russian foreign agent law and warning that it would jeopardize Georgia's Euro-Atlantic integration. The controversy sparked mass protests, ultimately forcing Parliament to withdraw the bill. [ref: Georgia drops bill on 'foreign agents' after two nights of protests, The Guardian] On 8 March 2023, tens of thousands of people gathered outside Parliament, demanding an end to further deliberations on the bill. Opposition leader Giorgi Vashadze issued an ultimatum, calling for the rejection of the bill and the release of those detained during the protests. [ref: Thousands protest as Georgia parliament advances 'foreign influence' bill] Amid the protests in Tbilisi, the Russian Foreign Ministry issued a statement warning against a violent change of government in Georgia. [ref: Russian concern over protests in Georgia, Eurasianet] On 10 March, the ruling party withdrew the foreign agents bill following two days of violent protests. [ref: Georgia drops bill on 'foreign agents' after two nights of violent protests, The Guardian] [ref: Update: Majority Pledges to Withdraw the "Foreign Agent" Bill, But Questions Loom, Civil Georgia] [ref: Georgia withdraws 'foreign influence' bill but opposition vows more protests, CNN]

In September 2023, the State Security Service of Georgia claimed to have uncovered an alleged plot by opposition groups and Western-funded organizations to stage a coup in Georgia, purportedly with the support of Georgian opposition politicians based in Ukraine. [ref: Georgia claims US contributes funds to coup preparations, Eurasianet] [ref: Georgia's security service accuses Ukrainian official of plotting coup, Al Jazeera English]

In December 2023, the European Union granted Georgia candidate status, with the EU primarily congratulating the Georgian people rather than the government. [ref: Press Remarks by the EU Ambassador to Georgia, Pawel Herczynski on the Publication of the EU Enlargement Report, eeas.europa.eu] By October 2023, the Georgian Dream government had fulfilled only three of the twelve priorities set by the EU as conditions for granting candidate status. [ref: Georgia Awaits EU Decision on Candidate Status, The Jamestown Foundation]

During her 2018 presidential campaign, incumbent President Salome Zourabichvili was endorsed by the ruling Georgian Dream party. However, following the 2020–2021 Georgian political crisis, Zourabichvili became increasingly estranged from the GD-led Georgian government, with the rift deepening after the 2023 Georgian protests. In September 2023, the ruling party initiated impeachment proceedings against Zourabichvili, whom it accused of aligning with the opposition, but failed to secure sufficient votes to impeach her. [ref: Georgian parliament fails to impeach President Zourabichvili, Interfax]
==Reintroduction of foreign agent bill==
In early February 2024, Irakli Kobakhidze and Irakli Garibashvili exchanged positions, with Garibashvili becoming chairman of Georgian Dream and Kobakhidze being confirmed as prime minister on 8 February. [ref: Georgia's prime minister steps down to prepare for national elections this fall, Associated Press] [ref: Georgia Parliament Approves West Sceptic As New PM, Barron's]

On 3 April 2024, Georgian Dream (GD) announced plans to reintroduce the foreign agents bill, replacing the term "foreign agent" with "organization carrying the interests of a foreign power". [ref: Georgia's ruling party brings back disputed Russia-style 'foreign agent' law] [ref: Georgia's ruling party to reintroduce aborted bill on 'foreign agents', Reuters] [ref: Georgian ruling party to resubmit controversial foreign influence bill] [ref: Mamuka Mdinaradze: The bill will be introduced with exactly the same text as last year, with the only difference, instead of the term "agent of foreign influence", the term "organization carrying the interests of a foreign power" will be used, Interpressnews]

On 11 May, a large protest rally took place in Tbilisi, widely described as one of the largest demonstrations in Georgia's modern history. Despite the rain, tens of thousands of people gathered at four locations: First Republic Square, Marjanishvili Metro Station, 300 Aragveli Metro Station, and Tsereteli Avenue. Demonstrators marched along both banks of the Kura River, with four streams of protesters converging at Europe Square in Metekhi to mark Europe Day. Estimates of attendance varied, with some reports suggesting at least 169,000 participants and others citing peak figures of up to 200,000 or even 300,000. [ref: Massive Tbilisi protest marks historic turnout, Telewizja Polska] [ref: Photo Story: Tens of Thousands Protest Against Foreign Agents Law, Civil Georgia] [ref: რამდენი ადამიანი იყო ევროპის მოედანზე 11 მაისს, ღამის 10 საათისთვის, On.ge]

Parliament passed the bill on 14 May 2024, and it was subsequently signed into law on 3 June. [ref: Shalva Papuashvili: today, I signed the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence, the primary objective of which implies the enhancement of the resilience of the political, economic and social systems of Georgia without external interventions, Parliament of Georgia] [ref: Parliament adopts bill On Transparency of Foreign Influence with third reading, 1st channel]

==2024 Georgian parliamentary election==
Parliamentary elections were held in Georgia on 26 October 2024. [ref: Georgia's Central Election Commission reveals date, procedures for 2024 parliamentary vote, Agenda.ge] [ref: CEC releases information on registration of political parties for 2024 elections, 1TV] [ref: President signs decree declaring October 26 as date for parliamentary elections, Georgian Public Broadcaster]

During its pre-election campaign, Georgian Dream emphasized the importance of "safeguarding peace" through a "pragmatic policy" towards Russia. [ref: October Elections: Odds, Context, Past Trends, Civil Georgia] [ref: What's at stake in Georgia's October election?, Reuters] [ref: Rising Stakes in Tbilisi as Elections Approach, Civil Georgia] [ref: Georgian Dream promises 'pragmatic policy' with Russia in election programme, OC Media] The party also campaigned on socially conservative policies, particularly the recently adopted "LGBT propaganda" law and a proposal to strengthen the status of the Georgian Orthodox Church in the Constitution. [ref: ივანიშვილმა დააკონკრეტა რის ჩაწერას აპირებენ კონსტიტუციაში ეკლესიისგან სახელმწიფო რელიგიაზე უარის შემდეგ, Netgazeti] The pre-election campaign marked the consolidation of Georgian Dream's shift towards social conservatism to appeal to Georgia's large socially conservative electorate, despite the party's origins as a center-left, social democratic party. While most Georgians support EU membership, only a small minority shares the EU's socially liberal values, although politicians had previously avoided tapping into this conservative sentiment. [ref: The Rise of Socially Conservative Georgia, Center for European Policy Analysis]

Georgian Dream blamed the former ruling party, the opposition United National Movement (UNM), for the 2008 war with Russia. The party also announced plans to seek a ban on the UNM and its allies, citing alleged "crimes" committed during the UNM's time in government, including the Gldani prison scandal, as well as what it described as "sabotage" while the party was in opposition. [ref: Georgia goes 'North Korea' with bombshell plan to ban main opposition parties, POLITICO] [ref: კობახიძე აკონკრეტებს, რომელი პარტიების აკრძალვას გეგმავს "ქართული ოცნება", Netgazeti] [ref: Speaker assesses reports on banning opposition parties as disinformation, 1st Channel of Georgia]

The party also adopted a Eurosceptic stance without outright rejecting Georgia's bid to join the EU, pledging to pursue membership while "playing by Georgian rules". [ref: Kakha Kaladze: The Georgian government will play by Georgian rules – if a political decision is made regarding not granting the status, they can keep it for themselves, Interpressnews] It also pledged to restore the country's territorial integrity, while party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili made overtures to the Kremlin. In one of his pre-election speeches, Ivanishvili blamed the UNM for the 2008 war with Russia over Georgia's separatist region of South Ossetia and said that Georgia would need to apologize to South Ossetians for the conflict. His remarks sparked controversy, including among war veterans, and prompted accusations that he was attempting to rewrite history in Russia's favor at Georgia's expense. [ref: Anger in Georgia after Ivanishvili vows to apologise to South Ossetians for 2008 War, OC Media] [ref: Ivanishvili: We Need Constitutional Majority to Restore Territorial Integrity, Georgian News]

Opposition parties, meanwhile, criticized what they described as Georgian Dream's pro-Russian shift and its failure to meet the European Commission's conditions for EU accession. They campaigned in support of European integration. [ref: Georgian Democratic Opposition Parties sign Declaration of Unity, European Parliament] [ref: პროდასავლური ოპოზიციური პარტიების ერთობლივი განცხადება, Droa.ge]

Based on preliminary results published by the Central Election Commission of Georgia on 28 October, Georgian Dream declared victory in the election, having received more than 53% of the vote. The four major opposition coalitions, which had agreed under the Georgian Charter not to cooperate with Georgian Dream in parliament, were reported to have received a combined total of 37.79% of the vote. [ref: Official Results of 2024 Vote: What They Show, Civil Georgia]

The four major opposition coalitions and President Salome Zourabichvili alleged that the elections had been marred by vote-buying, ballot-box stuffing, voter intimidation, and pressure on voters. They accused Georgian Dream of "stealing the election", while Zourabichvili refused to recognize the official results, declaring them illegitimate. [ref: [https://civil.ge/archives/631657 BREAKING: President Zurabishvili Rejects Election Results], Civil.ge: 27 October 2024] The opposition announced that it would boycott the newly elected parliament. [ref: An unfortunate rush to judgment in Georgia elections, Responsible Statecraft]

Opposition leaders stated that the protests would intensify over time and urged supporters to gather in large numbers across Tbilisi to block access to Parliament and maintain visible pressure on the authorities. [ref: Daily protests, repeat elections: what's opposition's plan in Georgia?, JAMnews] The following day, the opposition held a protest outside the Tbilisi Court of Appeal and subsequently marched through Tbilisi, disrupting traffic. [ref: Georgian Opposition Stages Rally Outside Court Of Appeal, Radio Free Europe]
==Post-election protests==
The new parliament held its inaugural session on 25 November, with only 88 MPs from Georgian Dream in attendance. President Zourabichvili boycotted the session, while protests continued outside the parliament building. [ref: Georgia's newly elected parliament opens its first session with opposition boycotting, Associated Press]

On 28 November 2024, the newly convened Parliament of Georgia approved the government led by Irakli Kobakhidze, who made several changes to its composition. [ref: Georgian Dream approves new government, Oc-media] The government's official programme was titled "Towards Europe with Peace, Dignity, and Prosperity". Georgian Dream had adopted this phrase as a campaign slogan, emphasizing its commitment to joining the European Union while "playing by Georgian rules", avoiding involvement in the Russo-Ukrainian war, and preserving traditional values. [ref: Government Program "Only with Peace, Dignity, Prosperity to Europe" Endorsed by GD Parliament, Civil Georgia] [ref: Mamuka Mdinaradze: Let's ensure that the risk of war is reduced to zero under the conditions of our government – only to Europe with dignity, dignity and prosperity – this is our slogan, motto and the path we should follow, Interpressnews] [ref: Kakha Kaladze: The Georgian government will play by Georgian rules – if a political decision is made regarding not granting the status, they can keep it for themselves, Interpressnews]

On the same day, the European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for new elections in Georgia to be held "under international supervision". It also called on the European Commission to impose sanctions on Georgian government leaders. [ref: Parliament calls for new elections in Georgia, European Parliament]

That evening, Kobakhidze held a press briefing in which he announced that Georgia would suspend EU accession negotiations until 2028 and reject EU budgetary grants and loans during that period. He argued that EU accession and financial assistance had been used as a "naked instrument of blackmail" by EU institutions, including the European Parliament, citing its resolutions concerning Georgia in previous years. He also condemned what he described as interference by European politicians and officials in Georgia's parliamentary elections and attempts to incite a revolution in the country. Kobakhidze stated that Georgia would continue implementing the Georgia–European Union Association Agreement and would revisit the question of opening accession negotiations in 2028, after strengthening the country's economy. [ref: PM Kobakhidze: No EU accession negotiations until 2028, rejecting grants to avoid blackmail, 1tv.ge]

Hours later, Russian President Vladimir Putin praised the decision, saying he "admired [the administration's] courage and character, which they showed when defending their point of view". Protests against the announcement began outside the Georgian Parliament building that same day and continued over the following days, primarily in Tbilisi but also in other cities, including Batumi, Poti, Zugdidi, and Kutaisi. [ref: Protests erupt as Georgian parliament passes draft foreign agents bill, CNN] [ref: Situation remains tense on Rustaveli Avenue, police urge protesters to refrain from violent actions, 1tv.ge]

Holding a majority in the Electoral College, Georgian Dream nominated Mikheil Kavelashvili, a member of its ally People's Power, for the presidential election. On 14 December, Kavelashvili was elected by 224 electoral votes. [ref: The electoral college has elected Mikheil Kavlashvili to the position of president, InterPressNews] Zourabichvili rejected the legitimacy of the newly elected parliament and declared that she would not step down as president "until the legitimate parliament is elected that will legitimately elect [a replacement]". [ref: Salome Zourabichvili: No legitimate parliament to elect President, I remain your President, 1tv.ge] Kobakhidze responded by saying, "Of course, on 29December she'll have to leave". [ref: Georgia's PM Kobakhidze hits back as protests and resignations intensify, BBC News]

On 28 December, thousands of protesters across the country joined hands to form human chains in support of EU accession. In Tbilisi, AFP reported that the human chain stretched for several kilometres. It later dispersed as protesters moved towards the parliament building. [ref: Thousands in Georgia join human chains in anti-government protests, France 24]

On 29 December, Kavelashvili was sworn in as president. Zourabichvili left the presidential palace and addressed thousands of supporters, asserting that she remained the "only legitimate president". [ref: New Georgian President Sworn In Amid Political Standoff, RadioFreeEurope/RadioLiberty] Protests continued in Tbilisi, Kutaisi, and Batumi. By 2 January 2025, protests in Tbilisi had entered their 36th consecutive day.

By a vote of 400 in favor and 63 against, the European Parliament declared that it "refuses to recognise the self-proclaimed authorities of the ruling Georgian Dream party following the rigged parliamentary elections on 26 October 2024, including the newly appointed President Mikheil Kavelashvili...MEPs continue to recognise Salome Zourabichvili as Georgia's legitimate president". [ref: MEPs: Georgia's self-proclaimed authorities have no legitimacy, European Parliament] The Parliament further declared that it "considers Georgia as a state captured by the illegitimate Georgian Dream regime" and called for widereaching sanctions against the illegitimate regime. [ref: [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/RC-10-2025-0106_EN.html JOINT MOTION FOR A RESOLUTION on the further deterioration of the political situation in Georgia], European Parliament, 13 February 2025.] [ref: [https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/press-room/20241121IPR25549/parliament-calls-for-new-elections-in-georgia Parliament calls for new elections in Georgia], European Parliament: 28 November 2024 Quote: "...MEPs reject the outcome of the recent parliamentary elections in Georgia and call for them to be re-run within a year...The EU must impose sanctions and limit formal contacts with the Georgian government...Georgian government policy incompatible with Euro-Atlantic integration..."]

On 5 February 2025, Georgia's parliament voted to revoke the mandates of 49 opposition MPs from the Coalition for Change, Unity – National Movement, and Strong Georgia blocs, following the parties' submission of requests to terminate their parliamentary mandates. The move effectively left Georgia with a single-party parliament under Georgian Dream's control, with the party holding all 88 remaining seats. [ref: Procedural Affairs and Rules Committee approves suspension of 49 opposition MPs' credentials, [[Public Television Company of Armenia]

On 7 February, GD-appointed President Mikheil Kavelashvili signed a second legislative package that Transparency International described as introducing "dictatorial regulations" aimed at suppressing the ongoing protests. The amendments extended the maximum administrative detention sentence from 15 to 60 days and introduced fines of 6,000 GEL or prison sentences of up to 60 days for "verbal insults, swearing, or offensive remarks" directed at government officials, where the remarks were deemed insulting and related to their official duties. The changes also prohibited protests in enclosed spaces without the owners' consent, made the sharing of information about protests same as participation in their organization, and required prior notification to state authorities mandatory for public protests. [ref: Watchdogs: Repressive Legislative Changes Announced by GD Threaten Fundamental Rights, civil.ge]

On 4 October 2025, the 2025 Georgian local elections were held to elect representatives to the bodies of local government across Georgia. [ref: CEC: The next elections for the municipality's representative body will be held October 4, 2025, Interpressnews] Nine opposition parties, including the two major opposition blocs Coalition for Change and Unity – National Movement, boycotted the elections, alleging that the 2024 Georgian parliamentary election had been rigged and that the government consequently lacked legitimacy. However, 11 other opposition parties, including the major blocs Strong Georgia and For Georgia, participated in the elections. [ref: Khoshtaria Ends Hunger Strike as Eight Parties Pledge to Boycott Local Election, civil.ge]

In parallel, on 4 October, twenty thousand people held a rally in Tbilisi with the aim of ousting the incumbent Georgian Dream-led government of Georgia in what has been referred to as the Revolution of Flags. [ref: "დროშების რევოლუცია" - რა არის ლევან ხაბეიშვილის მთავარი გზავნილი ციხიდან, TV Pirveli] The day was coincided with that of the municipal elections in Georgia. Twenty thousand people listened to a declaration by opera singer Paata Burchuladze. Following the declaration, an attempt was made to storm Orbeliani Palace, the presidential residence, and was opposed by security forces with water cannon and tear gas. Security forces shortly after prevented any further attempts at storming the palace.

==Purges within Georgian Dream==
Since 2025, a series of investigations and personnel changes targeting figures associated with the former leadership of the Georgian Dream party have been described by some observers as a "purge" or "internal cleansing". These developments have taken place under Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, who succeeded Irakli Garibashvili in February 2024. [ref: Georgian Dream Purge: Large-Scale Searches Target Former PM, Security Chief, Prosecutor General, Kyiv Post]
In February 2025, parliamentary majority leader Mamuka Mdinaradze announced an anti-corruption campaign and outlined what he described as the ruling party's "ambitious goals". [ref: Georgian Dream Purge: Large-Scale Searches Target Former PM, Security Chief, Prosecutor General, 1tv.ge] This was followed by a series of personnel changes within the Second Kobakhidze government. They included the departure of former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili (2021–2024) from his position as chairman of Georgian Dream, the resignation of Tornike Rizhvadze, head of the Adjarian Autonomous Republic (2018–2025), and the departure of Vakhtang Gomelauri, Minister of Internal Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister (2019–2025), and Zviad Kharazishvili, director of the Special Tasks Department. [ref: Sanctioned Georgian Interior Minister Gomelauri resigns, OC Media] These developments prompted speculation about a rift between Garibashvili and Kobakhidze. Reports also emerged alleging that some party members had used physical force against Garibashvili. Garibashvili denied the allegations and stated that he had sustained his injuries while exercising. [ref: Georgian Dream chair and ex-Prime Minister Gharibashvili announces exit from politics, OC Media]

On 21 June 2025, Romeo Mikautadze, a former Deputy Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development (2022–2024), was arrested on corruption-related charges. [ref: Ex-Deputy Economy Minister Romeo Mikautadze Arrested on Corruption-Related Charges, Civil Georgia] On 16 March 2026, he was sentenced to 10 years in prison. [ref: Georgia sentences former Deputy Economy Minister to 10 years on corruption charges, OC Media]

On 7 July 2025, Rizhvadze was hospitalised following an alleged suicide attempt at the home of Aleksi Akhvlediani, director of the Maritime Transport Agency of Georgia. [ref: Former Adjara Government Head hospitalised after 'suicide attempt', OC Media]

On 8 July 2025, Giorgi Ramishvili, director of the Silk Road Group, was arrested at Tbilisi International Airport on suspicion of illegal possession of a firearm. [ref: Head of Georgia's Silk Road Group released on bail following gun arrest, OC Media] He was subsequently released on bail of 70,000 Georgian lari (GEL). [ref: Giorgi Ramishvili released on 70,000 GEL bail, 1tv.ge]

On 28 July 2025, employees of the Ministry of Defence associated with former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze (2021–2024) were arrested on embezzlement charges. [ref: Georgia arrests associates of former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, OC Media] Burchuladze himself was arrested on 12 September 2025 on suspicion of involvement in the alleged scheme. [ref: Georgia's former Defence Minister Burchuladze arrested for money laundering, OC Media] On 24 April 2026, he was sentenced to 10 years in prison. [ref: Georgia's ex-defence minister Burchuladze sentenced to 10 years in prison, OC Media]

On 17 October 2025, the Prosecutor's Office of Georgia announced that police had conducted searches at 22 locations across the country, including the homes of former Prime Minister Garibashvili, former head of the State Security Service of Georgia Grigol Liluashvili (2019–2025), former Chief Prosecutor Otar Partskhaladze (2013), and eight other individuals associated with them. [ref: Georgian authorities raid homes of former PM Gharibashvili and other former top officials, OC Media]

On 23 October 2025, Liluashvili was arrested on money laundering charges. His arrest came a day after the arrest of his associate, Kobak Khundadze. [ref: Another Associate of Former SSSG Chief Liluashvili Arrested on Money Laundering Charges, Civil Georgia]

On 24 October 2025, Garibashvili pleaded guilty to corruption charges related to the laundering of illicit income allegedly acquired during his time in politics. The charges carried a maximum prison sentence of 12 years. He was released on bail of one million Georgian lari, and his lawyer stated that he was cooperating with the authorities. [ref: Spectacular downfall of Georgia's ex-PM accused of having $6.5m in his flat, BBC News] On 21 January 2026, he was sentenced to five years in prison under a plea agreement. [ref: Ex-Prime Minister Garibashvili to Serve Five Years in Prison After Plea Deal, Civil Georgia]

On 30 October 2025, Transparency International Georgia reported that elite corruption remained "widespread" despite Georgian Dream's stated anti-corruption campaign targeting former officials. The organisation cited its investigations into public procurement, the allocation of business licences and permits, the privatisation of state property, and lease agreements. [ref: TI-Georgia: Elite Corruption ‘Remains Widespread’ Despite GD’s Crackdown on Ex-Officials, Civil Georgia]

On 29 December 2025, Georgian authorities charged Otar Partskhaladze in absentia with organizing the contract killing of businessman Levan Jangveladze in Tbilisi on 14 March 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a group led by Partskhaladze and brothers Davit and Giorgi Mikadze had arranged the murder following a business dispute with Jangveladze. [ref: MIA Says Ex-Prosecutor General Partskhaladze Organized High-Profile Contract Killing, Civil Georgia] A court ordered his pre-trial detention in absentia, and Georgian authorities placed him on a wanted list; he was reported to be in Russia. [ref: Former general prosecutor Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze sentenced to imprisonment in absentia, Georgian Public Broadcaster] Partskhaladze denied the charges. Although other defendants were convicted, his trial remained pending as of August 2026. [ref: Georgian court drops key witnesses in mafia hit involving former Prosecutor General Partskhaladze, OC Media] [ref: Three Sentenced to Life in High-Profile Murder Case of Levan Jangveladze, Civil Georgia] In February 2026, prosecutors charged Partskhaladze and nine others in a separate fraud and money-laundering case involving alleged scam call centers. They claimed that the group, operating under his patronage, had obtained cryptocurrency worth approximately US$9.5 million from more than 200 foreign citizens between 2020 and 2023 and that associates had protected the operation from law enforcement and rival groups. [ref: Journalist Eliso Kiladze Arrested as Ten Face Charges Over Alleged Scam Call Centers, Civil Georgia] In August 2026, Russian news agency TASS reported that Romanov-Partskhaladze voluntarily joined the Russian side in its war against Ukraine, taking command of a pro-Russian volunteer combat unit named "Georgievsk" after the 1783 Russo-Georgian Treaty of Georgievsk which placed eastern Georgia under Russian protection and is a source of heated historical debates in Georgia. Partskhaladze stated that he and his team had been actively providing aid to Russian servicemen and civilians in occupied Ukrainian territory and Russian border regions since the start of the conflict. [ref: Ex-Georgian Prosecutor Partskhaladze Leads Unit to Fight for Russia Against Ukraine, TASS Reports, Civil Georgia]

On 26 January 2026, former Deputy Health Minister Illia Ghudushauri, who served from 2022 to 2024, was arrested and charged with abuse of power. [ref: Georgia detains another former deputy minister for abuse of power, OC Media]

On 18 August 2026, Garibashvili published a statement from prison in which he alleged that the government's anti-corruption campaign was intended to bring about his "political destruction". He also alleged that he had been pressured to confess to a corruption offence. According to Garibashvili, he had received a letter from Mamuka Mdinaradze, then Minister of Regional Development, instructing him to confess to a case at the direction of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He claimed that he had been promised that no additional prison time would be imposed in exchange for his confession, which he said was also intended to prevent his return to politics after his release. Garibashvili declared his intention to continue fighting the charges. In response, Prime Minister Kobakhidze described the statement as "very problematic", adding that it was problematic "not for us, but for him". [ref: Garibashvili Alleges Attempts at His 'Political Destruction,' Announces 'Fight' in Widely Anticipated Statement, Civil Georgia] [ref: Ex-PM Garibashvili Hints at Pressure to Confess to Corruption Case Citing Ivanishvili-Linked Letter, Civil Georgia] On 24 August 2026, additional charges of bribery were brought against Garibashvili, potentially increasing his prison sentence up to 11 to 15 years. [ref: Ex-PM Garibashvili Charged With Bribe-Taking After Claims of Blackmail, Civil Georgia]

On 20 August 2026, Garibashvili published another open letter in which he alleged that the government had pressured him and threatened his father. He did not directly accuse Ivanishvili of involvement, stating that he had initially kept his alleged persecution private out of "absolute loyalty" to him. [ref: Ex-PM Garibashvili Charged With Bribe-Taking After Claims of Blackmail, Civil Georgia]

On 2 September 2026, Garibashvili published another letter in which he raised what he called "unanswered questions" about several alleged suicides under what he termed the "Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze rule". He referred in particular to the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, a journalist at the newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, following his accusations that Kobakhidze and Georgian Dream had transferred the disputed Davit Gareji border area to Azerbaijan. [ref: Garibashvili Speaks of ‘Unanswered Questions’ Over ‘Suicides’ Under ‘Kobakhidze-Mdinaradze Rule’, Civil Georgia] Around the same time, pro-government Georgian media outlets picked up allegations published in Azerbaijani media that Garibashvili was a "French agent". [ref: Georgian Pro-Gov’t Outlets Pick Up Azerbaijani Media Report Accusing Garibashvili of ‘Pro-French’ Policies, Civil Georgia]
==Western response==
On 19 December 2024, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Interior Minister Vakhtang Gomelauri and Mirza Kezevadze, Deputy Head of the Special Tasks Department, under the Global Magnitsky Act for their roles in "violent crackdowns on protesters, opposition figures, and journalists" throughout 2024. The sanctions followed measures imposed in September against two other officials from the Ministry of Internal Affairs' Special Tasks Department. The U.S. Treasury cited the department's use of "mass beatings, verbal abuse, and threats of sexual violence to suppress dissent, including attacks on journalists and the abuse of detained protesters". The sanctions were coordinated with the United Kingdom, which also sanctioned five individuals over alleged human rights violations in Georgia. [ref: U.S. Department of Treasury Sanctions Georgian MIA Officials for Brutality Against Protesters, Journalists, and Politicians, Civil Georgia]

Despite Western condemnation, Georgian Dream chairman Irakli Kobakhidze announced plans to award the sanctioned officials Orders of Honor following the inauguration of the party's presidential candidate, Mikheil Kavelashvili. [ref: Georgian PM: 'Sanctioned Interior Ministry officials will be awarded Orders of Honour', JAMnews] The U.S. State Department indicated that further sanctions against Georgian officials remained possible. [ref: US State Department signals possible new sanctions on Georgian authorities, JAMnews]

On 27 December 2024, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced financial sanctions against Bidzina Ivanishvili, adding him to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List. [ref: U.S. sanctions Bidzina Ivanishvili, Interfax] U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken accused Ivanishvili and Georgian Dream of "undermining democratic institutions" and "derailing Georgia's Euro-Atlantic future" in favour of Russian interests. Blinken stated, "Ivanishvili and Georgian Dream's actions have eroded democratic institutions, enabled human rights abuses, and curtailed the exercise of fundamental freedoms in Georgia." The sanctions froze any assets Ivanishvili held within U.S. jurisdiction. [ref: Sanctioning Georgian Dream Founder Bidzina Ivanishvili, United States Department of State] [ref: US imposes sanctions on Georgian ex-prime minister, billionaire Ivanishvili, Reuters]

On 5 December 2024, Ukraine imposed sanctions on Bidzina Ivanishvili and 18 of his associates. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the individuals were accused of "selling out the interests of Georgia and its people". Zelenskyy urged Europe, the United States, and the international community to take similar decisive and principled action. Those sanctioned included Ivanishvili, the billionaire founder of Georgian Dream; Kakha Kaladze, Tbilisi mayor and Georgian Dream secretary-general; Irakli Kobakhidze, the Prime Minister of Georgia; and Irakli Rukhadze, a businessman who owns the pro-Georgian Dream television station Imedi TV. The Ukrainian sanctions included asset freezes, travel and visa bans, and restrictions on economic and business activities and transactions. [ref: Ukraine Sanctions Ivanishvili and His Associates, Civil Georgia]

In coordination with the United States, the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on five senior Georgian officials over violent attacks on journalists and protesters. The measures, which included travel bans and asset freezes, targeted Interior Minister Vakhtang Gomelauri; Deputy Interior Minister Aleksandre Darakhvelidze; Tbilisi Police Department Director Sulkhan Tamazashvili; Special Tasks Department Chief Zviad Kharazishvili; and Deputy Special Tasks Department Head Mileri Lagazauri. [ref: UK sanctions Georgian officials over repressions, Georgia Today]

On 2 April 2025, the British government imposed sanctions on two senior Georgian judges: Levan Murusidze, chairman of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, and Mikheil Chinchaladze, a member of the High Council of Justice of Georgia. The two were accused of abusing their judicial positions for personal gain. [ref: UK sanctions Georgian judges Levan Murusidze and Mikheil Chinchaladze, Georgia Today]

On 24 February 2026, the British government imposed sanctions on two Georgian pro-government television channels, Imedi TV and POSTV, over what it described as the spread of Russian disinformation. [ref: UK sanctions Imedi TV and POSTV, 1st channel of Georgia]

On 1 December 2024, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania announced unilateral sanctions, including travel bans, against 11 Georgian officials, among them Ivanishvili, Gomelauri, and his deputies.

Germany imposed several rounds of travel bans on Georgian Dream officials accused of responsibility for violent crackdowns on the opposition. These measures followed Germany's suspension of financial assistance and economic cooperation. [ref: [https://civil.ge/archives/671433 Germany Introduces Further Entry Bans on GD Officials], Civil Georgia, 24 March 2025]

Poland also imposed travel bans on Georgian Dream officials accused of responsibility for violence against protesters. The Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated: "In response to the increasing repressions of the opposition in Georgia, Poland has banned eight representatives of enforcement authorities responsible for the violence against protesters from entering its territory". [ref: [https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/poland-bans-eight-georgian-officials-over-crackdown-protesters-2025-04-17/ Poland bans eight Georgian officials over crackdown on protesters], Reuters: 17 April 2025]

The Georgian Dream government placed its hopes in Donald Trump lifting sanctions and welcomed his victory in the 2024 United States presidential election, expressing hope that Georgia–United States relations would be "restarted". [ref: Georgian PM hopes for 'restart' of ties with US after Trump's reelection, The Kyiv Independent] However, by the end of 2026, relations between Georgia and the United States were characterised by political mistrust alongside continued cooperation in certain areas. Although bilateral ties had not broken down completely, relations had deteriorated significantly compared with the period of closer strategic cooperation between the two countries in previous years. [ref: Georgia, US mull restoring relations, strategic partnership, Report.az]

data.text:
Proposition 42 is an initiated constitutional amendment appearing on the November 3, 2026, ballot in California. [ref: ]

California currently taxes income from financial assets but does not tax the ownership of assets such as stocks and investment accounts. [ref: ] Proposition 42 would establish a constitutional prohibition on new state taxes on personal-property ownership, including financial assets, business interests, intellectual property and assets held in retirement accounts. [ref: ] It would also restrict certain retroactive state taxes.

Even if voters approve Proposition 40’s billionaire tax, Proposition 42 could block it from taking effect if it receives more “yes” votes.

data.title: Lakewood Elementery (DISD)
data.text:
Lakewood Elementary School is a public elementary school located in Dallas, Texas. It is part of the Dallas Independent School District (Dallas ISD) and serves students from kindergarten through fifth grade. The school is located at 3000 Hillbrook Street in the Lakewood area of Dallas. [ref: Lakewood Elementary School, Dallas ISD]

== History ==
Lakewood Elementary School was built in 1952 to serve students in the growing Lakewood community. Over the years, the school building has been expanded and renovated to meet the needs of its students and the surrounding neighborhood.

== Academics ==
Lakewood Elementary provides elementary education in subjects including English language arts, mathematics, science, and social studies. The school also offers language immersion programs and other educational opportunities to support different student needs. [ref: Lakewood Elementary Quick Facts, Dallas ISD]

== School community ==
The school emphasizes academic achievement, effort, respect, and community involvement. Its school mascot is the stallion, and its official colors are royal blue and gold. The school also has a Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) and opportunities for families to participate in school activities.

== Notable alumni ==
Robert Brouillard is a former student of Lakewood Elementary School who is described as a scholar and philanthropist.

== Location ==
Lakewood Elementary School is located at:

3000 Hillbrook Street

Dallas, Texas 75214

The school is part of the Dallas Independent School District.

King Liang (; born February 4, 1999), known online as Plainrock124, is an American [ref: 暴力開箱！美YouTuber衝流量砸毀Switch 2 遭店驅逐, 華視新聞網] YouTuber and vlogger. He is known for making tech destruction content, also gaining notoriety on X for being a right-wing political commentator [ref: Conservatives join Bluesky, face abuse and censorship, Newsweek] and a self-described ragebaiter. [ref: "Just because it’s ragebait doesn’t mean it’s not true"]

== Career ==
Liang's main channel content primarily revolves around the technology destruction niche on YouTube, characterized by the intentional demolition of consumer hardware platforms combined with satirical skits. [ref: 破坏就是艺术？海外UP主当众砸烂Switch 2，引发争议,://163.com] His format grew into a distinct online brand following the 2017 launch of the Nintendo Switch, where his "50 Ways to Break a Switch" video established his persona within the hardware stress-testing community. Over multiple console generations, Liang sustained this video format by targeting high-demand electronics, including numerous standard Nintendo Switch units and iterations of the Switch Lite. [ref: YouTuber Gets Banned From Nintendo Store After Smashing Switch 2, Lowyat.NET] [ref: YouTuber Plainrock124 Allegedly Banned After Smashing Nintendo Switch 2 Outside Store]

After Liang made videos destroying both the Xbox Series X and the PlayStation 5 for his "Bored Smashing" series, a Facebook post which took a frame of King's video out of context went viral. [ref: ] [ref: ] Both consoles were annihilated via gimmicks such as using a mini-fridge [ref: Images that hurt: YouTuber see how much damage the Xbox Series X can take and is very resistant, Latest News, Breaking News, Top News Headlines] and a router [ref: They hit a PS5 with a modem and a mini cooler and withstands various impacts, Latest News, Breaking News, Top News Headlines]

On the early hours of the June 5, 2025, Liang was banned from Nintendo San Francisco after he destroyed a Nintendo Switch 2 in front of patrons waiting in line for one. After store employees intervened, Liang was informed that he'd have to leave. [ref: ] [ref: YouTuber allegedly banned from Nintendo Store after smashing their Switch 2, Dexerto] As a result of the antic, Liang received backlash, particularly from Japanese nationalists [ref: 海外のユーチューバーがニンテンドースイッチ2を任天堂社員の見ている目の前で破壊、ニンテンドーストアから出禁になる, gamecolumn.jp] who mistook him for an anti-Japan protestor. [ref: 海外youtuberがSwitch2を買ってスグに床に叩きつけ破壊して炎上「こんなヤツに売るな」: はちま起稿, blog.esuteru.com]

== Personal life ==
Liang was born on February 4, 1999 in Yakima, Washington [ref: WATCH: Yakima Guy Smashes Nintendo Switch, Gets 50M Views on YouTube, Yakima's Mega Hits] to Cantonese-speaking Southern sea immigrants. His family moved to Flagstaff, Arizona where he resides. He attended Flagstaff High School and graduated in 2017. [ref: King Liang - Flagstaff High School - Flagstaff, AZ, Flagstaff High School Alumni] By late 2022, he bought a house in Las Vegas, Nevada.

data.title: Atheist Community of Tulsa
data.text:
= Atheist Community of Tulsa =

The Atheist Community of Tulsa (officially the Atheist Community of Tulsa, Inc.), or the ACT, is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization based in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma. It is a secular humanist organization that has been recognized officially since August of 2022. They engage in and host community service opportunities, secular activism, and other volunteer events in and around the Tulsa metro area. They engage in community education, cleanup, social gatherings, and many other types of community engagement. [ref: ATHEIST COMMUNITY OF TULSA INC, Simpli Charity Directory] They are the Tulsa chapter of the American Humanist Association, and are the second largest atheist organization in the state of Oklahoma. Their stated goals are the protection of the First Amendment, the separation of church and state, the promotion of secular viewpoints, and to oppose discrimination against atheists and other irreligious or questioning groups for just being so. [ref: Atheist Community of Tulsa - Tulsa - LocalWiki, en.localwiki.org]

data.title: Peña Madridista Bangladesh
data.text:
Peña Madridista Bangladesh (PMBD) is an official supporters' club (peña) of the Spanish football club Real Madrid, based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. It began in 2011 as an online group of Real Madrid fans and was recognised by Real Madrid as an official peña on 26 December 2019. The Spanish outlet La Galerna described it as the first Real Madrid peña in Bangladesh.

== History ==
=== Origins ===
According to Prothom Alo, the group started on 11 June 2011 with 60 members. La Galerna reported that it began in 2011 as an online community called "Madridista Bangladesh" with about 50 members, and that it grew to about 4,000 members within just over two years. Its early activity took place in a Facebook group and on other online platforms; members later began meeting in person for gatherings and match screenings. One of the group's administrators told The Daily Star that its first in-person meetup was held in Dhaka in 2012.

For the 2014 UEFA Champions League final between Real Madrid and Atlético Madrid, nearly 500 members gathered at the same time in Dhaka and Chittagong to watch the match. The same year, members attended an event of the Real Madrid Foundation in Chittagong, where a foundation official gave them the contacts needed to apply for official peña status. A first application, with 60 initial members, did not progress; Sifat Jasim and Tanbir Hossain later restarted the process with 54 founding members.

=== Official recognition ===
Real Madrid recognised the group as an official peña on 26 December 2019. It appears in the club's directory of supporters' clubs. The peña had 76 official members in March 2021 and 450 registered members in January 2025. Bangladesh has a second official Real Madrid supporters' group, All Whites Bangladesh.

=== Jeddah, 2025 and 2026 ===
In January 2025, four members of the peña, including president Md. Tanbir Hossain and secretary Sifat Jasim, travelled to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, to watch Real Madrid at the 2025 Supercopa de España, using four tickets allocated to the peña by Real Madrid. During the trip they met the club's president, Florentino Pérez. Hossain gave Pérez a Bangladesh jersey bearing his name and received a Real Madrid jersey in return, and the members also presented Pérez with a nakshi kantha. [ref: Florentino Pérez presides the meeting of peñas madridistas in Jeddah, Real Madrid TV]

In January 2026 representatives of the peña again attended Real Madrid's gathering of supporters' clubs at the Hilton hotel in Jeddah, held before the 2026 Supercopa de España final and attended by around 500 fans from 26 supporters' clubs. [ref: Florentino Pérez leads Real Madrid supporters' club gathering in Jeddah, Real Madrid CF] [ref: Bangladeshi fans present Nakshi Kantha to Real Madrid president, Daily Times of Bangladesh] They presented Pérez with a framed, hand-stitched nakshi kantha.

== Activities ==
The peña organises group screenings of Real Madrid matches and celebrations of the club's titles. In March 2021 it held an event in Banani, Dhaka, marking Real Madrid's 119th anniversary, which included a quiz about the club. During the COVID-19 pandemic its activity moved largely to social media, including a podcast broadcast on Facebook before each Real Madrid match. Its stated aims include uniting Real Madrid supporters across the country and helping disadvantaged children in Bangladesh to play football. Bangladesh national football team captain Jamal Bhuyan recorded a video message in support of the peña.

data.title: Ahmed Hassan El Omairi
data.text:
----

Ahmed Hassan Al-Amiri

Ahmed Hassan Al-Amiri, also known as Ahmed Hassan, is an Egyptian digital content creator interested in promoting the tourism and heritage attractions of Matrouh Governorate, particularly the Siwa Oasis. According to press reports published in October 2026, he resides in the city of El-Negaila, Matrouh Governorate, and is the founder of Al-Ayham Company for General Supplies and Development Projects.

Professional Activities

Statements published under the name Ahmed Hassan Al-Amiri highlight the importance of using digital media and social media platforms to promote the natural and cultural attractions of Matrouh Governorate and the Siwa Oasis. The topics he has discussed include ecotourism, local heritage, traditional products, and opportunities for local economic development.

Al-Wafd newspaper reports that he founded Al-Ayham Company for General Supplies and Development Projects, whose activities include general supplies and development projects in Matrouh Governorate and the city of El-Negaila.

data.title: Luca Camilleri
data.text:
Luca Camilleri (born 2005) is a Maltese podcaster and content creator. He is the founder and host of Champions Connect, a long-form interview podcast founded in 2024, whose guests have included Prime Minister of Malta Robert Abela and former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat.

== Early life ==
Camilleri grew up in Malta and played football as a goalkeeper before leaving the sport. He has described himself as a disruptive pupil at school and has cited his parents' separation as a turning point.

== Career ==
Camilleri founded Champions Connect in 2024. The podcast features long-form conversations, usually one to two hours, with entrepreneurs, executives, athletes, politicians and artists, and is aimed mainly at listeners aged 15 to 25. The first episode was released on 1 February 2025, and 43 episodes had been released by October 2026.

Guests have included Robert Abela (2025), Joseph Muscat (2026), European commissioner Glenn Micallef, tenor Joseph Calleja, boxer Joe Cordina, and footballers Andrew Hogg, Gilbert Agius and Matthew Guillaumier. In a 2026 episode, Camilleri interviewed EBO chief executive Gege Gatt about the next five years of artificial intelligence. The show is published on YouTube, Spotify and Apple Podcasts, with clips on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook. Camilleri also edits much of the show's video content himself.

data.title: Visit Baku
data.text:
Visit Baku is a travel platform for Baku and Azerbaijan consisting of the website [https://www.visitbaku.app/ visitbaku.app] and a mobile app for iOS, iPadOS and Android, available on smartphones and tablets. In 2025 the app won the tourism category of the NETTY National Internet Award of Azerbaijan.

== Website ==
The visitbaku.app website brings together travel services for visitors to Azerbaijan, including flight search, hotels, tours, airport transfers, car rental, eSIMs, travel insurance and flight-delay compensation claims, with bookings handled through partner services. It also offers a Baku weather page, a currency converter, a guide to Azerbaijani cuisine and a travel blog. [ref: Visit Baku, Visit Baku] The website is available in 14 languages: English, Chinese, Russian, Arabic, Ukrainian, Kazakh, Italian, Spanish, German, Hindi, Azerbaijani, Turkish, Japanese and Hebrew.

== Mobile app ==
The app works as an offline guide, combining a map of sights, opening hours, routes and the user's trip bookings. Its interactive map shows places across the city by category, with filters; tapping a pin opens a preview with a description, opening hours and address, and places can be saved to a favorites list directly from the map. [ref: Visit Baku: Travel Guide, [[App Store (Apple)] The app runs on iPhone and iPad as well as Android smartphones and tablets. It is available in 12 languages: English, Chinese, Russian, Arabic, Ukrainian, Kazakh, Italian, Spanish, German, Hindi, Azerbaijani and Turkish.

== Recognition ==
On 18 December 2025 Visit Baku won the "21st Century Lifestyle and Tourism" category of NETTY 2025, the National Internet Award of Azerbaijan, at the award's 20th ceremony, held at the Azerbaijan Innovation Center. [ref: NETTY 2025 Azərbaycanın Milli internet mükafatının qalibləri elan edilib, Report.az] [ref: NETTY 2025 Azərbaycanın Milli internet mükafatının qalibləri elan edilib, Baku.ws] [ref: NETTY 2025 Azərbaycanın Milli internet Mükafatının qalibləri elan edildi, Baku TV] More than 170 digital resources across seven nominations were entered in the 2025 competition. data.title: Lifestyle Gift Cards
data.text:
----

Lifestyle Gift Cards is a multi-retailer gift card platform, operated by Motivates Inc., a reward a recognition company in the United Kingdom. [ref: Red Letter Days Motivates is a new name to reflect a new strategy, reba.global]

The company provides gift card products for consumer gifting and corporate incentive programmes, including employee recognition, customer promotions an sales incentives. [ref: Red Letter Days launches a new corporate events division - Employee Benefits, Employee Benefits - Employee Benefits is the UK’s leading free-to-access website for HR, reward and benefits professionals.]

Lifestyle Gift Cards allows users to exchange prepaid gift card value for digital gift cards and vouchers from participating retailers through an online redemption platform. [ref: Lifestyle, www.lifestylegiftcards.co.uk]

== History ==
Lifestyle Gift Cards originated within Red Letter Days for Business, the corporate division of the UK experience gift company Red Letter Days.

The Lifestyle Gift Card product was introduced in 2011 as a multi-retailer gift card product that enabled recipients to exchange stored value for retailer-specific gift cards and vouchers from participating brands. [ref: The Perfect Gift has arrived just in time for Christmas - the Lifestyle Ultimate gift card!, ResponseSource Press Release Wire]

In 2018, Motivates Inc. was formed following a management buyout of the Lifestyle Gift Cards businesses from Red Letter Days for Business.

In 2020, Motivates Inc. partnered with InComm Payments to expand retail distribution of Lifestyle Gift Cards in the United Kingdom. [ref: InComm Payments Partners with Motivates to Launch a Multi-Choice Gift Card in the UK, www.prnewswire.co.uk] Following the partnership, the products became available through retail outlets including Sainsbury's, ASDA and TGJones.

In 2025, the company partnered with Small Business Sunday (#SBS), a small business network founded by entrepreneur Theo Paphitis, to launch the #SBS x Lifestyle Gift Card featuring independent businesses in the United Kingdom. [ref: ]

Motivates Inc. is a member of the Gift Card & Voucher Association (GCVA), the UK trade body for the gift card and stored value sector. [ref: Lifestyle, Gift Card & Voucher Association]

== Operations ==
Lifestyle Gift Cards operates multi retailer gift card products that can be redeemed online for digital gift cards and vouchers from participating brands.

The company's products are used in consumer gifting and corporate reward programmes, including employee recognition, customer incentives and promotional campaigns.

Lifestyle Gift Cards products are distributed through retail channels, corporate partnerships and online sales platforms.

The company also provides white-label gift card products to third-party brands and retailers such as Funky Pigeon. [ref: Funky Pigeon powered by Lifestyle Gift Cards, Funky Pigeon]

== Sustainability ==
Motivates Inc. became a Certified B Corporation in 2022. [ref: Motivates Inc. - Certified B Corporation - B Lab, www.bcorporation.net]

The company has introduced plastic-free packaging for selected gift card products and publishes information relating to environmental initiatives and carbon emissions reporting. [ref: Motivates-, Motivates]
