data.title: History of Rajshahi
data.text:
The history of Rajshahi, a city on the northern bank of the Padma River in northern Bangladesh, spans the ancient kingdom of Pundravardhana, successive Hindu and Buddhist dynasties, Muslim rule from the 13th century, the Mughal and British colonial periods, and the city's growth after Bangladeshi independence in 1971. The city is the headquarters of Rajshahi District and Rajshahi Division.

The surrounding Varendra tract was part of Pundravardhana, one of the earliest recorded state formations in ancient Bengal, and later came under the Maurya, Gupta, Pala and Sena rulers. Muslim rule was established in northwestern Bengal after the campaigns of Bakhtiyar Khilji in the early 13th century, and the spread of Islam in the surrounding countryside is traditionally associated with Sufi preachers, among them Shah Makhdum Rupos, whose arrival local tradition dates to 1288–89. Under Mughal rule the area was absorbed into the imperial revenue system, and the founding of the modern city is conventionally dated to about 1634. The name Rajshahi is usually explained as a compound of raj, denoting a raja or zamindar, and the Persian shahi, denoting royal status.

Under British rule the settlement, then known as Rampur-Boalia, became a centre of the silk and indigo trades; Rajshahi District was created in 1772 and the district headquarters moved to Rampur-Boalia in 1825. The founding of Rajshahi College in 1873 and of the Varendra Research Museum in 1910 established the town as an educational centre. Rajshahi became part of East Pakistan after the partition of 1947 and saw large-scale killings during the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971, including at the University of Rajshahi. In 2016 the city attracted international attention for a sharp fall in airborne particulate pollution, although later reporting has described a deterioration in local air quality.

==Ancient period==
The Varendra tract of northern Bengal, which includes the area of present-day Rajshahi, has a documented history extending into antiquity. The region that now forms Rajshahi was part of the ancient territory of Pundravardhana, home to the Pundras, who are described in late Vedic literature as a non-Aryan people and who are said to have established one of the more prosperous Janapadas of ancient India by the 7th–8th centuries BCE. This early settlement lay within the Varendra (or Barind) tract, an elevated plateau of red clay soil bounded by the Ganges and Kosi rivers to the west, the Karatoya to the east and the Padma to the south. Archaeological evidence indicates that the riverine floodplains of Bengal have been inhabited for millennia, with sedentary settlement based on irrigated rice cultivation dating back at least 2,500 years.

The region's transition from a tribal polity to an imperial province began with the expansion of the Maurya Empire in the 3rd century BCE. The Mahasthangarh Brahmi inscription, the oldest written record found in Bangladesh, identifies the city of Pundranagara, at modern Mahasthan, as an administrative centre under Mauryan rule with a system for distributing grain during emergencies. Following the Mauryas the region came under the Gupta Empire of the 4th to 6th centuries CE, during which Pundravardhana became an administrative division known as a bhukti. Finds from this period in Rajshahi district include Gupta-style sculpture, such as a plainly carved Buddha image from Mandail.

The decline of the Guptas was followed by the rise of the Pala Empire in the 8th century, a period that O'Malley's gazetteer describes as a golden age of Varendra. The Pala kings, who were Buddhist, established an organised administration and supported the Varendra school of art, known for its black stone sculpture. Architectural work from the period includes the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, in the neighbouring area of present-day Naogaon District, built by King Dharmapala ( 770–810 CE), which became an important centre of Buddhist learning in South Asia. In the 12th century the Sena dynasty, originally from southern India, replaced the Palas and brought a shift toward orthodox Brahmanism; the Senas established a capital at Vijaynagara, near present-day Rajshahi city, and later moved it to Lakhnauti-Gaur.

==Medieval period==
Islam reached the Bengal delta by land at the start of the 13th century. In 1202–1204 CE Muhammad-i-Bakhtiyar Khilji, a Turkish officer, led a cavalry raid that overran northwestern Bengal. According to the traditional account, Bakhtiyar and his men entered the royal city of Nudiya disguised as horse dealers; the site of that city is disputed, and Van Schendel notes that it may have lain within the modern Rajshahi region rather than at Nabadwip. The Sena ruler Lakshmana Sena withdrew to eastern Bengal, and Bakhtiyar established a Muslim-ruled state with its capital at Lakhnauti-Gaur. For more than a century the region was administered by governors loosely subject to the Delhi sultans. Silk production in the area is recorded from this period, and the industry has continued into modern times.

Between 1338 and 1342 CE Bengal broke away from Delhi and was ruled by independent sultans for the next two centuries. The spread of Islam among the rural population during this era was assisted by Sufi preachers, who emphasised a direct spiritual relationship with the divine. Local tradition connects the Sufi saint Shah Makhdum Rupos with the settlement later known as Rampur-Boalia; his arrival is generally dated to 1288–89, though accounts vary.

In the early 15th century Raja Ganesha, a Hindu zamindar of Bhaturia, an area covering parts of the modern Rajshahi and Dinajpur districts, displaced the reigning sultan and took power in Bengal. His son Jadu converted to Islam and ruled as Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah, in a reign generally described as stable. The Bagha Mosque, built in 1523 CE during the reign of Nusrat Shah, is the district's principal surviving building from the Sultanate period; the jami mosque has ten domes, terracotta ornament and a raised platform intended as a prayer gallery for the ruler. [ref: Bagha Mosque, Asiatic Society of Bangladesh]

==Mughal period (1526–1757)==
The Mughal era brought significant administrative change, as the region moved from a frontier of local resistance to an integrated part of the imperial revenue system. Mughal control followed a long period of resistance by local Afghan and Hindu landholders known as the Baro Bhuiyans. Although the Mughals won a major victory in 1576, full control of the territory was not achieved until 1611–1612, during the viceroyalty of Islam Khan. To secure the province against Portuguese and Arakanese incursions, Islam Khan moved the provincial capital to Dhaka, renamed Jahangirnagar, in 1610. The territory was organised into a hierarchy of suba (province), sarkar (region), pargana (subdivision) and mouza (revenue village), the last of which remains a standard unit in Bangladesh.

The formal founding of the modern city, historically known as Rampur-Boalia, is generally dated to about 1634 on the basis of epigraphic records at the mausoleum of Shah Makhdum Rupos. The name "Rajshahi" is widely explained as a compound of raj, denoting a raja or zamindar, and the Persian shahi, denoting royal status. [ref: Rajshahi District, Asiatic Society of Bangladesh] Under the zamindari system, local territorial chiefs retained their lands on condition that they collected and remitted a fixed share of revenue to the imperial treasury. These zamindars formed a secular aristocracy that maintained local order and mediated between the rural population and the imperial court.

The weakening of central Mughal authority in the early 18th century allowed the rise of the Natore Raj, a family of Barendra Brahmins who became the dominant zamindars of the region. The family's prominence began with the brothers Raghunandan and Ramjivan: Raghunandan, a senior official under Nawab Murshid Quli Khan, secured land grants for his brother, formalising the estate around 1712. At its height the Rajshahi zamindari was among the largest estates in Bengal, extending over nearly 13,000 square miles (34,000 km2) across parts of what are now Murshidabad, Nadia and Jessore. Rani Bhabani (r. 1748–1802) managed the estate for roughly half a century and is remembered for her religious patronage, including the construction of temples and public works.

==British colonial period (1757–1947)==
Following the East India Company's victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, the region was brought into the colonial administrative framework, and Rajshahi District was formally established in 1772. The district was initially one of the largest in Bengal, corresponding to the Rajshahi zamindari and estimated in 1786 to cover nearly 13,000 square miles. The headquarters remained at Natore until 1825, when the seat was moved to Rampur-Boalia, the site of the modern city, on account of the prevalence of malaria at Natore.

Company rule met early armed resistance in the district during the Fakir–Sannyasi resistance, a movement of Muslim fakirs and Hindu sannyasis that began around 1760 and continued for four decades. Its targets included Company factories and the revenue offices of zamindars loyal to the new administration; in one episode the rebels attacked the Company kuthi at Rampur Boalia and captured its factory chief. [ref: Fakir-Sannyasi Resistance, Asiatic Society of Bangladesh] In the early 20th century the town became a centre of the Swadeshi movement, with local leaders and students taking part in boycotts of British goods and institutions.

During the 18th and 19th centuries Rajshahi was known for its silk trade, and the city is still commonly called the Silk City. The Dutch were the first Europeans to establish a significant presence, building a trading post known as the Bara Kuthi on the bank of the Padma, which the British later took over. The district was also a centre of indigo production, with numerous factories until the industry declined in the late 19th century following the introduction of synthetic dyes.

Several institutions founded in the colonial period shaped the town's later reputation as an educational centre. Rajshahi Collegiate School was established in 1828 and Rajshahi College in 1873, the latter becoming one of the leading colleges in North Bengal. The Varendra Research Museum, founded in 1910 as a private initiative by local aristocrats and scholars, was the first museum of its kind in East Bengal. The Sardaha Police Academy was established in 1912 and continues to serve as a training centre for the national police.

==Partition and East Pakistan (1947–1971)==
Following the Partition of India in 1947, Rajshahi became part of East Pakistan. Partition produced large-scale population movement, with Muslim migrants arriving from India and many Hindu families leaving for West Bengal, altering the city's demographic composition. The city retained its administrative role in North Bengal as the headquarters of Rajshahi Division.

The years immediately after partition saw sustained peasant activism in the greater Rajshahi region. The Tebhaga movement, a campaign by sharecroppers for a larger share of the harvest, took hold around Nachole, then a police station of Rajshahi district and now in Chapai Nawabganj District, where it was led by the communist organiser Ila Mitra among Santal and Bengali cultivators. After a clash between peasants and police on 5 January 1950, a large police force was deployed to the area, Mitra was arrested, and she was later tried for treason and sentenced to life imprisonment in Rajshahi Central Jail. [ref: Mitra, Ila, Asiatic Society of Bangladesh]

The establishment of the University of Rajshahi on 6 July 1953 was a significant development for a region considered poorly served by higher education, the only university in the province until then being in the capital. [ref: Welcome to the University of Rajshahi, University of Rajshahi] The university became home to a community of scholars and students who contributed to intellectual life in East Pakistan, and the Varendra Research Museum was placed under its jurisdiction in 1964. Rajshahi Medical College, which had begun as a private medical school in 1949 and became a government college in 1954, was launched as a full medical college in 1958. [ref: Brief history, Rajshahi Medical College] Rajshahi Engineering College, the forerunner of the Rajshahi University of Engineering & Technology, followed in 1964. [ref: Rajshahi University of Engineering and Technology, Asiatic Society of Bangladesh]

Rajshahi was also a centre of political activity during the Pakistan period, particularly during the Bengali language movement of 1952, when students from local colleges and the university joined protests and strikes against the imposition of Urdu as the sole state language. Unrest continued through the 1960s as the city became a base for the autonomy movement led by the Awami League and for the mass protests against the government of Ayub Khan.

==Bangladesh Liberation War (1971)==
Fighting broke out in Rajshahi on 25–26 March 1971 as the Pakistan Army moved to seize control from supporters of the Awami League. [ref: Eyewitness account of Rajshahi battle, The Hindustan Standard] The city was initially held by irregular resistance forces supported by the local population, while the Pakistani garrison remained in the Rajshahi Cantonment on the northern edge of the city. Early resistance in the surrounding countryside included villagers, often armed only with clubs and stones, clashing with small groups of Pakistani soldiers.

During the nine-month war the Pakistan Army established a camp at Zoha Hall of the University of Rajshahi, where large numbers of people were killed and buried in mass graves in the adjacent playground. Killings also took place at the Sardaha Police Academy and in villages such as Sonaikandi, and freedom fighters fought a series of engagements with Pakistani forces across the district, including an attack on an army patrol boat near Tahirpur in August 1971. In the final days of the conflict, pro-Pakistan militias carried out targeted killings of members of the city's intelligentsia.

Rajshahi was liberated following the surrender of Pakistani forces on 16 December 1971. The war left substantial damage to bridges and other infrastructure across the country. Memorials were subsequently built at the university, among them the sculpture Sabash Bangladesh.

==Since 1971==
Rajshahi Municipality, formed on 1 April 1876, was converted into a municipal corporation on 13 August 1987 and given city corporation status in 1991. Rajshahi Town Development Authority, later the Rajshahi Development Authority, had been created in 1976 to guide the expansion of the urban area. [ref: Rajshahi Development Authority, Government of Bangladesh] Post-war development concentrated on restoring connectivity and on the city's established economic base in sericulture and agriculture.

The city's institutional base expanded after independence. Rajshahi Engineering College became the Bangladesh Institute of Technology, Rajshahi, in 1986 and was upgraded to the Rajshahi University of Engineering & Technology in 2003. The region is also associated with gambhira folk performance and with mango cultivation, including the Fazli and Himsagar varieties. Rajshahi silk was registered as a geographical indication in September 2017, and the certificate was formally issued in June 2021. [ref: Six products get GI tag, The Financial Express]

From the early 2000s the city corporation pursued a series of environmental measures, including tree planting under a "zero soil" programme, the introduction of battery-powered rickshaws in 2004, daytime restrictions on heavy vehicles in the city centre, and changes to brick kiln technology. [ref: Rajshahi: the city that took on air pollution – and won, The Guardian] Drawing on World Health Organization data, The Guardian reported in 2016 that concentrations of PM10 particulates in the city had fallen from 195 micrograms per cubic metre in 2014 to about 64 in 2016, the largest such reduction recorded worldwide over that period. Later assessments have been more critical. A 2023 fact-check by Dismislab found that claims describing Rajshahi as the cleanest city in Asia were unsupported, noting that the 2016 finding concerned the rate of improvement rather than absolute air quality, [ref: Rajshahi is not the cleanest city in Asia, Dismislab] and in 2026 The Business Standard described a marked deterioration in the city's air and noise pollution, attributing it to unplanned construction and weak urban management. [ref: Why is Rajshahi city losing its clean, green, healthy image fast?, The Business Standard]

==References==

==Sources==

* Final Report on the Survey and Settlement Operations in the District of Rajshahi 1912–22, Bengal Secretariat Book Depot
* Bengal District Gazetteers: Rajshahi, Bengal Secretariat Book Depot

data.title: Sync.me
data.text:
----

Sync.me (originally SmartSync) is a caller ID and contact-management
mobile app developed by Sync.me Technologies Ltd for
Android and iOS. The app identifies incoming callers,
blocks spam and robocalls, offers reverse phone lookup, and
synchronises contact details and photos from social networks.

== History ==
The app was first released as SmartSync, a social contact-synchronisation app for the
iPhone that displayed a caller's latest Facebook status updates and photos when they
called. It was founded by Ken Vinner and Shlomo Unger with angel funding.

The company later renamed the app Sync.ME and, in November 2012, raised a US$4 million
funding round from undisclosed private investors. At that time it reported approximately five
million users and described itself as syncing more than one billion contacts each week, with
particular popularity in Japan after the addition of a Japanese-language search
algorithm.

The app subsequently added caller identification, spam-call blocking, reverse phone lookup and
spam-text filtering, which became its main focus. The company says
its caller identification draws on a database of several billion phone numbers together with
spam reports crowdsourced from its users.

== Features ==
On Android and iOS, Sync.me offers caller identification for incoming calls, including numbers
not saved in the user's contacts; blocking of spam and robocalls; reverse phone-number lookup;
filtering of spam and scam text messages; and contact synchronisation that backs up and updates
contact details and photos from social-network profiles. The
contact-syncing function, which originally drew photos and details from social networks, was
the app's initial focus before it added caller-identification tools.

== Reception ==
Reviewing an early version, TechCrunch described it as "the app that turns you into a
god", referring to the way it surfaced callers' social-media information during a
call.

data.title: Delius (Song of Summer)
data.text:
"Delius (Song of Summer)" is a song by the English singer-songwriter Kate Bush, released on her third studio album, Never for Ever (1980). [ref: Delius (Song Of Summer), Kate Bush Encyclopedia] The track served as a tribute to the English composer Frederick Delius and was additionally issued as the B-side to the single "Army Dreamers" in October 1980.

== Background and Composition ==
Bush wrote "Delius" after viewing Song of Summer, Ken Russell's 1968 BBC television film depicting the final years of the blind, paralyzed composer Frederick Delius and his amanuensis, Eric Fenby. [ref: Kate Bush's 50 greatest songs – ranked!, The Guardian] In a contemporaneous newsletter, Bush described the piece as a tribute to "an extraordinary man both in body and spirit."

Musically, the composition relies on acoustic piano, a prominent sitar line performed by Paddy Bush, and ambient vocal harmonies. The backing track features rhythmic accentuations generated by an early drum machine; the liner notes of Never for Ever credit the drum machine simply as "Roland". [ref: Never for Ever, EMI Records]

The lyrical themes detail Delius's dictation process to Fenby, featuring spoken-word style vocal fragments like "In B, Fenby!" alongside subtle Latin phrases ("Delius amat") and references to Delius's orchestral piece To Be Sung of a Summer Night on the Water.

== Release and Promotion ==
The track was recorded between January and June 1980 at Abbey Road Studios in London and released on 7 September 1980 as part of Never for Ever. Rather than being performed live in-studio, the song's music video was broadcast on television programs, including a Dr. Hook television special on 7 April 1980 and on The Russell Harty Show on 25 November 1980, where Bush appeared as a guest alongside Eric Fenby and Julian Lloyd Webber. [ref: Russell Harty Show (the), Kate Bush Encyclopedia]

== Personnel ==
Credits adapted from the Never for Ever album liner notes:

* Kate Bush – lead vocals, piano, production
* Paddy Bush – sitar, bass vocals, additional performance
* Alan Murphy – electric guitar
* Ian Bairnson – bass vocals
* Preston Heyman – percussion
* Jon Kelly – production, engineering
* "Roland" – drum machine

data.title: Pamela Lowell
data.text:
Pamela Lowell is an American licensed clinical social worker, watercolor artist, and author. [ref: BookShelf: Trauma Specialist Offers Ospreys As 'Gateway Drug' to Nature, SEJournal Online] She is known for her professional and creative work intersecting trauma psychotherapy, environmental stewardship, and wildlife art, which is the subject of her 2024 nature memoir My Summer with Ospreys. [ref: Meet Pamela Lowell, CanvasRebel]

== Education and Career ==
Lowell earned her Master of Social Work (MSW) from Rutgers University in 1984. [ref: Ms. Pamela A. Lowell LICSW, AAO Education Hub] She has operated a private psychotherapy practice since 2001, specializing in the clinical treatment of complex emotional trauma, anxiety, and depression.

From 2008 to 2015, Lowell served as a clinical consultant for Adoption Rhode Island, providing agency and state-wide training, program evaluation, and specialized supervision for complex foster care cases. [ref: Pamela Lowell, MSW, LICSW - Bio and Press, PamelaLowell.com] [ref: Pamela Lowell Profile, LinkedIn] For her contributions, she received the organization's Community Partner Award in 2008. She was also the clinical director at Turning the Corner Group Homes, where she designed and implemented agency-wide trauma-informed care using the Attachment, Regulation and Competency (ARC) framework. Additionally, she has served on the adjunct faculty at Rhode Island College.

== Art and Activism ==
As a visual artist, Lowell creates large-scale watercolor paintings depicting New England salt marshes and regional avian species. Her painting Breakfast on the Marsh (2023) was chosen for the Roger Tory Peterson Institute's juried exhibition Art that Matters to the Planet: Wild America, curated by ornithologist Kenn Kaufman. [ref: Art that Matters to the Planet: Wild America, Roger Tory Peterson Institute] In August 2024, the Cape Cod Museum of Art hosted her for a presentation focused on wildlife translocation and environmental art. [ref: Presentation: My Summer with Ospreys with Author, Artist, and Trauma therapist Pamela Lowell, Cape Cod Museum of Art] She volunteers for the Mass Audubon South Coast Osprey Project, assisting with nest monitoring and population data collection, and routinely donates portions of her art proceeds to environmental non-profits.

== Literary Works ==
Lowell has authored four books:

* Returnable Girl (Marshall Cavendish, 2006) – A young adult novel following a 13-year-old girl navigating the foster care and adoption systems. [ref: Returnable Girl Review, Booklist] The novel received the International Reading Association (IRA) Young Adult Choices designation and was named to VOYA's Top Shelf Fiction list.
* Spotting for Nellie (2010) – A young adult fiction novel.
* My Summer with Ospreys: A Therapist's Journey Toward Hope, Community, and Healing Our Planet (Stillwater River Publications, 2024) – A non-fiction narrative weaving wildlife monitoring with trauma therapy concepts, featuring original watercolor illustrations.

== Reception ==
Lowell's literary work has received recognition from major literary and conservation outlets. Kirkus Reviews praised Returnable Girl for its authentic, "convincing portrait" of troubled adolescents, citing Lowell's real-world clinical expertise as a family therapist. [ref: Returnable Girl, Kirkus Reviews] Booklist noted the novel sensitively captures the emotional reality of betrayal and longing within the foster care system.

Her 2024 memoir, My Summer with Ospreys, was reviewed by Tom Henry for the Society of Environmental Journalists, who described it as a "breezy, loose narrative" that effectively bridges mental health counseling with climate awareness. Rebecca Minardi of the American Birding Association commended the book's ability to frame environmental grief through the lens of trauma therapy while maintaining a heartfelt, human tone. [ref: Finding Community in Ospreys, American Birding Association] Additional commentary from the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy praised the integration of her watercolor artwork within the environmental narrative. [ref: Close-up with Ospreys: Book Review, West Virginia Highlands Conservancy]

data.title: 1974–75 Notre Dame Fighting Irish men's basketball team
data.text:

The 1974–75 Notre Dame Fighting Irish men's basketball team represented the University of Notre Dame during the 1974–75 NCAA Division I men's basketball season. The team was coached by Digger Phelps and was ranked in the Associated Press poll for the entirety of the season.

True sophomore Adrian Dantley was the team's leading scorer with 30.4 points and 10.2 rebounds and he was selected as a first-team player on the 1975 All-America team.

The team finished 19–10, losing by a 71–83 score against Maryland in the NCAA tournament, and going on to finish third in the Mideast Regional.

data.title: China Everbright Bank Europe S.A.
data.text:
China Everbright Bank (Europe) S.A. is a credit institution incorporated in Luxembourg. It serves as the European subsidiary of China Everbright Bank (中国光大银行), a Chinese joint-stock commercial bank founded in August 1992, headquartered in Beijing, and listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE: 601818) and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (SEHK: 6818).

When China Everbright Bank set up its Luxembourg operation in 2017, it did so through two separate legal structures: the subsidiary covered in this article, and a directly operated branch, the China Everbright Bank Luxembourg Branch. At the time, this made China Everbright the seventh Chinese bank with a presence in the Grand Duchy. Academic research on Chinese banks' European expansion has noted that Luxembourg's early diplomatic ties with China, dating to 1972, and its role as a financial gateway have made it a recurring choice for Chinese lenders structuring their EU market entry.

== History ==
China Everbright Bank obtained a banking licence from the European Central Bank and clearance from Luxembourg's financial regulator, the CSSF, to open the subsidiary in 2017. Press coverage at the time framed the move partly as a way of securing a foothold in the EU single market ahead of Brexit, and partly as part of the bank's wider push to support trade tied to China's Belt and Road Initiative.

The bank marked the opening with a launch event in Luxembourg on 8 September 2017, held alongside the "Forum for Belt and Road Initiative and Investment of Chinese Enterprises in Europe". Those attending included Luxembourg's then prime minister Xavier Bettel, finance minister Pierre Gramegna, CSSF director general Claude Marx, China's ambassador to Luxembourg Huang Changqing, and China Everbright Group and Bank chairman Tang Shuangning.

Research on the sector has characterised such moves by Chinese state-linked banks as part of a broader, legally-structured pattern of foreign direct investment into the European Union, in which a Luxembourg subsidiary combined with a parallel branch is a common structural choice.

== Operations ==
The subsidiary is built around corporate banking rather than retail services. Its business centres on deposits and loans for corporate clients, multi-currency accounts (it handles euros, US dollars and renminbi), trade finance instruments such as letters of credit and guarantees, and international settlement and money-market activity. In practice, its client base consists mainly of European firms doing business in China, Chinese companies investing into the EU, and other banks needing a correspondent relationship in Luxembourg.

== Regulation ==
As a Luxembourg-licensed credit institution, the bank is supervised jointly by the European Central Bank under the Single Supervisory Mechanism and, at national level, by the CSSF, the country's financial regulator. The entity is listed in the CSSF's public register of authorised credit institutions and in the European Central Bank's official list of supervised entities. The licence also gives it EU passporting rights, so it can offer services across the wider European Economic Area without separate authorisation in each country. Deposits are covered up to €100,000 per depositor under Luxembourg's deposit guarantee scheme, the *Fonds de garantie des dépôts Luxembourg*.

Its identifying codes are: BIC/SWIFT EVERLULX; LEI 22210018MLEVW7CTGU78; Luxembourg trade and companies register (RCS) number B213668; and ECB monetary financial institution code LUB00401. The company's registration and corporate filings can be consulted through the official Luxembourg Business Registers portal.

== Financial position ==
As of 2025, the bank reported total assets of around €105 million and net profit of roughly €2 million, with a small workforce of six employees. Its registered office is at 10, Avenue Émile Reuter, in Luxembourg City.

data.title: Ilaria Bernardini
data.text:
----

Ilaria Bernardini (born 1977) is an Italian novelist and screenwriter who writes in both Italian and English. Her works include several collections of short stories and graphic novels. [ref: Bernardini, Ilaria, Treccani] She has written screenplays for TV shows such as In Treatment, [ref: In treatment 2, Wildside] Citadel: Diana and along with several films including Chalk, Te l'avevo detto, Amata and The Echo Chamber. [ref: Citadel: Diana, Amazon MGM Studios] [ref: Te l'avevo detto – Commissione Nazionale Valutazione Film, Commissione Nazionale Valutazione Film] [ref: Amata - 2025 - films released 2000 - 2025, Filmitalia] [ref: The Echo Chamber, Cinema/Chicago] She co-authored the screenplay for the short film Chalk, which was nominated for the BAFTA Award for Best Short Film in 2012. [ref: Film Awards 2012, British Academy of Film and Television Arts] She also wrote the screenplay for Morten Tyldum's upcoming film Ibelin. [ref: Charlie Plummer, Stephen Graham, Toni Collette, Anthony Hopkins Starring in 'Ibelin,' Inspirational 'World of Warcraft' Drama, [[Variety (magazine)] [ref: Bill Nighy Joins 'Ibelin' As Production Begins In Oslo, Deadline]

== Early life and education ==
Born in Milan in 1977, Bernardini graduated in Philosophy of science. [ref: Domenica - Ilaria Bernardini - Feltrinelli Editore, feltrinellieditore.it] Her thesis was based on a year-long interview with the poet Alda Merini. [ref: Film card - Torino Film Fest, Torino Film Festival] [ref: La fine dell'amore, Artribune]

== Literary career ==
Bernardini's first novel, Non è niente, was published by Baldini Castoldi Dalai in 2005. [ref: Ilaria Bernardini: Libri e opere in offerta, Gruppo Feltrinelli] The short-story collection La fine dell'amore came out in 2006 and was a finalist for the Premio Chiara in 2007. [ref: Albo d'oro del Premio Chiara, Premio Chiara] Her other works are I supereroi (2009), Corpo libero (2010), Domenica (2012), another short-story collection L'inizio di tutte le cose (2015), [ref: ] Faremo foresta (2018), Il ritratto (2020), Il dolore non esiste (2024) and Amata (2025). Domenica made the finalist of the Premio Letterario Chianti. Faremo foresta was translated into English by Livia Franchini as We Will Be Forest. It was published in 2024 by Whitefox Publishing in London. [ref: We Will Be Forest [Translation], Goldsmiths, University of London]

Her first novel in English, The Portrait, was published by Atlantic Books in the UK in 2020 [ref: The Portrait – Atlantic Books, Atlantic Books] and by Pegasus Books in the US in 2021. [ref: ] Publishers Weekly called it a "mournful English-language debut". [ref: The Portrait, Publishers Weekly] Corpo libero, published in Italy by Feltrinelli and Mondadori, was acquired by HarperCollins for the UK and HarperFiction for the US as The Girls Are Good in 2022. [ref: HarperFiction pre-empts Bernardini's 'gripping' thriller set in world of elite gymnastics, The Bookseller] [ref: The Girls Are Good, HarperCollins Publishers] The book Il dolore non esiste (2024) deals with her relationship (in absence) with her missing father. [ref: «Mio padre non mi parla più. Volevo usare la mia storia per interrogare i vuoti di tutti», Domani] HarperCollins Italia published Amata in 2025. [ref: Amata – Premio Strega 2026, Premio Strega] Bernardini said that Amata was inspired by reporting about a newborn left at a hospital baby hatch in Milan and the public pressure subsequently placed on the child's mother. [ref: "Amata" da libro a film: La scrittrice Bernardini: narro echi di maternità, Avvenire]

Three of her novels have been proposed for the Strega Prize: Faremo foresta in 2018 by writer Caterina Bonvicini; [ref: I titoli proposti dagli Amici della domenica per concorrere alla LXXII edizione, Premio Strega] Il ritratto in 2020 by film director Paolo Sorrentino; [ref: Il ritratto, Premio Strega] and Amata in 2026 by journalist Simonetta Sciandivasci.

=== Graphic novels ===
In 2014, Hop! Edizioni published La fine dell'amore graphic short stories, an illustrated adaptation of stories from Bernardini's first collection with artwork by thirteen illustrators. [ref: La fine dell'amore, Linkiesta.it] [ref: "La fine dell'amore": tredici graphic short stories per tredici talenti italiani – Lo Spazio Bianco, Lo Spazio Bianco] Hop! also published the children's book Facciamo foresta! (2019), which was written together with Lorenza Tonani and inspired by Faremo foresta, narrating the story as a child's diary [ref: Rosicchialibri Facciamo f(or)esta!, Il Rosicchialibri] and a graphic-novel version of Corpo libero (2022), scripted by Chiara Barzini, Bernardini, Ludovica Rampoldi and Giordana Mari, with artwork by Giulia Rosa. [ref: Corpo libero, Hop! Edizioni] [ref: "Corpo libero", un thriller psicologico che svela il lato oscuro della ginnastica artistica, Fumettologica]

== Columnist ==
Bernardini has written for the Italian editions of Rolling Stone, Vogue, [ref: Il nuovo sesso, Vogue Italia] GQ, Amica and also for Vanity Fair. [ref: Ilaria Bernardini – Atlantic Books, Atlantic Books]

== Television ==
Bernardini created the MTV Italia documentary series Ginnaste - Vite parallele, about Italian top gymnasts. [ref: "La palestra è una grandissima metafora delle vicende della vita"- intervista a Ilaria Bernardini] [ref: Amore, iPod e ginnastica"Il nostro reality olimpico", la Repubblica] The series won Best MTV Show at the 2013 MTV Awards. [ref: Vite Paralelle e Carlotta Ferlito vincitori agli MTV Awards, OA Sport] [ref: Mtv Awards 2013: Firenze al centro della musica Rete impazzita: 600mila tweet FOTO/VIDEO/I TWEET, La Nazione] She was one of the writers of MTV's Very Victoria [ref: 2° romanzo classificato: Corpo Libero, di Ilaria Bernardini, [[Elle (magazine)] and La7's Victor Victoria - Niente è come sembra, [ref: Arisa e Melissa P. da Victoria, Tgcom24] created Ballerini - Dietro il sipario, [ref: "Faremo Foresta", il nuovo romanzo di Ilaria Bernardini, ilLibraio.it] [ref: Ilaria Bernardini, Peters Fraser and Dunlop] and was one of the writers of Sky's Italian adaptation of In Treatment. [ref: In Treatment (IT), FilmTV.it]

Corpo libero was adapted into a six-part series of the same name (English title The Gymnasts). Indigo Film and Network Movie produced it with ZDFneo, Rai Fiction, Paramount+ and All3Media International. [ref: Al via la serie Corpo Libero, Rai] [ref: Corpo libero, FilmTV.it] Bernardini wrote the series bible with Chiara Barzini and Ludovica Rampoldi. She also co-wrote the scripts with Barzini, Rampoldi, and Giordana Mari. [ref: The Gymnasts, Indigo Film] It premiered on Paramount+ in Italy on 26 October 2022. [ref: Corpo Libero: la serie tv sulla ginnastica artistica su Paramount+, Artribune]

Bernardini was one of the writers of Citadel: Diana, the Italian series in the Citadel franchise, which premiered on Prime Video on 10 October 2024.

== Film ==
In 2002 she wrote and directed the short film Che cosa vuol dire pensare that was shown at the 20th Torino Film Festival.

She and director Martina Amati co-wrote the short film Chalk (2011). [ref: British Council UK Films Database: Chalk, British Council] Chalk was nominated for Best Short Film at the 65th British Academy Film Awards. The nomination was credited to Amati, Bernardini, James Bolton and Gavin Emerson.

She co-wrote Te l'avevo detto (2023) together with its director, Ginevra Elkann, and Chiara Barzini. [ref: Cast Te l'avevo detto, MYmovies.it] [ref: I Told You So (Te l'avevo detto), tiff.net]

Bernardini adapted her own novel of the same name for the screenplay of Amata (2025). The film was directed by Elisa Amoruso. [ref: AMATA - Giornate degli Autori, Giornate degli Autori] It was a joint production of MeMo Films, Indiana Production and Rai Cinema. The film premiered in the Notti Veneziane section of the Giornate degli Autori at the 82nd Venice International Film Festival. [ref: 'Amata': corpo, desiderio e libertà di scelta, Cinecittà News]

Bernardini and Ludovica Rampoldi adapted Bernardo Bertolucci's last screenplay, The Echo Chamber. [ref: Andrea Pallaoro's The Echo Chamber is set to compete in Venice, Cineuropa] Andrea Pallaoro directed the film, which competed in the main competition at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival in 2026. The screenplay was credited to Bertolucci, Bernardini and Rampoldi. [ref: The Echo Chamber, [[Venice Biennale] Pallaoro said Bernardini and Rampoldi worked with him during development and pre-production to revise Bertolucci's initial screenplay into the version that was filmed. [ref: Andrea Pallaoro On Reviving Bernardo Bertolucci's 'The Echo Chamber', Deadline Hollywood]

Bernardini wrote the screenplay for the film Ibelin, directed by Morten Tyldum, on the life of the Norwegian gamer Mats Steen. Later Hossein Amini carried out additional writing. [ref: Anthony Hopkins, Toni Collette, Stephen Graham, Charlie Plummer Join Morten Tyldum's 'Ibelin', The Hollywood Reporter]

== Bibliography ==

=== Novels ===

* Domenica (Feltrinelli, 2012)

=== Short-story collections ===

* La fine dell'amore (I Libri di Isbn / Guidemoizzi, 2006)

=== Graphic novels ===

data.title: Firearms Import & Export
data.text:
Firearms Import and Export, also known as FIE, was a firearms manufacturer, importer, exporter and wholesale distributor of firearms, whose main office was located in Opa-Locka, Florida. FIE imported firearm components into the United States and had them assembled in the Miami area in order to comply with federal firearms laws. The company sold large numbers of inexpensive pistols, as well as imported sporting rifles and shotguns, from 1969 until the company filed for bankruptcy in 1990. [ref: Second try at the target: Gun loophole exploited, Ottawa Citizen] [ref: GT 27 Tanfoglio pistol: A gun that trumps the Gun Control Act of 1968, Guns.com] [ref: Cartridges and Firearm Identification, CRC Press]
[ref: IN RE FIREARMS IMPORT AND EXPORT CORP., Leagle] [ref: FIE, Blue Book of Gun Values] The company was an offshoot of Eig Cutlery, which had previously imported firearms from abroad, but was prohibited from continuing to import many types of firearms due to the Gun Control Act of 1968. [ref: GT 27 Tanfoglio pistol: A gun that trumps the Gun Control Act of 1968, Guns.com]

data.title: Francisco Saia
data.text:
Francisco Saia (born 18 September 1998) is an Italian film director and screenwriter.

== Early life and education ==
Saia was born in Savona, Liguria. In 2018, he graduated from the SDAC – Scuola d'Arte Cinematografica in Genoa, studying directing and screenwriting. He later studied DAMS (Discipline delle Arti, della Musica e dello Spettacolo) at the University of Turin. [ref: CinemaItaliano.info - Francisco Saia]

== Career ==
Saia directed the short films Abraham (2018) and The Double (2021). In 2020, he made his feature film debut with Boccaccio 2020 – Novella Trash, produced by FEDIC. The following year, he directed the science fiction film Dalì 2021.

In December 2021, he received the "Miglior talento ligure dell'anno" award from the Liguria regional administration. [ref: Il regista 26enne savonese Francisco Saia, l’enfant prodige partito da Villapiana, Il Secolo XIX]

In 2023, production began on his fantasy feature film The Thief of Falling Stars (Il ladro di stelle cadenti), which received funding from the Italian Ministry of Culture. [ref: 'Il ladro delle stelle cadenti': al via le riprese del fantasy italiano, Cinecittà News] The film, starring Daniel McVicar, premiered at the 70th Taormina Film Fest in July 2024 in the "Officina Sicilia" section [ref: Taormina Film Fest, presentato "Il ladro di stelle cadenti", TGR Sicilia] and was later released theatrically in Italy in October 2024. [ref: Il Ladro di stelle cadenti di Francisco Saia, la recensione di Cinecorriere, Cinecorriere]

data.title: Glen Burn Colliery
data.text:
The Glen Burn Colliery, known earlier as the Cameron Colliery and originally as the Gap mines, was an anthracite coal mine and breaker on the western edge of Shamokin, in Coal Township, Northumberland County, Pennsylvania. It lay in the Western Middle Anthracite Field. Coal was first mined in the Shamokin Creek water gap in the 1830s. Over the next century and a half the workings passed through a series of lessees, companies tied to the Pennsylvania Railroad, the Susquehanna coal companies and, from 1966, Kerris and Helfrick. The breaker shut down during a strike in 1984 and was demolished after the operation was liquidated in 1986. The colliery's culm bank still towers over Shamokin, and water from the old workings still drains into Shamokin Creek.

==History==
===Gap mines===
The first mines in the gap were opened in the late 1830s. On the east side, the landowners Dewart & Donnel drove several drifts beside the railroad and leased them to Yoxtheimer & Snyder of Sunbury, who failed after about a year. J. H. Purdy & Company began mining the west side at about the same time; their workings were later joined to those on the east side as part of the Cameron Colliery. The gap mines were among the four operations that shipped coal from the Shamokin district in 1839.

Fagely, Cleaver & Company took over the east-side mines in 1841. The partners, William and Reuben Fagely, Kimber Cleaver and William H. Kase, opened the Tape, or Skidmore, vein and soon became the district's leading shippers. The News-Item reports that William Cameron, a justice of the peace with experience building canals, tunnels, bridges and railroads, acquired the Gap mine in June 1841. In July 1855 the lessees, Kase, Reed & Company, sold their interest to Zimmerman & Pursell. The colliery's first breaker was built in 1857, a year in which Zimmerman & Pursell's "Lower Gap" shipped 14,887 tons.

===Cameron Colliery===
Haas & Bowen, who were already operating at Locust Gap, leased the Lower Gap in April 1862 and renamed it the Cameron Colliery. They sank a slope there, one of the first in the region. One archival record dates the name change to 1864 and says the colliery was named after William Cameron.

The colliery later passed to the Mineral Railroad and Mining Company, a Pennsylvania Railroad affiliate. Work on a new breaker began late in 1887 and was finished in January 1888, but the building burned that October. Its replacement, completed early in 1889, was described as "one of the largest and most complete structures in the State". That year the colliery shipped 101,418 tons.

Fire struck again in February 1890, this time in the gangway of the No. 1 slope, below the surface. The blaze was reportedly started by a miner's lamp and killed more than twenty mules. After weeks of firefighting, the company turned Shamokin Creek into the mine. By the officials' count, about a billion gallons of water flowed in over six days, eight hours and thirty minutes to fill workings that held more than of underground railroad. Pumping began in May, and the mine was dry again by November 2.

Another fire broke out on February 28, 1904, in the pump house on the second level of the No. 7 vein. Officials of the Mineral Railroad and Mining Company and the Susquehanna Coal Company closed off the area and smothered the fire with steam at for a full day, then spent three weeks putting out what was left with hoses. It was finally out on March 21.

The state mine inspectors' annual reports trace the mine's continued development. In 1910 a tunnel was driven from the No. 6 vein to the No. 1 Lykens Valley vein. In 1913 the company put up a concrete-block bathhouse,, with lockers and hot and cold showers, along with a reinforced-concrete emergency hospital for injured workers. In 1917 the No. 7 slope was extended and new jigs were installed in the breaker.

Cameron was one of seven Susquehanna Coal Company collieries in Northumberland County. Much of the company's stock was owned by the Pennsylvania Railroad and the Pennsylvania Canal Company, and the Pennsylvania State Archives call Cameron "one of the most famous mines in the Western Middle Coal Field". Bell's 1891 county history said much the same, calling it "one of the most famous collieries in the State". In 1917 the Susquehanna Coal Company transferred its mines to the Susquehanna Collieries Company, which was operating Cameron that year.

===Glen Burn===
The colliery's last breaker went up in 1939. In 1940 the colliery was renamed Glen Burn. Three miners were killed in an explosives detonation there on February 26, 1964.

Kerris and Helfrick, a Shamokin-area firm owned by Robert Kerris and Edward W. Helfrick, bought the colliery from the Susquehanna Coal Company on June 30, 1966. Working with the Lower Anthracite Regional Economic Development Organization (LAREDO), the new owners opened the mine to visitors on June 22, 1968. Tours ran on weekends and holidays, when the mine was idle, and were promoted as the world's first tour of a working anthracite mine. They continued until 1976.

==Closure and demolition==
The breaker's conveyor stopped for good on May 31, 1984, when more than 100 members of the United Mine Workers walked out. The strike ended on March 13, 1986, when Kerris and Helfrick announced that it would liquidate the operation. Within two years the breaker, which could process 500 tons of coal an hour, had been reduced to rubble. The miners' washhouse survived for a time but was eventually demolished as well.

==Present day==
The colliery's refuse banks, "draped over the nose of the Big Mountain water gap of the Shamokin Creek" in the words of a state environmental report, tower over the town. Before reclamation began, the bank held an estimated 33 million tons of waste. Smoke still rises from a pit near its summit, and a steel pipe sunk into the ground nearby is warm to the touch, signs that an underground mine fire may still be burning. For many years Shamokin launched its annual fireworks from the top of the bank. A mantrip once used on the mine tour has been restored by students at the Northumberland County Career and Technology Center and put on display at the Anthracite Outdoor Adventure Area.

===Mine drainage===
Water from the flooded workings reaches Shamokin Creek through two openings, the Cameron Air Shaft and the Cameron Drift, on the flood plain between Route 61 and the creek at the northern edge of Shamokin. Both carry drainage from the Hickory Ridge, Colbert, Hickory Swamp, Cameron, Glen Burn, Natalie and Luke Fidler collieries. During a United States Geological Survey study of the Shamokin Creek basin in 1999–2001, the air shaft discharged of acidic water (pH about 4) carrying roughly 50 mg/L of dissolved iron. The drift discharged with a pH of about 5.4. Ranked by dissolved metals load, the air shaft was the fourth-largest source of acid mine drainage in the basin and the drift the eighth.

data.title: Tahini's
data.text:
Tahini's is a Canadian fast-casual restaurant chain specializing in Mediterranean fusion cuisine. [ref: Tahini's goes global: London restaurant chain expanding to the U.S., CBC News] [ref: A Small Restaurant Chain Is Plowing All of Its Profits Into Bitcoin, Markets Insider] Founded in 2012 in London, Ontario, the company operates franchise and corporate locations across Canada and the United States. [ref: Tahini's Bitcoin Treasury: How A Family Chain Outsmarted Inflation, Bitcoin Magazine] The chain is notable in corporate finance for converting its cash reserves into Bitcoin as a treasury reserve asset beginning in August 2020. [ref: Canadian Restaurant, Tahini's, Goes All-In With Bitcoin, BNN Bloomberg]

== History ==
Tahini's was established in 2012 by brothers Omar and Aly Hamam after acquiring a restaurant in London, Ontario. The company initially operated as a single local restaurant before expanding into a franchise business model across Canada.

In February 2025, the company began international expansion into the United States, opening franchise locations in Illinois with further regional development planned in Chicago and New Jersey.

== Corporate treasury strategy ==
In August 2020, Tahini's converted 100% of its corporate cash reserves into Bitcoin to hedge against potential currency inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic. Co-founders Omar and Aly Hamam cited past personal experiences with currency devaluation in Egypt and corporate moves by MicroStrategy as primary influences for the treasury adoption.

The company instituted a monthly dollar-cost averaging strategy, sweeping excess operational profits into Bitcoin while maintaining three to six months of working capital in cash. The company also introduced Bitcoin ATMs at select restaurant franchise locations.

== Media coverage ==
The company's non-traditional balance sheet strategy and international franchise growth have been featured in corporate broadcast coverage on BNN Bloomberg as well as dedicated business reporting by Markets Insider and CBC News.

== History ==
Tahini's was established in 2012 by brothers Omar and Aly Hamam after acquiring a restaurant on Richmond Row in London, Ontario. The company originally operated a single location before launching a franchise expansion model across Ontario.

In 2025, the chain expanded internationally into the United States, opening locations in Illinois with further development planned for Chicago and New Jersey. [ref: Tahini's, Canada's fastest-growing Mediterranean brand, lands in the U.S., Retail Insider]

== Corporate treasury strategy ==
In August 2020, Tahini's converted its corporate cash reserves into Bitcoin as a treasury reserve asset intended to hedge against inflation and currency devaluation. Co-founders Omar and Aly Hamam cited past personal experiences with the devaluation of the Egyptian pound and financial moves by MicroStrategy as primary influences for the strategy.

The company instituted a monthly dollar-cost averaging (DCA) strategy, allocating excess operating profits into Bitcoin while retaining working capital in fiat currency.

== Public and media coverage ==
In March 2022, Conservative Party of Canada leader Pierre Poilievre visited a Tahini's location in London, Ontario, purchasing food using Bitcoin as part of a campaign event that was subsequently cited in national media and parliamentary debates. [ref: As the crypto chaos continues, Liberals remind voters of Poilievre's praise for bitcoin, CBC News] [ref: Poilievre blasted during Commons debate on cryptocurrency legislation, CBC News]

In September 2025, CEO Omar Hamam was featured in coverage by CBC News and business trade media discussing federal adjustments to Canada's Temporary Foreign Worker program and food service labor supply. [ref: Owners of Wendy's, a sushi shop and Tahini's on ending temporary foreign worker program, CBC News]

data.title: Nazareth German war cemetery
data.text:
The Nazareth German war cemetery () is a First World War military cemetery in Nazareth, Israel, near the Holy Family Hospital. It holds the graves of German soldiers who died in what became British Mandate Palestine and Transjordan during the Sinai and Palestine campaign of the war. This includes many airmen and members of the Royal Bavarian Flying Corps.

It was built by the German War Graves Commission (Volksbund Deutsche Kriegsgräberfürsorge) with a design by and dedicated on 30 June 1935.

It is the only German war cemetery in Israel.

== History ==
=== Wartime burials ===
During the First World War the Holy Family Hospital of the Austrian Brothers of Mercy in Nazareth served as Imperial German Field Hospital No. 213. Nazareth was also the headquarters of the Yildirim Army Group, the Ottoman army group under German command.

Fifty-one German soldiers who were killed in action or died in the hospital were buried next to it. Those not buried at Nazareth lay in small cemeteries and single graves across the country, most of them in poor condition by the late 1920s.

=== Construction and dedication ===
The Treaty of Versailles required of the British to care for the graves of enemy soldiers in Palestine. In December, 1928, British authorities in Palestine agreed with the German consul-general to establish a central German cemetery. It would be located at Nazareth for the burial of German dead of Palestine and Transjordan. Some German soldiers remained buried at smaller cemeteries in Jerusalem or in British war cemeteries.

The German War Graves Commission agreed in May 1931 to meet the cost. The High Commissioner for Palestine acquired a plot beside the hospital, and it was leased to the German Reich for 999 years without charge. The municipality of Nazareth issued the building permit on 11 August 1934.

The commission's architect, Robert Tischler, designed the cemetery, and construction began in 1934. Builders from Nazareth carried out the work. The dead were brought in from temporary graves across Palestine and Transjordan, including Anabta, Beersheba, Jenin, Ma'an, Mafraq, Salt, Samakh and Tulkarm, with the help of the British war graves authorities.

The cemetery was dedicated on 30 June 1935. Representatives of Germany's wartime allies, the Evangelical and Catholic churches, the Templers and the local Nazi Party attended and a swastika flag flew from the tower. Adolf Hitler sent a telegram regarding the dedication.

=== Later history ===
During the Arab revolt of 1936 Austrian brothers continued to tend the graves, keeping in touch with the German Foreign Office through the Spanish consul in Jerusalem until the end of the Second World War. The hospital and the care of the cemetery later passed to Italian brothers that were from the same Christian order.

The German War Graves Commission has paid for the upkeep since the end of Second World War. Major repairs were carried out in 1967 and 1982. In 1982 Cardinal Joseph Höffner donated a new bell frame and a motor for the bell.

The land is now owned by the State of Israel, from which it is leased. There is no war-graves agreement between Germany and Israel, but the Israeli government guarantees the permanent right of rest of the dead and the protection of the site.

== Description ==
The cemetery is reached through a locked gate to the right of the hospital, across the brothers' cemetery and up a narrow stair. As built, it consisted of a court of honor, a bell tower, a covered hall of honor and two rows of open tomb chambers.

The tower holds a bell cast in Munich, about across and weighing nearly two tonnes, one of the largest in Israel.

Wooden crosses made from the propellers of crashed aircraft hang on the tower walls. Red Weser sandstone slabs were shipped from Germany for its construction.

== Burials ==
The cemetery holds primarily German, but also some Austro-Hungarian, soldiers and airmen of the First World War. The number buried is somewhere between 217 and 261. Tablets give each man's name, dates and place of death and are arranged by place of death. A second row of tablets commemorates about 250 German and Austrian dead whose graves were never found.

Among those buried is Alfred Gerechter, a German Jewish soldier killed at Salt on 30 April 1918.

== Commemoration ==
Since the early 1980s the German embassy in Israel has held an annual ceremony at the cemetery on Volkstrauertag, the German day of national mourning. It is attended by foreign military attachés and Israeli soldiers.

The service is interfaith, and an Israel Defense Forces rabbi recites the Kaddish for the dead.

== Further reading ==
* Deutsche Soldatengräber in Israel: Der Einsatz deutscher Soldaten an der Palästinafront im Ersten Weltkrieg und das Schicksal ihrer Grabstätten, Aschendorff

data.title: Caroline Elliott
data.text:
----

Caroline Elliott is a political commentator, and former vice-president of the BC United party. [ref: BC Conservatives leadership vote to offer glimpse into party's vision, The Globe and Mail]
She was one of five candidates in the 2026 B.C. Conservative Party leadership election, losing by a narrow margin of 51% to 49%, after four rounds of voting.

Elliott was nominated as the Conservative Party of BC candidate in the 24 October 2026 British Columbia general election in the West Vancouver-Capilano constituency. [ref: Former B.C. Conservative leadership candidate Caroline Elliott will run in election, Vancouver CityNews]

==Background==
Caroline Elliot spent several years at BC Hydro working on the Site C dam project, including with the joint federal-provincial environmental assessment used by the province for its 2014 final investment decision. [ref: Caroline Elliott's theory of culture war: persuasion, not anger, National Post] [ref: Caroline Elliott brings B.C. Conservative leadership campaign to Vernon this Wednesday, Castanet]
She has run a communications business, providing advice for clients in the resource sector. [ref: BC United announce new candidate in West Vancouver-Capilano, North Shore News]

Elliott earned a PhD in aboriginal self-government and liberal democracy from Simon Fraser University. [ref: Completed Theses & Projects]
She has been a senior fellow with the Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy, a think tank; a director with the Public Land Use Society; and she is co-founder of the online opinion publication Without Diminishment. [ref: Caroline Elliott makes her case to become B.C. Conservative leader, CBC.ca]

Elliott is a former vice-president of the provincial political party BC United. [ref: BC Conservatives leadership vote to offer glimpse into party's vision, The Globe and Mail] [ref: New BC United candidate announced in West Vancouver-Capilano, North Shore News]

==2026 B.C. Conservative leadership election campaign==
Caroline Elliot was one of five candidates in the May 2026 Conservative Party of British Columbia leadership election. [ref: Has right's rise primed B.C. politics for a party that breaks the binary?, The Globe and Mail]
She was described as a "real conservative"
since she argued that while economic issues are "critically important", it is necessary to take on "cultural" issues like the catch-and-release criminal justice system, [ref: PODCAST: Caroline Elliott: 'This province is at a crucial time', Northern Beat] [ref: Can't fix B.C. without a culture war, says Conservative leadership runner-up, Vancouver Sun]
and B.C.'s DRIPA legislation which she said should be replaced by a made-in-Canada framework that would "unapologetically assert the public interest and defend private property rights". [ref: BC Conservative leadership race Q&A: Caroline Elliott, Business in Vancouver] [ref: Public interest comes second with B.C.'s Haida agreement, The Hub]

Elliott's campaign was supported by a number of well-known conservative advisors, although she was criticized for bringing in strategists from outside B.C., including Kory Teneycke, who ran Ontario Premier Doug Ford's 2025 election campaign. [ref: How a little-known B.C. Conservative built up a backroom dream team, National Post]
[ref: Will the B.C. Conservatives now become MAGA North?, The Globe and Mail]
She received the endorsement of former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell, [ref: Former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell back in the political game, The Globe and Mail] [ref: Campbell, Day throw support behind Elliott in race for BC Conservative leadership, The Castanet] and Harman Bhangu, a longtime B.C. Conservative. [ref: Bhangu's backing puts Elliott on offensive in BC Conservative race, Business in Vancouver]

Elliott narrowly lost the leadership election to former MP Kerry-Lynne Findlay by a vote of 51% to 49%, on the final of four ballots. [ref: Has right's rise primed B.C. politics for a party that breaks the binary?, The Globe and Mail]

data.title: Dane Lam
data.text:
Dane Lam is an Australian conductor. He is Music and Artistic Director of the Hawaiʻi Symphony Orchestra, Artistic Director of State Opera South Australia and Principal Conductor of the Xi'an Symphony Orchestra, and has been described as the only conductor holding simultaneous leadership positions at major institutions in the United States, Australia and Asia. [ref: Interview: Conductor Dane Lam on New Album, Globe-trotting, and Why 'Classical Music Is Better', Blogcritics] [ref: 'Orchestra of the Pacific': HSO extends inaugural music director's contract, Hawaiʻi Public Radio] [ref: New State Opera artistic director's international ambitions, InDaily]

Appointed in 2023 as the first music director in the Hawaiʻi Symphony Orchestra's history, Lam had his contract extended to 2031 in 2025. [ref: Hawai'i Symphony Orchestra appoints music director, BBC Music Magazine] At Xi'an, where he has led the orchestra since 2014, he was the first non-Chinese national to hold its chief conducting post. [ref: New State Opera South Australia Artistic Director announced, Government of South Australia] He was previously the first conductor to hold an official position with Opera Queensland.

In opera he has conducted for Opera Holland Park, Scottish Opera, Opera Australia and West Australian Opera. In 2025–26 he conducted The Magic Flute, the first co-production between Australian and Chinese opera companies, in Hong Kong, Adelaide and Beijing, where he made his debut with the London Philharmonic Orchestra at the Beijing Music Festival. [ref: Opera review: The Magic Flute, InDaily] [ref: Central Opera House, Beijing, London Philharmonic Orchestra] Reviewing his Scottish Opera Carmen, Opera Now described his conducting as "the best thing about this production". [ref: Bizet: Carmen at Scottish Opera – Live Review, Opera Now]

== Career ==

=== Hawaiʻi Symphony Orchestra ===
On 18 January 2023 the Hawaiʻi Symphony Orchestra announced Lam's appointment as its first music director, on a five-year contract beginning with the 2023–24 season; he had guest-conducted the orchestra in 2022. [ref: Hawai'i Symphony Orchestra Names First-Ever Music Director, The Violin Channel] In August 2023, in his first weeks in the post, he conducted the orchestra in Maui Ola, a benefit concert for victims of the Maui wildfires that raised more than one million dollars. [ref: Hawaii Symphony Orchestra joins benefit performance for Maui, Limelight]

In November 2025 the orchestra extended his contract through 2031 and gave him the title Music and Artistic Director. Under Lam the orchestra has broadened its programming to include collaborations with Hawaiian artists and premieres of music from across the Pacific, and he has campaigned for the orchestra to be recognised as the state orchestra of Hawaiʻi; Lam has described the ensemble as "the orchestra of the Pacific". In September 2026 the orchestra gave a free concert, Mele for Maui, in West Maui. [ref: Free 'Mele for Maui' concert in West Maui celebrates resilience, healing, Hawaii News Now]

=== State Opera South Australia ===
In September 2023 Lam was appointed Artistic Director of State Opera South Australia in Adelaide, succeeding Stuart Maunder. [ref: State Opera South Australia announces new AD, Limelight] On his appointment he said he intended to conduct at least one production each season, to commission works telling Australian and South Australian stories, and to develop locally made productions capable of touring internationally.

In 2025 Lam conducted a new production of Mozart's The Magic Flute, co-produced by State Opera South Australia, Opera Hong Kong, the Beijing Music Festival and the China National Opera House, described by Limelight as "the first major co-production between Australian and Chinese opera institutions". [ref: SOSA unveils "Opera without Borders" premieres, Limelight] It was staged in Hong Kong and then in Adelaide in August 2025, where Graham Strahle in InDaily wrote that Lam "imparts real energy and dynamism both as conductor and guiding light" and had the Adelaide Symphony Orchestra "playing with flowing tempos, neat articulation and great spirit", before its Chinese mainland premiere at the Beijing Music Festival in October 2026. [ref: The 29th Beijing Music Festival Celebrates Mozart and the Unifying Power of Music, Musical America] The Beijing performances, on 10 and 11 October 2026 at the Central Opera House, were given by the London Philharmonic Orchestra, the festival's orchestra-in-residence, and marked Lam's debut with the orchestra.

=== Xi'an Symphony Orchestra ===
Lam became Principal Conductor of the Xi'an Symphony Orchestra in 2014, [ref: Bach to Xi'an – UQ alumnus takes up post in Xi'an Symphony Orchestra, University of Queensland] the first non-Chinese national to hold the orchestra's chief conducting post. With the orchestra he conducted the 2016 CCTV-1 Mid-Autumn Festival Gala and, in 2017, a joint project with students of the University of Queensland Symphony Orchestra in China. At Xi'an he brought in international soloists including Sumi Jo and programmed works by living and neglected composers.

=== Opera in the United Kingdom ===
Lam made his London debut conducting Rossini's La Cenerentola at Opera Holland Park, where he later conducted Don Giovanni, Norma and a new production of Così fan tutte in 2018. [ref: New artist: conductor Dane Lam, Rayfield Allied] He was nominated for Best Newcomer at the 2018 International Opera Awards.

Lam first worked with Scottish Opera in 2017, sharing the conducting of the company's autumn tour of La traviata with David Parry. [ref: Scottish Opera's new season opens with La traviata, Scottish Opera] In 2023 he conducted the company's new production of Carmen in Glasgow and Edinburgh. [ref: Scottish Opera's new production of Carmen receives praise from critics and audiences, Scottish Opera] Susan Nickalls, writing in Opera Now, found that "the best thing about this production was conductor... Lam's fresh and pacey approach to this well-known score". He returned in 2026 for The Marriage of Figaro; David Kettle in The Scotsman praised a "beautifully light-footed but richly detailed account of Mozart's score", [ref: Scottish Opera: The Marriage of Figaro, Glasgow review: 'plenty to provoke', The Scotsman] and the British Theatre Guide wrote that he "conducts with his usual exuberant precision". [ref: The Marriage of Figaro from Scottish Opera at Theatre Royal, Glasgow, British Theatre Guide]

=== Australia ===
In December 2020 Lam was appointed Associate Music Director and Resident Conductor of Opera Queensland, the first conductor in the company's history to hold an official position, and led the company's return to performance after the COVID-19 lockdowns. [ref: Dane Lam, Hawaiʻi Symphony Orchestra] He was appointed an associate lecturer at the University of Queensland in 2021 to establish a conducting programme. He has conducted the Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Adelaide Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Sydney Symphony Orchestra, West Australian Symphony Orchestra and Canberra Symphony Orchestra, and has appeared with Opera Australia and West Australian Opera, for which he conducted a new production of Carmen in 2023. He was nominated for Artist of the Year by Limelight in 2021.

=== Guest conducting ===
In the 2026–27 season Lam makes his debut with the Buffalo Philharmonic Orchestra, conducting Mozart and Mahler with violinist Melissa White in January 2027, [ref: BPO Announces 2026–27 Concert Season, Buffalo Philharmonic Orchestra] and with the Ann Arbor Symphony Orchestra in April 2027, in a programme including the Midwest premiere of Nico Muhly's Concerto for String Quartet and Orchestra with Brooklyn Rider and Dvořák's Eighth Symphony. [ref: Sketches of Spring, Ann Arbor Symphony Orchestra]

=== Orchestras conducted ===
Beyond his titled posts, Lam has conducted the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra, London Philharmonic Orchestra, Munich Radio Orchestra, Residentie Orkest (The Hague), Beethoven Orchester Bonn, Orchestre National de France, RTÉ Concert Orchestra, City of London Sinfonia, Manchester Camerata, Southbank Sinfonia and the Verbier Festival Orchestra in Europe; the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Queensland Symphony Orchestra, Adelaide Symphony Orchestra, West Australian Symphony Orchestra, Canberra Symphony Orchestra and Dunedin Symphony Orchestra in Australasia; and the Beijing, Suzhou, Kunming and Shandong symphony orchestras in China. [ref: Xiaogang Ye: The Backyard of the Village – Orchestral Works, Europadisc]

== Recordings ==

* Xiaogang Ye: The Backyard of the Village – Orchestral Works. Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra, Diyang Mei (viola), Guy Johnston (cello), Dane Lam. Signum Classics, 2026.

== Views ==
Lam has spoken publicly about the economics and civic role of opera. On his appointment in Adelaide he rejected the charge that opera is elitist, saying that performers "shouldn't be apologetic that we have trained for years and years to be able to perform at the highest level", and argued for retaining the traditional repertoire while opening it to new voices and audiences. In October 2026 he appeared on CGTN's discussion programme The Hype to discuss the Beijing Magic Flute co-production and cultural exchange between China, Australia and the United States. [ref: Live: The Hype – Mozart's 'The Magic Flute', CGTN]

== Training ==
Lam was born in Brisbane to an Australian mother and a Singaporean-Chinese father. He played the piano as a child and later studied the clarinet, and made his first appearance with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra at the Sydney Opera House at the age of 18. He completed a Bachelor of Music with honours at the University of Queensland in 2006, studying conducting with Gwyn Roberts, and was accepted at 22 as a postgraduate student at the Juilliard School in New York, where he took a master's degree on a full scholarship under James DePreist. He subsequently held a Junior Fellowship in Conducting at the Royal Northern College of Music under Sir Mark Elder, Clark Rundell and Mark Heron, spent three years studying with Gianluigi Gelmetti, and was a protégé of Kurt Masur, for whom he served as assistant conductor at the Orchestre National de France. His student awards included the Bruno Walter Memorial Scholarship, the Boris Christoff Prize, the Brian Stacey Memorial Prize, the Pellegrino Scholarship, the Brian Boak Bursary and the Dalley-Scarlett Memorial Scholarship.

== Personal life ==
Lam is married to the soprano Sofia Troncoso. He has described Hawaiʻi as his home.
