data.title: Pealeism
data.text:
----

Pealeism, known by its namesake as Practical Christianity, or more commonly Positive Thinking, is a non-denominational Christian revivalist and new religious movement based on the preaching of Norman Vincent Peale and his book The Power of Positive Thinking. It emerged in the 1940s advocating for Christian revival in the United States, primarily emphasizing the practical, rather than creedal, aspects of Christian faith to improve daily life. Pealeism reached its height during the early Fourth Great Awakening before declining throughout the 1960s. [ref: Surge of Piety: Norman Vincent Peale and the Remaking of American Religious Life, Yale University Press]

Pealeism’s legacy remains politically, scientifically, and theologically controversial. Its approach to Christian faith, mental health, and politics has been respectively criticized as unbiblical, scientifically flawed, and having provided religious justification for conservatism and radical anti-communism during the Cold War.

The movement’s philosophy received renewed public attention during Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and first presidency, with Peale being cited by biographers and Trump himself as a formative influence on the latter’s worldview.

== History ==
=== Opposition to the New Deal ===
Beginning in 1942, Norman Vincent Peale travelled across the United States to court contacts in business, politics, industry, and religion, which would become a movement around his ministry. In 1945, Peale and his wife, Ruth Stafford Peale, established Guideposts magazine, which featured personal accounts claiming how Christian faith helped overcome personal difficulty.

Peale associated Christianity with American civic life, capitalism, anti-communism, opposing U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, and participated in conservative organizations including the Committee for Constitutional Government and Spiritual Mobilization. [ref: Norman Vincent Peale Was A Conservative Hero Known Well Beyond His Era, NPR] He belived Christian revival could encouraging Americans to treat faith as integral to personal wellbeing and thus be a counter to communist influence.

=== Post-World War II era and Cold War ===
After World War II, the Pealeist movement grew to include the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic and Foundation for Christian Living, which was the administrative arm of Peale’s ministry. The two organizations allowed Peale to preach to business executives, industrial workers, and youth outside his immediate congregation. In 1951, the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic was renamed the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry, [ref: Dr. Smiley Blanton Dead Here; Psychiatrist and Author Was 84; Co-Founder With Dr. Peale of Clinic to Aid Distressed Wrote 'Love or Perish', The New York Times] with Peale serving as its until 1962. The foundation promoted cooperation between clergy and psychiatrists, supported pastoral counselling, and sought to establish Christian faith as integral to mental health.

Peale’s relationships with Federal Bureau of Investigation director J. Edgar Hoover and U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, increased his public visibility and brought his views on religion and national identity to influential circles. He supported campaigns presenting the United States as “one nation under God,” which was part of a broader political and cultural trend towards the prominence of religious language in public life during the 1950s.

=== Decline and institutional reorganization ===
Peale’s ministry remained active after the 1950s, but growth in American religious observance started declining in the 1960s.

Peale stepped down as president of the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry in 1962. The foundation subsequently faced financial difficulties by the late 1960s and struggled to maintain the level of support in had the decade prior, reflecting broader changes in the relationship between Christian revivalism and mental-health care.

In 1972, the foundation merged with the Academy of Religion and Mental Health to create the Institutes of Religion and Health.

Peale continued to lecture, write, and participate in religious and media activities until he retired as senior minister of Marble Collegiate Church in 1984. He also received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the United States’ highest civilian honour.

=== 2016 United States presidential election and influence on Donald Trump ===
Peale’s influence received renewed attention during Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign through the latter’s public accounts of his religious upbringing. Trump attended Marble Collegiate Church with his family, and repeatedly identified Peale as a significant spiritual influence. [ref: How Trump got religion — and why his legendary minister’s son now rejects him, The Washington Post] Peale’s influence continues to be relevant in public discourse about Christianity’s role in contemporary American conservatism. [ref: ]

== Beliefs ==
Pealeism’s institutional leadership was theologically liberal, [ref: After Cloven Tongues of Fire: Ecumenical Protestantism and the Modern American Encounter with Diversity, The Journal of American History] with its namesake articulating such views through Faith is the Answer, A Guide to Confident Living, The Art of Real Happiness, and The Art of Living. These developed from his alma mater’s appreciation of Boston personalism; especially works by Marcus Aurelius, Ralph Waldo Emerson and William James, which were treated as an intellectual authority for the Methodist interpretation of Christ's real presence in the Eucharist. [ref: God's Salesman: Norman Vincent Peale and the Power of Positive Thinking, Oxford University Press] Peale further developed on this doctrine by incorporating practices and concepts from the Unity Church and Christian Science. Doing so, he emphasized the practical, rather than creedal, aspects of Christianity to improve life as popularized through The Power of Positive Thinking. [ref: Lehmann, William Jr. (1958) The Theology of Norman Vincent Peale, Concordia Theological Monthly: Vol. 29, Article 8. https://scholar.csl.edu/ctm/vol29/iss1/8]

Since 1984, Peale’s ministry has also been politically non-partisan. In an interview with Christian Science Monitor, he explained that if he could change what he did in his career, “(I wouldn't) get involved with a politician. A minister should deal (only) with the human soul.” [ref: Preacher's preacher most enjoys helping people one-to-one - CSMonitor.com, www.csmonitor.com] But during the early Fourth Great Awakening, his preaching religiously justified politically conservative values of Americanism, anti-communism, Christian nationalism, and laissez-faire individualism.

=== Theology ===
==== God as a person ====

God wasn’t a doctrinally defined subject within Pealeism, merely portrayed as personal in nature and emphasized through simple prayer language, forgiveness, and role as the Father. Peale further described God as a ubiquitous, natural, creative, and vital force, able to renew individuals mentally through continuous engagement. [ref: Business Ethics and the Protestant Spirit: How Norman Vincent Peale Shaped the Religious Values of American Business Leaders, Journal of Business Ethics]

==== Jesus as a teacher ====

Jesus Christ’s role of the Son of God wasn’t heavily emphasized either, instead being portrayed as the “Great Teacher” and embodying the “art of living;” a life of confidence, trust, and idealism, with followers meant to be living “in Christ.” Here, Christ taught how to live healthily and let go of guilt that affects mental well-being.

==== Nature of the soul ====
Given Christ’s role, Pealeism rejected original sin, instead grounding the soul's nature in lived experience and thought. Humans were therefore seen as capable of improvement through their thoughts and beliefs. Positive thinking therefore provided personal strength, while emotional pain, feelings of inferiority, fear, and negative thought engendered weakness.

==== Sin and mental state ====
This meant sin was actually a lack of mental wellness, which was believed to undermine personal livelihood and fulfillment, while moral failure was specifically emotional turmoil and lack of personal success. It could thus be remedied through moral knowledge of general precepts, conscience, reason, the teachings of Jesus, practical experience, and primarily faith; including trust in God’s forgiveness, personal confidence, and the settled expectation of improvement in one’s lived circumstances. Faith was sometimes equated with self-confidence or surrendering to God to overcome fear and act constructively. The regular reading and memorizing of uplifting biblical passages, along with church attendance was also recommended to support mental adjustment.

==== Universalism and salvation ====
Pealism’s understanding of sin led it to hold what is now criticized as a universalist stance on salvation, [ref: Norman Vincent Peale, Apostle of Self-Esteem, Way of Life Literature] with human beings sometimes described as “citizens of eternity,” not entirely meant to corporeally exist. Peale claimed that all people receive salvation after death, arguing this is the soul’s true state, with his eschatology being otherwise vague and simplified instead of systematic.

==== Approach to prayer ====
Prayer itself was presented as a simple, disciplined technique rather than a devotional practice, with followers urged to be specific, regular, and purposeful in its use. It was framed a means of sustained self-reflection and understanding of God, influencing personal conduct, and fostering positive mental focus per the principles of Matthew 7:7–8 and Philippians 4:13.

==== Role of the bible ====
Scripture itself had a selectively central role, with Peale’s ministry publishing the King James Bible. He praised the text as the best source of insight into human beings and as a source of curative power. And it was claimed this for the New Testament because the disciples of Christ copied his practice of “the art of living” in to its books. Peale even described the Bible as working “like penicillin,” excusing harmfully infectious thinking by providing practical wisdom, positive imagery, and remedial thought.

=== Politics ===
Peale argued through his preaching that the free market, business success, and economic growth were compatible with Christianity. In a 1950 article titled Let the Church Speak Up for Capitalism, he argued for a more active Christian justification of capitalism. His overall approach helped connect Protestant values with prevailing America’s business culture, as his preaching emphasized self-improvement, confidence, and perseverance.

After 1936, he also presented Christianity being in political conflict with communism. He specifically argued that Christian faith was counter communist influences by strengthening social stability and reinforcing national identity. This iteration of religious nationalism helped promote the idea that individual faith and faith in God were equivalent to faith in the United States. Peale argued that this improved individual health and strengthened the United States.

Since 1984, however, the organizations making up Peale’s ministry have largely refrained from partisan politics. Guideposts editor-in-chief Edward Grinnan explained that the publication does not cover such issues. [ref: The P Word, Guideposts Articles] The only public policy stance taken by the associated Blanton-Peale Institute & Counselling Center is to advocate for universal mental health care. [ref: ]

In 2016 however, Peale’s son John Stafford Peale, who was vice-president of the Peale Foundation and identifies with the Democratic Party, personally disavowed Trump’s invocation of his father’s influence. He claimed that what Trump espoused wasn’t related to his father’s preaching. [ref: How Trump got religion — and why his legendary minister’s son now rejects him, The Washington Post]

== Controversy ==
=== Psychological soundness ===
Despite the popularity of The Power of Positive Thinking, Peale’s approach was criticized by theologians, psychologists, psychiatrists, and other religious commentators. Some argued that his techniques reduced otherwise complicated emotional and social problems to appear readily solvable. They objected to the emphasis on avoiding negativity, arguing that optimism couldn’t simply dismiss anxiety, grief, anger, and suffering. Other critics questioned if these techniques were scientifically sound.

=== Credibility of the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry ===
The American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry experienced difficulties reconciling Christian counselling with psychiatry. Some medical professionals and researchers objected to its claims about the role of faith in treating mental illness, particularly questioning the veracity of its evidence for faith healing and the tendency to wards faith as a necessity for mental health. The foundation also faced disagreements over its research methods, professional standards, and the degree to which evangelism should be part of counselling.There was also misgivings within the foundation, including the precision of its scientific and clinical goals. Overall, this weakened the movement’s premise that Christian faith and psychology could be treated as a unified scientific approach.

=== 1960 United States presidential election and anti-Catholicism ===
During the 1960 United States presidential election, Peale was controversially associated with the Citizens for Religious Freedom, a group of Protestant clergy who objected to the candidacy of John F. Kennedy because he was Roman Catholic. They argued a Catholic president could be unduly influenced by the Holy See, which was widely criticized as religiously prejudiced, and damaged Peale’s reputation. He withdrew from the group and offered to resign as minister of Marble Collegiate Church, although they didn’t accept his resignation. Peale later described his involvement as a serious mistake. [ref: Norman Vincent Peale, 'Minister to Millions,' Dies: Religion: Mixing faith and psychology, author of 'The Power of Positive Thinking' spread inspiration worldwide., Los Angeles Times] [ref: National Affairs: Test of Religion, TIME] [ref: Protestant Clergy Vs. the Catholic Candidate, JFK, Time]

=== Theological criticism ===
Peale’s practical approach faith was criticized for reducing Christianity as a means to attaining individual goals while largely neglecting theological reflection, the meaning of suffering, and selflessness. Critics such as Reinhold Niebuhr argued that Peale overly emphasized self-assurance and individual success over obligations to Christian faith and role of original sin. Some regarded his approach as reducing religion to reassurance and practical achievement. William Lehmann Jr., a contributor of Concordia Theological Monthly, argued that Peale’s interpretations of the soul, God, sin, faith and Christ were inconsistent with traditional Christianity. He also criticized the latter for treating faith principally as an emotional experience.

== Notable figures ==
* Richard Nixon — 37th President of the United States (1969-1974), 36th Vice President of the United States (1953-1961), United States Senator from California (1950-1953), member of the United States House of Representatives from California’s 12th district (147-1953) [ref: NIXON, IN CHURCH, PRAISED BY PEALE AS A PEACEMAKER, The New York Times]
* Joel Osteen - senior pastor of Lakewood Church (1999-present)
* Bobby Schuller – lead pastor on Hour of Power (2012–present), senior pastor of Shepherd’s Grove (2013–present) [ref: How Norman Vincent Peale Inspired the New Book from Bobby Schuller, Guideposts Articles]
* Robert Schuller – lead pastor on Hour of Power (1970–2006), senior pastor of Crystal Cathedral (1980–2006) [ref: Died: Robert Schuller, Forerunner of the Seeker-Sensitive Movement, Christianity Today]
* W. Clement Stone – businessman, philanthropist, and author
* Donald Trump – chairman of The Trump Organization (1971–2017), Co-Chairman of the New York Vietnam Veterans Memorial Commission (1982–1985), 45th and 47th President of the United States (2017–2021, 2025–2029) [ref: Too Much and Never Enough: How My Family Created the World's Most Dangerous Man, Simon & Schuster] [ref: Never Enough: Donald Trump and the Pursuit of Success, Thomas Dunne Books, St. Martin's Press]
* Fred Trump – chairman of The Trump Organization (1929–1971)

Thomas Spencer () was an English politician. He sat as MP for Southwark in 1406, May 1413, and 1415. [ref: SPENCER, Thomas, of London and Southwark, Surr., History of Parliament Online]

He also served as tax collector of Southwark in November 1419.

By 1398, he was married to Joan, the daughter of Richard Burn of Southwark.

data.title: The Bernard Shaw
data.text:
----

The Bernard Shaw was a pub in Portobello, Dublin open from 2006 to October 2019. Housed in a late 19th century protected structure, the pub previously known as Bambrick's was taken over in 2006 by Bodytonic who refurbished, reopened, and renamed it after writer George Bernard Shaw, who was born on nearby Synge Street. It became a popular venue, associated with alternative bohemian subcultures, and incorporated a basement venue, food yard, and beer garden in addition to a traditional style pub.

After the adjoining buildings had gradually been demolished or left fall into dereliction, the bar was refused planning permission to retain the beer garden in May 2019, and four months later announced the bar would close entirely in October of that year. The closure was polarising, with commentators lamenting a great loss to Dublin cultural life, while others celebrated it as eliminating a source of anti-social behaviour and an obstacle to regeneration and progress.

==Design==
The Bernard Shaw is in an old-fashioned pub with mahogany panels and a brass rail at the front entrance on South Richmond Street, that opened onto both a small 60-person venue space in the basement and an outdoor beer garden at the back; [ref: Bernard Shaw owner to open new pub on Dublin’s north side, The Irish Times] to the side of the pub was "Eatyard", an open area featuring food vendors and seating.

===Prior history===
The pub was included in the Record of Protected Structures maintained by Dublin City Council. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage dates the building to 1895, while a 2019 article in The Irish Times dates it to 1859, and a 2019 San Francisco Chronicle article reported claims of there having been a pub on the site since the 12th century. The 1862 Thom's Directory notes a spirit distiller at the site. A 2017 appraisal of the building by the National Built Heritage Service described it thusly:

The pub ran as 'Bambrick's' before Bodytonic refurbished and reopened it as The Bernard Shaw in 2006. [ref: Closure of Dublin's Bernard Shaw pub 'just another sign the city is changing', The Irish Times] The name of the pub refers to writer George Bernard Shaw, who was born on nearby Synge Street. [ref: The Bernard Shaw, 11-12 South Richmond Street, Dublin 2, DUBLIN, National Inventory of Architectural Heritage] They received planning permission in 2008 for a smoking area beside the pub, which they converted into the beer garden three years later.

===Dilapidated appearance and artwork===
[[File:EATYARD NEXT DOOR THE THE BERNARD SHAW -9-18 SOUTH RICHMOND STREET DUBLIN 2--134830 (25537978058).jpg|thumb|left|The pub was known for exterior, which featured street art and murals. Irish political leader Daniel O'Connell and the band 12 Sundays shown depicted on its northern face here in December 2017.]]
A mural by artist Aches of Savita Halappanavar adorned the wall adjacent to the pub's facade during the campaign around the 2018 referendum on abortion. It became a shrine to her memory in May 2018 when mourners left over a thousand messages at its base. [ref: Post-it notes left at a 'shrine' to Savita Halappanavar photographed and archived, The Irish Times] The notes were collected and archived by the Dublin City Library and Archive (DCLA) in collaboration with the Digital Repository of Ireland. After the pub's closure, a barrier over the former Eatyard entrance was painted by ESTR with a mural for Concern Worldwide with a QR code linking to a recording of a poem. [ref: Bodytonic to replace Bernard Shaw with new venue on Dublin's north side, Newstalk.com]

Christopher Jones of Dublin Live considered it to not look like much from the outside, but said it did have a charming and easygoing look, noting that it was a "reflection of many of the people that hung out there: scruffy but interesting".
Journalist Una Mullally of The Irish Times commented that it was "symbolic too because it revelled in its dilapidation", calling it a compelling visual environment"

==Activities and offerings==
[[File:Andrew Weatherall 9 Aug 2009.jpg|thumb|left|DJ Andrew Weatherall (pictured in 2006) was one of many artists to peform in the basement space]]
Acts who performed in the basement venue include Mr Saturday Night, [ref: Over 15K people have signed a petition to keep The Bernard Shaw's beer garden open, Nialler9] Andrew Weatherall, Acid Granny, [ref: Here's what's happening in the Bernard Shaw before it closes down this month, Nialler9] Optimo, Niall Byrne, Blue Niall, [ref: Blue Niall: “We are a nation of poets, we were destined to fully embrace hip hop eventually”, District Magazine] and Motor City Drum Ensemble.

The pub was also a centre of political activity, hosting events for Dublin Pride, International Women’s Day, and the Repeal the 8th abortion rights referendum campaign.

The beer garden was named among the city's five best in a 2017 roundup in The Irish Independent, [ref: Anyone for sunny pints? Dublin’s top five beer gardens, The Irish Independent] and its pool table was named the city's finest by The Daily Edge in 2015. [ref: 9 of the best pub pool tables in Dublin, The Daily Edge] Following public complaints that drinkers along the popular hangout spot of the nearby Grand Canal were causing public nuisance by leaving litter behind during the summer of 2018, the pub launched a publicity stunt whereby punters were offered branded bin bags, which once returned filled with rubbish from the canal, would be exchanged for free pints. [ref: Dublin pub offering free pints - but there's a catch, The Irish Independent]

In 2018, the pub stocked Pabst Blue Ribbon, and beers from Bodytonic's Rascals Brewing, Five Lamps Brewery, Whiplash Brewery, and White Hag Brewery, while food vendors in the Eatyard included Kinara Kitchen, Box Burgers, Just Wing-It, Vish Shop and Mr Doughnut. In the beer garden, a large blue bus dispensed pizza. [ref: The Bernard Shaw might have to close its famous beer garden after planning permission refused, Dublin Live] A 2018 review of the food offerings by celebrity chef Darina Allen, which referred to the pub as "hipster central", concluded "the vendors in Eatyard vary in quality a little, but overall standards are high with the added bonus of getting to hang out with people far prettier and cooler than you." [ref: Restaurant review: EatYard at the Bernard Shaw, The Irish Examiner]

==2019 plannning permission refusal==
[[File:Gerard Mannix Flynn.jpg|thumb|Independent councillor Mannix Flynn (pictured 2016), who supported the refusal to extend planning permission for the beer garden to operate]]
The operators applied for permission to continue to run the beer garden in May 2019, invoking "brewing unease and scepticism [at how] once-lauded cultural institutions are being replaced by hotels and short-term accommodation" in reference to the recent closure and demolition of Tivoli Theatre and Andrews Lane Theatre. [ref: The Bernard Shaw loses planning bid to continue operating outside beer garden and Big Blue Bus area, [[The Journal (Ireland)] Local residents had objected due to the noise generated by pubgoers in the space. [ref: 'It's out of our hands now': Dublin's Bernard Shaw pub to close at end of October, [[The Journal (Ireland)]

An Bord Pleanála's inspector's report described it as "clearly a vibrant enterprise with its own unique character within an area notable for the extent of dereliction", and recommended requesting further submissions from the applicants detailing greater evidence of noise mitigation efforts. An Bord Pleanála instead refused the application outright, on the basis that it would hinder the “emerging pattern of development in the vicinity” given that the surrounding buildings were being redeveloped.

The decision was celebrated by independent city councillor Mannix Flynn, who concluded "A bunch of cool hipsters can think it’s an amazing place. But the level of anti-social behaviour that goes on is incredible, and the noise is appalling." A petition opposing the decision as "drastic and harmful to Dublin’s development as an attractive and vibrant cultural hub" attracted 15,000 signatures.

==Closure==
The operators Bodytonic announced in September 2019 that The Bernard Shaw would be closing the following month, [ref: Dublin's Bernard Shaw pub to close next month, RTÉ.ie] through a statement by company executive Trevor O'Shea:

In an article called "Mystery at The Bernard Shaw", The Phoenix observed with suspicion that the exact reason for the closure was not made clear by Bodytonic's statement. [ref: Mystery at The Bernard Shaw, [[The Phoenix (magazine)] A report in The Irish Times noted that the pub had been a highly successful business, earning €622,416 profit in 2018.

At the time of its closure The Bernard Shaw was described as "much loved" (Dublin Live, [ref: A fond farewell to The Bernard Shaw as the Portobello pub finally shuts its doors, Dublin Live] The Guardian [ref: Ireland: no country for the young, creative or homeless, The Guardian]), "iconic" (The Journal, Newstalk), "legendary" (The Irish Mirror), [ref: The Bernard Shaw pub in Dublin to close along with Eatyard, The Irish Mirror] and "a staple of the city’s creative communities" (San Francisco Chronicle). [ref: Fontaines D.C. sings lovingly to a disappearing Dublin on bracing debut album, San Francisco Chronicle]

===Reaction===
====Dublin City Council====

A cross party group of Dublin City Councillors cited the "great anger" of the public in response to the closure to demand a special meeting with the Lord Mayor. [ref: Call for special council meeting to discuss Dublin ‘cultural crisis’, The Irish Times] The group was composed of Claire Byrne, Patrick Costello, Hazel Chu, Donna Cooney, Michael Pidgeon, Janet Horner, Sophie Nicollaud, Caroline Conroy and Lawrence Hemmings from the Green Party, Rebecca Moynihan and Kevin Donoghue from the Labour Party, and Gary Gannon of the Social Democrats.

Their statement called for the Dublin City Development Plan to be updated to curtail the spread of hotels and protect cultural venues, to appoint a night mayor, and for action to be taken by the government ministers for Tourism, Culture and Justice. Byrne commented: "It’s not only a great pub and venue, but its closure is a symbol of Dublin’s cultural crisis. Unique spaces which build Dublin’s culture and character are being replaced with homogenous hotels and chain restaurants."

Within weeks, motions were passed by the council to appoint a night mayor, promote street art, change the development plan to inhibit hotel development, and to require audits of any commercial development over 5,000 metres to ensure no cultural spaces would be lost. [ref: Call for protection of cultural space in Dublin, RTÉ.ie]

A spokesperson for Dublin City Council remarked;"Recent office, hotel and student accommodation construction in the city has invariably been on long-standing, unsightly vacant sites. They have not resulted in the wholesale displacement of socio and cultural uses as stated in some media [...] Rather, they have contributed to employment and vitality in the city and are part of the rich fabric and character of the city as it evolves."

====Musicians====
[[File:Hozier at Lollapalooza, Chicago, 2014 02 (cropped).jpg|thumb|Musician Hozier (pictured in 2014) was one of many to express dismay at the pub's closure]]
Musician Hozier lamented "I’m sorry to read this. What is most special and unique about Dublin are Dubliners themselves, and spaces like this where culture and community is fostered & grows. Without interesting places like these the city loses its heartbeat."

Dublin post-punk band Fontaines D.C. and musician and podcaster Blindboy Boatclub also reacted despondently to the news, citing fond memories of the pub. [ref: Bernard Shaw pub closure: ‘Does anyone give a damn about cultural value?’, The Irish Times] Musician and TodayFM radio presenter Kelly-Anne Byrne condemned the Irish government in the wake of the closure, and added "If Leo Varadkar turns up at any of my gigs trying to look trendy, I might jst drop kick him 2 the head".

DJ and chair of the Give Us the Night campaign for greater government support for Irish nightlife Sunil Sharpe was quoted in The Times as calling The Bernard Shaw "probably the most important cultural and social hub in Dublin". [ref: Bernard Shaw pub latest Dublin venue to close, The Times] Sharpe criticised the proliferation of hotels, offices for tech companies, and chain pubs, and argued that their prioritisation over cultural spaces would result in a bland and inhospitable city that no-one would want to be in.

====Columnists and cultural commentators====
Peter McGoran of Hot Press called it a "seismic loss [that] will no doubt lead to people pushing even hard[er] for a change to Dublin's careless treatment of its social spaces". [ref: 'Dublin is changing, we can all see it': Anger and frustration as The Bernard Shaw announces closure, Hot Press] DJ Christopher Jones writing for Dublin Live remarked that the redevelopment surrounding the building lent an air of inevitability to the closure, saying "this part of Dublin has turned into something of a hostile environment for a bohemian drinking spot" and concluded "there’s no doubt that The Bernard Shaw will leave a colossal hole in Portobello’s nightlife, and in its many regulars’ lives."

Shane Morgan in Gay Community News remarked "To live in Dublin at the minute is to watch a play-by-play of a city’s slow death, and to be all the while conscious of the fact that the going rate for tickets to the funeral will be out of our price range" and wrote that the pub's closure should be seized upon as the start of a fight for the future of the city. [ref: Beloved as the Bernard Shaw was, the collective mourning of it means more, [[Gay Community News (Dublin)] This sentiment was echoed by The Irish Times columnist Una Mullally, a prominent commentator on Dublin culture and gentrification, who too issued a call to action:

The public uproar, and Mullally's article in particular, drew pushback from columnist Dónal Lynch, who in an opinion column for The Irish Independent entitled "Spare us the hysteria over the closure of the Bernard Shaw", contended that the local residents' success in having the beer garden closed was an example of "the people taking on The Man and winning, not the other way around". [ref: Donal Lynch: 'Spare us the hysteria over the closure of the Bernard Shaw', The Irish Independent] Lynch further accused devotees of the pub of confusing a bar with a community, and of "getting pissed in a place and calling it a cultural event".

==Successor==
[[File:The Bernard Shaw pub.jpg|thumb|The new Bodytonic bar of the same name opened in Glasnevin in November 2019]]
A month after the closure of The Bernard Shaw, Bodytonic opened a new pub of the same name in the former Porterhouse Whitworth building, at Cross Guns Bridge in Glasnevin on the north side of the city. A post they made to Instagram to announce the new opening, showing youths in hoodies and tracksuit bottoms with a machete, a baseball bat and making obscene gestures, captioned "Northsiders before the Bernard Shaw moved", contrasted with an "After" image showing people in hipster outfits drinking over an electronic keyboard. [ref: Social media row triggered by Bernard Shaw pub post on gentrifying northside, The Irish Times] The post drew immediate criticism on social media, calling out Bodytonic for being petty bourgeois, and classist capitalists profiting from gentrification of the area. The post was swiftly removed and replaced with an apology.

==Post-closure redevelopment==
In October 2023, Dublin City Council rejected a request for planning permission for a proposed redevelopment of the former The Bernard Shaw site, citing a lack of residential units in the scheme and the level of intervention proposed to the protected structure: "The protected structure will be subsumed and diminished by the proposed development. It is considered that it would overwhelm the protected structure and would cause serious injury to its amenity, architectural significance, legibility, special architectural character and setting."

In October 2024, an appeal to overturn the decision was approved by An Bord Pleanála. [ref: Plans to redevelop former Bernard Shaw pub site approved one year after appeal, Dublin Live] Although the report from An Bord Pleanálas inspector recommended upholding the rejection on the grounds of compromising the protected structure, An Bord Pleanála again decided against their inspector's recommendation, saying the substance of the appeal adequately addressed the cited concerns. The approved proposal entailed an eight storey mixed use development incorporating office space, hospitality, retail and an arts and cultural space.

==See also==
*The Cobblestone, a pub on Dublin's northside whose threated replacement by a hotel in 2021 sparked major protest

data.title: William D. Oliver
data.text:
William D. Oliver is an American physicist and electrical engineer. He is the Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a professor of physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), director of the MIT Center for Quantum Engineering, and associate director of the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE). His research focuses on superconducting qubits and on cryogenic control electronics for quantum and classical high-performance computing.

== Early life and education ==
Oliver received a B.S. in electrical engineering and a B.A. in Japanese from the University of Rochester in 1995. He earned an S.M. in electrical engineering and computer science from MIT in 1997, working with Tod Machover at the MIT Media Lab, and a Ph.D. in electrical engineering, with a minor in physics, from Stanford University in 2003 supervised by Yoshihisa Yamamoto.

== CareerYoshihisa Yamamoto ==
Oliver joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 2003 as a member of its Quantum Information and Integrated Nanosystems Group. He became a principal investigator at RLE in 2006 and later led its Engineering Quantum Systems Group. He spent 2013 as a JSPS Visiting Researcher at the University of Tokyo, and the MIT Department of Physics appointed him Professor of the Practice two years later. Lincoln Laboratory named him a Fellow in 2017. He was also appointed associate director of RLE, where he leads quantum information science research and is the liaison between RLE and Lincoln Laboratory.

MIT promoted Oliver to Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and of Physics in 2021 and named him the Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor. He is the founding director of the MIT Center for Quantum Engineering and holds Lincoln Laboratory Fellow Emeritus status.

Oliver was a co-author of the 2019 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine consensus study report Quantum Computing: Progress and Prospects. He is a member of the U.S. National Quantum Initiative Advisory Committee and the U.S. Committee for Superconducting Electronics.

Oliver and several current and former members of the Engineering Quantum Systems Group founded Atlantic Quantum in 2022 to develop superconducting quantum-computing hardware. The company raised a $9 million seed round led by The Engine and joined Google Quantum AI in October 2025. In a 2026 Scientific American feature on the state of the field, Oliver estimated that larger-scale quantum computers could arrive in about 20 years.

== Research ==
Oliver's research covers the materials growth, fabrication, design and measurement of superconducting qubits and their use in quantum processors. He also works on cryogenic packaging and on control electronics based on cryogenic complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) and single-flux-quantum digital logic.

His group studies the coherence of superconducting flux and fluxonium qubits. A 2016 paper in Nature Communications described a redesigned flux qubit with improved coherence and more reproducible fabrication. A separate 2016 study in Science showed that qubit relaxation could be suppressed by quasiparticle pumping.

== Awards and honors ==
* Fellow, American Association for the Advancement of Science (2023) [ref: ]
* Thornton Family Faculty Research and Innovation Fellowship, MIT (2021)
* Fellow, American Physical Society (2016), "for pioneering contributions to the physics and associated engineering of robust, reproducible, superconducting quantum systems and high-performance cryogenic control electronics" [ref: Division of Quantum Information Fellowship, www.aps.org]
* Fellow, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (2025) [ref: ]

== Selected publications ==
* The flux qubit revisited to enhance coherence and reproducibility, Nature Communications
* Suppressing relaxation in superconducting qubits by quasiparticle pumping, Science

data.title: Robyn Dixon
data.text:
Robyn Dixon (née Bragg; born March 31, 1979) is an American television personality, real estate agent, and entrepreneur. She is best known as an original cast member of the Bravo reality television series The Real Housewives of Potomac, which premiered in 2016. Dixon is also the co-host of the podcast Reasonably Shady with fellow Real Housewives of Potomac cast member Gizelle Bryant. She was previously married to former professional basketball player Juan Dixon, with whom she has two sons.

== Early life and education ==
Robyn Dixon was born Robyn Bragg in Baltimore, Maryland to parents Gladys and Guy Bragg. [ref: Who is Robyn Dixon? The Potomac 'Wife is Keeping Her Family Together, Bravo] She attended the University of Maryland, College Park, where she graduated with a bachelor’s degree in business administration in 2000. While in high school, she met basketball player Juan Dixon when his team played against her school. They began dating in 1996. [ref: ‘Real Housewives of Potomac’ Star Robyn Dixon and Juan Dixon’s Relationship Timeline: From High School Sweethearts to Rekindling Their Romance, Us]

== Career ==

=== Public Relations ===
Dixon began her career in public relations, working as a publicist and event manager for TAA PR, a Washington, D.C.-based public relations, marketing, and special events firm specializing in luxury lifestyle, fashion, and hospitality. [ref: Who Is Robyn Dixon? The 'Real Housewives Of Potomac' Star Is A Power PR Player, Bustle] She later served as the lead publicist for GLO30, a skincare company based in the Washington, D.C., area. [ref: Class Notes, Terp Magazine] [ref: Robyn Dixon’s latest corporate venture? A facial business in Howard Co., The Banner]

=== Real Estate ===
Dixon entered real estate investing with her mother, Gladys Bragg. [ref: RHOP Star Robyn Dixon Wants More Black Women To Invest In Real Estate, BAUCE] Bragg initially worked in real estate wholesaling, and after completing several wholesale deals, the pair began rehabbing properties. Dixon described their first rehabilitation project in an interview as a learning experience. In 2017, the two began renovating properties for resale with guidance from real estate investor Marcel Umphery. [ref: Robyn Dixon Just Revealed the (Not So) Glamorous Life of a House Flipper, Bravo] Their first renovation project was featured on The Real Housewives of Potomac during its third and fourth seasons. [ref: RHOP's Gizelle Bryant Apologizes to Robyn Dixon for Open House Fight: 'I Really Messed Up', People] Dixon and Bragg subsequently sold the property for a profit of more than $30,000. [ref: Robyn Dixon Reveals She Sold Her Flip House… and Made a Tidy Profit, Bravo]

=== She is Empowered ===

In 2017, Dixon founded She Is Empowered, a women’s entrepreneurship and professional development initiative that was part of the Visionary Events Group. [ref: Every Single One of Robyn Dixon's Business Ventures in Her Growing Empire, Bravo] The initiative hosted seminars and events in the Washington, D.C., area focused on entrepreneurship and developing multiple sources of income.

=== Embellished ===

In 2020, Dixon launched Embellished, an accessories and apparel brand featuring satin-lined baseball caps, graphic T-shirts, hoodies and masks. [ref: Here's Why Robyn Dixon's Embellished Hat Line Is So Good, Bravo] The satin lining was designed to protect hair from breakage. [ref: Satin lined fashion caps by Robyn Dixon, Embellished] The business was featured during the fifth season of The Real Housewives of Potomac, including an October 2020 episode in which Dixon presented the line. Following the episode’s airing, Dixon said the response was greater than anticipated, and the collection sold out. [ref: Robyn Dixon Shares "Amazing" News About Her Embellished Hat Line, Bravo] She subsequently expanded Embellished’s headwear offerings to include satin-lined ribbed beanies. [ref: Robyn Dixon Just Shared a Very Exciting Update on Her Embellished Hat Line, Bravo]

=== Television ===

==== The Real Housewives of Potomac ====

Dixon joined the Bravo reality television series The Real Housewives of Potomac as an original cast member when the series premiered in January 2016. [ref: ‘The Real Housewives’ Franchise Heads To Maryland And Texas, Deadline] [ref: Bravo Plots ‘Real Housewives’ Franchise Expansion for 2016, The Hollywood Reporter] Her early storylines centered on her relationship with former NBA player Juan Dixon, whom she had divorced but continued to live with while raising their two sons. [ref: ‘The Real Housewives of Potomac’: TV Review, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: 'Real Housewives of Potomac' premiere react: Meet Bravo's latest big, bold personalities..., Entertainment Weekly] During the series, the couple reconciled and became engaged for a second time in the fifth season. [ref: Love Is in the Air: All of the Celebrity Engagements of 2019, People] They married in a private ceremony in Maryland in August 2022, with their sons and Robyn’s parents in attendance; the wedding was featured in the seventh season finale. [ref: Robyn Dixon and Juan Dixon Are Married Again! RHOP to Air Surprise Wedding in Season 7 Finale, People]

During the show’s later seasons, Dixon’s drew criticism viewers over her handling of reports that Juan Dixon had been unfaithful. [ref: The 'Real Housewives' Shows Are in the Midst of an Authenticity Crisis, Rolling Stone] Dixon acknowledged that Juan had communicated with another woman but initially chose not to discuss the matter extensively on the show. [ref: RHOP’s Candiace Dillard Bassett Says Robyn Dixon Fueling Husband’s Affair Rumors Felt ‘Intentional’, Us] [ref: Why Gizelle Bryant Didn't Bring Up Those Juan Dixon Cheating Rumors on RHOP: 'I Forgot About It', People] Her decision to discuss aspects of the relationship on Reasonably Shady, the podcast she co-hosted with Bryant, rather than on the show also contributed to criticism that Dixon was unwilling to show aspects of her personal life. [ref: Robyn Dixon Grilled by Andy Cohen After Keeping Juan Dixon Relationship Woes Off RHOP, People]

Following the season eight reunion in April 2024, Dixon confirmed that she had been fired from the series and would not return for its ninth season. [ref: Robyn Dixon “Fired” From ‘The Real Housewives Of Potomac’ After 8 Seasons: “The Network Did Not Invite Me Back”, Deadline] [ref: Robyn Dixon Confirms Exit from 'Real Housewives of Potomac' After 8 Seasons: 'I Was Fired', People.com] Dixon said she was ultimately at peace with the decision, stating that she had a long run on the series and was grateful for the opportunity. [ref: Robyn Dixon, OG 'RHOP' cast member says she was 'fired' from the Bravo series, Entertainment Weekly] Bravo executive and reunion host Andy Cohen praised Dixon for being honest with viewers about the nature of her exit. [ref: Andy Cohen On Robyn Dixon & Candiace Dillard-Bassett’s ‘RHOP’ Exit & Being Crowned The Grand Duke Of Potomac, Deadline]

In 2026, she returned to The Real Housewives of Potomac for its eleventh season as a friend of the cast, marking her first appearance on the series in a recurring capacity since her departure as a full-time cast member two years earlier. [ref: ‘The Real Housewives Of Potomac’ Season 11 Cast Set At Bravo With Return Of Robyn Dixon As A “Friend” & Karen Huger After Jail, Deadline] [ref: Robyn Dixon Returning to ‘Real Housewives of Potomac’ 2 Years After Being Fired: Meet Season 11 Cast, Us]

==== The Traitors ====

In June 2024, Dixon was announced to join the cast of Peacock’s reality competition series The Traitors. [ref: ‘The Traitors’ Season 3 Trailer: Reality Stars Kill Off the Faithfuls in Peacock’s Murder Mystery Series, Variety] [ref: ‘Traitors’ Season 3 Books Tom Sandoval, Chrishell Stause, Sam Asghari and More — See the Full Cast, The Hollywood Reporter] Dixon competed as a Faithful on the third season of the series, which premiered in January 2025. [ref: ‘The Traitors’ Season 3 Cast: ‘Big Brother,’ ‘Real Housewives,’ ‘Survivor,’ & ‘Vanderpump Rules’ Stars Set For Peacock Competition, Deadline] [ref: 'The Traitors' season 3 cast portraits revealed (exclusive), EW.com] She placed 17th out of 23 contestants after being murdered by the Traitors in the fifth episode. After she was eliminated, Dixon stated she suspected Boston Rob Mariano was a Traitor and said she would have targeted him at the next roundtable had she remained in the game. [ref: Robyn Dixon Says Traitors Are a ‘Hot Mess’ After Latest Murder: ‘It’s Going to Implode’, Us]

==== BravoCon ====

Dixon has attended every edition of BravoCon since the inaugural convention in 2019. She appeared at the 2019, [ref: The Juiciest Reveals from Bravo Producers at BravoCon 2019, Bravo] 2022, [ref: Everything We Learned at BravoCon 2022, Variety] 2023, [ref: ‘Below Deck’ & ‘Real Housewives’ Among Stars Set For 2023 BravoCon Lineup In Las Vegas, Deadline] and 2025 [ref: How to Watch BravoCon 2025: Streamer, Schedule, Bravo Stars and More, Us] [ref: Robyn Dixon Says Biggest BravoCon 2025 Fights Were Over Golf Carts, Outs Housewives Who Stole Hers, Us] conventions with her castmates from The Real Housewives of Potomac.

=== Podcasting ===

Dixon and fellow The Real Housewives of Potomac cast member Gizelle Bryant launched the podcast Reasonably Shady in 2021. [ref: Gizelle Bryant and Robyn Dixon Unpack Their New Podcast "Reasonably Shady", Media Village] The podcast covers topics including relationships, popular culture, entrepreneurship, and their experiences on reality television. [ref: ] [ref: RHOP’s Gizelle Bryant and Robyn Dixon Say Only 2 of the Housewives on Ozempic Look Good, Us] Dixon continued co-hosting the podcast after leaving The Real Housewives of Potomac in 2024. [ref: RHOP's Gizelle Bryant and Robyn Dixon Break Silence on Karen Huger DUI Video — and Their Remarks Are Reasonably Shady, People]

Reasonably Shady was nominated for an NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Arts and Entertainment Podcast in 2022. [ref: ]

In 2023, rapper Eminem opposed Bryant and Dixon’s application to trademark the name Reasonably Shady, arguing that it could create confusion with his trademarks for Shady and Slim Shady. [ref: Real Slim Shady vs. Real Housewives: Eminem Tries to Block 'Reasonably Shady' Trademark, Rolling Stone] [ref: Eminem Files Opposition Against Gizelle Bryant and Robyn Dixon for Using 'Shady' in Podcast Title, People] Bryant and Dixon contested the opposition, arguing that their trademark was not confusingly similar and that their services were unrelated to Eminem’s. [ref: Eminem requests protective order against 'The Real Housewives of Potomac' stars Gizelle Bryant and Robyn Dixon over 'Shady' trademark dispute., Entertainment Weekly] The dispute remains ongoing before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board. [ref: Gizelle Bryant and Robyn Dixon Claim Eminem Demands Special Treatment as He Accuses ‘RHOP’ Stars of Harassment, Us]

=== Philanthropy ===

Dixon has served as a board member and director of the Holistic Life Foundation, a Baltimore-based nonprofit that provides wellness and mindfulness programs to children and adults in underserved communities. [ref: ] She joined the organization’s board in 2023.

== Personal life ==
Dixon met basketball player Juan Dixon while they were in high school and began dating in 1996. They married in 2005 and have two sons, Corey and Carter. The couple divorced in 2012 but continued living together and raising their children. [ref: RHOP's Robyn Dixon Blasts Juan Dixon Affair Rumors in Season 8 Premiere: 'The World Wants to Tear Us Apart', People] They even continued sharing a bedroom, and their unconventional post-divorce relationship became part of Dixon’s storyline when The Real Housewives of Potomac premiered in 2016. Over the following years, they gradually reconciled and resumed their romantic relationship.

Dixon and Juan became engaged for a second time in December 2019. [ref: Real Housewives of Potomac's Robyn and Juan Dixon Get Engaged (Again!), People] Their plans to remarry were delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, the construction of their home, and issues involving Juan’s communication with another woman. [ref: RHOP's Robyn Dixon Explained Why Juan Paid For A Woman's Hotel Room, Bustle] Dixon said Juan had communicated with the woman through Instagram but denied that he had been unfaithful, and said that the couple had resolved the matter. [ref: Robyn Dixon Admits 'Idiot' Husband Juan Dixon's DMs with Another Woman Stalled Their Wedding: 'We Worked Through It', People] [ref: RHOP’s Karen Huger Says She Can’t Support Robyn Dixon Until She Stops ‘Lying’ About Juan Dixon Drama, Us]

The couple obtained a marriage license in Maryland in August 2020. [ref: RHOP's Robyn and Juan Dixon Obtain Marriage License Nearly 3 Years After Second Engagement, People] They initially planned to marry in Jamaica in July 2022 but abandoned those plans shortly before the ceremony. On August 24, 2022, Dixon and Juan married for a second time in an intimate ceremony at The Bayfront Club in Edgemere, Maryland, with their sons present. [ref: RHOP Stars Robyn Dixon and Juan Dixon Marry Again 'Our Way' in Intimate Ceremony — See the Pics!, People]

data.title: Batuling Bantayao Gumander
data.text:
Datu Batuling Bantayao Gumander (November 15, 1937 – April 16, 1976) was a political leader, a community figure, and one of the most prominent symbols of revolution and resistance among the Moro people in the Philippines. He was known for his prominent political role in leading the community of the Sultan Kudarat municipality in Maguindanao province, and was famous for his leadership of the political wing in the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). [ref: The Life and Martyrdom of Datu Batuling Bantayao Gumander, Medium]

He is considered in local accounts and memory as the "First Martyr" of the Sultan Kudarat municipality after his summary execution by the Philippine Armed Forces during the martial law era under Ferdinand Marcos in 1972. [ref: The Life And Martyrdom Of Datu Batuling Bantayao Gumander] [ref: ] [ref: Infographic: The day Marcos declared Martial Law]

== Personal life ==
Batuling was born in the village of Bungabong in the municipality of Sultan Kudarat in Maguindanao province. He descends from the Gumander family; his father was Datu Salusub Gumander (known as "Ama i Angkog"), and his grandfather was the Muslim scholar and judge Datu Kali Gumander. [ref: Historical Biography: The Life and Martyrdom of Datu Batuling Bantayao Gumander, Zenodo]

He married Undang Ara Butuan, who belongs to the "Bilawatao" family [ref: 1st GRAND REUNION ""BILAWATAO CLAN"" MANOCOB DESCENDANTS] from the village of Mulawug in Sultan Kudarat, and had four children with her: Abdulhadie, Yaqub, Nusaibah, and Mujahid. [ref: "BRIEF HISTORY OF MAGUINDANAO" (PDF).]

== Political career ==

Batuling Gumander began his career in public service as an elected and appointed official in leadership positions, rising through the political ranks in the municipality of Sultan Kudarat, where he held several notable positions:
* Municipal Councilor (Kagawad): He was first elected as First Municipal Councilor for the term (1962–1965), and was re-elected for a second term (1965–1968).
* Vice Mayor: During his third term, he was appointed Vice Mayor of Sultan Kudarat (1968–1970).
* He continued to perform his duties as Vice Mayor until 1971, following the death of former Vice Mayor Datu Mamur Matabalao, working alongside then-Mayor Hajj Datu Sangacala Baraguir (who governed the municipality between 1956 and 1971).

When Mayor Sangacala Baraguir was appointed Governor of Maguindanao province, [ref: List of Municipal Officials and Employees in the Municipality of Sultan Kudarat (1970-1971), Internet Archive] an official offer was made to Datu Batuling to assume the position of Mayor of Sultan Kudarat municipality. However, he refused the position, preferring to abandon formal government work and join the ranks of the armed struggle to defend the rights of the Bangsamoro people.

== Role in the Bangsamoro struggle ==
Datu Batuling joined the ranks of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) early in its formative years, working as a co-founder of the protest and revolutionary movement. He adopted a nom de guerre in the Iranun language, "Langkom Pangulima" (LANGKOM PNGULIMA), which translates to "Commander-in-Chief". [ref: The Life and Martyrdom of Datu Batuling Bantayao Gumander] [ref: ]

He assumed a pivotal leadership role by taking the position of General Chairman of the Political Committee (POLCOM) of the Front. He was also a founding member of the "Ansarul Islam" movement in the Sultan Kudarat area, a movement formed to protect Islamic identity and communities against marginalization policies.

== Personality and social standing ==
Datu Batuling was known for his good character and altruistic leadership among the members of his community. He was distinguished by his extreme humility and dedication, often spending his own money to help young people unable to afford marriage costs, and to provide direct support to needy and poor families in his area. This generosity and community-oriented behavior made him a beloved leader whose services transcended the boundaries of politics and became woven into the social welfare fabric of his town.

== Death (Execution) ==
On April 16, 1976, during the strict implementation of martial law under President Ferdinand Marcos, Datu Batuling was attacked by members of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) while he was with some of his men at his farm in the "Tinedteban" area (which is currently located within the municipality of Sultan Mastura).

According to local accounts and testimonies, Datu Batuling fought fiercely, refusing to surrender or let go of his two personal handguns even after his ammunition ran out. Following his death, military forces decapitated him and hung his head on a military tank, parading it through the villages to terrorize the residents; the tank was seen crossing the Simuay River. The burial site of his body and head remains unknown to this day, and his family has been unable to retrieve them. [ref: Historical Biography: The Life and Martyrdom of Datu Batuling Bantayao Gumander, Zenodo] [ref: Martial Law, the dark chapter in Philippine history, RAPPLER]

As a result of this incident, the community bestowed upon him the title of "The First Martyr of Sultan Kudarat".

data.title: Out of Eden Walk
data.text:
----

The Out of Eden Walk is a long-form journalism project led by American journalist Paul Salopek, who began walking in 2013 along a route approximating the early human migration out of Africa. [ref: [https://gis.harvard.edu/out-eden-walk Center for Geographic Analysis, Harvard University, article and timeline]] The project is managed by an independent nonprofit organization and supported by the National Geographic Society. The combines travel writing, photography, audio, video, and mapping to document contemporary life along the journey.

== Background ==
The project was created by Paul Salopek as an experiment in "slow journalism", which would use walking as a method for reporting on different communities and landscapes at human scale, while following one of the broad migration routes associated Out of Africa theory. [ref: Out of Eden Walk, National Geographic Education] [ref: ‘Slow Journalist’ Paul Salopek Is in India on His Epic 10-Year Walk Across Continents, VICE] The project was originally planned as a seven-year trek from Africa's Rift Valley to Tierra del Fuego, [ref: Paul Salopek is on a foot journey across the world. He provides an extraordinary record of humanity at a new millennium, National Geographic] [ref: What Do You Pack For A Seven-Year Trip?, NPR] but due to delays and other factors has continued beyond its initial schedule. [ref: To walk the world: part one, National Geographic] [ref: A Twenty-Four-Thousand-Mile Walk Across Human History, The New Yorker]

A recurring feature of the project is the "milestone" in which a standardized record made at regular intervals along the route. These milestones include observations of landscape, sound, people, and other details from the walk. [ref: New Milestone, East to China, Out of Eden Walk] The project publishes written dispatches, photographs, audio recordings, videos, and map-based stories through the National Geographic Society's Out of Eden Walk platform. [ref: Out of Eden Walk, Out of Eden Walk Nonprofit]

== Route ==
The walk began at Herto Bouri, Ethiopia, in the Afar region near the Great Rift Valley. [ref: Baby Steps, Out of Eden Walk] [ref: Travel Pioneers: Paul Salopek, BBC Travel] The first chapter, "Out of Africa", covered Ethiopia, Djibouti, and a Red Sea crossing between January and May 2013. [ref: Out of Eden Walk, Out of Eden Walk] The project has organized the route into chapters including "Out of Africa", "Holy Lands", "Autumn Wars", "Silk Road", "Riverlands", "Middle Kingdom", "Asian Rim", "Ocean Crossing", and "Americas".

In a 2019 essay for The New Yorker, Salopek wrote that the route was intended to follow archaeological and genetic evidence for ancient human migration as closely as modern borders, wars, and practical conditions allowed. By that time, he had walked from Ethiopia through regions including Saudi Arabia, the Levant, Afghanistan, and India, and planned to continue across China and toward Alaska before proceeding down the Americas.

The walk was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, with Salopek having paused in Myanmar. [ref: Crossroad of Memory, Out of Eden Walk] He resumed the route in China in October 2021 after a quarantine in Shanghai. In April 2023, while Salopek was in China, PBS NewsHour described him as halfway through the journey. [ref: Explorer halfway through journey to walk around the world, PBS NewsHour]

By January 2025, Salopek reached the Pacific Rim, and wrote that he hoped to board a cargo ship from Japan to Alaska that spring. [ref: Bookend Oceans, Out of Eden Walk] In May 2025, he was in Nagano Prefecture. [ref: One long walk: National Geographic 'explorer' on global journey strolls into Victoria, Times Colonist] He crossed the North Pacific by container ship in 2025, with a November 2025 dispatch describing the crossing as the project's "Ocean Crossing" chapter. [ref: Blue Highway, Out of Eden Walk]

In October 2025, National Geographic announced that the project had entered North America, beginning a new phase of the journey in Alaska. [ref: Out of Eden Walk Global Storytelling Journey Arrives in North America, National Geographic Society] In January 2026, Salopek published a dispatch from Anchorage, Alaska. [ref: Reading Anchorage, Out of Eden Walk] In October 2026, he arrived in Victoria, BC. At that point, he was 5,000 days into his trip and had walked approximately 30,000 kilometres.

== Educational use and organization ==
The Out of Eden Walk has been used as an educational resource by National Geographic Education and the Pulitzer Center. [ref: Out of Eden Walk: An Introduction for Educators, Pulitzer Center] National Geographic Education describes the project as a resource for subjects including anthropology, genetics, geography, human geography, social studies, storytelling, and geographic information systems. The Pulitzer Center, an education partner of the project, has promoted the walk as a tool for teaching about migration and global storytelling.

The Out of Eden Walk is also associated with an independent nonprofit organization, Out of Eden Walk, which describes itself as a 501(c)(3) organization supporting Salopek's journey and related educational work. [ref: Out Of Eden Walk, ProPublica]

data.title: Woofy (TV series)
data.text:
Woofy is a French-Canadian animated television series created by Alexandre Révérend and directed by Dominique Etchecopar. [ref: Woofy, Gaumont] [ref: Woofy, Planète Jeunesse] Consisting of 65 five or six-minute episodes, the series was co-produced by animation studios Alphanim and Tooncan Productions XXV, inc. in association with France 5. [ref: Alphanim Scores Sales Ahead of MIPCOM, Animation Magazine]

== Premise ==
The series revolves around Woofy, a stray dog adopted by a four-year-old boy named Anthony (French: Antoine). Because Anthony's mother forbids pets in the household, Anthony pretends that Woofy is a plush toy won at a school fair. [ref: TV5MONDE February Highlights, Complete France] Woofy maintains a secret life whenever adults are not looking, leading to comedic situations as he and Anthony attempt to conceal his true identity.

== Voice cast & crew ==
=== French voice cast ===
* Laurent-Christophe de Ruelle as Woofy
* François-Nicolas Dolan as Antoine
* Rafaëlle Leiris as Antoine's Mother
* Jean-François Beaupré as Antoine's Father
* Rosemarie Houde as Muriel
* Aline Pinsonneault as Rémi

=== French crew ===
* François Sasseville – Voice Director

=== English cast ===
* Thor Bishopric as Woofy
* Aaron Grunfeld as Anthony (French: Antoine)
* Jane Wheeler as Anthony's Mother
* Mark Camacho as Anthony's Father
* Sonja Ball as Marina (French: Marine)
* Eleanor Noble as Bobby (French: Rémi)
* Bailey Stocker as Muriel

=== English crew ===
* Terrence Scammell – Voice Director [ref: Terrence Scammell credits, Behind The Voice Actors]

=== Voice recording ===
* Joe Petrella – Voice Recording
* Louis-Gabriel Pothier – Voice Recording

== Production and crew ==
The series was created by Alexandre Révérend, who also served as a writer alongside Valérie Baranski, Manon and Muguette Berthelet, Michel Coulon, Frédéric Révérend, Nathalie Reznikoff, Frédéric Sabrou and Nicolas Verpilleux. The series was directed by Dominique Etchecopar with an original score composed by Laurent Aknin.

== Episodes ==
The series premiered in France on 13 November 2004 on France 5 and in Canada on Télévision de Radio-Canada on 26 July 2005. It consists of 65 five or six-minute episodes.

data.title: Accelerated Resolution Therapy
data.text:
----

Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART) is a brief, manualized form of psychotherapy developed by licensed marriage and family therapist Laney Rosenzweig in 2008. It uses imagery-based techniques, attention to physical and emotional responses, and therapist-directed eye movements while a person recalls distressing memories. Clients do not have to describe the details of a traumatic event verbally to the therapist. [ref: Treatment of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A State-of-the-art Review, Current Neuropharmacology] [ref: USF Public Health awarded Army contract to train military clinicians in treatment of PTSD, USF Health News]

ART has been studied mainly as a treatment for Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and trauma-related symptoms. Clinical studies have reported reductions in PTSD symptoms as well as depression, anxiety, psychological distress, and sleep problems. A 2024 systematic review of five primary studies involving 337 enrolled adults described ART as a promising, time-efficient treatment for PTSD, while concluding that more high-quality research, particularly comparisons with established PTSD treatments, is needed. [ref: Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART) for the treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder in adults: A systematic review, PLOS Mental Health]

== History ==
ART was developed in 2008 by Laney Rosenzweig. She is a licensed marriage and family therapist who has worked in the mental health field since 1989. [ref: Introduction to Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART), National Association of Social Workers – California] The first clinical study of the therapy was published in 2012, [ref: Brief Treatment of Symptoms of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) by Use of Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART®), Behavioral Sciences] followed in 2013 by a randomized controlled trial involving U.S. service members and veterans. [ref: Randomized Controlled Trial of Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART) for Symptoms of Combat-Related Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Military Medicine]In 2015, ART was included in the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration's National Registry of Evidence-Based Programs and Practices (NREPP), which classified it as "effective" for psychological trauma and depression. [ref: Interventions with Special Relevance for the Family First Prevention Services Act (FFPSA), Ohio Department of Job and Family Services] In 2016, the U.S. Army awarded the University of South Florida a contract to train military mental health clinicians in ART at several Army installations.The first systematic review of ART for PTSD in adults was published in 2024.

== Technique ==
ART is a highly structured, manualized psychotherapy in which a therapist guides the client through the recall and processing of distressing memories while using sets of horizontal eye movements.The client brings a distressing event or image to mind while attending to associated emotional and physical sensations. ART places particular emphasis on processing physiological or somatic sensations associated with the recalled material. Detailed verbal narration of the traumatic experience is not required.

ART also uses a form of imagery rescripting known as Voluntary Image Replacement (VIR), in which distressing imagery associated with a memory is replaced with imagery selected by the client. The technique is intended to alter the distressing imagery without replacing the factual or narrative memory of the event.ART also incorporates visual imagery, metaphors, Gestalt-based techniques, and other prescribed interventions within its structured protocol. The client selects the replacement imagery, while the therapist guides the sequence of prescribed interventions. [ref: Practice comparisons between accelerated resolution therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing and cognitive processing therapy with case examples, Nurse Education Today]

ART and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) both use clinician-directed eye movements while distressing material is processed, but published descriptions identify differences in how the protocols structure reprocessing. ART uses different amounts of eye movements, incorporates attention to associated physiological sensations during processing, and uses Voluntary Image Replacement, in which the client deliberately rescripts distressing imagery. Published descriptions characterize ART's processing as more directive and less free-associative than EMDR.Several processes and mechanisms have been proposed to contribute to ART's effects, including exposure and imagery rescripting, along with hypotheses involving working memory and memory reconsolidation. It is not yet known which mechanisms or individual treatment components account for the clinical effects reported in studies. [ref: Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART): a Review and Research to Date, Current Psychiatry Reports]

== Research ==

=== Post-traumatic stress disorder ===
Most ART research to date has focused on PTSD.A 2012 prospective study of 80 adults with clinically significant PTSD symptoms reported reductions in PTSD symptoms and several related measures after one to five ART sessions. The study did not include a control group.

In 2013, a randomized controlled trial compared ART with an attention-control condition in 57 U.S. service members and veterans with combat-related PTSD symptoms. Participants in the ART group received an average of 3.7 treatment sessions. Participants receiving ART had greater reductions in self-reported PTSD symptoms and several related measures than those in the control condition. Improvements were maintained at three-month follow-up.

A 2024 systematic review included five primary studies with 337 enrolled participants, 250 of whom completed treatment. Two were randomized controlled trials, two were prospective observational studies, and one was a feasibility study. All five reported significant reductions in PTSD symptoms after treatment. Reductions in depression, anxiety, psychological distress, and sleep dysfunction were also reported.

The reviewers did not conduct a meta-analysis because they concluded that the studies differed in design and there were too few studies with low risk of bias. The comparative studies also used different control conditions, so the review could not determine how ART compares with other PTSD treatments. The authors described ART as a promising, time-efficient treatment and recommended further high-quality randomized trials.

The 2023 VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for PTSD found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against ART.

=== Other applications ===
ART has also been studied for complicated grief. In a 2020 randomized controlled trial of 54 older adults who had experienced the death of a hospice care recipient, participants receiving ART showed greater reductions in grief, PTSD, and depressive symptoms than those in a wait-list group. The researchers recommended testing the treatment in larger and more diverse samples. [ref: Accelerated Resolution Therapy: Randomized Controlled Trial of a Complicated Grief Intervention, American Journal of Hospice and Palliative Medicine]Depression, anxiety, sleep problems, and psychological distress have also improved as secondary outcomes in PTSD studies.

data.title: Tarek Elgindi
data.text:
Tarek M. Elgindi is an Egyptian-American mathematician and a professor of mathematics at Duke University. His research concerns partial differential equations and mathematical fluid dynamics, particularly singularity formation and the long-term behavior of solutions to the incompressible Euler equations.

Elgindi established finite-time singularity formation in three-dimensional incompressible Euler flows without a physical boundary. His construction concerns initial velocity fields in the regularity class C^{1,\alpha}, rather than infinitely differentiable initial data. His analytical methods were subsequently adapted by Jiajie Chen and Thomas Y. Hou in further proofs of singularity formation for the Euler and Boussinesq equations. He received a Sloan Research Fellowship in 2020 and a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2026.

== Education and academic career ==

Elgindi studied mathematics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where he received a Goldwater Scholarship in 2008. He earned his doctorate at New York University in 2014, supervised by Nader Masmoudi and Fang-Hua Lin.

He was an instructor at Princeton University from 2014 to 2017 and an assistant professor at the University of California, San Diego from 2017 to 2020. He joined Duke University in 2020, and was appointed professor of mathematics in 2024.

== Research ==

=== Singularity formation ===

Elgindi's work on the incompressible Euler equations examines whether initially regular fluid motion can develop a singularity in finite time. The equations describe an idealized fluid with no viscosity and constant density; a singularity can involve unbounded growth of vorticity, which measures local rotation within the fluid.

In work first circulated in 2019 and published in 2021, Elgindi constructed solutions on three-dimensional Euclidean space, \mathbb{R}^3, that develop finite-time singularities. The result demonstrated that short-time existence and uniqueness, known in the relevant regularity class since the 1920s, do not imply that solutions remain regular indefinitely. The construction uses axisymmetric flows without swirl: flows that are rotationally symmetric but have no velocity component around their symmetry axis. Their initial velocities belong to C^{1,\alpha} for sufficiently small positive \alpha, meaning that their first derivatives satisfy a Hölder continuity condition. The proof constructs self-similar solutions of a simpler model and uses their stability to obtain singular solutions of the Euler equations.

With Tej-Eddine Ghoul and Nader Masmoudi, Elgindi subsequently studied the stability of the blowup construction. They established the existence of finite-energy solutions with C^{1,\alpha} initial velocity that become singular in a locally self-similar manner.

== Honors and recognition ==

* Elgindi received a Sloan Research Fellowship in 2020.
* In 2024, he received a Frontiers of Science Award in mathematics from the International Congress of Basic Science for his work on finite-time singularity formation in the incompressible Euler equations.
* He was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2026.

data.title: Abdelrahman Mohamed (AI Researcher)
data.text:
Abdelrahman Mohamed (also written Abdel-rahman Mohamed); is an Egyptian-American computer scientist working in the United States, known for his research on deep learning for speech recognition and self-supervised speech representation learning. As a doctoral student at the University of Toronto under Geoffrey Hinton and Gerald Penn, he was part of the group that first applied deep belief networks to acoustic modelling, work that is credited with starting the deep learning era in speech recognition. He later created the HuBERT model and co-developed wav2vec 2.0 at Meta AI. He is a co-founder and chief AI scientist of the advertising-technology company Rembrand.

== Education ==
Mohamed received a bachelor's degree (2004) and a master's degree (2007) in computer science from Cairo University. After a research position at KU Leuven in Belgium, he began doctoral studies at the University of Toronto in 2008, where he was supervised by Gerald Penn and Geoffrey Hinton, receiving his PhD in 2014.

== Career ==
In 2009, Mohamed, George E. Dahl and Hinton showed that deep belief networks could outperform the Gaussian mixture models then standard in speech recognition on the TIMIT phone-recognition benchmark. The result was extended to large-vocabulary recognition by groups at Microsoft, Google and IBM, and Mohamed was a co-author of the 2012 overview paper in IEEE Signal Processing Magazine that summarised the shared findings of the four groups. With Alex Graves and Hinton he also published early work on deep recurrent neural networks for speech recognition, and with Ossama Abdel-Hamid and others on convolutional neural networks for speech.

Mohamed was a researcher at Microsoft Research in Redmond, Washington, from 2014 to 2017, and a principal scientist and manager in the Amazon Alexa AI group from 2017 to 2018. From 2018 to 2022 he was at Meta's Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) laboratory in Seattle, where his group worked on learning speech representations from unlabelled audio. He co-developed wav2vec 2.0, a contrastive self-supervised framework for speech, and led the development of HuBERT (Hidden-Unit BERT), which learns speech representations by predicting clustered "hidden units" of masked audio segments; both models are widely used as pre-trained foundations for speech systems. His group extended the approach to audio-visual speech with AV-HuBERT and co-organised SUPERB, a benchmark for evaluating self-supervised speech models. He was first author of a 2022 review of self-supervised speech representation learning in the IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing.

In December 2022 Mohamed left Meta, where he had been a director of AI research, to co-found Rembrand, a Palo Alto, California company that uses generative AI to insert virtual product placement into video, serving as its chief AI scientist. The company, led by Omar Tawakol, raised an $8 million seed round in 2023 and a $23 million Series A in 2025.

== Awards ==
* IEEE Signal Processing Society Best Paper Award, 2016, for "Convolutional Neural Networks for Speech Recognition" (with Abdel-Hamid, Jiang, Deng, Penn and Yu).
* IEEE Signal Processing Magazine Best Paper Award, 2022, for "Deep Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling in Speech Recognition: The Shared Views of Four Research Groups".

== Selected publications ==
* Deep belief networks for phone recognition
* Acoustic Modeling Using Deep Belief Networks, IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing
* Deep Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling in Speech Recognition: The Shared Views of Four Research Groups, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine

* Convolutional Neural Networks for Speech Recognition, IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing

* HuBERT: Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning by Masked Prediction of Hidden Units, IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing
* Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning: A Review, IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing
