data.title: Lydia Rodarte-Quayle
data.text:
Lydia Rodarte-Quayle is a fictional character in the crime drama television series Breaking Bad and its prequel series Better Call Saul. She is portrayed by Scottish actress Laura Fraser.

Introduced in fifth season, Lydia is a business executive at Madrigal Electromotive who is involved in the company's logistics operations. She secretly helps Gustavo Fring obtain chemicals for his methamphetamine operation and later becomes involved with Walter White and Todd Alquist's uncle Jack Welker with his criminal organization. Lydia is a single mother with a daughter, and her concern for her daughter is part of her motivation. She later helps expand the methamphetamine business into the Czech Republic. In series finale, Walter eventually poisons her with ricin concealed in the stevia she uses in her tea.

== Creation and characterization ==
[[File:Laura Fraser in 2017.png|thumb|233x233px|Laura Fraser, who plays Lydia Rodarte-Quayle]]
Lydia Rodarte-Quayle is portrayed by Scottish actress Laura Fraser. Fraser was cast after auditioning for the role and later performed a diner scene with Jonathan Banks, who plays Mike Ehrmantraut. Fraser had not watched Breaking Bad before getting the role, but watched the first four seasons after being cast. [ref: 'Breaking Bad' Post-Mortem: New Face Laura Fraser Talks About Her Role, The Hollywood Reporter] Fraser described Lydia as "extremely highly strung, calculating, enterprising" and said that she had learned to survive at all costs and developed skills to do so. She also said that her character was constantly trying to regain control of her situation and that she did not know whether the character would survive from one scene to the next.

Fraser said that Lydia's concern for her daughter influenced the way she understood the character's actions. She described the daughter as an important part of how Lydia justified her actions to herself. [ref: Breaking Bad's Lydia: 'Drinking camomile tea with milk is disgusting', The Guardian] Fraser also described her character as being in a constant state of "fight-or-flight" while discussing the physical strain of playing the character. Fraser discussed Lydia's position within the corporate world represented by Madrigal Electromotive. She said that Lydia's role allowed the series to show a side of the drug trade connected to large businesses rather than only street-level criminal activity. [ref: 'Breaking Bad' Q&A: Laura Fraser on the Mystery of Lydia, Rolling Stone]

In a 2013 interview with Rolling Stone, Fraser described Lydia as a "clean-cut, bonkers sociopath" and said that the character took herself seriously while believing that she was always right. She also discussed Lydia's Louboutin shoes, saying that the red soles represented the bloodshed for which Lydia was responsible. [ref: 'Breaking Bads Lydia: 'She's a Clean-Cut, Bonkers Sociopath', Rolling Stone] Fraser also described her character as "extremely self-righteous and irritating" and said that she took herself too seriously. In developing the character, Fraser imagined that Lydia had grown up in a group home, had an unhappy and uncertain childhood, and had been abandoned as a child, which she believed contributed to Lydia's loneliness and alienation. [ref: Breaking Bad's Laura Fraser Channels Her 'Inner Hate' To Play Lydia Rodarte-Quayle, CBS News]

Lydia's tea, which consists of chamomile tea with soy milk and stevia, was later discussed by creator Vince Gilligan. Gilligan said there was no hidden meaning behind the choice. He said that he personally put milk in chamomile tea and that soy milk was chosen because it sounded healthy. [ref: 'Breaking Bad' Creator Vince Gilligan Finally Explains Why Lydia Took Her Tea Like That, TheWrap] Fraser also discussed filming Lydia's final scene in the series finale, "Felina". She said that her final day on the set involved filming Lydia's death scene and that she was made to look physically ill after being poisoned with ricin. She recalled filming the scene with Bryan Cranston. [ref: Breaking Bad's Laura Fraser on the Finale, [[Vulture (magazine)]

== Appearances ==
=== Better Call Saul ===
Lydia is introduced in Better Call Saul during the events preceding Breaking Bad. In 2003, she accompanies Gustavo Fring while he examines an industrial laundry facility that Gus plans to use for a secret methamphetamine laboratory. The facility later becomes the location of Gus's underground laboratory. [ref: Off Brand] Lydia later meets Mike Ehrmantraut at Madrigal's Houston office. She explains her concerns about Mike's activities involving the company's security and becomes involved in arrangements connected to Gus's operation. Although she is nervous about the risks involved, she continues to work with Gus. [ref: Fall]

==== Season 4 ====
Lydia continues to work at Madrigal and becomes involved in the security arrangements surrounding the company's illegal activities. She asks Mike to stop testing the company's security, but Gus later allows Mike to continue working with Madrigal. [ref: Breathe]

==== Season 5 ====
Lydia meets with Peter Schuler and Gus to discuss Lalo Salamanca, who is causing problems for Gus's operation while in prison. Lydia suggests that Lalo be killed in prison, but Gus rejects the idea because of the attention it would bring to them. [ref: JMM]

=== Breaking Bad ===
Lydia works for Madrigal Electromotive and is involved in its logistics operations in Houston. Through her position, she secretly assists Gus in obtaining chemicals and other resources for his methamphetamine operation. She is also involved in plans to distribute Gus's methamphetamine to the Czech Republic before his death. [ref: Better Call Saul Season 5: Madrigal Enters the Story, Den of Geek]

==== Season 5 ====
After Gus is killed and Peter Schuler dies by suicide, Lydia attends a meeting between Madrigal executives and the Drug Enforcement Administration. Fearing that the people connected to Gus's operation could expose her involvement, she asks Mike to kill eleven imprisoned associates. Mike refuses, but Lydia later hires Chris Mara to kill Mike and the men on her list. [ref: Madrigal] Mike eventually enters Lydia's home in Houston intending to kill her. Lydia asks Mike to leave her body where her daughter will find it so that her daughter will not believe she abandoned her. Mike does not kill her and instead asks whether she can still obtain methylamine. Lydia agrees to help him obtain it.

Lydia provides methylamine to Mike's group and later helps them obtain more. She becomes involved with Walter White, Jesse Pinkman and Mike after learning that their supply is limited. Lydia also discovers that Mike has placed a tracking device on one of her methylamine barrels and becomes suspicious of him. [ref: Hazard Pay] Lydia later tells Walter, Jesse and Mike about a large shipment of methylamine being transported by train. Walter and Jesse use the information to plan a train robbery. During the robbery, Todd Alquist kills Drew Sharp, a young boy who witnesses the operation. [ref: Dead Freight] After Mike and Jesse leave the business, Lydia meets Walter and gives him the names of Mike's imprisoned associates. Walter later arranges their deaths. Lydia also proposes expanding the methamphetamine business into the Czech Republic, using Madrigal's international distribution network. [ref: Gliding Over All]

After Walter retires from the methamphetamine business, Lydia continues working with Todd and Jack Welker's group. She meets with Walter at the A1A Car Wash and asks him to return to the operation because Todd's methamphetamine does not meet her expectations. Walter refuses, and Lydia later approaches Declan, the distributor who took over Walter's operation. [ref: Blood Money] Lydia meets Declan and criticizes the quality of the methamphetamine being produced by his organization. She suggests that Todd should take over the cooking, but Declan refuses. Jack and his men subsequently kill Declan and the other members of his crew and take control of the laboratory. [ref: Buried] Lydia continues to work with Todd and Jack's organization as they produce methamphetamine for her distribution network. She remains dissatisfied with Todd's product and pushes him to improve its quality. [ref: To'hajiilee]

After Jesse is captured, Lydia becomes involved in the decision to keep him alive so that he can continue producing high-quality methamphetamine. Todd develops an interest in Lydia, while she remains focused on maintaining the business. Lydia later asks Jack's group to deal with Skyler White and other potential threats to her operation. [ref: Granite State] Lydia meets Todd, while Walter's return to the methamphetamine business becomes part of a plan that leads to Jack's compound. Lydia agrees to a meeting with Walter while secretly intending for Jack's group to kill him. After Walter attacks the compound, Lydia calls Todd to confirm that Walter has been killed. Walter answers Todd's phone and tells Lydia that he has replaced the stevia in her tea with ricin. Lydia is visibly ill during the call. [ref: Felina]

=== Fate ===
Following Walter's attack on Jack's compound, a news report heard in El Camino: A Breaking Bad Movie identifies an unnamed woman from Houston who was poisoned by Walter. The woman is reported to be in critical condition and not expected to survive. The report does not explicitly state that she dies, but the woman is understood to be Lydia. [ref: 'El Camino: A Breaking Bad Movie' Recap: Jesse Pinkman Is Born Again, Rolling Stone]

== Reception ==
=== Critical response ===
Lydia's role in the later part of Breaking Bad was discussed by several television critics. In his review of "Buried", Paul Martinovic of Den of Geek discussed Lydia's involvement in the attack on Declan's group. He described the scene in which Lydia kept her eyes closed while being led past the bodies as showing her attempt to distance herself from the violence she had helped create. [ref: Breaking Bad season 5 episode 10 review: Buried, Den of Geek] K.M. McFarland of Boing Boing described Lydia as someone who approached the drug trade from a removed perspective and wanted to keep her hands clean. He noted that her decision to have Todd and his associates take over the methamphetamine operation showed her lack of understanding of the violence involved in the business. [ref: 'Breaking Bad,' Season 5, Episode 10, 'Buried': review, Boing Boing]

Time also discussed Lydia's role in "Buried", focusing on the scene in which she is led past the bodies of the methamphetamine producers with her eyes closed. The recap described the scene as a reflection of Lydia's attempt to avoid confronting the consequences of her actions. [ref: Breaking Bad Watch: You Made Your Bed of Money, Now Lie on It, [[Time (magazine)] The Chicago Sun-Times described Lydia as an unlikely figure in the methamphetamine business and focused on her role in arranging the takeover of Declan's operation. The review also compared her reaction to the massacre to the "three wise monkeys", noting her efforts to avoid seeing the violence she had caused. [ref: 'Breaking Bad' recap, 'Buried': Girl power, activate, Chicago Sun-Times] Todd VanDerWerff of the Los Angeles Times was less positive about Lydia's storyline in "Buried", writing that the scenes involving Lydia and Todd seemed out of place and expressing hope that they would lead to a larger storyline. [ref: In the latest 'Breaking Bad,' Jesse and Hank meet up, Skyler decides not to turn on Walt, and Walt buries his money., Los Angeles Times]

In its review of "Felina", Slant Magazine discussed Lydia's poisoning by Walt and described her as a character who had repeatedly left the violent work of the drug trade to others. [ref: Breaking Bad Recap: Season 5, Episode 16, “Felina”, Slant Magazine] The WBUR review also noted Lydia's poisoning as part of the conclusion of Walt's story and described her as one of the characters affected by his final actions. [ref: 'Breaking Bad' Series Finale: The Tidy End Worked — But At Some Cost, WBUR] Hank Stuever of The Washington Post mentioned Lydia's poisoning in his review of the series finale, describing Walt's use of the Stevia packet as one of the acts of revenge carried out during the episode. [ref: 'Breaking Bad' finale: What happened to Walt — and to us, The Washington Post]

=== Analysis ===
Mollie Wilson O'Reilly of Commonweal viewed Lydia's death as part of the consequences left behind by the series' ending. In her review of "Felina", she noted that Lydia's daughter is left without a mother, placing Lydia's death alongside the effects of Walter's actions on the families of other characters. [ref: Breaking Bad #516: "Felina", [[Commonweal (magazine)]

== References ==

data.title: Criston Cole
data.text:
Criston Cole is a fictional character from George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire series of epic fantasy novel, appearing in the 2013 novella The Princess and the Queen, the 2014 novella The Rogue Prince and the 2018 novel Fire & Blood. In the HBO television adaptation House of the Dragon, he is portrayed by French-English actor Fabien Frankel.

In both the books and the show, Cole is a highly skilled knight who ascends to become a member of King Viserys I Targaryen's Kingsguard, initially acting as Rhaenyra Targaryen's sworn protector. He later rises to become Lord Commander of the Kingsguard and Hand of the King to King Aegon II Targaryen, fighting for the green faction during the Targaryen civil war known as the Dance of the Dragons. Cole acts as one of the greens' primary military commanders, leading campaigns throughout the Crownlands and Riverlands to ensure Aegon's continued reign.

Since his introduction in the television series, Cole has proven to one of House of the Dragons most polarising characters. [ref: ‘House of the Dragon’ Just Took One of Its Best Characters Off the Board, GQ] Though Frankel's performance received consistent acclaim, critical reception to the character's writing has been more mixed, whilst fans regularly cite him as one of the show's most hated characters. [ref: House of the Dragon Season 3 Has Undermined One Major Book Character, GameRant] [ref: Fans Are Very Happy About House of the Dragon's "Unceremonious" Episode 6 Death, Esquire]

== In the books ==

=== Fire and Blood ===
Criston was born in 82 AC to the son of Lord Dondarrion's steward. In 104 AC, during the tournament at Maidenpool to celebrate King Viserys I Targaryen's ascension to the Iron Throne, he won Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen's favour after beating Prince Daemon Targaryen during the melee by knocking his sword Dark Sister out of his hands with a morningstar. He later wore the princess' favour during the joust, where he again bested Daemon, as well as Ser Erryk and Arryk Cargyll of the Kingsguard. A year later, he was sworn in as a member of the Kingsguard, replacing Ser Ryam Redwyne, and was named Rhaenyra's sworn shield. [ref: Fire and Blood, Bantam Books]

In 113 AC, following the betrothal of Rhaenyra to Ser Laenor Velaryon, Criston reportedly confessed his love to Rhaenyra, offering to run away to the Free Cities with her, but she refused. However, an alternate source suggested that it was Rhaenyra who attempted to seduce him but was refused. Regardless, Criston went from being Rhaenyra's strongest supporter to her most hated enemy, and was replaced by Ser Harwin "Breakbones" Strong as her sworn protector.

In 114 AC, Criston fought in the joust at Rhaenyra's wedding to Laenor, during which he injured Harwin and Ser Joffrey Lonmouth, the latter of whom died from his injuries six days later. Though many were angered at Criston's actions, Queen Alicent Hightower chose him to be her sworn protector.

Following the death of King Viserys in 129 AC, Queen Alicent assembled the small council - Criston among them - to discuss the succession. Criston objected to the ascension of Rhaenyra, Viserys' chosen heir, on account of her children with Laenor Velaryon being supposed bastards, instead supporting her brother Aegon as the correct choice for the crown. During the meeting, Lord Lyman Beesbury, the only councillor to support Rhaenyra, declared that this was treason, leading to Criston slitting his throat with a dagger or throwing him out of a window to his death (depending on which source is to be believed). Criston then helped imprison the remaining Black supporters at court and personally crown Aegon as king in the Dragonpit. [ref: Fire and Blood, Bantam Books] As a result of his support of Aegon II and his hand in crowning him, Criston would be forever remembered in Westeros' history as 'The Kingmaker'. [ref: The World of Ice & Fire: The Untold History of Westeros and the Game of Thrones, Bantam]

Following Aegon II's coronation, the Dance of the Dragons officially began when Rhaenyra refused to support her half-brother's ascension. Many lords remembered King Viserys' wish for Rhaenyra to succeed him, and threw their support behind her. As the blacks started to gain more allies, Aegon II became frustrated at the slow progress of his grandfather and Hand of the King, Ser Otto Hightower, resulting in him stripping Otto of his office and appointing Criston as his new hand. [ref: Fire and Blood, Bantam Books]

In response to the death of Aegon's eldest son, Prince Jaehaerys Targaryen, at the hands of Blood and Cheese, Criston ordered Ser Arryk Cargyll to sneak into Dragonstone disguised as his twin brother Ser Erryk, who was guarding Rhaenyra on Dragonstone. The scheme ended up failing when the twins came encountered and killed one another in single combat.

Criston then began a military campaign throughout the crownlands, subduing any houses loyal to Rhaenyra, including Houses Rosby, Stokeworth and Darklyn, forcing them to join his army. He then launched an attack on the castle of Rook's Rest, the seat of House Staunton, in an attempt to bait Rhaenyra into sending a dragonrider to meet him, wherein he would ambush them using King Aegon II Targaryen on Sunfyre and Prince Aemond Targaryen on Vhagar. Princess Rhaenys Targaryen then arrived on her dragon Meleys, leading to the Battle at Rook's Rest, in which Rhaenys and Meleys were killed and Aegon and Sunfyre were badly crippled. Aemond was later appointed Prince Regent following Aegon's injuries, but kept Criston as Hand.

Following Rook's Rest, Aemond and Criston plotted to retake Harrenhal from Prince Daemon, who had gathered an army of rivermen to the castle in support of Rhaenyra. Criston then marched his army of four thousand greens to Harrenhal, only to find it abandoned when they arrived, as Daemon had emptied the castle and flown away on Caraxes to aid Rhaenyra in the fall of King's Landing. Criston attempted to convince an enraged Aemond to retreat south to join with the host of greens led by Lord Ormund Hightower and Prince Daeron Targaryen, but Aemond refused, abandoning Criston's forces to wreck havoc upon the Riverlands with Vhagar as revenge for Daemon's trickery. [ref: Fire and Blood, Bantam Books]

Criston attempted to march his remaining forces south to meet the Hightower host, but was met by strong resistance from the Riverlords allied to the blacks, who used ambush tactics and guerrilla warfare to wear down his army. This culminated when Criston's surviving host was trapped by an army of thousands of blacks, led by Ser Garibald Grey, Ser Pate of Longleaf, and Lord Roderick Dustin. Criston offered to surrender if the blacks would spare the lives of his men, but was refused, and so challenged all three of his foes to a duel. He was then killed when Pate ordered Red Robb Rivers and his archers to shoot Criston with three arrows, saying "I'll have no songs about how brave you died, Kingmaker. There's tens o' thousands dead on your account". Following his death, Criston's remaining men were wiped out by the rivermen and Winter Wolves, a massacre later known as 'The Butcher's Ball'. Criston's head was then mounted on a spear and carried to the First Battle of Tumbleton.

=== A Song of Ice and Fire ===
In the main A Song of Ice and Fire novels, Criston is mentioned as having embodied the best and worst aspects of the Kingsguard. In A Feast for Crows, Ser Arys Oakhart recalls a rumour that Criston had been Rhaenyra's lover prior to joining the Kingsguard, whilst Jaime Lannister tells Loras Tyrell that not all Kingsguard can be so easily classified as heroic or villainous, naming Criston as an example. [ref: A Feast for Crows, HarperCollins]

== Television adaptation ==

=== Season 1 ===
Criston is first introduced as a competitor in the Heir's Tournament, where he defeats several high-born lords in the joust, including Prince Daemon Targaryen, whom he also bests in single combat. Following his victory, Cole asks for the favor of Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen, who throws her laurel wreath to him and wishes him luck. Six months later, Criston is named to the Kingsguard at Rhaenyra's insistence, as he is the only candidate who has real combat experience. He later travels to Dragonstone as part of a detachment led by Ser Otto Hightower, the Hand of the King, to force Prince Daemon into giving up his occupation of the castle and returning an egg that he stole from the Dragonpit.

Three years later, King Viserys organizes a royal hunt in honor of his son Aegon's second nameday. During the hunt, Rhaenyra flees into the woods on horseback, prompting Criston to chase after her. As they walk back to camp, Rhaenyra expresses frustration at her lack of control over her own life, but Cole reminds her that it was only by her grace that he became a Kingsguard and bestowed such a great honour on his house. He later saves Rhaenyra from a wild boar after they make camp during the night. Some time later, Criston accompanies Rhaenyra on a tour of Westeros to find potential suitors for her hand, though the tour is cut short after a fight breaks out between suitors during an audience at Storm's End. Later that night, Rhaenyra seduces Cole whilst he stands guard in her bedroom, despite some initial reluctance on his part.

After Rhaenyra is betrothed to Lord Corlys Velaryon's son Laenor, Criston, still guilt-ridden over breaking his Kingsguard vow, tries to convince Rhaenyra run away to Essos with him so that they can secretly marry. Rhaenyra refuses, insisting that she must do her duty, but suggests that she and Criston continue their affair in secret. Criston angrily accuses Rhaenyra of using him, distraught at the fact that he believes he has soiled his white cloak for nothing. Criston is then summoned by Queen Alicent Hightower, who questions him about a rumor she heard about Rhaenyra (in reference to her and Daemon), leading Criston to confess his sexual encounter with the princess. During the welcoming feast for Rhaenyra's wedding, Criston is approached by Ser Joffrey Lonmouth, who admits to being Laenor's lover and hints that he knows Criston's secret. This causes Criston to snap, and he furiously beats Joffrey to death in front of the other wedding guests, much to their horror and Laenor's dismay. Criston then walks out to the godswood and prepares to commit suicide, but is interrupted by Alicent.

Ten years later, Criston is now the master-at-arms in King's Landing and a staunch ally of Queen Alicent, encouraging Alicent's sons, Aegon and Aemond, to develop an intense hatred of Rhaenyra's sons Jacaerys and Lucerys. During a training exercise, Harwin Strong interevenes and chastises Cole for his harsh instruction, causing Criston to mock Harwin by alluding to the rumour that he is the father of Rhaenyra's sons. Harwin violently beats Cole in response to his mockery and is forced to leave King's Landing as a result. Following Laena Velaryon's funeral, Criston is among the Kingsguard who separate Rhaenyra and Daemon's children from Aemond following a fight in which Aemond loses his eye. Viserys later berates Cole for failing to prevent the fight. Alicent orders Criston to cut out one of Lucerys' eyes as revenge, but he refuses, reminding her that he is only sworn to her as a protector, not an enforcer. He is then held back by Daemon when Alicent tries to attack Lucerys with a knife.

Six years later, Criston is still master-at-arms and has trained Aemond into becoming a highly competent warrior. Following the death of King Viserys, Criston attends the subsequent Small Council meeting and kills Lord Lyman Beesbury by slamming his face down on the table in an attempt to make him sit down when he protests Prince Aegon's ascension. Criston is then ordered by Lord Commander Harrold Westerling to drop his sword and cloak, but Criston refuses and draws his sword, confirming his loyalty to the Green cause.

Later that day, Criston is secretly ordered by Alicent find Aegon, who has disappeared from the Red Keep, and bring him to her. Criston takes Aemond with him and the two begin their search on the Street of Silk, during which Aemond vents about how he should be king over Aegon. The two later intercept Arryk and Erryk Cargyll, who have found Aegon on Otto's orders, and a fight breaks out, resulting in Aemond and Cole gaining control of the wayward prince. Criston is then appointed Lord Commander of the Kingsguard by Alicent for his loyalty, and he crowns Aegon with the Conqueror's own crown in the Dragonpit, hailing him as the true heir to the Iron Throne. The coronation is interrupted when Rhaenys Targaryen bursts through the floor on her dragon Meleys, who then flies away to warn Rhaenyra of the Greens' betrayal.

=== Season 2 ===
Following Aegon's coronation, Criston has been plotting with Aemond to wage war against Rhaenyra in the Riverlands whilst also having an affair with Alicent. He is later caught having sex with Alicent by Queen Helaena Targaryen after she rushes into the room following the murder of her son Prince Jaehaerys. At the following Small Council meeting, Criston is interrogated by an enraged Aegon II about where he was at the time of Jaehaerys' murder, to which he lies and says he was asleep. Consumed by guilt, Criston commands Ser Arryk Cargyll to infiltrate Dragonstone and slay Rhaenyra as revenge for Jaehaerys' death. However, the plan fails and Arryk is killed as a result. Criston is then appointed Hand of the King by Aegon after he dismisses Ser Otto from the post, insisting that Cole will be his "steel fist" for the wars to come.

During his first council meeting as Hand, both Jasper Wylde and Alicent declare Criston's scheme to with Ser Arryk as foolhardy, but Cole defends himself, saying the Greens cannot afford to wait for war to come to them. Criston points out that controlling Harrenhal is essential to the war effort, proposing that he lead a small force to begin gradually subduing the crownlands houses loyal to Rhaenyra and join them to his cause. Just before leaving for his march, Alicent tells Criston that her elder brother Gwayne Hightower will be joining him, who backhandedly insults Cole for his Dornish heritage and for replacing Otto as Hand. Alicent then offers to pray for Criston's safety and offers her favour in the form of a handkerchief at his request. Later, whilst out in the Crownlands, Criston saves Gwayne and a party of Hightower knights after they are spotted by Baela Targaryen and her dragon Moondancer whilst leaving for a nearby tavern.

Criston, Gwayne and their army continue their campaign throughout the Crownlands, recruiting houses Rosby and Stokeworth to the Green cause and beheading Lord Gunthor Darklyn after he refuses their terms of surrender. Instead of marching on Harrenhal, Cole then turns the army east towards Rook's Rest and insists upon attacking the castle in broad daylight, much to Gwayne's confusion. The army then attacks the castle, which is halted when Princess Rhaenys Targaryen arrives on Meleys and begins incinerating the Green forces. However, this is all revealed to be part of Criston's plan, who launches signal arrows to alert Aemond, who is lying in wait to ambush Rhaenyra's dragonriders with Vhagar. During the battle, Aegon unexpectedly arrives on Sunfyre, which Cole uses to boost his men's morale into continuing the attack as the dragons duel. Aemond then joins the fight on Vhagar and blasts Aegon and Sunfyre out of the sky, causing them to free-fall and crash into the forest. A horrifed Crison rides to the impact site but is knocked out en route when Vhagar violently crashes into the battlefield, reawakening to find that Rhaenys and Meleys are dead and that his army has been completely decimated by dragonfire. He then makes his way towards Aegon's crash site, finding the king's motionless body with a severly injured Sunfyre curled around him.

Upon returning to King's Landing, Criston parades Meleys's severed head through the city but is baffled at the muted reaction of the smallfolk, who consider the death of a dragon to be a bad omen. Aegon revealed to be alive but severly injured and comatose; Criston does not reveal to Alicent that Aemond had a hand in his brother's injuries. At the subsequent small council meeting, Alicent nominates herself as regent, but the council - including a shell-shocked Criston - overrule her and instead elect Aemond. Alicent furiously confronts Criston afterwards and declares him disloyal.

At a later Small Council meeting, Criston protests when Aemond orders him to march on Harrenhal against Daemon, as their losses at Rook's Rest mean they do not have the numbers to defeat him, but is overruled. He then shares a glance with Alicent before leaving the city with Gwayne and his army. On the march to Harrenhal, Gwayne sees Criston with Alicent's handkerchief, accusing him of sleeping with his sister and breaking his Kingsguard vows as a result. However, Criston, having been mentally destroyed following the carnage at Rook's Rest, expresses regret over his past choices and tells Gwayne that he believes they "march toward their annihilation" at the hands of Rhaenyra's dragons, much to Gwayne's horror.

=== Season 3 ===
During their march to Harrenhal, Gwayne confronts Criston about a soldier who he caught sexually assualting a local village girl, insisting that he be punished. However, Cole refuses to directly punish the man himself, nihilistically declaring that war brings out the worst in men and that "doom and ruin" awaits them regardless. He later sees Aemond approaching Harrenhal on Vhagar, spurring his men to march on.

The army reaches Harrenhal days later, finding it abandoned save for Alys Rivers, who insists that Aemond and Vhagar have fled and revealing that Rhaenyra has taken King's Landing from the greens. Gwayne pleads Cole to make for Tumbleton and join with Lord Ormund Hightower's forces, but Cole refuses, instead deciding to wage guerilla warfare against the Riverlords and Winter Wolves in a final stand.

Cole's forces successfully take out multiple Riverland camps, but their progress is stalled by caltrops left by Roderick Dustin and Oscar Tully. Having been forced to put down their horses, Cole leads his remaining soldiers on foot, only to find that the Riverlords have already crossed the river and burned the bridges behind them to prevent Cole from pursuing them. Despondent at their futile progress, Gwayne offers Cole to serve under the Hightowers, but Criston, having grown tired of serving highborn lords, vows to make a final stand against the blacks in the hope that he will die a glorious death. He then gives a speech to his tired men as Gwayne abandons the group to head for Tumbleton.

Cole's dwindling army continues to march until they find a seemingly abandoned Tully camp, which is revealed to be a trap laid by the Riverlords, who ambush them. They fight off their attackers, only to be surrounded on all sides by Oscar, Roderick, the Riverland army and the Winter Wolves, who demand Criston face justice for his treachery against the crown. Cole asks if they will spare his men if he surrenders but Oscar refuses, at which point Cole demands single combat against Oscar and Roderick, wrapping Alicent's handkerchief around his sword hilt as he prepares to make his final stand. This is short lived, however, as Criston is unceremoniously shot three times by Alysanne Blackwood in the chest, breast and face, killing him. As his lifeless body slumps to the ground, still clutching the handkerchief, the Black army rushes Cole's remaining men from all sides and wipes them out.

Following his death, Cole's head is mounted on a spear and carried by Roderick to the First Battle of Tumbleton. When asked by Daemon how Cole died, Roderick replies, "Badly".

== Reception ==
Cole is widely regarded as one of the most divisive characters in House of the Dragon. Some have praised the character's gradual descent into nihilism as complex and multi-faceted, such as William Goodman of GQ, who argued his obsession with absolution and transformation into a man who "found freedom in nihilism" resulted in an "utterly compelling" character arc. Domink Bošnjak from Game Rant similarly highlighted how Cole's "growing disillusionment with the war, and visible exhaustion have made him more human than he appears in a book structured as a collection of unreliable histories", though he criticised the TV series for downplaying the character's martial prowess in comparison to the novel.

However, some have expressed frustration at the character's vindictive and hypocritical nature, particularly towards Rhaenyra, which was frequently compared to that of a modern-day incel. [ref: Somehow, 'House of The Dragon' Found a Way To Make Ser Criston Cole Look Even Worse, The Mary Sue] Saloni Gajjar from A.V. Club referred to Cole as a "certified Westerosi incel", arguing that the character's behaviour had led to his death being regarded as "the moment every House Of The Dragon viewer has been waiting and loudly wishing for". [ref: House Of The Dragon burst its own bubble, AV Club] Similarly, Jessica Toomer of Collider wrote that Cole seemed "tailor-made for Tumblr fandom", only to reveal himself to be a "bitter, bloodthirsty incel" whose actions had caused fans to launch "memes and Reddit threads and summoning circles dedicated to his on-screen demise". [ref: Before HBO's 'Task,' This Star Played the Most Hated Man in Westeros in 'House of the Dragon', Collider] Goodman acknowledged the contradictory nature of the character, noting that he was "smug, pious, hypocritical, or even incel-adjacent", but praised Frankel's performance for bringing "so much depth to the character.

Critics were also divided on Cole's death scene in the episode 'Faceless Men', some feeling that it was far too anticlimactic for such a hated character. Gajjar argued that despite his death being highly anticipated by fans, the third season's uneven pacing caused the scene to feel "watered-down" in comparison to the deaths of other hated Game of Thrones characters such as Joffrey Baratheon, Ramsay Bolton and Littlefinger. Josh Rosenberg from Esquire argued that the episode glossed over the impact of Cole's death on the other characters, stating that the show "doesn't even bother to have anyone react to his departure", opining that the sequence would have been better placed at the end of episode five rather than the start of episode six. [ref: ‘House of the Dragon’ Season 3, Episode 6’s Major Death Deserved More, Esquire] Conversely, David Crow from Den of Geek argued that the character's "muted, unsung end" was a fitting end for Cole, as his desire for "an honour and chivalric destiny he never earned or deserved" went ultimately unfulfilled. [ref: House of the Dragon Season 3 Episode 6 Review: Butcher’s Work, Den of Geek]

Despite the character's mixed reception, Frankel was consistently praised for his performance, particularly during the third season. Commending Frankel's performance during Cole's death, Crow said that "the abject surprise of a final, bitter disappointment [...] in Frankel’s eyes is enough to almost make me pity this pathetic man". TVLine named Frankel "Performer of the Week" for his performance in the episode 'Unbowed and Unbent', writing, "Would we want to follow Ser Criston Cole into battle, especially after the events of this week's "House of the Dragon"? Hell no — the knight seems to have lost his damn mind. But were we captivated by Fabien Frankel's performance as his character made clear his fatalistic intentions? Absolutely." [ref: MSN, www.msn.com]

== References ==

data.title: Abdulla Avloniy Memorial Museum
data.text:
The Abdulla Avloniy Memorial Museum (; also rendered Abdulla Avloni Memorial Museum) is a memorial museum in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, dedicated to the life and work of the Jadid educator, writer and public figure Abdulla Avloniy (1878–1934). It is housed in the building of the Abdulla Avloni National Institute of Pedagogical Excellence. [ref: Muzey haqida, Abdulla Avloniy Memorial Museum]

== History ==
The museum was established in 1968 in the house where Avloniy had lived with his family from 1910 to 1934. On the initiative of the Uzbekistan Society of Book Lovers, it was officially opened as the Avloniy House Museum in December 1988, on the 110th anniversary of his birth. [ref: Toshkent: ensiklopediya, O‘zbekiston milliy ensiklopediyasi]

In 1993 the museum was moved to the building of the Abdulla Avloniy Central Institute for the Retraining and Advanced Training of Public Education Staff, the predecessor of the present institute, and was reopened there on 26 December 1993 as the Avloniy Memorial Museum. According to the 2009 encyclopedia Toshkent, the museum then held 682 items and consisted of a memorial section, with Avloniy's household and personal belongings and his books in Uzbek and Russian, and a literary section with photographs, documents, books and journals relating to his educational, journalistic, theatrical, literary and public activities.

After the institute's buildings were renovated and new ones were built, a new exhibition was created in 2024 to mark the 90th anniversary of the institute, which was founded in 1934. [ref: Activities of the National Institute of Pedagogical Excellence acquire new quality and content, President of the Republic of Uzbekistan] [ref: New opportunities for teachers: visit to the renovated building of the A. Avloni Institute, Xalqtaliminfo.uz] On 30 September 2024 the President of Uzbekistan, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, visited the institute and toured the museum and its library. [ref: Prezident Abdulla Avloniy nomidagi pedagogika institutiga tashrif buyurdi, Anhor.uz]

== Exhibition ==
According to the museum, about 400 items are on display. The exhibition presents the Jadids' attention to education, the education system founded by Avloniy, textbooks and stage works of the period, and the stages in the development of general education; portraits of Jadid enlighteners have been recreated with the help of artificial intelligence.

The museum's holdings include books from Avloniy's personal library; printed and manuscript works of the 18th and 19th centuries, among them works by Alisher Navoi, Bedil and Shams Tabrizi; newspapers and journals published in Turkestan, Turkey and Azerbaijan in the early 20th century; and early textbooks written for the Jadid new-method schools. Among the exhibits is a 1913 edition of Padarkush, a play by Mahmud Khoja Behbudiy. [ref: «Padarkush» — milliy dramaturgiyaning tamal toshi, Abdulla Avloniy Memorial Museum]

data.title: Ernst Schellenberg
data.text:
Ernst August Rudolf Schellenberg (20 February 1907 – 6 June 1984) was a German economist, social insurance administrator and politician of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). After the Second World War he headed the unified social insurance institution for Berlin, the Versicherungsanstalt Berlin (VAB). He was a member of the Bundestag for Berlin from 1952 to 1976 and chaired its committee on social policy from 1957 to 1976.

He was the SPD's spokesman on pensions in the debate on the 1957 pension reform and chaired the committee during the social legislation of the grand coalition and the first social–liberal coalition.

== Early life and education ==

Schellenberg was born in Berlin, the eldest of three children of Paul Schellenberg, a legal adviser, and his wife Anna, who ran a flower shop in Schöneberg. He attended the Paulsen-Realgymnasium in Steglitz from 1913 to 1922. After his parents divorced, his mother could not pay for further schooling, and he left with an intermediate certificate.

At fifteen he began an apprenticeship in social insurance at the Schmiede-Berufsgenossenschaft, the accident insurance association for the metalworking trades in Berlin. He then worked as a welfare worker and received state recognition as a Wohlfahrtspfleger in 1930.

In the mid-1920s he joined the Zentralverband der Angestellten, a union of salaried employees, and led its working group on social policy. In the last years of the Weimar Republic he did voluntary work for Rote Hilfe and was a sympathiser of the Communist Party of Germany.

From 1927 to 1929 he attended the social policy seminar of the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik. He then attended economics lectures at the University of Berlin as a guest student, and in 1931 he was admitted to regular study without the Abitur after passing a special examination. He also studied for a time in Heidelberg. In early 1933 he received a doctorate (Dr. rer. pol.) from the University of Berlin under Emil Lederer, with a dissertation on the voluntary labour service, Der freiwillige Arbeitsdienst auf Grund der bisherigen Erfahrungen.

== Nazi period ==

After the Nazis came to power, Schellenberg was briefly unemployed. In September 1933 he became a statistician with Allianz in Stuttgart. His attempt to obtain the habilitation at the University of Tübingen failed in 1936; the university cited his wife's Jewish family background and the Nuremberg Laws.

In 1938 he moved to Berlin as head of the calculation department of the national association of private insurers. From 1940 he also taught at the Hochschulinstitut für Versicherungswissenschaft of the University of Berlin, and after 1942 he acted for a time as deputy to its director, Theodor Süss. The education ministry refused on political grounds to extend his teaching. In 1944 he was released from military service after a few months as a recruit, having been found unfit.

== Social insurance in post-war Berlin ==

In May 1945 Ottomar Geschke, head of the social welfare department of Berlin's new Magistrat, appointed Schellenberg as his deputy. On 18 June 1945 Schellenberg proposed to the Magistrat that the city's fragmented insurance funds be replaced by a single institution. Ferdinand Sauerbruch, the councillor responsible for health, supported the proposal, and the Magistrat adopted it.

The Versicherungsanstalt Berlin began operating on 1 July 1945 under Schellenberg's direction. It combined health, pension and accident insurance. All employed persons were compulsorily insured, and a single contribution of 20 per cent of earnings was shared equally by employers and employees. Pension payments, suspended at the capitulation, resumed in August 1945 and were initially limited to 35 Reichsmarks a month. In January 1947 the Soviet Military Administration extended the Berlin model to the provinces of the Soviet occupation zone.

Schellenberg left the Magistrat in 1946. From the winter semester of 1946/47 he lectured on social insurance and social policy at the University of Berlin, later the Humboldt University, and in 1947 he was appointed extraordinary professor and director of its Institute for Social Policy and Insurance.

The SED-dominated Magistrat planned to change how the VAB's self-governing bodies were appointed. In February 1949 Schellenberg moved the VAB's headquarters from Mitte to Wilmersdorf in the western sector, and the institution split into eastern and western bodies. In May 1949 the Humboldt University announced that he was no longer a member of its teaching staff.

After West Berlin adopted federal legislation, the unified insurance was divided into separate branches in the early 1950s. Schellenberg headed the western institution's successor, the Krankenversicherungsanstalt Berlin, and became the first director of the AOK Berlin, the city's general local health insurance fund. He held these posts until 1958.

== Political career ==

Schellenberg joined the SPD in 1948.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

In February 1952 Otto Suhr resigned his Bundestag seat, and the Abgeordnetenhaus of Berlin elected Schellenberg as his successor. He represented Berlin in the Bundestag until 1976.

From 1952 he worked with Ludwig Preller and Walter Auerbach on the SPD's Sozialplan für Deutschland, a programme for reorganising the social security system. He held constituency surgeries in Spandau and Kreuzberg.

=== Pension reform of 1957 ===

In January 1956 he gave the main address on the SPD's position on social reform at a party congress in Cologne. On 18 April 1956 he introduced the SPD's bill on pension reform; Labour Minister Anton Storch presented the government's outline the following day. The SPD bill proposed a pension of 75 per cent of previous gross earnings and a single pension law for manual workers and salaried employees.

The positions of the government and the opposition converged during the committee stage and through amendments in the plenary. The final debate in January 1957 was called the "Rentenschlacht" (pension battle) in the press. Schellenberg spoke 57 times during the readings and made 64 interjections; his most frequent opponent was Margot Kalinke of the German Party.

The Bundestag passed the reform on 21 January 1957 with the votes of the governing parties and the SPD, against those of the FDP. The reform linked pensions to wage growth and moved the system to pay-as-you-go financing; pensions rose by about 60 per cent on average. In the third reading Schellenberg claimed the idea of the wage-indexed pension for the SPD.

=== Chair of the Committee on Social Policy ===

After the 1957 federal election Schellenberg became chairman of the Bundestag committee on social policy, renamed the Committee on Labour and Social Affairs in 1969. He held the chair until 1976.

In 1955 he was elected to the executive of the SPD parliamentary group. He led its working group on social policy from 1957 to 1972, was a member of the SPD party executive from 1960 to 1973, and also served as a deputy chairman of the parliamentary group.

In opposition he criticised the policies of Labour Minister Theodor Blank. In March 1961 he moved, on behalf of the SPD group, that the minister's salary be withheld until the next election; the motion was defeated. He also opposed Blank's health insurance reform bill of 1960.

In the mid-1960s he drew up a plan for a Volksversicherung (people's insurance), which proposed compulsory pension insurance for all employees and the self-employed, a flexible retirement age and a benefit formula based on points. After he presented a resolution on it to the 1964 party conference, it became SPD policy. He was a member of the SPD's shadow team in the 1965 and 1969 election campaigns.

During the grand coalition of 1966–1969 he supported the government's social policy. From 1955 he had called for manual workers to receive continued pay from their employers during sickness on the same terms as salaried staff; this was enacted in 1969.

When the SPD and FDP formed a government in 1969, Willy Brandt appointed the trade union leader Walter Arendt as labour minister. Schellenberg declined an offer from Herbert Wehner of the post of parliamentary state secretary.

As committee chairman he dealt with the Works Constitution Act of 1971, in which he opposed the special protection for enterprises with political, religious or press aims but was outvoted within his parliamentary group. He also dealt with the pension reform of 1972, which allowed insured persons with at least 35 years of contributions to draw a pension from the age of 63 and opened statutory pension insurance to the self-employed and to housewives, and with the Occupational Safety Act of 1973.

In the negotiations on codetermination from 1974 he called for full parity between employee and shareholder representatives on supervisory boards. Wehner instead sought a compromise with the FDP.

=== Withdrawal from politics ===

After the 1972 election the chair of the SPD group's working group on social policy passed to Eugen Glombig, and in 1973 Schellenberg did not stand again for the party executive. He was in poor health in 1974 and 1975 and did not stand for re-election in 1976. His last speech in the Bundestag, on 8 April 1976, concerned the 19th Pension Adjustment Act. He chaired the committee for the last time on 2 June 1976; Adolf Müller (Remscheid) of the CDU chaired it for the rest of the term. During Schellenberg's chairmanship the committee dealt with 262 bills in 565 sittings.

== Personal life ==

In the late 1920s Schellenberg met the law student Anneliese Meyer, whose father, a senior civil servant who had converted from Judaism to Christianity, lost his post under the Nazis. She was barred from legal training under the racial laws and later completed a doctorate in Switzerland. The couple had a daughter, Cora-Beate (born 1938), and a son, Dierk (born 1939). They separated during the war and divorced after it. In 1947 Schellenberg married Annemarie, a lawyer and daughter of Karl Geiler, the first post-war Minister-President of Hesse. She was an SPD member of the Berlin House of Representatives from 1963 to 1967.

After leaving parliament Schellenberg returned to Berlin, where he died of pneumonia on 6 June 1984.

== Honours ==

* 1965: Grand Cross of Merit with Star of the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany
* 1972: Grand Cross of Merit with Star and Sash
* 1976: Grand Cross

data.title: Erwin Horn
data.text:
Erwin Horn (2 May 1929 – 13 May 2006) was a German teacher and politician of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). He was a member of the Bundestag from 1969 to 1998, representing the Gießen constituency in Hesse by direct mandate for most of that period. He was deputy chairman of the Bundestag's Defence Committee from 1980 to 1983.

== Early life and education ==

Horn was born in Annerod, a village near Gießen that is now part of Fernwald. He was a Protestant. After attending a Volksschule and an Aufbauschule, he passed his Abitur in 1948. From 1949 to 1955 he studied history, German, English, philosophy and politics, and took the state examination for teachers in 1955.

== Teaching career ==

Horn worked as a Studienrat from 1955 to 1962. From 1962 to 1966 he was Fachleiter (subject supervisor) for social studies at the teacher training seminar (Studienseminar) in Gießen. From 1966 to 1969 he was headmaster (Oberstudiendirektor) of the Gymnasium in Nidda.

== Political career ==

=== Local politics ===

Horn chaired the SPD sub-district (Unterbezirk) of Gießen from 1962 to 1988. He was a member of the district council (Kreistag) from 1960 to 1976.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

Horn was elected to the Bundestag in the 1969 federal election. He won the Gießen constituency in each election from 1969 to 1994 except 1983, when he entered parliament through the SPD's Hesse state list. He did not stand in the 1998 election and left the Bundestag at the end of the 13th legislative term.

He was deputy chairman of the Defence Committee from 1980 to 1983 and the SPD's Obmann (lead member) on the committee from 1983 to 1990. From 1977 to 1988 he was a member of the executive board of the SPD parliamentary group. During the 13th legislative term he was a deputy member of the Foreign Affairs Committee and, from 1997, a deputy member of the Defence Committee.

In the Bundestag debate of 21–22 November 1983 on the deployment of American intermediate-range missiles under the NATO Double-Track Decision, Horn spoke for the SPD. He said the decision had become a source of dispute within the alliance and a burden on domestic politics in the countries where the missiles were to be stationed. He said the SPD had originally regarded the decision as a means of bringing the superpowers to negotiations on disarmament, and that the deployment would not change the global strategic balance. The Bundestag approved the deployment with the votes of the CDU/CSU and FDP.

In 1990, during the debate on the equipment of the former East German National People's Army, Horn proposed that the Bundeswehr take over all of its MiG-29 fighter aircraft and that Germany withdraw from the Jäger 90 project. He said that scrapping usable weapons while placing new arms contracts could not be justified given the level of public debt.

=== International assemblies ===

Horn was a member of the North Atlantic Assembly. He chaired its Military Committee from 1981 to 1985 and its socialist group from 1985 to 1988. He was part of the German delegation to the assembly's spring session in Paris in May 1990. He was a substitute member of the German delegation to the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe from 1981 to 1984 and from 1995 to 1999, and a deputy member of the Assembly of the Western European Union.

== Conviction ==

In 1990 a Schöffengericht (lay-judge court) in Cologne fined Horn 24,000 DM for false unsworn testimony and attempted obstruction of prosecution. The court found that he had made false statements in a traffic case against a master mason from Bornheim. Horn had been a passenger in the man's car in April 1988 when it damaged another vehicle while leaving a parking space in central Cologne and drove away. The driver was convicted of leaving the scene of an accident.

== Death ==

Horn died on 13 May 2006.

== Honours ==

* 1983: Cross of Merit, 1st Class (Verdienstkreuz 1. Klasse) of the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany
* 1988: Grand Cross of Merit (Großes Verdienstkreuz) of the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany

data.title: Mountaineer Mall
data.text:
The Mountaineer Mall and Professional Plaza is a shopping mall and business park located in Morgantown, West Virginia. It is the first of two malls built in Morgantown; the other being the Morgantown Mall. Major tenants are Senior Monongalians, Spark! Imagination and Science Center, and Osher Lifelong Learning Institutes. [ref: Mountaineer Mall, more than just stores, [[The Dominion Post (Morgantown)]
== History ==

=== 1975–1999: Early history, expansion, and decline ===
Mountaineer Mall was developed by First Union Management [ref: Shopping center takes new direction, Morgantown Dominion Post] on the south side of Morgantown, off of U.S. Route 119 and on a raised bluff near the Monongahela River. The mall started construction in 1973 [ref: Shop center name: 'Mountaineer Mall', Sunday Dominion-Post] and it partially-opened with 19 stores on August 5, 1975. [ref: 30,000 attend first day at mall, Morgantown Dominion Post] 32 stores were open by January the next year. [ref: Progress, [[The Dominion Post (Morgantown)] Anchors were Murphy's Mart (later Ames), JCPenney, and Montgomery Ward. [ref: Mountaineer Mall; Morgantown, West Virginia, labelscar.com] [ref: Adventures in West Virginia: day trips & longer travels, Huntington, W. Va.: Aegina Press] It was the first mall to open in the Morgantown metropolitan area and despite its compact size, was a big success. In 1987, the mall was expanded, which would include the construction of a freestanding Giant Eagle and a new anchor store, Stone & Thomas, [ref: Realty Stock Review Vol. XVIII, No. 5, Audit Investment Research, Inc. (New York)] which opened in November. [ref: Mrs. Hoffman Promotes Upcoming State Pageant, [[Cumberland Times-News]

In the 1990s, many tenants began leave the after the early 1990s recession and the opening of the newer Morgantown Mall. JCPenney followed suit, as they needed more space. [ref: Discount stores anchor Mountaineer Mall's comeback, The State Journal] The mall then transitioned to attract discount businesses. [ref: Mountaineer Mall finds identity with eclectic tenants, WV News] JCPenney was replaced by U.S. Factory Outlets in 1993, which became Gabriel Brothers in 1996. A Walmart opened in the former Ames space in January 1994. [ref: Mall bounced back from troubled times, Morgantown Dominion Post] Stone & Thomas became Elder-Beerman in 1998. Montgomery Ward closed in 1999.

=== 2000–present: Further decline and transition into business ===
TeleTech opened in 2000, in part of the former Montgomery Ward space. The rest was taken up by General Glass, which opened in February 2005. In 2002, Spark! opened as the Children's Discovery Museum of West Virginia. In April 2005, the International Council of Shopping Centers and the Environmental Protection Agency awarded the Mountaineer Mall with "Best Community Partnership (Large Shopping Center)" for its recycling program. [ref: ICSC and EPA Announce Winners of America’s Marketplace Recycles! Awards Program, icsc.org] Walmart closed in October 2006, when two new Supercenters opened near Morgantown. [ref: Wal-Mart selling all but walls, Morgantown Dominion Post] In 2007, Gabriel Brothers opened their flagship store in Morgantown Commons near Morgantown Mall, keeping the Mountaineer Mall location open but with a "smaller selection". [ref: Gabriel Brothers opens flagship store in Morgantown Commons, Morgantown Dominion Post] [ref: Mountaineer mall: Life after wal-mart, The State Journal] This would, however, close the next year. Elder-Beerman closed in January 2008 after its lease expiry, having become redundant as the chain had a store at Morgantown Mall. [ref: Elder-Beerman to close its doors in January, Morgantown Dominion Post] Rex Appliances, one of the last remaining large stores, closed in 2009 when the entire chain shut down.

In February 2010, Mylan Pharmaceuticals announced that it would renovate the former Walmart space into offices for its IT and legal departments. [ref: Mylan moving IT, legal staff to former Walmart, Morgantown Dominion Post] The next year, Mylan started renovating the former Gabriel Brothers to expand its offices. [ref: Mylan to lease at mall, Morgantown Dominion Post]

On February 15, 2020, Eloquence Antiques & Artisans moved and reopened in Mountaineer Mall. [ref: Eloquence Antiques & Artisans reopens in the Mountaineer Mall, The Dominion Post] The store expanded in 2026. [ref: Vintage, antique lovers take over Mountaineer Mall, [[WBOY-TV] In early August 2024, the United States Army Reserve held decontamination training drills at the mall. [ref: Mass casualty exercise held at Mountaineer Mall, WBOY] As of 2026, Mylan and TeleTech have vacated the site. [ref: ]

== Description ==
The Mountaineer Mall (as of 1975) is primary made up of rusted-brick wall with tiled flooring and carpets, facing its 65 stores; benches, trees, and planters laid throughout the walkways. The singular corridor had Montgomery Ward to the east, JCPenney in the center, and Murphy’s Mart to the west. The 80s addition extruded from the central area and had fake skylights and brass fixtures. The addition was built on a slight incline, so a ramp and accompanied stairs were needed to connect the two.

== Incidents ==
* On November 29, 2011, a woman sued GP-Mountaineer LLC after claiming that she was injured on the property due to "dangerous conditions". [ref: Morgantown woman sues for injuries at Mountaineer Mall, Legal Newsline]

data.title: Mila's Keeper
data.text:
----

Mila's Keeper is an American designer and manufacturer of eco-friendly, plastic-free breastfeeding and breast milk storage products. Founded by global public health professional Lara Vu, MPH, the company is recognized as a Certified B Corporation and is a certified women- and minority-owned business based in Long Beach, California. Its flagship product, the MilKeeper portable breast milk cooler, was named one of TIME's Best Inventions of 2024. [ref: Lara Vu, LinkedIn] [ref: Founder's Story, Mila's Keeper] [ref: Mila's Keeper – Certified B Corporation, B Lab Global] [ref: National WIC Association Page, Mila's Keeper] [ref: Motherhood Advocates Join Forces to Empower Breastfeeding Women, Mila's Keeper]

== History ==
The company was conceived by Lara Vu, a certified lactation educator and former UNICEF global health professional. [ref: How Mila's Keeper Was Born From a Failed UNICEF Project, Mila's Keeper] [ref: YSPH Alumna Launched Company to Empower Breastfeeding Mothers, Yale School of Public Health] While leading a UNICEF initiative in Vietnam to establish corporate lactation spaces for female factory worker populations, Vu observed that the lack of convenient cold storage options frequently resulted in a premature cessation of breastfeeding. Drawing from her background in public health and her personal experiences as a traveling, breastfeeding mother, Vu founded Mila's Keeper to engineer modern, portable temperature-controlled solutions for pumping parents. [ref: Fabulous People: Lara Vu, Fabulous California] The company launched its products commercially during World Breastfeeding Week in August 2022.

== Products and design ==
Mila's Keeper specializes in plastic-free, multi-use components designed to transition with a child's developmental phases, later serving as food storage or water bottles.

* The MilKeeper: The brand's signature product is an insulated, vacuum-sealed double-walled steel flask designed to fit wide- and standard-neck baby bottles, breast milk bags, or direct liquid. Paired with a custom high-density polyethylene cold pack, it maintains safe milk storage temperatures for up to 20 hours without melting ice. [ref: Mila's Keeper Portable Insulated Breast Milk Cooler, Amazon] [ref: Mila's Keeper MilKeeper, TIME] [ref: Press, Mila's Keeper]
* 3-in-1 storage bottles: The company manufactures medical-grade glass storage bottles and 100% silicone pumping/feeding bottles designed to connect directly with major breast pump brands, minimizing milk transfer and plastic degradation risk. [ref: Mila's Keeper Silicone Bottles, Genuine Lactation] [ref: Instagram post, Instagram] [ref: Silicone Breast Milk Storage, Mila's Keeper]

== Reception ==
The MilKeeper has been included in gift and registry roundups by several publications, including Forbes, [ref: The Best Baby Gifts, From Toys To Travel Cribs, Forbes] [ref: Mother's Day Gift Guide: The Best Travel Gear For New Moms, Forbes] Harper's Bazaar, [ref: The Best Gifts for Moms, Harper's Bazaar] New York magazine's The Strategist, [ref: The Strategist Baby Registry Hall of Fame, New York Magazine] [ref: The Best Baby Registry List, According to Experts, New York Magazine] Motherly, [ref: 12 Best Breastmilk Coolers That Will Keep Your Breastmilk Fresh and Cold for Hours, Motherly] HGTV, [ref: First Mother's Day Gift Ideas, HGTV] and The Cut. [ref: The Best Mother's Day Gifts for New Moms, The Cut] The product has also appeared in registry and shopping guides published by Babylist. [ref: What to Pack in Your Breast Pump Bag, Babylist] [ref: How to Store Breast Milk, Babylist]

== Corporate responsibility and awards ==
In January 2025, Mila's Keeper achieved Certified B Corporation status via B Lab, meeting verified standards of social and environmental performance. The business operates as a California benefit company, dedicating a minimum of 2% of its profits to female empowerment and environmental non-profits, including membership in 1% for the Planet. The company also actively partners with the National WIC Association to provide accessible cold-storage solutions to low-income postpartum communities.

* 2024: Named to TIME's Best Inventions list under the parenting category.
* 2026: Awarded Best Breastfeeding Accessory by Parents magazine. [ref: Mila's Keeper, Mila's Keeper]
* 2026: Awarded the U.S. Small Business Administration Los Angeles District's Manufacturer of the Year Award. [ref: Small Business Week celebration honoring Lara Vu, MPH, LinkedIn]

== References ==

data.title: Helene Verin
data.text:
----

Helene Verin is an American designer, author, and curator. Across a career documented in The New York Times from 1988 onward she has designed shoes, wallpaper, furniture, rugs, tiles and interiors; the paper has described her variously as "a designer of shoes and home furnishings", "a designer of furniture, wallpaper, rugs and shoes", and "a product and interior designer". [ref: Like a Fly On the Wall, The New York Times] [ref: CURRENTS; Making Furniture 'Seem Like Clouds', The New York Times] [ref: CURRENTS: INNOVATIONS; Skateboards That Step, The New York Times] She later taught at the Fashion Institute of Technology and wrote Beth Levine Shoes (2009), a monograph on the American shoe designer Beth Levine, whose work she presented in three museum exhibitions. [ref: Beth Levine: The First Lady of Shoes, Face to Face]

== Early life and education ==
Verin grew up in Highland Park, Illinois, the daughter of Bernard D. Verin, a former president of Chicago Aligraphy Inc. She graduated from the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Before entering design she worked as assistant director of special projects at KTCA-TV in Minneapolis and, by 1979, as a management consultant for arts organizations. [ref: Helene Verin Wed in Illinois To Rodney Ripps, an Artist, The New York Times]

== Design career ==

=== Shoes ===
The New York Times reported in 1992 that Verin had designed shoes for Bernardo and Keds. [ref: Sometimes the Art on the Wall Happens to Be the Wallpaper, The New York Times] In later coverage the paper described her as a shoe and accessories designer, a housewares and shoe designer, and a designer of "shoes, purses, pillows, floor tiles, rugs and wallpaper". [ref: CURRENTS; Where the Accessories Are for Deaccessioning, The New York Times] [ref: Bringing the Party to Sotheby's, The New York Times] [ref: Habitats/East 22nd Street; They're Living Together, But Four Floors Apart, The New York Times]

=== Massachusetts Museum of Culture and Accessories ===
In May 1988 Verin opened the Massachusetts Museum of Culture and Accessories, a 200-square-foot shop in Lenox, Massachusetts, selling avant-garde housewares and fashion accessories by twenty artists. She said the name was partly a joke at the expense of the much larger Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, then being developed in North Adams. Verin displayed the stock as art, with lamps and glass on pedestals and jewelry hung in gilded frames: she "wanted to showcase the designs in a museum setting where they wouldn't get lost, as they do when they are sold in a department store." The shop also carried her own work, including a rug designed to resemble a wood floor.

=== Wallpaper ===
Verin designed and hand-printed wallpaper in Lenox under the company name Fern I. Tchur. Her pattern Flypaper, introduced at the International Contemporary Furniture Fair in Manhattan in 1991, scattered gold-rendered flies, butterflies, ladybugs and beetles at wide intervals against plain grounds; she consulted entomology books for the renderings. A companion pattern, Tape Measure, staggered six measuring tapes so the repeat appeared random. "Very few wallpapers are hip," she told the Times. "Most are those all-over rose patterns with vines, and they don't appeal to me."

A 1992 Times survey of artist-designed wallpaper discussed her work alongside that of Roy Lichtenstein, Gerhard Richter and Donald Judd, and described a second Verin design, Truth, printed with the words serenity, liberty, justice, sublime, honesty, artistry and strength. "Covering the walls is such an ancient art," she said. "Since the caves of Lascaux, people have been decorating their walls." The papers were sold through the John Boone showroom in Manhattan. Her hand-printed wallpaper was covered again in The New York Times Magazine in 1996. [ref: Back in Prints, The New York Times Magazine]

In 1991 Verin and the decorative painter Benjamin Pasteur created a sitting room called "Rome at Dusk" for a designer show house at Edith Wharton's home The Mount, covering the ceiling in her hand-painted royal blue paper with gilt stars. [ref: Producing Illusions in an Edith Wharton Show House, The New York Times]

=== Furniture and interiors ===
After buying a small studio apartment in Greenwich Village in 1993, Verin designed a line of lightweight solid maple furniture — two desks, two consoles, a coffee table and chairs — that could be recombined for different uses, with tapered ends and edges carved to follow the grain. She cited Charles Eames's bentwood chairs and "his feeling of lightness" as the inspiration: "This room is not an architectural wonder. Anything heavy or bold would overwhelm it. I wanted to make the furniture seem like clouds and disappear."

In 1999 she and the artist Mike Stoughton built a staircase to her son's loft bed from painted skateboards: "Aliens, thunderbolts and bull's-eyes are on backgrounds of brilliant oranges, apple greens and electric blues," she said. "They're the canvases of young artists." In 2000 the Times commissioned her as one of three Manhattan designers asked to produce a budget concept kitchen, for which she combined inexpensive IKEA frosted-glass cabinets lit from within with custom-cut solid walnut counters, and cut the pass-through to the dining room in the shape of an egg — the thick walnut sill beneath it, she said, being "the shadow of the egg." [ref: TRADE SECRETS; 4-Star Kitchens Delivered on a Takeout Budget, The New York Times]

== Teaching ==
Verin has taught as an adjunct professor at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York City. [ref: Helene Verin Publishes Book on Shoe Designer Arsho Baghsarian, Fashion Institute of Technology]

== Work on Beth Levine ==
Verin met Beth Levine (1914–2006), the principal designer behind the Herbert Levine shoe label, after moving to New York in the late 1970s to become a shoe designer. Writing for the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery, Verin described Levine as a mentor and friend, and recounted that after returning to New York in 1996 she visited Levine several times a week to work through her archives and record her recollections; Levine gave her samples, shoe ornaments and press materials from the company's former factory storage. Verin has said she pursued the work because her students had never heard of Levine.

=== Beth Levine Shoes ===
Verin's monograph Beth Levine Shoes, with photography by David Hamsley, was published by Stewart, Tabori & Chang, an imprint of Harry N. Abrams, in 2009. [ref: Beth Levine Shoes, Stewart, Tabori & Chang]

=== Exhibitions ===
* Beth Levine: The First Lady of Shoes, Dutch Leather and Shoe Museum, Waalwijk, Netherlands, 2009, co-curated with Inge Specht. [ref: Beth Levine: First Lady of Shoes, Bellevue Arts Museum]
* Beth Levine: First Lady of Shoes, Bellevue Arts Museum, Bellevue, Washington, 2010, with more than 100 pairs of shoes and boots.
* Beth Levine: The First Lady of Shoes, The Long Island Museum, Stony Brook, New York, 21 August 2015 – 3 January 2016, as guest curator. The exhibition comprised nearly 150 artifacts and works of art, anchored by Philip Pearlstein's 1985 portrait of Levine, lent by the National Portrait Gallery. Joshua Ruff, the museum's director of collections and interpretation, wrote that Verin was the right person to lead the project. [ref: Beth Levine, The Long Island Museum] It was reviewed in The New York Times. [ref: Exploring Beth Levine's High-Fashion Footwear at the Long Island Museum, The New York Times]

== Arsho Baghsarian: A Life in Shoes ==
Verin's second book covers the shoe designer Arsho Baghsarian, who designed for four decades for labels including Christian Dior, Andrew Geller and Stuart Weitzman. Published by Schiffer Fashion Press in 2019, it reproduces sketches, prototypes and shoes Baghsarian donated to the Fashion Institute of Technology; Stuart Weitzman wrote the introduction and Karen Trivette, head of FIT Special Collections, the foreword.

== Portraits by Warhol and Pearlstein ==
Verin sat for Andy Warhol in 1980. A Polaroid from the sitting, catalogued Verin, Helene (Mrs. Rodney Ripps) and dated April 1980, is in the permanent collection of the Chazen Museum of Art at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, a gift of The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts. [ref: Verin, Helene (Mrs. Rodney Ripps), Chazen Museum of Art] The resulting painting, Portrait of Helene Verin, acrylic and silkscreen ink on canvas, was shown at Betty Cuningham Gallery in the 2016 exhibition Pearlstein, Warhol, Cantor: From Carnegie Tech to New York, reviewed in The Brooklyn Rail. [ref: Pearlstein, Warhol, Cantor: From Carnegie Tech to New York, The Brooklyn Rail]

In 2016 she sat for Philip Pearlstein over fourteen sittings. Artsy reported that she may be the only person portrayed by both artists. [ref: This Woman Sat for Warhol, and 36 Years Later She Sat for Philip Pearlstein, Artsy] She wrote Musing: Sitting for a Portrait by Philip Pearlstein (Betty Cuningham Gallery, 2017) to accompany Pearlstein's exhibition Facing You. [ref: Musing by Helene Verin, Betty Cuningham Gallery]

== Personal life ==
Verin married the artist Rodney Ripps on 2 December 1979 at her parents' home in Highland Park, Illinois, and kept her own name. Their son is the conceptual artist Ryder Ripps. [ref: Ryder Ripps: An Artist of the Internet, The New York Times] The marriage lasted eighteen years; afterwards Verin returned to New York from the Berkshires and bought a loft on East 22nd Street in the Flatiron district, which she renovated for herself and her son.

Verin later moved to Palm Springs, California, buying a home in Royal Hawaiian Estates, the 1959 Donald Wexler development in Twin Palms built for the architect's mother and her friends, who as Jews had been excluded from other neighborhoods in the area. Her home, where her Warhol and Pearlstein portraits hang together, is profiled in the photography book Inside Palm Springs (Vendome Press, 2025) by Don Flood with text by Peter Haldeman. [ref: New Book Spotlights Desert Creatives in Their Homes, Palm Springs Life]

== Publications ==
* Beth Levine Shoes. New York: Stewart, Tabori & Chang, 2009.
* Musing: Sitting for a Portrait by Philip Pearlstein. New York: Betty Cuningham Gallery, 2017.
* Arsho Baghsarian: A Life in Shoes. Atglen, PA: Schiffer Fashion Press, 2019.

data.title: Irra Ariella Khi
data.text:
----

Irra Ariella Khi is a technology entrepreneur and humanitarian founder based in the United Kingdom. [ref: Meet the Ukrainian tech entrepreneur who has raised £300,000 of humanitarian relief from London, Sky News] [ref: What happened when this entrepreneur put her startup on hold to help Ukraine, and told VCs to donate, TechCrunch] She is the co-founder and chief executive of Zamna, an aviation technology company focused on digital identity and border compliance, [ref: Zamna raises $5M to automate airport security checks between agencies using blockchain, TechCrunch] [ref: Zamna raises $5m as it secures deal with IAG for airport security tech, City A.M.] and the founder of Sunflower Relief, a humanitarian initiative supporting civilians in Ukraine following the Russian invasion of the country in 2022. She also serves on the Communities Committee of the Harpur Trust, an educational charity based in Bedfordshire. [ref: Ready2Lead?, The Harpur Trust]

== Humanitarian work ==
Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Khi founded Sunflower Relief, a humanitarian initiative focused on supporting civilians affected by the conflict. Sky News reported that the organisation raised funds and coordinated aid efforts from the United Kingdom, with an emphasis on delivering assistance to civilians in conflict-affected areas of Ukraine.

In an interview with TechCrunch, Khi described pausing aspects of her technology work in order to focus on humanitarian relief efforts, including fundraising and coordination with aid networks. Coverage highlighted the rapid formation of Sunflower Relief and its role in mobilising private donations and logistical support in response to the humanitarian crisis.

== Technology career ==
Khi is the co-founder and chief executive of Zamna, an aviation technology company working in the area of digital identity and compliance for airlines and border authorities. In 2023, WestJet expanded its use of Zamna's digital intelligence system to verify travel documents across its network, following a pilot that reduced manual document checks. [ref: WestJet accelerates seamless passenger check-in with invisible digital intelligence system, Future Travel Experience]

== Other activities ==
Khi serves on the Communities Committee of the Harpur Trust, an educational charity based in Bedfordshire, England.

== Recognition ==
In 2025, Khi was named on Computer Weekly longlist of the Most Influential Women in UK Tech. [ref: Most Influential Women in UK Tech: The 2025 longlist, Computer Weekly] In 2019, she was named one of Management Today "35 Women Under 35", listed under VChain, Zamna's former name. [ref: 35 Women Under 35 2019: profiles, Management Today]
