data.title: Charge collection narrowing
data.text:
Charge collection narrowing (CCN) is a mechanism used to obtain spectrally selective (narrowband) photodetection from a semiconductor that absorbs light over a broad spectral range, without an optical filter. Instead of restricting which photons are absorbed, CCN restricts which photogenerated charge carriers are collected: the active layer is made optically thick, so that strongly absorbed photons generate carriers in a region from which they cannot be extracted, while weakly absorbed photons near the absorption edge penetrate deeper into the device and are collected. The external quantum efficiency therefore peaks near the absorption onset, and the response to the main absorption band is suppressed.

== Principle of operation ==
The absorption coefficient of a semiconductor varies with wavelength, so the depth at which light is absorbed (the penetration depth) is wavelength dependent. In a device whose charge collection efficiency is not uniform across the active layer, this converts a spectral difference into a spatial one. Carriers generated in a poorly collecting region near the illuminated contact are lost, whereas carriers generated beyond it contribute to the photocurrent. Narrowband response is obtained by matching the thickness of the absorbing layer to the spectrally dependent penetration depth of the light. The mechanism has been described as selectively collecting long-wavelength photogenerated carriers by exploiting the difference between the carrier drift length and the penetration depth of the light, giving a narrow response at the absorption cut-off edge of the active material.

Reported origins of the non-uniform collection include electrical doping of the active layer and imbalanced charge-carrier mobilities.

== History ==
CCN was introduced in 2015 by Armin and co-workers, who reported organic photodiodes with optically thick bulk heterojunctions showing sub-100 nm full width at half maximum (FWHM), visible-blind red and near-infrared responses, and named the concept charge collection narrowing. Filterless narrowband visible photodiodes based on the same principle were reported in the same year. A 2018 review of organic near-infrared photodiodes lists manipulation of internal quantum efficiency via charge collection narrowing as one of three primary strategies for narrowband organic photodiodes, alongside truly narrowband absorbers and optical cavity structures.

== Implementations ==
CCN has been applied across several material systems:
* Organic semiconductors. Thick bulk-heterojunction photodiodes; a 2025 device based on a low-bandgap random terpolymer reached an FWHM of 68 nm at 916 nm, an effect attributed to a hole mobility exceeding the electron mobility by more than an order of magnitude.
* Doped organic junctions. Intentional n-type doping of an optically thick polymer:non-fullerene blend through an electron-donating amine interlayer produced a sub-50 nm response in the near-infrared.
* Metal-halide perovskites. The mechanism has been used to make perovskite narrowband photodetectors, with the spectral position tuned through the composition-dependent bandgap.
* Wide-bandgap semiconductors. A filterless narrowband 4H-silicon carbide photodetector using a sufficiently thick absorbing layer showed an FWHM of 14.5 nm at a peak wavelength of 355 nm.

== Limitations ==
Because the mechanism works by discarding the carriers generated by strongly absorbed light, narrowband response obtained through CCN is accompanied by a reduced external quantum efficiency, and the thick absorbing layers required lead to slower response times than thin-film photodiodes of the same materials.

== Comparison with other narrowband strategies ==
Alternative routes to filterless narrowband detection include semiconductors with intrinsically narrow absorption bands, optical microcavity and light management structures, and mechanisms based on exciton dissociation rather than charge collection.

* Photodiode
* Quantum efficiency
* Organic semiconductor

data.title: Ann Ingle
data.text:
Ann Ingle (born 1939, Hackney, London) [ref: Openhearted by Ann Ingle: compelling memoir by a woman ahead of her time, Irish Independent] is a British-Irish writer. Originally from London, she has lived in Dublin since the 1960s. She founded the Dublin 4 community newspaper News Four in the 1980's. She co-wrote the memoir of Irish rally driver Rosemary Smith, Driven (2018), before publishing her own memoir, Openhearted, in 2021. [ref: Openhearted: Ann Ingle on publishing her first book aged 82, RTÉ] [ref: Ann Ingle: 'People don't think about older people as exciting', The Irish Times] She is the mother of journalist Róisín Ingle.

==Early life and career==
Originally from London, Ingle moved to Ireland in the 1960s after meeting her future husband, Peter Ingle, while on holiday in Cornwall. [ref: 'Forget saving to leave it all to your kids - spend it!', Irish Independent] The couple had eight children. She worked as a typist, preparing manuscripts for writers, and later edited News Four, a community newspaper serving the Sandymount area of Dublin. She returned to education as a mature student, graduating from Trinity College Dublin with a degree in English and history. [ref: Ann Ingle, NewsFour]

In 2018, Ingle co-wrote Driven, the memoir of rally driver Rosemary Smith. The book was shortlisted for an Irish Book Award. She has collaborated with daughter Róisín, a journalist and columnist for The Irish Times, through interviews, and mentions in newspaper columns. [ref: Mother-daughter duo Ann and Róisín Ingle on ghostwriting for a rally legend, RTÉ]

==Books==
Ingle's memoir Openhearted: Eighty Years of Love, Loss, Laughter and Letting Go was shortlisted for the Irish Book Awards Biography of the Year award. [ref: Openhearted, Irish Book Awards] Still Here: Everything I Know About Being Older was published by The O'Brien Press in 2026. [ref: Still Here, O'Brien Press]

==Selected works==
* Driven, HarperCollins
* Openhearted: Eighty Years of Love, Loss, Laughter and Letting Go (2021)
* Still Here: Everything I Know About Being Older (2026)

data.title: Russification of Georgia
data.text:
The Russification of Georgia includes a system of measures, actions and legislations undertaken by the Russian Empire, later Soviet Union and currently Russian-occupied Abkhazia, aimed at linguistical and cultural assimilation of Georgians to eredicate their identity, terminate Georgia's cultural uniqueness and fully integrate it into Russia.
==Imperial Russification policy in Georgia==
Russian conquest of the South Caucasus began in the late 18th century and included various territorial acquisitions from Qajar Iran and the Ottoman Empire. Various Georgian kingdoms and principalities, threatened by Iran and the Ottoman Empire, voluntarily placed themselves under the protection of the Russian Empire. Georgian and Armenian attitudes towards the Russian Empire contrasted with the Muslim struggle against Russian expansion, as broad sections of the Georgian and Armenian populations sought ties with Russia to liberate themselves from Islamic rule. However, they also expected Russia to grant them political and cultural autonomy, which was not respected. Russia instead proceeded to outright annex Georgia while abolishing its local dynasties, suppressing its dynastic autonomy and violating the bilateral treaties. The eastern Georgian king Erekle II placed his kingdom under Russian protection through the Treaty of Georgievsk in 1783. However, in September 1801, the eastern Georgian kingdom was unilaterally and directly annexed by Russian Empire, which was rationalized by the need to defend Russia's new subjects against domestic discord and external enemies, but actually ran contrary to previous agreements between Kartli-Kakheti (Eastern Georgia) and Russia. The western Georgian principalities, which were part of the Ottoman Empire, placed themselves under Russian protection from 1803 to 1811 and were able to preserve their autonomy under the native princely families for several decades, with the exception of the Kingdom of Imereti.

In 1811, the centuries-old autocephaly of the Georgian Orthodox Church was abolished, and it was forcibly integrated into the Russian Orthodox Church. In 1817, it was placed under an ethnic Russian exarch. The liturgy of the Georgian Church was gradually brought into line with the Church Slavonic Russian rite. The Georgian language was excluded from schooling and replaced by the Russian-language school system. This contrasted with the policy towards the Muslims of Transcaucasia and the Armenian Church, whose autonomy was recognized in 1836 and which was initially viewed as an ally in the campaigns of expansion against the Ottoman Empire. The policy towards Georgia resembled that towards the Romanians in Bessarabia, who were subjected to early assimilatory measures because they were Orthodox Christians and were therefore considered closer to Russians in religious and sociocultural terms.

Under Nicholas I, the Transcaucasus was regarded as a colony, while the peoples of Transcaucasia were viewed as "uncivilized Asiatics", which was followed by repressive policies aimed at fully integrating Transcaucasia into Russia. In 1833, the Russian State Council identified its goal as linking Transcaucasia to Russia "as one body, and its population be brought to speak, think, and feel Russian". The repressive policies led to numerous Georgian uprisings,, 1832, and 1841, as well as Muslim uprisings in the 1830s. By the middle of the 19th century, the system of far-reaching local autonomies under native vassals was eventually replaced by the Russian gubernia (province) system. The provinces of Tiflis and Kutais were created and headed by non-native civil servants appointed by St. Petersburg, although local anomalies persisted in the judicial and local administration.

The ongoing resistance in both the South and North Caucasus, as well as the failure of forced integration and the absence of economic profit from the colony, led to a shift towards a more pragmatic and flexible policy under Mikhail Vorontsov, the viceroy of the Caucasus from 1845 to 1855, who sought cooperation with the non-Russian elites. Vorontsov implemented reforms aimed at fully integrating the Georgian nobility into the regional administration, army, and bureaucracy, and introduced an estate-based organization of the nobility. The reforms aimed to transform the rebellious noble layer of society into a loyal and uniform official service nobility, while the peasants lost their traditional rights.

In the 1860s and 1870s, there was again an increase in Russification efforts in Transcaucasia due to the more systematic Russification and standardization program adopted by the Russian Empire across the country. Judicial and municipal reforms were introduced, and the office of the viceroy was abolished in 1883. While there was a certain revival of the Georgian language in the middle of the century, in the 1870s and especially the 1880s, Georgian was systematically excluded from schools. In 1872, the theological seminary in Tiflis replaced Georgian with Russian as the language of instruction. In 1882, the use of the term "Georgia" in the print press was forbidden. In 1886, the director of the Tiflis Theological Seminary, Reverend Chudetsky, who opposed the introduction of Georgian and called it a "language for dogs", was murdered by Ilia Laghiashvili, one of his expelled students.

The policy of Russification led to strong opposition from the Georgian national movement, which championed the Georgian language, literature, and culture, and successfully opposed the repressive Russian policy, which refused to recognize the Orthodox Georgians, with their ancient high culture and written language, as the equals of the Russians. After Russia concluded that the Russification of Georgia had failed, it switched to another tactic—attempting to deny the existence of a distinct Georgian nation. In the 1897 census, 11 ethnic groups were separated from Georgians by the Russian authorities. A similar policy of dividing homogeneous nations was adopted in the North Caucasus after its rebellions, notably towards the Circassians. These policies promoted distinct identities among minority groups in Georgia: schools were opened in Mingrelian and Svan languages. The teaching of the Russian language to Abkhazians led to the replacement of Georgian by Russian as their second language. This process continued in the Soviet Union, which treated Russian as the "language of inter-ethnic communication", and led to the further alienation of Abkhazians from Georgians, despite their common historical heritage and the relatively few historical problems between them. The Russian Empire created alphabets and elementary textbooks for the Mingrelian, Abkhaz, and Svan languages. The goal of this policy was to obviate the use of Georgian by these groups, leading them to replace Georgian with Russian as a vehicle of high culture, as well as to discourage the use of the Georgian script for everyday literacy. Georgian writers, by contrast, had attached special significance to Georgian as the common language of scholarship, culture, religion, law, and inter-ethnic communication in Georgia since the time of Pharnavaz I. Russian policies devalued the Georgian language in the second half of the 19th century, as knowledge of Russian was required to find a job in the administration. By the late 1890s, the Caucasus was ruled directly by Russian generals, and Georgians were denied official positions.

==Soviet Union==

In the Soviet Union, the Georgian language was granted official status in the 1921 and 1937 constitutions of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. However, the 1960s saw a push in the USSR towards linguistic Russification, which was rationalized by a theory of the gradual elimination of ethnic differences in the USSR and the emergence of a new, unitary "Soviet nationality". The Russification attempts were met with resistance in Ukraine, the Baltics, and the Caucasus. Russian became the language of instruction for various courses at Tbilisi State University, which was criticized by Georgian writers at the Georgian Writers' Union, an official organization. There were bombings in Georgia in 1975 and 1976, perpetrated by Vladimir Zhvania. According to dissident sources, he was motivated by opposition to the Russification drive. The discontent ultimately culminated in mass protests in 1978 against the Russification policy, which aimed to replace Georgian with Russian as the official language of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic, as part of the adoption of the "Brezhnev" constitution to replace the Stalin constitution. Soviet Georgian leader Eduard Shevardnadze sided with the protesters, and the popular demonstrations forced the Soviet authorities to retreat from their planned constitutional changes. [ref: Demonstrators Win Victory in Georgia (May 1978), Labour Focus on Eastern Europe]
==Russification of Georgains in Russian-occupied Abkhazia==
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the War in Abkhazia saw Georgia lose control of the region of Abkhazia to Russian-backed separatist forces. Despite the ethnic cleansing of Georgians, the Georgian population continued to constitute a majority in southern Gali District of Abkhazia. In 1994, Russian was imposed as the official language of Abkhazia alongside the poorly known Abkhaz language. Due to a lack of teachers in Russian, a transitional plan was announced in 2015, and education in Russian became mandatory in all Gali schools in 2021, while the use of the Georgian language was banned. Before the war, Georgian was the language of instruction in 52 of the 58 schools operating in Gali District. [ref: Abkhazia: Erasing the Georgian language, Institute for the Study of War]

data.title: Proposed Guinea-Bissau hepatitis B vaccine trial
data.text:
The proposed hepatitis B vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau, also known as the HBV-NSE trial, was a proposed randomized controlled trial assertedly intended to investigate the effects of administering the hepatitis B vaccine to newborn infants in Guinea-Bissau. The study was developed by researchers affiliated with the Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, and funded by an award of US$1.6 million from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, under the authority of Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. [ref: Notice of Award of a Single Source Unsolicited Grant To Fund University of Southern Denmark (SDU), Federal Register] [ref: Controversial HBV vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau halted, The Lancet Infectious Diseases] [ref: CDC awards $1.6 million for hepatitis B vaccine study by controversial Danish researchers, Center for Infectious Disease Research & Policy-CIDRAP] It was ostensibly intended to evaluate whether administration of the vaccine at birth affected childhood mortality, illness, and development beyond its established protective effect against hepatitis B infection, [ref: US awards no-bid contract to Denmark scientists studying hepatitis B vaccine in African babies, Associated Press] but experts questioned the intent of the experiment, and the ethics of its design. [ref: The Hepatitis B Foundation and The African Hepatitis B Advocacy Coalition denounce the unethical HepB birth dose study in Guinea-Bissau, Hepatitis B Foundation] [ref: Guest post: The CDC hepatitis B study is unethical and must never be published, Retraction Watch] [ref: The U.S. Health Research Project Rejected by Guinea Bissau was Absurd and Deadly, CounterPunch.org] [ref: Every accusation is a confession (or a statement of intent): MAHA’s new Tuskegee experiment, Science-Based Medicine] [ref: The US must never support research and policies that inflict harm on Black communities, BMJ] [ref: US-funded Guinea-Bissau vaccine study to undergo ethical review, African health officials say, Reuters] The proposed trial was ultimately formally rejected by the government of Guinea-Bissau in October 2026, and the country's judicial police subsequently searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project and seized vaccine supplies intended for the study. The trial was never conducted, and no participants were enrolled.

==Background==
===Hepatitis B vaccination===
Hepatitis B is a viral infection that can cause chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Infection acquired during infancy is particularly likely to become chronic, with approximately 90% of newborns infected during childbirth developing chronic infection. The hepatitis B vaccine, first approved in 1981, has an established record of safety and effectiveness in preventing infection and its complications. Serious adverse effects are rare, and studies have found that vaccination can provide protection against clinical disease and chronic infection for at least 30 years. [ref: Hepatitis B vaccines: WHO position paper – July 2017, Relevé Épidémiologique Hebdomadaire] [ref: Ask the Experts: Hepatitis B, Immunize.org]

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all newborns receive an initial dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 24 hours, followed by two or three additional doses. The birth dose is particularly important in preventing vertical transmission of the virus from an infected mother to her infant. According to the WHO, timely birth-dose vaccination prevents an estimated 70–95% of mother-to-child hepatitis B transmission. For newborns whose mothers are infected, administering hepatitis B immune globulin in addition to vaccination provides greater protection than vaccination alone. [ref: Hepatitis B immunisation for newborn infants of hepatitis B surface antigen-positive mothers, The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews]

Guinea-Bissau has a high prevalence of hepatitis B infection, with the WHO estimating in 2026 that more than 12% of adults were living with chronic infection in 2022 and that approximately 2% of children younger than five were infected in 2020. At the time of the proposed trial, the country's routine childhood immunization schedule did not include a hepatitis B birth dose, with infants instead receiving their first hepatitis B vaccination at approximately six weeks of age. In 2024, Guinea-Bissau decided to introduce universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth, with implementation planned by 2028. The WHO identified the timely introduction of the birth dose as an important measure for reducing hepatitis B transmission in the country.

===Questioning of Bandim Health Project research practices===
The Bandim Health Project has investigated the possible non-specific effects of vaccines, including effects on health outcomes other than the diseases against which vaccines are intended to protect. Researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn have contributed to this line of research, which has also been the subject of scientific criticism.

A 2025 article in Vaccine said that strong claims previously made by Benn and Aaby about non-specific vaccine effects were not supported by the evidence presented: "We were surprised to find several instances of questionable research practices, such as unpublished primary outcomes, outcome switching, reinterpretation of trials based on statistically fragile subgroup analyses, and frequent promotion of cherry-picked secondary findings as causal, even when primary outcomes yielded null results. Sample size calculations appeared to be driven by unwarranted optimism regarding effect-sizes and event rates leading to underpowered studies". [ref: What is actually the emerging evidence about non-specific vaccine effects in randomized trials from the Bandim Health Project?, Vaccine] [ref: Randomized trials show no evidence of non-specific vaccine effects, Aarhus University] Bandim Health Project requested the retraction of meta-analysis.

A 2026 article—also in Vaccine—reported on 10 pre-registered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) performed at the Bandim Health Project where the primary outcomes are partly or completely missing from the scientific records. Altogether these 10 RCTs included more than 74,000 children. [ref: Non-emerging primary trial results from the Bandim health project, Vaccine]

==Proposed study==
===Funding and institutional involvement===
In December 2025, the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, under the authority of Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., awarded approximately US$1.6 million to the University of Southern Denmark for a proposed study of the timing of the hepatitis B vaccine birth dose in Guinea-Bissau. Christine Stabell Benn, a Professor of Global Health at the University of Southern Denmark, was identified as one of the leaders of the research team. The award was made without a competitive bidding process. Additional support from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation brought the total reported funding commitments to approximately $3.2 million. According to The BMJ, the researchers submitted an application for American funding within hours of a 19 September 2025 meeting of the United States Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), at which the committee considered changing the longstanding recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth. Emails obtained by Danish newspaper Weekendavisen indicated that Lyn Redwood and Stuart Burns, two senior health department officials appointed under Kennedy, helped guide the application through the funding process, with Burns characterizing the proposal as a funding priority. [ref: Controversial African vaccine trial likened to Tuskegee is "cancelled"—but US funders insist it will continue, BMJ]

Kennedy had previously praised the research of Peter Aaby and Stabell Benn, and the award followed efforts by bodies under Kennedy's control to change United States hepatitis B vaccination recommendations. Stabell Benn had served as a consultant to a working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices that considered the timing of hepatitis B vaccination. [ref: Guinea-Bissau suspends Trump-backed hepatitis B vaccine study for ethical review, Associated Press] The researchers disputed suggestions that the trial had been developed to advance Kennedy's vaccination policies, maintaining that the research proposal had originated independently of subsequent American policy decisions.

===Proposed design===
The original proposed randomized controlled trial was intended to enroll approximately 14,000 newborns. One group would receive the vaccine at birth, while the other would follow the country's existing schedule and receive it six weeks later. Researchers aimed to examine mortality, illness and developmental outcomes. [ref: America First, Africa Last? Health data deals and the new scramble for pathogens, PLOS Global Public Health]

==Scientific and ethical controversy==
The study attracted criticism from public-health researchers who argued that withholding the birth dose from some newborns would expose them to preventable infection. The Bandim research team responded that Guinea-Bissau did not routinely administer the vaccine at birth and argued that the study would evaluate the vaccine before the country's planned introduction of a universal birth dose. [ref: Hepatitis B Guinea-Bissau trial: Researchers behind controversial study weigh in as confusion reigns over its fate, BMJ]

The World Health Organization subsequently stated that it had significant concerns about the study's scientific justification, ethical safeguards and compliance with accepted principles for research involving human participants. [ref: Statement on the planned hepatitis B birth dose vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau, World Health Organization]

==Suspension and institutional review==
In January 2026, the government of Guinea-Bissau suspended the study pending an ethical and technical review, after the health minister said that the committee associated with its original approval had not formally met to evaluate it. [ref: Guinea-Bissau suspends US-funded vaccine trial as African scientists question its motives, [[Nature (journal)] Conflicting public statements exacerbated uncertainty about the status of the trials. On 19 January 2026, Africa CDC official Yap Boum stated that the study had been canceled following criticism by researchers and ethicists, but two days later, the United States Department of Health and Human Services told The BMJ that the study was proceeding as planned, with protocols being finalized. On 22 January, in the wake of a November 2025 military coup in the country that had brought a transitional government to power, health minister Quinhi Nantot again stated that the study had been suspended pending ethics review. [ref: Guinea-Bissau suspends US-funded vaccine trial as African scientists question its motives, Nature] [ref: Controversial Danish vaccine research group faces new allegations, Science] Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, emphasized that African public health authorities should determine whether the study could proceed and supported additional ethical review.

In March 2026, the University of Southern Denmark said it had paused all work associated with the proposed trial while seeking an independent ethical evaluation. United States health officials stated that the study remained under review and could proceed only after approval from the relevant authorities. [ref: Experts fear 'unethical' vaccine trial in Africa is 'prototype' for US studies under RFK Jr, The Guardian]

==Rejection and police investigation==
On 16 October 2026, Guinea-Bissau's Council of Ministers formally reaffirmed its decision not to accept the proposed trial. The decision was confirmed by Stabell Benn in correspondence with Ars Technica, published on 22 October. She expressed regret over the decision but acknowledged the government's authority to determine whether the research could take place in the country. [ref: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry, Ars Technica]

On 19 October 2026, Guinea-Bissau's judicial police searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project and seized hepatitis B vaccine doses intended for the trial. According to the police, the investigation concerned the circumstances surrounding the acquisition, transportation, storage and traceability of the vaccines. Authorities indicated that the seizure did not imply that the vaccines themselves were defective or unsafe. [ref: RFK Jr's 'deities of vaccine research' raided by police in Guinea-Bissau, The Guardian]

data.title: Peter Dutkewich
data.text:
----

Meletius Peter Dutkewich (1871–1939) was an American photographer. [ref: US Passport Application, Family Search] He was known as an adventurer, big game hunter, and for his attempt to climb Mount Kilimanjaro with Peter MacQueen in 1909.

==Early life==
Dutkewich was born in Warsaw in 1871 and emigrated to the United States as a teenager. He became a US citizen in 1895. [ref: Another Dimension: Stereoscopic Photography and the Press, c. 1896–1911, Doctoral thesis, Durham University]

==Early African travels==
Between 1908 and 1909, Dutkewich and Peter MacQueen plotted an expedition from the Nile to East Africa and Kilimanjaro, for the purpose of recording their adventures. The excursion was later published in a book titled In Wildest Africa: The record of a hunting and exploration trip through Uganda, Victoria Nyanza, the Kilimanjaro region and British East Africa, with an account of an ascent of the snowfields of Mount Kibo, in East/Central Africa, and a description of the various native tribes, [ref: In Wildest Africa PDF] which contained sixty-four of Dutkewich's photographs along with MacQueen's narrative. [ref: In Wildest Africa, Seattle Post-Intelligencer] The book was published in advance of Theodore Roosevelt's travels to Africa which heightened American interest in the region. [ref: New Books, Etc., Scientific American]

During their expedition, Dutkewich was reported lost in Central Africa for three weeks, fell into animal traps, and suffered a fall on Kilimanjaro where he broke three ribs. [ref: Peter Dutkewich, The Times-Union] [ref: Rev Peter M'Queen is a Climber Too, The Buffalo News] [ref: Kilimanjaro: To the roof of Africa, National Geographic Society] They completed their Kilimanjaro ascent on July 17, 1908. [ref: Peter McQueen on the Heights, Vermont Journal] Some of Dutkewich's photographs of his African travels – big game hunters, ceremonies and dances, mountain peaks and other African scenes – were published as stereographs by Underwood & Underwood. [ref: In Advance of Roosevelt, Ottawa Daily Republic] He was described in 1909 as having "a genius for adventure". Dutkewich was said to have made more than 12,000 negatives of the African continent and his photography was used to illustrate other contemporary books about Africa and appeared in the Burr McIntosh Monthly. [ref: My African neighbors: man, bird, and beast in Nyasaland, Little, Brown, and Company] [ref: Peter MacQueen: "the fighting parson", Puzzlebox Press]

==Later career==
In the 1920s, Dutkewich met Bert Underwood of Underwood & Underwood while both were traveling in Athens during the Greco-Turkish War. According to his memoir, Underwood offered Dutkewich a job on the spot, but was turned down until Dutkewich fulfilled his ongoing contract with another photographic house. He continued to do freelance work for Underwood & Underwood and other American stereoscopic companies such as B.W. Kilburn & Co., of New York. Over the course of his life, Dutkewich took photographs of many countries and territories, including Australia, New Guinea, New Zealand, Japan, India, China, Siberia, Turkey, the Philippines, the Canadian Rockies, Mexico, Zimbabwe, and Kenya.

The Esher Novices' Chase is a Grade 2 National Hunt steeplechase in Great Britain which is open to horses aged four years or older. It is run at Doncaster Racecourse over a distance of about 3 miles (3 miles 42 yards, or 4,866 metres), and during its running there are 22 fences to be jumped. The race was added to the programme in 2023, replacing both the John Francome Novices' Chase and the December Novices' Chase, run at Newbury and Doncaster respectively. data.title: Gregor Herten
data.text:
Leonhard Gregor Herten (born April 29, 1955 in Korschenbroich, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany) is a German physicist.

== Career ==
Gregor Herten studied physics at RWTH Aachen, where he received his doctorate in 1983
[ref: "Messung der Ladungsasymmetrie in der Reaktion e^+ e^- \to \mu^+ \mu^- mit dem MARK-J Detektor bei PETRA"]
under the supervision of
Albrecht Böhm.
He subsequently worked as a Research Fellow at the European Centre for Nuclear and Particle Physics, CERN, from 1984 to 1986. From 1986 to 1992, he was a Professor of Physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Cambridge, MA, USA, first as an Assistant Professor and later as an Associate Professor
[ref: MIT LNS 1992 Symposium: On the Matter of Particles - L. Gregor Herten - The Future of L3 at LHC].
From 1992 to 2023, he was Professor
[ref: Experimentelle Teilchenphysik, Prof. Dr. Gregor Herten]
of Experimental Physics
at the Albert Ludwigs University of Freiburg;
he has been retired since October 2023.

== Research ==
Gregor Herten's research focuses on the investigation of the elementary building blocks of matter and their interactions using high-energy particle accelerators. He contributed to the discovery of the gluon
[ref: Discovery of Three Jet Events and a Test of Quantum Chromodynamics at PETRA Energies, Phys. Rev. Lett. 43 (1979), p. 830.]
and to the observation
[ref: Measurement of e^+ e^- \to \mu^+ \mu^- Charge Asymmetry, Phys. Rev. Lett. 48 (1982), p. 1701.]
of
electroweak processes
at the
PETRA storage ring of the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron, DESY, Hamburg.

Together with his research group at the University of Freiburg, he developed and built
[ref: The ATLAS Experiment at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, JINST 3 (2008) S08003.]
large, precision
particle detectors for
muons for the
ATLAS experiment at the
Large Hadron Collider, LHC at CERN, which contributed to the discovery of the Higgs boson
[ref: Observation of a new particle in the search for the Standard Model Higgs boson with the ATLAS detector at the LHC, Phys. Lett. B, 716 (2012)].
Further contributions include measurements of Z boson decays at the
Large Electron-Positron Collider (LEP), as well as the search for new particles beyond the Standard Model and the study of heavy
quarks at the LHC
[ref: Gregor Herten: Complete list of publications on InspireHEP (Gregor Herten) (https://inspirehep.net/authors/1006125)].

In 2024, he published a textbook in german language together with Christoph Berger entitled "Elementarteilchenphysik"
[ref: Textbook: Elementarteilchenphysik, Springer Nature].
The English version of the book was published in 2025 under the title "Particle Physics"
[ref: Textbook: Particle Physics, Springer Nature].

== Administration ==
Gregor Herten served as Vice-Rector for Research at the University of Freiburg from 1995 to 2000 and received the Freiburg University Medal in recognition for his service to the university
[ref: Universitaetsmedaille/2000-2009].
He was the German scientific delegate to the CERN Council, and its Vice-President from 2007 to 2009
[ref: Presidents and vice-Presidents of CERN Council].
He was a member and, from 2005 to 2008, Chair of Commission C11 on Particles and Fields
[ref: IUPAP C11 Members]
[ref: Gregor Herten, Report from IUPAP-C11]
of the
International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP).
From 2013 to 2015, he led the Section Matter and Cosmos (SMuK) and the Division of Particle Physics of the German Physical Society (DPG). In addition, Gregor Herten served as a scientific advisor on boards and committees of DESY, CERN, the
German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMBFTR)
and the
German Research Foundation (DFG).

data.title: Paul Kenny (Composer, Pianist, Educator)
data.text:
----

Paul Kenny  –  A Life in Music. Beginnings The story of Paul Kenny begins in a house where silence was never truly silent. Even in the quietest hours of early morning, before the world stirred awake, sound lived there, the faint hum of the wind through a window crack, the rhythm of rain on a tin roof, the soft, steady breathing of a family still asleep. To a child attuned to the subtleties of the world, these were not random noises; they were the first fragments of music. From the earliest days, Paul seemed to hear differently. Where others heard routine, he heard patterns. Where most would pass by a songbird's tweet without notice, he paused to catch its phrasing, its pauses, its echoes. This gift, or perhaps this calling, would shape the course of his entire life. There was an old piano in the corner of his grandparents home, one that had seen better days. Its wood bore scratches and its keys had yellowed slightly with age. Yet for Paul, it was an entire universe waiting to be discovered. He would sit before it long before he was formally taught, stretching his small hands across the keys, pressing down gently at first, and then with growing curiosity. The notes, however uneven, stirred something deep within him, a sense of purpose that transcended the moment.

Music became his first language. It spoke to him in ways words could not. The harmonies he found by accident seemed to reveal truths beyond expression, beauty, longing, and an unexplainable peace. As the years passed, the piano was no longer simply an instrument. It became a friend, a confidant, and later, a mirror through which Paul would come to understand himself and the world around him.  Formal lessons began soon after. Teachers noticed quickly what his family had already seen, that this was not an ordinary student. Paul absorbed theory, technique, and interpretation with rare ease. Paul's natural learning and understanding of the language of writing music, music theory and performance meant that he outgrew teachers extremely quickly as they simply could not keep up with the Maestro in the making. Yet even as he mastered scales, études, sonatas and concertos his imagination reached beyond the printed notes. He wanted to understand why music moved people, why a certain chord could summon joy, or a modulation could bring tears. That question would become the quiet pursuit of his life. The Maroochy River holds a special place in his childhood, shaped by long, unhurried days spent with my grandparents along its banks. Fishing was never rushed. Lines were cast gently into the moving water, and we waited together in comfortable silence, watching the river breathe with the tide. The mangroves framed the day, alive with birds and the soft sounds of water against mud. In those moments, time seemed to slow, and Paul learnt that patience was not something you forced, it arrived naturally when you allowed yourself to be still. Mud crabbing was both exciting and grounding. Paul remembers lifting the heavy pots from the river, thick with mud and anticipation, Paul's grandfather guiding and reminding him to be careful. He showed Paul how to handle the crabs properly, which ones to keep and which to return, and why respect for the river mattered. These were practical lessons, but they carried something deeper, an understanding of responsibility, balance, and gratitude for what nature provided. Chess belonged to a different world, taught by his grandfather on his mothers side, far from the river's edge. With him, the lessons were quieter and more deliberate. Sitting across a small board, he explained the logic behind each move, encouraging me to think ahead and consider the whole picture rather than chasing quick wins. His teaching was calm and thoughtful, shaping the way Paul approached not only the game, but problem-solving itself. Together, these memories form two distinct threads of his early life, one rooted in river mud and sunlight, the other in quiet rooms and careful thought. Each grandfather taught Paul in his own way, and both left lasting impressions. One gave him a love of the natural world and its rhythms; the other gave him a way of thinking that would guide Paul long after the board was packed away. Paul's grandfather carried his history quietly, never with show or ceremony, but with a steady sense of gravity that made you listen when he spoke. Through him, Paul became aware of the family's long association with the Masonic lodge, a lineage bound not by power or secrecy, but by values: discipline, service, knowledge, and moral responsibility. Freemasonry, as he described it, was less about what was hidden and more about what was expected of a man, integrity in private, fairness in public, and loyalty to something greater than oneself. He spoke of the Freemasons and the Lodge with respect, emphasising their role as custodians of tradition and symbolism rather than holders of authority. The rituals, the tools, and the language all pointed toward self-improvement and the shaping of a person's character. Listening to him, Paul understood that the lodge was a place of reflection and fraternity, where men were reminded to build their lives as carefully as a mason shapes stone, deliberately, honestly, and with purpose. Alongside this Masonic heritage was the deeper, older thread of the Knights Templar, spoken of not as myth, but as an ancestral memory. To Paul's grandfather, the Templars represented duty, sacrifice, and faith in God and oneself under pressure, men bound by oath and belief, navigating turbulent times with courage and conviction. Whether preserved through family story, symbol, or tradition, the Templar connection carried a sense of guardianship, the idea that knowledge and values must be protected and passed forward unaltered and intact. These stories were never delivered as boasts or claims to importance. Instead, they felt like a quiet inheritance and a reminder that identity is shaped not only by where we come from, but by how we choose to carry what we've been given. Through my grandfather, the lineage of Freemasonry and the echo of the Knights Templar and Rosslyn Church became less about history and more about responsibility, to live thoughtfully, act justly, and honour the past through the choices made in the present. Paul's grandfather was a 33rd Degree Mason. The 33rd Degree is a prestigious, honorary recognition within the Scottish Rite for extraordinary achievement and commitment to Masonic ideals, representing the culmination of a Mason's journey with the Lodge and with God Eternal. As adolescence arrived, so too did the awareness that music would not be a pastime for him any longer, it would be his vocation. While others his age spoke of practical futures, he spoke of sound, of composition, of creating something as a lasting legacy. To Paul, a melody was never just a sequence of tones, it was a living entity, breathing and evolving in time. He composed instinctively, sketching short piano pieces that hinted at the expressive lyricism that would later define his mature work. When a new piano arrived at the family home Paul seemed to come alive. The late nights at the new piano, often until 3:00am or 4:00am became sacred rituals. The house would grow still, and Paul would sit alone, guided only by a dim lamp and the soft glow of the keys. Sometimes he would play through entire symphonies in his head, conducting invisible orchestras, hearing textures that no one else could yet imagine. It was not ambition that drove him but an unshakable inner necessity, the same force that has always driven true artists to translate the invisible into sound. Paul seemed to be able to hear and create music from the sounds around him.  Those formative years were filled with both beauty and struggle. The path of the artist, even then, was uncertain. Yet Paul's resolve deepened with every challenge. Music was not simply what he did, it was who he was becoming. He felt the weight of something larger than himself, a sense that his life would be devoted not merely to performing music, but to understanding it, teaching it, and giving it back to others. By the time he reached adulthood, that path had become unmistakable. What began as curiosity had matured into craft; what began as wonder had become vocation. The boy who once listened to rain on a roof had found his own sound, and it was unmistakably his, the "Sounds of Nature and the Music of Paul Kenny".  Throughout his life, Paul's parents have been a constant source of unwavering support, standing beside him through every challenge, triumph, and turning point in his musical journey. Both worked hard to provide Paul with exceptional musical instruments such as a beautiful professional upright piano and new digital style electronic organ. They encouraged his earliest explorations at the piano, nurtured his curiosity, and never once questioned the legitimacy of a life devoted to creativity. Paul's parents even added an extra room to the back of the family home where it became Paul's music studio and tuition room. Their never failing belief in him, quiet, steady, and unconditional, became the foundation on which he built his confidence as a composer, performer, and educator. In moments when the path ahead felt uncertain, their reassurance reminded Paul of who he was and what he was capable of. So much of his music, his resilience, and his achievements trace back to the love and encouragement they offered so freely. They didn't just support his career, they helped shape the person that Paul became.

The Bike Paul had entered a music competition playing the organ, something he loved but if being completely honest, there was another very strong motivation driving him at the time... he desperately wanted a BMX bike. There had been a few serious accidents on pushbikes in Paul's  neighbourhood, so his Mum and Dad were understandably cautious. Eventually, though, they made Paul a deal. If he won the organ competition, they would buy him a bike. That was all the incentive Paul needed. The night of the competition arrived, and Paul and his parents sat waiting... and waiting... and waiting for his name to be called in the Under 14 section. One by one, the categories were announced, but somehow Paul's name never came up. Before he knew it, they had moved on to the Under 16s. Paul remembers thinking something must have gone wrong. Paul was only 12 or 13 at the time and definitely not meant to be in the senior group. Somehow, his name had been placed in the wrong category. Then, suddenly, Paul was called to the stage to compete with the older students. Paul and his parents didn't have time to question it. He just remembers thinking, well, if I'm here, I'd better give it everything I've got. So he did. Paul added repeats, changed sounds, experimented with the instrument pushing himself far beyond what he had originally planned. If Paul was going to compete with the older players, he needed to step it up. At the end of the evening, the winners were announced. Under 10s... Under 12s... Under 14s... all called and applauded. Then came the Under 16 category. "Highly Commended" was awarded. Then third place. Then second place. Paul and his parents sat there quietly, already convinced there would be no BMX bike for him. Paul was not even meant to be in this section. And then came the announcement: first place in the Under 16s—the senior section went to Paul Kenny. They praised the use of the instrument, the sound changes and the overall performance. They called it a highlight of the night. Everyone was clapping, Mum and Dad were in complete disbelief... and all Paul could think about was one thing... When are we going to buy the bike? In fact, Paul was so caught up in that thought that he barely noticed them calling his name again to come up and collect the certificate and trophy. People were looking at Paul, wondering why he hadn't moved. Eventually, Paul made his way to the stage but in his mind, the real prize wasn't the trophy at all. It was that BMX bike waiting just around the corner. It was, without a doubt, one of the funniest and most memorable nights of Paul's childhood.

Paul's childhood and high school years were a strange balancing act between two completely different worlds. By day, he was just another student quietly moving through classes, careful not to draw attention to myself, especially in music. Yet the moment the final school bell rang, Paul's real life began. Paul spent most afternoons teaching younger students, nurturing their musical growth while further shaping his own. Weekends were filled with performances, concert work and engagements that saw Paul playing for audiences both small and large who had no idea he would be back in a school uniform on Monday morning. Alongside this, Paul worked for various piano and musical instrument companies, demonstrating instruments, performing for clients and immersing himself in the professional music scene from a very young age. At school, however, Paul carefully protected this secret life. He was determined that no teacher would ever discover just how capable he was at music and at the piano. He even went so far as to deliberately achieve lower results in his written music tests, all in an effort not to stand out. His reasoning was simple,he didn't want to be cornered into becoming the music director or accompanist for the school musical productions. Paul had seen that the role involved the endless rehearsals, the pressure, the responsibility and he wanted desperately to avoid being tied down by it due to his already busy music schedule.  So his double life continued. Paul taught music most afternoons, worked in music stores, and spent his Friday and Saturday nights performing at restaurants, functions and events. One such evening found him playing at a corporate function for the Jaguar car company, held at the local Yacht Club to showcase their new vehicle range. A beautiful white grand piano had been hired especially for the occasion, and Paul was asked to perform a full program of Richard Clayderman pieces, which were incredibly popular at the time. The evening was flowing perfectly, until the moment he became uncomfortably aware not of the audience, but of a familiar presence. As he glanced at the polished surface of the piano, Paul saw the unmistakable reflection of one of his school teachers standing right beside him. "Well, well, well... this is a surprise," the teacher said with a knowing smile. Paul pretended not to see him, but the secret was already out. By the following Monday, Paul was summoned into the school office and presented with the very role he had spent years trying to dodge as musical director and pianist for the school production. Paul's carefully guarded escape plan had finally unravelled, and the life he had hidden so carefully from my school had caught up with him in the most spectacularly ironic and funny way.

Another moment that remains etched in Paul's memory with a gentle glow, like soft stage lights that framed the beautiful Judith Durham of "The Seekers".  She stood with such grace and quiet strength, the very embodiment of Australian musical elegance, as she prepared to present Paul with a music award. What made it all the more extraordinary was that she had no idea that Paul was still just a high school student, merely the pianist who had accompanied her before with complete devotion. When she called Paul's name and he began walking toward the stage, she looked at Paul with a knowing smirk and a warm, genuine smile, as though something suddenly made perfect sense to her. As she placed the certificate into Paul's hands and shook his hand firmly and kindly, there was a spark in her eyes, a recognition, perhaps of more than just a musician, but a shared spirit. Then, she leaned in, kissed Paul softly on the cheek as he accepted the award, and whispered in his ear with that unmistakable sweetness, "Are you still okay to play piano for me Saturday evening?"  In that quiet, tender moment, time seemed to pause. Paul was no longer just a schoolboy pianist, he was becoming part of something magical, woven briefly yet forever into the fabric of Australian music history, guided by one of its most radiant stars.

Growing up with a younger brother five years Paul's junior brought a particular kind of rhythm to the house, one that shifted and evolved as they both found their own paths. Paul's brother showed a natural curiosity for music in his early years, picking up the clarinet and later the violin, and for a while it seemed as though the two of them might share that creative journey side by side. Paul remembers hearing him practise in the next room, the familiar scales weaving through the house, adding their own colour to those formative years. But while music held his attention for a time, it soon became clear that his true passion lived elsewhere. Golf captured him completely. What began as a hobby gradually grew into a genuine talent, and before long he was excelling with a confidence and precision that impressed everyone who watched him play. Where Paul's world gravitated toward pianos, orchestras, and composition, his brother moved to fairways, greens, and long, focused hours perfecting his swing. During this time cars and girls came and went but both boys kept focused on their dreams. Together they grew up under the same roof, each discovering their own calling, different disciplines, perhaps, but grounded in the same spirit of dedication and love for what they did.

One of the funniest and most awkward moments of Paul's musical life happened at a huge dance event where over 400 tickets had been sold. Paul was booked to play a magnificent big theatre organ in a grand ballroom complete with chandelier, so he arrived early to set up and do a sound check. Paul was dressed very casually, suit pants and an old T-shirt, with his good shirt, tie and suit jacket neatly hanging in the back of the car, ready to change before the evening began. Paul's parents were there too, seated at a table near the entrance, quietly watching as he laid out his music and explored the organ's rich array of sounds and volume levels. Out of nowhere, a flustered man came charging across the dance floor, shouting at Paul to get off the organ and off the stage immediately. He insisted that a world-class organist was arriving soon and called Paul a "young punk," ordering him to leave the building altogether. The whole situation was shockingly embarrassing and very uncomfortable, and Paul's parents could hardly believe what they were witnessing. Trying to keep his dignity (for a change... haha), Paul calmly gathered his music, stepped down from the stage, and in a very polite voice told the man, "No problem at all, I'll head out to my car now and leave." Just before walking away, Paul politely asked who this famous organist was that he was apparently delaying. Without hesitation, the man declared, "Paul Kenny." Paul smiled, offered a gentle, knowing smirk and simply replied, "Ahhh OK, have an outstanding evening," as Paul turned toward the exit. That's when his parents stood up, and Paul's Dad quietly corrected the guy in a soft voice saying, "You do realise that's Paul Kenny... the one you've just told to get off the organ and get out of the building." The colour drained from the man's face instantly. Moments later, he came running across the car park, breathless and mortified, as Paul stood by his car ready to leave. As he reached Paul, his eyes fell on Paul's formal shirt, tie and suit jacket hanging neatly in the back of his car, the clear signs that Paul had been preparing to perform all along. His expression shifted from authority to sheer embarrassment as he stumbled through a series of desperate apologies, realising fully the mistake he had made. By then, all Paul could do was smile and laugh. The tension dissolved into something almost comical, and what had begun as a deeply awkward moment transformed into a story that still makes Paul laugh today, a gentle reminder that sometimes even the most grand and formal musical evenings can begin with the most wonderfully human confusion.  After that evening the man that had come running across the dance floor and telling Paul to get off the stage and out of the building actually became one of Paul's greatest advocates for his music and performances. Almost every time Paul performed the man was always there with his wife and friends in the audience.

== We certainly live in a funny world!! ==

The Making of a Musician As Paul grew older, the horizon widened before him, yet it was music that continued to guide his every step. The piano, that steadfast companion of his youth, had become more than a familiar presence, it was now the instrument through which his imagination found its fullest expression. In every chord he played, he sensed echoes of the natural world, fragments of stories, and the intricate architecture of human emotion. The late 1980s became a defining era in his musical journey, marking the moment Paul stepped from the familiar discipline of the acoustic piano into the exhilarating world of keyboards, synthesizers, and emerging computer music. Suddenly, the boundaries of sound dissolved, analog synths shimmered with warmth, digital keyboards offered precision and clarity, and sequencers opened doors to textures and rhythms he had never imagined. This technological shift didn't pull Paul away from his classical roots, it expanded them, allowing him to blend the expressive nuance of piano with the bold, futuristic energy of electronic instruments. During this period, Paul played in jazz quartets, cover bands, and countless ensembles, bringing these new sounds to life on stages large and small. The 1980s and 1990s became a whirlwind of musical activity performing at hundreds of weddings, corporate events, parties, and community functions, sometimes several in a single weekend. Those years taught Paul versatility, stamina, and the joy of adapting his playing to every possible style and setting. Looking back, that era not only shaped Paul's musicianship but also cemented the foundation for the eclectic, technology-embracing composer he would become. The discipline of formal study refined his instincts. Hours spent practicing evolved into years of disciplined artistry, scales, sonatas, counterpoint, harmony. He learned to hear not only with the ear but with the mind, looking through the printed notes at the true beauty of the song. He understood that technique was not a constraint, but a pathway toward freedom: a structure that allowed the imagination to soar without collapsing under its own weight. As he began to perform more widely in front of a few people for small private performances through to larger crowds of 7,000 or more, audiences sensed something distinctive about his playing. It was not flamboyant nor self-conscious. Rather, it carried a quiet conviction, a kind of sincerity that drew listeners inward instead of dazzling them outwardly. His interpretations of classical works were personal yet respectful, each phrase shaped with an awareness that every note had purpose and lineage.

But even while mastering the repertoire of others, Paul's mind was already turning toward creation. The urge to compose became impossible to ignore. Sketchbooks filled with ideas, short motifs, fragments of melody, harmonic progressions that hinted at deeper landscapes. It was as if each new piece revealed not only a new sound, but a new aspect of his own identity. He came to understand that composition was a kind of reflection, not merely of one's technique or intellect, but of one's spirit. His early works, though modest in scale, were sincere explorations of emotion and colour. He began to blend traditional classical structures with the intuitive lyricism that would later define his voice. The piano was always central, but around it grew the textures of strings, woodwinds, and the occasional touch of modern harmony, hints of the expansive orchestral writing to come. In time, Paul's path led him beyond performance and composition into the broader world of music itself, its instruments, its mechanics, its industry. He possessed an innate curiosity not only about how music was made, but about how it was built, how wood, wire and felt combined to form the instrument that had shaped his life. This curiosity led him to study the inner workings of pianos, to tune and restore them, to understand their personalities as intimately as a craftsman might understand the grain of timber. This mechanical understanding did not distract him from artistry, it deepened it. To tune a piano was, in a sense, to listen with ultimate precision. Each string, each vibration, carried within it the possibility of beauty. Over time, Paul's name became known not just as a performer and composer, but as someone who understood the piano completely, inside and out. Parallel to this, his professional journey expanded into realms that demanded both artistry and intellect. His managerial and business acumen grew from genuine curiosity rather than ambition. When he later held national positions, managing the Piano Division of Samick Corp (Alex Steinbach Pianos Australia), and serving as Accounts Manager for ASUS and also Head of Design and Marketing for an International Tool Company, he brought to those roles the same qualities that defined his musicianship, precision, creativity, and integrity. Yet even at the height of these professional responsibilities, music remained his compass. No matter how complex the day's work became, the evenings would return him to the piano, the instrument that had never left his side. There, in the stillness of night, the melodies came again, sometimes gentle, sometimes grand, but always honest. It was during this time that Paul's dual identity as artist and craftsman fully took shape.

Through years of performance, tuning, and leadership, he came to see that all these aspects were not separate callings but parts of a single truth: that music is both art and architecture, inspiration and structure, passion and patience. Every element of his life seemed to reflect one of those pairs, the balance between the creative and the practical, between soul and discipline. The seeds of his future work as a composer, pianist and educator were already present in this balance. He began to see how the worlds of performance, composition, and teaching could converge, how knowledge could flow from one to the other. His experiences had taught him that mastery was not an endpoint, but a cycle, learning, creating, teaching, and learning again. The path that music leads you down is never a straight line, but it is always rich with people, extraordinary, unexpected, and often unforgettable. Along the way, Paul found himself crossing paths with musicians whose talent left me in awe, actors whose faces were familiar from the big screen yet whose warmth felt quietly human. Actors, musicians, authors, famous chefs and even politicians whose lives momentarily intersected with Paul through the universal language of music. These encounters were rarely planned. They happened in concert halls, backstage corridors, gala events, dusty rehearsal rooms, and fleeting moments between soundcheck and silence. Music has an uncanny way of dissolving hierarchy, titles fade, and what remains is simply one soul recognising another through shared creation. What surprised Paul most was not the status of those he met, but the genuine friendships that formed in these moments. Conversations that began with a simple comment about a song or a melody or arrangement often grew into lasting bonds, built on mutual respect and a shared understanding of the sacrifices and devotion that a life in music demands. Some offered guidance, others laughter, and a few became companions through different chapters of my life, each one leaving a quiet imprint on my journey.

Through music, the world opened itself in ways Paul could never have imagined. It introduced him to people from every corner of the world, of life and society, yet it reminded Paul that beyond fame, success, and influence, we are all connected by the same emotional language. Every handshake, every shared stage, every late-night conversation over coffee or a few bottles of wine became part of a larger story, not just of music, but of humanity, connection, and the enduring friendships that continue to echo long after the final note has faded.

The day already carried a special glow, it was Paul's 30th birthday  yet he had no idea just how extraordinary it was about to become. Paul  found himself at a friend's piano factory in Sydney, wandering among rows of beautifully crafted instruments, when his hands settled on a stunning Steinway concert grand. This was no ordinary piano, it had been carefully prepared and was awaiting delivery to the Sydney Opera House for an upcoming concert. As Paul played, the room filled with a rich, commanding sound that seemed to echo off the high factory walls, each note reminding Paul how deeply music had shaped every chapter of his life. It was in that moment of quiet immersion that the telephone rang. His  friend answered, his expression shifting from casual curiosity to astonishment as he listened. On the line was the manager for Jerry Lewis, the world-famous comedian and entertainer, explaining that Jerry's pianist had suddenly fallen ill and could not attend the important rehearsal. Without missing a beat, Paaul's friend gestured toward him and said to the person on the phone, "Paul Kenny is here playing the Steinway right now, and he knows all Jerry's material." Hearing his name spoken so confidently into that phone, against such a backdrop, felt almost unreal, as if fate itself had chosen his birthday to present the ultimate gift.

For a few breathless emotional moments, the idea hung in the air, that Paul, on his 30th birthday, might be called upon to play for one of the most iconic performers of our time, seated at the very piano that would grace the Opera House stage. But timing, cruel and uncompromising, had other plans. Paul was flying out to Perth in just a few hours to deliver a presentation at a music event, a commitment that could not be undone. No matter how much his heart pleaded, the logistics of reality refused to bend. And so, Paul left the piano factory that day with a strange mixture of exhilaration, quiet melancholy and a bottle of red wine his friend gave him as a birthday gift. While most people mark their 30th birthday with cake and candles, Paul's had offered something far rarer, a brush with history, a moment when his path almost crossed with Jerry Lewis under the glow of fame and music. It became a story not of what was, but of what might have been, a memory wrapped in wonder, destined to live forever in the pages of his life and music.

The Shadow Never Spoken There was a period of several years in Paul's life so carefully hidden that even those closest to him would never have imagined it existed. While the world saw a quiet music teacher, a composer, a man of intellect, gentle discipline and creativity, another version of Paul lived in the margins of shadows, secrecy and silence. He was called upon not for melody or his song, but for his discipline and precision. Not for applause, but for anonymity. In this secret chapter of Paul's life, he trained to be a ghost for a role that demanded calm under impossible pressure, absolute loyalty, and a willingness to carry future burdens no one could ever know. With truth and integrity always leading the way.  Paul was trained not to destroy, but to observe, to anticipate, to protect from afar, heightening his senses and sharpening his mind to foresee people, body language, actions and events. The title that was given to him was never spoken aloud, only implied through secret training. He was trained to be a ghost moving through existence as though nothing had changed, while every heartbeat carried the knowledge that his decisions could alter unseen destinies. There were no medals, no recognition, no stories, no discussions at dinner tables, only silence and the heavy responsibility of duty. What few understood was that the greatest battle was never external. It was the conflict between the man who created beauty through music and the one tasked with operating in the cold stillness of necessity. Each part of his precision training stripped a little more colour from his world, and in response, Paul poured himself deeper into the piano, his compositions and his inner self. Music became his sanctuary, his confession, his redemption. In the stillness of night, when the world slept without knowing how fragile and close it was to chaos, Paul would sit alone and play softly, as though each note rewrote a fragment of his soul. Paul stepped away from the training and the precise art of what he was being trained for. The secret life faded, as all shadows do, but it left behind a sharpened awareness of fragility, of life's delicate thread, and the extraordinary power of foreseeing and choosing compassion over conflict.  There are those who walk a different path—quietly, beneath the noise of the world, where recognition never reaches and applause is never heard. They move through the shadows carrying knowledge, purpose, and stories that may never be told, leaving no footprints for others to follow. While the world celebrates those who stand in the light, these silent travellers continue onward, unseen and unacknowledged, guided by something deeper than fame or praise. Perhaps their greatest secret is not who they are, but why they chose the path that few will ever understand.

By the time Paul reached full artistic maturity, the foundations were well and truly laid. The boy who once played with wonder had become the man who could shape that wonder into form. His compositions began to gather the hallmarks that would come to define them, clarity of line, emotional resonance, and an ever-present sense of atmosphere. He no longer composed merely to express, but to communicate. Music, for him, had become a bridge between the seen and unseen, a way to reveal what words could never capture.

The Composer's Voice There comes a point in every musician's life when sound becomes more than sound, when it turns into language, philosophy, and memory all at once. For Paul, that threshold arrived quietly, as most profound things do. It was not marked by applause or public acclaim, but by a deep, unspoken realization that composition was no longer a choice or pastime. It was the truest way he could make sense of the world. He began to compose more consistently, almost instinctively, as though guided by a voice that had long waited to be heard. His music evolved with the patience of nature itself, each piece growing organically from a single idea, a small fragment of melody or harmony that slowly unfolded into something much larger. What distinguished Paul's writing was not complexity for its own sake, but clarity and an insistence that every note serve meaning and emotion and the space of silence was also valued.  His compositions carried traces of the landscapes around him. Australia's wide skies and quiet coasts, the stillness of dawn over the Pacific and Tasman, the hum of cicadas in the late afternoon heat and all of these found their way, somehow, into his harmonic and melodic language. The natural world did not merely inspire him; it conversed with him. In these sounds of place, he heard rhythm, pulse, and form. He once described the wind in the gum trees as "a symphony no one conducts but everyone hears."  Paul has the ability to see and hear music in everything that the world has to offer.  Out of this sensibility emerged works that listeners would later describe as modern classical music that bridged the precision of the concert tradition with the warmth of human experience. From his earliest albums "Rainforest Dreaming" to "Pictures in My Mind", one of his defining projects, captured this aesthetic perfectly. Each composition on the album offered a glimpse into an inner landscape: moments of self reflection rendered in tone. The album progresses through song to tell a story with each piece a reflection of life and time itself.  Among them, "Visions of Vienna" stood out as a statement of both homage and independence. While its title evoked the city of Mozart and Schubert, the piece itself was unmistakably Paul's lyrical yet contemporary, rich in harmony, and shaped by a distinct emotional narrative. A sweeping string orchestra framed the piano like light around glass, allowing melody to move freely between nostalgia and renewal. Listeners heard in it not imitation but continuation, the timeless conversation between tradition and modern life. In this period of creative expansion, Paul's work became increasingly interdisciplinary. He has collaborated with poets, blending the spoken word with original compositions that extended the emotional texture of language. These collaborations, numbering more than a hundred poems over the years, explored everything from the sacred and spiritual to the raw and those that are extremely unfiltered. Through them, Paul discovered new dimensions of expression: how music could give breath to text, and how silence itself could become part of the dialogue. At the same time, his work as a private music teacher for over 40 years deepened. Standing before a class of students, he recognized the same spark he once carried as a child, the fascination with sound, the hunger to understand. Teaching became not merely instruction but continuation,  a passing on of the very flame that had once lit his own journey. He encouraged students to hear music not as notation, but as emotion shaped by structure. When he began developing his songbooks which are used globally for various graded piano exams and his music theory workbooks, it was with this same philosophy. Each piece, each lesson was designed to demystify complexity, to lead students from curiosity to comprehension through clear steps, gentle humour, and real musical examples. The workbooks and songbooks were not cold manuals; they were invitations, ways for young musicians to enter the world of the piano and music theory without fear or boredom. In time, Paul's class became more than a place of education, it was a studio of discovery. Students not only learned notes and rhythms but experienced what it meant to think musically, to see connections, to understand harmony as a kind of architecture of feeling. Many would later speak of how his teaching shaped not just their musicianship but their character... patience, precision, imagination, humility. Outside the classroom, Paul's professional life continued to weave between performance, composition, and craftsmanship. His understanding of pianos remained intimate, he tuned instruments for schools, colleges, and private studios, concert halls and student pianos ensuring that every note could speak as purely as it was intended. The combination of artistry and technical mastery gave him a rare authority, he was both creator and caretaker of sound. Alchemist of tone, turning sound frequencies into masterpieces enjoyed around the world.  But for all the practical work, the heart of his world remained creation. Each new composition revealed a facet of his evolving voice, music that seemed to listen as much as it spoke. There was often a reflective stillness in his writing, a sense of somehow time being suspended. Listeners described it as cinematic, spiritual, and deeply human. His melodies seemed to make you remember something ancient even as they moved forward. Paul's personal philosophy of music was simple yet profound, that beauty must be truthful, and truth, when fully realized, is beautiful. He never chased trends or abstraction for their own sake. Instead, he sought resonance, that mysterious quality that makes music linger in the heart long after the final chord fades. In interviews and public appearances, he often spoke not about fame or success, but about the privilege of being able to share something meaningful. "A composer's task," he once said, "is to hold a mirror to emotion, not to dramatize it, but to remind people of what they already feel inside." "The purpose of music is to paint emotion on the canvas of silence and silence itself is also music". That humility, coupled with his unwavering dedication to craft, earned him a reputation not only as a gifted musician but as a generous human being. As the years passed, recognition followed naturally. His compositions began to appear in concerts and recordings across educational and community contexts, documentaries, tv radio, background music in coffee shops, used in hospitals for mental health and more. His name became associated with modern classical compositions, new age music and personal integrity, work that was polished but never pretentious, emotive yet never indulgent. For many, hearing his pieces was like being invited into a private conversation between heart and mind.
