data.title: George J. Magovern Jr.
data.text:
George J. Magovern Jr. (born March 4, 1952) is a prominent retired American cardiothoracic, vascular and transplantation surgeon [ref: Health Care Heroes: Celebrating Magovern's career of milestones, Pittsburgh Business Times] who spent 40 years at Allegheny General Hospital (AGH) in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. His career focused on cardiac and vascular surgery, transplantation, mechanical circulatory support, surgical education, and clinical research. From 1985 until his retirement in 2025, Magovern held a number of clinical, academic and administrative leadership positions at AGH and later Allegheny Health Network (AHN), including chairman of the Department of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery and chairman of the AHN Cardiovascular Institute.

Magovern is a member of a family closely associated with the development of cardiothoracic surgery nationally, [ref: Mending hearts: Dr. Magovern had a healing effect on Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette] and in Pittsburgh: His father, George J. Magovern Sr. [ref: In Memoriam: George J. Magovern, Sr. (1923–2013), Texas Heart Institute Journal] (1923–2013), was a pioneering cardiac surgeon who, working with engineer Harry Cromie, developed a sutureless prosthetic aortic valve [ref: ] in 1962. In 1957, the elder Magovern and thoracic surgeon Edward M. Kent introduced open-heart surgery using the heart-lung machine to Western Pennsylvania. [ref: George Jerome Magovern, MD, November 17, 1923–November 4, 2013, The Annals of Thoracic Surgery]

Magovern's brother, James A. Magovern [ref: Obituary: Dr. James Anthony Magovern / Nationally known heart surgeon, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette] (1954–2007), was also a cardiac surgeon and conducted cardiovascular research at AHN until his death from cancer.

== Early years ==
George J. Magovern Jr. was born on March 4, 1952, in Brooklyn, New York, to George J. Magovern Sr. and Ann Magovern. [ref: Obituary: Ann Magovern / Longtime supporter of Allegheny General Hospital, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette] Both of his parents were born and raised in New York. The family moved to Pittsburgh in 1957, when his father joined the medical staff at Allegheny General Hospital, and settled in the Fox Chapel area in 1960. Magovern was raised in an Irish Catholic community, and attended the former St. Scholastica grade school in Aspinwall.

He was the oldest of six children; his younger siblings were James, Mary, Susan, Frances and Ann. James Magovern followed his father and older brother into cardiac surgery and cardiovascular medicine. Magovern attended Shady Side Academy in Pittsburgh, graduating in 1970. [ref: News Post, www.shadysideacademy.org] As a student, he participated in football, wrestling and tennis.

== Education ==
Magovern attended the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester, Massachusetts, where he majored in biology and graduated in 1974. He then attended the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, graduating in 1978. While in medical school, he served as president of his class.

Following medical school, Magovern completed his surgical training at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore from 1978 to 1985. His training included general surgery, vascular surgery, general thoracic surgery and cardiac surgery. Upon completing his residency, Magovern returned to Pittsburgh and joined Allegheny General Hospital in 1985, beginning an association with the hospital that continued until his retirement four decades later.

== Career ==
Clinical practice and transplantation

During his career, Magovern performed several thousand cardiac surgical procedures. Most were performed at Allegheny General Hospital, although he also operated at West Penn Hospital, Forbes Hospital, Beaver Medical Center [ref: Jun 29, 1994, page 122 - Pittsburgh Post-Gazette at Newspapers.com™, Newspapers.com] and Westmoreland Hospital. His clinical practice encompassed the surgical treatment of coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease, heart failure and thoracic aortic disease, as well as thoracic organ transplantation [ref: Allegheny Health Network completes 500th heart transplant - Becker's ASC, Becker’s ASC] and ventricular assist device implantation. [ref: Jul 15, 2000, page 1 - Pittsburgh Post-Gazette at Newspapers.com™, Newspapers.com]

In 1987, Magovern established AGH's heart transplant and left ventricular assist device program. The heart transplant program launched in 1985 [ref: ] and received approval from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) in 1988 and became one of the country's longest continually approved heart transplant programs.

Magovern also performed AGH's first single-lung transplant in 1992. He subsequently served as director of the lung transplant program from 1992 to 2000.

Leadership at Allegheny General Hospital

In 1992, Magovern was appointed director of the Division of Cardiothoracic Surgery at AGH. Two years later, he became program director of the hospital's Cardiothoracic Surgery Residency Program. He was a member of the Thoracic Surgery Directors Association from 1995 to 2013. In 1995, he was elected to membership in the American Association for Thoracic Surgery. The following year, he was promoted to professor of cardiothoracic surgery at Drexel University College of Medicine.

In 1998, Magovern became the first chairman of AGH's newly established Department of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. In 2005, Magovern established the McGinnis Cardiovascular Institute, [ref: AGH opens 'one-stop' cardiac facility, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette] with support from businessman and philanthropist Gerald E. McGinnis and George J. Magovern Sr. The institute was created to encourage greater collaboration between cardiology and cardiac surgery and to support the development and adoption of new cardiovascular procedures and technologies at Allegheny. [ref: Media Professional Press Release Information for AHN, www.ahn.org]

Magovern also helped to establish [ref: Students get rare look at heart surgery, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette] an educational surgery observation program at AGH. [ref: Saturday Diary: Open heart, open eyes, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]

Allegheny Health Network

Following the formation of Allegheny Health Network in 2013, Magovern was named system chairman of the Department of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery.

Three endowed academic positions were established in connection with the Magovern family's work at Allegheny: the George J. Magovern Sr. Endowed Chair in Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery, the James A. Magovern Endowed Chair in Cardiovascular Research, and the George J. Magovern Jr., M.D., Endowed Professorship in Cardiac Surgery.

The [https://www.ahn.org/locations/hospitals/allegheny-general/patients-visitors/magovern-conference-center George J. Magovern Education Conference Center at Allegheny General Hospital] also commemorates the family's contributions to thoracic and cardiovascular surgery at the institution.

Research, awards and professional service

A prominent researcher, over the course of his Magovern authored or co-authored more than 50 peer-reviewed publications and more than 15 book chapters. [ref: George J. Magovern - ScienceDirect research bibliography, Science Direct]

From 2004 to 2018, Magovern served as a reviewer for the Annals of Thoracic Surgery and the Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. In 2011, he was elected to the American Board of Thoracic Surgery (ABTS). Magovern and his father were the first father and son to serve on the ABTS since the board was established in 1948. [ref: History: The Allegheny General Hospital Conference Center, AHN.org]

Magovern received a number of professional honors during his career. In 2015, he received the American Heart Association's Peter Safar "Pulse of Pittsburgh" Award. [ref: Pittsburgh cardiology leader Samir Saba, M.D., named 2026 Peter J. Safar Pulse of Pittsburgh honoree, American Heart Association] In 2018, the Allegheny County Medical Society presented him with its Ralph C. Wilde Leadership Award.

Magovern retired from active practice in April 2025 after 40 years at Allegheny General Hospital.

== Personal life ==
Magovern married Jamie Hall Magovern [ref: GEORGE MAGOVERN Obituary (2013) - Legacy Remembers, Legacy.com] in 1979. The couple met while Magovern was attending the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and Hall was an undergraduate at Carnegie Mellon University studying fine arts. They have lived in Sewickley Heights, Pennsylvania, for four decades and have three children.

As of 2026, Magovern is the mayor of Sewickley Heights. [ref: Sewickley Heights police chief gets new contract, terms reluctantly released, TribLIVE.com]

data.title: Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan
data.text:
----

Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan (1940 – 23 October 2024), also known as Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan Bahawalpuri or by his childhood name Jind Badda, was an eminent Pakistani classical vocalist, master musicologist, and ancestral chief of the **Walyani tribe**. He represented the orthodox Gwalior Gharana tradition and was historically recognized as the last direct custodian of the ancestral Shahi Singers (royal court musicians) of the princely state of Bahawalpur Riyasat. Khan spent over five decades broadcasting classical art music across South Punjab and the Siraiki belt, maintaining a legendary reputation for his strict adherence to Hindustani classical ragas, his leadership of the Walyani clan, and his highly specialized renditions of spiritual Siraiki Kafi structures. [ref: A short brief on Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan by Radio Pakistan Multan, Radio Pakistan Multan] [ref: استاد مبارک علی خان کی برسی عقیدت واحترا م سے منائی گئی, Daily Raigzar Bahawalpur]

== Ancestral History, Tribal Leadership, and Royal Migration ==
Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan belonged to an ancient, multi-generational dynasty of classical vocalists who simultaneously held hereditary leadership within the **Walyani tribe**. For centuries, his family line had been deeply intertwined with the royal court music traditions of the subcontinent. His ancestors were originally residents of the Bikaner State in Rajasthan, India, where they served as the celebrated state musicians under the patronage of Maharaja Ganga Singh.

Prior to the partition of India, a historic transition of patronage occurred when the grandfather of the final ruler of Bahawalpur, Nawab Sir Sadiq Muhammad Khan V, visited Bikaner. Deeply captivated by the family's melodic prowess, the Nawab formally requested Maharaja Ganga Singh to allow the family to relocate to the Bahawalpur royal court. The family migrated to the Bahawalpur Riyasat, where they were officially designated as Shahi Singers (Royal Court Musicians). At the time of this transition, the family collective was led by Mubarak Ali Khan's father, Ustad Kayam Ali Khan, alongside his paternal uncle, Ustad Jivan Khan. Khan eventually inherited the traditional mantle of leadership, serving as the official **Chief (Head) of the Walyani tribe** throughout his later life in Bahawalpur.

== Early Life, Training, and Discipleship ==
Born in Bahawalpur in 1940, Mubarak Ali Khan initiated his musical training and initial accompaniment (Sangat) under the guidance of Ustad Ali Bux Khan, a resident of Bahawalpur and father of the notable musician Ustad Nazar Hussain Khan.

Following this foundational phase, he moved during his youth to Hyderabad, Sindh, to seek advanced mentorship from the legendary maestro Ustad Umeed Ali Khan (son of Ustad Pyare Khan), one of the grandest proponents of the Gwalior and Kotwali Gharana systems in United India. Khan spent approximately seven years in Hyderabad undergoing rigorous training in Khayal gayaki under Umeed Ali Khan's direct supervision, and subsequently earned the distinction of performing alongside his master on stage, as well as with Ustad Asad Ali Khan. [ref: Official Request and Statement to the Executive Director, Punjab Arts Council]

== Performance Artistry and Raga Repertoire ==
Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan possessed a comprehensive master-level repertoire over a vast catalog of Hindustani classical frameworks. While he possessed mastery over folk idioms, his core musical focus remained strictly classical, characterized by flawless note execution (Swar Shuddhi) and deep microtonal development. He was particularly famous for his exceptional live renditions of the following classical modes:
* Abhogi and Bageshree
* Bhairavi, Bhoopali, and Yaman
* Darbari Kanada and Jaunpuri
* Desh, Kedar, and Hansadhwani (Huns Dhuni)
* Malkauns: Celebrated for his classical interpretation of the spiritual Sufi bandish "Peer E Nizam Ud Din" dedicated to Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya. [ref: محفلِ موسیقی ’خیال‘ میں استاد مبارک علی خان کی شاندار کارکردگی, Daily Vintage Archive]
* Pratap Varali (Partab Varali): An exceptionally rare raga in the Hindustani system that very few classical practitioners attempt, which Khan famously performed and preserved during a private assembly recording using mobile-media documentation.

Khan seamlessly brought the classical structural weight of Gwalior vocalization into regional Urdu poetry—notably rendering Abdul Hamid Adam's ghazals—as well as the mystical Siraiki Kafis of Khwaja Ghulam Farid, such as "Chola Mera Rut Nal Ratiya" and "Dukhan Lagi Tey Yar Bhoven".

== Strategic Broadcasting Career and Peer Praise ==
Khan was an essential pillar across regional public broadcasting centers in South Punjab, building a historic recording career:
* Radio Pakistan Multan & Bahawalpur: Long before the establishment of the Bahawalpur station, Khan was a frontline contracted classical artist for Radio Pakistan Multan, where his early classical خیال (Khayal) and folk کافیاں (Kafis) were recorded. Upon the inception of Radio Pakistan Bahawalpur, he brought structural weight to their live and recorded scheduling, eventually earning the highest **"AA" Class Category Artist** ranking from the Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation (PBC). [ref: To Whom It May Concern (Ref No. PMB (5)/13-351), Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation]
* Praise from Contemporary Maestros: Khan commanded immense respect among peer musicians for his immaculate humility and artistic stature. During a prominent archival live gathering, the legendary rhythm maestro and tabla virtuoso **Ustad Tafu Khan** publicly presented a ceremonial monetary tribute (Nazar) to Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan on stage, accompanied by profound praises, declaring his deep admiration for Khan's vocal mastery and darvesh-like persona. [ref: Ustad Tafu khan Praises Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan, Abuzar Ali Archive]
* Academic Footprint: Khan established a formal music training setting in Bahawalpur, personally instructing over 100 regional disciples, including Liaqat Cholistani, Ustad Nawaz, Mohammad Ashraf, Shazia Talib, Tariq Khan Cholistani, and Sonam Khan.

== Death ==
Ustad Mubarak Ali Khan passed away in Bahawalpur on 23 October 2024 at the age of 84 after a prolonged illness. His funeral proceedings marked the symbolic conclusion of the state-patronized royal classical era in Bahawalpur, drawing respect from cultural circles and the members of his tribe. His lineage and musical inheritance continue to be maintained by his descendants and family members, including his sons Nawazish Ali Khan and Nadir Ali Khan, his paternal grandson Mustajar Ali (son of Nawazish Ali Khan), and his maternal grandson Abuzar Ali Khan, alongside Mazahir Ali, Ali Naqi, and other members of the Walyani clan.

data.title: KubeVirt
data.text:
----

KubeVirt is an open-source virtualization project that extends Kubernetes to manage traditional Virtual machine (VM) workloads. It allows organizations to deploy, run, and manage VMs side-by-side with containerized applications within the same Kubernetes cluster, utilizing the same underlying orchestration, networking, and tooling. [ref: What is KubeVirt?, Red Hat] The project is heavily adopted by organizations seeking to unify their infrastructure platforms and is an incubating project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). [ref: KubeVirt - Cloud Native Computing Foundation, CNCF]

== History and timeline ==
KubeVirt was developed as Kubernetes emerged as a standard platform for application deployment. The project was designed to directly complement Kubernetes by extending its control plane to natively host and manage legacy VM workloads alongside containers. This design allowed organizations adopting Kubernetes to use a single foundational layer for both modern containerized applications and traditional virtual machines. KubeVirt entered the CNCF Sandbox and later graduated to an Incubating project as its adoption across the cloud-native ecosystem grew.

KubeVirt aligns its release cycle closely with Kubernetes, typically trailing standard Kubernetes minor releases by roughly two months to allow for proper stabilization.

Key milestones:
* June 2016: Initial commit.
* September 2019: KubeVirt was accepted into the CNCF Sandbox.
* April 2022: The project was promoted to the CNCF Incubating maturity level.
* July 2023: KubeVirt v1.0 was officially released, marking a major maturity milestone for the project.
* August 2025: A formal [https://github.com/cncf/toc/issues/1822 pull request] for CNCF Graduation was opened, signaling the project's push toward the foundation's highest maturity tier.

== Architecture and dependencies ==
KubeVirt extends the Kubernetes API using custom resource definitions (CRDs) to represent virtual machine objects. It relies on the Linux virtualization stack rather than inventing a new hypervisor stack. From the perspective of Kubernetes, a KubeVirt VM is simply treated as a pod with specific resource requests. From the Kubernetes perspective KubeVirt is a cloud-native application and implemented using the Kubernetes controller (VM life-cycle management) and operator (KubeVirt lfie-cycle management) patterns.

=== Core dependencies ===
* Kubernetes: The foundational orchestration engine.
* KVM: The underlying Linux hypervisor used to execute the virtual machines.
* QEMU & libvirt: Used to configure, execute, and manage the VM processes.

data.title: Science in School
data.text:
----

Science in School is a free online magazine that provides inspiring resources covering subjects from sciences. It aims to support teachers in the delivery of their STEM curricula by connecting them to inspiring, cutting-edge science and technology, in order to foster positive attitudes towards the science that shapes our lives, and attract students to careers in these fields.
The main language of publication is English, but it also provides translations in other European languages. [ref: EIROforum > Activities https://www.eiroforum.org/activities/science-in-school/]

The magazine's web-site: https://scienceinschool.org/

Published and funded by EIROforum, a collaboration between eight of Europe’s largest inter-governmental scientific research organizations (CERN – European Organization for Nuclear Research; EMBL – European Molecular Biology Laboratory; ESA – European Space Agency; ESO – European Organisation for Astronomical Research in the Southern Hemisphere; ESRF – European Synchrotron Radiation Facility; EUROfusion – European Consortium for the Development of Fusion Energy; European XFEL – European X-ray Free-Electron Laser Facility; ILL – Institut Laue-Langevin), the journal is a non-profit project and is hosted by the European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL) in Heidelberg, Germany. [ref: EMBL Communications https://www.embl.org/about/info/communications/publications/]

The publication was founded in 2006, and has published 3-5 issues each year. Initially, the magazine was published in print format (as a magazine distributed free of charge in Europe), but in 2013 it transitioned to an online-only platform.

data.title: GIOYA Higher Education Institution
data.text:
----

GIOYA Higher Education Institution is a higher education institution based in San Ġwann, Malta. It operates within Malta's higher education accreditation and quality assurance framework overseen by the Malta Further and Higher Education Authority (MFHEA). [ref: External Quality Assurance, Malta Further and Higher Education Authority]

== History ==
The institution was founded in March 2019 as GIOYA Academy by a group of professionals with backgrounds including business management, higher education administration and international organisations. [ref: GIOYA Higher Education Institution – External Quality Assurance Audit Report, Malta Further and Higher Education Authority]

It subsequently adopted the name GIOYA Higher Education Institution.

== Academic activities ==
GIOYA offers higher education programmes in areas including business administration and entrepreneurship, commercial diplomacy and management. [ref: Academic Programmes, GIOYA Higher Education Institution]

Its programmes include the Bachelor in International Business Administration and Entrepreneurship, which is part of a double-degree arrangement with the University of Turin. [ref: Double degree programs/Joint degree programs, University of Turin]

In the field of commercial diplomacy, GIOYA has collaborated with the University for Peace (UPEACE). In 2023, the two institutions entered into an agreement concerning the Executive Doctorate in Commercial Diplomacy. [ref: First executive doctorate in commercial diplomacy, Times of Malta]

== Quality assurance ==
In 2024, GIOYA underwent an external quality assurance audit by the Malta Further and Higher Education Authority. The audit report was published on 21 October 2024.

The assessment found the institution compliant with the majority of the standards examined while identifying areas where improvements were required. The MFHEA subsequently published a follow-up report in November 2025. [ref: External Quality Assurance, Malta Further and Higher Education Authority]

== Institutional collaborations ==

=== University of Turin ===
GIOYA has a double-degree agreement with the University of Turin involving the university's degree programme in Information and Business Communication Management.

In July 2025, the University of Turin's Board of Directors approved the renewal of the agreement concerning the structured mobility programme leading to the award of the two degrees. [ref: Resoconto del Consiglio di Amministrazione del 18 luglio 2025, University of Turin]

=== UNITAR and NAVIGO ===
In 2025, GIOYA, NAVIGO and the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) announced a collaboration to develop an executive programme on sustainability and management in the maritime sector. [ref: NAVIGO, GIOYA and UNITAR Join Forces for an Executive Programme on Sustainability and Management in the Maritime Sector, United Nations Institute for Training and Research]

=== Sport-related education ===
In 2025, GIOYA and The Embassy Sport Premium launched an initiative focused on the professional transition of athletes following their competitive careers. [ref: NBA star Jose Calderón helping athletes' transition beyond sport, Times of Malta]

In March 2026, GIOYA signed a memorandum of understanding with the Authority for Integrity in Maltese Sport (AIMS) concerning education and professional development for athletes and sports professionals in Malta. [ref: AIMS signs Memorandum of Understanding with GIOYA Higher Education Institution, Times of Malta]

data.title: Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce
data.text:
The Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce (OJC or OJCC) is an American business membership organization serving Orthodox Jewish business owners and professionals. It was founded by Duvi Honig, who serves as its chief executive officer, and is headquartered on Wall Street in Manhattan. [ref: "MBDA and Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce Unite to Boost Economic Opportunities for MBEs." Minority Business Development Agency, January 2025. https://www.mbda.gov/news/press-releases/2025/01/mbda-and-orthodox-jewish-chamber-commerce-unite-boost-economic] [ref: "Democrats Are Left Off the Guest List at White House Hanukkah Party." The New York Times, December 7, 2017. https://www.nytimes.com/2017/12/07/us/politics/democrats-white-house-hanukkah-party.html] [ref: "Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce (OJC)." InfluenceWatch, Capital Research Center. https://www.influencewatch.org/organization/orthodox-jewish-chamber-of-commerce-ojc/] The chamber describes itself as a global umbrella of businesses of all sizes together with professionals, elected officials and communal activists, and says it exists to help members network with one another and to use that network to stimulate economic opportunity and shape public policy internationally. [ref: "About." Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce. https://www.ojchamber.com/about] Its activities combine business networking and expositions with public policy advocacy at municipal, state and federal level.

== History ==

The chamber grew out of Parnassah Network, an employment and business-networking organization Honig founded in Lakewood, New Jersey in response to the 2008 financial crisis. Beginning with a program pairing Torah study with job training and networking, the effort expanded into the Parnassah Expo, first held in Lakewood in 2012 and subsequently at the Meadowlands Exposition Center and in Edison. [ref: "Parnassah Expo To Be Held In Lakewood." The Yeshiva World, 2012. https://www.theyeshivaworld.com/news/human-interest/117861/parnassah-expo-this-sunday-in-lakewood.html] [ref: "Learn & Network Announces Nationwide Parnassah Expo At Meadowlands Expositions Center." The Lakewood Scoop, 2012. https://thelakewoodscoop.com/news/learn-network-announces-nationwide-parnassah-expo-at-meadowlands-expositions-center/] [ref: "PHOTOS & VIDEO: Parnassah Expo Draws Unprecedented Crowd." The Lakewood Scoop, 2013. https://thelakewoodscoop.com/news/photos-video-parnassah-expo-draws-unprecedented-crowd/] [ref: "Edison, NJ – Business Expo Hopes To Provide Parnassah Opportunities For Thousands." VINnews, January 22, 2014. https://vinnews.com/2014/01/22/edison-nj-business-expo-hopes-to-provide-parnassah-opportunities-for-thousands/] Honig has said the success of that network prompted the creation of a year-round chamber of commerce. [ref: "Orthodox Community's First Ever Chamber of Commerce Launched to Service the Jewish Business World." Matzav. http://matzav.com/orthodox-communitys-first-ever-chamber-of-commerce-launched-to-service-the-jewish-business-world/] Honig organized the first Parnassah Expo in February 2012 at Bais Yaakov High School in Lakewood, which organizers said drew more than 7,000 attendees. The following year the event moved to the Meadowlands Exposition Center in Secaucus as the Nationwide Parnassah Expo and Networking Event, occupying more than 60,000 square feet; attendees included New Jersey Lieutenant Governor Kim Guadagno, Lakewood Mayor Isaac Akerman and Assemblyman Gary Schaer. By its third year the expo had moved to Edison and was described by organizers as the largest business-to-business expo of its kind in the United States.

The chamber opened a New York City office in 2017 and launched an Israel division in Jerusalem in 2018, later opening an office in Tel Aviv and Bnei Brak. Its annual exposition was subsequently renamed the JBiz Expo.

== Activities ==
=== Expositions and conferences ===

The chamber's principal public event is the JBiz Expo and Business Conference, an annual business-to-business exposition. During the COVID-19 pandemic it held an outdoor exposition in Lakewood aimed at businesses affected by the pandemic. [ref: "In hard-hit New Jersey, Jewish group seeks to boost small businesses." JNS, November 24, 2020. https://www.jns.org/news/in-hard-hit-new-jersey-jewish-group-seeks-to-boost-small-businesses] In December 2025 it held the JBiz Economic Summit in Atlantic City, at which New Jersey Lieutenant Governor-elect Dale G. Caldwell made his first public appearance since the election and delivered a keynote; Governor Phil Murphy sent a recorded message and Senator Andy Kim sent a letter of commendation. [ref: "Lt. Governor–Elect Dr. Dale G. Caldwell Makes First Post-Election Public Appearance at JBiz Economic Forum." The Lakewood Scoop, December 14, 2025. https://thelakewoodscoop.com/news/lt-governor-elect-dr-dale-g-caldwell-makes-first-post-election-public-appearance-at-jbiz-economic-forum-as-governor-phil-murphy-acknowledges-chambers-eight-year-economic-partnershi/] The summit included panels on banking, artificial intelligence and New Jersey economic development, the last featuring the chief executive of the New Jersey Economic Development Authority.

=== Publishing ===

The chamber operates JBizNews, an online business news publication launched to cover business, economic development and public policy affecting the New York, New Jersey and Connecticut region. [ref: JBizNews. https://www.jbiznews.com/]

== World Trade Week NYC ==

The U.S. Department of Commerce appointed the chamber as a partner organization for World Trade Week NYC, an annual program promoting international trade in the New York metropolitan region. [ref: Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce partner listing, World Trade Week New York. https://www.worldtradeweeknyc.org/orthodox-jewish-chamber-of-commerce.html] The chamber hosts an annual World Trade Week reception in Manhattan in conjunction with the Greater New York Chamber of Commerce and the New York City mayor's office for international affairs, attended by consuls general, foreign trade ministers and U.S. trade officials. [ref: "Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce Host U.S. World Trade Week in NYC." Matzav, 2025. https://matzav.com/orthodox-jewish-chamber-of-commerce-host-u-s-world-trade-week-in-nyc-features-u-s-border-and-custom-control-tariff-policy-commisioner-honors-korean-air/]

== New Jersey Economic Development Day ==

In 2019 the New Jersey Legislature passed Senate Joint Resolution 72, designating the second Monday in May as New Jersey Economic Development Day; Governor Phil Murphy signed it on May 13, 2019. Senator Robert Singer, the lead sponsor, credited the chamber and Honig with prompting the effort, and said in 2025 that the designation had been inspired by Honig. [ref: "Governor Murphy Signs Resolution Designating 'Economic Development Day'." Office of the Governor, State of New Jersey, May 13, 2019. https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/news/562019/20190513e.shtml] [ref: "If you are one of New Jersey's 800,000 businesses, you need to know this." ROI-NJ, March 6, 2025. https://www.roi-nj.com/2025/03/06/industry/if-you-are-one-of-new-jerseys-800000-businesses-you-need-to-know-this/] The observance has continued to be marked in subsequent years, including through a pre-observance summit held at Georgian Court University in 2025.

== Government engagement ==
=== Department of Commerce ===

In April 2024 the Department of Commerce hosted the first National Chambers of Commerce Leaders Roundtable in Washington, D.C., convened by its Office of Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships in partnership with the chamber. Invitations were issued by the Secretary of Commerce's office to roughly 30 chamber presidents selected by the chamber's leadership, and the session was hosted by Deputy Secretary Don Graves and Eric Morrissette of the Minority Business Development Agency. [ref: "Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce Leads Mission to Washington DC with Top 30 US Chamber of Commerce Presidents." The Lakewood Scoop, April 2024. https://thelakewoodscoop.com/news/orthodox-jewish-chamber-of-commerce-leads-mission-to-washington-dc-with-top-30-us-chamber-of-commerce-presidents/] In a December 2024 letter, Graves credited the roundtable to Honig's initiative and described it as a bottom-up effort that empowered chamber leaders nationally. [ref: "LANDMARK VICTORY in USA: Orthodox Jewish Businesses Gain Federal Minority Status." JFeed, January 2025 — reports the contents of Deputy Secretary Graves's letter. https://www.jfeed.com/jewish-world/sptu1y]

=== Minority Business Development Agency ===

On January 13, 2025, in the final week of the Biden administration, the Minority Business Development Agency and the chamber signed a memorandum of understanding at the Department of Commerce, described by the agency as intended to improve access to capital, contracts and global markets for minority business enterprises in the Jewish community. The agreement was reported as extending minority business enterprise recognition to Jewish-owned businesses, and professional accounting and tax firms subsequently published client guidance on the change. [ref: "US government agrees to confer 'minority' status on Jewish-owned businesses." JNS, January 2025. https://www.jns.org/us-government-agrees-to-confer-minority-status-on-jewish-owned-businesses/] [ref: "Jews react strongly to a new minority designation for US Jewish businesses." The Jerusalem Post, 2025. https://www.jpost.com/diaspora/article-819629] [ref: "Understanding the New Minority-Owned Business Designation for Jewish-Owned Businesses." Bonadio & Co., February 2025. https://www.bonadio.com/article/understanding-new-minority-owned-business-designation-jewish-owned-businesses/] [ref: Kahn Tax Law, client advisory, January 2025. https://www.kahntaxlaw.com/jews-granted-minority-status-by-u-s-department-of-commerce-opening-access-to-billions-in-benefits/] The designation drew mixed reactions within the Jewish community.

In March 2025 an executive order signed by President Donald Trump named the agency among several federal entities to be eliminated to the extent permitted by law; Congress had permanently authorized it in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, and members of Congress objected. [ref: Meng, Grace. Statement on the executive order concerning MBDA, March 2025. https://meng.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/meng-issues-statement-executive-order-shutting-down-minority-business] [ref: "Trump seeks to gut a minority business agency decried by white conservatives." March 17, 2025. https://www.ms.now/top-stories/latest/trump-minority-business-development-agency-dei-rcna196756]

=== Department of Health and Human Services ===

Honig took part in the Department of Health and Human Services roundtable on Lyme disease convened by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on December 15, 2025, and was subsequently appointed to the evaluation panel of the TOPx HHS Tech Sprint for AI and Invisible Illness. [ref: "WTAS: Secretary Kennedy Convenes Lyme Disease Patients and Providers to Announce New Diagnostic Efforts." HHS, December 16, 2025. https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/wtas-secretary-kennedy-convenes-lyme-disease-patients-providers-announce-new-diagnostic-efforts.html] [ref: Duvi Honig, person page, C-SPAN. https://www.c-span.org/person/duvi-honig/147160/] [ref: "Duvi Honig appointed to HHS AI evaluation panel." Israel National News, 2026. https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/430410]

== Legal advocacy ==

The chamber has joined amicus curiae briefs before the Supreme Court of the United States as part of coalitions of Orthodox Jewish organizations, most prepared by the National Jewish Commission on Law and Public Affairs and authored by attorney Nathan Lewin.

In Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018) it joined a brief arguing that Jewish law can forbid meaningful participation in conduct it prohibits. [ref: Brief amicus curiae of COLPA on behalf of Orthodox Jewish organizations, Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission, No. 16-111, September 7, 2017 — chamber named at page 2. https://www.scotusblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/16-111_tsac_the_national_jewish_commission_on_law_and_public_affairs_colpa_.pdf] In Groff v. DeJoy (2023) it joined a brief asking the Court to overrule the standard set in Trans World Airlines v. Hardison, under which employers could refuse religious accommodation at more than minimal cost; the Court ruled unanimously for Groff, adopting a substantially higher threshold in a decision described as significantly expanding protections for religious employees. [ref: Brief amici curiae of COLPA and other Jewish organizations, Groff v. DeJoy, No. 22-174, February 28, 2023 — chamber named at page 2. https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/22/22-174/255774/20230228124631518_22-174%20tsac%20COLPA%20Final.pdf] [ref: Groff v. DeJoy, decided June 29, 2023. https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/22-174_k536.pdf] [ref: "Groff v. DeJoy is the rare Supreme Court decision that every Jew can celebrate." Jewish Telegraphic Agency, July 12, 2023. https://www.jta.org/2023/07/12/ideas/groff-v-dejoy-is-the-rare-supreme-court-decision-that-every-jew-can-celebrate] The chamber has also joined briefs in Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Small v. Memphis Light, Gas & Water, a case on the ministerial exception, the emergency application in Yeshiva University v. YU Pride Alliance, and Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael v. Education for a Just Peace in the Middle East. [ref: "Coalition Of Jewish Organizations Files Brief In Supreme Court Religious Freedom Case." Agudath Israel of America, 2020. https://agudah.org/coalition-of-jewish-organizations-files-brief-in-supreme-court-religious-freedom-case] [ref: "Orthodox Jewish Coalition Supports Sweeping Application of the 'Ministerial Exception'." Agudath Israel of America, 2020. https://agudah.org/orthodox-jewish-coalition-supports-sweeping-application-of-the-ministerial-exception-in-a-supreme-court-case] [ref: COLPA amicus brief, Small v. Memphis Light, Gas & Water, No. 19-1388, 2020. https://lewinlewin.com/about/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Small_v_-Memphis-No_19-1388-COLPA_Amicus_Brief.pdf] [ref: Amicus brief, Yeshiva University v. YU Pride Alliance, No. 22A184, September 2022. https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/22/22A184/236926/20220901162958571_22A184%20Amicus%20Brief%20National%20Orthodox%20Jewish%20Organizations.pdf] [ref: Amicus brief, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael v. Education for a Just Peace in the Middle East, No. 23-208, December 2023. https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/23/23-208/293901/20231220154601336_23-208%20Amicis%20COC%20PDFA.pdf]

== Multicultural Business Coalition ==
Honig co-founded the Multicultural Business Coalition, an alliance of ethnic and immigrant-led chambers of commerce, and serves as its secretary. [ref: Fickenscher, Lisa. "Mamdani's city-owned supermarkets to face off against new immigrant-led business group that has already raised more than $1M, prepared to sue." The New York Post, May 13, 2026. https://nypost.com/2026/05/13/business/mamdanis-city-owned-supermarkets-to-face-off-against-new-immigrant-led-business-group-that-has-already-raised-more-than-1m-prepared-to-sue/] Formed as a 501(c)(4) advocacy organization, the coalition brought together roughly 50 to 65 member chambers representing Asian, African, Caribbean, Hispanic, Middle Eastern, South Asian and Jewish business communities, concentrated in the New York and New Jersey region. [ref: "Multicultural Business Coalition (MBC) Announces…" Greater New York Chamber of Commerce, 2026. https://chamber.nyc/news/142784]
In 2026 the coalition became a prominent opponent of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's proposal for city-owned grocery stores, arguing that subsidized municipal stores would compete unfairly with immigrant-owned grocers and bodegas. Its campaign received coverage in Time, the New York Post, Spectrum News NY1 and Fox Business. [ref: "What We Know About Mamdani's First Planned City-Owned Grocery Stores." Time, May 21, 2026. https://time.com/article/2026/05/21/mamdani-city-owned-grocery-stores-east-harlem-manhattan-the-bronx/] [ref: "Grocery groups planning fight against city grocery stores." Spectrum News NY1, May 29, 2026. https://ny1.com/nyc/all-boroughs/politics/2026/05/29/grocery-groups-planning-fight-against-city-grocery-stores] [ref: "Business owner says NYC's grocery store initiative is 'embarrassing'." Fox Business, May 29, 2026. https://www.foxbusiness.com/video/6396998831112]

== International activity ==

In December 2021 the chamber signed a memorandum of understanding with the Panama-US Chamber of Commerce at a reception in New York, witnessed by Panama's consul general, aimed at promoting trade between the two countries; it had signed a comparable agreement involving Turkish officials earlier that year. [ref: "Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce signs MOU with Panama." Israel National News, December 13, 2021. https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/318585] At its 2025 World Trade Week event the Korean government recognized Honig as a trade ambassador for that year's World Korean Business Convention.

== Humanitarian activity ==

Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the chamber organized an emergency evacuation fleet of buses, ambulances and other vehicles to move civilians out of the conflict zone and assist them at border crossings. [ref: Reporting on the chamber's Ukraine evacuation fleet, Asbury Park Press, March 15, 2022. https://www.app.com/story/news/world/2022/03/15/orthodox-jewish-chamber-evacuation-fleet-ukraine-refugees/7003432001/] [ref: "Orthodox Jewish Chamber Creates First Emergency Evacuation Fleet in Ukraine." The Lakewood Scoop, March 2022. https://thelakewoodscoop.com/news/orthodox-jewish-chamber-creates-first-emergency-evacuation-fleet-in-ukraine/] Israel's then-Diaspora Affairs Minister Nachman Shai wrote to the chamber in December 2022 acknowledging the operation. [ref: Letter from Israel's Diaspora Affairs Minister Nachman Shai, December 1, 2022. (unpublished; supporting only)]

== Holocaust education ==

Through the Morris Katz Foundation the chamber distributes the Presidential Collection, a series of portraits of United States presidents by Morris Katz, a Holocaust survivor who emigrated to the United States in 1949. In February 2022 the New Jersey Commission on Holocaust Education circulated a memorandum to school administrators statewide describing the collection as a free classroom resource, and the New Jersey Department of Education hosts the accompanying materials on its Holocaust education website. [ref: New Jersey Commission on Holocaust Education materials, New Jersey Department of Education. https://www.nj.gov/education/holocaust/curriculumn/addresources/]

== Starbucks boycott ==

In October 2023, following a since-deleted social media post by Starbucks Workers United expressing solidarity with Palestinians shortly after the Hamas attack on Israel, the chamber called for a widespread boycott of Starbucks, issuing a statement headlined "Drinking a Cup of Starbucks is Drinking a Cup of Jewish Blood." [ref: "Jewish orgs. call to boycott Starbucks over union's support of Hamas." The Jerusalem Post, October 18, 2023. https://www.jpost.com/business-and-innovation/banking-and-finance/article-768968] [ref: "Why Starbucks is being targeted on Israel-Gaza by both sides." The Forward, October 2023. https://forward.com/fast-forward/574222/starbucks-protests-israel-gaza-union-boycott/] Starbucks had publicly condemned the attack and disavowed the union's statement, and the union and the company subsequently filed competing lawsuits.

The chamber said that former Starbucks chief executive Howard Schultz had contacted it and that the company would supply a list of the roughly 300 unionized stores. [ref: "Starbucks' Founder Schultz Phones Chief of Jewish Chamber of Commerce to End Boycott." VINnews, October 19, 2023. https://vinnews.com/2023/10/19/read-after-boycott-starbucks-sends-letter-to-orthodox-jewish-chamber-of-commerce/] Workers United then filed an unfair labor practice charge with the National Labor Relations Board alleging that Starbucks had shared a list of unionized stores and addresses with the chamber in order to initiate a boycott of those stores; a Starbucks spokesperson denied that the company had provided the list. [ref: "Starbucks accused of assisting boycott of union stores." Restaurant Business, October 20, 2023. https://www.restaurantbusinessonline.com/operations/starbucks-accused-assisting-boycott-union-stores] [ref: "Starbucks Hit With Claim Alleging Boycott List To Jewish Org." Law360, October 20, 2023. https://www.law360.com/employmentauthority/articles/1735434] The chamber later called off the boycott.

== Organization ==

The chamber is headquartered on Wall Street in Manhattan and has operated divisions covering regions including Israel and the U.S. West Coast, as well as sector-specific groups. It states that small businesses make up more than 80 percent of its membership, and that its Executive Public Policy Committee conducts advocacy with the White House, Congress and the Knesset.

data.title: Kanaya Maru
data.text:
The Kanaya Maru is a Japanese roll-on/roll-off passenger and vehicle carrier operated by Tokyo-Wan Ferry.

== Construction ==
The ship was laid down in August 1991 and completed in February 1992 by the Niihama Shipbuilding yard in Tamano, Japan. Built as a steel-hulled roll-on/roll-off passenger and vehicle carrier, the vessel was specifically designed to handle the choppy, heavily trafficked waters of the Uraga Channel at the mouth of Tokyo Bay. [ref: Kanaya Maru (3rd Generation) Vessel Specifications, Wakanatsu Marine Database]

== Career ==
The ship entered service in April 1992 [ref: ], operating on the route between Kurihama Port in Yokosuka, Kanagawa Prefecture, and Kanaya Port in Futtsu, Chiba. For over three decades, the vessel has served alongside its sister ship, the Shirahama Maru [ref: ], as a vital marine bypass. [ref: 料金案内と船内設備のご案内, Tokyo-Wan Ferry Official]

== Maintenance==
To comply with domestic Japanese maritime safety regulations and regular ship inspection codes, the ship undergoes mandatory drydocking procedures once per year. [ref: 空飛ぶ船ジェットフォイルの「翼」その意外すぎる形 ドックでの検査, Traffic News] The annual overhaul typically takes place in December at the Kanazashi Heavy Industries shipyard (Kanasashi Shipbuilding yard) located in Shimizu Port, Shizuoka Prefecture. [ref: 東京湾フェリー公式アカウント: かなや丸ドック報告, Tokyo-Wan Ferry Official Instagram] During this offline period, which spans approximately two to three weeks, the ferry is removed from the Uraga Channel route entirely, triggering temporary timetable adjustments for the fleet. Drydock maintenance protocols include complete hull sandblasting and anti-fouling repainting, detailed safety inspections of the lower bow thruster units, dual-propeller adjustments, steering rudder overhauls, and deep-engine compartment load tests. [ref: かなや丸ドライドック入渠の様子, Tokyo-Wan Ferry Official Facebook]

== References ==

data.text:

= Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku =

=== Executive Director | Entrepreneur | Philanthropist | Leadership Advocate ===

== Professional Overview ==
Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku is an entrepreneur, executive leader, philanthropist, author, and social-impact advocate whose work spans business development, FMCG distribution, technology, education, youth empowerment, women’s advancement, and community development.

She is the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Mertesacker Nigeria Limited, a business operating within the fast-moving consumer goods and distribution sector. She is also associated with SackerTech, a technology-driven enterprise focused on digital transformation, business systems, and innovative solutions.

Beyond business, she is the Founder and Executive Director of the Minugiano Onduku Foundation, a nonprofit organisation established to inspire change and empower lives through education, youth development, healthcare support, community development, and practical empowerment initiatives.

Her leadership philosophy is built around the belief that sustainable progress is achieved when people are equipped with knowledge, opportunities, structure, and the confidence to create meaningful change.

== Early Life and Background ==
Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku was born on March 14, 1981, in Okoroba, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Her early life and personal journey have shaped her commitment to resilience, service, discipline, faith, and community advancement.

Her professional and personal story reflects a transition from humble beginnings to executive leadership, entrepreneurship, philanthropy, and public advocacy. Her experiences have influenced her belief that a person’s starting point should not determine the extent of their future.

== Education and Professional Development ==
Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku’s educational journey reflects continuous academic advancement, professional development, leadership training, and lifelong learning.

Her educational qualifications include:

l Doctor of Business Administration (DBA), Information Technology — European Institute of Applied Science and Management.

l Master of Business Administration (MBA), Logistics and Supply Chain Management — European Global School–University.

l ChLogMP, Chartered Institute of Management and Leadership — Commonwealth of Kentucky, USA, 2025

l Bachelor of Science (B.Sc.), Accounting — University of Port Harcourt

l First School Leaving Certificate (FSLC) — State Primary School, Churchill, Rivers State, Nigeria

She has also undertaken leadership, entrepreneurship, and professional development programmes, including:

l Basic Certificate Course at Word of Faith Bible Institute.

l Leadership Certificate Course at Word of Faith Bible Institute.

l Entrepreneurship Masterclass at Garden City Premier Business School.

l Certified Management Consultant qualification.

l Fellowship of the Institute of Management Consultants.

l Fellowship of the Institute of Professional Managers and Administrators.

l Honorary Special Marshal recognition with the Federal Road Safety Corps.

Her continuous investment in professional development reflects her commitment to leadership excellence, organisational growth, and lifelong learning.

== Professional Career ==

=== Mertesacker Nigeria Limited ===
Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku is the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Mertesacker Nigeria Limited.

The company operates within the FMCG distribution and business services space, with activities connected to retail, wholesale distribution, logistics, and consumer products.

Under her leadership, the company’s work is shaped by a focus on:

Operational efficiency.

Distribution excellence.

Customer service.

Business growth.

Team development.

Strategic partnerships.

Sustainable enterprise development.

Her leadership approach combines commercial discipline with people development, enabling the organisation to pursue growth while strengthening its internal systems and relationships.

=== SackerTech ===
Minugiano is also connected with SackerTech, a technology-focused enterprise committed to digital transformation and business innovation.

SackerTech’s work includes technology-enabled business solutions, enterprise systems, process improvement, and tools designed to help organisations improve accountability, productivity, and operational performance.

Her involvement reflects her interest in connecting traditional business structures with technology, innovation, and modern management practices.

== Entrepreneurship and Business Development ==
Minugiano’s entrepreneurial interests extend across consumer products, technology, logistics, business systems, and enterprise development.

Her wider business interests have included initiatives connected to consumer-focused brands, digital business solutions, enterprise resource planning, and business support.

She is passionate about helping organisations move from informal operations to structured and sustainable business models. Her approach places emphasis on:

Clear business systems.

Strong leadership structures.

Effective communication.

Customer-focused operations.

Accountability.

Innovation.

Long-term sustainability.

She also mentors young entrepreneurs and women in business, encouraging them to develop practical skills, strengthen their confidence, and build businesses capable of creating value and employment.

== Minugiano Onduku Foundation ==

=== Founder and Executive Director ===
The Minugiano Onduku Foundation was established in 2023 as a philanthropic organisation focused on transforming compassion into action and creating opportunities for individuals and communities to thrive.

The Foundation operates under the guiding philosophy:

=== Inspiring Change, Empowering Lives. ===
Its work is centred on education, healthcare access, community development, youth empowerment, and practical support for vulnerable people.

The Foundation’s stated areas of focus include:

i. Education for empowerment.

ii. Healthcare access and wellbeing.

iii. Community development.

iv. Vocational training.

v. Youth development.

vi. Women’s advancement.

vii. Community support and humanitarian assistance.

== Foundation Projects and Community Impact ==

=== 1. Education and Scholarship Support ===
Education is one of the central pillars of the Minugiano Onduku Foundation.

Through its educational initiatives, the Foundation supports students and young people who may face financial, social, or infrastructural barriers to completing their education.

Its education-focused work includes:

Scholarship support.

School outreach.

Educational resources.

Learning support.

Youth development programmes.

School infrastructure assistance.

Skills and capacity-building initiatives.

The Foundation’s approach recognises education as a tool for breaking cycles of poverty and helping individuals develop the confidence and skills required to contribute meaningfully to society.

=== 2. Bayelsa Medical University Scholarship and Borehole Project ===
One of the Foundation’s documented initiatives involved students of Bayelsa Medical University.

The project included the provision of a borehole to improve access to potable water for students, as well as the award of five scholarships.

According to the Foundation, the borehole was intended to benefit more than 1,000 students, while the scholarship component prioritised vulnerable students from low-income families. The Foundation also stated that the scholarships were distributed through a fair raffle process because many of the applicants faced similar economic circumstances.

This project reflects the Foundation’s combined approach to education and community wellbeing by addressing both academic support and basic infrastructure needs.

=== 3. MOF Goes to School ===
The “MOF Goes to School” initiative forms part of the Foundation’s educational outreach activities.

The programme is designed to take support directly to schools and learning communities. Its broader purpose is to encourage learning, improve access to educational resources, and strengthen the relationship between the Foundation and young people.

The initiative aligns with the Foundation’s commitment to school support, youth development, and educational empowerment.

=== 4. HERITAGE Programme ===
The HERITAGE Programme is described as the flagship initiative of the Minugiano Onduku Foundation.

Its central theme is:

=== Reclaiming Heritage. Building Futures. ===
HERITAGE is designed as an immersive learning and development experience that brings together students, educators, parents, and community leaders. It combines practical learning, cultural workshops, mentorship, leadership development, and opportunities for participants to present their work.

The programme is structured around four major learning tracks:

==== Graphics Design ====
Participants are introduced to visual communication, creative design, and the process of transforming ideas into practical design outputs.

==== Digital Marketing and Content Creation ====
This track focuses on content development, digital communication, audience building, personal branding, and the use of digital platforms to create opportunities.

==== Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity ====
The programme introduces young people to emerging technology, artificial intelligence, digital safety, and the importance of responsible technology use.

==== Civic Leadership ====
This track explores public speaking, governance, community organising, leadership, and the role of young people in shaping their communities.

Beyond technical learning, HERITAGE includes cultural immersion, mentorship circles, leadership activities, and a showcase where participants present their work and celebrate their progress.

The programme’s 2026 editions were scheduled for Port Harcourt and Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, reflecting the Foundation’s interest in reaching young people across the region.

=== 5. Youth Empowerment and Skills Development ===
Youth empowerment is a major part of Minugiano’s philanthropic vision.

Through the Foundation’s programmes, young people are encouraged to develop practical skills, discover their interests, build confidence, and explore opportunities for personal and professional growth.

The Foundation’s youth-focused approach includes:

Ø Digital skills.

Ø Leadership development.

Ø Entrepreneurship education.

Ø Mentorship.

Ø Career exposure.

Ø Cultural awareness.

Ø Creative development.

Ø Community participation.

The emphasis is not only on training but also on helping young people understand their capacity to become responsible leaders and contributors to society.

=== 6. Community Development and Infrastructure ===
The Foundation’s community development work focuses on practical interventions that respond to identified needs.

Its stated community development interests include sustainable infrastructure, vocational training, empowerment, and initiatives that promote self-reliance.

The borehole project at Bayelsa Medical University is an example of this approach, as it addressed a basic infrastructure need while supporting the wellbeing of students.

=== 7. Humanitarian and Community Support ===
On March 24, 2024, the Minugiano Onduku Foundation visited Living Faith Church, GRA Phase 3, Port Harcourt, as part of a support initiative connected to an anonymous donor.

The Foundation assisted with the disbursement of ₦2 million to selected youth workers in the church. The process reportedly involved interviews and background checks to ensure that the intended beneficiaries met the donor’s requirements.

The Foundation also presented bags of rice, beans, and garri to the church and its members ahead of the Easter holiday.

This intervention reflects the Foundation’s willingness to support both structured empowerment initiatives and immediate community needs.

=== 8. Women’s Advancement and Entrepreneurial Support ===
Minugiano is committed to helping women develop confidence, skills, and economic independence.

Her work with women and entrepreneurs focuses on practical knowledge, leadership, business structure, and access to opportunities.

She encourages women to:

1. Build sustainable enterprises.

2. Develop financial awareness.

3. Improve their professional confidence.

4. Strengthen their leadership capacity.

5. Participate in community development.

6. Create opportunities for others.

Her advocacy is connected to the broader belief that empowering women strengthens families, businesses, and communities.

=== 9. Giano Karaoke Idol ===

=== Giano Karaoke Idol therefore stands not simply as a karaoke competition, but as part of Minugiano’s broader legacy of discovering potential, nurturing talent, and opening doors. Its story is ultimately a story about what can happen when young people are given a platform, when their abilities are taken seriously, and when someone is willing to invest in the possibilities within them. ===

=== The initiative also reflects a recurring theme throughout Minugiano’s work: empowerment through opportunity. Whether through entrepreneurship, philanthropy, mentorship, or creative development, her approach has consistently centred on creating platforms that enable people—particularly young people—to recognise their potential and pursue meaningful pathways for growth. ===

=== For Minugiano, these journeys speak to something larger than competition victories. They illustrate the potential of creating grassroots platforms where young talent can take its first meaningful steps toward wider opportunities. Giano Karaoke Idol became part of that journey by bringing young performers into an environment where talent was celebrated, confidence was cultivated, and ambition was given room to grow. ===

=== The impact of this vision became particularly significant in the journeys of Idyl and Pere Jason, who went on to achieve national recognition through The Voice Nigeria. Idyl, whose real name is Daniel Diongoli, emerged as the winner of The Voice Nigeria Season 2 in 2017. Pere Jason later emerged as the winner of The Voice Nigeria Season 4 in 2023. These achievements stand as notable milestones in the journeys of talents associated with the platform. ===

=== Over the years, the platform became associated with the development of talents including Idyl, Pere Jason, and Kendrix, providing an early platform through which their musical abilities could be expressed and nurtured. Their journeys represent the broader purpose behind Minugiano’s initiative—to create opportunities for young people whose abilities might otherwise remain undiscovered. ===

=== From its inception, Giano Karaoke Idol was built around a simple but powerful conviction: talent can change the course of a young person’s life when it is discovered early, nurtured intentionally, and given the opportunity to flourish. Through the platform, emerging singers were encouraged to step beyond their comfort zones, build confidence, develop their vocal abilities, perform before audiences, and experience the discipline and exposure required to pursue music professionally. ===

=== Among Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku’s most distinctive contributions to youth development is the creation of Giano Karaoke Idol, a talent-discovery and development platform established to give young people more than a stage—it gave them an opportunity to be seen, heard, encouraged, and developed. ===

=== 10. Mentorship and Human Capital Development ===
Minugiano’s leadership extends beyond organisational management to the development of people.

Across her professional and philanthropic activities, she places importance on mentorship, discipline, teamwork, confidence, and continuous improvement.

She is particularly interested in supporting:

l Young entrepreneurs.

l Women in business.

l Students.

l Emerging leaders.

l Creative talents.

l Community volunteers.

Her approach is based on the conviction that people become more effective when they are given guidance, encouragement, practical tools, and opportunities to lead.

== HER VOICE MATTERS ==
HER VOICE MATTERS is a women-centred initiative associated with Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku.

The initiative creates space for women to discuss their experiences, express their truths, reflect on their challenges, and engage in meaningful conversations around identity, leadership, confidence, family, society, and personal growth.

Its central message is connected to the importance of listening to women and recognising their voices as valuable contributions to social and community development.

Through HER VOICE MATTERS, Minugiano’s public advocacy extends beyond business and philanthropy into conversations about women’s experiences, personal agency, and societal participation.

== Leadership Philosophy ==
Minugiano’s leadership philosophy is anchored in:

Ø Faith.

Ø Integrity.

Ø Discipline.

Ø Service.

Ø Collaboration.

Ø Innovation.

Ø Resilience.

Ø Accountability.

Ø Human-capital development.

She believes leadership should produce measurable value, develop people, and create opportunities that outlive the leader.

Her approach combines commercial responsibility with social impact. In business, she focuses on structure, efficiency, growth, and sustainability. In philanthropy, she focuses on compassion, inclusion, education, empowerment, and community transformation.

== Faith and Personal Values ==
Minugiano is a Christian and describes her personal philosophy through the expression:

=== Giving is Living. ===
Her faith influences her approach to service, leadership, family, and philanthropy.

She views generosity not simply as the distribution of resources but as the intentional creation of opportunities, dignity, hope, and long-term empowerment.

== Authorship ==
Minugiano is the author of the book Against the Tide: The Dream of the Waterside Girl.

The work is presented as a story of resilience, faith, determination, and transformation. It reflects themes connected to humble beginnings, personal development, courage, and the pursuit of purpose.

== Recognition and Professional Standing ==
Minugiano’s professional profile includes recognition through management consultancy, professional fellowships, leadership training, and service-related honours.

Her documented professional distinctions include:

n Certified Management Consultant.

n Fellow, Institute of Management Consultants.

n Fellow, Institute of Professional Managers and Administrators.

n Honorary Special Marshal, Federal Road Safety Corps.

n Leadership and entrepreneurship training through recognised institutions.

Specific award titles, dates, awarding bodies, and official citations should be added to the profile only when independently verified through appropriate documentation.

== Public Profile and Continuing Work ==
Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku continues to operate across business, philanthropy, leadership advocacy, and community development.

Her work brings together enterprise development and social responsibility, with a focus on building systems, developing people, and creating practical opportunities.

Through Mertesacker Nigeria Limited, SackerTech, the Minugiano Onduku Foundation, HERITAGE, HER VOICE MATTERS, and related initiatives, she continues to promote a model of leadership that connects business growth with education, empowerment, and community impact.

Her public identity is defined by three central commitments:

=== Building Enterprises. ===

=== Developing People. ===

=== Transforming Communities. ===

== Conclusion ==
Minugiano Abrahams Salome Onduku’s professional journey reflects the intersection of entrepreneurship, leadership, philanthropy, faith, and service.

From business operations and technology-enabled enterprise development to scholarships, school support, youth training, community infrastructure, humanitarian assistance, and women’s advocacy, her work demonstrates a commitment to turning ideas into practical outcomes.

Her enduring philosophy is that leadership should not be measured only by personal achievement, but also by the number of people empowered, the systems strengthened, and the communities positively affected.

data.title: Gas Gang Group of Companies
data.text:
Gas Gang Group of Companies, also known as Gas Gang, is a privately held energy infrastructure investment platform based in Fort Worth, Texas, United States. The company is described in business database profiles as focusing on natural gas infrastructure, power generation, and related energy assets. [ref: Gas Gang Group of Companies, Crunchbase]

The platform operates through separately organized investment funds and affiliated entities. Gas Gang, LLC is identified in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) as the sponsor and investment manager of Gas Gang Fund IV, L.P. [ref: Gas Gang Fund IV, L.P. — Form D/A, U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]

== History and organization ==

Gas Gang is a private infrastructure investment platform headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas. The database identifies Matthew Brown as its founder.

The company uses separately organized investment vehicles for its investment activities. Each fund is a distinct legal entity with its own governing documents, assets, liabilities, and investment arrangements.

== Management ==

Matthew Brown is identified in the SEC filing for Gas Gang Fund IV, L.P. as the manager of Gas Gang Fund IV GP, LLC, the fund's general partner, and as the person who controls Gas Gang, LLC, the sponsor and investment manager. Tristen York is listed as the Interim-President.

Brown is listed in management roles associated with Gas Gang Fund IV and Gas Gang Fund V. [ref: Gas Gang Fund IV, L.P., Crunchbase] [ref: Gas Gang Fund V, L.P., Crunchbase]

== Investment strategy ==

Gas Gang as an infrastructure investment platform focused on natural gas, power generation, and related energy infrastructure in the United States and selected international markets.

The company's stated investment approach emphasizes assets that may generate contracted or recurring revenues. The arrangements described in its company profile include long-term power purchase agreements, tolling arrangements, capacity payments, transportation and storage contracts, equipment leases, and offtake agreements.

The investment categories described in the profile include:

* Natural gas infrastructure: pipelines, gathering and transportation systems, compression and processing facilities, and underground storage.
* Liquefied natural gas: LNG facilities and terminal infrastructure.
* Power generation: gas-fired generation, turbines, modular generation equipment, and related grid infrastructure.
* Equipment finance and leasing: financing arrangements for energy infrastructure equipment.
* Project and structured finance: potential investments through equity, preferred equity, structured credit, project debt, equipment finance, leases, and joint ventures.

The company profile describes an investment approach that considers contractual cash flows, asset value, infrastructure positioning, counterparty quality, and contractual protections. These descriptions represent the stated strategy and do not independently establish that the company has completed investments in every listed category.

== Investment funds ==

=== Gas Gang Fund IV, L.P. ===

Gas Gang Fund IV, L.P. is a Delaware limited partnership registered with the SEC as an issuer of securities. Its Form D/A filing, dated 14 August 2026, identifies Gas Gang Fund IV GP, LLC as its general partner and Gas Gang, LLC as its sponsor and investment manager.

The filing reports a proposed offering of US$125 million and a minimum investment of US$5 million. The filing indicated that the first sale had yet to occur and reported no capital sold at that point. Consequently, the offering amount should not be interpreted as capital raised.

The filing identifies Matthew Brown as the manager of the fund's general partner.

=== Gas Gang Fund V, L.P. ===

Gas Gang Fund V, L.P. is a Delaware limited partnership associated with Gas Gang, LLC. A Form D filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), dated 8 September 2026, reports a proposed securities offering of US$450 million. [ref: Gas Gang Fund V, L.P. — Form D, U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]

The US$450 million figure represents the reported offering amount, not necessarily capital raised or assets under management. The fund's sponsor, investment manager, general partner, and management arrangements should be described according to the fund's regulatory disclosures and governing documents.

== Headquarters ==

Crunchbase lists Gas Gang Group of Companies in Fort Worth, Texas, United States. The SEC filing for Gas Gang Fund IV, L.P. also identifies a business address in Fort Worth.

Rivan IT Institute (also known as RivanCyber Training Institute) is a private information technology training provider based in Makati, Metro Manila, Philippines. It offers short-course "bootcamp" preparation for industry certifications in computer networking, cybersecurity and cloud computing, most prominently the Cisco Certified Network Associate (CCNA) examination.

== History ==
Rivan was founded by Robert Victor, a network engineer and instructor who personally taught many of the institute's early CCNA classes. According to the company, it was established in 1999.

== Programs ==
The institute's best-known program is an intensive CCNA course consisting of five days of on-site instruction followed by a period of guided home-laboratory practice. It also offers preparatory courses for the Cisco Certified Network Professional (CCNP) and CompTIA Security+ certifications, as well as training related to Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Linux, VMware and Fortinet products.

== Locations ==
The institute's main facility is in La Paz, Makati. It also operates a branch in Cebu.
