data.title: Lyubov Zapolskaya
data.text:
Lyubov Nikolaevna Zapolskaya (;; 7 August 1871 – 3 November 1943) was a Russian mathematician and the first woman to receive a master's degree in mathematics from a Russian university.

== Early life and education ==
Zapolskaya was born on 7 August 1871 in the village of Bigildino in the Ryazan Governorate of the Russian Empire to secondary school teachers Sofya Zapolskaya (née Kochurova) and Nikolay Zapolsky.

When she was five years old, her family moved to St. Petersburg, where her father taught Russian language and literature at the Second Military Gymnasium, and her mother taught at Vasileostrovskaya Girls' Gymnasium.

In 1880, she enrolled in the after receiving financial support from her cousin. She studied there for seven years and completed her studies in 1887 at the age of sixteen, receiving a gold medal for her grades and academic achievements. She then took a three-year pedagogical course for women and received another medal for her efforts.

She then enrolled in the mathematics department of St. Petersburg Higher Courses for Women in late 1890. There, she studied analytic geometry, calculus, physics, and astronomy, and she developed an enthusiasm for higher algebra. She completed her studies in 1894. Russian universities did not admit women at the time, so Zapolskaya, inspired by Sofya Kovalevskaya, continued her education abroad. After obtaining permission from Ivan Delyanov, the Minister of Public Education, she traveled to Germany in October 1895 and attended the University of Göttingen.

At Göttingen, Zapolskaya studied under David Hilbert and Felix Klein. Her research focused on relatively abelian cubic number fields. Her research drew from Hilbert's prior work on algebraic number fields and his influential The Theory of Algebraic Number Fields. Her thesis defense took place in 1902, with Hilbert praising Zapolskaya's work, and she was awarded a Doctor of Philosophy in Mathematics, magna cum laude. She subsequently returned to Russia to pursue a career in teaching.

== Career ==
On 19 November 1902, Zapolskaya attended a meeting held by the Moscow Mathematical Society and presented her thesis. Her work impressed the attendees, including Nikolai Bugaev and Sergey Chaplygin, and she was made a member of the Moscow Mathematical Society.

From 1903, she taught at the Higher Women's Courses in Moscow and at the Imperial Moscow University. The university published her thesis in 1905 and invited her to defend it. She accepted and defended it on 8 March 1905, with and Dmitri Egorov acting as the examiners. She succeeded and was granted a master's degree, becoming the first woman to receive a master's in mathematics in Russia. Following her defense, she became a professor at the university.

== Later years and death ==
Zapolskaya died in Ryazan on 3 November 1943. She was buried at the Skorbyashchenskoye Cemetery.

David S. Lawrence is the Fred Eshelman Distinguished Professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He is known for his work in chemical biology, developing strategies for the design of self-assembling molecular systems, methods for detecting and manipulating protein kinase activity, and the construction of light-responsive proteins and drug delivery systems. [ref: Lawrence, David – APS2025] [ref: David S. Lawrence: Biology and Biochemistry Researcher – H-Index, Publications & Awards, Research.com]

== Education ==
Lawrence received his Bachelor of Science degree in the biological sciences from the University of California at Irvine. He earned his Doctor of Philosophy in chemistry from the University of California at Los Angeles in 1982, where he pursued the total synthesis of steroids and Vitamin D analogs. [ref: Vitamin B12: A Tunable, Long Wavelength, Light-Responsive Platform for Launching Therapeutic Agents, Accounts of Chemical Research]

== Career ==
Lawrence was a National Institutes of Health postdoctoral fellow at the Rockefeller University in New York City. He subsequently served as a professor in the Department of Chemistry at the State University of New York at Buffalo for 10 years. He joined the Department of Biochemistry at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in 1996, and then moved to the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 2007 as the Fred Eshelman Distinguished Professor. He was elected a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 2005. [ref: Faculty in the American Association for the Advancement of Science, UNC Research] He holds affiliated appointments across multiple schools at the University of North Carolina and chaired the Division of Chemical Biology and Medicinal Chemistry in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy from 2011 to 2025.

== Research ==
Lawrence's research in chemical biology explores the design of molecules that emulate or control biological processes. His work intersects the areas of supramolecular chemistry, cellular signaling, and targeted drug delivery. In the area of supramolecular chemistry, he created "self-assembling molecules by selecting component molecules whose parts carry different electric charges or are either attracted to or repelled by water...the molecules snap together automatically, like a self-assembling jigsaw puzzle." [ref: Chemists Make Molecule With Hint of Life, The New York Times] The assembled multicomponent entities mimic the oxygen carrying protein hemoglobin and the cytochrome P-450 family of proteins. [ref: Self-Assembly of Porphyrin Complex, Chemical & Engineering News Archive]

Lawrence also developed molecules programmed to target protein kinases, [ref: Purely Peptidic Enzyme Inhibitor Made, Chemical & Engineering News Archive] [ref: Cell Signaling Pathway Controlled By Light, Chemical & Engineering News Archive] signaling enzymes that, if mutated, can promote various cancers, as well as neurological, autoimmune, and cardiovascular diseases. Light-activated analogs of these protein kinase targeting molecules were designed as well, in order to "turn [signaling] pathways on and off non-invasively”. A collaborative research program with Zhong-Yin Zhang at Purdue University generated bidentate inhibitors for another family of signaling enzymes, protein tyrosine phosphatases, thereby furnishing "opportunities for drug discovery against diseases such as diabetes, cancer, autoimmune diseases, and tuberculosis". [ref: Bidentate Inhibitors of Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases, Antioxidants & Redox Signaling] Lawrence's lab also created a technology for delivering drugs to diseased sites using laser light. [ref: This Revolutionary New Tech Uses Light to Activate Medicine, Fortune] [ref: UNC-Chapel Hill researchers use light to launch drugs from red blood cells, Drug Discovery News] [ref: Using light, red blood cells and a honey bee peptide to deliver therapeutic proteins, ScienceDaily] [ref: Targeted Drug Delivery through Optical Control of Cell Lysis, ACS Central Science] This therapeutic platform has been licensed by Covalt Bio, a biotechnology company. [ref: Covalt Bio, Covalt Bio]

== Pedagogy ==
Lawrence developed a laboratory safety course built around case studies in response to the spate of deaths and serious injuries in academic research laboratories. [ref: Chemistry 701 - Introduction to Laboratory Safety, guides.lib.unc.edu] [ref: Academic Lab Safety Under Exam, Chemical & Engineering News] The course was subsequently transformed into an online American Chemical Society training exercise. [ref: ACS Case Studies for Research Lab Safety] In addition, Lawrence created "virtual laboratory experiences...emphasizing laboratory safety and bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application".

data.title: Alejandro Cifuentes
data.text:
Alejandro Cifuentes (born 6 June 1965) is a Spanish analytical chemist and food scientist. [ref: Quick Update: Foodomics Alejandro Cifuentes on how foodomics could lead to new ways of treating Alzheimer’s disease, The Analytical Scientist] He is a research professor at the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC). He is known for introducing the concept of Foodomics. [ref: ] He is an editor of TrAC – Trends in Analytical Chemistry. [ref: ]

== Education and career ==
Cifuentes received a Ph.D. in Chemistry in 1992 from the University of Valladolid. He held postdoctoral research at the University of Amsterdam between 1993 and 1995 through a European Union fellowship. [ref: Alejandro Cifuentes Founding Director of the Institute of Food Science Research (, ICBC]

Cifuentes has spent his academic career at the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC). He has headed the Laboratory of Foodomics since 1999 and directed the Metabolomics Platform at the Institute of Food Science Research (CIAL), a joint CSIC–Autonomous University of Madrid facility, since 2012. [ref: Prof. Alejandro Cifuentes and Prof. Elena Ibañez Appointed Editors-in-Chief of Exploration of Foods and Foodomics, Open Exploration] He was deputy director of the Institute of Industrial Fermentations before serving as CIAL's founding director from 2007 to 2010. He became a full research professor in 2007. [ref: Alejandro Cifuentes - Laboratorio de Alimentómica, www.cial.uam-csic.es]

He serves as Editor of TrAC – Trends in Analytical Chemistry, and Specialty Chief Editor of Frontiers in Nutrition. [ref: ] He has also served as editor of Elsevier's reference work. [ref: Comprehensive Foodomics, ScienceDirect]

== Research ==
Cifuentes' research focuses on analytical chemistry, separation science, food science and foodomics. [ref: ] His laboratory develops and applies high-resolution analytical platforms including liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) [ref: Online Extraction Followed by LC-MS/MS Analysis of Lipids in Natural Samples: A Proof-of-Concept Profiling Lecithin in Seeds, Foods], gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS), capillary electrophoresis–mass spectrometry (CE–MS), multidimensional chromatography, and molecular biology techniques for the characterization of food composition.

He also introduced the concept of Foodomics. [ref: Foodomics: Analytical Opportunities and Challenges, Analytical Chemistry]

His group has investigated molecular signatures related to cancer, Alzheimer's disease, obesity, inflammation, and other chronic disorders, using metabolomic, lipidomic, transcriptomic and proteomic approaches to understand the mechanisms through which dietary compounds influence disease prevention and progression. [ref: Exhaustive Search of Dietary Intake Biomarkers as Objective Tools for Personalized Nutrimetabolomics and Precision Nutrition Implementation, Nutrition Reviews]

== Selected publications ==

*Foodomics: Advanced Mass Spectrometry in Modern Food Science and Nutrition, John Wiley & Sons
* Fundamentals of advanced omics technologies: from genes to metabolites, Elsevier
* Applications of Advanced Omics Technologies From Genes to Metabolites
* Green Extraction Techniques: Principles, Advances and Applications
* Comprehensive Foodomics
* The role of Food Science and Foodomics in the implementation of One-Health, Frontiers in Nutrition
* In vivo neuroprotective capacity of a Dunaliella salina extract - comprehensive transcriptomics and metabolomics study, npj Science of Food
* Recent applications of high resolution mass spectrometry for the characterization of plant natural products, TrAC Trends in Analytical Chemistry

data.title: List of international presidential trips made by Nicolas Sarkozy
data.text:
Nicolas Sarkozy, the 23rd President of France, made 92 presidential trips to 54 states internationally during his presidency, which began with his inauguration on 16 May 2007 and ended with the inauguration of François Hollande on 15 May 2012.

==Summary==
The number of visits per country where President Sarkozy traveled are:
* One visit to Afghanistan, Algeria, Andorra, Angola, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Bulgaria, Canada, Czech Republic, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, Egypt, Gabon, Haiti, Iraq, Israel, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Mexico, Monaco, Morocco, Niger, Oman, Qatar, Republic of the Congo, Romania, Rwanda, Saudi Arabia, Senegal, South Korea, Switzerland, Syria, Trinidad and Tobago, Tunisia and Turkey.
* Two visits to Brazil, Georgia, India, Italy, Libya, the United Arab Emirates and Vatican City.
* Three visits to China, Poland, Portugal, Russia, and Spain.
* Four visits to United Kingdom.
* Five visits to Belgium, and Germany.
* Eleven visits to the United States.

data.title: Hugh Clout
data.text:
Hugh Donald Clout (born 29 April 1944) is a British historical and rural geographer and emeritus professor of geography at University College London (UCL). His research focuses on the historical geography of France [ref: Book review essays: French historical geography: de Planhol, X. editor, 1978: Etudes de géographie historique. Bulletin de la Section de Géographie, Comité des Travaux Historiques et Scientifiques 82 (années 1975-77), 7-203. Paris: Bibliothèque Nationale. 203 pp. FF 90, Progress in Human Geography], rural landscapes [ref: An Overview of the Fluctuating Fortunes of Viticulture in England and Wales, EchoGéo] and regional development, postwar reconstruction, and the history of geographical scholarship. [ref: Hugh Clout, After the Ruins: Restoring the Countryside of Northern France After the Great War, Material Culture Review] He is an Emeritus Fellow of the British Academy [ref: Professor Hugh Clout FBA, The British Academy], a Fellow of University College London [ref: Hugh Clout, UCL Faculty of Social & Historical Sciences], and the Academia Europaea. [ref: ]

== Education and Career ==
He earned a BA, MPhil and PhD from University College London, a Doctorat from the Université Paris I, and a DLit from the University of London. Sorbonne University later awarded him an honorary doctorate. [ref: Sorbonne University honours eight outstanding achievers, Sorbonne Université]

Clout joined University College London's Department of Geography as a lecturer in 1967 [ref: Academy of Europe: Clout Hugh, www.ae-info.org] and later became professor of geography. He introduced rural geography teaching at UCL in the late 1960s and served as Dean of Social and Historical Sciences from 1995 to 2004. He was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1997 and a Fellow of UCL in 2008. In 2005, he shared the Newbigin Prize of the Royal Scottish Geographical Society with Iain Stevenson. [ref: Newbigin Prize, The Royal Scottish Geographical Society]

== Research and scholarly work ==
Clout's research has focused on rural and historical geography, particularly France and Western Europe. His books include Agriculture in France on the Eve of the Railway Age (1980) [ref: H. D. Clout. Agriculture in France on the Eve of the Railway Age, Norois], The Land of France, 1815–1914 (1983) [ref: Book Review: The Land of France 1815–1914, Progress in Human Geography] and After the Ruins: Restoring the Countryside of Northern France after the Great War (1996), which examined agricultural change and postwar reconstruction. [ref: Reconstitution des paysages dévastés par la Grande Guerre: H. Clout, After the ruins. Restoring the Countryside of Northern France after the Great War, Annales de géographie]

He has also written on French geographers, the history of geographical thought and the development of geography as an academic discipline. His other works include Histoire de Londres [ref: Clout H., Histoire de Londres, Géocarrefour] and The Times History of London. [ref: ]

data.title: Death Letter Blues (2023 film)
data.text:
Death Letter Blues, originally titled The Banality, is a 2022 American Southern Gothic mystery thriller film written and directed by Michael Stevantoni and Strack Azar. It stars Sherman Augustus as a small-town Mississippi priest who becomes involved in the aftermath of the death of a teenager known locally as Feral Boy. Karole Foreman, Ramsay Midwood, Arianna Ngnomire and Keylor Leigh also star.

The film premiered at the Newport Beach Film Festival in October 2022 and played other festivals under its original title before Dark Sky Films released it in the United States as Death Letter Blues on August 8, 2025. Critics generally praised its atmosphere, cinematography and lead performance, with some finding its pacing slow and its ending unresolved.

== Plot ==
In a small Mississippi town, Father Moss, a priest struggling with his faith, arranges for a boy found living in the woods to be raised by a childless couple, Ed and Marcy. Eleven years later the boy, still known around town as "Feral Boy", is killed after a party in the woods. As Moss counsels the couple, he is also left a car and a letter of confession by a recently deceased parishioner, and begins to see parallels between the two deaths and his own recurring nightmares.

== Cast ==

* Sherman Augustus as Father Moss
* Karole Foreman as Marcy
* Ramsay Midwood as Ed
* Arianna Ngnomire as Riley
* Keylor Leigh as Jo
* Layton Miller as Feral Boy
* Woodrow Wilkins as Deacon Graham
* Diana Stevan as Ms. Webb

== Production ==
The film was Stevantoni's second feature and was shot in the Mississippi Delta, with many of the supporting roles cast from the local community. [ref: The Filmmakers, Comox Valley International Film Festival] [ref: Film Review: Death Letter Blues, CineGods] Augustus also served as a producer. Thomas Taugher was the cinematographer and Daniel McClure composed the score. [ref: Death Letter Blues, Dark Sky Films]

== Release ==
The film premiered as The Banality at the Newport Beach Film Festival in October 2022. [ref: The Banality, Newport Beach Film Festival] It went on to screen under that title at festivals including the Popcorn Frights Film Festival in August 2023 and the Woods Hole Film Festival in 2025, [ref: Mike's Review: The Banality (2023 Popcorn Frights Film Festival), The Scariest Things] [ref: The Banality, Woods Hole Film Festival] and won Best Mississippi Narrative Feature at the Oxford Film Festival. [ref: Death Letter Blues, Dark Sky Films]

Dark Sky Films released a trailer under the title Death Letter Blues in July 2025, [ref: Official Trailer for 'Death Letter Blues' Small Town Priest Horror Film, FirstShowing.net] and released the film in limited theaters and on digital platforms in the United States on August 8, 2025. [ref: Trailer for Death Letter Blues teases a supernatural mystery, Flickering Myth]

== Critical response ==
In Dread Central, the reviewer praised the film's cinematography and Augustus's performance as the tormented priest but found the pacing slow and the ending unresolved, with several characters' fates left unclear. [ref: 'Death Letter Blues' Review: A Southern Gothic Thriller That Burns Too Slowly, Dread Central] Australian critic Jim Schembri rated it three stars out of five, calling it an atmospheric Southern noir that plays subtly with genre conventions. [ref: A Stranger in the Woods: Death Letter Blues, jimschembri.com]

In a column for Crooked Marquee, Josh Bell gave the film a B, comparing it to the work of Flannery O'Connor and the early films of Jeff Nichols while finding its storytelling somewhat muddled and its pace slow. [ref: VODepths: What to See (and Avoid) on Demand This Week, Crooked Marquee] Tim Cogshell of CineGods was more positive, describing it as a sharp piece of Southern Gothic storytelling with a touch of magical realism. Louisa Moore of Screen Zealots praised its command of light, shadow and atmosphere, while noting that its lack of full resolution might frustrate some viewers. [ref: Death Letter Blues, Screen Zealots] Reviewing it at Popcorn Frights, Mike Campbell of The Scariest Things gave it four stars out of five, praising its cinematography and roots-music score and likening its contemplative approach to the films of Terrence Malick.

data.title: Tamami Honma
data.text:
----

Tamami Honma is a Japanese-American concert pianist, chamber musician, educator and recording artist. In 2024, she became the first female pianist to record the complete cycle of 35 Beethoven piano sonatas, released as a 10-CD set by Divine Art Recordings. [ref: Tamami Honma plays Beethoven's Complete 35 Piano Sonatas, Pianist Magazine] She is an advocate for 20th and 21st-century repertoire, having premiered and recorded works by several British and Lithuanian composers. She serves on the music faculties at Stanford University and Santa Clara University. [ref: Tamami Honma, Stanford Department of Music] [ref: Tamami Honma Faculty Profile, Santa Clara University] [ref: ]

== Education and early history ==
Honma studied with Byron Janis, one of the few students of Vladimir Horowitz, at the Manhattan School of Music where she earned a bachelor's degree in piano performance. She subsequently studied with Christopher Elton at the Royal Academy of Music in London, earning a master's degree, and joined the academy's academic faculty; she was later awarded an honorary ARAM degree.

Early in her career, she won first prize at several national and international piano competitions, including the Yamaha Competition at the MTNA (Music Teachers National Association) in Little Rock, Arkansas, [ref: Logan Pianists Get 2 Top Music Contest Awards, Deseret News] the Stravinsky Awards International Piano Competition, [ref: Nine Young Utahns Picked to Solo on 30th Annual 'Salute to Youth', Deseret News] the Gina Bachauer International Young Artists Piano Competition (1990), [ref: Return recital part of circle of learning and sharing, Deseret News] and the Kingsville (Isabel Scionti) International Young Performers Competition (1991). [ref: Utah People in the Arts, Deseret News] [ref: Isabel Scionti Piano Solo First Place Winners, Kingsville Young Performers Competition] She has also appeared as a soloist at Bolshoi Hall in Moscow with the Moscow Radio Symphony Orchestra.

== Contemporary music advocacy ==
Honma maintained a long-standing collaboration with composer John McCabe. In 2001, she released Star Preludes (Metier), featuring her performance of McCabe's title work alongside violinist Peter Sheppard Skærved. [ref: Star Preludes, Divine Art Recordings] In 2002, she gave the world premiere of McCabe's solo piano study Scrunch at Weill Recital Hall in New York; Allan Kozinn of The New York Times wrote that she "negotiated the work's thickets easily and produced an eloquent, powerful performance". [ref: Works, John McCabe official website] [ref: Music Review; Capturing Eclectic Energy and South Asia's Melodies, The New York Times] On November 28, 2003, she premiered McCabe's "Snowfall in Winter" — like Scrunch, a study dedicated to her — at St John's Smith Square in London; reviewing the concert for The Independent, Robert Maycock wrote that she "played with both flair and immediate understanding". [ref: Operest, St John's, Smith Square, London, The Independent] That same year, she released a recording of McCabe's Piano Concerto No. 2 (Sinfonia Concertante) with the St. Christopher Chamber Orchestra (Dutton Digital). [ref: Composition Discography, John McCabe official website] This partnership culminated in the 2005 recording Two Pianos (Dutton Digital), on which she performed alongside the composer. [ref: Two Pianos: Stravinsky, McPhee, McCabe, Copland, Britten, Presto Music] She contributed the chapter "The Piano Music" to Landscapes of the Mind: The Music of John McCabe (2008), a collection of essays on the composer edited by George Odam. [ref: Landscapes of the Mind: The Music of John McCabe, Ashgate] In 2006, she performed piano duets by Alan Rawsthorne and Constant Lambert with McCabe on his recording of Rawsthorne's complete solo piano music (Dutton Digital), which received a Gold Star rating from Gramophone. [ref: 'Gramophone' Gold Star for Rawsthorne CD, John McCabe official website] Beyond McCabe's music, she has also premiered and recorded music by British composer Nigel Clarke on the album Premonitions (2002). [ref: Nigel Clarke: Premonitions, Divine Art Recordings]

Honma has also been a prominent advocate of Lithuanian music. On October 2, 2003, she made her Wigmore Hall solo recital début, in a program including the world premiere of Cascades-3 by Lithuanian composer Osvaldas Balakauskas; [ref: Tamami Honma's Wigmore Hall solo recital début, Music & Vision] her recording of the work appeared the following year on the compilation Zoom In 3: New Music from Lithuania. [ref: Zoom In 3: New Music from Lithuania, Music Information Centre Lithuania] At the St John's Smith Square concert that November, she also premiered an arrangement made for her by Lithuanian composer of his percussion work No moon, no flowers, no friend – and he drinks sake. By decree of President Valdas Adamkus of January 10, 2006, Honma was awarded the Medal of the Order of the Lithuanian Grand Duke Gediminas. [ref: Apdovanotų asmenų duomenų bazė: Tamami Honma, Office of the President of the Republic of Lithuania] [ref: Dėl Lietuvos Respublikos ir užsienio valstybių piliečių apdovanojimo Lietuvos valstybės ordinais ir medaliais Vasario 16-osios – Lietuvos valstybės atkūrimo dienos proga, President of the Republic of Lithuania]

In June 2017, Honma was the soloist in the world premiere of a piano concerto by Luis Andrei Cobo, written in collaboration with her, performed with the Cambrian Symphony; the performance was voted "Best New Music Performance" in San Francisco Classical Voice 2016–17 Best of the Bay readers' poll. [ref: Best of the Bay 2016–2017 Winners, San Francisco Classical Voice] [ref: Cambrian Symphony Announces "A Tale of Three Cities" – World premiere of Piano Concerto by Luis Andrei Cobo, Cambrian Symphony] Her performance of Beethoven concertos with the Cal Arte Ensemble made her a finalist for Best Instrumental Recital Performance in the following year's poll. [ref: Best of the Bay 2017–2018 Winners, San Francisco Classical Voice]

In October 2023, Honma performed Busoni's Piano Concerto (1904) with the Saratoga Symphony. [ref: Tamami Honma, pianist, Meet the Artist] The massive, rarely performed work lasts over an hour and is among the most demanding in the piano repertoire; the San Francisco Symphony had given its first performances of the concerto only a few months earlier. [ref: A 100-Year-Old Concerto That Inspires Awe and Wonder at SF Symphony, San Francisco Classical Voice]

== Major recording projects ==
Honma's 2008 recording of Chopin's Piano Concertos Nos. 1 and 2 (SOMM), performed in a chamber arrangement with the Vilnius String Quartet, was named The Observer CD of the week; critic Stephen Pritchard wrote that Honma "plays exquisitely" and called the recording "a complete delight". [ref: Chopin: Piano Concertos Nos 1 and 2, Honma/Vilnius String Quartet, The Observer] [ref: Chopin's Concertos in chamber versions as "The Observer" CD of the Week, PWM Edition]

In 2024, Honma completed a multi-year project to record all 35 of Beethoven's piano sonatas for the Divine Art label, following the ABRSM critical edition edited by Barry Cooper and presenting the sonatas in broadly chronological order. [ref: Beethoven: Complete Piano Sonatas (Tamami Honma), International Piano] The recordings grew out of a "Beethoven Odyssey" Honma began in February 2016, in which she performed the cycle of 32 piano sonatas in concert along with the ten violin sonatas, the five piano concertos and the Choral Fantasy. Most recorded cycles include only the 32 sonatas to which Beethoven assigned opus numbers; Honma's set also includes the three early Kurfürstensonaten, making it one of very few complete recordings of all 35. [ref: Beethoven: Complete 35 Piano Sonatas, [[Fanfare (magazine)] Reviewing the set in Fanfare, Jerry Dubins described the cycle as "transcendental", comparing aspects of Honma's playing to interpreters including Alfred Brendel, Wilhelm Kempff, Vladimir Ashkenazy and Maurizio Pollini. Writing in International Piano, Guy Rickards praised the consistency of Honma's interpretations across the cycle, noting that "the strengths of Honma's interpretations of the earlier works persist to the end, whether in the lyrical warmth of Op 90's finale or the stratospheric heights of the final three." Honma was also the subject of a lengthy profile and interview in Fanfare by Marc Medwin, discussing her artistic development and approach to the Beethoven Sonatas. [ref: Point, Journey, Universe: An Interview with Tamami Honma, [[Fanfare (magazine)] In a separate review, Medwin contrasted her approach with Brendel's, describing the cycle as "remarkably complete and endlessly rewarding". [ref: Beethoven: Complete 35 Piano Sonatas, [[Fanfare (magazine)]

Honma has also written on Beethoven interpretation: her article "Performance Practice in Beethoven: Tempo Modifications and the Role of the Performer in the Creative Process", appeared in Arietta, the journal of the Beethoven Piano Society of Europe, in 2000. [ref: Performance Practice in Beethoven: Tempo Modifications and the Role of the Performer in the Creative Process, Arietta]

data.title: Golden jackals in Italy
data.text:
Golden jackals of the subspecies C. a. moreoticus have been present in Italy since the mid-1980s. They expanded into Italy from neighbouring Slovenia and established several isolated populations in the northeast, particularly in Friuli-Venezia Giulia and Veneto. This expansion accelerated throughout the 2010s and 2020s, with the species reaching as far west as Piedmont and as far south as Lazio.

Data on the diet of jackals in Italy indicate they are primarily scavengers that feed on animal remains discarded by humans. Parasitological examinations of jackal carcasses show that the species is host to over a dozen endoparasite species. They dominate red foxes, but are outcompeted and sometimes killed by wolves.

The Italian golden jackal population is fully protected and classed as least-concern, though because its range is still fragmentary, poaching and vehicular collision still pose a serious threat, with the potential of causing localised extinctions. Public perception of jackals in Italy is largely negative among hunters and urban citizens living in regions where jackals are present.

==Species overview==
The golden jackal is a medium-sized canid whose basic fur colour is golden, though seasonal variations occur, from pale creamy yellow to dark tawny. [ref: Canids: Foxes, Wolves, Jackals, and Dogs:Status Survey and Conservation Action Plan, IUCN, The World Conservation Union] It can be distinguished from the red fox by its slightly larger size, shorter tail and light-coloured ruff around the neck. The jackal also lacks the fox's white tail tip and the backs of its ears are the same colour as the rest of its body rather than black. In winter, when its fur is longer and gives the impression of larger size, the golden jackal can be mistaken for a wolf, but is distinguished by its more slender build, shorter tail, more pointed muzzle and its more fulvous colour. It is an opportunistic, omnivorous forager that can live in a variety of different habitats, from deserts to evergreen forests.

The golden jackal populations in Italy have been classed, together with all other populations in Europe, as belonging to the subspecies C. a. moreoticus, which was first described by French naturalist Isidore Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire during the Morea expedition. It is the largest subspecies, measuring in length and cm in height, with males weighing and females kg.

==Range and population==
The jackal is present in most of Northern Italy, both in alpine/prealpine regions and the Po Valley, where it ranges westwards from Friuli-Venezia Giulia to Piedmont and southwards from Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol to Ravenna in Emilia-Romagna. As of 2024, the jackal has been reported in ten regions of Italy: Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Veneto, Trentino-Alto Adige, Lombardy, Piedmont, the Aosta Valley, Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany, Marche and Lazio.

In 2021, it was estimated that 196-250 jackals, divided into 37-47 family groups, inhabited Italy based on bio-acoustic monitoring. The largest population, consisting of 2-5 packs, is found in Friuli-Venezia Giulia, in large part due to the low number of wolves there. As of 2024, the population of jackals in Friuli-Venezia Giulia has been calculated at 400. This region is considered the core area of the Italian jackal population, as it contains the largest number of reproducing individuals and provides a genetic link to neighbouring populations from the Balkans. Packs present in the karsts of Isonzo, Gorizia and Trieste near the Slovenian border seem to be the only self-sustaining populations in Italy.

==History==
===Background===
Several pre-Holocene fossil canids found in Italy and neighbouring countries initially attributed to the golden jackal were later found to have belonged to wolves, dogs or unrelated extinct canids. The species is therefore a relatively recent arrival to southeastern Europe, colonising the area during the Late Pleistocene from Anatolia via a land bridge on the Bosporus. Its expansion into the Balkan peninsula was however limited by climate, extensive woodland and the presence of wolves, thus limiting its range to the coastline, some islands, and steppe zones.

The species' eventual arrival in Italy coincided with its expansion throughout neighbouring Yugoslavia from the 1950s onwards, which had been facilitated by the elimination of government-sponsored bounties, an increase in pastoral activity in Slovenia, and a reduction in wolf populations. Jackals were already reported in the Slovenian village of Smast, a few kilometres from the Italian border, as early as 1953, and an increase in jackal populations on the Dalmatian and Montenegrin coasts resulted in the species colonising northwestern Istria during the early 1980s.

===Expansion===
Comparative studies undertaken in 2014 on the mtDNA control region and autosomal microsatellite loci of golden jackals in Italy and eastern Europe showed that the Italian populations descend from admixed Dalmatian and Slavonian jackals, thus conferring high genetic diversity.

The expansion of jackals into Italy underwent three phases: the initial phase (1984–1996) led to the species' first recorded appearance in prealpine Veneto, its occasional reproduction in the provinces of Udine and Belluno, and its colonisation of the Isonzo karst in Gorizia; the second phase (1997–2008) saw a deceleration in expansion and an overall decrease in sightings, but nevertheless resulted in reproductive events near Muggia and in the valleys of the Natisone, as well as an increased presence in Gorizia; the third phase (2009–2018) saw a rapid expansion characterised by further reproductions in Belluno, Carnia, Alto Adige, Natisone, Gorizia and the steppe areas of the province of Pordenone.

====First phase====
On 24 January 1984, after numerous reports were received concerning a pair of "giant foxes" and several predation events on roe deer, a male jackal was captured at Ponte Orsina near San Vito di Cadore in the province of Belluno, though it would not be positively identified until 1993. In September 1985, a female jackal was killed during a fox hunt, and was found to have been no older than six months of age, thus leading to the conclusion that it had been born in Italian territory, given the unlikelihood of such a young specimen dispersing many kilometres from its birthplace. A second specimen was later discovered as roadkill that year.

In the summer of 1987, reports were made of "coyotes" in Udine. On 23 August, an adult female was killed there during an anti-rabies campaign against red foxes. An examination of the carcass definitively precluded it from being an imported pet coyote or coydog, and showed that the specimen was very similar to jackals in neighbouring Yugoslavia. The animal was also shown to be relatively old and displayed signs of having recently raised pups.

Several more sightings were reported between 1988 and early 1992. On 25 June 1992, a young male jackal, erroneously identified as a "big fox", was killed in a vehicular colision in Treviso, and correctly identified after being examined at the Museo Friulano di Storia Naturale di Udine. Two months later, a large adult male was observed frequenting. Another, possibly the same animal, was later observed near. At the same time, jackals were reported in the karst of Trieste and by the middle section of the Tagliamento. It was concluded that the species had by then fully established itself in Veneto and Friuli-Venezia Giulia, having expanded westwards by since the first records. By 1994, jackals were reported in the karst of Gorizia and a family group was sighted in Rivamonte Agordino.

====Second phase====
In 1998, camera traps confirmed the presence of a jackal pair near Doberdò del Lago. Nevertheless, the expansion of the species in Italy seemed to stop by the late 1990s, probably due to hunting pressures and a simultaneous decrease in Balkan jackal populations. A survey of the Julian Prealps undertaken between 2003-2009, however, showed that the species was expanding into the high Adriatic Hinterland, though still in small numbers, with perhaps 2-4 specimens being present. It was nevertheless considered likely that there were at least two family groups located along the Italian-Slovenian border.

====Third phase====
On 30 April 2009, a subadult male was caught at San Donà di Piave in the province of Venice, in close proximity to a location in Treviso where another jackal was sighted in the 1990s, thus indicating the possible presence of a reproductive population in the Venetian Prealps penetrating into the Venetian floodplain via the Piave River Valley. In the summer and winter of 2009, the presence of jackals was ascertained in South Tyrol in the Dolomites and Socchieve in Udine respectively.

By 2011, the species' had established reproductive groups in the mountainous regions of Friuli-Venzia Giulia, Veneto and parts of Trentino-Alto Adige, with occasional incursions into the lowlands of Udine, Treviso and Venice by dispersing young males. At least one reproduction was recorded in Udine.

In 2017, the jackal population on the Italo-Slovenian border increased significantly, leading to a wave of dispersals which brought the species to Emilia-Romagna, where it crossed the Po River into Mirandola, and established itself in Val Brembana in Lombardy.

====2020 – present====
In 2020, jackals were confirmed to be present in the province of Verona, with at least one family group establishing itself near Lake Garda. In August of that year, a dispersing jackal, thought to be from the Verona population, entered the in Piedmont. In December 2020, a specimen was sighted in in Parma. Further sightings in the area in 2021-2023 confirmed that the species was reproducing, despite the area's high level of industrialisation.

The species reached the Tuscan Apennines in 2021-2022, with two specimens being reported in Prato. In 2022, the golden jackal was confirmed to be present in Lazio through camera trap footage dating from 6-21 March 2020 in the Circeo National Park. On 5 March 2023, a dead specimen was found in the countryside of Potenza Picena in the Marche region, with a live jackal being sighted later that month near the Esino in Ancona.

==Ecology==
===Habitat===
Golden jackals inhabit humid areas and human-modified habitats, but they will move to shrubby and forested areas during the mating season, where they make use of abandoned badger setts or other natural cavities to raise their young. In plains areas, they favour agricultural areas, humid zones, disturbed lands and suburban areas, where they feed on the refuse of farms, cultivations, landfills and recycling depots. They generally prefer areas of low or medium elevation, though they have been recorded at elevations of 1,900 metres in South Tyrol and at 2,600 metres ASL on Mount Motto in Lombardy.

===Reproduction===
In Italy, jackal family groups consist of around 3-7 individuals that patrol a home range of 300-500 hectares. As of 2018, there is little data on the reproduction of jackals in Italy, though the mating season typically occurs in late February, with pups being born in late April or early May.

===Diet===
Data on the diet of golden jackals in Italy are scarce and largely come from direct examination of the stomach contents of roadkilled specimens, with faecal analyses proving unreliable due to the similarity of jackal faeces with those of foxes, wolves and dogs. Most of the species' diet consists of the remains of game and livestock discarded by hunters and butchers, as well as crops and animal feed, though the remains of hares and voles have also been found. Jackals have been reported to prey occasionally on beech martens, as well as ungulates like roe deer and sheep, though the killing of the latter two rarely occurs. They also feed on fruits and vegetables taken from farms.

===Competitors===
Non-invasive studies carried out in three areas in Friuli-Venzia Giulia containing both golden jackals and red foxes in 2017-2018 showed marked niche differentiation between the two species: the jackals were found to primarily prey on wild ungulates, whereas red foxes targeted small mammals, and while both overlapped in their diurnal cycles, having predominantly crepuscular and nocturnal activity patterns, they showed differing habitat preferences, with jackals actively avoiding human-modified habitats and cultivated areas, unlike foxes. This differentiation was hypothesied to be the result of active avoidance of jackals by red foxes, as jackals in the same study areas had been found to consume foxes.

In areas where they are sympatric, wolves exclude jackals from forested areas, pushing them into humid wetland, Mediterranean scrub and traditionally managed cultivated areas. Jackals living in wolf-inhabited areas have been reported to stop answering recorded jackal howls, an antipredator adaptation reported in other regions of Europe. In 2017, a pair of wolves was thought to have displaced the jackals in the area of Pordenone and, as of 2021, there are five known cases of wolves killing jackals in Italy. Nevertheless, it was hypothesied that the expansion of jackals into Marche was due in part to their seeking out wolves in order to feed on their kills. It is possible that future expansion of wolves eastwards will cause jackals to become segregated to plains areas.

===Diseases and parasites===
Data on the diseases and parasites of the golden jackal in Italy are still scarce. In 2009, a jackal was found to be the host of the first case of Metagonimus yokogawai in Italy. In 2022, the Department of Agri-Food, Environmental and Animal Sciences of the University of Udine, the Friulian Museum of Natural History and the FVG Region conducted the first study on the parasitofauna of the jackal in Friuli-Venezia Giulia, using 47 jackal specimens collected from various areas between 2009-2021. 91.5% of the specimens were found to be infected by at least one parasite species. Among the species found were 17 endoparasites, including Sarcocystis, the first incidence of the species in Italy, which infected 59% of the examined jackals.

A discrete presence of parvovirus, both 1 and 2, was also detected in the specimens. Monitoring of the epidemiology and parasitology of the jackal is undertaken by the Istituto Zooprofilattico delle Venezie, together with analogous institutions in Piacenza and Turin, as well as several natural history museums and universities.

==Relationships with humans==
===Common names===
The golden jackal is known in Italian as sciacallo dorato or simply sciacallo, which derives from the Turkish çakal, itself derived from the Persian shagāl. Recent neologisms referring to the species in Friulian and Venetian include coiòte and sciacàl.

===Livestock predation===
The first recorded case of livestock predation by golden jackals in Italy occurred in 2013 in a farm in Gorizia, during which several lambs were killed. Another small farm raising Istriana sheep in the same area was attacked in 2015–2016. Both cases occurred in summer at night. The golden jackal was added to the list of compensable species in 2018, as per DPR n.05/2018. [ref: Decreto n° 05 / Pres.]

===Public attitudes===
As the species is a relatively new arrival to Italy, it does not feature prominently in local idioms, though the phrase Non fidarti, è uno sciacallo! () is used to describe untrustworthy people. A survey on the public perception and knowledge of the golden jackal in the Italian part of the Karst Plateau among excursionists, hunters and farmers between 2017–2018 showed that none of the three categories considered the species dangerous to people. The most negative opinions were expressed by hunters, who blamed jackals for declines in roe deer populations. This same category also displayed the least knowledge of the jackals' biology and ecology. Another survey taken across ten Italian cities showed that jackals rated negatively in cities where the species is present, while the inhabitants of cities where jackals are absent, like Naples and Syracuse, showed more positive attitudes.

==Conservation==
===Legislation===
The IUCN classes the golden jackal population in Italy as least-concern, and does not consider it an invasive species, as its arrival in Italy was through natural processes rather than through human intervention. In Italy, the golden jackal is protected under the following regulations:
*"Ratification of the Berne Convention"
*"Regulations for the protection of homeothermic wild fauna and hunting"
*Council Regulation (EC) No. 338/97 of 9 December 1996 on the protection of species of wild fauna and flora by regulating trade therein
*"On the implementation of Directive 92/43/EEC on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora"

===Threats===
The range of the jackal in Italy is very irregular, with a high risk of local extinction. Vehicular collision is a major source of mortality, with over 30 specimens having been recorded to have been killed in this manner as of 2018. Most roadkilled jackals were found to be young dispersing males or yearling pups. It has been estimated that vehicular collisions reduce jackal populations by almost 10% annually. Poaching is also a significant threat to the species in Italy: two subadult jackals were poisoned in 2018 in the Gorizian karst, while another was illegally shot in the Triestine karst in 2020. As of 2025, there are no reports of hybridisation with dogs, though it may become an issue once jackals come into contact with large free-ranging dog populations in south-central Italy.

data.title: William Gill (surgeon)
data.text:
----

William Gill (1795 – 14 September 1863) was a British-born surgeon and naturalist who practiced in the Cape Colony. He is best known for the large bequest in his will that established Gill College in Somerset East (today KwaNojoli), one of the older educational institutions in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa. [ref: Gill College – Sursum Prorsusque – Upwards and Onwards]

== Early life and training ==
Gill was born in Market Harborough, Leicestershire, in 1795 to the Reverend George Gill and his wife (name unknown). [ref: Cape Province. Probate Records 1861–1862, 1863] He started work in Wellingborough, Northamptonshire in 1810 as a medical apprentice to Thomas Peck, under whom he was indentured for five years, subsequently studying medicine at the University of Glasgow. He became a member of the Royal College of Surgeons of England in 1817 and a licentiate of the Society of Apothecaries in 1818. He spent a year travelling in continental Europe, during which he developed a lasting interest in botany. [ref: S2A3 Biographical Database of Southern African Science, www.s2a3.org.za]

== Career in the Cape Colony ==
Gill arrived at the Cape Colony in June 1818 and was licensed to practise as a surgeon, obstetrician and pharmacist later that year. [ref: Cape of Good Hope Government Gazette, 16 September 1862, "List of the medical practitioners in the Cape Colony"] He initially served as the district surgeon at Caledon and later settled in the Zwartland district (near present-day Malmesbury) in 1822, where he was noted for his work during a typhoid outbreak.

In 1826 he undertook an expedition northward for hunting and natural-history collecting, reaching as far as Kuruman, where he met the explorer and geologist Andrew Geddes Bain. He suffered heavy losses when his wagons were destroyed and returned to Cape Town in 1827, before trekking inland again. Around 1830 he collected plant and shell fossils along the Sundays River near Uitenhage. [ref: Botanical Exploration of Southern Africa, SANBI] [ref: Notes on South African geology, South African Quarterly Journal, 1830, No. 4]

On the recommendation of Dr James Barry and the Reverend George Thom, Gill was appointed district surgeon of the newly established settlement of Somerset (later Somerset East) in 1829 at £100 per annum. [ref: South Africa: its medical history 1652-1898; a medical and social study, Struik] He maintained a private practice there for many years and was a respected member of the local community, with a wide circle of friends and known for his generosity. When the district surgeoncy was abolished in 1845, Gill declined an alternative appointment as resident surgeon on Robben Island, instead opting for an annual pension of £50 and continued to practice medicine in the town. He acquired a number of farms in the district and became a wealthy merino sheep farmer.

He co-founded the Somerset Reading Society in 1832 and was a member of the Literary, Scientific and Medical Society of Grahamstown [ref: Grahamstown Journal, 15 March 1856, p. 2, "Literary, Scientific and Medical Society"]. He continued to collect botanical specimens, particularly orchids, and sold approximately 400 specimens to Thom that eventually reached the Herbarium at Kew Gardens. Several plant species, including Myrsine gilliana [ref: [https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A589125-1 Myrsine gilliana Sond. | Plants of the World Online | Kew Science]], Aspalathus gillii (renamed Aspalathus setacea) [ref: ] and Erica gillii [ref: ], were named after him.
== Death and legacy ==
Gill, unmarried, died of oedema on 14 September 1863 in Somerset East, aged 68. [ref: Obituary, Eastern Province Herald] [ref: Dictionary of South African biography, Nasional Boekhandel Bpk. for National Council for Social Research, Dept. of Higher Education] In his will dated 19 January 1863 he left the bulk of his estate, approximately £23 000, for the formation and future maintenance of a higher educational institution in the Eastern Province. Local residents raised funds for the buildings. The Gill College Corporation was formed, land was granted in 1867, and the college opened on 18 March 1869. Its architecture was modelled on that of the University of Glasgow. [ref: Dr William Gill of Somerset East] Originally intended as a university college, it later became a high school (from 1903) and continues today as a co-educational dual-medium school.

Gill was originally laid to rest in the town's cemetery at the foot of the Boschberg. In 1916 his remains were reinterred in front of the college, and a monument to him was erected in 1923 alongside his grave.

== References ==

==Further reading==
* A History of Medicine in South Africa Up to the End of the Nineteenth Century, A.A. Balkema
* Journals of Andrew Geddes Bain: trader, explorer, soldier, road engineer and geologist, Van Riebeeck Society

data.title: 2027 World Climbing Championship
data.text:
The 2027 World Climbing Championship, the 20th edition of the event, will be held at the newly built Arena Brno [ref: 2027 WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS TO BE HELD IN BRNO, CZECHIA, World Climbing] in Brno, Czechia, from 13 to 22 August 2027. The competition climbing championship consists of lead, speed, and bouldering, and for the first time ever, Paraclimbing World Climbing Championship will be held at the same time as the other climbing disciplines. [ref: World Cups, World Championships & Olympic Qualification: World Climbing presents its 2027 season calendar, LaCrux.com]

World Climbing (then known as International Federation of Sport Climbing) chose Brno ahead of host city candidates in China, France, and Indonesia. Adam Ondra, Czech climber, resident of Brno, and four-time world champion, served as the face of the host city bid. [ref: Brno Will Host Climbing World Championships in 2027, Brno Daily]

The World Championship will double as the first opportunity for athletes to qualify for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. [ref: Here’s Where the World Cup Is Going in 2027, Gripped]

data.text:
Aditya Rikhari is an Indian singer, songwriter from New Delhi. He is well known for "Sahiba", and appearing at the reality show I-Popstar as a Mentor. [ref: Who is Aditya Rikhari? The Sahiba singer whos topping every chart, mirchi.in] [ref: Faasle, Paro, Sahiba: A night of music with Aditya Rikhari, The New Indian Express]

Rikhari was nominated at the 70th Filmfare Awards for Best Music Album, for his contribution to the Bhool Bhulaiyaa 3 soundtrack. [ref: Filmfare Awards 2025 Winners List Out: Alia, Kartik, Abhishek & Laapataa Ladies Win Big, MensXP]

He started his career in the 2020 during the COVID, releasing cover tracks. His initial tracks "Kya Karein", and "Tu Rehti Hai" received breakthrough. In 2023, His release "Sahiba" received major breakthrough. [ref: ] In 2024, his release "Jaana Samjho Na" was picked up for the Bollywood film Bhool Bhulaiyaa 3, marking his debut entry in film. data.title: Karel Havlíček (composer)
data.text:
----

Karel Havlíček (born 31 July 1974), also known by the pseudonym Karzi, is a Czech composer, pianist and music producer whose work includes film and television scores, advertising music and solo instrumental compositions. [ref: Karel Havlíček, Filmový přehled] He was a member of the Czech indie rock band Southpaw before concentrating on screen composition. [ref: Hudební skladatel Karel Havlíček: Největší hvězdy mají největší pokoru, Novinky.cz] His screen credits include the films Ghoul, Němá tajemství and Bratři, as well as the television series Terapie, Mamon (TV series), Vzteklina and Profesor T. His score for Bratři was nominated for Best Music at the 2024 Czech Lion Awards. [ref: Bratři, Český lev]

== Biography ==
Havlíček was born in Prague in 1974 and has also worked under the name Karzi. In 1996, Havlíček co-founded the Prague indie rock band Southpaw with Jiří Burian. He worked as a keyboardist, composer, programmer and sound engineer. [ref: SOUTHPAW MAJÍ PLNÝ HEART DISK, iREPORT] The group released several albums during the 2000s, including Pop Secret, Pleasure You Can Measure, Boys Make Noise and Heart Disk.

Southpaw ended its original run in 2011. The group returned in 2021 with the album I'm Really Gonna Miss These Songs When I'm Dead, on which Havlíček and Burian collaborated again. [ref: Na desce je náš pohled na vztahy, duševní svobodu i smrt, říká kapela Southpaw, iDNES.cz]

After his work with Southpaw, Havlíček concentrated on composing and producing music for film and television. The National Film Archive records his work in several capacities, including composer, musician, producer and sound engineer. His film credits include the American documentary Lion Ark (2013), the horror film Ghoul (2015), Carpe Noctem (2022), Němá tajemství (2023) and Bratři (2023). [ref: Lion Ark – Full Cast & Crew, TV Guide] His television work includes the Czech adaptation of the Israeli drama series Terapie and the series Mamon, Vzteklina, Profesor T and Polda.

Havlíček composed the music for Czech Television's news programming, including the news channel ČT24 and the main news programme Události. Czech Television reported on the news themes and identified him as their composer. [ref: Znělky zpravodajství ČT se začaly používat před deseti lety. Složil je hudební skladatel Karel Havlíček, ČT24]

In 2023, Havlíček composed the scores for Němá tajemství and Bratři, both directed by Tomáš Mašín. [ref: Karel Havlíček, Czech Film Center] Bratři, a historical drama concerning the Mašín brothers, received several nominations at the 2024 Czech Lion Awards. Havlíček's score was nominated in the Best Music category.

In addition to film and television scores, Havlíček has worked on advertising music and trailer soundtracks. His work includes music for the Penny Market Christmas 2018 advertising campaign, which became a finalist in the Film Craft – Direction category at the 2019 New York Festivals Advertising Awards. [ref: Penny Market Christmas 2018, New York Festivals Advertising Awards]

In 2024, Havlíček composed music for the official trailer of the HBO series The Penguin. [ref: HBO Releases Official Trailer For The Penguin, Starring Colin Farrell, Debuting September 19, Warner Bros. Discovery Pressroom] In 2026, he also worked on trailer music for ELLE, a television series associated with the Legally Blonde franchise. [ref: Karel Havlíček — Czech Film & Television Composer, Karel Havlíček]

Havlíček released the solo album Spoken in 2020. The instrumental recording combines piano, orchestral textures and electronic elements. [ref: RECENZE: Album Spoken je luxusně zařízený byt, v němž nikdo nežije, iDNES.cz] In his review, music critic Jindřich Göth discussed the album's atmospheric arrangements and its relationship to the idea of a soundtrack for an imaginary film.

In October 2022, KlasikaPlus published a review of a concert based on Spoken. The review discussed the work's extended melodic lines, recurring musical patterns and dramatic development, as well as the integration of music with lighting and visual effects. [ref: Karel Havlíček v bazénu, KlasikaPlus]

In 2023, Havlíček presented Electric Universe, an audiovisual concert project combining orchestral and electronic music. Czech Radio covered the project and interviewed him about the eight-hour musical event. [ref: Propojím svět klasické a elektronické hudby, zve na osmihodinovou show skladatel Karel Havlíček, Rádio Praha]

On 11 June 2025, Havlíček appeared with composer Vadim Petrov in a programme of their compositions at Czech Radio's Studio S1 in Prague, presented in association with the Prague Philharmonia. [ref: Special concert: Between classical and electronic music — Vadim Petrov & Karel Havlíček, Prague Philharmonia] The concert was reviewed by OperaPlus, which discussed five of Havlíček's compositions and their combination of ambient, minimalist, melodic and electronic elements. [ref: Dva skladatelé, dvě cesty. Havlíček a Petrov na jednom pódiu, OperaPlus] KlasikaPlus also reviewed the concert in the context of contemporary music and its accessibility to audiences. [ref: Že je soudobá hudba přístupná, může překvapit, KlasikaPlus]

In 2025, Havlíček released the two-part project It's Never Late to See the Light, consisting of Part 1 and Part 2. [ref: It's Never Late To See The Light, Part (1), Apple Music] [ref: It's Never Late to See the Light, Part (2) – EP, Apple Music]

In March 2026, Havlíček was included on Moderna, a compilation released by Czech Radio Vltava documenting contemporary Czech neoclassical, modern classical, electroacoustic, ambient and film music. [ref: Pokřtili jsme ambientní a elektroakustické album Moderna za osobní účasti autorek a autorů. Poslechněte si záznam koncertu, Vltava]

Havlíček co-founded Kabelovna Studios in Prague with sound designer Vladimír Chorvatovič. The studio provides sound post-production, recording, mixing and music-production services for film, television and advertising. [ref: Kabelovna Studios, Czech Film Commission]

He joined the PETROF Art Family in 2023, an artist community associated with the Czech piano manufacturer Petrof. [ref: Karel Havlíček is a new member of the PETROF Art Family, PETROF]

== Personal life ==

Havlíček's twin brother is the Czech-American painter Maxim Havlíček. [ref: Umělec Maxim Havlíček o zvláštním poutu, které má se svým dvojčetem Karlem, Lifee.cz]

== Selected works ==

data.title: Redcoat Air Cargo Flight 103
data.text:
----

Redcoat Air Cargo Flight 103 was an international cargo flight from Massachusetts, United States to Shannon, Ireland. On February 16, 1980, the Bristol Britannia lost lift and stalled shortly after take-off. It crashed into a wooded area near Billerica, Massachusetts, leaving only the flight engineer survived of the eight on board. [ref: ] [ref: Bristol Britannia: the turboprop airliner and its legacy, Ready For Take-Off Book] [ref: Remembering the Billerica plane crash of 1980, Lowell Sun]

== Background ==

=== Aircraft ===
The aircraft involved was a Bristol Britannia manufactured in 1959. Before the accident, the plane had accumulated 21,963 flight hours and 8,310 hours.

=== Victims ===

* The captain of the flight was George William Coburn, aged 56, having certification for the Bristol Britannia and British Aerospace 125. He had acquired 11,600 flight hours, 7,600 of which were in the Bristol Britannia.
* The first officer of the flight was Jack Kingston Jones, aged 54, who had logged in 7,600 flight hours, 4,760 of which were in the Bristol Britannia.
* The flight engineer of the flight was Richard Alfred Creer, aged 59, who had logged in 20,000 flight hours, 12,000 of which were in the Bristol Britannia. He was the only survivor of the crash.
* The navigator of the flight was Anthony John Beckett, aged 49, who had logged in 14,000 flight hours, 8,000 of which were in the Bristol Britannia.
* The loadmaster was David Esmond Whike.
* The ground engineer was William Brady. [ref: ]
* The two passengers were Lionel Heady and Susan Parker.

== Accident ==
Before the accident, witness found that there were ice built up on the fuselage, wings, horizontal stabilizer, and the engine pipes. The ice were swept off before applying the deicing fluid. The aircraft was still parking for 20-25 minutes before being cleared to taxi at runway 15R. However, it was then changed to runway 33L. Following the traffic conflict, the flight had to hold position. During that time, witness found the accumulation of ice on the control surface.

At 14:08, the aircraft took off from Logan International Airport. As it reached an altitude of 1,700 feet, it suddenly lost altitude and crashed into a wooded area located in Billerica. Only the flight engineer survived with severe injuries. Numerous witnesses found the aircraft falling down in a nose-up configuration, exploded on impact and caught fire.

== Investigation ==
The final report stated that the probable cause of the crash was:

"Degraded aerodynamic performance, resulting from an accumulation of ice and snow on the airframe before take-off and a further accumulation of ice when the aircraft was flown into moderate to severe icing conditions following take-off.

Contributing were encounters with windshear, downdraughts and turbulence during the climb. The failure of the flight crew to obtain an adequate pre-flight weather briefing and the failure of the National Weather Service to advise the crew of a SIGMET for severe icing conditions were also contributing factors." [ref: AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT REPORT, NTSB] [ref: Accident Bristol 175 Britannia 253 G-BRAC, Saturday 16 February 1980, aviation-safety.net] [ref: When the sky fell over Billerica, Burlington Retro]

== See also ==

* Sol Lineas Aereas Flight 5428: a crash with almost the same circumstances

== References ==

data.title: TAM Airlines Flight 540
data.text:
TAM Airlines Flight 540 was a domestic flight in Brazil from São Paulo to Bauru. On 12 February 1990, the Fokker F27 Friendship crashed while go-around after a failed attempt to land at Bauru Airport, killing the instructor and two individuals on ground. [ref: Accident Fokker F-27 Friendship 200 PT-LCG, Monday 12 February 1990, aviation-safety.net] [ref: ] [ref: Matéria para o Jornal Nacional sobre a queda do avião Fokker da TAM em Bauru, G1] [ref: JCNET: Queda matou 2 em 1990, sampi]

This plane crash was considered to be the most serious air accident in the Bauru region.

== Background ==

=== Aircraft ===
The aircraft involved was a Fokker F27 Friendship, manufactured in 1962. [ref: RELATÓRIO FINAL, CENIPA]

=== Crew member ===
On board was the instructor named Paulo Sérgio Espósito, who have acquired 5,706 flight hours with 3,578 of them were in the F27. He was the only fatality on the plane. [ref: Folha de S.Paulo - TAM diz que família não aceitou valor - 7/11/1996, www1.folha.uol.com.br]

The pilot flying was Minoru Kawakubo, who have acquried 10,010 flight hours with 1,286 of them were in the F27. He was under training during the flight. After the crash, he was fired and became a flight instructor for Pantanal Linhas Aéreas.

== Accident ==
At around 9:40 AM, at an altitude of 4000 feet, the crew decided to make a direct approach instead of the IFR plan. The plane was found to be too high for a proper descent but the instructor decided to continue the approach by pushing back the throttles and pushing the nose down steeply to bring back to the flight level. The plane touch down 775 meters from the threshold, nose gear first. The plane bounced and touched again 959 meters from the threshold. They realized they won't be able to stop the plane in time, so they initiated a go-around. However, the aircraft then stalled, fell down rapidly and crashed into obstacles. [ref: Queda de avião da TAM que matou mãe e filho em carro e marcou a aviação em Bauru completa 35 anos; relembre o caso, G1]

The plane struck a vehicle carrying Gisele Marie Savi Pinto and her son, Guilherme - all died at the scene. The captain initially survived, but was unconcious, trapped at the scene and died 27 days later due to smoke intoxication. Apart from the mother and child, other residents were not injured or affected. 25 passengers escaped unharmed, 11 passengers were injured. The co-pilot and flight attendant were also injured.

== Investigation ==
The investigation was conducted by CENIPA. On November 14, 1990, the final report was finalized. The reason for the stall during the go-around was found to be an abrupt throttle acceleration done by the instructor. This cause the engine combustion to gain too much fuel, insufficient air was received to ignite the kerosene-oxygen mixture and the temperature rose to a critical level, which hampered the propellor to produce energy for the lift. The flap was still retracted during the touchdown and go-around, lowering down the critical angle of attack. Those factors combined led to the aircraft's stalling condition.

== Lawsuit ==
Relatives of the victims demand compensation from the airline at Superior Court of Justice. The airline initially was ordered but then able to appeal as the crash was not the airlines' fault. Howevery, it was later denied after the court recognized the need for reimbursement of personal belongings damaged or lost in the accident. The company also need to cover funeral expenses not covered by social security institutions. In total, the airline had to pay 500 minimum wage per victims. [ref: G1 > Edição São Paulo - NOTÍCIAS - STJ mantém condenação a TAM por morte de mãe e filho atingidos por avião, g1.globo.com] [ref: TAM deve indenizar família por acidente em tentativa frustrada de pouso, Consultor Jurídico]

The airline also had to compensate R$116,000 for a passenger named Carlos Salles as he suffered from spinal injuries in the accident leading to a 20% loss of his work capacity. [ref: TAM é condenada a indenização por avião que bateu em carro, Exame]

data.title: Dionys Jobst
data.text:
Dionys Jobst (5 September 1927 – 25 March 2017) was a German lawyer, railway official and politician of the Christian Social Union (CSU). He was a member of the Bundestag from 20 October 1969 to 26 October 1998, representing the Burglengenfeld constituency, later renamed Schwandorf, by direct mandate. He chaired the Bundestag's Committee on Transport from 1988 to 1998.

== Early life and education ==

Jobst was born in Teublitz in the Upper Palatinate and attended an Oberrealschule. From 1943 to 1945 he served as a Flakhelfer, in the Reich Labour Service and in the Wehrmacht. He was wounded and taken prisoner. On 20 March 1944 he applied for membership of the Nazi Party (NSDAP) and was admitted on 20 April 1944, with membership number 10,116,768.

He completed his Abitur in 1947 and studied law at the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München until 1950. He passed the first state law examination in 1951, received a doctorate in law in 1954 and passed the second state examination in 1955.

== Civil service career ==

Jobst worked as a Regierungsassessor for the government of the Upper Palatinate in Regensburg and then as a legal officer at a district office. In January 1956 he joined the Deutsche Bundesbahn, where his last post was as a department head (Dezernent) at the Regensburg railway directorate.

He was a member of the supervisory board of Erste Bayerische Basaltstein AG Steinmühle, a member of the administrative board of the Deutsche Siedlungs- und Landesrentenbank and a board member of the German friends' association of Tel Aviv University.

== Political career ==

Jobst joined the CSU in 1959. He was a member of the Teublitz town council from 1960 to 1991, the Burglengenfeld district council from 1960 to 1972 and the Schwandorf district council from 1972 to 1996. From 1965 to 1972 he chaired the CSU district association in Burglengenfeld.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

Jobst won the Burglengenfeld constituency in the 1969 federal election and sat in the CDU/CSU parliamentary group. He was re-elected at each election until 1994. He did not stand in the 1998 election and left the Bundestag on 26 October 1998.

He was president of the cross-party parliamentary group on railways and chairman of the German–Japanese parliamentary friendship group. In 1990 the Japanese government awarded him the Order of the Rising Sun, Grand Cordon.

On 9 July 1993 Bild published a front-page story stating that members of the Bundestag were considering leasing or buying Majorca from Spain for 50 billion marks and make it the country's seventeenth state. [ref: Kein Anschluss unter dieser Nummer, BILDblog] Jobst said, the idea was meant as a joke during a conversation about transport matters and that some readers took it literally. [ref: Ich habe verstanden: Das Sommerloch fällt aus, Der Tagesspiegel]

=== Chair of the Committee on Transport ===

Jobst was a member of the Bundestag's Committee on Transport from 1980 and its chairman from 1988 until he left parliament in 1998. As chairman he presented the committee's reports and recommendations to the plenary.

== Personal life and death ==

Jobst was Roman Catholic, married, and had three children. He lived in Teublitz and died on 25 March 2017 at the age of 89.

== Honours ==

* Cross of Merit on ribbon (1978)
* Bavarian Order of Merit (1980)
* Cross of Merit, 1st Class (1983)
* Order of the Rising Sun, Grand Cordon (Japan, 1990)

data.title: Erwin Lange
data.text:
Erwin Lange (10 May 1914 – 30 October 1991) was a German politician of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). He was a member of the Bundestag from 1949 to 1980 and in the European Parliament from 1970 to 1984. In the European Parliament he chaired the economic committee and the budget committee. In 1937 a Nazi court convicted him of preparing high treason.

== Early life ==

Lange was born in Essen and was a Protestant. He left Mittelschule and started a commercial apprenticeship in 1930, then switched in 1931 to an apprenticeship as a typesetter. He joined the socialist youth movement in 1928 and the trade union movement in 1930.

== Persecution and war ==

Lange was arrested by the Nazi authorities in 1936 for political reasons. In 1937 he was convicted of preparing to commit high treason and sentenced to three and a half years in a penitentiary (Zuchthaus) and three years' loss of civil honour rights. After the sentence he did labour on moorland, was held in protective custody and was placed under police supervision. He is among the members profiled in Olaf Ihlau's 1969 study of the Rote Kämpfer (Red Fighters), a council communist resistance group broken up by the Gestapo in 1936–37.

In autumn 1942 Lange was conscripted into the punishment unit 999 and sent to Africa. He was taken prisoner by American forces in 1943 and released in 1946.

== Political career ==

After the war Lange passed the master's examination in his trade in 1947 and became manager of a printing company in Essen. [ref: Friedrich Ebert Foundation Library: Social Democratic Press Service: 1946–1995, library.fes.de] In the SPD he belonged to the Essen sub-district (Unterbezirk) and chaired the Niederrhein Bezirk.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

Lange was elected to the first Bundestag at the 1949 federal election and sat through the eighth legislative term, which ended in 1980. [ref: Biographisches Handbuch der Mitglieder des Deutschen Bundestages 1949–2002, Walter de Gruyter] Until 1969 he was on the executive committee of the SPD parliamentary group.

=== Member of the European Parliament ===

Lange sat in the European Parliament from 21 January 1970 to 23 July 1984. He chaired the economic committee until 1975 and then the budget committee. From 17 July 1979 to 23 July 1984 he was a member of the Socialist Group in the first directly elected Parliament, and from 20 July 1979 he chaired the Committee on Budgets. On 11 April 1983 he joined the delegation for relations with the United States.

== Death ==

Lange died in Essen on 30 October 1991.

data.title: Faith Tabernacle Congregation
data.text:
Faith Tabernacle Congregation is a Christian Fundamentalist non-denominational church based in Philadelphia. The church was started in 1897 as an off-shoot of John Alexander Dowie's faith-healing ministry. Faith Tabernacle Congregation has been the subject of controversy due to its belief in faith healing and rejection of modern medicine. Faith Tabernacle Congregation was prominently involved in the 1990-91 Philadelphia measles outbreak.

== Origin ==
In 1896, Jacob Wilhide established a divine healing ministry in Philadelphia. [ref: Out of Zion Into Philadelphia and West Africa: Faith Tabernacle Congregation, 1897-1925, Pneuma] He aimed to spread John Alexander Dowie's faith healing ministry and establish a divine healing church. This church was not officially associated with the Dowie's Christian Catholic Church, but Dowie later integrated Wilhide's Philadelphia Ministry into his own church.

John Wesley Ankins was a member of Wilhide's faith healing mission, and was one of the first people baptized into it. Ankins quickly rose into a leadership role alongside Wilhide. In 1897, he established his own separate meeting in 1897. He called this Gospel Mission, and associated himself with Wilhide's mission in 1898. However, by 1899, Ankins had separated his own mission from Wilhide and Dowie's.

In 1904, Ankins's Gospel Mission purchased a church building that it had been using for the past seven years and renamed itself to Faith Tabernacle Congregation. In 1907, Faith Tabernacle opened a healing home, modeled after those of the Christian Catholic Church.

Faith Tabernacle Congregation gathered new members through distributing free literature. The primary publications were entitled Sword of the Spirit and Leaves of Healing. Correspondence was also published internationally, which led to the formation of branches of Faith Tabernacle Congregation in Nigeria and Ghana.

== Beliefs ==
Faith Tabernacle follows a fundamentalist interpretation of the bible. Most notably, the church preaches a literal belief in praying to heal the sick, as well as rejection of modern medicine. [ref: Bad Faith: When Religious Belief Undermines Modern Medicine, Basic Books] This includes prohibition of vaccination, glasses, hearing aids, and over-the-counter painkillers. [ref: God's will vs. medicine: Does Faith Tabernacle beliefs put children at risk?, pennlive] Faith Tabernacle Congregation also prohibits drinking alcohol, smoking cigarettes, and premarital sex. Women are forbidden to wear pants and are expected to be subservient to their husbands. [ref: When Prayer Fails: Faith Healing, Children, and the Law, Oxford Academic] Faith Tabernacle Congregation preaches against associating with members not in the church, which leads to members who leave the church being shunned. Some former members have called Faith Tabernacle Congregation a cult. [ref: From fear to freedom: Family urges others to leave faith-healing church they call a cult, WHP] [ref: Former 'cult' members call for Pennsylvania church to be shut down, investigated, WHP]

== 1990–1991 Philadelphia measles outbreak ==

Faith Tabernacle Congregation gained national attention during the 1990-91 measles outbreak in Philadelphia. The outbreak was declared in October 1990. On January 16, 1991, the Philadelphia Health Commission received an anonymous call detailing the caller's granddaughter who was sick with measles. [ref: A 1990 Measles Outbreak Shows How the Disease Can Roar Back, The New York Times] The caller believed that measles was spreading at Faith Tabernacle School, a private school for children of church members. On February 7, a 9-year-old Faith Tabernacle School Student died of measles. The Philadelphia Health Commissioner, Dr. Robert Ross, then asked Pastor Charles Reinert to vaccinate Faith Tabernacle School Students. He refused, citing a belief in prayer to heal the sick, but did agree to give Ross addresses and phone numbers of members of the church. The commissioner started calling members of the church and asked them to report sick children. However, a child from one of the families Ross had called died a few days after he had called them. Due to the refusal of members of the church to report sick children, Commissioner Ross obtained a court order allowing him to compel medical treatment for sick children against their parents' will and to compel vaccinations for children.

Out of the 9 children that died in the outbreak, 6 of them were members of Faith Tabernacle Congregation and First Century Gospel Church, an off-shoot with similar faith-healing beliefs. [ref: 1991: The Philly measles outbreak that killed 9 children, 6abc Philadelphia] 438 of the 1,424 measles cases reported were among members of Faith Tabernacle Congregation and First Century Gospel Church. [ref: High attack rates and case fatality during a...: Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal, Ovid] Members of the two churches were roughly 1,000 times more likely to catch the disease than non-members, and roughly 4 times more likely to die from the disease than non-members.
