data.title: Aristide Saggino
data.text:
Aristide Saggino is an Italian psychologist and psychotherapist, and former full professor of psychometrics at the University of Chieti–Pescara. [ref: Curriculum vitae – Aristide Saggino, Open Science Framework] He is co-author of the Teate Depression Inventory and served two terms as national president of the Italian Association for Behaviour Analysis and Modification and Behavioural and Cognitive Therapy (AIAMC). He is known for his advocacy of scientifically grounded, evidence-based psychotherapy.

== Education and career ==
Saggino graduated in psychology from Sapienza University of Rome in 1979 and completed a specialization in clinical psychology there in 1992. He received a PhD in psychology from the Pontifical Salesian University in 2000, with a dissertation on the Myers–Briggs Type Indicator.

From 1979 to 2001 he worked as a psychologist in the Italian national health service in Campania, while conducting research on psychological testing at Sapienza University from 1985 to 1999. In 1994, supported by a CNR–NATO Senior Fellowship, he was a research fellow at the University of Exeter with psychometrician Paul Kline, with whom he co-authored studies of the Italian Myers–Briggs Type Indicator. [ref: Item factor analysis of the Italian version of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, Personality and Individual Differences] Between 1998 and 2007 he was repeatedly a visiting professor at the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London, working on personality theory and assessment.

He joined the University of Chieti–Pescara as associate professor in 2001 and was full professor from 2006 until his retirement in 2026. Since October 2026 he has been scientific director of the postgraduate schools of cognitive behavioural psychotherapy of the Centro per lo Studio della Personalità (CSP), which are recognised by the AIAMC. He chaired the undergraduate programme in psychological sciences from 2005 to 2012 and headed the university's Psychometrics Laboratory and its laboratory for research on cognitive behavioural and evidence-based psychotherapy (LARIPSI).

He was national president of the AIAMC from 2014 to 2017 and again from 2020 to 2024. [ref: Psicoterapia e Salute Mentale: incontro con il Prof. Saggino a EXPO, State of Mind] [ref: Gli organi sociali – Past Presidents, AIAMC] [ref: 12a Conferenza Internazionale di Applied Behavior Analysis – programma ECM, University of Chieti–Pescara] [ref: La Psicoterapia Cognitiva e Comportamentale in Italia oggi – Intervista al Prof. Aristide Saggino, State of Mind] During his first term, in March 2016, the AIAMC became the first Italian association to have its training programmes accredited by the European Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Therapies (EABCT). [ref: Accredited associations, European Association for Behavioural and Cognitive Therapies] From 2017 to 2023 he was the AIAMC's representative to the EABCT. Since 2019 he has been vice-president of IACABAI, the Italy Associate Chapter of the Association for Behavior Analysis International formed by AIAMC and AARBA. [ref: About us, IACABAI] From 2012 to 2020 he chaired the Abruzzo–Molise section of CICAP, the Italian skeptics' organization.

== Research ==
Saggino's research covers the construction and validation of psychological tests, individual differences with a focus on psychometric theories of intelligence, and cognitive behavioural therapy.

With Michela Balsamo he developed the Teate Depression Inventory (TDI), a self-report measure of depression built using the Rasch model. [ref: TDI – Teate Depression Inventory. Manuale, Hogrefe] [ref: Building a new Rasch-based self-report inventory of depression, Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment] In the United States, the construct validity of the TDI has been the subject of graduate theses at Eastern Illinois University, including studies with Black/African American and Middle Eastern/Arab American samples. [ref: Construct Validity of the Teate Depression Inventory with a Black African American Sample, Eastern Illinois University] [ref: Construct Validity of the Teate Depression Inventory (TDI) with a Middle Eastern/Arab American Sample, Eastern Illinois University] [ref: Construct Validity of the Teate Depression Inventory: Convergent and Discriminant Validity and Equivalence for Black/African American and White/Caucasian Samples, Eastern Illinois University]

He has also led Italian adaptations of several instruments, including the Myers–Briggs Type Indicator, the Eysenck Personality Profiler and the WPPSI-IV.

Since 2022 he has served on the scientific advisory board of the Treatments That Work series of Oxford University Press, edited by David H. Barlow. [ref: Treatments That Work – Editorial Board, Oxford University Press]

He has also been active in public outreach on evidence-based psychotherapy; in 2015, for example, he spoke at Expo 2015 in Milan in a round table titled "Towards an evidence-based psychotherapy". On 26 October 2023 he testified as an expert before the 10th Standing Committee of the Italian Senate during its examination of bills on the employment of people with autism spectrum disorders. [ref: 10ª Commissione Affari sociali, sanità, lavoro pubblico e privato, previdenza sociale del Senato della Repubblica, Radio Radicale]

He has also expressed critical views on the scientific status of contemporary cognitive behavioural therapy: at the 2022 CBT-Italia congress in Florence, speaking as president of the AIAMC, he described the field's crisis as "pathological" rather than healthy, a view discussed critically by Giovanni Maria Ruggiero. [ref: La prima giornata del congresso CBT-Italia, State of Mind]

== Awards ==
In 2024 he received the "Buona Sanità" (Good Healthcare) award, presented in Naples by the Buona Sanità association, for his contribution to research on and public dissemination of evidence-based psychotherapies. [ref: Al professor Aristide Saggino della d'Annunzio il premio Buona Sanità 2024, ChietiToday]

== Selected works ==
* Saggino, A., & Kline, P. (1996). "The location of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator in personality factor space". Personality and Individual Differences, 21, 591–597.
* Saggino, A. (2000). "The Big Three or the Big Five? A replication study". Personality and Individual Differences, 28, 879–886.
* Saggino, A. (2002). La teoria dei tipi psicologici. Una verifica empirica. Bari: Laterza.
* Ebisch, S. J., et al., & Saggino, A. (2012). "Common and unique neuro-functional basis of induction, visualization, and spatial relationships as cognitive components of fluid intelligence". NeuroImage, 62, 331–342.
* Balsamo, M., & Saggino, A. (2013). TDI – Teate Depression Inventory. Manuale. Florence: Hogrefe.
* Balsamo, M., Giampaglia, G., & Saggino, A. (2014). "Building a new Rasch-based self-report inventory of depression". Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment, 10, 153–165.
* Saggino, A., Pezzuti, L., Tommasi, M., Cianci, L., Colom, R., & Orsini, A. (2014). "Null sex differences in general intelligence among elderly". Personality and Individual Differences, 63, 53–57.
* Saggino, A., & Collevecchio, A. (2014). Psicoterapia e metodo scientifico. Un'analisi critica. Milan: FrancoAngeli.
* Tommasi, M., Pezzuti, L., Colom, R., Abad, F. J., Saggino, A., & Orsini, A. (2015). "Increased education level is related with higher IQ scores but lower g-variance: Evidence from the standardization of the WAIS-R for Italy". Intelligence, 50, 68–74.
* Carlucci, L., Saggino, A., & Balsamo, M. (2021). "On the efficacy of the unified protocol for transdiagnostic treatment of emotional disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis". Clinical Psychology Review, 87, 101999.

data.title: Limnes, Argolis
data.text:
Limnes () is a village in Argolis, Greece. It forms a community of the municipality of Argos-Mykines, within the municipal unit of Mykines. [ref: ΔΗΜΟΣ ΑΡΓΟΥΣ – ΜΥΚΗΝΩΝ ΠΕ ΑΡΓΟΛΙΔΑΣ, Kallikratis] The village had 553 permanent residents at the 2021 Greek census. [ref: Αποτελέσματα Μόνιμου Πληθυσμού κατά οικισμό, Απογραφή 2021, Hellenic Statistical Authority]

== Geography and economy ==
Limnes is a mountain village. Livestock farming became the main local occupation after tobacco cultivation was abandoned. [ref: Εκπληκτικά ντοκουμέντα για την λαϊκή μουσική παράδοση της Αργολίδας από τις Λίμνες (βίντεο), Argolikes Eidiseis]

== Language and traditions ==
Limnes is one of the Arvanite villages of Argolis, where Arvanitika has traditionally been spoken. [ref: Learning Arvanitic in Late 19th and Early 20th Century Greece: Linguistic Maintenance and Cultural Idiosyncrasies in Greece's Arvanitic Speaking Communities, Zeitschrift für Balkanologie]

The village celebrates the feast of the Presentation of Christ on 2 February. Its central church is dedicated to the feast, and traditional singing and dancing form part of the celebrations. [ref: Sui canti tradizionali degli arbëreshë della Grecia oggi, tenendo conto specialmente dei canti delle nozze. Notizie di una ricerca sul campo]

data.title: Basht. (band)
data.text:
Basht. are an Irish post-punk and alternative rock band formed in Dublin in 2021. The band consists of Jack Leavey (vocals and guitar), Lughaidh Armstrong-Mayock (lead guitar), Louis Christle (bass) and Ryan McClelland (drums). [ref: Irish band Basht crash the Top Ten with debut album, RTÉ]

The group released two EPs, Dirty White Lies (2024) and Bitter and Twisted (2025), before their debut studio album, Poor Advice, was released through LAB Records on 9 October 2026. The album reached number seven on the Irish Albums Chart and number one on the Irish Independent Albums Chart. [ref: Official Irish Albums Chart on 16/10/2026, Official Charts Company] [ref: Irish Charts: Top 50 Independent, 10 October 2026 – 16 October 2026, Irish Recorded Music Association]

== History ==

=== Formation and early releases (2021–2025) ===

Basht. were formed in Dublin in 2021 by vocalist and guitarist Jack Leavey, who had initially been looking for musicians to accompany a solo project. After meeting bassist Louis Christle, the two began developing the project as a band. [ref: Una-Basht., Dork]

Their first EP, Dirty White Lies, was released in 2024, followed by Bitter and Twisted in 2025. The band toured the United Kingdom and Ireland and supported acts including Wunderhorse, DEADLETTER, Everything Everything and Miles Kane.

The lineup changed during this period. Lughaidh Armstrong-Mayock initially joined as a touring guitarist before becoming involved in the band's songwriting. Drummer Ryan McClelland subsequently joined, completing the four-member lineup in 2025.

=== Poor Advice (2026) ===

In April 2026, Basht. announced their debut studio album, Poor Advice, and released its lead single, "Perfume". The song was produced by Ali Chant. Leavey described its subject as a son looking back on the breakdown of his parents' marriage, with the lyrics also addressing the historical influence of the Catholic Church on private life in Ireland. [ref: Basht announce debut album Poor Advice, Hot Press]

The band worked on material for the album while touring, developing songs during rehearsals and soundchecks. The recording sessions were undertaken with producer Ali Chant.

Poor Advice was released on 9 October 2026 through LAB Records. The ten-track album addresses institutional authority, religion and political conflict. In an interview with Hot Press, Leavey discussed the use of biblical imagery in the lyrics and the influence of contemporary conflicts on songs including "Terror TV" and "Circadia". [ref: Basht.: "It's just our nature – Irish people question authority, and we've always had the ability to put two fingers up to it", Hot Press]

The album entered the Irish Albums Chart at number seven on 16 October 2026. It also debuted at number one on the Irish Independent Albums Chart.

Following the album's release, Basht. announced a headline tour of the United Kingdom beginning in October 2026 and a sold-out concert at the Button Factory in Dublin in November. Leavey's father had previously managed the venue when it was known as the Temple Bar Music Centre. [ref: Basht., Morgana and The Wran debut in Top 10 of Irish Albums Chart, Hot Press]

== Musical style ==

Basht.'s music has been described as post-punk and alternative rock. Their songs feature distorted guitars, bass-driven arrangements and changes between quieter passages and heavier sections. The Irish Times compared their sound to a combination of Radiohead and Nirvana in its review of Poor Advice. [ref: New Irish albums reviewed and rated: Basht, Meryl Streek, Morgana, Wasps vs Humans, Whozyerman?, The Irish Times]

The band's members have discussed their interest in music outside conventional guitar-based rock. In an October 2026 interview with Hot Press, Christle described listening to 1990s house and 1980s Detroit techno, particularly the use of drum machines.

The lyrics of Poor Advice draw on religious imagery and political subjects. Leavey has identified the relationship between religious and political authority in Ireland as one of the album's recurring concerns.

== Critical reception ==

Poor Advice received a five-star review from Tony Clayton-Lea of The Irish Times. Clayton-Lea compared the band's sound to Radiohead and Nirvana and noted the album's changes in dynamics and politically focused lyrics.

Riccardo Dwyer of Hot Press awarded the album 7.5 out of 10. His review discussed the album's intensity and its treatment of religion and political conflict. [ref: Album Review: Basht., Poor Advice, Hot Press]

== Band members ==

=== Current members ===

data.title: Inter-University Accelerator Centre
data.text:
The Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC), known until 2005 as the Nuclear Science Centre (NSC), is an autonomous research institute in New Delhi, India, that operates particle accelerators and associated experimental facilities as a national user facility for researchers from Indian universities, colleges and research institutions. It was the first Inter-University Centre set up by the University Grants Commission (UGC), and is funded by the UGC. [ref: Inter University Accelerator Centre (formerly Nuclear Science Centre), University Grants Commission] [ref: About IUAC, Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

The centre's main accelerator is a 15 UD Pelletron tandem electrostatic accelerator, which has delivered ion beams to users since 1991 and is supplemented by a superconducting linear accelerator booster, several smaller accelerators, and a compact free-electron laser producing terahertz radiation. It also hosts a PARAM Rudra supercomputer under India's National Supercomputing Mission. [ref: Nuclear reaction and structure studies using experimental facilities at Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC), The European Physical Journal A]

== History ==
The UGC conceived the Inter-University Centre model in the early 1980s to give university researchers access to expensive research infrastructure that individual universities could not afford. The proposal for an accelerator-based centre was approved by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in 1984, and the institute was set up that year as the Nuclear Science Centre, the first of the UGC's Inter-University Centres. [ref: Historical dates of events, Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

The centre was built as a greenfield project on about 25 acres of land provided by Jawaharlal Nehru University, in the institutional area near the Qutub in south Delhi. [ref: Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC), New Delhi, Vikaspedia] Construction began in December 1986. The centre was registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 on 30 September 1988 and became autonomous on 19 December 1988.

The Pelletron accelerator was commissioned and dedicated to the nation by the Minister of Human Resource Development on 19 December 1990, and the first user experiment was carried out on 8 July 1991, from which date the centre has functioned as a national user facility.

Through the 1990s and 2000s the centre added beamlines and detector systems for nuclear physics, materials science and radiation biology, and developed a superconducting linear accelerator (LINAC) to boost the energy of beams from the Pelletron. Its first LINAC module was commissioned in September 2004. In June 2005 the Nuclear Science Centre was renamed the Inter-University Accelerator Centre, reflecting its role as a multidisciplinary accelerator facility rather than a nuclear physics laboratory alone. [ref: Inter-University Accelerator Centre (Formerly Nuclear Science Centre), Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

== Accelerators ==
=== 15 UD Pelletron ===
The centre's principal machine is a 15 UD Pelletron, a vertical tandem electrostatic accelerator capable of terminal voltages of about 15 MV. It accelerates beams of ions ranging from protons to heavy ions to energies of tens to hundreds of MeV, and has been in near-continuous operation as a user facility since 1991. [ref: IUAC information brochure 2020, Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

=== Superconducting LINAC ===
To reach higher beam energies, the centre designed and built a superconducting linear accelerator that boosts ions from the Pelletron. It uses niobium quarter-wave resonators, a number of which were fabricated in-house at the centre's resonator fabrication facility, and is cooled by liquid helium from an on-site cryogenic plant.

=== Other accelerators and ion sources ===
* A 1.7 MV Pelletron used mainly for ion beam analysis techniques such as Rutherford backscattering spectrometry.
* A Low Energy Ion Beam Facility (LEIB), based on a high-temperature superconducting electron cyclotron resonance ion source, providing low-energy, highly charged ion beams for materials and atomic physics research.
* A dedicated accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) system based on a 500 kV Pelletron, used for measuring long-lived radionuclides such as beryllium-10 and aluminium-26 in geological and environmental samples.

=== Delhi Light Source ===
The Delhi Light Source (DLS) is a compact, pre-bunched free-electron laser facility built at the centre with support from the Board of Research in Nuclear Sciences. A photocathode radio-frequency electron gun driven by a fibre laser produces short electron bunches of a few MeV, which pass through an undulator to generate tunable terahertz radiation in roughly the 0.18–3 THz range. Later phases of the project envisage a superconducting electron gun and accelerating structures to raise the electron energy to about 40 MeV, for infrared radiation and X-ray production by inverse Compton scattering. [ref: Status of Design and Development of Delhi Light Source at IUAC, Delhi] [ref: Free Electron Laser, Inter-University Accelerator Centre] The design and development involved collaboration with KEK in Japan and with Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin and DESY in Germany. [ref: An upcoming compact THz radiation and electron beam facility at IUAC, Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

== Experimental facilities ==
Beams from the accelerators are delivered to experimental stations in two beam halls. Major facilities include:
* Heavy Ion Reaction Analyser (HIRA), a recoil mass spectrometer for studying nuclear reaction products.
* Hybrid Recoil mass Analyzer (HYRA), a gas-filled and vacuum-mode separator for studies of heavy and superheavy nuclei and reactions near the Coulomb barrier.
* Indian National Gamma Array (INGA), a national array of Compton-suppressed clover germanium detectors for gamma spectroscopy, which is periodically moved between Indian accelerator laboratories.
* National Array of Neutron Detectors (NAND), used for neutron measurements in fusion–fission studies.
* General Purpose Scattering Chamber and other set-ups for reaction studies.
* Materials science beamlines for swift heavy ion irradiation and ion implantation, with facilities for in-situ characterisation.
* A radiation biology beamline for studying the effects of heavy-ion irradiation on biological systems.
* Atomic physics set-ups for ion–atom collision studies.

== High-performance computing ==
In September 2024 the centre became one of three host sites for the PARAM Rudra supercomputers, built in India by the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing under the National Supercomputing Mission and dedicated to the nation by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 26 September 2024. The other two systems were installed at the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope in Pune and the S. N. Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences in Kolkata, and the three machines together cost about. [ref: PM Modi unveils India-made Param Rudra supercomputers; what you need to know, [[Business Today (India)] [ref: India unveils three supercomputers to boost HPC ambitions, [[DatacenterDynamics]

The IUAC system, with a capacity of about 3 petaflops, is the most powerful of the three. It is intended mainly for computational research in materials science and atomic physics, complementing the centre's experimental facilities, and, like other National Supercomputing Mission systems, is available to researchers from academic institutions across India who apply for accounts through the mission's user portal. [ref: Access to PARAM Systems, National Supercomputing Mission]

== Research ==
Research at the centre is conducted both by visiting users from universities and institutes and by the centre's own scientists, who have the dual role of operating the facilities for users and pursuing their own research. Main research areas include:
* Nuclear physics, particularly nuclear structure and heavy-ion reaction dynamics such as fusion, fission and quasi-fission near the Coulomb barrier
* Materials science, including the modification of materials by swift heavy ions and the synthesis of nanostructures
* Atomic physics
* Radiation biology
* Accelerator mass spectrometry applied to earth, environmental and archaeological sciences

The centre's facilities have been used by several hundred researchers from about 70 universities, dozens of colleges and numerous national laboratories in India, as well as by researchers from abroad.

== Technology development and industry collaboration ==
Alongside its user facilities, the centre has developed expertise in superconducting magnets, cryogenics and related accelerator technologies, which it has applied outside basic research. As part of India's contribution to the PIP-II upgrade of the Fermilab accelerator complex in the United States, the centre and the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre supplied two single-spoke superconducting resonator cavities for testing at Fermilab. [ref: India sets its sights on linac innovation, CERN Courier]

=== Indigenous MRI magnet ===
The centre is a partner in the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology's Indigenous Magnetic Resonance Imaging (IMRI) national mission, led by the Society for Applied Microwave Electronics Engineering and Research (SAMEER), Mumbai, alongside two centres of the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing and other partners, to design and build India's first domestically developed 1.5 tesla magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner. [ref: AIIMS to launch human trials on indigenous MRI machine system in October] Within the mission, IUAC was responsible for the scanner's core component: an actively shielded, whole-body 1.5 T superconducting magnet with a zero-boil-off liquid-helium cryostat, technology that had previously been held by only a few foreign manufacturers. [ref: Development of a 1.5 T Actively-shielded Superconducting MRI Magnet System (MeitY-funded IMRI project), Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

The cryostat, designed at IUAC, was fabricated by the industrial firm INOXCVA and completed in April 2023. The magnet system was named I-Amrit 1.5 (Indian Advanced MRI Technology 1.5), and the project partners described India as the sixth country able to manufacture MRI magnet systems. [ref: India's first indigenously designed 4K Helium cryostat for lowering cost of Magnetic Resonance Imaging, BioSpectrum India] The first prototype scanner, which SAMEER agreed in March 2025 to install at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi for clinical trials, was integrated with a procured magnet while the indigenous magnet was being completed.

To take the technology to commercial production, IUAC worked with Paras Defence and Space Technologies, which co-developed the MRI magnet in consultation with the centre and planned to manufacture it at its Ambernath facility. [ref: Paras Defence to manufacture critical magnets for India's first indigenous MRI machines, BioSpectrum India] In November 2025 the two signed a memorandum of understanding to jointly develop a commercial-grade superconducting MRI magnet system for manufacture in India. [ref: Paras Defence shares jump 2% after MoU with IUAC for MRI magnet system, The Economic Times] [ref: Paras Defence, IUAC to develop commercial-grade MRI magnet system, [[Business Today (India)]

== Academics and training ==
Although it does not award degrees itself, the centre supports doctoral research for students registered at Indian universities, who carry out experimental work at the centre and return to their home institutions. It runs a training programme for new research students and scientist trainees that is open to university research scholars, and a summer programme in experimental and accelerator physics for physics students, in which each participant completes a short project under a mentor.

== Governance ==
The centre is a registered society funded by the UGC. Its Governing Council is chaired by the Chairman of the UGC, and its other statutory bodies include a Governing Board, a Finance Committee and an Accelerator Users Committee drawn from the national research community. [ref: Organizations, Inter-University Accelerator Centre] The Director of the centre is its chief executive and serves as member secretary of the Governing Council.

data.title: Yangjiaping
data.text:
Yangjiaping (杨家坪) most commonly refers to a major, bustling commercial and residential subdistrict located in the Jiulongpo District of Chongqing, China. Known historically as one of the city's oldest industrial hubs, it has evolved into a vibrant urban destination famous for its massive pedestrian shopping street, modern high-rises, and unique multi-layered transit infrastructure. A major hub on Line 2 and Line 18 of the Chongqing Rail Transit network. Line 2 is famous for its monorail trains that weave dramatically through and around the city's mountainous high-rises. Historically, Yangjiaping is also famous in religious history as the location of the Our Lady of Consolation Abbey. Established in 1883 by French Catholic Trappist monks in the rugged mountains of Hebei province (just outside the Great Wall), it grew into a prominent monastery. However, it was tragically destroyed in August 1947 during the Chinese Civil War when Communist forces burned it down during what is known as the Yangjiaping Massacre. Thus, the name historically means "The Yang Family's Flat Land," indicating that these locations originally began as settlements established by families sharing the Yang surname on level terrain.

data.title: Central Maine Healthcare
data.text:
Central Maine Healthcare (CMH) is a non-profit integrated healthcare delivery system based in Lewiston, Maine. It serves approximately 400,000 residents in central, western, and mid-coast Maine. Since February 2026, it has been a member of the Prime Healthcare Foundation.

== History ==
Central Maine Healthcare was established as an integrated system in 1982. It originally operated as an independent regional health system centered around Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston.

In January 2025, CMH announced an agreement to affiliate with the California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation. The transaction closed on February 16, 2026, making Prime Healthcare Foundation the sole corporate member and parent organization of Central Maine Healthcare. As part of the agreement, Prime Healthcare Foundation committed to investing $150 million over five years in facilities, services, and infrastructure across the CMH system. CMH hospitals and facilities retained their names. Local leadership structures were retained in the initial period after closing, though subsequent leadership changes have occurred, including the appointment of a new chief executive officer in March 2026.

== Facilities ==
Central Maine Healthcare includes the following main facilities:
* Central Maine Medical Center (Lewiston) — flagship hospital (formerly a Level III Trauma Center; ACS verification lapsed in December 2025, with state conditions requiring re-establishment by 2028)
* Bridgton Hospital (Bridgton)
* Rumford Hospital (Rumford)
* Central Maine Comprehensive Cancer Center
* Central Maine Heart and Vascular Institute
* Maine College of Health Professions
* Rumford Community Home
* Bolster Heights (assisted living)
* More than 40 outpatient physician practices

== Affiliation with Prime Healthcare Foundation ==
On February 16, 2026, Prime Healthcare Foundation completed its affiliation with Central Maine Healthcare, becoming the sole corporate member and parent organization. The transaction expanded Prime Healthcare Foundation’s portfolio to 21 not-for-profit hospitals across eight states. Under the structure, Central Maine Healthcare continues to operate its facilities under their existing names while becoming part of the larger Prime Healthcare network. The affiliation was subject to regulatory conditions imposed by the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, including commitments regarding essential services and trauma-center status.

== Services ==
CMH provides a full range of healthcare services, including:
* Primary and specialty care
* Emergency and trauma services
* Cancer care
* Cardiovascular services
* Surgical services
* Medical education through the Maine College of Health Professions

data.title: CUYAHOGA BUILDING
data.text:
Burnham and Root Cuyahoga Building was a skyscraper located in Cleveland, Ohio, United States. The building had 8 floors at a height of 152 ft (46.3 m).

==History==
The Burnham and Root Cuyahoga Building was constructed from 1892 to 1893 by Myron T. Herrick and Jas. Parmalee. It was the first steel-frame structure in Cleveland. Architectural design by Burnham & Root. The mayor of Cleveland, Tom L. Johnson, had his office in the building. Major tenets included: Cleveland Electric Illuminating Company, Schroeder's Drugs, and Schroeder's Bookstore. [ref: CUYAHOGA BUILDING, Encyclopedia of Cleveland History]

In 1982 the Cuyahoga building along with the adjacent Williamson Building was demolished to make way for the construction of the 200 Public Square, also know has the Sohio building.

The terra cotta entrance was saved and re-installed in the Western Reserve Historical Society library building.

data.title: Leslie James Milton
data.text:
Leslie James Milton, Sr is an American drummer, singer and bandleader born in 1938 [ref: Leslie Milton, Discogs].  His career includes music played in and around New Orleans, LO [ref: Modern Jazz Concert, L.L.A Auditorium, 2700 S. Claiborne Ave, New Orleans LO, The Louisiana Weekly] [ref: Talented Musicians have new 'Jazz" Idea, The Louisiana Weekly], San Francisco, CA [ref: Jazz, The Beat of the City, San Francisco Examiner], Los Angeles, CA [ref: Sonny, Cher Impressive, Los Angeles Citizens News], Long Beach, CA [ref: In Person: Judy, Les, John and Steve are 'Something New' and they are Truly Something Special, The Independent], and the Pacific Northwest (WA [ref: Put me on the Guest List: Strypes, Isaac Scott, Blue Lights, The Rocket] [ref: Blues Calendar, The Rocket] [ref: Leslie Milton's Stardoms Big Band Laser Blues, The Rocket] [ref: Jolly Roger 8721 Lake City Way, The Rocket] [ref: Thursday 3: Leslie Milton's Star Drums, The Rocket] [ref: Special: Leslie Milton's "Star Drums", The News Tribune] [ref: Meadow Park Golf Course, The News Tribune] [ref: Big-mama blues, The Spokesman-Review Spokane Chronicle] [ref: Leslie Milton's Star Drums, The Rocket] [ref: Bluestars know their business, The Spokane Review Spokane Chronicle] [ref: Owl Cafe, The News Tribune] [ref: Ticket Alert, The News Tribune] [ref: Hot Summer Jazz, The Rocket] [ref: New Orleans Restaurant, The Rocket] [ref: Melody Ballroom, The Oregonian]).

Early Life and Education

Leslie James Milton, Sr., better known by his current stage name Leslie “Star Drums” Milton [ref: The Chat: Talkin' blues, space and loose garbage with Leslie 'Star Drums' Milton, Heraldnet.com] [ref: Leslie "Star Drums" Milton & the Star Drums Light Show, https://wablues.org/bluesletter/], is an American drummer and bandleader.   His motto is: ”Listen, Concentrate, and have Fun!”

Milton was born in New Orleans, Louisiana. He began his drumming career "at about 5 years old, playing little toy drums. It was a passion. I saw my uncle play drums and he took me under his wing. That was it, I was a drummer." His uncle was Ernest ‘The Kid’ Milton, a well-known show drummer in New Orleans, [ref: ] who taught him the art of drumming and showmanship.   While attending Joseph S. Clark Sr. High School, [ref: ] Milton joined the marching band led by Yvonne V. Bush [ref: Yvonne Busch Obituary (2014) - New Orleans, LA - The Times-Picayune, Legacy.com] [ref: ].   Milton met his wife Janice Carol Thornton while in 9th grade and they married when he was 19 years old.

Early Career

As a teenager and through his early 20s, Milton played drums professionally in and around New Orleans and traveled with Roy "Good Rockin" Brown [ref: ] to New York to play in Brown's orchestra at the Apollo Theater. Milton also played in a variety of burlesque halls and night clubs in New Orleans including one led by Bill Senegal [ref: Bill Sinegal, wikilink].

In 1961, Milton moved to Los Angeles, CA where he had an active career as a session and touring musician.  Milton worked with "Robert Bumps Blackwell"   [ref: Robert Blackwell, wikilinks] for Mercury Records. Blackwell at the time was managing Sam Cooke and Little Richard with whom Milton participated in session recordings.  "Bumps" hired Milton to back "Bessie Griffin and the Gospel Pearls" for the "Ed Sullivan Show". [ref: Bessie Griffin, wikipedia]  Milton was an active session musician working on studio tracks with a variety of musicians including Johnny Otis, Etta James, Little Richard, Jackie DeShannon, Roy Brown, Ike & Tina Turner and Connie Stevens. He performed regularly with "Sonny and Cher". [ref: Leslie "Star Drums" Milton Still Having Fun Doing What He Loves, The Seattle Times]. Milton played with the Watts' 103rd Street Rhythm Band on American Bandstand performing their hit called "Spreading Honey" [ref: American Bandstand Episode #11.4, YouTube]. In 1962, Milton recorded "Papa-Oom-Mow-Mow" with The Rivingtons. [ref: Papa-Oom-Mow-Mow, Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia]. Milton also appeared, uncredited, in the movie, The Hotel [ref: The Hotel, Hotel (1967 film)], playing drums in the scenes showing the cabaret go-go dancers, visible at about 90 minutes in the film.

Milton also performed in bands supporting musical scenes in several "Alfred Hitchcock" thrillers. For instance, in the TV episode of Alfred Hitchcock Presents (1961), "You Can't Trust a Man", [ref: Alfred Hitchcock Presents season 6, Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia] he can be heard playing drums for a nightclub vocalist who walks into her room and says "I asked for drums in the last number, not an active uprising. Musicians!"

In 1976, inspired by America's Bicentennial Celebration, Milton created his persona as Leslie 'Star Drums' Milton.  He used his 'extra-terrestrial' imagination to take the audience on an imaginary journey into space using special effects and show drumming. At that time, Milton was the drummer for the Something New group. He performed drum solos including the 'Space Odyssey' show that included special lighting effects, creating a feeling of a rocket flight deep into outer space. These 'show drumming' performances evolved into his persona as Leslie 'Star Drums' Milton. The band also played several original songs by Milton including Gator Joe and Somebody Make it Right.

Moving to Seattle, WA

In 1977, Milton moved to Seattle, WA and started playing with The Blue Lights band and recorded the song 'Mount St. Helen Blues' prior to the mountain explosion 6 months later. This song became an opening act for Muddy Waters and Willie Dixon at the Show Box events venue. He was a special guest drummer for the Isaac Scott Band and with Louis Erlanger, Kin Field and Mark Dalton, Milton was a member of The Slamhound Hunters. [ref: Kim Field hunts for a magic moment, The Daily Herald] [ref: Slamhound Hunters, The Rocket] The Slamhound Hunters released three recording projects including two albums ("4/1 Mind"and Private Jungle), and a single ("Cadillac Walk"). Private Jungle was selected by Rocket Magazine as one of the top 10 albums of all time in the Pacific Northwest. This later album includes Milton's original song, "Swamp Crab".

In the late 1980's, Milton joined Freddy James (pianist/organist 'extraordinaire') and the Rocking 88's'. He was with Freddy's band for 10 years. The group recorded several CD's together and performed 7 nights a week in clubs all over Seattle and western Washington.

Milton has since written and recorded many originals songs (see Discography below) and one instrumental track of the Duke Ellington composition "Caravan” (ref his album).

Milton was the co-writer with King Floyd ( Ref. ) for the song:  Heartaches (1971 release.)  (See his Discography pages I wrote and the Discogs page for this….)

Star Drums and Lady Keys

Milton always wanted to sing so, in in the late 1990's, he teamed up with Gael 'Lady Keys' Kurath [ref: Getting Back in the Groove, Bluesletter, Washington Blues Society] who hails originally from Chicago, and is a classically trained pianist and scientist [ref: Viral fitness: definitions, measurement, and current insights, Current opinions in Virology].  Kurath adopted the moniker of “Lady Keys”.  The musical partnership of *”Star Drums & Lady Keys'” has endured over several decades. They are known for their steady gig at the Alligator Restaurant in Everett WA as well as playing local nightclubs, private parties and special benefit shows.

In view of the contributions Leslie Milton has made throughout his lifetime, The Washington Blues Society presented Milton with several awards including Drummer of the year (1993/1995), Entertainer of the year (1994), and a Living Blues Legend (1999).  He was also inducted into the Washington Blues Society Hall of Fame (1995) and performed for former President William Clinton (1996) at the Paramount Theatre in Seattle.

data.title: Bayou Boy
data.text:
Bayou Boy is a 1971 American television adventure film produced by Walt Disney Productions. [ref: The Wonderful World of Disney Television, Hyperion Books] [ref: Disney A to Z: The Official Encyclopedia: Third Edition, Disney Editions] Directed by Gary Nelson and written by Louis Pelletier, it originally aired in two parts on NBC's The Wonderful World of Disney on February 7 and February 14, 1971. [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23] [ref: Louis Pelletier; Wrote 500 Episodes of 'FBI' Radio Series, Los Angeles Times]

Filming took place at Pine Island Point at Caddo Lake, on the Texas-Louisiana border near Shreveport. [ref: Dynamite, cowboy boots, horse falls, and toupee hijinks with Steve McQueen's costar Mitch Vogel, Medium] [ref: Disney filming at Caddo Lake, Shreveport Times] [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] [ref: Louisiana to be Spotlighted in Disney TV Series on NBC, The Marksville Weekly News] [ref: Page 28, The Jeffersonian] In one instance when a stuntman failed to show up, a local highway patrolman was asked to fall 25 feet in a lake. [ref: City Beat, The Mexia Daily News] After filming Governor Preston Smith made the cast of the film honorary Texas citizens. [ref: 'Bayou Boy' Cast Honorary Texas Citizens, The Salt Lake Tribune]

A $12,000 replica of the bayou was constructed at Disney Studio in Burbank for the alligator fight scene. [ref: Bayou Boy, Chronique Disney] [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] [ref: TV Scout, The Index-Journal]

Co-stars John McIntire and Jeanette Nolan were married in real life, and often appeared in the same shows and movies. [ref: Husband, Wife Acting Team in 'Bayou Boy', Idaho State Journal] [ref: Behind the Scenes, The Daily Herald]

The musical score was composed by Buddy Baker. [ref: Norman "Buddy" Baker Collection, NYU Special Collections Finding Aids] The opening title song, "Bayou Boy", was written by Terry Gilkyson and performed by his daughter Lisa. [ref: Dynamite, cowboy boots, horse falls, and toupee hijinks with Steve McQueen's costar Mitch Vogel, Medium]

The Robesonian called it an “exciting two-part action adventure drama,” [ref: Percy Rodrigues Fights Alligator on 'Disney World' Bayou Drama, The Robesonian] and The Oneonta Star felt that it was “suitable family fare.” [ref: Top TV, The Oneonta Star] The Daily Herald referred to it as a “mystery adventure,” [ref: Mitch Vogel in Title Role for Disney's 'Bayou Boy', The Daily Herald] and the Albuquerque Journal wrote that “kids should eat it up.” [ref: TV Key Previews, Albuquerque Journal]

The film was rebroadcast by NBC in 1979 under the title The Boy from Dead Man's Bayou. [ref: The Magical World of Disney Season 17 Episodes, TV Guide] [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23]

data.title: San Diego County Bar Association
data.text:
----

The San Diego County Bar Association (SDCBA) is a professional association for lawyers and other members of the legal community in San Diego County, California. Founded in 1899, the organization supports the legal profession through professional education, public service, lawyer referral, judicial candidate evaluations, pro bono initiatives, and community programs. Over its history, the SDCBA has also helped establish and support organizations serving people who need legal assistance. [ref: 100 years and counting for San Diego's lawyers, archive.calbar.ca.gov]

== History ==

The SDCBA was founded on April 22, 1899 as the Bar Association of San Diego. During a meeting at the newly established San Diego Superior Court, San Diego lawyer Eugene Daney Sr. was elected as the organization's first president. [ref: Footprints of Justice in San Diego: Profiles of senior members of the bench and bar, San Diego County Law Library] A graduate of Hastings College of the Law, Daney would later become the president of the San Diego Lawyers Institute, established in 1919 by a group of lawyers interested in discussing law review articles, ethics and fee cutting. The Institute, which later merged with the SDCBA, became one of the nation's first regulatory law organizations, screening applicants, disciplining attorneys, and working to simplify legal proceedings.

Over time, the SDCBA participated in the launch of several organizations and programs that provide legal assistance or conflict resolution services in San Diego. For instance, In 1919, the SDCBA created the first Office of the Public Attorney. Local attorney DeWitt C. Mitchell died in 1918 while serving in the Army Air Corps during World War I. DeWitt's dream of creating a public attorney to represent the rights of all citizens, as well as a bequest of $20,000 to the SDCBA from DeWitt's estate, spurred the formation of the Office of the Public Attorney, providing people living in poverty with access to a free civil lawyer. In 1953, the Office incorporated and changed its name to the Legal Aid Society of San Diego (LASSD). LASSD continues to operate as a nonprofit law firm, providing free legal services to lower income San Diego residents. [ref: About, Legal Aid Society of San Diego]

The SDCBA played a major role in the creation of Appellate Defenders, Inc. (ADI) in 1972. Originally known as Defenders, Inc., ADI was formed to improve the quality of representation in appointed criminal appeals. With SDCBA sponsorship and federal grant funding, ADI used experienced staff attorneys to handle appeals and supervise a panel of private attorneys. In 1980, all ADI employees were hired by the State Public Defender, and the organization became inactive. In 1983, the budget cuts led to the closure of the State Public Defender's office in San Diego. To help it reorganize, ADI sought a $30,000 start-up loan from the SDCBA, which was approved. ADI then resumed operations in 1983, and the loan helped kickstart the organization back into service. [ref: Public defenders for poor restored, The San Diego Union] ADI eventually expanded its work across California's Fourth Appellate District. [ref: ADI's History, Appellate Defenders, Inc.]

In 1983, the SDCBA teamed with the University of San Diego School of Law to create the San Diego Volunteer Lawyer Program (SDVLP). The program was designed to be a clearinghouse for pro bono legal services, connecting volunteer legal professionals with people who could otherwise not afford legal representation. SDVLP continues to provide free legal assistance to disadvantaged individuals and families across San Diego County. [ref: ]

SDCBA and University of San Diego School of Law also teamed up in 1983 to launch the San Diego Mediation Center, which provided community-based alternative dispute resolution services. The center later became known as the National Conflict Resolution Center (NCRC). Through mediation, conflict resolution, and other related services, NCRC strives to reduce conflict, intolerance, and incivility in our modern society. [ref: About NCRC – Conflict Resolution & Mediation Experts, National Conflict Resolution Center]

The SDCBA and its members are often on the frontlines of disaster relief and pro bono service. Following the Southern California wildfires of 2003, the SDCBA led the San Diego County Disaster Relief Coalition, bringing together more than 20 bar-related organizations and law firms to help those affected by the fires. The Coalition setup a toll-free information hotline, recruited and trained volunteer lawyers, and helped arrange legal assistance for homeowners and others displaced. For its efforts, the Coalition was recognized by the State Bar of California with the Distinguished Pro Bono Service Award in 2004. [ref: California Bar Journal, archive.calbar.ca.gov]

== Lawyer Referral and Information Service ==
In 1952, the SDCBA launched the Lawyers Reference Plan, which intended to help members of the public connect with attorneys who handle particular legal matters. Lawyer referral services help members of the public identify appropriate legal assistance and, depending on the service, obtain an initial consultation at a reduced or no cost. [ref: ] The service, one of the first of its kind, is known today as the Lawyer Referral and Information Service and is certified by the State Bar of California. [ref: ]

== Judicial Candidate Evaluations ==
Contested elections for the Superior Courts of California occur in even-numbered years as nonpartisan, six-year term races. However, the nature of these elections meant that voters often had limited information about judicial candidates prior to Election Day. [ref: Bar Association Ranks 7 Superior Court Candidates: 'Exceptional' to 'Lacking', Times of San Diego]

In 1978, the San Diego County Bar Association began publishing evaluations of candidates running in contested judicial elections to help inform the public. [ref: San Diego County Bar Association evaluates judges on June primary ballot, KPBS Public Media]

The SDCBA's 23-member Judicial Election Evaluation Committee (JEEC) evaluates candidates based on 15 different criteria, including ability, experience, competence, and integrity. [ref: San Diego County Bar rates judges candidates, Daily Journal] Political affiliation, religion and type of law practiced are among factors not considered. [ref: Bar Association Evaluates Eleven San Diego Judicial Candidates, NBC 7 San Diego] As the largest law-related organization in San Diego, the SDCBA's Judicial Candidate Evaluations are frequently cited by media in the months leading up to a primary election. [ref: Bar Association Ranks 5 Superior Court Candidates as 'Exceptionally Qualified', Times of San Diego]

== Bench-Bar-Media ==
Every year, the San Diego County Bar Association hosts the Bench-Bar-Media Conference, a collaboration among the San Diego Superior Court, the SDCBA, and the San Diego Society of Professional Journalists. The event is designed to help build public confidence in the justice system by bringing judges, attorneys, and journalists together to discuss issues at the intersection of law, courts, and public information. Past topics have included cameras in the courtroom, eroding trust in the courts, and how the COVID-19 pandemic impacted the bar, courts, and news outlets. [ref: Events, San Diego Society of Professional Journalists]

== Wills for Heroes ==
The San Diego County Bar Association’s Wills for Heroes program connects volunteer attorneys with first responders, healthcare professionals, military personnel, and other eligible heroes to provide essential estate-planning documents at no cost. It is one of the Bar's signature pro bono initiatives, serving hundreds of local heroes since 2013. [ref: Free estate planning service for first responders this year includes new group – healthcare workers, San Diego Union-Tribune] Through this pro bono program, participants receive assistance preparing wills, durable powers of attorney, and advance healthcare directives. These legal documents help protect families and ensure that those who serve the public have access to basic estate-planning protections. The Wills for Heroes program is open to participants with an estate of $500,000 or less. Held annually during the month of October, Wills for Heroes is part of the SDCBA's commitment to serving those who put their lives on the line to protect the community. [ref: San Diego County Bar Association initiates pro bono estate planning services for first responders, military] [ref: Attorneys to offer free wills, estate planning documents for first responders, San Diego Union-Tribune]

== Youth Programming ==
The SDCBA participates in educational activities that introduce students to the court system and legal profession. One of the most popular examples is the San Diego County High School Mock Trial Program, in which students take part in simulated courtroom proceedings by assuming roles such as lawyers, bailiffs, and witnesses. Teams also alternate who gives the opening and closing statements. SDCBA members volunteer as team coaches and attorney scorers, while judges and other judicial officers from both state and federal courts preside over competitions. [ref: ] [ref: La Jolla’s Bishop’s School takes first in San Diego Mock Trials, San Diego Union-Tribune]

The SDCBA also promotes legal and civic education through its annual Law Week programming, including a student poster contest. Dating back to the 1970s, the Law Week Poster Contest invites students to interpret a designated Law Day theme through artwork, video, and other creative submissions. Themes draw from the American Bar Association’s national Law Day initiative, which encourages public dialog on the rule of law, justice, liberty, and constitutional principles. Student entries have been displayed as part of local Law Week activities, giving young people an opportunity to engage with legal concepts while showcasing their creativity. [ref: San Diego Students Create Inspiring Law Week Contest Posters and Videos, California Lawyers Association] [ref: County bar association holds student Law Week poster, video contest, The Coast News Group]

== San Diego Bar Association Auxiliary ==
In 1952, the wives of members of the San Diego County Bar Association were invited to join a new Auxiliary, dedicated to providing assistance and raising funds for the Legal Aid program of San Diego. By the end of that same year, membership in the San Diego Bar Association Auxiliary totaled 123. Funds were raised through rummage sales, theater, and concert tickets. The group’s largest event was the Blackstone Ball, a formal gala honoring the judiciary which raised funds for the Crime Victims Fund, the Legal Aid Society, and the YMCA. In 1981, San Diego Bar Auxiliary Philanthropies, Inc. was established to help collect and distribute funds raised by the Auxiliary. Beneficiaries of the Auxiliary included the San Diego County Bar Foundation, the San Diego Volunteer Lawyer Program, the Juvenile Court Book Club and Libraries, the Child Abuse Prevention Foundation, Youth Leadership Conference, Center for Women’s Studies, Battered Women’s Services, and many others. The Auxiliary lasted until 2001, when members voted to end the Auxiliary's activities as an organization. The San Diego History Center is now the repository of records from the Auxiliary. [ref: MS 244 San Diego Bar Association Auxiliary Records, San Diego History Center]

data.title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight
data.text:
----

Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight is a 2026 children's novel written and illustrated by American author Jeff Kinney. It is the 21st book in the Diary of a Wimpy Kid series. The book was published by Amulet Books, an imprint of Abrams Books, on October 20, 2026. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight, Wimpy Kid]

== Premise ==
Greg Heffley has compiled a three-ring binder filled with notes on his middle school's biggest bullies and strategies for avoiding them. When the binder falls into the wrong hands, Greg finds himself targeted and must decide how to respond. His best friend Rowley Jefferson has been taking karate lessons, giving Greg some support, though an unexpected complication arises. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight (Book 21), Penguin Books]

In interviews, Kinney described the book as addressing bullying through humor. He noted that Greg begins by viewing himself as part of a "long line of cowards" and proud of avoiding confrontation, only to attract the attention of the school's worst bully. [ref: Jeff Kinney Launches 'Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight', Fun 107]

== Development and publication ==
The book continues the series' pattern of annual releases established in recent years. The cover features a scrambled-eggs background with Greg depicted as a chicken wearing a boxing glove, surrounded by feathers. An earlier version of the cover used a bacon-patterned spine, which was later changed to burnt toast. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight, Diary of a Wimpy Kid Wiki]

The title and cover were publicly revealed in early 2026, including an appearance related to The Kelly Clarkson Show. Kinney supported the launch with a multi-city tour featuring an interactive stage show themed around the book. [ref: Fight or Flight Tour Wimpy Kid Press Release, Abrams Books] [ref: 'Wimpy Kid' at Home and on the Road: Jeff Kinney's Wildly Busy Year, Publishers Weekly]

== Reception ==
As a newly released title, critical reception is still emerging. Early reader responses on platforms such as Goodreads have been generally positive, consistent with the series' established popularity. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight, Goodreads] The broader Diary of a Wimpy Kid series has sold more than 300 million copies worldwide.

data.title: James Baca
data.text:
James Baca (born April 21, 1983) is an American journalist, author, podcaster, and consumer advocate based in Las Cruces, New Mexico. He is the founder and publisher of AGGREGATOR, an independent publication covering New Mexico State University athletics, and has produced consumer advocacy commentary under the name The Notorious Banker.

Baca's reporting on New Mexico State athletics has been credited by the Albuquerque Journal, the Las Cruces Sun-News, and Sports Illustrated. [ref: NMSU fires running backs coach, general manager, Albuquerque Journal] [ref: NMSU GM, RBs coach David Cobb fired, Las Cruces Sun-News] [ref: Former New Mexico State Softball Coaches Speak Out After Sexual Misconduct Allegations, Sports Illustrated]

== Early life and education ==

Baca grew up in Socorro, New Mexico, and graduated from Socorro High School in 2001.

He attended Eastern New Mexico University–Roswell, where he earned an associate degree in 2008. He subsequently attended Eastern New Mexico University in Portales, earning a bachelor's degree.

== Career ==

=== Banking and consumer advocacy ===

Baca worked for Bank of America from 2005 to 2018. Following his banking career, he began producing consumer-oriented commentary concerning banking practices, customer service, financial institutions, and consumer rights.

He developed the podcast The Notorious Banker, originally known as Why Your Bank Sucks. The program discussed retail banking, consumer experiences, financial products, and corporate accountability. [ref: The Notorious Banker, Apple Podcasts] [ref: The Notorious Banker, Spotify]

His consumer commentary has also appeared through independent publications, including Consumer Beast and Terms & Conditions.

=== Journalism and AGGREGATOR ===

In November 2023, Baca founded AGGREGATOR, an independent, subscription-supported publication based in Las Cruces, primarily covering New Mexico State University athletics.

According to Baca, the publication was established in response to what he considered insufficient local media coverage of New Mexico State's football program during its successful 2023 season. The Aggies finished that season with a 10–5 record and appeared in the Conference USA Football Championship Game. Baca argued that the program's accomplishments were not receiving sustained coverage from traditional local news organizations. [ref: About AGGREGATOR, AGGREGATOR]

Baca has also identified his dissatisfaction with coverage of controversies surrounding the university's men's basketball program as a factor in establishing the publication. These included the November 2022 shooting involving New Mexico State basketball player Mike Peake and the hazing scandal that led to the cancellation of the remainder of the 2022–23 men's basketball season.

Baca has criticized what he perceived as sensationalized coverage of those controversies, arguing that some local reporting emphasized negative developments while providing comparatively limited attention to other university athletic programs. These views formed part of his stated motivation to develop an alternative source of coverage focused on New Mexico State athletics.

AGGREGATOR publishes game reports, statistical analysis, interviews, commentary, and coverage of athletic administration. Its reporting includes football, men's and women's basketball, volleyball, soccer, and other university sports.

The publication also addresses conference realignment, collegiate athletics finances, media rights, and issues affecting Southern New Mexico.

In July 2026, the Albuquerque Journal and Las Cruces Sun-News credited Baca and AGGREGATOR with first reporting the dismissal of New Mexico State running backs coach and general manager David Cobb.

In September 2026, Sports Illustrated referenced Baca's reporting concerning statements obtained from former New Mexico State softball coaches Kathy Rodolph and Cat Heifner during coverage of allegations involving the university's softball program.

=== Athlon Sports ===

Baca has stated that he contributed freelance material to Athlon Sports, including its annual college football preview publication.

His work included material concerning New Mexico State's football program, including team analysis and depth-chart information. [ref: Jody Adams Resurfaces as Head Coach, AGGREGATOR]

== Recognition ==

Baca was listed among the finalists for Best Local Newspaper Columnist in the Las Cruces Bulletin annual Bulletin's Best recognition for 2024–25. [ref: Bulletin's Best 2024–25, Las Cruces Bulletin]

== Writing and public commentary ==

=== Local journalism and media ownership ===

Baca has written critically about the consolidation of local newspapers and television stations under national media companies, including Gannett, Nexstar Media Group, and Sinclair Broadcast Group.

His commentary has addressed newsroom staffing reductions, centralized editorial decision-making, and the effects of corporate ownership on reporting about local institutions.

He has argued that reduced newsroom resources can diminish coverage of community affairs and collegiate athletics, particularly in smaller media markets such as Southern New Mexico.

=== Mental health awareness ===

Baca has expressed support for mental health awareness and has criticized what he considers inadequate institutional responses to mental health crises.

His commentary has addressed access to mental health services, public understanding of mental illness, and the responsibilities of institutions and public agencies when responding to individuals experiencing mental health emergencies.

== Bibliography ==

Baca has published books addressing personal finance, consumer experiences, and other subjects. Selected works include:

* Baca, James (2021). Please Try Your Call Again Later: My Journey Through Customer Service Hell for Pandemic Relief. Independently published. ISBN 9798758478219.

* Baca, James (2022). High-Risk Transaction: The Ryan Coogler–Bank of America Incident. Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing. ISBN 9798444550342. [ref: High Risk Transaction, Google Books]

* Baca, James. BROKE AF: Hustling, Surviving, and Never Looking Back.

* Baca, James. Predicando.

== Personal life ==

Baca has lived in Las Cruces, New Mexico, since 2008.

Higher Up Texas (HUT) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization based in Dickinson, Texas, that provides life skills education, professional development, financial literacy, critical thinking, and career exploration and guidance to young adults transitioning from high school into adulthood. [ref: Higher Up Texas Inc, ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer] [ref: Dickinson program helping students 'bloom' in high school and beyond, ABC13 Houston]

Founded in 2019, the organization serves students attending Dickinson High School, La Marque High School, and Texas City High School in Galveston County, Texas. [ref: Higher Up Texas, Cause IQ] [ref: FAQs, Higher Up Texas]

Higher Up Texas operates a three-phase program beginning with classroom instruction during students' senior year of high school. Following graduation, the organization provides individualized guidance, career development support, and connections to professional opportunities. The program also engages alumni as mentors and speakers. [ref: FAQs, Higher Up Texas] [ref: Dickinson program helping students 'bloom' in high school and beyond, ABC13 Houston]

== History ==

Higher Up Texas originated in 2018, when Rick Gornto and Tony Annunziato began discussing gaps in resources, opportunities, and professional networks available to young adults transitioning from high school into adulthood. Later that year, the founders met with leadership at Dickinson High School to propose a program addressing these challenges. [ref: HUT Happenings – April 2022, Higher Up Texas]

In June 2019, Hillary Gramm joined the organization and developed its initial life skills curriculum. The program launched in August 2019 with a founding class of 27 seniors at Dickinson High School. [ref: Learning for Life, The Daily News]

In spring 2020, the organization adapted its programming in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The disruption contributed to the development of its second program phase, which provides continued guidance and support following high school graduation. [ref: Learning for Life, The Daily News]

In 2023, Higher Up Texas expanded into Texas City Independent School District, adding programs at Texas City High School and La Marque High School. [ref: Higher Up Texas, Higher Up Texas] The organization operates a three-phase model encompassing high school preparation, post-graduation guidance, and alumni engagement. [ref: FAQs, Higher Up Texas]

Lohenette (Lohenette Ky) is a Finnish family-owned limited partnership (kommandiittiyhtiö) founded in 1992, with its registered domicile in Helsinki, Finland, specializing in e-commerce and commercial operations. [ref: Lohenette - yritystiedot, päättäjät, taloustiedot, Finder]

== Early Years ==
Originally, Lohenette supplied illuminated signs, neon lights, and related accessories such as transformers to large and medium-sized enterprises. [ref: Lohenette historical products page, Internet Archive] As the emergence of the internet transformed both domestic and international markets, Lohenette positioned itself as an early pioneer in e-commerce. The company expanded its operations to offer consumer goods and retail products online in 1995, famously becoming one of the first vendors to sell Leatherman multi-utility tools online in Finland in the mid-1990s. [ref: Lohenette historical snapshot, Internet Archive]

== Current State ==
Currently, Lohenette operates as a B2B supplier specializing in furniture and office products. [ref: Lohenette – Welcome to the world of Lohenette – B2B business no more no less.]

data.text:
= Uthumalai, Tamil Nadu =
Uthumalai, also spelled Uttumalai, is a village in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu. It is situated in Veerakeralampudur taluk of Tenkasi district, in the southern part of the state. The settlement is associated with the agricultural landscape and historical political structures of the former Tirunelveli region. Uthumalai is also notable for its historical connection with the poligar and zamindari systems that shaped local administration during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.[1][2]

== Geography and location ==
Uthumalai is located in southern Tamil Nadu, in the region historically administered as part of Tirunelveli district. Following the reorganisation of district boundaries in 2019, the village falls within Tenkasi district.[1][3] The surrounding region includes rural settlements and agricultural land, and the area forms part of the wider cultural and economic landscape of southern Tamil Nadu.

The village is situated within Veerakeralampudur taluk, an administrative subdivision of Tenkasi district. Surandai is identified as a nearby town in village-directory records.[1] Its geographical position connects it to a region characterised by rural communities, agriculture and longstanding local administrative institutions.

== History ==
Uthumalai has a historical association with the poligar system of southern India. Poligars, also known as palaiyakkarars, were local political and military authorities who exercised varying degrees of control over territories and settlements. Their responsibilities could include revenue collection, the maintenance of armed forces and the administration of local affairs. The relationship between these rulers and larger political powers changed considerably during the expansion of British colonial rule.[2]

Historian Nicholas B. Dirks examined Uthumalai in his research on the transformation of local rulers into landlords under British administration. His 1986 study, “From Little King to Landlord: Property, Law, and the Gift under the Madras Permanent Settlement”, discusses how colonial revenue arrangements altered the political and economic status of traditional ruling families.[2]

During the early nineteenth century, Uthumalai became associated with the zamindari system under the Madras Presidency. Under this arrangement, recognised estate holders were responsible for revenue obligations to the colonial administration, while retaining certain rights over their estates. The establishment of zamindari arrangements in southern Tamil Nadu formed part of a broader transformation of land ownership, taxation and political authority following conflicts involving the poligars.[2]

The history of Uthumalai therefore provides an example of the wider changes experienced by rural estates in southern India during the colonial period. The transition from local political authority to a more formalised landlord system affected relationships between ruling families, agricultural communities and the colonial state.[2]

== Administration ==
Uthumalai is administered within the present-day framework of local government in Tamil Nadu. The village is listed in village-directory records under Veerakeralampudur taluk in Tenkasi district.[1] Local administration operates within the state's wider system of district, taluk and village-level governance.

Tenkasi district was established in November 2019 after being separated from the former Tirunelveli district. The district administration oversees public services and development activities across its rural and urban areas.[3] This administrative change placed Uthumalai within the newly constituted district while maintaining its connection to the historical Tirunelveli region.

== Demographics ==
According to figures reported from the 2011 Census of India, Uthumalai had a population of 7,737 people living in 2,168 households. The recorded population consisted of 3,788 males and 3,949 females.[1] These figures provide a historical demographic reference for the village rather than a current population estimate.

The 2011 population data also indicate that the village was a substantial rural settlement within the surrounding area. Census records are useful for examining population distribution, household numbers and other characteristics of rural communities in Tamil Nadu.[4]

More recent population figures should be established through an updated official census or other authoritative government publication before being added to this article.

== Economy ==
Agriculture has historically played an important role in the economy of the wider Tenkasi region. The district administration describes agriculture and related activities as major sources of livelihood and identifies rivers, reservoirs and irrigation tanks as important water resources supporting cultivation in the district.[3]

Uthumalai's rural setting places it within this broader agricultural environment. However, the principal crops, employment distribution and present-day occupational structure of the village require confirmation from village-level government statistics or reliable published studies.

The historical development of the Uthumalai estate is also relevant to understanding the area's agricultural past. Under the zamindari system, land revenue and the relationship between estate holders and cultivators formed important parts of rural economic organisation.[2] Such arrangements linked village agriculture to the larger political and fiscal systems of the Madras Presidency.

== Language and culture ==
Tamil is the principal language of the wider region and the official language of Tamil Nadu. The cultural environment of Uthumalai is part of the broader Tamil-speaking society of southern India.

Local customs, religious observances, festivals and community traditions are important subjects for documenting the cultural history of rural settlements. Nevertheless, detailed claims about particular temples, annual festivals, folk traditions or notable cultural institutions in Uthumalai should be supported by reliable local histories, government records or independent publications before inclusion in an encyclopaedic article.

== Regional significance ==
Uthumalai is of historical interest because of its association with the former poligar and zamindari systems of southern Tamil Nadu. Research into the estate contributes to wider discussions about colonial land-revenue policies, local political authority and the changing relationship between landowners and the state.[2]

The village also illustrates the importance of examining rural settlements through several kinds of historical evidence. Census records help establish demographic characteristics, administrative publications document changes in district boundaries, and historical scholarship provides context for understanding political and economic institutions.[1][2][3][4]

Further research using official village records, historical maps, land-revenue documents and independently published studies could provide additional information about Uthumalai's development, local institutions and contemporary economy.

data.title: Liu HanYuan
data.text:
Liu Hanyuan (Chinese: 刘汉元; born December 1964) is a Chinese billionaire-businessman and is the founder and chairman of Tongwei Group. [ref: Liu Hanyuan, Forbes] He is the National People's Congress deputy and vice chairman of All-China Federation of Industry & Commerce. [ref: 刘汉元, All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce]

As of 2026, Liu has a net worth of US$5.9 billion.

==Early Life==
Liu was born in December 1964 to a peasant family background in Meishan, Sichuan. [ref: 通威40年变迁，如何穿越市场周期？, China Business Journal] He trained at Sichuan Fisheries School where he graduated in 1981, and worked as a technician in a state-run reservoir fishery. At age 19, he started an experimental fish cage initiative, where he developed the "flowing-water cage culture" technique, where he built mesh/metal cages and anchored them in a moving water source. [ref: 刘汉元：从网箱养鱼的年轻人到水产大亨, Yicai] At the time, aquaculture technology in China was limited to raising fish in an open pond, which limited yield based on the available oxygen and food in the water. Liu's development resulted in record yields, and his technique was later promoted nationwide by China's agriculture ministry. His success helped him realize that technique would require specialized feed, which inspired his founding of Sichuan Tongwei Feed Co., Ltd.

=== Founding of Tongwei ===
In 1992, Liu founded the company Sichuan Tongwei Feed Co., Ltd., which is the predecessor company of Tongwei Group. Under Liu's leadership, the company grew into China's largest producer of aquaculture feed. The company went public on the Shanghai Stock exchange in 2004.

=== Diversification into solar energy ===
Starting in 2006, Liu led the company to diversify into high-purity polysilicon production for the solar industry.

Tongwei was a latecomer to the PV industry in China. Liu led the company through a strategy that combined his expertise in aquatic fishing with solar energy. PV power stations were placed over aquaculture ponds to generate electricity while farmers harvested at lower costs with higher efficiency. [ref: 刘汉元"追光"40年创富950亿 通威股份抛650亿扩张欲再创奇迹, Sina Finance]

In 2013, Tongwei acquired LDK Solar Hi-Tech (Hefei) Co, a solar cell and module manufacturing unit from LDK Solar Co. [ref: Poly maker Tongwei acquires cell and module business, pv magazine] [ref: 8.7亿通威收购合肥赛维 布局光伏产业链, China Economic Net] The acquisition meant Tongwei could now manufacture solar cells and modules using its own polysilicon. [ref: 通威布局全产业链 光伏业频现"抄底"并购, China Securities Journal (CNStock)]

In 2019, Liu stepped down from operational leadership roles at the listed subsidiary Tongwei Co., Ltd., while remaining chairman and controlling shareholder of the unlisted parent, Tongwei Group. [ref: Chinese Silicon Giant Tongwei Names Founder's Daughter as New Chair, CEO, Yicai Global]

== Honors ==
In October 2018, Liu was named one of the "100 Outstanding Private Entrepreneurs of the 40 Years of Reform and Opening-up" (改革开放40年百名杰出民营企业家), an honor jointly conferred by central Chinese government and party bodies to mark the fortieth anniversary of China's reform era. [ref: 改革开放40年百名杰出民营企业家名单发布, All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce]

== Personal life ==
Liu is married to Guan Yamei; they have one daughter, Liu Shuqi (born 1989), who has served as chairwoman and chief executive of Tongwei Co., Ltd. since 2023.

== Philanthropy ==
In 2007, Liu established the "Siyuan–Sunshine Plan" with an initial donation of ¥50 million (around US$6.6 million at the time) to fund poverty-alleviation projects built around small-scale solar power, including installations in Sichuan's Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture and in Xinjiang. [ref: 以新质生产力创造新未来——访全国人大代表、通威集团董事局主席刘汉元, The Paper (澎湃新闻)]
