Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Limited (DOSCEL) is an Australian Catholic education organisation responsible for the governance and operation of Catholic primary and secondary schools with in Diocese of Sale in Victoria, Australia. [ref: education - Catholic Diocese of Sale, www.cdsale.org.au] Established in 2018, the organisation provides system leadership, governance and educational support to schools across south-eastern Victoria and the Gippsland region. [ref: Governance - Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Ltd]

DOSCEL is a company limited by guarantee, with the Bishop of Sale its sole member. Is governance is overseen by a board of directors, supported by an executive leadership team. The organisation's central office is Sion House, Warragul.

== History ==
Before the establishment of DOSCEL, the governance of Catholic schools in the Diocese of Sale was traditionally the responsibility of parish priests. In 2018, school governance was transferred to DOSCEL which was newly established. [ref: Priests out of school admin, Latrobe Valley Express] The transition was intended to provide coordinated governance and support for schools while allowing parish priest to focus more closely on their pastoral and spiritual responsibilities. Under the new structure, DOSCEL assumed responsibility for the employment of school staff and the governance of the schools under its authority.

Maria Kirkwood served as the organisation's inaugural chief executive officer and Director of Catholic Education. She retired in December of 2022 after a decade as Director of Catholic Education in the diocese. [ref: Catholic Education leader to retire after 50 years of service, Dandenong Star Journal]> Paul Velten was appointed as her successor in 2022. [ref: Announcement of Director Catholic Education, CEO of DOSCEL, www.cdsale.org.au]

== Governance and structure ==
DOSCEL operates as a company limited by guarantee. The Bishop of Sale is the company's sole member and appoints a board of directors to oversee its governance. The executive leadership team manages the organisation's day-to-day operations and provides leadership and services to schools within its jurisdiction.

Its responsibilities include school governance, educational improvement, staff support, child safety, regulatory compliance and the maintenance of Catholic identity across its schools.

== Curriculum ==
All DOSCEL schools are required to complete Religion Education through the use of the Diocesan curriculum 'To Live in Christ Jesus'. This curriculum aims to teach from the Catholic perspective through the invitation of other faiths along the journey. The 'To live in Christ Jesus' framework is based on four core learning strands; Triune God, The Life and Mission of Jesus, Sacramental Church and Christian Life and Catholic Social Teaching. [ref: Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Limited (DOSCEL), Catholic School Parents Victoria]

== Schools ==
DOSCEL governs and operates 44 Catholic schools, comprising 39 primary schools and five secondary colleges, according to its official website in 2026. [ref: Overview, Victorian Catholic Education Authority] The organisation's schools are distributed across south-eastern Victoria, extending from the outer south-eastern suburbs of Melbourne, including Narre Warren and Cranbourne, through Phillip Island and Gippsland to Orbost. [ref: About - Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Ltd]

Two Catholic secondary colleges within the Diocese of Sale are governed separately from DOSCEL: Lavalla Catholic College, which is governed by Marist Schools Australia, and Catholic College Sale, which is governed by Catholic College Sale Limited. [ref: Schools, Marist Schools Australia] These schools remain part of the wider Catholic education community of the diocese but are not directly governed by DOSCEL.

=== Future Schools ===
DOSCEL is developing three additional Catholic primary schools to serve growing communities in south-eastern Victoria and Gippsland. [ref: Building Projects, Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Limited]

Our Lady of Sion Catholic Primary School – Sale. The project involves the redevelopment of the historic Our Lady of Sion Convent and campus into a modern educational facility. [ref: Former Sale convent to undergo $40m development, CathNews] The development will also accommodate St Thomas' Primary School, which is to be renamed Our Lady of Sion Catholic Primary School. [ref: Major redevelopment of Our Lady of Sion Convent to enhance 21st century learning, Catholic Diocese of Sale]

St Oscar Romero Catholic Primary School – Drouin. The school is being constructed to accommodate growing demand for Catholic primary education in the Drouin area. Its development is planned in stages, with the first two stages intended to provide classrooms, administration facilities, a library, an art room and outdoor learning spaces. [ref: St Oscar Romero Catholic Primary School – Drouin, Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Limited] [ref: St Oscar Romero Catholic Primary School (Drouin), www.schoolbuildings.vic.gov.au]

St Carlo Acutis Catholic Primary School – Clyde. The school is being developed in the Cardinia Creek South growth area to serve families in Clyde and surrounding suburbs. Its first stage includes administration facilities, learning areas and outdoor facilities. The school is planned to open in Term 1 of 2027. data.title: European Biotechnology Thematic Network Association EBTNA
data.text:
----

The European Biotechnology Thematic Network Association (EBTNA) is a non-profit scientific association operating in the domain of biotechnology. These networking activities of European biotechnologies resulted in the formal establishment of the association in 2007, in Perugia, Italy. [ref: ]

== History ==
The European Biotechnology Thematic Network Association (EBTNA) originated as a thematic network in biotechnology established in 1996. Between 1996 and 2006, the network carried out four projects within the European Union’s Socrates and Erasmus programmes. In 2007, it was formally registered as a non-profit association in Perugia, Italy [ref: ].

== European Biotechnology Congress ==
Since 2011, EBTNA has organized an annual congress under the title "European Biotechnology Congress" [ref: ]. The 2025 congress, held in Tirana, Albania, from 11 to 13 September 2025, was co-organized with the Academy of Sciences of Albania and the University of Tirana [ref: Academy of Sciences of Albania Joins European Biotechnology Network, RTSH]. The 2026 congress took place in Varna, Bulgaria, on 23-24 March 2026 [ref: European Biotechnology Congress 2026].

== The EuroBiotech Journal ==
EBTNA publishes The EuroBiotech Journal, an English-language scientific periodical founded in 2017. The journal is listed in the ISSN International Center as a quarterly publication with electronic ISSN 2564-615X. [ref: The EuroBiotech Journal, Paradigm]

data.title: Belraj Kalarickal
data.text:
Belraj Kalarickal (Malayalam: ബെൽരാജ് കളരിക്കൽ, 19 August 1999 – 17 October 2026) was a Indian film director, associate director and assistant director. [ref: Filmmaker found dead days after series debut, The New Indian Express]

Born in Manimala, Kalarickal would be an associate director and assistant director of multiple films, including Nizhal, Madhuram, and Dakini. He would also be one of the founding members of First Print Studios, which created Ottamuri Velichan, among other films.

In October 2026, Kalarickal would release his first independent series as director, Kappi Squad. [ref: New JioHotstar Malayalam series Kappi Squad launched, The New Indian Express] [ref: Kappi Squad: If FRIENDS tried to open a coffee shop instead of chilling in one, India Today] However, on 17 October 2026, he would die in Kochi.

Kalarickal would also marry Athira Bindu Sabu on 12 September 2026.

== Early life ==
Kalarickal was born in Manimala, Kerala on 19 August 1999. [ref: Belraj Kalarickal Dies At 27: Who Was Kaapi Squad Director Found Dead In Kochi Hotel? Cause Of Death, Wife, Family And Career, The Sunday Guardian]

== Career ==
Kalarickal worked on seven feature films, including Nizhal, Madhuram, and Dakini. He was one of the founding members of First Print Studios, which created Ottamuri Velicham, and other films. Kalarickal worked with Rahul Riji Nair in films such as Dakini, Keedam, and Kho Kho. He would also be involved in the crime drama Kerala Crime Files. [ref: Balraj Kalarickal, Malayalam director, dies at 28 a day after Kappi Squad began streaming on Jio Hotstar, India TV News] In 2024, he would be involved in the streaming television series Jai Mahendran. [ref: Malayalam Director Belraj Kalarickal Biography, News, Photos, Videos, nettv4u]

His first independent web series, Kappi Squad [ref: Malayalam Director Belraj Kalaricka, 27, Found Dead In Hotel, Weeks After First Wedding Anniversary, BollywoodShaadis], released on JioHotstar on October 15.

== Personal life and death ==
Kalarickal married Athira Bindu Sabu in September 2026, after a six-year relationship. [ref: Who Is Athira Bindu Sabu? All You Need To Know About Kappi Squad Director Belraj Kalarickal's Wife, TimesNow]

On 17 October 2026, Kalarickal died in a hotel room in Kochi, at the age of 27. [ref: Kappi Squad director Belraj Kalarickal passes away, Cinema Express] [ref: Kappi Squad director - Belraj Kalarickal passes away: నిన్న వెబ్‌ సిరీస్‌ రిలీజ్‌.. నేడు దర్శకుడి మృతి, EENADU] His exact death has beet not confirmed [ref: 'Kappi Squad' director Belraj Kalarickal, 27, found dead; cast devastated by 'cruel' loss, Deccan Herald], however preliminary reports suggest a heart attack. [ref: 27 வயதில் காலமான மலையாள இயக்குநர்!, தினமணி] [ref: Kappi Squad director - Belraj Kalarickal passes away: నిన్న వెబ్‌ సిరీస్‌ రిలీజ్‌.. నేడు దర్శకుడి మృతి, EENADU]

After his death, Rahul Riji Nair paid tribute to his death. [ref: Kappi Squad director Belraj Kalarickal found dead; producer, cast pay tribute, India Today]

data.text:
The Works transformed Swindon from a small 2,500-population market town into a bustling railway town. Built to the north of the town centre, the works had need for locally accessible housing and services for the workers. The development of the railway village was on the lines of similar Victorian era socially-encompassing lifestyle concepts, such as that at Bournville but architect/builder Rigby's signed an agreement in February 1841 to build 300 cottages at their own expense. [ref: Swindon The Legacy of a Railway Town, HMSO] The completed village provided to the town medical and educational facilities that had been sorely lacking, The large St Mark's Church was built in 1843-45. The Bakers Arms public house was built as a shop with accommodation above in 1846. [ref: Former Bakers Arms Public House, 16 Emlyn Square, Historic England] The Cricketers' public house was built in 1846. [ref: 14 Emlyn Square, formerly The Cricketers Public House, Historic England]

Construction of the Railway Village began in 1841. In 1891 it had around 287 houses, a large mechanics' institute, a market with capacity for 32 shops and standings for thirty stalls, a cottage hospital, a park, an Anglican church, a Methodist chapel, swimming baths and a medical dispensary. The financial difficulties of the contractors J.D. & C. Rigby, who undertook to build 300 cottages but only completed 130, delayed the completion of the village until the 1850s. The cottages to the west of Emlyn Square were built first (1842–43), followed by those on the east side (1845–1847). The end blocks towards Emlyn Square, having corner shops on the ground floor, were built in 1845–1847, and the remainder, mostly end blocks on the outer ends of the streets, in 1853–1855. In 1966, the local authority acquired the cottages from British Rail and restored them. The village is one of Britain’s best-preserved and architecturally most ambitious railway settlements. [ref: 30-50, Exeter Street, Swindon, SN1 5EF, Historic England] [ref: Made in Swindon a social history 1840s-1940s; The Architectural Legacy of Swindon Railway Village, The Hobnob Press]

The terraced two-storey cottages were built on two blocks of four parallel streets, not dissimilar in appearance to passing trains. Each road was named after the destinations of trains that passed nearby: Bristol, Bath, Taunton, London, Oxford and Reading among them. Built in the nearby open area, named Emlyn Square after GWR director Viscount Emlyn (later known as John Campbell, 1st Earl Cawdor), was the Mechanics Institute (MI). Designed and constructed by Edward Roberts, the MI was completed in 1855. It contained one the UK's earliest public lending libraries and provided health services to workers. The GWR Medical Fund Baths and Dispensary (which housed Victorian Turkish baths from 1906) were built in 1891–92, becoming the NHS Health Centre and Milton Road Baths in 1947 and the Health Hydro in 1986. The Mechanics' Institute (founded in 1843) moved into a purpose-built building in 1854. [ref: Made in Swindon a social history 1840s to 19140s, The Hobnob Press] The Mechanics' Institute building was closed in February 1986 [ref: We're Left in the Cold, Swindon Advertiser] and remains unoccupied. The Barracks were built in 1853–55 as a lodging house but became a Wesleyan chapel in 1867, the GWR Museum in 1962 and then The Platform (Swindon Music Service) in 2000. The Armoury, built in 1862, became the GWR Hospital in 1871, a Workers' Club in 1960 and the Central Community Centre in 1979. [ref: Swindon in 50 Buildings, Amberley Publishing] The GWR Park, adjacent to St Mark's Church, was acquired in 1844. The Octagonal Market started in 1892 and was demolished in 1977. A house and shop built in the 1840s became a public house in the 1850s and is now the Glue Pot public house. [ref: Swindon An Illustrated History, The Breedon Books Publishing Company Limited]

In 1846-1847 a terrace of 16 cottages was built on the north side of Faringdon Road (Nos 4-34). One of the last houses to be built, 34 Faringdon Road, originally 1 Faringdon Street is now the 'Railway Village Museum' and is maintained as a typical railwayman's house of about 1900. It retains original features such as glazing, window sashes, margin lights and plank door. [ref: 4-34, Faringdon Road, Swindon, SN1 5BJ, Historic England] [ref: Railway Village Museum, Swindon Heritage Preservation]
link=File:20261022_Park_House.jpg|thumb|Park House
1876 saw the GWR directors agree to build a house and surgery combined. The house, Park House, was for the company’s chief medical officer and his family and was built in 1876-77. Built in yellow brick with stone dressings and a slate roof. Three stories and basement. [ref: Park House, Church Place, Swindon, SN1 5ED, Historic England] [ref: A Century of Medical Service, Great Western Railway Medical Fund Society] Park House today provides serviced offices. [ref: Park House, total Guide to Wiltshire]

In the 1960s, the Borough of Swindon municipal council applied to demolish much of the village, but poet and railway enthusiast John Betjeman [ref: No 3: GWR Railway Village, Born Again Swindonian] led a successful campaign to preserve it. Today the Railway Village is part of the Swindon Railway Conservation Area, and many structures within it are listed buildings. [ref: Railway Village, Swindon.co] [ref: Swindon railway conservation area appraisal and management plan, Swindon Borough Council]

data.title: Andion CH4 Renewables
data.text:
----

Andion CH4 Renewables SAS, also known as Andion CH4, is a Luxembourg-based renewable energy company with its operational headquarters in Milan. The company develops, finances and operates facilities that produce biogas and biomethane from organic waste. [ref: Goldman Sachs Alternatives backs European biogas developer Andion with €67m credit facility, Bioenergy News] Founded in 2017, it has operations and projects in countries including Italy and Sweden. [ref: Andion CH4 Renewables, LinkedIn] [ref: Andion CH4 gets EUR-24m loan for its 1st biomethane plant in Italy, Renewables Now] [ref: Groundbreaking held for Eskilstuna Biogas bioLNG, Bioenergy International] Jonas Martin-Löf is the company's chief executive officer and chairman, while Mattias Pihlgren is deputy chief executive officer and CIO. [ref: About, Andion CH4 Renewables]

== History and financing ==
The company was founded in 2017. For a period, it was legally domiciled in Canada before returning to Luxembourg. The move was completed before a capital raise announced in January 2025. Investors included Equitix New Generation Fund, which was funded by an investment company associated with Ikea. [ref: GSK Stockmann advises Andion CH4 Renewables on the first capital raise after its migration from Canada to Luxembourg, GSK Stockmann]

In February 2026, Andion secured a €67 million credit facility from Goldman Sachs Alternatives. The financing, together with new equity from existing shareholders, was intended to support the company's project portfolio in Italy and the Nordic region. In March that year, the company was reported to have secured €24 million in project financing for a facility in Mirandola in northern Italy.

== Operations and projects ==
Andion's activities include the development, construction, financing and operation of facilities that convert organic residues into biogas or biomethane.

The company and its technology operations have delivered more than 50 anaerobic digestion facilities, as well as numerous advanced wastewater treatment facilities in Europe and North America. Andion owns or holds stakes in several biogas and biomethane facilities in Italy and Sweden. [ref: Andion Global, BDC Capital]

=== Sweden ===
Andion is involved in the development of Eskilstuna Biogas, a liquefied biogas facility outside Eskilstuna. The project has been carried out with partners including Gotlandsbolaget and Equitix New Generation Fund. In 2025, Wärtsilä announced that Andion Scandinavia AB had commissioned it to supply biogas upgrading and liquefaction technology for the facility. Its planned production capacity was stated as up to 17 tonnes of bio-LNG per day. [ref: Wärtsilä to supply Andion Scandinavia AB with bioLNG solution for new biogas plant in Sweden, Wärtsilä]

The Swedish company Andion Scandinavia AB was registered in 2021. According to its company registration, its activities include the development, construction, management and maintenance of waste and energy facilities. [ref: Andion Scandinavia AB, Allabolag.se]

=== Italy ===
In Mirandola, in the Emilia-Romagna region, Andion is developing a facility to produce biomethane from organic residues. In 2025, industrial gas company SOL Group acquired a 20 per cent minority stake in Biomethan Green 1, the project company controlled by Andion Italy. Investment in the facility was reported to exceed €20 million. [ref: SOL Group joins Andion in €20m+ bioLNG plant project with offtake deal, Gasworld]

During 2026, Andion expanded its portfolio of facilities in Italy. In January, it became the majority owner of the Enerland facility in Baricella, in the province of Bologna. The facility had a capacity of approximately 11 GWh and was intended to be converted from biogas-based electricity generation to biomethane production. [ref: Acquisition of the Enerland plant in Northern Italy, Andion CH4 Renewables] [ref: Explore our assets, Andion CH4 Renewables]

In February 2026, the company announced that it had signed a binding agreement to acquire the Cella Dati facility in the province of Cremona. Its existing capacity was stated as approximately 44–45 GWh, with a planned expansion to 56 GWh. [ref: Acquisition of the Cella Dati plant, Andion CH4 Renewables] In May, Andion signed a binding agreement to acquire the Q Energia facility in Quargnento, in the province of Alessandria. The facility had a capacity of approximately 22 GWh and was to be converted from biogas-based electricity generation to biomethane production. [ref: Acquisition of the Q Energia plant, Andion CH4 Renewables]

In June 2026, Andion signed a binding agreement to acquire a majority stake in the Agromet facility in Barbianello, in the province of Pavia. The press release stated an installed capacity of approximately 42 GWh, while the company's subsequent overview of its assets listed 44 GWh. [ref: Acquisition of the Agromet plant, Andion CH4 Renewables]

== Management ==
Jonas Martin-Löf is the company's chief executive officer and chairman. Mattias Pihlgren is deputy chief executive officer and CIO. He has worked at Andion since 2017, including in business development and fundraising. [ref: Mattias Pihlgren, Andion CH4 Renewables]

data.title: Mattappilly Raman
data.text:
Mattappilly Raman (1885–1971), also known as Raman Master, was an Indian painter, sculptor and art educator from the Kingdom of Cochin, in present-day Kerala. He studied art in Calcutta, founded the Cochin School of Arts in Ernakulam in 1932, and was given the title of "Palace Artist" by the Maharaja of Cochin. Under his direction the school became known for casting life-size bronze statues, including one of Sree Narayana Guru. [ref: The artists we forgot, The Hindu] [ref: Census of India 1961, Volume VII: Kerala, Part VII-A: Selected Crafts, Manager of Publications, Government of India] His sons M. R. D. Dattan and M. R. Baburam also became artists. [ref: 'To make it better, State should support biennale', The Hindu]

== Early life and education ==
Raman was born in 1885 in Cochin. His family at first opposed his wish to study art. According to The Hindu, his father met Sree Narayana Guru at Alwaye, and the Guru encouraged the family to support him, giving him ten rupees towards his journey to Calcutta.

At the College of Art, Calcutta, he was taught by Percy Brown and Jamini Prasad Ganguly. He then spent time at Santiniketan before travelling across India painting portraits.

== Career ==
=== Cochin School of Arts ===
Raman returned to Cochin and founded the Cochin School of Arts in 1932, the first school of its kind in the region. [ref: Art tutors should be given freedom, The New Indian Express] The school taught wall-poster design, clay modelling, book illustration, Indian-style painting, and commercial and applied art. It prepared students for the Madras government technical examinations and awarded diplomas in drawing and painting, and at the time was the only aided fine-arts institution in the state to do so.

The 1965 Kerala District Gazetteer for Ernakulam listed the Cochin School of Arts as one of the district's three main schools of fine arts. The school was housed in the premises of the Ernakulam Public Library and received a government grant. Alongside drawing and painting classes leading to Group Certificates and a Diploma in Art, it specialised in teaching statue-making; the certificate course took three years and the diploma five. The Gazetteer described it as "the only institution in the whole of Kerala where a six-feet likeness statue in bronze has been tried successfully". [ref: Kerala District Gazetteers: Ernakulam, Government Press] By the early 1970s the school was run by Dattan and taught a realistic style of painting. [ref: Art and the man, The Hindu] Several artists from Kerala trained at the school, among them the painter T. Kaladharan, who studied there for a year around 1972, the painter and sculptor Jeevan Lal [ref: The human in the divine, The Hindu] and the graphic designer B. S. Satyaraj, who designed a 2014 Brazilian postage stamp marking 100 years of Indian cinema. [ref: A post from Brazil, The Hindu]
=== Palace Artist ===
The Maharaja of Cochin gave Raman the title of "Palace Artist". His works are held at the Hill Palace, the Guest House and the Port Trust buildings in Cochin.

=== Sculpture ===
Raman was also a sculptor. The Hindu credits him with one of the earliest bronze statues in India made by lost-wax casting. The 1961 Census of India's survey of Kerala crafts noted that the Cochin School of Arts, "run by Artist Sri. M. Raman", had made a valuable contribution to the manufacture of life-size statues. Among the school's works it described a six-foot standing statue of Sree Narayana Guru at Koorkancherry, which it said bore a close resemblance to the Guru and was "the only one of its kind". A statue of the Guru made by Raman and his sons was unveiled by S. Radhakrishnan in 1969, and later portraits and statues of the Guru have drawn on Raman's depiction.

== Family ==
Raman died in 1971. His sons M. R. D. Dattan (1935–2006) and M. R. Baburam trained at the Cochin School of Arts and became artists, and a younger son, M. Dilipkumar, is also an artist.

Dattan studied at the Madras School of Art and later became director of the Cochin School of Arts. His statues include those of Mahatma Gandhi, Swami Vivekananda, B. R. Ambedkar, R. Venkataraman and the elephant Guruvayur Kesavan, and he received a Kerala Lalithakala Akademi fellowship. [ref: Artist and sculptor M R D Dattan passes away, The Hindu]

Baburam was known for pastel portraiture and designed pavilions with theme murals for exhibitions and trade fairs in India and abroad. He was the founder of Pavilions and Interiors (India) Pvt. Ltd., an exhibition design and fabrication company established in 1972. [ref: About Us, Pavilions and Interiors]

data.title: Parakode N. R. Kurup
data.text:
----

Parakode N. R. Kurup (died 3 July 2024) was an Indian poet, translator, editor, and literary worker associated with Janayugam, Malayalanadu, the Sarvavijnanakosham (Kerala Encyclopaedia), and the [https://ksicl.org/ State Institute of Children’s Literature(KSICL)]. Known for his romantic and lyrical style, Kurup authored several notable works and contributed significantly to Malayalam literary translation, including the Malayalam translation of Laila–Majnu.

== Biography ==

=== Early Life and Education ===
N. R. Kurup was born into a middle‑class farming family in Parakode, Pathanamthitta district, Kerala. He went to NSS College Pandalam and then to University College Thiruvananthapuram for his post-graduation. He wrote several poems while he was a student, as well as lyrics and articles in various periodicals. In his youth, he became acquainted and worked closely with prominent political workers and student activists like Adoor Ramachandran,Thirunalloor Karunakaran, C. Achuthamenon, Vayalar Ramavarma, Thoppil Bhasi which made him a staunch sympathiser of the Communist Party of India. and later joined Janayugam.

=== Career ===

==== Early Association with Janayugam ====
N R Kurup became involved with Janayugam, the Malayalam daily aligned with the Communist movement, during the 1950s. He contributed significantly to the Party’s efforts during the 1954 Adoor constituency election. In 1958, he formally joined Janayugam as a member of the editorial committee and served until 1964.

==== Editorial and Literary Roles ====
After leaving Janayugam in 1964, Kurup served as:

* Chief Editor, Malayalanadu [ref: Malayalanadu, Wikipedia] [ref: Sahitya Varaphalam – Column by Critic M. Krishnan Nair, Malayala Manorama] weekly
* Editor, Sarvavijnanakosham (1970–1983)
* Editor, [https://ksicl.org/ State Institute of Children’s Literature(KSICL)] (1983–1986)

Kurup was known for his disciplined editorial work and his contributions to major state‑sponsored literary projects. He played a significant role in the translation of Ambedkar’s works undertaken by the [https://keralabhashainstitute.org/ Kerala State Language Institute (Kerala Bhasha Institute)].

== Literary contributions ==

=== Poetry ===
Kurup was widely regarded as a poet of love and emotion. His major works include:

* Nee Entethanu
* Dheerasameere Yamuna Theere
* Balance Sheet [ref: Library Catalogue Record – 222929, University of Calicut Library Catalogue]
* Chuvanna Theeyilekku
* Sreeraman Enna Manushyan [ref: Library Catalogue Record – 205549, University of Calicut Library Catalogue]
* Delhi Muthal Helsingi Vare

His first work, Nee Ente Thaane, carried a foreword by noted poet Prof. Thirunalloor Karunakaran, who was an early mentor and influence on Kurup’s literary development.

=== Translations ===
Kurup’s Malayalam translation of the celebrated romantic epic Laila–Majnu is considered one of his most notable contributions. His translation work was recognized for its sensitivity and literary finesse.

* [http://[ip]/cgi-bin/koha/opac-detail.pl?biblionumber=25141 Doctor Ambedkar sampoorna krithikal] [ref: Library Catalogue Entry – Biblio Record 25141, Kerala State Central Library OPAC] [ref: Library Catalogue Record – SSU.11093, VuFind OPAC] [ref: Library Catalogue Entry – Biblio Record 25141, Kerala State Central Library OPAC] [ref: Library Catalogue Record – ch.10997, University of Calicut Library Catalogue]
* Lailayum Majnuvum

Additionally, during his time on the editorial board of Janayugam and the Malayalanadu weekly, he translated numerous contemporary socio-political essays and literary critiques from English into Malayalam to support the publications' weekly runs.

== Legacy ==
Although N. R. Kurup made notable contributions to Malayalam literature—as a poet, translator, and editor—he did not receive the level of recognition many felt he deserved. His works, especially his romantic poetry and translations, continue to be remembered by those familiar with his literary journey.

===== Yuvakala Sahithi   =====
Parakode N. R. Kurup was one of the early leaders of Yuva Kala Sahithi [ref: യുവകലാസാഹിതി, Malayalam Wikipedia],, a prominent cultural and literary youth movement in Kerala. He served as the organisation’s first president, helping shape its initial activities and literary outreach. His involvement in Yuvakala Sahithi reflects his broader engagement with progressive cultural platforms and his influence on Kerala’s literary activism..

Ahead of the first World Malayalam Conference held in Thiruvananthapuram, it was N. R. Kurup who led the Deepashikha Rally conducted from Kasaragod to Thiruvananthapuram. In 1965, he participated as the Indian representative at the World Peace Conference held in Helsinki. He had written multiple travelogues such as "Delhi Multhal Helsingi Vare" [ref: Library Catalogue Record – uok2.54781, University Library Catalogue (VuFind)] and "Hiroshima Diary" [ref: Library Catalogue Record – uok2.54871, University Library Catalogue (VuFind)] during his various travels during this period.

Parakode N. R. Kurup Foundation

The Parakode N. R. Kurup Foundation honors his memory, hosting annual memorial events (Parakode N. R. Kurup Anusmaranam) [ref: Parakode N. R. Kurup Anusmaranam, In My City Today] and literary award ceremonies (the inaugural award was presented to Prof. O. N. V. Kurup in 2014)

== Selected works ==

* Nee Ente Thaane
* Dheerasameere Yamuna Theere
* Chuvanna Theeyilekku
* Sreeraman Enna Manushyan
* Delhi Muthal Helsingi Vare [ref: Library Catalogue Record – uok2.54781, University Library Catalogue (VuFind)]
* Laila–Majnu (Malayalam translation)

data.title: Iya Agbebi system in precolonial Lagos
data.text:
Iya Agbebi System in Pre-Colonial Lagos

Iya Agbebi system in precolonial Lagos refers to the traditional Yoruba institution of midwifery and maternal healthcare as it operated in the Lagos region before the British colonization of 1861, and its role in trade and economic development. The system was maintained by women known as Iya Agbebi or Iya Abiye, who provided childbirth care, herbal medicine, and postnatal support.

The Iya Agbebi were part of a wider network of female economic actors in precolonial Lagos, alongside women potters, traders, and market leaders.

== Historical background ==
In precolonial Awori and Yoruba societies of Lagos, midwifery was a hereditary female occupation transmitted within family compounds. Training was by apprenticeship, from mother to daughter or from senior female relative to junior wife, similar to other craft guilds. [ref: Nigerian Women in Historical Perspective, Sankore] Their practice combined herbal knowledge, spiritual rites, and practical obstetric care.

== Relationship to trade and economic development ==

=== Labor preservation and population growth ===
The economy of precolonial Lagos relied on human labor for fishing, farming, boat-building, and long-distance trade across the Lagos Lagoon. By providing maternal and infant care, Iya Agbebi contributed to the preservation of human capital and the maintenance of household labor, which supported market expansion. [ref: Slavery and the Birth of an African City: Lagos, 1760-1900, Indiana University Press]

=== Economic role and compensation ===
While anchored in communal welfare, Iya Agbebi were compensated through gifts, agricultural produce, cowries, and specialized trade goods. This exchange contributed to local circulation of currency and goods. Many midwives also engaged in market trading, using the social networks built through their healthcare work to establish customer bases. [ref: Women Traders, Chiefs and the Market, Journal of African History]

=== Support for women's productivity ===
Community-based prenatal and postnatal care reduced periods of incapacity for female traders and artisans, enabling them to return to productive activities. The apprenticeship model of the Iya Agbebi mirrored other female occupational guilds in Yorubaland. [ref: Where Women Work: A Study of Yoruba Women in the Marketplace and at Home, University of Michigan]

=== Medical supply chain ===
The practice relied on medicinal plants, roots, bark, and palm oils, collectively known as egbogi. Sourcing these materials involved herbal merchants and medicine suppliers (onisegun) and created demand for forest products from the Yoruba interior, linking coastal Lagos with inland communities. [ref: Yoruba Medicine, Oxford University Press]

== Decline and transformation ==
With the introduction of colonial biomedical services and Christian missionary maternity centers in late 19th and early 20th century Lagos, the formal role of the Iya Agbebi declined, though the practice continued informally.

data.title: Aleksandër Frangaj
data.text:
Aleksandër Frangaj (born 4 October 1968) is an Albanian media entrepreneur and former journalist. He is the founder and majority shareholder of TV Klan, a television network established in 1997. [ref: TVSH, Klan dhe Top Channel dominojnë tregun televiziv në vend, Reporter.al]

== Early life and education ==

Frangaj was born in Lezhë, Albania, on 4 October 1968. He completed secondary education at Mujo Ulqinaku school in Durrës in 1987 and subsequently studied directing at the Academy of Fine Arts in Tirana, completing his studies in 1994. [ref: Aleksandër Frangaj: Hyj në politikë për t’u shërbyer njerëzve, Koha Jonë]

== Media career ==

In 1991, Frangaj became involved in the newspaper Koha Jonë, which was founded in Lezhë by Nikollë Lesi and became an independent publication that year. [ref: Koha Jonë, Media Ownership Monitor] Frangaj served as an editor at the newspaper during the early 1990s. [ref: Human Rights in Post-Communist Albania, Human Rights Watch]

In 1993, Frangaj and fellow journalist Martin Leka were arrested in connection with reporting about military affairs. The case was documented by human-rights organisations and press-freedom groups. [ref: Frangaj-Leka, Lesi: Si arrestoi Berisha dy gazetarët në '94, Shqiptarja.com]

In 1997, Frangaj established Media 6 with businessmen Julian Roche and Marsel Skëndo. The company published the weekly magazine Klan and launched the television station TV Klan.

TV Klan received a national terrestrial broadcasting licence in 2001. Its programming includes news, current affairs and entertainment. The programme Opinion (Albanian TV program))|Opinion]], hosted by journalist Blendi Fevziu, is among its current-affairs programmes.

In 2013, Media 6 changed its name to TV Klan. Frangaj holds 60% of the company's shares and his wife, Alba Gina, holds 40%.

data.title: Marina Shmatova
data.text:
Marina Shmatova (also spelled Schmatova) is a social entrepreneur and philanthropist based in Mozambique. She is the founder of the Nia Safi Charity Foundation. [ref: Mentalidade Ecológica, Meio Ambiente]

== Environmental and humanitarian work ==

Since 2020, Shmatova has been carrying out the "Mentalidade Ecológica" (EcoMindset) program in Sofala and Manica provinces in Mozambique. According to the Mozambican magazine Meio Ambiente, the initiative focuses on environmental education and volunteer actions. [ref: Mentalidade Ecológica, Meio Ambiente]

In March 2023, the Nia Safi Charity Foundation began rehabilitation works of the EPC de Mungassa Primary School in Beira, which was destroyed by Cyclone Idai in March 2019. As reported by Diário de Moçambique, the project includes the rehabilitation of four classrooms and an administrative block, serving 3,843 students. [ref: Nia Safi Charity Foundation reabilita Escola de Mungassa, Diário de Moçambique]

The Foundation has also implemented housing projects for vulnerable families in Beira, including the delivery of a house in Vila Massane and a commitment to build additional houses. [ref: Fundação Nia Safi promete construir mais casas para famílias vulneráveis, Diário de Moçambique]

data.title: OnsaFX
data.text:
----

Onsafx (stylised OnsaFX) is an online foreign exchange (forex) and contracts for difference (CFD) trading brand based in Johannesburg, South Africa. It is operated through Onsa FX (Pty) Ltd and a separate company registered in Saint Lucia. [ref: Licence & Regulation, OnsaFX] The brand has been an official partner of the Spanish football club Getafe CF since the 2024–25 season [ref: We Proudly Welcome OnsaFX as an Official Partner for the 2024–2025 Season, Getafe CF] and has worked with former Chelsea captain John Terry and market strategist Roger Hirst.

== Company and regulation ==
Onsa FX (Pty) Ltd is registered in South Africa under registration number 2023/648987/07. It states that it is an authorised financial services provider (FSP) with the Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA) under FSP number 53192, and that it provides advice and intermediary services without acting as counterparty to client trades.

Trades are executed by a company registered in Saint Lucia as an international business company (registration number 2025-00284), which the website describes as the counterparty to client trades. The website does not name a Saint Lucia financial regulator for this entity. Clients are introduced through the South African company and then enter a trading agreement with the Saint Lucia company.

The company states that its website is directed at residents of South Africa and that its services are not offered to residents of several jurisdictions, including the United States. The company also states that it is registered with the United States Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). [ref: OnsaFX – Trade Forex, CFDs, OnsaFX]

== Partnerships ==
=== Getafe CF ===
In the 2024–25 season, Getafe CF announced OnsaFX as an official partner. The club said the brand's logo would appear on the club's digital platforms and at matchday events. The club later announced that the partnership would continue for the 2025–26 season, and said the two organisations planned community initiatives relating to youth talent and financial education. [ref: Getafe CF and OnsaFX continue their strategic alliance for the 2025-2026 season, Getafe CF]

=== John Terry ===
In June 2026, a corporate news item published by Gulf News reported that former Chelsea and England captain John Terry had joined OnsaFX as a brand ambassador. [ref: From the pitch to the financial markets, Gulf News]

=== Roger Hirst ===
In November 2025, OnsaFX announced a collaboration with Roger Hirst, a macro and foreign exchange strategist and former managing editor at Real Vision. Under the arrangement, Hirst produces monthly macro analysis videos, weekly foreign exchange updates and educational content for the company's clients. [ref: We are excited to launch our new collaboration with Roger Hirst, OnsaFX]

== Awards ==
The company's website lists a number of industry awards for the years 2024 to 2026, including "Fastest Growing Online Broker" (2025) and "Best Customer Service" (2025). [ref: Awards & Recognition, OnsaFX]

data.title: Luciano Perrone
data.text:
Luciano Perrone è un medico chirurgo italiano attivo nei campi della chirurgia generale, della chirurgia del seno e della medicina e chirurgia estetica. [ref: Dott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

== Formazione e carriera ==
Perrone si è laureato in Medicina e Chirurgia presso l'Università degli Studi di Roma Tor Vergata nel marzo 2008. La sua tesi riguardava la correlazione tra fibrosi epatica e infiammazione nei pazienti sottoposti a trapianto di fegato per epatite C; lo stesso argomento è stato trattato in una pubblicazione scientifica alla quale ha partecipato come coautore. [ref: Correlation between liver fibrosis and inflammation in patients transplanted for HCV liver disease, PubMed]

Tra il 2008 e il 2010 ha lavorato nell'unità di trapianto di Tor Vergata, occupandosi di chirurgia epatobiliare e trapianti di fegato e rene. Successivamente ha svolto attività presso l'Aurelia Hospital di Roma e, dal 2013, ha maturato esperienze in chirurgia del pavimento pelvico, chirurgia laparoscopica e chirurgia colorettale. Tra il 2014 e il 2016 ha proseguito la formazione in chirurgia epatobiliare e laparoscopica presso strutture italiane e britanniche, tra cui il Noble's Hospital, il Colchester Hospital e l'ICENI Centre. [ref: Curriculum vitae del dottor Giovanni Domenico Tebala, Azienda ospedaliero-universitaria Sant'Andrea]

Nel 2012 ha completato un percorso di perfezionamento in Medicina Estetica presso l'Università di Camerino. Nel luglio 2015 ha conseguito la specializzazione in Chirurgia Generale e Chirurgia del Seno presso Tor Vergata. [ref: Dr. Luciano Perrone, Chirurgo Plastico, iDoctors]

La successiva formazione in chirurgia estetica ha incluso periodi presso il Dolan Park Hospital di Bromsgrove e nell'area di Harley Street a Londra, oltre a esperienze formative a Buenos Aires sotto la supervisione del chirurgo J. C. Pavani. [ref: Dott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

== Attività professionale ==
Dal 2013 Perrone ha svolto attività in chirurgia estetica nel Regno Unito, con esperienze professionali a Londra, Birmingham e Manchester. I suoi ambiti di attività comprendono la chirurgia del seno, del viso e del corpo, la chirurgia intima, i trattamenti non chirurgici di medicina estetica e il trapianto di capelli. [ref: Dott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

In Italia è direttore sanitario delle Cliniche Dr. Peròn, con sedi a Parma, Milano e Bologna. I profili professionali disponibili lo indicano iscritto all'Ordine dei Medici di Parma con il numero 7488 e a quello di Roma con il numero 56818. È inoltre indicato come membro dell'Associazione Italiana di Chirurgia Plastica ed Estetica (AICPE) e registrato presso il General Medical Council britannico. [ref: Chi siamo, Cliniche Dr. PerònDott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

Perrone presenta un approccio alla mastoplastica additiva denominato Mastoplastica Argentina, associato alle sue esperienze formative in Argentina. In un'intervista pubblicata da Guidaestetica ha descritto un percorso che comprende la valutazione delle aspettative della paziente, l'esame delle caratteristiche anatomiche e la scelta dell'impianto. La tecnica chirurgica descritta prevede il posizionamento della protesi secondo la tecnica dual plane, con scelte adattate alle caratteristiche individuali. [ref: Il metodo della Mastoplastica Argentina del Dr. Luciano Perrone, un seno naturale su misura senza sorprese, Guidaestetica]

== Attività scientifica ==
L'attività scientifica di Perrone si è concentrata prevalentemente sulla chirurgia dei trapianti, la chirurgia laparoscopica e la chirurgia colorettale. Tra le pubblicazioni a cui ha contribuito figurano studi sulla fibrosi epatica dopo trapianto, sui regimi immunosoppressivi nei pazienti sottoposti a trapianto renale e sui programmi di recupero postoperatorio. [ref: Correlation between liver fibrosis and inflammation in patients transplanted for HCV liver disease, PubMedEarly Discharge After Colorectal Resection: The Positive Impact of an Enhanced Recovery Program on a Rural Colorectal Surgery Service, PubMed]

=== Pubblicazioni selezionate ===

* L. Baiocchi, M. Angelico, A. Petrolati, L. Perrone et al., Correlation between liver fibrosis and inflammation in patients transplanted for HCV liver disease, American Journal of Transplantation, vol. 8, n. 3, 2008, pp. 673–678. DOI.
* M. Manuelli, L. De Luca, G. Iaria, P. Tatangelo, D. Sforza, L. Perrone et al., Conversion to rapamycin immunosuppression for malignancy after kidney transplantation, Transplantation Proceedings, vol. 42, n. 4, 2010, pp. 1314–1316. DOI.
* G. Iaria, F. Pisani, L. De Luca, D. Sforza, M. Manuelli, L. Perrone et al., Prospective study of switch from cyclosporine to tacrolimus for fibroadenomas of the breast in kidney transplantation, Transplantation Proceedings, vol. 42, n. 4, 2010, pp. 1169–1170. DOI.
* G. D. Tebala, L. Perrone, I. Selvaggio, Tractions and countertractions in laparoscopic cholecystectomy, Surgical Chronicles, vol. 17, n. 3, 2012, pp. 178–181.
* M. Shah, A. Q. Khan, M. V. Cavalletti, L. Perrone, C. Ratnavel, G. D. Tebala, Self resolving non-parasitic splenic cyst: A case report, International Journal of Case Reports and Images, vol. 5, n. 5, 2014, pp. 365–369. DOI.
* G. D. Tebala, S. Keane, A. Osman, M. Ip, A. Q. Khan, L. Perrone, Early Discharge After Colorectal Resection: The Positive Impact of an Enhanced Recovery Program on a Rural Colorectal Surgery Service, Surgical Laparoscopy, Endoscopy & Percutaneous Techniques, vol. 26, n. 6, 2016, pp. e137–e144. DOI.

== Attività divulgativa e riconoscimenti ==
Il 2 agosto 2021 Perrone è intervenuto nella trasmissione radiofonica Non Stop News di RTL 102.5, parlando di trattamenti estetici e degli errori da evitare nella chirurgia plastica. [ref: Luciano Perrone, il chirurgo estetico ci ha parlato di ritocchi e degli errori da non commettere, RTL 102.5 Play] Nell'ottobre dello stesso anno è stato citato dalla Gazzetta dello Sport in un articolo sulle precauzioni da adottare per riprendere l'attività fisica dopo la mastoplastica additiva. [ref: Fare sport dopo la mastoplastica additiva: come e quando è possibile? Ce lo spiega l'esperto, La Gazzetta dello Sport]

Il 10 settembre 2026 ha ricevuto il riconoscimento Beauty for Cinema durante il Gran Galà Premio Cinema & Industria, organizzato a Venezia in occasione dell'83ª Mostra internazionale d'arte cinematografica. La notizia è stata riportata da diverse testate nell'ottobre dello stesso anno. [ref: Medico di Parma riceve il premio «Beauty for Cinema» a Venezia, ParmaTodayVenezia, Luciano Perrone tra i premiati del Gran Galà Premio Cinema & Industria, Italia News Radio TVBeauty for Cinema, premiato il dottor Luciano Perrone, Il Roma]

data.title: Stumble Guys
data.text:
----

Stumble Guys is a 2020 free-to-play platform battle royale game developed by the american game developer Scopely and was published by the former developer Kitka Games. The game tends to be heavily inspired by the 2020 video game Fall Guys although Stumble Guys tends to not use the bean-like characters from Fall Guys. The game was first released on Android on 24 September, 2020, but was then released on iOS on 12 February, 2021 and was released on Steam on 7 October, 2021. The game was released on consoles like Xbox One, Xbox Series X and Series S in January 2024, [ref: Mobile smash hit Stumble Guys is coming to consoles, Polygon.com] [ref: Mobile Hit 'Stumble Guys' Will Be A Timed Console Exclusive For Xbox, Pure Xbox] [ref: Stumble Guys trips onto console, first to Xbox, GAMINGTREND] [ref: ] [ref: “Stumble Guys” is bringing its massively multiplayer mayhem to Console, www.scopely.com] PlayStation 4, and PlayStation 5 in May 2024, [ref: Stumble Guys Debuts On PS4 And PS5 Today, Cross-Progression Update Now Live, GameSpot] [ref: Stumble Guys confirmed for PS5, PS4, Gematsu] and was last released on Nintendo Switch on August 2024. [ref: ]

== Gameplay ==
Similar to Fall Guys, about 24 to 32 players are put in battle royal matches where the players must pass through obstacles without trying to not get knocked out or fall. When they finish all of the obstacles, up to 12 people will win if they make it to the finish. Progressively, the same gameplay happens but with less players and different maps. Players can dive, slide, and more, just like Fall Guys. The aim is to qualify for subsequent rounds by successfully completing each of the randomly selected mini-games from a spinning wheel-like selector which many of have randomly selected variations.
====Currency====
The game uses a currency called Gems where players can buy spinning wheels, avatar skins, and change their username.
====Features====
There are features in the game such as prize wheels where players can use 9 free spins on the Free prize wheels before they have to wait 12 or 24 hours to get those free prize wheel spins again. Players can buy prize wheels with the currency Gems which may cost around 99 or 149 Gems. Players can also get free Stumble Boxes where it contains points where when the player gets enough points, they will get a avatar skin.

== Development ==
The game was originally developed and published by Kitka Games with a small team. The idea was to make a mobile version of Fall Guys since Android and iOS didn't have Fall Guys and it wasn't available on Android and iOS. [ref: Stumble Guys Analysis: How a Clone Game Became a Massive Success, [[Medium (website)] Since the rise of Fall Guys, Kitka Games made Stumble Guys, a highly inspired version of Fall Guys but on mobile. The game was made from using the video game engine Unity just like Fall Guys. The game didn't get popular until 2021 when it grew viral growth in parts of regions in India.

In September 2022, Scopely officially acquired the game from Kitka Games. [ref: Welcome “Stumble Guys” to the Scopely portfolio!, www.scopely.com] [ref: Scopely acquires Stumble Guys battle royale game from Kitka Games, GamesBeat]

====Collaboration events====
On 15 December, 2022, the game collaborated with Hot Wheels, releasing a hot wheels track which allowed players to race other players. [ref: “Stumble Guys” players can now tear up the race track with new driving mode powered by Mattel's Hot Wheels™, www.scopely.com] [ref: Stumble Guys hits the tracks with Hot Wheels, GamesBeat] This was Stumble Guys first ever official brand partnership between a major company called Mattel.

On 25 April, 2023, the game collaborated with Nerf, an American toy company that is known for making Nerf Blasters released an update where players would be in a first-person shooter map where the players would have to shoot other players. [ref: New first-person game mode, powered by NERF, is launching into “Stumble Guys”, www.scopely.com] [ref: Grab your blaster! 🔫 @[user] is officially here!!! 🔥 Check out our newest trailer and play our new Blaster Base level in the Nerf Arena NOW! 😎🎉 #StumbleGuys]

On 27 July, 2023, the game collaborated with MrBeast, releasing MrBeast avatar skins and oversized obstacle courses were added in the update. On November 2023, a new part of the update was released, releasing a stage called MrBeast's Dangerous Traps was introduced, mimicking his channel's high-stakes endurance challenges. The final update was in February 2024 where a music-themed elimination level named Disco Drop. Alongside this level, the developers launched the Stumble Workshop MrBeast Toolkit, allowing players to use lasers, blimps, and giant fans to build their own custom MrBeast obstacle courses. [ref: Stumble Guys launches the Stumble Workshop MrBeast Toolkit and other collab goodies in latest update, www.pocketgamer.com] [ref: Design your own MrBeast course in “Stumble Guys” with the Stumble Workshop MrBeast Toolkit, www.scopely.com]

On 10 November, 2023, a collaboration came to the game such as Spongebob Squarepants being added to the game. [ref: Ohhh…Who’s Coming to “Stumble Guys” on Mobile and PC? SpongeBob SquarePants!, Games Press] Krabby patties were a temporary currency in the collaboration. The Spongebob Squarepants collaboration was re-released on 25 June, 2024 due to community demand. [ref: Stumble Guys sees two major new additions, and the return of its SpongeBob collaboration, www.pocketgamer.com]

Other collaboration events like Barbie, [ref: Barbie™ Brings Her Summer Beach Party to “Stumble Guys” With New Barbie Dream Dash Level, www.scopely.com] Avatar: The Last Airbender, [ref: ] [ref: Stumble Guys adds Avatar: The Last Airbender to its lineup, GamesBeat] [ref: ] Monopoly, Pac-Man, and other various collaborations were released into the game throughout 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026.

====Release====
The game was first released on Android on 24 September, 2020 and iOS on 12 February, 2021 and on Steam on 7 October, 2021. The game was released on consoles in 2024 such as Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S, [ref: Stumble Guys - Official Xbox Launch Trailer - IGN] PlayStation 4 and 5, and Nintendo Switch. [ref: Stumble Guys Coming To Consoles; Beta, Cross-Play, And Cross-Progression Confirmed, GameSpot]
====Merchandise====
Since May 2024, Stumble Guys has been selling official merchandise such as action figures, plushies, mini-collectables, and clothing. [ref: Stumble Guys - Merch, Stumble Guys]

== Reception ==
The reception of the game is mostly positive. Mobile gaming critics from outlets like Pocket Gamer and GamesBeat noted that the Avatar: The Last Airbender crossover perfectly matched the "wild spirit" of the game. They praised Scopely's ongoing strategy of using massive pop-culture franchises to continuously keep the multiplayer title feeling fresh. [ref: Stumble Guys brings Avatar: The Last Airbender into the fray, www.pocketgamer.com]

On PCGamesN, Danielle Rose said "If you're looking for something similar to Fall Guys, then you can't get much more similar than Stumble Guys. Probably could have done with a slightly more original name but who are we to criticize? While Stumble Guys is a fun and suitable alternative to the Mediatonic original, it's so similar that there aren't many reasons to choose it over Fall Guys since the latter became free to play. It's fun, it's free, and it's worth at least an evening of your time to check out some different courses." [ref: The best games like Fall Guys on PC 2024, PCGamesN]

data.title: University of Health Sciences (Somalia)
data.text:
----

University of Health Sciences (UOHS; Somali: Jaamacadda Culuumta
Caafimaadka) is a private non-profit higher-education institution in Bosaso,
Bari, Puntland, Somalia. It provides education and training in health sciences
and has a Faculty of Medicine listed in the World Directory of Medical
Schools.University of Health Sciences Faculty of Medicine, World Directory of Medical Schools
== History ==
The university's institutional history states that the University of Health Sciences
was established in September 2000 as a health institute. It was promoted to college
status in 2003 and obtained university status in 2012. The institution attributes its
establishment to the shortage of medical professionals in Somalia following the
country's civil war.UOHS History and Background of the University, University of Health Sciences
The university identifies Prof. Abdirisak Hussein Hassan as its founding father.
According to the university, he established a nursing institute in response to
shortages of trained medical personnel in Somalia.UOHS Founding Father, University of Health Sciences
A 2013 report by the Heritage Institute for Policy Studies listed the University of
Health Sciences among the higher-education institutions surveyed in Puntland. The
report recorded the institution as having been established in 2006 and, at the time of
the survey, listed five faculties and 947 students.The State of the Higher Education Sector in Somalia, Heritage Institute for Policy Studies
== Administration ==
The university's current rector is Dr. Najma Abdirisak H. Hassan. The university's
rector page identifies her as rector, and the Somali Research and Education Network
lists her as a member of its board of directors in the same capacity.Rector's Message, University of Health SciencesBoard of Directors, Somali Research and Education Network
== Academics ==
The university's academic structure includes eight health sciences faculties: the
Faculty of Medicine and Surgery, Faculty of Clinical Midwifery, Faculty of Clinical
Nursing, Faculty of Food Sciences and Nutrition, Faculty of Clinical Pharmacy,
Faculty of Public Health, Faculty of Medical Laboratory, and Faculty of Radiological
Sciences and Medical Imaging.UOHS History and Background of the University, University of Health SciencesUndergraduate Programs, University of Health Sciences

The University of Health Sciences Somalia (UOHS) is a member institution of the Somali Research and Education Network (SomaliREN), a non-profit organization that connects higher education and research institutions in Somalia.Member Institutions, Somali Research and Education Network

The Faculty of Medicine provides a Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery
(MBBS) programme. The World Directory of Medical Schools records the school
as a private, currently operational medical school in Bosaso. It lists 2014 as the year
instruction began, a five-year curriculum, and admission of both men and
women.University of Health Sciences Faculty of Medicine, World Directory of Medical Schools
The university also offers undergraduate programmes in clinical nursing, clinical
midwifery, food sciences and nutrition, public health, medical laboratory sciences,
clinical pharmacy, and radiological sciences and medical imaging.Undergraduate Programs, University of Health Sciences
The radiological sciences and medical imaging programme was inaugurated in 2021,
according to the university, which describes it as an undergraduate programme in
the field.Faculty of Radiological Sciences & Medical Imaging, University of Health Sciences
== Affiliations and partnerships ==
The University of Health Sciences is a member institution of the Association of
Puntland Universities (APU). The association identifies UOHS as one of its
member universities and describes the network as a cooperative body for higher
education institutions in Puntland.Member Universities, Association of Puntland Universities
The university has participated in activities of the Inter-University Council for East
Africa (IUCEA). In 2024, the university reported that it joined IUCEA and that a
university representative participated in the 13th East African Higher Education
Quality Assurance Forum in Nairobi, Kenya.University of Health Sciences, University of Health Sciences
The university's membership and affiliation listings are also included in highereducation directories such as uniRank, which lists associations including the
Association of African Universities, Association of Somali Universities, Somali
Research and Educational Network, Tuning Africa, and the Association of Arab
Private Universities.University of Health Sciences, uniRank
== Campus ==
The university's main campus is located in Bosaso, Puntland, on Airport Road
near Bosaso Public Secondary School.UOHS History and Background of the University, University of Health Sciences
The same location is given independently by the World Directory of Medical
Schools, which lists Airport Street, Bosaso, Puntland, Somalia as the main address of
the Faculty of Medicine.University of Health Sciences Faculty of Medicine, World Directory of Medical Schools
A 2024 Bosaso City Strategy published by the United Nations Development
Programme identified six universities operating in Bosaso and named the
University of Health Sciences among the city's larger universities, alongside the
University of Bosaso and East Africa University.Bosaso City Strategy & Extension Plan, United Nations Development Programme
== Institutional profile ==
uniRank describes the University of Health Sciences as a private, non-profit,
coeducational higher-education institution established in 2000 and recognised by
Somalia's Ministry of Education, Culture and Higher Education. Its profile gives an
estimated student-enrolment range of 2,000 2,999 and an academic-staff range of 50
99.University of Health Sciences UOHS, uniRank
The same directory lists the institution's motto as Towards a Better Health and its
colours as green and orange.University of Health Sciences, uniRank

data.title: Ian McBride (cyclist)
data.text:
I

I have a conflict of interest regarding the cyclist Ian McBride. I am submitting data and sources for review by independent editors via the Articles for Creation process.

=== Ian McBride (cyclist) ===

* Subject Description: Ian McBride (born c. 1970s) is a New Zealand-born, London-based ultra-distance and audax cyclist who has competed internationally in premier long-distance randonnées. After moving from New Zealand to the UK in the late 1990s, he transitioned from triathlons to ultra-endurance cycling, joining the night-riding group "The Fridays". He completed the 1,200 km Paris–Brest–Paris (PBP) event in 2019, and returned in the 2023 edition to finish with a time of 51 hours and 39 minutes, cementing his record as the fastest New Zealander in the event's history. He also finished the 1,540 km London–Edinburgh–London (LEL) event in 2022 in joint 2nd with 2x winner Dutchman Anco De Jong, despite suffering from Shermer's neck in the final stages. Following his cycling achievements, he was voted by the membership and awarded the 2025 Audax UK Male Merit Award (The Paul Castle Cup), given annually to the cyclist whose performance is considered the most meritorious of the year.

McBride achieved widespread national and international cycling media coverage during the August 2025 iteration of the London–Edinburgh–London event. Setting off at 4:00 AM on 3 August 2025, McBride intentionally paced his ride to outrun an impending severe weather system. He successfully crossed into Scotland and reached the Edinburgh turnaround point, with a 3 hour lead over the 2nd placed rider, just before event organisers officially suspended the brevet due to 100 mph winds brought by Storm Floris. Because thousands of trailing participants were ordered to stop or turn back from wherever they had reached, McBride became the only rider out of 2,500 entrants to complete the full, original 1,500 km scheduled route back to London. His feat is a primary subject of the 2025 non-fiction book "Riders of the Storm: The Inside Story of London Edinburgh London".

data.title: Die Gstettensaga: The Rise of Echsenfriedl
data.text:
Die Gstettensaga: The Rise of Echsenfriedl is a 2014 Austrian post-apocalyptic science fiction comedy film directed by Johannes Grenzfurthner and written by Grenzfurthner and Roland Gratzer. Produced by the art group monochrom and the media collective Traum & Wahnsinn, it premiered on ORF III on 10 March 2014 as part of the broadcaster's Artists in Residence series. [ref: ORF III am Dokumontag: Der Arabische Frühling und seine Auswirkungen zwischen Traditionalismus und Freiheitswillen, APA-OTS]

Set in post-apocalyptic Austria, the film satirizes media monopolies, hacker culture and the politics of technological change. [ref: Österreichischer Mad Max II, Telepolis] [ref: Film Review: Die Gstettensaga: A Call to Class Consciousness for Hackers, 2600: The Hacker Quarterly]

== Plot ==
In the early 21st century, a conflict between China and Google escalates into the nuclear "Google Wars", destroying much of civilization. Decades later, a new society has formed among the ruins of Austria. In Mega City Schwechat, media proprietor Thurnher von Pjölk dominates public information through his newspaper and claims to have reinvented printing with movable type. His position is threatened by technologically minded "nerds" who have rediscovered television.

Pjölk sends journalist Fratt Aigner and technician Alalia Grundschober into the wasteland of Niederpröll to find the inventor Echsenfriedl and conduct a televised interview. Along the way they encounter armed postal workers, farmers who revere surviving European Union paperwork, undead miners and a community of traders. They also learn that several inventions credited to Pjölk may have originated with Echsenfriedl.

When they finally reach the inventor, they discover that he is a basilisk whose gaze turns people to stone. Pjölk intends to broadcast his image, killing the early adopters of television and protecting his newspaper monopoly. The scheme is exposed through the broadcast, and Pjölk is overthrown. Echsenfriedl subsequently takes over Pjölk's media empire, becoming the new media mogul and pushing for rapid technological innovation. Fratt and Alalia are hired to work for him.

== Production ==
The film was commissioned for ORF III's Artists in Residence series. In a September 2014 interview with Jungle World, Grenzfurthner said that ORF III had approved the proposal in late October 2013 for a March 2014 broadcast, and that the film had been shot in five days with €5,000 available for production. [ref: »Das Schockmoment ist nur noch Selbstmarketing«, Jungle World] [ref: Die Gstettensaga: The Rise of Echsenfriedl, pressplay]

Grenzfurthner and Gratzer developed the screenplay in November 2013, incorporating material from monochrom's earlier role-playing theatre project Campaign. Filming took place in December 2013 and January 2014, followed by approximately five weeks of post-production. Rather than commissioning an original score, the filmmakers used existing electronic, chiptune and synth-pop music. [ref: Die GstettenSaga: The Rise of Echsenfriedl. A post-apocalyptic aftermath of the 'Google Wars', Furtherfield]

The dialogue incorporates German, English, Austrian dialects and invented forms of speech. English subtitles sometimes deliberately depart from the spoken dialogue for comic effect.

An additional financing stunt was incorporated into the film itself: a notice resembling an anti-piracy warning invited viewers to report an allegedly unauthorized copy by calling a premium-rate telephone number. pressplay reported that the calls generated approximately €350. The filmmakers referred to the stunt as "crowdratting".

== Release ==
ORF III first broadcast the film on 10 March 2014. It was subsequently shown at the 2014 Slash Filmfestival in Vienna. The film was made available online in December 2015. [ref: Die Gstettensaga: a science fiction movie about the Google Wars, Boing Boing]

== Reception ==
Peter Mühlbauer, reviewing the film for Telepolis, discussed its post-apocalyptic media satire, performances and extensive cultural references. He singled out the deliberately inaccurate English subtitles as a further source of jokes and observed that much of the film's humor depended on the viewer recognizing its literary and cultural allusions.

Sebastian Vetter, writing for the Austrian cultural magazine skug, interpreted the film as a critique of failed revolutionary aspirations and of the political limits of technological subcultures. Comparing its post-apocalyptic landscape with the traditional Western, he argued that the film depicts progress as the recovery of a lost past rather than the creation of an alternative future. [ref: Pröll for ever – die Linke ist tot!, skug]

A May 2014 segment of Place de la Toile on France Culture described the film as an underground discovery for nerds, comparing it with Monty Python and the Frères Denis. [ref: Politique de l'algorithme, France Culture]

Bianca Hofbauer rated the film 8 out of 10 in pressplay. She praised the costumes, performances, dialogue and use of different languages, as well as the locations chosen to depict the post-apocalyptic landscape. She also found that the film's 72-minute running time felt overlong and prevented complete immersion in its fictional world.

A VICE report on the 2014 Slash Filmfestival praised the film's production quality and some of its humor but criticized its heavy-handed use of political and media-theoretical commentary. [ref: Die verdammten Highlights des diesjährigen /slash Filmfestivals, VICE]

The Autumn 2014 issue of 2600: The Hacker Quarterly examined the film's treatment of class, technology and economic power, interpreting its depiction of hackers as a call for collective political consciousness rather than faith in technological innovation alone.

In the November 2014 issue of Lotek64, Georg Fuchs praised the film's production design, soundtrack and visual details, as well as its references to Austrian society, hacker culture and science-fiction classics. [ref: Film: Die Gstettensaga (Ö, 2014) – The Rise of Echsenfriedl, Lotek64]

Writing for the media-art magazine Neural, Aurelio Cianciotta examined the film's mixture of genres, its use of improvised and do-it-yourself technologies, and the way its apparent technological revolution leaves existing relations of power substantially intact. [ref: Die Gstettensaga: The Rise of Echsenfriedl, [[Neural (magazine)]

Didi Neidhart reviewed the film in issue 24 of the German-language cultural magazine testcard. He interpreted the characters' faith in the "wisdom of the crowd" as a substitute for political organization and class consciousness, and linked their willingness to embrace Echsenfriedl to the film's satire of market ideology. [ref: Die Gstettensaga: The Rise of Echsenfriedl, testcard]

In Furtherfield, Lutschinger discussed the film's DIY approach, cultural references, subtitles and distribution.

== References ==

data.title: Tom Joel Obengo
data.text:
Tom Joel Obengo is a Kenyan bioethicist, philosopher, educator and academic administrator. He is Vice-Principal for Academic Affairs and Senior Lecturer at Moffat Bible College, Kijabe, Kenya, and a recent Postdoctoral Research Fellow in Epidemic Ethics in the Department of Medicine at the University of Cape Town.

== Early life and education ==

Obengo earned a Bachelor of Theology (B.Th.) from Scott University in 1994 and an Honours Bachelor of Arts (Hons.B.A.) in Ethics and Philosophy from the University of South Africa in 1999.

He completed his Master of Theology (M.Th.) in Medical Ethics (Systematic Theology) at Stellenbosch University in 2013 with a thesis titled The quest for human dignity in the ethics of pregnancy termination: a theological-ethical evaluation of the church's approach in Kenya, which was supervised by Professor Chris Jones.. [ref: Browsing by Author Obengo, Tom Joel, SUNScholar, Stellenbosch University] [ref: The quest for human dignity in the ethics of pregnancy termination, SUNScholar]

He undertook M.Phil. courses in Philosophy specialising in Applied Ethics at Stellenbosch University (2016–2017) and completed his Doctor of Philosophy (D.Phil.) in Applied Ethics in March 2020 with a dissertation titled A Utilitarian Assessment of the Relevance of Genetic Therapies for HIV-AIDS in Africa, with Special Reference to the Situation in Kenya, supervised by Professor Anton A. van Niekerk, Distinguished Professor of Philosophy at Stellenbosch University. [ref: A Utilitarian Assessment of the Relevance of Genetic Therapies for HIV-AIDS in Africa, with Special Reference to the Situation in Kenya, University of Stellenbosch, Department of Philosophy, Faculty of Arts & Social Sciences]

== Academic career ==

Since 2014, Obengo has served as Vice-Principal for Academic Affairs and Senior Lecturer at Moffat Bible College, Kijabe, where he teaches ethics, philosophy, critical thinking, apologetics and theology. [ref: Faculty, Moffat Bible College]Some pPublic records list him as Rev. Tom Obengo (Vice Principal Academics) explaining courses offered at the college. [ref: Moffat Bible College, Moffat Bible College via Haylla]

He previously served as Academic Registrarsuccessively at Scott University, at International Leadership University–Kenya, and at Great Lakes University of Kisum.uHe once served ass Academic Dean and Acting Principal at Ahero Bible Training College.

From 2021 to 2024, he was Post-Doctoral Research Fellow in Epidemic Ethics in the Department of Medicine at the University of Cape Town, based at the EthicsLab, where he focused on epidemic ethics and published articles and a book chapter. [ref: Dr Tom J. Obengo, University of Cape Town EthicsLab]

His university teaching and examination roles include:

* External examiner in bioethics, University of Nairobi and University of the Witwatersrand
* Adjunct teaching roles, University of Virginia and Stellenbosch University
* Postgraduate teaching in bioethics, Kabarak University and Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI)

== Research and publications ==

Obengo is the author of:

* The Quest for Human Dignity in the Ethics of Pregnancy Termination (Wipf and Stock, 2016)

and co-author of:

* Research Ethics in Epidemics and Pandemics: A Casebook (Springer Nature, 2024) – Chapter 2. [ref: Research Ethics in Epidemics and Pandemics: A Casebook, Springer Nature]

His research interests include utilitarian bioethics, genetic therapies for HIV-AIDS, epidemic ethics, human dignity, and African Christian ethics.

== Professional service ==

* Managing Editor, African Christian Theology Journal [ref: Editorial Team, African Christian Theology Journal]
* Editorial board member, Journal of Interdisciplinary Ethical Research [ref: Editorial Team, Journal of Interdisciplinary Ethical Research]
* Member, Institutional Scientific and Ethical Review Committee (ISERC), AIC Kijabe Hospital (since 2015)
* Member, Epidemic Ethics Team, The Global Health Network
* Member, Bioethics Society of Kenya

----

Bilal Dayani (; born 22 July 1964) is a media executive based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. He is the chief operating officer of Eagle Films Middle East, a film distribution and production company. [ref: Abu Dhabi Film Commission announces multifaceted enhancements to the 35% rebate programme, Abu Dhabi Media Office] He previously spent fourteen years as executive general manager of the Saudi music label and distributor Megastar, [ref: «شعبية الكرتون» إلى الإنجليزية, Emarat Al Youm] and in 2004 was president of the Arab Music Academy in Dubai, which organised the first Arab Music Awards. [ref: المستمعون يصوّتون للفنانين والفنانون يصوّتون لبعضهم: المهرجان الأول لجوائز الموسيقى العربية, As-Safir] In 2005 Ahlan! magazine included him in its list of the 100 most prominent faces of UAE society. [ref: بلال دياني, Ahlan! (Arabic edition)]

== Early life ==
Dayani was born on 22 July 1964. He is of Syrian nationality and worked in Saudi Arabia before moving to Dubai in the late 1990s.

== Career ==

=== Saudi Arabia and the music industry (1985–2009) ===
Dayani worked in the Saudi media sector from the mid-1980s. In 1995 he joined Al Faisaliah Group as executive general manager of Megastar Home Entertainment, a music label and distributor, a post he held until 2009. At Megastar he was responsible for the production and regional distribution of Arabic albums and music videos by artists including Samira Said, Amal Arafa, Fairuz and Nancy Ajram, and for the distribution of international record labels in the MENA region.

In February 2004 he became president of the Arab Music Academy, a Dubai-based body formed to promote Arabic music and to address piracy and intellectual-property issues facing producers and distributors. The academy organised the first Arab Music Awards, in which winners in 24 categories were chosen by public vote and the ceremony, in Dubai, was to be broadcast by Future TV. Dayani hosted the awards ceremony.

=== Eagle Films Middle East ===
Dayani joined Eagle Films Middle East in the mid-2010s [ref: «لف ودوران».. كوميديا السهل الممتنع, [[Al Bayan (newspaper)] and is the company's chief operating officer. The company distributes international films in the Middle East and produces Arabic television series and films. [ref: تعرف على تفاصيل "قصتي" الذي يجسد حياة محمد بن راشد وموعد العرض والقنوات الناقلة, UAE Barq]

In 2020 he was operations manager of My Story (Qesaty), a docudrama series executive-produced by Eagle Films for the Executive Office of Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum and broadcast on Dubai TV by Dubai Media Incorporated, based on the memoir My Story: 50 Memories from Fifty Years of Service. [ref: «قصتي» سيرة محمد بن راشد في برنامج وثائقي درامي, [[Al Bayan (newspaper)] [ref: إطلالة تلفزيونية جديدة بأسلوب درامي مبتكر, Emarat Al Youm] [ref: العمل الدرامي التوثيقي الأول من نوعه "قصتي" يعرض مراحل حياة محمد بن راشد على مدار 50 حلقة, Government of Dubai Media Office]

In December 2022 Eagle Films received the Excellence in Arabic-Language Productions award at the ASBU BroadcastPro ME Awards in Dubai; Dayani accepted the award on the company's behalf. [ref: Raising the curtain: applauding the best of the best in MENA media and entertainment at the 2022 BroadcastPro Awards, BroadcastPro ME] According to the Abu Dhabi Film Commission, Eagle Films produced the series From Al Haram Street To... and Milh Wa Samrah in Abu Dhabi under his supervision, using the emirate's production rebate programme, [ref: Eagle Films ME, COO, Bilal Dayani, has produced numerous successful projects in Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi Film Commission] and in December 2024 he was quoted in the Commission's announcement of enhancements to that programme.

In April 2019, Eagle Films was among the film distributors and cinema operators that signed memoranda of understanding with the UAE National Media Council under its National Program to Support Emirati Films, an initiative to extend the theatrical run and promotion of Emirati films. [ref: 16 جهة متخصصة تدعم تسويق السينما المحلية, Emarat Al Youm] [ref: «الوطني للإعلام».. برنامج لدعم صنّاع السينما الإماراتية, [[Al-Ittihad (newspaper)] [ref: "الوطني للإعلام" يطلق البرنامج الوطني لدعم الأفلام الإماراتية, Emirates News Agency]

=== Media appearances ===
Dayani has appeared as a commentator on CNBC Arabia, discussing the commercial state of Arab cinema [ref: السينما العربية.. هل هي في المقاعد الخلفية؟, CNBC Arabia] and whether streaming platforms will displace traditional television. [ref: هل تنجح المنصات الرقمية في إنهاء عصر التلفزيون التقليدي؟, CNBC Arabia] He spoke on the panel "Ramadan and Beyond: The Year-Round Content Formula" at the Dubai International Content Market in 2025. [ref: Speakers, Dubai International Content Market]
