data.title: Sicariid and bacterial phospholipase D toxins
data.text:
----

Sicariid and bacterial phospholipase D (PLD) toxins are proteins found in recluse spider venom, most infamously the brown recluse (Loxosceles reclusa), as well as certain types of bacteria. The term PLD broadly refers to a family of enzymes that are the primary active toxins in the venoms of recluse spiders (genus Loxosceles). PLD toxins function molecularly by chemically modifying certain types of lipids in cell membranes, forming lipids containing ring-structures called cyclic phospholipid products, which are thought to disrupt cell surfaces. Physiological symptoms of envenomation can result in the formation of dermonecrotic lesions, hemolysis, and a systemic syndrome called loxoscelism. [ref: Forty Years of the Description of Brown Spider Venom Phospholipases-D, Toxins] [ref: Loxoscelism: Old obstacles, new directions, Annals of Emergency Medicine] Closely-related enzymes are also expressed in tick saliva, [ref: Biochemical characterization of a novel sphingomyelinase-like protein from the Rhipicephalus microplus tick, Experimental Parasitology] and are pathogenicity factors in certain pathogenic bacteria [ref: Toxic phospholipases D of Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis, C. ulcerans and Arcanobacterium haemolyticum: cloning and sequence homology, Gene] and fungi. [ref: Identification of New Sphingomyelinases D in Pathogenic Fungi and Other Pathogenic Organisms, PLOS ONE] [ref: The Toxicogenomic Multiverse: Convergent Recruitment of Proteins Into Animal Venoms, Annual Review of Genomics and Human Genetics]

== Structure ==

PLD toxins are around 31 kDa in size and consist of alternating beta sheets and alpha helices in a circle that overall form a hollow cylindrical structure called a beta barrel. One side of the opening to the beta barrel forms the active site that engages with lipids in cell membranes. Disordered loops around the active site have been shown in computer simulations to dip into the membrane, to hold on, as the enzyme binds to the surface. [ref: Specificity of Loxosceles α Clade Phospholipase D Enzymes for Choline-Containing Lipids: Role of a Conserved Aromatic Cage, Biophysical Journal] The structures of four members of the PLD toxin family have been solved via protein X-ray crystallography, including PLDs from Loxosceles intermedia, [ref: Structure of a novel class II phospholipase D: Catalytic cleft is modified by a disulphide bridge, Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications] Loxosceles laeta, Sicarius terrosus, [ref: Variable Substrate Preference among Phospholipase D Toxins from Sicariid Spiders, Journal of Biological Chemistry] and the bacterium Arcanobacterium haemolyticum. [ref: Crystal Structure of PLD From Arcanobacterium haemolyticum Identifies a Novel Class IIa-α Variant With Unusual Thermostability, Journal of Molecular Biology] Structures of the PLD toxin from Sicarius terrosus were solved in 2026 at high resolution with lipid substrate and cyclic lipid product bound. [ref: Spider venom phospholipase D toxin structure: Interfacial binding site, mechanism, activation, and head group preference, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]

== Substrates and molecular mechanism ==
PLD toxins catalyse a chemical reaction called transphosphatidylation, which involves the formation of a bond between part of the lipid carbon chain and the phosphorus in the lipid head group; this reaction forms lipids with either hexagonal or pentagonal ring structures, called cyclic phosphate products. PLD toxins were originally called sphingomyelinase D (SMaseD) toxins because the original characterization showed activity against sphingomyelin. However, after the discovery that PLD toxins could also catalyze the cyclization of other types of lipids, including certain lysophospholipids including lysophosphatidylcholine, the enzyme was renamed phospholipase D (PLD) to more accurately reflect its target profile. [ref: Brown recluse spider (Loxosceles reclusa) venom phospholipase D (PLD) generates lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), Biochemical Journal] Targets include both sphingolipids and lysophospholipids containing a hydroxyl (OH) group on the lipid backbone, which is what forms the chemical bond to the phosphate, and that have a positive or neutral head group recognized by the PLD, including sphingomyelin (SM), lysophosphatidylcholine (LysoPC), ceramide phosphoethanolamine (CPE), and lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE). Enzyme activity is magnesium dependent, with the target lipid coordinated in the active site by a covalently bound Mg2+ ion. [ref: Structural Basis for Metal Ion Coordination and the Catalytic Mechanism of Sphingomyelinases D, Journal of Biological Chemistry]

The enzyme catalyzes cyclization by deprotonation of the hydroxyl (OH) nucleophile via an active site catalytic histidine. The substrate hydroxyl then nucleophilically attacks at the phosphorus center, resulting in loss of the (typically choline or ethanolamine) head group, which is protonated by a second histidine. The resulting molecule is either cyclic ceramide phosphate (CCP) from SM or CPE, or cyclic phosphatidic acid (CPA) from LPC or LPE. CCP has been poorly characterized, but it is thought to be resistant to hydrolysis in vivo [ref: Detection and characterization of ceramide-1-phosphate phosphatase activity in rat liver plasma membrane., Journal of Biological Chemistry] and there is one structure solved bound to enzyme, showing how the molecule is oriented in the active site of the enzyme.

=== Cyclic product ===
SMaseD/PLD was originally proposed to catalyze the cleavage (hydrolysis) of substrates sphingomyelin and lysophosphatidylcholine to form the linear products ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P) or lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), respectively, which is the mechanism catalysed by unrelated mammalian SMaseD and PLD enzymes. However, in 2013, experiments measuring the reaction by 31-phosphorous (31P) NMR, which enables characterization of chemical bonds to the phosphorus atom, showed that the product was a novel cyclic lipid: 6 ceramide-1,3-cyclic phosphate (N-hexanoyl-ceramide-1,3-cyclic-phosphate; CCP) from SM, and cyclic phosphatidic acid (1-acyl-sn-glycerol-2, 3-cyclic phosphate; CPA) from LPC. [ref: Phospholipase D Toxins of Brown Spider Venom Convert Lysophosphatidylcholine and Sphingomyelin to Cyclic Phosphates, PLOS ONE] In 2026, the cyclic product was crystallized in the active site for the first time, further confirming the mechanism and cyclic product. Despite clear NMR and direct structural evidence, acceptance of the cyclic product has been contentious and the linear product C1P has been erroneously claimed in multiple papers.

== Toxicity ==
All Sicariid spiders express at least three different groups of genes, for a total of around twenty various enzyme paralogues of PLD toxins present in each venom. The alpha-clade members of the family are generally toxic to mammalian cells, because they target substrate with choline head groups. In contrast, the beta-clade SMaseD/PLD members are neurotoxic to insects, because they target substrate with ethanolamine head groups, consistent with a role in prey immobilization and capture. [ref: Sphingomyelinase D in sicariid spider venom is a potent insecticidal toxin, Toxicon]

=== Cellular mechanism ===
The cellular mechanism of PLD toxicity is still highly contested. It has been shown that addition of PLD/SMaseD to liposomes causes membrane remodelling as seen by fluorescent microscopy. [ref: Sphingomyelinase D Activity in Model Membranes: Structural Effects of in situ Generation of Ceramide-1-Phosphate, PLOS ONE]

== Targeted therapies ==
Polyclonal antivenom is available in some countries for the treatment of loxoscelism. However, most therapies involve supportive care such as elevation and immobilization of the affected area, hypobaric oxygen, dapsone, glucocorticoids, and antihistamines. [ref: Bites of Brown Recluse Spiders and Suspected Necrotic Arachnidism, New England Journal of Medicine] No small-molecule targeted inhibitors currently exist for PLD/SMaseD toxins, although several have been investigated.

== Evolution ==
The mechanism described for recluse PLD toxins is believed to be the reverse of that for the ancient ancestral enzyme glycerophosphodiesterases. [ref: Evolutionary dynamics of origin and loss in the deep history of phospholipase D toxin genes, BMC Evolutionary Biology] Thus, these enzymes have also been referred to as glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase-like sphingomyelinase D/phospholipase D (GDPD-like SMaseD/PLD). The gene encoding the PLD toxin is thought to have been horizontally transferred from bacteria into spiders, followed by recruitment into the venom gland. [ref: Lateral gene transfer of a dermonecrotic toxin between spiders and bacteria, Bioinformatics]

== References ==

data.title: Kimaya Diggs
data.text:
Kimaya Diggs (born 1992 or 1993) is an American singer-songwriter based in Northampton, Massachusetts. Her music combines acoustic and indie-folk foundations with elements of soul, R&B and jazz. She has released three studio albums as an independent artist: Breastfed (2018), Quincy (2023) and Green (2026).

== Early life ==
Diggs grew up in western Massachusetts, the daughter of a Black father and an Indian mother. As a child she played music with her two sisters, learning instruments including cello, violin and viola. She attended college in Pennsylvania before returning to western Massachusetts.

== Career ==
=== Breastfed (2018) ===
Diggs released her debut album, Breastfed, in 2018. It was made with bassist Jacob Rosazza. Most of the songs feature Diggs accompanying herself on acoustic guitar, with occasional cello. WBUR later described the record as contemplative and self-produced in character.

=== Quincy (2023) ===
Diggs began work on her second album before the COVID-19 pandemic and continued it through 2020. In 2021 her mother died of cancer, a close friend and musical mentor was killed in a bicycle accident, and her dog, a retired racing greyhound named Quincy, died. The album was named after the dog. Diggs aimed for a fuller sound than on her debut, and her father contributed flute to three tracks.

Quincy was released on March 9, 2023, preceded by the singles "If You Love Me" and "Rainbow". Under the Radar characterized the album's style as indie pop with R&B and soul elements. In a 2023 profile, WBUR highlighted the album's retro-influenced R&B arrangements and noted that Diggs did not regard it as an album about grief. Later that year she released an EP of live versions of songs from the album.

=== "Everything Is Not Lost" (2024) ===
In 2024 Diggs released the single "Everything Is Not Lost", which she described as more dance-oriented than her earlier work. She photographed the single's cover art herself.

=== Green (2026) ===
Diggs released three singles ahead of her third album: "I Know That I'm Perfect", a rock-influenced track, followed by "Dance with Me" and "Plants (Still Grow)". Green was released on October 2, 2026. It is the first of her albums on which she is credited in a production role: she co-produced the record and engineered roughly a quarter of it. She and her partner, also a musician, converted the basement of their Northampton home into a studio and rehearsal space. Eighty-two artists from western Massachusetts contributed to the album.

The album explores the question of what makes a place feel like home and Diggs's relationship with the region where she grew up. The song "A Sense of Place" addresses the racial isolation she experienced in New England. The title refers to the point each spring when trees leaf out almost all at once.

== Live performance ==
Diggs has performed as a supporting act for artists including Mavis Staples, Trombone Shorty, Emily King and Tank and the Bangas.

data.title: Vaccine law
data.text:
Vaccine law, also known as vaccination law or immunization law, is a field of law concerning the development, testing, approval, manufacture, distribution, financing, administration, and use of vaccines, as well as legal responsibility for vaccine-related injuries and governmental policies concerning vaccination. [ref: Vaccine Law and Policy, Springer] [ref: Vaccine, Vaccination, and Immunization Law, Third Edition, Bloomberg Law] [ref: Vaccine Law 101, Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics] It draws on multiple areas of law, including administrative law, public health law, intellectual property law, tort law, constitutional law, and health law. Vaccine law encompasses legal questions arising throughout the life cycle of a vaccine, from initial research and clinical trials through approval, production, distribution, administration, safety monitoring, and potential injury compensation, [ref: A Proper Introduction to Vaccine Law, and a Very Necessary National Vaccine Law Conference, American Bar Association] often with special rules to be implemented in response to public health emergencies. [ref: Legal Issues in COVID-19 Vaccine Development and Deployment, Congressional Research Service]

Vaccination policy is a related field concerned particularly with decisions about recommending, promoting, providing, or requiring vaccination. Vaccine law also encompasses legal frameworks governing the vaccines themselves, independently of policies concerning their use.

==Scope==

The scope of vaccine law extends beyond vaccination mandates and other measures intended to increase vaccination rates. It includes the legal conditions under which vaccines are developed and marketed, the rights and responsibilities of manufacturers and healthcare providers, and the mechanisms through which governments and other institutions make vaccines available to the public. Hargan and colleagues have described the field in terms of the regulatory framework governing the production, procurement, distribution, and administration of vaccines, as well as liability arising from their use. Yang and Reiss examine these subjects alongside the legal treatment of vaccination requirements, vaccine safety, intellectual property, and public health policy.

Areas within the field include:

* Regulation of vaccine clinical trials
* Vaccine licensure, as an aspect of regulation of therapeutic goods
* Vaccine intellectual property, primarily patents
* Vaccine equity; Vaccine access, funding and distribution
* Vaccination mandates and exemptions
* Vaccine injury compensation
* Legal responses to vaccine misinformation

The COVID-19 pandemic brought renewed attention to these issues, including emergency authorization of vaccines, the allocation of initially limited supplies, government vaccination requirements, and the legal treatment of injuries attributed to emergency countermeasures.

===Development and regulation===
The development and approval of vaccines are governed by laws regulating clinical research, pharmaceutical products, and biological products. These laws establish requirements for testing vaccine safety and efficacy, obtaining authorization to market vaccines, maintaining manufacturing standards, and monitoring safety after authorization. Legal requirements governing vaccine research include informed consent, the protection of human research participants, oversight of clinical trials, and the collection and reporting of research results. Research involving vaccine candidates may raise additional questions concerning the use of control groups, the participation of minors and other vulnerable populations, the recruitment of sufficiently representative trial participants, and liability for injuries or misconduct during clinical research.

Regulatory agencies also oversee vaccine manufacturing, labeling, advertising, and postmarketing surveillance. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration regulates human vaccines under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Public Health Service Act. The agency may inspect manufacturing facilities, impose product requirements, and take enforcement action for violations of applicable law. Special regulatory pathways may permit access to vaccines that have not received ordinary marketing approval. In the United States, an emergency use authorization may permit the use of certain medical products during a qualifying public health emergency, subject to statutory conditions. Legal systems often provide mechanisms to accelerate the development or regulatory review of vaccines intended to prevent serious diseases, including expedited development and review procedures, such as fast-track designation and priority review, as well as accelerated approval based on qualifying evidence.

===Intellectual property===
Intellectual property protections for vaccines, and the technologies used in their development and production, include patents for vaccine compositions, components, manufacturing processes, and methods of use, as well as trade secrets and, to a lesser extent, trademarks.

Public funding of vaccine research can affect ownership and licensing of resulting inventions. In the United States, the Bayh–Dole Act permits certain recipients of federal research funding to retain patent rights while reserving specified rights for the federal government. These include authority, under certain conditions, to require licensing of federally funded inventions to other parties. Also, under 28 U.S.C. § 1498, the federal government may use patented inventions without obtaining the patent holder's permission, subject to an obligation to provide compensation. These provisions become relevant when patent rights affect the affordability or availability of vaccines.

===Financing, distribution, and access===
Vaccine law addresses the financing of vaccine research, procurement, distribution, and administration, including government purchasing programs, insurance coverage, and charitable initiatives. Public financing may support both the development of new vaccines and access to existing vaccines. Legal questions also arise concerning the authority of healthcare professionals to prescribe and administer vaccines, consent to vaccination, and access for populations dependent on institutional or governmental assistance.

The allocation of limited vaccine supplies raises additional questions concerning equality, public health priorities, and administrative decision-making. In a 2021 examination of COVID-19 vaccine distribution, legal scholars Kristen Underhill and Olatunde C. A. Johnson argued that allocation and appointment systems had contributed to racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic disparities in early vaccine access. They proposed regulatory measures to address such disparities, including more specific federal guidance, data reporting, and distribution arrangements designed to serve underserved communities. [ref: Vaccination Equity by Design, Yale Law Journal Forum]

Questions of vaccine equity extend beyond whether a vaccine is legally available or publicly funded. They include whether distribution policies, geographic availability, eligibility requirements, and administrative procedures allow different populations to obtain vaccination in practice.

===Vaccination mandates and exemptions===

Vaccination requirements may be imposed by governments as a condition of attending school, entering particular professions, serving in the military, or participating in other activities. Some laws require individuals to receive specified vaccines, while others direct institutions to offer or make vaccination available to certain populations.

In the United States, the United States Supreme Court upheld a compulsory smallpox vaccination law in Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905). In Zucht v. King (1922), the Court upheld the exclusion of unvaccinated students from schools. These decisions became important precedents concerning governmental authority to impose vaccination requirements for public health purposes. States exercise general police powers to protect public health, subject to constitutional limitations, while federal vaccination requirements must be supported by one or more of the powers granted to the federal government by the Constitution. Potential bases for federal action include the Spending Clause and Commerce Clause, although the use of these powers is subject to constitutional restrictions. Disputes over governmental vaccination requirements may therefore involve both individual rights and questions concerning the allocation of authority between federal and state governments. In Europe, the 2021 case of Vavřička and Others v. the Czech Republic, [ref: Vavřička and Others v. the Czech Republic, applications 47621/13, 3867/14, 73094/14, 19306/15, 19298/15, and 43883/15 (ECtHR April 8, 2021).] decided by the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), held that the nation of the Czech Republic did not violate the European Convention on Human Rights by imposing a vaccination mandate on children in that country. [ref: European Court Backs Mandatory Vaccinations For Children, NPR] [ref: Op-Ed: "It’s about proportionality! Strasbourg clarifies human rights standards for compulsory vaccination programmes", EU Law Live]

The availability of exemptions from vaccination requirements differs among jurisdictions. Medical exemptions generally concern circumstances in which vaccination would be medically contraindicated or pose a particular risk to the recipient. Other common exemptions concern religious beliefs or nonreligious philosophical objections. Legal disputes have addressed whether exemptions are constitutionally required, whether a claimed belief qualifies under an exemption statute, who may certify an exemption, and whether exempt individuals may be excluded from certain settings during outbreaks.

===Employment and private vaccination requirements===
Private employers and other institutions may establish vaccination requirements independently of governmental vaccination mandates. These requirements raise legal questions concerning employment law, occupational safety and health, collective bargaining, and protections against discrimination.

In the United States, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration requires certain employers to offer hepatitis B vaccination to workers with occupational exposure to bloodborne pathogens. Employer vaccination policies may also be subject to the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, including requirements for reasonable accommodation in applicable circumstances. In unionized workplaces, vaccination policies have been held to implicate obligations under the National Labor Relations Act of 1935.

===Vaccine safety surveillance and adverse-event reporting===
Requirements for reporting and investigating adverse events occurring after vaccination forms part of the practice of pharmacovigilance, the continuing monitoring of medical products after authorization. The World Health Organization uses the term adverse event following immunization (AEFI) to describe events occurring after vaccination, which may result from the vaccine itself, defects in its manufacture, errors in administration, or causes unrelated to vaccination. [ref: Adverse events following immunization (AEFI) reporting form, Public Health Agency of Canada] An adverse-event report does not necessarily establish that vaccination caused the reported condition. [ref: VAERS Overview, U.S. Food and Drug Administration] National legal systems vary in their adverse-event reporting requirements. Some countries have reporting systems specifically designed for vaccines, while others incorporate vaccine-related events into broader systems for reporting adverse reactions to medical products.

In the United States, the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), jointly administered by the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, collects reports of medical events occurring after vaccination. Healthcare providers and vaccine manufacturers are legally required to report certain events, while patients and other individuals may submit reports voluntarily. [ref: About the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] VAERS is a passive surveillance system intended to identify possible safety signals requiring further investigation. Because reports may be incomplete, unverified, or coincidental, the reports alone cannot establish causation or reliably measure the incidence of vaccine injuries.

Other surveillance methods supplement passive reporting. The Vaccine Safety Datalink, for example, uses healthcare data to investigate possible associations between vaccination and subsequent medical conditions. Findings from vaccine safety surveillance may lead regulators to require further studies, revise product labeling, issue safety communications, or take other regulatory action. The distinction between an event reported after vaccination and an injury legally attributable to vaccination is also relevant to vaccine injury compensation. Compensation programs may establish separate requirements for proving causation, including presumptions applicable to specified injuries, which differ from the standards used to report suspected adverse events.

===Vaccine injury liability and compensation===

In very rare instances, vaccination may cause injury, and legal systems differ in how claims of vaccine-related injury are resolved. Ordinarily, such claims are governed by product liability, medical malpractice, or other principles of tort law. In some jurisdictions, however, no-fault compensation programs have been established, which generally provide compensation for qualifying vaccine injuries without requiring claimants to prove negligence by manufacturers or healthcare providers. [ref: Global landscape analysis of no-fault compensation programmes for vaccine injuries: A review and survey of implementing countries, PLOS ONE]

In the United States, Congress established the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (NVICP) through the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986. The legislation responded to concerns that vaccine-related litigation threatened vaccine supplies while ordinary tort litigation could be costly, lengthy, and uncertain for persons seeking compensation. Claims under the NVICP are filed in the United States Court of Federal Claims and initially decided by special masters. The program provides for compensation for certain injuries identified in a Vaccine Injury Table, while allowing claims involving other injuries upon the required showing of causation. The statutory scheme also places limitations on the circumstances under which claimants may pursue civil litigation against vaccine manufacturers or administrators.

No-fault compensation systems differ internationally. A comparative study published in 2020 identified differences among existing programs in eligibility, funding, decision-making procedures, standards for establishing causation, and the relationship between compensation claims and ordinary civil litigation. Separate legal regimes may govern vaccines used during declared public health emergencies. In the United States, the Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness Act authorizes liability protections for designated medical countermeasures, including qualifying vaccines, their manufacturers, distributors, and administrators. The Act also provides a limited exception to immunity for specified willful misconduct and establishes the Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program as a separate mechanism for compensating qualifying injuries. This program differs from the NVICP in its statutory basis, coverage, eligibility requirements, and available benefits.

===Anti-vaccine activity and legal responses===

Opposition to vaccination has generated legal disputes concerning the authority of governments and private institutions to require vaccination, the availability and application of exemptions, and the regulation of vaccines. Opponents of vaccination have challenged laws and administrative actions on constitutional, statutory, and procedural grounds, including claims involving individual liberty, religious freedom, and the limits of governmental authority. The legal treatment of challenges to vaccination requirements depends in part on the source of the requirement. Challenges to governmental mandates may involve constitutional or other protections, and questions regarding the authority delegated to public officials, while disputes over private vaccination policies may concern employment discrimination, collective bargaining agreements, or the interpretation of institutional rules. Courts have distinguished challenges to the general validity of vaccination requirements from claims that particular requirements were imposed without sufficient legal authority or that an available exemption was improperly denied.

Legal responses to vaccine misinformation raise separate questions involving freedom of speech, consumer protection, and the professional regulation of healthcare providers. The regulation of false or misleading vaccine-related statements may depend on whether the statements constitute ordinary political expression, commercial advertising, or professional conduct. Disputes have also concerned government communications promoting vaccination and the moderation of vaccine-related content by private online platforms. Conduct associated with opposition to vaccination may also give rise to civil or criminal liability independently of the expression of anti-vaccination views. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the falsification of vaccination cards and immunization records led to criminal investigations and prosecutions in several countries. Other controversies have involved fraudulent exemption documentation and alleged violations of legal duties concerning the prevention of infectious disease.

===International and comparative vaccine law===
Vaccine research, manufacturing, distribution, and public health programs frequently cross national borders. International legal issues include the importation and regulation of vaccines, intellectual property rights, access to vaccine supplies, international travel requirements, and the coordination of vaccination programs by governments and international organizations. The World Health Organization, UNICEF, and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance participate in international efforts concerning vaccination and vaccine access. International regulatory cooperation also includes arrangements intended to harmonize pharmaceutical manufacturing and inspection standards. However, decisions about vaccine approval, vaccination requirements, and compensation for injuries are generally made under national or subnational legal systems. The vaccination laws of different countries also vary considerably, with some jurisdictions imposing extensive childhood vaccination requirements, and others relying more heavily on recommendations, incentives, or cultural and traditional support for vaccination. National approaches also differ with respect to the availability of medical and religious exemptions, the public financing of vaccination, adverse-event reporting, and compensation for vaccine injuries.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the COVAX initiative established multinational arrangements for vaccine procurement and distribution, including an international mechanism for compensating certain asserted vaccine injuries. The COVAX No-Fault Compensation Program was established to provide lump-sum compensation for qualifying serious adverse events attributed to COVID-19 vaccines supplied through COVAX and administered in economies eligible for support under the Gavi COVAX Advance Market Commitment. The program provided an international alternative to seeking compensation through national legal systems, subject to its eligibility requirements. [ref: Program Protocol, COVAX No-Fault Compensation Program for AMC Eligible Economies] COVAX officially closed on December 31, 2023, after delivering nearly two billion doses of COVID-19 vaccines to 146 economies. [ref: COVAX officially closes, The Lancet Infectious Diseases] [ref: COVAX Initiative Ending After 2 Billion COVID Vaccines Delivered, Respiratory Therapy] Participating organizations estimated that the vaccines distributed through COVAX had averted approximately 2.7 million deaths in lower-income participating economies, contributing to the broader worldwide reduction in COVID-19 mortality attributable to vaccination. [ref: COVID-19 vaccinations shift to regular immunization as COVAX draws to a close, World Health Organization] Following the closure of COVAX, eligible lower-income economies continued to have access to COVID-19 vaccines and delivery support through regular programs administered by Gavi.

==History and literature==
Although laws governing vaccination have existed nearly since the advent of vaccines in the 18th century, the field of vaccine law was not well-recognized as a separate field until the 2000s. A 2007 article in the Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics, titled "Vaccine Law 101", by Eric Hargan, Daniel O'Brien, Susan Sherman, and Georges Benjamin, examined the federal and state legal frameworks governing vaccine research, licensing, manufacturing, procurement, distribution, administration, and liability. Abramson and Ransom have described the field as comprising distinct areas of legal practice that can be organized around the successive stages of vaccine development and use. They identify regulation, intellectual property, public health policy, vaccine access and equity, vaccination mandates, injury compensation, and legal responses to misinformation as interconnected subjects within the field.

In 2018, the first comprehensive legal treatise in the field, Vaccine, Vaccination, and Immunization Law, was co-published by the Book Division of Bloomberg Law and the American Health Law Association, [ref: Brian Dean Abramson '05 authors Vaccine, Vaccination, and Immunization Law, Florida International University College of Law] [ref: FIU Law: Brian Dean Abramson] co-authored by Brian Dean Abramson with John R. Thomas and Peter O. Safir. [ref: Vaccine, Vaccination, and Immunization Law, Georgetown University Law Library] [ref: Is Biden's COVID-19 vaccine mandate a law? What happens to those who don't get the shot?, USA Today] The treatise was "the first to comprehensively cover all aspects of vaccine law". [ref: GW Spring 2019 Class Notes: Brian Dean Abramson, LLM '09, GW Magazine]

A 2020 Congressional Research Service report examined legal issues in COVID-19 vaccine development and deployment, organizing its analysis around vaccine testing and regulatory approval, intellectual property and access, governmental vaccination requirements, and liability and injury compensation. A second edition of the treatise, Vaccine, Vaccination, and Immunization Law, was published in 2022, additionally co-authored by Dorit Rubinstein Reiss. The second edition contained updated content covering COVID-19 vaccines, as well as "pandemic response and other pandemic-related materials; employer/ employee vaccination mandates; international vaccine law; and legal responses to anti-vaccine activism". [ref: GW Summer 2022 Class Notes: Brian Dean Abramson, LLM '09, GW Magazine] A third edition, with numerous additional authors, was published in 2025, and received a four-star rating from Doody's Reviews, also being placed on the Doody's Core Titles list in Health Policy for 2026, a designation given to works recommended by health-sciences specialists and librarians as core resources for professional and academic collections. [ref: Vaccine, Vaccination, and Immunization Law, 3rd Edition: Doody's Core Title (2026 Edition)]

In 2022, the first National Vaccine Law Conference was held at the Antonin Scalia Law School of George Mason University, in Northern Virginia, featuring panels and speakers addressing different areas of the field. [ref: From Mandates to Exemptions to Misinformation, Vaccine Law Conference Addresses Top Legal Issues, DC Bar] [ref: Conference Examines Historical and Contemporary Issues Around Vaccines, D.C. Bar]

data.title: Hickmanolobus nimorakiotakisi
data.text:
Hickmanolobus nimorakiotakisi is a species of spider in the family Orsolobidae. It is endemic to Queensland, Australia, and was described in 2011 from male specimens collected in rainforest at Lamington National Park.

==Taxonomy==
The species was described in 2011 by Barbara Baehr, Robert Raven and Wendy Hebron in a paper on the Orsolobidae collected during the IBISCA-Queensland Project, a survey of invertebrates along an altitudinal gradient in Lamington National Park. It is placed in the genus Hickmanolobus, which was established by Forster and Platnick in 1985, and is listed as an accepted species in the World Spider Catalog.

The holotype is a male collected at IBISCA site 1100C in Lamington National Park (about above sea level) on 26 October 2006 by C. Burwell using a pyrethrum knockdown; it is held in the Queensland Museum (registration number QM S86313). A second male, collected at Mount Asplenium in January 1993 by G. Monteith, was also examined.

===Etymology===
The specific epithet is a patronym in honour of Dr Bill Nimorakiotakis, then Deputy Director of the Australian Venom Research Unit at the University of Melbourne, whom the authors credit with supporting spider taxonomy "with great passion".

==Description==
Only the male is known. Photomicrographs of the male in dorsal, frontal, lateral and ventral views are published in the original description. [ref: Orsolobidae (Araneae) of the IBISCA-Queensland Project at Lamington National Park, Australia, Memoirs of the Queensland Museum – Nature] The holotype has a total length of, with the carapace long and wide, and the abdomen long and wide. The carapace is yellow-brown and the legs are yellow-brown. There are six well-developed eyes. The abdomen is purple, with five pale, inverted V-shaped chevrons along the midline. The male pedipalp has a pyriform (pear-shaped) bulb with a long, thin embolus.

The authors distinguished the species from Hickmanolobus mollipes of Tasmania, which it resembles, by its abdominal pattern of five inverted V-shaped chevrons (rather than five transverse bars) and by a more slender male palpal bulb.

==Distribution and habitat==
Hickmanolobus nimorakiotakisi is known only from Queensland. The holotype was collected in rainforest at Lamington National Park at about, and the second known specimen at Mount Asplenium at about. In the IBISCA-Queensland survey, all five orsolobid species recorded were collected only above about; the authors suggested that orsolobids could be useful for monitoring the effects of climate change on the park's fauna.

data.title: San Pedro Daijingū
data.text:
San Pedro Daijingū () was a Shinto shrine serving the Japanese American fishing community on Terminal Island in Los Angeles, California. Its Japanese name appears in the 1937 community history San Pidoro Dōhō Hattenroku. [ref: 第32回 「サンピドロ同胞発展録」― 日本の海岸線の旅の途中で①, Discover Nikkei]

== History ==
Shinkichi Miyoshi proposed establishing the shrine in 1930. A lease for its site at 226 Terminal Way was approved in March 1931, and a ceremony marking construction of its foundation took place on 6 December that year. In 1933, the organization incorporated in California under the name San Pedro Daijin-Gu. [ref: Terminal Island: Lost Communities on America's Edge, Angel City Press]

Following the forced removal of Terminal Island's Japanese American residents in 1942, the United States Navy demolished the shrine along with most of the settlement's buildings. [ref: Japanese American History at Terminal Island, Los Angeles Conservancy]

== Architecture ==
The shrine consisted of a small, single-room building in Japanese architectural design. A torii and two fox statues marked the entrance to the property. [ref: Fishermen Far from the Sea: Excavation of the Block 9 Mess Hall Japanese Garden, National Park Service]

== Legacy ==
The Terminal Island Japanese Memorial, dedicated in 2002, includes a torii recalling the community's former Shinto shrine. [ref: Terminal Island, Preserving California's Japantowns]

data.title: Liban Ahmed Hassan
data.text:
Liban Ahmed Hassan, also known as Liibaan Shuluq (), is a Somali politician and businessman who was elected president of Galmudug State on 22 October 2026. [ref: Somalia’s Galmudug elects new president and vice-president, Somalia Today] [ref: JSP candidate wins Galmudug presidential election with 72 votes, Hiiraan Online]

== Political career ==
Hassan was nominated by the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP) as its candidate for the Galmudug presidency in June 2026. His nomination followed the withdrawal from the race of the outgoing president, Ahmed Abdi Kariye. [ref: JSP Candidate Liban Hassan Receives Certificate to Contest Galmudug Presidential Election, Goobjoog English] [ref: ]

On 22 October 2026, members of the Galmudug State Assembly elected Hassan president in a vote held in Dhusamareb. [ref: ] He received 72 of the 89 votes cast, defeating Abdulkadir Abdullahi Diriye, who received 14 votes; three ballots were declared invalid. [ref: Liban Shuluq Rebukes Opposition as Galmudug Election Race Intensifies, WardheerNews] [ref: Liban Ahmed Hassan Elected Galmudug President in Landslide Win Against Opponents – Goobjoog English, en.goobjoog.com]

Hassan's election followed the September 2026 repeat parliamentary elections, in which the JSP won 67 of the assembly's 89 seats. The repeat election took place after Somalia's Supreme Court annulled the results of the parliamentary vote held in July over constitutional and procedural violations. [ref: JSP Galmudug Candidate Pledges Security and Reconciliation in Gaalkayo, Dawan Africa] [ref: Maxkamadda Sare oo laashay natiijadii doorashada Galmudug, Radio Muqdisho] [ref: Maxkamadda Sare oo go'aan kama dambeys kasoo saartay doorashadii Galmudug, Caasimada Online]

data.title: Neon (A2O Lite song)
data.text:
"Neon" is the debut single by the South Korean girl group A2O Lite. It was released by A2O Entertainment on October 13, 2026.

==Background and release==
In 2023, the South Korean record producer Lee Soo-man left SM Entertainment, the agency he founded in 1989 and built into one of South Korea's largest entertainment companies, where he pioneered the K-pop idol system. [ref: SM Founder Introduces Alien-themed Idols, Cutting-edge Technology in Return to K-pop, Korea JoongAng Daily] [ref: How Lee Soo-man's Idol System at SM Paved the Way for K-pop as We Know It, The Hankyoreh] The next year, he established A2O Entertainment, where he was joined by his longtime SM collaborator Yoo Young-jin, a record producer and vocal trainer. On October 8, 2026, A2O Entertainment launched official social media accounts for its first K-pop girl group, A2O Lite, announcing that they would be introduced at a showcase set to be held at the Korea International Exhibition Center in Goyang on October 12, broadcast by Mnet. [ref: Sports Kyunghyang] At the showcase, A2O Lite performed their debut single, "Neon", for the first time, before A2O Entertainment officially released it for digital download and streaming the following day.

==Composition==
Written and produced by Yoo and Dem Jointz, "Neon" is a dance-pop song. [ref: No Cut News]

==Live performances==
"Neon" intro was choreographed by the South Korean hip-hop dancer. [ref: Money Today]

data.title: The Once and Future World Order
data.text:
----

The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West is a 2025 book by international relations scholar Amitav Acharya,. [ref: ] published by Basic Books in April 2025. [ref: The Once and Future World Order, John Murray Press] The book explores the historical development of world order across different civilizations and regions, beginning with ancient Sumer and Egypt and extending through Persia, Greece, India, China, Rome, the Islamic world, Africa, the Americas, and Europe to the contemporary international system. [ref: The once and future world order: why global civilization will survive the decline of the West, Basic Books] The book examines the development of political ideas, institutions, and practices associated with relations among states and societies, including diplomacy, trade, political organization, war, and interstate cooperation, and concludes with a discussion of the changing international order and the implications of declining Western dominance.

== Contents ==
The book traces the development of different world orders and interactions among societies throughout history, before turning to the contemporary international system and its possible future.

The book starts by examining the different ideas and institutions commonly associated with the "Western" world order emerged in non-Western civilizations thousands of years before the rise of the West. These range from peace treaties and interstate cooperation to freedom of the seas and environmental protection. Acharya argues that these contributions have often been overlooked in the mainstream history.

The book examines how the dominance of the European perspective over the last 500 years has contributed to two forms of historical misrepresentation: the sin of commission and the sin of omission. The sin of commission is largely the misinterpretation or distortion of the achievements of non-Western cultures and civilizations. The sin of omission occurs when facts about them are overlooked. The book also considers the achievements and failures of both Western and non-Western civilizations. [ref: Review of the Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West, International Studies Review]

The book also explores three fears in the West today about the end of the American-led Western order: the fear of the rise of the "civilization states," the fear of the Chinese-built and Chinese-led order, and the fear of "chaos, violence, and conflict."

== Reception ==
Writing in The New York Times, historian Abhishek Kaicker reviewed the book together with historian William Dalrymple’s The Golden Road. He discussed the two works as attempts to reconsider conventional accounts of how the international order developed. [ref: Worried the World Is Falling Apart? That's OK. It's Happened Before., The New York Times] In The Christian Science Monitor, it appeared on the 10 best books of April 2025 [ref: 10 best books of April 2025 make a bouquet of great reads, The Christian Science Monitor] and Abhijnan Rej examined Acharya’s claim that the principles and institutions of political order arose across several civilizations rather than exclusively in the modern West. [ref: Democratic ideals and the rule of law have persisted across nations and eras, Christian Science Monitor]

The book was included in Foreign Policy’s The Most Anticipated Books of 2025. [ref: The Most Anticipated Books of 2025, Foreign Policy]

Academic reviews include International Studies Review [ref: Review of the Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West, International Studies Review] and Commonwealth & Comparative Politics [ref: The once and future world order: why global civilization will survive the decline of the West: by Amitav Acharya, New York, Basic Books, 2025, 464 pp., $32.50 (hardback), ISBN 9781541604148, Commonwealth & Comparative Politics]

The Aztecs finished the 2025–26 season 27–6, 19–1 in Mountain West play, to win the regular season title. As a No. 1 seed in the Mountain West tournament, they lost in the quarterfinals to Air Force. This is San Diego State's last season as members of the Mountain West Conference, as they will join the newly reformed Pac-12 Conference, effective July 1, 2026. [ref: Pac-12 adding four Mountain West schools Boise State, San Diego State, Fresno State, Colorado State, USA Today]

data.title: Bayou Boy
data.text:
Bayou Boy is a 1971 American television adventure film produced by Walt Disney Productions. [ref: The Wonderful World of Disney Television, Hyperion Books] [ref: Disney A to Z: The Official Encyclopedia: Third Edition, Disney Editions] Directed by Gary Nelson and written by Louis Pelletier, it originally aired in two parts on NBC's The Wonderful World of Disney on February 7 and February 14, 1971. [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23] [ref: Louis Pelletier; Wrote 500 Episodes of 'FBI' Radio Series, Los Angeles Times] The film was rebroadcast by NBC in 1979 under the title The Boy from Dead Man's Bayou. [ref: The Magical World of Disney Season 17 Episodes, TV Guide] [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23]

== Plot ==
Jeannot Boudreau is determined to locate a sunken silver church bell that is lost in Dead Man’s Bayou in the Louisiana backwoods, after a hurricane destroyed the church it was located in. [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23] He wants to retrieve it to honor his father, who helped cast the bell. [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] To find the bell he must contend with a giant alligator who patrols the bayou. [ref: The Magical World of Disney Season 17 Episodes, TV Guide]

== Cast ==

* Mitch Vogel as Jeannot Boudreau
* Mike Lookinland as Claude
* Vito Scotti as Mr. Bob
* Paul Fix as Captain Pierre
* John McIntire as Father Boudreau
* Jeanette Nolan as Tante Louise
* Marcel Hillaire as M. Verret
* Frank Silvera as Uncle Maxim
* Percy Rodrigues as Charbot
* Michael Ontkean as Alcide
* Brad David as Phillipe

== Production ==
Co-stars John McIntire and Jeanette Nolan were married in real life, and often appeared in the same shows and movies. [ref: Husband, Wife Acting Team in 'Bayou Boy', Idaho State Journal] [ref: Behind the Scenes, The Daily Herald]

Filming took place at Pine Island Point at Caddo Lake, on the Texas-Louisiana border near Shreveport. [ref: Disney filming at Caddo Lake, Shreveport Times] [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] [ref: Louisiana to be Spotlighted in Disney TV Series on NBC, The Marksville Weekly News] [ref: Page 28, The Jeffersonian] In one instance when a stuntman failed to show up, a local highway patrolman was asked to fall 25 feet in a lake. [ref: City Beat, The Mexia Daily News] After filming Governor Preston Smith made the cast of the film honorary Texas citizens. [ref: 'Bayou Boy' Cast Honorary Texas Citizens, The Salt Lake Tribune]

A $12,000 replica of the bayou was constructed at Disney Studio in Burbank for the alligator fight scene. [ref: Bayou Boy, Chronique Disney] [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] [ref: TV Scout, The Index-Journal]

== Music ==
The musical score was composed by Buddy Baker. [ref: Norman "Buddy" Baker Collection, NYU Special Collections Finding Aids] The opening title song, "Bayou Boy", was written by Terry Gilkyson and performed by his daughter Lisa. [ref: Dynamite, cowboy boots, horse falls, and toupee hijinks with Steve McQueen's costar Mitch Vogel, Medium]

== Reception ==
The Robesonian called it an “exciting two-part action adventure drama,” [ref: Percy Rodrigues Fights Alligator on 'Disney World' Bayou Drama, The Robesonian] and The Oneonta Star felt that it was “suitable family fare.” [ref: Top TV, The Oneonta Star] The Daily Herald referred to it as a “mystery adventure,” [ref: Mitch Vogel in Title Role for Disney's 'Bayou Boy', The Daily Herald] and the Albuquerque Journal wrote that “kids should eat it up.” [ref: TV Key Previews, Albuquerque Journal]

data.title: Ruhr miner's strike (1889)
data.text:
----

The Ruhr miner's strike of 1889 was one of the largest labor strikes in German history, and the largest at the time. [ref: Bismarck Urpreuße und Reichsgründer]. It took place in the highly industrial Ruhr area of the German Empire as a consequence of the 1873 Stock Market Crash, poor working conditions and the anti-socialist laws imposed by Chancellor Otto Von Bismarck [ref: Deutsche Gesellschaftsgeschichte, München: C.H. Beck]. It saw over 100.000 people participating in the strike and it was active during the months of April and May [ref: This Day in Labor History: May 14, 1889, Lawyers, Guns & Money] and it led to the creation of the Union of Miners of Germany (which would later be called the "Old Union" and is the modern day IG Bergbau, Chemie, Energie)

== Background ==
The strike originated as a result of the poor working and living conditions of working class families in this era. Most of them, like in many other industrialized regions of Europe, lived with their families in closed, cramped, and poorly maintained apartments with costly rent. Conditions in the mines as well were rather miserable, with barely any safety regulations in place and over 10 hour work shifts, alongside minimal pay.

Because of this, many workers in different areas of the empire started supporting workers movements, such as the Free Trade Unions or the SDAP (Sozialdemokratische Arbeiterpartei Deutschlands, which later turned into the modern-day SPD). However, with the "Bismarckian" anti-socialist laws passed by the Reichstag in 1878, many social democrat politicians and supporters were repressed or prosecuted.

Workers in the Ruhr organized a strike of about 21,000 miners in 1872. Although this was largely unsuccessful and it led to the workers subsequently organizing better, albeit initially without an official union or clear leadership.

Mining workers wanted wage increases like that of the mining entrepreneurs. The aim was a 15-20% wage increase, no more extra shifts, a reduction to 8 hours of working time, including entrances and exits, and, overall, better working conditions. [ref: Chronologie der deutschen Gewerkschaftsbewegung von 1794 bis 1918 / von Dieter Schuster. - Teil: Chronologie 1888-1889, library.fes.de]

== Strike ==

The strike began on the 25th of April in Bochum. At first, the strikers managed to get an 8.2% increase in pay and a short period of calm went onwards. However, the strikes quickly resumed on the 4th of May after police repression had started and about 80 union miners were fired from their positions and a full-on General Strike had begun, with numerous other workforces in Herne, Dortmund, Hörde, Witten, Oberhausen, Essen, and Recklinghausen deciding to join the strike. [ref: ]

As the strike continued, the two sides became increasingly aggressive. In order to “protect” their facilities and the miners that were willing to work, many mines requested police or even military protection, and the tense atmosphere of the strikes erupted into violence and the use of weapons against the miners, which, on May 12th, resulted in several workers being shot and a substantial increase in police brutality.

After the incident, on May 14, the strike committee decided to send a delegation to Kaiser Wilhelm II. The delegates (Friedrich Bunte, August Siegel and Ludwig Schröder) were received in Berlin by the emperor, whom they intended to appeal to as the supreme mining authority. [ref: Colorado Historic Newspaper Collection] Although the emperor criticized the strike, he did agree to have the grievances officially investigated. The talks with the emperor brought the strikers a great deal of attention, particularly among the middle classes of the empire, who tended to be skeptical on socialist ideas.

Through the mediation of Friedrich Hammacher, a member of the Reichstag, a protocol was finalized the following day, establishing an 8 hour workday for the miners, including a half-hour each for entering and exiting the mine. In addition, overtime shifts were to be worked on after prior agreement between the mine administration and the workers’ unions. When the association signaled a willingness to accommodate the miners’ interests, the strike initially subsided. However, they started once again on May 21st as the mining companies failed to comply with, and ignored, the agreements made in Berlin, and even introduced blacklists containing the names of many of striking miners in to make it impossible for them to find employment in the mining industry. In early June 1889, the strikes lost force and came to an end without any immediate lasting gains for the workers. [ref: Sozialpolitik—Description and Documentation: The Quest for Clarity, German History]
[[File:German soldiers coal strikers.png|thumb|Drawing of German mounted troops attacking strikers.]]
The strike triggered the founding of the Union of Miners of Germany in the Rhineland and Westphalia, [ref: Historisches Bochumer Ehrenfeld - Geschichte des alten Verbandes, www.historisches-ehrenfeld.de] the starting point for the breakthrough of the trade union movement in the Ruhr mining industry.

== Consequences ==
The strike and its reception by the general public would indirectly clear the path for progressive labor laws to be passed in the empire, such as the Workers' Protection Act of June 1st, 1891. In addition, regulations on the protection of women, protection against child labor, restrictions to night work and a reduction of the 10-hour work day and were also implemented partly thanks to this strike and the movement that led to it. It also contained provisions for a 24-hour Sunday rest for all workers in factories, workshops, mines, construction sites and shipyards.

This strike also massively contributed to the popularizing of leftist ideas in Germany and the radicalization of said ideas and groups, such as the SPD which was already in a path of changing its political approach, eliminating any sort of of compromise or collaboration with the federal government in Berlin [ref: ]

data.title: Native Officer Ali
data.text:
----

Native Officer Ali D.C.M, ADC, was a native officer originally from Katsina in His Majesty King Edward the Seventh's Hausas [ref: ARIBA ALI V. ALHAJI MAMA ALI, judy.legal] who served in the British colonial forces in West Africa and the recognized Head of the Hausa community (Sarkin Hausawa) the year 1907 in the British colony, Gold Coast. [ref: The Power of Space in the Evolution of an Accra Zongo, Ethnohistory] [ref: Native Tribunals of the Akras (Continued from p. 330), Journal of the Royal African Society] [ref: The Muslim Association Party: A Test of Religious Politics in Ghana, Transactions of the Historical Society of Ghana]

== Early life and military career ==
Native Officer Ali enlisted in a military unit established by governor Sir John Hawley, known as "Glover Hausas or the "Hausa Force" in the year 1863 during a period of British expansion in West Africa and he subsequently served in several British military expeditions in West Africa. [ref: The Slaves of Salaga, The Journal of African History] He served as a Sargeant Major commanding troops at Prasu during the third Anglo-Ashanti War of 1873-1874. He and other officer were sent to the United Kingdom for further training in 1875-1876.

Ali later took part in several military campaigns and expeditions including one where he and 60 Hausa troops landed on an Island and searched it from end to end [ref: A History of the Gold Coast and Ashanti from the Earliest Times to the Commencement of the Twentieth Century, John Murray] He received a medal for his service during the Awuna expedition of 1885 and Denkyira expedition in 1890. [ref: Danborno, shardowfamilyweb] He served as an aide-de-camp to Gold Coast governors including Sir Matthew Nathan, Sir John Pickersgill Rodger and Frederick Mitchell Hodgson. He continued his military career into the early twentieth century, serving with the 2nd Gold Coast Regiment before retiring.

== Retirement and leadership ==
After Native Officer Ali retired from the service of Government in June 1902, and he was receiving a pension of £48 per anum. [ref: The Muslim Community in Accra (An Historical Survey), University of Ghana] Ali settled in Accra Ussher Town, Horse Road where he built his Zongo quarters, this location was where the current Accra General Post Office sits. [ref: A History of Accra's "Zongos": Heterogeneity and Social Change, Indiana University]

In 1907, the Hausa Community led by High Priest Mama Fulata Bornu, who was then the Chief Imam, together with Mallam Abubakare (Priest), Mallam DanJimba (Priest), Native Officer Harri Zanuah of (The Gold Coast Regiment) and Mallam Bukare (Priest) petitioned through the Colonial Government to officially recognize Native Officer Ali as Head Chief of the Hausa Community (Sarkin Hausawa), they wrote,

"As Hausas we have so far been under a great disadvantage in having no head chief, and whenever it has been necessary to wait upon the Government, it has always been difficult to obtain a spokesman.

"We are writing solely on behalf of the Hausas residing here. We have nothing to do with the Yorubas or other tribes who have their own head-chiefs."

On October 26, the Hausa community's request was approved by Governor John Pickersgill Rodger through Sir William Charles Fleming Robertson secretary for native affairs. [ref: Letter from the Acting Secretary for Native Affairs to Mama Fulata Bornu, Mallam Abubakare, Malam DanJimba, Native Officer Harri Zenuah, and Malam Bukare, Public Records and Archives Administration Department (PRAAD)] Native Officer Ali held the position until his death on 2nd day of February 1908. [ref: Migrant Chiefs in Stranger Communities in Ghana: The Challenge of their Inclusion into the Houses of Chiefs, Contemporary Journal of African Studies]

== Death and legacy ==
Native Officer Ali died on February 2, 1908. [ref: Gold Coast Leader] Remained Native Officer in the Gold Coast Regiment of the West African Frontier Force (also known as Native Officer in Chief of the Gold Coast Hausas) and Head Chief (or headman) of the Hausa community in Accra until his death.

He is regarded as one of the three principal early migrant leaders in the Gold Coast, alongside Mallam Naino (Nenu) and Alhaji Brimah

After his death, his name and ceremonial titles lived on in the person of his son by a Fanti woman from Elmina, Alhaji Mohammed Ali.

data.title: Spring Break Fiji
data.text:
----

Spring Break Fiji is an annual music festival and retreat organised by New Zealand tourism company TourismHQ. [ref: Fiji Spring Break holiday turns into nightmare for Kiwis, The New Zealand Herald] The five-day event is held at Beachcomber Island in Fiji's Mamanuca Islands. [ref: Spring Break Fiji 2.0 – a revamped rite of passage for first-time travellers by Tourism HQ, NZBusiness] [ref: SpringBreak: The exclusive island get-away you don't want to miss out on, Remix Magazine] It was founded by Rich Henry in 2013. [ref: Max Key: Party Animal, [[Metro (magazine)]

== History ==
TourismHQ earlier ran a Fiji trip branded Blue Sky. Spring Break Fiji was established in 2013 as a packaged festival holiday aimed mainly at young travellers from New Zealand and Australia. [ref: Young Kiwis get Spring Break experience, The New Zealand Herald] Coverage has described exclusive use of Beachcomber Island, yacht transfers, island activities, and DJ performances as part of the itinerary.

In 2015, Max Key (son of then New Zealand prime minister John Key) performed at the event as part of the DJ duo Troskey with Joshua Troskie. [ref: What on earth is Spring Break?, [[Stuff (website)] During that edition a fire destroyed one bure at Beachcomber Island Resort; guests were evacuated and no injuries were reported. [ref: PM's son among Kiwi partygoers forced off Beachcomber Island by blaze, The New Zealand Herald] [ref: Investigations continue into Beachcomber Resort bure fire, FijiVillage] [ref: PM's son Max Key caught up in Fiji party island blaze, [[Stuff (website)] Organisers and resort staff said the fire was contained to a single building.

The January 2023 edition drew criticism after guests reported power outages, drinking-water shortages, and related problems. [ref: 'Holiday from Hell': Spring Break Fiji organisers could face legal action, Consumer NZ says, [[Stuff (website)] Former employees described the event as being "poorly organised". [ref: ] Organisers apologised and attributed difficulties to rough weather and a resort generator failure, and advised guests to contact their insurers. Consumer NZ said organisers could face legal action under consumer law.

In 2024 Beachcomber Island Resort was acquired by interests associated with Vision Hotels / the Deeley brothers, who announced a FJ$10 million renovation and expansion of the resort. [ref: Deeley brothers commit $10m to transform Beachcomber Resort, FBC News] [ref: Beachcomber Island Resort to undergo $10M renovation after purchase by Deeley brothers, FijiVillage]

data.title: Robert Perks
data.text:
Robert Perks (Dec 1919 – July 2005) was a New Zealand music educator, conductor, composer and multi-instrumentalist. He founded the Christchurch School of Instrumental Music in 1955 and served as its musical director until 1975. [ref: Let the Children Play: A 25-Year History of the Christchurch School of Instrumental Music, University of Canterbury]. Perks was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire for services to music education in 1985. [ref: Award to Musician, The Press]

== Biography ==

=== Early life ===
Robert Perks was born in St Clair Dunedin, New Zealand, in December 1919 to John Alfred Perks (a newsagent or delivery agent for the "Evening Star") [ref: Many high notes in a lifetime of music, The Christchurch Star] and Mabel May Perks. He attended St Clair Primary School from 1925 to 1931. He entered Dunedin Technical High School (also known as King Edward Technical College) in 1932.

While at the Dunedin Technical College, he came under the influence of T Vernon Griffiths, and credits his musical career to Professor Griffiths: "He started me on my musical career. What a great man he is. I owe him more than any other man." Griffiths paid for his advanced piano tuition out of his "own meagre pay". According to Perks, it was the intervention of Griffiths and Perks' headmaster, that meant the young Perks did not become a butcher and was able to pursue a music education career.

He married Myrtle Wood of Roxburgh in 1942.

=== Education ===
In 1938, Perks began studying at Dunedin Teachers' Training College, specialising in music and received a University of Otago music bursary. He completed a Bachelor of Music degree in 1941. [ref: NZ Composers' Festival - Centennial Composition of Robert Perks, The Press]

Perks enlisted in the Army in 1941 and later transferred to the Navy and was able to continue his studies while a Petty Officer radio mechanic in the Navy. While at the Devonport Base he became the official organist and took lessons from the Auckland Cathedral organist, Edgar Randal. He gained the Licentiate of the Royal Schools of Music diploma in organ in 1944. [ref: Music Appointment, The Press]

=== Career ===
In 1945, Perks became music master at Christchurch Technical College, where he worked for eight years before joining Christchurch Teachers’ College in 1955. [ref: Pupils 9 Orchestras To Give Concert, The Press] He had broad experience teaching young people and wrote two school music publications that were widely used in New Zealand schools. In 1955, Perks began an experimental instrumental scheme for 50 primary-school pupils under a subcommittee of the Primary Schools’ Music Festival Association. The scheme aimed to provide affordable group tuition and practical experience of orchestral playing. This grew quickly and became the Christchurch School of Instrumental Music (later the Christchurch School of Music | Te Kura Puoro), which regularly celebrates its founding by Robert Perks in 1955. This work provided music education to over a thousand students each year while he was the Music Director of that organisation from 1955 to 1975.

Perks was also an award-winning composer, winning the composition competition run by the Canterbury Centennial Association in 1950 [ref: Awards in NZ Composers' Contest, Greymouth Evening Star], among other awards. An Allegro was performed by the Christchurch Chamber Music Players in 1952 [ref: Works by NZ Composers - Concert in the Civic Theatre, The Press]. He regularly composed music for young musicians to play.

== Published works ==
Robert perks wrote a series of books for music teachers, learners and families. They were published by local publishers AH and AW Reed. The series was called Music in School, A modern approach in the classroom. Book 1 was the Teacher's Manual, book 2 was Short Score, and book 3 was The Main Progression (for beginners) Supplementary Parts. The series included scores for playing in groups for different instruments including recorder (descant), cello, bass, B Flat clarinet, percussion, melodica and autoharp, chime bar, and guitar. He also wrote Music Making in School and Home, also published by Reeds in 1965. [ref: Music Making in School and Home, A H Reed & A W Reed]

As an academic, Perks published a few accounts of his musical education endeavours, or as he termed them, "experiments". In the London journal, "Music in Education" he described his work in mass music education as, "an interesting New Zealand experiment." [ref: An interesting New Zealand experiment, Music in Education] Similarly, a year earlier he published "Christchurch music experiment: schools instrumental scheme" in the New Zealand journal "National Education". [ref: Christchurch music experiment: schools instrumental scheme, National Education]

== Honours and legacy ==
Perks was awarded life membership of the Christchurch School of Instrumental Music in 1978. At the time the newspaper, The Press, commented, "The success attending Mr Perks' efforts has aroused interest abroad, and the numbers of players in orchestras from the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra downwards, who began their training in the C.S.I.M. orchestras, is sufficient tribute to the worth of the training. They and the many hundreds of others who owe their present love of music and attendant broadening of their experiences to Mr Perks and his work must be a constant satisfaction to him in his retirement." [ref: Fine Progress shows in young orchestras, The Press]

He continued to conduct former pupils at the school’s 25th-anniversary celebrations in 1980, conducting the CSIM Alumnae Orchestra. [ref: Spirited concert by C.S.I.M. orchestras, The Press] He was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire for services to music education in the 1985, and his legacy is recognised through the Robert Perks Scholarship. [ref: Christchurch School of Instrumental Music [advertisement for donations to the Robert Perks scholarship]] He died in July 2005, aged 85. [ref: Music Educator Dies at 85, The Press]

data.title: Roger Humberston
data.text:
Roger Humberston () was an English politician. He sat as MP for Leicester in January 1397. [ref: HUMBERSTON, Roger, of Leicester., History of Parliament Online]

He was the son of the merchant William Humberston Sr. of Leicester and the brother of MP William Humberston. Before September 1392, he married Margaret, the daughter of John Tansley, and widow of John Samon of Nottingham and they had one daughter.

He also served as Mayor of Leicester from Michaelmas 1398 till 1399, and 1410 till 1411.

The Online Media Practitioners Association of Nigeria (OMPAN) is a Nigerian association of digital news practitioners founded in March 2018 to bring together bloggers, online publishers and other digital media practitioners. [ref: OMPAN inaugurates new National Executives as two Cross Riverians make list, The Daily News NG] [ref: The Importance of the Online Media Practitioners of 2018 Convention, PUO REPORTS] [ref: Owerri2018: Online Media Practitioners Nat. Convention Holds 30–31st March 2018, PUO REPORTS] [ref: Imo State Govt Expresses Willingness to Support Online Media Convention (Owerri2018), PUO REPORTS] [ref: Imo State Govt Approves World Class Imo Trade & Investment Centre for 2018 Online Media Practitioners Convention, PUO REPORTS]

The association promotes professional ethics, responsible online publishing and cooperation among practitioners. [ref: Online Media Practitioners get new Excos, as Convention Ends in Owerri, OtownGist Media] [ref: PRESS RELEASE: ONLINE MEDIA PRACTITIONERS ASSOCIATION OF NIGERIA (OMPAN) GETS NEW NATIONAL EXECUTIVE COUNCIL, DòtunRoy.com] [ref: OMPAN IN BRIEF, Imo Ompan] [ref: Enough of Intimidation and Harassment of Our Members, Online Media Practitioners Warns, PUO REPORTS] [ref: Enebeli Cautions Online Publishers Against Unverified News Says Its Anti-People, Anti-Development, Asaba Metro News]

In 30-31st of March 2018, the new media association held its first national convention in Owerri, Imo State where members appointed a National Executive Council to oversee its affairs. [ref: Online Media Practitioners' Association Berths in Oyo, MegaIcon Magazine] [ref: OMPAN Anchors in Cross River, Holds First Meeting with New Excos Appointed, The Daily News Nigeria] [ref: New Media Practitioners Close Ranks on Media Round Table, Chat New Course, The City Pulse News]

OMPAN operates within Nigeria's wider online media sector, which includes other professional organisations representing online publishers and journalists. data.title: Cyclone Arnab
data.text:
----

Cyclone Arnab is a currently active cyclone in the Bay of Bengal threatening South India. The eighth depression and first cyclone of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season, Arnab originated from a low-pressure area in the eastern Bay of Bengal that had been meandering for several days.

==Meteorological history==

On 20 October, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) began to monitor the Bay of Bengal for a low-pressure area that was likely to develop within 24 hours. [ref: REGIONAL SPECIALISED METEOROLOGICAL CENTRE -TROPICAL CYCLONES, NEW DELHI TROPICAL WEATHER OUTLOOK, India Meteorological Department] Three days later, a low-pressure area formed over the eastcentral–southcentral Bay of Bengal under the influence of an upper-level cyclonic circulation. Favourable conditions prevailed over the central Bay of Bengal, with the Madden–Julian oscillation enhancing thunderstorm activity. Sea surface temperatures were, while wind shear was moderate. [ref: REGIONAL SPECIALISED METEOROLOGICAL CENTRE -TROPICAL CYCLONES, NEW DELHI TROPICAL WEATHER OUTLOOK, India Meteorological Department] By 12:00 UTC on 24 October, the well-marked low pressure area concentrated into a depression over the central Bay of Bengal. [ref: REGIONAL SPECIALISED METEOROLOGICAL CENTRE -TROPICAL CYCLONES, NEW DELHI SPECIAL TROPICAL WEATHER OUTLOOK, India Meteorological Department] [ref: REGIONAL SPECIALISED METEOROLOGICAL CENTRE -TROPICAL CYCLONES, NEW DELHI SPECIAL TROPICAL WEATHER OUTLOOK, India Meteorological Department] The system, marked Invest 98B by the United States Navy's Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC), consisted of a partially exposed but consolidating low-level circulation and developing banding features to the south and east of the depression’s vicinity as a TCFA was issued at 11:00 UTC. On 25 October at 09:30 UTC, the IMD reported that the system intensified to a deep depression. [ref: REGIONAL SPECIALISED METEOROLOGICAL CENTRE -TROPICAL CYCLONES, NEW DELHI SPECIAL TROPICAL WEATHER OUTLOOK, India Meteorological Department] The next day, the system strengthened into a cyclonic storm and was assigned the name Arnab. [ref: NATIONAL BULLETIN NO. 8 (BOB/08/2026), rsmcnewdelhi.imd.gov.in] 12 hours later, Arnab intensified into a severe cyclonic storm. [ref: NATIONAL BULLETIN NO. 12 (BOB/08/2026), mausam.imd.gov.in] Six hours later, Arnab intensified into a very severe cyclonic storm. [ref: NATIONAL BULLETIN NO. 14 (BOB/08/2026), mausam.imd.gov.in]

==Preparations==
===India===
====Andhra Pradesh====
The IMD declared red alerts in seven districts in Andhra Pradesh on 26 October. 15 teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) were mobilised in Andhra Pradesh while ₹27 crore in relief was released by the state. Schools in 10 districts were closed. [ref: Schools closed tomorrow in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha amid Cyclone Arnab, India Today] By 27 October, at least 89,000 people were evacuated in Andhra Pradesh. [ref: India evacuates tens of thousands as Cyclone Arnab nears eastern coast in Andhra Pradesh state, Associated Press]

Andhra Pradesh called on boats to return from sea and identified 570,000 people as vulnerable in preparation for evacuations. [ref: India to evacuate thousands as Cyclone Arnab nears eastern coast, Reuters] By 26 October, Andhra Pradesh officials stated that over 30,000 fishing boats had returned to harbour. [ref: ] The Chintoor Integrated Tribal Development Officer directed the suspension of tourism boat operations to the Papikonda hills in Godavari Valley. [ref: Cyclone Arnab: Over 4,800 fishing vessels return safely to Kakinada coast, The Hindu] Rail service on 53 routes in southern India were suspended on 27–28 October, [ref: Thousands evacuate India's eastern coast ahead of Cyclone Arnab, Reuters] including the Godavari Express, Gowthami Express, Visakha Express, Falaknuma Express, Narasapur Express, and the Garib Rath Express. 21 flights were cancelled at Vijayawada Airport and Visakhapatnam Airport, with cancellations also occurring at Gannavaram Airport. [ref: Cyclone Arnab Live: Schools shut, evacuations begin in Andhra, Odisha ahead of landfall, India Today]

====Odisha====
The government of Odisha declared that over 1,700 shelters were prepared in the state's southern districts. Eight NDRF teams and 40 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force teams were mobilised. [ref: A.P., Odisha on alert as cyclone ‘Arnab’ nears land, The Hindu] The closure of schools and colleges in five districts was announced for 28–29 October.

==Impacts==
===India===
====Andhra Pradesh====
As Arnab approached landfall, trees were uprooted in Visakhapatnam. A man died after touching a fallen live wire in Visakhapatnam. [ref: ]

====Elsewhere====
Persistent rainfall in the Nilgiris district in Tamil Nadu caused as many as 69 landslips on 25 and 26 October, damaging power lines, revetments, and 16 huts. [ref: Nilgiris district hit by 62 minor landslips in a day till October 25 morning, The Hindu]

data.title: Koumaros, Tinos
data.text:
Koumaros () is a village in the centre of the island of Tinos, in the Cyclades, Greece. [ref: Εγκυκλοπαίδεια Νέα Δομή, Τεγόπουλος-Μανιατέας] It lies near Exomvourgo, the hill of the island's old castle town, and belongs to the municipal unit of Exomvourgo.

== History ==
After Ottoman rule, the village was officially attached in 1835 to the then municipality of Steni. [ref: Κουμάρος Κυκλάδων, ΕΕΤΑΑ] It has been listed as a traditional settlement since 1988. [ref: Κουμάρος, estia – Ministry of Environment and Energy]

== Population ==
The village had 103 inhabitants in 1928 and 19 permanent residents in the 2021 Greek census. [ref: ΦΕΚ αποτελεσμάτων ΜΟΝΙΜΟΥ πληθυσμού απογραφής 2021, Hellenic Statistical Authority]

== Association ==
The "O Koumaros" Association was founded in 1976 by people from the village living in Athens. [ref: The Association, "O Koumaros" Association of Tinos] [ref: Ο Σύλλογος των Κουμαριανών Τήνου έκοψε την Πρωτοχρονιάτικη Πίτα στην Αθήνα, Tinos News]
